rxn00351.other_comments: This is the glutathione synthetase (GSH synthase) reaction, the second step of glutathione biosynthesis. It ligates glycine to gamma-glutamylcysteine using ATP, which is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + glycine + gamma-glutamylcysteine yields ADP + phosphate + glutathione (GSH) + H+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced.

rxn02201.other_comments: This is the dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) reaction. ABEE is 4-aminobenzoate (PABA), which condenses with 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin pyrophosphate (the diphosphate substrate) to form dihydropteroate, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) and a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: the diphosphate leaving group departs as PPi, and the amine of PABA attacks the methylene carbon, releasing H+. Atoms and charges balance.

rxn00836.other_comments: This reaction represents hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT) written in the reverse (degradative) direction. The forward physiological reaction is: PRPP + hypoxanthine -> IMP + PPi. As written here (PPi + H+ + IMP <=> PRPP + hypoxanthine), it is the reverse of the biologically favored salvage direction. Stoichiometry is balanced: IMP + PPi yields PRPP + hypoxanthine, with the proton accounting for charge/protonation balance. In vivo, the salvage direction (toward IMP formation) is strongly favored due to PPi hydrolysis by pyrophosphatase.

rxn00364.other_comments: This is the cytidylate (UMP-CMP) kinase reaction, transferring a phosphate from ATP to CMP yielding ADP and CDP. The core phosphotransfer (ATP + CMP = ADP + CDP) is stoichiometrically balanced in atoms and charge; nucleoside monophosphate kinases operate near equilibrium and are physiologically reversible.

The stoichiometry is balanced (24 UDP-glucose donate 24 glucosyl groups, yielding 24 UDP and the glucose-substituted product). Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in vivo.

rxn01094.other_comments: This is the EntA-catalyzed reaction (2,3-dihydro-2,3-dihydroxybenzoate dehydrogenase) in enterobactin/siderophore biosynthesis. It oxidizes 2,3-dihydro-2,3-dihydroxybenzoate (2,3-dihydroxy-2,3-dihydrobenzoate) to 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate, reducing NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (C7H10O4 + NAD+ -> C7H6O4 + NADH + H+, losing 2H total: 2e- + 1H+ to NAD+ giving NADH, plus one released H+).

rxn03408.other_comments: This is the MurG-catalyzed reaction in bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis. MurG transfers N-acetylglucosamine from UDP-GlcNAc to the lipid intermediate (lipid I, undecaprenyl-diphospho-MurNAc-pentapeptide), forming lipid II and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one GlcNAc unit is transferred via a beta-1,4 glycosidic bond, with UDP as the leaving group. The reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02177.other_comments: This is the isochorismate pyruvate-lyase / hydrolase reaction (e.g., PhzD-type) where isochorismate is hydrolyzed with water to yield pyruvate and 2,3-dihydro-2,3-dihydroxybenzoate (2,3-dihydroxy-2,3-dihydrobenzoate). The reaction is atom and charge balanced: isochorismate (C10H8O6 as acid) + H2O yields pyruvate (C3H4O3) + 2,3-dihydro-2,3-dihydroxybenzoate (C7H8O4). Carbon: 10+0 = 3+7; balanced.

rxn05250.other_comments: This is a fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (long-chain) reaction, specifically for palmitate (fa6, C16:0). The reaction activates the fatty acid: ATP + CoA + palmitate -> AMP + PPi + palmitoyl-CoA. Stoichiometry is balanced and mass/charge conserved. The two-step mechanism proceeds via an acyl-adenylate intermediate. Although written as reversible, in vivo it is driven forward by rapid hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making fatty acid activation essentially irreversible.

rxn00646.other_comments: This is the glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL/gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase) reaction, the first and rate-limiting step of glutathione biosynthesis. ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi to drive the amide (gamma-glutamyl) bond formation between the gamma-carboxyl of glutamate and the amino group of cysteine. Stoichiometry is balanced: charges and atoms account for the released proton. In vivo this ATP-driven ligation is essentially irreversible and proceeds toward gamma-glutamylcysteine formation.

rxn01673.other_comments: This is the nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDPK) reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to dCDP, producing ADP and dCTP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (4 P, ignoring adenine) donates one phosphate to dCDP (2 P) yielding ADP (2 P) and dCTP (3 P); atoms balance. NDPK enzymes are intrinsically reversible in vitro, but in vivo the high ATP/ADP ratio drives net synthesis of the dNTP, so the physiological flux is in the forward direction.

rxn05440.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid biosynthesis (branched-chain elongation). It reduces the trans-2 double bond of 7-methyl-trans-oct-2-enoyl-ACP to give the saturated 7-methyl-octanoyl-ACP, using NADH + H+ as the reductant and producing NAD+. The reaction is stoichiometrically and redox balanced: the C=C double bond consumes one hydride from NADH and one proton, adding two H atoms across the double bond. In vivo, enoyl-ACP reductase strongly favors the reductive (forward) direction toward chain elongation.

rxn01452.other_comments: This reaction is the NADP-dependent oxidation/reduction interconverting (S)-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA. Oxidation of the secondary hydroxyl to a ketone transfers a hydride to NADP+, generating NADPH and a proton. The atoms and charges balance: NADP+ + (S)-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA <=> NADPH + H+ + acetoacetyl-CoA. As a typical NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenase/reductase, it is thermodynamically reversible, though physiological flux often favors the reductive (acetoacetyl-CoA -> hydroxybutyryl-CoA) direction during fatty acid synthesis or PHB biosynthesis.

rxn00935.other_comments: This reaction represents malate:quinone oxidoreductase / FAD-dependent malate dehydrogenase activity, oxidizing L-malate to oxaloacetate while reducing FAD to FADH2. The stoichiometry is balanced: malate (C4H6O5) loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) to form oxaloacetate (C4H4O5), and FAD gains them to form FADH2. While the classic NAD-linked malate dehydrogenase is freely reversible, the membrane-bound FAD/quinone-linked enzyme (e.g., Mqo) is essentially irreversible toward oxaloacetate in vivo because electrons are passed to the quinone pool. As written with free FAD/FADH2, the thermodynamics make it functionally forward-driven, but I list it as reversible given the abstract acceptor formulation.

rxn02342.other_comments: This is the second step of the pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 component reaction. The hydroxyethyl-ThPP (2-(alpha-hydroxyethyl)-thiamine diphosphate) transfers its acetyl-derived group to lipoamide, reducing the disulfide and forming S-acetyldihydrolipoamide while regenerating TPP (thiamine diphosphate). The reaction is mass and charge balanced: the C2 carbon-bound hydroxyethyl group is transferred to the lipoamide sulfur as an acetyl group, with the reduced lipoamide carrying the additional hydrogen. In vivo this step is essentially irreversible, driving the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate forward.

rxn02000.other_comments: This reaction represents the dTDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-D-glucose 3,5-epimerase (RmlC, EC 5.1.3.13) step in the dTDP-L-rhamnose biosynthesis pathway. The substrate dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose (also called dTDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-D-glucose) is epimerized at C3 and C5 to give dTDP-4-oxo-L-rhamnose (dTDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-L-mannose). The reaction is a double epimerization with no net change in atoms, so it is stoichiometrically balanced.

rxn02632.other_comments: This is the (S,S)-butane-2,3-diol dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.76). NAD+ oxidizes (S,S)-2,3-butanediol to (S)-acetoin, producing NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced in atoms (one secondary alcohol oxidized to a ketone, removing 2H as NADH + H+) and charge. Although written as reversible and biochemically reversible, in vivo bacterial fermentation typically favors butanediol formation (reverse direction) to regenerate NAD+ and avoid acidification.

rxn03239.other_comments: This is the third step of fatty acid beta-oxidation, the oxidation of (S)-3-hydroxyhexadecanoyl-CoA (3-hydroxypalmitoyl-CoA) to 3-oxopalmitoyl-CoA (3-ketopalmitoyl-CoA) by 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, using NAD+ as electron acceptor. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: NAD+ + hydroxyacyl-CoA yields NADH + H+ + oxoacyl-CoA. Although thermodynamically favoring the reverse (reduction) direction in isolation, in beta-oxidation the reaction proceeds forward and is generally considered reversible; the same enzyme operates in reverse during fatty acid synthesis/elongation pathways.

rxn05457.other_comments: This reaction transfers a myristoyl group between acyl-carrier-protein (ACP) and coenzyme A: CoA + Myristoyl-ACP <=> Myristoyl-CoA + ACP. The acyl group (myristoyl, C14) is conserved on both sides, and the thiol carrier (CoA vs ACP) is exchanged. Stoichiometry is balanced as written, with one acyl group transferred from ACP to CoA. As a thioester-to-thioester acyl transfer, the free energy change is near zero, so the reaction is thermodynamically reversible; the in vivo direction depends on the relative pools of acyl-ACP/ACP and acyl-CoA/CoA.

rxn00107.other_comments: This is a nucleoside diphosphate kinase-type reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to a deoxynucleoside diphosphate (5-hydroxymethyl-dCDP) to form the corresponding triphosphate (5-hydroxymethyl-dCTP). Atoms and charges are balanced: ATP + dNDP <=> ADP + dNTP. NDK reactions are catalytically near-equilibrium and generally reversible, but in vivo high ATP/ADP ratios drive net synthesis of the dNTP in the forward direction. This pathway is notable in phage T-even biology where hydroxymethyl-dCTP replaces dCTP in DNA.

rxn00199.other_comments: This is the decarboxylation of oxalosuccinate to 2-oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate), part of the isocitrate dehydrogenase reaction in the TCA cycle. Oxalosuccinate (a 6-carbon dicarboxylic acid with a keto group) loses CO2 to form 2-oxoglutarate (5-carbon). Stoichiometry and charge balance are correct: oxalosuccinate plus a proton yields CO2 and 2-oxoglutarate. The decarboxylation is essentially irreversible in vivo due to the release of CO2.

rxn02944.other_comments: This is the succinylornithine aminotransferase (AstC/SuccinylOrnithine transaminase) reaction in the arginine succinyltransferase (AST) degradation pathway. It transfers an amino group from N2-succinyl-L-ornithine to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and N-succinyl-L-glutamate 5-semialdehyde. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (atoms and charge) and, like most PLP-dependent transaminases, is freely reversible; in vivo the catabolic flux drives it toward N-succinylglutamate semialdehyde production.

rxn01867.other_comments: This is the betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction: betaine aldehyde + NAD+ + H2O -> betaine (BET) + NADH + 2 H+. The reaction is stoichiometrically and charge balanced (aldehyde oxidation to carboxylate adds an oxygen from water and releases 2 H+ with one going as hydride to NAD+). Note the listed enzyme name 'p-cumic alcohol:NAD+ oxidoreductase' does not match the substrates given (betaine aldehyde/betaine), which is an annotation inconsistency but not a stoichiometric error. In vivo this aldehyde dehydrogenase strongly favors the oxidation (forward) direction.

rxn10231.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol--serine O-phosphatidyltransferase (phosphatidylserine synthase) reaction. rxn12637.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide glycyl-L-aspartate (Gly-Asp) into glycine and L-aspartate, consuming one water molecule. The stoichiometry is balanced: the dipeptide plus water yields the two free amino acids. Peptide bond hydrolysis by peptidases is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction.

rxn01219.other_comments: This is the dCMP kinase (cytidylate kinase) reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to dCMP, yielding ADP and dCDP. Atoms and charges balance: ATP (-4) + H+ (+1) + dCMP (-2) = -5 on the left; ADP (-3) + dCDP (-2) = -5 on the right. Phosphate transfer is conserved (ATP has 3 phosphates -> ADP has 2; dCMP has 1 -> dCDP has 2). The H+ is appropriately included given the protonation states. In vivo, nucleoside monophosphate kinases catalyze phosphorylation toward NDP formation driven by ATP, though these enzymes are generally reversible in principle.

rxn10270.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylglycerophosphate phosphatase (PGP phosphatase) reaction with branched-chain isohexadecanoyl (iso-C16) acyl groups. Water hydrolyzes the phosphomonoester bond of phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP) to yield phosphatidylglycerol (PG), releasing inorganic phosphate and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the phosphate monoester is cleaved, removing one phosphate group and freeing a proton. This is a committed step in cardiolipin/phosphatidylglycerol biosynthesis.

rxn00172.other_comments: This is the acetate-CoA ligase (ADP-forming) reaction, EC 6.2.1.13, also known as acetyl-CoA synthetase (ADP-forming). It activates acetate to acetyl-CoA using ATP, with ATP being hydrolyzed to ADP + inorganic phosphate (Pi). The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + Acetate yields ADP + Pi + Acetyl-CoA, with charges and atoms conserved. This ADP-forming enzyme (common in archaea and some anaerobes) is notably reversible in vivo, capable of substrate-level ATP synthesis from acetyl-CoA during acetate formation, unlike the AMP-forming acetyl-CoA synthetase (EC 6.2.1.1) which is typically driven forward by PPi hydrolysis.

rxn09177.other_comments: This is the phosphopantothenoylcysteine synthetase reaction (CoenzymeA biosynthesis), in which CTP activates 4-phosphopantothenate to form a cytidylyl intermediate, then L-cysteine is condensed via amide bond formation, releasing CMP and PPi. Mass and charge balance check: reactants CTP + Cys + 4-phosphopantothenate yield PPi + CMP + N-substituted amide product. Atoms and charges balance with 2 H+ released, consistent with the bacterial CTP-dependent enzyme (e.g., CoaB).

The reaction is balanced: H2O cleaves the thioester bond, releasing free CoA (with its thiol), the carboxylate of 3-hydroxyisobutyrate, and a proton. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn00800.other_comments: This is adenylosuccinate lyase (ASL/ADSL) acting on adenylosuccinate (N6-(1,2-dicarboxyethyl)AMP), cleaving it to AMP plus fumarate. The stoichiometry is balanced: adenylosuccinate (C14H18N5O11P) yields AMP (C10H14N5O7P) and fumarate (C4H4O4). In vivo, this is the second step of the purine nucleotide cycle / de novo AMP synthesis and proceeds in the direction of AMP and fumarate formation.

rxn00192.other_comments: This is the N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS, EC 2.3.1.1) reaction, the first committed step of arginine/ornithine biosynthesis. Acetyl-CoA transfers its acetyl group to the alpha-amino group of L-glutamate, producing N-acetyl-L-glutamate, CoA, and a proton. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge (acetyl-CoA C23 plus glutamate C5 yields CoA C21 plus N-acetylglutamate C7, with H+ released).

rxn01218.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of dCMP (2'-deoxycytidine 5'-monophosphate) by a 5'-nucleotidase/phosphohydrolase, producing inorganic phosphate and deoxycytidine. The stoichiometry is balanced: dCMP + H2O yields deoxycytidine + Pi. Phosphate ester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of dephosphorylation.

rxn00179.other_comments: This is glutamate 5-kinase (EC 2.7.2.11), the first committed step in proline/ornithine biosynthesis. ATP phosphorylates the gamma-carboxyl of L-glutamate to form L-glutamyl 5-phosphate (gamma-glutamyl phosphate) and ADP. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ATP + glutamate -> ADP + glutamyl-5-phosphate, with the phosphate transferred from ATP. In vivo, the product is unstable and rapidly consumed by the next enzyme (gamma-glutamyl phosphate reductase), driving the reaction forward despite being thermodynamically unfavorable in isolation.

rxn00211.other_comments: This is UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase (UGDH, EC 1.1.1.22), which oxidizes the C6 primary alcohol of UDP-glucose to a carboxylic acid, producing UDP-glucuronate. The reaction consumes 1 water and 2 NAD+ (two sequential 2-electron oxidations through an aldehyde intermediate), yielding 2 NADH. Charge and atom balance: oxidation of -CH2OH to -COOH releases 4 H (as 2 NADH carry 2 H equivalents plus 2 protons), and the additional H+ accounting gives 2 NADH + 3 H+. Mass and charge are balanced as written.

rxn00962.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 4-hydroxybenzoate 3-monooxygenase (EC 1.14.13.2), a flavin-dependent monooxygenase. It hydroxylates 4-hydroxybenzoate at the 3-position to form protocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxybenzoate), using NADPH and molecular O2. One oxygen atom is incorporated into the substrate (hydroxyl group) and the other is reduced to water. The stoichiometry is balanced: substrate + O2 + NADPH + H+ yields hydroxylated product + H2O + NADP+. Carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and charge balance correctly. Monooxygenase reactions consuming NADPH and O2 are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn00509.other_comments: This is the NADP+-dependent succinate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase reaction (succinic semialdehyde + NADP+ + H2O -> succinate + NADPH + H+). 4-Oxobutanoate is succinate semialdehyde. The reaction is balanced: atoms and charges balance with H2O + NADP+ + succinate semialdehyde (C4H6O3) giving NADPH + succinate (C4H4O4 as dianion / C4H6O4 neutral) + 2 H+. The proton count of 2 H+ is consistent with the deprotonated succinate form. Stoichiometry and mass/charge balance check out.

rxn08807.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase reaction (PldB/TesA type) hydrolyzing the remaining acyl ester bond of a monoacyl-glycerophosphoethanolamine (1-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine bearing a hexadec-9-enoyl/C16:1 group). Water cleaves the ester to yield glycerophosphoethanolamine (GPE) plus the free fatty acid hexadecenoate (palmitoleate) and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acyl ester + H2O gives the deacylated headgroup-glycerol backbone plus the carboxylate anion and H+.

rxn01210.other_comments: This reaction describes the ATP-dependent ligation of L-glutamate to 10-formyltetrahydrofolate, forming a polyglutamylated folate (10-formyl-THF-L-glutamate) with release of ADP and inorganic phosphate. This is consistent with folylpolyglutamate synthetase-type chemistry. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the energy via hydrolysis to ADP + Pi, the amide/peptide bond formation between the glutamate gamma-carboxyl of the folate and the amino group of incoming glutamate releases an H+, and atoms balance.

rxn05614.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction for L-methionine R-oxide (one diastereomer of methionine sulfoxide). The substrate L-methionine R-oxide appears on both sides because transport reactions move the metabolite across a membrane compartment (e.g., extracellular to cytoplasm); compartment labels are implied. The reaction couples ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to import. Mass and charge balance are correct, with the transported metabolite identical on both sides aside from compartment. [directionality_note] ATP-driven primary active transport is effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the import direction.

rxn03384.other_comments: This is the uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase reaction acting on the type I isomer. Uroporphyrinogen I has four acetate side chains that are decarboxylated to methyl groups, yielding coproporphyrinogen I and releasing 4 CO2. The stoichiometry of 4 H+ + uroporphyrinogen I -> 4 CO2 + coproporphyrinogen I is balanced (each decarboxylation of -CH2-COOH to -CH3 consumes one H+ and releases one CO2). Note that coproporphyrinogen I is a dead-end metabolite (not a substrate for the next enzyme, coproporphyrinogen oxidase), so this type I pathway is not productive for heme biosynthesis.

rxn00501.other_comments: This is the malonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (acylating) reaction (EC 1.2.1.18). 3-Oxopropanoate (malonate semialdehyde) is oxidatively decarboxylated and CoA is added, yielding acetyl-CoA, CO2, and NADH. Atoms balance: malonate semialdehyde (C3H3O3-) + CoA + NAD+ gives acetyl-CoA (C2 acyl) + CO2 + NADH. Carbon (3 = 2+1) and the redox/CoA accounting are consistent. The decarboxylation makes the reaction effectively irreversible toward acetyl-CoA in vivo.

The general scheme (2 PG -> CL + glycerol) is biologically correct and proceeds in the synthetic (forward) direction in vivo, though the reaction is in principle reversible enzymatically; net flux favors cardiolipin formation, especially in stationary phase.

rxn10262.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PGP synthase, CDP-diacylglycerol--glycerol-3-phosphate 3-phosphatidyltransferase) reaction with branched-chain (isopentadecanoyl, anteiso/iso C15) acyl groups. The CDP-diacylglycerol transfers its phosphatidyl moiety to sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP). Stoichiometry is balanced: the phosphatidyl group is transferred and CMP is released. A proton (H+) is sometimes shown as a product but is commonly omitted.

rxn00262.other_comments: This is L-aspartate oxidase (EC 1.4.3.16), which oxidatively deaminates L-aspartate to iminoaspartate, which spontaneously hydrolyzes to oxaloacetate. The reaction shown combines these steps: L-aspartate + O2 + H2O -> oxaloacetate + NH3 + H2O2. The atoms balance (C4H7NO4 + O2 + H2O -> C4H4O5 + NH3 + H2O2: C4, H9, N1, O7 on each side). Note that with O2 as electron acceptor producing H2O2, the H2O is not strictly required as a substrate for the FAD-dependent oxidase mechanism (the imine hydrolysis water and the oxidase water balance differently), but as written the equation is mass-balanced.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: NADP+ reduction to NADPH involves transfer of a hydride and consumes 2 electrons plus a proton; combined with H2O addition the H and O balance does not match between substrates and products as written. The conversion of DMAPP (dimethylallyl diphosphate, C5H12O7P2) plus H2O to 1-hydroxy-2-methyl-2-butenyl 4-diphosphate (HMBPP, C5H12O8P2) is a reduction step, but the listed direction and cofactor usage are inverted relative to the physiological reaction.

Cofactor directionality error: the IspH/LytB enzyme uses reduced electron donors (reduced ferredoxin in vivo) to convert HMBPP into a mixture of DMAPP and IPP; the enzyme reduces HMBPP, so DMAPP is a product, not a substrate, and NADPH/reduced equivalents are consumed in that direction.
rxn04996.other_comments: This corresponds to the final step of the MEP (non-mevalonate) isoprenoid pathway catalyzed by HMBPP reductase (IspH/LytB). Physiologically HMBPP is reduced to DMAPP (and IPP) using reduced ferredoxin (or NADPH in some assay setups), releasing water. As written (DMAPP + H2O + NADP+ -> HMBPP + NADPH), the reaction is reversed and the electron carrier direction is wrong; the in vivo direction proceeds from HMBPP toward DMAPP.

rxn10126.other_comments: This represents the reoxidation of FADH2 by ubiquinone-8 (the half-reaction of succinate dehydrogenase / Complex II that transfers electrons to the quinone pool). FADH2 + Ubiquinone-8 -> FAD + Ubiquinol-8 is balanced: both electrons and two protons are transferred from FADH2 to ubiquinone, yielding FAD and ubiquinol. In vivo this step is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds toward ubiquinol formation, feeding electrons into the respiratory chain. Note this is only part of the full succinate dehydrogenase reaction (which also includes succinate + FAD -> fumarate + FADH2).

rxn10209.other_comments: This is a glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) reaction, the first committed step of glycerophospholipid/triacylglycerol biosynthesis. Glycerol-3-phosphate is acylated at the sn-1 position by an anteiso-pentadecanoyl-CoA (fa4coa, a 15-carbon branched-chain acyl-CoA), producing 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and releasing free CoA. Stoichiometry is balanced: one acyl group transferred from CoA thioester to the hydroxyl, with CoA released. In vivo this thioester-driven acyl transfer is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn08084.other_comments: This is the second acylation step in phosphatidic acid biosynthesis (PlsC / 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase), transferring a myristoyl group from myristoyl-ACP to the sn-2 position of 1-tetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid), yielding 1,2-ditetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (phosphatidic acid) and free ACP. Atom and charge balance: the acyl-thioester bond is replaced by an ester bond, releasing ACP-SH; the H+ accounts for proton balance of the released ACP thiol and the consumed hydroxyl. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as written.

rxn00898.other_comments: This is the dihydroxy-acid dehydratase (DHAD) reaction (EC 4.2.1.9) in branched-chain amino acid (valine/isoleucine) biosynthesis. It converts 2,3-dihydroxy-3-methylbutanoate (2,3-dihydroxyisovalerate) to 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate (2-oxoisovalerate/ketovaline) with loss of water. The stoichiometry is balanced: C5H10O4 -> H2O + C5H8O3. In vivo it operates in the biosynthetic (dehydration) direction.

rxn10225.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol synthase (phosphatidate cytidylyltransferase, EC 2.7.7.41) reaction with a branched-chain (isohexadecanoyl) phosphatidate. CTP reacts with the phosphatidic acid to form CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: CTP + phosphatidate yields CDP-DAG + PPi + H+. The charge and atom balance are correct. Although nominally reversible, in vivo the subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase drives the reaction strongly in the forward (CDP-DAG-forming) direction.

rxn10205.other_comments: This represents a glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) reaction, transferring an isoheptadecanoyl (branched C17) acyl group from acyl-CoA (fa11coa) to the sn-1 position of glycerol-3-phosphate, producing 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and free CoA. Stoichiometry is balanced: the acyl group transferred from CoA to glycerol-3-phosphate, releasing CoA. This is the first committed step of glycerophospholipid biosynthesis and is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven toward acylation.

rxn05040.other_comments: This reaction represents 3,4-dihydroxy-2-butanone 4-phosphate synthase (RibB, EC 4.1.99.12), which converts D-ribulose 5-phosphate into L-3,4-dihydroxy-2-butanone 4-phosphate plus formate. The carbon balance checks out: ribulose 5-phosphate (C5) loses one carbon as formate (C1), yielding the C4 product. Charge and mass balance appear correct with release of H+ and formate. This is a committed step in riboflavin biosynthesis and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn01598.other_comments: This is the cyclohexanone monooxygenase (Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase, EC 1.14.13.22) reaction. The enzyme uses NADPH and O2 to insert an oxygen atom into cyclohexanone, producing the seven-membered lactone 2-oxepanone (epsilon-caprolactone), with NADP+ and water as co-products. The reaction is balanced: C6H10O (cyclohexanone) + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> C6H10O2 (caprolactone) + H2O + NADP+. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn05444.other_comments: This is the enoyl-ACP reductase step of fatty acid synthesis (FabI-type), reducing the trans-2 double bond of a 15-methyl-hexadecenoyl-ACP to the saturated 15-methyl-hexadecanoyl-ACP using NADH as the electron donor. Atoms balance: the enoyl group gains 2 H (one from NADH hydride, one from the proton), converting C=C to C-C, and NADH is oxidized to NAD+. The reaction is written and balanced correctly (NAD shown without explicit charge but interpreted as NAD+). In vivo, enoyl reductase strongly favors the reductive (forward) direction as part of the elongation cycle.

rxn01636.other_comments: This is the ornithine acetyltransferase (OAT, ArgJ) reaction, which transfers the acetyl group from N-acetylornithine to glutamate, producing ornithine and N-acetylglutamate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: both sides carry the acetyl group and the glutamate/ornithine carbon skeletons are conserved. In vivo, this glutamate recycling step in arginine biosynthesis proceeds in the direction written (acetyl transfer to glutamate, releasing ornithine), regenerating N-acetylglutamate to feed the cyclic pathway, though the enzyme reaction is intrinsically reversible.

errors: Name/substrate mismatch: the reaction name refers to (3R)-3-Hydroxybutanoyl-ACP (a C4 substrate), but the actual reactants/products are C8 species ((R)-3-Hydroxyoctanoyl-ACP and (2E)-Octenoyl-ACP)

Stereochemistry inconsistency: typical fatty acid biosynthesis dehydratase (FabA/FabZ) acts on the (3R)-hydroxyacyl-ACP, but the dehydratase mechanism in FAS commonly involves the (R)-3-hydroxy isomer being dehydrated to trans-2-enoyl - this is consistent, though naming conventions vary
rxn05334.other_comments: This is a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase reaction (beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase, FabA/FabZ type) for the C8 chain, removing water to form a trans-2-enoyl-ACP. Atom and charge balance is satisfied: hydroxyacyl-ACP -> enoyl-ACP + H2O. In fatty acid biosynthesis the reaction proceeds toward the enoyl product (chain elongation cycle).

rxn05582.other_comments: This is a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN) moving glycine and a proton (H+) across a membrane, likely a glycine:proton symporter. The identical species on both sides represent the same molecules in different cellular compartments (e.g., extracellular/cytoplasm). Stoichiometry is balanced (1 glycine and 1 H+ on each side). Such symporters are typically reversible depending on the electrochemical gradient, though the physiological direction is usually proton-coupled import.

rxn04792.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by S-(hydroxymethyl)glutathione dehydrogenase (also known as glutathione-dependent formaldehyde dehydrogenase, ADH3/class III alcohol dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.284). S-(hydroxymethyl)glutathione (the spontaneous adduct of formaldehyde and glutathione) is oxidized to S-formylglutathione, with NAD+ reduced to NADH + H+. The reaction is correctly balanced in atoms (a CH-OH is oxidized to C=O, releasing 2 [H] = NADH + H+) and charge.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction includes H+ on the left side but the products as written do not balance the extra proton; if NH3 is protonated to NH4+ the H+ would be consumed, otherwise the H+ is unbalanced
Ambiguous abbreviation 'PACT' should be explicitly defined as phenylacetate (phenylacetic acid)
rxn01843.other_comments: This is an amidohydrolase (amidase) reaction hydrolyzing 2-phenylacetamide into phenylacetate (PACT) and ammonia. The atoms (C8H9NO + H2O -> C8H8O2 + NH3) balance correctly for mass, but proton/charge handling depends on protonation states. Amide hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn01117.other_comments: This is the aldose-ketose isomerization between D-arabinose-5-phosphate (an aldose) and D-ribulose-5-phosphate (a ketose), catalyzed by arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase (KdsD/GutQ, EC 5.3.1.13). Stoichiometry is balanced 1:1 since these are isomers (both C5H11O8P). Isomerase reactions are typically reversible; in vivo the direction toward D-arabinose-5-phosphate is favored for KDO/LPS biosynthesis.

rxn02988.other_comments: This is quinolinate synthase (NadA), which condenses glycerone phosphate (dihydroxyacetone phosphate, DHAP) with iminoaspartate (iminosuccinate) to form quinolinate, releasing 2 H2O and inorganic phosphate. As written, the reaction is in the direction of quinolinate breakdown; the physiological biosynthetic direction is the reverse (DHAP + iminoaspartate -> quinolinate + 2 H2O + Pi). The stoichiometry appears mass- and charge-balanced for the condensation/cyclization. The proton balance is approximately correct given the loss of water and phosphate.

rxn01021.other_comments: This is the MTA nucleosidase (MtnN/Pfs) reaction hydrolyzing the N-glycosidic bond of 5-methylthioadenosine (MTA) to yield adenine and 5-methylthio-D-ribose. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: MTA (C11H15N5O3S) + H2O yields adenine (C5H5N5) + 5-methylthioribose (C6H12O4S). C, H, N, O, and S all balance. Physiologically this hydrolysis is essentially irreversible, driven by glycosidic bond cleavage and salvage of the products.

errors: Stoichiometry is unbalanced. The correct reaction (PdxJ, pyridoxine 5'-phosphate synthase) produces 3 H2O and 1 inorganic phosphate. With only 2 H2O on the product side, the oxygen/hydrogen balance does not close.

Mass/atom balance fails: pyridoxine 5'-phosphate synthase converts 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate + 1-amino-3-(phosphooxy)propan-2-one (3-amino-2-oxopropyl phosphate) into pyridoxine 5'-phosphate + Pi + 3 H2O; the listed product water count (2) leaves the equation unbalanced.
rxn04070.other_comments: This is the PdxJ-catalyzed condensation of 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate (DXP) with 1-amino-acetone-3-phosphate (3-amino-2-oxopropyl phosphate) to form pyridoxine 5'-phosphate, releasing inorganic phosphate and water. In vivo this committed biosynthetic step proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction (toward pyridoxine 5'-phosphate). The main issue is the water stoichiometry; it should be 3 H2O rather than 2.

rxn00001.other_comments: This is inorganic pyrophosphatase (diphosphate phosphohydrolase), hydrolyzing one PPi (diphosphate) with one water to yield two orthophosphate ions plus a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: PPi (P2O7, charge -4 at physiological pH approximation used here, but written here with H+ released) + H2O -> 2 HPO4/Pi + H+. Stoichiometry of phosphorus (2 P in, 2 P out) and oxygen are conserved. In vivo this reaction is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible, driving many biosynthetic reactions by removing PPi.

errors: Unbalanced reaction: the equation as written is missing a water molecule on the substrate side. Atom balance check: L-Serine (C3H7NO3) -> Pyruvate (C3H4O3) + NH3 (H3N) gives C3H7NO3 vs C3H7NO3, so atoms actually balance as written.
rxn00165.other_comments: This is the L-serine ammonia-lyase (L-serine dehydratase) reaction, EC 4.3.1.17. The enzyme catalyzes elimination of ammonia from L-serine, initially forming aminoacrylate that spontaneously hydrolyzes to pyruvate and ammonia. The atoms do balance: serine C3H7NO3 = pyruvate C3H4O3 + ammonia NH3.

The standard net reaction (e.g., CDP-DAG + serine -> phosphatidylserine + CMP + H+) typically balances with 1 H+.
rxn10228.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol--serine O-phosphatidyltransferase (phosphatidylserine synthase, EC 2.7.8.8) reaction using isotetradecanoyl (anteiso/iso C14) acyl chains. Serine's hydroxyl attacks the phosphatidyl group of CDP-DAG, displacing CMP to form phosphatidylserine. The acyl groups (diisotetradecanoyl) are conserved on both sides.

rxn00671.other_comments: This is methylmalonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (acylating, EC 1.2.1.27), part of valine catabolism. It oxidatively decarboxylates 2-methyl-3-oxopropanoate (methylmalonate semialdehyde) using NAD+ and CoA to form propionyl-CoA, NADH, and CO2. The reaction is balanced: C atoms (4 in substrate = 1 CO2 + 3 in propionyl portion), with CoA incorporation. Charge and mass balance hold when accounting for the implicit proton/H balance; the overall oxidative decarboxylation is correct.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the product side should account for the released peptide fragment(s). Cleaving the D-Ala->A2pm cross-bridge between two tetrapeptides yields uncrosslinked tetrapeptides, but the equation as written consumes 2 H2O to break what appears to be a single peptide bond. A single D,D-endopeptidase cleavage of one cross-link requires only 1 H2O, so the water stoichiometry (2.0) does not match a single bond hydrolysis.
The substrate is described as 'tetrapeptide crosslinked tetrapeptide' (one cross-link), but 2 H2O implies two hydrolytic events, creating a mass/atom imbalance unless two cross-links are broken.
rxn08895.other_comments: This describes a murein (peptidoglycan) D,D-endopeptidase that hydrolyzes the D-Ala-meso-A2pm (DAP) cross-link between two adjacent murein tetrapeptide strands, converting crosslinked murein into uncrosslinked murein units in the periplasm. Hydrolytic peptide-bond cleavage is essentially irreversible in vivo.

The reaction does not represent the named function (phosphate ABC transporter permease) which should involve phosphate transport across a membrane coupled to ATP hydrolysis.

Missing ATP hydrolysis components (ATP, ADP, Pi) expected for an ABC transporter.
PPi (pyrophosphate) is not the typical substrate of a phosphate ABC transporter, which transports inorganic phosphate (Pi).

rxn00710.other_comments: This is orotidine-5'-monophosphate decarboxylase (OMP decarboxylase, EC 4.1.1.23), which catalyzes the decarboxylation of orotidine-5'-monophosphate (OMP/orotidylic acid) to form UMP and CO2 in de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis. The reaction is balanced: OMP (C10H11N2O11P, with the carboxyl) plus H+ yields UMP (C9H11N2O9P) plus CO2. Carbon: 10 = 9 + 1. The decarboxylation is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven by release of CO2, proceeding in the UMP-forming direction.

rxn02305.other_comments: This is the thiamine phosphate synthase (TMP synthase, ThiE) reaction. It condenses 4-amino-2-methyl-5-(diphosphomethyl)pyrimidine (HMP-PP) with 4-methyl-5-(2-phosphoethyl)thiazole (THZ-P), forming thiamine phosphate and releasing pyrophosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the diphosphate leaving group from the pyrimidine becomes PPi, and the methylene carbon links the two ring systems via the thiazole nitrogen.

rxn08137.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of Ap5A (diadenosine pentaphosphate, P1,P5-bis(5'-adenosyl)pentaphosphate) by a bis(5'-nucleosyl)-tetraphosphatase/asymmetric Ap5A hydrolase. Ap5A has 5 phosphates linking two adenosines. Asymmetric cleavage yields ATP (3 phosphates) + ADP (2 phosphates), accounting for all 5 phosphate groups, both adenosines, and consuming one water. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced. As a hydrolysis of a high-energy phosphoanhydride bond, it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn08817.other_comments: This reaction represents lysophospholipase L2 hydrolyzing 2-dodecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a 2-acyl lysophosphatidic acid) into glycerol-3-phosphate and dodecanoate (ddca, lauric acid, C12:0). The ester bond hydrolysis consumes one water and releases the free fatty acid. Charge and mass balance: the acyl-glycerophosphate carries the fatty acyl ester; cleavage yields glycerol-3-phosphate + free dodecanoate. The release of a carboxylic acid (deprotonated) plus a phosphate-containing product is consistent with the production of 2 H+ to maintain charge/proton balance at physiological pH. Hydrolysis of an ester bond is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn08296.other_comments: This is diacylglycerol kinase, transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the sn-3 hydroxyl of a 1,2-diacylglycerol (with two tetradec-7-enoyl, i.e. C14:1, acyl chains) to form the corresponding phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) plus ADP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: a phosphoryl group is transferred and the carbon/acyl chains are conserved. Kinase reactions coupling ATP hydrolysis to phosphorylation are strongly exergonic and proceed in the forward (kinase) direction in vivo.

rxn00470.other_comments: This is ornithine decarboxylase (ODC, EC 4.1.1.17). L-ornithine is decarboxylated to putrescine with release of CO2. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ornithine (C5H13N2O2+, net +1 charge) plus H+ gives putrescine (C4H14N2 2+, net +2 charge) plus CO2 (neutral). Counting atoms: ornithine C5 + 1 CO2 carbon = C5 on right (C4 putrescine + C1 CO2). H: 13 + 1 = 14 on putrescine. N2 conserved. O2 in ornithine accounted by CO2 (2 O). Charge: +1 (orn) + 1 (H+) = +2 = putrescine +2. Balanced.

rxn05647.other_comments: This is a PEP-dependent phosphotransferase system (PTS) reaction transporting salicin into the cell while phosphorylating it. PEP donates its phosphate group to salicin, producing salicin-6-phosphate and pyruvate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (one phosphate transferred from PEP to the salicin substrate). PTS group translocation reactions are physiologically driven in the import/phosphorylation direction due to the high phosphoryl transfer potential of PEP.

As written, both sides are identical with no compartment labels, so it represents no net transformation. Properly written, it should move H+ and putrescine from the extracellular to the cytoplasmic compartment.

rxn00910.other_comments: This reaction is methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR, EC 1.5.1.20). The written direction shows oxidation of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate using NADP+ as electron acceptor. Stoichiometry is balanced: 5-methyl-THF (one extra hydride/reduction level) is oxidized to 5,10-methylene-THF, transferring electrons to NADP+ to form NADPH + H+. In vivo, MTHFR catalyzes the physiologically irreversible reduction of 5,10-methylene-THF to 5-methyl-THF (i.e., the reverse of how written), committing folate to methionine synthesis.

rxn05654.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport of succinate across the membrane (extracellular to cytoplasm). Proton symport-driven succinate uptake is typically directional (into the cell) but can be modeled as reversible depending on gradients.

rxn01297.other_comments: This is xanthine dehydrogenase acting on hypoxanthine (HYXN) to form xanthine (XAN), using NAD+ as electron acceptor and water as oxygen source. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn10254.other_comments: This is a diacylglycerol kinase (DAGK) reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the sn-3 hydroxyl of 1,2-dianteisoheptadecanoyl-sn-glycerol to form the corresponding phosphatidic acid. Carbon/acyl backbone is conserved between substrate DAG and product phosphatidic acid, and ATP-to-ADP conversion is consistent. The only stoichiometric issue is charge/proton balance.

rxn01682.other_comments: This represents the reaction catalyzed by the alpha subunit of tryptophan synthase (TrpA, EC 4.1.2.8), which cleaves indole-3-glycerol phosphate to indole and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. rxn03181.other_comments: This is the LpxK reaction (4'-kinase) in lipid A biosynthesis. ATP phosphorylates the 4'-position of the tetraacyldisaccharide-1-phosphate (lipid A disaccharide) to yield lipid IVA (the 1,4'-bisphosphorylated species), producing ADP and a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: the transferred phosphate plus released H+ account for the conversion of ATP to ADP. The reaction is physiologically driven in the forward (kinase) direction.

rxn02331.other_comments: This is KDO-8-phosphate synthase (KdsA, EC 2.5.1.55). The physiological reaction condenses phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) and D-arabinose-5-phosphate with release of inorganic phosphate to form 3-deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate-8-phosphate (KDO-8-P), consuming water. The reaction as written is the reverse of the biological direction (it shows Phosphate + KDO-8-P producing H2O + PEP + arabinose-5-P). Atoms and charges balance correctly; the issue is only directionality. In vivo this enzyme is essentially irreversible, driving toward KDO-8-P (LPS biosynthesis).

rxn12846.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide Gly-Phe (glycyl-L-phenylalanine) into its constituent amino acids glycine and L-phenylalanine, catalyzed by an aminopeptidase. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water molecule is consumed to cleave the single peptide bond, yielding the two free amino acids. Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible under physiological conditions, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn08796.other_comments: This reaction represents lysophospholipase L1 activity hydrolyzing the ester bond of 1-dodecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a lysophosphatidic acid with a C12:0 acyl chain at sn-1). Hydrolysis adds H2O to release dodecanoate (ddca, the C12:0 fatty acid) plus a proton and glycerol-3-phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acyl ester is cleaved into the free fatty acid and glycerol-3-phosphate, consuming one water and releasing one proton from the carboxylic acid. Mass and charge balance hold (the carboxylate carries a negative charge accompanied by the released H+).

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: hydrolysis of the gamma-beta phosphoanhydride bond of a nucleoside triphosphate to release pyrophosphate yields the nucleoside monophosphate plus one proton, not two. The standard reaction XTP + H2O -> XMP + PPi + H+ requires only 1.0 H+ for charge and atom balance.
rxn01962.other_comments: This reaction represents an XTP pyrophosphohydrolase cleaving xanthosine triphosphate (XTP) into xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) and inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi). Such nucleotide pyrophosphohydrolase/house-cleaning reactions (e.g., Nudix-type hydrolases) are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn06493.other_comments: This is the dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3) reaction, transferring electrons from dihydrolipoyl-protein to NAD+. The reaction NAD+ + dihydrolipoyl-protein <=> NADH + H+ + lipoyl-protein (oxidized lipoamide with disulfide) is balanced in atoms and charge: the dihydrolipoyl (dithiol) form loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons), one H pair goes to form NADH + H+, restoring the disulfide of the lipoyl group. Stoichiometry is correct. While the in vivo flux as part of the pyruvate/2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes runs toward NADH production (regeneration of oxidized lipoamide), the isolated enzyme is freely reversible.

rxn00337.other_comments: This is aspartate kinase (aspartokinase), the first committed step in the biosynthesis of aspartate-derived amino acids (lysine, threonine, methionine). ATP transfers its gamma-phosphate to the beta-carboxyl group of L-aspartate, producing L-aspartyl-4-phosphate (4-phospho-L-aspartate) and ADP. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge (1 ATP + 1 Asp -> 1 ADP + 1 phospho-Asp). Although the phosphorylation is thermodynamically unfavorable in isolation, in vivo it is pulled forward by the subsequent reduction step (aspartate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase) and is the entry point into the pathway.

errors: The reaction lacks compartment designations; for a symporter, substrates and products must be in different compartments (e.g., extracellular vs. cytoplasmic). As written, both sides are identical (L-Proline + Na+ = L-Proline + Na+), making it a null/empty transformation with no net change.
rxn05221.other_comments: This represents a Na+/L-proline symporter, which co-transports sodium ions and proline across a membrane in the same direction. Stoichiometrically the chemical species are balanced (1 proline and 1 Na+ on each side), but transport reactions require compartment labels (e.g., L-Proline[e] + Na+[e] <=> L-Proline[c] + Na+[c]) to be meaningful. The 1:1 Na:proline coupling is plausible.

rxn00208.other_comments: This is the pyridoxamine-5'-phosphate oxidase (PNPO) reaction (EC 1.4.3.5). The reaction oxidatively deaminates pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate using molecular oxygen and water to yield pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, ammonia, and hydrogen peroxide. Stoichiometry is balanced: C8H13N2O5P + O2 + H2O -> C8H10NO6P + NH3 + H2O2. Atoms balance (C8, N2, P1, and H/O check out).

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: hydrolysis of one ester bond consumes one H2O and releases one carboxylate (octadecenoate) plus regenerates a hydroxyl; this produces at most one proton, not 2 H+. The stoichiometry of 2.0 H+ is incorrect.

Mass balance should be checked: the substrate is a monoacyl-glycerophosphate (lysophosphatidic acid); cleaving the single acyl group yields glycerol-3-phosphate + the free fatty acid, which is consistent, but the proton count is off.
rxn08823.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase (acylglycerophosphate hydrolase) reaction hydrolyzing 2-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (a lysophosphatidic acid bearing an 18:1 oleoyl chain) into glycerol-3-phosphate and oleate (octadecenoate). Hydrolysis of an ester bond is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction.

rxn05346.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthase condensation (KAS) reaction. Butyryl-ACP (C4) condenses with malonyl-ACP, releasing CO2 to form the beta-ketoacyl product 3-oxohexanoyl-ACP (C6) and free ACP. Atoms balance: the malonyl carboxyl carbon is lost as CO2, the acetyl unit is transferred and condensed with butyryl, extending the chain by two carbons. The decarboxylation makes this essentially irreversible in vivo, driving chain elongation forward.

rxn05434.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase reaction in the fatty acid elongation cycle. NADH reduces the trans-2 double bond of 6-methyl-trans-oct-2-enoyl-ACP to yield the saturated 6-methyl-octanoyl-ACP, oxidizing NADH to NAD+. The stoichiometry is balanced: the enoyl group plus 2 H (from NADH + H+) gives the saturated acyl-ACP plus NAD+. In vivo the enoyl reductase step strongly favors reduction (saturated product formation), so the physiological direction is forward as written.

rxn00867.other_comments: This is the histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase, HAL/HutH) reaction, the first step of histidine catabolism. It deaminates L-histidine via a non-oxidative elimination to form urocanate (trans-urocanic acid) and ammonia. The stoichiometry is balanced: L-histidine (C6H9N3O2) yields urocanate (C6H6N2O2) plus NH3. In vivo this reaction proceeds in the catabolic (forward) direction toward urocanate.

rxn00140.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of cyclic AMP (cAMP) to AMP by cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase (EC 3.1.4.x). The reaction adds water across the 3',5'-cyclic phosphodiester bond, opening the ring to yield 5'-AMP. Stoichiometry is balanced: cAMP (C10H11N5O6P) + H2O yields AMP (C10H13N5O7P, shown as ionized minus a proton) + H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly. As a hydrolysis reaction of a high-energy cyclic phosphodiester, it is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo in the forward direction.

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: the product is described as UDP-MurNAc joined to the full tetrapeptide (L-Ala-D-Glu-meso-DAP-D-Ala), but UDP-MurNAc already lacks any peptide. Adding the intact tetrapeptide L-alanine-D-glutamate-meso-DAP-D-Ala as a single substrate to UDP-MurNAc would form a peptide bond between MurNAc lactyl group and L-Ala, releasing water, not phosphate. The listed products (ADP + Pi + H+) imply ATP hydrolysis consistent with a Mur ligase, but the substrate naming implies the entire peptide is added at once, which is not how the Mur ligase pathway works (MurC/D/E/F add residues sequentially). This combined reaction is not a single physiological enzymatic step.
The reaction as written conflates a multi-step ligase pathway into one reaction; mass balance only works if one peptide bond is formed with release of H2O, but no H2O is shown as a product.
rxn09360.other_comments: This is annotated as a Mur-type ATP-dependent amide/peptide ligase (UDP-MurNAc:peptide ligase). Such ligases couple ATP hydrolysis (to ADP + Pi) to peptide bond formation, releasing H+; they are physiologically essentially irreversible in the biosynthetic (forward) direction. However, the substrate naming suggests addition of an entire pre-formed tetrapeptide to UDP-MurNAc, which does not correspond to a single in vivo Mur ligase step and likely has a missing water on the product side for proper balance.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: S-Adenosyl-L-methionine carries a positive charge (sulfonium center), so the methyl transfer to homocysteine to form neutral S-adenosyl-homocysteine and methionine does not release an additional H+. The reaction as written is not charge-balanced; the H+ on the product side is spurious.
rxn00452.other_comments: This is the homocysteine S-methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.10), transferring the methyl group from SAM to homocysteine, yielding S-adenosyl-homocysteine (SAH) and methionine. Atom-wise (ignoring the extra proton) the transfer is balanced: methyl group moves from SAM to the thiol of homocysteine.

rxn05386.other_comments: This is a beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis. The substrate 5-methyl-3-hydroxy-hexanoyl-ACP loses water to form the trans-2-enoyl-ACP product (5-methyl-trans-hex-2-enoyl-ACP). The reaction is mass-balanced: removal of H2O from the beta-hydroxy group and an alpha-hydrogen creates the trans double bond between C2 and C3. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms balance correctly.

rxn03248.other_comments: This is a thiolase (acetyl-CoA C-acyltransferase, beta-ketothiolase) reaction. In the synthetic/degradative direction shown, acetyl-CoA condenses with hexanoyl-CoA to form 3-oxooctanoyl-CoA (a C8 beta-ketoacyl-CoA) plus free CoA. Atom balance: acetyl-CoA (C2 acyl) + hexanoyl-CoA (C6 acyl) gives a C8 3-oxoacyl-CoA, releasing one CoA. Carbon, hydrogen, and CoA moieties balance correctly. Thiolases are inherently reversible enzymes; in beta-oxidation the reaction runs toward thiolytic cleavage (right-to-left as written, producing acetyl-CoA + hexanoyl-CoA), while in biosynthesis it runs toward condensation.

rxn01729.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing glutarate semialdehyde (5-oxopentanoate) to glutarate, using NAD+ as electron acceptor and consuming water. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde carbon (CHO) is oxidized to a carboxylate (COOH), with H2O providing the oxygen, NAD+ accepting a hydride to form NADH, and releasing 2 H+. Charge and mass balance check out. Aldehyde dehydrogenases are typically thermodynamically driven strongly toward the carboxylic acid (oxidation) direction in vivo.

errors: Proton (H+) imbalance: the reaction produces 2.0 H+, but the correct stoichiometry releases only 1 H+. The condensation of serine's hydroxyl with the CDP-diacylglycerol phosphate releases CMP and one proton, giving a charge- and mass-balanced equation with 1 H+.
rxn09206.other_comments: This is the CDP-diacylglycerol-serine O-phosphatidyltransferase (PS synthase) reaction for the di-C14:0 (ditetradecanoyl) species. L-serine attacks CDP-1,2-ditetradecanoylglycerol to form phosphatidylserine plus CMP. In vivo this proceeds in the biosynthetic direction toward phosphatidylserine.

rxn08308.other_comments: This is the CDP-diacylglycerol synthase reaction (CDS) using a phosphatidic acid species with two tetradec-7-enoyl (C14:1) acyl chains. CTP reacts with the phosphatidate to form CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing pyrophosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the phosphate of PA attacks the alpha-phosphate of CTP, displacing PPi and forming the CDP-DAG linkage. The H+ release accounts for proton balance. Although written as reversible, in vivo the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase.

rxn02376.other_comments: This is the second step of the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (E1/E2 reaction). 3-Carboxy-1-hydroxypropyl-ThPP (the alpha-carbanion/enamine adduct of succinyl semialdehyde on thiamine pyrophosphate) transfers its succinyl group to the oxidized lipoamide cofactor, regenerating TPP (ThPP) and producing S-succinyldihydrolipoamide. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the C4 succinyl moiety is transferred from ThPP to the lipoamide sulfur, with concomitant reduction of the lipoamide disulfide. Carbon, oxygen, and sulfur atoms balance across the equation.

errors: The cadmium ion (Cd2+) appears on both sides of the equation without compartment distinction; for a transport reaction the substrate and product Cd2+ should be in different compartments (e.g., Cd2+[cytoplasm] -> Cd2+[extracellular/periplasm]). As written, Cd2+ cancels out, making the transport step meaningless.
No charge/compartment annotation is provided, so the transport function is not properly represented.
rxn05516.other_comments: This is a P-type ATPase that uses ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to drive efflux/translocation of Cd2+ across a membrane. The hydrolysis stoichiometry is correct and balanced. The reaction is physiologically driven in the forward direction (ATP-dependent cadmium export), but the Cd2+ should be in distinct compartments.

rxn08556.other_comments: This is the glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (aerobic/respiratory, GlpD/GlpABC type) reaction. sn-Glycerol 3-phosphate is oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerone phosphate), with two electrons transferred to ubiquinone-8 to form ubiquinol-8. The reaction is stoichiometrically and redox balanced: glycerol-3-phosphate loses 2 H (2e- + 2H+) which reduce ubiquinone-8 to ubiquinol-8. In vivo this membrane-bound respiratory enzyme operates essentially irreversibly in the forward (oxidation) direction, feeding electrons into the respiratory chain via the quinone pool.

rxn08017.other_comments: This is a fatty acyl-ACP synthetase reaction activating hexadecenoate (C16:1) using ATP, forming hexadecenoyl-ACP with release of AMP and PPi. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides AMP + PPi, the carboxylate of the fatty acid is esterified to the ACP thiol. The 2 H+ accounts for protons released upon adenylate formation and thioester bond formation from the carboxylate/thiol groups. Charge and mass balance is consistent. In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by pyrophosphatase, making acyl-ACP formation strongly favored.

rxn12512.other_comments: This is the phosphopantothenoylcysteine synthetase reaction (CoA biosynthesis), condensing 4'-phosphopantothenate with L-cysteine using ATP, releasing AMP and PPi. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the AMP and PPi, the amide bond formation between the carboxyl of phosphopantothenate and the amino group of cysteine releases water, and charge balance is maintained with 2 H+ released. The subsequent PPi hydrolysis typically drives the reaction forward in vivo.

rxn08669.other_comments: This is the glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase (GlpQ/UgpQ) reaction. The hydrolysis of glycerophosphoglycerol (a glycerophosphodiester) by water yields glycerol-3-phosphate and glycerol, releasing a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the diester bond is cleaved hydrolytically, distributing the phosphate to one glycerol moiety. As a hydrolysis reaction, it is strongly exergonic and proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn01739.other_comments: This is shikimate kinase (EC 2.7.1.71), part of the shikimate pathway for aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. ATP phosphorylates shikimate at the 3-hydroxyl position to form shikimate 3-phosphate (3-phosphoshikimate), producing ADP and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced in atoms and charge. Although kinase reactions can be reversible in vitro, in vivo the reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction driven by ATP hydrolysis and metabolic flux through the pathway.

rxn00649.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by cysteine synthase (O-acetylserine sulfhydrylase, EC 2.5.1.47). H2S reacts with O-acetyl-L-serine to form L-cysteine and acetate. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2S (H2S) provides the sulfur and reacts with O-acetyl-L-serine, displacing the acetyl group as acetate and releasing a proton, yielding L-cysteine. Mass and charge balance hold (H2S contributes 2 H, S; the acetyl group leaves as acetate plus H+).

rxn02400.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of nicotinate D-ribonucleotide (nicotinate mononucleotide, NaMN), removing the 5'-phosphate group to yield nicotinate riboside (nicotinate D-ribonucleoside) and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: a phosphomonoester bond is cleaved by water, releasing one phosphate and producing the dephosphorylated nucleoside. Phosphomonoester hydrolysis is strongly exergonic and physiologically essentially irreversible in the hydrolytic direction.

rxn01268.other_comments: This is prephenate dehydrogenase (TyrA), which oxidatively decarboxylates prephenate to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate) using NAD+ as electron acceptor, producing NADH and CO2. The reaction is balanced: prephenate (C10H8O6, accounting for protonation state) loses CO2 and is oxidized; atoms balance with the NAD+/NADH and CO2 products. A proton (H+) is often included for full charge/H balance depending on protonation states used. The reaction strongly favors the forward direction in vivo due to the irreversible decarboxylation step.

rxn00641.other_comments: This is GTP:alpha-D-mannose-1-phosphate guanylyltransferase (mannose-1-phosphate guanylyltransferase, GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase, EC 2.7.7.13). The reaction GTP + alpha-D-mannose 1-phosphate -> GDP-mannose + diphosphate (PPi) is correctly balanced in atoms and charge (each nucleotidyltransfer releases PPi). Stoichiometry is correct. Although the enzymatic reaction is intrinsically reversible, in vivo the forward direction toward GDP-mannose synthesis is favored, driven by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase.

errors: The substrate should be bicarbonate (HCO3-) rather than carbonic acid (H2CO3); under physiological conditions the active species used by biotin carboxylase is HCO3-

Proton (H+) balance should be checked: with HCO3- as substrate the reaction is typically ATP + HCO3- + holo-carboxylase -> ADP + Pi + carboxy-biotin-carrier-protein, requiring no free H+ release; if H2CO3 is used the H+ accounting changes
rxn06672.other_comments: This is the biotin carboxylase half-reaction (e.g., acetyl-CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase), in which ATP-dependent carboxylation of the biotin moiety on the biotin carboxyl carrier protein (BCCP) forms carboxybiotin, consuming bicarbonate and producing ADP and inorganic phosphate. The overall ligase reaction is generally considered reversible in vitro, though in vivo it is typically driven forward by ATP hydrolysis and consumption of carboxyphosphate intermediate.

errors: Proton (H+) stoichiometry is incorrect: the phosphatidylserine synthase reaction (base-exchange/transfer of the phosphatidyl group from CDP-diacylglycerol to serine) releases CMP and should produce only 1 H+, not 2 H+. The reaction as written is charge-unbalanced.
Charge imbalance: L-serine is zwitterionic (net 0), CDP-DAG carries a net negative charge; products CMP plus phosphatidylserine plus 2 H+ do not balance the charges of the substrates.
rxn09209.other_comments: This is the CDP-diacylglycerol-dependent phosphatidylserine synthase (PSS, EC 2.7.8.8) reaction with C16:1 (palmitoleoyl) acyl chains. The phosphatidyl moiety from CDP-1,2-dihexadec-9-enoylglycerol is transferred to L-serine, releasing CMP and forming the corresponding phosphatidylserine. In vivo this reaction is driven essentially irreversibly toward PS synthesis.

errors: Charge and proton imbalance: thiosulfate (H2S2O3) should typically be represented as the ionized species (S2O3^2-) at physiological pH; the proton balance does not reconcile correctly as written

Mass/sulfur accounting concern: thiosulfate provides two sulfur atoms; one is incorporated into cysteine and one is released as sulfite, which is consistent, but the redox bookkeeping with thioredoxin (trdrd/trdox) and the proton/charge balance is not fully balanced as written
rxn05733.other_comments: This is the cysteine synthase B (CysM)-type reaction where O-acetyl-L-serine reacts with thiosulfate to form S-sulfocysteine, which is then reduced (here coupled to thioredoxin) to L-cysteine plus sulfite, releasing acetate. The overall transformation makes biological sense for thiosulfate-dependent cysteine biosynthesis.

rxn00361.other_comments: This is the adenylylsulfate kinase (APS kinase) reaction, EC 2.7.1.25. ATP phosphorylates the 3'-hydroxyl of adenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (APS) to form 3'-phosphoadenylyl sulfate (PAPS), producing ADP and a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced (ATP4- + APS2- -> ADP3- + PAPS4- + H+; charges: -6 = -6, atoms balanced). In vivo this reaction proceeds toward PAPS formation, driving sulfate activation for sulfation reactions.

rxn00902.other_comments: This is the 2-isopropylmalate synthase reaction (EC 2.3.3.13), the first committed step of leucine biosynthesis. As written, the reaction shows the reverse (hydrolysis/cleavage) direction: 2-isopropylmalate + CoA -> acetyl-CoA + 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate (2-oxoisovalerate). The biosynthetic direction in vivo is acetyl-CoA + 2-oxoisovalerate + H2O -> 2-isopropylmalate + CoA + H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly: C25 on each side, CoA condenses an acetyl group onto the 2-oxo acid. The physiological flux is toward 2-isopropylmalate formation, so as written this points in the reverse direction.

rxn02679.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (ACAD) reaction in fatty acid beta-oxidation. Octanoyl-CoA (medium-chain) is dehydrogenated at the alpha,beta positions to form trans-2-octenoyl-CoA, with FAD reduced to FADH2. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (2 H atoms transferred from substrate to FAD). In vivo, electrons from the enzyme-bound FADH2 are passed to electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF), driving the reaction in the dehydrogenation (forward) direction.

rxn01974.other_comments: This is the diaminopimelate epimerase (DapF, EC 5.1.1.7) reaction, which interconverts LL-2,6-diaminopimelate and meso-2,6-diaminopimelate in the lysine biosynthesis pathway. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as it simply interconverts two stereoisomers (epimerization at one chiral center). As an epimerase, the reaction is thermodynamically near-equilibrium and reversible; however, in vivo the net flux is toward meso-DAP, which is the substrate for the downstream diaminopimelate decarboxylase producing L-lysine.

rxn12641.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide L-alanylglycine, cleaving the peptide bond with water to yield L-alanine and glycine. The stoichiometry is balanced: the dipeptide plus one water gives the two free amino acids. This is a typical dipeptidase/peptidase reaction. Hydrolysis of peptide bonds is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction toward the free amino acids.

rxn00242.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of ppGpp (guanosine 3',5'-bis(diphosphate)) by SpoT/3'-pyrophosphohydrolase activity. Water cleaves the 3'-diphosphate group, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) and yielding GDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: ppGpp contributes a 5'-diphosphate (which becomes GDP) and a 3'-diphosphate (released as PPi), with water providing the hydrolytic cleavage. This is part of the stringent response regulation.

rxn03887.other_comments: This is galactarate dehydratase (GarD, EC 4.2.1.42), which catalyzes the dehydration of D-galactarate (galactaric/mucic acid) to 5-dehydro-4-deoxy-D-glucarate plus water. Both galactarate (C6H8O8) and 5-dehydro-4-deoxy-D-glucarate (C6H6O7) plus H2O (H2O) are balanced: 6 C, 8 H, 8 O on each side. The reaction is the first step in galactarate catabolism and proceeds in the dehydration (forward) direction physiologically.

rxn08971.other_comments: This reaction represents NADH dehydrogenase transferring electrons from NADH to menaquinone-8 (MK-8), producing NAD+ and menaquinol-8 (MKH2-8). Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + H+ donates 2 electrons and effectively 2 H to reduce menaquinone (quinone) to menaquinol (quinol). Charge and atoms balance (NADH carries the extra H+ needed along with the proton consumed). The variant noted specifies 0 protons translocated across the membrane. In vivo, this oxidation of NADH coupled to quinone reduction is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward direction.

rxn00060.other_comments: This is the porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase) reaction. Four molecules of porphobilinogen condense with loss of four ammonia to form the linear tetrapyrrole hydroxymethylbilane (preuroporphyrinogen). The reaction consumes one water for the hydroxymethyl group. Stoichiometry is balanced: 4 PBG provide 4 pyrrole units, releasing 4 NH3, and water provides the terminal hydroxyl. In vivo this proceeds toward hydroxymethylbilane in the heme biosynthesis pathway.

errors: The reaction is a trivial identity: the substrate and product are identical (Inosine and H+ on both sides), resulting in no net chemical transformation
No net change in metabolites; this represents a transport reaction where the compound identifiers should differ by compartment (e.g., extracellular vs cytosolic Inosine and H+)
rxn05316.other_comments: This appears to be a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN prefix) involving the symport or facilitated movement of inosine, possibly coupled with a proton. As written, both sides are identical, which is stoichiometrically valid (mass and charge balanced) but biologically meaningless unless the two sides represent different cellular compartments. The compartment annotations are missing from the displayed metabolite names.

errors: Charge and hydrogen imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced. For an FMNH2-dependent monooxygenase oxidizing sulfoacetate to glyoxylate plus sulfite, one O atom from O2 is incorporated and the other is reduced to water, while FMNH2 is oxidized to FMN. A balanced form requires explicit protons. Typical balance: Sulfoacetate + O2 + FMNH2 -> Glyoxylate + Sulfite + FMN + H2O (+ H+). Without protons the charge does not balance (sulfoacetate 2-, sulfite 2-, glyoxylate 1-).
rxn08471.other_comments: This is a desulfonation/monooxygenase reaction in which reduced flavin (FMNH2) activates O2 to cleave the C-S bond of sulfoacetate, yielding glyoxylate and sulfite, with FMN and water as products. The note spells glyoxylate as 'Glyoxalate' and the reaction needs proton accounting to fully balance H and charge.

rxn09198.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (Psd) reaction converting the dimyristoyl (di-C14:0) species of phosphatidylserine to the corresponding phosphatidylethanolamine, releasing CO2. The decarboxylation of the serine carboxyl group yields the ethanolamine headgroup.

rxn05350.other_comments: This is a fatty acid elongation condensation step (KAS, beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase). Hexanoyl-ACP (C6) condenses with malonyl-ACP, releasing CO2 and the free ACP, to yield 3-oxooctanoyl-ACP (C8 beta-ketoacyl-ACP). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: carbons (6 + 3 from malonyl = 9, products give 8-carbon acyl chain + 1 CO2 = 9), and the decarboxylation/Claisen condensation mechanism is correct. In vivo this condensation is essentially irreversible due to the loss of CO2 driving it forward.

rxn01102.other_comments: This is glycerate kinase (EC 2.7.1.31), transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to D-glycerate to form 3-phosphoglycerate (or 2-phosphoglycerate depending on the isoform). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP + glycerate -> ADP + 3-phosphoglycerate + H+. The proton release accounts for charge balance. Note that some glycerate kinases produce 2-phosphoglycerate rather than 3-phosphoglycerate, so the specific product depends on the enzyme.

rxn08838.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase L2 reaction hydrolyzing the ester bond of 2-dodecanoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine. Water cleaves the acyl group, yielding free glycerophosphoethanolamine and dodecanoate (ddca, C12:0). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the substrate carries a 2-acyl ester, hydrolysis produces the free fatty acid (deprotonated, with H+ released) plus glycerophosphoethanolamine. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn03906.other_comments: This reaction represents 1-hydroxy-2-naphthoate 1,2-dioxygenase-type/monooxygenase activity in the bacterial naphthalene degradation pathway. The salicylate-type hydroxylase-decarboxylase converts 1-hydroxy-2-naphthoate to 1,2-naphthalenediol with consumption of NADH and O2, releasing CO2 and water. Stoichiometry balances: atoms (C11 on each side counting CO2, H, O, N) and charges balance with the 2 H+ included. The NAD/NADH and oxygen consumption with oxidative decarboxylation strongly favor the forward direction as written in vivo.

rxn05569.other_comments: This is a PEP-dependent phosphotransferase system (PTS) reaction transporting D-glucosamine (GLUM) across the membrane while phosphorylating it to D-glucosamine 6-phosphate. PEP donates its phosphate group, becoming pyruvate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced (one phosphate transferred from PEP to glucosamine; one carbon/phosphorus accounting is consistent). PTS group translocation reactions are physiologically irreversible due to the high free energy of PEP hydrolysis driving transport and phosphorylation.

rxn00100.other_comments: This is the final step of CoA biosynthesis catalyzed by dephospho-CoA kinase (EC 2.7.1.24). ATP phosphorylates the 3'-hydroxyl of dephospho-CoA to yield CoA and ADP. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP donates a phosphate to dephospho-CoA, producing ADP, CoA, and a proton. Atoms and charges balance correctly. In vivo this reaction strongly favors CoA synthesis (forward direction) as part of the committed biosynthetic pathway.

rxn00789.other_comments: This is the first step of histidine biosynthesis catalyzed by ATP phosphoribosyltransferase (HisG). The reaction as written shows the synthesis direction running right-to-left: ATP + PRPP -> Phosphoribosyl-ATP (N1-(5-phospho-beta-D-ribosyl)-ATP) + PPi. The stoichiometry is balanced: PRPP + ATP combine, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). The proton balance is reasonable for the condensation. As written (PPi + Phosphoribosyl-ATP -> ATP + PRPP), the biological/physiological flux actually proceeds in the reverse direction toward PR-ATP formation, pulled forward by subsequent pyrophosphate hydrolysis.

rxn00568.other_comments: This is the nitrite reductase (NAD(P)H) reaction (assimilatory). Written form shows ammonia oxidation to nitrite coupled to NAD reduction. In vivo, nitrite reductase runs in reverse: nitrite + NADH -> ammonia, consuming reducing equivalents. The 6-electron reduction of nitrite to ammonia uses 3 NADH. The reaction as written (ammonia -> nitrite producing NADH) is thermodynamically unfavorable in vivo.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: hydrolysis of ITP to IMP + PPi releases 1 H+, not 2 H+. The balanced reaction is H2O + ITP -> IMP + PPi + H+
rxn00514.other_comments: This is the ITPase (inosine triphosphate pyrophosphatase) reaction, hydrolyzing ITP to IMP and pyrophosphate. The cleavage of the phosphoanhydride bond plus subsequent PPi hydrolysis makes this strongly exergonic and physiologically irreversible in the forward direction. The reaction serves a housekeeping role removing non-canonical (deaminated) nucleotides.

rxn00327.other_comments: This is intended to represent hydrolysis of (S)-ureidoglycolate to glyoxylate, releasing the ureido carbon as CO2 and nitrogen as ammonia (a step in purine/allantoin degradation). The decarboxylating amidohydrolase splits the ureido group. As written the H2O count and proton/charge balance appear off; the carbon balance (C3 ureidoglycolate -> C2 glyoxylate + CO2) is plausible, and nitrogen (2 N -> 2 NH3) balances, but oxygen/hydrogen require 2 H2O.

rxn05390.other_comments: This is a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase reaction in branched-chain fatty acid synthesis. It removes water from 7-methyl-3-hydroxy-octanoyl-ACP to form the trans-2-enoyl-ACP (7-methyl-trans-oct-2-enoyl-ACP). Stoichiometry is balanced: the substrate loses H2O (dehydration) to yield the enoyl product. In FAS elongation cycles this dehydratase step is typically reversible, though in vivo it is pulled forward by the subsequent enoyl reductase step.

rxn05560.other_comments: This is the PEP:carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS) reaction for D-fructose import. PEP donates its phosphoryl group through the PTS cascade (EI, HPr, EIIA, EIIB) to phosphorylate fructose during transport across the membrane, yielding pyruvate and intracellular fructose-1-phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphoryl group is transferred from PEP to fructose, converting PEP to pyruvate. In vivo this is essentially irreversible due to the large free energy of PEP hydrolysis and its coupling to vectorial transport.

rxn03436.other_comments: This is the ketol-acid reductoisomerase (KARI, IlvC) reaction in branched-chain amino acid (isoleucine) biosynthesis. The full reaction should be: 2-aceto-2-hydroxybutanoate + NADPH + H+ <=> (R)-3-hydroxy-3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate + NADP+. As written, the redox cofactors are omitted, making it stoichiometrically unbalanced. In vivo it proceeds toward the hydroxy product for isoleucine synthesis.

rxn00781.other_comments: This is the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) reaction. It oxidizes G3P while phosphorylating it with inorganic phosphate to form 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, reducing NAD+ to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced for both atoms and charge (the released proton is accounted for). The enzyme operates reversibly in vivo, functioning in glycolysis (forward) and gluconeogenesis (reverse).

rxn08976.other_comments: This reaction represents the reduction of 2-demethylmenaquinone-8 (a quinone form) to 2-demethylmenaquinol-8 (the reduced quinol form) using NADH as the electron donor. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADH provides 2 electrons and a hydride, with H+ supplying the additional proton needed for the 2-electron, 2-proton reduction of the quinone to the quinol. NADH is oxidized to NAD+. Atom and charge balance are consistent (quinone + 2H+ + 2e- -> quinol, with NADH/H+ supplying the reducing equivalents). In vivo, NADH-driven quinone reduction typically proceeds in the forward direction (quinone reduction) as part of the respiratory electron transport chain, given the favorable redox potential difference.

rxn05437.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid biosynthesis (specifically branched-chain, iso/anteiso fatty acid synthesis). NADH + H+ reduces the trans-2-enoyl double bond of the 12-methyl-trans-tetra-dec-2-enoyl-ACP substrate to give the saturated 12-methyl-tetradecanoyl-ACP, producing NAD+. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge (NADH + H+ provides the hydride and proton needed to reduce the C2-C3 double bond). Note: the product side lists 'NAD' which should be NAD+ for proper charge balance, but this is likely just a notation issue.
