rxn00881.other_comments: This is the inositol monophosphatase (IMPase) reaction, hydrolyzing inositol 1-phosphate to free inositol and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (H2O + inositol-1-phosphate -> inositol + Pi). In vivo it proceeds essentially irreversibly toward free inositol due to the exergonic phosphate ester hydrolysis.

rxn08336.other_comments: This is the dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) reaction using menaquinone-8 as the electron acceptor, characteristic of class 2 DHODH enzymes in many bacteria. S-Dihydroorotate is oxidized to orotate, transferring two electrons (and protons) to menaquinone-8, reducing it to menaquinol-8. The reaction is balanced: dihydroorotate loses 2 H (one as hydride, one as proton) and menaquinone gains 2 H to become menaquinol. Stoichiometry of atoms and electrons is consistent.

rxn05298.other_comments: This is intended to be a sodium-glutamate symport transport reaction, where Na+ and L-glutamate are co-transported across a membrane. As written without compartment labels, both sides are identical and represent a null reaction. Correctly, it should be written as L-Glutamate[out] + Na+[out] <=> L-Glutamate[in] + Na+[in].

rxn00292.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase (hydrolyzing, EC 3.2.1.183). It hydrolyzes UDP-N-acetylglucosamine, simultaneously epimerizing at C2 to release UDP and N-acetyl-D-mannosamine (ManNAc). The atoms balance: UDP-GlcNAc (C17H27N3O17P2) + H2O yields UDP (C9H14N2O12P2) + ManNAc (C8H15NO6). Both C, H, N, O, P balance. As an irreversible hydrolytic step, it proceeds in the direction of UDP and ManNAc formation in vivo, committing flux toward sialic acid biosynthesis.

errors: Urea appears on both sides of the reaction without a compartment distinction; for a transport reaction the substrate should be denoted in different compartments (e.g., Urea[extracellular] -> Urea[cytoplasm]), otherwise it cancels out and the net transport is not represented
rxn05157.other_comments: This is an ABC-type urea importer coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to translocation of urea across the membrane. As written, urea is identical on both sides because compartment tags are missing, making the transport meaningless stoichiometrically. With proper compartmentalization the reaction balances. ABC transporters use ATP hydrolysis irreversibly, so the reaction proceeds in the import (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn09202.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (PSD) reaction with distearoyl (di-C18:0) acyl chains. The serine head group is decarboxylated to ethanolamine, releasing CO2 and converting PS to PE. The carboxylate of serine is lost as CO2, requiring one proton to balance charge/mass.

rxn01451.other_comments: This is the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.35/1.1.1.157), oxidizing the 3-hydroxyl group of (S)-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA to a keto group, yielding acetoacetyl-CoA, with NAD+ reduced to NADH. The reaction is balanced in carbon, hydrogen (NAD+ + substrate-OH gives NADH + H+ + keto product), and the CoA and redox cofactors are correctly paired. In the beta-oxidation direction it runs forward toward acetoacetyl-CoA; in biosynthesis it runs in reverse, so the enzyme is physiologically reversible.

rxn00097.other_comments: This is the adenylate kinase (myokinase) reaction, ATP:AMP phosphotransferase. The core reaction ATP + AMP <=> 2 ADP is correct and freely reversible in vivo, with direction governed by the adenylate energy charge. The extraneous H+ is the stoichiometric problem.

rxn05198.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport of cytidine across the membrane (likely extracellular to cytoplasm). The stoichiometry (1 H+ : 1 cytidine) is plausible for a symporter, but the lack of compartment annotation makes the reaction appear to do nothing. Proton symport-driven nucleoside uptake is typically driven inward by the proton motive force, so it would functionally favor import.

rxn02264.other_comments: This reaction represents uroporphyrinogen III synthase (EC 4.2.1.75), which converts hydroxymethylbilane (preuroporphyrinogen) into uroporphyrinogen III with release of water, involving inversion of ring D. Stoichiometry is balanced: hydroxymethylbilane (C40H38N4O17) loses one H2O to form the cyclic tetrapyrrole uroporphyrinogen III (C40H36N4O16). In vivo this is the committed step in heme/siroheme/cobalamin biosynthesis and proceeds in the forward (cyclizing) direction.

rxn00191.other_comments: This is alanine aminotransferase (ALT/GPT), transferring an amino group from L-alanine to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding pyruvate and L-glutamate. The reaction is balanced: C5H4O5 (2-oxoglutarate) + C3H7NO2 (L-alanine) gives C3H3O3 (pyruvate) + C5H8NO4 (L-glutamate). Atoms and charges balance correctly. This PLP-dependent transamination is freely reversible in vivo, with net direction set by metabolic context.

rxn00250.other_comments: This is pyruvate carboxylase (EC 6.4.1.1), an ATP-dependent carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate. The reaction is balanced: ATP + pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + H2CO3 yields ADP + Pi + oxaloacetate (C4H3O5-) + H+. Carbon balance (3+1=4), atoms, and charges balance correctly. In vivo, this anaplerotic reaction is driven forward by ATP hydrolysis and is essentially irreversible.

rxn02212.other_comments: This is the 3-dehydroquinate synthase (AroB) reaction, the second step of the shikimate pathway. DAHP (3-deoxy-D-arabino-heptulosonate 7-phosphate) is converted to 3-dehydroquinate (5-dehydroquinate) with release of inorganic phosphate. The reaction is intramolecular and atom-balanced: the phosphate is eliminated and a new carbocyclic ring is formed. Although the enzyme uses NAD+ catalytically (transient oxidation/reduction), no net redox cofactor change occurs, so it is correctly omitted from net stoichiometry. The mechanism involves cyclization (aldol condensation) and is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn10481.other_comments: This represents a primary active transport reaction where ATP hydrolysis drives copper translocation across a membrane via an ABC transporter. rxn00692.other_comments: This is the serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) reaction. rxn00311.other_comments: This is a lysine N6-monooxygenase (e.g., IucD/flavin-dependent hydroxylase) reaction that hydroxylates the epsilon-amino group of L-lysine to form N6-hydroxy-L-lysine, consuming NADPH and molecular oxygen, producing water and NADP+. rxn00802.other_comments: This is argininosuccinate lyase (ASL, EC 4.3.2.1), which cleaves L-argininosuccinate into L-arginine and fumarate as part of the urea cycle. The reaction is correctly balanced: argininosuccinate (C10H18N4O6) yields arginine (C6H14N4O2) plus fumarate (C4H4O4). In vivo, the enzyme catalyzes the cleavage direction (forward toward arginine + fumarate) under urea cycle conditions, though the reaction is thermodynamically reversible and EC class assignment as a lyase reflects this.

rxn08440.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of lauroyl-CoA (a 12-carbon acyl-CoA thioester) by a thioesterase/acyl-CoA hydrolase. Water cleaves the thioester bond, yielding free CoA (CoA-SH) and dodecanoate (ddca = laurate, the C12 fatty acid anion), plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the thioester C-S bond is hydrolyzed, releasing the carboxylate (deprotonated at physiological pH, hence the H+) and free CoA. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn03535.other_comments: This is the cob(I)alamin/cobyrinate adenosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.5.1.17), transferring the adenosyl group from ATP to the cobalt center of cob(I)yrinate a,c-diamide, releasing triphosphate. rxn00913.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of GMP (guanosine 5'-monophosphate) by a 5'-nucleotidase, releasing inorganic phosphate and guanosine. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: GMP + H2O yields guanosine + Pi. Hydrolysis of the phosphate monoester is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible, proceeding in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn01492.other_comments: This reaction describes 1-phosphofructokinase (PfkB family, e.g., FruK), which phosphorylates the 6-position of D-fructose-1-phosphate using ATP to produce D-fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, ADP, and a proton. The atoms balance: ATP transfers a gamma-phosphate to fructose-1-phosphate, generating ADP and the bisphosphate plus a released H+. Stoichiometry and charge are consistent.

rxn02761.other_comments: This reaction represents allantoin racemase, which interconverts the (S)-(+) and (R)-(-) enantiomers of allantoin. The substrate 'Allantoin' here refers to the (S)-form and the product is the (R)-form. Racemases are inherently reversible enzymes that catalyze the stereochemical inversion at a chiral center. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced since it is simply an interconversion of optical isomers (same molecular formula, C4H6N4O3, on both sides). Racemization approaches a 1:1 equilibrium mixture, so directionality depends on the relative concentrations of the two enantiomers.

rxn02720.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction for lauroyl-CoA (C12 saturated acyl-CoA), oxidizing it at the 2,3 (alpha-beta) position to form trans-2-dodecenoyl-CoA. Strictly, the enzyme-bound FADH2 is typically reoxidized by an electron acceptor (ETF) rather than released as free FADH2, but written with free FAD/FADH2 it is stoichiometrically acceptable.

rxn10230.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylserine synthase (CDP-diacylglycerol-serine O-phosphatidyltransferase) reaction in which L-serine is transferred onto a CDP-activated diacylglycerol (here with anteiso-pentadecanoyl acyl chains), releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylserine. rxn08802.other_comments: This represents a lysophospholipase (L1) reaction in the periplasm hydrolyzing the ester bond of 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid with an 18:1 oleoyl chain) to release glycerol-3-phosphate and oleate (octadecenoate, 18:1). rxn01997.other_comments: This is the dTDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase reaction (EC 4.2.1.46), which converts dTDP-D-glucose to dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose (dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-glucose) with release of water. The reaction is an intramolecular oxidoreduction using a tightly bound NAD+ cofactor that is regenerated in the catalytic cycle, so it does not appear in the net stoichiometry. The stoichiometry is balanced: dTDP-glucose loses one water molecule (net dehydration/oxidation), producing the 4-keto-6-deoxy product. This is a committed step in dTDP-L-rhamnose biosynthesis.

rxn08809.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase L1 reaction hydrolyzing 2-acyl-glycerophosphoethanolamine (with an oleate/C18:1 chain at the sn-2 position) to release the fatty acid (octadecenoate, C18:1) and glycerophosphoethanolamine. The stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the ester bond, releasing one fatty acid carboxylate plus a proton, leaving the glycerophosphoethanolamine backbone. Mass and charge balance hold (the carboxylic acid is released as octadecenoate anion plus H+).

rxn03958.other_comments: This is the DXR (1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate reductoisomerase, IspC) reaction in the MEP/non-mevalonate isoprenoid pathway. The reaction as written shows the reverse physiological direction: it depicts 2-C-methyl-D-erythritol-4-phosphate (MEP) being oxidized by NADP+ to form 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate (DXP) plus NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry and charge/atom balance are correct (DXP and MEP are isomers with the same formula C5H11O7P; the redox couple NADP+/NADPH+H+ is balanced). In vivo, the enzyme catalyzes the conversion of DXP to MEP using NADPH, i.e., the reverse of how it is written here.

rxn00178.other_comments: This is the thiolase (acetyl-CoA C-acetyltransferase, EC 2.3.1.9) reaction: two molecules of acetyl-CoA condense to form acetoacetyl-CoA plus free CoA. Carbon balance: 2 acetyl-CoA = 2x(2 carbons in acetyl) = 4 carbons; acetoacetyl-CoA has a 4-carbon acetoacetyl moiety, plus one CoA released. CoA balance: 2 CoA in, 1 free CoA + 1 CoA attached to acetoacetyl out. Stoichiometry is correct and balanced.

rxn03264.other_comments: This is the selenium analog of methionine adenosyltransferase (MAT, EC 2.5.1.6). The enzyme transfers the adenosyl group from ATP to selenomethionine, producing Se-adenosylselenomethionine, with concomitant cleavage of the triphosphate into orthophosphate (Pi) and pyrophosphate (PPi). The reaction consumes water for hydrolysis of the triphosphate. Mass and charge balance: ATP provides adenosyl + triphosphate; the triphosphate is split into Pi + PPi using H2O, releasing one H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly. Like the standard MAT reaction, this is physiologically essentially irreversible due to the energetically favorable cleavage of both phosphoanhydride bonds (tripolyphosphate hydrolysis driving the reaction forward).

rxn03903.other_comments: This is the MraY reaction (phospho-N-acetylmuramoyl-pentapeptide-transferase), the first lipid-linked step in peptidoglycan biosynthesis. Stoichiometry is balanced: the UDP donor (UMP + phosphate carrying MurNAc-pentapeptide) is split such that UMP leaves and the diphospho-MurNAc-pentapeptide is linked to undecaprenol. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn01362.other_comments: This is the orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (OPRT) reaction, EC 2.4.2.10. As written, it shows OMP (orotidine-5'-monophosphate, orotidylic acid) plus pyrophosphate forming PRPP plus orotate. The mass balance is correct: orotate + PRPP <=> OMP + PPi. The proton (H+) accounting is consistent with this transfer. In vivo, the physiological direction is the biosynthetic one (orotate + PRPP -> OMP + PPi), driven forward by subsequent pyrophosphate hydrolysis. Since this reaction is written in the opposite (degradative/PRPP-forming) direction, the biologically favored flow corresponds to the reverse of how it is written.

rxn00225.other_comments: This is acetate kinase (EC 2.7.2.1), catalyzing the reversible phosphotransfer from ATP to acetate, forming ADP and acetyl phosphate. The reaction is balanced in both atoms and charge (ATP + Acetate <=> ADP + Acetyl phosphate). Although the standard free energy favors ATP formation (the reverse direction), the enzyme operates reversibly in vivo depending on substrate concentrations; in fermentative organisms it commonly runs toward ATP/acetate production, while in acetate assimilation it runs toward acetyl phosphate.

rxn00549.other_comments: This is fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase, EC 3.1.3.11), which hydrolyzes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate and inorganic phosphate. rxn05161.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter ATPase coupling ATP hydrolysis to import of a nonpolar amino acid (L-Leucine). rxn00264.other_comments: This is the malate oxidase reaction (S)-malate:oxygen oxidoreductase, oxidizing L-malate to oxaloacetate using molecular oxygen as the electron acceptor and producing hydrogen peroxide. rxn03951.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD-dependent oxidation of 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine (4-(phosphonooxy)-threonine) to 2-amino-3-oxo-4-phosphonooxybutyrate (3-amino-2-oxo... commonly written as (2S)-2-amino-3-oxo-4-phosphonooxybutanoate), catalyzed by PdxA in the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate biosynthesis pathway. The reaction oxidizes a secondary hydroxyl to a ketone, transferring a hydride to NAD+ to form NADH and releasing a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: the substrate loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD, one as H+), consistent with NAD + RCH(OH) -> NADH + H+ + RC(=O).

rxn02933.other_comments: This is the 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction (HSD17B10/MHBD, EC 1.1.1.178), part of isoleucine degradation. It oxidizes the 3-hydroxyl group to a ketone using NAD+, producing 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA, NADH, and H+. Atoms and charges balance: oxidation of a secondary alcohol to ketone removes 2 H (one to NAD+ as hydride, one as H+). Stoichiometry is correct. In vivo, this catabolic pathway proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction toward 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA.

rxn00506.other_comments: This is the aldehyde dehydrogenase (NAD+) reaction, oxidizing acetaldehyde to acetate. The stoichiometry is balanced: acetaldehyde (C2H4O) + H2O + NAD+ -> acetate (C2H3O2-) + NADH + 2 H+. Carbon (2=2), oxygen (1+1=2), hydrogen (4+2 acetaldehyde+water = 6 on left; acetate 3 + 2 H+ + NADH H = 6) and charge balance correctly. In vivo this reaction is essentially irreversible in the oxidative direction due to the favorable thermodynamics of aldehyde oxidation.

rxn00171.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (acylating), EC 1.2.1.10. It oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetyl-CoA using NAD+ as electron acceptor and CoA as the acyl acceptor. The stoichiometry is balanced: acetaldehyde (C2H4O) + CoA + NAD+ yields acetyl-CoA + NADH + H+. Atoms and charge balance correctly. The reaction is thermodynamically reversible and used in both directions in vivo, for example in acetaldehyde/ethanol metabolism (bifunctional AdhE enzymes) where it runs in the reductive direction toward acetaldehyde during fermentation.

rxn00584.other_comments: This corresponds to the oxidative decarboxylation/aromatization step converting a 1,6-dihydroxy-2,4-cyclohexadiene-1-carboxylate (a dihydrodiol of benzoate) to catechol, releasing CO2 and reducing NAD+ to NADH. The release of CO2 and aromatization make this step strongly favorable and effectively irreversible in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn00727.other_comments: This is the anthranilate synthase reaction (EC 4.1.3.27), the first committed step in tryptophan biosynthesis. Chorismate plus the amide nitrogen donor L-glutamine yields anthranilate, pyruvate, L-glutamate, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: glutamine provides the amino group to form anthranilate while the chorismate side chain is released as pyruvate, and glutamine is hydrolyzed to glutamate. Atoms and charge balance correctly. In vivo this reaction is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn05617.other_comments: This is a PEP-dependent phosphotransferase system (PTS) reaction for mannitol uptake. PEP donates its phosphoryl group (via the phosphorelay of EI, HPr, EIIA, EIIB, EIIC) to translocate and phosphorylate extracellular mannitol, producing intracellular mannitol-1-phosphate and pyruvate. The stoichiometry is balanced: PEP + mannitol -> pyruvate + mannitol-1-phosphate. One phosphoryl group is transferred, and atoms balance. [directionality_note] PTS group translocation is effectively irreversible in vivo due to the high phosphoryl-transfer potential of PEP and the coupling to substrate import.

rxn09105.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP) phosphatase reaction, hydrolyzing the phosphate group from PGP to yield phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and inorganic phosphate, here specified with the di-C16:1 (dihexadec-9-enoyl) acyl chains. The stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the phosphomonoester bond, releasing Pi and H+ while converting PGP to PG. Mass and charge balance correctly with the H+ released.

errors: TTP and dTDP are inconsistent: TTP (thymidine triphosphate, also written dTTP) is a deoxyribonucleotide, so the product should be dTDP, which is correct, but the substrate label 'TTP' should be 'dTTP' for consistency

Stoichiometry imbalance: NAD kinase phosphorylates NAD to NADP, transferring one phosphate from dTTP to NAD. NAD + dTTP -> NADP + dTDP is charge/mass balanced only if H+ accounting is considered; the H+ on product side is questionable since phosphoryl transfer to the 2'-OH typically does not release a free proton in this stoichiometry
rxn10060.other_comments: This is an NAD kinase reaction using dTTP (TTP) as the phosphoryl donor instead of ATP, converting NAD to NADP and producing dTDP. The reaction is essentially a phosphoryl transfer. In vivo, kinase reactions consuming a triphosphate to make a phosphorylated product strongly favor the forward direction.

rxn01445.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of dGMP (2'-deoxyguanosine 5'-monophosphate) by a 5'-nucleotidase, cleaving the phosphate group to yield deoxyguanosine and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: dGMP + H2O yields deoxyguanosine + Pi. Phosphomonoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of dephosphorylation.

rxn05248.other_comments: This is a fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (ligase) reaction for a 15-carbon anteiso branched fatty acid (fa4). The reaction activates the free fatty acid: ATP + CoA + fatty acid -> AMP + PPi + fatty acyl-CoA. Stoichiometry is balanced as written (ATP provides AMP + PPi, and CoA is esterified to the carboxylate releasing water, which is sometimes omitted in lumped models). In vivo this proceeds in the forward (activation) direction because the released pyrophosphate is rapidly hydrolyzed by pyrophosphatase, pulling the reaction toward acyl-CoA formation.

rxn08766.other_comments: This is the FabH (beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase III) reaction that initiates fatty acid biosynthesis. It condenses acetyl-CoA with malonyl-ACP to form acetoacetyl-ACP, releasing CoA and CO2. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA condenses with the malonyl-ACP, with decarboxylation providing the thermodynamic driving force (loss of CO2). Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: The substrate name 'gly-pro-L' indicates a glycylproline dipeptide (Gly-Pro), which is not a typical substrate for methionyl aminopeptidase. Methionyl aminopeptidase (MetAP) specifically removes N-terminal methionine residues from nascent polypeptides, not glycyl-proline dipeptides.
The enzyme-reaction assignment appears incorrect; cleavage of Gly-Pro dipeptides is characteristic of prolidase/Xaa-Pro dipeptidase or aminopeptidase P, not methionyl aminopeptidase.
Although prolyl bonds (Xaa-Pro) are generally resistant to most aminopeptidases, the hydrolysis chemistry itself is otherwise stoichiometrically balanced.
rxn12638.other_comments: The reaction describes hydrolysis of the dipeptide glycyl-L-proline (Gly-Pro) into glycine and L-proline, consuming one water molecule. The mass balance and atom balance of the hydrolysis are correct (one peptide bond broken, one water added). However, the assigned enzyme name (methionyl aminopeptidase) does not match this substrate.

rxn00305.other_comments: This is phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (GTP-dependent, PEPCK, EC 4.1.1.32). Oxaloacetate is decarboxylated and phosphorylated by GTP to form PEP, CO2, and GDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: carbons (OAA C4 = PEP C3 + CO2 C1), and phosphate transfer from GTP to PEP yields GDP. The reaction is freely reversible in vitro, though in vivo it typically operates in the PEP-forming (gluconeogenic) direction in the cytosol/mitochondria depending on tissue.

rxn05329.other_comments: This is the dehydration step in fatty acid biosynthesis (FabA/FabZ type 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase), converting (R)-3-hydroxybutanoyl-ACP to but-2-enoyl-ACP (crotonyl-ACP) plus water. Stoichiometry is balanced: the hydroxyl and a hydrogen are removed as water, forming a C2-C3 double bond. In vivo, in the context of the fatty acid synthesis elongation cycle, the reaction proceeds toward dehydration (forward).

rxn00612.other_comments: This is glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (NADP+), EC 1.1.1.94. It oxidizes sn-glycerol-3-phosphate to glycerone phosphate (dihydroxyacetone phosphate, DHAP) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The reaction is balanced: glycerol-3-phosphate (C3H7O6P, includes the 2-hydroxyl) is oxidized to DHAP (C3H5O6P), releasing 2H (one as H+ and a hydride to NADP+). Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: Oxygen atom imbalance: O2 (2 O atoms) on the left cannot balance with 2.0 H2O (2 O atoms) on the right; however the hydrogen balance is the key issue - acyl-CoA dehydrogenase/oxidase reactions remove 2 H per substrate. For 2 substrates, 4 H are removed, which combined with O2 gives 2 H2O (correct H2O2 vs H2O distinction matters)

Acyl-CoA oxidases typically produce H2O2, not H2O. If this is an oxidase using O2, the product should be H2O2 (O2 + 2 substrate -> 2 product + ... actually O2 + substrate -> product + H2O2). The stoichiometry with 2.0 H2O implies an oxidase coupled differently or a mixed-function oxidase
rxn02268.other_comments: This represents the oxidation of (S)-2-methylbutyryl-CoA to tiglyl-CoA (2-methylcrotonyl-CoA / (E)-2-methylbut-2-enoyl-CoA), introducing a double bond between C2 and C3. This is the first dehydrogenation step in isoleucine catabolism. The reaction is written as an oxidase using O2. Atom balance: 2 substrate molecules each lose 2 H (4 H total), O2 + 4 H -> 2 H2O, which balances. However, biologically this dehydrogenation is normally catalyzed by an FAD-dependent acyl-CoA dehydrogenase using electron transfer flavoprotein (not molecular O2 directly), or by an acyl-CoA oxidase that yields H2O2.

rxn12405.other_comments: This is a passive transport reaction moving (R)-3-hydroxybutanoate between the extraorganism (extracellular) compartment and the cytosol. The same metabolite appears on both sides, which is correct for a transport reaction where the species differ only by compartment. Stoichiometry is balanced (1:1). Passive (facilitated/diffusion) transport is driven by the concentration gradient and is therefore reversible in vivo.

rxn05461.other_comments: This is the NADPH-dependent reduction of a 3-oxoacyl-ACP (beta-ketoacyl-ACP) to a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP, catalyzed by 3-oxoacyl-ACP reductase (FabG) in the fatty acid elongation cycle. The substrate is an 18-carbon (octadecanoyl) beta-ketoacyl-ACP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: NADPH + H+ reduces the 3-oxo group to a 3-hydroxy group, yielding NADP+. Note: the name uses 'octodecanoyl' which is a misspelling of 'octadecanoyl' (C18). In the fatty acid synthesis cycle this reductive step proceeds in the forward (reduction) direction in vivo.

rxn10222.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol synthase (phosphatidate cytidylyltransferase, EC 2.7.7.41) reaction with a specific branched-chain (isotetradecanoyl/iso-C14:0) phosphatidate substrate. CTP reacts with phosphatidic acid to form CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing pyrophosphate. The reaction is balanced: CTP provides CMP transfer with loss of PPi, and a proton is released. Charges and atoms balance with the H+ accounting. In vivo this enzyme is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible toward CDP-diacylglycerol synthesis.

rxn10263.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PgsA) reaction transferring the phosphatidyl group from CDP-diacylglycerol to sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, producing phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP) and CMP. With the anteiso-pentadecanoyl (15:0 anteiso) acyl chains, the stoichiometry is balanced: the phosphatidyl moiety is transferred to the glycerol-3-phosphate, releasing CMP. Mass and charge balance hold as written.

rxn00269.other_comments: This is glycine oxidase (EC 1.4.3.19), which oxidatively deaminates glycine using O2. The reaction: H2O + O2 + Glycine -> NH3 + H2O2 + Glyoxylate. Atom balance: C2, N1, and checking H: left H2O(2) + Glycine(C2H5NO2, 5H) = 7H; right NH3(3) + H2O2(2) + Glyoxylate(C2H2O3 as acid, or glyoxylate anion). Glyoxylic acid is C2H2O3 (2H). 3+2+2=7H. Balanced. O: left H2O(1) + O2(2) + Glycine(2) = 5; right H2O2(2) + Glyoxylate acid(3) = 5. Balanced. The reaction is stoichiometrically correct assuming neutral/protonated species.

rxn03586.other_comments: This is vanillate O-demethylase (vanillate demethylase / monooxygenase), catalyzing the oxidative demethylation of vanillate to protocatechuate. It consumes NADH, O2, and a proton, producing water, NAD+, formaldehyde, and protocatechuate. Atom and charge balance check: C8H7O4(-) vanillate + CH3 group is removed as formaldehyde (CH2O), yielding C7H5O4(-) protocatechuate. The mass and charge balance correctly (one O incorporated, the other reduced to water by NADH). The reaction is balanced for C, H, O, N, and charge.

rxn02159.other_comments: This is the histidinol dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.23), here representing the first oxidation step of L-histidinol to L-histidinal. The reaction as written (NAD+ + L-histidinol -> NADH + H+ + L-histidinal) is stoichiometrically and charge balanced: histidinol is oxidized (loss of 2H, gain of =O effectively, releasing 2 electrons and 2 protons; one H+ appears in solution, the hydride goes to NAD+). In vivo, histidinol dehydrogenase normally proceeds in the biosynthetic direction toward histidine, oxidizing histidinol via histidinal to histidine (a 4-electron oxidation using 2 NAD+). The partial oxidation step is thermodynamically driven forward in the context of the overall pathway.

rxn08814.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase (L1) reaction hydrolyzing the ester bond of 1-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol (carrying a hexadec-9-enoyl/C16:1 group) using water to release the free fatty acid (hexadecenoate) and glycerophosphoglycerol, plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acyl-ester hydrolysis consumes one H2O and produces one free fatty acid (deprotonated, hence the H+) and the deacylated glycerophosphoglycerol backbone. Hydrolytic lipase/esterase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn08845.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase (L2) reaction hydrolyzing the ester bond of 2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol bearing a dodecanoyl (C12:0) chain. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acyl group plus water yields the free fatty acid (carboxylate + H+) and the deacylated glycerophosphoglycerol.

rxn02798.other_comments: This is the steroid sulfatase (STS, arylsulfatase C) reaction hydrolyzing estrone 3-sulfate to estrone and inorganic sulfate. Mass and charge balance: H2O + estrone-3-sulfate (C18H21O5S-, charge -1) yields estrone (C18H22O2, neutral) + sulfate (SO4 2-) + H+. Atom balance checks out (C18, S1, and O/H balance) and charge balances (-1 = -2 +1). The reaction is essentially irreversible toward hydrolysis under physiological conditions.

rxn08078.other_comments: This represents a beta-N-acetylglucosaminidase (a lytic transglycosylase-related/exo-glycosidase) cleaving the glycosidic bond in a 1,6-anhydro-MurNAc-containing muropeptide, releasing free GlcNAc and the 1,6-anhydro-MurNAc-tetrapeptide. Hydrolytic glycosidase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn05174.other_comments: This is a nickel ABC transporter reaction coupling ATP hydrolysis to Ni2+ import. The reaction shows ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+), which is mass and charge balanced. The Ni2+ appears on both sides because compartmental localization (e.g., extracellular vs cytoplasmic) is not annotated here, but it represents the transported substrate. ABC import systems use ATP hydrolysis to drive uptake against a gradient, making this effectively irreversible (forward).

At physiological pH, palmitate (carboxylate, -1) and glycerol-3-phosphate (-2) carry the negative charges; balancing the reactant 1-hexadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (-2) plus H2O requires only 1 H+ on the product side, not 2.0 H+.
rxn08799.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase (L1) reaction hydrolyzing the ester bond of 1-hexadecanoyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (a lysophosphatidic acid / monoacyl-glycerophosphate) to yield glycerol-3-phosphate and palmitate (C16:0). Atomically the mass balance is correct, but the proton stoichiometry appears off.

Standard gamma-glutamyl transfer uses an existing gamma-glutamyl donor (e.g., glutathione or a glutamyl peptide), not free L-glutamate, because the gamma-carboxyl amide bond formation from free glutamate plus an acceptor amine releasing only water is thermodynamically unfavorable as written.

Atom balance: L-Glutamate (C5H9NO4) + L-3-cyanoalanine (C4H6N2O2) = C9H15N3O6; products gamma-glutamyl-beta-cyanoalanine (C9H13N3O5) + H2O (H2O) = C9H15N3O6. The mass balance actually checks out, but the implied direct condensation of an amide bond with only water release does not reflect the enzyme's true (transpeptidation) mechanism.
rxn02791.other_comments: This represents a gamma-glutamyltransferase (transpeptidation) forming gamma-glutamyl-beta-cyanoalanine. The written form is a net condensation of L-glutamate with the amino acid beta-cyanoalanine (L-3-cyanoalanine) losing water. Atom counts balance, but physiologically GGT-type enzymes use an activated gamma-glutamyl donor rather than free glutamate.

rxn05957.other_comments: This is O-succinylhomoserine sulfhydrylase (MetZ/direct sulfhydrylation pathway, EC 2.5.1.49), which combines O-succinyl-L-homoserine with hydrogen sulfide to yield L-homocysteine and succinate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written: H2S + O-succinyl-L-homoserine -> homocysteine + succinate. In vivo it proceeds toward homocysteine biosynthesis in methionine metabolism.

rxn00433.other_comments: This is sarcosine oxidase (EC 1.5.3.1). Sarcosine (N-methylglycine) is oxidatively demethylated to glycine, with the methyl group released as formaldehyde, consuming O2 and water and producing H2O2. The reaction is balanced: sarcosine (C3H7NO2) + O2 + H2O -> glycine (C2H5NO2) + formaldehyde (CH2O) + H2O2 (H2O2). Atom check: C 3=2+1, N 1=1, O 2+2+1=5 vs 2+1+2=5, H 7+2=9 vs 5+2+2=9. Stoichiometrically correct.

errors: The reaction is not balanced. GTP (C10H12N5O14P3, charge -4 at physiological pH) plus 3 H2O should yield the products. Checking carbon: GTP has 10 carbons; products are formate (1 C) + dihydroneopterin precursor 2,5-diamino-6-(5'-phosphoribosylamino)-4-pyrimidinone (9 C) = 10 C, OK. Phosphate balance: GTP has 3 P; products PPi (2 P) + product (1 P) = 3 P, OK. However, the hydrogen/charge balance with '3.0 H+' on the product side combined with 3 H2O appears inconsistent and should be verified; the conventional GTP cyclohydrolase II reaction releases formate, PPi and the diaminopyrimidine intermediate.
rxn00300.other_comments: This is GTP cyclohydrolase II (EC 3.5.4.25), which hydrolyzes GTP to 2,5-diamino-6-(5'-phosphoribosylamino)-4(3H)-pyrimidinone, releasing formate and pyrophosphate. This is the first committed step in riboflavin/FMN/FAD biosynthesis. The atom count for C, N, P generally matches; the reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo due to PPi release and hydrolysis.

rxn10256.other_comments: This is a diacylglycerol kinase reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the sn-3 hydroxyl of 1,2-diisopentadecanoyl-sn-glycerol, producing the corresponding phosphatidic acid (1,2-diisopentadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) and ADP. Atoms balance: the phosphate transferred from ATP to DAG accounts for the product PA and ADP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as written.

rxn08792.other_comments: This represents L-lactate dehydrogenase (respiratory, quinone-dependent), e.g. LldD in E. coli, which oxidizes L-lactate to pyruvate while reducing ubiquinone-8 to ubiquinol-8. The reaction is balanced: L-lactate (C3H5O3) + ubiquinone-8 yields pyruvate (C3H3O3) + ubiquinol-8, with the two H/electrons transferred from lactate to the quinone. Mass and charge are balanced (two electrons and two protons effectively move to ubiquinone). In vivo this enzyme operates in the direction of lactate oxidation, feeding electrons into the respiratory chain, so it is effectively physiologically forward.

errors: The transported substrate hexanesulfonate appears on both sides of the equation without compartment designations, making the transport reaction stoichiometrically uninformative. For an ABC transport reaction, hexanesulfonate should be shown in distinct compartments (e.g., hexanesulfonate[extracellular] -> hexanesulfonate[cytosol]).
Without compartment annotations the reaction as written is a futile cycle (hexanesulfonate cancels out), leaving only ATP hydrolysis.
rxn05585.other_comments: This represents an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the import of hexanesulfonate. The ATP hydrolysis chemistry is balanced and correct, and ABC importers are effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo. The main issue is the absence of compartment labels for the transported metabolite.

rxn03419.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolytic cleavage of the formamido group from a formamidopyrimidine nucleoside triphosphate, releasing formate and yielding a 2,5-diaminopyrimidine nucleoside triphosphate. This is an amidohydrolase (deformylase-type) reaction. Mass and charge balance appear consistent: the formamido carbonyl carbon is removed as formate with addition of water, generating a free amine and releasing a proton. This step is part of riboflavin/deazaflavin or related cofactor biosynthesis pathways where the formamidopyrimidine intermediate is deformylated. Such hydrolytic deformylation reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, driven forward by the release of formate.

The reaction is mass/charge unbalanced as written. A correct form would not include H+ as a reactant, or would release H+ if accounting for the proton from the glycerol hydroxyl.
rxn08551.other_comments: This is the glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT/PlsB-type) reaction that esterifies the sn-1 position of glycerol-3-phosphate using octadecanoyl (stearoyl)-ACP as the acyl donor, producing 1-octadecanoyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and free ACP. The thioester bond cleavage makes this strongly thermodynamically favorable and committed in the forward direction in vivo.

errors: Carbon chain length mismatch: (3R)-3-Hydroxypalmitoyl-ACP is a C16 substrate, but the product (2E)-Tetradecenoyl-ACP is a C14 acyl chain. The dehydration of 3-hydroxypalmitoyl-ACP should yield (2E)-hexadecenoyl-ACP (C16), not the C14 tetradecenoyl species.
The abbreviation 'HMA' is ambiguous/non-standard for (3R)-3-hydroxypalmitoyl-ACP.
rxn05335.other_comments: This is intended to be a beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase (FabZ/FabA-type) reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis, removing water from a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP to form a trans-2-enoyl-ACP. In vivo, FAS dehydratase steps proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward enoyl-ACP formation.

rxn00679.other_comments: This is 2-methylcitrate synthase (PrpC), which condenses propionyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form 2-methylcitrate, releasing CoA. As written (CoA + H+ + 2-methylcitrate -> H2O + oxaloacetate + propionyl-CoA), it is the reverse of the biological direction. The stoichiometry balances: 2-methylcitrate (C7H8O7) hydrolytic cleavage of the thioester forms the C-C bond with oxaloacetate and propionyl-CoA. Atom and charge balance are consistent with the aldol-type condensation analogous to citrate synthase.

rxn00758.other_comments: This is the glycerophosphodiesterase (GPCPD) reaction, hydrolyzing sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine into glycerol-3-phosphate and choline. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: substrate glycerophosphocholine plus water yields glycerol-3-phosphate (which carries a negative charge), choline (positively charged), and the released proton, accounting for atoms and charges correctly. Hydrolysis of the phosphodiester bond is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn05607.other_comments: This is a PEP-dependent phosphotransferase system (PTS) reaction for maltose uptake. PEP donates a phosphate group to maltose during translocation across the membrane, producing pyruvate and intracellular maltose-6-phosphate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one phosphate is transferred from PEP (yielding pyruvate) to maltose (yielding maltose-6-phosphate). PTS transport is essentially irreversible in vivo due to the high phosphoryl-transfer potential of PEP coupling to vectorial transport.

rxn01746.other_comments: This is allantoicase (allantoate amidinohydrolase, EC 3.5.3.4), which hydrolyzes allantoate. Allantoate (C4H7N4O4-) + H2O yields ureidoglycolate (C3H5N2O4-) + urea (CH4N2O). Checking stoichiometry: allantoate C4H7N4O4 + H2O (H2O) = C4H9N4O5; products ureidoglycolate C3H5N2O4 + urea CH4N2O = C4H9N4O5. Atoms and charge balance correctly. This is a hydrolytic reaction in purine degradation and proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn09111.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PgsA) step, transferring the phosphatidyl moiety from CDP-diacylglycerol (with two C16:0/palmitoyl chains) to the sn-1 position of glycerol-3-phosphate, releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP). Note: the label says 'Phosphatidylglycerol synthase' but the product is phosphatidylglycerophosphate, so this is actually PGP synthase (EC 2.7.8.5), an earlier step than PG formation (which requires subsequent dephosphorylation). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: G3P provides the glycerol-phosphate head group, CDP-DAG provides the diacylglycerol-phosphate, and CMP is released.

rxn00672.other_comments: This is methylmalonyl-CoA decarboxylase. The reaction shows (R)/(D)-methylmalonyl-CoA being decarboxylated to propionyl-CoA plus CO2, consuming a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced (mass and charge): D-methylmalonyl-CoA (C25, charge -5) + H+ yields propionyl-CoA (C24, charge -4) + CO2. Note the enzyme name references (S)-methylmalonyl-CoA but the substrate listed is D-(R)-methylmalonyl-CoA; the natural substrate of the decarboxylase is indeed the (R)/(S) epimer-dependent on system, a minor naming inconsistency. In vivo, decarboxylation is thermodynamically favorable (forward toward propionyl-CoA + CO2), though it is often represented as reversible in databases.

rxn05348.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthesis condensation step (KAS/FabB-FabF type). Decanoyl-ACP (C10) condenses with malonyl-ACP, releasing CO2 and free ACP, yielding 3-oxododecanoyl-ACP (C12 beta-ketoacyl-ACP). Carbon balance: C10 acyl + C3 malonyl moiety = C13 minus CO2 = C12 product, consistent. Stoichiometry is balanced and the decarboxylative condensation is thermodynamically driven forward in vivo.

errors: No net chemical transformation; both sides are identical (H+ + K+ <=> H+ + K+). This is a transport reaction where the lack of compartment annotation makes it appear as a null reaction. To be meaningful, the metabolites should be distinguished by compartment, e.g., H+[out] + K+[in] <=> H+[in] + K+[out].
rxn05595.other_comments: This is a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN) representing a K+/H+ antiporter or exchanger, where a proton and a potassium ion are translocated across a membrane in exchange. As written, no compartment distinction is shown, so it reads as an identity (no net change). Stoichiometrically the atom and charge balance is trivially satisfied. The biological function is proton/potassium exchange across a membrane, often driven by the proton motive force; direction depends on the electrochemical gradients of both ions.

Compartment designations (extraorganism vs cytosol) are not encoded in the metabolite identifiers, so the transport across the membrane is not represented
For a proper secondary symport, the stoichiometry should show both Malonate and Na+ moving in the same direction (e.g., Malonate[e] + Na+[e] -> Malonate[c] + Na+[c])
rxn12432.other_comments: This is described as a sodium-coupled secondary symport importing malonate from the extracellular space into the cytosol. As written the metabolites lack compartment tags, so the equation reduces to an identity (no net change). The intended reaction is the cotransport of malonate with Na+ down the sodium electrochemical gradient. Driven by the inward Na+ gradient, such uptake symporters typically operate in the import direction in vivo, though thermodynamically they can be reversible depending on gradients.
