rxn00206.other_comments: This is the superoxide dismutase (SOD) reaction, dismutation of superoxide radical anion into molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. As written it lacks the 2 protons needed for both charge and mass balance.

rxn01871.other_comments: This is the dihydrolipoyllysine-residue acetyltransferase (E2) reaction of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (EC 2.3.1.12). Acetyl-CoA transfers its acetyl group to the dihydrolipoamide moiety, producing CoA and S-acetyldihydrolipoamide. The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced as written: one acetyl group is transferred from CoA to a free thiol of dihydrolipoamide. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1:1).

errors: The substrate 'apolipoprotein' is misspelled as 'applipoprotein' in the equation

The reaction as written may not be elementally balanced; the apolipoprotein gains an acyl group to become the mature lipoprotein, but the H+ stoichiometry should be verified - the N-acylation of the apolipoprotein cysteine amine typically releases the H+ but charge/mass balance depends on protonation states
rxn08119.other_comments: This represents the Lnt (apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase) reaction, the final step in bacterial lipoprotein maturation. Lnt transfers an acyl chain (here C16:0/palmitoyl) from the sn-1 position of phosphatidylethanolamine to the free alpha-amino group of the N-terminal diacylglyceryl-cysteine of apolipoprotein, producing the mature triacylated lipoprotein and a 2-acyl-lyso-phosphatidylethanolamine. This occurs at the periplasmic/outer face of the inner membrane.

rxn08306.other_comments: This is the CDP-diacylglycerol synthase reaction (CDS, EC 2.7.7.41) with dodecanoyl (C12:0) acyl chains. CTP reacts with phosphatidic acid (1,2-didodecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) to form CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). The reaction is balanced in mass and charge: CTP provides the CMP-phosphate transferred to the phosphate of PA, with release of PPi and a proton. In vivo the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate, making it physiologically essentially irreversible toward CDP-diacylglycerol synthesis.

errors: Reaction is missing a proton (H+) on the NADPH side; the balanced reaction should be 3-oxododecanoyl-ACP + NADPH + H+ <=> (3R)-3-hydroxydodecanoyl-ACP + NADP+
rxn05340.other_comments: This is the 3-oxoacyl-ACP reductase (FabG) step of fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing 3-oxododecanoyl-ACP to (3R)-3-hydroxydodecanoyl-ACP using NADPH. As written, the reaction proceeds left-to-right as oxidation (hydroxy to oxo, producing NADPH), but in vivo the biosynthetic direction is reduction (oxo to hydroxy, consuming NADPH), i.e., the reverse of how it is written.

rxn02143.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction (EC 2.8.3.6) transferring the CoA moiety from succinyl-CoA to 3-oxoadipate, yielding succinate and 3-oxoadipyl-CoA. It is part of the beta-ketoadipate pathway for aromatic compound degradation. Atoms and CoA groups balance: one CoA is transferred, both sides carry equivalent C, H, O, N, P, S. CoA-transferases typically operate near equilibrium and are reversible, though physiological flux favors the forward (succinyl-CoA-consuming) direction in the degradative pathway.

errors: This is a transport reaction where the same metabolite (L-Serine) and proton (H+) appear identically on both sides, but the compartment annotations are not shown in the provided string, making it impossible to verify the transport. As written literally, the reaction is a null/trivial identity (substrates equal products) with no net chemical change.
If intended as a symport/transport, the compartment designations (e.g., cytosol vs extracellular) are missing from the displayed equation.
rxn05307.other_comments: The reaction appears to be a proton-coupled L-serine transport reaction (SER:H+ symport) based on the reaction ID 'SER_SER' and 'TRANS-RXN' prefix. Transport reactions move identical species across membranes, so the same metabolite legitimately appears on both sides differing only by compartment. As displayed without compartment tags, it reduces to a no-op identity.

rxn08546.other_comments: This is the glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (PlsB-type) reaction, transferring a dodecanoyl (C12:0) acyl group from acyl-ACP to the sn-1 position of glycerol-3-phosphate to form 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and free ACP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one acyl group is transferred, producing one ACP and one monoacyl-G3P. This is the committed first step of phospholipid biosynthesis and is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the acylation direction.

rxn08900.other_comments: This represents the FAD-dependent malate dehydrogenase (malate:quinone oxidoreductase, MQO, EC 1.1.5.4) reaction. L-Malate is oxidized to oxaloacetate, with the electrons transferred to the membrane quinone pool (ubiquinone-8 reduced to ubiquinol-8). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: malate (C4H4O5, 2- at physiological pH) loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) to become oxaloacetate (C4H2O5, 2-), and ubiquinone-8 + 2H+ + 2e- becomes ubiquinol-8. Atoms and charges balance. Although written as reversible, in vivo MQO strongly favors malate oxidation (forward direction) because the reaction is essentially irreversible due to the favorable thermodynamics of quinone reduction, unlike the NAD-dependent malate dehydrogenase.

rxn05735.other_comments: This reaction is the oxidation of aminoacetaldehyde to glycine, catalyzed by an aldehyde dehydrogenase using NAD+ as electron acceptor. Balancing: aminoacetaldehyde (C2H5NO) + H2O + NAD+ -> glycine (C2H5NO2) + NADH + 2 H+. Carbon (2=2), nitrogen (1=1), oxygen (1 from aldehyde + 1 from water = 2 in glycine) all balance. Hydrogen: aminoacetaldehyde (5) + water (2) = 7 on left; glycine (5) + NADH adds H + 2 H+ = balances when accounting for NAD/NADH hydride transfer. Charge is balanced with the 2 H+ produced. Aldehyde dehydrogenase reactions are thermodynamically strongly favorable and considered essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn01133.other_comments: This is the maltose O-acetyltransferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.79), transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to maltose, producing CoA and acetyl-maltose (6-O-acetyl-maltose). The reaction is balanced: acetyl-CoA donates the acetyl moiety to the sugar hydroxyl, releasing free CoA. Stoichiometry is correct with one acetyl transferred. In vivo, the thioester bond of acetyl-CoA is high-energy and its hydrolysis/transfer to the alcohol drives the reaction toward acetylation of maltose.

rxn12639.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide L-alanyl-L-glutamine (Ala-Gln) into its constituent amino acids L-alanine and L-glutamine, consuming one water molecule. The reaction is balanced: the dipeptide plus water yields the two free amino acids (the peptide bond is cleaved by addition of water). Stoichiometry is correct. Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible under physiological conditions, so it proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn01015.other_comments: This reaction is an aldose-ketose isomerization between hydroxypyruvate (a 3-carbon ketoacid, HOCH2-CO-COOH) and tartronate semialdehyde (OHC-CHOH-COOH). Both are C3H4O4 isomers, so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (1:1 conversion with no additional substrates or products). Isomerase reactions of this type are typically reversible, with directionality determined by metabolic context and downstream consumption.

rxn00875.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction (EC 2.8.3.8) transferring the CoA moiety from butyryl-CoA to acetate, producing acetyl-CoA and butyrate. The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: acetate + butyryl-CoA <=> acetyl-CoA + butyrate. CoA-transferases generally operate near equilibrium and are reversible; in vivo direction depends on the relative concentrations of the acyl-CoA and free acid substrates. In many anaerobic/gut bacteria (e.g., butyrate-producing species) this enzyme runs toward butyrate formation, but it is thermodynamically reversible.

rxn03159.other_comments: This is the LpxB (lipid A disaccharide synthase) reaction in the Raetz pathway of lipid A biosynthesis. UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine donates its 2,3-bis(3-hydroxytetradecanoyl)glucosamine moiety to Lipid X (2,3-bis(3-hydroxytetradecanoyl)-alpha-D-glucosaminyl-1-phosphate), forming the beta(1->6)-linked lipid A disaccharide and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced (glycosyl transfer with UDP leaving group). The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the biosynthetic direction.

errors: The substrate name 'Toxopyrimidine' is incorrect; the correct substrate is 4-amino-5-hydroxymethyl-2-methylpyrimidine (HMP). Toxopyrimidine refers to a different toxic analog (pyrithiamine-related). The intended substrate based on the enzyme name (HMP kinase) is the hydroxymethyl form.

The product '4-Amino-5-phosphomethyl-2-methylpyrimidine' should more correctly be named 4-amino-2-methyl-5-(phosphooxymethyl)pyrimidine (HMP-P), reflecting that a phosphate is added to the hydroxymethyl group, not a 'phosphomethyl' group.
rxn02484.other_comments: This is the HMP kinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.49) phosphorylating 4-amino-5-hydroxymethyl-2-methylpyrimidine to its monophosphate using ATP, part of thiamine biosynthesis. Stoichiometry (ATP + HMP -> ADP + H+ + HMP-P) is balanced if the correct substrate is the hydroxymethyl compound. ATP-dependent kinase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (phosphorylation) direction.

rxn01000.other_comments: This is prephenate dehydratase (EC 4.2.1.51), which converts prephenate to phenylpyruvate in phenylalanine biosynthesis. The reaction consumes a proton and prephenate, releasing water, CO2, and phenylpyruvate. Atom and charge balance: prephenate (C10H8O6, charge -2) + H+ yields phenylpyruvate (C9H7O3, charge -1) + H2O + CO2. Carbon: 10 = 9 + 1. Charge: -2 + 1 = -1. The reaction is balanced and correct.

rxn00647.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction (cysteine aminotransferase / cysteine transaminase, EC 2.6.1.3) transferring the amino group from L-cysteine to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and 3-mercaptopyruvate (the keto acid of cysteine). Atom and charge balance: 2-oxoglutarate (C5H4O5, -2) + H+ + L-cysteine (C3H6NO2S, -1 zwitterion as written, actually C3H7NO2S neutral / C3H6NO2S anion) -> L-glutamate (C5H8NO4, -1) + mercaptopyruvate (C3H3O3S, -1). With the explicit H+ included the equation balances for atoms and charge. Aminotransferases are PLP-dependent and characteristically reversible.

rxn00363.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of CMP (cytidine-5'-monophosphate) by a 5'-nucleotidase, yielding cytidine and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: H2O + CMP gives Pi + cytidine. Atoms and charges balance correctly. Phosphomonoester hydrolysis is highly exergonic, so in vivo it proceeds strongly in the direction of dephosphorylation.

errors: The reaction name (UDP-L-rhamnose:flavonol-3-O-D-glucoside L-rhamnosyltransferase) does not match the actual chemistry described, which is a SAM-dependent C-methylation, not a rhamnosyltransfer reaction
The enzyme name references UDP-L-rhamnose and a flavonol glucoside substrate, neither of which appear in the reaction equation
rxn03397.other_comments: The reaction equation itself is a stoichiometrically balanced SAM-dependent methyltransferase reaction: SAM + 2-octaprenyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinone yields SAH + H+ + 2-octaprenyl-3-methyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinone. This is a step in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis, catalyzed by 2-methoxy-6-polyprenyl-1,4-benzoquinol methylase (UbiE). The atoms and charges balance correctly. However, the assigned enzyme name/EC annotation is completely mismatched with the chemistry shown.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the acyl group transferred from phosphatidylglycerol to the lipoprotein N-terminus is one fatty acyl chain, but the product 2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol retains one acyl chain while the substrate dihexadecanoyl-PG has two; this accounts correctly for one acyl transfer, however a free H+ release should be checked and the apolipoprotein must already be a diacylglyceryl-modified prolipoprotein (the substrate label 'apolipoprotein' is imprecise)
Mass balance cannot be fully verified due to ambiguous/generic metabolite names ('applipoprotein', 'Lipoprotein')
Typo: 'applipoprotein' should be 'apolipoprotein'
rxn08120.other_comments: This represents Lnt (apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase), which transfers an acyl group from the sn-1 position of phosphatidylglycerol to the alpha-amino group of the N-terminal diacylglyceryl-cysteine of apolipoprotein, forming mature triacylated lipoprotein and releasing lyso-phosphatidylglycerol (2-acyl-GPG). The net acyl transfer (one C16 acyl moved, leaving a monoacyl-GPG) is consistent.

rxn12643.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide L-alanyl-L-leucine (Ala-Leu) into its constituent amino acids L-alanine and L-leucine, catalyzed by a dipeptidase. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: H2O cleaves the single peptide bond, yielding one molecule each of the two amino acids. Peptide bond hydrolysis is strongly thermodynamically favorable (large negative delta G) and proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn01462.other_comments: This reaction is guanidinobutyrase (EC 3.5.3.7), which hydrolyzes 4-guanidinobutanoate using water to produce urea and 4-aminobutanoate (GABA). The stoichiometry is balanced: C5H11N3O2 (4-guanidinobutanoate) + H2O yields CH4N2O (urea) + C4H9NO2 (GABA). Carbon (5 = 1+4), nitrogen (3 = 2+1), and other atoms balance correctly. As a hydrolase reaction, it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn01670.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), referred to here as nicotinamide ribonucleotide, by a 5'-nucleotidase/phosphohydrolase. Water attacks the phosphate ester bond, releasing inorganic phosphate and yielding nicotinamide riboside (N-ribosylnicotinamide). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: NMN (C11H15N2O8P) + H2O yields nicotinamide riboside (C11H15N2O5) + phosphate (HPO4/H2PO4). Mass and charge balance hold when protonation states are accounted for.

errors: The transported metabolite (D-Methionine) appears on both sides of the equation without compartment designations; in a proper ABC transport reaction it should be distinguished by compartment (e.g., D-Methionine[e] -> D-Methionine[c]). As written, with identical metabolites on both sides, D-Methionine cancels out and the reaction reduces to simple ATP hydrolysis, which is not the intended transport reaction.
rxn05183.other_comments: This is intended to represent ABC-transporter-driven import of D-methionine coupled to ATP hydrolysis. Stoichiometry of the ATP hydrolysis component (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) is balanced. ABC transport reactions are energetically driven and effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo. The key issue is the missing compartment labels on the substrate.

errors: The product of glycerate oxidation should be hydroxypyruvate, not tartronate semialdehyde. Oxidation of (R)-glycerate at the C2 hydroxyl yields hydroxypyruvate (2-oxo-3-hydroxypropanoate). Tartronate semialdehyde (2-hydroxy-3-oxopropanoate) would arise from oxidation at the terminal C3 hydroxyl, which is a distinct enzymatic activity (tartronate semialdehyde reductase / glyoxylate carboligase pathway).
NADP should be written as NADP+ for proper charge balance representation, though this is a notation issue.
rxn01281.other_comments: This is intended to be a glycerate dehydrogenase/reductase type reaction coupling NADP+/NADPH to a glycerate/aldehyde or ketoacid pair. As written, the carbonyl product is mislabeled; for the (R)-glycerate:NADP+ oxidoreductase activity the expected product is hydroxypyruvate. If the intended reaction is tartronate semialdehyde reductase, then it should be tartronate semialdehyde + NADPH + H+ <=> glycerate + NADP+, and the named substrate/product pairing here is inconsistent.

rxn05217.other_comments: This is a transport reaction (proton symport/antiport of L-aspartate across a membrane). The same metabolites appear on both sides because the reaction moves L-aspartate and H+ from one compartment to another. Mass and charge are balanced since identical species appear on each side. Although written symmetrically, the intended interpretation is translocation of L-aspartate coupled with H+ between compartments; without explicit compartment annotations the net chemical change is null, making true directionality uncertain in practice.

rxn03908.other_comments: This is the CMK reaction (4-diphosphocytidyl-2-C-methyl-D-erythritol kinase, EC 2.7.1.148) in the MEP/non-mevalonate isoprenoid biosynthesis pathway. ATP phosphorylates the 2-hydroxyl of 4-diphosphocytidyl-2-C-methyl-D-erythritol (CDP-ME) to yield CDP-ME 2-phosphate (CDP-MEP), ADP, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced in mass and charge: a gamma-phosphate is transferred from ATP to the substrate hydroxyl, releasing ADP and H+.

rxn00321.other_comments: This is the lysine 2,3-aminomutase (KAM/LAM) reaction, which interconverts L-lysine (alpha-lysine) and L-beta-lysine (3,6-diaminohexanoate). The reaction is an intramolecular amino group migration from the C2 (alpha) to the C3 (beta) position, requiring S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as a cofactor along with a [4Fe-4S] cluster and pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP). The mass balance is correct as written since it is an isomerization (substrate and product are both C6H14N2O2). In vivo it operates in the direction of L-beta-lysine formation, which feeds into lysine fermentation pathways (e.g., in Clostridium).

rxn00601.other_comments: This is the first step of the arginine succinyltransferase (AST) pathway for arginine catabolism. The enzyme (AstA, EC 2.3.1.109) transfers the succinyl group from succinyl-CoA to the alpha-amino (N2) nitrogen of L-arginine, releasing CoA and a proton. The atoms balance: arginine (C6H14N4O2) + succinyl-CoA contributes a succinyl group (C4H4O3 added), yielding N2-succinyl-L-arginine (C10H18N4O5) plus free CoA and H+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is incorrect; phosphatidylserine decarboxylation consumes one proton, not two. The balanced reaction is: H+ + phosphatidylserine -> CO2 + phosphatidylethanolamine
rxn09197.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (PSD) reaction with didodecanoyl (di-C12:0) acyl chains. The serine head group is decarboxylated to yield ethanolamine, converting phosphatidylserine to phosphatidylethanolamine and releasing CO2. This decarboxylation is metabolically irreversible in vivo.

errors: Proton (H+) stoichiometry and balance is incorrect; the oxidation of a hydroxyl to a keto group with NADP+ reduction to NADPH should consume/produce one H+, not 2.0 H+. As written (forward direction: NADP+ + 2 H+ + 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP -> NADPH + 3-oxoacyl-ACP), the equation is not charge- or hydrogen-balanced.

The reaction as written in the forward direction has reactant NADP+ being reduced to NADPH while a hydroxyl is oxidized to a ketone; this is chemically inconsistent because oxidizing a substrate (hydroxy to oxo) requires NADP+ to be the oxidant going to NADPH only if 2 electrons + H+ are transferred, but the correct balanced form is: 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP + NADP+ -> 3-oxoacyl-ACP + NADPH + H+ (H+ on product side, not reactant side).
rxn05336.other_comments: This is the beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase (FabG) reaction of fatty acid biosynthesis. The enzyme normally catalyzes reduction of 3-oxoacyl-ACP to (3R)-3-hydroxyacyl-ACP using NADPH. The named direction (oxidoreductase forming the oxo compound) is opposite to the physiological direction; in vivo the reaction proceeds toward the 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP (i.e., reverse of how it is written here).

rxn01300.other_comments: This is homoserine kinase (EC 2.7.1.39), which phosphorylates L-homoserine using ATP to form O-phospho-L-homoserine, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP donates a phosphate to homoserine's hydroxyl group, releasing ADP and H+. This is a key step in threonine biosynthesis.

rxn00838.other_comments: This is adenylosuccinate synthase (purA), which condenses IMP and L-aspartate using GTP to form adenylosuccinate (N6-(1,2-dicarboxyethyl)-AMP), releasing GDP and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: GTP + Asp + IMP -> adenylosuccinate + GDP + Pi + 2 H+. In vivo it proceeds in the direction of adenylosuccinate synthesis as part of de novo AMP biosynthesis.

rxn00831.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of inosine 5'-monophosphate (IMP) to inosine and inorganic phosphate, catalyzed by a 5'-nucleotidase. The stoichiometry is balanced: IMP + H2O yields inosine + phosphate. Atoms and charges are conserved as the phosphomonoester bond is hydrolyzed.

rxn00512.other_comments: This reaction is glycolate dehydrogenase/oxidoreductase: Glycolate + NAD+ <=> Glyoxylate + NADH + H+. The atoms balance: glycolate (C2H3O3-) loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one as H+) to yield glyoxylate (C2HO3-). Charge and mass are balanced as written. Thermodynamically, the oxidation of glycolate by NAD+ is unfavorable (high redox potential of glyoxylate/glycolate couple), so in vivo the reaction generally proceeds in the reverse direction (reduction of glyoxylate to glycolate), though dedicated glycolate oxidases use FAD/electron acceptors rather than NAD+.

rxn01100.other_comments: This is the phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) reaction. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP + 3-phospho-D-glycerate <=> ADP + 1,3-bisphospho-D-glycerate. Although enzymatically reversible, in vivo during glycolysis the dominant flux runs in the opposite direction to that written (1,3-BPG + ADP -> 3-PG + ATP, substrate-level phosphorylation). As written (ATP-consuming direction), this corresponds to the gluconeogenic direction, so relative to the written equation the typical glycolytic flux is 'reverse'.

rxn01352.other_comments: This is the dGTP triphosphohydrolase reaction (e.g., E. coli dgt gene product), which hydrolyzes dGTP into deoxyguanosine and inorganic triphosphate (PPPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: dGTP + H2O yields deoxyguanosine + triphosphate + H+. Mass and charge balance hold (dGTP is -4, deoxyguanosine is neutral, triphosphate PPPi is -5, plus H+). As a hydrolase, it is thermodynamically driven and physiologically irreversible in the direction of hydrolysis.

rxn02004.other_comments: This is the trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase (TPS2/OtsB) reaction, hydrolyzing trehalose 6-phosphate to free trehalose (TRHL) and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: one water and trehalose-6-phosphate yield phosphate plus trehalose. As a phosphate ester hydrolysis it is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn12634.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of the dipeptide glycyl-glutamate (Gly-Glu) into free glycine and L-glutamate, using one molecule of water. The stoichiometry is balanced: the dipeptide plus water yields the two constituent amino acids. However, the enzyme name 'methionyl aminopeptidase' is inconsistent with the substrate, as methionyl aminopeptidases specifically cleave N-terminal methionine residues, not an N-terminal glycine. This appears to be a generic aminopeptidase/dipeptidase activity rather than a methionyl-specific one. Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn00786.other_comments: This is the fructose-bisphosphate aldolase reaction (EC 4.1.2.13). D-fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is cleaved into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerone-phosphate) and D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the 6-carbon FBP splits into two 3-carbon triose phosphates. Although thermodynamically unfavorable in the cleavage direction (positive standard free energy), the reaction is pulled forward in glycolysis by downstream removal of products, and it runs in reverse during gluconeogenesis; thus it is physiologically reversible.

errors: The product 'L-Inositol' is incorrect; the dephosphorylation of 1D-myo-inositol 3-phosphate yields myo-inositol, not 'L-inositol'. myo-Inositol is the meso (achiral) form and is the correct product.
rxn00883.other_comments: This is the inositol monophosphatase (IMPase) reaction. It hydrolyzes 1D-myo-inositol 3-phosphate (= L-myo-inositol 1-phosphate) using water to release inorganic phosphate and free myo-inositol. Stoichiometry of atoms is balanced (one phosphate group transferred to water). In vivo this hydrolysis is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the dephosphorylation direction, a key step in inositol biosynthesis and the lithium-sensitive phosphoinositide cycle.

errors: Incorrect electron acceptor: acyl-CoA dehydrogenase uses FAD/FADH2, not NAD/NADH

The enzyme is typically FAD-dependent and reduces the FAD cofactor, which is then reoxidized by ETF (electron-transfer flavoprotein); writing NAD+/NADH as the cofactor pair is mechanistically and thermodynamically incorrect
rxn10014.other_comments: This represents the first oxidation step of fatty acid beta-oxidation, converting myristoyl-CoA (tetradecanoyl-CoA) to (2E)-tetradecenoyl-CoA. The carbon skeleton transformation and stoichiometry of the acyl moiety are correct, but the cofactor should be FAD/FADH2 rather than NAD/NADH. In vivo this dehydrogenation step proceeds in the forward (oxidation) direction as part of beta-oxidation.

rxn05485.other_comments: This is a PEP:carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS) reaction transporting N-Acetyl-D-glucosamine (GlcNAc) across the membrane while phosphorylating it. PEP donates its phosphate group to the incoming sugar, yielding pyruvate and GlcNAc 6-phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphate is transferred from PEP to the sugar, with conservation of atoms and charge.

rxn05406.other_comments: This is a fatty acid biosynthesis dehydratase reaction (3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase, FabZ/FabA type) acting on a branched-chain (15-methyl, iso/anteiso) C16 hydroxyacyl-ACP substrate. The 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP loses water to form a trans-2-enoyl-ACP. Stoichiometry is balanced: removal of one H2O converts the 3-hydroxy group plus adjacent C-H into a trans-2,3 double bond. Atoms and ACP carrier are conserved on both sides.

rxn10299.other_comments: This reaction represents the glycosylation (glucose substitution) of a myristoyl-lipoteichoic acid polymer with 24 repeating units. UDP-glucose serves as the glucosyl donor, transferring 24 glucose moieties onto the lipoteichoic acid backbone and releasing 24 UDP. The 24:24 stoichiometry between UDP-glucose consumed and UDP produced is balanced and consistent with one glucose transfer per repeat unit (n=24). Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugars are strongly exergonic due to the high group-transfer potential of the UDP-sugar bond, so this proceeds in the forward (glycosylation) direction in vivo.

rxn01255.other_comments: This is chorismate synthase (EC 4.2.3.5), which converts 5-enolpyruvylshikimate-3-phosphate (EPSP) to chorismate plus inorganic phosphate via a 1,4-elimination of phosphate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: EPSP (C10H12O10P, accounting for ionization) yields chorismate (C10H8O6, accounting for ionization) plus phosphate. Note that this enzyme requires a reduced FMN cofactor, though FMN is not net consumed and is typically omitted from the net equation.

rxn00214.other_comments: This is the UDP-glucose 4-epimerase (GALE) reaction, EC 5.1.3.2, which interconverts UDP-glucose and UDP-galactose via a transient oxidation/reduction at C4 using a tightly bound NAD+ cofactor. The reaction is balanced 1:1 (both are C15H24N2O17P2 isomers) and is mass- and charge-balanced as written.

rxn05251.other_comments: This is a fatty acyl-CoA ligase (synthetase) reaction. The reaction name FACOAL170(anteiso) and identifier fa12/fa12coa indicate activation of a fatty acid to its CoA thioester. The general stoichiometry ATP + CoA + fatty acid -> AMP + PPi + fatty acyl-CoA is balanced and standard for acyl-CoA synthetases (EC 6.2.1.x). In vivo, this reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible. Note: the fatty acid placeholder (fa12) should consistently match the acyl-CoA product (fa12coa); ensure the metabolite definitions correspond to the intended 17-carbon anteiso fatty acid implied by the name.

rxn01211.other_comments: This is the methenyltetrahydrofolate cyclohydrolase reaction (EC 3.5.4.9). The hydrolysis of the methenyl bridge in 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate yields 10-formyltetrahydrofolate. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O is consumed, and H+ plus 10-formyl-THF are produced. The methenyl form carries a +1 charge that is neutralized upon ring opening, consistent with H+ release. The enzyme is physiologically reversible and operates in both directions depending on folate one-carbon pool demands; in mammals it is part of the trifunctional MTHFD1 enzyme.

rxn00527.other_comments: This is the tyrosine aminotransferase reaction (EC 2.6.1.5), transferring the amino group from L-tyrosine to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate). The reaction is balanced in both atoms and charge: each side has the equivalent number of C, H, N, and O atoms. Aminotransferase reactions are PLP-dependent and generally near-equilibrium, hence reversible in vivo, though physiologically it often proceeds toward tyrosine degradation (forward direction).

As written, it shows oxidation of the 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP to the 3-oxoacyl-ACP using NADP+. In vivo during fatty acid synthesis, the physiological direction is the reduction of 3-oxohexanoyl-ACP to (3R)-3-hydroxyhexanoyl-ACP using NADPH, i.e. the reverse of how it is written here.

rxn00994.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction transferring the CoA moiety from butyryl-CoA to acetoacetate, yielding butyrate and acetoacetyl-CoA. The reaction is balanced: each side has the butanoyl/butyrate and acetoacetyl/acetoacetate moieties, with CoA conserved. CoA-transferases typically operate near equilibrium and the net direction depends on substrate concentrations in vivo.

rxn01917.other_comments: This is N-acetylglutamate kinase (EC 2.7.2.8), catalyzing phosphorylation of N-acetyl-L-glutamate by ATP to form N-acetyl-L-glutamyl-5-phosphate (N-acetylglutamyl-phosphate) and ADP, a step in the arginine biosynthesis pathway. The reaction is balanced: ATP donates a phosphate to the gamma-carboxyl group, with conservation of all atoms and charges. Kinase reactions of this type are thermodynamically reversible in vitro, though in vivo the flux is typically toward N-acetylglutamyl-phosphate formation as part of arginine biosynthesis.

rxn03147.other_comments: This is the SAICAR synthetase reaction (PurC, EC 6.3.2.6) in de novo purine biosynthesis. ATP + L-aspartate + CAIR (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxyribonucleotide) yields ADP + Pi + SAICAR (5-aminoimidazole-4-(N-succinylocarboxamide) ribonucleotide). The atoms balance: the carboxylate of CAIR is activated by ATP (forming an acyl-phosphate intermediate) and the aspartate amino group is ligated, releasing ADP and inorganic phosphate. Charge balance is consistent with release of 2 H+ at physiological pH.

rxn01477.other_comments: This is the Entner-Doudoroff pathway enzyme 6-phosphogluconate dehydratase (EC 4.2.1.12). It catalyzes the dehydration of 6-phospho-D-gluconate to form 2-keto-3-deoxy-6-phosphogluconate (KDPG) and water. The reaction is balanced: 6-phosphogluconate (C6H10O10P, as anion) loses one H2O to yield KDPG (C6H8O9P). Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn00474.other_comments: This is the tryptophan synthase beta reaction (EC 4.2.1.20), where L-serine condenses with indole to form L-tryptophan plus water. The reaction is balanced: L-serine (C3H7NO3) + indole (C8H7N) yields L-tryptophan (C11H12N2O2) + H2O (H2O). Carbon: 3+8=11; nitrogen: 1+1=2; the atoms balance correctly. Physiologically the reaction strongly favors tryptophan formation as part of biosynthesis.

rxn08073.other_comments: This is a hydrolytic amidase reaction in the periplasm that cleaves the bond between the peptide stem (L-Ala-D-Glu-meso-DAP tripeptide) and the N-acetylmuramic acid (anhydro-MurNAc) of a peptidoglycan degradation product (GlcNAc-anhMurNAc-tripeptide). Water is consumed, releasing the free tripeptide and the disaccharide (GlcNAc-anhMurNAc). Stoichiometry appears balanced and mass-conserving for an amide hydrolysis. As a hydrolase acting on a muropeptide turnover product, the reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the catabolic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn10224.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol synthase (phosphatidate cytidylyltransferase) reaction with anteiso-pentadecanoyl (a15:0) acyl chains on the phosphatidate. CTP reacts with the phosphatidic acid to form CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) and a proton. The mass and charge balance is correct: CTP + PA yields CDP-DAG + PPi + H+. In vivo this reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible toward CDP-DAG synthesis.

rxn08557.other_comments: This is the anaerobic glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction (GlpABC-type), oxidizing sn-glycerol-3-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerone-phosphate) with reduction of menaquinone-8 to menaquinol-8. The stoichiometry is balanced: glycerol-3-phosphate is oxidized (loses 2H), and menaquinone-8 is reduced to menaquinol-8 (gains 2H), so atoms and charges balance. In vivo this respiratory dehydrogenase functions in the oxidative (forward) direction, feeding electrons into the quinone pool.

rxn01116.other_comments: This is the ribulose-5-phosphate 3-epimerase (Rpe, EC 5.1.3.1) reaction, interconverting D-ribulose-5-phosphate and D-xylulose-5-phosphate via epimerization at C3. As an isomerase/epimerase with no net change in atoms, the reaction is balanced (both are C5H11O8P) and freely reversible. It is a key step in the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway.

rxn01802.other_comments: This is the glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.3.8.6). It catalyzes both oxidation (dehydrogenation) of glutaryl-CoA to glutaconyl-CoA and decarboxylation to yield crotonyl-CoA and CO2. The overall reaction consumes glutaryl-CoA and FAD, producing crotonyl-CoA, CO2, and FADH2. Atom balance: glutaryl-CoA (C5 dicarboxylic acyl-CoA) loses one carboxyl as CO2 and 2 H to FAD, giving crotonyl-CoA (C4 acyl-CoA). Carbon, hydrogen, and charge are balanced as written. The H+ on the left properly balances charge given the decarboxylation and FADH2 formation.

rxn10258.other_comments: This is a diacylglycerol kinase reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the sn-3 hydroxyl of 1,2-diisohexadecanoyl-sn-glycerol, producing the corresponding phosphatidic acid (1,2-diisohexadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) and ADP. Atoms and charges balance: the phosphoryl group transferred from ATP becomes the phosphate ester on glycerol. Diacylglycerol kinase reactions are strongly exergonic due to ATP hydrolysis coupling and proceed in the forward (DAG to PA) direction in vivo.

rxn01653.other_comments: This is the 5-formyltetrahydrofolate cyclo-ligase reaction (EC 6.3.3.2, MTHFS), which uses ATP to convert 5-formyltetrahydrofolate into 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate via an intramolecular cyclization. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + phosphate, providing energy to drive the dehydrative ring closure that converts the formyl group into a methenyl bridge. Atoms and charges balance. Physiologically this reaction is essentially irreversible in the forward direction (toward methenyl-THF) due to ATP hydrolysis, serving to recycle 5-formyl-THF (folinic acid) back into the active one-carbon folate pool.

rxn00670.other_comments: This is phosphate acetyltransferase (Pta) acting on the propionyl analog (phosphotransacetylase family). It transfers the propionyl group from CoA to inorganic phosphate, forming propionyl phosphate (propanoyl phosphate) and free CoA. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: phosphate + propionyl-CoA <=> CoA + propionyl phosphate. This enzyme is freely reversible in vivo; physiologically it can run toward propionyl-CoA synthesis (with propionate kinase) or toward propionyl phosphate, depending on metabolic conditions.

rxn00863.other_comments: This is the final step of histidine biosynthesis (histidinol dehydrogenase, hisD), oxidizing L-histidinal to L-histidine. The reaction is an aldehyde-to-carboxylic-acid oxidation requiring water and NAD+, producing NADH and two protons, which is stoichiometrically balanced for atoms and charge. Note that hisD typically performs the four-electron oxidation of L-histidinol all the way to L-histidine using 2 NAD+, with L-histidinal as an enzyme-bound intermediate; this half-reaction (histidinal to histidine) is the second oxidation step.

rxn02811.other_comments: This is the isopropylmalate isomerase (3-isopropylmalate dehydratase) reaction in the leucine biosynthesis pathway. 3-Isopropylmalate (2-hydroxy-4-methyl-2,3-dicarboxypentanoate / specifically 3-isopropylmalate, also called (2R,3S)-3-isopropylmalate) loses water to form 2-isopropylmaleate (2-isopropylmaleate is the dehydration intermediate). The enzyme IPMI catalyzes interconversion between 2-isopropylmalate and 3-isopropylmalate via the dehydrated intermediate 2-isopropylmaleate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (loss of H2O), and as an aconitase-family hydro-lyase it is freely reversible in vivo.

rxn08847.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase (L2) reaction hydrolyzing the ester bond of a 2-acyl-lysophosphatidylglycerol (with a C14:1 tetradec-7-enoyl chain) to release the free fatty acid (tetradecenoate) and glycerophosphoglycerol (GPG). The stoichiometry is balanced: one water hydrolyzes the acyl ester, producing the free fatty acid (carrying the proton released, hence H+) and the deacylated glycerophosphoglycerol. Hydrolytic lysophospholipase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and operate in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn00711.other_comments: This reaction represents uracil phosphoribosyltransferase (UPRT, EC 2.4.2.9). As written, it shows UMP + PPi being converted to uracil + PRPP. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: UMP (C9H11N2O9P, charge -2) + PPi (HP2O7, charge -3) + H+ yields uracil (C4H4N2O2, neutral) + PRPP (C5H8O14P3, charge -4). Atoms and charges balance correctly. Physiologically, UPRT operates in the salvage pathway favoring the direction uracil + PRPP -> UMP + PPi, so the written direction (UMP + PPi -> uracil + PRPP) is the reverse of the in vivo favored direction.

rxn08299.other_comments: This is a diacylglycerol kinase reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the sn-3 hydroxyl of 1,2-dioctadecanoyl-sn-glycerol (1,2-distearoyl-DAG), producing the corresponding phosphatidic acid (1,2-dioctadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) and ADP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: one phosphoryl group is transferred, with conservation of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and phosphorus atoms across both sides. Kinase reactions coupled to ATP hydrolysis are strongly exergonic and operate in the forward (DAG phosphorylation) direction in vivo, regenerating phosphatidic acid.

rxn09113.other_comments: This reaction represents phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PgsA), which transfers the phosphatidyl group from CDP-diacylglycerol (here distearoyl, n-C18:0) to the sn-1 hydroxyl of glycerol-3-phosphate, releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP). Stoichiometry is balanced: the phosphatidyl moiety is transferred and CMP is released, with the phosphate of glycerol-3-phosphate retained in the PGP product. Note the enzyme name labels it as 'Phosphatidylglycerol synthase' but the product is actually phosphatidylglycerophosphate, requiring a subsequent dephosphorylation step (PgpA/PgpB) to yield phosphatidylglycerol.

rxn08291.other_comments: This is the D-amino acid dehydrogenase (DadA) reaction acting on D-alanine. The reaction performs oxidative deamination: D-alanine + H2O + FAD yields pyruvate + ammonia + FADH2. Atoms balance: D-alanine (C3H7NO2) + H2O (H2O) = pyruvate (C3H4O3) + NH3 (NH3) + reduced flavin (2H transferred to FAD). Carbon (3=3), nitrogen (1=1), and oxygen (3=3) balance. The hydrogen balance works when accounting for the 2H transferred from substrate/water to FAD forming FADH2. In vivo, FADH2 is reoxidized via the respiratory chain, driving the reaction toward deamination/oxidation.

errors: The product stereochemistry is incorrect: condensation of isopentenyl diphosphate with (all-trans) farnesyl diphosphate by a trans-prenyltransferase yields all-trans (2E,6E,10E)-geranylgeranyl diphosphate, not a cis isomer. A cis-prenyltransferase acting on FPP would not be named a 'farnesyl cistransferase' producing GGPP in this configuration; the enzyme name and product stereochemistry are inconsistent.
An H+ is included as a product; the standard prenyltransferase condensation releases diphosphate (PPi) but the proton balance/charge should be checked depending on protonation states.
rxn03843.other_comments: This is a prenyltransferase chain-elongation reaction adding a C5 isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) unit to a C15 farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) to form a C20 geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP), releasing diphosphate. The carbon balance (C5 + C15 = C20) is correct and PPi release is expected.

rxn00941.other_comments: This reaction is the reverse of the nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT, EC 2.4.2.12) reaction. The physiological direction is Nicotinamide + PRPP -> Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) + PPi. As written here (PPi + NMN <=> PRPP + Nicotinamide), the forward direction shown corresponds to the thermodynamically unfavorable reverse phosphoribosyltransfer. Stoichiometry is balanced: ribose-phosphate moiety, phosphate groups, and the nicotinamide base are conserved. The salvage pathway in vivo proceeds toward NMN synthesis, so relative to the written equation the biological direction is reverse.

errors: The reaction name (L-arogenate:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase) does not match the substrates shown; the name implies 2-oxoglutarate and glutamate as the amino donor/acceptor pair, but the equation uses oxaloacetate and L-aspartate

Mechanistically, the transamination is correct as written: oxaloacetate + arogenate (pretyrosine) <=> L-aspartate + prephenate (the amino group transfers from arogenate to oxaloacetate forming aspartate, regenerating prephenate)
rxn01270.other_comments: Pretyrosine is a synonym for L-arogenate, and prephenate is its keto-acid (deaminated) counterpart. This is an aminotransferase (transamination) reaction, which transfers an amino group between an amino acid and a 2-oxo acid. Transaminases are generally reversible. The stoichiometry of atoms and charges is balanced for the transamination between arogenate/prephenate and aspartate/oxaloacetate pairs. The main issue is that the enzyme name specifies 2-oxoglutarate/glutamate as the amino acceptor/donor, which is inconsistent with the oxaloacetate/aspartate pair in the equation.

rxn12845.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide glycyl-L-leucine (Gly-Leu) by an aminopeptidase, cleaving the peptide bond with water to release free glycine and L-leucine. The reaction is balanced: the dipeptide plus one water yields the two constituent amino acids, with mass and charge conserved.

rxn05465.other_comments: This is malonyl-CoA:ACP transacylase (FabD, EC 2.3.1.39), transferring the malonyl group from malonyl-CoA to the phosphopantetheine thiol of ACP, releasing CoA. Stoichiometry is balanced (the malonyl moiety is conserved, and the H+ accounts for the protonation state difference between the CoA/ACP thiols). The enzyme is freely reversible in vitro, though in vivo it is driven forward by consumption of malonyl-ACP in fatty acid synthesis.

errors: Charge imbalance: the product side lists 2.0 H+ but hydrolysis of one ester bond releases only 1 proton (carboxylate plus the phosphate/hydroxyl protonation states must balance). At physiological pH, palmitate is anionic (palmitate-) and glycerol-3-phosphate carries -2 charge; the reactant 2-acylglycerophosphate carries -2 charge. Balancing requires only 1 H+ on the product side, not 2.
rxn08820.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase (acylhydrolase) reaction: water hydrolyzes the ester bond of 2-hexadecanoyl(palmitoyl)-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate to yield glycerol-3-phosphate and palmitate (free fatty acid). The reaction concept is correct; only the proton stoichiometry appears off.

errors: The reaction as written is not balanced in terms of compartments; a proton symport transport reaction should show metabolites in two distinct compartments (e.g., extracellular and cytosolic). As written, both sides are identical, making it a null/trivial reaction with no net transformation.
No compartment annotations are provided to distinguish substrate and product, so the transport process is not actually represented.
rxn05494.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transporter for D-alanine, where a proton and D-alanine are co-transported across a membrane (typically extracellular to cytoplasm). As written, both sides are identical (H+ + D-Alanine on each side), so it represents no chemical change and is mass/charge balanced only trivially. Properly, it should read: H+[e] + D-Alanine[e] <=> H+[c] + D-Alanine[c]. Symport transport is generally reversible thermodynamically, though physiologically driven by the proton motive force toward import.

rxn05347.other_comments: This is the condensing step catalyzed by beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (e.g., FabB/FabF or the initiation enzyme FabH). Acetyl-ACP condenses with malonyl-ACP to yield acetoacetyl-ACP, releasing CO2 and free ACP. Carbon balance: acetyl (C2 acyl) + malonyl (C3 acyl) -> acetoacetyl (C4 acyl) + CO2 (C1), so carbons balance (5 acyl carbons in, 4 + 1 out). ACP carriers also balance (2 in, 2 out as acetoacetyl-ACP + free ACP). The decarboxylation of malonyl drives the reaction essentially irreversibly toward condensation.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction for the catalyzed thermodynamics: methionine sulfoxide reductase reduces L-methionine S-oxide to L-methionine using reduced thioredoxin, not the reverse. As written, this depicts oxidation of methionine by oxidized thioredoxin, which is not how this enzyme operates.

Mass/charge balance check: the conversion of trdox to trdrd corresponds to a 2-electron reduction (gaining 2 H), but only one H+ appears on the product side, indicating an apparent imbalance in protons/hydrogens when paired with sulfoxide formation.
rxn06077.other_comments: This represents the methionine sulfoxide reductase (Msr) reaction. The biologically favored direction is reduction of L-methionine S-oxide to L-methionine, oxidizing reduced thioredoxin (trdrd -> trdox). As written (forward), it shows the unfavorable oxidation of methionine, so in vivo the reaction proceeds in reverse relative to how it is written.

rxn08547.other_comments: This reaction represents glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (PlsB-type) using myristoyl-ACP (C14:0) as the acyl donor to acylate the sn-1 position of glycerol-3-phosphate, producing 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and free ACP. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acyl group transfers from ACP to the glycerol backbone, releasing free ACP. In vivo this is the committed first step of phospholipid biosynthesis and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the acylation (forward) direction.

rxn00145.other_comments: This is flavocytochrome b2 (L-lactate:ferricytochrome-c oxidoreductase, EC 1.1.2.3). L-lactate is oxidized to pyruvate, transferring 2 electrons to 2 cytochrome c (Fe3+ reduced to Fe2+), with release of 2 H+. The reaction is balanced: carbon (3=3), and the 2 electrons plus 2 protons released account for the 2-electron oxidation of the alpha-carbon. Charge balances: left side 2(+3) from cytochrome c + lactate (-1) = +5; right side pyruvate (-1) + 2 H+ (+2) + 2 cytochrome c2+ (+4) = +5. In vivo this is a catabolic oxidation strongly favored toward pyruvate.

rxn03062.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 3-isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (LeuB, EC 1.1.1.85) in leucine biosynthesis. 3-Isopropylmalate is oxidized by NAD+ to form the unstable intermediate 2-isopropyl-3-oxosuccinate (3-isopropyloxalacetate), producing NADH and H+. The stoichiometry is balanced for this oxidation step. Note that in the full enzymatic mechanism the oxosuccinate intermediate undergoes spontaneous decarboxylation to 2-oxoisocaproate (4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate) plus CO2, but as written here (just the dehydrogenation), the atoms and charges balance. In vivo this proceeds in the oxidative direction toward leucine biosynthesis.

rxn03407.other_comments: This reaction represents the amidation of the alpha-carboxyl group of D-glutamate (gamma-D-glutamyl) to form D-isoglutamine (D-isoglutaminyl) in the lipid II precursor of peptidoglycan, catalyzed by an ATP-dependent amidoligase (MurT/GatD-type or AsnB-type activity). Ammonia serves as the amide nitrogen donor. The ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi (ADP-forming ligase). Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + NH3 provides the amide group, releasing ADP, phosphate, and a proton. Mass and charge balance are consistent with conversion of a free carboxylate to a carboxamide.

errors: Incorrect electron acceptor: acyl-CoA dehydrogenase uses FAD/FADH2 (or via ETF), not NAD/NADH. The reaction as written with NAD+ is biochemically incorrect.
If FAD were the cofactor, the product would be trans-2-hexadecenoyl-CoA with FADH2; stoichiometry of H+ is also questionable for the FAD-dependent reaction.
rxn05732.other_comments: This represents the first step of fatty acid beta-oxidation: dehydrogenation of palmitoyl-CoA to form (2E)-hexadecenoyl-CoA (trans-2-enoyl-CoA). The correct enzyme acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is FAD-dependent, transferring electrons to electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF), not to NAD+. In vivo this proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction toward chain shortening.

errors: Oxygen mass imbalance: the left side has 2 oxygen atoms from O2 plus 2 from benzoate carboxylate (4 O total in O2+COO-), and benzoate dioxygenation should incorporate both atoms of O2 into the ring to form a cis-dihydrodiol, but the product 'cis-1,2-dihydrobenzoate' (cis-1,2-dihydroxy-3,5-cyclohexadiene-1-carboxylate / benzoate cis-diol) requires careful accounting; written as shown the H/O balance does not close.

Product nomenclature is ambiguous/incorrect: benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase yields cis-1,2-dihydroxycyclohexa-3,5-diene-1-carboxylate (benzoate-cis-diol), not 'cis-1,2-dihydroxybenzoate' which would be a fully aromatic dihydroxybenzoate (catechol-type), inconsistent with an NADH-dependent dioxygenase reaction.
Reducing equivalents: NADH + H+ should be consumed to incorporate O2; ensure both O atoms of O2 appear in the diol product.
rxn03897.other_comments: This corresponds to benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase (benzoate-cis-dihydrodiol formation), a Rieske-type dioxygenase that uses NADH, H+, and O2 to convert benzoate into a cis-dihydrodiol carboxylate, regenerating NAD+. Such dioxygenase reactions are physiologically essentially irreversible (forward).

errors: Incorrect product: oxidation of D-lactaldehyde (an aldehyde) by NAD+ should yield the carboxylic acid (R)-lactate/D-lactate, not 2-oxopropanal (methylglyoxal). Methylglyoxal is the product of dehydrogenation/oxidation at the hydroxyl carbon, not aldehyde oxidation. The named enzyme '(R)-Lactaldehyde:NAD+ oxidoreductase' corresponds to lactaldehyde dehydrogenase producing D-lactate.

Atom/redox inconsistency: converting lactaldehyde (C3H6O2) to methylglyoxal (C3H4O2) plus NADH + H+ does not balance hydrogens/redox correctly; oxidation of the secondary alcohol to a ketone giving methylglyoxal would not simultaneously generate the listed products from this substrate as written.
rxn01831.other_comments: The reaction is intended to be an NAD+-dependent oxidation of (R)/D-lactaldehyde. As written it lists 2-oxopropanal (methylglyoxal) as the product, but aldehyde dehydrogenase activity should yield D-lactate. The substrate stereochemistry is also inconsistently labeled (D- vs R- vs the proper (R)-lactaldehyde naming).

rxn00297.other_comments: This is the UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase (EC 5.1.3.14) reaction, an epimerization at C-2 interconverting UDP-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine and UDP-N-acetyl-D-mannosamine. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (same molecular formula, just stereochemical inversion at C-2). Note: some 2-epimerases (e.g., the bifunctional human GNE) are hydrolyzing and produce free ManNAc plus UDP, but the non-hydrolyzing bacterial enzyme written here retains the UDP linkage as shown.

rxn08901.other_comments: This reaction represents malate dehydrogenase using menaquinone-8 as the electron acceptor: L-malate is oxidized to oxaloacetate while menaquinone-8 (MK-8) is reduced to menaquinol-8 (MKH2-8). The stoichiometry is balanced: malate (C4H4O5 as L-malate dianion) is oxidized by losing 2 H (2e- + 2H+) to oxaloacetate, and these are transferred to menaquinone-8 forming menaquinol-8. Mass and charge balance hold given proper protonation states. The redox potential of the malate/oxaloacetate couple (~ -0.17 V) is more negative than the menaquinone/menaquinol couple (~ -0.07 to -0.08 V), so coupling to menaquinone reduction makes the oxidation thermodynamically feasible in the forward direction, consistent with its role in fumarate/anaerobic respiration-linked metabolism.

rxn00113.other_comments: This is the carbamoyl phosphate synthetase reaction (using ammonia as nitrogen source, as in CPS-I). It consumes 2 ATP, CO2, and NH3 to produce carbamoyl phosphate, 2 ADP, and 1 Pi. Mass and charge are balanced: left has C1, right has C1; N balances (1 each); P balances (2 ATP provide ATP-phosphates, products are 2 ADP + 1 Pi + carbamoyl-P, total P = 4 each side); H+ release of 3 makes the charges balance. The reaction is highly exergonic with two ATP hydrolyzed, so it is physiologically essentially irreversible in the forward direction.

rxn00745.other_comments: This is a PEP-dependent phosphotransfer reaction transferring the phosphoryl group from phosphoenolpyruvate to glycerone (dihydroxyacetone), yielding pyruvate and glycerone phosphate (dihydroxyacetone phosphate). The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: PEP (C3) + DHA (C3) gives pyruvate (C3) + DHAP (C3), with one phosphate transferred. This corresponds to the dihydroxyacetone kinase (PTS-dependent) activity in many bacteria.

errors: Mass imbalance: D-fructose-1-phosphate (C6H11O9P, with one phosphate) cleaves into glycerone-phosphate (dihydroxyacetone phosphate, C3H5O6P) plus D-glyceraldehyde (C3H6O3); the products are correct and balanced, so there is no actual imbalance. Note: the product glyceraldehyde is unphosphorylated, NOT glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate as the enzyme name suggests.
rxn01870.other_comments: This is fructose-1-phosphate aldolase (aldolase B / fructose-bisphosphate aldolase class I acting on fructose-1-phosphate, EC 4.1.2.13/4.1.2.-). It cleaves D-fructose-1-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerone-phosphate) and free D-glyceraldehyde. The atoms balance (C6 -> C3 + C3; single phosphate retained on DHAP). The enzyme name string 'D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate-lyase' is misleading since the actual product is D-glyceraldehyde, not glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.

rxn00137.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate (PAP) by a 3'-phosphatase (e.g., the CysQ/HAL2 family), removing the 3'-phosphate to yield AMP and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate yields AMP (which retains the 5'-phosphate) plus free phosphate. In vivo this hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically directed forward to recycle PAP produced during sulfation reactions.

rxn00611.other_comments: This is glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.8). It oxidizes sn-glycerol-3-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerone-phosphate) with concomitant reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: glycerol-3-phosphate (C3H7O6P, with appropriate protonation) plus NAD+ yields DHAP plus NADH plus H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn01678.other_comments: This is the nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDK) reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to dUDP, producing ADP and dUTP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: ATP (donates one phosphate) + dUDP yields ADP + dUTP. Atoms and charges balance. NDK enzymes are catalytically reversible in vitro, but in vivo the net flux favors NTP/dNTP formation due to high cellular ATP concentrations driving the reaction toward dUTP production.

rxn02286.other_comments: This is the MurC reaction (UDP-N-acetylmuramate--L-alanine ligase). It adds L-alanine to UDP-MurNAc using ATP, producing ADP, inorganic phosphate, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written. In vivo it proceeds in the biosynthetic direction toward UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine, driven by ATP hydrolysis.

rxn00872.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase) reaction, which oxidizes butyryl-CoA to crotonyl-CoA (trans-2-butenoyl-CoA) with reduction of FAD to FADH2. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: C and H balance, and two electrons/two hydrogens transfer from the substrate to FAD. The enzyme name 'oxygen oxidoreductase' is a misnomer since the physiological electron acceptor is electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF), not molecular oxygen directly; FAD/FADH2 is the prosthetic group involved. While the dehydrogenase chemistry is reversible in principle, in vivo it typically operates in the oxidative (forward) direction during beta-oxidation, whereas the crotonyl-CoA reductase (using NADPH) often handles the reductive direction in biosynthesis.

rxn00360.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate, also called 3'-phospho-5'-adenylyl sulfate) at its 3'-phosphate position by water, yielding APS (adenosine-5'-phosphosulfate) and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: PAPS minus a 3'-phosphate group (released as Pi, consuming one water) leaves APS. The enzyme is a 3'-phosphohydrolase (3'(2'),5'-bisphosphate nucleotidase / PAPS 3'-phosphatase type activity). Atom and charge balance are consistent with phosphomonoester hydrolysis.

rxn10193.other_comments: This reaction represents poly(glycerol-phosphate) alpha-glucosyltransferase, which transfers glucose from UDP-glucose to the glycerol-phosphate units of teichoic acid. The stoichiometry of 45 UDP-glucose donating 45 glucose residues to a teichoic acid polymer with 45 glycerol-phosphate repeat units (Prenol-45n) is internally consistent, yielding 45 UDP plus the glucosylated teichoic acid product. Glycosyltransferase reactions using nucleotide-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo due to release of UDP.

errors: This reaction as written is not stoichiometrically balanced. IMP (inosine monophosphate, C10H13N4O8P) plus H2O does not equal FAICAR. The correct product of IMP cyclohydrolase acting in the reverse (hydrolytic ring-opening) direction is FAICAR (5-formamido-4-imidazolecarboxamide ribotide), but the proper reaction is FAICAR <=> IMP + H2O. As written (H2O + IMP -> FAICAR), water is added to the reactant side along with IMP, which would not balance; FAICAR contains one more oxygen and two more hydrogens than IMP, consistent with addition of one H2O, so atomically H2O + IMP = FAICAR is actually balanced (C10H13N4O8P + H2O = C10H15N4O9P).
Reaction name 'IMP 1,2-hydrolase (decyclizing)' corresponds to EC 3.5.4.10 (IMP cyclohydrolase); the physiological direction is FAICAR -> IMP + H2O (ring closure), not the reverse.
rxn00832.other_comments: The reaction describes IMP cyclohydrolase (EC 3.5.4.10) in the hydrolytic ring-opening direction. Atomically, IMP + H2O = FAICAR is balanced. However, in vivo this enzyme operates in the direction of purine biosynthesis: FAICAR -> IMP + H2O (ring closure to form the purine), so as written it is reversed relative to physiological flux.

rxn01106.other_comments: This reaction is the interconversion of 2-phospho-D-glycerate (2-PG) and 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PG), catalyzed by phosphoglycerate mutase (the enzyme moves the phosphate group between the C2 and C3 positions). It is mass- and charge-balanced as written (both metabolites are C3H4O7P with identical atomic composition, just differing in phosphate position). In glycolysis the reaction proceeds 3-PG to 2-PG, while in gluconeogenesis it proceeds in the opposite direction; the equilibrium constant is near unity, so the reaction is freely reversible in vivo.

rxn01188.other_comments: This is the 3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase reaction (EC 4.2.1.118), converting 3-dehydroshikimate to protocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxybenzoate) with release of water via dehydration and aromatization. The atoms balance: 3-dehydroshikimate (C7H8O5) yields protocatechuate (C7H6O4) plus H2O. In vivo this catabolic, aromatization-driven reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly toward protocatechuate.

rxn00066.other_comments: This is the NADH peroxidase reaction (EC 1.11.1.1), where NADH reduces hydrogen peroxide to water. Atoms balance: left side has NADH + H2O2 + H+ providing the H and O; right side gives 2 H2O + NAD+. Charge balance: NADH(-1) + H2O2(0) + H+(+1) = 0 on left; 2 H2O(0) + NAD+(+1)... this gives +1 on right, suggesting a charge imbalance unless NAD is written as the cation NAD+ without explicit charge tracking. Treating 'NAD' as NAD+ leaves a charge discrepancy of 1, which typically indicates a missing proton balance. With H+ on the reactant side the protons balance for atoms but charge should be rechecked.

errors: The enzyme is named methionyl aminopeptidase, but the substrate dipeptide is Ala-Glu, which does not have an N-terminal methionine; the reaction substrate is inconsistent with the enzyme name
Methionyl aminopeptidase (MetAP) specifically cleaves N-terminal methionine residues, so hydrolysis of Ala-Glu is not a reaction this enzyme catalyzes
rxn12640.other_comments: The reaction shown is hydrolysis of the dipeptide Ala-L-Glu into L-Alanine and L-Glutamate using water. Stoichiometrically the hydrolysis is balanced (one peptide bond cleaved by one water yields the two free amino acids). However, the enzyme annotation (methionyl aminopeptidase) does not match the substrate, since MetAP removes N-terminal Met, not Ala.

errors: Charge and hydrogen imbalance: the reaction as written produces 2 H+ but the correct stoichiometry for proline oxidation to 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate releases NADPH + H+ (1 H+), not 2 H+. Oxidation of proline removes 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+, one as H+), so balanced form is L-Proline + NADP+ <=> 1-Pyrroline-5-carboxylate + NADPH + H+
rxn00931.other_comments: This is the proline dehydrogenase / pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase type interconversion. P5C reductase (ProC) normally runs in the reductive direction (P5C + NADPH + H+ -> proline) in vivo for proline biosynthesis, but the enzyme reaction as named (oxidoreductase) is often written reversibly. The main issue is the H+ stoichiometry.

rxn08756.other_comments: This reaction corresponds to the final step of the MEP (non-mevalonate) pathway catalyzed by IspH (HMBPP reductase, also called LytB). HMBPP (1-hydroxy-2-methyl-2-butenyl 4-diphosphate, also written as (E)-4-hydroxy-3-methyl-but-2-enyl diphosphate) is reductively dehydrated to isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) and water. The atoms balance: HMBPP (C5H12O8P2 as the protonated form / C5 skeleton) loses an OH (as water) and is reduced by NADH. Note that in vivo IspH uses reduced ferredoxin/flavodoxin rather than NAD(P)H as the physiological electron donor, so the NADH/NAD+ representation is a simplification. The reaction produces both IPP and DMAPP in roughly a 5:1 ratio; here only IPP is shown.

rxn00938.other_comments: This is the nicotinamidase (nicotinamide amidohydrolase, EC 3.5.1.19) reaction. Nicotinamide is hydrolyzed using water to release ammonia and produce nicotinic acid (niacin). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: C6H6N2O (nicotinamide) + H2O yields C6H5NO2 (niacin) + NH3. In vivo, this amide hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible, proceeding in the forward direction as written.

errors: Reaction is not charge-balanced: butanesulfonate carries a -1 charge and sulfite carries a -2 charge, while the proton balance is not accounted for. Including an H+ on the product side would balance both charge and hydrogen (typical formulation: O2 + FMNH2 + butanesulfonate -> H2O + FMN + sulfite + butanal + H+).
Hydrogen atoms are not balanced as written without an explicit proton; FMNH2 contributes 2 reducing equivalents and the standard product set requires release of a proton.
rxn08470.other_comments: This represents an alkanesulfonate monooxygenase (SsuD-type) reaction, where an FMNH2-dependent two-component monooxygenase oxidatively cleaves the C-S bond of an alkanesulfonate (here butanesulfonate) to yield the corresponding aldehyde (butanal) and sulfite, using O2 and consuming FMNH2 to FMN. The overall transformation is essentially irreversible in vivo because it consumes O2 and FMNH2 and releases sulfite for sulfur assimilation under sulfate starvation.

rxn01544.other_comments: This reaction is xanthine phosphoribosyltransferase, which normally catalyzes the salvage reaction XAN + PRPP -> XMP + PPi (forward, releasing pyrophosphate). The reaction as written shows the thermodynamically unfavorable reverse direction (PPi + XMP -> PRPP + XAN). Stoichiometry and atom balance are correct: the phosphoribosyl group and phosphate/proton accounting are consistent on both sides. In vivo, the salvage direction (toward XMP formation, i.e., the reverse of how this is written) is favored, driven by subsequent pyrophosphate hydrolysis.

rxn01303.other_comments: This is homoserine O-acetyltransferase (MetX, EC 2.3.1.31), which transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the hydroxyl of L-homoserine, producing O-acetyl-L-homoserine and CoA. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: the acetyl moiety is transferred, with one product (CoA) and one acetylated product. In vivo this is the committed first step of methionine biosynthesis (via the direct sulfhydrylation/transsulfuration pathway) and proceeds in the forward direction driven by the thioester energetics of acetyl-CoA.

errors: Incorrect electron acceptor: acyl-CoA dehydrogenase reactions use FAD (or ETF/electron-transfer flavoprotein), not NAD. The product should be FADH2 (or reduced ETF), not NADH + H+.
The reaction as written with NAD/NADH is not biochemically correct for acyl-CoA dehydrogenase; the proper form is: FAD + Decanoyl-CoA <=> FADH2 + (2E)-Decenoyl-CoA
rxn10012.other_comments: This represents the first oxidation step of fatty acid beta-oxidation, converting decanoyl-CoA to trans-2-decenoyl-CoA via dehydrogenation across the C2-C3 bond. The atom balance for the carbon skeleton (introducing a double bond by removing 2 H) is conceptually correct, but the cofactor is wrong. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenases are flavoproteins using FAD, with electrons passed to ETF, not NAD. In vivo this proceeds in the catabolic (forward) direction toward the enoyl-CoA product.

rxn04938.other_comments: This is the S-(hydroxymethyl)glutathione dehydrogenase / S-formylglutathione-forming reaction (EC 1.1.1.284). It oxidizes S-(hydroxymethyl)glutathione to S-formylglutathione, transferring a hydride to NADP+ producing NADPH and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: 2 electrons and a proton released, NADP+ reduced to NADPH, and one additional H+ accounts for charge/mass balance. Although the enzyme is often described with NAD(H) as cofactor, the NADP-dependent variant exists. Physiologically, in the formaldehyde detoxification pathway the reaction proceeds toward S-formylglutathione formation, but it is thermodynamically reversible.

errors: Reaction has identical substrates and products (H+ + Cytosine on both sides), representing no net chemical transformation
If intended as a transport reaction, the compartment annotations are missing or identical, making the reaction a futile null transformation as written
rxn05527.other_comments: This appears to be a proton-coupled cytosine transport reaction (TRANS-RXN-199), where H+ and cytosine are moved across a membrane. As written, both sides are identical, so the membrane compartments (e.g., extracellular vs cytosolic) need to be specified for the reaction to be meaningful. The atoms balance trivially since both sides are the same.

rxn00650.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide cysteinylglycine (Cys-Gly) by a dipeptidase (e.g., membrane dipeptidase/dehydropeptidase or aminopeptidase N), yielding free L-cysteine and glycine. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one water molecule cleaves the single peptide bond to produce the two free amino acids. This is a key step in the gamma-glutamyl cycle and glutathione degradation.

rxn00412.other_comments: This is CTP synthase (EC 6.3.4.2), which aminates UTP to form CTP using glutamine as the nitrogen donor, with ATP hydrolysis to ADP and phosphate. Glutamine is hydrolyzed to glutamate, releasing ammonia that is transferred to UTP. The stoichiometry is balanced: atoms and charges balance with the 2 H+ produced. In vivo this reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward CTP production driven by ATP hydrolysis.

rxn02402.other_comments: This is the quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT, EC 2.4.2.19) reaction written in reverse. The physiological direction is: Quinolinate + PRPP + H+ -> Nicotinate ribonucleotide (nicotinate mononucleotide) + CO2 + PPi. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: quinolinate is decarboxylated and the resulting nicotinate moiety is transferred to the ribose-5-phosphate from PRPP, releasing pyrophosphate. As written here (left to right), it would be the reverse/non-physiological direction.

rxn03167.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of 7,8-dihydroneopterin 3'-triphosphate to dihydroneopterin, releasing 3 phosphate groups and 3 protons, consuming 3 water molecules. This is the alkaline phosphatase-type dephosphorylation step in folate/tetrahydrobiopterin biosynthesis pathways. Stoichiometry is balanced: removal of three phosphate groups (triphosphate to free hydroxyl) requires three hydrolytic water additions, yielding three inorganic phosphates and three protons. Note that in classical folate biosynthesis the conversion involves a pyrophosphohydrolase (releasing pyrophosphate) followed by phosphatase action; this particular enzyme account treats it as complete hydrolysis to free phosphates.

rxn05115.other_comments: This reaction represents the N5-CAIR mutase (PurE) step in de novo purine biosynthesis, converting N5-carboxyaminoimidazole ribonucleotide (N5-CAIR) to 4-carboxy-5-aminoimidazole ribonucleotide (CAIR). The substrate 5-phosphoribosyl-5-carboxyaminoimidazole is N5-CAIR and the product 5'-phosphoribosyl-4-carboxy-5-aminoimidazole is CAIR. The reaction is a carboxyl group migration (mutase). Stoichiometry is balanced as an intramolecular rearrangement; the H+ accounts for the protonation state difference between substrate and product. In vivo this reaction proceeds in the direction of CAIR formation toward IMP synthesis.

rxn01313.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADH-dependent reduction of dihydrobiopterin (7,8-dihydrobiopterin) to tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), catalyzed by dihydrofolate reductase or dihydropteridine reductase activity. The reaction is balanced: NADH + H+ + dihydrobiopterin yields NAD+ + tetrahydrobiopterin. Note that classical dihydropteridine reductase (QDPR) prefers NADH and acts on quinonoid dihydrobiopterin, while dihydrofolate reductase reduces 7,8-dihydrobiopterin using NADPH. The atom and charge balance is consistent (transfer of a hydride plus proton reducing the dihydro to the tetrahydro form).

rxn00515.other_comments: This is a nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDK) type reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to IDP, producing ADP and ITP. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ATP + IDP <=> ADP + ITP, with one phosphate transferred between nucleotides. NDK reactions are well known to be reversible due to the ping-pong mechanism and similar free energies of the phosphoanhydride bonds involved.

rxn01353.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDK/NDPK), transferring a phosphate from ATP to dGDP, yielding ADP and dGTP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (ATP + dGDP <=> ADP + dGTP). NDPK operates via a ping-pong mechanism with a phosphohistidine intermediate and is broadly substrate-nonspecific. The equilibrium constant is near unity, and the reaction direction in vivo is driven by relative concentrations of the nucleotide pools, so it is physiologically reversible.

errors: L-Aspartate appears on both sides of the reaction with identical compartment designation, indicating the transport (compartmental) distinction is missing. As written, the substrate being transported is not represented as moving between compartments, making the transport reaction stoichiometrically meaningless. A proper ABC transporter reaction should show L-Aspartate in an external compartment on the reactant side and an internal compartment on the product side (e.g., L-Aspartate[e] -> L-Aspartate[c]).
rxn05152.other_comments: This is intended to be an ABC-type polar amino acid (L-Aspartate) importer coupled to ATP hydrolysis. The ATP hydrolysis portion (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) is balanced and correct. ATP-driven import is thermodynamically driven and physiologically irreversible in the import direction.

rxn12633.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide L-alanyl-L-aspartate into L-alanine and L-aspartate, catalyzed by a peptidase/dipeptidase. The reaction is balanced: the dipeptide bond is cleaved with addition of one water molecule, yielding the two free amino acids. Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction.

rxn03437.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by dihydroxy-acid dehydratase (IlvD, EC 4.2.1.9) in the isoleucine biosynthesis pathway. (R)-2,3-dihydroxy-3-methylpentanoate (2,3-dihydroxy-3-methylvalerate) is dehydrated to form (S)-3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (3MOP, the 2-keto acid precursor of isoleucine) plus water. The stoichiometry is balanced: loss of one water from the dihydroxyacid yields the 2-oxo acid.

errors: Charge imbalance: phosphatidylserine decarboxylation does not consume 2 H+; the standard reaction consumes 1 H+ (PS + H+ -> PE + CO2). The decarboxylation of the serine carboxyl group releases CO2 and the resulting amine, with net consumption of one proton to balance charge.
rxn10235.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (PSD) reaction converting a phosphatidylserine species (diisopentadecanoyl-PS) to the corresponding phosphatidylethanolamine plus CO2. Decarboxylation reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to CO2 release, so direction is forward toward PE.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the conversion of N-formyl-GAR (FGAR) to GAR releases a formyl group, which should appear as formate or be transferred to tetrahydrofolate as 10-formyl-THF, not as 5,10-methenyl-THF in a simple single step

Charge/proton imbalance: condensation of formate with THF to form 5,10-methenyl-THF requires ATP-dependent activation and proper H+ accounting; the given 2 H+ on the substrate side does not correctly balance the formation of methenyl-THF plus water
The standard reaction interconverting FGAR/GAR with folate cofactors uses 10-formyl-THF (formyltransferase, EC 2.1.2.2), not 5,10-methenyl-THF directly
rxn03005.other_comments: This appears to represent a glycinamide ribonucleotide (GAR) transformylase-type step in de novo purine biosynthesis, interconverting GAR and N-formyl-GAR (FGAR) coupled to a one-carbon folate carrier. As written with 5,10-methenyl-THF and 2 H+ on one side and water on the other, the stoichiometry is questionable; the biologically standard cofactor is 10-formyl-THF.

errors: Product should be myo-inositol, not L-inositol; dephosphorylation of 1D-myo-inositol 4-phosphate yields myo-inositol (a meso compound), so the 'L-Inositol' naming is incorrect/misleading
rxn00882.other_comments: This is a phosphomonoesterase (phosphatase) reaction hydrolyzing the 4-phosphate group of 1D-myo-inositol 4-phosphate, releasing inorganic phosphate and free inositol. Stoichiometry is balanced (one phosphate group transferred to water). Phosphate ester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn08846.other_comments: This reaction represents lysophospholipase L2 hydrolyzing the ester bond of 2-tetradecanoyl (myristoyl) sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol. Water is consumed and the acyl group is released as myristic acid (tetradecanoic acid, C14:0), yielding glycerophosphoglycerol and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: 1 H2O cleaves 1 ester bond, releasing 1 free fatty acid and the deacylated glycerophosphoglycerol backbone, with 1 H+ from the carboxylic acid ionization. Hydrolysis of the acyl ester is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible.

rxn03244.other_comments: This is the beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase step of fatty acid beta-oxidation, oxidizing (S)-3-hydroxydecanoyl-CoA to 3-oxodecanoyl-CoA with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is balanced in atoms (C, H, O, N, P, S) and charge: the carbinol C-H and O-H are oxidized to a ketone, releasing 2 electrons and 2 H (one to NAD+ as hydride and one as free H+). Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn02949.other_comments: This is the enoyl-CoA hydratase-type reaction (3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydro-lyase, EC 4.2.1.17/related, part of valine catabolism). Water is added across the double bond of methacrylyl-CoA to yield (S)-3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: methacrylyl-CoA (C25H38N7O17P3S) plus H2O gives 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA (C25H40N7O18P3S). Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and charge balance.

rxn00616.other_comments: This is glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (FAD-dependent, EC 1.1.5.3). It oxidizes sn-glycerol-3-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerone-phosphate), reducing the enzyme-bound FAD to FADH2. The reaction is balanced (atoms and charges): the two electrons and two protons removed from glycerol-3-phosphate (one from C2-OH, one from C2-H) are transferred to FAD. In vivo this membrane-bound enzyme funnels electrons to the quinone pool of the respiratory chain, making the reaction effectively unidirectional toward DHAP formation as part of the glycerophosphate shuttle.

rxn00313.other_comments: This is diaminopimelate decarboxylase (DapDC, EC 4.1.1.20), the final step in lysine biosynthesis via the DAP pathway.
