The physiological ferredoxin-glutamate synthase reaction is reductive (consumes reduced ferredoxin), not oxidative as written here (consumes oxidized ferredoxin).
rxn12822.other_comments: This represents glutamate synthase (Fd-GOGAT, EC 1.4.7.1). The biologically relevant in vivo direction is L-glutamine + 2-oxoglutarate + 2 reduced ferredoxin -> 2 L-glutamate + 2 oxidized ferredoxin, i.e., the reverse of how this reaction is written.

rxn00260.other_comments: This is aspartate aminotransferase (AST/GOT). It transfers an amino group from L-aspartate to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding oxaloacetate and L-glutamate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: each side has the same atoms (transamination swaps an amino group for a keto group). Aminotransferases catalyze near-equilibrium reactions and are physiologically reversible, with net direction depending on substrate/product concentrations.

errors: The reaction does not distinguish between cellular compartments; both substrates and products appear identical, making it a null reaction as written. A proper proton symport transport reaction should specify periplasm/extracellular versus cytoplasm, e.g., H+[e] + D-Glucarate[e] <=> H+[c] + D-Glucarate[c].
rxn05572.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction in which D-glucarate is co-transported with a proton across the membrane. As written, the metabolites on both sides are identical with no compartment labels, so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced but biologically meaningless (zero net transformation). The stoichiometry of 1 H+ to 1 D-glucarate is plausible for symport. With proper compartment annotation, proton symport is typically driven by the proton motive force and would be effectively directional toward uptake into the cytoplasm, though it can be modeled as reversible.

errors: This reaction has identical substrate and product (Guanosine + H+ on both sides), making it a null/trivial reaction with no net chemical transformation
No actual metabolic conversion occurs
rxn05204.other_comments: This appears to be a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN prefix) where guanosine is moved across a membrane along with a proton, likely a proton-coupled symporter. The identical chemistry on both sides represents compartment translocation rather than a chemical change. As written without compartment annotations, it is stoichiometrically trivial and uninformative.

errors: Phosphonate appears on both sides without a compartment distinction; for an ABC-type transporter, the substrate should be shown in two different compartments (e.g., Phosphonate[out] -> Phosphonate[in]), otherwise it cancels out and the reaction is not properly balanced as a transport process
rxn13892.other_comments: This represents a phosphonate-transporting ABC ATPase coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to import of phosphonate. The hydrolysis component is mass and charge balanced. The transport is driven by ATP hydrolysis and is effectively irreversible in vivo, hence the forward direction. The substrate should be annotated with distinct compartments.

rxn00461.other_comments: This is the MurA reaction (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 1-carboxyvinyltransferase, EC 2.5.1.7), the first committed step in peptidoglycan biosynthesis. PEP transfers its enolpyruvyl moiety to the 3'-OH of UDP-GlcNAc, releasing inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one UDP-GlcNAc and one PEP yield one enolpyruvyl-UDP-GlcNAc and one phosphate. In vivo this committed biosynthetic step proceeds in the forward direction toward UDP-GlcNAc-enolpyruvate.

rxn02803.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase step of fatty acid beta-oxidation acting on myristoyl-CoA (C14). FAD accepts two hydrogens (one H and one electron pair effectively two H atoms) from C2 and C3 of the acyl chain to form the trans-2-enoyl-CoA (trans-2-tetradecenoyl-CoA) and FADH2. Stoichiometry is balanced: the substrate loses 2 H, FAD gains 2 H. In vivo this proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction during beta-oxidation; the electrons from FADH2 are passed to ETF, making the physiological flux essentially unidirectional toward dehydrogenation.

rxn00858.other_comments: This is agmatinase (EC 3.5.3.11), which hydrolyzes agmatine to putrescine and urea. The reaction is balanced: agmatine (C5H14N4) + water yields putrescine (C4H14N2) + urea (CH4N2O). Atoms and charges balance correctly. As a hydrolysis reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn05247.other_comments: This is a fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (long-chain) reaction, specifically for tetradecanoate (C14:0, myristate). The generic metabolites fa1 (a fatty acid) and fa1coa (the corresponding fatty acyl-CoA) are activated using ATP, CoA, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate (PPi). The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced as written symbolically: ATP + CoA + fatty acid -> AMP + PPi + acyl-CoA. Physiologically this acyl-CoA synthetase reaction (ACS/FACOAL) proceeds via an acyl-adenylate intermediate. Although written as reversible, in vivo it is driven forward by the subsequent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate to two phosphate ions, making fatty acid activation effectively irreversible toward acyl-CoA formation.

errors: Stoichiometric/structural inconsistency: thiolase (C-acyltransferase) condenses an acyl-CoA with acetyl-CoA to form a 3-oxoacyl-CoA that is two carbons longer than the starting acyl-CoA. Decanoyl-CoA (C10) + acetyl-CoA (C2) should yield 3-oxododecanoyl-CoA (C12), which is consistent here; however the net carbon balance: C10 + C2 = C12 is correct. Atoms balance for C, but the reaction as written is actually balanced.
rxn03243.other_comments: This is a beta-ketothiolase (acetyl-CoA C-acyltransferase) reaction. As written (condensation direction), decanoyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA -> 3-oxododecanoyl-CoA + CoA, the carbons balance (C10+C2=C12). Thermodynamically the thiolytic cleavage (3-oxoacyl-CoA + CoA -> shorter acyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA) is strongly favored in vivo during beta-oxidation. The biosynthetic condensation direction is unfavorable. Therefore the physiological direction is the reverse of how written (toward thiolytic cleavage of 3-oxododecanoyl-CoA).

rxn03136.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by adenylosuccinate lyase (SACAIR lyase activity) in de novo purine biosynthesis. SAICAR (1-(5-Phosphoribosyl)-5-amino-4-(N-succinocarboxamide)-imidazole) is cleaved to release fumarate, yielding AICAR (5-amino-4-imidazolecarboxamide ribonucleotide, here as the carboxamide form, properly named 1-(5-Phosphoribosyl)-5-amino-4-imidazolecarboxamide). The stoichiometry is balanced: removal of the succinyl moiety as fumarate is consistent. This beta-elimination is freely reversible thermodynamically, though in vivo flux through purine biosynthesis proceeds in the SAICAR-to-AICAR direction.

rxn10303.other_comments: This reaction describes glycosylation (glucose substitution) of a lipoteichoic acid polymer with 24 repeating glycerophosphate units. UDP-glucose serves as the glucosyl donor, transferring glucose moieties to the LTA backbone and releasing UDP. The 24:1 stoichiometry (24 UDP-glucose to substitute 24 positions on the n=24 polymer) is internally consistent. Mass balance is plausible: each glucosyl transfer adds C6H10O5 to the LTA and converts UDP-glucose to UDP. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible.

errors: Proton balance is incorrect: the reaction produces only 1 H+, not 2. The phosphotransfer from CDP-diacylglycerol to serine releases CMP and one proton, so the correct stoichiometry should show 1.0 H+ rather than 2.0 H+.
rxn10229.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylserine synthase (CDP-DAG-dependent, PssA-type) reaction in which L-serine is condensed with CDP-diisopentadecanoylglycerol to form phosphatidylserine and CMP. The acyl chains are branched-chain (isopentadecanoyl, C15) species. In vivo this reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic direction toward phosphatidylserine formation, driven by subsequent decarboxylation to phosphatidylethanolamine.

rxn01387.other_comments: This is the first step of the NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.42), in which isocitrate is oxidized to the unstable intermediate oxalosuccinate, reducing NADP+ to NADPH. The mass and charge balance: isocitrate (C6H5O7^3-) loses 2H (as hydride to NADP+ plus a proton), yielding oxalosuccinate (C6H4O7^3- in its dianion/trianion form) plus NADPH and H+. This partial reaction is freely reversible; the overall physiological reaction is pulled forward by the subsequent decarboxylation of oxalosuccinate to alpha-ketoglutarate.

rxn08810.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase L1 reaction hydrolyzing the ester bond of 2-acyl-glycerophosphoglycerol (C12:0 dodecanoyl form). Water cleaves the acyl group, releasing dodecanoate (ddca, lauric acid) plus a proton and glycerophosphoglycerol (the deacylated backbone). Stoichiometry is balanced: the acyl ester + H2O yields free fatty acid (with H+) and the alcohol product. Hydrolysis reactions of this type are thermodynamically favorable and operate in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn02937.other_comments: This is the AIR synthetase (PurM) reaction, step 5 of de novo purine biosynthesis. FGAM (formylglycinamidine ribonucleotide) is cyclized using ATP to form AIR (5-aminoimidazole ribonucleotide), yielding ADP and inorganic phosphate. The reaction also releases water, which is sometimes written explicitly; the substrate name '2-(Formamido)-N1-(5-phosphoribosyl)acetamidine' corresponds to FGAM. Stoichiometry is balanced when water is included as a product (ATP + FGAM -> ADP + Pi + AIR + H2O).

rxn03137.other_comments: This is the AICAR transformylase reaction (EC 2.1.2.3), the penultimate step of de novo purine biosynthesis. 10-Formyltetrahydrofolate donates a formyl group to AICAR (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide), producing FAICAR (5-formaminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide) and tetrahydrofolate. The reaction is balanced: the formyl group (CHO) is transferred from the cofactor to the amino group of AICAR, accounting for all atoms.

rxn05613.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter reaction for L-methionine S-oxide import, coupled to ATP hydrolysis. The substrate L-methionine S-oxide appears on both sides because it is transported across the membrane (extracellular to intracellular), so it is not chemically transformed. ATP + H2O is hydrolyzed to ADP + Phosphate + H+, providing energy. Stoichiometry is balanced (the metabolite on each side cancels; ATP hydrolysis is mass- and charge-balanced).

errors: The named enzyme (S-Aminomethyldihydrolipoylprotein:(6S)-tetrahydrofolate aminomethyltransferase, the glycine cleavage system T-protein, EC 2.1.2.10) does not correspond to the reaction shown; the T-protein reaction involves aminomethyldihydrolipoylprotein + THF -> dihydrolipoylprotein + 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate + NH3
The chemistry shown (5,10-methenyl-THF + H2O -> 5-formyl-THF) does not match the enzyme name

rxn01652.other_comments: The reaction text describes hydration of 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate to 5-formyltetrahydrofolate, which is the activity of 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate cyclohydrolase-type chemistry (5-formyl-THF is normally produced/interconverted differently). However, the enzyme name given belongs to the glycine cleavage system aminomethyltransferase (T-protein), which is a completely different reaction. There is a mismatch between the enzyme annotation and the displayed substrates/products.

rxn00350.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of glutathione (gamma-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine, GSH) at the gamma-glutamyl bond, releasing L-glutamate and the dipeptide cysteinylglycine (Cys-Gly). The stoichiometry is balanced: GSH (C10H17N3O6S) + H2O yields L-glutamate (C5H9NO4) + Cys-Gly (C5H10N2O3S). Atoms balance (C10, N3, S1, O7, H19 on each side). This is a hydrolytic cleavage characteristic of gamma-glutamyl hydrolase / gamma-glutamyltransferase-type activity in glutathione catabolism.

rxn05462.other_comments: This is the dehydratase step of fatty acid biosynthesis (FabA/FabZ type), converting 3-hydroxyoctadecanoyl-ACP (C18 beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP) to trans-2-octadecenoyl-ACP plus water. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: removal of water from the 3-hydroxyacyl group yields the trans-2-enoyl product. In vivo, the overall fatty acid synthesis cycle is pulled forward (dehydration direction) toward elongation, though the dehydratase enzyme itself catalyzes a freely reversible step.

rxn00992.other_comments: This is 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.30). It oxidizes (R)-3-hydroxybutanoate to acetoacetate, transferring a hydride to NAD+ to form NADH and releasing a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: C4H7O3- + NAD+ -> C4H5O3- + NADH + H+. Atoms balance (4 C, 6 H net on substrate side plus NAD, and consistent charges). The enzyme is physiologically reversible, with net direction governed by NADH/NAD+ ratio and ketone body metabolism (synthesis vs utilization).

rxn09101.other_comments: This represents PgsP/PgpA/PgpB-type phosphatidylglycerophosphate phosphatase activity, hydrolyzing the phosphate from PGP to yield phosphatidylglycerol (PG) plus inorganic phosphate. This is a key step in PG biosynthesis. The hydrolysis of a phosphomonoester is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, so it proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction.

rxn10163.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction (tetradecanoate/myristate import via proton symport across a membrane). The reaction name describes the oxidoreductase in the PAPS-forming (reverse) direction, but the written equation proceeds in the PAPS-consuming (sulfite-forming) direction, an inconsistency between name and equation.
rxn05239.other_comments: This is PAPS reductase (thioredoxin-dependent), reducing 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) to sulfite and PAP, using reduced thioredoxin (trdrd) as electron donor, yielding oxidized thioredoxin (trdox). In vivo this is the sulfate assimilation pathway and runs in the PAPS-to-sulfite direction.

rxn00161.other_comments: This is the NADP-dependent malic enzyme reaction (EC 1.1.1.40). L-malate is oxidatively decarboxylated to pyruvate, releasing CO2 and reducing NADP+ to NADPH. The reaction is balanced: malate (C4H6O5) + NADP+ yields pyruvate (C3H4O3) + CO2 + NADPH + H+. Note that a proton (H+) is typically released to balance charge/hydrogen, and many databases write it explicitly. In vivo this generally proceeds in the decarboxylating (forward) direction toward pyruvate, providing NADPH and a link between glycolysis/TCA intermediates.

rxn08312.other_comments: This is the CDP-diacylglycerol synthase (CDS) reaction using oleoyl (C18:1, cis-11/vaccenic-like) phosphatidic acid. CTP reacts with phosphatidic acid to form CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing pyrophosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: CTP provides CMP moiety transferred to the phosphate of PA, with PPi and H+ released. Although written as reversible, in vivo the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase.

rxn10267.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylglycerophosphate phosphatase (PGP phosphatase) reaction with isotetradecanoyl (anteiso/iso C14) acyl chains. It hydrolyzes the phosphomonoester of phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP) to yield phosphatidylglycerol (PG), inorganic phosphate, and a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O cleaves the terminal phosphate group, releasing Pi and a proton, with the lipid PGP converted to PG. This is a key step in PG biosynthesis.

rxn01517.other_comments: This is the phosphorylation of dUMP (2'-deoxyuridine 5'-monophosphate) to dUDP using ATP as the phosphate donor, catalyzed by a nucleoside monophosphate kinase (UMP-CMP kinase / dUMP kinase activity). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (-4) + H+ (+1) + dUMP (-2) = -5 on the left; ADP (-3) + dUDP (-2) = -5 on the right. Phosphorus is conserved (3 ATP + 1 dUMP = 2 ADP + 2 dUDP). The inclusion of the proton accounts for the protonation state change upon phosphoryl transfer.

rxn00371.other_comments: This is formate dehydrogenase (EC 1.2.1.2), catalyzing the oxidation of formate to CO2 with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is balanced: formate (CHO2-) + NAD+ -> CO2 + NADH. Atoms balance (C:1, O:2, H accounted for with the proton/hydride transfer) and charge is conserved when formate carries a -1 charge. In vivo, this reaction strongly favors CO2 formation due to the highly negative free energy of formate oxidation and the irreversible release of CO2, making it effectively unidirectional toward NADH and CO2 production.

rxn00952.other_comments: This is O-acetylhomoserine sulfhydrylase (O-acetylhomoserine (thiol)-lyase, EC 2.5.1.49). O-acetyl-L-homoserine reacts with hydrogen sulfide (H2S) to form L-homocysteine and acetate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: H2S provides the sulfur, the acetyl group is released as acetate, and the homoserine backbone becomes homocysteine. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1:1).

rxn08896.other_comments: This is a murein (peptidoglycan) D,D-endopeptidase reaction. It hydrolyzes the D-Ala-meso-A2pm (DAP) cross-link between two adjacent peptidoglycan strands, converting a cross-linked tripeptide-tetrapeptide dimer into two separate uncrosslinked strands bearing tripeptide and tetrapeptide stems. The single water molecule appropriately hydrolyzes the single peptide cross-bridge, so the stoichiometry is balanced. D,D-endopeptidases catalyze hydrolytic cleavage of the peptide cross-link, which is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically directional toward bond cleavage.

rxn01961.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of xanthosine 5'-monophosphate (XMP) into xanthosine and inorganic phosphate, catalyzed by a 5'-nucleotidase/phosphohydrolase. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O cleaves the phosphomonoester bond, releasing one phosphate and the dephosphorylated nucleoside (xanthosine). Phosphomonoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (hydrolysis) direction.

rxn05006.other_comments: This reaction represents precorrin-2 methyltransferase (SUMT/CysG/CobI type), specifically the methylation of precorrin-1 to precorrin-2 using SAM as the methyl donor, producing S-adenosyl-homocysteine and releasing a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group is transferred from SAM, converting precorrin-1 to precorrin-2, with SAH and H+ as byproducts. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn03141.other_comments: This is the MurF reaction (UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-tripeptide:D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase) adding the D-Ala-D-Ala dipeptide to the UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide to form the UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide in peptidoglycan synthesis. Atoms and charges otherwise balance (ATP -> ADP + Pi + H+, peptide bond formation).

rxn12206.other_comments: This represents malonate decarboxylase (malonate carboxy-lyase) converting malonate to acetate plus CO2. Mass balance checks: Malonate (C3H2O4, 2- charge) + H+ gives CO2 (CO2) + Acetate (C2H3O2, 1- charge). Carbon: 3 = 1 + 2 (balanced). Hydrogen: 2 + 1 = 0 + 3 (balanced). Oxygen: 4 = 2 + 2 (balanced). Charge: -2 + 1 = -1 (balanced). The reaction is stoichiometrically correct. Decarboxylation reactions releasing CO2 are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn10226.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol:serine O-phosphatidyltransferase (phosphatidylserine synthase, PSS/CHO1-type) reaction. L-serine attacks the CDP-diacylglycerol, transferring the phosphatidyl moiety to form phosphatidylserine and releasing CMP. The acyl chains are the isoheptadecanoyl (iso-C17) variants. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven toward phosphatidylserine synthesis.

errors: Proton imbalance: the reaction produces 2.0 H+, but the CDP-diacylglycerol + serine to phosphatidylserine + CMP reaction should release at most 1 H+ (the displaced proton balance depends on protonation states). Charge/mass balance is not satisfied with 2 H+ on the product side.
Atom balance should be verified: transfer of the phosphatidyl group from CDP-DAG to serine yields phosphatidylserine + CMP, but the net hydrogen count appears off by one proton.
rxn09211.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol-dependent phosphatidylserine synthase (PSS, prokaryotic/yeast-type) reaction using dioleoyl (18:1, n-C18:1 cis-11 vaccenoyl) CDP-diacylglycerol. L-serine attacks the CDP-DAG, displacing CMP and forming phosphatidylserine. The substrate naming (1,2-dioctadec-11-enoylglycerol) corresponds to the vaccenoyl/oleoyl-type acyl chains.

rxn09234.other_comments: This is ribonucleotide reductase acting on UDP to produce dUDP (2'-deoxyUDP), using reduced glutaredoxin as the electron donor. The reaction removes the 2'-OH from the ribose, with the oxygen released as water and glutaredoxin becoming oxidized (forming a disulfide). Stoichiometry is balanced: the 2'-OH oxygen leaves as H2O, and the two electrons/protons come from the dithiol of glutaredoxin. In vivo this reaction proceeds in the reductive (forward) direction toward deoxyribonucleotide synthesis.

rxn01299.other_comments: This is the inosine ribohydrolase (inosine nucleosidase) reaction, EC 3.2.2.2. Inosine is hydrolyzed to D-ribose and hypoxanthine (HYXN). The stoichiometry is balanced: inosine (C10H12N4O5) + water (H2O) yields D-ribose (C5H10O5) + hypoxanthine (C5H4N4O). Atoms balance: C10, H14, N4, O6 on each side. As a hydrolytic glycosidase reaction, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of nucleoside cleavage.

rxn00533.other_comments: This is the acetyl-CoA carboxylase reaction (EC 6.4.1.2), forming malonyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA and bicarbonate/CO2, using ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi. The reaction is balanced: ATP + Acetyl-CoA + H2CO3 yields ADP + Phosphate + H+ + Malonyl-CoA. Carbon, phosphorus, and charge appear balanced (H2CO3 provides the carboxyl carbon and the proton released). In vivo this ATP-driven carboxylation is essentially irreversible and committed to fatty acid biosynthesis, so it runs in the forward direction.

rxn08309.other_comments: This is the CDP-diacylglycerol synthase reaction (CdsA) using a fully saturated dipalmitoyl phosphatidic acid (1,2-dihexadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate). CTP reacts with phosphatidic acid to form CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the CMP moiety from CTP is transferred to the phosphate of phosphatidic acid, releasing PPi. Mass and charge balance check out (the proton release is consistent with the chemistry). In vivo this reaction is driven forward by the subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase.

rxn02476.other_comments: This is the EPSP synthase (AroA) reaction in the shikimate pathway. PEP + shikimate-3-phosphate yields 5-enolpyruvylshikimate-3-phosphate (EPSP) + inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass-balanced: the enolpyruvyl moiety from PEP is transferred to the 5-hydroxyl of shikimate-3-phosphate, releasing phosphate. Although the enzyme is intrinsically reversible in vitro, in vivo it proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward chorismate/aromatic amino acid synthesis.

rxn05331.other_comments: This is a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase reaction (FabA/FabZ type) in fatty acid biosynthesis, removing water from D-3-hydroxydodecanoyl-ACP to form trans-2-dodecenoyl-ACP (a C12 step). Atoms balance: loss of H2O converts the beta-hydroxy group to a trans-2,3 double bond. In vivo, coupled to the irreversible reductase steps of the fatty acid synthesis cycle, it proceeds toward the enoyl-ACP.

rxn03841.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate lyase (ADCL, PabC), which converts 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate (ADC) into 4-aminobenzoate (ABEE/PABA) plus pyruvate, with release of a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ADC (C10H10NO5-) yields PABA (4-aminobenzoate, C7H6NO2-) + pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + H+. This is the final step in PABA biosynthesis, a precursor of folate.

rxn04954.other_comments: This reaction represents methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR, EC 1.5.1.20) written in the oxidation direction (5-methyl-THF to 5,10-methylene-THF using NAD+). Stoichiometry is balanced: the 2-electron oxidation of the methyl to methylene group yields NADH + H+. Note that in mammals MTHFR physiologically uses NADPH (EC 1.5.1.20 historically/bacterial uses NADH), but the carbon/electron balance shown here is correct as written.

rxn04748.other_comments: This is a salicylate 1-monooxygenase (decarboxylating) type reaction acting on m-cresotic acid (3-methylsalicylate / 2-hydroxy-6-methylbenzoate). The enzyme uses NADH and O2 to hydroxylate and decarboxylate, releasing CO2 and producing 4-methylcatechol, NAD+, and water. Stoichiometry balances: NADH + O2 + 2 H+ + substrate (C8H8O3) gives H2O + NAD+ + CO2 + 4-methylcatechol (C7H8O2). Atom and charge balance check out.

errors: The reaction as written is reversed relative to the biosynthetic direction; the acyltransferase (LpxL/HtrB) transfers the lauroyl (dodecanoyl) group FROM dodecanoyl-ACP TO Kdo2-lipid IVA, releasing free ACP. As written, lauroyl-Kdo2-lipid IVA + ACP gives Kdo2-lipid IVA + dodecanoyl-ACP, which describes the reverse (thiolysis) reaction.
Stoichiometry is otherwise balanced: the acyl (C12) group is conserved between the lipid and ACP carriers.
rxn06865.other_comments: This is the LpxL (HtrB) lauroyltransferase step in lipid A (Kdo2-lipid A) biosynthesis. Physiologically, dodecanoyl-ACP (lauroyl-ACP) acylates Kdo2-lipid IVA to produce lauroyl-Kdo2-lipid IVA plus free ACP. The acyltransfer is thermodynamically driven toward acylation in vivo, so the biological direction is the formation of the lauroyl-lipid product (i.e., the reverse of how this reaction was written).

rxn08818.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase L2 reaction hydrolyzing the ester bond of 2-tetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a 2-acyl lysophosphatidic acid with myristoyl/C14:0). Hydrolysis releases myristic acid (C14:0) and glycerol-3-phosphate. The mass balance is correct: the acyl-glycerophosphate plus H2O yields the free fatty acid plus glycerol-3-phosphate. The two H+ account for ionization states of the phosphate and carboxylate groups, which is consistent with charge balancing at physiological pH. Hydrolytic reactions of this type are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the hydrolysis (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn04113.other_comments: This is the IspH (LytB) reaction, the final step of the MEP/non-mevalonate isoprenoid pathway. It converts (E)-4-hydroxy-3-methyl-but-2-enyl diphosphate (HMBPP) to isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) using two electrons (here from NADPH). The reaction is mass-balanced: substrate C5H12O8P2 + reduction yields IPP (C5H12O7P2) + H2O. The enzyme physiologically uses reduced ferredoxin/flavodoxin in vivo rather than NADPH directly, but the stoichiometry as a 2-electron reduction with loss of the hydroxyl as water is correct. Note IspH actually produces a mixture of IPP and DMAPP (~5:1), but the IPP-forming reaction is valid.

errors: The reaction as written is stoichiometrically trivial/null: identical species (H+ and Aminoethanol/ethanolamine) appear on both sides, so it represents no net chemical change unless compartments are specified
Compartment annotations are missing; a proton symport transport reaction must distinguish extracellular and cytoplasmic species, e.g. H+[e] + Aminoethanol[e] <=> H+[c] + Aminoethanol[c]
rxn05551.other_comments: This is intended to be an ethanolamine:proton symport transport reaction (uptake driven by the proton motive force). As written without compartment labels both sides are identical, so it cannot be evaluated for true mass/charge transfer. Assuming proper compartmentalization (e to c), the stoichiometry of 1 H+ symported with 1 ethanolamine is reasonable. Net direction in vivo is typically import (extracellular to cytoplasm) driven by the PMF, though transporters can be modeled as reversible.

errors: The reaction does not specify cellular compartments; a proton symport transport reaction must distinguish extracellular and intracellular (cytoplasmic) species, e.g. H+[e] + D-Malate[e] <=> H+[c] + D-Malate[c]. As written, both sides are identical and the net reaction is null (no actual transport or transformation occurs).
rxn05603.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction in which D-malate is imported across the membrane coupled to the inward movement of a proton (proton symport), driven by the proton motive force. The intent is clear, but the compartment annotations are missing, making the equation appear as a trivial identity (same metabolites on both sides). Stoichiometry of 1 H+ per D-malate is plausible for a symporter, though the charge balance depends on the protonation state of malate (D-malate is typically a dianion at physiological pH, so additional protons might be expected for electroneutral symport).

errors: Stoichiometric mass imbalance: condensation of acetyl-CoA (C23) and propionyl-CoA (C24) releasing one free CoA should yield a C4 acyl-CoA product (2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA), but the carbon/atom balance must be checked carefully. The reaction as written is actually a Claisen-type condensation: acetyl-CoA contributes a 2-carbon acetyl unit and propionyl-CoA acts as the acceptor. The product 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA contains 5 carbons in the acyl portion (CH3-CO-CH(CH3)-CO-SCoA), which equals acetyl (2C) + propionyl (3C). One CoA is released. This balances if elements are tracked properly.

The product naming/regiochemistry: condensation of acetyl-CoA + propionyl-CoA via thiolase typically gives 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA, which is consistent. No clear stoichiometric error if H atoms balance (one H2O is not involved in thiolase Claisen condensation).
rxn00676.other_comments: This is a thiolase-type (acetyltransferase) Claisen condensation: acetyl-CoA + propionyl-CoA giving 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA + free CoA. This is the reverse of the thiolytic cleavage in isoleucine degradation. Thiolases are physiologically reversible, though in vivo the degradative (thiolytic cleavage) direction is usually favored.

rxn00943.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of palmitoyl-CoA (a thioester) by palmitoyl-CoA hydrolase (acyl-CoA thioesterase, EC 3.1.2.2). Water attacks the thioester bond, releasing free CoA and palmitate. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + palmitoyl-CoA yields CoA + H+ + palmitate, with mass and charge conserved (the H+ accounts for proton release upon carboxylate formation). Thioester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn09272.other_comments: This represents the succinate dehydrogenase / fumarate reductase reaction with the ubiquinone/ubiquinol couple. The reaction as written (succinate + ubiquinone-8 -> fumarate + ubiquinol-8) is balanced in atoms and electrons (succinate to fumarate releases 2H+ and 2e-, reducing ubiquinone to ubiquinol). However, the fumarate reductase complex (FRD) operates physiologically in the direction of fumarate reduction (fumarate + ubiquinol-8 -> succinate + ubiquinone-8) during anaerobic respiration, using menaquinol/quinol as electron donor. Thus the in vivo flux for FRD is in the reverse direction relative to how the reaction is written.

errors: L-Cysteate appears on both sides without compartment labels, making the transport reaction stoichiometrically ambiguous; in a proper ABC transport reaction the substrate should be shown in two different compartments (e.g., L-Cysteate[external] -> L-Cysteate[cytoplasm])
rxn05599.other_comments: This represents an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the import of L-cysteate. The ATP hydrolysis portion is correctly balanced. The transported metabolite should differ in compartment between substrate and product sides; as written without compartment annotations, L-cysteate cancels out and the net transport is not represented.

rxn01257.other_comments: This is the aminodeoxychorismate synthase (PabA/PabB) reaction in folate biosynthesis. L-Glutamine donates its amide nitrogen to chorismate, producing 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate (ADC) and L-glutamate. The reaction is balanced: chorismate (C10H10O6) plus glutamine amide nitrogen yields ADC (4-amino-4-deoxychorismate) with displacement of the 4-hydroxyl as water, and glutamine is converted to glutamate. Mass and charge balance hold when water is accounted for.

rxn03249.other_comments: This is a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction (part of fatty acid beta-oxidation) acting on a C6 substrate. (S)-3-Hydroxyhexanoyl-CoA is oxidized to 3-oxohexanoyl-CoA with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Atoms and charges balance: the secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, removing 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+ giving NADH, one released as H+). Stoichiometry is correct. Although written reversibly and the enzyme is mechanistically reversible, in vivo flux during beta-oxidation runs in the oxidation (forward, hydroxyacyl to oxoacyl) direction.

rxn00980.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by phosphoglycolate phosphatase (EC 3.1.3.18). It hydrolyzes 2-phosphoglycolate to glycolate and inorganic phosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: 2-phosphoglycolate (C2H2O6P, charge -3 at physiological pH) + H2O yields glycolate (C2H3O3, charge -1) + phosphate (HPO4, charge -2). Atoms and charges balance. As a phosphatase hydrolysis, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of phosphate release.

errors: The reaction as written is identical on both sides (H+ + K+ + Cd2+ <=> H+ + K+ + Cd2+), so it represents no net chemical transformation
Transport reactions must specify compartments (e.g., cytoplasm vs extracellular) to be meaningful; without compartment annotations the reaction is a null transformation
Stated as an antiport but no opposing directional movement of species across compartments is indicated
rxn05517.other_comments: This is intended to be a cadmium efflux antiport reaction (likely Cd2+/H+ or cation antiporter such as CzcD-type). As written it lacks compartment labels, so both sides are identical and the equation conveys no net transport or chemistry. A correct form would be something like Cd2+[c] + H+[e] <=> Cd2+[e] + H+[c], showing Cd2+ exported in exchange for H+ import. The inclusion of K+ on both sides unchanged is also questionable.

rxn00056.other_comments: This is the oxidation of ferrous iron (Fe2+) to ferric iron (Fe3+) by molecular oxygen. The reaction O2 + 4 H+ + 4 Fe2+ -> 2 H2O + 4 Fe3+ is balanced: charge (4 H+ gives +4, 4 Fe2+ gives +8, total +12 on left; 4 Fe3+ gives +12 on right), atoms (2 O, 4 H, 4 Fe each side), and electrons (4 Fe2+ each lose 1 electron = 4 electrons; O2 + 4 H+ + 4 e- -> 2 H2O). This corresponds to ferroxidase/ceruloplasmin-type activity. The reaction is thermodynamically strongly favorable in the oxidative direction.

rxn00016.other_comments: Chitobiose (N,N'-diacetylchitobiose) is a disaccharide of two GlcNAc units linked by a beta-1,4 glycosidic bond. Hydrolysis with one water yields 2 N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, which is correctly balanced (one glycosidic bond cleaved by one H2O). Glycoside hydrolase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn02213.other_comments: This is the third step of the shikimate pathway, catalyzed by 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase (DHQ dehydratase). It converts 3-dehydroquinate (5-dehydroquinate is a synonym) to 3-dehydroshikimate via dehydration, releasing one water molecule. The reaction is balanced: dehydroquinate (C7H10O6) loses H2O to form dehydroshikimate (C7H8O5). Mass and atoms balance correctly.

errors: Charge and proton imbalance: the reaction is missing an H+ (one proton). Balanced form: O2 + FMNH2 + ethanesulfonate -> H2O + FMN + acetaldehyde + sulfite + H+. Ethanesulfonate (C2H5O3S-, charge -1) and sulfite (SO3^2-, charge -2) require an additional H+ on the product side to balance charge and hydrogen.
rxn08469.other_comments: This is the alkanesulfonate monooxygenase (SsuD-type) reaction, where reduced flavin (FMNH2) and molecular oxygen oxidize ethanesulfonate to release sulfite and the corresponding aldehyde (acetaldehyde). The flavin is provided by an associated NAD(P)H-FMN reductase. The reaction consumes O2 and FMNH2 irreversibly in vivo, driving it strongly in the forward direction (sulfur scavenging under sulfate starvation).

rxn05441.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2 double bond of a 9-methyl-branched enoyl-ACP (C10 chain with methyl branch) using NADH/H+ to give the saturated acyl-ACP and NAD+. Stoichiometry is balanced: the trans-2 double bond is reduced by addition of 2 H (one as hydride from NADH, one as H+). Mass and charge balance hold (NADH + H+ -> NAD+ provides 2H, consistent with C=C reduction). In vivo this enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI/FabK-type) step strongly favors the reductive forward direction toward the saturated acyl-ACP.

rxn08668.other_comments: This reaction describes glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase (GDPD) hydrolyzing glycerophosphoserine into L-serine and glycerol-3-phosphate. The phosphodiester bond is cleaved with water, releasing the serine headgroup and yielding sn-glycerol-3-phosphate plus a proton. Atom and charge balance: glycerophosphoserine + H2O yields L-serine + glycerol-3-phosphate + H+, which is consistent. The H+ accounts for the proton released upon phosphodiester hydrolysis.

rxn00903.other_comments: This is the branched-chain amino acid aminotransferase (BCAT) reaction for valine. L-Valine donates its amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, forming L-glutamate and 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate (2-oxoisovalerate, the keto acid of valine). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: each side has matching atoms (C, H, N, O) and the amino/keto group transfer is correct. Aminotransferase reactions are near-equilibrium and physiologically reversible.

errors: The H+ on the left side is not balanced; the standard adenylate kinase-type reaction (ATP + dAMP <=> ADP + dADP) does not consume or produce a proton, so the H+ should be removed for charge and mass balance
rxn01127.other_comments: This is a nucleoside monophosphate kinase reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to dAMP, producing ADP and dADP. Apart from the spurious H+, the phosphate transfer is otherwise balanced (adenine moieties and phosphate counts match). Such kinase reactions operate near equilibrium and are physiologically reversible.

errors: Proton balance is incorrect: acyl transfer from acyl-ACP to glycerol-3-phosphate does not consume 2 H+; the reaction should be balanced without added protons (the released ACP thiol and the formed ester do not require 2 H+ consumption)
rxn08548.other_comments: This is a glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) reaction transferring a C14:1 (tetradecenoyl) group from acyl-ACP onto the sn-1 position of glycerol-3-phosphate, yielding 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and free ACP. The acyl chain (tetradecenoyl) and product (1-tetradec-7-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) are consistent.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance protons. The standard methanesulfonate monooxygenase reaction is O2 + FMNH2 + methanesulfonate -> H2O + FMN + formaldehyde + sulfite + H2O (two waters) or requires explicit H+ balancing. Sulfite (SO3^2-) carries charge that must be accounted for.
rxn08468.other_comments: This represents methanesulfonate monooxygenase (FMNH2-dependent two-component monooxygenase), which oxygenatively cleaves methanesulfonate (CH3SO3-) to release formaldehyde and sulfite, consuming O2 and reduced flavin (FMNH2). One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated. The oxygen and carbon/sulfur backbone roughly balance, but proton/charge balancing is incomplete and a second water (or H+) is typically needed for full mass/charge balance.

rxn05341.other_comments: This is the beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase (FabG) reaction in fatty acid synthesis, here written for the C8 intermediate. The forward reaction as written oxidizes (R)-3-hydroxyoctanoyl-ACP to 3-oxooctanoyl-ACP, reducing NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry and charge/atom balance are correct (NADP+ + hydroxyacyl-ACP <=> NADPH + H+ + ketoacyl-ACP). In vivo, FabG runs in the reductive direction (3-oxoacyl-ACP + NADPH + H+ -> 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP + NADP+), so relative to how it is written here the physiological flux is the reverse direction.

rxn00298.other_comments: This is the UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 6-dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.136). It oxidizes the C6 primary alcohol of UDP-GlcNAc to a carboxylate (UDP-N-acetylglucosaminuronate), a 4-electron oxidation requiring 2 NAD+ and 1 H2O, producing 2 NADH and 3 H+. The stoichiometry is balanced for both atoms and charge: oxidation of -CH2OH to -COOH releases 4 electrons (2 NADH) plus the gem-diol intermediate hydration accounts for the water and proton balance.

rxn05226.other_comments: This is the phosphoenolpyruvate:carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS) for glucose uptake. Extracellular D-glucose is transported and concomitantly phosphorylated to D-glucose-6-phosphate, with PEP serving as the phosphoryl donor and being converted to pyruvate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (1:1:1:1 for glucose, PEP, pyruvate, G6P). Strictly, the substrate glucose is extracellular and the product G6P is intracellular, so this represents a coupled transport-phosphorylation process. In vivo this is strongly forward (toward glucose uptake) due to the high energy of the PEP-to-pyruvate conversion making it essentially irreversible.

rxn05445.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2 double bond of 4-methyl-trans-pent-2-enoyl-ACP to give the saturated 4-methylpentanoyl-ACP. NADH provides the reducing equivalents (2 electrons + H from NADH plus a proton). Stoichiometry is balanced: the enoyl substrate (C=C) plus NADH + H+ yields the saturated acyl-ACP + NAD+. The naming as NAD+ oxidoreductase (A-specific) reflects hydride transfer stereochemistry. Physiologically, enoyl reductase strongly favors reduction (saturation) toward the saturated acyl-ACP, consistent with chain elongation/branched-chain fatty acid synthesis.

errors: Charge and mass imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance. Nitrite reductase (NAD(P)H) physiologically reduces nitrite to ammonia, consuming reducing equivalents (NADPH), not producing them. The forward direction shown produces NADPH while oxidizing ammonia, which is thermodynamically and biologically backwards.
Hydrogen/oxygen balance: reduction of nitrite (NO2-) to NH3 plus 2 H2O requires 6 electrons and proper proton accounting; the written stoichiometry of protons is inconsistent for the direction shown.
Possible missing water/proton balance check: 3 NADPH provide 6 electrons, consistent with nitrite-to-ammonia, confirming the reaction is written in the reverse of the physiological direction.
rxn00569.other_comments: This is assimilatory nitrite reductase using NAD(P)H. Physiologically it converts nitrite + 3 NADPH (+ H+) into ammonia + water + 3 NADP. As written (NH3 + NADP -> nitrite + NADPH), it is the reverse of the biological direction. The number of electrons (6 from 3 NADPH) matches a 6-electron reduction of nitrite to ammonia, but the proton/charge balance and the direction shown are problematic.

rxn05449.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2-enoyl double bond of a branched-chain (12-methyl-tridecanoyl, an iso-C14 precursor) acyl-ACP using NADH. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: NADH + H+ donate a hydride and proton across the C2=C3 double bond, yielding the saturated 12-methyl-tridecanoyl-ACP and NAD+. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn00615.other_comments: This is glycerol kinase (EC 2.7.1.30), which phosphorylates glycerol using ATP to produce glycerol-3-phosphate, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is correctly balanced: ATP (C10H16N5O13P3) + glycerol (C3H8O3) yields ADP (C10H15N5O10P2) + glycerol-3-phosphate (C3H7O6P) + H+. Atoms and charges balance. In vivo this reaction is essentially irreversible toward glycerol-3-phosphate due to the favorable thermodynamics of ATP hydrolysis coupling, committing glycerol to metabolism.

rxn00083.other_comments: This is a transhydrogenase reaction transferring a hydride between NAD(H) and NADP(H). NADPH reduces NAD+ to NADH, producing NADP+. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge (NAD+ + NADPH <=> NADH + NADP+). The naming convention 'NADPH:NAD+ oxidoreductase' matches this hydride transfer.

rxn00291.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by N-succinylglutamate desuccinylase (AstE, EC 3.5.1.96), the final step of the arginine succinyltransferase (AST) pathway for arginine/glutamate catabolism. Hydrolysis of the amide bond in N-succinyl-L-glutamate yields L-glutamate and succinate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (C9H13NO7 + H2O -> C5H9NO4 + C4H6O4) and is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic direction.

rxn00562.other_comments: This is the ureidoglycolate lyase (ureidoglycolate urea-lyase) reaction, EC 4.3.2.3. (S)-ureidoglycolate is cleaved into glyoxylate and urea. The reaction is mass-balanced: ureidoglycolate (C3H6N2O4) yields glyoxylate (C2H2O3) plus urea (CH4N2O), with C, H, N, and O all balanced. In vivo this is part of purine degradation and proceeds in the direction of glyoxylate and urea formation.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: hydrolysis of a single amide bond by an amidase releases the peptide and the anhydro-muramate moiety but should not generate 2 H+; a typical amide hydrolysis is charge-neutral or produces at most a net change of 1 proton depending on protonation states, so 2.0 H+ appears incorrect

The cleaved product is named as the full tetrapeptide (L-Ala-D-Glu-meso-DAP-D-Ala), which is correct for the peptide moiety, but the enzyme is an amidase cleaving the lactyl-amide bond linking muramate to L-Ala; stoichiometry of carbon/nitrogen balances only if naming is exact
rxn08124.other_comments: This is the cell wall recycling amidase (e.g., AmpD-type) that hydrolyzes the amide bond between 1,6-anhydro-N-acetylmuramate and the stem peptide L-Ala-D-Glu-meso-DAP-D-Ala, releasing the free peptide and 1,6-anhydro-N-acetylmuramate. The hydrolysis consumes one water. In vivo this is a catabolic/recycling hydrolysis and runs essentially irreversibly in the forward direction.

rxn00743.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of glycerone phosphate (dihydroxyacetone phosphate, DHAP) by a phosphohydrolase, releasing inorganic phosphate and glycerone (dihydroxyacetone). The stoichiometry is balanced: DHAP (C3H7O6P) + H2O yields dihydroxyacetone (C3H6O3) + phosphate (HPO4/H3PO4). As a phosphomonoester hydrolysis, the reaction is highly exergonic and proceeds in the direction of hydrolysis in vivo.

errors: Acyl-CoA substrate mismatch: the reaction names the product as 1-anteisoheptadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a C17 anteiso acyl group), but the donor is given as fa12coa (dodecanoyl/lauroyl-CoA, C12). The acyl-CoA should be anteisoheptadecanoyl-CoA (C17) to match the product.
Atom/mass imbalance results from the acyl chain mismatch between substrate (C12) and product (C17 acyl group).
rxn10206.other_comments: This is a glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) reaction transferring an acyl group from acyl-CoA to the sn-1 position of glycerol-3-phosphate, releasing free CoA. The general reaction scheme (glycerol-3-P + acyl-CoA -> 1-acyl-glycerol-3-P + CoA) is correct and proceeds in the acylation direction in vivo.

rxn07438.other_comments: This represents methionine sulfoxide reductase (MsrB for the R-form). The enzyme reduces peptide-bound methionine-(R)-S-oxide back to methionine, using reduced thioredoxin as the electron donor and producing oxidized thioredoxin and water. As written, the substrates are H2O + oxidized thioredoxin (trdox) + Peptide-L-methionine, with products including Peptide-L-methionine-(R)-S-oxide. This written direction is the thermodynamically unfavorable oxidation; the physiological reaction proceeds in the reverse direction (sulfoxide reduction coupled to thioredoxin oxidation). The reaction is mass/atom balanced as written (an oxygen from the sulfoxide and reducing equivalents are transferred appropriately, with water and the disulfide states accounting for atoms).

rxn02483.other_comments: This is the gamma-carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.44) in the protocatechuate branch of the beta-ketoadipate pathway. 4-Carboxymuconolactone (gamma-carboxymuconolactone) is decarboxylated to yield 3-oxoadipate-enol-lactone (beta-ketoadipate enol-lactone) plus CO2. The reaction consumes a proton along with the substrate and releases CO2, which balances mass and charge (loss of a carboxyl group as CO2). Decarboxylations releasing CO2 are physiologically essentially irreversible.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the acyltransferase reaction (glycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferase, GPAT) does not consume a proton. The balanced reaction is Glycerol-3-phosphate + Palmitoyl-CoA -> CoA + 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, with no H+ on the substrate side. Including H+ as a reactant introduces a charge imbalance.
rxn10202.other_comments: This is the GPAT reaction (EC 2.3.1.15) transferring a palmitoyl (16:0) group from palmitoyl-CoA to glycerol-3-phosphate, forming 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and releasing CoA. The carbon/acyl mass balance is correct; only the proton balance is questionable.

rxn00834.other_comments: This is the IMP dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.205). IMP is oxidized to XMP (xanthosine 5'-monophosphate) using NAD+ as the electron acceptor, producing NADH and H+, with water incorporated. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: IMP (C10H11N4O8P, charge -2) + NAD+ (charge -1) + H2O yields XMP (C10H11N4O9P, charge -2) + NADH (charge -2) + H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly. In vivo, this is the committed and rate-limiting step in guanine nucleotide biosynthesis and proceeds in the direction of XMP formation.

rxn00782.other_comments: This is the NADP-dependent glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction (non-phosphorylating vs phosphorylating; here phosphorylating). It oxidizes G3P with NADP+ and inorganic phosphate to form 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, NADPH, and H+. The reaction is balanced for atoms and charge as written (C3 backbone conserved, phosphate added, redox transfer to NADP+/NADPH, with H+ release). In the Calvin cycle direction, this enzyme typically runs in reverse (1,3-BPG + NADPH -> G3P + NADP+ + Pi), but the enzyme is intrinsically reversible.

rxn02369.other_comments: This reaction describes 4-carboxymuconolactone (2-carboxy-2,5-dihydro-5-oxofuran-2-acetate) being converted by a lyase (decyclizing) to 3-carboxy-cis,cis-muconate plus a proton. This is the ring-opening/lactone hydrolysis step in the protocatechuate branch of the beta-ketoadipate pathway, catalyzed by 4-carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase-related or muconolactone-type enzymes. The atom and charge balance is consistent: the lactone ring opening yields the carboxymuconate dicarboxylate and releases a proton.

errors: Reaction as written is missing CO2 and is not properly balanced; the physiological quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase reaction involves quinolinate, not niacin/nicotinate ribonucleotide as a simple PRPP exchange

The forward decarboxylation requires quinolinate + PRPP -> nicotinate ribonucleotide + CO2 + PPi; the substrate 'Niacin' (nicotinate) does not match the enzyme name which refers to nicotinate D-ribonucleotide formation
rxn01265.other_comments: This appears to describe quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (EC 2.4.2.19), which normally converts quinolinate + PRPP into nicotinate D-ribonucleotide + CO2 + PPi. The given equation lists 'Niacin' instead of quinolinate and omits CO2, so it does not balance. In vivo this enzyme runs in the direction of nicotinate ribonucleotide synthesis (NAD de novo pathway), driven by decarboxylation.

rxn00704.other_comments: This is phosphoglucomutase (EC 5.4.2.2), which interconverts alpha-D-glucose 1-phosphate and D-glucose 6-phosphate via a glucose 1,6-bisphosphate intermediate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (both sides are C6H11O9P, a single phosphate group moved internally). It is freely reversible in vivo with an equilibrium favoring glucose-6-phosphate (~95:5), so the net direction depends on metabolic context (glycogenolysis pushes G1P->G6P, while glycogen synthesis/UDP-glucose formation pulls toward G1P).

errors: Charge imbalance: the production of an H+ is not justified by the group transfer; methyl transfer from S-methylmethionine to homocysteine produces 2 methionine without net proton release. The reaction should balance without the extra H+.
Homocysteine should be specified as L-homocysteine for biological relevance
rxn08703.other_comments: This is the homocysteine S-methyltransferase (S-methylmethionine:homocysteine methyltransferase) reaction. S-methyl-L-methionine donates a methyl group to homocysteine, yielding two molecules of L-methionine. The core stoichiometry (1 homocysteine + 1 SMM -> 2 methionine) is correct, but the extra H+ creates a charge/proton imbalance.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction as written loses a CoA moiety and is unbalanced. The correct thiolase-type condensation should be Butyryl-CoA + Acetyl-CoA -> 3-Oxohexanoyl-CoA + CoA, but mass balance requires careful checking of carbon and the thioester. 3-Oxohexanoyl-CoA (C6 acyl) is formed from a C4 (butyryl) and C2 (acetyl) unit with release of one CoA, which is correct for a Claisen condensation; thus the atoms balance and there may be no real stoichiometric error.
rxn00874.other_comments: This is a thiolase (acetyl-CoA C-acyltransferase) type reaction: condensation of butyryl-CoA and acetyl-CoA to give 3-oxohexanoyl-CoA plus free CoA. The C2 + C4 acyl chains combine to a C6 3-oxoacyl-CoA. Mechanistically this is a Claisen condensation. In vivo, the thiolytic (degradative) direction toward acetyl-CoA + acyl-CoA is usually favored, but in fatty acid/butyrate synthesis the condensation direction is used, so it is treated as reversible.

rxn01459.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of 4-aminobutanal (4-aminobutyraldehyde) to GABA (4-aminobutanoate/gamma-aminobutyrate) using NADP+ as the electron acceptor, with water as a co-substrate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (C4H9NO) plus water minus 2 hydrogens (2 H+ released, but net redox transfer to NADPH) yields the carboxylic acid (GABA, C4H9NO2). Carbon (4), nitrogen (1), and the redox/proton balance are consistent with an aldehyde dehydrogenase mechanism. Note the enzyme name cites NAD+ but the reaction uses NADP+; this is a cofactor discrepancy worth flagging in the source annotation.

rxn00241.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP and inorganic phosphate. The reaction H2O + GTP -> Phosphate + GDP + H+ is correctly balanced for mass and charge: GTP (4-) + H2O yields GDP (3-) + HPO4 (2-) + H+, balancing both atoms and charge. GTP hydrolysis is strongly exergonic and proceeds in the forward (hydrolysis) direction in vivo.

rxn05252.other_comments: This is a fatty acid-CoA ligase (acyl-CoA synthetase) reaction for an isoheptadecanoic acid (C17 iso fatty acid, fa11). The reaction activates a free fatty acid to its CoA thioester. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + fatty acid -> AMP + PPi + acyl-CoA. The two high-energy bonds released (ATP to AMP + PPi) plus subsequent PPi hydrolysis make this reaction effectively irreversible in vivo, driving it in the acyl-CoA forming direction.

rxn12642.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide L-alanyl-L-histidine (also related to carnosine-type dipeptides) by a dipeptidase, cleaving the peptide bond to yield L-alanine and L-histidine. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the dipeptide plus one water gives the two free amino acids. Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible under physiological conditions.

rxn05620.other_comments: This represents ABC-transporter-mediated import of MOPS (3-(N-morpholino)propanesulfonic acid, a buffer/osmolyte) coupled to ATP hydrolysis. The ATP hydrolysis portion (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) is stoichiometrically balanced. ABC transport powered by ATP hydrolysis is effectively irreversible in vivo, driving uptake against a gradient.

rxn01512.other_comments: This reaction represents nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDPK) activity acting on dTDP. ATP phosphorylates dTDP (thymidine diphosphate) to form dTTP (shown as TTP), generating ADP. The reaction is balanced: ATP + dTDP gives ADP + dTTP, with one phosphate transferred. Note that 'TTP' here should properly be 'dTTP' (thymidine is a deoxyribonucleoside; there is no ribo-TTP in standard nomenclature), but this is a notation convention rather than a stoichiometric error. NDPK reactions are well known to be reversible due to the similar phosphoryl transfer potential of nucleoside triphosphates.

rxn05627.other_comments: This is intended to represent nitrate uptake coupled to proton symport across the cell membrane. As written, both sides are identical (H+ + Nitrate <=> H+ + Nitrate), which is only meaningful if compartment annotations are added (e.g., H+[e] + Nitrate[e] <=> H+[c] + Nitrate[c]). Physiologically, proton symport uses the proton motive force to drive nitrate import into the cytoplasm.

rxn08130.other_comments: This is the menG-catalyzed (2-demethylmenaquinone methyltransferase) final step of menaquinone biosynthesis. SAM methylates 2-demethylmenaquinol-8 (the reduced quinol form) at the C-2 position to yield menaquinol-8, releasing S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The reaction is balanced: a methyl group (CH3, i.e. CH2 + H+ accounted for) is transferred from SAM to the substrate; the carbon and hydrogen mass and charge balance correctly with the H+ released. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the forward direction (toward menaquinol-8) is appropriate.

rxn10010.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADH-dependent reduction of trans-2-hexenoyl-CoA (an enoyl-CoA with a 2E double bond) to hexanoyl-CoA, catalyzed by an enoyl-CoA reductase (trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase). The double bond between C2 and C3 is reduced, consuming NADH + H+ and producing NAD+. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH contributes the hydride and the proton balances charge/H. Carbon (6-carbon acyl chain) and CoA moiety are conserved on both sides. Although written as reversible, in vivo this enoyl-CoA reductase reaction (e.g., in reductive/fatty acid elongation or fermentation pathways) strongly favors the reductive (forward) direction.

rxn01571.other_comments: This is the feruloyl-CoA synthetase (4-coumarate-CoA ligase / ferulate:CoA ligase, AMP-forming) reaction. Ferulate is activated by ATP to feruloyl-AMP, then thioesterified with CoA to form feruloyl-CoA, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the carboxyl group of ferulate is esterified to CoA, ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi, and one proton is released, consistent with the AMP-forming ligase mechanism. In vivo this proceeds in the forward direction (toward feruloyl-CoA) because the released pyrophosphate is hydrolyzed by inorganic pyrophosphatase, pulling the reaction forward.

rxn01332.other_comments: This is the DAHP synthase reaction (EC 2.5.1.54), the first committed step of the shikimate pathway. PEP condenses with erythrose-4-phosphate, releasing inorganic phosphate and consuming water, to form 3-deoxy-D-arabino-heptulosonate-7-phosphate (DAHP). The reaction is balanced: PEP (C3H5O6P) + E4P (C4H9O7P) + H2O -> DAHP (C7H13O10P) + Pi (H3PO4). Carbon, phosphorus, and overall mass balance check out.

rxn00693.other_comments: This is methionine synthase (EC 2.1.1.13/2.1.1.14), transferring a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, producing methionine and tetrahydrofolate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: both sides carry the methyl group and the relevant atoms are conserved. In vivo this reaction proceeds toward methionine synthesis, regenerating tetrahydrofolate (the folate cycle), and is the key step linking folate and methionine metabolism.

rxn00785.other_comments: This is the transketolase reaction (EC 2.2.1.1) from the pentose phosphate pathway. Transketolase transfers a two-carbon glycolaldehyde unit from a ketose donor (fructose-6-phosphate, 6C) to an aldose acceptor (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, 3C), yielding xylulose-5-phosphate (5C) and erythrose-4-phosphate (4C). Carbon balance: 6+3 = 5+4 = 9 carbons, balanced. Phosphate atoms also balance (2 = 2). The reaction is stoichiometrically correct.

rxn01351.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of dGTP (2'-deoxyguanosine 5'-triphosphate) to dGMP plus pyrophosphate (PPi). The enzyme is a diphosphohydrolase that cleaves the beta-gamma phosphoanhydride bonds, releasing the two terminal phosphates as PPi and leaving dGMP. Mass and charge balance check out: dGTP (charge -4 at physiological pH) + H2O yields dGMP (-2) + PPi (-3) + 2 H+ (+2), giving -4 = -3 -2 +2 = -3... charge balance requires 2 H+ to reconcile, which is included. Atom balance for P: dGTP has 3 P, products dGMP (1 P) + PPi (2 P) = 3 P, correct.

rxn03909.other_comments: This is the DXP synthase (Dxs) reaction, which condenses pyruvate and D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate in a thiamine diphosphate (TPP)-dependent decarboxylation to form 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate (DXP) and release CO2. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written: C3H3O3- (pyruvate) + H+ + C3H5O6P2- (G3P) gives CO2 + C5H9O7P2- (DXP). Atoms balance (C6, H9, O9, P1 on each side) and charge balances (-3 on each side). This is the committed first step of the MEP/non-mevalonate isoprenoid biosynthesis pathway.

rxn03084.other_comments: This is the FGAM synthetase reaction (PurL, EC 6.3.5.3) in purine biosynthesis. Glutamine donates an amide nitrogen to N-formylglycinamide ribonucleotide (FGAR) to form formylglycinamidine ribonucleotide (FGAM), with ATP hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi and glutamine converted to glutamate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: nitrogen from the glutamine amide is transferred to the substrate, and the 2 H+ released balance the proton accounting. Stoichiometry checks out.

rxn06600.other_comments: This is the glycine cleavage system T-protein (aminomethyltransferase, GcvT) reaction. It transfers the aminomethyl moiety carried on the lipoyl arm of the H-protein (S-aminomethyldihydrolipoylprotein) to tetrahydrofolate, producing 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate, ammonia, and the regenerated dihydrolipoyl-H-protein. The stoichiometry is balanced (the aminomethyl group CH2NH is split into CH2 transferred to THF and NH3 released; the lipoamide is reduced/regenerated). In vivo this operates in the glycine cleavage direction.

rxn03439.other_comments: This is the KdtA (WaaA) catalyzed transfer of a second KDO (3-deoxy-D-manno-oct-2-ulosonate) residue from CMP-KDO onto KDO-lipid IVA to form KDO2-lipid IVA, releasing CMP and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the KDO group (donor) is transferred from CMP-KDO leaving CMP, and the glycosidic bond formation releases H+. This is part of LPS/lipid A biosynthesis.

rxn01101.other_comments: This is the phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase reaction (PHGDH, EC 1.1.1.95), the first committed step of serine biosynthesis. It oxidizes 3-phosphoglycerate to 3-phosphohydroxypyruvate (3-phosphonooxypyruvate) using NAD+ as electron acceptor. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced in both mass and charge: 3-PG (carbon backbone with 2-OH) is oxidized to the 2-keto compound, releasing 2 electrons (NAD+ to NADH) plus a proton. As written (NAD+ + 3-PG -> NADH + H+ + 3-phosphohydroxypyruvate), this is the physiological/biosynthetic direction in vivo, which corresponds to the left-to-right (forward) direction here. Although the standard equilibrium thermodynamically favors the reverse (reduction), the reaction is pulled forward in vivo by coupling to subsequent transamination and removal of products.

rxn05117.other_comments: This is the aspartate oxidase / aspartate dehydrogenase type reaction (L-aspartate:NADP+ oxidoreductase, deaminating), oxidizing L-aspartate to iminoaspartate (2-iminosuccinate) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: L-aspartate (C4H6NO4-, actually C4H7NO4 neutral) loses 2 H (2 electrons + proton equivalents) to form iminoaspartate; NADP+ + 2e- + H+ -> NADPH, with one H+ released. Atoms and charges balance. This enzyme (e.g., AspDH / NadB-type in NAD(P)+ biosynthesis) typically runs in the oxidative deamination direction toward iminoaspartate in vivo to feed quinolinate/NAD synthesis, but the dehydrogenase reaction is intrinsically reversible.

rxn10233.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (PSD) reaction converting dianteisoheptadecanoyl-phosphatidylserine to the corresponding phosphatidylethanolamine with release of CO2. PSD reactions are physiologically irreversible due to the loss of CO2.

rxn00558.other_comments: This is the phosphoglucose isomerase (PGI) reaction interconverting glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate. The reaction is an intramolecular aldose-ketose isomerization, so it is stoichiometrically balanced 1:1 (both are C6H13O9P). It operates near equilibrium in vivo and the net direction depends on the metabolic context (glycolysis: G6P to F6P; gluconeogenesis: F6P to G6P).

rxn02005.other_comments: This is a PEP:carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS) reaction for trehalose uptake. Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) donates its phosphate group to incoming trehalose (TRHL) during translocation across the membrane, producing pyruvate and intracellular trehalose 6-phosphate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one phosphate is transferred from PEP to trehalose, yielding pyruvate and trehalose 6-phosphate. PTS systems couple transport with phosphorylation and are physiologically driven in the uptake (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn12635.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide glycyl-methionine (Gly-Met) into its constituent amino acids, glycine and L-methionine, with the consumption of one water molecule. The stoichiometry is balanced: the peptide bond is cleaved by water, releasing the two free amino acids. Peptide hydrolysis catalyzed by peptidases is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of hydrolysis.

rxn00346.other_comments: This is the aspartate 1-decarboxylase (PanD, EC 4.1.1.11) reaction, converting L-aspartate to beta-alanine and CO2 with consumption of a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: L-aspartate (C4H6NO4-, with the proton effectively neutralizing) yields beta-alanine (C3H7NO2) plus CO2. Atom and charge balance check out when accounting for the H+ consumed during decarboxylation.

rxn00806.other_comments: This is the branched-chain amino acid aminotransferase (BCAT) reaction. L-Leucine donates its amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-Glutamate and 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (4MOP, also known as ketoleucine or 2-oxoisocaproate). The reaction is balanced: C5+C6 reactants (2-oxoglutarate C5H6O5 + L-Leucine C6H13NO2) yield C5+C6 products (L-Glutamate C5H9NO4 + 4MOP C6H10O3). Atoms (C, H, N, O) and charges balance for a transamination, which is a simple amino/keto group exchange.

rxn08808.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase reaction (Lysophospholipase L1, encoded by pldB in E. coli, periplasmic). It hydrolyzes 2-acyl-glycerophosphoethanolamine (1-lyso, with the acyl group being stearate, C18:0) at the ester bond, releasing the free fatty acid (octadecanoate/stearate, ocdca) and glycerophosphoethanolamine. The H2O acts as the nucleophile in hydrolysis. Charge and mass balance: lysoPE (1-) + H2O is consumed with H+; products are glycerophosphoethanolamine (anion) and stearate (1-). The H+ appears as a substrate to balance protonation states. Stoichiometry of the acyl/glycerol/ethanolamine groups is conserved. Note: depending on the protonation conventions of the model, the H+ placement should be verified, but the overall hydrolysis is balanced.

rxn01851.other_comments: This is the aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction (ABALDH/gabaldh) oxidizing 4-aminobutanal to 4-aminobutanoate (GABA) with NAD+ as electron acceptor. Stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (C4H9NO) plus H2O is oxidized to the carboxylate (GABA, C4H8NO2-) with concomitant reduction of NAD+ to NADH and release of 2 H+, which is the standard mass- and charge-balanced form for NAD-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenases. This oxidative decarboxylation coupled to quinone reduction is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible.

The ATP hydrolysis stoichiometry (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) is balanced and correct. rxn01388.other_comments: This is the second half-reaction of aconitase (EC 4.2.1.3), the dehydration of isocitrate to cis-aconitate plus water. In vivo aconitase catalyzes the reversible interconversion of citrate, cis-aconitate, and isocitrate; net flux direction depends on TCA cycle demand but the enzyme operates near equilibrium and is reversible.

The carbon skeleton (C7 branched chain) is conserved, and the loss of one water molecule across the C2-C3 bond to form the double bond is correct. Stoichiometry is balanced.

rxn03638.other_comments: This is the GlmU acetyltransferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.157), transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to glucosamine-1-phosphate to form N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate. rxn09174.other_comments: This reaction describes a CoA transferase (propionate CoA-transferase, EC 2.8.3.x) transferring the CoA moiety from propionyl-CoA to succinate, yielding succinyl-CoA and propionate. Such CoA-transferase reactions are thermodynamically near-equilibrium and biologically reversible, with net direction set by relative substrate/product concentrations.

rxn00991.other_comments: This reaction represents HMG-CoA lyase (EC 4.1.3.4), which cleaves (S)-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA into acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate. The reaction is atom-balanced: HMG-CoA (C27H44N7O20P3S as the CoA thioester) yields acetyl-CoA plus acetoacetate (a free carboxylic acid). Stoichiometry is 1:1:1 and balances for carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur. This is the final step of ketogenesis in the mitochondria.

rxn10260.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PgsA) reaction with specific anteiso-C17:0 acyl chains. CDP-diacylglycerol reacts with sn-glycerol-3-phosphate to transfer the phosphatidyl group, releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylglycerophosphate. rxn03242.other_comments: This is the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase step of beta-oxidation, oxidizing (S)-3-hydroxydodecanoyl-CoA to 3-oxododecanoyl-CoA with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. rxn02277.other_comments: This is the dethiobiotin synthetase (BioD) reaction. rxn00166.other_comments: This is D-serine dehydratase/ammonia-lyase (EC 4.3.1.18), a PLP-dependent enzyme that deaminates D-serine. rxn01480.other_comments: This is 3-hydroxyisobutyrate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.31), which oxidizes 3-hydroxyisobutyrate to 2-methyl-3-oxopropanoate (methylmalonate semialdehyde) using NAD+ as electron acceptor. The reaction is balanced: 3-hydroxyisobutyrate (C4H7O3-) loses 2H (as hydride to NAD+ and a proton), giving the oxo product (C4H5O3-) plus NADH and H+. Atoms and charges balance. In vivo, this is part of the valine catabolism pathway and proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction toward methylmalonate semialdehyde.

rxn09199.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (PSD) reaction with ditetradec-7-enoyl (n-C14:1) acyl chains. rxn00851.other_comments: This is the D-alanine:D-alanine ligase (Ddl, EC 6.3.2.4) reaction. It condenses two D-alanine molecules to form D-alanyl-D-alanine (D-Ala-D-Ala), a key precursor in peptidoglycan biosynthesis. rxn01200.other_comments: This is the transketolase reaction (EC 2.2.1.1) of the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway. rxn00141.other_comments: This is the S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase (AHCY, EC 3.3.1.1) reaction. It hydrolyzes S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) into adenosine and L-homocysteine using water. rxn03075.other_comments: This is the thiazole kinase (ThiM, EC 2.7.1.50) reaction, which phosphorylates 4-methyl-5-(2-hydroxyethyl)thiazole (THZ) to 4-methyl-5-(2-phosphoethyl)thiazole (THZ-P) in the thiamine salvage/biosynthesis pathway. rxn08558.other_comments: This is the anaerobic glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GlpABC) reaction. rxn01241.other_comments: This is the dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3) reaction, EC 1.8.1.4. Dihydrolipoamide is oxidized to lipoamide with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Atoms and charge balance correctly.

rxn02003.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidoreductase interconversion between dTDP-L-rhamnose and dTDP-4-oxo-L-rhamnose (dTDP-4-dehydrorhamnose), coupled with NADP+/NADPH. rxn05332.other_comments: This is the beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase step (FabA/FabZ type) of fatty acid biosynthesis, dehydrating (3R)-3-hydroxypalmitoyl-ACP (C16) to trans-2-hexadecenoyl-ACP plus water. rxn00438.other_comments: This reaction represents thiamine phosphate kinase (EC 2.7.4.16), which phosphorylates thiamine monophosphate (TMP) to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, thiamine diphosphate) using ATP. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP transfers a phosphate group to thiamine phosphate yielding ADP and TPP. The H+ accounts for charge/proton balance in the transfer. In vivo this kinase-type phosphotransfer reaction proceeds predominantly in the forward (TPP-synthesizing) direction.

rxn00288.other_comments: This is the succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) reaction. Succinate is oxidized to fumarate while FAD is reduced to FADH2. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: succinate (C4H6O4) loses two hydrogens (2H, as 2H+ + 2e-) to form fumarate (C4H4O4), and FAD accepts them to become FADH2. In vivo, this reaction proceeds in the forward (oxidative) direction as part of the TCA cycle, coupled to the electron transport chain via the FAD/FADH2 cofactor bound to the enzyme. The enzyme transfers electrons to the quinone pool (ubiquinone), which makes the physiological reaction effectively forward-driven.

rxn08550.other_comments: This is a glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) reaction transferring a hexadec-9-enoyl (C16:1) group from acyl-ACP to glycerol-3-phosphate, yielding 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and free ACP. rxn05249.other_comments: This is a fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (ligase) reaction for a 15-carbon iso-branched fatty acid (fa3 = isopentadecanoate/isopentadecanoic acid). The stoichiometry is balanced and correct: ATP + CoA + fatty acid yields AMP + PPi + acyl-CoA. Although written as reversible, in vivo the reaction is driven forward by the subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making fatty acid activation effectively irreversible.

rxn00763.other_comments: This reaction is glycerol dehydrogenase (NAD+-dependent) oxidizing glycerol to D-glyceraldehyde, with NAD+ reduced to NADH. rxn00377.other_comments: This is S-formylglutathione hydrolase (EC 3.1.2.12), which hydrolyzes the thioester S-formylglutathione into glutathione (GSH) and formate. rxn01275.other_comments: This is gluconokinase (ATP:D-gluconate 6-phosphotransferase, EC 2.7.1.12), which phosphorylates D-gluconate (GLCN) using ATP to form 6-phospho-D-gluconate, ADP, and a proton. rxn02473.other_comments: This is the imidazoleglycerol-phosphate dehydratase (HisB) reaction in histidine biosynthesis. rxn08347.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 2,5-diketo-D-gluconate reductase (e.g., EC 1.1.1.346/1.1.1.274). rxn09069.other_comments: This is the PAPS reductase (CysH) reaction in assimilatory sulfate reduction. rxn01434.other_comments: This is argininosuccinate synthase (EC 6.3.4.5), which condenses citrulline and aspartate using ATP to form argininosuccinate, releasing AMP and PPi. rxn02345.other_comments: This is an epimerization reaction interconverting the (S) and (R) stereoisomers of 3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA. This step is relevant in fatty acid beta-oxidation, where the (S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA produced by some pathways must be converted to the (R) form (or vice versa) for further processing.

rxn00912.other_comments: This is the ketopantoate hydroxymethyltransferase (PanB) reaction. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced in atoms (C, H, O, N) and charge as written. In vivo it proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward pantothenate/CoA biosynthesis.

rxn00122.other_comments: This is FAD synthetase (FMN adenylyltransferase, EC 2.7.7.2), which transfers an adenylyl group from ATP to FMN, producing FAD and releasing pyrophosphate. rxn08294.other_comments: This is a diacylglycerol kinase reaction with didodecanoyl (di-C12:0) acyl chains. rxn03068.other_comments: This is ketol-acid reductoisomerase (KARI, EC 1.1.1.86) in the valine/isoleucine/leucine biosynthesis pathway. As an O2-consuming oxygenase reaction, it is physiologically irreversible.

rxn03061.other_comments: This is the 2-methylaconitate hydratase (aconitase-family) reaction in the methylcitrate cycle for propionate metabolism. rxn05344.other_comments: This is a fatty acid elongation condensation step (KAS / beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase type reaction). Carbon balance: C14 acyl + C3 malonyl moiety -> C16 3-oxoacyl product (3-oxohexadecanoyl, C16) plus CO2. The carbons and acyl-carrier proteins balance correctly. In vivo, the decarboxylative Claisen condensation is essentially irreversible due to CO2 release, driving the reaction forward.

rxn03241.other_comments: This is the enoyl-CoA hydratase (crotonase) reaction acting on the C14 fatty acyl-CoA. Stoichiometry is balanced: C35H60N7O18P3S on the hydroxyacyl-CoA side equals the trans-2-enoyl-CoA (C35H58N7O17P3S) plus H2O. Note the canonical fatty acid beta-oxidation enzyme acts on the (S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA stereoisomer, and in beta-oxidation flux runs toward hydration (enoyl-CoA + H2O -> 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA), but the enzyme is freely reversible.

rxn01521.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of dUMP (2'-deoxyuridine 5'-monophosphate) by a phosphohydrolase (nucleotidase), removing the phosphate group to yield deoxyuridine and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: dUMP + H2O yields deoxyuridine + Pi. Phosphomonoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the dephosphorylation direction as written.

errors: Incorrect directionality as written; physiologically the enzyme (dihydrofolate reductase, DHFR) reduces folate/dihydrofolate using NADPH, not oxidizes dihydrofolate to folate
