The named reaction (folate + NADPH -> dihydrofolate + NADP+) is the reverse of what is written
Proton (H+) balance: when written in the biological direction, H+ should be on the NADPH/substrate side
rxn01602.other_comments: This corresponds to dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR, EC 1.5.1.3). The biologically relevant reaction is folate + NADPH + H+ -> dihydrofolate + NADP+ (and dihydrofolate + NADPH + H+ -> tetrahydrofolate + NADP+). As written, the substrate/product roles are reversed: dihydrofolate is shown being oxidized to folate while NADP is reduced to NADPH, which is thermodynamically unfavorable in vivo. The atom stoichiometry between folate (C19H19N7O6) and dihydrofolate (C19H21N7O6) differs by 2H, consistent with the NADPH/H+ pair, so the equation is balanced; the issue is direction.

errors: Charge imbalance: the H+ on the left side is not balanced by any product; hydrolysis of a dipeptide does not consume or produce a net proton in this representation. The substrate Met-Ala (neutral peptide) + H2O yields zwitterionic L-Met + L-Ala without need for an extra H+. As written with an added H+, charge is not conserved.
rxn12636.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide methionyl-L-alanine (Met-Ala) by methionyl aminopeptidase, cleaving the N-terminal methionine to release free L-methionine and L-alanine. Peptide bond hydrolysis consumes one water.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass/charge balanced for the standard succinylarginine dihydrolase (AstB) reaction. The accepted AstB reaction is: N2-succinyl-L-arginine + 2 H2O + 2 H+ -> N2-succinyl-L-ornithine + CO2 + 2 NH4+. Whether this is unbalanced depends on protonation states: with NH3 as product, the 2 H+ on the substrate side are not consumed and charge does not balance. Atom balance: succinylarginine (C10H18N4O5) + 2 H2O gives C10H22N4O7 on substrate side; products succinylornithine (C9H16N2O5) + CO2 (CO2) + 2 NH3 (N2H6) sum to C10H22N4O7. Atoms balance, but the 2 H+ are extra and cause a charge imbalance (+2 on left unaccounted).
rxn02927.other_comments: This is the N-succinylarginine dihydrolase (AstB) step of the arginine succinyltransferase (AST) degradation pathway, converting N2-succinyl-L-arginine to N2-succinyl-L-ornithine, releasing 2 ammonia and CO2 (from the guanidino group hydrolysis). The reaction is hydrolytic and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the catabolic (forward) direction.

rxn02663.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of epsilon-caprolactone (2-oxepanone, a 7-membered cyclic ester/lactone) by 1,4-lactonase or caprolactone lactonohydrolase, opening the ring to yield 6-hydroxyhexanoate. Atom balance: 2-oxepanone is C6H10O2; adding H2O (H2O) gives C6H12O3, which equals 6-hydroxyhexanoate (C6H12O3) as the protonated acid, or C6H11O3- plus H+ as written. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge. Lactone hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable due to ring strain relief and is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn04786.other_comments: This is the diaminobutyrate aminotransferase (DABA AT, EctB-type) reaction. It transfers an amino group from L-glutamate to L-aspartate-4-semialdehyde (ASA), forming 2-oxoglutarate and L-2,4-diaminobutyrate. The reaction is atom and charge balanced: glutamate (C5H8NO4-/donor) plus aspartate semialdehyde yields 2-oxoglutarate and L-2,4-diaminobutyrate. Aminotransferase reactions are intrinsically reversible; in vivo, in the ectoine biosynthesis pathway, the net flux is toward DABA production.

rxn03394.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydroxylation step in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis, converting 2-octaprenylphenol to 2-octaprenyl-6-hydroxyphenol. It is a monooxygenase reaction: O2 is split, with one oxygen atom incorporated into the substrate as a hydroxyl group and the other reduced to water. NADPH serves as the electron donor (oxidized to NADP+). The stoichiometry balances: NADPH + O2 + H+ provides the reducing equivalents and oxygen, yielding H2O, NADP+, and the hydroxylated product. Note that in E. coli this step (UbiB/related) is more commonly described with NADH, but the NADPH-dependent version is chemically valid.

rxn00338.other_comments: This is L-aspartate oxidase (NadB, EC 1.4.3.16), the first step in NAD biosynthesis in many bacteria. It oxidizes L-aspartate to iminoaspartate (2-iminosuccinate). The reaction is balanced: L-aspartate (C4H6NO4-) loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) to form iminoaspartate (C4H4NO4-), and O2 accepts these to form H2O2. Atoms and charge balance: C4, N1, O6 on each side, and the charge is consistent. While NadB can use either O2 or fumarate as electron acceptor (functioning aerobically or anaerobically), the oxygen-dependent reaction proceeds in the direction of aspartate oxidation in vivo.

rxn02373.other_comments: This is glutamate-5-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (also called N-acetyl-gamma-glutamyl-phosphate reductase analog, EC 1.2.1.41), the second step of proline biosynthesis from glutamate. The reaction is written in the oxidation direction: L-glutamate-5-semialdehyde + NADP+ + Pi -> L-glutamyl-5-phosphate + NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry and atom/charge balance are correct. In vivo, the biosynthetic flux proceeds in the reverse direction as written here, namely reduction of L-glutamyl-5-phosphate to L-glutamate-5-semialdehyde with consumption of NADPH and release of phosphate.

errors: Stoichiometry is unbalanced: the substrate 3-hydroxy-3-(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)propionyl-CoA contains the vanillin aryl moiety plus a CoA-thioester portion. A retro-aldol-type cleavage would yield vanillin (4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde) plus acetyl-CoA, but the atom count must be verified. The C3-hydroxy propionyl-CoA (Ar-CH(OH)-CH2-CO-SCoA) cleaved between C-aryl and the rest gives Ar-CHO (vanillin) and CH2=CO... but to form acetyl-CoA (CH3-CO-SCoA) two hydrogens must be accounted for. As written, the reaction is missing balance of H atoms; the lyase aldol cleavage should be balanced but no explicit cofactor/water shown.
rxn04025.other_comments: This is the retro-aldol (lyase) cleavage step in vanillin/ferulate degradation, where 3-hydroxy-3-(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)propionyl-CoA (the hydrated/HHM-CoA intermediate) is split into vanillin and acetyl-CoA, catalyzed by an HCHL-type lyase. Aldol lyases are generally reversible in vitro; in vivo the degradative direction (toward vanillin + acetyl-CoA) is typically favored.

rxn08667.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of P1,P4-bis(5'-guanosyl) tetraphosphate (Gp4G, GppppG) by a symmetrically cleaving Gp4G hydrolase. The substrate has 4 phosphates bridging two guanosines; symmetrical hydrolysis of the central phosphoanhydride bond by water yields two GDP molecules. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: GppppG (C20H25N10O21P4) + H2O yields 2 GDP (each C10H13N5O11P2). Atom counts balance correctly. Hydrolysis of a high-energy phosphoanhydride bond is strongly exergonic and physiologically irreversible.

errors: Charge and proton imbalance: the H+ on the left side is not needed for this phosphotransfer reaction; standard formulation is ATP + UMP <=> ADP + UDP, which is already mass and charge balanced. Including H+ introduces a charge imbalance.
rxn00119.other_comments: This is the UMP kinase (adenylate-kinase-like) phosphotransfer reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to UMP, yielding ADP and UDP. Atom balance for P, C, N is fine (ATP=3P, UMP=1P -> ADP=2P, UDP=2P), but the extra H+ unbalances charge.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: combining two L-glutamate to form 2-oxoglutarate plus L-glutamine does not balance. Correct glutamate synthase (GOGAT) reaction is L-glutamine + 2-oxoglutarate + NADPH + H+ -> 2 L-glutamate + NADP+. The reaction as written has the substrates and products reversed in terms of which species are consumed/produced.

The enzyme name 'L-Glutamate:NADP+ oxidoreductase (transaminating)' describes glutamate synthase, but the written direction is incorrect; it should consume NADPH, glutamine, and 2-oxoglutarate to produce two glutamate.
rxn00085.other_comments: This is glutamate synthase (NADPH-dependent GOGAT, EC 1.4.1.13). The physiologically correct/biosynthetic direction is: L-glutamine + 2-oxoglutarate + NADPH + H+ -> 2 L-glutamate + NADP+. As written, the reaction proceeds in the wrong direction and the proton placement is inconsistent with NADPH consumption.

rxn01893.other_comments: This reaction represents 2-oxopent-4-enoate (also called 2-keto-4-pentenoate) hydratase (EC 4.2.1.80), which adds water across the C=C double bond of 2-oxopent-4-enoate to form 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate (4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate). This is part of the meta-cleavage pathway for aromatic compound degradation (e.g., catechol/protocatechuate degradation). The stoichiometry is balanced: addition of H2O to the substrate yields the hydroxylated product. In vivo, in the context of degradation pathways, the reaction proceeds in the hydration direction toward 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate, which is subsequently cleaved by an aldolase. The enzyme reaction is technically reversible, but the pathway flux drives it forward.

errors: Charge imbalance: ATP (-4) + H2O (0) = -4 on left; AMP (-2) + PPi (-3) + 2 H+ (+2) = -3 on right. The reaction is not charge balanced. Correct form releases only 1 H+: ATP + H2O -> AMP + PPi + H+, giving -4 = -4.
rxn00063.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of ATP to AMP and inorganic pyrophosphate (apyrase/ATP diphosphohydrolase type activity). Mass balance for atoms is correct (water cleaves the alpha-beta phosphoanhydride bond), but the proton stoichiometry causes a charge imbalance at physiological pH.

errors: Stoichiometric/chemical inconsistency: conversion of acrylate (CH2=CH-COO-) to acrylamide (CH2=CH-CONH2) is an amidation, but combining NH3 with acrylate to give acrylamide plus water requires the carboxylate, not the free acid; mass balance only works if the acid form (CH2=CH-COOH) is used. With acrylate as written and NH3, the products NH3+CH2=CHCOO- -> CH2=CHCONH2 + OH- (not H2O). The atom balance as written (acrylate vs acrylamide + water) is essentially that of acid + ammonia -> amide + water, so charge/protonation state should be specified.

This reaction as drawn (direct condensation of ammonia with carboxylate to amide releasing water) is thermodynamically unfavorable and not the physiological route; amidation of carboxylic acids by NH3 is not spontaneous in vivo without ATP activation.
rxn03839.other_comments: The reaction depicts amidation of acrylate by ammonia to form acrylamide and water. Biologically, the relevant enzyme (amidase/nitrilase family) typically hydrolyzes acrylamide to acrylate + ammonia, i.e., the reverse direction is favored. Direct condensation of a carboxylate with NH3 to an amide plus water is endergonic and would not proceed forward without energy input.

rxn01466.other_comments: This is farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FPPS) catalyzing the head-to-tail condensation of geranyl diphosphate (C10) with isopentenyl diphosphate (C5, IPP) to yield farnesyl diphosphate (C15), releasing pyrophosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: C10+C5 = C15, with PPi released and a proton produced upon formation of the new bond. The reaction is strongly exergonic due to PPi release and proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn05233.other_comments: This is the ribonucleotide reductase reaction (class I/II type using thioredoxin) reducing GDP to dGDP. The 2'-OH of the ribose is replaced by H, and the reducing equivalents come from reduced thioredoxin (trdrd), which becomes oxidized thioredoxin (trdox). The stoichiometry is balanced: GDP + H+ + reduced thioredoxin -> H2O + dGDP + oxidized thioredoxin. The proton and water account for the removal of the 2'-OH oxygen as water. In vivo this reaction proceeds in the reductive (forward) direction toward deoxyribonucleotide synthesis for DNA replication.

rxn04453.other_comments: This is the 5-hydroxyisourate hydrolase (HIU hydrolase, EC 3.5.2.17) reaction in the purine degradation/urate oxidation pathway. 5-hydroxyisourate (HIU) is hydrolyzed by addition of water to yield 2-oxo-4-hydroxy-4-carboxy-5-ureidoimidazoline (OHCU), here named 5-hydroxy-2-oxo-4-ureido-2,5-dihydro-1H-imidazole-5-carboxylate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced (water adds across a ring bond, releasing a proton). Although HIU can decay nonenzymatically to allantoin, the enzyme accelerates and directs hydrolysis to the specific OHCU product, which is then decarboxylated stereospecifically by OHCU decarboxylase.

errors: Proton (H+) stoichiometry is incorrect; the acyl transfer from acyl-ACP to glycerol-3-phosphate does not produce or consume 2 protons. The reaction is charge- and mass-unbalanced as written. No net protons should be released for this esterification at the relevant ionization states.
rxn08549.other_comments: This is the glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) reaction, transferring a palmitoyl (C16:0) group from palmitoyl-ACP to the sn-1 position of glycerol-3-phosphate, yielding 1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) and free ACP. The acyl-ACP thioester is high-energy, driving the reaction toward product (lysophosphatidic acid) formation in vivo.

rxn05447.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2 double bond of 8-methyl-non-2-enoyl-ACP to the saturated 8-methyl-nonanoyl-ACP using NADH as the electron donor. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the C=C double bond is reduced by two electrons and two hydrogens (one from NADH as hydride, one from H+), converting NADH + H+ to NAD+. The named enzyme uses NAD+/NADH as cofactor (A-specific hydride transfer). In vivo, enoyl-ACP reductase strongly favors the reductive (saturating) direction during fatty acid elongation, consuming NADH.

errors: Vitamin B12 appears on both substrate and product sides with identical compartment designation, which is incorrect for a transport reaction; the transported metabolite should differ by compartment (e.g., Vitamin B12[e] -> Vitamin B12[c]) to represent translocation
rxn05187.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter that uses ATP hydrolysis to import Vitamin B12. The ATP/ADP/Phosphate/H+ stoichiometry is balanced and correct for ATP hydrolysis. However, as written the Vitamin B12 is not assigned distinct compartments, so the reaction does not actually represent transport (no net movement). ABC importers are effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo due to ATP hydrolysis driving uptake.

rxn00974.other_comments: This is the aconitase-catalyzed dehydration of citrate to cis-aconitate, releasing water. The reaction is part of the citrate-isocitrate interconversion in the TCA cycle. Stoichiometry is balanced: citrate (C6H5O7^3-) yields cis-aconitate (C6H3O6^3-) plus H2O. Mass and charge are conserved. Aconitase is a classic reversible enzyme, and in vivo flux direction depends on the cellular state, though net TCA cycle flux proceeds toward isocitrate.

rxn02008.other_comments: This is the MurD reaction (UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine:D-glutamate ligase, EC 6.3.2.9), which adds D-glutamate to UDP-MurNAc-L-Ala in peptidoglycan biosynthesis. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi, releasing a proton, while the amide bond between the carboxyl of L-Ala and the amino group of D-Glu is formed. Mass and charge balance check out for the standard ligase mechanism.

rxn03409.other_comments: This reaction represents the ATP-dependent amidation of the D-glutamate residue to D-glutamine (D-iso-glutamine) on the lipid II-like peptidoglycan precursor (undecaprenyl-diphospho-MurNAc-GlcNAc-pentapeptide). The enzyme is an amidotransferase/amidoligase (similar to MurT/GatD or AsnB-type activity). Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + NH3 are consumed to convert the glutamyl carboxyl to a glutaminyl amide, releasing ADP + Pi + H+. The product is correctly described as containing L-alanyl-D-glutaminyl-meso-DAP-D-alanyl-D-alanine, consistent with amidation of the substrate's D-glutamyl residue.

rxn01171.other_comments: This reaction represents aldose 1-epimerase (mutarotase) activity interconverting the anomeric forms of D-glucose. The substrate 'D-Glucose' likely denotes alpha-D-glucose, which is interconverted with beta-D-glucose. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (a single isomerization between anomers, same molecular formula C6H12O6). As an epimerization/anomerization, it is freely reversible and equilibrates between alpha and beta forms.

rxn00605.other_comments: This is the trehalose-6-phosphate synthase (OtsA, TPS) reaction. UDP-glucose donates a glucosyl group to glucose-6-phosphate, forming trehalose-6-phosphate and UDP plus an H+ (a proton is released that could be added for full charge balance). Atom balance: UDP-glucose (C15H22N2O17P2 as charged species) + glucose-6-phosphate yields UDP + trehalose-6-phosphate; carbons (15+6=21=15+6) and the glucosyl transfer are consistent. In vivo this reaction is essentially irreversible in the synthetic direction driven by hydrolysis of the glycosidic bond energy.

rxn02288.other_comments: This is the uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) reaction in heme biosynthesis. Uroporphyrinogen III (with 4 acetate side chains) undergoes sequential decarboxylation of the four acetate groups to yield coproporphyrinogen III (with 4 methyl groups) plus 4 CO2. The stoichiometry is mass and charge balanced: each of the four acetate side chains (-CH2-COOH) loses CO2, and the 4 H+ consumed balance the protons. UROD is metal- and cofactor-independent. The reaction is physiologically driven in the decarboxylation (forward) direction.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is incorrect; the decarboxylation of phosphatidylserine to phosphatidylethanolamine consumes 1 H+, not 2 H+. Balanced reaction: H+ + phosphatidylserine -> CO2 + phosphatidylethanolamine
rxn09203.other_comments: This is phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (PSD), which converts phosphatidylserine to phosphatidylethanolamine with release of CO2. The acyl chains are dioctadecenoyl (di-C18:1, oleoyl/vaccenoyl). The carbon and acyl backbone balance, but the proton count is wrong: serine head group (-CH2-CH(NH3+)-COO-) loses CO2 to form ethanolamine (-CH2-CH2-NH3+), which requires only one proton.

rxn01225.other_comments: This is guanine deaminase (guanine aminohydrolase, EC 3.5.4.3), which hydrolytically deaminates guanine to xanthine (XAN) with release of ammonia. The reaction is: H2O + Guanine -> NH3 + Xanthine. The stoichiometry is balanced if the H+ is considered carefully: guanine (C5H5N5O) + H2O -> xanthine (C5H4N4O2) + NH3. Checking atoms: C5 = C5, left H = 5+2 = 7 plus H+ = 8, right H = 4 (xanthine) + 3 (NH3) = 7, so the H+ on the left side leaves a 1-proton imbalance. N: left 5, right 4+1 = 5 (balanced). O: left 1+1 = 2, right 2 (balanced). The extra H+ on the substrate side creates a charge/mass imbalance; the standard reaction is H2O + Guanine -> Xanthine + NH3 without the additional H+, or it should appear as a product depending on protonation states.

errors: Nomenclature inconsistency: the substrate is named with '6-carboxy-L-lysyl' while the enzyme name and product use 'meso-2,6-diaminopimeloyl'; 6-carboxy-L-lysine is meso-DAP, so these refer to the same residue but the naming should be consistent
Minor: stoichiometry is balanced as written (transfer of phospho-MurNAc-pentapeptide from UDP to undecaprenyl phosphate, releasing UMP)
rxn03904.other_comments: This is the MraY reaction (phospho-N-acetylmuramoyl-pentapeptide-transferase), forming lipid I. Undecaprenyl phosphate attacks UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide, releasing UMP and producing undecaprenyl-diphospho-MurNAc-pentapeptide (lipid I). The atom balance is essentially correct; the phosphomuramyl-pentapeptide moiety plus a phosphate are transferred to undecaprenyl phosphate, giving the diphosphate linkage and releasing UMP.

rxn10199.other_comments: This represents the transglycosylation step of peptidoglycan polymerization. Lipid II (undecaprenyl-diphospho-MurNAc-GlcNAc-pentapeptide with the meso-DAP-containing stem peptide typical of Gram-negative/Bacillus-type peptidoglycan) is added to the growing glycan chain, releasing undecaprenyl (bactoprenyl) diphosphate. The growing polymer goes from n-1 to n subunits, consistent with addition of one disaccharide-peptide unit. Stoichiometry is balanced: one lipid II donor plus polymer(n-1) yields polymer(n) plus the released lipid carrier diphosphate.

rxn08015.other_comments: This is an acyl-ACP synthetase (fatty acyl-ACP ligase) reaction for myristoleate (C14:1). It activates the free fatty acid tetradecenoate using ATP, forming an acyl-ACP thioester with release of AMP and pyrophosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides AMP + PPi, the carboxylate condenses with the ACP thiol, and 2 H+ are released, consistent with the charge balance (ATP loses both gamma and beta phosphates as PPi). The reaction is typically driven forward in vivo by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi.

rxn00409.other_comments: This is the nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDPK) reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to CDP, yielding ADP and CTP. The reaction is balanced: ATP (C10H12N5O13P3) + CDP (C9H12N3O11P2) gives ADP (C10H12N5O10P2) + CTP (C9H12N3O14P3). Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn01107.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of D-glucono-1,5-lactone (gluconolactone) to D-gluconate (GLCN). The reaction consumes water and produces gluconate plus a proton (from the carboxylic acid group). Stoichiometry is balanced: gluconolactone (C6H10O6) + H2O (H2O) yields gluconate (C6H11O7-) + H+, balancing carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge. In vivo, lactonase-catalyzed lactone ring opening is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible, proceeding in the forward (hydrolysis) direction.

rxn00598.other_comments: This is the beta-ketothiolase (3-oxoadipyl-CoA thiolase) reaction in aromatic compound degradation (e.g., the beta-ketoadipate pathway). Acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA condense to form 3-oxoadipyl-CoA, releasing one CoA. The reaction is balanced: combining acetyl-CoA (C2 acyl) and succinyl-CoA (C4 acyl) yields the C6 3-oxoadipyl-CoA plus free CoA. Atoms and CoA moieties balance correctly. Physiologically the thiolytic cleavage direction is favored, so in the degradative pathway the reaction runs in reverse (thiolysis of 3-oxoadipyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA), but as written for biosynthetic condensation it proceeds left-to-right; in vivo the net flux in the beta-ketoadipate pathway is toward succinyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA. Given the written direction (synthesis of 3-oxoadipyl-CoA), the condensation is thermodynamically unfavorable.

rxn08842.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase L2 reaction hydrolyzing the acyl ester bond of 2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (with a C16:1 hexadec-9-enoyl group) to yield glycerophosphoethanolamine and the free fatty acid (hexadecenoate). Mass and charge balance: the lysophospholipid carries one acyl ester; hydrolysis with H2O releases the carboxylic acid (deprotonated as hexadecenoate) plus a proton (H+), and the deacylated backbone glycerophosphoethanolamine. Stoichiometry is balanced. Hydrolysis of an ester bond is strongly thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible.

rxn02518.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of dITP (2'-deoxyinosine-5'-triphosphate) to dIMP plus pyrophosphate, catalyzed by an ITPase/dITP pyrophosphohydrolase (e.g., RdgB/ITPA family). Stoichiometry is balanced: dITP has 3 phosphates, removal of PPi (2 phosphates) leaves dIMP (1 phosphate). Mass and charge balance check out with H2O consumed and 2 H+ released. Such hydrolytic phosphatase/pyrophosphohydrolase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to release of PPi and water-driven hydrolysis.

rxn01258.other_comments: This is the isochorismate synthase (also called chorismate mutase/isochorismate hydroxymutase, e.g. EntC, MenF, PchA) reaction, EC 5.4.4.2. It is an isomerization that converts chorismate to isochorismate by transferring the hydroxyl group. The reaction is intramolecular (a 1,5 shift of the hydroxyl with a transient water exchange), so it is mass- and charge-balanced with no additional substrates or products needed. Both metabolites are C10H8O6 (2-) at physiological pH. The enzyme is Mg2+-dependent. In vivo it typically proceeds toward isochorismate to feed siderophore (enterobactin), menaquinone, or salicylate biosynthesis, but the isomerization itself is thermodynamically near-equilibrium and is generally treated as reversible.

errors: Atom and charge balance cannot be verified because mRNA is a lumped biomass-type macromolecule without a defined formula

The sum of NTP coefficients (0.7706 + 0.9496 + 0.5853 + 0.6331 = 2.9386) equals the PPi coefficient, which is consistent with one PPi released per nucleotide incorporated; however the mass/charge balance for the polymerized mRNA cannot be confirmed without its composition
rxn05295.other_comments: This is a lumped biomass/macromolecular synthesis reaction (typical of genome-scale metabolic models) representing mRNA polymerization from the four ribonucleotide triphosphates (ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP) with release of pyrophosphate. The fractional coefficients reflect average nucleotide composition normalized so that the total NTPs sum to ~2.9386, matching the PPi stoichiometry. Note that PPi released per nucleotide should be 1:1, so the sum of NTPs should equal PPi, which it does.

errors: Substrate mismatch: the enzyme name indicates pantothenate as the phosphoryl acceptor (pantothenate kinase, EC 2.7.1.33), but the reaction uses pantetheine as substrate
If the intended reaction is pantetheine kinase (EC 2.7.1.34), the enzyme name is incorrect; if pantothenate kinase is intended, the substrate/product should be pantothenate/4'-phosphopantothenate
rxn02128.other_comments: This is written as a kinase reaction phosphorylating pantetheine to phosphopantetheine using ATP, yielding ADP and a proton. Stoichiometrically the reaction as written (ATP + pantetheine -> ADP + H+ + phosphopantetheine) is balanced for atoms and charge. However, the named enzyme (ATP:pantothenate 4'-phosphotransferase = pantothenate kinase) does not match the listed substrate (pantetheine). The pantetheine-phosphorylating activity corresponds to pantetheine kinase (EC 2.7.1.34).

rxn05621.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction for methanesulfonate, coupling ATP hydrolysis (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to substrate import. The methanesulfonate appears on both sides representing the same metabolite in different compartments (e.g., periplasm/extracellular and cytoplasm); in a properly compartmentalized model these should carry different compartment tags but the species and stoichiometry are otherwise balanced. ATP hydrolysis drives the transport, making it physiologically irreversible (import direction).

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: hydrolysis of the diphosphate to monophosphate + phosphate releases only 1 H+ at physiological pH, not 2 H+. Bactoprenyl diphosphate (C55-PP, charge -3) + H2O -> undecaprenyl phosphate (C55-P, charge -2) + phosphate (HPO4 2-, charge -2) + 1 H+ balances charge; as written with 2 H+ the equation is charge-unbalanced by +1 on the product side.
rxn03901.other_comments: This is undecaprenyl diphosphate (bactoprenyl/C55-PP) phosphohydrolase, which hydrolyzes one terminal phosphoanhydride bond of the lipid carrier to yield undecaprenyl monophosphate (the active lipid carrier) plus inorganic phosphate. Hydrolysis of a phosphoanhydride bond is thermodynamically strongly favorable and physiologically unidirectional in the forward direction.

rxn00193.other_comments: This is the glutamate racemase (MurI, EC 5.1.1.3) reaction, interconverting L-glutamate and D-glutamate. As a racemase, it is a cofactor-independent isomerization that is freely reversible and mass/charge balanced (both stereoisomers share the molecular formula C5H8NO4-). D-glutamate produced is important for bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan biosynthesis.

errors: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase uses FAD as the electron acceptor, not NAD. The correct cofactors are FAD/FADH2, producing trans-2-dodecenoyl-CoA. Using NAD/NADH here is incorrect.
Charge/proton balance is inconsistent with the wrong cofactor; the FAD-dependent reaction does not release a free H+ in the same manner.
rxn10013.other_comments: This represents the first oxidation step of fatty acid beta-oxidation, dehydrogenating lauroyl-CoA (dodecanoyl-CoA) to (2E)-dodecenoyl-CoA. In vivo this proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction, but it is physiologically catalyzed by an FAD-dependent acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, with electrons passed to ETF, not by an NAD-dependent enzyme.

rxn00946.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction (first step of fatty acid beta-oxidation). Palmitoyl-CoA is oxidized to trans-2-hexadecenoyl-CoA (2E-hexadecenoyl-CoA) with FAD reduced to FADH2. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: C, H, O, N, P, and S atoms balance, and a C-C single bond is converted to a trans double bond with two H atoms transferred to FAD. The enzyme name 'Palmitoyl-CoA:oxygen 2-oxidoreductase' implies O2 as acceptor, but in vivo the immediate electron acceptor is FAD (electrons subsequently pass to ETF and the respiratory chain), so the written acceptor (FAD/FADH2) is correct for the dehydrogenase step. In vivo this beta-oxidation step proceeds in the forward direction toward the enoyl-CoA.

errors: Charge imbalance: H+ on the left side is not balanced. AMP(2-) + H+ + triphosphate(5-) gives net charge -6 on left; ADP(3-) + PPi(3-) gives net charge -6 on right, so the H+ creates a charge mismatch of +1. The H+ should not be present for charge balance.

Atom balance check: AMP + triphosphate (P3O10) vs ADP + PPi (P2O7). Phosphorus: AMP has 1 P, triphosphate has 3 P (total 4 P on left); ADP has 2 P, PPi has 2 P (total 4 P on right) - P balances. Oxygen and phosphate distribution are consistent with phosphoryl transfer, but the proton inclusion disrupts the charge balance.
rxn10052.other_comments: This is an adenylate kinase-type reaction using inorganic triphosphate as the phosphoryl donor: a terminal phosphate from triphosphate (PPPi) is transferred to AMP, producing ADP and releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). Kinase/phosphotransfer reactions of this type are generally near-equilibrium and reversible in vivo. The main issue is the unbalanced H+.

rxn02517.other_comments: This reaction represents a nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDK)-type phosphotransfer, where ATP donates a gamma-phosphate to dIDP (deoxyinosine diphosphate), yielding ADP and dITP (deoxyinosine triphosphate). The reaction is balanced: ATP + dIDP -> ADP + dITP, with conserved phosphates, ribose/deoxyribose moieties, and bases. NDK enzymes are broad-specificity and typically catalyze such phosphate exchanges. Although the enzyme itself is mechanistically reversible (ping-pong via phosphohistidine intermediate), in vivo the net flux generally favors triphosphate formation due to high ATP/ADP ratios.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (H+ + Uracil) on both sides, with no net transformation or compartmental distinction specified
For a permease/transport reaction, the substrates should be distinguished by compartment (e.g., H+[e] + Uracil[e] <=> H+[c] + Uracil[c]) to represent symport across the membrane
rxn05197.other_comments: This is a uracil permease (symporter) reaction coupling proton transport with uracil uptake. As written, it lacks compartment annotations, making it appear as a null reaction (same species on both sides). The intended biology is a proton-coupled uracil symport across the cell membrane. With proper compartment tags it represents uracil import driven by the proton motive force, which is typically directional toward uptake into the cytoplasm in vivo, though transporters can be modeled as reversible.

rxn03251.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase step of fatty acid beta-oxidation, converting hexanoyl-CoA to trans-2-hexenoyl-CoA with reduction of FAD to FADH2. The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: 2 hydrogens are removed from the C2-C3 positions of the acyl chain and transferred to FAD. In vivo, the enzyme-bound FADH2 is reoxidized via electron transfer flavoprotein, driving the reaction in the dehydrogenation (forward) direction.

errors: The substrate should be CO2 rather than H2CO3 (carbonic acid) in the canonical N5-CAIR synthetase reaction; if H2CO3 is used, the proton balance is off. With CO2 as substrate (ATP + CO2 + AIR -> ADP + Pi + N5-CAIR + H+), only 1 H+ is produced, not 2.
rxn05114.other_comments: This is the N5-carboxyaminoimidazole ribonucleotide (N5-CAIR) synthetase reaction (PurK), where AIR is carboxylated using ATP-driven phosphorylation/dehydration of bicarbonate to form N5-CAIR. The product named '5-phosphoribosyl-5-carboxyaminoimidazole' is N5-CAIR. The mass/charge balance depends on whether the carbon source is written as CO2, HCO3-, or H2CO3, which affects the number of protons.

errors: L-Glutamine appears on both sides of the equation with no net transport indicated; for an ABC importer reaction the substrate should be shown as translocated (e.g., L-Glutamine[external] on the left and L-Glutamine[cytoplasm] on the right). As written, the amino acid cancels out, leaving only ATP hydrolysis with no actual import.
Compartment labels are missing, which are essential to represent an importer reaction correctly.
rxn05155.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter reaction coupling ATP hydrolysis to the import of L-glutamine (a polar amino acid). The chemistry of ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) is balanced, but the transport aspect is not represented because glutamine appears identically on both sides without compartmentalization.

errors: Hydrogen imbalance: oxidation of L-proline to 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate releases 2 electrons and effectively 1 proton net, but the written reaction shows 2 H+ on the product side which does not balance. The correct balance is NAD+ + L-proline <=> NADH + H+ + 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate, releasing only 1 H+.
Charge imbalance arising from the incorrect proton count.
rxn00929.other_comments: This represents proline dehydrogenase / proline oxidase chemistry (EC 1.5.1.2 is actually pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase using NAD(P)H). The reaction oxidizes the secondary amine of L-proline to form the cyclic imine 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The redox conversion is sound, but the stated proton stoichiometry (2 H+) is incorrect; one proton is the standard balance.

errors: The reaction name describes a full fatty acid elongation cycle (a C-acyltransferase with decarboxylation, oxoacyl-reduction, and enoyl-reduction), but the written reaction only depicts a single oxidation/dehydrogenation step. The name and the equation are inconsistent.

The written equation is itself an oxidation (acyl-ACP to enoyl-ACP) using NAD, which is the reverse direction of the enoyl-ACP reductase step normally found in fatty acid biosynthesis. In FAS, enoyl-ACP is reduced to acyl-ACP using NADPH/NADH, not the oxidation shown.

Stoichiometry of the written equation is balanced for the simple dehydrogenation (loss of 2 H as NADH + H+), but it does not match the named multi-step reaction which would require malonyl-CoA, release of CO2 and CoA, and produce a C8 product.
rxn05326.other_comments: The input has a mismatch: the enzyme name implies a complete two-carbon elongation cycle (condensation with malonyl-CoA, decarboxylation, then reduction steps yielding 3-oxo, 3-hydroxy, enoyl, and saturated acyl-ACP), whereas the equation given is just the oxidation of hexanoyl-ACP to trans-2-hexenoyl-ACP with NAD. As written, this oxidative direction is not favored in vivo; the physiological flux in fatty acid synthesis runs from enoyl-ACP toward saturated acyl-ACP.

rxn05433.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase type reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2-enoyl double bond of 4-methyl-trans-hex-2-enoyl-ACP to give the saturated 4-methyl-hexanoyl-ACP, using NADH + H+ as the reductant and producing NAD+. The atoms and electrons balance: addition of 2 H (one from NADH hydride, one from H+) across the C2-C3 double bond. Stoichiometry is correct. NAD should formally be written as NAD+ for charge balance, but this is a common notation convention. In vivo, enoyl reductase steps in fatty acid/branched-chain elongation strongly favor the reductive (forward) direction.

rxn02166.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of 4-nitrophenyl phosphate (a common chromogenic substrate for phosphatase assays) into inorganic phosphate and 4-nitrophenol (PNP). The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O cleaves the phosphoester bond, yielding one phosphate and one 4-nitrophenol. Phosphate hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically strongly favored and physiologically irreversible.

errors: Proton (H+) stoichiometry is incorrect: hydrolysis of one ester bond by water yields one carboxylate (hexadecenoate) and the free hydroxyl on glycerol-3-phosphate; only one proton is released upon ionization of the fatty acid carboxyl group at physiological pH, not 2.0 H+. The mass/charge balance should produce 1 H+, not 2.
rxn08800.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase/acylhydrolase reaction: a monoacyl-glycerophosphate (1-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, C16:1) is hydrolyzed by water to release the free fatty acid (hexadec-9-enoate) and glycerol-3-phosphate. Hydrolytic ester cleavage is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so direction is forward as written.

rxn00256.other_comments: This is citrate synthase (EC 2.3.3.1) written in the reverse (citrate cleavage) direction. The forward physiological reaction is: Acetyl-CoA + Oxaloacetate + H2O -> Citrate + CoA + H+. The stoichiometry is balanced for atoms and charge. In vivo, citrate synthase strongly favors citrate formation (highly exergonic due to thioester hydrolysis), so as written here the reaction would proceed in reverse (right to left, i.e., toward Citrate consumption is NOT favored). The biologically favored direction is toward citrate synthesis.

rxn00342.other_comments: This is the asparaginase reaction (EC 3.5.1.1), hydrolyzing L-asparagine to L-aspartate and ammonia. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: H2O + L-asparagine (C4H8N2O3) yields L-aspartate (C4H6NO4 as the anion, or C4H7NO4 neutral) plus NH3. Mass and charge balance hold when proper protonation states are considered. As a hydrolysis reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn08335.other_comments: This is dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH, class 2), oxidizing (S)-dihydroorotate to orotate while reducing ubiquinone-8 to ubiquinol-8. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: dihydroorotate loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) which are transferred to ubiquinone-8 to form ubiquinol-8. In vivo, this is the fourth step of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis and proceeds in the forward direction, coupling orotate formation to the respiratory chain via ubiquinone.

errors: Oxygen is not balanced: the forward direction (reduction of 3-aminopropanal to beta-alanine would require addition of an oxygen, but beta-alanine has one more oxygen atom than 3-aminopropanal; the reaction as written has H2O on the product side but no compensating oxygen source, and the oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid requires water as a reactant, not a product)

The reaction as written is unbalanced: oxidation of 3-aminopropanal (an aldehyde) to beta-alanine (a carboxylic acid) should consume H2O and NAD+, producing NADH + H+; the cofactor usage is reversed relative to the listed direction
Stoichiometry/charge inconsistency: an aldehyde-to-acid oxidation produces one NADH and one H+, and consumes one H2O, but here H2O appears as a product and 2 H+ are on the reactant side
rxn00653.other_comments: The enzyme is named 3-aminopropanal:NAD+ oxidoreductase, implying the physiological reaction is oxidation of 3-aminopropanal to beta-alanine using NAD+ as electron acceptor (requiring H2O). As written, the equation has the oxidation occurring in the reverse direction (NADH reducing the carboxylic acid beta-alanine back to the aldehyde), which is thermodynamically unfavorable and inconsistent with the enzyme name. The correct balanced reaction is: 3-aminopropanal + NAD+ + H2O -> beta-alanine + NADH + H+.

rxn03004.other_comments: This is the GAR transformylase (PurN) reaction in de novo purine biosynthesis. 10-Formyltetrahydrofolate transfers its formyl group to glycinamide ribonucleotide (GAR) producing N-formyl-GAR (FGAR) and tetrahydrofolate, releasing a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced for carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and charge: the formyl group (CHO) is transferred from 10-formyl-THF to the amine of GAR, leaving THF, and one H+ is released consistent with the transfer. Atoms and charge balance.

rxn00138.other_comments: This is NAD+ synthetase (EC 6.3.1.5), catalyzing the ATP-dependent amidation of deamido-NAD+ (nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide) using ammonia to form NAD+, releasing AMP and PPi. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: ATP + NH3 + deamido-NAD -> NAD + PPi + AMP + 2 H+. The atoms and charges balance, with two protons released (one from the carboxyl/amide conversion and the ligase mechanism). In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making it essentially irreversible.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is incorrect; phosphatidylserine decarboxylase consumes 1 H+ (not 2) along with the substrate to yield CO2 and phosphatidylethanolamine. The balanced reaction is: H+ + phosphatidylserine -> CO2 + phosphatidylethanolamine.
rxn10232.other_comments: This represents phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (PSD) acting on a phosphatidylserine species with two isoheptadecanoyl (iso-C17:0) acyl chains, decarboxylating the serine head group to form phosphatidylethanolamine. The decarboxylation releases CO2 and is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn00347.other_comments: This is the aspartase (aspartate ammonia-lyase, EC 4.3.1.1) reaction. L-Aspartate is deaminated to fumarate plus ammonia. The reaction is balanced: L-aspartate (C4H7NO4) yields fumarate (C4H4O4) plus NH3 (NH3). Atoms balance (C4, H7, N1, O4 on both sides). The enzyme is reversible in vitro, though physiologically the deamination direction (toward fumarate + NH3) is typically favored; the reverse amination can also occur depending on substrate concentrations. Note that protonation states may be written variously (NH4+ vs NH3).

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the addition of a free H+ on the substrate side is not justified for an acyl transfer reaction; this acyltransferase reaction (LpxA) should be balanced without an extra H+
Stoichiometric ambiguity: HMA (3-hydroxymyristoyl-ACP) as written should be (R)-3-hydroxymyristoyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] to match the enzyme name and product
rxn06729.other_comments: This is the LpxA reaction, the first step of lipid A biosynthesis: transfer of a (R)-3-hydroxymyristoyl (beta-hydroxymyristoyl) group from acyl-ACP to the 3-OH of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine, releasing holo-ACP. The reaction is thermodynamically unfavorable and known to be reversible/near-equilibrium in vitro, pulled forward in vivo by the subsequent LpxC deacetylation step.

rxn02167.other_comments: This is the enoyl-CoA hydratase (crotonase) reaction acting on a C4 substrate. (S)-3-Hydroxybutyryl-CoA undergoes dehydration to yield crotonyl-CoA (trans-2-butenoyl-CoA) and water. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: C25H42N7O18P3S (hydroxybutyryl-CoA) gives H2O plus C25H40N7O17P3S (crotonyl-CoA). Note that the canonical enoyl-CoA hydratase typically uses the (S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA stereoisomer, so this is consistent.

rxn01364.other_comments: This is the quinate dehydrogenase (PQQ-dependent) reaction. Quinate is oxidized to 5-dehydroquinate (3-dehydroquinate), with the prosthetic group PQQ being reduced to PQQH2. The reaction is balanced: quinate (C7H12O6) is oxidized by removal of two hydrogens (2H+ + 2e-) to give 5-dehydroquinate (C7H10O6), and PQQ accepts these to form PQQH2. Atoms and charge balance correctly.

rxn07977.other_comments: This is a fatty acid biosynthesis dehydratase (FabA/FabZ-type) reaction acting on a C14 hydroxyacyl-ACP. It removes water from (R)-3-hydroxy-cis-7-myristoleoyl-ACP to form a trans-2-enoyl (here written as trans-3) intermediate. The mass balance is consistent: loss of one H2O converts the 3-hydroxyacyl group to the 2,3-enoyl group, with the additional cis-7 double bond preserved. In the FAS elongation cycle this dehydration step is committed forward, although FabA can catalyze isomerization steps reversibly.

rxn01858.other_comments: This is the deoxyadenosine deaminase reaction (EC 3.5.4.- / adenosine deaminase family). Deoxyadenosine plus water undergoes hydrolytic deamination to form deoxyinosine and ammonia. The H+ on the substrate side balances the charge: the amino group nitrogen leaves as NH3 (or NH4+), and water provides the oxygen for the resulting carbonyl (inosine has a keto group at C6 replacing the amino group). Mass balance: deoxyadenosine (C10H13N5O3) + H2O + H+ -> deoxyinosine (C10H12N4O4) + NH4+ (writing NH3 + H+ as NH4+) checks out for atoms (C10, appropriate H, N5, O4).

rxn00231.other_comments: This is the amidase (acetamidase) reaction hydrolyzing acetamide. H2O + acetamide (CH3CONH2) yields acetate (CH3COO-) + ammonia (NH3/NH4+). Atom balance: acetamide C2H5NO + H2O (H2O) gives acetate C2H3O2 (or C2H4O2 for acetic acid) + NH3. Using neutral species acetic acid C2H4O2 + NH3 (NH3) balances C2, H: 5+2=7 vs 4+3=7, N1, O: 1+1=2 vs 2. Balanced. Hydrolysis of amides is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: oxidation of choline (an alcohol) to betaine aldehyde requires removal of two hydrogen atoms (2H), but the reaction shows only one NAD reduced to NADH + H+. The hydrogen/proton balance is incorrect as written.

Charge and atom balance not satisfied: choline (C5H14NO+) to betaine aldehyde (C5H12NO+) loses 2 H, which should be captured as NADH + H+, so the equation as written is short one hydrogen on the right side.
rxn10770.other_comments: This represents the choline dehydrogenase / NAD-dependent oxidation of choline to betaine aldehyde, the first step of betaine (glycine betaine) biosynthesis. Physiologically the reaction proceeds in the oxidative direction (choline to betaine aldehyde). Note that the canonical enzyme choline dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.99.1) uses an electron acceptor like FAD/quinone rather than NAD, though NAD(P)-dependent choline dehydrogenases exist.

rxn02297.other_comments: This is the 8-amino-7-oxononanoate synthase (BioF/KAPA synthase) reaction in biotin biosynthesis. Pimeloyl-CoA condenses with L-alanine, releasing CoA and CO2 to form 8-amino-7-oxononanoate (KAPA). The reaction is correctly balanced: L-alanine (C3H7NO2) + pimeloyl-CoA contributes the carbons, with decarboxylation of alanine releasing CO2 and PLP-dependent Claisen condensation. Charge and atom balance check out with the H+ consumed. This decarboxylative condensation is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn08396.other_comments: This is the enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI) reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing trans-2-octadecenoyl-ACP (C18:1 enoyl) to octadecanoyl-ACP (stearoyl-ACP, C18:0) using NADH. Stoichiometry is balanced: the enoyl double bond is reduced by addition of two hydrogens (NADH + H+ donates a hydride and a proton). In vivo this step is essentially irreversible and drives the elongation cycle toward saturated acyl-ACP synthesis.

rxn10161.other_comments: This is a transport reaction for octadecanoate (ocdca, stearate) coupled with a proton symport across a membrane. The reaction shows H+ and ocdca on both sides, which is correct for a transport reaction where compartment designations (e.g., extracellular vs cytoplasmic) distinguish the two sides. The stoichiometry is balanced (1:1 proton-to-substrate symport). Without explicit compartment tags shown in the formula, the species appear identical, but for symport transport this is expected. Proton symport transporters are typically driven by the proton motive force and can be considered reversible depending on the gradient.

rxn08021.other_comments: This is acyl-ACP synthetase activating decanoate (C10:0). ATP + decanoate + ACP yields decanoyl-ACP + AMP + PPi + H+. The reaction is balanced for atoms and charge: ATP provides AMP + PPi, the carboxylate of decanoate is esterified to the ACP thiol, releasing one proton. Mechanism proceeds via an acyl-adenylate intermediate. The hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase makes this effectively irreversible toward acyl-ACP formation in vivo.

rxn00504.other_comments: This is the P5C dehydrogenase / ALDH4A1-type reaction oxidizing 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (in equilibrium with glutamate-5-semialdehyde) to L-glutamate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: left side 2 H2O + NADP+ + P5C (C5H7NO2), right side NADPH + L-glutamate (C5H9NO4) + H+. Carbon (5=5), nitrogen (1=1), and oxygen/hydrogen balance correctly when accounting for the hydrolytic ring opening of P5C to the semialdehyde. The two waters supply oxygen for oxidation to the carboxylate.

rxn09104.other_comments: This is phosphatidylglycerophosphate phosphatase (PgpA/PgpB/PgpC type), hydrolyzing the phosphate from PGP to yield phosphatidylglycerol (PG) plus inorganic phosphate. With dihexadecanoyl (di-C16:0) acyl chains, the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: water cleaves the phosphomonoester bond, releasing Pi and a proton. This is the committed final step of PG biosynthesis.

errors: No stoichiometric imbalance: K+ appears on both sides with equal amounts, but the reaction lacks compartment specification to indicate transport
rxn05206.other_comments: This appears to be a potassium ion transport reaction (TRANS-RXN-187), where K+ is moved across a membrane between two compartments (e.g., cytosol and extracellular space). As written, both sides show K+ without compartment labels, making it appear as a trivial identity. For a transport reaction, the two K+ species should be in different compartments (e.g., K+[out] <=> K+[in]). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced. Directionality depends on the electrochemical gradient and whether transport is passive or active.

errors: The substrate dipeptide should be D-alanyl-D-alanine (D-Ala-D-Ala), not generic Ala-Ala; the enzyme name specifies D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase activity

The product naming is inconsistent with the substrate: the substrate is the meso-DAP (meso-2,6-diaminopimelate / 6-carboxy-lysine equivalent) tripeptide-nucleotide while the product is written as the same tetrapeptide-nucleotide core, so naming should remain consistent (UDP-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-Glu-meso-DAP-D-Ala-D-Ala)
rxn03164.other_comments: This is the MurF reaction adding D-Ala-D-Ala to the UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide (with meso-DAP) to form the UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide in peptidoglycan synthesis. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi + H+ drives amide bond formation. The reaction is mass- and charge-consistent if the dipeptide is D-Ala-D-Ala.

errors: The product 'D-Glucosamine phosphate' is ambiguous; for a 1,6-phosphomutase reaction the product should be specified as D-Glucosamine 6-phosphate

As written, substrate and product appear to have identical molecular formulas (both are glucosamine monophosphates), so the equation is formally balanced, but the positional information needed to confirm the isomerization is missing
rxn01485.other_comments: This is intended to be a phosphomutase reaction interconverting D-glucosamine 1-phosphate and D-glucosamine 6-phosphate (intramolecular transfer of the phosphate group between the 1 and 6 positions). Phosphomutase reactions of this type are generally reversible. The interconversion is stoichiometrically balanced as an isomerization (1:1), though mechanistically it typically requires a glucosamine 1,6-bisphosphate intermediate/cofactor.

errors: Charge and hydrogen imbalance: the left side includes an extra H+ that is not balanced. For H2O2 + trdrd -> 2 H2O + trdox, the reduced thioredoxin (with two thiol -SH groups) provides 2 H and 2 electrons; balanced as H2O2 + trdrd -> 2 H2O + trdox without an additional free H+. Including H+ makes hydrogen count unequal (left has 2+1+2 thiol H = effectively imbalanced).
rxn09296.other_comments: This is the thioredoxin-dependent peroxiredoxin/peroxidase reaction reducing hydrogen peroxide to water using reduced thioredoxin (trdrd), oxidizing it to trdox (disulfide form). Physiologically this proceeds strongly toward H2O2 detoxification.

rxn00441.other_comments: This is the first step of the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (E1 component, oxoglutarate decarboxylase). 2-Oxoglutarate (a 5-carbon dicarboxylic acid) is decarboxylated with TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate/ThPP) to release CO2 and form the TPP-bound 3-carboxy-1-hydroxypropyl intermediate (succinyl-semialdehyde-TPP adduct). Carbon balance: 2-oxoglutarate (C5) = CO2 (C1) + 3-carboxy-1-hydroxypropyl moiety (C4) attached to ThPP. The reaction is mass and charge balanced as written.

rxn03250.other_comments: This is an enoyl-CoA hydratase (crotonase-type) reaction. (S)-3-Hydroxyhexanoyl-CoA undergoes dehydration to form trans-2-hexenoyl-CoA ((2E)-hexenoyl-CoA) plus water. The atoms balance: removal of water (H2O) from the beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA yields the alpha,beta-unsaturated enoyl-CoA. Note the substrate name says 'Hydroxyhexanoyl-CoA' but the hydratase mechanism specifically requires the 3-hydroxy (beta) position; the product double bond at 2E is consistent with this. The stereochemistry shown (S) is typical for the substrate of enoyl-CoA hydratase, though biological beta-oxidation usually generates/uses the (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA isomer.

errors: The proton (H+) on the left side is not balanced; the reaction ATP + GMP <=> ADP + GDP is balanced without the extra H+, so including H+ creates a charge/mass imbalance
rxn00239.other_comments: This is guanylate kinase (GMP kinase, EC 2.7.4.8), which transfers a phosphate from ATP to GMP, producing ADP and GDP. The core phosphoryl transfer is correctly represented, but the added H+ is incorrect. Guanylate kinase reactions are physiologically near-equilibrium and readily reversible in vivo.

rxn02465.other_comments: This is N-acetyl-gamma-glutamyl-phosphate reductase (ArgC, EC 1.2.1.38). The reaction as written shows N-acetylglutamate-5-semialdehyde (2-acetamido-5-oxopentanoate) + NADP + Pi being oxidized/phosphorylated to N-acetylglutamyl-phosphate + NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced (atoms and charges consistent with the oxidative phosphorylation of the aldehyde to the acyl-phosphate). In vivo, during arginine biosynthesis, the physiological flux runs the opposite way: N-acetylglutamyl-phosphate + NADPH + H+ -> semialdehyde + NADP + Pi. Thus relative to how it is written here, the biologically favored direction is reverse.

rxn02222.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of indole-3-acetamide (IAM) to indole-3-acetate (IAA, auxin) plus ammonia, catalyzed by indole-3-acetamide hydrolase (e.g., bacterial iaaH in Agrobacterium/Pseudomonas IAM pathway). The reaction is balanced: H2O + C10H10N2O -> NH3 + C10H9O2 (indoleacetate). Atoms balance (C10, H consistent when accounting for protonation state of carboxylate and NH3). As an amide hydrolysis, it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds essentially irreversibly toward IAA in vivo.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the reaction produces 2.0 H+, but the standard phosphatidylserine synthase (CDP-DAG pathway) reaction releases only 1 H+ (CDP-DAG + L-serine -> phosphatidylserine + CMP + H+). The displacement of CMP from the CDP-diacylglycerol by the serine hydroxyl generates a phosphodiester bond and releases one proton, not two.
rxn09207.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylserine synthase reaction (CDP-DAG pathway, e.g., bacterial/yeast type) using a specific tetradecenoyl (C14:1) CDP-diacylglycerol. Serine attacks the CDP-DAG, transferring the phosphatidyl moiety to serine and releasing CMP. The acyl chains are conserved between substrate and product, which is consistent. In vivo this committed biosynthetic step proceeds in the forward direction toward phosphatidylserine.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (H+ + Thymine) on both sides without distinguishing intracellular and extracellular compartments. A valid transport reaction must specify compartments, e.g., H+[e] + Thymine[e] <=> H+[c] + Thymine[c]. As written, it is a null/empty reaction with no net change.
rxn05659.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction moving thymine across the membrane coupled to proton movement. Stoichiometrically the substrates and products are balanced (1 H+ and 1 thymine on each side), but the lack of compartment labels makes it appear as a do-nothing reaction. Transport reactions of this type are typically modeled as reversible unless driven by the proton motive force.

rxn01791.other_comments: This is pantothenate synthetase (PanC, EC 6.3.2.1), which condenses pantoate and beta-alanine to form pantothenate (PAN), with ATP cleaved to AMP and PPi. Mass and charge balance check: ATP provides AMP + PPi upon adenylation; the amide bond formation between pantoate carboxyl and beta-alanine amino group releases water, but here it is balanced as releasing 2 H+. The reaction is properly written with PAN as pantothenate. In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent PPi hydrolysis, making it physiologically irreversible toward pantothenate synthesis.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: hydrolysis of the UDP-sugar to UMP and lipid X (a sugar 1-phosphate) releases one phosphate-bearing product; the cleavage of a phosphoanhydride bond by water typically yields 1 H+ rather than 2 H+ at physiological pH, though exact proton count depends on protonation states

Possible atom imbalance: UMP retains one phosphate while lipid X carries the 1-phosphate, so the two phosphates of the original UDP must be accounted for - verify P balance between UDP-diacylglucosamine substrate and UMP + lipid X products
rxn03130.other_comments: This is the LpxH (or LpxI/LpxG) reaction in lipid A biosynthesis: hydrolysis of UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine to release UMP and lipid X (2,3-diacylglucosamine 1-phosphate). The reaction is a phosphoanhydride hydrolysis driven essentially irreversibly toward product formation in vivo.

errors: The product 'Optal' is not a recognized metabolite name; the expected product of propanal reduction by NADH is propan-1-ol (1-propanol), not 'Optal'. This appears to be a typo or incorrect compound name.

The enzyme name 'Propane-1,3-diol:NAD+ 1-oxidoreductase' implies the substrate/product should be propane-1,3-diol (a diol with hydroxyls at positions 1 and 3) and 3-hydroxypropanal, but the reaction shows propanal/propanol chemistry, creating an inconsistency between the enzyme name and the listed substrates.
rxn01710.other_comments: The reaction depicts an NAD+/NADH-dependent alcohol/aldehyde oxidoreductase. The enzyme name suggests propane-1,3-diol oxidation, but the listed substrate is propanal and the product 'Optal' is undefined. Stoichiometrically, NADH + H+ + aldehyde <=> NAD+ + alcohol is balanced (2 H transferred), so if 'Optal' were propan-1-ol the reaction would balance. Alcohol/aldehyde oxidoreductases are generally reversible, though direction depends on the NADH/NAD+ ratio in vivo.

rxn09107.other_comments: This is phosphatidylglycerophosphate phosphatase (PgpA/PgpB/PgpC type), which hydrolyzes phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP) to phosphatidylglycerol (PG) plus inorganic phosphate. The acyl chains here are di-C18:1 (dioctadec-11-enoyl, i.e., cis-vaccenic acid, common in E. coli). The hydrolysis of a phosphomonoester releasing Pi and a proton is correctly balanced: H2O attacks the terminal phosphate, yielding free phosphate, a proton, and PG. Stoichiometry of mass and charge is consistent.

rxn00183.other_comments: This is the glutamate-5-semialdehyde dehydrogenase-type reaction (EC 1.2.1.41 family, related to P5C/glutamate metabolism). It oxidizes L-glutamate 5-semialdehyde to L-glutamate using NAD+ and water, producing NADH and 2 H+. Mass and charge balance: left side has the aldehyde + H2O + NAD+; right side has glutamate (with new carboxyl from the aldehyde carbon) + NADH + 2 H+. Carbon (5 each), nitrogen, oxygen, and charge all balance correctly. Physiologically the relevant pathway typically runs in the proline biosynthesis/degradation direction; this NAD-dependent oxidation step is generally treated as reversible thermodynamically, though in vivo it commonly favors glutamate formation.

rxn06526.other_comments: This reaction describes thioredoxin reductase-type chemistry (protein-dithiol:NADP+ oxidoreductase, e.g. EC 1.8.1.9). As written, the protein dithiol reduces NADP+ to NADPH while the protein forms a disulfide. Stoichiometry is balanced: the two protein thiols (-SH groups) provide 2 electrons and 2 H; NADP+ + H+ + 2e- + 2H -> NADPH accounts for the hydrogens and the released H+. However, in vivo the physiological direction is the reverse: NADPH reduces protein disulfides (NADPH + Protein disulfide -> NADP+ + Protein dithiol), as thioredoxin reductase uses NADPH to maintain reduced thiols. The named oxidoreductase convention writes the substrate (dithiol) on the left, but the thermodynamically and biologically favored flux is toward dithiol formation (reverse of the EC nomenclature direction).

rxn00623.other_comments: This is the assimilatory sulfite reductase (NADPH) reaction, EC 1.8.1.2. The reaction is written in the oxidative direction (H2S + 3 NADP+ -> sulfite + 3 NADPH). Checking stoichiometry: sulfite (SO3 2-) has S at +4, sulfide (S 2-) at -2, a 6-electron change. 3 NADPH provide 6 electrons (2 each), consistent. Atom balance: left H2O(3) + H2S gives O3, H8 (6 from water + 2 from H2S), plus N from NADP; right side sulfite SO3 (O3), 3 NADPH + 3 H+ provide H balance. Charge and mass balance reasonably. In vivo this enzyme runs in the reductive (assimilatory) direction, i.e., sulfite + NADPH -> sulfide, which is the reverse of how it is written here.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass-balanced; opening the imidazole ring of GTP by GTP cyclohydrolase-type/8,9-hydrolase activity adds water but the product formamidopyrimidine nucleoside triphosphate retains all atoms of GTP plus H2O - this is actually balanced for a ring-opening hydration, so the apparent imbalance depends on the exact formula used. Verify atom and charge balance explicitly (the formyl/amino group from C8 must be accounted for).
rxn00302.other_comments: This represents hydrolytic ring opening of the imidazole portion of GTP, converting the purine ring into a formamidopyrimidine (FAPy) species while retaining the triphosphate moiety. Such ring-opening hydrolysis reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (hydrolysis) direction.

rxn01757.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction where the amino group of L-cysteate is transferred to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and 3-sulfopyruvate (the keto acid corresponding to cysteate). Atom and charge balance are consistent: L-cysteate (C3H6NO5S-) plus 2-oxoglutarate yields L-glutamate plus 3-sulfopyruvate (C3H3O6S-). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced for C, H, N, O, and S.

errors: Stoichiometrically incomplete as written without a cofactor; phosphomutase reactions require a catalytic bisphosphate intermediate (e.g., D-mannose 1,6-bisphosphate) but the net reaction D-mannose 6-phosphate <=> D-mannose 1-phosphate is mass- and charge-balanced as a simple isomerization
rxn01329.other_comments: This is a phosphomutase reaction interconverting the phosphate group between the C6 and C1 positions of mannose (D-mannose 6-phosphate to D-mannose 1-phosphate). Analogous to phosphoglucomutase. Net reaction is an intramolecular phosphate transfer and is balanced in atoms and charge. Such mutase reactions are freely reversible in vivo.

rxn00950.other_comments: This is the cystathionine gamma-lyase (CSE/CTH) reaction acting on L-cystathionine. Hydrolytic/eliminative cleavage of cystathionine yields L-homocysteine, pyruvate, and ammonia. The stoichiometry is balanced: cystathionine (C7H14N2O4S) + H2O gives homocysteine (C4H9NO2S) + pyruvate (C3H4O3) + NH3 (charges and atoms balance). This beta/gamma-elimination is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of cleavage.

rxn10268.other_comments: This is the dephosphorylation of phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP) to phosphatidylglycerol (PG) by PGP phosphatase, with isopentadecanoyl (anteiso/iso-C15) acyl chains. The reaction hydrolyzes the terminal phosphate group, releasing inorganic phosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O cleaves the phosphomonoester bond, yielding free phosphate, a proton, and the PG product. This is the final step of PG biosynthesis.

rxn01029.other_comments: This is agmatine deiminase (EC 3.5.3.12), which hydrolyzes agmatine to N-carbamoylputrescine and ammonia. Stoichiometry is balanced: agmatine (C5H14N4) + H2O yields N-carbamoylputrescine (C5H13N3O) + NH3. The reaction is the first step of the agmatine deiminase pathway and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn02507.other_comments: This is the indole-3-glycerol phosphate synthase (IGPS, TrpC) reaction in tryptophan biosynthesis. It converts 1-(2-carboxyphenylamino)-1-deoxy-D-ribulose 5-phosphate (CdRP) into indole-3-glycerol phosphate (IGP), releasing CO2 and H2O. The reaction is a ring closure with decarboxylation and dehydration. Mass and charge balance check: CdRP (C12H14NO9P with appropriate protonation) plus H+ yields IGP (C11H12O6P-) + CO2 + H2O. Atoms balance: one carbon lost as CO2, one water released during cyclization. Charge balances with the consumed proton.

rxn10220.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol synthase (phosphatidate cytidylyltransferase) reaction with isoheptadecanoyl (C17 branched) acyl chains. CTP reacts with phosphatidic acid (1,2-diisoheptadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) to form CDP-diacylglycerol plus pyrophosphate and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: CTP provides the CMP moiety attached to the phosphate of PA, releasing PPi. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: Charge imbalance: allophanate is typically represented as a -1 anion (urea-1-carboxylate, C2H3N2O3-), and with 3 H+ on the left the charges do not balance with neutral products (left side net charge +2, right side 0)

Mass/atom balance issue: allophanate (C2H3N2O3-) + H2O + 3 H+ gives C2H8N2O4 on the left, while 2 CO2 + 2 NH3 = C2H8N2O4; atoms (C2 H8 N2 O4) actually balance, but the proton count is tied to the protonation state assumption and the products are written as neutral CO2/NH3 rather than the physiological HCO3-/NH4+ forms
rxn00002.other_comments: This is the allophanate hydrolase (urea carboxylase pathway) reaction, EC 3.5.1.54, which degrades allophanate to 2 CO2 + 2 NH3. As a hydrolytic decarboxylation step in urea/atrazine catabolism it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (degradative) direction in vivo.

rxn03031.other_comments: This is the tetrahydrodipicolinate N-succinyltransferase reaction (DapD, EC 2.3.1.117) in the lysine/DAP biosynthesis pathway. The cyclic tetrahydrodipicolinate (2,3,4,5-tetrahydropyridine-2,6-dicarboxylate) is hydrolytically opened and succinylated, transferring the succinyl group from succinyl-CoA to the amino group, yielding N-succinyl-L-2-amino-6-oxopimelate and free CoA. The reaction consumes water and is balanced in atoms and charge as written (H2O + succinyl-CoA + THDPA -> CoA + N-succinyl-2-amino-6-oxopimelate). Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn08043.other_comments: This is the acetohydroxybutanoate synthase (AHAS) reaction in isoleucine biosynthesis. Pyruvate is decarboxylated (releasing CO2) and the resulting 2-carbon hydroxyethyl-TPP unit is transferred to 2-oxobutyrate to form 2-aceto-2-hydroxybutanoate. The atoms balance: pyruvate (C3H3O3-) plus 2-oxobutyrate (C4H5O3-) plus H+ gives CO2 (CO2) plus 2-aceto-2-hydroxybutanoate (C6H9O4-). Carbon: 3+4 = 7 = 1+6. The reaction is essentially irreversible due to CO2 release.

rxn10300.other_comments: This reaction represents glycosylation (glucosylation) of a stearoyl-lipoteichoic acid polymer with 24 repeating units, transferring glucose from 24 UDP-glucose donors to the unsubstituted lipoteichoic acid backbone, releasing 24 UDP and producing the glucose-substituted product. The stoichiometry is balanced 24:1 substrate to polymer, consistent with one glucose added per repeat unit. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo due to the high group-transfer potential of UDP-glucose.

rxn14333.other_comments: This is a cis-prenyltransferase (chain elongation) reaction adding one isopentenyl diphosphate (C5) to ditrans,dicis-pentaprenyl diphosphate (C25) to yield ditrans,tricis-hexaprenyl diphosphate (C30), releasing pyrophosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: each condensation extends the chain by one isoprene unit and releases one PPi and one H+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written.

rxn00990.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction (EC 2.8.3.x family) transferring CoA between acetoacetate and acetate. Atoms balance: acetate (C2H3O2-) + acetoacetyl-CoA yields acetyl-CoA + acetoacetate (C4H5O3-). Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and CoA moiety all balance. CoA-transferases typically operate near equilibrium and are reversible, though physiological direction depends on metabolic context (e.g., in ketone body utilization the analogous succinyl-CoA transferase runs toward acetoacetyl-CoA formation).

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: AIR (5-aminoimidazole ribonucleotide, C8H13N3O7P) plus H2O and NAD cannot balance to the products as written; carbon and nitrogen counts do not reconcile with HMP (4-amino-2-methyl-5-hydroxymethylpyrimidine phosphate, C6H10N3O4P) plus 2 formate.
Charge imbalance: the 4 H+ produced along with NAD->NADH do not balance the proton/charge accounting for this conversion.
Incorrect cofactor usage: the ThiC-catalyzed conversion of AIR to HMP-P is a complex radical SAM rearrangement, not an NAD-dependent oxidation; NAD/NADH should not appear.
Byproduct accounting incomplete: the actual ThiC reaction releases formate, CO, and other fragments along with 5'-deoxyadenosine (from SAM); these are not represented correctly.
rxn08131.other_comments: This reaction represents the biosynthesis of HMP-P (4-amino-2-methyl-5-phosphomethylpyrimidine) from AIR, normally catalyzed by ThiC, a radical SAM enzyme. The conversion is physiologically essentially irreversible (forward), but the equation as written is not properly balanced and uses NAD/NADH instead of SAM-dependent radical chemistry.

rxn08816.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of a monoacyl-glycerophosphoglycerol (2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol bearing an oleoyl/octadec-11-enoyl chain) by lysophospholipase L1 in the periplasm. Water hydrolyzes the ester bond, releasing the free fatty acid (octadecenoate) and glycerophosphoglycerol, plus a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: one acyl-GPG + H2O yields GPG + free fatty acid + H+. Note: the substrate name says '1-Acyl' while the enzyme description says '2-acyl', a minor naming inconsistency but does not affect stoichiometry.

rxn05464.other_comments: This is the enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI/FabK-type) step in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2 double bond of an 18-carbon enoyl-ACP (trans-octadec-2-enoyl-ACP) to octadecanoyl (stearoyl)-ACP using NADH as the reducing cofactor. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: NADH + H+ provide the 2 electrons and 2 protons (hydride + proton) needed to saturate the alpha,beta double bond, yielding NAD+ and the saturated acyl-ACP. In vivo the enoyl reductase step is essentially irreversible and drives the fatty acid elongation cycle in the reductive (biosynthetic) direction.

rxn01964.other_comments: This is the overall tryptophan synthase reaction (EC 4.2.1.20), combining the alpha reaction (indoleglycerol phosphate -> indole + G3P) and the beta reaction (indole + L-serine -> L-tryptophan + H2O). Atoms and charges balance: L-serine (C3H7NO3) + indoleglycerol phosphate (C11H14NO6P) yields L-tryptophan (C11H12N2O2) + G3P (C3H7O6P) + H2O. Carbon (14=14), nitrogen (2=2), phosphorus (1=1) all balance. In vivo this proceeds toward tryptophan biosynthesis.

rxn01519.other_comments: This is the dUTPase (dUTP nucleotidohydrolase) reaction. dUTP is hydrolyzed at the alpha-beta phosphate position, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) and dUMP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: dUTP (4- at physiological pH) + H2O yields dUMP (2-) + PPi (3-) + 2 H+, conserving atoms and charge. Physiologically, dUTPase drives this reaction strongly in the hydrolytic direction to keep dUTP pools low and prevent uracil misincorporation into DNA, while supplying dUMP for thymidylate synthesis.

rxn01137.other_comments: This is adenosine deaminase (EC 3.5.4.4), catalyzing the hydrolytic deamination of adenosine to inosine. The reaction H2O + Adenosine -> NH3 + Inosine is mass and charge balanced if the released amino group is captured as NH3 and the proton balances out. Note: typically written as Adenosine + H2O -> Inosine + NH3, where the H+ on the substrate side accounts for the protonation/deamination chemistry. The atoms balance: adenosine (C10H13N5O4) + H2O -> inosine (C10H12N4O5) + NH3 (NH3). Carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen all balance.

rxn10261.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PGS) type reaction (CDP-diacylglycerol:sn-glycerol-3-phosphate 3-phosphatidyltransferase, EC 2.7.8.5) using a CDP-diacylglycerol bearing isotetradecanoyl (iso-myristoyl, 13-methyltetradecanoyl) acyl chains. The phosphatidyl group is transferred from CDP-diacylglycerol to the hydroxyl of glycerol-3-phosphate, releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP). Stoichiometry is balanced: the glycerol-3-phosphate provides the 3-phosphate and free hydroxyl, CDP is cleaved to CMP, and the phosphatidyl moiety forms the new ester bond.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is incorrect; a standard decarboxylation of phosphopantothenoylcysteine consumes 1 H+ (not 2) to balance charge/protons. The reaction as written: substrate (C13H24N2O9PS, charge typically -2) + 2 H+ -> CO2 + phosphopantetheine (C11H23N2O6PS, charge -1 typically). Balancing one H+ is correct, two leaves a hydrogen/charge imbalance.
rxn02341.other_comments: This is the phosphopantothenoylcysteine decarboxylase (PPCDC) reaction in CoA biosynthesis, removing the cysteine carboxyl group as CO2 to yield 4'-phosphopantetheine. Decarboxylations are essentially irreversible in vivo due to CO2 release.

rxn03182.other_comments: This is the KdtA (WaaA) catalyzed transfer of 3-deoxy-D-manno-oct-2-ulosonate (KDO) from CMP-KDO to lipid IVA, producing KDO-lipid IVA, CMP, and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the KDO moiety is transferred from CMP-KDO to the acceptor lipid, releasing CMP. Mass and charge balance hold (the glycosidic bond formation releases CMP and a proton). In Escherichia coli KdtA is bifunctional and adds two KDO residues, but this single-transfer step is correctly represented here.

rxn08076.other_comments: This is an amidase reaction cleaving the amide bond between the lactyl group of anhydro-N-acetylmuramic acid and the L-alanine of the peptide stem in a peptidoglycan turnover product (GlcNAc-anhMurNAc-tetrapeptide). Water hydrolyzes the bond, releasing the tetrapeptide (L-Ala-D-Glu-meso-DAP-D-Ala) and the disaccharide GlcNAc-anhMurNAc. This corresponds to AmpD-type N-acetylmuramyl-L-alanine amidase activity in the periplasm/cytoplasm. Mass and atoms balance: hydrolysis splits one substrate into two products with addition of H2O.

rxn09108.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PgsA) reaction, transferring the phosphatidyl group from CDP-diacylglycerol (here with two C12:0 dodecanoyl chains) onto glycerol-3-phosphate, releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP). Stoichiometry balances: the CMP-leaving group and the new phosphodiester bond to G3P are consistent. In vivo this CDP-DAG-consuming step is essentially irreversible and proceeds toward PGP synthesis.

rxn00224.other_comments: This is the ferrochelatase reaction (EC 4.99.1.1, protoheme ferro-lyase). It inserts ferrous iron (Fe2+) into protoporphyrin IX to form protoheme (heme b), releasing 2 protons. The stoichiometry is balanced: protoporphyrin IX has two NH groups that lose protons upon Fe2+ chelation, accounting for the 2 H+ released; net charge balances (Fe2+ in, 2 H+ out, neutral porphyrin to neutral heme). The reaction is the final step of heme biosynthesis and proceeds in the heme-forming direction in vivo.

rxn08797.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase (acylglycerophosphate hydrolysis) reaction. The substrate 1-tetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a lysophosphatidic acid with a C14:0/myristoyl group) is hydrolyzed by water to release myristic acid (C14:0 fatty acid) and glycerol-3-phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: cleavage of one ester bond consumes one H2O and releases one fatty acid (carboxylic acid, hence the H+) and the deacylated glycerophosphate backbone. Mass and charge balance: the ester hydrolysis adds H and OH across the bond, generating the carboxylic acid and alcohol; releasing a proton from the carboxylic acid accounts for the H+. This is a thermodynamically favorable hydrolysis reaction and proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn01513.other_comments: This is thymidylate kinase (dTMP kinase, EC 2.7.4.9), catalyzing the transfer of a phosphate from ATP to dTMP, yielding ADP and dTDP. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: ATP (-4) + dTMP (-2) + H+ (+1) = -5 on the left; ADP (-3) + dTDP (-2) = -5 on the right. Note that some databases write the kinase reaction without the explicit H+; the inclusion here keeps charge balance consistent. In vivo, the reaction proceeds toward dTDP formation as part of dTTP biosynthesis, though kinases are intrinsically reversible.

rxn08307.other_comments: This is the CDP-diacylglycerol synthase reaction (EC 2.7.7.41) using a phosphatidic acid with two myristoyl (C14:0) chains. CTP reacts with phosphatidate to form CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing pyrophosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: the cytidylyl group is transferred from CTP to the phosphate of phosphatidate, releasing PPi, and the proton balance is correct. In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase.

errors: The substrate ALCTT (acetolactate, specifically 2-acetolactate / (S)-2-hydroxy-2-methyl-3-oxobutanoate) is the correct substrate, but the product shown is the result of a combined isomerization and reduction; this is acceptable for ketol-acid reductoisomerase (EC 1.1.1.86). Stoichiometry of atoms and charge appears balanced when ALCTT = 2-acetolactate and product = 2,3-dihydroxy-3-methylbutanoate (2,3-dihydroxyisovalerate).
