rxn02186.other_comments: This is the ketol-acid reductoisomerase reaction in branched-chain amino acid (valine) biosynthesis. It converts (2S)-2-acetolactate to (2R)-2,3-dihydroxy-3-methylbutanoate (2,3-dihydroxyisovalerate) using NADPH. In vivo it proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward the dihydroxy product.

errors: Reaction name and substrate mismatch: the enzyme is named '(3R)-3-Hydroxybutanoyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] hydro-lyase' (a C4 substrate) but the actual substrate given is (R)-3-Hydroxydecanoyl-ACP (a C10 substrate)

Charge/proton balance is inconsistent: a simple dehydration releases only H2O, not both H2O and H+ separately; the extra H+ makes the equation unbalanced unless ACP protonation states are explicitly defined
rxn05333.other_comments: This is a beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase (FabA/FabZ-type) reaction converting (R)-3-hydroxydecanoyl-ACP to trans-2-decenoyl-ACP plus water. The chemistry (dehydration to form an enoyl-ACP) is correct in principle, but the enzyme name corresponds to a C4 substrate while the reaction shows a C10 substrate. FabA-type dehydratases catalyze reversible dehydration/hydration.

rxn10255.other_comments: This is a diacylglycerol kinase reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the sn-3 hydroxyl of 1,2-diisotetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol (a diacylglycerol with two isotetradecanoyl/iso-C14 chains), producing the corresponding phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) and ADP. The reaction is stoichiometrically and charge balanced: one phosphate is transferred from ATP to DAG. Kinase reactions coupled to ATP hydrolysis are thermodynamically strongly favorable in the phosphorylation direction in vivo.

rxn00209.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by pyridoxine 5'-phosphate oxidase (PNPOx, EC 1.4.3.5). It oxidizes pyridoxine 5'-phosphate using molecular O2 to produce pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (the active vitamin B6 cofactor) and hydrogen peroxide. The reaction is balanced: pyridoxine phosphate (C8H12NO6P) plus O2 yields pyridoxal phosphate (C8H10NO6P) plus H2O2, conserving atoms and charge. Physiologically, this FMN-dependent oxidase drives PLP biosynthesis in the salvage pathway and is essentially irreversible toward PLP formation in vivo.

rxn03246.other_comments: This is a beta-oxidation step: 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidizes (S)-3-hydroxyoctanoyl-CoA to 3-oxooctanoyl-CoA using NAD+ as the electron acceptor, producing NADH and H+. The atoms balance: the substrate loses 2 H (one from the hydroxyl, one from the carbon), which are transferred as a hydride to NAD+ (yielding NADH) plus a free proton. Note that the enzyme physiologically acts on (S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA; the name 'hydroxyoctanoyl' should specify the 3-position. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced.

rxn02474.other_comments: This is the riboflavin biosynthesis reaction catalyzed by 5-amino-6-(5-phosphoribosylamino)uracil reductase (RibD/RibG). The reaction converts the ribosyl compound (an amino-ribitylamino vs ribosylamino distinction): the reductase reduces the ribose moiety to a ribitol moiety, consuming NADPH. As written (NADP + ribitylamino <=> NADPH + H+ + ribosylamino), the forward direction shows oxidation of ribitylamino to ribosylamino, which is the reverse of the physiologically relevant reductive direction. Stoichiometry is balanced (a 2-electron/hydride transfer with NADP/NADPH and H+).

rxn04783.other_comments: This reaction represents the ATP-dependent formylation of glycinamide ribonucleotide (GAR) using free formate, catalyzed by the formate-dependent GAR transformylase (PurT, also called GAR transformylase T). The standard PurN enzyme uses N10-formyl-THF, but the PurT variant uses formate plus ATP. The reaction mechanism proceeds via a formyl-phosphate intermediate, hydrolyzing ATP to ADP and Pi while transferring the formyl group to the amino group of GAR to form N-formyl-GAR (FGAR). Atoms and charges balance: ATP + formate + GAR yields ADP + Pi + H+ + FGAR.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the hydrolysis of the thioester bond in (R)-S-lactoylglutathione yields glutathione (GSH) and D-lactate. At physiological pH, this reaction produces one proton (from the carboxylate of lactate), not two. The stoichiometry of 2.0 H+ is incorrect; it should be 1.0 H+.
rxn01274.other_comments: This is glyoxalase II (hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase, EC 3.1.2.6), which hydrolyzes (R)-S-lactoylglutathione to GSH and D-lactate, completing the glyoxalase pathway that detoxifies methylglyoxal. Thioester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn02144.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by 3-oxoadipate enol-lactonase (EC 3.1.1.24), part of the beta-ketoadipate pathway for aromatic compound degradation. It hydrolyzes the enol-lactone (3-oxoadipate enol-lactone) by adding water to open the lactone ring, yielding 3-oxoadipate (beta-ketoadipate). The stoichiometry is balanced: the lactone (C6H6O4) plus H2O (H2O) gives 3-oxoadipate (C6H6O5, present as the dianion 3-oxoadipate with release of H+). As a hydrolase acting on an irreversible ring-opening of a strained/activated lactone, the reaction proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn12645.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide glycyl-L-asparagine (Gly-Asn) into glycine and L-asparagine, consuming one water molecule. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: Gly-Asn + H2O yields free glycine and free L-asparagine. Note that the enzyme name 'methionyl aminopeptidase' is somewhat inconsistent with the substrate, since methionyl aminopeptidases typically cleave N-terminal methionine residues; here the N-terminal residue is glycine. However, the chemistry of peptide bond hydrolysis as written is correct.

errors: No net chemical transformation: identical species (L-Phenylalanine + H+) appear on both sides; this represents a transport reaction but lacks compartment annotations to distinguish substrate from product
rxn05306.other_comments: This appears to be a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN) moving L-phenylalanine along with a proton across a membrane, likely a proton-coupled amino acid symporter. As written without compartment identifiers (e.g., cytosol vs extracellular), the two sides are identical, making the reaction stoichiometrically trivial/null. Mass and charge are formally balanced only because both sides are the same.

errors: Proton imbalance: with NADH + O2 + 1 H+ the reaction balances for H and charge; the stoichiometry of 2.0 H+ leaves an excess of one H and one positive charge on the left side
Charge balance is off by +1 as written (left side carries net +1 from the two protons plus NADH/NAD+ couple not cancelling)
rxn04745.other_comments: This is a salicylate 1-monooxygenase-type reaction: a flavin-dependent monooxygenase using NADH and O2 to hydroxylate and decarboxylate a hydroxymethylsalicylate to the corresponding catechol, releasing CO2 and water. Monooxygenase decarboxylation reactions of this type are physiologically irreversible (forward).

rxn02929.other_comments: This is dihydrodipicolinate reductase (DapB) in lysine/DAP biosynthesis. The enzyme reduces 2,3-dihydrodipicolinate to 2,3,4,5-tetrahydrodipicolinate using NAD(P)H. As written, the reaction shows oxidation of tetrahydrodipicolinate to dihydrodipicolinate with NADP+ reduction; in vivo the physiological direction is the reverse (reduction of dihydrodipicolinate using NADPH/NADH), so the biologically relevant flux goes right-to-left as written. Stoichiometry is balanced (one NADPH, one H+, and the substrate differ by 2 H, i.e. one hydride plus proton).

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance as written: the beta-ketothiolase (thiolase) condensation of acetyl-CoA with a fatty acyl-CoA combines a C12 (lauroyl, C12) with a C2 (acetyl) unit to give a C14 3-oxoacyl-CoA, but this also releases CoA. As written the carbon count works (12 + 2 = 14) and one CoA is liberated, so the reaction is actually balanced. No real stoichiometric error.
rxn06510.other_comments: This is the thiolase (3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase / acetyl-CoA C-acyltransferase) reaction. Written direction is the synthetic (condensation) direction: acetyl-CoA + lauroyl-CoA -> 3-oxotetradecanoyl-CoA + CoA. In vivo during beta-oxidation the thiolase runs in the thiolytic (degradative) direction (cleaving 3-oxoacyl-CoA + CoA -> shorter acyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA), which is the reverse of how this is written. The condensation direction is thermodynamically unfavorable and is normally only used in biosynthetic contexts.

errors: The reaction shows identical species (H+ + L-Malate) on both sides with no net transformation as written
Transport reactions must distinguish compartments; substrates should be labeled with compartment identifiers (e.g., H+[e] + L-Malate[e] <=> H+[c] + L-Malate[c]) to represent translocation
The enzyme annotation (Maltose permease MAL31) is inconsistent with the substrate (L-Malate); MAL31 is a maltose/H+ symporter, not a malate transporter
rxn05605.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport (transport) reaction for L-Malate. As written it is a null reaction because both sides are identical, lacking the extracellular/cytoplasmic compartment distinction needed to represent transmembrane movement. Also, the named transporter does not match the substrate.

rxn08849.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase reaction hydrolyzing the ester bond of 2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol (with a hexadec-9-enoyl/palmitoleoyl group) to yield glycerophosphoglycerol and the free fatty acid hexadecenoate. The stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the acyl ester, releasing the carboxylate (hexadecenoate) and a proton, leaving the deacylated glycerophosphoglycerol. Mass and charge balance are consistent.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass/phosphate balanced. ATP (with 3 phosphates) + PPi (2 phosphates) = 5 phosphates on the left; ADP (2 phosphates) + Triphosphate (3 phosphates) = 5 phosphates on the right, so phosphate count balances. However, the conventional polyphosphate kinase (PPK) reaction is ATP + (polyP)n <=> ADP + (polyP)n+1, transferring a phosphate to a polyphosphate chain rather than to free PPi to form a discrete triphosphate. The substrate should be polyphosphate, not pyrophosphate.
rxn00104.other_comments: This represents a polyphosphate kinase reaction where ATP transfers its terminal gamma-phosphate to an acceptor. As written, ATP + PPi yields ADP + triphosphate (PPPi). Atom-wise the phosphate counts balance (5 P each side), and the reaction is chemically reversible, though physiologically PPK typically uses growing polyphosphate chains. The enzyme can run in both directions depending on cellular ATP/polyP ratios; in vivo it commonly favors polyP synthesis (ATP consumption) but can regenerate ATP under high polyP conditions.

rxn01019.other_comments: This is ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC, EC 2.1.3.3), transferring the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine, producing citrulline and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is correctly balanced: ornithine (C5H12N2O2, charge 0 at physiological pH but often written +1) plus carbamoyl phosphate (CH2NO5P, -2) yields citrulline (C6H13N3O3) plus phosphate (HPO4 2-) plus H+. Atoms (C, N, O, P) and charges balance with the proton released. In vivo this proceeds essentially irreversibly toward citrulline synthesis in the urea cycle.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced for protons/charge. The arogenate dehydrogenase reaction should include an H+ on the product side. Balanced form: L-arogenate + NAD+ <=> L-tyrosine + CO2 + NADH (the net releases NADH; a proton balance check shows H+ is typically released, giving ... + NADH + H+ or accounted by the decarboxylation).
rxn00525.other_comments: This is the arogenate dehydrogenase (TyrA) reaction, where pretyrosine (L-arogenate) undergoes oxidative decarboxylation using NAD+ to yield L-tyrosine, CO2, and NADH. Pretyrosine is a synonym for L-arogenate. In vivo this proceeds in the biosynthetic direction toward tyrosine, driven by CO2 release.

rxn08295.other_comments: This is diacylglycerol kinase, which phosphorylates 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol (here with two C14:0/myristoyl chains, ditetradecanoyl) using ATP to produce phosphatidic acid (1,2-ditetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) and ADP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: one phosphate is transferred from ATP to the DAG hydroxyl, yielding ADP and the phosphorylated lipid. ATP-dependent kinase reactions are strongly exergonic and physiologically essentially irreversible in the forward (phosphorylation) direction.

errors: Proton (H+) stoichiometry appears incorrect; the reaction should produce 1 H+ rather than 2.0 H+. The base-exchange/CDP-DAG pathway: CDP-DAG + L-serine -> phosphatidylserine + CMP + H+ (charge balance gives one proton released).
rxn09208.other_comments: This is the CDP-diacylglycerol-dependent phosphatidylserine synthase (PSS) reaction using dipalmitoyl (di-16:0) species. L-serine displaces CMP from CDP-1,2-dihexadecanoylglycerol to form phosphatidylserine. In vivo this is essentially irreversible in the synthetic direction due to consumption of the high-energy CDP-DAG and release of CMP.

rxn09448.other_comments: This is a fatty acid--CoA ligase (long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase) reaction activating octadecenoate (e.g., oleate, C18:1) to octadecenoyl-CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + fatty acid yields AMP + PPi + acyl-CoA. The mechanism proceeds via an acyl-adenylate intermediate. Although written as reversible, in vivo the reaction is driven forward by hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible toward acyl-CoA formation.

rxn05638.other_comments: This is a proton-coupled L-proline transport reaction (symport/antiport). The metabolites are identical on both sides (H+ and L-Proline), indicating a transmembrane transport event where the same species move across compartments. Stoichiometry is balanced (1 H+ and 1 L-Proline on each side). The compartment labels are not shown in the string but the reaction type (TRANS-RXN) implies movement between cellular compartments. As written, with no compartment distinction visible, it appears as a trivial identity; assuming proper compartmentalization, it represents proton-coupled proline transport.

rxn05439.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase reaction (fatty acid biosynthesis), reducing the trans-2-enoyl double bond. NADH + H+ donates two electrons and a proton to convert the alpha,beta-unsaturated 5-methyl-trans-hex-2-enoyl-ACP to the saturated 5-methyl-hexanoyl-ACP, producing NAD+. The reaction is stoichiometrically and redox balanced (2 H from NADH+H+ added across the C=C double bond). In vivo, enoyl-ACP reductase strongly favors the reductive (forward) direction during fatty acid chain elongation.

errors: TTP (thymidine triphosphate, dTTP) hydrolysis to dTMP releasing PPi should produce only 1 H+ under standard biochemical conventions, not 2 H+; charge/proton balance is inconsistent
Nomenclature ambiguity: 'TTP' is used for dTTP (deoxythymidine triphosphate); thymidine has no ribonucleotide form in standard metabolism so this is likely dTTP
rxn09014.other_comments: This represents hydrolysis of a nucleoside triphosphate (dTTP) to the monophosphate (dTMP) plus pyrophosphate, catalyzed by a nucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphohydrolase. Such hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically strongly favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo (forward direction toward hydrolysis products).

rxn01603.other_comments: This is dihydrofolate synthase (folC), EC 6.3.2.12, which ligates L-glutamate to 7,8-dihydropteroate to form dihydrofolate, driven by ATP hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP + glutamate + dihydropteroate yields ADP + Pi + H+ + dihydrofolate. ATP-dependent ligase reactions strongly favor the forward synthetic direction in vivo.

rxn09232.other_comments: This is the ribonucleotide reductase reaction reducing GDP to dGDP using glutaredoxin as the electron donor. The 2'-OH of the ribose is replaced by H, and the released oxygen leaves as water; the reducing equivalents come from glutaredoxin (reduced -> oxidized via a disulfide). Atom and charge balance is consistent: ribose 2'-OH reduction yields dGDP plus H2O, with glutaredoxin dithiol being oxidized to disulfide. The reaction is physiologically driven in the direction of deoxyribonucleotide synthesis.

rxn09112.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PgsA) reaction with C16:1 acyl chains. Glycerol-3-phosphate attacks the CDP-diacylglycerol (CDP-1,2-dihexadec-9-enoylglycerol), releasing CMP and forming phosphatidylglycerophosphate (PGP). The stoichiometry is balanced: the glycerophosphate moiety is transferred and CMP is displaced from the CDP-DAG. In vivo this reaction is driven forward as part of phosphatidylglycerol biosynthesis, with the subsequent dephosphorylation by PGP phosphatase pulling flux toward product.

rxn00686.other_comments: This is dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR, EC 1.5.1.3). The reaction as written shows oxidation of tetrahydrofolate (THF) to dihydrofolate (DHF) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The atoms and charges balance: THF + NADP+ <=> DHF + NADPH + H+. In vivo, however, DHFR strongly favors the reduction direction, converting DHF to THF using NADPH (essentially irreversible toward THF). Therefore, as written (oxidation direction), the biologically relevant flux runs in reverse.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the reaction should include a proton (H+) to be balanced. The balanced form is typically NADPH + H+ + trdox <=> NADP+ + trdrd
rxn05289.other_comments: This is thioredoxin reductase (NADPH-dependent), reducing oxidized thioredoxin (trdox, disulfide form) to reduced thioredoxin (trdrd, dithiol form) using NADPH. In vivo this strongly favors reduction of thioredoxin to maintain the reduced cellular redox state, so it proceeds in the forward direction as written.

rxn02914.other_comments: This is the phosphoserine aminotransferase (PSAT, EC 2.6.1.52) reaction, the second step of the phosphorylated pathway of L-serine biosynthesis. The reaction is a PLP-dependent transamination: phosphoserine (O-phospho-L-serine) and 2-oxoglutarate yield L-glutamate and 3-phosphonooxypyruvate (3-phosphohydroxypyruvate). Stoichiometry is balanced (1:1:1:1) for both atoms and charge in the transamination. In vivo, the physiological direction in serine biosynthesis runs from 3-phosphohydroxypyruvate + glutamate toward phosphoserine + 2-oxoglutarate, i.e., the reverse of how this reaction is written.

rxn00689.other_comments: This is the folylpolyglutamate synthetase (FPGS, EC 6.3.2.17) type reaction, forming the gamma-glutamyl bond between the terminal glutamate of tetrahydrofolate and an additional L-glutamate. ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + phosphate (Pi), consistent with the ADP-forming ligase mechanism. The proton (H+) released balances charge. Stoichiometry is mass- and charge-balanced. As an ATP-driven ligation, it proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction relative to the enzyme name and biochemistry; ribonucleotide reductase reduces UDP to dUDP, not the reverse
Stoichiometry as written is unbalanced for the proton/oxygen accounting: oxidation of dUDP back to UDP would require an oxygen source, but the listed direction (UDP -> dUDP) consumes trdrd not trdox
trdrd (reduced thioredoxin) should be the reductant consumed when forming dUDP; here trdox is the substrate on the dUDP side, which is inconsistent
rxn06075.other_comments: This represents the ribonucleotide reductase reaction. The correct biological reaction is UDP + trdrd -> dUDP + trdox + H2O (reduction of ribonucleotide using reduced thioredoxin, releasing oxidized thioredoxin and water). As written, the left side (dUDP + trdox + H2O) and right side (UDP + trdrd + H+) are reversed; the natural in vivo direction proceeds toward dUDP formation, i.e., the reverse of how this equation reads.

rxn01973.other_comments: This is N-succinyl-LL-2,6-diaminopimelate desuccinylase (DapE, EC 3.5.1.18), a hydrolase in the succinylase branch of lysine/DAP biosynthesis. It hydrolyzes the amide bond of N-succinyl-LL-2,6-diaminopimelate to release succinate and LL-2,6-diaminopimelate. The reaction is balanced: H2O is consumed, one amide is cleaved yielding free succinate and the free amino group. In vivo this biosynthetic hydrolysis runs in the direction of DAP/lysine formation.

errors: Atom imbalance: the product cis-1,2-dihydro-1,2-dihydroxybenzoate (cis-benzoate dihydrodiol) has formula C7H8O4, but benzoate is C7H5O2; the reaction as written shows only one oxygen incorporated whereas dioxygenase adds two oxygen atoms from O2
Oxygen balance: O2 contributes 2 oxygen atoms, but only one new OH appears in the stated product 'cis-1,2-dihydroxybenzoate' - the proper product is the cis-dihydrodiol bearing two hydroxyls
Charge/H balance is not satisfied as written; product name is ambiguous (should be cis-1,2-dihydro-1,2-dihydroxybenzoate, the non-aromatic dihydrodiol)
rxn03898.other_comments: This represents a benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase (reductase-coupled) reaction. NADPH and O2 reduce/oxygenate benzoate to a cis-dihydrodiol. Such aromatic ring dioxygenase reactions are effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (degradative) direction. The product should be the cis-1,2-dihydrodiol of benzoate, incorporating both atoms of molecular oxygen.

rxn01520.other_comments: This is thymidylate synthase (EC 2.1.1.45), which transfers and reduces a one-carbon unit from 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate to dUMP, producing dTMP and dihydrofolate. The atoms balance: the methylene carbon plus two hydrogens from the folate cofactor are added to C5 of the uracil ring, oxidizing tetrahydrofolate to dihydrofolate. Stoichiometry is correct as written.

rxn01286.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of D-glyceraldehyde to D-glycerate, catalyzed by an aldehyde dehydrogenase (NAD+) type enzyme (EC 1.2.1.3 family). The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde carbon is oxidized to a carboxylic acid, consuming water and NAD+ to produce NADH, glycerate, and 2 protons. Carbon (3), oxygen, hydrogen, and charge all balance. Aldehyde dehydrogenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the favorable thermodynamics of carboxylic acid formation and NADH release, driving the reaction in the forward (oxidation) direction.

rxn05343.other_comments: This is a fatty acid elongation condensation step catalyzed by beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (KAS, e.g. FabB/FabF). Octanoyl-ACP (C8) condenses with malonyl-ACP, releasing CO2 and free ACP, to give 3-oxodecanoyl-ACP (C10). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the malonyl group provides 2 carbons to extend the acyl chain while one carbon is lost as CO2. Atoms and charges balance (1 octanoyl + 1 malonyl -> 1 CO2 + 1 3-oxodecanoyl + 1 free ACP).

rxn03395.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis, corresponding to UbiG activity. SAM methylates the hydroxyl group of 2-octaprenyl-6-hydroxyphenol to form 2-octaprenyl-6-methoxyphenol, releasing S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The atom and charge balance is consistent: the methyl group is transferred from SAM, and the released H+ accounts for the deprotonation of the phenolic hydroxyl during methylation. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the high transfer potential of the methylsulfonium group.

rxn05736.other_comments: This is the fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (long-chain) reaction activating myristic acid (C14) to myristoyl-CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + myristate yields myristoyl-CoA + AMP + PPi, with one proton released. The thioester bond is formed via an acyl-AMP intermediate. In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making fatty acid activation effectively irreversible.

rxn00117.other_comments: This is the nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDK) reaction, transferring a phosphate from ATP to UDP, producing ADP and UTP. The reaction is balanced: ATP (C10H12N5O13P3) + UDP (C9H11N2O12P2) gives ADP (C10H12N5O10P2) + UTP (C9H11N2O15P3). Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn02246.other_comments: This reaction represents O-acetylserine sulfhydrylase acting with thiosulfate (H2S2O3) instead of sulfide. O-Acetyl-L-serine reacts with thiosulfate to form S-sulfocysteine, releasing acetate and a proton. The atoms balance: thiosulfate (S2O3H2) plus O-acetylserine yields acetate (C2H3O2), a proton, and S-sulfocysteine, which carries the additional sulfonate group. This is the cysteine synthase (CysM-type) thiosulfate pathway.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction relative to the named enzyme (malate synthase, EC 2.3.3.9); the catalyzed reaction is the condensation of acetyl-CoA and glyoxylate to form malate and CoA, i.e. the reverse of what is written here
The named enzyme function 'acetyl-CoA:glyoxylate C-acetyltransferase' describes acetyl-CoA + glyoxylate + H2O -> malate + CoA, not the hydrolysis/cleavage direction shown
rxn00330.other_comments: This is malate synthase. The reaction as written (CoA + H+ + L-malate -> H2O + acetyl-CoA + glyoxylate) is stoichiometrically and charge balanced (C6 on each side: malate C4 + acetyl-CoA acetyl C2; H balance accounts for H+ and H2O). However, in vivo malate synthase strongly favors malate formation due to thioester hydrolysis providing a large negative free energy change, so the physiological direction is acetyl-CoA + glyoxylate + H2O -> malate + CoA + H+, the reverse of what is depicted.

rxn03445.other_comments: This is the PdxA-related/SerC (PdxC, PhosphoSerine aminotransferase) step in pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (vitamin B6) biosynthesis. The reaction is the transamination between 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine (O-phospho-4-hydroxy-L-threonine) and 2-oxoglutarate, producing 2-oxo-3-hydroxy-4-phosphobutanoate (the corresponding 2-keto acid) and L-glutamate. The carbon and nitrogen balance: amino acid + keto acid <=> keto acid + amino acid, which is stoichiometrically balanced. In vivo, the physiological direction in the B6 biosynthetic pathway runs from 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine toward the keto acid intermediate (catalyzed by PdxA in some annotations), so the productive direction is the one shown as reverse relative to the name (i.e., consuming 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine + 2-oxoglutarate). Note: the canonical PdxB/SerC steps; this aminotransferase step is the SerC-catalyzed transamination running in the direction that consumes phosphohydroxythreonine.

rxn00493.other_comments: This is the aromatic amino acid aminotransferase reaction (EC 2.6.1.57). L-Phenylalanine donates its amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, producing phenylpyruvate and L-glutamate. The reaction is balanced: each side has the same atoms (transamination simply swaps an amino group for a keto group). C: phenylalanine C9 + 2-OG C5 = 14; glutamate C5 + phenylpyruvate C9 = 14. N: 1 on each side. Charges balance as well.

rxn08298.other_comments: This is diacylglycerol kinase transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the sn-3 hydroxyl of a 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol bearing two C16:1 (hexadec-9-enoyl) chains, producing phosphatidic acid (the diacylglycerol 3-phosphate) and ADP. Atoms and charges balance: ATP + DAG -> ADP + phosphatidic acid. Phosphoryl transfer from ATP to a diacylglycerol acceptor is strongly exergonic and proceeds in the kinase (phosphorylation) direction in vivo.

rxn01834.other_comments: This is the glyoxalase I (lactoylglutathione lyase) reaction. The reaction as written shows the breakdown of (R)-S-lactoylglutathione into glutathione (GSH) and methylglyoxal (2-oxopropanal). Stoichiometry is balanced: the hemithioacetal/thioester adduct of GSH with methylglyoxal isomerizes from the non-enzymatic hemithioacetal. In vivo, glyoxalase I drives the forward direction, converting the hemithioacetal of GSH and methylglyoxal into S-D-lactoylglutathione (i.e., GSH + methylglyoxal -> S-lactoylglutathione). As written here, the favored biological direction is the reverse (formation of S-lactoylglutathione from GSH + methylglyoxal).

rxn01226.other_comments: This is the guanosine ribohydrolase (purine nucleosidase) reaction, hydrolyzing guanosine into D-ribose and guanine. The reaction is balanced: guanosine (C10H13N5O5) + H2O (H2O) yields D-ribose (C5H10O5) + guanine (C5H5N5O). Atoms balance (C10, H15, N5, O6 on each side). Hydrolytic nucleoside cleavage is thermodynamically favorable and operates in the catabolic/forward direction in vivo.

rxn00293.other_comments: This is the UDP-N-acetylglucosamine pyrophosphorylase (GlmU) reaction. UTP reacts with N-acetyl-alpha-D-glucosamine 1-phosphate to form UDP-N-acetylglucosamine and pyrophosphate (PPi). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: both sides carry the appropriate phosphate and nucleotide moieties, with PPi released. In vivo, although the enzyme is intrinsically reversible, the reaction is typically driven forward (biosynthetic direction) by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making UDP-GlcNAc synthesis favored. Thermodynamically the uridylyltransferase step itself is near-equilibrium/reversible.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: 4-(phosphonooxy)-threonine (C4H10NO7P) oxidatively decarboxylated to 3-amino-2-oxopropyl phosphate (C3H8NO5P) plus CO2 requires correct H and O balancing; the equation as written is missing an H+ on the NADH side and does not balance hydrogens/oxygens properly

The substrate is normally 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine, and the product of PdxA (4-phosphohydroxy-threonine dehydrogenase) is 2-amino-3-oxo-4-phosphonooxybutanoate, which spontaneously decarboxylates to 3-amino-2-oxopropyl phosphate; combining these steps without an H+ leaves charge/atom imbalance
Charge imbalance: NAD+ to NADH transfer should release a proton (H+), which is not shown
rxn11663.other_comments: This represents the PdxA reaction in pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (vitamin B6) biosynthesis: NAD-dependent oxidation and decarboxylation of 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine to give 3-amino-2-oxopropyl phosphate (3-amino-1-hydroxyacetone 1-phosphate). The oxidative decarboxylation with concomitant NAD+ reduction drives it forward in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides (L-Lysine + H+ <=> L-Lysine + H+), which is a null reaction with no net change
No compartment annotations are shown; a transport reaction requires distinct compartments (e.g., L-Lysine[c] + H+[e] <=> L-Lysine[e] + H+[c]) to represent the antiport translocation
The name says 'proton antiport' but the stoichiometry shows H+ on the same side as L-lysine on each side, which is inconsistent with antiport (substrates moving in opposite directions)
rxn05305.other_comments: This is intended to be a transmembrane transport reaction for L-lysine coupled to proton movement (antiport). As written, without compartment tags, both sides are identical and the reaction is meaningless. A correct lysine/proton antiport would have lysine and proton crossing the membrane in opposite directions, e.g., Lys[in] + H+[out] <=> Lys[out] + H+[in].

rxn04024.other_comments: This is the hydratase reaction (enoyl-CoA hydratase type) where water is added across the alpha-beta double bond of feruloyl-CoA to give the beta-hydroxypropionyl-CoA derivative (3-hydroxy-3-(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)propanoyl-CoA). It is part of the CoA-dependent, beta-oxidative ferulic acid degradation pathway catalyzed by feruloyl-CoA hydratase/lyase (HCHL/Ech-type enzymes). Stoichiometry is balanced: one water added to the unsaturated thioester yields the hydroxylated saturated thioester. The hydration step is typically committed toward the hydroxy product in the degradation direction, although enoyl-CoA hydratases are intrinsically reversible.

errors: The reaction has identical reactants and products (H+ + Adenine on both sides), making it a null/trivial reaction with no net chemical transformation
If intended as a proton-coupled transport reaction, the compartmental designations (e.g., periplasm vs cytoplasm) are missing, so the transport nature is not represented
rxn05491.other_comments: The reaction as written (rxn05491, TRANS-RXN-198) shows H+ + Adenine on both the substrate and product side. This appears to be intended as a proton/adenine symport transport reaction across a membrane, but without distinct compartment labels the two sides are chemically identical, yielding a net-zero (empty) reaction. Stoichiometry is balanced trivially but biologically meaningless as displayed.

rxn00839.other_comments: This is the nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDK/NDPK) reaction transferring a gamma-phosphate from ATP to dADP, producing ADP and dATP. The reaction is balanced: ATP (C10H16N5O13P3) + dADP (C10H15N5O9P2) yields ADP (C10H15N5O10P3) + dATP (C10H16N5O12P3), with atoms and charges conserved. NDP kinase has broad substrate specificity for both ribo- and deoxyribonucleotides.

rxn21857.other_comments: This is the ketoreductase step in the biosynthesis of the polyketide-like methyl ester acyl carrier protein intermediates (e.g., in biotin/pimeloyl-ACP methyl ester pathway). NADPH and H+ reduce the 3-keto group of 3-oxoglutaryl-ACP methyl ester to the 3-hydroxy group, regenerating NADP+. The reaction is balanced: NADPH + H+ provides the hydride and proton to convert the ketone (C=O) to a secondary alcohol (CH-OH), with NADP+ released. Carbon, hydrogen, and redox balance are consistent.

rxn14011.other_comments: This is a cis-prenyltransferase (UppS-type) reaction adding one isopentenyl diphosphate (C5) unit to ditrans,pentacis-octaprenyl diphosphate (C40, 8 isoprene units) to yield ditrans,hexacis-nonaprenyl diphosphate (C45, 9 isoprene units), releasing pyrophosphate and a proton. The condensation creates a new cis double bond. Stoichiometry balances: C40 substrate + C5 IPP = C45 product + PPi, with H+ released from the condensation. Carbon, phosphorus, and charge are balanced. This is a chain-elongation step in undecaprenyl/polyprenyl diphosphate biosynthesis.

rxn00367.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of CTP to CMP and pyrophosphate (PPi), releasing protons. Checking the mass and charge balance: CTP has formula C9H12N3O14P3 (charge -4), water adds H2O, products are CMP (C9H12N3O8P, charge -2) plus PPi (HP2O7, charge -3) plus 2 H+. Atom balance: CTP (9C, 14N->3N, 14O, 3P) + H2O. Phosphorus: 3 on CTP = 1 (CMP) + 2 (PPi), balanced. The breaking of the bond between the alpha and beta phosphate yields CMP + PPi. Charge: left CTP(-4) = right CMP(-2) + PPi(-3) + 2H+(+2) = -3, while left including H2O is -4. There appears to be a charge imbalance of 1; the proton count may need adjustment (likely only 1 H+ released rather than 2 depending on protonation states).

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: hydrolysis of a methyl ester releases the free carboxylic acid, so the product should be the carboxylate form (pimelyl-ACP carrying a free carboxyl group) plus methanol; if pimelyl-[ACP] is written as the protonated acid the proton balance should be checked, but as written the reaction is essentially balanced for the methyl ester hydrolysis
rxn16573.other_comments: This is the BioH-catalyzed step in biotin biosynthesis: hydrolysis of the methyl ester of pimelyl-ACP to yield free pimelyl-ACP (carboxyl form) and methanol. Hydrolysis of an ester with water consuming H2O is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically proceeds in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn14159.other_comments: This is the ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase (FNR) reaction. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADP+ + H+ + 2 reduced ferredoxin yields NADPH + 2 oxidized ferredoxin. rxn23042.other_comments: This is the thiamine phosphate synthase reaction. rxn15395.other_comments: This is the cystathionine gamma-synthase reaction (EC 2.5.1.48). L-Cysteine displaces the succinate from O-succinyl-L-homoserine to form L-cystathionine plus succinate. rxn15466.other_comments: This is the ketol-acid reductoisomerase (KARI, EC 1.1.1.86) reaction in branched-chain amino acid (valine/leucine) biosynthesis. rxn47768.other_comments: This is a Claisen-type condensation reaction (FabB/FabF-like, KAS condensing enzyme). rxn15021.other_comments: This is acetolactate synthase (AHAS), which condenses two pyruvate molecules to form (S)-2-acetolactate plus CO2 (the decarboxylation of one pyruvate). Carbon balances (6=5+1), and charge/H balance with the H+ shown. In vivo this enzyme strongly favors acetolactate formation, so the biological direction is opposite to how this reaction is written.

rxn08475.other_comments: This is a transport reaction moving Fe2+ from the extracellular space to the periplasm via passive diffusion. Passive diffusion is driven by the concentration gradient, so the reaction is appropriately modeled as reversible.

Stoichiometric H2O usage is questionable; the dithiolene formation generally releases water rather than (or in addition to) consuming it, so a single H2O on the substrate side may be incorrect
rxn41896.other_comments: This represents the MPT synthase (MoaD/MoaE) catalyzed reaction converting Precursor Z (cPMP) to molybdopterin using two thiocarboxylated MPT synthase small subunits, regenerating two thiol-form (Thi-S) subunits. This sulfur-transfer/dithiolene-forming step is essentially irreversible in vivo (the thiocarboxylate is a consumed activated sulfur donor).

rxn16583.other_comments: This represents the final step of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis catalyzed by MoeA/gephyrin-type molybdate transferase. Adenylated molybdopterin (Mo-MPT-AMP) reacts with molybdate, inserting molybdenum and releasing AMP and water to form the mature Mo cofactor. The stoichiometry is balanced: the adenylyl group leaves as AMP, the H+ and molybdate are consumed, and water is released. In vivo this hydrolytic, biosynthetic insertion step proceeds in the forward direction toward mature Moco formation.

rxn10506.other_comments: This is the deaminase step in riboflavin biosynthesis, converting 2,5-diamino-6-ribitylamino-4(3H)-pyrimidinone 5'-phosphate to 5-amino-6-(5-phosphoribitylamino)uracil. The reaction is a hydrolytic deamination: water and a proton are consumed, ammonia is released. Stoichiometry is balanced with H2O + H+ in giving NH3 (as NH4+ effectively) plus the product. The deamination is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven physiologically in the biosynthetic direction.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is unbalanced in a functional sense: 2.0 H+ appears on both sides and cancels out, leaving no net proton translocation. A true membrane-bound (energy-linked) transhydrogenase couples hydride transfer to translocation of one proton across the membrane, so protons on opposite sides/compartments should not cancel. As written it reduces to a soluble (energy-independent) transhydrogenase: NADH + NADP+ <=> NAD+ + NADPH.
If intended as the proton-translocating periplasmic/membrane enzyme, the H+ should be in different compartments (e.g., periplasm vs cytoplasm) and not cancel.
rxn09295.other_comments: This is a pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase reaction transferring a hydride between NADH/NAD+ and NADP+/NADPH. The hydride transfer itself is thermodynamically near-equilibrium and intrinsically reversible; in vivo direction depends on proton-motive force and nucleotide ratios. As written the protons cancel, so it behaves like the soluble UdhA-type enzyme rather than the proton-pumping PntAB.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction relative to the enzyme name and known biochemistry; the physiological reaction is the reductive direction (NADPH + 2,3-dihydrodipicolinate -> NADP+ + tetrahydrodipicolinate), not an oxidation producing a 4-hydroxy product
The substrate/product pairing is incorrect: dihydrodipicolinate reductase (DapB) reduces 2,3-dihydrodipicolinate to tetrahydrodipicolinate, it does not produce a 4-hydroxy-tetrahydrodipicolinate
H2O is not a participant in the dihydrodipicolinate reductase reaction as written

The redox bookkeeping is inconsistent: converting tetrahydrodipicolinate to a hydroxylated product while generating NADPH (reduced cofactor) violates electron balance, since adding a hydroxyl/oxidizing the substrate should consume NADPH, not produce it
rxn39452.other_comments: This appears intended to represent dihydrodipicolinate reductase (DapB) chemistry in the lysine/DAP biosynthesis pathway, which normally reduces 2,3-dihydrodipicolinate to 2,3,4,5-tetrahydrodipicolinate using NAD(P)H. As written, the reaction couples NADP+ reduction (to NADPH) with formation of a 4-hydroxy-tetrahydrodipicolinate from tetrahydrodipicolinate, which is both stoichiometrically and redox-inconsistent.

rxn41452.other_comments: This is a malonyl-ACP O-methyltransferase reaction (BioC, EC 2.1.1.197). SAM donates a methyl group to the free carboxylate of malonyl-ACP, producing the malonyl-ACP methyl ester and S-adenosyl-homocysteine. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced with a 1:1:1:1 ratio of substrates and products, and is part of the biotin biosynthesis pathway. SAM-dependent methyltransferases strongly favor the forward (methyl transfer) direction in vivo.

rxn21864.other_comments: This is the BioB/BioF-type reaction catalyzed by 8-amino-7-oxononanoate synthase (AONS, bioF). It is the decarboxylative condensation of pimeloyl-ACP with L-alanine to form 8-amino-7-oxononanoate (AON, also called 7-keto-8-aminopelargonate), releasing CO2 and free ACP. The atoms balance: pimeloyl group (C7 diacid thioester) condenses with alanine (C3), losing CO2 (C1) to give the C9 product AON. The H+ and CoA/ACP bookkeeping are consistent. This is a key step in biotin biosynthesis. [directionality_note] The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo due to decarboxylation (loss of CO2), driving the reaction forward.

rxn21858.other_comments: This is a dehydration reaction in fatty acid/polyketide-type biosynthesis. 3-Hydroxyglutaryl-ACP-methyl-ester loses water to form the enoyl (alpha,beta-unsaturated) glutaryl-ACP-methyl-ester. The stoichiometry is balanced: removal of one H2O from the hydroxyl-containing substrate yields the unsaturated product plus water. This is analogous to the beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase (FabA/FabZ-type) step, which proceeds in the dehydration direction in vivo during chain elongation.

errors: The reaction is not mass/atom balanced as written: condensation of GTP with the molybdenum cofactor (Mo-MPT) to form the bis-MGD (molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide) cofactor releases pyrophosphate (PPi), but the formula 'bis(molybdenum cofactor)' and product 'Mo(Dtpp-mGDP)2' are nonstandard/ambiguous and cannot be confirmed to balance phosphate, Mo, and guanine atoms
The conversion of Mo-MPT to Mo-MGD via MobA actually consumes GTP and Mg2+; Mg2+ cofactor is not shown
Stoichiometry of 2 GTP per Mo center requires 2 MPT moieties; the substrate naming 'bis(molybdenum cofactor)' implies two pterins already present, which should be made explicit
rxn44539.other_comments: This appears to represent the MobA-catalyzed maturation of the molybdenum cofactor: attachment of two GMP groups to the molybdopterin (MPT) dithiolene-pyranopterin to form the bis-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide (bis-MGD) cofactor, releasing 2 pyrophosphate. The biosynthetic guanylylation step is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven by PPi release/hydrolysis.

errors: Charge and proton balance not explicitly shown; adenylyltransferase reactions transferring AMP to a phosphate group typically release pyrophosphate (PPi), which is consistent here, but the molybdopterin terminal phosphate is required as the acceptor and should be specified
rxn16574.other_comments: This represents the MoaB/MogA-type (or molybdopterin adenylyltransferase) activation step where ATP adenylylates molybdopterin to form adenylated molybdopterin (MPT-AMP) plus pyrophosphate. The reaction is part of the Mo-cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis pathway. Stoichiometry (one ATP consumed, one PPi released, one AMP transferred to molybdopterin) is balanced in principle. In vivo, subsequent rapid hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase drives the reaction toward adenylylation, making it effectively forward.

errors: The reaction as written is incorrect. The enzyme dihydrodipicolinate reductase (DapB, EC 1.17.1.8 / 1.3.1.26) catalyzes the REDUCTION of 2,3-dihydrodipicolinate to 2,3,4,5-tetrahydrodipicolinate, not a hydroxylation. The actual reaction is: 2,3-dihydrodipicolinate + NAD(P)H + H+ <=> 2,3,4,5-tetrahydrodipicolinate + NAD(P)+

The product (2S,4S)-4-hydroxy-2,3,4,5-tetrahydrodipicolinate is not a recognized product of this pathway; the standard DAP/lysine biosynthesis does not include a 4-hydroxylated tetrahydrodipicolinate intermediate via NAD-dependent oxidation

Stoichiometric/redox inconsistency: oxidation of a substrate by NAD+ to give NADH should remove hydrogens (dehydrogenation) or, if hydroxylation occurs, typically requires O2 (monooxygenase) rather than H2O + NAD+; coupling H2O addition with NAD+ reduction to introduce a hydroxyl is not balanced for a simple oxidoreductase as written
rxn39451.other_comments: The named enzyme (2,3,4,5-tetrahydrodipicolinate:NAD+ 4-oxidoreductase) implies oxidation of tetrahydrodipicolinate at C4 to form a 4-hydroxy product with NAD+ as electron acceptor. This appears to be a non-standard or erroneous reaction; the well-characterized biology here is the reverse direction (reduction of dihydrodipicolinate by DapB in lysine biosynthesis).

rxn40439.other_comments: This is the adenosylmethionine-8-amino-7-oxononanoate aminotransferase-like reaction but using L-lysine as the amino donor. The enzyme (related to BioA) transfers an amino group from L-lysine to 8-amino-7-oxononanoate (KAPA/AON), producing 7,8-diaminononanoate (DAPA) and converting L-lysine to allysine (2-aminoadipate 6-semialdehyde / L-2-aminoadipate-6-semialdehyde). The amino group transfer is balanced: lysine loses its epsilon-amino group (becoming allysine, the 6-semialdehyde) and donates it to the keto carbon of AON. Stoichiometry and atom balance are consistent for a transamination. Aminotransferase reactions are generally reversible, though in vivo this typically proceeds toward DAPA formation in biotin biosynthesis.

errors: Proton (H+) balance is not shown; the conversion of cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate (Precursor Z) to molybdopterin typically releases protons that should appear in a balanced reaction

Water as a reactant is questionable; the sulfur transfer mechanism incorporates two sulfur atoms from the thiocarboxylated synthase C-termini, and the byproduct is more accurately the carboxylated (or carboxy-terminal Gly) form of the synthase rather than simply regenerated MPT-synthase without accounting for the oxygen/water exchange
rxn24830.other_comments: This is the molybdopterin synthase reaction: Precursor Z (cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate) is converted to molybdopterin (MPT) by incorporation of two sulfur atoms donated by the thiocarboxylated C-termini of two MoaD subunits (thiocarboxylated MPT-synthase), regenerating the carboxylate form of MPT-synthase. The 2:1 stoichiometry of synthase subunits to product reflects the two dithiolene sulfurs added.

Electron balance mismatch: reduction of 2 Co(II) to Co(I) (the reactive intermediate that attacks ATP) requires 2 electrons, but Reduced-Flavoprotein typically donates 2 electrons (1 FADH2), so the 1:2 ratio of flavoprotein to cobinamide for a two-electron-per-cobalt reduction is inconsistent

Adenosyl cobinamide is formed by transfer of the 5'-deoxyadenosyl moiety from ATP, releasing triphosphate (PPPi); this part appears reasonable but the elemental/cobalt redox state balance should be verified
rxn42230.other_comments: This represents the adenosylation of cobinamide (a cobalamin/B12 biosynthetic intermediate), where Co(II)-cobinamide is reductively adenosylated using ATP and electrons from a reduced flavoprotein (corrinoid adenosyltransferase, e.g. CobA/PduO/EutT type). The 5'-deoxyadenosyl group is transferred to the cobalt, releasing inorganic triphosphate. In vivo this is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

errors: Reaction is not mass/charge balanced as written: MobA transfers a GMP moiety from GTP to molybdopterin (Mo-MPT) forming molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide (MGD/bis-MGD) and releasing pyrophosphate. The phosphate accounting requires that GTP donates GMP while releasing PPi, which is consistent, but the substrate should be specified as the molybdopterin form of the molybdenum cofactor (Mo-MPT) rather than a generic 'Molybdoenzyme molybdenum cofactor'.
rxn26021.other_comments: This represents the MobA-catalyzed guanylylation reaction: GTP + molybdopterin (Mo-MPT) -> MGD (molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide) + PPi. The reaction is driven forward in vivo by subsequent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making it essentially irreversible toward MGD synthesis.

rxn42530.other_comments: This is the D-lysine oxidase / amino acid oxidase type reaction. D-Lysine is oxidatively deaminated using O2 and H2O, producing the corresponding 2-oxo acid (2-oxo-6-aminohexanoate, i.e. 2-keto-6-aminocaproate), ammonia (NH3), and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). The stoichiometry is balanced: D-Lysine (C6H14N2O2) + H2O + O2 -> 2-oxo-6-aminocaproate (C6H11NO3) + NH3 + H2O2. Carbon (6=6), nitrogen (2=1+1), and the overall atom/charge balance check out. Flavin oxidase reactions consuming O2 and generating H2O2 are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the oxidative deamination direction.

errors: Reaction is not mass-balanced as written; the combination of molybdopterin and a molybdenum cofactor to form bis(molybdenum cofactor) (MGD-type or Mo-bisMGD) typically requires additional substrates such as GTP/CTP and Mg2+, and the stoichiometry of Mo and pterin atoms is not clearly conserved
Molybdenum atom balance is unclear: 'Molybdopterin' generally lacks Mo whereas the products are Mo-containing cofactors; a Mo source is needed
The participants are poorly defined generic entities making elemental balance impossible to verify
rxn41683.other_comments: This appears to represent biosynthesis/maturation of a bis-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide (bis-Mo-cofactor) type cofactor from molybdopterin and a molybdenum cofactor, with water release. As written the entities are ill-defined and the equation cannot be confirmed as balanced; biologically such maturation steps are generally driven forward, but no clear data here.

rxn07436.other_comments: This reaction describes the QueF-catalyzed reduction of preQ0 (7-cyano-7-deazaguanine) to preQ1 (7-aminomethyl-7-carbaguanine, Base Q). As written, it shows the oxidation direction (Base Q + 2 NADP+ -> preQ0 + 2 NADPH + 3 H+). The nitrile reduction to a primary amine consumes 4 electrons (2 NADPH) and is balanced with respect to H and charge. In vivo, QueF strongly favors the reductive direction (preQ0 -> preQ1), so relative to the way it is written here (left-to-right being oxidation), the biological flux is in the reverse direction.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: ureidoacrylate (C4H6N2O3) + H2O should yield products that conserve atoms; the listed products (carbamate CH3NO2 + aminoacrylate C3H5NO2) plus H+ do not balance. Ureidoacrylate hydrolysis typically yields 2-aminoacrylate plus carbamate (which decomposes to CO2/NH3), but the H+ and atom counts as written should be verified.
The product 'Aminoacrylate' (2-aminoacrylate) is unstable and tautomerizes/hydrolyzes spontaneously to pyruvate and ammonia in vivo.
rxn16826.other_comments: This represents the RutB-type ureidoacrylate amidohydrolase (peptidase) reaction in the pyrimidine utilization (Rut) pathway, hydrolyzing ureidoacrylate to 2-aminoacrylate and carbamate. The hydrolytic cleavage of the amide/ureido bond is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn16829.other_comments: This represents the hydrolytic deamination of 2-aminoacrylate (2-aminoprop-2-enoate, an enamine/imine tautomer) to yield ammonia and malonate semialdehyde (3-oxopropanoate). 2-Aminoacrylate is an unstable, reactive enamine that spontaneously hydrolyzes; via its keto tautomer (2-iminopropanoate) it undergoes hydration and loss of ammonia. The reaction balances: C3H5NO2 (aminoacrylate) + H2O + H+ gives NH4+ (or NH3) + C3H4O3. Atoms and charge balance depending on protonation states used; with H+ on the left and neutral NH3 the mass balance is consistent (C3, sums of H and O check out).

rxn16776.other_comments: This represents an RutA-type flavin-dependent monooxygenase step in pyrimidine (uracil) degradation. RutA uses FMNH2 (provided by an NADH-dependent flavin reductase, RutF) and O2 to oxygenate uracil, opening the ring to give (Z)-3-ureidoacrylate peracid, which is subsequently processed by RutB. The FMNH2 is oxidized to FMN. Biologically this is a catabolic, essentially irreversible oxygenation; oxygen incorporation into the peracid product makes the reverse infeasible.

errors: Atom imbalance: the products as written do not balance with the substrates. (Z)-3-Ureidoacrylate peracid (C4H6N2O4) + H2O (H2O) gives C4H8N2O5 on the left; carbamate (CH3NO2 / NH2COO-, ~CH3NO2) + (Z)-3-peroxyaminoacrylate must account for the remaining atoms, but the named '(Z)-3-Peroxyaminoacrylate' is not a standard well-defined species and the split of the ureido group into carbamate + aminoacrylate-peroxide appears atom-inconsistent
Charge balance uncertain: H+ is released, implying anionic products (carbamate as carbamate ion), but neutral product names are used inconsistently
Product '(Z)-3-Peroxyaminoacrylate' is poorly defined / likely nonstandard nomenclature
rxn16794.other_comments: This is a putative hydrolytic cleavage (amidohydrolase) of a ureido/peracid intermediate, analogous to RutB-type ring-opening hydrolysis in pyrimidine degradation, releasing carbamate. Hydrolases typically proceed in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo. However, the specific peracid/peroxyamino species are unusual and the written stoichiometry cannot be confirmed as balanced.

errors: Mass imbalance: the product 2-Octaprenyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinone has one more oxygen than the substrate 2-Octaprenyl-6-methoxyphenol, but only one H2O is produced. Atom balance: substrate phenol C(n)H(m)O2 (one OH + one OCH3) gains a carbonyl oxygen to form the para-quinone (two C=O plus OCH3 = 3 O). One O comes from O2 (hydroxylation), the other O of O2 becomes H2O. Hydrogen balance must be checked but appears off by accounting for the H released on quinone formation.
rxn03396.other_comments: This is the UbiH/UbiF-type monooxygenase (hydroxylase) step in ubiquinone biosynthesis, converting 2-octaprenyl-6-methoxyphenol to the corresponding benzoquinone using molecular oxygen and NADPH. Oxygenase reactions consuming O2 and NADPH are physiologically irreversible (forward) in vivo. The stoichiometry as written should be carefully checked for H and O balance.

rxn13741.other_comments: This is the proline dehydrogenase (proline oxidase, PutA) reaction. L-Proline is oxidized to (S)-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate, with electrons transferred via FAD to ubiquinone-8, producing ubiquinol-8. Atoms balance: proline (C5H9NO2) loses 2 H (2 H equivalents) to form P5C (C5H7NO2), and ubiquinone-8 + 2H -> ubiquinol-8. The proton on the right balances charge/H accounting given the redox couple. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: Incorrect product stereochemistry/identity: the product of 6-phosphogluconate dehydratase (EDD, EC 4.2.1.12) should be 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-6-phospho-D-gluconate (KDPG), not 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-galactonate 6-phosphate; the named product corresponds to a different enzyme/substrate series (galactonate)
rxn15296.other_comments: This is the Entner-Doudoroff dehydratase reaction converting 6-phospho-D-gluconate to KDPG with loss of water. Atom balance (C6, P, with water release) is internally consistent, but the stated product name uses the galactonate configuration rather than the expected gluconate-derived KDPG.

errors: The reaction as written is identical on both sides (L-Arginine + Ornithine on both reactant and product side), which is meaningless. A proper antiporter transport reaction must specify compartments, e.g., L-Arginine[periplasm] + Ornithine[cytosol] <=> L-Arginine[cytosol] + Ornithine[periplasm]. Without compartment designations, no net transport or transformation is represented.
rxn08153.other_comments: This is intended to be an arginine/ornithine antiporter (e.g., ArcD), which exchanges extracellular/periplasmic arginine for intracellular ornithine. As written, both sides are identical because compartment tags are missing, so the equation is a null reaction. Antiporters are typically modeled as reversible, with net direction driven by concentration gradients (arginine in, ornithine out in the arginine deiminase pathway).

errors: Reactant and product are identical (H+ + Shikimate on both sides), so no net chemical transformation occurs.

rxn09256.other_comments: The reaction ID (TRANS-RXN-27) and the .cp suffix indicate this is a transport reaction, likely a proton-coupled shikimate symporter. As written without compartment labels, both sides are identical and the reaction is stoichiometrically trivial/null. Transporters are often treated as reversible depending on electrochemical gradients.

rxn22316.other_comments: This represents adenylyl-sulfate reductase (thioredoxin), EC 1.8.4.10. The physiological reaction is APS + reduced thioredoxin -> AMP + sulfite + oxidized thioredoxin, i.e., reduction of APS to sulfite using thioredoxin as electron donor (part of the assimilatory sulfate reduction pathway). As written here (AMP + sulfite + Ox-Trx -> APS + Red-Trx), the equation is in the reverse (non-physiological) direction. The atom stoichiometry of substrates/products is otherwise consistent.

errors: The product 2-C-methyl-D-erythritol 2,4-cyclodiphosphate (MEcPP) is incorrect for the forward direction shown; this reaction (IspG/GcpE) converts MEcPP into HMBPP, so the substrate and product are swapped relative to the listed direction

Electron/proton balance is questionable: the reductive ring-opening requires 2 electrons (from reduced flavodoxin) plus protons, but here oxidized flavodoxin appears on the substrate side which contradicts a reductive reaction
rxn43581.other_comments: This corresponds to the IspG (GcpE) step of the MEP/non-mevalonate isoprenoid pathway. The physiological reaction is the reductive ring-opening of MEcPP to form HMBPP (1-hydroxy-2-methyl-2-butenyl 4-diphosphate), consuming reduced flavodoxin and releasing water. As written, the equation has substrates and products reversed and the water/cofactor placement is inconsistent with the in vivo biochemistry.

rxn08241.other_comments: This is a passive diffusion transport reaction moving Co2+ ions from the extracellular space to the periplasm. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (one Co2+ on each side, representing the same species in two different compartments). Passive diffusion driven by concentration gradient is inherently reversible, with net direction determined by the electrochemical gradient of Co2+ across the outer membrane.

rxn25971.other_comments: This is the archaetidylserine synthase reaction (RXN-9996), part of archaeal phospholipid biosynthesis. L-Serine is transferred to the CDP-activated glycerol backbone CDP-2,3-bis-O-(geranylgeranyl)-sn-glycerol, releasing CMP and producing archaetidylserine. The stoichiometry is balanced: the serine hydroxyl attacks the phosphate, displacing CMP and releasing a proton. This is analogous to phosphatidylserine synthase in bacteria/eukaryotes (CDP-DAG pathway). The CMP-displacing reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of archaetidylserine synthesis.

rxn09193.other_comments: This is a passive diffusion transport reaction moving L-proline from the extracellular space to the periplasm. The metabolite is identical on both sides (L-proline), differing only in cellular compartment. Stoichiometry is balanced 1:1, which is correct for a simple transport/diffusion process. Passive diffusion is inherently bidirectional and driven by concentration gradients, so it is properly modeled as reversible.

errors: Hg2+ appears unchanged on both sides of the equation; for an ABC transporter the transported substrate should be distinguished by compartment (e.g., Hg2+[periplasm] -> Hg2+[cytoplasm]), otherwise the metal ion cancels out and the reaction reduces to simple ATP hydrolysis

rxn08715.other_comments: This is intended to represent an ATP-driven ABC transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to translocation of Hg2+ across a membrane. The ATP hydrolysis portion is correctly balanced (atoms and charge). The directionality is effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo because ATP hydrolysis drives active transport.

errors: This is a transport reaction where the same metabolites (L-Lysine and H+) appear on both sides; without compartment annotations distinguishing the two sides, the reaction appears trivially balanced but biologically meaningless as written
Missing compartment localization tags (e.g., periplasm/extracellular vs cytosol) needed to represent the actual translocation
rxn08854.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled L-lysine symport/transport reaction (TRANS-RXN-58), moving L-Lysine and H+ across a membrane. As written it shows identical species on both sides; the implied physiological process is co-transport of lysine with a proton, typically driven by the proton motive force.

rxn24134.other_comments: This is the OHCU decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.97) in the purine/urate degradation pathway. 2-oxo-4-hydroxy-4-carboxy-5-ureidoimidazoline (OHCU) is decarboxylated to produce (S)-allantoin and CO2. The atom balance is correct: OHCU (C5H6N4O5, as the carboxylate anion C5H5N4O5-) plus H+ yields allantoin (C4H6N4O3) plus CO2 (CO2). Carbon: 5 = 4+1; nitrogen 4=4; the H+ provides the proton for decarboxylation. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo and serves to ensure formation of the pure S-enantiomer of allantoin (non-enzymatic decarboxylation of OHCU yields racemic allantoin).

errors: The substrate naming and stoichiometry are ambiguous; cyanophycin synthesis adds an aspartate residue to the growing cyanophycin polymer, but the product 'cyanophycin primer-L-aspartate' does not clearly reflect addition to the [L-4-(L-arginin-2-N-yl)aspartate]3 primer shown as substrate

rxn46365.other_comments: This appears to represent cyanophycin synthetase (CphA) activity, which uses ATP to add L-aspartate to the cyanophycin primer/polymer backbone, releasing ADP, phosphate, and H+. The ATP-dependent ligation makes the reaction effectively irreversible in vivo toward biosynthesis (forward), though the polymer-elongation stoichiometry as written is unclear.

errors: Proton balance/translocation issue: the cytochrome bd oxidase oxidizes menaquinol releasing 2 H+ to the periplasm, but it also consumes protons from the cytoplasm when reducing the cofactor/oxygen; as written without compartments and without an electron acceptor (O2), the reaction is incomplete. The named acceptor 'cytochrome-bd-ox' to 'cytochrome-bd-red' implies a 2-electron reduction, but menaquinol oxidation yields 2 electrons and 2 H+, so charge/electron balance between the cofactor states must account for 2 electrons.
Missing compartmental annotation for the 2 H+ (these are released to a specific side of the membrane)
rxn14420.other_comments: This represents menaquinol being oxidized to menaquinone by cytochrome bd, releasing 2 protons and reducing the oxidized cytochrome bd to its reduced form. In vivo this is part of the respiratory chain and proceeds in the direction of menaquinol oxidation (forward as written). The redox states of the cytochrome must each accept the 2 electrons for electron balance.

rxn23336.other_comments: This reaction represents the octanoyltransferase (LipB/LipM) reaction, transferring an octanoyl group from octanoyl-ACP to the lipoyl-domain lysine of the glycine cleavage system H protein (GcvH). The stoichiometry is balanced: octanoyl-ACP donates the octanoyl moiety to a lysine residue of GcvH, releasing free ACP and a proton. This is the committed first step of lipoic acid biosynthesis/salvage on GcvH and is physiologically directed toward octanoylation of GcvH.

rxn15467.other_comments: This is the dihydroxy-acid dehydratase reaction (EC 4.2.1.9) in branched-chain amino acid (valine) biosynthesis. rxn01208.other_comments: This corresponds to KEGG R01652, a carboxylation of 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (4MOP, ketoleucine) to form 2-isopropyl-3-oxosuccinate (oxalylmethylvalerate intermediate). The CO2 fixation in this context is part of leucine/branched-chain metabolism. In vivo, biotin-dependent or related carboxylation favors the carboxylation (forward) direction.

rxn10570.other_comments: This represents passive diffusion of methanol across a membrane (likely between two compartments, e.g., extracellular/periplasm and cytoplasm). The reactant and product are the same metabolite (methanol) in different compartments. Stoichiometry is balanced 1:1. Simple diffusion is inherently reversible, driven by the concentration gradient.

errors: Charge imbalance: the H+ on the left side is not consumed in this addition reaction. Formaldehyde (CH2O) adds directly to the thiol of glutathione to form S-(hydroxymethyl)glutathione (the hemithioacetal); no proton is gained or lost. rxn04791.other_comments: This is the spontaneous (or glutathione-dependent) formation of the hemithioacetal S-(hydroxymethyl)glutathione from reduced glutathione and formaldehyde. The thiol of GSH adds across the carbonyl of formaldehyde. Atom balance is correct (C, H, O, N, S match) only if the spurious H+ is removed. errors: This reaction conflates two separate enzymatic steps. 5-Hydroxyisourate (HIU) is first hydrolyzed by HIU hydrolase (EC 3.5.2.17) to 2-oxo-4-hydroxy-4-carboxy-5-ureidoimidazoline (OHCU), which is then decarboxylated by OHCU decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.97) to yield (S)-allantoin and CO2. There is no single enzyme converting HIU directly to allantoin plus CO2.

Mass/atom balance is incorrect for a single step: the net conversion of HIU to allantoin + CO2 requires the addition of two water molecules across the two steps (one for hydrolysis/ring opening of HIU to OHCU, and the decarboxylation), not one. Carbon and oxygen do not balance with only one H2O.

The stereochemistry of the product is wrong: the enzymatic OHCU decarboxylase yields (S)-allantoin, not (R)-allantoin. Non-enzymatic decarboxylation gives racemic allantoin, but the directed enzymatic product is the (S) enantiomer.
rxn04132.other_comments: This represents part of the uric acid degradation (purine catabolism) pathway downstream of urate oxidase. HIU is unstable and is converted to allantoin via OHCU; the overall process is thermodynamically driven forward by decarboxylation (loss of CO2), making it effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the conversion of 2-amino-3-carboxymuconate semialdehyde to quinolinate is a non-enzymatic cyclization/dehydration that releases water and ammonia. Going in the written forward direction (quinolinate to ACMS), the equation does not balance - quinolinate + H2O does not provide the nitrogen needed for the amino group of ACMS, and the atoms do not match.
Mass/atom imbalance: quinolinate (C7H3NO4 as anion) plus H2O cannot yield 2-amino-3-carboxymuconate semialdehyde (C7H7NO5) - nitrogen and hydrogen/oxygen counts are inconsistent.
rxn02989.other_comments: This reaction relates to the kynurenine pathway. 2-amino-3-carboxymuconate semialdehyde (ACMS) undergoes spontaneous (non-enzymatic) cyclization with loss of water to form quinolinate. So the biologically favored direction is ACMS -> quinolinate + H2O, i.e., the reverse of how it is written here. The written direction also appears unbalanced because the nitrogen of the amino group is unaccounted for.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction as written includes a free H+ on the left but ATP and ITP are typically represented as charged species; with H+ added, charge is not balanced. The correct deamination releases NH3 (or NH4+) and the proton balance should yield H+ on the product side, not consumed.
If species are written as neutral (ATP, ITP, NH3), then the extra H+ on the substrate side is incorrect and breaks both mass and charge balance.
rxn00064.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic deamination of ATP to ITP, converting the adenine 6-amino group to a 6-oxo (hypoxanthine) group with release of ammonia. Mass balance of the heavy atoms (the amino N leaves as NH3, replaced by O from water) is essentially correct, but the proton/charge accounting (the lone H+ on the left) is questionable.

errors: This reaction has identical substrate and product (O2 = O2), so it has no net chemical transformation
No stoichiometric imbalance exists since both sides are identical, but the reaction is biochemically meaningless as written unless it represents a transport process across a membrane
rxn05468.other_comments: The input represents molecular oxygen (O2) on both sides of the reaction. The reaction ID (TRANS-RXNAVI) and naming convention suggest this is intended to be a transport reaction, where O2 is moved between compartments (e.g., extracellular to cytosol or across an organelle membrane). As written without compartment annotations, it appears as a trivial identity reaction. If it is a transport reaction, the two O2 species should be in different compartments (e.g., O2[e] <=> O2[c]). errors: No compartment annotation distinguishes the two BDOH species; a transport reaction must specify different compartments (e.g., BDOH[e] <=> BDOH[c]), otherwise the reaction is trivial/null as written
rxn11322.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction for (R,R)-butanediol (2,3-butanediol). rxn05467.other_comments: This is a transport reaction representing the passive diffusion of carbon dioxide (CO2) across a membrane between two compartments (e.g., extracellular and cytoplasm). The species CO2 is identical on both sides, and the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (1 CO2 in, 1 CO2 out). As a passive diffusion process, it is correctly modeled as reversible, with net flux determined by the concentration gradient.

errors: The product should be 'Glyoxylate' (not 'Glyoxalate'), a spelling/naming error.
rxn23589.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic deamination of iminoglycine (2-iminoacetate / dehydroglycine) to glyoxylate and ammonia. Iminoglycine is the unstable imine product of glycine oxidation (e.g., by glycine oxidase or D-amino acid oxidase). The reaction is balanced: iminoglycine (C2H3NO2) + H2O -> glyoxylate (C2H2O3) + NH3. This spontaneous hydrolysis of the imine strongly favors the forward direction in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometry is not balanced. 5-hydroxyisourate (C5H4N4O4) + H2O (H2O) = C5H6N4O5; products CO2 (CO2) + allantoin (C4H6N4O3) = C5H6N4O5. Atom balance actually checks: C5 vs C5, H6 vs H6, N4 vs N4, O5 vs O5 - the reaction IS balanced. However, this is a simplified/lumped reaction.

The conversion of 5-hydroxyisourate to allantoin is actually a two-step enzymatic process: HIU hydrolase produces 2-oxo-4-hydroxy-4-carboxy-5-ureidoimidazoline (OHCU), and OHCU decarboxylase then produces (S)-allantoin with release of CO2. The single-step lumped reaction omits the OHCU intermediate.
rxn04133.other_comments: This represents the net conversion of 5-hydroxyisourate (HIU) to allantoin in the purine/urate degradation pathway downstream of urate oxidase. The net atom balance (C5H6N4O5 on both sides) is correct, but biologically this lumps two enzymatic steps (HIU hydrolase and OHCU decarboxylase). The decarboxylation step makes this effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn08032.other_comments: This is a transport reaction moving acetaldehyde from the extracellular space to the periplasm via passive diffusion. The same metabolite appears on both sides (differing only by compartment), which is correct for a diffusion transport reaction. Mass and charge are balanced (1 acetaldehyde to 1 acetaldehyde). Passive diffusion driven by concentration gradient is inherently reversible, so the direction depends on the relative concentrations across the membrane.

rxn08428.other_comments: This is a passive diffusion transport reaction moving ethanol from the extracellular compartment to the periplasm. The two sides represent ethanol in different compartments (extracellular and periplasmic). Stoichiometry is balanced (1:1). Passive diffusion follows the concentration gradient and is inherently reversible.

errors: Hydrogen atom imbalance: left side has H2O2 (2 H) + 2-oxo-6-aminocaproate (C6H11NO3, 11 H) = 13 H; right side has H2O (2 H) + CO2 (0 H) + 5-aminopentanoate (C5H11NO2, 11 H) = 13 H, so H balances; however the oxygen and overall balance should be checked: left O = 2 (H2O2) + 3 (substrate) = 5; right O = 1 (H2O) + 2 (CO2) + 2 (5-aminopentanoate) = 5, O balances; carbon: left C6, right C5 + C1 = C6, balances; nitrogen: 1 = 1. rxn24718.other_comments: This is an H2O2-dependent oxidative decarboxylation of 2-oxo-6-aminocaproate (an alpha-keto acid) to 5-aminopentanoate (5-aminovalerate), releasing CO2 and water. The atoms appear to balance (C6, N1, O5, H13 on each side). Such peroxide-driven decarboxylations of 2-oxo acids are strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn08691.other_comments: This represents simple passive diffusion of molecular hydrogen (H2) across the outer membrane from the extracellular space into the periplasm. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (one H2 on each side, identical species in different compartments). Diffusion-based transport reactions are inherently reversible and driven by the concentration gradient, so directionality depends on relative H2 concentrations in each compartment.

rxn09008.other_comments: This is a passive diffusion transport reaction moving nitric oxide (NO) across a membrane from the extracellular space to the periplasm. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (1 NO on each side, same molecule in different compartments). Diffusion-driven transport is inherently reversible and follows the concentration gradient.

errors: Charge imbalance: producing 9 H+ is incorrect; enterobactin formation from 3 DHB-AMP and 3 Ser-AMP releases 6 AMP and a smaller number of protons. The H+ stoichiometry of 9 is not balanced with the formation of 3 amide bonds and 3 ester bonds.
Mass/atom balance should be rechecked: condensation releasing 6 AMP plus the cyclic trilactone backbone formation must account for water/protons consistently.
rxn13827.other_comments: This represents enterobactin (enterochelin) biosynthesis by the EntF/nonribosomal peptide synthetase machinery, condensing three 2,3-dihydroxybenzoyl groups with three L-serine residues to form the cyclic triester siderophore enterobactin, releasing AMP. The overall biosynthesis is thermodynamically driven and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms do not balance. Aminoacetone (C3H7NO) + CO2 (CO2) gives C4 on the left, but L-2-amino-acetoacetate (C4H6NO3, deprotonated form) plus H+ does not balance correctly. rxn02666.other_comments: The biologically relevant reaction is the decarboxylation of L-2-amino-3-oxobutyrate (2-amino-acetoacetate) to aminoacetone + CO2, which is spontaneous and essentially irreversible in vivo. As written (carboxylation direction), the forward reaction is thermodynamically unfavorable; the in vivo flow is from amino-acetoacetate to aminoacetone + CO2, i.e., the reverse of the written direction.

rxn09330.other_comments: This is a transport reaction moving thiosulfate (H2S2O3, thiosulfic acid form) across the outer membrane from the extracellular space to the periplasm via diffusion. The reactant and product are the same chemical species in different compartments, so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced. Diffusion-based transport is inherently bidirectional and driven by concentration gradients, making it reversible.

rxn08689.other_comments: This is a transport reaction moving hydrogen sulfide (H2S) between two compartments, indicated as periplasmic transport. The two H2S species represent the same molecule in different cellular compartments (e.g., cytoplasm and periplasm). The reaction is mass-balanced and charge-balanced since H2S is neutral and identical on both sides. As a passive diffusion transport of a small neutral gas-like molecule, this is appropriately modeled as reversible.

rxn09260.other_comments: This is a transport reaction moving sulfite across a membrane (extracellular to periplasm) via passive diffusion. Both sides show the same species (Sulfite), with the same metabolite in two different compartments. Stoichiometry is balanced 1:1, which is correct for a simple diffusion transport reaction. Passive diffusion follows the concentration gradient and is inherently reversible.

rxn00062.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi). The reaction is balanced: ATP (C10H12N5O13P3 with appropriate protonation) + H2O yields ADP + Pi + H+. Mass and charge are conserved when considering the standard protonation states of the species. ATP hydrolysis is strongly exergonic (delta-G ~ -30 kJ/mol) and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo, though enzymes typically couple this hydrolysis to drive other reactions rather than performing simple hydrolysis.

rxn08350.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for D-lactate across the membrane (cytoplasm/periplasm). Although written without explicit compartment labels in the metabolite formulas shown, the reaction name indicates H+ and D-lactate are co-transported from the periplasm into the cytoplasm. Stoichiometry is balanced (1 H+ and 1 D-lactate on each side, representing different compartments). Such proton symport transporters are typically reversible depending on the proton motive force and concentration gradients.

rxn00738.other_comments: This is the ACC deaminase (1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate deaminase, EC 3.5.99.7) reaction. It hydrolytically deaminates ACC, with ring opening, to yield 2-oxobutyrate (alpha-ketobutyrate) and ammonia. The atoms balance: ACC (C4H7NO2) + H2O (H2O) gives 2-oxobutyrate (C4H6O3) + NH3 (NH3); C, H, N, O all balance. In vivo, this reaction is essentially irreversible toward deamination/ring-opening.

rxn01331.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of D-erythrose 4-phosphate to 4-phosphoerythronate (4-phospho-D-erythronate) by the enzyme erythrose-4-phosphate dehydrogenase (E4PDH, gene epd in E. coli), part of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (vitamin B6) biosynthesis. The aldehyde group of E4P is oxidized to a carboxylic acid using NAD+ as electron acceptor, consuming water. Stoichiometry is balanced: an aldehyde + H2O + NAD+ yields a carboxylic acid + NADH + 2 H+. Mass and charge balance check out.

The decarboxylation (releasing CO2) is performed separately by SAM decarboxylase. As written with SAM, the products would not balance because SAM still contains the carboxyl group; CO2 release would require an extra decarboxylation step not catalyzed by this enzyme.
