rxn00144.other_comments: This reaction describes 2,3-diaminopropanoate ammonia-lyase activity, where 2,3-diaminopropionate (L-2,3-diaminopropanoate) is converted to pyruvate with release of two ammonia molecules and consumption of one water. Atom and charge balance are consistent for a P450 hydroxylation.

rxn03303.other_comments: This is a 3-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-type reaction. Urocortisol (3alpha,11beta,17alpha,21-tetrahydroxy-5beta-pregnan-20-one, i.e., tetrahydrocortisol) is oxidized at the 3-position to yield the 3-oxo product (5beta-pregnane-11beta,17alpha,21-triol-3,20-dione), with NADP+ reduced to NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: removal of two hydrogens (one as hydride to NADP+ giving NADPH, one as a proton) from the 3-hydroxy to form the 3-keto. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance check out. 3-keto/3-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases are generally reversible, though in vivo direction depends on enzyme and cofactor pool (NADPH/NADP+ ratio often favors reduction/synthesis of the 3-hydroxy form).

rxn02559.other_comments: This is an alcohol dehydrogenase / oxidoreductase reaction (EC 1.1.1.x type). Indan-1-ol (a secondary alcohol) is oxidized to 1-indanone (indanone) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH and release of a proton. The reaction is balanced: indan-1-ol (C9H10O) loses 2H to become 1-indanone (C9H8O), and NADP+ gains a hydride (becoming NADPH) plus a free H+ is released, accounting for the two hydrogen atoms. Charge and mass are balanced.

errors: The reaction lists Aniline and Benzenamine as if they are distinct species, but Aniline and Benzenamine are synonyms for the same compound (C6H5NH2); the substrate should be Aniline and the product should be the N-sulfo derivative (N-sulfanilic acid / N-phenylsulfamate)

Charge/proton balance is questionable: PAPS sulfo transfer to an amine yields the sulfamate (R-NH-SO3-) plus PAP; the H+ accounting should be verified since the sulfamate product carries the negative charge
Product naming 'Benzenamine sulfate' is ambiguous - it should denote the N-sulfonated aniline (phenylsulfamate), not a sulfate salt of aniline
rxn01357.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase reaction transferring the sulfo group from PAPS to the amino nitrogen of aniline, producing PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate) and N-sulfonated aniline. PAPS-dependent sulfotransferases proceed strongly in the sulfo-transfer (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn09560.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of 3',5'-cyclic IMP (cyclic inosine monophosphate) by a 3',5'-cyclic-nucleotide phosphodiesterase, producing 5'-IMP. The reaction is balanced: H2O + cyclic IMP yields IMP + H+, with the water adding across the cyclic phosphodiester bond to open the ring and release a free hydroxyl plus a proton. Mass and charge balance check out (the cyclic phosphate -1 charge plus water gives the open-chain phosphate -2 charge plus H+). Phosphodiesterase-catalyzed hydrolysis of cyclic nucleotides is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding strongly toward hydrolysis.

rxn06276.other_comments: This represents the primary photochemical event in vision: light-induced isomerization of the 11-cis-retinal chromophore in rhodopsin to all-trans-retinal, forming the high-energy intermediate bathorhodopsin. The reaction is a photoisomerization and conserves mass (it is an intramolecular conformational change of the same molecular species). In vivo it proceeds in the forward direction upon photon absorption, after which bathorhodopsin relaxes through subsequent intermediates (lumirhodopsin, metarhodopsin) rather than reverting to rhodopsin.

errors: The reaction is missing a proton (H+) on the product side. UDP-glucose transfer to an acceptor hydroxyl typically releases UDP and forms a new glycosidic bond; the charge/mass balance should be checked, and a H+ is commonly required to balance the equation.
rxn10278.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to monoglucosyl-diacylglycerol, producing diglucosyl-diacylglycerol and UDP. The diacyl groups are anteiso-pentadecanoyl (anteiso-C15) chains. This is part of glycolipid biosynthesis (e.g., in Gram-positive bacteria). UDP-glucose-dependent glycosyltransfer reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to release of UDP and the energetically favorable cleavage of the UDP-sugar bond.

rxn07782.other_comments: This reaction represents the intramolecular cyclization of homoeriodictyol chalcone (a chalcone) to homoeriodictyol (a flavanone), catalyzed by chalcone isomerase (EC 5.5.1.6). It is an isomerization with no net change in molecular formula, so it is stoichiometrically balanced as written (1:1). Although chalcone isomerases can in principle catalyze a reversible reaction, the cyclization to the flavanone is strongly favored thermodynamically and proceeds in the forward direction in vivo as part of flavonoid biosynthesis.

rxn00557.other_comments: This is an ITP-dependent variant of phosphofructokinase, transferring a phosphate from ITP to fructose-6-phosphate to form fructose-1,6-bisphosphate plus IDP and a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ITP (-4) + F6P (-2) = -6 on the left; H+ (+1) + IDP (-3) + FBP (-4) = -6 on the right. Atoms balance with the gamma-phosphate transfer.

rxn04271.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction converting trans-2-Methyl-5-isopropylhexa-2,5-dienal to the corresponding carboxylic acid. The aldehyde is oxidized using NAD+ as the electron acceptor, with water as the oxygen source. Stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (R-CHO) plus H2O minus 2H (transferred as hydride to NAD+ plus a proton) yields the carboxylic acid (R-COOH), NADH, and 2 H+. Mass and charge balance check out.

rxn08934.other_comments: This reaction represents maltodextrin glucosidase (EC 3.2.1.20, alpha-glucosidase activity) hydrolyzing maltopentaose (5 glucose units, alpha-1,4 linked) by cleaving a terminal glucose to yield D-glucose plus maltotetraose (4 glucose units). The stoichiometry is balanced: maltopentaose (C30H52O26) + H2O (H2O) yields glucose (C6H12O6) + maltotetraose (C24H42O21). Carbon: 30 = 6 + 24; hydrogen: 52 + 2 = 12 + 42; oxygen: 26 + 1 = 6 + 21. All balanced.

rxn03474.other_comments: This reaction represents the isomerization between neopinone and codeinone in the morphine biosynthesis pathway. Neopinone and codeinone are isomers (both C18H19NO3) differing in the position of the double bond and ketone, and they interconvert via an allylic isomerization. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a simple isomerization with a 1:1 ratio. In the morphine biosynthetic pathway, the net flux proceeds from neopinone to codeinone (then to codeine), but the isomerization itself is chemically reversible and can occur spontaneously.

rxn02089.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by CDP-ribitol pyrophosphorylase (ribitol-5-phosphate cytidylyltransferase, e.g. TarI/Tcl1 or the bifunctional Tag/Tarl). CTP attacks ribitol 5-phosphate, transferring the cytidylyl (CMP) moiety and releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) to form CDP-ribitol. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (CTP + ribitol-5-P -> CDP-ribitol + PPi). In vivo the reaction is driven toward CDP-ribitol formation because PPi is rapidly hydrolyzed by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making the overall process effectively irreversible toward nucleotide-sugar synthesis for teichoic acid biosynthesis.

rxn04641.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.236) transferring an L-rhamnose moiety from UDP-L-rhamnose to apigenin 7-O-beta-D-glucoside (cosmetin/apigenin-7-glucoside). The product rhoifolin is apigenin 7-O-neohesperidoside, formed by adding rhamnose to the 2'' position of the glucose. Stoichiometry is balanced: one UDP-rhamnose plus the glucoside yields UDP plus the rhamnosyl-glucoside. UDP-sugar dependent glycosyltransferases are thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic (forward) direction due to the energy of the UDP-sugar bond.

rxn05392.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthase elongation (condensation) step (ketoacyl-ACP synthase / KAS type). Malonyl-ACP condenses with the acyl-ACP primer (7-methyl-octanoyl-ACP) to form a beta-ketoacyl-ACP elongated by two carbons, releasing CO2 and free ACP. Carbon balance checks: 7-methyl-octanoyl (C9 acyl) + 2 carbons from malonyl (after loss of CO2 carboxyl) gives 9-methyl-3-oxo-decanoyl (C11 acyl, beta-keto). Stoichiometry of products (CO2 + ACP + beta-ketoacyl-ACP) is balanced.

rxn09412.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by glutamate-5-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (gamma-glutamyl phosphate reductase, ProA, EC 1.2.1.41) in proline biosynthesis. L-glutamyl 5-phosphate is reduced by NADPH (note: physiologically NADPH/NADP+ rather than NADH/NAD+) to L-glutamate-5-semialdehyde with release of inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: substrate phosphate ester is cleaved and the acyl phosphate is reduced to an aldehyde. In vivo this proceeds toward proline biosynthesis (semialdehyde formation).

errors: FADH2 should be written as FADH2 but the product enoyl-CoA naming is inconsistent: oxidation of OPC8-CoA (3-oxo-2-(2-pentenyl)-cyclopentaneoctanoyl-CoA) by acyl-CoA oxidase/dehydrogenase yields the 2,3-dehydro (trans-2-enoyl) product, so the carbon count should be retained; the listed name 'trans-2-Enoyl-OPC8-CoA' is acceptable but should specify trans-2-enoyl-OPC8-CoA = OPC8-trans-2-enoyl-CoA

If this is the peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase step, the electron acceptor is O2 producing H2O2, not FADH2 reoxidation in situ; FAD/FADH2 as written represents the enzyme-bound cofactor and is formally balanced but physiologically the reoxidation differs
rxn07678.other_comments: This is a beta-oxidation-type first dehydrogenation step in the jasmonate biosynthesis pathway, converting OPC8-CoA to its trans-2-enoyl-CoA derivative with reduction of FAD to FADH2. Atoms are conserved (loss of 2 H from substrate to FAD). The reaction proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction in vivo as part of peroxisomal beta-oxidation shortening OPC8 to OPDA-derived jasmonate precursors.

rxn05431.other_comments: This is a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase reaction in the fatty acid elongation cycle (FabZ/FabA type), specific to a branched-chain (isohexadecanoyl/14-methyl-pentadecanoyl) substrate. It removes water from the beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP to form the trans-2-enoyl-ACP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one water is released and the carbon/ACP framework is conserved. The enzyme is mechanistically a hydro-lyase and operates reversibly, though in vivo the elongation cycle pulls flux toward the enoyl product (dehydration direction).

rxn04600.other_comments: This is the dehydrogenation of a cis-dihydrodiol intermediate in the bacterial degradation of cinnamate (phenylpropanoid catabolism). The substrate cis-3-(3-carboxyethenyl)-3,5-cyclohexadiene-1,2-diol is oxidized by NAD+ to yield 2,3-dihydroxycinnamic acid (the aromatic/catechol product) plus NADH and H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: a two-electron, two-proton oxidation removes 2H from the diol, with one H going to NAD+ (forming NADH) and one released as H+. This rearomatization step is thermodynamically favorable and drives the catabolic pathway forward.

rxn04681.other_comments: This is the second methylation step in the phosphobase methylation pathway (e.g., in plants/Plasmodium for phosphocholine biosynthesis). SAM donates a methyl group to N-methylethanolamine phosphate, producing N,N-dimethylethanolamine phosphate (phosphodimethylethanolamine), SAH, and a proton. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge: SAM (net +1 charge as commonly represented) plus the substrate yields SAH plus the methylated product plus H+. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are thermodynamically driven forward by the favorable SAM-to-SAH conversion.

rxn07966.other_comments: This reaction represents an acyltransferase coupling octadecenoate (oleate/vaccenate, C18:1) to a 2-acyl-glycerophosphoglycerol acceptor to form phosphatidylglycerol with two C18:1 chains. The mechanism uses ATP to activate the fatty acid, releasing AMP and PPi (an acyl-AMP intermediate type mechanism). Stoichiometry balances: ATP provides AMP + PPi, the carboxylate is esterified releasing the equivalent of one H+ (mass and charge are consistent for an acyl-AMP forming ligase/acyltransferase). The naming '(n-C18:1)' and 'octadec-11-enoyl' indicate vaccenate-type C18:1.

rxn01358.other_comments: This is purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) acting on inosine. The reaction is: inosine + phosphate <=> hypoxanthine (HYXN) + alpha-D-ribose 1-phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced (the N-glycosidic bond of inosine is cleaved by phosphate, transferring the ribosyl group to phosphate to form ribose 1-phosphate and releasing the free base hypoxanthine). PNP is well known to catalyze a readily reversible reaction in vivo, though under physiological conditions it typically favors phosphorolysis (forward direction toward base + ribose-1-phosphate).

rxn02997.other_comments: This is the norcoclaurine synthase (NCS) reaction (EC 4.2.1.78), a Pictet-Spengler condensation between dopamine and 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde to form (S)-norcoclaurine with release of water. This is the committed first step of benzylisoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis. The stoichiometry is balanced: dopamine (C8H11NO2) plus 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde (C8H8O2) condense to form (S)-norcoclaurine (C16H17NO3) plus water (H2O). In vivo, the enzyme drives the condensation toward norcoclaurine formation.

rxn00099.other_comments: This reaction corresponds to ATP-dependent NADH hydratase / NAD(P)H-hydrate dehydratase (EC 4.2.1.93), which dehydrates the (6S)-hydrate of NADH back to functional NADH using ATP hydrolysis. The atoms balance: removal of water (hydro-lyase) from the hydrated NADH regenerates NADH, while ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi + H+. Stoichiometry of charge and mass is consistent (the water released from the substrate combines into the ADP + Pi products).

errors: Stoichiometry is ambiguous/incomplete: glycogen (or starch) phosphorylase removes one glucosyl unit per reaction, so the polymeric substrate and product should differ by one glucose residue (e.g., Starch(n) + Phosphate <=> Starch(n-1) + Glucose-1-phosphate). Representing both polymers as distinct named species (Starch vs Amylose) without an explicit (n) and (n-1) chain-length relationship makes the mass balance incorrect.

Starch and Amylose are not appropriate as separate reactant/product species; both are alpha-1,4-glucan polymers, so using two different polymer names misrepresents the reaction (the product should be the shortened glucan of the same type).
rxn06096.other_comments: This is the phosphorylase reaction (EC 2.4.1.1), phosphorolytic cleavage of the terminal alpha-1,4 glucosidic bond yielding glucose-1-phosphate. Although chemically reversible in vitro, in vivo the high cytosolic Pi/G1P ratio drives it in the degradative (phosphorolytic) direction, producing glucose-1-phosphate.

errors: The reaction name describes a complex multi-step fatty acid elongation (condensation with malonyl-CoA, decarboxylation, ketoreduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction, thioester hydrolysis), but the written equation only represents a single oxidation step (butyryl-ACP to but-2-enoyl-ACP), so the name and equation are inconsistent

Stoichiometry is unbalanced: the written reaction shows oxidation of butyryl-ACP to enoyl-ACP, which should consume an oxidizing equivalent (produce NADPH from NADP) but the H balance is incorrect; oxidation of a C-C single bond to a double bond removes 2 H, so NADP should appear with reduced product yielding NADPH + H+ (1 H+), not 2 H+
The malonyl-CoA, CoA, CO2, and water that the enzyme name implies are entirely absent from the equation
rxn05353.other_comments: The written equation is the oxidation/desaturation of butyryl-ACP to but-2-enoyl-ACP coupled to NADP reduction. This is the reverse of the physiological enoyl-ACP reductase step (FabI/FabG-type), which normally reduces enoyl-ACP to acyl-ACP using NADPH. The given equation also does not match its own enzyme name, which describes a full ketoacyl synthase/elongation module.

errors: Atom imbalance: thiamin (C12H17N4OS+) plus the substrates does not balance to thiamine acetic acid plus products. Thiamine acetic acid differs from thiamin by oxidation of the 5-(2-hydroxyethyl) side chain to a carboxylic acid (-CH2CH2OH -> -CH2COOH), which is a net change requiring loss of 4 H and gain of 1 O (2 dehydrogenation steps). The given stoichiometry of 1 H2O + 2 O2 -> 2 H2O2 does not properly balance oxygen and hydrogen for this conversion.
Oxygen balance issue: 2 O2 (4 O) on left vs 2 H2O2 (2 O) on right plus 1 O incorporated and 1 O from water; mass balance should be rechecked.
Charge balance should be verified: thiamin carries a +1 charge (thiazolium); product side has H+ and thiamine acetic acid.
rxn01536.other_comments: This represents oxidation of the hydroxyethyl side chain of thiamin to a carboxylic acid (thiamine acetic acid) by an oxidase using O2 and producing H2O2. Oxidase reactions with O2/H2O2 are essentially irreversible in vivo, so forward direction is appropriate, but the stoichiometry as written appears unbalanced.

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: the glucosyl moiety is transferred from indole-3-acetyl-beta-1-D-glucoside to inositol, so the released product should be free D-glucose only if the IAA-glucose bond were hydrolyzed; in the transferase reaction the indole-3-acetyl group is transferred, releasing free D-glucose and forming IAA-inositol, but the carbon/atom balance requires water if glucose is liberated as free sugar. As written without water, the equation is mass-imbalanced.
Substrate naming inconsistency: 'L-Inositol' should be 'myo-inositol' (the biologically relevant isomer named in the enzyme and product). myo-Inositol is meso, not L-configured.
rxn03009.other_comments: This is the indole-3-acetyl glucose:myo-inositol indoleacetyltransferase reaction, transferring the IAA group from glucose to myo-inositol, producing IAA-myo-inositol and free D-glucose. The overall transfer is plausible, but the inositol substrate is mislabeled as L-inositol and atom balance is questionable as written.

rxn00511.other_comments: This is the saccharopine dehydrogenase (NADP+, L-lysine-forming) reaction, part of the lysine biosynthesis aminoadipate pathway. Saccharopine is hydrolyzed/oxidized with water and NADP+ to yield 2-oxoglutarate, L-lysine, NADPH, and H+. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: saccharopine (the N6-(L-1,3-dicarboxypropyl)-L-lysine adduct) is cleaved oxidatively at the C-N bond to release lysine and regenerate 2-oxoglutarate.

rxn04761.other_comments: This represents the reaction catalyzed by 9-cis-epoxycarotenoid dioxygenase (NCED), the key regulatory step in abscisic acid (ABA) biosynthesis. The enzyme oxidatively cleaves the 11,12 double bond of 9'-cis-neoxanthin using molecular O2, producing the C15 product xanthoxin and a C25 allenic apo-aldehyde. Stoichiometry is balanced in terms of the cleavage products (one O2 incorporated across the cleaved double bond). The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of carotenoid cleavage.

rxn05057.other_comments: This is the cyanuric acid amidohydrolase (AtzD/TrzD) reaction in the s-triazine/atrazine degradation pathway. Cyanuric acid (C3H3N3O3) is hydrolyzed with one water to ring-open and release CO2, yielding biuret (C2H5N3O2). Mass balance checks: left side C3H5N3O4 (cyanuric acid C3H3N3O3 + H2O), right side CO2 (CO2) + biuret (C2H5N3O2) = C3H5N3O4. Atoms balance (C3 H5 N3 O4 on both sides). The reaction is physiologically catabolic and essentially irreversible in vivo due to CO2 release.

rxn03284.other_comments: This is the CYP27A1-catalyzed sterol 26-hydroxylation step in bile acid biosynthesis. The substrate 3alpha,7alpha,12alpha-trihydroxycoprostane (5beta-cholestane-3alpha,7alpha,12alpha-triol) is hydroxylated at C26 to form the tetrol, consuming NADPH and O2 and releasing water plus NADP+. The reaction is balanced: one O atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate hydroxyl, the other reduced to water using NADPH-derived electrons and the proton. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: The reaction is missing a proton (H+) on the product side; balanced form should be: NAD+ + GSH + Formaldehyde -> NADH + S-Formylglutathione + H+

Strictly, the enzyme acts on the spontaneously formed S-hydroxymethylglutathione adduct (GSH + formaldehyde), so a water-balanced representation including the hemithioacetal intermediate is more accurate
rxn09567.other_comments: This describes glutathione-dependent (NAD-linked) formaldehyde dehydrogenase (ADH3/class III alcohol dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.284). Formaldehyde reacts non-enzymatically with GSH to form S-hydroxymethylglutathione, which is oxidized to S-formylglutathione with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. In vivo this serves formaldehyde detoxification and runs in the oxidative (forward) direction.

errors: The substrate name is misspelled; the correct compound is 'muconolactone' (not 'mucolactone'). The enzyme is muconolactone isomerase (muconolactone Delta-isomerase, EC 5.3.3.4).
Stoichiometry is balanced as an isomerization (1:1, same molecular formula C6H6O4).
rxn12679.other_comments: This is the muconolactone isomerase step of the beta-ketoadipate (ortho-cleavage) pathway for aromatic compound degradation. Muconolactone is converted to 3-oxoadipate-enol-lactone (beta-ketoadipate enol-lactone), an intramolecular double-bond shift/isomerization. In vivo this proceeds in the catabolic (forward) direction toward beta-ketoadipate.

rxn03086.other_comments: This is the N-acetyl-LL-diaminopimelate aminotransferase reaction (EC 2.6.1.-) in the acetylated DAP/lysine biosynthesis pathway. It transfers the amino group from N-acetyl-LL-2,6-diaminopimelate to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and N-acetyl-6-oxo-pimelate (L-2-acetamido-6-oxopimelate). The reaction is atom-balanced: an amino group is exchanged for a keto group between the two substrate pairs, which is stoichiometrically consistent for a transamination.

rxn01577.other_comments: This is a branched-chain amino acid aminotransferase (BCAT) reaction. L-Valine donates its amino group to 3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (3MOP, the keto acid corresponding to isoleucine), producing 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate (the keto acid of valine) and L-Isoleucine. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: both sides have matching carbon, nitrogen, and other atoms, since the amino and keto groups are simply exchanged between the valine/isoleucine carbon skeletons. BCAT reactions are typically PLP-dependent and freely reversible in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the proton (H+) should not be released; the reaction is a simple diphosphate elimination/cyclization that produces a neutral diterpene plus PPi without a net free proton. The substrate copalyl-PP (formula approximately C20H36O7P2 as diphosphate) loses PPi (HP2O7 3-) to give a C20H32 hydrocarbon; mass and charge balance do not require an extra H+.

Product/name inconsistency: the enzyme name specifies an ent-abieta-8(14),12-diene-forming activity, but the listed product is levopimaradiene; these are distinct diterpene isomers, so the named activity and the written product do not match.
rxn04176.other_comments: This is a class II/class I-type diterpene synthase reaction in which copalyl (labdadienyl) diphosphate undergoes ionization-dependent cyclization with loss of diphosphate to form a bicyclic/tricyclic diterpene olefin. Such carbocation-driven, diphosphate-eliminating cyclizations are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding strongly in the direction of olefin formation.

rxn03473.other_comments: This reaction is codeinone reductase (NADPH), which interconverts codeinone and codeine. As written, it shows the oxidation of codeine to codeinone with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: the secondary alcohol of codeine is oxidized to a ketone (codeinone), transferring a hydride to NADP+ to form NADPH plus a proton. In vivo (in opium poppy alkaloid biosynthesis), the physiological direction is the reduction of codeinone to codeine (reverse of as written), using NADPH. NADP+ should formally be written as NADP+, but the chemistry is correct.

rxn04648.other_comments: This is a catechol 1,2-dioxygenase (intradiol) type reaction acting on 3,4,6-trichlorocatechol. Molecular oxygen cleaves the aromatic ring between the two hydroxyl-bearing carbons to yield the corresponding cis,cis-muconate derivative (2,3,5-trichloromuconate). The two catechol hydroxyl protons are released as 2 H+ as the ring opens and carboxylate/dione groups form. Atom and charge balance are consistent (O2 incorporated, 2 H+ released).

rxn07266.other_comments: This is the cholinephosphotransferase reaction (EC 2.7.8.2-like, specifically the alkylacylglycerol cholinephosphotransferase). CDP-choline donates a phosphocholine group to the free sn-3 hydroxyl of 1-alkyl-2-acylglycerol, producing the phosphocholine-containing product (a precursor in ether/plasmanyl lipid synthesis) and releasing CMP. The proton balance and atom transfer are consistent: phosphocholine is transferred, CMP and H+ are released. The product '1-Radyl-2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine' uses 'radyl' as a general term encompassing the alkyl substituent, which is appropriate here.

rxn08002.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (KAS) condensation reaction in fatty acid elongation. Malonyl-ACP condenses with the cis-9-hexadecenoyl-ACP (C16:1) acyl chain, releasing CO2 and free ACP, and producing the elongated 3-oxo-cis-11-octadecenoyl (cis-vaccenoyl precursor, C18:1) chain bound to ACP. Atoms balance: the two-carbon addition from malonyl group (minus released CO2) extends the acyl chain by two carbons. Decarboxylative Claisen condensations of this type are essentially irreversible and proceed in the elongation (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: ribonucleotide reduction removes one oxygen from the 2'-OH of the ribose, but this requires two electrons and two protons. The product should be water (H2O) plus oxidized flavodoxin, but the reaction as written is not balanced for hydrogen/protons. A balanced form is: ATP + flavodoxin (reduced) + 2 H+ -> dATP + flavodoxin (oxidized) + H2O
Flavodoxin redox typically carries 1 or 2 electrons; the proton balance must accompany the 2-electron reduction. As written, protons are missing on the substrate side.
rxn09235.other_comments: This is a class III (anaerobic) ribonucleotide reductase-type reaction reducing the 2'-OH of a ribonucleotide (ATP) to the deoxyribonucleotide (dATP), using reduced flavodoxin as the electron donor. The conversion of ribonucleotide to deoxyribonucleotide is physiologically committed (forward) for DNA precursor synthesis.

rxn01317.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by N-acetylneuraminate-9-phosphatase (EC 3.1.3.29). It hydrolyzes N-acetylneuraminate 9-phosphate (Neu5Ac-9-P) to release inorganic phosphate and free N-acetylneuraminate (Neu5Ac). The stoichiometry is balanced: one water and one substrate phosphate ester yield one free phosphate and the dephosphorylated sugar acid. This is the final step in sialic acid (Neu5Ac) biosynthesis.

errors: Product should be D-Glucono-1,5-lactone (delta-lactone), not D-Glucono-1,4-lactone. Glucose dehydrogenase oxidizes the C1 anomeric hydroxyl, and the resulting lactone forms a 6-membered ring (1,5-lactone) from the C5 hydroxyl, which is the standard product.
rxn00218.other_comments: This is glucose 1-dehydrogenase (NADP+-dependent), oxidizing the anomeric carbon (C1) of D-glucose to the corresponding lactone, reducing NADP+ to NADPH. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (assuming the lactone identity is corrected). In vivo it proceeds toward glucono-lactone formation/NADPH production.

errors: Hydrogen/charge imbalance: oxidation of 2 chalcone molecules by O2 to form 2 H2O requires removal of 4 H (4 electrons + 4 protons). The oxidative cyclization to aurone (aureusidin) involves loss of hydrogens, but the equation as written needs verification of H balance. For 1 O2 + 2 substrate -> 2 H2O + 2 product, each substrate must lose 2 H atoms (one to form water, plus cyclization). The stoichiometry of O2:substrate at 1:2 is consistent with aureusidin synthase (a polyphenol oxidase) producing water rather than H2O2.
rxn07800.other_comments: This represents the aureusidin synthase reaction, where pentahydroxychalcone 4'-O-glucoside undergoes oxidative cyclization to form the aurone aureusidin 6-O-glucoside using molecular oxygen. The enzyme is a polyphenol oxidase. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo (O2-dependent oxidation), proceeding in the forward direction toward aurone (yellow pigment) formation.

rxn04079.other_comments: This reaction (R05847) is the NADPH-dependent reduction of cathenamine to ajmalicine, catalyzed by cathenamine reductase / vinorine synthase-related enzymes in the monoterpenoid indole alkaloid biosynthesis pathway. The stoichiometry is balanced: cathenamine + NADPH + H+ yields ajmalicine + NADP+. Note that as written it shows 2.0 H+ on the left; the balanced reduction of an iminium/enamine double bond typically consumes one H+ along with the hydride from NADPH, so the proton count may be slightly off (likely should be 1 H+). Biologically this is a committed reductive biosynthetic step favoring ajmalicine formation.

rxn02259.other_comments: This is the oxidation of (R)-pantolactone (pantoyl-lactone) to 2-dehydropantolactone (ketopantolactone) with NADP+ as electron acceptor, producing NADPH and H+. rxn01326.other_comments: This is the tyrosine hydroxylase (tyrosine 3-monooxygenase) reaction. rxn12172.other_comments: This reaction represents an acetyltransferase transferring the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the monoterpenol (+)-neomenthol, producing neomenthyl acetate and free CoA. rxn14222.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 8-hydroxygeraniol dehydrogenase (involved in iridoid/monoterpene indole alkaloid biosynthesis). It oxidizes both the primary alcohol groups of 8-hydroxygeraniol to aldehydes, yielding 8-oxogeranial, consuming 2 NADP+ (or NADPH in reverse). The atoms appear to balance: removal of 4 H corresponds to 2 NADPH + 2 H+.

errors: The reaction as written is not balanced and is reversed. Cyclohexane-1,2-dione hydrolase (decyclizing) hydrolyzes cyclohexane-1,2-dione to 6-oxohexanoate, requiring addition of water (ring opening with water), not release of water.

Mass/atom balance: cyclohexane-1,2-dione (C6H8O2) + H2O (H2O) should yield 6-oxohexanoate (C6H10O3, as the anion C6H9O3-). The written direction consuming H+ and 6-oxohexanoate to produce water and the dione is incorrect; water and the diketone substrate are swapped.
The H+ stoichiometry is questionable given the carboxylate product would release a proton rather than consume one.
rxn03456.other_comments: This is the EC 3.7.1.11 cyclohexane-1,2-dione hydrolase reaction. Physiologically it catalyzes hydrolytic ring opening of cyclohexane-1,2-dione plus water to form 6-oxohexanoate. The reaction as written runs in the wrong (reverse) direction and has the water on the wrong side.

rxn00078.other_comments: This is NAD kinase acting on the reduced form (NADH 2'-phosphotransferase, EC 2.7.1.86). ATP phosphorylates the 2'-hydroxyl of NADH to form NADPH, generating ADP and a proton. The reaction is balanced: atoms and charges match (ATP + NADH yields NADPH + ADP + H+). Phosphoryl transfer from ATP is strongly exergonic, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (NADPH-forming) direction in vivo.

rxn01196.other_comments: This is the 4,5-dihydroxyphthalate decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.55), part of the phthalate degradation pathway. 4,5-Dihydroxyphthalate is decarboxylated to form protocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxybenzoate) plus CO2. The reaction is balanced: 4,5-dihydroxyphthalate (C8H6O6) plus H+ yields protocatechuate (C7H6O4) plus CO2 (CO2). Carbon: 8 = 7+1. The H+ consumed balances the loss of the carboxylate proton during decarboxylation.

errors: Reaction is not charge/proton balanced as written: an oxidation of coformycin to 8-oxocoformycin coupled to NADP+ reduction to NADPH requires an additional water on the substrate side and a released proton (H+). A balanced form would be: Coformycin + NADP+ + H2O <=> 8-Oxocoformycin + NADPH + H+
rxn02606.other_comments: This represents a coformycin:NADP+ 8-oxidoreductase converting coformycin to 8-oxocoformycin with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The carbon backbone (coformycin to its 8-oxo derivative) is consistent, but H2O and H+ are missing for a balanced oxidoreductase reaction.

errors: The reaction is written identically on both sides (L-Valine + Na+ <=> L-Valine + Na+), so no net chemical transformation or transport vector is represented. A proper transport reaction must distinguish compartments, e.g., L-Valine[extracellular] + Na+[extracellular] <=> L-Valine[cytosol] + Na+[cytosol]. As written, it is a null/identity reaction.
rxn05242.other_comments: This is intended to be a sodium-coupled symport of L-valine into the cell. Stoichiometrically the 1:1 valine:Na+ ratio is plausible, but the reaction as written lacks compartment annotations, making both sides identical. In vivo, Na+ symport is driven by the inward sodium electrochemical gradient, so transport proceeds in the import direction (extracellular to cytosol).

rxn10572.other_comments: This reaction represents monomethylamine methyltransferase (MtmB/MtbC system) in methylotrophic methanogens, transferring a methyl group from monomethylamine to coenzyme M (CoM, 2-mercaptoethanesulfonate) to form methyl-CoM (2-(methylthio)ethanesulfonate) and releasing ammonia. Atom balance: CoM (C2H5O3S2-, the thiol with -SH) + CH3NH2 (monomethylamine) yields methyl-CoM (C3H7O3S2-) + NH3. Carbon: 2+1=3 on each side; the methyl is transferred from amine to the thiol sulfur. Charge and mass balance appropriately if CoM and methyl-CoM are written in matching protonation states. In vivo this is the committed methyl-transfer step feeding methanogenesis and is essentially irreversible (favored forward toward methyl-CoM).

rxn05194.other_comments: This is an ABC-type import reaction for 2-(beta-D-Glucosyl)-sn-glycerol coupled to ATP hydrolysis. The substrate appears on both sides representing transport between compartments (e.g., extracellular to cytoplasmic). Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+ is correct for ATP hydrolysis. The transported metabolite is conserved across the membrane. Note: in a proper representation the two glucosylglycerol instances should carry distinct compartment tags to indicate translocation.

rxn04969.other_comments: This is benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase (reductase component coupled), a Rieske-type dioxygenase that converts benzoate to cis-1,2-dihydroxycyclohexa-3,5-diene-1-carboxylate (cis-dihydrodiol). The stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + O2 + H+ + benzoate yields NAD+ and the cis-diol product. Both atoms of O2 are incorporated into the product (one as a hydroxyl, with NADH providing reducing equivalents). Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance correctly.

errors: Charge imbalance: the left side includes an extra H+ that is not balanced on the product side. Hydration of an enoyl-CoA (addition of H2O across the double bond) does not consume or release a proton, so the H+ should not be present.
If the H+ is removed, the reaction H2O + Tiglyl-CoA <=> 3-Hydroxy-2-methyl-butyryl-CoA is mass- and charge-balanced (water adds OH and H across the C2=C3 double bond).
rxn13450.other_comments: This is an enoyl-CoA hydratase (crotonase-family) reaction. Tiglyl-CoA (2-methyl-2-butenoyl-CoA, an intermediate of isoleucine catabolism) is hydrated to 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA. Enoyl-CoA hydratases catalyze reversible syn-addition of water across the alpha,beta double bond; in the isoleucine degradation pathway the net flux is toward the hydroxyacyl-CoA (hydration direction).

rxn05407.other_comments: This is the enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI-type) step in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2 double bond of a 15-methyl (branched) hexadecenoyl-ACP using NADPH. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: NADPH + H+ provides the hydride and proton needed to saturate the C2-C3 double bond, yielding NADP+ and the saturated 15-methyl-hexadecanoyl-ACP. In vivo, enoyl reductase strongly favors the reductive (forward) direction as part of the fatty acid elongation cycle.

errors: Cyclohexane (C6H12) to Hexalin/cyclohexanol (C6H12O) is a monooxygenase reaction; the oxygen balance requires only one O incorporated into the product while the second O goes to water. Balanced equation: NADH + O2 + H+ + Cyclohexane -> H2O + NAD+ + cyclohexanol. This appears stoichiometrically balanced (C6H12 + 2[H] + O2 -> C6H12O + H2O). Atom check: left C6H12 + O2 + NADH(+H+) ; right cyclohexanol C6H11OH = C6H12O + H2O. The reaction as written is essentially balanced for a cytochrome P450/monooxygenase reaction.
rxn04754.other_comments: This is a monooxygenase (cytochrome P450-type) hydroxylation of cyclohexane to cyclohexanol (hexalin), using NADH and molecular O2, producing water and NAD+. The reaction is balanced as a typical monooxygenase reaction.

errors: This is a transport reaction representing translocation of guanine across a membrane, but both sides show identical species (H+ + Guanine) without compartment distinction; as written it is a null/trivial reaction with no net change
Missing compartment annotations (e.g., guanine[c] vs guanine[e]) to indicate actual transport
If intended as proton symport/antiport, the H+ stoichiometry and direction across compartments must be specified and may not be balanced relative to the transport event
rxn05203.other_comments: The input is a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN) for guanine, likely coupled to a proton. As written it shows H+ + Guanine on both sides which is identical and thus a no-op; presumably the two sides represent different compartments (e.g., extracellular and cytosolic guanine and/or proton) but compartment tags are absent.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction for a decarboxylase/decarboxy-lyase; physiologically the substrate 5-hydroxykynurenine is decarboxylated to produce 5-hydroxykynurenamine + CO2, not the reverse

Charge/mass balance issue: as written, CO2 + 5-hydroxykynurenamine on the left does not balance an H+ on the right without proper accounting of the amino/carboxyl protonation states; the decarboxylation should release CO2 and consume an H+
Atom balance does not appear correct; 5-hydroxykynurenine (which bears a carboxyl group) minus CO2 should equal 5-hydroxykynurenamine, so the equation orientation and proton are inconsistent
rxn03360.other_comments: This is an amino acid decarboxylase (decarboxy-lyase) reaction. Biologically, 5-hydroxykynurenine is decarboxylated to yield 5-hydroxykynurenamine and CO2. The reaction as written shows the carboxylation (reverse) direction, which is thermodynamically unfavorable in vivo due to CO2 release driving decarboxylases forward. The correct in vivo direction is 5-hydroxykynurenine + H+ -> 5-hydroxykynurenamine + CO2.

rxn07779.other_comments: This represents the type III polyketide synthase (chalcone synthase-like) reaction where feruloyl-CoA serves as the starter unit and is extended by three malonyl-CoA units, with three decarboxylations releasing 3 CO2 and 4 CoA total (1 from feruloyl-CoA + 3 from malonyl-CoA), followed by cyclization to form the chalcone (homoeriodictyol chalcone). The stoichiometry balances: starter C4-CoA backbone plus 3 C2 units from malonyl decarboxylation. Carbon, CoA, and charge/proton balance are consistent with chalcone synthase chemistry. Such PKS condensation/cyclization reactions are thermodynamically driven forward by decarboxylation and are physiologically essentially irreversible.

rxn02193.other_comments: This reaction represents the conversion of 5(S)-HPETE (5(S)-hydroperoxy-6,8,11,14-eicosatetraenoic acid) to leukotriene A4 (LTA4) with release of water. It is catalyzed by 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX), which has dual activity: first oxygenating arachidonate to 5-HPETE, then dehydrating 5-HPETE to the epoxide LTA4. The reaction is mass-balanced: 5-HPETE (C20H32O4) loses H2O to form LTA4 (C20H30O3), so C20H32O4 = H2O + C20H30O3. Both atoms and charges balance.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (H+ + D-Methionine) on both sides without compartment distinction, making it a null/trivial reaction. A proper proton symport transport reaction requires compartment annotations, e.g., H+[extracellular] + D-Methionine[extracellular] <=> H+[cytoplasm] + D-Methionine[cytoplasm].
rxn12531.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction where D-methionine is co-transported with a proton across the membrane. As written, both sides are identical so no net transport or chemical change is represented; the missing compartment labels prevent it from being a meaningful transport reaction. Stoichiometrically the atoms balance trivially (identical), but biologically it conveys nothing without compartmentalization.

rxn11631.other_comments: This is an aldehyde oxidase / aldehyde dehydrogenase (oxidase-type) reaction converting 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde to 5-hydroxyindoleacetate (5-HIAA), a key step in serotonin degradation. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (RCHO) plus H2O plus O2 yields the carboxylate (RCOO-) plus H2O2 plus H+. Atom and charge balance check out (the carboxylate carries a -1 charge balanced by the released H+). Oxygen-dependent oxidations producing H2O2 are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn00316.other_comments: This reaction represents acetyl-CoA:L-lysine N6-acetyltransferase activity, transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the epsilon-amino group (N6) of L-lysine, producing N6-acetyl-L-lysine and CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred to lysine, releasing CoASH. The proton (H+) is released because the amine nitrogen loses a proton upon acetylation, consistent with charge and mass balance. Acetyltransferases using acetyl-CoA are typically thermodynamically favorable in the acetyl-transfer (forward) direction due to the high-energy thioester bond.

errors: Substrate mismatch: the enzyme name specifies D-xylulose as the phosphate acceptor, but the reaction lists D-Lyxulose instead. D-Lyxulose and D-Xylulose are distinct epimers (differing at C3). If the product is D-Xylulose 5-phosphate, the substrate should be D-Xylulose, not D-Lyxulose.

Carbon/atom balance issue: phosphorylating D-Lyxulose would yield D-Lyxulose 5-phosphate, not D-Xylulose 5-phosphate. As written, the substrate and product are not the same sugar backbone, so the reaction is not properly balanced as a simple phosphotransfer.
rxn01199.other_comments: This is intended to be an ATP-dependent kinase (xylulokinase-type) reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the 5-OH of a ketopentose, producing a sugar 5-phosphate, ADP, and a proton. The phosphoryl transfer charge/proton balance is otherwise reasonable, but the sugar identities are inconsistent.

errors: Product naming inconsistency: the substrate is N6,N6,O-Trimethylpuromycin-5'-phosphate but the acetylated product is named N-Acetyl-N6,N6,O-tridemethylpuromycin-5'-phosphate, which implies loss of three methyl groups. An acetyltransferase reaction should only add an acetyl group, not remove methyls. The product name should retain the trimethyl groups (e.g., N-Acetyl-N6,N6,O-trimethylpuromycin-5'-phosphate).
rxn03942.other_comments: This is an acetyl-CoA-dependent N-acetyltransferase step in puromycin biosynthesis (transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to an amino group, releasing CoA and H+). The atom balance for the acetyl transfer (acetyl-CoA + amine -> CoA + N-acetyl-amine + H+) is correct in principle, but the product nomenclature is contradictory regarding the methylation state.

rxn00545.other_comments: This is the phosphofructokinase (PFK-1) reaction, EC 2.7.1.11. ATP phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate to form fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, producing ADP and a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ATP (4-) + F6P (2-) = ADP (3-) + H+ + FBP (4-), giving -6 charge on each side and balanced atoms. In vivo this is a highly exergonic, essentially irreversible committed step of glycolysis, proceeding in the forward direction.

errors: This reaction is not catalyzed by threonine dehydrogenase; the named enzyme (L-threonine 3-dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.103) produces L-2-amino-3-oxobutanoate + NADH, not these products
Stoichiometric/atom balance issues: the products (acetate + glycine) imply a multi-step degradation rather than a single dehydrogenase step
Carbon balance check: L-threonine (C4) yields acetate (C2) + glycine (C2) = C4, which balances for carbon, but the reaction conflates several enzymatic steps
Oxygen/water handling is inconsistent for a simple dehydrogenase reaction
rxn13143.other_comments: The input describes a net conversion of L-threonine to acetate and glycine with reduction of NAD+ to NADH, which corresponds to the overall threonine cleavage pathway (threonine dehydrogenase followed by 2-amino-3-ketobutyrate CoA ligase and aldehyde/acetate steps) rather than the single threonine dehydrogenase reaction. As written it mislabels a lumped pathway as one enzyme.

errors: Incorrect product: the enzyme ribose-phosphate diphosphokinase (PRPP synthetase, EC 2.7.6.1) transfers a pyrophosphate (diphosphate) group from ATP to ribose-5-phosphate, producing AMP and 5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate (PRPP), not ADP and ribose 1,5-bisphosphate

Charge/mass imbalance: as written, ATP donates only a single phosphate to yield ADP, but the named product Ribose 1,5-bisphosphate would require this single-phosphate transfer; however the standard reaction transfers diphosphate yielding AMP + PRPP
The H+ stoichiometry and overall balance do not match the biologically known reaction
rxn00771.other_comments: The reaction is labeled as an ATP:D-ribose-5-phosphate 1-phosphotransferase, but this corresponds biologically to PRPP synthetase, which transfers a pyrophosphoryl group (not a single phosphate). The known products are AMP + 5-phospho-D-ribose 1-diphosphate (PRPP), not ADP + ribose-1,5-bisphosphate. In vivo this reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction toward PRPP formation.

rxn01913.other_comments: This reaction represents L-gulonate 3-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.45), which oxidizes L-gulonate at the C3 position to 3-dehydro-L-gulonate (3-keto-L-gulonate) with concomitant reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is balanced: atoms and charges are conserved (a secondary hydroxyl is oxidized to a ketone, releasing 2 [H], captured as NADH + H+). Mass and charge balance correctly.

rxn10886.other_comments: This reaction describes spectinomycin 3''-adenylyltransferase (aminoglycoside adenylyltransferase, ANT/AAD family), which catalyzes the transfer of an AMP moiety from ATP to the 3'' hydroxyl of spectinomycin, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). The product is 3''-adenylylspectinomycin, an inactivated form conferring antibiotic resistance. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP donates the adenylyl (AMP) group to spectinomycin and the beta-gamma phosphates leave as PPi. Although written as reversible, the reaction proceeds in the adenylylation (forward) direction in vivo, especially because PPi is rapidly hydrolyzed by pyrophosphatase, driving the reaction forward.

errors: Proton (H+) imbalance: the oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylate consumes O2 and NADPH but the charge/H balance is not satisfied. A balanced form would be: aldehyde + NADPH + H+ + O2 -> carboxylate + NADP+ + H2O. As written, the left side has an extra H and the charges do not balance (carboxylate carries -1 charge, NADP is shown without charge).
rxn04003.other_comments: This is a sterol C4-demethylation step (SMO/CYP51-related pathway, specifically the sterol 4-alpha-methyl oxidase / NAD(P)H-dependent oxidation of the 4-alpha-aldehyde to the 4-alpha-carboxylic acid intermediate in cholesterol biosynthesis). The substrate aldehyde is oxidized to the carboxylate using O2 and NADPH. Mechanistically this monooxygenase-type oxidation is irreversible in vivo.

rxn09960.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing tetradecanal (myristaldehyde, C14 aldehyde) to myristic acid (tetradecanoic acid, C14 carboxylic acid), with NAD+ reduced to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde RCHO plus H2O gives RCOOH, releasing 2 electrons and 2 protons; one H goes to form NADH (hydride) and the net 2 H+ are released, consistent with the written equation. Atoms and charges balance. Aldehyde dehydrogenases are essentially irreversible in vivo, favoring oxidation of the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid.

rxn02930.other_comments: This is the D-2,4-diaminopentanoate dehydrogenase reaction involved in ornithine degradation (Stickland-type fermentation in clostridia). It oxidatively deaminates the C4 amino group of 2,4-diaminopentanoate to form 2-amino-4-oxopentanoate, releasing ammonia and reducing NAD+ to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: water provides the oxygen, the C4-amine is released as NH3, and the redox is accounted for by NAD+/NADH plus a proton. Mass and charge balance check out (H2O + NAD+ + substrate -> NADH + NH3 + H+ + product).

errors: Proton stoichiometry incorrect: thioester hydrolysis releases 1 H+ (net), not 2 H+. The reaction H2O + R-CoA -> R-COO- + CoA-SH + H+ balances with one proton when carboxylate and CoA thiol charges are accounted for.
rxn08445.other_comments: This is a thioesterase (thioester hydrolase) cleaving octadecenoyl-CoA (e.g., oleoyl-CoA) into the free fatty acid octadecenoate and CoA. Thioester hydrolysis is highly exergonic and essentially irreversible in vivo, so it proceeds in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn13649.other_comments: This is the 5'-deoxyadenosine nucleosidase reaction, hydrolyzing the N-glycosidic bond of 5'-deoxyadenosine to yield adenine and 5-deoxy-D-ribose. The stoichiometry is balanced: 5'-deoxyadenosine (C10H13N5O3) plus H2O yields adenine (C5H5N5) and 5-deoxy-D-ribose (C5H10O4). Hydrolytic nucleosidase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction. This enzyme is important for salvaging 5'-deoxyadenosine, a byproduct of radical SAM enzyme reactions.

rxn01234.other_comments: This is taurine dehydrogenase (EC 1.4.2.-/1.4.99.2 type), which oxidatively deaminates taurine to sulfoacetaldehyde and ammonia, transferring electrons to cytochrome c. Atom balance: Taurine (C2H7NO3S) + H2O provides the necessary atoms. Products: NH3 (N, 3H) + sulfoacetaldehyde (C2H4O4S, i.e. OHC-CH2-SO3H). Checking: C2H7NO3S + H2O = C2H9NO4S on left; right = NH3 + 2H+ + sulfoacetaldehyde (C2H4O4S) = N: 1, C: 2, H: 3+2+4=9, O: 4, S: 1. Balanced for atoms and charge (2 cyt c3+ -> 2 cyt c2+ gains 2 negative charge, balanced by 2 H+).

errors: This is a symport transport reaction, but the compartment designations are missing from the metabolites. Both H+ and ALCTT (acetolactate) appear identical on both sides, which makes the reaction a null/empty transformation as written. A proper proton symport transport reaction should show the metabolites in two different compartments, e.g., H+[e] + ALCTT[e] <=> H+[c] + ALCTT[c].
rxn10438.other_comments: The reaction is intended to represent the reversible transport of acetolactate (ALCTT) across a membrane coupled to proton symport. As written, it is stoichiometrically balanced (same atoms on both sides) but biologically meaningless because no compartment transition is indicated. The reaction name explicitly states reversible transport via proton symport.

rxn05087.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of 5,6,7,8-tetrahydropteridine to dihydropteridine, coupled with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: tetrahydropteridine loses 2 hydrogens (2H = 2e- + 2H+), with one hydride transferred to NAD+ forming NADH and one proton released. In vivo, the physiologically relevant direction is typically the reverse: dihydropteridine reductase (EC 1.5.1.34) regenerates tetrahydropteridine (e.g., tetrahydrobiopterin) from dihydropteridine using NAD(P)H, which is essential for aromatic amino acid hydroxylase cofactor recycling. The forward (oxidation) direction as written is thermodynamically unfavorable under cellular conditions.

errors: The transacylation appears mass-unbalanced as written: transferring one acyl chain from phosphatidylglycerol (ditetradecanoyl) to the 2-acyl-GPE should yield a monoacyl-phosphatidylglycerol (lyso-PG) plus a diacyl-PE, not glycerophosphoethanolamine. Glycerophosphoethanolamine (GPE) is the fully deacylated product, which is inconsistent with adding an acyl group to the 2-acyl-GPE substrate.

Product side: removing an acyl group from 2-acyl-GPE to form GPE means the GPE substrate is acting as an acyl DONOR, but the enzyme name indicates it should be an acyl ACCEPTOR forming diacyl-PE. The acyl-balance between substrates and products does not match.
rxn08825.other_comments: This is annotated as a lysophospholipase L2 acyltransferase reaction. Lysophospholipase L2 (e.g., E. coli PldB) transfers an acyl chain from a lyso-phospholipid to another lipid acceptor. Here 2-acyl-GPE (a lyso-PE, C14:0) donates its acyl group, releasing glycerophosphoethanolamine (GPE) and acylating phosphatidylglycerol to form acyl-PG. Interpreted this way the reaction is actually stoichiometrically plausible (acyl transfer from lyso-PE to PG), but the labeling/balance of acyl chains on each species needs verification.

rxn02764.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA ligase (4-chlorobenzoate:CoA ligase, EC 6.2.1.33) reaction. The substrate 4-chlorobenzoate is activated by ATP to form an acyl-adenylate intermediate, then thioesterified with CoA to yield 4-chlorobenzoyl-CoA, releasing AMP and PPi. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + 4-chlorobenzoate gives AMP + PPi + H+ + 4-chlorobenzoyl-CoA. Mass and charge balance check out (the proton accounts for charge balance of the thioester formation). In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible.

errors: Proton (H+) imbalance: the reaction shows 2.0 H+ produced, but methyl transfer from SAM to xanthosine N7 should produce at most 1 H+ (or be charge-balanced with 1 H+). The N7-methylation forms a quaternary nitrogen, and the released SAH plus 7-methylxanthosine accounting yields net 1 H+, not 2.
rxn07707.other_comments: This is the caffeine biosynthesis pathway reaction (7-methylxanthosine synthase / xanthosine N7-methyltransferase) where SAM methylates xanthosine at N7 to produce 7-methylxanthosine and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are strongly thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn02390.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of the cyclic phosphate (1D-myo-inositol 1,2-cyclic phosphate) by inositol-1,2-cyclic-phosphate 2-phosphohydrolase (EC 3.1.4.-), opening the cyclic phosphodiester ring with water to yield myo-inositol 1-phosphate. Atoms balance: cyclic phosphate (C6H11O9P) + H2O (H2O) gives inositol 1-phosphate (C6H13O9P, i.e., C6H12O9P as 1- anion) plus H+. Counting C6, the H and P and charge balance once the proton release is accounted for, so the stoichiometry is correct.

rxn00030.other_comments: This is an acyloin (benzoin-type) condensation reaction. Two molecules of propanal (C3H6O) condense to form propioin (4-hydroxy-3-hexanone, C6H12O2), which is the acyloin condensation product. Stoichiometry is balanced: 2 x C3H6O = C6H12O2. The enzyme name indicates a lyase cleaving propioin into 2 propanal in the forward direction as written here (propanal-forming), but the reaction as listed (2 Propanal => Propioin) is the condensation direction. Such acyloin condensations are typically catalyzed by thiamine-dependent enzymes and can proceed in either direction depending on substrate concentrations.

errors: This is a transport reaction where the substrate D-Psicose and a proton appear identically on both sides, but the compartments are not distinguished in the provided string; as written (without compartment labels) it is a null/identity reaction with zero net change
No net chemical transformation: identical species (H+ and D-Psicose) on both reactant and product sides cancel out
rxn05697.other_comments: This appears to be intended as a proton-coupled symport/transport reaction for D-Psicose (a C-3 epimer of D-fructose, a ketohexose). Transport reactions move a metabolite between compartments (e.g., extracellular to cytoplasm), so the same chemical species appears on both sides but in different compartments. The provided string lacks compartment annotations, making it read as an identity reaction.

rxn08603.other_comments: This is the gamma-glutamylputrescine oxidase reaction (PuuB/YgjG, EC 1.4.3.-) in the putrescine utilization (Puu) pathway of E. coli. It is an FAD-dependent amine oxidase that oxidizes the primary amine of gamma-glutamyl-putrescine to the corresponding aldehyde (gamma-glutamyl-gamma-aminobutyraldehyde), consuming O2 and water, and releasing ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. The stoichiometry is balanced: oxidative deamination converts a -CH2-NH2 group to -CHO with release of NH3, and O2 + 2[H] yields H2O2. Atoms and charge are consistent.

rxn02425.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of methylmalonyl-CoA thioester by a thioesterase/hydrolase, yielding free CoA and methylmalonate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: H2O + methylmalonyl-CoA (assuming the dianion form -2) gives CoA (-4) + H+ + methylmalonate (-2). Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and sulfur atoms balance. Thioester hydrolysis is highly exergonic (large negative delta G due to loss of the high-energy thioester bond), so it strongly favors the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance charge or protons. The correct half-reaction is 2 monodehydroascorbate (ascorbate radical) + NADH + H+ -> 2 ascorbate + NAD+. Forming radicals from ascorbate is an oxidation requiring an electron acceptor, not NAD+ reduction.

Direction of electron flow is reversed: NADH (not NAD+) is the electron donor that reduces the ascorbate radical (monodehydroascorbate) back to ascorbate. As written, NAD+ is shown oxidizing ascorbate, which is thermodynamically and biologically incorrect.

rxn00071.other_comments: This is monodehydroascorbate reductase (MDHAR, EC 1.6.5.4), which uses NADH to reduce the ascorbate radical (monodehydroascorbate) back to ascorbate. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

Racemases catalyze reversible interconversion driven toward racemic equilibrium.
