Thermodynamically, the standard reduction potential of NAD+/NADH (about -320 mV) is far more negative than Fe3+/Fe2+ (about +770 mV), so under standard conditions the reaction strongly favors NADH oxidation and Fe3+ reduction (the reverse of how written).

rxn02325.other_comments: This is ornithine aminotransferase activity acting via the 2-oxoglutarate/glutamate amino donor-acceptor pair. Ornithine (2,5-diaminopentanoate) transfers its delta-amino group (C5) to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and 2-oxo-5-aminovalerate (glutamate-5-semialdehyde, which exists in equilibrium with 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate). The reaction is atom-balanced: C5H12N2O2 (ornithine) + C5H6O5 (2-oxoglutarate) -> C5H9NO4 (glutamate) + C5H9NO3 (2-oxo-5-aminovalerate). Aminotransferase reactions are generally reversible, though in ornithine catabolism it typically proceeds toward glutamate-5-semialdehyde formation.

rxn10242.other_comments: This is a phosphatidic acid phosphatase (lipin-type/PAP) reaction acting on a specific diacylglycerophosphate (1,2-dianteisopentadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate, i.e. phosphatidic acid with two anteiso-C15 acyl chains). Hydrolysis of the 3-phosphate yields the corresponding diacylglycerol plus inorganic phosphate. Mass and charge balance check out: H2O + PA(2-) -> DAG + Pi(2-) + H+, accounting for water-mediated phosphate ester hydrolysis releasing a proton along with phosphate.

rxn11895.other_comments: This represents an aldehyde oxidase type reaction converting 9-cis-retinal to 9-cis-retinoic acid. The aldehyde (CHO) is oxidized to a carboxylic acid (COOH), incorporating one oxygen from water and reducing molecular O2 to H2O2. Mass and charge balance check: left side has retinal (C20H28O) + H2O + O2; right side retinoic acid (C20H28O2) + H2O2 + H+. Carbon balances (20=20). Oxygen: 1+1+2=4 left; 2+2=4 right. As written (neutral retinoic acid named), there is an extra H+ on the right giving a charge/proton imbalance unless retinoate is the deprotonated species.

rxn00762.other_comments: This reaction represents glycerol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.6), oxidizing glycerol to glycerone (dihydroxyacetone) with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is balanced: glycerol (C3H8O3) loses 2 H (as a hydride to NAD+ and a proton), yielding dihydroxyacetone (C3H6O3). Atoms and charges balance correctly. In vivo, glycerol oxidation to dihydroxyacetone proceeds in the forward direction, though the enzyme can catalyze the reverse under high NADH conditions; physiologically forward is favored.

rxn04459.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase (NADPH-dependent, oxygen-utilizing 2'-hydroxylase) reaction. Such monooxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (driven forward by O2 consumption and NADPH oxidation).

rxn00930.other_comments: This is the dehydrogenation of L-proline to 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (a cyclic imine, the 2,3-dehydro tautomer/Delta1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate), coupled to reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Such reductase/dehydrogenase reactions involving an unstable cyclic imine typically run in the reductive (reverse) direction in vivo, with NADPH reducing the pyrroline carboxylate to proline.

rxn04830.other_comments: This is a glutathione S-transferase-type conjugation: nucleophilic opening of the arene oxide (1-nitronaphthalene-7,8-oxide) by GSH thiol yields the 7-hydroxy-8-glutathionyl dihydronaphthalene adduct. Biologically, GSH conjugation to reactive epoxides is strongly favored in the conjugation (forward) direction as a detoxification step. rxn03113.other_comments: This is the 15-hydroxyprostaglandin/HETE dehydrogenase-type oxidoreductase reaction. 15(S)-HETE (the 15-hydroxy alcohol) is oxidized to 15-oxo-ETE (the ketone), with NADP+ reduced to NADPH + H+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the secondary alcohol loses two hydrogens (one as hydride to NADP+, one as proton), giving the keto product. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: Mass imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance. 1,4-Dihydroxy-2-naphthoate (C11H8O4) + phytyl diphosphate (C20H40O7P2) gives products CO2 + PPi (HP2O7, i.e. H2P2O7 / diphosphate) + 2 H+ + demethylphylloquinone (C31H44O2). rxn04673.other_comments: This is the MenA/phytyl-DHNA reaction in phylloquinone (vitamin K1) biosynthesis: 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoate is decarboxylated and prenylated by phytyl diphosphate to yield demethylphylloquinone (demethylmenaquinol/2-phytyl-1,4-naphthoquinol type product), releasing CO2 and PPi. The release of CO2 and PPi drives the reaction essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn04065.other_comments: This represents the cytochrome P450 (CYP72A) monooxygenase reaction converting 7-deoxyloganate to loganate via hydroxylation at C-7. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH provides reducing equivalents, O2 is split with one oxygen atom incorporated into the substrate (hydroxylation) and the other reduced to water. Atoms and charges balance correctly. As a P450 monooxygenase reaction, it is physiologically irreversible in the forward (hydroxylating) direction.

rxn03292.other_comments: This is an oxidation of the 3-hydroxyl group of 5beta-cholestane-3alpha,7alpha-diol to a 3-keto group, with NAD+ accepting the hydride (B-specific). Stoichiometry is balanced: the alcohol loses two hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one released as H+) to form the ketone. This is part of bile acid biosynthesis catalyzed by 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity. The enzyme reaction is thermodynamically reversible, though in vivo it generally proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction toward bile acid synthesis.

rxn01003.other_comments: This reaction represents the decarboxylation of phenylpyruvate to form phenylacetaldehyde (alpha-tolualdehyde) and CO2, consuming a proton. Stoichiometry balances: phenylpyruvate (C9H7O3-) + H+ yields CO2 (CO2) + phenylacetaldehyde (C8H8O). Carbon: 9 = 1+8; balanced. The decarboxylation releases CO2 and is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (decarboxylation) direction.

rxn05104.other_comments: This is the methionine salvage pathway dehydratase step (MtnB / DK-MTP-1-P dehydratase, EC 4.2.1.109), converting S-methyl-5-thio-D-ribulose-1-phosphate to 2,3-diketo-5-methylthiopentyl-1-phosphate with release of water. The enzyme name 'hydro-lyase' confirms a dehydration reaction.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance for hydrogen and charge. 1-Pyrroline-4-hydroxy-2-carboxylate (C5H6NO3-, the deprotonated form) + H2O + H+ should yield 2,5-dioxopentanoate (C5H5O4-) + NH4+ (or NH3 + H+). With NH3 as product, the extra H+ on the left is unbalanced; the standard balanced form is: 1-Pyrroline-4-hydroxy-2-carboxylate + 2 H2O = 2,5-dioxopentanoate + NH3 (with appropriate H+ handling)
rxn01635.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 1-pyrroline-4-hydroxy-2-carboxylate deaminase (EC 3.5.4.22) in the hydroxyproline degradation pathway. It hydrolytically opens the cyclic imine ring and releases ammonia, producing 2,5-dioxopentanoate (alpha-ketoglutarate semialdehyde). The hydrolytic ring-opening/deamination is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (degradative) direction.

errors: The reaction as written may not be charge-balanced or mass-balanced depending on exact structures; DDMS (1-chloro-2,2-bis(4-chlorophenyl)ethane) losing HCl to form DDNU (1,1-bis(4-chlorophenyl)ethylene, an unsaturated/olefin product) is consistent, but the listed products H+ + Cl- account for HCl elimination, which appears balanced as a dehydrohalogenation
rxn03686.other_comments: This represents a dehydrochlorination (HCl elimination) step in the microbial degradation of DDT metabolites: DDMS is converted to DDNU (an unsaturated compound) by a chloride-lyase, releasing HCl as H+ and Cl-. Elimination of HCl to form an alkene is thermodynamically favorable and typically irreversible in vivo.

rxn06345.other_comments: This is prolyl 3-hydroxylase (EC 1.14.11.7), an Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase. It hydroxylates a proline residue in procollagen at the 3-position, splitting molecular O2 so one oxygen atom is incorporated into the hydroxyproline and the other into the succinate/CO2 product (oxidative decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate). The stoichiometry is balanced: one O2, one 2-oxoglutarate, and one proline residue yield one CO2, one succinate, and one 3-hydroxyproline residue. The two oxygen atoms of O2 are accounted for (one to the hydroxyl, one to succinate). In vivo this reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (hydroxylation) direction due to the thermodynamically favorable decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate.

rxn02671.other_comments: This reaction describes a delta23-oxidoreductase acting on 23,24-dihydrocucurbitacin. As written, the dihydro (reduced) form is oxidized to cucurbitacin (with the C23-C24 double bond), reducing NADP+ to NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of the saturated bond removes 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons), one hydride goes to NADP+ to form NADPH and one proton is released. In vivo, NADPH/NADP+-dependent reductases typically operate in the reductive direction (consuming NADPH to reduce the double bond), so the physiological flux likely favors cucurbitacin + NADPH -> dihydrocucurbitacin + NADP+, i.e., the reverse of as-written. Note: 'cucurbitacin' is a generic class name; a specific cucurbitacin should be specified for a precise mass balance.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the oxidation of thiomorpholine-3-carboxylate to its 3,4-dehydro form removes 2 H (one hydride to NADP+ giving NADPH, plus one H+), so the correct form should produce NADPH + 1 H+, not 2 H+. As written with 2 H+ on the product side, hydrogen and charge are not balanced.
rxn03015.other_comments: This is an oxidoreductase reaction where thiomorpholine-3-carboxylate is oxidized (dehydrogenated) at the 3,4-position with concomitant reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. This type of imine-forming dehydrogenation (analogous to dihydropyrimidine/related dehydrogenases) is typically reversible, though physiological direction may favor the reductive (NADPH-consuming) direction toward the saturated ring. The standard oxidation of a C-N bond to form a C=N (dehydro) compound releases 2[H], appearing as NADPH + 1 H+.

rxn01906.other_comments: This is the cysteine sulfinate aminotransferase (aspartate aminotransferase side activity) reaction. 3-Sulfinoalanine (L-cysteine sulfinate) transfers its amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and 3-sulfinopyruvate (beta-sulfinylpyruvate). Atoms and charges balance: the amino group is transferred from the amino acid donor to the 2-oxoacid acceptor. The unstable 3-sulfinopyruvate spontaneously decomposes to pyruvate and sulfite in vivo, which can pull the reaction forward, but the aminotransferase reaction itself is mechanistically reversible.

rxn09665.other_comments: This is a transport reaction moving adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate (PAP) between two compartments (e.g., extracellular and cytosol). The same metabolite appears on both sides, which is correct for a transport reaction where compartment labels distinguish the species. Stoichiometry is balanced 1:1. Without additional coupling (e.g., proton symport/antiport or ATP), simple facilitated diffusion transporters are typically modeled as reversible.

rxn03057.other_comments: This reaction represents the isomerization of 5-methylthio-5-deoxy-D-ribose-1-phosphate (an aldose phosphate) to 5-methylthio-5-deoxy-D-ribulose-1-phosphate (a ketose phosphate), catalyzed by methylthioribose-1-phosphate isomerase (MtnA) in the methionine salvage pathway. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a simple intramolecular aldose-ketose isomerization with no atoms gained or lost. Although isomerases are intrinsically reversible, in vivo this step is driven forward by the irreversible downstream dehydratase and subsequent steps of the methionine salvage pathway.

errors: The H+ on the substrate side is incorrect; glucosyltransferase reactions of this type typically release a proton rather than consume one, so the H+ should appear on the product side (or be omitted)

Substrate naming inconsistency: the reaction name refers to N-hydroxy-2-phenylethanethioamide (a phenethyl-derived thiohydroximate) but the actual substrate given is the indolylmethyl thiohydroximate; the enzyme name does not match the metabolite
rxn11701.other_comments: This is an S-glucosyltransferase (UGT74-type) reaction forming a desulfoglucosinolate from a thiohydroximate using UDP-glucose as the glucosyl donor, releasing UDP. Glucosyl transfer to the sulfur yields the desulfoglucosinolate. Atom balance is otherwise reasonable (glucose moiety transferred, UDP released), but the proton handling and the enzyme/substrate name mismatch are issues.

errors: Oxygen/electron balance: reduction of a nitro group (R-NO2) to a hydroxylamino group (R-NHOH) is a 4-electron reduction requiring 2 NADH and removing one oxygen (as water); 2 NADH + 2 H+ provides 4 electrons and 4 H+, while the reaction shows only 1 H2O released. Mass balance check: R-NO2 (2 O) -> R-NHOH (1 O) loses 1 O as H2O, consistent. Hydrogen balance: left has 2 NADH H + 2 H+ donated = need to account; product side gains 1 H on N and 1 OH, plus 1 H2O. The equation appears approximately balanced for the 4-electron nitro-to-hydroxylamine reduction.
Charge/proton convention should be verified (NAD shown as NAD rather than NAD+).
rxn02951.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD(P)H-dependent reduction of 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4-NQO), a known mutagen, to its more reactive metabolite 4-hydroxyaminoquinoline N-oxide (4-HAQO). This is a 4-electron reduction of the nitro group to a hydroxylamine, consuming 2 NADH and producing 1 water and 2 NAD+. The stoichiometry is essentially balanced for this transformation.

rxn01947.other_comments: This is an aminotransferase (transaminase) reaction transferring the amino group from 5-hydroxy-L-tryptophan to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and 5-hydroxyindolepyruvate (the keto acid analog). The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: amino group transfer between an amino acid and a 2-oxo acid pair. Aminotransferase reactions are typically reversible due to the PLP-mediated ping-pong mechanism and near-equilibrium thermodynamics.

rxn11623.other_comments: This is the epoxide hydrolase reaction (cholesterol 5,6-epoxide hydrolase, EC 3.3.2.11) where water hydrolyzes the 5,6-alpha-epoxide ring of 5,6alpha-epoxy-5alpha-cholestane to yield the corresponding trans-diol, 5alpha-cholestane-5alpha,6beta-diol. Stoichiometry is balanced: addition of one H2O across the epoxide gives the vicinal diol with no extra atoms required. Epoxide hydrolysis is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding strongly toward diol formation.

rxn04936.other_comments: This is a 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3-oxidoreductase) reaction acting on 3beta-hydroxy-5alpha-pregnan-20-one (allopregnanolone-type isomer). Oxidation of the 3beta-hydroxyl group to a 3-keto group yields 5alpha-pregnane-3,20-dione (allopregnanedione), with concomitant reduction of NADP+ to NADPH + H+. The reaction is balanced in carbon, hydrogen, and redox equivalents: a hydroxyl/CH center is oxidized to a ketone, releasing 2 electrons and a proton to NADP+, releasing one H+ into solution. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: condensation of polyprenyl-mannose (mannosyl donor) with keto-meroacid-3-mycolate (acceptor) releasing water does not balance with the listed substrates; a mannosyl transfer should release the polyprenyl-phosphate carrier rather than only H2O, so the product/byproduct accounting appears incomplete

rxn13521.other_comments: This is depicted as a mannosyltransferase/condensation step in mycobacterial cell-envelope lipid biosynthesis using a polyprenyl-mannose lipid carrier as the sugar donor onto a keto-meroacid mycolate intermediate. As written the equation does not properly balance atoms because a glycosyl transfer from a polyprenyl-mannose donor should release the polyprenyl carrier (e.g., polyprenyl-phosphate) rather than just water.

rxn00021.other_comments: This is the benzaldehyde lyase (EC 4.1.2.38) / benzoin aldolase type reaction. Benzoin (2-hydroxy-1,2-diphenylethanone, C14H12O2) is cleaved into 2 molecules of benzaldehyde (C7H6O). Atom balance: C14H12O2 = 2 x C7H6O = C14H12O2, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. Although named as a lyase (cleavage) reaction, the enzyme catalyzes both benzoin condensation and cleavage in a thiamine diphosphate-dependent manner, so it is functionally reversible.

rxn04411.other_comments: This reaction represents the interconversion between the chalcone isoliquiritigenin and the flavanone liquiritigenin via an intramolecular cyclization (Michael-type addition of the 2'-hydroxyl onto the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone). The two compounds are isomers (both C15H12O4), so the reaction is balanced 1:1 with no atoms gained or lost. In vivo this is typically catalyzed by chalcone isomerase (EC 5.5.1.6), which strongly favors flavanone formation, though the cyclization can also occur spontaneously and non-enzymatically. The enzyme reaction is stereospecific producing the (2S)-flavanone. Given the isomerase nature, the reaction is formally reversible, but biologically it proceeds predominantly toward liquiritigenin.

rxn03374.other_comments: This is a cystathionine gamma-lyase type beta/gamma elimination reaction acting on the selenium analog. Selenocystathionine (Se-bridged analog of cystathionine) is cleaved with water to yield 2-oxobutyrate, ammonia, and selenocysteine. Mass and charge balance: selenocystathionine (C7H14N2O4Se) + H2O gives selenocysteine (C3H7NO2Se) + 2-oxobutyrate (C4H5O3-) + NH3 + H+, which balances atoms and charge. The reaction is analogous to cystathionine gamma-lyase, a deaminating gamma-elimination, and is physiologically essentially irreversible in the catabolic (lyase/elimination) direction.

rxn02436.other_comments: This is a kinase reaction (dihydrostreptomycin-6-phosphate 3'alpha-phosphotransferase) transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the 3'alpha position of dihydrostreptomycin 6-phosphate, producing the 3'alpha,6-bisphosphate and ADP plus a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: one phosphate is transferred from ATP to the substrate, yielding ADP and H+. Stoichiometry is correct. As an ATP-dependent phosphotransferase (aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme conferring antibiotic resistance), the reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo due to ATP hydrolysis driving phosphoryl transfer.

rxn04384.other_comments: This is the cobinamide phosphate synthase reaction (CbiB/CobD) in the cobalamin biosynthesis pathway. ATP-dependent amide bond formation links the (R)-1-aminopropan-2-yl phosphate to a carboxyl group of adenosylcobyric acid (one of the f side chain), yielding adenosyl cobinamide phosphate, with ATP hydrolyzed to ADP and inorganic phosphate. Atoms and charges balance: the new amide bond releases water-equivalent components captured by phosphate plus H+. Stoichiometry is consistent with an ATP-driven ligase.

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: the transfer of one acyl group from the diacyl-phosphatidylglycerol donor to the 2-acyl-monoacyl acceptor should yield a triacyl product plus a deacylated (glycerophosphoglycerol) product, but the formula balance depends on correct acyl counts. As written, the donor (diacyl-PG, 2 x C14:1) loses one acyl to give monoacyl-PG (lyso-PG), while the acceptor (2-acyl-PG, 1 x C14:1) gains one acyl to give diacyl-PG. The product names ('acyl phosphatidylglycerol' = monoacyl/lyso and 'Glycerophosphoglycerol' = deacylated) are inconsistent: an acyltransferase moving an acyl onto the 2-acyl acceptor would produce a diacyl product, not glycerophosphoglycerol, and would convert the donor to lyso-PG, not to fully deacylated GPG.
rxn08833.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase L2 / acyltransferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.-/3.1.1.5 family) involving transfer of a tetradec-7-enoyl (C14:1) acyl group between phosphatidylglycerol species. The mechanism takes two lyso/acyl-PG molecules and forms one diacyl-PG plus one fully deacylated glycerophosphoglycerol (transacylation/disproportionation). The labeling of intermediates in this reaction appears internally inconsistent regarding which product is the diacyl vs deacylated species.

rxn14355.other_comments: This reaction represents the S-glucosyltransferase step (UGT74-type enzyme, e.g., UGT74B1) in glucosinolate biosynthesis. UDP-glucose donates a glucose moiety to the thiol group of thiohydroximate, forming the S-beta-D-glucosyl thiohydroximate (desulfoglucosinolate) and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: the glucosyl group transferred from UDP-glucose accounts for the difference between thiohydroximate and desulfoglucosinolate, with UDP as the leaving group. Generic substrate names (R groups) are used, so atom-by-atom balance cannot be fully verified, but the group transfer is consistent.

rxn09913.other_comments: This reaction represents L-amino acid ligase (Lal) forming the dipeptide glycyl-L-phenylalanine (Gly-Phe) from glycine and L-phenylalanine, using ATP hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: peptide bond formation releases water, but the ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi consumes water, so atoms and charges balance with the release of one H+. The energetically favorable ATP hydrolysis (to ADP + Pi) drives the otherwise unfavorable peptide bond synthesis in the forward (synthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn06382.other_comments: This is the dinitrogen reductase ADP-ribosyltransferase (DraT) reaction, which transfers an ADP-ribosyl group from NAD+ onto an arginine residue of dinitrogen reductase (the Fe protein of nitrogenase), releasing nicotinamide and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: NAD+ donates the ADP-ribosyl moiety while nicotinamide and H+ are released. In vivo this modification inactivates nitrogenase and proceeds in the direction of ADP-ribosylation; the reverse (removal) is catalyzed by a separate enzyme (DraG, a glycohydrolase), so this reaction is effectively physiologically forward.

rxn01306.other_comments: This is a class II aldolase reaction (2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-pentonate aldolase, EC 4.1.2.28). The substrate 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-pentonate (a 5-carbon keto-acid) is cleaved into pyruvate (3 carbons) and glycolaldehyde (2 carbons). Carbon balance is correct (5 = 3 + 2). The reaction is part of D-arabinose/D-xylose degradation pathways. Although aldol cleavages are formally reversible, in vivo this operates in the cleavage (forward) direction within catabolic pathways.

rxn08201.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol pyrophosphatase reaction. CDP-diacylglycerol (with two C14:1 tetradec-7-enoyl chains) is hydrolyzed at the diphosphate bridge by water, releasing CMP and yielding phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) plus a proton. Mass and charge balance: CDP-DAG carries the cytidine diphosphate moiety; hydrolysis cleaves the pyrophosphate to give CMP and the monophosphate (PA). Atoms (C, N, P) and charges balance with the released H+. This pyrophosphatase/hydrolase reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo due to phosphoanhydride bond hydrolysis.

errors: Oxygen mass/electron balance appears incorrect: oxidation of an aldehyde (5'-oxoinosine, a 5'-aldehyde) to a carboxylic acid (9-riburonosylhypoxanthine) by O2 should also produce water or H2O2; as written, the oxygen and hydrogen atoms do not balance. For 2 aldehyde -> 2 carboxylic acid using one O2, the balanced form would typically be O2 + 2 aldehyde -> 2 carboxylic acid (with O atoms accounted) but the released 2 H+ without a reduced oxygen acceptor (H2O or H2O2) leaves electrons unbalanced.
rxn11662.other_comments: This is an aldehyde oxidase / dehydrogenase-type reaction oxidizing the 5'-aldehyde of 5'-oxoinosine to the 5'-carboxylate (9-riburonosylhypoxanthine, the uronic acid). Such O2-dependent oxidations are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (oxidation) direction. The main concern is atom/redox balance of the oxygen species.

rxn04358.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction (AveBI, the avermectin oleandrosyltransferase) that transfers an L-oleandrose sugar from dTDP-L-oleandrose to the avermectin B1b monosaccharide, producing the disaccharide avermectin B1b and releasing dTDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the glycosyl moiety is transferred from the nucleotide-sugar donor to the aglycone acceptor, releasing dTDP. In vivo this proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward avermectin formation, driven by the favorable cleavage of the nucleotide-sugar bond.

rxn01676.other_comments: This reaction is the thymidylyltransferase reaction where TTP (dTTP) reacts with alpha-D-galactose 1-phosphate to form dTDP-galactose and pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: the nucleotidyl (TMP/dTMP) moiety is transferred to the sugar phosphate, releasing PPi. Atoms and charges balance correctly. In vivo, the released PPi is rapidly hydrolyzed by pyrophosphatase, driving the reaction toward dTDP-sugar synthesis.

rxn09661.other_comments: This is a transport reaction representing passive diffusion of D-glucitol/D-sorbitol (D-gulitol is a synonym for D-glucitol/sorbitol) across a membrane. The same metabolite appears on both sides, which is standard notation for transport reactions where the compartment differs (e.g., extracellular vs cytoplasmic). Stoichiometry is balanced 1:1, which is correct for facilitated/passive diffusion. The reaction name mentions L-sorbitol while the metabolite is D-gulitol; this naming inconsistency should be noted but does not affect mass balance.

errors: The reaction name (L-2-Aminoadipate-6-semialdehyde:NAD(P)+ 6-oxidoreductase) does not match the reaction shown, which describes an adenylylation/thioester-loading step rather than an NAD(P)+-dependent oxidoreduction; no NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H appears

rxn06802.other_comments: This represents the loading of alpha-aminoadipate (already activated as the alpha-aminoadipoyl-AMP adenylate) onto the phosphopantetheine thiol of the holo-Lys2 enzyme (aminoadipate reductase), releasing AMP and forming the enzyme-bound thioester (aminoadipoyl-S-enzyme). In vivo this thioester-forming step is driven strongly toward the loaded intermediate to subsequently undergo NADPH-dependent reductive release of the semialdehyde.

rxn04419.other_comments: This is an SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction. Daidzein (4',7-dihydroxyisoflavone) is methylated at the 4'-hydroxyl to form formononetin (7-hydroxy-4'-methoxyisoflavone), with SAM converted to S-adenosyl-homocysteine and release of a proton. The atoms balance: one methyl group is transferred from SAM to the 4'-O of daidzein, and the H+ released accounts for the deprotonation of the hydroxyl. Stoichiometry and charge are correct.

rxn08436.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of palmitoyl-ACP (acyl-ACP thioesterase reaction). Water cleaves the thioester bond between palmitate and acyl carrier protein, releasing free palmitate and holo-ACP. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge (with one H2O consumed and the thioester converted to a carboxylate and free thiol). This is the typical FatA/FatB acyl-ACP thioesterase chain-terminating step in plant/bacterial fatty acid synthesis.

errors: Proton imbalance: the reaction as written produces 2 H+, but the correct balance for an acyl-AMP forming ligase (ATP + acid + ACP -> AMP + PPi + acyl-ACP) typically yields 1 H+ when accounting for ionization states; the stoichiometry of 2.0 H+ is likely incorrect.
rxn10752.other_comments: This represents an acyl-ACP synthetase (ligase) reaction in which 4-hydroxybenzoate is activated using ATP (forming an acyl-AMP intermediate, releasing PPi) and then transferred to acyl carrier protein (ACP) to form 4-hydroxybenzoyl-ACP plus AMP. The general chemistry (ATP + carboxylic acid + ACP -> AMP + PPi + acyl-ACP) is plausible.

rxn04264.other_comments: This is a monooxygenase reaction where limonene is oxidized to limonene 1,2-epoxide (limonene oxide). One atom of molecular oxygen is incorporated into the substrate (forming the epoxide) while the other oxygen atom is reduced to water using electrons from NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + H+ provide 2 electrons and 2 protons; O2 is split with one O going into the epoxide and one O combining with 2H to form H2O, regenerating NAD+. Monooxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the consumption of O2 and NADH and the highly exergonic oxygen activation.

rxn02555.other_comments: This is an amidohydrolase reaction where N-feruloylglycine is hydrolyzed at the amide bond, consuming one water molecule to release glycine and ferulate. The reaction is balanced: N-feruloylglycine (C12H13NO5) + H2O (H2O) yields glycine (C2H5NO2) + ferulate (C10H9O4-, or C10H10O4 protonated). Mass and charge balance are consistent. Hydrolysis of amide bonds is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn14372.other_comments: This is the N-succinylornithine carbamoyltransferase (SOTCase) reaction, part of the alternative arginine biosynthesis pathway found in organisms like Bacteroides. Carbamoyl phosphate transfers its carbamoyl group to the delta-amino group of N2-succinyl-L-ornithine, producing N-succinyl-L-citrulline and releasing phosphate plus a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: carbamoyl phosphate (CH4NO5P) + N2-succinyl-L-ornithine donates carbamoyl, yielding phosphate + H+ + N-succinyl-L-citrulline. Atoms and charges balance.

rxn02888.other_comments: This is an enoyl-CoA hydratase-type reaction. 3-Hydroxyisovaleryl-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylbutyryl-CoA) undergoes dehydration to yield 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA (dimethylacryloyl-CoA, 3,3-dimethylacryloyl-CoA) plus water. The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: removal of H2O from the beta-hydroxy acyl-CoA gives the alpha,beta-unsaturated acyl-CoA. Hydro-lyase reactions of this type are typically reversible, though physiological direction depends on context (e.g., leucine degradation favors the hydration/synthesis side).

rxn02046.other_comments: This reaction describes phosphoserine phosphatase activity on the D-isomer: hydrolysis of D-O-phosphoserine (D-phosphoserine) to D-serine and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced (one water consumed, phosphate ester bond hydrolyzed yielding free phosphate and free amino acid). Phosphate monoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction toward D-serine and phosphate.

rxn13400.other_comments: This reaction describes the dehydration of 3-(4-hydroxyphenyl)lactate (HPL) to form 4-coumarate (4-hydroxycinnamate) plus water, catalyzed by a hydro-lyase. Removing water (H2O) from the lactate (which bears a hydroxyl on the beta carbon) yields the alpha,beta-unsaturated 4-coumarate. The atoms balance: loss of one H2O from HPL gives the unsaturated acid. Hydro-lyase (dehydratase) reactions are generally reversible, though direction in vivo depends on substrate/product concentrations. The mass balance is correct as written.

errors: Substrate/product mismatch with enzyme name: the enzyme is described as precorrin-4 C20-methyltransferase, but the reaction uses precorrin-2 as substrate and precorrin-3A as product
The methylation of precorrin-2 to precorrin-3A is catalyzed by precorrin-2 C20-methyltransferase (CobI/CbiL, EC 2.1.1.130), not precorrin-4 C11-methyltransferase (EC 2.1.1.133)
rxn02775.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent C-methyltransferase reaction in the cobalamin/siroheme biosynthesis pathway. The reaction as written (precorrin-2 + SAM -> precorrin-3A + SAH + H+) is stoichiometrically balanced and chemically correct for the C20 methylation step. However, the enzyme name (precorrin-4 C20-methyltransferase) is inconsistent with the substrates listed. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions of this type proceed essentially irreversibly in the forward (biosynthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn04144.other_comments: This represents a step in the phototransduction cascade of rhodopsin. After light absorption, rhodopsin progresses through a series of conformational intermediates: bathorhodopsin to lumirhodopsin to metarhodopsin (I and II). Lumirhodopsin thermally decays to metarhodopsin. These are isomerization/conformational transitions of the same chromophore-protein complex (with all-trans retinal), so the conversion is mass-balanced. The transition is thermally driven and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo as the protein relaxes toward the active metarhodopsin II state.

errors: The reaction is written identically on both sides (H+ + 2',3'-Cyclic UMP on both reactant and product sides) without compartment annotations. For a transport reaction, the metabolites must be designated to different compartments (e.g., periplasm/extracellular vs cytoplasm) to represent translocation across the membrane. As written, it is a null reaction with no net transformation.
rxn11402.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction moving 2',3'-cyclic UMP across the membrane along with a proton. Although the input lacks compartment labels, the implied transport (uptake driven by the proton motive force) would proceed in the import direction. Stoichiometry of 1 H+ per substrate is reasonable for a proton symporter, but compartment specification is required.

rxn04977.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by liquiritigenin 2-hydroxylase / licodione synthase (CYP93B-type cytochrome P450 monooxygenase). It converts the flavanone liquiritigenin into licodione via 2-hydroxylation followed by ring opening of the heterocyclic C-ring, yielding a 1,3-diketone (licodione). As a P450 monooxygenase reaction, the stoichiometry is correct: one atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (and ultimately leads to ring opening) and the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Charge/atom balance is consistent (NADPH + O2 + substrate -> H2O + NADP + product). P450 monooxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of oxygenation.

rxn03335.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing 3,4-dihydroxymandelaldehyde to 3,4-dihydroxymandelic acid (dihydroxymandelic acid). The stoichiometry is balanced: an aldehyde plus water plus NAD+ yields the carboxylic acid plus NADH plus 2 H+. The mass and charge balance check out (the aldehyde gains an oxygen from water and loses 2 H as NADH + H+). rxn04607.other_comments: This is intended to represent a cytochrome P450 (2-hydroxyisoflavanone synthase, CYP93C) type monooxygenase reaction converting a flavanone/flavone to a 2-hydroxyisoflavanone, here apigenin to 2-hydroxy-2,3-dihydrogenistein. errors: The reaction is not mass-balanced. Oxidation of spheroidene (C41H60O, contains one methoxy group) to spheroidenone introduces a keto group (=O). The balanced reaction requires O2 + spheroidene -> spheroidenone + H2O, but checking atoms: spheroidene C41H60O + O2 -> spheroidenone C41H58O2 + H2O. Left H: 60, Right H: 58+2=60 (H balanced); Left O: 1+2=3, Right O: 2+1=3 (O balanced); C: 41=41. Actually the reaction is balanced as written for a monooxygenase-type reaction. No stoichiometric error if formulas are as stated.

Note: a true monooxygenase reaction typically also requires a reductant (e.g., NAD(P)H or reduced acceptor) to account for the second oxygen atom of O2; the simplified equation may omit this cofactor.
rxn07368.other_comments: This is the spheroidene monooxygenase (CrtA) reaction converting spheroidene to the ketocarotenoid spheroidenone in purple photosynthetic bacteria. As written (O2 + spheroidene -> H2O + spheroidenone), atoms balance assuming one O incorporated as keto group and one reduced to water. Biologically it is an irreversible oxygenation proceeding in the forward direction.

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance is unlikely here; this is a phosphotransfer where the phosphate moves from phosphohistidine to ascorbate. The reaction as written appears balanced (phosphoryl group transferred from protein N-pros-phosphohistidine to ascorbate yielding ascorbate 6-phosphate and dephosphorylated protein histidine).
rxn07486.other_comments: This represents the phosphoenolpyruvate:carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS)-like phosphoryl transfer for the ascorbate-specific PTS (EC 2.7.1.194). A phosphohistidine residue on an enzyme (EIIB) transfers its phosphoryl group to L-ascorbate, producing L-ascorbate 6-phosphate during import. The donor is the N-pros (N1) phosphohistidine of the protein and the product is the dephosphorylated histidine residue.

rxn02842.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent oxidation of 2-deoxy-D-gluconate at the C3 hydroxyl group, producing 3-dehydro-2-deoxy-D-gluconate (a ketone) plus NADH and H+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one as H+), which is correctly represented. This corresponds to KEGG R04049, catalyzed by 2-deoxy-D-gluconate 3-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.125).

rxn02281.other_comments: This is the N-methylhydantoin amidohydrolase (ATP-hydrolyzing) reaction (EC 3.5.2.14). It hydrolyzes the ring of N-methylhydantoin to N-carbamoylsarcosine, coupled to ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi. The atom balance checks out: ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi releases 1 H+, and ring hydrolysis of N-methylhydantoin with one H2O adds atoms to give N-carbamoylsarcosine. The stoichiometry of 2 H2O, ATP -> ADP + Pi + 2 H+ + product is consistent with mass and charge balance. The ATP-driven step makes the reaction effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction (hydantoin degradation).

rxn02634.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.114) transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the hydroxyl group of trans-2-hydroxycinnamate, forming beta-D-glucosyl-2-coumarate and releasing UDP. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: UDP-glucose (donor) plus the aglycone acceptor yields the glucoside plus UDP. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo due to the high group-transfer potential of the UDP-glucose anomeric bond.

rxn12185.other_comments: This is galactose dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.48 / 1.1.1.120), oxidizing D-galactose at C1 using NAD+ to produce D-galactono-1,5-lactone (the gamma/delta lactone form) plus NADH and H+. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: each side carries one oxidation/reduction event, the carbon/oxygen/hydrogen atoms balance when accounting for the loss of 2 H (one as H+ and one transferred as hydride to NADH), and charge is balanced. In vivo, the lactone is typically hydrolyzed to galactonate, pulling the reaction toward oxidation (forward direction).

errors: The reaction is a transport reaction but as written it shows identical species (H+ + Indoleacetate) on both sides without compartment annotations, making it appear as a null/identity reaction with no net change
No distinction between compartments (e.g., cytosol vs extracellular/periplasm) is indicated, so the proton symport/antiport coupling cannot be verified
Stoichiometry appears balanced only trivially because both sides are identical; a meaningful transport reaction would show the same metabolites in different compartments
rxn10560.other_comments: This appears to be a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN) for indoleacetate (likely indole-3-acetate, a plant auxin / bacterial metabolite) coupled with a proton. As written, the substrates and products are identical, which represents a transport across a membrane where the compartment labels have been stripped. Without compartment information the reaction is effectively a no-op.

rxn14160.other_comments: This reaction represents gluconate 2-dehydrogenase (NADP+), oxidizing D-gluconate (GLCN) at the C2 position to 2-keto-D-gluconate (2-dehydro-D-gluconate), with NADP+ reduced to NADPH plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: gluconate (C6H11O7-) loses 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+, one released as H+) to form 2-keto-D-gluconate. Carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and charge balance correctly. While the enzyme is named as a 2-oxidoreductase favoring oxidation, NADP-dependent oxidoreductases of this type are generally reversible; in vivo the direction depends on the NADPH/NADP+ ratio, with the reductive (2-ketogluconate to gluconate) direction often favored when NADPH is abundant.

rxn07677.other_comments: This is the activation of OPC-8:0 (3-oxo-2-(2'-pentenyl)cyclopentane-1-octanoic acid), an intermediate in jasmonic acid biosynthesis, to its CoA thioester (OPC8-CoA). The reaction is catalyzed by OPCL1 (4-coumarate:CoA ligase-like / OPC-8:0 CoA ligase). Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + carboxylic acid yields AMP + PPi + the CoA thioester, with one proton released. This is the standard acyl-adenylate forming mechanism. Atoms and charges balance with the proton accounted for.

rxn09023.other_comments: This represents the O16 antigen polymerase (Wzy) reaction in E. coli, which elongates the growing O-antigen chain. The polymerase transfers the nascent polysaccharide chain from one undecaprenyl-diphosphate carrier onto a single O-antigen repeat unit attached to another undecaprenyl-diphosphate carrier. Here a chain of 2 repeat units plus a single repeat unit yields a chain of 3 repeat units, releasing undecaprenyl (bactoprenyl) diphosphate. Stoichiometry balances: the two substrate undecaprenyl-PP carriers yield one elongated chain on a single carrier plus one free undecaprenyl-PP. Note that 'Bactoprenyl diphosphate' and 'undecaprenyl diphosphate' are synonyms, so the released carrier is correctly accounted for.

errors: Mass imbalance: reduction of a nitro group (-NO2) to a hydroxylamino group (-NHOH) requires 2 NADPH and consumes water/protons but produces water. The given equation produces H2O on the product side while consuming NADPH; for nitro-to-hydroxylamino reduction the net reaction typically is R-NO2 + 2 NADPH + 2 H+ -> R-NHOH + 2 NADP+ + H2O, so the single H2O product is consistent, but the substrate 4-Hydroxylamino-2,6-dinitrotoluene to 2,4-Dihydroxylamino-6-nitrotoluene converts one of the remaining nitro groups to hydroxylamino, which is balanced as written
Charge/proton balance should be verified: NADP is typically written as NADP+; ensure 2 H+ consumed matches the reduction stoichiometry
rxn07805.other_comments: This is a nitroreductase-type reaction reducing a nitro group on the dinitrotoluene to a hydroxylamino group, using NADPH as electron donor. As written it converts 4-hydroxylamino-2,6-dinitrotoluene to 2,4-dihydroxylamino-6-nitrotoluene. The stoichiometry (2 NADPH, 2 H+, 1 H2O) is appropriate for a two-electron-equivalent nitro-to-hydroxylamino reduction (actually 4-electron, requiring 2 NADPH). [directionality_note] NADPH-dependent reductions strongly favor the forward (reductive) direction in vivo

rxn10523.other_comments: This is a prenyltransferase (chain elongation) reaction where isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP, C5) condenses with 3-hydroxy-farnesyl diphosphate (C15) to form 3-hydroxy-geranylgeranyl diphosphate (C20), releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: C20 = C15 + C5, and the diphosphate from IPP is released as PPi with one H+. The condensation of IPP onto an allylic diphosphate is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically proceeds in the elongation (forward) direction.

errors: Substrate/product naming inconsistency: the reaction is named galactosyltransferase but uses UDP-glucose as the sugar donor, which would transfer glucose, not galactose. A galactosyltransferase should use UDP-galactose as donor. Either the donor should be UDP-galactose or the product/enzyme name should reflect glucose transfer.
rxn08583.other_comments: This represents a glycosyltransferase step in LPS core biosynthesis, transferring a sugar from a nucleotide-sugar donor (UDP-sugar) to a growing oligosaccharide acceptor on lipid A, releasing UDP. Stoichiometry of atoms balances (UDP-sugar + acceptor -> UDP + sugar-acceptor). Such Leloir-type glycosyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo due to cleavage of the high-energy sugar-nucleotide bond.

rxn11201.other_comments: This is an aromatic aminotransferase reaction transferring an amino group between L-Phenylalanine and p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, producing L-Tyrosine and Phenylpyruvate. Stoichiometry is balanced: the amino group from phenylalanine is transferred to the keto acid (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate), yielding tyrosine and converting phenylalanine to its corresponding keto acid (phenylpyruvate). Aminotransferase reactions are typically near-equilibrium and freely reversible in vivo.

errors: Glycerol-3-phosphate appears on both sides of the equation without distinguishing intracellular and extracellular compartments; as written it is not a transport reaction and the substrate is not consumed or produced, making the inclusion of glycerol-3-phosphate meaningless without compartment annotation
rxn05158.other_comments: This is intended to be an ABC-type transporter reaction coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to import of glycerol-3-phosphate. The ATP hydrolysis portion is correctly balanced, but the transported metabolite should be written as Glycerol-3-phosphate[external] -> Glycerol-3-phosphate[cytoplasm] to reflect the import. As written, both glycerol-3-phosphate terms are identical and cancel.

rxn09264.other_comments: This is the spermidine N1-acetyltransferase (SSAT) reaction. Acetyl-CoA transfers an acetyl group to spermidine, producing N1-acetylspermidine, CoA, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: acetyl-CoA + spermidine yields CoA + N1-acetylspermidine + H+. In vivo, SSAT-catalyzed acetylation strongly favors the forward (acetylation) direction as the committed step in polyamine catabolism/back-conversion, driven by the favorable thioester cleavage of acetyl-CoA.

rxn03518.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by HPP epoxidase (HppE), the final step in fosfomycin biosynthesis. HppE oxidatively cyclizes (S)-2-hydroxypropylphosphonate (2-HPP) to fosfomycin, an epoxide-containing antibiotic. The enzyme is a non-heme iron(II)-dependent oxidase that uses O2 as the oxidant and produces water (formally an oxygenase-type 2-electron oxidation forming the C-O epoxide bond and reducing O2). The stoichiometry shown (O2 + 2-HPP -> H2O2 + fosfomycin) is balanced overall in atoms (C3H9O4P + O2 -> C3H7O4P + H2O2), and represents the dehydrogenative epoxidation. In vivo this is committed biosynthetic step driven strongly toward fosfomycin formation.

rxn10792.other_comments: This is the cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) reaction: reduction of half an O2 to water using two reduced cytochrome c molecules and two protons (chemical/scalar protons), producing oxidized cytochrome c. The equation balances: O (1=1), H (2 from H+ vs 2 in H2O), and charge (2+ from 2 H+ plus 2 Fe2+ = +4 on left; 2 Fe3+ = +6 on right minus... note charge needs care). Checking charge: left = 2(+1) + 2(+2) = +6; right = H2O neutral + 2(+3) = +6. Charge balances. Note this representation only includes the scalar protons consumed in water formation, not the protons pumped across the membrane.

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: ring-cleavage dioxygenases (catechol-type) incorporate O2 without consuming H2O; the H2O on the left appears unnecessary or indicates an unbalanced equation

Atom balance issue: 3-sulfocatechol (C6H4O5S, as sulfonate) cleaved with release of sulfite should yield 2-hydroxymuconate, but oxygen/hydrogen/sulfur balance must be checked - releasing sulfite (SO3) plus 2-hydroxymuconate from sulfocatechol + O2 does not balance without additional water/oxygen accounting
Charge balance must be verified: 2 H+ on product side against anionic sulfite and muconate species
rxn07602.other_comments: This represents an extradiol-type ring cleavage of 3-sulfocatechol (2,3-dihydroxybenzenesulfonate) by a dioxygenase, releasing sulfite and forming a hydroxymuconate. Dioxygenase ring-cleavage reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo (driven by O2 incorporation), so forward direction is appropriate. The stoichiometry should be carefully rechecked, particularly the role of H2O and the H+ count, as ring-cleavage dioxygenases typically use O2 alone.

errors: N-Acetyl-D-chondrosamine is a synonym for N-Acetyl-D-galactosamine, so the substrate and product (N-Acetyl-D-galactosamine 6-phosphate) represent the unphosphorylated and phosphorylated forms of the same sugar; this is consistent, not an error, but the naming is inconsistent/confusing

The enzyme name specifies N-pros (N(pi)/N(pros)) phosphohistidine in the title but the reaction substrate is written as 'N-pros-phosphohistidine' while the enzyme name says 'N(pai)' (N-tele); there is an inconsistency between N(pi)/N(pros) and N(pai)/N(tele) histidine tautomer designation
rxn11878.other_comments: This is a PTS (phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase system) type transfer where a phospho-histidine protein donates its phosphate to N-Acetyl-D-galactosamine, producing GalNAc 6-phosphate and dephosphorylated (histidine) protein. N-Acetyl-D-chondrosamine is the same molecule as N-Acetyl-D-galactosamine. Stoichiometry of phosphate transfer balances (1 phosphate moves from protein to sugar).

errors: Incorrect stoichiometry and chemistry: the conversion of IMP to GMP requires NAD+ (or NADP+) as an oxidant to first form XMP (oxidative step producing NADH/NADPH), followed by an amination step that consumes glutamine (or ammonia) plus ATP; it is not a single oxidoreductase reaction

Redox direction is wrong: forming GMP from IMP via XMP is an oxidation of IMP, which should produce NADPH from NADP+, but the amination of XMP to GMP consumes ATP and glutamine, none of which are included
Atom/charge imbalance: NADP+ + NH3 + IMP cannot yield NADPH + 2 H+ + GMP because GMP has an additional carbon-nitrogen (amino) group and the redox bookkeeping does not balance
Missing required substrates: ATP and glutamine (or the AMP, PPi, glutamate products) are not represented
rxn00837.other_comments: The reaction attempts to combine IMP dehydrogenase and GMP synthase activities into a single mis-formulated step. In vivo, IMP is converted to XMP by IMP dehydrogenase (IMP + NAD+ + H2O -> XMP + NADH + H+) and then XMP to GMP by GMP synthase (XMP + ATP + glutamine + H2O -> GMP + AMP + PPi + glutamate). The given equation is both stoichiometrically and mechanistically incorrect.

rxn10681.other_comments: This reaction describes the dephosphorylation of decaprenylphosphoryl-beta-D-5-phosphoribofuranose (DPA precursor) to form decaprenylphosphoryl-beta-D-arabinofuranose (DPA), the arabinose donor for arabinan biosynthesis in mycobacterial cell walls. The reaction hydrolyzes a phosphate group, releasing inorganic phosphate and a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: the substrate phosphate ester is cleaved by water, yielding the dephosphorylated arabinofuranose product, free phosphate, and H+. Mass and charge balance are consistent with a hydrolytic phosphatase reaction.

rxn04725.other_comments: This is a monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction in which 1-methylnaphthalene is oxidized to 1-naphthalenemethanol. One atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (the methyl carbon becomes hydroxymethyl) and the other oxygen atom is reduced to water using electrons from NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + O2 + H+ provides the reducing equivalents and oxygen, yielding H2O + NAD+ + the hydroxylated product. As a typical NAD(P)H-dependent oxygenase reaction, this proceeds essentially irreversibly in the oxidative (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction is not balanced. Acetophenone is C8H8O. With O2 (2 oxygen atoms) and 2 acetophenone, the left side has 2 oxygen atoms added. 2 2-Hydroxyacetophenone (C8H8O2) would require 2 additional oxygen atoms, which is provided by O2. However, the hydrogen balance must be checked: 2 C8H8O + O2 = 2 C8H8O2 gives C16H16O4 on both sides, so atoms balance. The issue is mechanistic: monooxygenase hydroxylation typically requires a reductant (e.g., NAD(P)H) and produces water, consuming only one atom of O2 per substrate, so the simple stoichiometry shown is likely missing cofactors.
rxn03727.other_comments: The reaction shows hydroxylation of acetophenone at the alpha (methyl) position to form 2-hydroxyacetophenone (phenacyl alcohol / 2-hydroxy-1-phenylethanone) using molecular oxygen. Atom counting (C16H16O4 both sides) balances, but oxygenation/hydroxylation reactions in vivo generally require electron donors like NAD(P)H and yield water.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction for an amidohydrolase; the named enzyme catalyzes hydrolysis, which would consume H2O and the gamma-glutamyl amide to produce L-Glutamate and 3-Aminopropiononitrile, not the reverse condensation as written

As written, this is a condensation (amide bond formation) that releases water but lacks an energy source such as ATP; spontaneous amide synthesis from free amino acid and amine is thermodynamically unfavorable in vivo
rxn14123.other_comments: The reaction depicts gamma-Glutamyl-beta-aminopropiononitrile being formed from L-Glutamate and 3-Aminopropiononitrile with release of water. The enzyme name (amidohydrolase) indicates the physiological reaction is hydrolysis of the gamma-glutamyl amide bond, so the biologically relevant direction is the reverse of how it is written. Atoms appear to balance for the condensation/hydrolysis equilibrium.

rxn06135.other_comments: This reaction represents one elongation cycle of fatty acid synthesis: stearoyl-CoA (C18) is condensed with malonyl-CoA, accompanied by decarboxylation, and the resulting beta-ketoacyl group is reduced (oxoacyl-reducing) and dehydrated/enoyl-reduced to yield icosanoyl-CoA (C20). Carbon balance: stearoyl (C18 acyl) + malonyl (C3, contributing 2 carbons after losing CO2) = C20 acyl, correct. The two NADH provide the two reduction steps (ketoreduction and enoyl reduction). H2O is released from the dehydration step. CoA is released from decarboxylative condensation. Stoichiometry of NADH/NAD+ (2 each), CO2, CoA, and H2O is balanced and consistent.

errors: The substrate name in the reaction title (N,6-O-Disulfo-D-glucosamine) differs from the substrate in the equation (N2,6-Disulfo-D-glucosamine); naming should be consistent
The product 'N-Sulfo-D-glucosamine' should specify the position (N-sulfo, i.e., 2-N-sulfo) to be unambiguous, but stoichiometry is otherwise balanced
rxn02301.other_comments: This is a sulfatase (sulfohydrolase) reaction hydrolyzing the 6-O-sulfate group from N,6-disulfo-D-glucosamine to yield N-sulfo-D-glucosamine plus sulfate and a proton. Atoms and charges balance: H2O hydrolyzes the sulfate ester releasing inorganic sulfate and H+. Hydrolytic sulfatase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn04585.other_comments: This is the amide bond formation step in novobiocin biosynthesis catalyzed by the amide synthase NovL. ATP activates the carboxyl group of 3-dimethylallyl-4-hydroxybenzoate (forming an acyl-AMP intermediate), which is then condensed with the amino group of 3-amino-4,7-dihydroxy-8-methylcoumarin (novobiocic acid aminocoumarin moiety) to form the amide bond, releasing AMP, PPi, and H+, and yielding novobiocic acid. The stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphoanhydride bond of ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi, consistent with adenylation-dependent amide synthetases.

errors: This is a transport reaction but lacks compartment annotations to distinguish the two sides of the membrane. As written, both sides are identical (Succinate + 3.0 H+ on both sides), making it a null reaction with no net change. Proper notation would be: Succinate[e] + 3.0 H+[e] <=> Succinate[c] + 3.0 H+[c]
rxn10157.other_comments: This represents a secondary active transport of succinate coupled to proton symport (3 protons per succinate). The intent is to move succinate across a membrane driven by the proton motive force. The reaction is mass and charge balanced trivially since both sides are written identically, but it is missing compartment designators that are essential for a transport reaction. Symport reactions are often modeled as reversible, with the in vivo direction determined by the proton gradient (typically import of succinate driven by inward proton flux).

rxn06578.other_comments: This is a PTS (phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase system) reaction. The phosphoryl group is transferred from a phospho-histidine residue on a protein (such as HPr or an EII component) to L-sorbose, producing L-sorbose 1-phosphate and regenerating the dephosphorylated histidine residue. The stoichiometry is balanced (one phosphate transferred). In vivo this is the sugar-uptake/phosphorylation step and proceeds in the direction of sugar phosphorylation.

rxn09265.other_comments: This reaction represents diamine/spermidine N8-acetyltransferase activity, transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the N8 position of spermidine, yielding CoA, a proton, and N8-acetylspermidine. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: acetyl-CoA + spermidine yields CoA + H+ + N8-acetylspermidine, which conserves atoms (the acetyl group transferred) and charge.

errors: The reaction has identical reactants and products (Acyl-CoA on both sides) with no compartment specification shown, making it appear as a null reaction; for a valid transport reaction, the metabolite should be annotated with distinct compartments, e.g., Acyl-CoA[c] <=> Acyl-CoA[m]
No stoichiometric or compartmental distinction is provided to represent actual transport
rxn12632.other_comments: This is described as an Acyl-CoA transport reaction. As written, it shows Acyl-CoA converting to Acyl-CoA, which is a trivial/null reaction without compartment tags. Transport reactions typically move a metabolite between compartments (e.g., cytosol to mitochondria), but no compartments are indicated here. Note that intact Acyl-CoA is generally not directly transported across membranes; instead, the acyl group is shuttled via the carnitine system.

errors: Proton (H+) should not be generated in this acyl transfer reaction; the transfer of an acyl group from CoA thioester to ACP thiol is thioester-to-thioester exchange and does not release a free proton. The reaction should balance as Isobutyryl-CoA + ACP <=> CoA + isobutyryl-ACP.
rxn05408.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase reaction transferring the isobutyryl (2-methylpropionyl) group from CoA to the phosphopantetheine thiol of ACP. Both substrates are thioesters of similar energy, so the reaction is thermodynamically near-equilibrium and reversible; in vivo direction depends on downstream consumption of isobutyryl-ACP.

rxn07737.other_comments: This reaction is part of the nicotine degradation pathway (KEGG R07947). It involves the dehydration/cyclization between 2,6-dihydroxypseudooxynicotine and 2,6-dihydroxy-N-methylmyosmine. As written, the substrate is the open-chain ketone (2,6-dihydroxypseudooxynicotine) forming the cyclic imine (2,6-dihydroxy-N-methylmyosmine) plus water. Atom balance is consistent: loss of one water molecule converts the amino-ketone into a cyclic Schiff base (imine). In the catabolic direction in vivo, the hydrolytic ring opening (hydration) of 2,6-dihydroxy-N-methylmyosmine to the open-chain compound is favored, so the physiological flow proceeds opposite to the way written.

rxn11674.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 4-hydroxymandelate synthase (HMS), an Fe(II)/alpha-keto acid-dependent dioxygenase. It converts 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate plus O2 to (S)-4-hydroxymandelate plus CO2. The reaction is balanced: substrate C9H8O4 + O2 yields product C8H8O4 + CO2 (carbon: 9+0 = 8+1; oxygen: 4+2 = 4+2; hydrogen: 8 = 8). Mechanistically this is an oxidative decarboxylation incorporating one oxygen atom into the product hydroxyl group. The enzyme is mechanistically irreversible (decarboxylation drives the reaction forward).

rxn03608.other_comments: This is the meta-cleavage pathway hydrolase reaction (e.g., from p-cresol/4-methylcatechol or toluene degradation). The substrate 2-hydroxy-5-methyl-cis,cis-muconic semialdehyde is hydrolytically cleaved by water to release formate plus 2-oxohex-trans-4-enoate (2-oxo-trans-hex-4-enoate). Atom and charge balance: substrate (C7H7O4-, after deprotonation) + H2O yields formate (CHO2-) + 2-oxohex-4-enoate (C6H7O3-) + H+. Carbon (7=1+6), oxygen, and charge appear balanced. The enzyme is a hydrolase acting essentially irreversibly in the catabolic direction in vivo.

rxn05097.other_comments: This represents a cytochrome P450-type / flavonoid 3'-hydroxylase reaction. A flavanone is hydroxylated at the 3' position using molecular oxygen, with NADPH serving as electron donor. One oxygen atom is incorporated into the substrate (as the hydroxyl group) and the other is reduced to water, consistent with a monooxygenase mechanism. Atom and charge balance: NADPH + O2 + H+ + Flavanone yields H2O + NADP+ + 3'-Hydroxyflavanone, which is balanced (the flavanone gains an O and H; the other O plus 2 H from NADPH/H+ form water; NADPH loses H- to become NADP+).

rxn04877.other_comments: This reaction represents the non-enzymatic (or epoxide hydrolase-independent) rearrangement of bromobenzene-2,3-oxide (an arene oxide) to 2-bromophenol via the NIH shift. Arene oxides are reactive intermediates formed during cytochrome P450 metabolism of bromobenzene, and they spontaneously isomerize to phenols. Both species share the same molecular formula (C6H5BrO), so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a simple isomerization.

errors: Substrate should be CO2 or bicarbonate (HCO3-) rather than carbonic acid (H2CO3); if H2CO3 is used as written, a water molecule is missing on the product side to balance oxygen and hydrogen
Charge/proton imbalance depending on protonation states; the free H+ released may not balance correctly with bicarbonate vs carbonic acid as the carboxyl donor
rxn01355.other_comments: This is propionyl-CoA carboxylase activity, an ATP-dependent biotin carboxylase that carboxylates propionyl-CoA to form (S)-methylmalonyl-CoA. Note that the physiological product is typically (S)-methylmalonyl-CoA (D-methylmalonyl-CoA in older nomenclature can map to the S isomer, so stereochemistry naming should be verified). The carbon source is bicarbonate/CO2. The reaction consumes ATP, hydrolyzing it to ADP + Pi, which strongly favors the carboxylation direction in vivo.

rxn03088.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase reaction (EC 2.8.2.-) where PAPS (3'-phosphoadenylylsulfate) transfers a sulfate group to the 6-position of UDP-N-acetyl-D-galactosamine 4-sulfate, producing the 4,6-bissulfate product and PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate) plus a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the sulfate group is transferred from PAPS to the sugar acceptor, and the H+ accounts for the proton released upon sulfate ester formation. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: The reaction shows identical species (H+ and Ethanol) on both sides without distinguishing intracellular and extracellular compartments. As written, this is a null reaction with no net change. For a proton antiport transport reaction, the metabolites must be assigned to different compartments, e.g. H+[e] + Ethanol[c] <=> H+[c] + Ethanol[e].

The name 'proton antiport' is mechanistically inconsistent: in an antiport, the proton and the substrate move in opposite directions, but ethanol transport across membranes is typically passive diffusion, not coupled antiport. The stoichiometry and mechanism described do not match.
Without compartment annotations, stoichiometric balance across membranes cannot be verified.
rxn05553.other_comments: I understand this is intended to be a transport reaction moving ethanol out of the cell, purportedly coupled to proton antiport. However, as written there are no compartment tags, so both sides are identical and the reaction is trivially balanced but biologically meaningless. Ethanol generally crosses membranes by passive diffusion.

rxn02876.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the chromogenic substrate BAPNA (N-benzoyl-DL-arginine-4-nitroanilide) by an amidase/protease activity, cleaving the amide bond to release p-nitroaniline (yellow, measured spectrophotometrically) and N-benzoyl-arginine. The reaction consumes water and produces a proton, which balances charge and mass. Stoichiometry is correct: the amide C-N bond is hydrolyzed, giving a carboxylic acid (N-benzoylarginine) and a free amine (p-nitroaniline).

rxn01030.other_comments: This is the agmatine kinase reaction (EC 2.7.3.10), transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the guanidino nitrogen of agmatine to form N-phosphoagmatine (a phosphagen), producing ADP and a proton. rxn01787.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (limonene 3-monooxygenase, EC 1.14.13.47) reaction. rxn01700.other_comments: This is cellobiose dehydrogenase (cellobiose:quinone 1-oxidoreductase, EC 1.1.5.1). Cellobiose (CELB) is oxidized to cellobiono-1,5-lactone (Cellobiose-1,5-lactone) with concomitant reduction of a quinone to a quinol (hydroquinone). The reaction is a 2-electron, 2-proton transfer and is stoichiometrically balanced as written (one quinone accepting the two electrons/protons released in lactone formation). In vivo this enzyme operates in the oxidative direction, oxidizing cellobiose to drive quinone/electron-acceptor reduction.

rxn02649.other_comments: This is an O-methyltransferase reaction transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to the 3'-hydroxyl of isoorientin, producing isoscoparin (the 3'-O-methyl derivative) and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). The proton release is consistent with methylation of a hydroxyl group. Atom and charge balance are consistent: SAM (net +1 charge in many representations) yields SAH plus the methylated product and a proton. The methyl transfer is correctly accounted for between SAM and the flavone substrate.

rxn00614.other_comments: This is the glycerol-3-phosphate oxidase reaction (EC 1.1.3.21), oxidizing sn-glycerol-3-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerone-phosphate) using molecular oxygen and producing hydrogen peroxide. The reaction is atom-balanced: glycerol-3-phosphate (C3H9O6P) loses two hydrogens to O2, forming DHAP (C3H7O6P) and H2O2. Charges/protonation states depend on convention but mass is balanced.

errors: Electron/oxygen balance is incorrect. The conversion of 2 o-aminophenol to 2 1,2-benzoquinone monoimine removes 4 electrons and 4 hydrogen atoms (one O2 accepts 4 H to form 2 H2O). The correct balanced reaction is: 2 o-aminophenol + O2 -> 2 1,2-benzoquinone monoimine + 2 H2O, which is actually atom-balanced. Each o-aminophenol (C6H7NO) loses 2 H to become the monoimine (C6H5NO); 2 substrates lose 4 H total, and O2 + 4 H -> 2 H2O, so the equation as written IS balanced.
rxn14084.other_comments: This is the o-aminophenol oxidase reaction (EC 1.10.3.4 type chemistry), oxidizing 2-aminophenol to 1,2-benzoquinone monoimine (2-aminophenoxazinone precursor chemistry). Checking atoms: LHS C12H14N2O2 + O2 = C12H14N2O4; RHS 2 H2O (H4O2) + 2 C6H5NO (C12H10N2O2) = C12H14N2O4. The reaction is correctly balanced.

rxn09957.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing undecanal (C11 aldehyde) to undecanoate (C11 carboxylate) using NAD+ as the electron acceptor. Stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (R-CHO) plus water and NAD+ yields the carboxylate (R-COO-), NADH, and 2 H+. Mass balance: undecanal C11H22O + H2O adds the extra oxygen and hydrogens; charge balance also holds (NAD+ +1 on left; NADH 0, undecanoate -1, 2 H+ +2 on right, net +1).

rxn13022.other_comments: This is the 3-isopropylmalate dehydrogenase reaction (LeuB) in leucine biosynthesis. It catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of (2R,3S)-3-isopropylmalate, but the listed substrate is given as 2-isopropylmalate (3-isopropylmalate is the true substrate; if 2-isopropylmalate is meant, that is a substrate mismatch). The product 4MOP is 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (2-oxoisocaproate / ketoleucine). Stoichiometry is balanced: NAD+ + isopropylmalate -> NADH + CO2 + 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate, with an implicit H+ release. The reaction proceeds physiologically in the forward (decarboxylation) direction due to loss of CO2.

rxn07670.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase (BAHD family) reaction transferring a 4-coumaroyl group from 4-coumaroyl-CoA to the 6-position of the 5-O-glucose of pelargonin (pelargonidin 3,5-diglucoside), releasing CoA and producing the acylated anthocyanin. Stoichiometry is balanced: the coumaroyl moiety is transferred from CoA to the glucoside, with CoA released. The acyl-CoA thioester provides the thermodynamic driving force, so the reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn09355.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of UDP-glucuronate by a pyrophosphohydrolase, cleaving the diphosphate bridge to yield UMP and D-glucuronate 1-phosphate. The atoms balance: UDP-glucuronate (C15H22N2O18P2) + H2O yields UMP (C9H13N2O9P), glucuronate 1-phosphate (C6H11O10P), and H+. Mass and charge are conserved. Such hydrolytic cleavage reactions involving water are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: The transported substrate Alkylphosphonate appears on both sides of the equation with identical compartment designation; a proper transport reaction must distinguish the substrate by compartment (e.g., Alkylphosphonate[e] on the reactant side and Alkylphosphonate[c] on the product side). As written, the alkylphosphonate cancels out, leaving only ATP hydrolysis with no net transport.
rxn05191.other_comments: This represents an ABC-type transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the import of alkylphosphonate across a membrane. ATP-driven ABC import is essentially irreversible in vivo, hence forward directionality.

rxn03001.other_comments: This reaction describes a 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase acting on etiocholan-3alpha-ol-17-one (3alpha-hydroxy-5beta-androstan-17-one). The 3alpha-hydroxyl group is oxidized to a ketone, forming 5beta-androstane-3,17-dione, with NADP+ reduced to NADPH + H+. The atoms and electrons balance: oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes two hydrogens (one as hydride to NADP+, one as H+), consistent with the stoichiometry shown.

rxn05116.other_comments: This is the decarboxylation step in pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (vitamin B6) biosynthesis, catalyzed by PdxA-type or related enzymes. 2-Amino-3-oxo-4-phosphonooxybutyrate (1-amino-propan-2-one 3-phosphate precursor) loses CO2 to form 3-amino-2-oxopropyl phosphate (1-amino-acetone 3-phosphate / 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine derived intermediate). The reaction consumes a proton and releases CO2. Atoms balance: substrate C4H7NO7P + H+ gives CO2 (CH... carbon) + product C3H7NO5P. Carbon: 4 = 1 + 3. The decarboxylation is essentially irreversible in vivo due to CO2 release.

rxn03123.other_comments: This is the alpha-1,3-galactosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.87). UDP-galactose donates a galactose to the 3-position of the terminal beta-D-galactose of N-acetyllactosamine, forming the alpha-Gal epitope (Gal-alpha-1,3-Gal-beta-1,4-GlcNAc) and releasing UDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: UDP-galactose contributes galactose plus UDP, with one galactose transferred to the acceptor. Glycosyltransferase reactions using nucleotide-sugar donors are strongly exergonic due to cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn01193.other_comments: This is the protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase (LigAB, EC 1.13.11.8) reaction, which cleaves the aromatic ring of protocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxybenzoate) at the 4,5 (meta) position, incorporating both atoms of O2 to yield 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde. Stoichiometry balances: protocatechuate (C7H5O4-, as the carboxylate anion) plus O2 gives the ring-opened product (C7H4O6, here written as 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde) plus the released H+. Atom and charge balance are consistent. As a dioxygenase incorporating molecular oxygen with ring cleavage, the reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn02511.other_comments: This is a sulfatase (4-sulfohydrolase) reaction that hydrolytically removes the 4-sulfate group from the N-acetyl-D-galactosamine residue of an unsaturated disaccharide derived from chondroitin/dermatan sulfate degradation. The unsaturated uronic acid (4-deoxy-beta-D-gluc-4-enuronosyl) arises from prior lyase action. Stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the sulfate ester, releasing inorganic sulfate and a proton, leaving the desulfated disaccharide. Mass and charge balance check out (sulfate ester + H2O -> alcohol + sulfate + H+).

rxn11733.other_comments: This is the isoprene synthase reaction: dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) is cleaved to release isoprene plus diphosphate (PPi) and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: DMAPP (C5H9O7P2, charge -2 at physiological pH) yields isoprene (C5H8), PPi (HP2O7, charge -3) and H+ (+1). Carbon (5=5), phosphorus (2=2), and net charge (-2 = -3 + 1 + 0) balance correctly. In vivo this is essentially irreversible, driven strongly toward isoprene release (volatile product) and PPi hydrolysis.

rxn02768.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydration of glutaconyl-CoA (a 2,3-unsaturated dicarboxylic acyl-CoA, specifically (E)-glut-2-enedioyl-CoA) to 2-hydroxyglutaryl-CoA via addition of water across the double bond. Stoichiometrically the reaction balances: glutaconyl-CoA (C26H36N7O19P3S, the acyl-CoA thioester of glutaconate) plus H2O yields 2-hydroxyglutaryl-CoA (C26H38N7O20P3S). Atoms (one H2O added across C=C giving an OH and an H) and charges balance. This corresponds to 2-hydroxyglutaryl-CoA dehydratase (EC 4.2.1.-), a key enzyme in glutamate fermentation in anaerobic bacteria such as Acidaminococcus fermentans and Clostridium symbiosum. In vivo the physiological flux is in the dehydration direction (2-hydroxyglutaryl-CoA -> glutaconyl-CoA + H2O) during glutamate degradation, but the enzyme catalyzes a reversible enol/radical-based dehydration and is written reversibly; the in vivo driving direction depends on the metabolic context.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides (H+ + sorbate <=> H+ + sorbate) with no compartment distinction; a transport reaction must specify different compartments, e.g. H+[e] + sorbate[e] <=> H+[c] + sorbate[c]
rxn12536.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport of sorbate, where one proton and one sorbate are co-transported across the membrane. The stoichiometry (1:1 H+:sorbate) is reasonable, but the reaction is missing compartment annotations, making it appear as a null/identity reaction. Transport via proton symport is typically driven by the proton motive force and is often modeled as reversible.

rxn13209.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by branched-chain alpha-keto acid decarboxylase (or the E1 component / a thiamine-dependent decarboxylase). 4MOP is 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (alpha-ketoisocaproate), the keto acid derived from leucine. Non-oxidative decarboxylation yields CO2 and 3-methylbutanal (isovaleraldehyde). Stoichiometry balances: 4MOP (C6H9O3-, as anion) plus H+ gives CO2 (C1) + 3-methylbutanal (C5H10O), so carbon (6=1+5), hydrogen and oxygen balance with proton consumption. Decarboxylations releasing CO2 are essentially irreversible in vivo, hence forward.

rxn04036.other_comments: This is ComB, (R)-2-phospho-3-sulfolactate phosphohydrolase, involved in coenzyme M biosynthesis. It hydrolyzes the phosphate ester of (2R)-phosphosulfolactate to yield (2R)-3-sulfolactate and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: H2O + phosphate monoester yields sulfolactate + Pi. Phosphate monoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolysis (forward) direction.

rxn00655.other_comments: This is an opine dehydrogenase-type reaction. Beta-alanopine is the secondary amine condensate of pyruvate and beta-alanine. The reaction couples reductive condensation (pyruvate + beta-alanine + NADH + H+ -> beta-alanopine + NAD+ + H2O) with the reverse oxidative cleavage. As written (beta-alanopine + NAD+ + H2O -> pyruvate + beta-alanine + NADH + H+), the atoms and charges balance: each side carries the secondary amine carbon backbone, one oxygen added by water on cleavage, and one proton released. Opine dehydrogenases are generally reversible, though physiologically they often favor the reductive (opine-forming) direction during anaerobic conditions to regenerate NAD+.

rxn10239.other_comments: This is a phosphatidic acid phosphatase (PAP) reaction. The substrate is a diacylglycerol-3-phosphate (phosphatidic acid) with two anteiso-heptadecanoyl (C17 branched) acyl chains. Hydrolysis of the phosphate monoester releases inorganic phosphate and yields the corresponding 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol (DAG). The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O cleaves the phosphate ester bond, producing free phosphate, a proton, and DAG.

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: the glucose product should be beta-D-glucose retaining the glycosidic configuration, but more importantly the substrate '1-O-trans-cinnamoyl-beta-D-glucopyranose' transfers the cinnamoyl group leaving free beta-D-glucose, which is consistent; however listing 'D-Glucose' (anomerically unspecified) is a minor inconsistency
The reaction as written balances in atoms: cinnamoyl-glucose + methanol -> glucose + methyl cinnamate, so no major mass imbalance
rxn06683.other_comments: This is an O-cinnamoyltransferase (acyltransferase) that transfers the trans-cinnamoyl moiety from the activated 1-O-acyl-beta-D-glucose donor to an acceptor alcohol (methanol), yielding methyl cinnamate and free glucose. The 1-O-acylglucose serves as the activated acyl donor. Such transacylations are generally reversible, though in vivo flux typically favors transfer to the alcohol acceptor.

errors: Substrate mismatch: the enzyme name specifies N-acetyl-D-glucosaminyl-1,3-D-galactosyl-1,4-D-glucosylceramide (Lc3Cer) as the acceptor, but the reaction lists Ceramidetrihexoside (Gb3Cer / globotriaosylceramide), which is a different glycolipid
Product inconsistency: transfer of galactose to Lc3Cer correctly yields Lc4Cer, but starting from Ceramidetrihexoside (Gb3Cer) the proper product would be globotetraosylceramide (Gb4Cer), not Lc4Cer
rxn03162.other_comments: This represents a galactosyltransferase reaction transferring galactose from UDP-galactose to a glycolipid acceptor, releasing UDP. The enzyme name (beta-D-galactosyltransferase acting on Lc3Cer to form Lc4Cer) is internally consistent, but the listed substrate 'Ceramidetrihexoside' typically refers to Gb3Cer, creating an ambiguity/mismatch between the named acceptor and the listed acceptor. Atom balance for the glycosyl transfer (UDP-Gal + acceptor -> UDP + Gal-acceptor) is otherwise sound.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the proposed equation does not balance.
