Mass balance: 2-oxo-5-aminovalerate (C5H9NO3) + urea (CH4N2O) = C6H13N3O4; products 2-oxo-5-guanidinopentanoate (C6H11N3O3) + H2O (H2O) = C6H13N3O4. The atoms actually balance.
No net stoichiometric error after recounting; the reaction is balanced as written (amino group converted to guanidino by transfer of the carbamoyl/amidino moiety from urea, releasing water).
rxn02327.other_comments: This reaction transfers a guanidino group, forming 2-oxo-5-guanidinopentanoate (the 2-oxo analog of arginine) from 2-oxo-5-aminovalerate (the 2-oxo analog of ornithine) using urea, releasing water. It is the deamino/keto-acid counterpart of the ornithine-to-arginine condensation type chemistry. Atom balance checks out (C6H13N3O4 on both sides).

rxn03200.other_comments: This is a 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase-type reaction (Estriol:NAD+ 17-oxidoreductase). Estriol (16alpha-hydroxyestradiol) is oxidized at the C17 hydroxyl to a keto group using NAD+ as the electron acceptor, producing 16alpha-hydroxyestrone, NADH, and H+. The reaction is balanced: estriol (C18H24O3) + NAD+ -> 16alpha-hydroxyestrone (C18H22O3) + NADH + H+, with the loss of two hydrogens (2H = H- transferred to NAD+ plus released H+) accounting for the conversion of the C17 secondary alcohol to a ketone. Atoms and charges balance. 17beta-HSD enzymes are generally reversible in vitro, though in vivo direction depends on isoform and NAD(H)/NADP(H) pool ratios; here it is annotated as reversible.

rxn00443.other_comments: This is L-galactono-1,4-lactone dehydrogenase (GLDH, EC 1.3.2.3), the final step of ascorbate biosynthesis in plants. It oxidizes L-galactono-1,4-lactone to L-ascorbate, transferring two electrons to two molecules of cytochrome c (reducing ferricytochrome c3+ to ferrocytochrome c2+). The stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of the substrate removes 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons), which reduces 2 cytochrome c and releases 2 H+. Atoms and charges balance. Physiologically the enzyme is coupled to the mitochondrial electron transport chain and operates in the direction of ascorbate production.

errors: Reaction is not charge balanced as written: the left side (NADP+ + HCOO-) carries net charge -1 (treating NADP as NADP+), while the right side (NADPH + CO2) carries net charge -2; proper balancing requires a proton, e.g. NADP+ + Formate -> NADPH + CO2 has unbalanced charge unless written as Formate(-) + NADP(+) <=> CO2 + NADPH with H accounting

Hydrogen/proton balance should be checked: formate (CHO2-) provides the hydride; CO2 has no H, so the H is transferred to NADP+ forming NADPH - this is consistent, but explicit charges/protons are needed for a fully balanced equation
rxn00103.other_comments: This is the NADP-dependent formate dehydrogenase reaction, oxidizing formate to CO2 with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The overall hydride transfer is correct (formate carbon goes from +2 to +4 oxidation state). The main concern is explicit charge/proton balancing rather than the underlying chemistry.

rxn04068.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the bile acid conjugate glycocholate (cholic acid conjugated to glycine via an amide bond) by bile salt hydrolase (choloylglycine hydrolase, EC 3.5.1.24). Water hydrolyzes the amide bond, releasing free glycine and cholate (cholic acid). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (C26H42NO6- + H2O -> C2H4NO2- (glycine, zwitterion/anion) + C24H39O5-; the carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen counts balance). As a hydrolase reaction it is thermodynamically favorable in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Proton (H+) should not appear on the substrate side; glucosyltransferase reactions typically release a proton or have no net proton change. The balanced reaction is: UDP-glucose + Luteolin <=> UDP + Luteolin 7-O-glucoside + H+, with H+ on the product side
rxn02562.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent O-glucosyltransferase transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the 7-hydroxyl of luteolin (5,7,3',4'-tetrahydroxyflavone), producing luteolin 7-O-glucoside and UDP. Glycosyltransferases of this type strongly favor the forward (glycosylation) direction in vivo due to the high-energy UDP-sugar donor.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance atoms. In the beta-oxidation thiolase step, the correct reaction is 3-Oxo-OPC4-CoA + CoA <=> Acetyl-CoA + OPC2-CoA (jasmonyl-CoA / (+)-7-isojasmonic acid CoA being OPC4-CoA). The product of the 3-oxoacyl-CoA thiolase cleavage should be a shortened CoA ester (acetyl-CoA + the chain-shortened acyl-CoA), not the conversion shown.
Carbon count mismatch: combining Acetyl-CoA (2C acyl) with OPC4-CoA cannot yield CoA + 3-Oxo-OPC4-CoA as written; the acyl chain lengths and oxidation states do not reconcile.
rxn07689.other_comments: This corresponds to a 3-oxoacyl-CoA thiolase (acetyl-CoA C-acyltransferase) step in jasmonate biosynthesis / peroxisomal beta-oxidation. In vivo the thiolytic cleavage proceeds toward acetyl-CoA release (i.e., 3-Oxo-OPC4-CoA + CoA -> Acetyl-CoA + OPC2-CoA), so as written (with acetyl-CoA on the left) it runs in the reverse direction physiologically. I interpreted the metabolites as CoA esters in the OPC (oxo-pentenyl-cyclopentane) beta-oxidation pathway.

errors: The product Glycerone (dihydroxyacetone, C3H6O3) is incorrect for this transketolase-type transfer; transfer of a glycolaldehyde (2-carbon) unit from 2-(1,2-dihydroxyethyl)-TPP to formaldehyde (1-carbon acceptor) would yield a 3-carbon aldose, glyceraldehyde, not glycerone (a ketose)
Atom/charge balance should be checked: the glycolaldehyde (C2H3O2) unit transferred to formaldehyde (CH2O) gives a C3 product; glyceraldehyde (C3H6O3) is the expected product rather than glycerone
rxn04677.other_comments: This is a transketolase/dihydroxyethyl-TPP transferase reaction in which the activated 2-carbon (glycolaldehyde) unit carried on TPP is transferred to an aldehyde acceptor (formaldehyde), regenerating free TPP. Such transketolase reactions are generally freely reversible in vivo.

rxn04415.other_comments: This is the isoflavone 2'-hydroxylase (CYP81E) reaction, a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that hydroxylates formononetin at the 2' position. The reaction consumes NADPH, O2, and a proton; one oxygen atom is incorporated into the substrate (yielding 2'-hydroxyformononetin) and the other is reduced to water. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + formononetin -> H2O + NADP+ + 2'-hydroxyformononetin. P450 monooxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (forward) due to O2 consumption and the energetics of oxygen activation.

errors: Stoichiometric/charge imbalance: the redox cofactors are written in the wrong direction. This is a monooxygenase (CYP, e.g. CYP2R1/CYP27A1) hydroxylation that consumes O2 and reduced ferredoxin (or NADPH), not produces O2. As written, oxidized ferredoxin appears on the reactant side and reduced ferredoxin on the product side, which is inverted.

Direction of the substrate/product pair is reversed: calcidiol (25-hydroxyvitamin D3) is the hydroxylated product of vitamin D3, so vitamin D3 should be the substrate and calcidiol the product in the hydroxylation direction.

Electron/proton balance is inconsistent: a typical 25-hydroxylation reads Vitamin D3 + O2 + Reduced ferredoxin (2e-/2H+) -> Calcidiol + H2O + Oxidized ferredoxin; the given equation does not balance O and H consistently with this.
rxn06424.other_comments: This corresponds to the cytochrome P450-catalyzed 25-hydroxylation of vitamin D3 to form calcidiol (25-OH-D3). The reaction is a monooxygenase reaction that incorporates one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate, producing water, and uses reducing equivalents (ferredoxin/NADPH). As written, the O2 and the ferredoxin redox states are on the wrong sides.

rxn05422.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid biosynthesis (here for a branched/methyl-branched chain). NADPH reduces the 3-oxo (beta-keto) group of 10-methyl-3-oxo-undecanoyl-ACP to the 3-hydroxy product, consuming NADPH + H+ and producing NADP+. The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced (2 H from NADPH + H+ are added: one to C3 as the hydride and one as the proton forming the hydroxyl). In vivo this reductive step in FAS proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn01378.other_comments: This is aminoglycoside 3'-phosphotransferase (APH(3')), an antibiotic resistance enzyme transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the 3'-hydroxyl of kanamycin A. The reaction is balanced: ATP + kanamycin yields ADP + kanamycin 3'-phosphate + H+. The proton balance is correct since the transferred phosphate group contributes the proton. Phosphoryl transfer from ATP is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically drives strongly toward phosphorylation (detoxification of the antibiotic).

rxn00402.other_comments: This is octopine dehydrogenase (EC 1.5.1.11) operating in the reverse (oxidative deamination) direction. Octopine is N2-(D-1-carboxyethyl)-L-arginine. The reaction shown oxidizes octopine using NAD+ and water to yield pyruvate, L-arginine, NADH, and H+. Stoichiometry balances: octopine (C9H18N4O4) + H2O + NAD+ gives L-arginine (C6H14N4O2) + pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + NADH + H+. Carbon (9 = 6+3), nitrogen (4 = 4), and charge balance check out.

errors: Atom balance error: the reaction as written does not balance. 2-Chloro-3-oxoadipate (C6H6ClO5, as the dianion) plus H2O cleaving between C2 and C3 would yield chloroacetate (C2 fragment) and a C4 succinate-derived fragment, but the carbon and oxygen counts do not match cleanly. Succinate is C4H4O4 (dianion); chloroacetate is C2H2ClO2 (anion). Reactant side: C6 + H2O = C6, products C4 + C2 = C6 carbons OK, but hydrogen/oxygen/charge must be rechecked.

Charge balance should be verified: products carry succinate(2-) + chloroacetate(1-) + H+ = net -2, reactant 2-chloro-3-oxoadipate(2-) = -2, water neutral; charge balances only if proton accounting is correct.
Likely a hydrolytic C-C bond cleavage; if O/H counts are off this is a stoichiometric error in the reaction definition.
rxn04670.other_comments: This appears to be a hydrolytic cleavage of 2-chloro-3-oxoadipate into succinate and chloroacetate, a step in chloroaromatic/2,4-D-type degradation pathways. Such hydrolase-catalyzed C-C cleavage reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo and proceed in the catabolic (forward) direction.

rxn03110.other_comments: This is a glycoside hydrolase (glucuronohydrolase) reaction in which water hydrolyzes the glycosidic bond between the glucuronosyl residue and the N2,6-disulfo-D-glucosamine, releasing free glucuronate and N2,6-disulfo-D-glucosamine. The reaction is mass-balanced: the disaccharide plus water yields the two monosaccharide products, with the glucuronate carrying the elements of the broken glycosidic bond plus water. Atom and charge balance are consistent assuming the sulfo groups are retained on the glucosamine product. Hydrolytic cleavage by hydrolases is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Mass imbalance: condensation of acetyl-CoA (2-carbon donor) with OPC6-CoA should yield a beta-ketoacyl-CoA with 2 additional carbons (3-oxo-OPC8-CoA), but this is a Claisen condensation that releases CoA from acetyl-CoA, not directly. The standard reaction for OPC8 biosynthesis is a 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase-type condensation: Acetyl-CoA + OPC6-CoA -> CoA + 3-Oxo-OPC8-CoA. Atom balance appears consistent if OPC8 = OPC6 + C2 unit, so the equation may actually be balanced.
rxn07681.other_comments: This reaction is part of jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis via beta-oxidation. OPC stands for 3-oxo-2-(2-pentenyl)cyclopentane-1-octanoic acid derivatives. The enzyme is a 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (KAT). Thiolase reactions are written as condensation (acetyl-CoA + acyl-CoA -> 3-ketoacyl-CoA + CoA), but in the beta-oxidation/JA shortening direction the physiological flux is the thiolytic cleavage (reverse), converting 3-oxo-OPC8-CoA + CoA -> acetyl-CoA + OPC6-CoA, shortening the carbon chain by two. The reaction as written is the condensation direction.

rxn12681.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing protocatechualdehyde (3,4-dihydroxybenzaldehyde, 34dhbald) to protocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxybenzoate). The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (RCHO) plus H2O plus NAD+ yields the carboxylate (RCOOH) plus NADH plus 2 H+. Mass and charge balance check out (one H+ from carboxylic acid formation/oxidation and the proton balance with NADH gives 2 H+).

rxn07476.other_comments: This is the ArnC-catalyzed reaction transferring 4-deoxy-4-formamido-L-arabinose (Ara4FN) from UDP-Ara4FN to undecaprenyl phosphate, forming undecaprenyl phosphate alpha-L-Ara4FN and releasing UDP. The atoms balance: the glycosyl group transfers from UDP donor to the lipid acceptor, with the phosphoanhydride cleavage releasing UDP. The H+ accounts for charge/proton balance. This is part of the lipid A modification pathway conferring polymyxin/cationic peptide resistance. Glycosyltransferase reactions of this type are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn04559.other_comments: This represents the cocaine esterase / cocaine benzoylhydrolase reaction (EC 3.1.1.84), the hydrolysis of the benzoyl ester bond of cocaine to yield benzoate and ecgonine methyl ester (methyl ecgonine). Stoichiometry is balanced: cocaine (C17H21NO4) + H2O yields benzoate (C7H5O2-) + methylecgonine (C10H17NO3) + H+. Mass and charge balance correctly when benzoate is treated as the deprotonated carboxylate.

rxn07272.other_comments: This reaction represents a 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase oxidizing the 3-beta-hydroxyl group of campest-4-en-3beta-ol to a 3-keto group, using NAD+ as the electron acceptor and producing NADH and H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: the oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes two hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one released as H+), which is correctly represented. Atom and charge balance are consistent. In vivo, this type of oxidation coupled to NAD+ reduction is typically driven in the forward (oxidative) direction, particularly in sterol biosynthesis pathways where the 3-keto intermediate is formed; however, such dehydrogenase reactions can be thermodynamically reversible depending on the NAD+/NADH ratio.

rxn10248.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to a diglucosyl-diacylglycerol (with anteisoheptadecanoyl acyl chains), producing a triglucosyl-diacylglycerol and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one glucosyl unit is transferred from UDP-glucose, converting UDP-glucose to UDP and adding one glucose to the lipid acceptor. UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases are generally strongly exergonic and proceed in the biosynthetic direction due to release of UDP and the high energy of the sugar-nucleotide bond.

rxn03799.other_comments: This is a CoA transferase reaction (propionate CoA-transferase / acrylate CoA-transferase type). The CoA group is transferred from acetyl-CoA to acrylate, yielding acetate and acrylyl-CoA. The reaction is balanced: both sides carry one CoA moiety, and atoms/charges are conserved (acetyl-CoA + acrylate = acetate + acrylyl-CoA). CoA-transferase reactions are typically near-equilibrium and reversible in vivo, with directionality driven by relative substrate/product concentrations.

errors: The product 3-fluorocyclohexadiene-cis,cis-1,2-diol-1-carboxylate is missing a fluoride/proton balance check, but the main issue is that the dihydrodiol product should retain the carboxylate and incorporate two oxygen atoms from O2 plus two hydrogens from NADH; the equation as written is atom-balanced if NADH provides the reducing equivalents and both O atoms are added to the ring
Charge balance should be verified: NADH (-2) + H+ (+1) + 3-fluorobenzoate (-1) = -2 on left; NAD+ (+1) + diol-carboxylate (-1) = 0 on right, indicating a charge imbalance of 2
rxn07896.other_comments: This represents a benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase (reductase-coupled) type reaction acting on a fluorinated benzoate analog, converting 3-fluorobenzoate to the corresponding cis-dihydrodiol carboxylate with consumption of NADH and molecular oxygen.

rxn03208.other_comments: This is the coclaurine N-methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.140) in the benzylisoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis pathway. SAM donates a methyl group to the nitrogen of (S)-coclaurine, producing (S)-N-methylcoclaurine and S-adenosyl-homocysteine, with release of a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: SAM (carrying the transferred methyl) becomes SAH, and the methyl group is added to the substrate nitrogen, with H+ released to balance charge.

rxn02525.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of alpha-aminopropiononitrile (the nitrile of alanine, also known as 2-aminopropanenitrile) to form alanine and ammonia. Nitrile hydrolysis (nitrilase-type activity) requires 2 water molecules to convert the nitrile group (C#N) into a carboxylic acid (COOH) with release of NH3. The carbon and nitrogen balance checks out: substrate C3H6N2 (containing nitrile N and amino N) plus 2 H2O yields alanine C3H7NO2 plus NH3. Charge/proton balance is reasonable given protonation states.

errors: Atom balance is not satisfied as written; AIR (5-aminoimidazole ribonucleotide, C8H13N4O7P) does not balance against the listed products. Carbon count is off: AIR has 8 carbons, while products (glycolaldehyde C2 + toxopyrimidine/HMP C6) give 8 carbons but nitrogen and oxygen must be checked carefully. Nitrogen: AIR has 4 N; HMP (4-amino-5-hydroxymethyl-2-methylpyrimidine) has 3 N, glycolaldehyde 0 N - leaving 1 N unaccounted.
The release of 0.5 O2 is biochemically implausible; ThiC (HMP-P synthase) is a radical SAM enzyme, and the real reaction is not an O2-releasing process.

The actual ThiC reaction consumes AIR and SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) and produces HMP-P (the phosphorylated form), 5'-deoxyadenosine, methionine, CO, and formate - not free toxopyrimidine plus glycolaldehyde and O2.
Product should be HMP-P (phosphorylated) rather than free toxopyrimidine if phosphate is balanced; as written phosphate is released separately, which conflicts.
rxn09997.other_comments: This represents the ThiC-catalyzed conversion of AIR (5-aminoimidazole ribonucleotide) to HMP/HMP-P (4-amino-5-hydroxymethyl-2-methylpyrimidine phosphate, i.e., toxopyrimidine precursor) in thiamine biosynthesis. The reaction as written omits the required SAM cofactor and radical SAM chemistry, and incorrectly invokes O2 release. The carbon-skeleton rearrangement is real and the reaction is physiologically irreversible (forward), but the stoichiometry given is incorrect.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: oxidation of L-arabinose (open-chain aldose, C5H10O5) to L-arabinono-1,4-lactone (C5H8O5) involves loss of 2 H (as in NADH + H+), but the lactone is a cyclic ester formed with loss of water relative to the free acid. The direct dehydrogenase product is L-arabinono-1,5-lactone or the open-chain acid; if lactone is the product an explicit H2O balance should be checked. As written: arabinose C5H10O5 -> lactone C5H8O5 + 2[H] is balanced for C, H, O, so atom balance holds, but the typical product is the 1,5-lactone (gamma vs delta lactone) - verify which lactone.
rxn01289.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent aldose dehydrogenase oxidizing the anomeric carbon (C1) of L-arabinose to the corresponding lactone, part of the bacterial/fungal oxidative L-arabinose catabolic pathway. Atom balance: C5H10O5 + NAD+ -> C5H8O5 + NADH + H+ is internally consistent. The main concern is the specific lactone isomer (1,4 vs 1,5). In vivo the reaction proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction toward the lactone.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides (Cytidine + Na+ <=> Cytidine + Na+) with no compartmental distinction, making it a null/trivial reaction with no net transformation. A proper transport reaction must specify different compartments, e.g., Cytidine[extracellular] + Na+[extracellular] <=> Cytidine[cytosol] + Na+[cytosol].
rxn10857.other_comments: This is annotated as a sodium-cytidine symport (secondary active transport) importing cytidine into the cell coupled to Na+ influx down its electrochemical gradient. Stoichiometry of substrate-to-substrate (1 cytidine : 1 Na+) is plausible, but the missing compartment labels make the equation appear as no net reaction. In vivo, the inward sodium gradient drives net uptake, so the reaction is effectively forward (import).

errors: Atom imbalance: the conversion of indole-3-acetaldoxime plus L-cysteine to S-(indolylmethylthiohydroximoyl)-L-cysteine adds a sulfur and forms a C=N-OH thiohydroximate; mass/atom balance should be checked carefully. The oxime to aci-nitro/thiohydroximate conversion in glucosinolate biosynthesis typically proceeds via an aci-nitro compound intermediate, and the direct combination with cysteine as written may not balance H and O exactly.

This step (CYP83B1/CYP83A1 type reaction) usually oxidizes the aldoxime to an aci-nitro compound or nitrile oxide, which then conjugates non-enzymatically with a thiol (glutathione/cysteine); writing cysteine directly as a substrate oversimplifies the mechanism.
rxn12018.other_comments: This represents the cytochrome P450 (CYP83) mediated oxidation of indole-3-acetaldoxime in glucosinolate/IAA biosynthesis, consuming NADPH and O2 to form an S-alkyl-thiohydroximate via thiol conjugation. The reaction is physiologically essentially irreversible (forward) due to O2/NADPH consumption.

errors: The reaction as written appears unbalanced. Hydrolytic cleavage of a 2-hydroxy-2-enoate (enol/oxoacid intermediate) to pyruvate typically releases the remaining fragment as a carboxylic acid/aldehyde, but the carbon and oxygen balance between the indene-containing substrate and the proposed indanone product should be verified; the indene-derived portion likely does not match the named '1-Formyl-2-indanone' product in mass/formula.
rxn03833.other_comments: This represents a hydrolytic carbon-carbon bond cleavage of a meta-cleavage-type product (a 2-hydroxy-but-2-enoate/oxo-acid) releasing pyruvate and an aldehyde-bearing fragment, analogous to bacterial aromatic ring degradation hydrolase reactions. Such C-C hydrolase steps are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward pyruvate release.

rxn00491.other_comments: This is the L-phenylalanine:pyruvate aminotransferase reaction. The transamination transfers an amino group from L-phenylalanine to pyruvate, yielding phenylpyruvate and L-alanine. The reaction is balanced: both sides have matching atoms (C, H, N, O) and charge. Transaminase reactions are generally near-equilibrium and freely reversible in vivo, with direction governed by relative substrate/product concentrations.

rxn02717.other_comments: This reaction represents the 11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11beta-HSD) reaction, oxidizing corticosterone to 11-dehydrocorticosterone using NAD+ as the cofactor. Stoichiometry is balanced: corticosterone (C21H30O4) loses 2H (one to NAD+ forming NADH, plus one released as H+) to form 11-dehydrocorticosterone (C21H28O4). The NAD+/NADH and H+ accounting is correct. The NAD-dependent enzyme (11beta-HSD2) predominantly catalyzes oxidation (dehydrogenase direction) in vivo, favoring formation of 11-dehydrocorticosterone, though the reaction is intrinsically reversible.

errors: Charge imbalance: hydrolysis of a phosphoanhydride bond (ADP-like to AMP-like) releases inorganic phosphate and typically generates one H+, not 2 H+; the stoichiometry of 2.0 H+ produces a charge/proton imbalance
rxn07851.other_comments: This reaction represents hydrolysis of the beta-phosphate (diphosphate to monophosphate) of an isopentenyl-adenosine diphosphate derivative, yielding the corresponding monophosphate plus inorganic phosphate. Phosphoanhydride hydrolysis is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the forward (hydrolytic) direction is favored.

rxn03487.other_comments: This is a hydrolysis reaction catalyzed by 1,4-beta-D-glucan glucohydrolase (beta-glucosidase/exoglucanase, EC 3.2.1.74). It cleaves a single glucose unit from the non-reducing end of celloheptaose (a beta-1,4-linked glucose 7-mer), producing one D-glucose and cellohexaose (6-mer). Stoichiometry is balanced: celloheptaose (C42H72O36) + H2O yields glucose (C6H12O6) + cellohexaose (C36H62O31). Hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn02449.other_comments: This reaction represents the SpoT/RelA-type 3'-pyrophosphohydrolase activity, specifically the conversion of pppGpp (guanosine 5'-triphosphate 3'-diphosphate) to ppGpp (guanosine 3',5'-bis(diphosphate)) by hydrolysis of the gamma-phosphate from the 5' triphosphate. H2O cleaves a terminal phosphate yielding inorganic phosphate plus a proton. Mass and charge are balanced: removing one phosphate (Pi + H+) from the 5'-triphosphate converts it to a 5'-diphosphate, consistent with the 3',5'-bis(diphosphate) product. This is the canonical gpp/GppA-mediated step in (p)ppGpp metabolism during the stringent response.

rxn04550.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction in the mithramycin biosynthetic pathway. The mycarosyltransferase MtmGIV transfers a D-mycarose sugar from the activated donor dTDP-beta-D-mycarose to the acceptor Premithramycin A2', producing Premithramycin A3 and releasing dTDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: the mycarosyl moiety is transferred from the dTDP-sugar to the aglycone, with dTDP as the leaving group. Glycosyltransferase reactions using NDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable due to cleavage of the activated glycosidic bond and are physiologically committed in the forward (biosynthetic) direction.

rxn04598.other_comments: This is a cinnamate 2,3-dioxygenase type reaction (Rieske non-heme iron dioxygenase). trans-Cinnamate is dihydroxylated at positions 2,3 using molecular O2, with NADH providing reducing equivalents. The stoichiometry balances: NADH + O2 + H+ + cinnamate yields NAD+ and the cis-dihydrodiol product. Both atoms of O2 are incorporated (one into each hydroxyl), and NADH/H+ reduces the substrate plus enables dioxygen activation. Mass and charge balance check out (the dihydrodiol gains 2 O and 2 H net relative to cinnamate, accounting for O2 and the NADH/H+).

rxn00354.other_comments: This is the oxidation of UDP-galactose to UDP-galacturonate (the UDP-sugar 6-dehydrogenase type reaction, analogous to UDP-glucose dehydrogenase). The C6 primary alcohol (CH2OH) is oxidized to a carboxylate (COOH), a 4-electron oxidation requiring 2 NAD+ and producing 2 NADH plus water consumed. Mass and charge balance: H2O + 2 NAD+ + UDP-galactose -> 2 NADH + 3 H+ + UDP-galacturonate. Carbon, oxygen, hydrogen and charge balance correctly (2 NAD+ vs 2 NADH + 2 H+ for the dehydrogenations, plus 1 additional H+ from carboxyl formation with water).

rxn01624.other_comments: This reaction represents prostacyclin synthase (CYP8A1, EC 5.3.99.4), which catalyzes the intramolecular isomerization of prostaglandin H2 (PGH2) to prostacyclin (PGI2). The substrate name '(5Z,13E)-(15S)-9alpha,11alpha-Epidioxy-15-hydroxyprosta-5,13-dienoate' is the systematic name for PGH2. This is an isomerase reaction with no net change in molecular formula, so it is stoichiometrically balanced (C20H32O5 on both sides). The enzyme rearranges the endoperoxide bridge of PGH2 to form the bicyclic prostacyclin structure.

errors: Atom imbalance: O2 (2 oxygen atoms) on the left does not balance with the products. Adding the ring-opening/oxygenation product 2-carboxy-2-hydroxychromene to a dihydroxynaphthalene substrate plus one H+ does not balance oxygen and hydrogen atoms. The dioxygenase-type cleavage of a dihydroxynaphthalene typically yields a ring-cleavage product incorporating both oxygen atoms, but here the stated product retains only the carbons with apparent loss of mass balance.

Hydrogen imbalance: a single H+ on the product side is inconsistent with insertion of molecular O2 into the aromatic diol; ring-cleavage dioxygenase reactions do not release a free proton without a corresponding electron/proton balance.
Charge imbalance likely if the carboxy groups are deprotonated and only one H+ is accounted for.
rxn04730.other_comments: This appears to be a ring-cleavage dioxygenase reaction (KEGG R06921) acting on a dihydroxy aromatic substrate (1,2-dihydroxy-8-carboxynaphthalene) with O2 incorporation to form a chromene/muconate-type ring-opened product. Such oxygenase reactions consuming O2 are physiologically essentially irreversible (forward). However, as written the equation does not appear atom-balanced.

rxn05021.other_comments: This is the GDP-mannose:undecaprenyl-phosphate D-mannosyltransferase reaction. GDP-mannose transfers a mannosyl group to undecaprenyl phosphate, yielding mannosyl-1-phosphoundecaprenol and GDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: the mannosyl moiety (C6H11O5) is transferred from GDP-mannose to the phosphate of undecaprenyl phosphate, releasing GDP, with a proton consumed/released to balance charges. Atom and charge balance hold as written. Biologically, glycosyltransferases using sugar-nucleotide donors are highly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of glycolipid synthesis.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction produces 2 H+ but a hydrolytic phosphoanhydride cleavage of UDP-GlcNAc to UMP + GlcNAc-1-phosphate releases only 1 H+ under physiological conditions; the proton stoichiometry should be 1.0 H+ to maintain charge and mass balance
rxn09341.other_comments: This represents hydrolysis of the UDP-GlcNAc pyrophosphate (phosphoanhydride) bond, splitting it into UMP and N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate. Hydrolysis of a high-energy phosphoanhydride bond is strongly exergonic and essentially irreversible in vivo, so it should proceed in the forward direction as written.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (H+ and BIOT/biotin) on both sides with identical stoichiometry, so it has no net chemical transformation as displayed. For a transport reaction, the species should be annotated with distinct compartments, e.g., H+[e] + BIOT[e] <=> H+[c] + BIOT[c], to represent translocation across a membrane.
rxn09693.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled biotin uptake (symport) reaction, importing biotin into the cell driven by the proton motive force. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (1 H+ and 1 biotin on each side), but the compartment labels distinguishing extracellular from cytosolic species are missing in the input. Biologically, biotin uptake via a proton symporter (e.g., BioY/H+ symport systems) proceeds in the import direction.

rxn02170.other_comments: This is the deamination of L-3-aminobutyryl-CoA, catalyzed by 3-aminobutyryl-CoA ammonia-lyase (EC 4.3.1.14). The enzyme removes ammonia from the beta-position to form the alpha,beta-unsaturated thioester crotonyl-CoA (but-2-enoyl-CoA). Atoms balance: L-3-aminobutyryl-CoA (C4 aminoacyl moiety on CoA) loses NH3 to give crotonyl-CoA. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced for C, H, N, O, and S.

rxn01348.other_comments: This reaction describes the phosphorylation of sedoheptulose 7-phosphate at the C1 position to form sedoheptulose 1,7-bisphosphate, using ITP as the phosphate donor (an unusual alternative to the canonical ATP). The reaction is atomically and charge balanced: ITP (4-) + S7P (2-) -> H+ + IDP (3-) + SBP (4-), with phosphoryl transfer releasing one proton. Physiologically, phosphofructokinase-type reactions transferring a gamma-phosphate from a nucleoside triphosphate to a sugar phosphate are essentially irreversible and proceed in the kinase (forward) direction due to the large negative free energy of NTP hydrolysis.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: ring-cleavage dioxygenase reactions incorporate both atoms of O2 into the product. For 4-chlorocatechol (C6H5ClO2) + O2 (O2) yielding 3-chloro-cis,cis-muconate (C6H4ClO4 as the diacid, or C6H2ClO4(2-) as the dianion), the proton balance does not match. Balanced as dianion: C6H5ClO2 + O2 -> C6H2ClO4(2-) + 2 H+ would require checking carbon/hydrogen: left H=5, right H=2+2(from protons)=4, so hydrogen is unbalanced (5 vs 4)
Charge balance must be verified; the muconate species charge state is not explicitly indicated, making the 2 H+ stoichiometry ambiguous
rxn02969.other_comments: This is a catechol 1,2-dioxygenase (intradiol) type ring-cleavage reaction acting on 4-chlorocatechol to form 3-chloro-cis,cis-muconate, incorporating molecular O2. Such intradiol dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the ring-cleavage (forward) direction.

rxn04141.other_comments: This is a 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/oxidoreductase reaction. The substrate 3beta-hydroxy-5beta-pregnane-20-one (with a hydroxyl at C3) is oxidized to 5beta-pregnane-3,20-dione (with a keto at C3), with NADP+ accepting the hydride to form NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced: the oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH, one as proton), consistent with the products shown. NADP-dependent oxidoreductases of this type are typically reversible in vitro and in vivo, with direction set by the NADPH/NADP+ ratio and substrate concentrations.

rxn07752.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-type N-demethylation of theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine) to 7-methylxanthine, releasing formaldehyde from the 3-methyl group. The reaction consumes NADPH, O2, and H+, producing H2O, NADP+, formaldehyde, and the demethylated xanthine. Atoms balance: the methyl carbon is removed as formaldehyde, one O2 oxygen incorporated into formaldehyde/water consistent with monooxygenase chemistry. Charge and mass are balanced as written. Such oxidative demethylations are physiologically irreversible.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the ring-cleavage product 2-hydroxy-2H-benzo[h]chromene-2-carboxylate (a carboxylate, charge -1) plus H+ does not balance against phenanthrene-3,4-diol + O2; mass and charge are not conserved as written. A proper extradiol/intradiol dioxygenase cleavage of a catechol (diol) with O2 typically yields a ring-opened muconate-type product without releasing a free H+ in this manner, and oxygen atoms from O2 must be accounted for in the product.
rxn03922.other_comments: This represents a dioxygenase-catalyzed oxidative ring cleavage of phenanthrene-3,4-diol (a catechol substrate from phenanthrene degradation) incorporating molecular O2 to give a ring-fission product. Such dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the cleavage (forward) direction.

errors: D-Lyxitol is a synonym for D-arabinitol (D-arabitol), but the product D-Ribulose is inconsistent with the substrate; oxidation of D-arabinitol at C2 yields D-xylulose, while D-ribulose would be produced from oxidation of ribitol (adonitol), not arabinitol

The enzyme name 'D-arabinitol:NADP+ oxidoreductase' implies a D-xylulose or D-ribulose product depending on the position oxidized; the EC 1.1.1.11 D-arabinitol 4-dehydrogenase produces D-xylulose, and EC 1.1.1.250 D-arabinitol 2-dehydrogenase produces D-ribulose, so the product depends on the specific enzyme
rxn04942.other_comments: This is a polyol dehydrogenase reaction interconverting a sugar alcohol (D-arabinitol/D-lyxitol) and a ketose (D-ribulose) using NADP+/NADPH. The stoichiometry (charges, atoms, redox equivalents with H+) is balanced. The main concern is the substrate-product pairing: D-arabinitol 2-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.250) does yield D-ribulose, so the naming may be acceptable depending on the position oxidized.

rxn14153.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of 3beta-hydroxy-9beta-pimara-7,15-diene-19,6beta-olide to Momilactone A, catalyzed by a NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase (momilactone A synthase). The secondary 3beta-hydroxyl group is oxidized to a 3-keto group, transferring a hydride to NAD+ to form NADH and releasing a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the loss of two hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+, one as H+) accounts for the hydroxyl-to-ketone conversion. This is a step in momilactone biosynthesis in rice (Oryza sativa).

errors: Stoichiometric mass/group imbalance: the substrates and products do not balance. The mycolate moiety on 'alpha-meroacyl-1-mycolate-ppm' is transferred to trehalose-6-phosphate to form trehalose-monomycolate-phosphate, but the leaving carrier should be the polyprenyl-phosphate (decaprenyl-phosphate / Pol), not 'Polyprenyl-mannose'.
The product 'Polyprenyl-mannose' is inconsistent: there is no mannose donor in the substrates, so mannose cannot appear in a product. This indicates a mislabeled or incorrect carrier lipid.
Charge/proton balance is questionable: the role of the free H+ is not justified by the proposed group transfer.
Carrier lipid naming inconsistency: 'ppm' (polyprenyl-phospho-mannose?) versus the actual mycolate carrier (typically a polyprenyl/decaprenyl phosphate) is ambiguous.
rxn13554.other_comments: This appears to represent trehalose monomycolate (TMM) biosynthesis, in which a mycolate group is transferred from a polyprenyl-phosphate-linked mycolate donor (mycolyl-decaprenyl-phosphate) to trehalose-6-phosphate, yielding trehalose-monomycolate-6-phosphate and releasing the polyprenyl-phosphate carrier. As written, the reaction has carrier-lipid/mannose inconsistencies and does not balance.

rxn05385.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid biosynthesis. NADPH reduces the 3-oxo (beta-keto) group of 5-methyl-3-oxo-hexanoyl-ACP to the corresponding 3-hydroxy product, with NADPH oxidized to NADP+. The reaction is stoichiometrically and redox balanced (2 electrons + 1 H+ from NADPH reduce the ketone to a secondary alcohol). NADP should formally be written as NADP+ for charge balance, but this is a notation convention.

rxn04022.other_comments: This is the UDP-glucose:hydroquinone-O-beta-D-glucosyltransferase reaction (arbutin synthase). UDP-glucose transfers a glucosyl group to hydroquinone (quinol), forming arbutin (ursin) and UDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: UDP-glucose (C15H22N2O17P2 + glucose moiety) plus quinol (C6H6O2) yields the glucoside arbutin (C12H16O7) plus UDP. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugars are strongly exergonic due to the energy of the UDP-sugar bond, so the reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn03013.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction transferring the amino group from S-(4-Bromophenyl)-L-cysteine to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and the corresponding 2-oxo acid (S-(4-Bromophenyl)-mercaptopyruvate, i.e. 3-((4-bromophenyl)thio)-2-oxopropanoate). The stoichiometry is balanced: the amino acid donates -NH2 and becomes a keto acid, while 2-oxoglutarate accepts it to form glutamate. Transaminase (PLP-dependent) reactions are typically near-equilibrium and freely reversible in vivo.

rxn02133.other_comments: This is the sphinganine kinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.91), transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the primary hydroxyl of sphinganine to form sphinganine 1-phosphate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ATP donates a phosphate to sphinganine yielding ADP, a proton, and sphinganine 1-phosphate.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is unbalanced as written: menaquinol oxidation releases 2 H+ from the quinol, so the left side should have no extra protons beyond those bound, and the right side should show the released protons. As balanced chemistry: Menaquinol6 -> Menaquinone6 + 2 H+ + 2 e-, and 2 Cytochrome c3+ + 2 e- -> 2 Cytochrome c2+. Net: Menaquinol6 + 2 Cyt c3+ -> Menaquinone6 + 2 Cyt c2+ + 2 H+. The reaction as written adds 2 H+ on the left and 4 H+ on the right (net 2 H+ released), which is actually charge/mass consistent if the extra 2 H+ on each side represent scalar/translocated protons. However, written this way the explicit 2 H+ on the left appear superfluous unless representing vectorial (translocated) protons across a membrane, which is not annotated.
rxn10990.other_comments: This is a quinol:cytochrome c oxidoreductase type reaction (menaquinol-6 oxidized while reducing two cytochrome c from ferric Fe3+ to ferrous Fe2+). Electron balance (2 e-) and Fe redox are correct. The proton bookkeeping suggests an electrogenic/proton-translocating step (Q-cycle-like), but it is not clearly labeled as transmembrane.

rxn03092.other_comments: This reaction represents a keto-enol tautomerization between 4-carboxy-2-oxo-3-hexenedioate (the keto form) and 4-carboxy-2-hydroxyhexa-2,4-dienedioate (the enol form). The two species are tautomers with identical molecular formula (C7H6O7 in their fully protonated/deprotonated states depending on pH), so the reaction is mass-balanced as a 1:1 isomerization. Tautomerase/isomerase reactions of this type are intrinsically reversible. This step is associated with the meta-cleavage (catechol/protocatechuate) degradation pathways of aromatic compounds.

rxn03468.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase-type reaction (KEGG R05119) oxidizing 3-butyn-1-al to 3-butynoate, coupled to NAD+ reduction to NADH. The atom and charge balance is correct: the aldehyde plus water gains an oxygen, loses 2 [H] (electrons plus 2 H+ released, one of which goes to NAD+ forming NADH and the other released as H+), yielding the carboxylate. Mass and charge balance check out. Such NAD+-dependent aldehyde oxidations are strongly favored thermodynamically and operate essentially irreversibly in the forward (oxidative) direction in vivo.

rxn02875.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine (an amide bond between the lactyl group of N-acetylmuramate and L-alanine) by N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine amidase (EC 3.5.1.28). One water is consumed to cleave the amide bond, releasing free L-alanine and N-acetyl-D-muramate. The stoichiometry is balanced (one amide bond cleaved per water consumed). As a hydrolytic amidase reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolysis direction.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the conversion of dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose (a ketone) to dTDP-L-olivose (a deoxysugar with the keto reduced to hydroxyl) is a simple ketoreduction requiring one NADPH + H+, which appears balanced for the reduction step, but the epimerization at C3/C5 implied by the L-configuration of olivose is not accounted for by a reductase alone

The substrate dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose differs from the product dTDP-L-olivose by both reduction at C4 and stereochemical inversion; a single NADPH-dependent reduction cannot generate the L-sugar configuration without a separate epimerase step
rxn04293.other_comments: This represents an NADPH-dependent 4-ketoreductase step in dTDP-deoxysugar biosynthesis, converting a 4-keto sugar intermediate to dTDP-L-olivose. Biosynthetically, ketoreduction with NADPH proceeds toward the reduced sugar product.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: NADPH carries a 2- charge and NADP+ a 1- charge; with 7 NADPH + 7 H+ on the left producing 7 NADP, the protonation/charge accounting is inconsistent and likely should be written as 7 NADP+ with the H+ balancing charges

Hydrogen atom balance should be verified: full saturation of two geranylgeranyl-derived chains (each having multiple C=C double bonds) requires a specific number of NADPH equivalents; the geranyl/geranyl-to-phytanyl conversion involves reduction of the unsaturated isoprenoid chains and the count of 7 should match the total double bonds reduced
rxn10554.other_comments: This is a saturation (hydrogenation) reaction reducing unsaturated geranylgeranyl/geranyl chains of an archaeal glycerophospholipid intermediate to fully saturated phytanyl chains using NADPH. Such geranylgeranyl reductase reactions in archaeal ether lipid biosynthesis are physiologically driven in the reductive (forward) direction.

rxn01468.other_comments: This is a monoterpene synthase (cyclase) reaction. Geranyl diphosphate (GPP, C10H20O7P2) is cyclized with addition of water to form sabinene hydrate (a bicyclic monoterpenoid alcohol, C10H18O) plus diphosphate (PPi) and a proton. Mass and charge balance check out: GPP carries the diphosphate which is released as PPi, water provides the hydroxyl, and a proton is released. The stoichiometry is correct.

rxn03405.other_comments: This is the MurG reaction in peptidoglycan biosynthesis. UDP-GlcNAc transfers its GlcNAc moiety to lipid I (undecaprenyl-PP-MurNAc-pentapeptide) to form lipid II, releasing UDP. The pentapeptide shown (L-Ala-D-Glu-L-Lys-D-Ala-D-Ala) is the typical Gram-positive/E. coli-type stem peptide. Stoichiometry is balanced: one GlcNAc transferred, one UDP released. In vivo this glycosyltransfer is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the lipid II-forming direction.

errors: Mass imbalance: 4-Hydroxy-L-threonine (C4H9NO4) minus CO2 (CO2) does not equal 3-Aminopropane-1,2-diol (C3H9NO2); a decarboxylation of 4-hydroxy-L-threonine would yield C3H9NO3 (e.g., an aminotriol), not C3H9NO2
Oxygen imbalance: left side has 4 O (excluding H+), right side has 2 (CO2) + 2 (aminopropanediol) = 4, but H and overall atom balance fails when accounting for the H+ and product hydroxyl count
Hydrogen imbalance: reactants H = 9 (substrate) + 1 (H+) = 10; products H = 0 (CO2) + 9 (aminodiol) = 9
rxn03447.other_comments: This is intended to be a decarboxylation of 4-hydroxy-L-threonine, an intermediate in pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (vitamin B6) biosynthesis. Decarboxylation reactions releasing CO2 are typically essentially irreversible (forward) in vivo. However, the listed product 3-aminopropane-1,2-diol appears to be missing an oxygen relative to the expected decarboxylation product, indicating a stoichiometric error.

rxn01779.other_comments: D-Arginine amidinohydrolase (an arginase-type enzyme, EC 3.5.3.10) hydrolyzes D-arginine to D-ornithine and urea. The reaction is balanced: D-arginine (C6H14N4O2) + H2O yields urea (CH4N2O) + D-ornithine (C5H12N2O2). Atoms balance (C6, N4, O3, H16 on each side). As a hydrolase reaction, it proceeds in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn06731.other_comments: This is the core 2 beta-1,6-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.102). UDP-GlcNAc donates a GlcNAc residue via beta-1,6 linkage to the GalNAc of the core 1 structure (beta-D-Gal-1,3-GalNAc-R), forming the core 2 O-glycan branch and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one GlcNAc transferred from the sugar nucleotide donor, UDP released. Glycosyltransferase reactions using sugar nucleotide donors are thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible.

rxn14017.other_comments: This is the FAD-dependent glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GlpD/GPD2) reaction, the mitochondrial/membrane-bound component of the glycerol phosphate shuttle. It oxidizes sn-glycerol 3-phosphate to glycerone phosphate (dihydroxyacetone phosphate, DHAP) while reducing ubiquinone (Q) to ubiquinol (QH2). The reaction is balanced: glycerol-3-phosphate (C3H7O6P, minus 2H = DHAP C3H5O6P) and Q + 2H -> QH2. Atoms and charges balance.

rxn00707.other_comments: This reaction represents a nucleoside (cytidine) kinase activity using ITP as the phosphate donor instead of the more common ATP. ITP donates a phosphate to cytidine, forming CMP and IDP, releasing a proton. The reaction is balanced: ITP (C10H11N4O14P3) + cytidine (C9H13N3O5) yields CMP (C9H12N3O8P) + IDP (C10H11N4O11P2) + H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly. Kinase reactions of this type are generally driven thermodynamically toward phosphorylation of the nucleoside (forward) in vivo due to the favorable hydrolysis of the high-energy phosphoanhydride bond.

errors: Charge and proton imbalance: phosphoryl transfer from GTP to cytidine to form CMP does not generate a free proton; GTP + Cytidine -> GDP + CMP should be balanced without an extra H+. The hydroxyl acceptor reaction (R-OH + GTP -> R-O-PO3 + GDP) typically releases one H+, so the H+ may be acceptable, but the net charge should be checked. As written, the proton inclusion makes the charge balance off by one.
rxn00369.other_comments: This is a phosphotransferase (kinase-type) reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of GTP to the 5'-OH of cytidine, yielding GDP and CMP. Cytidine kinases normally use ATP, but a GTP-dependent variant is plausible. Mass balance of the carbon/phosphate skeleton is essentially correct; the main concern is the proton/charge balance.

errors: No net transformation is represented; substrates and products are identical. A proton symport transport reaction should distinguish compartments, e.g. H+[extracellular] + Acetylcysteine[extracellular] <=> H+[cytosol] + Acetylcysteine[cytosol]. As written, both sides are identical and the reaction is trivially balanced but biologically meaningless without compartment annotation.
rxn12528.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport of N-acetylcysteine across a membrane. The mass and charge are formally balanced (1 H+ and 1 acetylcysteine on each side), but because compartment labels are missing, both sides appear identical and no actual transport is encoded.

rxn08530.other_comments: This is the FrlB-catalyzed reaction in the fructoselysine degradation pathway. Fructoselysine 6-phosphate undergoes deglycation (hydrolysis), releasing free L-lysine and converting the Amadori sugar moiety to glucose-6-phosphate. The atoms balance: fructoselysine 6-phosphate (the Amadori product of lysine and glucose) plus water yields lysine and glucose-6-phosphate, with release of a proton. Stoichiometry and mass/charge are consistent.

rxn05961.other_comments: This is the 4-chlorobenzoate dehalogenase (4-chlorobenzoate hydrolase) reaction. The hydrolytic dehalogenation replaces the chlorine substituent on the aromatic ring with a hydroxyl group from water, releasing chloride and a proton, yielding 4-hydroxybenzoate. The stoichiometry is balanced: C7H4ClO2- (4-chlorobenzoate) + H2O -> C7H5O3- (4-hydroxybenzoate) + Cl- + H+. Mass and charge balance check out (left charge -1, right charge -1+-1+1 = -1). Note that the true enzyme (EC 3.8.1.6) actually proceeds via a CoA-thioester intermediate in many bacteria (4-chlorobenzoyl-CoA dehalogenase pathway), but this net hydrolytic reaction is correct as written.

errors: Transport reaction lacks compartment designations; the same metabolites appear on both sides without indicating movement between compartments (e.g., extracellular vs cytosolic). As written, the reaction is null/identity with no net transformation.
rxn12608.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction for the glycyl-L-aspartate dipeptide, where H+ and gly-asp-L are co-transported across a membrane. However, without distinct compartment tags (e.g., [e] for extracellular and [c] for cytosolic), both sides are identical and the reaction is stoichiometrically void. Proton symporters typically transport substrates inward driven by the proton motive force.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (S-Adenosyl-L-methionine + H+) on both sides without specifying compartments; for a transport (permease) reaction, the substrate and proton should be annotated with distinct compartments such as [extracellular] and [cytosol] to represent translocation across the membrane.
rxn09696.other_comments: This is intended to be a membrane transport reaction catalyzed by the SAM3 permease, moving S-adenosylmethionine (likely co-transported with a proton, a symport) across the plasma membrane. As written it is missing compartment designations, so it appears as a futile/null reaction. With proper compartmentalization it would represent SAM uptake, typically driven by the proton gradient.

rxn02489.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphorylation of inositol 1,3,4,6-tetrakisphosphate at the 5-position by ATP, catalyzed by inositol-tetrakisphosphate 5-kinase (e.g., IPMK/Ipk2 or related kinases), yielding inositol 1,3,4,5,6-pentakisphosphate (InsP5), ADP, and H+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP transfers one gamma-phosphate to the inositol substrate, with one proton released, which is consistent with kinase chemistry.

rxn05026.other_comments: This is trehalose phosphorylase (alpha,alpha-trehalose:phosphate alpha-D-glucosyltransferase, EC 2.4.1.64). It catalyzes phosphorolysis of trehalose (TRHL = alpha,alpha-trehalose) using inorganic phosphate to yield D-glucose and beta-D-glucose-1-phosphate. The reaction is atom-balanced: trehalose (C12H22O11) + phosphate yields glucose (C6H12O6) + glucose-1-phosphate (C6H13O9P). Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: The reaction as written is likely mislabeled or reversed. The enzyme 4-carboxy-4-hydroxy-2-oxoadipate aldolase (EC 4.1.3.17) typically catalyzes an aldol cleavage producing oxaloacetate and pyruvate, not a simple dehydration. If treated as a hydro-lyase, the dehydration product (4-carboxy-2-oxo-3-hexenedioate / oxalocitramalate-type enol) should be verified; the conventional physiological reaction is the aldol synthesis (condensation) direction.
rxn03272.other_comments: The input describes 4-carboxy-4-hydroxy-2-oxoadipate undergoing a dehydration (hydro-lyase, loss of water) to form an unsaturated dicarboxy-oxo compound. Stoichiometrically, removing H2O from the hydroxyl-bearing substrate to yield an alpha,beta-unsaturated product is balanced (C7H8O8 -> C7H6O7 + H2O), so mass balance appears consistent. This compound is associated with the protocatechuate/gallate degradation pathway.

rxn04382.other_comments: This is the dihydroceramide desaturase/4-hydroxylase (DES2) reaction, which introduces a 4-hydroxyl group into dihydroceramide to form phytoceramide (Ceramide II in some databases). The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + dihydroceramide -> H2O + NADP+ + hydroxylated ceramide. One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the hydroxyl group, the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. As a monooxygenase/hydroxylase reaction coupled to NADPH oxidation and O2 consumption, it is thermodynamically and physiologically irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn04590.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in the novobiocin biosynthetic pathway (NovO or related). S-Adenosyl-L-methionine donates a methyl group to Novclobiocin 105, producing the methylated Novclobiocin 104 plus S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: SAM transfers a methyl group, becoming SAH, and a proton is released, consistent with O-methylation chemistry. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction toward methylation.

errors: Stoichiometric/charge imbalance: a free H+ is generated on the product side without a corresponding source, making the reaction unbalanced for hydrogen and charge
The substrate 'Hexadecenoyl-CoA' is ambiguous; an isomerization should specify the starting double-bond position/geometry (e.g., a cis-3 isomer) to be meaningful
rxn08706.other_comments: This is described as a cis-trans isomerization of a hexadecenoyl-CoA species to (2E)-hexadecenoyl-CoA. Such enoyl-CoA isomerase reactions (e.g., 3,2-enoyl-CoA isomerase in unsaturated fatty acid beta-oxidation) shift double-bond position/geometry without net atom change, so no H+ should be released; the reaction is intrinsically near-equilibrium and reversible.

rxn11780.other_comments: This is a condensation (amide bond formation) between the amino group of glycine and the carboxylic acid of isonicotinic acid, releasing water to form isonicotinylglycine (an N-acyl glycine conjugate). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: glycine (C2H5NO2) + isonicotinic acid (C6H5NO2) yields water (H2O) + isonicotinylglycine (C8H8N2O3). In vivo, such glycine conjugation reactions are driven by an activated acyl group (e.g., isonicotinyl-CoA via glycine N-acyltransferase) and serve as detoxification/elimination pathways, making them effectively forward (biosynthetic) toward the conjugate. Note: physiologically the acid is activated to a CoA thioester rather than reacting as the free acid directly, but as written the net transformation favors the conjugate.

errors: Charge imbalance: formononetin is a neutral molecule, but the products include a free H+ which is not consumed elsewhere. The correct dehydration should yield only H2O + formononetin without an extra proton. As written, the right side carries an extra positive charge that the left side does not balance.
rxn07537.other_comments: This is the 2-hydroxyisoflavanone dehydratase (HID) reaction, which removes water from 2,7-dihydroxy-4'-methoxyisoflavanone to form the isoflavone formononetin. Mass balance for C/H/O works if you account for water loss (C16H14O5 -> C16H12O4 + H2O), but the spurious H+ on the product side breaks charge balance.

errors: Reaction name refers to L-arabinose but the substrate listed is D-Arabinose; metabolite naming is inconsistent with the reaction annotation

The transported metabolite (D-Arabinose) appears identical on both sides with no compartment designation; a proper transport reaction should show the substrate in different compartments (e.g., D-Arabinose[e] -> D-Arabinose[c])
rxn10822.other_comments: This is intended to be an ABC-type transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to the import of arabinose. The ATP hydrolysis portion is stoichiometrically balanced. However, without compartment tags the transport is not represented (substrate is the same on both sides). ABC importers are effectively irreversible in vivo due to ATP hydrolysis driving uptake.

rxn03095.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of taurodeoxycholate (a conjugated bile acid) by bile salt hydrolase (BSH/choloylglycine hydrolase, EC 3.5.1.24), cleaving the amide bond to release taurine and deoxycholate. The reaction is balanced: taurodeoxycholate + water yields the free bile acid (deoxycholate) plus taurine. Atoms and charges balance assuming standard protonation states. As an amidohydrolase reaction, it is strongly favored thermodynamically in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo, carried out by gut microbiota.

rxn05922.other_comments: This reaction describes 3-chloro-D-alanine chloride-lyase (EC 4.5.1.2), which catalyzes the deamination and dechlorination of 3-chloro-D-alanine to form pyruvate, ammonia, and chloride. 3-chloro-D-alanine (C3H6ClNO2) plus water yields pyruvate (C3H3O3-), NH3, H+, and Cl-. Mass balance: left C3H8ClNO3, right C3H3O3 + NH3 + H + Cl = C3H7ClNO3... checking H: left H2O(2)+substrate(6)=8 H; right pyruvate(3)+NH3(3)+H(1)=7 H. Charge: left substrate is zwitterion/neutral, right pyruvate(-1)+H+(+1)+Cl-(-1)=-1. There appears to be a slight imbalance depending on protonation states, but using neutral 3-chloro-alanine and ionized pyruvate the overall scheme is consistent with one extra H needed. The reaction as commonly written balances when pyruvate is taken as pyruvic acid or with appropriate proton accounting.

rxn01220.other_comments: This is deoxycytidine kinase (EC 2.7.1.74), which transfers the gamma-phosphate from ATP to deoxycytidine, producing dCMP and ADP. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ATP (C10H12N5O13P3, charge -4) + deoxycytidine (C9H13N3O4, neutral) yields ADP (C10H12N5O10P2, charge -3) + dCMP (C9H12N3O7P, charge -2) + H+. Atoms balance (gamma-phosphate transferred) and charges balance (-4 = -3 -2 +1).

rxn11935.other_comments: This reaction represents choline dehydrogenase activity using PQQ (pyrroloquinoline quinone) as the cofactor/electron acceptor. Choline is oxidized to betaine aldehyde while PQQ is reduced to PQQH2 (the reduced quinol form). The stoichiometry is balanced: choline loses 2 H (2 electrons and 2 protons) which are accepted by PQQ to form PQQH2. In vivo, PQQ-dependent choline oxidoreductases (e.g., in methylotrophic and halotolerant bacteria) function in the oxidative direction as part of glycine betaine biosynthesis from choline, an osmoprotectant pathway, driven by reoxidation of PQQH2 by the respiratory chain.

rxn10615.other_comments: This reaction represents thiosulfate reductase activity, cleaving thiosulfate (H2S2O3) into sulfite and sulfide (H2S) using H2 as the reductant/electron donor. Mass balance: left side has S2, O3, and H4 (H2S2O3 + H2); right side has Sulfite (SO3, H? as HSO3- or SO3 2-), H2S (SH2), plus H+. Atoms appear balanced for S (2=2) and O (3=3); hydrogen and charge balance depend on the protonation states assumed for sulfite. Treating sulfite as SO3(2-) gives H+ + SO3 + H2S = H3SO3S, matching H2S2O3 + H2 = H4S2O3 only if charges are reconciled. The thiosulfate S-S bond is reductively cleaved, releasing the outer sulfane sulfur as sulfide and the inner sulfonate sulfur as sulfite.

rxn04180.other_comments: This is the acetyltransferase step in Taxol (paclitaxel) biosynthesis, catalyzed by taxadien-5alpha-ol O-acetyltransferase (TAT/TDAT). Acetyl-CoA donates its acetyl group to the C5 hydroxyl of taxa-4(20),11(12)-dien-5alpha-ol, producing the 5alpha-acetate ester and free CoA. The reaction is balanced: the acetyl group is transferred from CoA to the alcohol oxygen, conserving atoms. In vivo, acetyl-CoA-dependent acyltransfers are thermodynamically driven by the high-energy thioester bond, so the reaction proceeds essentially in the forward (acetylation) direction.

errors: The reaction as written does not balance. 3-Propylmalate (C7H12O5, deprotonated forms vary) should cleave into glyoxylate plus a 5-carbon acyl unit, but the proposed mechanism requires a CoA-dependent condensation/cleavage that does not conserve atoms as written.

Carbon balance: 3-propylmalate has 7 carbons; glyoxylate (2C) + pentanoyl-CoA acyl moiety (5C) = 7C, so carbon balances, but the reaction is missing the redox/dehydration accounting. A malate-type C-C lyase cleavage yields a carbonyl product, not a saturated acyl-CoA, unless an additional reduction step is included.

Oxygen/hydrogen imbalance: forming pentanoyl-CoA (CH3CH2CH2CH2-CO-CoA) from the 3-propylmalate fragment requires removal of a hydroxyl as water plus reduction; as written with only CoA + H+ -> H2O, the H and O atoms are not balanced.
Proton/charge balance should be rechecked once a valid mechanism is established.
rxn02178.other_comments: This is presented as a retro-aldol/lyase-type cleavage of 3-propylmalate into glyoxylate and a 5-carbon acyl-CoA (pentanoyl-CoA), analogous to malate synthase/citrate lyase chemistry run in reverse. The carbon count matches (7 = 2 + 5), but a simple aldol cleavage of a 2-hydroxy-dicarboxylate would yield a keto/aldehyde-acyl product (e.g., an oxo-acyl-CoA), not a fully saturated pentanoyl-CoA, so an extra reduction equivalent appears to be unaccounted for, breaking the H/O balance.

errors: Reaction is missing a proton (H+) on the product side; the standard PGP synthase reaction releases CMP plus a proton: CDP-diacylglycerol + glycerol-3-phosphate -> CMP + phosphatidylglycerophosphate + H+. As written it is charge/H-unbalanced.
rxn10694.other_comments: This is phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase (PgsA, CDP-diacylglycerol--glycerol-3-phosphate 3-phosphatidyltransferase, EC 2.7.8.5). It transfers the phosphatidyl group from CDP-diacylglycerol (with C16:0 and C19:0/tuberculostearoyl acyl chains) onto glycerol-3-phosphate, yielding CMP and PGP. The acyl chain bookkeeping is consistent between substrate and product.

rxn02528.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADPH-dependent reduction of butanal (butyraldehyde) to n-butanol, catalyzed by an alcohol/aldehyde reductase (e.g., EC 1.1.1.- ). Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ provides 2 electrons and a proton to reduce the aldehyde carbonyl to a primary alcohol, regenerating NADP+. Carbon (C4), oxygen, and hydrogen atoms balance correctly. In vivo, the high NADPH/NADP+ ratio and favorable thermodynamics typically drive aldehyde reduction toward the alcohol, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (butanal -> n-butanol) direction, as in butanol fermentation pathways.

rxn00566.other_comments: This is the cysteine desulfhydrase reaction (L-cysteine hydrogen-sulfide-lyase, deaminating, pyruvate-forming). L-Cysteine plus water yields pyruvate, ammonia, and hydrogen sulfide. Atom balance checks out: cysteine (C3H7NO2S) + H2O (H2O) gives NH3 + pyruvate (C3H4O3) + H2S. Carbon: 3=3, nitrogen: 1=1, sulfur: 1=1, oxygen: 2+1=3, hydrogen: 7+2=9 = 3(NH3)+4(pyruvate)+2(H2S)=9. Balanced. [directionality_note] This catabolic lyase/desulfhydrase reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of cysteine degradation.

rxn03814.other_comments: This reaction represents the N,N-dimethylation of dTDP-3-amino-3,4,6-trideoxy-alpha-D-glucose to form dTDP-desosamine, catalyzed by an N,N-dimethyltransferase using SAM as the methyl donor. Two methyl groups are transferred to the amino group, consuming 2 SAM and producing 2 SAH plus 2 H+. The product dTDP-desosamine has a 3-dimethylamino group, consistent with the two-fold methylation. Stoichiometry is balanced: 2 methyl groups transferred, 2 SAH formed, 2 protons released from the amine.

errors: The product of dehydration of a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA is a 2-enoyl-CoA (double bond between C2 and C3), so the product should be named trans-2-enoyl-CoA or cis-2-enoyl-CoA, not 2,3-dehydroacyl-CoA in the literal sense; the term 'cis-2,3-Dehydroacyl-CoA' is ambiguous/nonstandard.

Crotonase (enoyl-CoA hydratase) typically interconverts (S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA with trans-2-enoyl-CoA, while the (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA stereochemistry is associated with the auxiliary R-hydratase yielding trans-2-enoyl-CoA; pairing the (R)-isomer with a cis-2-enoyl-CoA is geometrically inconsistent for the standard anti elimination.
rxn06347.other_comments: This is a hydro-lyase (hydratase/dehydratase) reaction interconverting a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA and an enoyl-CoA with loss/addition of water. Atom balance for the dehydration itself is correct (substrate = product + H2O). The main concerns are nomenclature of the unsaturated product and the stereochemical pairing of (R)-hydroxy with a cis double bond.

rxn10567.other_comments: This reaction represents the activation of 2-phospho-L-lactate by GTP to form lactyl-2-diphospho-5'-guanosine (LPPG) with release of pyrophosphate (PPi). It is catalyzed by 2-phospho-L-lactate guanylyltransferase (CofC/LPPG synthetase), an enzyme in the F420 cofactor biosynthesis pathway. Stoichiometry is balanced: the guanylyl (GMP) group of GTP is transferred to the phosphate of 2-phospho-L-lactate, releasing PPi. In vivo this nucleotidyltransferase reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase.

errors: The reaction as written uses NAD/NADH, but the enzyme name specifies NADP+ as the cofactor (UDP-N-acetylmuramate:NADP+ oxidoreductase); however, MurB (UDP-N-acetylenolpyruvoylglucosamine reductase, EC 1.3.1.98) actually uses NADPH. Cofactor inconsistency.

The product is named 'UDP-N-acetylglucosamine enolpyruvate' which should be UDP-N-acetylglucosamine enolpyruvate (UDP-GlcNAc-enolpyruvate), the substrate for MurB reduction; the substrate UDP-MurNAc (UDP-N-acetylmuramate) is the reduced product, so the substrate/product assignment is internally consistent for an oxidoreductase but reversed relative to physiological MurB direction.
rxn02284.other_comments: This represents the MurB reaction (UDP-N-acetylenolpyruvoylglucosamine reductase) in cell wall peptidoglycan biosynthesis. In vivo, the enolpyruvyl intermediate (UDP-GlcNAc-enolpyruvate) is reduced by NADPH to form UDP-MurNAc (UDP-N-acetylmuramate). The reaction as written goes oxidatively (UDP-MurNAc -> enolpyruvate intermediate), which is the reverse of the biological direction.

rxn13688.other_comments: This is cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV). The chemistry consumes 0.5 O2, 2 reduced cytochrome c (Fe2+), and protons to form water and 2 oxidized cytochrome c (Fe3+). The net chemical reaction needs 2 protons (scalar/chemical protons): 0.5 O2 + 2 H+ + 2 cyt c2+ -> H2O + 2 cyt c3+. The notation here shows 4 H+ consumed on the left and 2 H+ produced on the right, giving a net of 2 protons consumed, consistent with 2 protons translocated across the membrane plus the chemical protons. The reaction is mass and charge balanced as written (left charge: +4 +2(2+) = +8 minus implicit; right: +2 + 2(3+) = +8). It is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction toward water formation.

rxn09898.other_comments: This reaction represents an ATP-dependent L-amino acid ligase forming a dipeptide bond between two L-threonine molecules. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the energy, hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi, releasing one H+ as the peptide bond forms (condensation eliminates water, captured by ATP hydrolysis). Mass and charge are balanced. Lal-type ligases (e.g., RizA, BacD family) drive peptide bond formation via ATP hydrolysis, making the reaction thermodynamically favorable in the synthetic direction in vivo.

rxn00592.other_comments: This is the decarboxylation of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate to form catechol and CO2, catalyzed by 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate decarboxylase (2,3-DHBD). Stoichiometry and atom/charge balance are correct: 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate (C7H5O4-) plus H+ yields catechol (C6H6O2) plus CO2 (CO2). Carbons: 7 = 6 + 1; charge balances. In vivo, while the enzyme can catalyze reversible carboxylation under high CO2/bicarbonate, the physiological/thermodynamically favored direction is decarboxylation (forward).

rxn02203.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by (2R,3S)-2,3-dimethylmalate hydro-lyase (dimethylmaleate-forming), EC 4.2.1.85. It is a dehydration (hydro-lyase) reaction in which (2R,3S)-2,3-dimethylmalate loses water to form dimethylmaleic acid (dimethylmaleate). The stoichiometry is balanced: dimethylmalate (C6H10O5) yields water (H2O) plus dimethylmaleic acid (C6H8O4). In the nicotinate fermentation pathway (e.g., in Eubacterium barkeri), this enzyme operates physiologically in the hydration direction (dimethylmaleate to dimethylmalate), but the enzyme reaction itself is biochemically reversible.

errors: The H+ should not appear as a reactant in this phosphoryl transfer reaction; kinase reactions of this type are typically proton-neutral or release H+, and the addition of a proton on the left side is not stoichiometrically justified
Charge and mass balance cannot be fully verified because 'Deoxynucleoside phosphate' and 'Deoxynucleoside diphosphate' are generic placeholders rather than specific defined species
rxn06630.other_comments: This is a nucleoside monophosphate kinase (NMP kinase) type reaction transferring a gamma-phosphate from ATP to a deoxynucleoside monophosphate (dNMP) to form a deoxynucleoside diphosphate (dNDP), regenerating ADP. The phosphoryl transfer itself is balanced (ATP + dNMP <=> ADP + dNDP). In vivo this reaction strongly favors dNDP formation as part of the pathway feeding dNTP synthesis for DNA replication.

rxn02639.other_comments: This is the peroxisomal bile-acid forming thiolase (SCPx/EC 2.3.1.176) step. In vivo it proceeds as thiolytic cleavage: 24-oxo-THCA-CoA + CoA -> choloyl-CoA + propionyl-CoA. The reaction as written (propionyl-CoA + choloyl-CoA -> CoA + 24-oxo-THCA-CoA) is the reverse of the physiological direction.

rxn03948.other_comments: This is an alcohol dehydrogenase-type reaction. Sulcatol (6-methyl-5-hepten-2-ol) is a secondary alcohol that is oxidized to the ketone Sulcatone (6-methyl-5-hepten-2-one), with NAD+ accepting the hydride to form NADH plus a proton. The atoms and charges balance: oxidation of the secondary alcohol removes two hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+, one as H+). NAD dehydrogenase reactions of this type are generally reversible, though the in vivo direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio and the specific physiological context.

rxn00870.other_comments: This reaction (butanal:NADP+ oxidoreductase, CoA-acylating) describes the interconversion of butanal and butyryl-CoA. In the written direction, butanal + CoA + NADP+ yields butyryl-CoA + NADPH + H+. Atoms and charges balance: butanal (C4H8O) + CoA forms the thioester butyryl-CoA (acyl group C4H7O attached to CoA), with the redox change of two electrons captured by NADP+ to NADPH. This is the aldehyde dehydrogenase (acylating) reaction. While the oxidative direction is written here, this enzyme physiologically often operates in the reductive direction (butyryl-CoA to butanal) as part of solventogenesis/alcohol-aldehyde formation, so it is best classified as reversible with biological context-dependent direction.

rxn09477.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA oxidase reaction (peroxisomal beta-oxidation, first step). Myristoyl-CoA (C14 saturated acyl-CoA) is oxidized by molecular O2 to form (2E)-tetradecenoyl-CoA (the trans-2-enoyl-CoA) plus hydrogen peroxide. The stoichiometry is balanced: the enzyme introduces a double bond between C2 and C3, removing two hydrogens that reduce O2 to H2O2. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn10445.other_comments: This represents beta-lysine acetyltransferase, transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the epsilon-amino group of L-beta-lysine, producing N-epsilon-acetyl-beta-lysine, CoA, and a proton. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: acetyl-CoA (C23) plus beta-lysine (C6) yields CoA (C21) plus acetyl-beta-lysine (C8) plus H+. Acetyl group (C2H3O) transfer accounts correctly. This enzyme is involved in betaine/ectoine-like osmolyte synthesis in some organisms.

errors: Mass imbalance: combining L-Arginine (C6H14N4O2) and Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (C3H7O6P) to form Phosphate (HO4P) + H+ + L-N2-(2-Carboxyethyl)arginine (C9H18N4O4) does not balance. Sum of reactants = C9H21N4O8P; sum of products = C9H19N4O8P. There is a deficit of 2 H on the product side (an additional H2O or loss of 2[H] is needed to balance).

The reaction concept is correct but the written formula equation is not properly H-balanced. [directionality_note] This is the carboxyethylarginine synthase (CEAS) reaction in clavulanic acid biosynthesis, which proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward CEA.

rxn11789.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) reaction transferring glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronate to the 6-hydroxyl of codeine, forming codeine-6-glucuronide and releasing UDP. This is a Phase II drug metabolism conjugation reaction.

rxn05563.other_comments: This is intended to be a glucose-6-phosphate transport reaction coupled to phosphate antiport across a membrane. The correct form should be: G6P[e] + Pi[c] <=> G6P[c] + Pi[e] (1:1 antiport).

rxn08979.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of 2-demethylmenaquinone-8 (oxidized quinone form) to 2-demethylmenaquinol-8 (reduced quinol form). The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH provides a hydride (2 electrons + 1 H), and with the additional H+, two H atoms are transferred to the quinone to form the quinol, regenerating NADP+. This is consistent with quinone reductase activity. Note: the cofactor is more commonly written as NADP+ with the explicit positive charge.

rxn00830.other_comments: This reaction represents isopentenyl-diphosphate delta-isomerase (IDI, EC 5.3.3.2), which interconverts isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) and dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP). Both substrate and product are C5 isomers (C5H12O7P2), so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a 1:1 isomerization. As an isomerase reaction, it is thermodynamically reversible; although the equilibrium favors DMAPP, in vivo flux direction depends on downstream demand (consumption of DMAPP in prenyltransferase reactions and continuous IPP supply from the MEP/MVA pathways).

errors: The reaction is not properly balanced; a Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenation of menthone to mentholactone (a lactone) requires insertion of an oxygen atom and produces only one water, but the oxygen and hydrogen balance should be checked. Menthone (C10H18O) + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> lactone (C10H18O2) + H2O + NADP+; oxygen balance: left has 1(menthone)+2(O2)=3 O, right has 2(lactone)+1(water)=3 O - oxygen balances. Carbon: 10=10 OK. Hydrogen: left 18(menthone)+1(NADPH adds H)... net appears balanced, so no major stoichiometric error.

rxn13988.other_comments: This represents a Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase (cytochrome P450 / flavin monooxygenase type) reaction converting (-)-menthone to mentholactone (menthone 1,2-monooxygenase / menthone lactonase pathway). NADPH and O2 driven monooxygenations are strongly exergonic and physiologically irreversible.

errors: The reaction as written is trivial/null: the same species (H+ and Histamine) appear identically on both sides with no compartment designations, so no net chemical or transport change is represented. A proper proton symport transport reaction should specify distinct compartments, e.g. H+[e] + Histamine[e] <=> H+[c] + Histamine[c].
rxn05706.other_comments: This is annotated as a histamine import via proton symport. The intended reaction couples movement of histamine into the cell with a proton down its electrochemical gradient. As written, both sides are identical (missing compartment labels), so it conveys no net transport. With proper compartment annotation, such proton-coupled import is typically driven inward (extracellular to cytoplasm) and is usually treated as effectively unidirectional (forward, import) in vivo, though formally reversible depending on gradients.

rxn03807.other_comments: This is described as a dTDP-sugar 2,3-dehydratase (hydro-lyase) acting on dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose, a step in deoxysugar biosynthesis. Such dehydratases typically eliminate water to form a 2,3-glucoseen intermediate; the stated 3,4-dioxo product naming is chemically suspect as written.
