rxn00928.other_comments: This reaction is the NAD+-dependent oxidation of L-proline at the alpha-carbon (C2-N bond) to form the cyclic imine 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (also called 3,4-dihydro-2H-pyrrole-2-carboxylate). Note this is distinct from proline dehydrogenase, which oxidizes the delta position to give 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate. The reaction is written with one extra proton.

rxn02395.other_comments: This is the NADP+-dependent oxidation of (R)-3-(4-hydroxyphenyl)lactate to p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, catalyzed by an (R)-hydroxyphenyllactate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.222). The reaction is balanced: the secondary alcohol (lactate) is oxidized to a ketone (pyruvate derivative), releasing 2 electrons and 1 proton, transferred to NADP+ to form NADPH + H+. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance correctly.

rxn00668.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of acrylyl-CoA (2-propenoyl-CoA) to propionyl-CoA (propanoyl-CoA), catalyzed by acrylyl-CoA reductase. The stoichiometry is balanced: the C=C double bond of acrylyl-CoA is reduced by addition of two electrons and two protons (one hydride from NADPH and one H+), yielding propionyl-CoA and NADP+. Atoms and charges balance correctly. In vivo, this reductive step (e.g., in the 3-hydroxypropionate cycle and certain propionate metabolism pathways) strongly favors the reduction direction toward propionyl-CoA due to the high reducing potential of NADPH.

rxn10472.other_comments: This is the hydration of cis-homoaconitate to form (2R,3S)-homoisocitrate (threo-isohomocitrate), part of the alpha-aminoadipate (AAA) lysine biosynthesis pathway. The reaction is catalyzed by homoaconitase (homoaconitate hydratase, an aconitase-family iron-sulfur enzyme). Stoichiometry is balanced: a single water molecule is added across the double bond of the unsaturated tricarboxylate to give the hydroxy-tricarboxylate, with no extra atoms or charges unaccounted for. Like aconitase-type hydratases, this reaction is freely reversible in vivo, though it proceeds toward homoisocitrate in the biosynthetic direction.

rxn01661.other_comments: This is the (+)-delta-cadinene synthase reaction (EC 4.2.3.13), a sesquiterpene cyclase. Farnesyl diphosphate (C15H25O7P2, 3- at physiological pH) undergoes ionization-cyclization to yield the bicyclic sesquiterpene (+)-delta-cadinene (C15H24) and releases diphosphate (PPi). Stoichiometry balances: C15 on each side; the FPP carbon skeleton becomes cadinene, the diphosphate group is released as PPi, and a proton is released to balance charge/H. Mass and charge are conserved.

rxn02161.other_comments: This is the rhamnulokinase reaction (RhaB, EC 2.7.1.5), phosphorylating L-rhamnulose at the 1-position using ATP to yield L-rhamnulose 1-phosphate, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP donates the gamma-phosphate, producing ADP and releasing H+. As an ATP-dependent kinase step in L-rhamnose catabolism, it is physiologically driven forward.

rxn04928.other_comments: This is the UlaD reaction (3-keto-L-gulonate-6-phosphate decarboxylase, EC 4.1.1.85) in the L-ascorbate utilization (ula) pathway of E. coli. It catalyzes decarboxylation of 3-keto-L-gulonate-6-phosphate to L-xylulose-5-phosphate, releasing CO2 and consuming a proton. The atoms balance: the C6 keto-acid substrate loses one carbon as CO2 to yield the C5 product, and the proton consumption is consistent with the decarboxylation. As an essentially irreversible decarboxylation, it proceeds in the forward (decarboxylation) direction in vivo.

rxn04378.other_comments: This is written as a phosphatase hydrolysis: ceramide-1-phosphate + water -> ceramide + inorganic phosphate. This is the reaction catalyzed by ceramide-1-phosphate phosphatase, not the named 3-sn-phosphatidate phosphohydrolase (lipid phosphate phosphatases can have broad specificity, however). Phosphomonoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn00503.other_comments: This is the P5C dehydrogenase (ALDH4A1) reaction. 1-Pyrroline-5-carboxylate is in equilibrium with L-glutamate-5-semialdehyde, which is oxidized by NAD+ to L-glutamate. The reaction consumes 2 H2O (one for hydration/ring opening of P5C and the overall oxidation) and produces NADH, L-glutamate, and H+. The atoms balance: P5C (C5H7NO2) + 2 H2O + NAD+ -> L-glutamate (C5H9NO4) + NADH + H+. Charge and mass are balanced.

rxn02723.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase reaction transferring a sinapoyl group from sinapoyl-CoA to a lactone acceptor, releasing free CoA. rxn00927.other_comments: This is the adenosine ribohydrolase (nucleoside hydrolase) reaction: hydrolysis of adenosine with water yields D-ribose and adenine. rxn07555.other_comments: This is a malonyltransferase reaction transferring a malonyl group from malonyl-CoA to the 6'' position of the glucose moiety of (-)-medicocarpin (medicarpin 3-O-glucoside), yielding CoA and the 6''-O-malonylated product (medicarpin 3-O-glucoside-6''-O-malonate). rxn04043.other_comments: This is the ADP-dependent phosphofructokinase (PFK) reaction, common in many Archaea (e.g., Pyrococcus, Thermococcus). rxn03851.other_comments: This represents the oxidative N-dealkylation of atrazine to deethylatrazine, releasing the ethyl carbon as acetaldehyde. This is an irreversible, oxygen-dependent catabolic (degradation) step, so it proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

Hydrolytic cleavage of the phosphoanhydride bond is thermodynamically strongly favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so it proceeds in the forward (hydrolysis) direction.

rxn04893.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-mediated monooxygenation of 1,1-dichloroethylene (vinylidene chloride). The reaction consumes NADPH, O2, and a proton, transferring one oxygen atom to the substrate and reducing the other to water. The epoxide intermediate of vinylidene chloride rearranges; chloroacetyl chloride is a known reactive metabolite of this oxidation. Stoichiometry balances: NADPH + O2 + H+ provide reducing equivalents and oxygen, yielding H2O, NADP+, and the oxidized product. rxn01481.other_comments: This is the (R)-3-amino-2-methylpropanoate:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase reaction (EC 2.6.1.40). rxn12582.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for D-glucose 1-phosphate. Transport directionality typically follows the proton motive force, generally importing the substrate, but can be modeled as reversible.

rxn09233.other_comments: This is the ribonucleotide reductase reaction reducing CDP (cytidine 5'-diphosphate) to dCDP (2'-deoxycytidine 5'-diphosphate). rxn01954.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction. 4-hydroxyphenylacetonitrile (4-hydroxybenzyl cyanide) is hydroxylated at the benzylic carbon to form 4-hydroxymandelonitrile, consuming NADPH and O2 and producing NADP+ and water. rxn13456.other_comments: This represents a fatty acid/polyketide-type elongation that extends a C42-ACP intermediate to a C56-ACP by 7 rounds of 2-carbon addition using malonyl-ACP. rxn07630.other_comments: This reaction (R07839) represents the tautomerization/isomerization between 4-oxalomesaconate (a keto form) and 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate / 4-carboxy-2-hydroxyhexa-2,4-dienedioate (the enol form, also called 2-hydroxy-4-carboxymuconate). Both compounds share the formula C7H4O7 (as anions), so the conversion is an internal isomerization/tautomerization with no atoms gained or lost; the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. It is part of the protocatechuate 4,5-cleavage (meta-cleavage) pathway, catalyzed by 4-oxalomesaconate tautomerase (EC 5.3.2.8, LigI/related). As a tautomerase-catalyzed isomerization, it is freely reversible in vivo though pulled forward in the degradative pathway.

rxn02426.other_comments: This is a kinase reaction where ATP phosphorylates scyllo-inosamine (1-amino-1-deoxy-scyllo-inositol) at the 4-position to form 1-amino-1-deoxy-scyllo-inositol 4-phosphate, producing ADP and a proton. This reaction is part of aminocyclitol/streptomycin-type antibiotic biosynthesis. The atoms balance: ATP transfers a phosphate group to the inositol substrate, releasing ADP and H+.

rxn04960.other_comments: This represents CoA-disulfide reductase chemistry. As written (oxidizing CoA to disulfide), the in vivo favored direction is the reverse (reduction of CoA-disulfide).

rxn05122.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of digalacturonate (a disaccharide of two galacturonic acid residues linked by an alpha-1,4 glycosidic bond) into two molecules of D-galacturonate, catalyzed by an exo- or oligogalacturonase/glycoside hydrolase. The stoichiometry is balanced: digalacturonate plus one water yields two galacturonate monomers. Hydrolytic cleavage of a glycosidic bond is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (hydrolysis) direction.

rxn10432.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by (S)-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase (or related D2HGDH-type enzymes for the corresponding enantiomer). The oxidation of (S)-2-hydroxyglutarate to 2-oxoglutarate uses NAD+ as electron acceptor, producing NADH and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: both carbon (C5 substrate to C5 product) and the hydride/proton transfer to NAD+ are accounted for, and charges balance with the explicit H+. While written as reversible, in vivo the physiological direction is typically oxidation (forward, toward 2-oxoglutarate) to clear the L-2-hydroxyglutarate metabolite; however thermodynamically the reaction can proceed in either direction depending on the NAD+/NADH ratio.

rxn06242.other_comments: This is a beta-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase reaction (iGnT/B3GNT family) that transfers GlcNAc from UDP-GlcNAc onto the terminal galactose of N-acetyllactosamine (Gal-beta-1,4-GlcNAc-R), forming GlcNAc-beta-1,3-Gal linkage and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one UDP-GlcNAc donates GlcNAc, releasing UDP, with the acceptor gaining one GlcNAc residue. This is a poly-N-acetyllactosamine chain elongation step. [directionality_note] Glycosyltransferase reactions using nucleotide-sugar donors are strongly favored in the forward (biosynthetic) direction in vivo due to the energetically favorable hydrolysis of the high-energy sugar-nucleotide bond and rapid clearance of UDP.

rxn02893.other_comments: This is a KEGG reaction (R04142) involved in lysine/cadaverine-related acetylated amino acid metabolism, proposed as a reductive carboxylation converting 5-acetamidopentanoate to 2-oxo-6-acetamidocaproate (a 2-oxo acid one carbon longer). rxn10285.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to a diacylglycerol (1,2-diisotetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol), producing UDP and a monoglucosyldiacylglycerol. Atoms and charges balance assuming the glycosidic bond formation releases the glucose with loss of UDP. Glycosyltransferases using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable in the synthetic (forward) direction in vivo due to the high-energy nucleotide-sugar bond.

rxn00920.other_comments: This is the phosphodiesterase-catalyzed hydrolysis of cyclic GMP (cGMP) to 5'-GMP. Water hydrolyzes the cyclic 3',5'-phosphodiester bond, opening the ring to yield GMP and releasing a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced (H2O + cGMP(1-) -> GMP(2-) + H+). In vivo this hydrolysis is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the forward direction, terminating cGMP signaling.

rxn02271.other_comments: This is the E2 (dihydrolipoyl transacylase) component reaction of the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex, specifically for the isoleucine-derived substrate 2-methylbutyryl. As written, the substrates are Dihydrolipoamide + 2-Methylbutyryl-CoA and products are CoA + S-(2-methylbutanoyl)-dihydrolipoamide. Atoms balance: the 2-methylbutanoyl group is transferred between the thiol of CoA and the dihydrolipoamide thiol, with one free thiol released on each side. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1:1).

rxn01442.other_comments: This reaction describes the phosphorylation of D-glucosamine (GLUM) using ITP as the phosphate donor, producing IDP and D-glucosamine 6-phosphate, with release of a proton. rxn03321.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (likely CYP11A1/side-chain cleavage) monooxygenase reaction hydroxylating 20alpha-hydroxycholesterol at C22 to form 20alpha,22-dihydroxycholesterol. rxn00995.other_comments: This is acetoacetate decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.4), which catalyzes the decarboxylation of acetoacetate to acetone and CO2. rxn02097.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of L-theanine (N5-ethyl-L-glutamine) catalyzed by gamma-glutamyltransferase/amidohydrolase activity. rxn02014.other_comments: This is the cholate:CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction, which activates cholate to choloyl-CoA. Physiologically (e.g., in respiratory complex I), this reaction is strongly exergonic and proceeds in the forward direction of NADH oxidation and quinone reduction.

rxn00422.other_comments: This is serine-pyruvate aminotransferase (EC 2.6.1.51). The amino group is transferred from L-serine to pyruvate, yielding L-alanine and hydroxypyruvate. rxn03500.other_comments: This is the 6-O-methyltransferase (6OMT) reaction in benzylisoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis. rxn01489.other_comments: This reaction represents the first committed step of carotenoid biosynthesis, catalyzed by phytoene synthase (CrtB/PSY). The stoichiometry is balanced: quercetin (C15H10O7) + O2 yields CO + the depside product (C14H10O8). Both carbon and oxygen atoms balance correctly.

rxn02260.other_comments: This reaction couples cleavage of the 3-hydroxypropanoyl-CoA thioester (releasing free CoA and 3-hydroxypropanoate/hydracrylic acid) to phosphorylation of ADP to ATP using inorganic phosphate, analogous to acyl-CoA synthetase (ADP-forming) chemistry proceeding in the synthesis direction reverse. It is the type of reaction catalyzed by an ADP-forming acyl-CoA synthetase/acetyl-CoA synthetase-like enzyme.

errors: No net chemical transformation is represented; both sides are identical (Glycogen <=> Glycogen) with no compartment annotation distinguishing substrate from product

rxn05580.other_comments: This is described as a glycogen transport (import) reaction. As written, glycogen on the left equals glycogen on the right with no compartment specification, so it cannot be properly evaluated. Stoichiometrically it is mass-balanced trivially, but it conveys no transport information without compartment tags. Biologically, glycogen is a large intracellular polymer and is not transported across membranes intact, so a true glycogen transport reaction is physiologically questionable.

rxn01298.other_comments: This is the xanthine oxidase reaction (EC 1.17.3.2) converting hypoxanthine (HYXN) to xanthine (XAN). The stoichiometry is balanced: hypoxanthine (C5H4N4O) + H2O + O2 yields xanthine (C5H4N4O2) + H2O2. Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen all balance. In vivo this oxidation proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the substrate 2,4,5-trichloro-2,5-cyclohexadiene-1-ol (C6H3Cl3O) does not balance against the products. 2,5-DCP (2,5-dichlorophenol, C6H4Cl2O) plus H+ plus Cl- accounts for C6H5Cl3O on the product side, leaving an extra hydrogen unbalanced
Hydrogen imbalance: substrate has 3 H plus the OH (total relevant H), product side gives 2,5-DCP (4 H) + H+ (1 H) = 5 H versus 4 H (3 ring/OH H + ...) on substrate; H count does not balance
rxn03780.other_comments: This is a dehydrohalogenation/aromatization step: 2,4,5-trichloro-2,5-cyclohexadien-1-ol eliminates HCl to form the aromatic 2,5-dichlorophenol (2,5-DCP), part of chlorophenol/2,4,5-T degradation pathways. The chemistry (loss of HCl to aromatize) is correct conceptually, but the written stoichiometry appears to have a proton/hydrogen imbalance that should be verified.

errors: Hydrogen and charge are not balanced; the reaction as written has 2 H+ on the left side that are not accounted for on the product side. A balanced reductive dehalogenation typically would be: 2 GSH + 2,3,6-trichlorohydroquinone -> GSSG + HCl + 2,6-dichlorohydroquinone (i.e., releasing H+ and Cl-, not consuming 2 H+). The proton stoichiometry appears incorrect.

Element balance: reactant chlorine count (3 from trichlorohydroquinone) vs product (1 Cl- + 2 from dichlorohydroquinone = 3) is balanced for Cl, but H balance is off due to the 2 H+ on the substrate side.
rxn03703.other_comments: This is a glutathione-dependent reductive dehalogenation (tetrachlorohydroquinone reductive dehalogenase, PcpC-type) converting 2,3,6-trichlorohydroquinone to 2,6-dichlorohydroquinone, using 2 GSH to form GSSG and releasing chloride. The reaction direction (dehalogenation toward dichlorohydroquinone) is the physiologically relevant degradation step.

errors: Mass imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced. 2,3-dihydroxyindole (C8H7NO2 in neutral form) plus O2 yielding anthranilate (C7H6NO2-, anthranilic acid C7H7NO2) plus CO2 (CO2) leaves a carbon/hydrogen/oxygen discrepancy. Balancing requires additional oxygen and/or water. With one O2 only one extra O is unaccounted; producing CO2 + anthranilate from dihydroxyindole typically needs more oxygen or water to balance O and H.
Charge balance should be verified: anthranilate (-1) + H+ on product side; reactant side dihydroxyindole and O2 are neutral, so net charge differs unless protonation states are reconciled.
rxn00724.other_comments: This represents an oxidative ring-cleavage (dioxygenase-type) reaction converting 2,3-dihydroxyindole to anthranilate with release of CO2. Oxygenase reactions consuming O2 with oxidative decarboxylation are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the reaction forward.

rxn12918.other_comments: This reaction represents a sterol C5-desaturase step (ERG3-type), converting episterol (5alpha-cholesta-7,24(28)-dien... ergosta-7,24(28)-dien-3beta-ol) to 5,7,24(28)-ergostatrienol by introducing a C5-C6 double bond. The desaturation uses O2 and NADPH (via cytochrome b5 system), reducing one oxygen atom to water and the other being incorporated/eliminated to form the double bond, yielding 2 H2O. Stoichiometry balances: NADPH + O2 + H+ are consumed, producing 2 H2O, NADP+, and the desaturated sterol. Charge and atoms are balanced as written.

errors: Mass/carbon imbalance: condensation of malonyl-ACP (C3 acyl) with 8-methyl-decanoyl-ACP (C11 acyl) should yield a 3-oxo product with 13 carbons in the acyl chain (10-methyl-3-oxo-tridecanoyl-ACP would be wrong too; correct length is C12 backbone plus methyl branch, i.e. the chain extension adds 2 carbons giving a C13 acyl). The named product '10-methyl-3-oxo-dodecanoyl-ACP' (dodecanoyl = C12) is missing one carbon. A C11 acyl (8-methyl-decanoyl = decanoyl C10 + methyl branch) extended by 2 carbons gives a C12 backbone + methyl branch = 10-methyl-3-oxo-dodecanoyl-ACP, so positions/naming of the methyl branch (8-methyl to 10-methyl) shift by 2, which is consistent. Re-check: the branch position is internally consistent, but the proton balance (H+ release) is typically not shown.
rxn05371.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthase elongation (KAS / 3-oxoacyl-ACP synthase) condensation step: malonyl-ACP condenses with an acyl-ACP primer, releasing CO2 and free ACP and forming a 3-oxoacyl-ACP elongated by two carbons. The methyl branch shifts numbering from C8 to C10 due to two added carbons, which is consistent. The decarboxylative condensation is essentially irreversible in vivo, driving fatty acid chain elongation forward.

rxn02092.other_comments: This is sorbitol dehydrogenase (acceptor) (EC 1.1.99.21), oxidizing D-sorbitol to L-sorbose using FAD as the electron acceptor (forming FADH2). The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: sorbitol (C6H14O6) loses 2 H (2 electrons and 2 protons) to become L-sorbose (C6H12O6), and FAD gains 2 H to become FADH2. This is the key reaction in industrial vitamin C precursor production via Gluconobacter/Acetobacter membrane-bound dehydrogenases, which oxidize sorbitol to sorbose. In vivo this enzyme operates physiologically in the oxidative direction.

errors: Reaction is not mass-balanced as written: indole-3-acetate (C10H8NO2-) plus O2 should yield 2-formaminobenzoylacetate, but the atoms do not balance without accounting for additional oxygen incorporation and ring cleavage products; the formula 2-formaminobenzoylacetate (C10H8NO4) requires both oxygen atoms of O2 to be incorporated, which is consistent only if no water or other product is released. Carbon balance is acceptable (10 C each side), but oxygen/hydrogen balance should be verified.
rxn02223.other_comments: This is the dioxygenase step in anaerobic/aerobic indole-3-acetate degradation, where indoleacetate 2,3-dioxygenase cleaves the pyrrole ring incorporating molecular O2 to form 2-formaminobenzoylacetate. Dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of ring cleavage.

rxn07659.other_comments: This reaction represents the lipoxygenase (13-LOX) catalyzed oxygenation of alpha-linolenate (alpha-linolenic acid, C18:3 omega-3) by molecular oxygen to form 13(S)-hydroperoxy-9,11,15-octadecatrienoate, i.e., 13(S)-HPOT. The stoichiometry is balanced: one molecule of O2 is incorporated into linolenate to yield the hydroperoxide. Lipoxygenases catalyze the dioxygenation of polyunsaturated fatty acids containing a cis,cis-1,4-pentadiene system, and the reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly toward hydroperoxide formation in vivo.

rxn09146.other_comments: This is a Phospholipase A2 reaction hydrolyzing the sn-2 ester bond of a phosphatidate (1,2-ditetradec-7-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate). Water cleaves the acyl group, releasing one tetradecenoate (C14:1) fatty acid and forming the lyso-phosphatidate (1-tetradec-7-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) plus a proton. The mass and charge balance check out: each side has the diacyl substrate splitting into one acyl chain plus the monoacyl product, with H2O consumed and H+ released, consistent with ester hydrolysis.

rxn01717.other_comments: This is the SAM-dependent N-methylation of tyramine to N-methyltyramine, producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. The reaction is balanced: SAM transfers a methyl group to the primary amine of tyramine, yielding N-methyltyramine and SAH, with release of a proton. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: This reaction is not balanced as written. 2-Oxobutyrate (C4H5O3-) cleaved into formate (CHO2-) and a propionyl group (C3H5O) attached to CoA accounts for the carbons, but a redox/electron issue exists. The correct pyruvate formate-lyase analog reaction (2-ketobutyrate formate-lyase / keto-acid formate-lyase, TdcE) is: 2-Oxobutyrate + CoA <=> Propionyl-CoA + Formate. Carbon: C4 = C3 (propionyl) + C1 (formate), OK. Mass/charge balance is actually correct for this radical-enzyme cleavage. No stoichiometric error after reassessment.
rxn04794.other_comments: This is the 2-ketobutyrate formate-lyase reaction (analogous to pyruvate formate-lyase, enzyme TdcE in E. coli). It cleaves the 2-oxoacid using CoA to yield the acyl-CoA (propionyl-CoA) and formate, via a glycyl-radical mechanism. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven toward formate and propionyl-CoA production under anaerobic conditions.

errors: Reaction has identical substrate and product (TTP <=> TTP), resulting in no net chemical transformation
No stoichiometric change occurs; this is a null/identity reaction
If intended as a transport reaction, compartment annotations are missing to distinguish the two TTP pools
rxn09686.other_comments: The reaction shows TTP (thymidine triphosphate, or possibly thiamine triphosphate) converting to itself. The identifier (TRANS-RXN) suggests this may be intended as a transport reaction moving TTP between cellular compartments, but as written both sides are identical with no compartment labels, making it stoichiometrically meaningless as a metabolic conversion.

rxn07584.other_comments: This reaction represents the adenylylation (activation) of lipoate by ATP to form lipoyl-AMP (lipoyl-adenylate) with release of pyrophosphate, catalyzed by lipoate-protein ligase (LplA) as the first step before transfer of the lipoyl moiety to apoproteins. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP (adenine + ribose + triphosphate) reacts with the carboxylate of lipoate, the AMP moiety becomes attached to lipoate carboxyl forming a mixed anhydride (lipoyl-AMP), and the beta-gamma phosphates leave as PPi. In vivo, this activation step is driven forward, and is rendered effectively irreversible by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, which pulls the reaction toward lipoyl-AMP formation.

rxn01124.other_comments: This is the NAD+-dependent oxidation of 2-keto-3-deoxygluconate (2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-gluconate) at the C5 hydroxyl position, yielding 2,5-diketo-3-deoxy-D-gluconate, NADH and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically and redox balanced: a secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, transferring two electrons and a hydride to NAD+ with release of one H+. Carbon and electron balance are consistent.

rxn01849.other_comments: This is the trans-2,3-epoxysuccinate hydrolase (EC 3.3.2.4) reaction, which catalyzes the hydrolytic ring-opening of the epoxide trans-2,3-epoxysuccinate by addition of water to form meso-tartrate. The stoichiometry is balanced: trans-2,3-epoxysuccinate (C4H2O5, as dianion) plus H2O yields tartrate (C4H4O6). Carbon (4=4), oxygen (5+1=6), and hydrogen balance when accounting for protonation states. As an epoxide hydrolysis, the reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding strongly toward the hydrolysis product (meso-tartrate).

rxn03211.other_comments: This reaction represents 1,2-dehydroreticuline reductase, which reduces the iminium intermediate 1,2-dehydroreticuline to (R)-reticuline using NADPH as the cofactor. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ provide the hydride and proton needed to reduce the C=N double bond, yielding NADP+ and (R)-reticuline. In vivo this step is part of the morphine/benzylisoquinoline alkaloid biosynthetic pathway, converting (S)-derived dehydroreticuline to (R)-reticuline, and proceeds in the reductive (forward, NADPH-consuming) direction.

rxn00434.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by N6-methyl-lysine oxidase (EC 1.5.3.4). It oxidatively demethylates N6-methyl-L-lysine using O2 and water, producing L-lysine, formaldehyde, and hydrogen peroxide. Stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl carbon and two hydrogens are released as formaldehyde; oxygen and water provide the oxidation, generating H2O2. Atom and charge balance check out.

rxn03742.other_comments: This is a monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction in which o-xylene is hydroxylated to 2-methylbenzyl alcohol. One atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (forming the alcohol) and the other is reduced to water, with NADH + H+ serving as the electron donor (oxidized to NAD+). Atom balance: o-xylene (C8H10) + O2 -> 2-methylbenzyl alcohol (C8H10O) accounts for one O; the second O combines with 2H (from NADH and H+) to form H2O. C, H, and O balance check out. As a monooxygenase reaction consuming O2 and NADH, it is physiologically irreversible (forward).

rxn11765.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphoribosyltransfer of mercaptopurine (6-mercaptopurine) to form 6-thioinosine 5'-monophosphate (thioinosine monophosphate, TIMP), catalyzed by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate) provides the ribose-phosphate moiety; the pyrophosphate (PPi) is released, along with a proton from the N9 nitrogen of the purine base. Stoichiometry is balanced: one purine base plus PRPP yields one nucleotide plus PPi and H+. This is the basis of mercaptopurine activation as a chemotherapeutic/immunosuppressive agent.

errors: The reaction has identical substrate and product (N-Acetyl-D-chondrosamine on both sides), making it a null/trivial reaction with no net chemical transformation
H+ appears on both sides without net change
No actual metabolic conversion occurs as written
rxn11396.other_comments: N-Acetyl-D-chondrosamine is N-acetyl-D-galactosamine. The reaction shows the same compound and proton on both sides, which represents a transport reaction (indicated by TRANS-RXN in the identifier) where the metabolite is moved across a membrane (e.g., proton-coupled symport/antiport). If intended as a transport step, the two compartments should be distinguished by compartment labels; as written without compartmentalization, it is a meaningless identity reaction.

rxn03133.other_comments: This is the prostaglandin delta13-reductase reaction (EC 1.3.1.48 region; part of 15-keto-PG metabolism). The enzyme name describes the oxidation of the saturated C13-C14 single bond product to introduce a delta13 double bond, but physiologically the relevant flux is reductive: NADPH/NADH-dependent saturation of the 13,14 double bond in 15-keto-prostaglandins (e.g., 13,14-dihydro-15-keto-PG formation). Stoichiometry is balanced: one hydride transfer (NAD+/NADH) plus one proton accounts for the loss/gain of the delta13 double bond (2H). The substrate with the delta13-ene (right side) is reduced to the saturated dioxoprostanoate (left side) in vivo, so the biological direction runs right-to-left relative to how this equation is written.

errors: The product is incorrect. Galactose oxidase (EC 1.1.3.9), the D-galactose:oxygen 6-oxidoreductase, oxidizes the C6 hydroxyl to an aldehyde, producing D-galacto-hexodialdose (galactose 6-aldehyde), not D-galactonate.
D-Galactonate would result from oxidation at C1 (the anomeric carbon), which is inconsistent with the named 6-oxidoreductase activity.
As written with H2O on the left, the equation is unbalanced; the correct galactose oxidase reaction is: D-galactose + O2 -> D-galacto-hexodialdose + H2O2 (no water consumed, no free proton released).
rxn00814.other_comments: This is intended to represent galactose oxidase (EC 1.1.3.9), which couples oxidation of a galactose hydroxyl with reduction of O2 to H2O2. The enzyme acts on the C6 primary alcohol, yielding an aldehyde product rather than a carboxylic acid (galactonate). Reactions producing H2O2 from O2 reduction are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn00306.other_comments: This is succinyl-CoA synthetase (GDP-forming, EC 6.2.1.4), part of the TCA cycle. The reaction couples GTP hydrolysis (GTP + H2O equivalent) to forming the thioester bond of succinyl-CoA, releasing GDP and inorganic phosphate. Stoichiometry is mass- and charge-balanced as written (succinate + CoA + GTP <=> succinyl-CoA + GDP + Pi). In vivo this enzyme is physiologically known to operate in the direction of succinate + GTP formation (substrate-level phosphorylation) in the TCA cycle, but it is a freely reversible enzyme thermodynamically.

rxn02181.other_comments: This is the 3-hydroxypropionyl-CoA dehydratase (hydro-lyase) reaction (EC 4.2.1.116), interconverting 3-hydroxypropionyl-CoA and acryloyl-CoA (acrylyl-CoA) with release/addition of water. Stoichiometry is balanced: 3-hydroxypropanoyl-CoA (C3 hydroxyacyl-CoA) loses water to form acryloyl-CoA (an alpha,beta-unsaturated acyl-CoA). Both carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and the CoA moiety balance. As a hydro-lyase, this is typically reversible, though in pathways such as the 3-hydroxypropionate cycle the physiological direction can favor hydration (acryloyl-CoA to 3-hydroxypropionyl-CoA) or dehydration depending on context.

rxn07747.other_comments: This is an N-demethylase reaction (cytochrome P450 type / CYP1A2-mediated). Paraxanthine (1,7-dimethylxanthine) undergoes N3-demethylation to yield 7-methylxanthine, releasing the methyl group as formaldehyde. The reaction consumes O2 and NADH (as electron donor via reductase), producing water and NAD+. Stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl carbon lost from paraxanthine is accounted for by formaldehyde, one O2 oxygen goes into formaldehyde and the other into water (with reducing equivalents from NADH). Atom and charge balance check out.

rxn04286.other_comments: This reaction represents the interconversion of dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose (dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-glucose) and dTDP-3-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose, an isomerization that shifts the keto group from C4 to C3. This type of transformation occurs in deoxysugar biosynthesis pathways and is typically catalyzed by isomerases/dehydratases. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a simple isomerization (same molecular formula on both sides, just repositioning of the oxo and hydroxyl groups). Such ketose isomerizations are thermodynamically near-equilibrium and generally reversible, though the in vivo direction depends on the metabolic context and downstream pull toward specific deoxysugar products.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: AMP appears on the substrate side but should be a product of the ligase/acylation step, while the meroacid-AMP intermediate is on the product side, which is inconsistent with the AMP being consumed

ATP/PPi not accounted for: a Fatty-Acid-Ligase-AMP (adenylating) reaction typically uses ATP to form an acyl-AMP intermediate releasing PPi; the given AMP usage as a reactant is mechanistically incorrect for forming an acyl-AMP product
Charge/H+ balance questionable: 2 H+ on the substrate side is not clearly justified by the indicated transformation
Transfer logic inconsistent: converting an ACP-bound meroacid to an AMP-bound meroacid should release ACP and form acyl-AMP, but the role of free AMP as a reactant contradicts this
rxn13465.other_comments: This appears to represent a FadD32-type fatty acyl-AMP ligase step in mycolic acid biosynthesis, generating a meroacyl-adenylate. As written, the cofactor accounting is wrong: an adenylation/ligase reaction should consume ATP and release AMP/PPi (or transfer the acyl group with concomitant release of ACP), not consume free AMP to make an acyl-AMP. The intended transformation is acyl-ACP -> acyl-AMP + ACP, which is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn04621.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase reaction transferring a 4-coumaroyl group from 4-coumaroyl-CoA to a hydroxyl on the terminal glucose of kaempferol 3-sophorotrioside, releasing free CoA. The reaction is balanced: the coumaroyl moiety is transferred from the thioester to form an ester bond on the sugar, and CoA-SH is released. Atom and charge balance are consistent for an acyl transfer. Acyl-CoA-dependent acyltransferases are thermodynamically driven by cleavage of the high-energy thioester bond, so the reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn13427.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction (butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA-transferase, EC 2.8.3.8) transferring the CoA moiety from acetyl-CoA to butyrate, yielding acetate and butyryl-CoA. Atoms and charges balance: the CoA group is simply swapped between the two carboxylic acids. The H+ on the substrate side is reasonable for charge balancing depending on the protonation states used (acetate -1, butyrate -1, acetyl-CoA and butyryl-CoA each -4 at physiological pH); transferase reactions like this are near-equilibrium. In organisms such as butyrate-producing gut bacteria the physiological direction is typically toward butyryl-CoA formation (consuming acetate), but thermodynamically the reaction is freely reversible.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: methyl transfer from SAM to a thiol (R-SH -> R-S-CH3) releases a proton, but here the substrate 'Thiopurine' and product naming is inconsistent; the methylation of a thiol sulfur typically does not generate an extra H+ unless the thiol is deprotonated first - the H+ stoichiometry depends on protonation state and may be incorrect

Nomenclature issue: the product should be an S-methylthiopurine (thioether), not a 'thiopurine S-methylether'; 'methylether' implies an O-methyl bond, whereas thiopurine methyltransferase forms an S-CH3 (thioether) bond
rxn02629.other_comments: This represents thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT), which transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to the sulfur of a thiopurine (e.g., 6-mercaptopurine), producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) and the S-methylated thiopurine. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are essentially irreversible in vivo in the methyl-donation direction.

rxn01119.other_comments: This is the first committed step of various O-antigen and exopolysaccharide biosynthesis pathways, catalyzed by a UDP-galactose:undecaprenyl-phosphate galactose-1-phosphate transferase (e.g., WbaP/RfbP). The enzyme transfers galactose-1-phosphate from UDP-galactose to undecaprenyl phosphate, releasing UMP and forming galactosyl-diphosphoundecaprenol (galactose-PP-undecaprenol). The reaction is correctly balanced: the phosphate of undecaprenyl-phosphate combines with the galactose-phosphate moiety to form the pyrophosphate linkage, and UMP is released. In vivo this proceeds in the synthesis direction toward the lipid carrier intermediate.

rxn02716.other_comments: This reaction represents protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase (POR, EC 1.3.1.33), which reduces protochlorophyllide a to chlorophyllide a. As written, the substrates are NADP+ and chlorophyllide producing NADPH + H+ + protochlorophyllide, which is the oxidation direction. The stoichiometry is balanced: the reduction of protochlorophyllide consumes NADPH + H+ and reduces the C17-C18 double bond of ring D. In vivo, the physiologically relevant direction is the reduction (protochlorophyllide -> chlorophyllide), which is the reverse of how this equation is written.

rxn00424.other_comments: This is the serine-glyoxylate aminotransferase reaction (EC 2.6.1.45). L-serine donates its amino group to glyoxylate, producing glycine and hydroxypyruvate. The reaction is balanced: serine (C3H7NO3) + glyoxylate (C2H2O3 / C2HO3-) yields glycine (C2H5NO2) + hydroxypyruvate (C3H4O4 / C3H3O4-). Atoms and charges balance. This enzyme is key in the photorespiratory glycolate pathway in plants, where it operates strongly toward glycine and hydroxypyruvate formation in vivo.

rxn00532.other_comments: This reaction is malonyl-CoA reductase / malonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (acylating). 3-Oxopropanoate is malonate semialdehyde. The written forward direction oxidizes malonate semialdehyde + CoA + NADP+ to malonyl-CoA + NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry and charge balance are correct (C, H, O, N, P, S balanced; the aldehyde carbon is oxidized to a thioester, releasing 2 electrons captured as NADPH). In vivo, this enzyme (e.g., in the 3-hydroxypropionate cycle of autotrophs) typically runs in the reductive direction, reducing malonyl-CoA to malonate semialdehyde, i.e., the reverse of the way written.

rxn06694.other_comments: This is the citrate lyase ligase (acetyltransferase activation) reaction, where ATP and acetate are used to acetylate the thiol form of citrate lyase, converting it to the active acetyl form. ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi (forming an acetyl-AMP intermediate), with release of H+. The reaction is balanced: the acetyl group from acetate is transferred to the enzyme's prosthetic group thiol, and the AMP/PPi release with H+ accounts for the ATP hydrolysis. Mass and charge appear balanced.

rxn00956.other_comments: This is a thiol-disulfide exchange/oxidoreductase reaction. Two molecules of reduced glutathione (GSH) reduce homocystine (the disulfide-linked dimer of homocysteine) to yield two homocysteine molecules and one oxidized glutathione (GSSG). The stoichiometry is balanced: 2 GSH contribute 2 thiol hydrogens, and the disulfide bond in homocystine is cleaved to form 2 free thiols, while a new disulfide forms in GSSG. Atom and charge balance check out with the 2 H+ included. Thiol-disulfide exchange reactions are generally reversible, with direction governed by the cellular GSH/GSSG redox ratio.

rxn10586.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction activating indoleacetate (indole-3-acetate) to indol-3-acetyl-CoA. ATP + CoA + carboxylic acid yields AMP + PPi + acyl-CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: the carboxylate (Indoleacetate, anionic) plus CoA-SH plus ATP gives the thioester, AMP, PPi, and one H+. Mass and charge balance are consistent with typical AMP-forming ligase reactions.

rxn00767.other_comments: This reaction represents diphosphate:glycerol 1-phosphotransferase (related to EC 2.7.1.79), transferring a phosphate from pyrophosphate (PPi) to glycerol, producing glycerol-3-phosphate (technically glycerol-1-phosphate by stereochemistry, but often labeled G3P) plus orthophosphate. Charge and mass balance check: PPi (PPi^3- typically, or as P2O7) donates one phosphoryl group; the released H+ balances the proton accounting. Stoichiometry is balanced with one PPi yielding one Pi and one phosphorylated glycerol. The hydrolysis of the pyrophosphate bond makes this thermodynamically favorable in the forward (synthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn03258.other_comments: This is a catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) type reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to the 2-hydroxyl of 2-hydroxyestrone, forming 2-methoxyestrone, with production of S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group is transferred from SAM to the catechol oxygen, releasing SAH, and the displaced phenolic proton accounts for the H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn03935.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase (NADP+-dependent) reaction oxidizing m-tolualdehyde to m-toluate. The reaction is: aldehyde + H2O + NADP+ -> carboxylic acid + NADPH + 2 H+. Atom and charge balance check: aldehyde (RCHO) + H2O provides the oxygen and the extra atoms; oxidation removes 2 H (2 electrons) transferred to NADP+ forming NADPH plus a released proton, with the second proton coming from carboxylic acid formation/water. The stoichiometry with 2 H+ on the product side is standard for this conversion and balances mass and charge.

errors: Mass imbalance: Cholate (C24H40O5, the 3alpha,7alpha,12alpha-trihydroxy-5beta-cholanoate) losing H2O would yield a dihydroxy-cholenoate that retains a double bond. The product 3alpha,12alpha-dihydroxy-5beta-chol-6-enoate (C24H38O4) is consistent with dehydration of cholate (loss of the 7-hydroxyl as water forming a 6-ene). Atoms balance: C24H40O5 = H2O (H2O) + C24H38O4. Stoichiometry appears balanced.
rxn02016.other_comments: This represents a dehydration/hydration at the C7 hydroxyl of cholate, forming a delta-6 double bond. Cholate (C24H40O5) loses water to give the 6-ene dihydroxy product (C24H38O4). The atoms balance (C24, H40, O5 on left equals H2O plus C24H38O4 on right), so the reaction is stoichiometrically correct.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: naphthalene 1,2-oxide (C10H8O) rearranges to 1-naphthol (C10H8O), so atoms are balanced, but if the substrate is drawn as the diol or hydrated form the balance would differ; as written with epoxide to naphthol the conversion is an intramolecular isomerization and is atom-balanced
rxn04816.other_comments: This represents the spontaneous (or epoxide hydrolase/non-enzymatic) NIH-shift rearrangement of naphthalene 1,2-oxide to 1-naphthol. The arene oxide opens and aromatizes to the phenol. This is essentially irreversible in vivo because aromatization to the stable phenol is highly thermodynamically favorable.

rxn04011.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by threo-3-hydroxy-L-aspartate ammonia-lyase (EC 4.3.1.16). It performs an alpha,beta-elimination of ammonia from L-threo-3-hydroxyaspartate, yielding oxaloacetate and ammonia. The atoms balance: L-threo-3-hydroxyaspartate (C4H7NO5) yields NH3 (NH3) plus oxaloacetate (C4H4O5). C: 4=4, H: 7=3+4, N: 1=1, O: 5=5. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. Note: the enzyme requires PLP as cofactor, which acts catalytically and is typically not shown in net stoichiometry.

rxn05721.other_comments: This is a transport reaction (proton symport) for adenosine 2'-monophosphate (2'-AMP). The same metabolites (H+ and AMP 2'-phosphate) appear on both sides because they represent extracellular and intracellular compartments, which is standard notation for transport reactions. Stoichiometry is balanced 1:1 for both proton and substrate, consistent with symport. As written without compartment labels it appears as a trivial identity, but the intended meaning is co-transport across a membrane. In vivo, proton symport directionality typically depends on the proton motive force, generally driving uptake into the cell, but transporters can be reversible.

rxn01642.other_comments: This is the imidazolonepropionase reaction (EC 3.5.2.7) in the histidine degradation pathway. It hydrolyzes 4-imidazolone-5-propanoate (the ring-opened, hydrolyzed product) to N-formimino-L-glutamate by hydrolytic ring opening. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O adds across the ring (C6H8N2O3 + H2O -> C6H10N2O4). As a hydrolase reaction in the catabolic histidine pathway, it proceeds physiologically toward N-formimino-L-glutamate.

errors: Oxygen atoms are unbalanced: reduction of sophorol to maackiain via NADPH should consume the oxygen, but the equation produces H2O on the product side while removing an oxygen function; as written the mass balance of O does not close correctly without an explicit accounting of the removed hydroxyl/keto oxygen
The enzyme name (maackiain:NADP+ 2'-oxidoreductase) implies oxidation of maackiain in the forward direction, which is inconsistent with the written direction (reduction of sophorol to maackiain)
rxn07562.other_comments: This is the pterocarpan biosynthesis step catalyzed by vestitone/pterocarpan synthase-type reductases. Sophorol (an isoflavanone with a 2'-hydroxyl) is reduced by NADPH and undergoes dehydration/ring closure to form the pterocarpan (+)-maackiain, releasing water. In vivo this proceeds toward maackiain formation. The reductive ring-closure consuming NADPH and releasing H2O is chemically reasonable, but the redox balance should be checked carefully.

rxn03952.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of 1,5-anhydro-D-glucitol (1,5-anhydroglucitol, a polyol) to 1,5-anhydro-D-fructose, with NADP+ being reduced to NADPH + H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of a secondary hydroxyl (CH-OH) to a ketone (C=O) removes two hydrogens (two electrons plus two protons), which are accounted for as hydride transfer to NADP+ (forming NADPH) plus one free H+. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge are balanced. As an NADP-dependent oxidoreductase acting on a CH-OH/C=O pair, the reaction is thermodynamically reversible; the direction in vivo depends on the NADP+/NADPH ratio and substrate concentrations.

rxn09064.other_comments: This is a phosphatidate phosphatase (lipin/PAP) reaction hydrolyzing a phosphatidic acid (1,2-ditetradec-7-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) into a diacylglycerol (1,2-ditetradec-7-enoyl-sn-glycerol) plus inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: water provides the OH and H for hydrolysis, releasing Pi and H+. The acyl chains (two C14:1, tetradec-7-enoyl) are conserved on both sides. Phosphate ester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the dephosphorylation direction.

rxn00856.other_comments: This is the putrescine aminotransferase (PuuE/YgjG-type) reaction where putrescine donates an amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and 4-aminobutanal (which spontaneously cyclizes to 1-pyrroline). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: 2-oxoglutarate (C5H6O5) + putrescine (C4H14N2 as protonated, or C4H12N2 neutral) yields L-glutamate (C5H9NO4) + 4-aminobutanal (C4H9NO). Carbon (5+4=9), nitrogen, and oxygen balance. In vivo this transamination proceeds in the catabolic direction toward GABA formation as part of putrescine degradation.

rxn02189.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by cinnamyl-alcohol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.195). Styrylcarbinol is a synonym for cinnamyl alcohol (cinnamic alcohol). The reaction reduces cinnamaldehyde to cinnamyl alcohol using NADPH, with NADP+ as the oxidized cofactor. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ + cinnamaldehyde (C9H8O) yields NADP+ + cinnamyl alcohol (C9H10O). The enzyme name describes the reverse (oxidation) direction (cinnamyl-alcohol:NADP+ oxidoreductase). Although named as an oxidoreductase, the enzyme is physiologically important in lignin biosynthesis where it favors reduction of the aldehyde to the alcohol; however the reaction is generally considered reversible in vitro.

rxn07664.other_comments: This reaction represents anthocyanidin 3,5-O-glucosyltransferase activity (EC 2.4.1.x). UDP-glucose serves as the glucosyl donor, transferring a glucose moiety to the 5-O position of pelargonidin 3-glucoside to form pelargonin (pelargonidin 3,5-diglucoside), releasing UDP. The reaction is atom-balanced: the glucosyl group transferred from UDP-glucose (which becomes UDP) is added to the acceptor anthocyanin, converting a monoglucoside to a diglucoside. In vivo, UDP-glucose-dependent glycosyltransferases strongly favor the glycosylation (forward) direction.

errors: Stereochemistry inconsistency: the enzyme name specifies '(R)-2-Hydroxyacid' but the substrate listed is '(S)-3-Sulfolactate'
Charge/proton balance should be verified: oxidation of the secondary alcohol to a ketone yields NADPH + H+, which appears balanced for the redox transfer
rxn03964.other_comments: This is an NADP-dependent oxidoreductase (sulfolactate dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.272-like) interconverting 3-sulfolactate and 3-sulfopyruvate. The hydroxyl at C2 is oxidized to a ketone with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Atom/redox balance is consistent (2H removed, one as hydride to NADP+ and one as H+). The main concern is the stereochemical descriptor mismatch between the enzyme name (R) and the substrate (S).

rxn08067.other_comments: This is an adenylate kinase reaction using ITP as the phosphate donor instead of ATP. The reaction transfers a phosphate group: AMP + ITP <=> ADP + IDP. Mass and charge balance: AMP (C10H12N5O7P, charge -2) + ITP (C10H11N4O14P3, charge -4) + H+ gives ADP (C10H12N5O10P2, charge -3) + IDP (C10H11N4O11P2, charge -3). Phosphate count: left side has 1 (AMP) + 3 (ITP) = 4 P; right side has 2 (ADP) + 2 (IDP) = 4 P, balanced. Charge: left -2 + -4 + 1 = -5; right -3 + -3 = -6. The H+ inclusion appears to make charge unbalanced; a proton-free formulation (AMP + ITP <=> ADP + IDP) would balance charges at -6 vs -6, so the explicit H+ may be erroneous depending on the protonation states used.

rxn02437.other_comments: This is an oxidoreductase reaction where GDP-6-deoxy-D-talose is oxidized at the C4 position to GDP-4-dehydro-D-rhamnose (also called GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose), with NAD+ reduced to NADH. GDP-6-deoxy-D-talose and GDP-6-deoxy-D-mannose (GDP-D-rhamnose) are C4 epimers, both deoxy sugars, and the 4-keto intermediate is shared. The reaction is balanced: atoms and charges (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus) are conserved with the transfer of a hydride to NAD+ and release of H+.

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: the oxidation of nitrite to nitrate adds an oxygen atom derived from water, not directly from O2; the balanced reaction should involve H2O. As written, oxygen and hydrogen atoms do not balance. A balanced version: 2 NO2- + O2 + ... Actually the canonical nitrite oxidoreductase reaction is NO2- + H2O -> NO3- + 2 H+ + 2 e-, with O2 as terminal electron acceptor. The given equation '2 NO2- + O2 -> 2 NO3- + 2 H+' has unbalanced oxygen: left O = 4(nitrite) + 2(O2) = 6 O plus N; right = 6 O (nitrate). Oxygen balances (6=6), but hydrogen does not balance: left has 0 H, right has 2 H. Charge: left 2(-1) = -2; right 2(+1) + 2(-1) = 0. Both H and charge are unbalanced.
rxn14184.other_comments: This represents nitrite oxidation to nitrate (nitrite oxidoreductase / NXR) using O2 as the ultimate oxidant. The biological oxygen atom incorporated into nitrate comes from water, so a proper equation needs H2O on the left and the H/charge accounting corrected. As written it is hydrogen- and charge-unbalanced. In vivo this reaction (nitrite to nitrate by nitrite-oxidizing bacteria) proceeds in the forward (oxidation) direction.

rxn14339.other_comments: This is the C-S lyase reaction in glucosinolate biosynthesis (SUR1/superroot1 type enzyme). The S-alkyl-thiohydroximate-cysteine conjugate is cleaved with water to release the thiohydroximic acid plus the cysteine moiety, which is deaminated to pyruvate and ammonia. Atom balance: substrate C9H18N2O3S3 + H2O yields NH3 + pyruvate (C3H4O3, with H+) + thiohydroximate (C6H13NO2S3). Carbon (9=3+6), nitrogen (2=1+1), and sulfur (3=3) balance; the cysteine portion is converted to pyruvate + ammonia consistent with a PLP-dependent C-S beta-lyase mechanism. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo due to elimination/deamination chemistry, proceeding in the lyase direction.

rxn11724.other_comments: This is a thioester hydrolysis reaction where an acyl-CoA thioesterase cleaves docosapentaenoyl-CoA (DPA-CoA, 22:5 omega-3) into free docosapentaenoic acid and CoA. The reaction consumes water and releases a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: the thioester bond hydrolysis transfers the acyl group from CoA to a hydroxyl, releasing free CoA-SH and the carboxylic acid, with H+ released consistent with the carboxylate/proton balance.

errors: The reaction as written is missing a hydrogen balance; oxidative decarboxylation coupled to NAD reduction typically releases H+ (e.g., NAD+ + substrate -> NADH + CO2 + product + H+).
Without explicit molecular formulas for 'zymosterol intermediate 1' and 'zymosterol intermediate 2', full atom balance (C, H, O) cannot be verified.

This step (C-3 sterol dehydrogenase/decarboxylase, ERG26/NSDHL) physiologically uses NAD+ as the cofactor and produces a 3-keto sterol; pairing the dehydrogenation with CO2 release in a single equation conflates the decarboxylase and dehydrogenase activities.
rxn09625.other_comments: This represents the C4-decarboxylation/C3-dehydrogenation step in sterol biosynthesis (zymosterol intermediate), catalyzed by the NAD-dependent C-3 sterol dehydrogenase/C-4 decarboxylase. The oxidative decarboxylation makes it effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (NADH + CO2 producing) direction.

rxn03669.other_comments: This is a hydrolytic dehalogenation reaction where cis-1,3-dichloropropene reacts with water to release chloride, a proton, and cis-3-chloro-2-propene-1-ol (cis-3-chloroallyl alcohol). The atoms balance: cis-1,3-dichloropropene (C3H4Cl2) + H2O yields C3H5ClO + H+ + Cl-. Carbon (3=3), chlorine (2=1+1), hydrogen (4+2=5+1), and oxygen (1=1) all balance, and the net charge is balanced (0 = +1 -1 + 0).

rxn11791.other_comments: This is the UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) reaction transferring a glucuronosyl group from UDP-glucuronate (UDP-glucuronic acid) to morphine, forming morphine-6-glucuronide and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: the glucuronate moiety is transferred to morphine's hydroxyl group, leaving UDP as the product. Glucuronidation is a key phase II conjugation reaction (catalyzed by UGT2B7 for morphine). In vivo, glucuronidation reactions are essentially irreversible and proceed in the forward (conjugation) direction.

errors: Oxygen mass imbalance: the product Quinoline-4,8-diol does not account for all oxygen atoms; the reaction as written is not balanced. The aldehyde product (4,8-dihydroxyquinoline-aldehyde) or the corresponding aldehyde from oxidative deamination is missing, and a water molecule should typically be a substrate in amine oxidase deamination reactions (R-CH2-NH2 + O2 + H2O -> R-CHO + NH3 + H2O2). The stated product Quinoline-4,8-diol implies cyclization and does not retain the carbon/oxygen balance of the substrate side.
rxn03358.other_comments: This is an amine oxidase (flavin-containing) reaction acting on 3-hydroxykynurenamine, using molecular oxygen to oxidatively deaminate the primary amine, releasing ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. Such flavin-dependent oxidative deaminations are essentially irreversible in vivo (driven by O2 consumption and H2O2 release). However, the written equation appears unbalanced: standard oxidative deamination requires water as a co-substrate and produces an aldehyde intermediate; the listed Quinoline-4,8-diol product likely results from spontaneous cyclization but the stoichiometry of C/H/O should be re-checked.

errors: Stoichiometric/identity mismatch: enol-oxaloacetate (C4H4O5) losing one water (H2O) yields C4H2O4, but the named product 2-butynedioic acid (acetylenedicarboxylic acid, C4H2O4) would require formation of a C-C triple bond, which is not chemically plausible from enol-oxaloacetate dehydration

The expected dehydration product of enol-oxaloacetate would be oxaloacetate-derived species or an unsaturated acid, not acetylenedicarboxylate; the chemistry implied (formation of an alkyne) is highly unlikely under physiological conditions
Product naming likely incorrect: dehydration of enol-oxaloacetate would more plausibly give a substituted maleate/fumarate-type compound (oxaloacetate enol -> oxaloacetate), not a butynedioic acid
rxn02917.other_comments: The reaction proposes a hydro-lyase removing water from enol-oxaloacetate to form 2-butynedioic acid (acetylenedicarboxylic acid). While atom counts (C4H4O5 -> H2O + C4H2O4) balance superficially, the formation of a carbon-carbon triple bond by simple dehydration is not biochemically reasonable, suggesting the product is misidentified.

rxn01159.other_comments: This is the gamma-glutamylmethylamide synthetase (GMA synthetase) reaction, catalyzing the ATP-dependent ligation of L-glutamate and methylamine (methanamine) to form N5-methyl-L-glutamine (gamma-glutamylmethylamide). The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the energy, hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi, with release of one proton, while the amine condenses with the gamma-carboxyl of glutamate. Mass and charge are balanced. Like other ATP-dependent ligases (glutamine synthetase family), the ATP hydrolysis drives the reaction strongly forward in vivo.

rxn04855.other_comments: This reaction represents the conversion of arachidonate and molecular oxygen to 9(S)-HPETE (9(S)-hydroperoxy-eicosatetraenoic acid), catalyzed by a lipoxygenase (9-LOX) or via cyclooxygenase activity. Stoichiometrically, arachidonate (C20H32O2) plus O2 yields 9(S)-HPETE (C20H32O4), which is balanced: the two oxygen atoms from O2 are incorporated as a hydroperoxy group. This is an oxygenation/dioxygenase reaction that proceeds in the forward direction in vivo, being thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible.

errors: Carbon/hydrogen imbalance: a saturated iso-C17 acyl chain would be produced from isovaleryl-CoA (5 carbons) plus 6 malonyl-CoA elongation cycles (each adding 2 carbons = 12 carbons), giving 17 carbons, but a single unsaturated (C17:1) product requires only 11 NADPH if one double bond is left unreduced; with 6 elongation cycles requiring 2 NADPH each (12 total) for full saturation, 11 NADPH is consistent with one unsaturation, so this part may be acceptable, but the overall atom balance should be verified

Stoichiometric check needed: 6 malonyl-CoA decarboxylation yields 6 CO2 (correct), and 7 CoA released (6 from malonyl-CoA + 1 from isovaleryl-CoA, correct), and 5 H2O (one per condensation/dehydration cycle, but 6 cycles would typically give 6 H2O - possible water imbalance)
Proton (H+) balance of 16 H+ should be recomputed against the NADPH/NADP and dehydration steps; likely imbalanced
rxn10038.other_comments: This is a lumped fatty acid synthesis reaction producing an iso-branched C17:1 fatty acid from isovaleryl-CoA primer and 6 malonyl-CoA extender units via repeated condensation/reduction/dehydration cycles. The CoA (7) and CO2 (6) counts are internally consistent, but the H2O count (5 vs expected ~6) and H+/NADPH balance appear off, suggesting minor stoichiometric imbalance.

rxn01045.other_comments: This is the valine dehydrogenase (NAD+) reaction: oxidative deamination of L-valine to 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate (2-oxoisovalerate). The reaction is balanced - C5H11NO2 (valine) + H2O loses 2H (to NAD+ forming NADH + H+) and releases NH3, yielding the 2-oxo acid C5H8O3. Atoms and charges balance. While the enzyme catalyzes a reversible reaction, in vivo it is typically directed toward oxidative deamination (valine catabolism).

rxn03283.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP27A1) sterol 26-hydroxylase monooxygenase reaction in the classic bile acid biosynthesis pathway. One atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate to form the 26-hydroxyl group, the other is reduced to water, with NADPH as the electron donor. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + diol yields H2O + NADP+ + triol, conserving mass and charge.

errors: The reaction as written is not stoichiometrically/charge balanced and the metabolite 'ALCTT' is ambiguous; the named enzyme (pyruvate:pyruvate acetaldehydetransferase, decarboxylating) corresponds to acetolactate synthase, which converts 2 pyruvate to 2-acetolactate + CO2. If ALCTT is 2-acetolactate, the correct reaction is 2 Pyruvate + H+ -> 2-acetolactate + CO2, so the direction written here (toward 2 pyruvate) is reversed.
Proton (H+) balance does not match a simple decarboxylation as written; for acetolactate synthase the H+ should be a substrate together with 2 pyruvate, not a product alongside pyruvate.
rxn00003.other_comments: The enzyme name indicates acetolactate synthase (acetohydroxyacid synthase), which condenses two pyruvate molecules with loss of CO2 to form 2-acetolactate. I interpret ALCTT as 2-acetolactate. In vivo this reaction proceeds toward acetolactate + CO2 (i.e., consuming 2 pyruvate), which is the reverse of how it is written here.

errors: The product 2-Oxopropanal (methylglyoxal) is incorrect; oxidation of L-lactaldehyde (an aldehyde) at the carbonyl carbon yields a carboxylic acid, namely L-lactate (L-lactic acid), not methylglyoxal. Methylglyoxal would require oxidation at the C2 hydroxyl, which is inconsistent with an aldehyde:oxidoreductase forming an acid.

Charge/mass imbalance: as written with the wrong product, the equation does not balance properly. The proper oxidation NADP+ + lactaldehyde + H2O -> NADPH + 2 H+ + lactate requires a water molecule, which is missing.
NADP should be written as NADP+ to reflect the correct redox state.
rxn01618.other_comments: The reaction is named as an (S)-lactaldehyde:NADP+ oxidoreductase, implying oxidation of lactaldehyde to lactate coupled to NADP+ reduction. The listed product 2-oxopropanal (methylglyoxal) does not match this enzymatic chemistry; the expected product is L-lactate, and water is needed as a co-substrate. Aldehyde dehydrogenases (NADP-dependent) typically operate in the oxidative direction in vivo, though such oxidoreductases can be reversible depending on cofactor ratios.

rxn04740.other_comments: This is a cis-dihydrodiol dehydrogenase reaction in which a cis-1,2-dihydrodiol of a hydroxymethyl-naphthalene is oxidized (with rearomatization) to the corresponding 1,2-dihydroxynaphthalene (catechol-type diol), with NAD+ reduced to NADH + H+. The atoms balance: the substrate loses 2 H (one from each carbinol C with rearomatization), which are transferred as hydride to NAD+ plus a released proton. This type of dihydrodiol dehydrogenase step in PAH degradation pathways operates physiologically in the oxidative (forward) direction toward the dihydroxylated aromatic.

rxn08044.other_comments: This is the MurNAc-6-phosphate etherase (MurQ) reaction, which cleaves the lactyl ether of N-acetylmuramate 6-phosphate to yield GlcNAc 6-phosphate and (R)-lactate. The reaction is a hydro-lyase (etherase) hydrolyzing the ether bond. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + MurNAc-6-P yields D-lactate + GlcNAc-6-P. In vivo this operates in the catabolic direction (degradation of cell wall amino sugars), strongly favoring lactate release.

rxn10510.other_comments: This reaction represents a step in coenzyme F430 biosynthesis, specifically a NADH-dependent reduction step converting coenzyme F430 precursor 2 to precursor 3. F430 is the nickel-containing tetrapyrrole cofactor of methyl-coenzyme M reductase in methanogenic archaea. The stoichiometry is balanced as written for a typical NADH-dependent reduction: NADH + H+ donate a hydride and proton (two reducing equivalents) to reduce the substrate, regenerating NAD+. The reaction is part of the late steps of F430 maturation where the Ni-sirohydrochlorin a,c-diamide framework is reduced. Reduction reactions driven by NADH are typically thermodynamically favorable in the forward (reductive) direction in vivo.

rxn04645.other_comments: This is a decarboxylation reaction. 2-Aminomalonate semialdehyde (aminomalonate semialdehyde) loses a carboxyl group as CO2 to form aminoacetaldehyde. Mass balance: 2-aminomalonate semialdehyde is OHC-CH(NH2)-COOH (C3H5NO3). Adding H+ and decarboxylating: product aminoacetaldehyde is OHC-CH2-NH2 (C2H5NO) plus CO2 (CO2). Left: C3H6NO3+ (with H+). Right: CO2 (CH0O2 wait CO2) + C2H5NO = C3H5NO3, plus the H+ adds one H giving C3H6NO3. Atoms balance (C3, H6, N1, O3) and charge balances. Decarboxylations are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn01610.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADH-dependent reduction of (E)-cinnamate (trans-cinnamate, a phenylpropenoate with a C2-C3 double bond) to phenylpropanoate (3-phenylpropanoate, hydrocinnamate), reducing the alpha,beta double bond. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + H+ provide 2 reducing equivalents (2H) to saturate the C=C bond, yielding NAD+ and the saturated product. Carbon (C9), oxygen, and charge all balance. The enzyme name (oxidoreductase, delta2) is consistent. Such enzymatic enoate reductions using NADH are thermodynamically favorable and typically proceed in the reduction direction in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: XAN (xanthine) to theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) requires addition of 2 methyl groups, which consumes 2 SAM and produces 2 SAH; however the proton balance is questionable. Each N-methylation transfers a methyl and releases one H+, so 2 H+ is consistent with 2 methylations. The main issue is substrate identity: theophylline is 1,3-dimethylxanthine, requiring methylation at N1 and N3 of xanthine, so 2 SAM is correct.

Atom balance appears approximately correct if XAN = xanthine and 2 methyl groups are added; the reaction is plausibly balanced for C, H, N when accounting for the two methyl transfers and two H+ released.
rxn12060.other_comments: This represents N-methylation of xanthine to theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) using two SAM-dependent methyltransferase steps lumped into one reaction. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are strongly forward-driven (reverse is thermodynamically unfavorable). Note KEGG R08410 actually concerns 7-methylxanthine/theobromine pathways; the lumped 2-SAM step is unusual.

rxn08954.other_comments: This is a KDO transferase reaction transferring a 3-deoxy-D-manno-octulosonic acid (KDO) moiety from the activated sugar donor CMP-KDO onto the LPS core acceptor (phospho-heptosyl-phospho-heptosyl-heptosyl-kdo2-lipidA), releasing CMP and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the KDO group is transferred to the acceptor, CMP is released, and the glycosidic bond formation releases an H+. Glycosyltransferases using CMP-activated sugars (CMP-KDO) are thermodynamically driven by hydrolysis of the high-energy CMP-glycoside bond, making the reaction essentially irreversible in vivo (forward direction toward LPS biosynthesis).

rxn02616.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.105) transferring a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the 2'' position of the C-glucosyl moiety of isovitexin, producing isovitexin 2''-O-beta-D-glucoside and UDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose, releasing UDP, and the acceptor gains one glucosyl group. Atoms balance correctly assuming standard structures.

errors: Reaction is not mass-balanced as written; the conversion of cobalt-precorrin 8 (also called cobalt-precorrin-8X / hydrogenobyrinate-type intermediate) to cobyrinate is a 1,3-intramolecular methyl migration that does not consume a free H+; the listed substrate/product pairing and the H+ stoichiometry do not yield a balanced equation

Naming/identity issue: 'Cobalt-precorrin 8' to 'cobyrinate' is catalyzed by cobyrinate a,c-diamide synthase precursor enzyme CbiC (precorrin-8X methylmutase), and the true product of the mutase step is cobyrinic acid / cobyrinate, but the H+ does not balance the rearrangement
rxn04052.other_comments: This is the precorrin-8X methylmutase step (KEGG R05814) in the anaerobic (early cobalt insertion) vitamin B12 biosynthetic pathway, converting cobalt-precorrin-8 to cobyrinate via a 1,3 methyl shift. The reaction is an isomerization (methyl migration) and should be atom/charge balanced; a lone H+ on the left typically indicates an incomplete or improperly balanced equation. [directionality_note] The methylmutase (CbiC) reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward cobyrinate in the anaerobic cobalamin biosynthesis pathway

rxn10981.other_comments: This reaction couples the oxidation of FADH2 to FAD with the reduction of menaquinone-6 (oxidized form) to menaquinol-6 (reduced form). The reaction is balanced: FADH2 donates 2 electrons and 2 protons, reducing menaquinone to menaquinol, while FADH2 is oxidized to FAD. Atoms and charges balance (2 H and 2 e- transferred). In vivo, this is thermodynamically favorable because the redox potential of the menaquinone/menaquinol couple (~ -74 mV) is higher than that of the FAD/FADH2 couple (~ -220 mV for free flavin), so FADH2-bound flavoenzymes (e.g., succinate dehydrogenase-like complexes) reduce menaquinone, driving the reaction in the forward direction as written.

rxn02438.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of GDP-D-rhamnose (GDP-6-deoxy-D-mannose) at the C4 position by NAD+, producing GDP-4-dehydro-D-rhamnose (4-keto sugar), NADH, and H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: one hydride and one proton are removed from the substrate, consistent with NAD+/NADH redox coupling. The enzyme name indicates a 4-oxidoreductase acting on GDP-6-deoxy-D-mannose. In vivo, such NAD-dependent 4,6-dehydratase/oxidoreductase steps are often part of nucleotide-sugar biosynthesis pathways and can operate reversibly, though physiological flux often favors the dehydro (4-keto) intermediate during deoxysugar biosynthesis.

rxn00677.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction (EC 2.8.3.1) transferring the CoA moiety from acetyl-CoA to propionate, yielding acetate and propionyl-CoA. The reaction is balanced: C23H38N7O17P3S (acetyl-CoA) + C3H6O2 (propionate, as propanoate) on the left maps to C2H4O2 (acetate) + C24H40N7O17P3S (propionyl-CoA) on the right. Atoms and charges balance. CoA-transferases are thermodynamically near-equilibrium and operate reversibly depending on relative concentrations of the acyl donor/acceptor pair.

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: as written the reaction does not balance. Nitroethane (C2H5NO2) has formula CH3CH2NO2; combining acetaldehyde (C2H4O) + nitrite (NO2-) gives C2H4NO3, which does not match nitroethane. The correct enzymatic reaction (nitroethane oxidase / EC 1.7.3.1) is: nitroethane + O2 + H2O -> acetaldehyde + nitrite + H2O2. The reaction as written is the reverse and also the atom/charge balance should be checked: nitroethane + O2 + H2O = C2H5NO2 + O2 + H2O (C2H7NO4) vs acetaldehyde + nitrite + H2O2 = C2H4O + NO2 + H2O2 (C2H7NO5) - oxygen mismatch indicates imbalance.
Oxygen atom imbalance between the two sides.
rxn00573.other_comments: This is nitroethane oxidase (EC 1.7.3.1). The physiological direction is nitroethane + O2 + H2O -> acetaldehyde + nitrite + H2O2, so as written (right-to-left for the named enzyme) it is reversed. The reaction also appears stoichiometrically unbalanced in oxygen.

rxn07622.other_comments: This reaction (KEGG R07831) is catalyzed by dihydrophloroglucinol hydrolase (EC 3.7.1.-), a ring-opening hydrolytic step in phloroglucinol degradation. Dihydrophloroglucinol (a cyclohexane-1,3-dione/diol) is hydrolytically cleaved by addition of one water to yield the linear product 3-hydroxy-5-oxohexanoate. The atom balance is consistent: dihydrophloroglucinol (C6H10O3) + H2O (H2O) gives 3-hydroxy-5-oxohexanoate (C6H10O4 / C6H9O4-), accounting for the added water across the cleaved C-C/ring bond. The reaction is mass-balanced.

rxn11798.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (likely CYP2D6) catalyzed aromatic hydroxylation of N-desmethyltamoxifen to form endoxifen. A monooxygenase reaction: one atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (hydroxylation) and the other is reduced to water using NADPH as the electron donor. Stoichiometry balances: NADPH + O2 + H+ + substrate -> H2O + NADP+ + hydroxylated product. In vivo this proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (oxidation) direction.

rxn04323.other_comments: This is the cytochrome P450 PikC-catalyzed hydroxylation of the 12-membered macrolactone YC-17 to neomethymycin in the pikromycin/methymycin biosynthetic pathway of Streptomyces venezuelae. rxn05480.other_comments: This is intended to be a symport reaction co-transporting a proton with 3'-UMP (3'-uridine monophosphate) across the membrane. Stoichiometry of mass (1 H+, 1 substrate) is balanced, but the missing compartment annotations make the written reaction a no-op. Proton symport is typically driven by the proton motive force, often favoring uptake (import) in vivo.

rxn07111.other_comments: This reaction is an acyltransferase reaction where the p-coumaroyl group from 4-coumaroyl-CoA is transferred to the 6-O position of the glucose moiety of cyanidin 3-O-glucoside, producing cyanidin 3-O-(6-O-p-coumaroyl)glucoside and releasing free CoA. The atoms balance: the acyl group (p-coumaroyl) is transferred from CoA thioester to the hydroxyl group of the glucoside, forming an ester bond. Stoichiometry is 1:1:1:1 and appears balanced. This is a typical anthocyanin acyltransferase (BAHD family) reaction, which proceeds in the biosynthetic direction toward the acylated anthocyanin in vivo due to the thermodynamically favorable cleavage of the CoA thioester bond.

rxn03184.other_comments: This is a sialyltransferase reaction (ST8Sia family) transferring N-acetylneuraminate from CMP-N-acetylneuraminate (CMP-Neu5Ac) to the ganglioside GD1a, producing GT1a, with release of CMP and a proton. Adding one Neu5Ac (alpha-2,8 linkage) to GD1a yields GT1a, which is consistent. The stoichiometry is balanced: the sialyl group is transferred from CMP-Neu5Ac to the acceptor, leaving CMP and a released H+. Glycosyltransferases using CMP-sugar nucleotide donors are essentially irreversible in vivo, driven by donor hydrolysis/transfer.

rxn02819.other_comments: This is the SAM-dependent N-methyltransferase reaction in the vindoline biosynthesis pathway (Catharanthus roseus). SAM donates a methyl group to the indole nitrogen of 16-methoxy-2,3-dihydro-3-hydroxytabersonine, producing deacetoxyvindoline plus S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group transferred from SAM to substrate, releasing SAH and H+. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the methylation direction.

NADP should be written as NADP+ for charge clarity
rxn14063.other_comments: This is annotated as an NADP-dependent oxidoreductase. The enzyme name corresponds to 2-dehydro-L-idonate:NADP+ 5-oxidoreductase (EC 1.1.1.346), which interconverts 2-dehydro-L-idonate and 2,5-diketo-D-gluconate. As written the redox half (NADP+ -> NADPH + H+) is consistent with an oxidation, but the carbon substrate/product pairing is questionable.

rxn05640.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-symport transport of O-phospho-L-serine, where one proton is co-transported with phosphoserine across the membrane.
