rxn12590.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport of trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline across a membrane. As written it is mass-balanced trivially (identical species on both sides) but lacks the essential compartment notation (e.g., H+[e] + hyp[e] <=> H+[c] + hyp[c]) needed to represent transport. Symport directionality is typically driven by the proton motive force, favoring uptake (extracellular to cytoplasm) in vivo.

rxn04911.other_comments: This reaction represents soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH/EPHX2) acting on 14,15-epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (14,15-EET). The epoxide ring is hydrolyzed by addition of water to yield the corresponding vicinal diol, 14,15-dihydroxyeicosatrienoic acid (14,15-DHET). The stoichiometry is balanced: the epoxide oxygen and the two atoms from water are incorporated into the diol product (one C-O-C epoxide + H2O gives two C-OH groups). In vivo this hydrolysis is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the forward direction toward the diol.

rxn08080.other_comments: This is a hydrolysis reaction catalyzed by an N-acetylglucosaminidase (related to lytic transglycosylase products). The substrate is the disaccharide GlcNAc-(beta-1,4)-1,6-anhydro-N-acetylmuramic acid (anhydro-disaccharide). Water cleaves the beta-1,4 glycosidic bond releasing free N-acetyl-D-glucosamine and 1,6-anhydro-N-acetylmuramate. Stoichiometry balances: one disaccharide plus one water yields the two monosaccharide products. Naming in the input is awkward but the chemistry is a standard glycoside hydrolysis.

rxn06295.other_comments: This is a hydrolysis reaction where monoterpenyl diphosphate is cleaved by water to release inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi) and a monoterpenol, with a proton released. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: water provides the OH for the alcohol and H for the proton/PPi. Phosphatase/pyrophosphohydrolase reactions of this type are thermodynamically favorable due to phosphoanhydride bond hydrolysis and proceed essentially irreversibly toward hydrolysis in vivo.

rxn02758.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase (CAD, EC 1.1.1.195), reducing sinapaldehyde to sinapyl alcohol using NADPH as the electron donor. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ + sinapaldehyde yields NADP+ + sinapyl alcohol. Sinapyl alcohol is a key monolignol precursor in lignin biosynthesis. While the enzyme is biochemically reversible, in vivo the reaction proceeds toward alcohol formation to feed the lignin pathway.

rxn11210.other_comments: This is a branched-chain aminotransferase-type reaction. 3MOP is (S)-3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate), the keto-acid precursor of L-Isoleucine. The amino group from L-Phenylalanine is transferred to 3MOP, yielding Phenylpyruvate (the keto acid of phenylalanine) and L-Isoleucine. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one amino acid + one 2-oxo acid yield the corresponding 2-oxo acid + amino acid, conserving atoms and the single amino group transferred. Aminotransferase reactions are typically freely reversible due to near-equilibrium thermodynamics (small free energy change).

rxn03626.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase oxidizing the 3-hydroxyl of (1S,3R,4S)-3,4-dihydroxycyclohexane-1-carboxylate to the corresponding 3-oxo product, yielding (1S,4S)-4-hydroxy-3-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylate plus NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced: one secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, consistent with the transfer of a hydride to NAD+ and release of a proton. Atoms and charges balance. Alcohol/aldehyde-ketone dehydrogenases coupled to NAD+/NADH are generally reversible, with direction set by cofactor and substrate concentrations in vivo.

rxn01965.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction. Cholesterol is hydroxylated at the C22 position to form 22-hydroxycholesterol, consuming molecular oxygen and NADPH. One oxygen atom is incorporated into the substrate (the new hydroxyl group) and the other is reduced to water. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + Cholesterol -> H2O + NADP+ + 22-hydroxycholesterol. The naming convention (22beta) reflects the stereochemistry of the product; the side-chain hydroxylation by CYP11A1 normally yields 22R-hydroxycholesterol, but the stoichiometry holds regardless. This monooxygenase reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of hydroxylation.

rxn03555.other_comments: This is the CmtB reaction in the p-cumate degradation pathway. A cis-dihydrodiol dehydrogenase oxidizes cis-2,3-dihydroxy-2,3-dihydro-p-cumate to 2,3-dihydroxy-p-cumate (the catechol), reducing NAD+ to NADH and releasing one proton. The reaction is balanced: removal of two hydrogens (2H = 2e- + 2H+) where the hydride goes to NAD+ forming NADH and one H+ is released. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn01479.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by ethanolamine-phosphate cytidylyltransferase (EC 2.7.7.14, PCYT2), the rate-limiting step in the CDP-ethanolamine (Kennedy) pathway. CTP reacts with phosphoethanolamine to form CDP-ethanolamine and pyrophosphate. The reaction is balanced: CTP (cytidine triphosphate) transfers a CMP moiety to phosphoethanolamine, releasing PPi. Atoms and charges balance correctly. In vivo, the subsequent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate by inorganic pyrophosphatase drives the reaction strongly toward CDP-ethanolamine synthesis.

rxn03947.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of N-acetylpuromycin, where an amide/ester acetyl group is cleaved by water to yield acetate and puromycin. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: H2O + N-acetylpuromycin yields acetate + puromycin (the acetyl group plus the water's components are accounted for). Hydrolysis of an acetylated substrate is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn00712.other_comments: This reaction represents a uridine 5'-phosphotransferase (uridine kinase-type) activity where UTP donates a phosphate to uridine, yielding UMP and UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: phosphate transfer from UTP (gamma-phosphate) to uridine produces UMP, leaving UDP. Mass and charge balance check out, with the H+ accounting for the deprotonation accompanying phosphoryl transfer to the 5'-hydroxyl. Note that uridine phosphorylation is more commonly catalyzed by uridine kinase using ATP as the donor (yielding UMP + ADP); UTP as donor is less typical but stoichiometrically valid.

rxn02307.other_comments: This is a 16alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (oxidoreductase, EC 1.1.1.x) reaction. It oxidizes a 16alpha-hydroxysteroid to a 16-oxosteroid, transferring a hydride to NAD+ to form NADH and releasing a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one hydroxyl group is oxidized to a ketone (loss of 2 H, as one hydride to NAD+ giving NADH and one H+). Charge and atom balance are consistent.

errors: HPA is an ambiguous abbreviation; in this context it should represent heptanoic acid (the carboxylic acid product of heptanal oxidation), but HPA commonly denotes hydroxyphenylacetate or 3-hydroxypropionate. The product name/ID should be clarified.
Stoichiometry is otherwise balanced: aldehyde + H2O + NAD+ -> carboxylic acid + NADH + 2 H+
rxn09974.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing heptanal to heptanoic acid (HPA) using NAD+ as electron acceptor, producing NADH. The reaction consumes water and NAD+ and releases two protons (one from the oxidation of the aldehyde hydrate, one accompanying hydride transfer to NADH). Charge and mass balance check out if HPA = heptanoate/heptanoic acid. Aldehyde dehydrogenases strongly favor the oxidative (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The hydrogen (H+) stoichiometry is incorrect; the GMP synthetase reaction (with NH3 as the amide donor) should produce approximately 2 H+, not 3 H+, to balance charge. Specifically: ATP(4-) + NH3 + XMP(2-) -> AMP(2-) + PPi(3-) + GMP(2-) + 2 H+ balances charge (left: -6, right: -7 + 2 = -5; recheck). Proper balancing yields 2 H+ rather than 3 H+.
rxn00916.other_comments: This is the GMP synthetase reaction (EC 6.3.5.2 / 6.3.4.1 ammonia-dependent variant), converting XMP to GMP using ATP and ammonia, producing AMP and PPi. The reaction is metabolically driven forward by subsequent PPi hydrolysis. Atom balance is essentially correct (N, P, C); the main concern is the proton/charge balance which appears off by one (3 H+ vs expected 2 H+).

rxn02477.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 3-hydroxy-2-methylpyridine-4,5-dicarboxylate 4-decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.51), part of the vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) degradation pathway in bacteria such as Mesorhizobium loti. The substrate is decarboxylated at the 4-position, consuming a proton and releasing CO2 to yield 3-hydroxy-2-methylpyridine-5-carboxylate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: substrate (C9H7NO5, charge -2 in the dicarboxylate form) plus H+ gives CO2 plus product (C8H7NO3, charge -1). Carbon (9 = 8+1), oxygen (5 = 2+3), nitrogen (1), and hydrogen all balance.

rxn02750.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydration of citraconate (2-methylmaleate / methylmaleate, a four-carbon dicarboxylic acid with a methyl branch) to form D-threo-3-methylmalate (3-methylmalate). The atoms balance: citraconate (C5H6O4 in protonated form, or C5H4O4 2- as dianion) plus H2O yields 3-methylmalate (C5H8O5 protonated, or C5H6O5 2- as dianion). This is a fumarase-type / 2-methylmalate dehydratase (citraconase) reaction, part of the nicotinate/methylaspartate or itaconate-related metabolism. Hydratase reactions of this type are typically reversible and the in vivo direction depends on metabolic context.

As written it is not a valid single enzymatic step: luteolin (flavone, lacks 3-OH) cannot be directly converted to myricetin (a 3-hydroxyflavone/flavonol with an additional B-ring OH). rxn05681.other_comments: This represents a proton symport transport reaction for 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-gluconate (2-keto-3-deoxygluconate, KDG). Product O: serine(3)+mercaptoheptanoate(2)=5. No water (H2O) is included; the net replacement of a ketone oxygen with sulfur should release H2O, which is missing from the equation, leaving the reaction unbalanced for O and H.
rxn10424.other_comments: The reaction couples a reductive sulfurtransfer from L-cysteine to a 7-oxo fatty acid, generating L-serine and a thiol-bearing fatty acid (likely a step in a thiol-cofactor/biotin-like biosynthetic context). The overall chemistry (cysteine as sulfur donor, NADH as reductant) is plausible conceptually, but as written it is unbalanced: a missing water and inconsistent H balance for the carbonyl-to-thiol reduction.

rxn08615.other_comments: This is glycogen synthase using ADP-glucose as the glucosyl donor (typical of bacteria, plants, and some archaea, rather than the UDP-glucose-dependent eukaryotic version). The reaction transfers a glucose unit from ADP-glucose to a growing glucan chain: ADP-glucose + glycogen(n-1 residues) -> ADP + glycogen(n residues). The stoichiometry is balanced: glucose is transferred from ADP-glucose, releasing ADP, and the polysaccharide is extended by one glucose unit. In vivo this is the biosynthetic glycogen/starch synthesis step and proceeds in the synthesis direction, driven by the high-energy ADP-glucose donor.

The reaction omits required reducing equivalents and molecular oxygen needed to introduce ketone and carboxyl oxygens into ABA
rxn01659.other_comments: The reaction proposes a one-step conversion of farnesyl diphosphate (C15) directly to (-)-abscisic acid plus pyrophosphate. While ABA is formally a C15 sesquiterpenoid, in higher plants it is derived from C40 carotenoid cleavage (xanthoxin pathway), not from FPP cyclization. Even in fungi where a direct sesquiterpenoid route exists, multiple oxidative steps (requiring O2/NADPH) are needed; a single bimolecular step releasing only PPi is not stoichiometrically balanced for the oxygen atoms and oxidation state of ABA.

Cleaving the C-N bond and adding water would give lumichrome + ribitol only if a different bond connectivity existed; the listed products account for C17H22N4O7 which exceeds reactants (riboflavin + H2O = C17H22N4O7), so atom count may balance but the chemistry is incorrect

Mechanistic error: enzymatic conversion of riboflavin typically yields lumichrome by loss/oxidative cleavage of the ribityl chain, not by simple hydrolysis to free ribitol; lumichrome formation is generally photochemical/oxidative rather than hydrolytic
rxn01271.other_comments: The reaction is written as a hydrolysis of riboflavin into ribitol and lumichrome. Atom balance: riboflavin C17H20N4O6 + H2O = C17H22N4O7; lumichrome C12H10N4O2 + ribitol C5H12O5 = C17H22N4O7, so it is formally balanced. However, lumichrome retains the methyl groups of the dimethylbenzene ring and represents the isoalloxazine after removal of the ribityl chain, and the actual biochemical/photochemical conversion does not cleanly release free ribitol via hydrolysis.

errors: The dipeptide Gly-Phe appears identical on both substrate and product sides, so no chemical transformation or transport compartmentalization is represented; transport reactions normally distinguish the substrate by compartment (e.g., Gly-Phe[extracellular] vs Gly-Phe[cytoplasm]). As written, the peptide cancels out and the net reaction reduces to simple ATP hydrolysis.
rxn12850.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis to import of the dipeptide Gly-Phe. The ATP/H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+ portion is stoichiometrically and charge balanced. ABC importers are driven irreversibly in the import (forward) direction by ATP hydrolysis in vivo. The main issue is the missing compartment labels on Gly-Phe, which makes the transport step invisible.

rxn00472.other_comments: This reaction represents ornithine racemase (EC 5.1.1.12), which interconverts L-ornithine and D-ornithine. The substrate 'Ornithine' typically refers to L-ornithine, and the product is D-ornithine. As an isomerization (racemization) reaction, the stoichiometry is balanced 1:1 with no atoms gained or lost, since both species are stereoisomers (C5H12N2O2). Racemases are inherently reversible enzymes operating near equilibrium, with the direction driven by the relative concentrations of the two enantiomers.

errors: The product name 'Glyoxalate' should be 'Glyoxylate' (HOOC-CHO); this appears to be a spelling/naming issue rather than a stoichiometric one

rxn06514.other_comments: This is the second step of the peptidylglycine amidation pathway, catalyzed by peptidyl-alpha-hydroxyglycine alpha-amidating lyase (PAL). Peptidylamidoglycolate (peptidyl-alpha-hydroxyglycine) is cleaved to yield the C-terminally amidated peptide (peptidyl amide) plus glyoxylate. In vivo this reaction proceeds strongly in the amidation (forward) direction to produce bioactive amidated peptides.

rxn06255.other_comments: This represents a monooxygenase (epoxidase) reaction. One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the alkene to form the epoxide, while the other oxygen atom is reduced to water using electrons from NADH. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + O2 + H+ provides 2 electrons and 2 H+, one O atom goes to the epoxide (added across the C=C double bond) and the other to H2O, with NAD+ released. This is a typical irreversible monooxygenase reaction driven forward by O2 consumption and NADH oxidation.

rxn01518.other_comments: This is the deoxyuridine kinase reaction, transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the 5'-hydroxyl of deoxyuridine to form dUMP, with ADP and a proton released. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge: ATP (-4) + deoxyuridine (0) = ADP (-3) + H+ (+1) + dUMP (-2), giving -4 on each side. Atom counts also balance. Kinase reactions of this type are strongly exergonic due to ATP hydrolysis coupling and proceed in the phosphorylation (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical reactants and products (2 H+ + Mucic acid on both sides), so there is no net chemical transformation indicated. A transport reaction must distinguish compartments (e.g., extracellular vs cytoplasmic) for the protons and substrate, such as: 2 H+[e] + Mucic acid[e] <=> 2 H+[c] + Mucic acid[c].
Without compartment annotations, the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced trivially but biologically meaningless as a transport process.
Galactarate symporters typically couple 1 H+ per substrate; a 2:1 stoichiometry should be verified against experimental evidence.
rxn12599.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction for galactarate (mucic acid / galactaric acid). Proton symport import is driven by the proton motive force, so it normally proceeds in the import direction (extracellular to cytoplasmic), though transporters can be reversible depending on gradients.

rxn07947.other_comments: This is a coupled reaction combining fatty acid activation (acyl-CoA synthetase-like step using ATP yielding AMP + PPi) with acyltransferase activity to acylate a 2-acyl-glycerophosphoethanolamine. ATP + myristic acid forms an activated acyl intermediate (myristoyl-AMP), which then acylates the sn-1 position of the lysophospholipid (2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine with a C14:0 at sn-2) to yield dimyristoyl phosphatidylethanolamine. Mass balance appears consistent: myristic acid (C14:0) is incorporated, ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi + H+, and the lysophospholipid becomes a fully acylated PE. The ATP-driven activation makes this thermodynamically driven and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn04092.other_comments: This is D-amino acid oxidase acting on D-alanine. The reaction: D-alanine + O2 + H2O -> pyruvate + NH3 + H2O2. The oxidase deaminates D-alanine to the imino acid, which hydrolyzes to pyruvate and ammonia, with O2 reduced to H2O2. Atoms balance: D-alanine (C3H7NO2) + H2O (H2O) + O2 = C3H9NO5; products pyruvate (C3H4O3) + NH3 (NH3) + H2O2 (H2O2) = C3H9NO5. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: Hydroxyquinol (1,2,4-benzenetriol) has three hydroxyl groups, while quinol (hydroquinone, 1,4-benzenediol) has two; adding one oxygen as a hydroxyl to quinol gives a benzenetriol, so the atom balance for the aromatic substrate is plausible. However, the oxygen balance is incorrect: a monooxygenase using O2 incorporates one O atom into the substrate and reduces the other to H2O, which is consistent here. The H balance should be checked: NADPH + O2 + H+ + C6H6O2 -> H2O + NADP+ + C6H6O3. Counting: left H = (NADPH H) + 1 (H+) + 6 (quinol) ; right = 2 (H2O) + (NADP H) + 6 (hydroxyquinol). NADPH has one more H than NADP+, so left adds NADPH(=NADP+ +H) +H+ = effectively 2 extra H, matching the 2 H in water. The reaction is balanced as a monooxygenase reaction.
rxn04666.other_comments: This represents an NADPH-dependent aromatic ring monooxygenase (hydroxylase) converting quinol (hydroquinone) to hydroxyquinol (1,2,4-benzenetriol), with O2 split into one hydroxyl on the ring and one water. Such NAD(P)H/O2-dependent oxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (hydroxylation) direction.

rxn03595.other_comments: This is an NAD-dependent oxidation of 6-hydroxyhexanoate (a primary alcohol) to 6-oxohexanoate (the corresponding aldehyde, adipate semialdehyde). The reaction is stoichiometrically and elementally balanced: the alcohol loses two hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one released as H+). Charge is also balanced. This corresponds to a 6-hydroxyhexanoate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.258), part of the epsilon-caprolactone/adipate degradation pathway. Alcohol dehydrogenases are generally reversible in vitro, though in vivo direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio and downstream reactions; in degradative pathways it typically proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction.

rxn08712.other_comments: This represents heptosyltransferase III (WaaQ) in the LPS inner core biosynthesis, transferring the third heptose (HepIII) from ADP-L-glycero-D-manno-heptose to the HepII residue of the lipid A-Kdo2-Hep2 acceptor. The reaction is balanced: ADP-heptose donor transfers a heptosyl group to the acceptor, releasing ADP. Atoms balance with the glycosyl transfer producing the elongated core plus ADP.

errors: The proton stoichiometry is inconsistent with a proton symport mechanism: for transport via proton symport, the protons and substrate should be on the same side as compartment-specific (e.g., periplasm/extracellular) on the left and cytoplasm on the right, but here both sides are identical with no compartment distinction shown
No compartmentalization is indicated; substrate and protons appear identical on both sides, making this a null (zero net) reaction as written
A 3:1 proton:substrate ratio is unusually high for a symport and is not clearly justified for 3-oxalomalate
rxn12545.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction moving 3-oxalomalate across a membrane coupled to 3 protons (proton symport). As written, both sides are identical (3 H+ + 3-Oxalomalate on each side), so the reaction is balanced trivially but lacks the compartment labels (e.g., [e] vs [c]) needed to represent actual transport. Without compartment annotation the net transformation is zero.

rxn07980.other_comments: This is a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase (FabA/FabZ type) step in fatty acid biosynthesis/elongation. The substrate (R)-3-hydroxy acyl-ACP loses water to form a trans-2-enoyl-ACP (here named trans-3-... but conceptually a trans-2,3 double bond plus the existing cis-11 double bond). Stoichiometry is balanced: one hydroxyacyl-ACP yields one enoyl-ACP plus one water. The naming is slightly ambiguous but the dehydration concept is sound. In vivo, dehydration in the elongation cycle proceeds toward enoyl-ACP formation, so the reaction is effectively forward, though the enzyme reaction itself is chemically reversible.

rxn06666.other_comments: This is an O-acyltransferase reaction transferring an acyl group from acyl-CoA to the sn-3 position of 1-O-alkyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycerol, producing CoA and 1-O-alkyl-2-acetyl-3-acyl-sn-glycerol. The reaction is balanced: the acyl group is transferred from CoA to the free hydroxyl at sn-3, and CoA is released. Mass and charge are conserved. Biologically, this resembles a step in ether lipid (alkyl-acylglycerol) biosynthesis catalyzed by an acyltransferase.

rxn11803.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP2B6/CYP3A4/CYP2C9) catalyzed hydroxylation of cyclophosphamide at the 4-position, the bioactivation step. A monooxygenase reaction: one atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (forming 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide) and the other is reduced to water, using NADPH and a proton as the electron/proton source. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + substrate -> H2O + NADP+ + hydroxylated product. P450 monooxygenations are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of substrate oxidation.

rxn02381.other_comments: This reaction is part of the fungal melanin (DHN-melanin) biosynthesis pathway. Vermelone is reduced from 1,3,8-trihydroxynaphthalene (1,3,8-naphthalenetriol) by the enzyme 1,3,8-trihydroxynaphthalene reductase (T4HN/T3HN reductase, an NADPH-dependent reductase). The stoichiometry as written is balanced for the redox couple (NADP+ + NADPH + H+) with one reduction equivalent transferred. However, the biologically favored direction is the reduction of 1,3,8-naphthalenetriol to vermelone using NADPH, which is the reverse of how this reaction is written. The reaction as written (vermelone being oxidized to the triol with NADP+) is thermodynamically and physiologically the non-favored direction.

rxn00636.other_comments: This is the mannose isomerase reaction (EC 5.3.1.7) interconverting D-mannose (an aldose) and D-fructose (a ketose). The reaction is an aldose-ketose isomerization, identical in atom count (both are C6H12O6 hexoses), so it is stoichiometrically balanced with a 1:1 ratio. As an isomerase-catalyzed reaction with a near-zero standard free energy change, it is thermodynamically reversible; the in vivo direction depends on relative substrate/product concentrations.

rxn01295.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by threonine aldolase / phenylserine aldolase (EC 4.1.2.5), a PLP-dependent aldol cleavage. L-threo-3-Phenylserine is cleaved into glycine and benzaldehyde. The reaction is mass-balanced: C9H11NO3 = C2H5NO2 (glycine) + C7H6O (benzaldehyde). Although classified as a lyase favoring cleavage, aldolases catalyze reversible aldol reactions and are commonly exploited synthetically in the condensation (reverse) direction.

errors: The myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (phytate) backbone is myo-inositol, not L-inositol; the product should be myo-inositol

Charge balance is not explicitly verifiable without protonation states, but phytate carries multiple negative charges and the hydrolysis releases inorganic phosphate (HPO4 or H2PO4), so proton balance should be checked
rxn09119.other_comments: This represents phytase-catalyzed hydrolysis of phytate (myo-inositol hexakisphosphate, InsP6) using 6 water molecules to release 6 inorganic phosphate groups and free inositol. The hydrolysis of all six phosphoester bonds is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, so it proceeds in the forward direction.

errors: The acceptor in the EC name is described as lipoyllysine (the protein-bound lipoyl group), but the reaction uses free Lipoamide; this is an acceptable model substitute though technically the physiological acceptor is the enzyme-bound lipoyllysine residue
Stoichiometry is balanced: 3MOP (C6H9O3-) provides the 2-methylbutanoyl group (C5H9O) after loss of CO2; the remaining carbons and the thioester linkage to dihydrolipoamide account for all atoms
rxn06621.other_comments: This is the second (E1-type, decarboxylating) step of branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex acting on (S)-3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (the keto acid derived from isoleucine). Oxidative decarboxylation transfers the 2-methylbutanoyl moiety to the lipoamide cofactor, releasing CO2. The decarboxylation makes this essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn02539.other_comments: This is a toluene dioxygenase reaction (EC 1.14.12.11) converting toluene (Toluol is German for toluene) plus O2 and NADH into toluene-cis-dihydrodiol (cis-toluene dihydrodiol) plus NAD+. Both oxygen atoms from O2 are incorporated into the diol product, and NADH provides the reducing equivalents. The stoichiometry balances: NADH + O2 + H+ + toluene yields NAD+ + cis-dihydrodiol. This dioxygenase-catalyzed step is the first committed step of aerobic toluene degradation.

rxn00719.other_comments: This reaction represents dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (NAD+) activity (EC 1.3.1.1), interconverting 5,6-dihydrouracil and uracil. Written direction: dihydrouracil + NAD+ -> uracil + NADH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced for atoms and charge (NAD+ accepts 2 electrons and a hydride, releasing NADH and a proton). In vivo, however, pyrimidine catabolism proceeds in the reductive direction (uracil + NAD(P)H -> dihydrouracil), so the physiological flux is opposite to the way this reaction is written; the reductive degradation pathway typically favors dihydrouracil formation.

errors: Mass/redox imbalance: the L-threonine dehydrogenase + cleavage pathway does not produce H2; reducing equivalents are carried by NAD(H), not released as molecular hydrogen
Missing NAD+/NADH cofactors required for the oxidation step
Charge and hydrogen balance incorrect as written
rxn13847.other_comments: This appears to represent the combined action of L-threonine dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.103), which oxidizes L-threonine to 2-amino-3-oxobutanoate using NAD+, followed by 2-amino-3-ketobutyrate CoA ligase (EC 2.3.1.29), which cleaves the product with CoA to yield glycine and acetyl-CoA. The net conversion of threonine + CoA + NAD+ to glycine + acetyl-CoA + NADH + H+ is correct, but the equation as written incorrectly shows H2 instead of NADH/NAD+.

errors: The reaction name specifies NAD+ as the cofactor (Cholest-5-ene-3beta,7alpha-diol:NAD+ 3-oxidoreductase), but the reaction as written uses NADP/NADPH; this is a cofactor mismatch

The substrate 7alpha-hydroxycholesterol (cholest-5-ene-3beta,7alpha-diol) to product 7alpha-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one involves both an oxidation at C3 (hydroxyl to ketone) and an isomerization of the double bond (Delta5 to Delta4); these are two distinct catalytic steps and the equation only accounts for the redox cofactor balance, not the isomerization step explicitly (though atom balance is maintained)
Atom/charge balance: oxidation of a 3beta-hydroxyl to a 3-oxo removes 2[H], consistent with NADP -> NADPH + H+, so the redox balance is correct
rxn02973.other_comments: This corresponds to the 3beta-hydroxy-Delta5-C27-steroid oxidoreductase (HSD3B7) reaction in the classic bile acid synthesis pathway, converting 7alpha-hydroxycholesterol to 7alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one. Note the enzyme physiologically uses NAD+, not NADP+, so the cofactor in the written equation appears incorrect. [directionality_note] In vivo this is the 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase step of bile acid biosynthesis, which proceeds in the oxidative direction toward the 4-en-3-one product

rxn04919.other_comments: This is a glutathione S-transferase type reaction where the thiol of GSH (glutathione) attacks the alpha-carbon of 2-bromoacetaldehyde (BrCH2CHO), displacing bromide and forming S-(formylmethyl)glutathione (GS-CH2-CHO). Stoichiometry balances: GSH (C10H17N3O6S) + C2H3BrO -> HBr + C12H19N3O7S. Atoms balance (C:10+2=12, H:17+3=19+1, N:3, O:6+1=7, S:1, Br:1). The conventional product notation lists HBr though physiologically Br- + H+ would be released. As a nucleophilic substitution detoxification reaction, it is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn02719.other_comments: This reaction as written shows oxidation of lauroyl-CoA (dodecanoyl-CoA, C12 saturated acyl-CoA) to trans-2-dodecenoyl-CoA, with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry and atom/charge balance are correct: removing two hydrogens (as H- to NADP+ giving NADPH, plus H+) introduces the 2,3-double bond. However, the enzyme name 'trans-Dodec-2-enoyl-CoA reductase' (an enoyl-CoA reductase, e.g. in fatty acid elongation/synthesis) physiologically catalyzes the NADPH-dependent reduction of the enoyl-CoA to the saturated acyl-CoA. Thus the biologically favored direction is the reverse of how it is written (consuming NADPH and trans-2-dodecenoyl-CoA to make lauroyl-CoA and NADP+).

rxn07444.other_comments: This is an epoxide hydrolase reaction where cis-stilbene oxide undergoes hydrolysis with water to yield the vicinal diol (1R,2R)-1,2-diphenylethane-1,2-diol. The stoichiometry is balanced: cis-stilbene oxide (C14H12O) plus H2O gives the diol (C14H14O2). Epoxide hydrolases catalyze the addition of water to the epoxide ring, producing the trans-diol from the cis-epoxide via anti-attack. The reaction is thermodynamically favorable in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn04363.other_comments: This reaction describes an isomerase converting eicosapentaenoic acid (5Z,8Z,11Z,14Z,17Z configuration) into a conjugated triene isomer (5Z,7E,9E,14Z,17Z). The transformation shifts and conjugates double bonds, converting the 8Z,11Z arrangement into a conjugated 7E,9E system while retaining the 5Z, 14Z, and 17Z double bonds. The molecular formula (C20H30O2) is conserved on both sides, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. Isomerases are generally near-equilibrium and reversible, though specific directionality in vivo may depend on downstream metabolism.

errors: The reaction is missing the UDP-N-acetylglucosamine donor; lipid II formation/polymerization requires incorporation, not just release of undecaprenyl diphosphate

Mass imbalance: the substrate (lipid II) cannot be converted simply to bactoprenyl diphosphate plus a polymeric peptidoglycan subunit without consuming an acceptor glycan chain or releasing the disaccharide-pentapeptide unit
Product 'Peptidoglycan subunit of Escherichia coli' is ill-defined and likely not stoichiometrically balanced against the single lipid II substrate
rxn10076.other_comments: This represents the transglycosylation/transfer step of peptidoglycan biosynthesis where lipid II (undecaprenyl-PP-MurNAc-GlcNAc-pentapeptide with meso-DAP) transfers its disaccharide-peptide unit into the growing peptidoglycan polymer, releasing undecaprenyl (bactoprenyl) diphosphate. The chemistry (cleavage of the pyrophosphate-glycosyl bond, release of C55-PP) is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven forward as part of cell wall synthesis.

rxn13999.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of CDP-4-keto-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose (CDP-4-dehydro-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose) to CDP-abequose, catalyzed by CDP-abequose synthase (RfbJ / Abe). The stoichiometry is balanced: the keto group at C4 is reduced to a hydroxyl using NADPH + H+, yielding NADP+ and CDP-abequose. This is the final step of abequose biosynthesis in Salmonella O-antigen pathways. The reaction name written as 'oxidoreductase' with NADP+ suggests the reverse oxidation direction, but in vivo the biosynthetic reduction toward CDP-abequose is favored.

rxn01278.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 5-keto-D-gluconate 5-reductase (EC 1.1.1.69), which interconverts D-gluconate and 5-dehydro-D-gluconate (5-keto-D-gluconate) using the NADP+/NADPH cofactor pair. The stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of the C5 hydroxyl of gluconate to a ketone removes two hydrogens (one as hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH, one released as H+). Atoms and charges balance. The enzyme is known to operate reversibly, with the in vivo direction depending on the NADPH/NADP+ ratio and substrate concentrations; physiologically it often favors reduction of 5-keto-gluconate to gluconate, but the reaction is genuinely reversible.

rxn03713.other_comments: This is an extradiol ring-cleavage dioxygenase reaction (KEGG R05413), part of dibenzofuran/diaryl ether degradation. 2,2',3-trihydroxydiphenyl ether undergoes meta-cleavage of the trihydroxylated aromatic ring by incorporation of both atoms of molecular O2, yielding the ring-opened 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-(2-hydroxyphenoxy)-hexa-2,4-dienoate. Stoichiometry is balanced: one O2 incorporated, one H+ released upon ring opening and carboxylate formation.

rxn06357.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphorylation of the beta-adrenergic receptor by a kinase (beta-adrenergic receptor kinase, GRK2/BARK1), transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the receptor protein, yielding ADP, a proton, and the phosphorylated receptor. Stoichiometry is balanced if one phosphate group is transferred (one Ser/Thr residue phosphorylated), with the H+ accounting for the proton released. Kinase reactions of this type are strongly exergonic due to ATP hydrolysis and are effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the phosphorylation direction.

rxn07656.other_comments: This reaction (R07866) is catalyzed by allene oxide cyclase (AOC, EC 5.3.99.6), which converts the allene oxide 12,13(S)-EOT (or 9,10-EOT in the 9-LOX branch) into 12-OPDA (or 10-OPDA, cis-(+)-10,11-epoxide product) in the jasmonate/oxylipin biosynthesis pathway. The reaction shown converts 9,10-EOT (an unstable allene oxide derived from linolenic acid via 9-lipoxygenase and allene oxide synthase) into 10-OPDA (10-oxo-11,15-phytodienoic acid). Stoichiometrically, this is an intramolecular cyclization/isomerization with no net atom change, so it is balanced as a 1:1 conversion. Because the substrate allene oxide is chemically very unstable and the cyclization establishes the specific stereochemistry of the cyclopentenone product, the reaction proceeds strongly in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn09936.other_comments: This represents an ATP-dependent L-amino acid ligase (Lal-type) forming a dipeptide bond between L-alanine and L-serine, releasing ADP and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi provides energy for peptide bond formation, and the released H+ accounts for charge/proton balance. Mass and charge balance are consistent. The reaction is thermodynamically driven toward dipeptide synthesis by ATP hydrolysis, so it proceeds in the forward (biosynthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn04014.other_comments: This is the epoxyalkane:CoM transferase (EaCoMT) reaction from bacterial propylene/epoxide metabolism. (R)-2-Hydroxypropyl-CoM is cleaved to release coenzyme M (2-mercaptoethanesulfonate) and (R)-1,2-epoxypropane (propylene oxide). The reaction is balanced: the C-S bond between the hydroxypropyl group and CoM is broken, with the hydroxyl oxygen forming the epoxide ring. In vivo, the physiological direction during epoxide degradation is the reverse (epoxide ring opening: addition of CoM to epoxypropane to form 2-hydroxypropyl-CoM), so the written forward direction (ring formation) is not the typical biological direction.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction produces a free H+ but the substrate sn-glycero-3-phospho-1-inositol and product inositol 1-phosphate carry phosphate groups; at physiological pH the hydrolysis of the phosphodiester does not release a free proton in this simple form. As written, mass balance is approximately maintained (C9H19O11P + H2O -> C3H8O3 + C6H13O9P), but the H+ on the product side creates a charge imbalance unless protonation states are explicitly accounted for.
rxn02389.other_comments: This is a glycerophosphoinositol inositolphosphohydrolase reaction: hydrolysis of the phosphodiester bond in sn-glycero-3-phospho-1-inositol yielding glycerol and inositol 1-phosphate. Hydrolytic phosphodiesterase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: The acyl group transferred must match the acyl-CoA substrate. The generic 'fa1coa' (a fatty acyl-CoA) is inconsistent with the product, which specifically gains an isotetradecanoyl group; the acyl-CoA should be isotetradecanoyl-CoA (anteiso/iso-C14:0-CoA) to yield the diisotetradecanoyl product.

If interpreted literally as written with a non-isotetradecanoyl acyl-CoA, the product would not be 1,2-diisotetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate, making the reaction stoichiometrically/chemically inconsistent.
rxn10216.other_comments: This is an LPAAT-type (1-acylglycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferase) reaction acylating the sn-2 position of lysophosphatidic acid (1-isotetradecanoyl-G3P) using a fatty acyl-CoA to form phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-G3P), releasing CoA and a proton. Atom/charge balance otherwise looks reasonable; the main issue is the generic vs specific acyl-CoA naming.

errors: Nebularine is the nucleoside of the base purine (9-beta-D-ribofuranosylpurine); the product 'Purine' should be the free base purine (nucleobase), which is consistent. The stoichiometry is balanced: phosphate + nucleoside yields free base + ribose 1-phosphate, analogous to purine nucleoside phosphorylase activity. No mass-balance error is evident.
rxn01684.other_comments: This is a purine-nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)-type reaction. Nebularine (9-ribosylpurine) is phosphorolytically cleaved to free purine base plus alpha-D-ribose 1-phosphate. PNP reactions are thermodynamically reversible, though in vivo the phosphorolysis (forward as written) direction is typically favored due to consumption of products.

errors: The product stereochemistry is incorrect for fatty acid biosynthesis. The FabG enzyme (3-oxoacyl-ACP reductase) produces the (3R)-hydroxyacyl-ACP; however, in standard nomenclature for FAS, the physiologically relevant product is the (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-ACP, so this may actually be correct depending on convention. Stoichiometry is balanced.
rxn07987.other_comments: This is the FabG-catalyzed reduction step in type II fatty acid synthesis, reducing a 3-oxoacyl-ACP (C12:1, cis-5) to the (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-ACP using NADPH. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (1 NADPH + 1 H+ reduces the ketone to a hydroxyl, yielding NADP+). In vivo this proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction as written.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance hydrogen and oxygen properly. A standard monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction is: substrate + NADPH + H+ + O2 -> hydroxylated-substrate + NADP+ + H2O. Here only one O atom of O2 is incorporated into the product (as the hydroxyl) and the other is reduced to water, which is consistent, but the proton/charge balance should be checked. With NADPH (charge typically written) + H+ consumed and NADP+ produced, the listed components are qualitatively correct, but explicit elemental balancing of the large branched fatty acid cannot be verified without molecular formulas.

Substrate naming inconsistency: 'octa-methyl tetracontatricosanoic acid' labeled as C34:0 is internally inconsistent. 'Tetracontatricosanoic' implies ~43 carbons (tetraconta = 40, tricosa = 23), not 34, and adding 8 methyl branches further changes the total carbon count. The C34:0 designation conflicts with the name.
rxn10747.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 / fatty acid hydroxylase-type monooxygenase reaction that uses NADPH and molecular O2 to introduce a single hydroxyl group onto a methyl-branched long-chain fatty acid, producing water and NADP+. NADPH-dependent oxygenase reactions are physiologically essentially irreversible, so the reaction proceeds in the hydroxylation (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn12026.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphorylation of 6-thioinosine-5'-diphosphate (a thiopurine drug metabolite analog) to its triphosphate form, with ATP serving as the phosphate donor and being converted to ADP. This is catalyzed by a nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDK)-type activity. Atomically, one phosphate is transferred from ATP to the diphosphate substrate, so the reaction is balanced (ATP + NDP <=> ADP + NTP). While NDK reactions are intrinsically reversible due to similar phosphoanhydride bond energies, in vivo the high ATP/ADP ratio and downstream incorporation of the triphosphate drive the reaction predominantly in the forward direction.

rxn02786.other_comments: This is a flavin-dependent monooxygenase (2-hydroxybiphenyl 3-monooxygenase) reaction. NADH provides reducing equivalents, O2 is incorporated as one atom into the substrate (2-hydroxybiphenyl/2-biphenylol) to form 3-phenylcatechol, and the other oxygen atom is reduced to water. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + O2 + H+ + substrate-OH yields H2O + NAD+ + substrate-(OH)2. Mass and charge are balanced (NADH carries 2 H + electrons, with H+ consumed). The reaction is physiologically irreversible in the oxygenation direction.

rxn11659.other_comments: This reaction represents nucleoside oxidase activity (EC 1.1.3.39), oxidizing the 5'-hydroxymethyl group of adenosine (a primary alcohol) to a carboxylic acid (the uronic acid, giving 9-riburonosyladenine). This two-step oxidation (primary alcohol -> aldehyde -> carboxylic acid) consumes 2 O2 and produces 2 H2O2. Mass balance: adenosine (C10H13N5O4) + H2O + 2 O2 = C10H11N5O6 (9-riburonosyladenine, the uronic acid) + 2 H2O2 + H+. Checking C: 10=10; N: 5=5. H: 13+2=15 on left; product 11 + (2x2=4) + 1 = 16 on right. There appears to be a one-hydrogen imbalance; the oxidation of a CH2OH to COOH removes 4 H (as 2 H2O2 from 2 O2), giving product C10H11N5O6 which balances without an extra H+. The free H+ produced from carboxylic acid deprotonation at physiological pH could account for an apparent charge/H discrepancy if the product is written as the carboxylate anion. As written with neutral acid, the proton is extra.

errors: Stoichiometry is likely incorrect/generic: arabinan is a polymer of variable length, so a fixed 3:1 water-to-substrate ratio and exactly 3 L-arabinose products is an oversimplification
The product should be alpha-L-arabinofuranose (the furanose form released by arabinofuranosidase), though it equilibrates to L-arabinose

Enzyme name mismatch: alpha-N-arabinofuranosidase typically cleaves terminal arabinofuranose residues rather than fully hydrolyzing arabinan; an endo-arabinanase plus arabinofuranosidase would be needed for complete depolymerization
rxn09988.other_comments: This represents the hydrolysis of arabinan (an L-arabinose polymer found in plant cell walls) into L-arabinose monomers, consuming water. Hydrolytic glycosidase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward the free sugar.

rxn00981.other_comments: This is an ether-bond lyase reaction. Carboxymethyloxysuccinate (an oxydiacetate-type compound, structurally -OOC-CH2-O-CH(COO-)-CH2-COO-) is cleaved at the ether linkage to yield fumarate (from the succinate portion via elimination) and glycolate (HOCH2-COO-). Stoichiometrically the atoms balance: the substrate C6H6O7 splits into fumarate C4H2O4 plus glycolate C2H4O3, with carbon (6=4+2), hydrogen (6=2+4) and oxygen (7=4+3) all conserved. Lyase reactions of this elimination type are often considered reversible in vitro, though in vivo the forward (cleavage) direction predominates as part of degradation pathways.

errors: The product should be beta-D-mannose specifically, but D-Mannose is acceptable as a generic form
Charge/protonation: GDP-mannose hydrolysis typically releases GDP plus mannose; mass and atom balance are correct as written
rxn08599.other_comments: This is the GDP-mannose mannosyl hydrolase (Nudix hydrolase, Gmm) reaction. It hydrolyzes the glycosidic bond of GDP-mannose using water to yield GDP and free D-mannose. The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced as written (H2O + GDP-mannose -> GDP + D-mannose). As a hydrolase reaction it is thermodynamically strongly favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn03144.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.202) transferring a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to DIMBOA (2,4-dihydroxy-7-methoxy-1,4-benzoxazin-3-one), forming DIMBOA-glucoside and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced 1:1 for both substrates and products, and the glucosyl moiety transfer is conserved.

errors: The product name 'D-Alanyl-alanyl-poly(glycerolphosphate)' appears inconsistent with the substrate '(D-Ala1->2Gro-1-P)n'; the product should represent the chain extended by one D-alanyl residue, i.e. (D-Ala)n+1-poly(glycerophosphate), but the nomenclature is ambiguous/poorly formed

Charge balance cannot be fully verified due to ambiguous polymer notation, but if a free hydroxyl of glycerophosphate is esterified by D-alanine, the production of ADP + Pi + H+ from ATP is consistent with a ligase mechanism
rxn06669.other_comments: This is the D-alanine--poly(glycerophosphate) ligase reaction involved in D-alanylation of teichoic acids (DltA-type activity). The enzyme activates D-alanine using ATP and transfers it to the poly(glycerophosphate) backbone. The hydrolysis of ATP to ADP + Pi makes the reaction thermodynamically driven toward synthesis in vivo, so it operates in the forward (alanylation) direction.

errors: The reaction is not charge or mass balanced as written; cardiolipin hydrolysis to phosphatidylglycerol plus phosphatidic acid releases the bond at the central glycerol, but the proton balance must be checked. Hydrolysis of one phosphodiester bond consumes one H2O and yields a free phosphate group on the phosphatidic acid (PA) and a free hydroxyl on the phosphatidylglycerol (PG). At physiological pH the products carry additional negative charges relative to substrate plus a proton should be released, so an H+ term is typically required for charge balance.
rxn08219.other_comments: This represents cardiolipin (a dimeric phospholipid, bis-phosphatidylglycerol) being hydrolyzed by a phospholipase D-type cardiolipin hydrolase into phosphatidic acid (1,2-didodecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) and phosphatidylglycerol, both with the C12:0 acyl chains. Hydrolytic cleavage of a phosphodiester bond is thermodynamically favorable and biologically irreversible in vivo, hence forward direction.

errors: The reaction is not properly balanced. Catechol (C6H6O2) reacting with O2 should yield products with consistent atom counts. rxn01478.other_comments: This is phosphoethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PEAMT, EC 2.1.1.103), which catalyzes the first methylation step in phosphocholine biosynthesis in plants and parasites like Plasmodium. rxn03992.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-catalyzed monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction, specifically the 3-hydroxylation of quinine by CYP3A4 to form 3-hydroxyquinine. rxn02545.other_comments: This is a NADPH-dependent monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction converting m-cresol (3-cresol) to 3-methylcatechol. It incorporates one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate (forming the new hydroxyl group) while the other oxygen is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. rxn04987.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP39A1)-catalyzed 7alpha-hydroxylation of 24-hydroxycholesterol (cerebrosterol = (24S)-cholest-5-en-3beta,24-diol). Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ -> NADP+ + H2O with one O incorporated into the substrate.

rxn07591.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 2-hydroxyisoflavanone synthase (IFS, CYP93C), a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. It converts the flavanone liquiritigenin into 2,7,4'-trihydroxyisoflavanone via a 1,2-aryl migration. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ provide reducing equivalents and oxygen for the monooxygenase reaction, yielding H2O, NADP+, and the hydroxylated isoflavanone product. As a P450 monooxygenase reaction with O2 and NADPH consumption, it is physiologically irreversible in the forward direction.

rxn02338.other_comments: This is a cis-trans isomerization of farnesol at the 2-position double bond, converting 2-trans,6-trans-farnesol to 2-cis,6-trans-farnesol. Isomerase reactions of this type are typically near-equilibrium and reversible in vivo, though the equilibrium position depends on the specific enzyme and cellular context.

rxn04446.other_comments: This reaction (R06593) represents the dehydration of 2-amino-2-deoxy-5-dehydroquinate (AminoDHQ) to form 2-amino-2-deoxy-5-dehydroshikimate (AminoDHS) plus water, catalyzed by 2-amino-2-deoxy-5-dehydroquinate dehydratase (aminoDHQ dehydratase). rxn01379.other_comments: This is an aminoglycoside N6'-acetyltransferase (AAC(6')) reaction transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the 6'-amino group of bekanamycin (kanamycin B), producing N6'-acetylkanamycin B, CoA, and a proton. rxn02538.other_comments: This reaction represents a UDP-glucose-dependent glucosyltransferase transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to saligenin (salicyl alcohol, 2-hydroxybenzyl alcohol), forming salicin (the beta-D-glucoside) and releasing UDP. rxn13723.other_comments: This is a menaquinol:Mn(IV) oxidoreductase reaction in which menaquinol-7 donates 2 electrons to reduce solid MnO2 (Mn4+) to soluble Mn2+, oxidizing menaquinol to menaquinone-7 and consuming protons to form water. rxn02584.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of N-methylhexanamide (an amide) by an amidase/amidohydrolase, adding water across the C-N bond to yield hexanoate (the carboxylic acid, deprotonated at physiological pH) and methanamine (methylamine).
