With 2 O2 reduced to 2 H2O2, oxygen balance requires 4 H on each side: 2 O2 + 4 H -> 2 H2O2. The substrate provides only those 4 H from dehydrogenation, so the extra H+ on the left is incorrect. A balanced form would be: Tetrahydropalmatine + 2 O2 -> Palmatine(+) + 2 H2O2 + (charge balance issue). The written equation has an unbalanced proton and unaccounted positive charge of palmatine.
rxn13952.other_comments: This represents an oxidase-type aromatization of the protoberberine alkaloid tetrahydropalmatine to the fully oxidized quaternary alkaloid palmatine, with O2 acting as electron acceptor forming H2O2. Such oxidative dehydrogenation/aromatization reactions are thermodynamically driven and physiologically essentially irreversible in the forward (oxidation) direction.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: luteolin and quercetin differ by one oxygen (luteolin C15H10O6, quercetin C15H10O7), but the substrate-product pair is wrong - this enzyme (flavonoid 3'-hydroxylase) should convert apigenin to luteolin, not luteolin to quercetin

Quercetin (a flavonol) cannot be produced from luteolin (a flavone) by a single 3'-hydroxylation; quercetin has an additional 3-hydroxyl on the C-ring compared to luteolin's structure, so these are not related by 3'-hydroxylation
Proton balance is incorrect: a monooxygenase reaction (RH + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> ROH + H2O + NADP+) requires only 1 H+, not 2
rxn04393.other_comments: This is described as a flavonoid 3'-hydroxylase (cytochrome P450 monooxygenase) reaction consuming NADPH and O2. The general monooxygenase form is correct, but the specific substrate (luteolin) and product (quercetin) are mismatched - 3'-hydroxylation of luteolin would not yield quercetin. Quercetin already possesses a 3'-OH; luteolin is the 3'-hydroxylated flavone. The correct substrate/product pairing for this EC class is typically apigenin -> luteolin or naringenin -> eriodictyol.

rxn03750.other_comments: This is the 4-hydroxyphenylacetate 3-monooxygenase (or related hydroxylase) type reaction. It uses NADH and molecular O2 to hydroxylate 2-hydroxyphenylacetate (o-hydroxyphenylacetate), incorporating one oxygen atom into the substrate to form homogentisate (2,5-dihydroxyphenylacetate) and the other into water. The stoichiometry balances: NADH provides 2 electrons and a hydride, plus H+, reduces one O of O2 to water while the other O is added to the aromatic ring. Atom and charge balance check out (NADH + H+ + O2 + substrate -> NAD+ + H2O + hydroxylated product).

rxn02974.other_comments: This reaction (R04265) represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of CDP-4-keto-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose (CDP-4-dehydro-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose) to CDP-paratose (CDP-3,6-dideoxy-D-ribo-hexose, i.e. CDP-paratose), catalyzed by CDP-paratose synthase (paratose synthase, an NADPH-dependent 4-keto reductase). The atoms balance: the 4-keto group is reduced to a hydroxyl using NADPH + H+, yielding NADP+. The standard notation 'NADP' should be 'NADP+', but the species is correctly identified.

rxn12040.other_comments: The reaction shown is the hydrolysis of trypanothione (TSH, also called N1,N8-bis(glutathionyl)spermidine) by glutathionylspermidine amidase activity. The enzyme bifunctional trypanothione synthetase/amidase (TryS) or glutathionylspermidine synthetase/amidase (GspSA) hydrolyzes one amide bond of trypanothione, releasing one glutathione (GSH) and yielding glutathionylspermidine (Gsp). This consumes one water. Stoichiometrically the reaction H2O + TSH -> GSH + Gsp is balanced, as it is a simple amide hydrolysis cleaving one GSH-spermidine amide bond. Note: full degradation of trypanothione to two GSH plus spermidine requires two hydrolysis steps; this reaction represents only the first amidase step.

rxn00273.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 2-amino-3-ketobutyrate CoA ligase (glycine C-acetyltransferase, EC 2.3.1.29). The reaction as written shows Acetyl-CoA + Glycine condensing to form CoA + 2-amino-3-oxobutanoate (2-amino-acetoacetate). Stoichiometry is balanced: acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred from CoA to glycine, releasing free CoA and forming the C-acetylated amino acid. In vivo the reaction predominantly proceeds in the direction of glycine + acetyl-CoA formation (i.e., cleavage of 2-amino-3-ketobutyrate), as part of threonine degradation; thus the physiological flux is opposite to the way it is written here (reverse).

rxn04136.other_comments: This is the (R)-limonene synthase reaction (EC 4.2.3.20). Geranyl diphosphate (C10H20O7P2 with appropriate charge) undergoes ionization-cyclization to form (+)-(R)-limonene (C10H16) plus diphosphate (PPi). Atom and charge balance: GPP carries the diphosphate leaving group; release of PPi and a proton accompanies cyclization. The mass balance (C10 substrate -> C10 monoterpene + diphosphate) is correct, and proton release balances the charge.

errors: The redox cofactor stoichiometry is conventionally written with FAD being reduced to FADH2 as the electron pair is transferred from the substrate; this is balanced for the two hydrogens removed. However, the product is named trans-2-Enoyl-OPC4-CoA which implies a 2,3-dehydrogenation; the substrate should be a saturated acyl-CoA (OPC4-CoA) which is consistent. No clear stoichiometric error if H count balances: substrate loses 2 H (one from C2, one from C3) and FAD gains 2 H to form FADH2.
rxn07686.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (ACX) step in the jasmonate biosynthesis beta-oxidation pathway, oxidizing OPC4-CoA to trans-2-enoyl-OPC4-CoA. The FAD-dependent dehydrogenation removes two hydrogens to introduce the C2-C3 double bond. In vivo this acyl-CoA oxidase/dehydrogenase reaction proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction; in peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase systems the FADH2 is reoxidized by O2, making the reaction essentially irreversible toward enoyl-CoA.

rxn03105.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to the 6-hydroxyl of 3',4',5,6-tetrahydroxy-3,7-dimethoxyflavone, producing SAH and the 6-O-methylated product (3',4',5-trihydroxy-3,6,7-trimethoxyflavone). The stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl transferred from SAM to a hydroxyl, converting a tetrahydroxy-dimethoxy substrate to a trihydroxy-trimethoxy product. Methyltransferases are strongly driven forward by SAM/SAH thermodynamics in vivo.

rxn03024.other_comments: This is a glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) reaction transferring a glucuronic acid moiety from UDP-glucuronate to the 3-alpha-hydroxyl group of etiocholan-3alpha-ol-17-one (a steroid/androsterone-type substrate), forming the steroid 3-glucuronide and releasing UDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the glucuronosyl group is transferred from UDP-glucuronate to the acceptor, with UDP released. Atom balance checks out as the glucuronosyl transfer accounts for the difference between UDP-glucuronate and UDP. [directionality_note] UGT-catalyzed glucuronidation is physiologically a detoxification/conjugation reaction driven strongly toward the conjugated product.

rxn00484.other_comments: This is the decarboxylation of L-tryptophan to form tryptamine, catalyzed by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (a PLP-dependent enzyme). The reaction is balanced: L-tryptophan (C11H12N2O2) plus a proton yields CO2 plus tryptamine (C10H12N2). Carbon (11 = 1 + 10), nitrogen (2 = 2), and charge are balanced when accounting for the H+ consumed during decarboxylation. Decarboxylation reactions release CO2 and are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the loss of CO2.

rxn00405.other_comments: This is arginine decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.19). L-Arginine (C6H14N4O2) is decarboxylated to agmatine (C5H14N4, charged +1 form). Mass/charge balance: left side C6H14N4O2 + H+ gives C6H15N4O2(+1); right side CO2 (CO2) + agmatine (C5H14N4 as +1) gives C6H14N4O2(+1) plus one extra H. Checking: arginine neutral C6H14N4O2, plus H+ = C6H15N4O2 charge +1. Products: CO2 = CO2, agmatine protonated = C5H15N4 charge +1. Sum products = C6H15N4O2 charge +1. Balanced. Decarboxylations are physiologically essentially irreversible due to CO2 release.

errors: The reaction as written is not redox/mass balanced for the standard radical SAM mechanism. Oxygen-independent coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (HemN) cleaves SAM to give 5'-deoxyadenosine plus L-methionine, but typically the products listed should include the dehydrogenated/decarboxylated porphyrinogen. Charge and hydrogen balance should be verified; protons (H+) are likely missing from the product side to balance the two decarboxylations.
rxn04704.other_comments: This represents the anaerobic (oxygen-independent) coproporphyrinogen III oxidase reaction (HemN, EC 1.3.98.3), a radical SAM enzyme that converts coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX by oxidative decarboxylation of two propionate side chains to vinyl groups. Each decarboxylation uses one SAM, generating one 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical (yielding 5'-deoxyadenosine and methionine) and releasing CO2. The 2:1 stoichiometry of SAM and the two CO2/methionine/deoxyadenosine products is mechanistically correct.

rxn02076.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase reaction transferring the sinapoyl group from sinapoyl-CoA to D-glucarate, producing O-sinapoylglucarate and releasing free CoA. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the sinapoyl moiety is transferred and the thioester bond to CoA is replaced by an ester bond to glucarate. Acyltransfer from an acyl-CoA thioester is thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy thioester bond, so it proceeds predominantly in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Charge and proton imbalance: hydrolysis of a phosphoanhydride bond (GDP-mannose + H2O -> GMP + mannose-1-phosphate) releases only 1 H+, not 2 H+
Stoichiometric H+ coefficient should be 1.0, not 2.0, to balance both mass and charge
rxn00639.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of GDP-mannose at the phosphoanhydride bond, cleaving it into GMP and D-mannose-1-phosphate. Hydrolysis reactions of high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo (forward direction). The atom balance is correct, but the proton stoichiometry is wrong: cleavage of a single phosphoanhydride bond by water yields one inorganic proton, so 1.0 H+ is expected rather than 2.0 H+.

rxn04901.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase reaction (RH-hydroxylating/epoxidizing). TCE (trichloroethene) is oxidized using molecular oxygen and NADPH as the electron donor, producing TCE epoxide, water, and NADP+. Stoichiometry is balanced: one oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate (epoxide) and the other is reduced to water. The reaction is balanced for atoms and charge (NADPH + H+ provides 2 electrons and 2 protons). P450 monooxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible due to consumption of O2 and NADPH.

rxn02625.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by methylaspartate ammonia-lyase (EC 4.3.1.2), which deaminates L-threo-3-methylaspartate to produce mesaconate (2-methylfumarate) and ammonia. The reaction is part of the glutamate fermentation pathway via the mesaconate route in anaerobic bacteria. Stoichiometry is balanced: L-threo-3-methylaspartate (C5H9NO4) yields NH3 (NH3) plus mesaconate (C5H6O4). Carbon (5=5), hydrogen (9=3+6), nitrogen (1=1), and oxygen (4=4) all balance.

rxn01169.other_comments: This is glucokinase/hexokinase acting on the beta anomer of D-glucose. ATP phosphorylates glucose at the 6-position to give glucose 6-phosphate, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (phosphate donor) plus glucose yields ADP plus glucose 6-phosphate plus H+, consistent with phosphoryl transfer chemistry.

errors: The reaction as written is unbalanced for oxygen and hydrogen. m-Toluate dihydroxylation by a Rieske dioxygenase incorporates both atoms of O2 into the substrate along with two reducing equivalents (NADH + H+), so the product should be a cis-dihydrodiol with NAD+ released. The product 1,2-dihydroxy-3-methylcyclohexa-3,5-dienecarboxylate accounts for both oxygen atoms, which is consistent, but the proton/charge balance should be checked: NADH + H+ + O2 + m-toluate -> NAD+ + cis-dihydrodiol. With these species the H and charge appear to balance, so the main concern is correct protonation state notation rather than a gross imbalance.
rxn03936.other_comments: This is the toluate/m-toluate 1,2-dioxygenase reaction (aromatic ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase), converting m-toluate to its cis-dihydrodiol using O2 and NADH as electron donor. This is a key step in the TOL plasmid (xylXYZ) degradation pathway. [directionality_note] Dioxygenase reactions consuming O2 and NADH are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the dihydroxylation (forward) direction.

rxn14301.other_comments: This is the L-arginine:taurine amidinotransferase reaction (EC 2.1.4.2), which transfers the amidino group from L-arginine to taurine, producing L-ornithine and taurocyamine (guanidinotaurine). The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced as written: the amidino/guanidino group is transferred from arginine to taurine, leaving ornithine and forming the guanidino derivative of taurine. Stoichiometry is 1:1:1:1 and correct. In vivo, this amidinotransferase reaction proceeds toward taurocyamine synthesis (the direction of guanidino compound biosynthesis, analogous to glycine amidinotransferase forming guanidinoacetate).

rxn02667.other_comments: This is the L-1-amino-2-propanol oxidoreductase reaction (EC 1.1.1.75). The secondary alcohol of (R)-1-aminopropan-2-ol is oxidized to a ketone, yielding aminoacetone. NAD+ accepts a hydride (becoming NADH) plus a proton (H+) is released. Stoichiometry balances: carbon (3C), nitrogen, and redox (2-electron oxidation paired with NAD+ to NADH + H+) are all conserved.

rxn01878.other_comments: This reaction is the phenylacetyltransferase (glutamine N-acyltransferase, EC 2.3.1.14) reaction in which the phenylacetyl group from phenylacetyl-CoA is transferred to the alpha-amino group of L-glutamine, forming alpha-N-phenylacetyl-L-glutamine and releasing free CoA and a proton. This is a key human/primate detoxification pathway for phenylacetic acid (ammonia disposal via phenylacetylglutamine excretion). Stoichiometry is balanced: phenylacetyl group (C8H7O) transferred to glutamine amine, thioester cleaved releasing CoA-SH and H+. Mass and charge balance check out.

rxn03091.other_comments: This is the first methylation step in diphthamide biosynthesis (DPH5 family methyltransferase). SAM transfers a methyl group to the amino group of 2-(3-carboxy-3-aminopropyl)-L-histidine, producing the monomethylated intermediate and SAH plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group transferred from SAM, generating SAH, the methylated product, and a released proton from the amine becoming methylammonio.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the dehydrogenation removes 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) from the substrate. The correct form is 2-Methylbutyryl-CoA + FAD <=> 2-Methyl-but-2-enoyl-CoA + FADH2, with no separate H+ added on the left. Adding an H+ on the substrate side overcounts hydrogens by one.
Hydrogen mass imbalance: as written, left side has substrate plus extra H+ while FADH2 already accounts for the two transferred hydrogens, leaving the equation unbalanced by one hydrogen.
rxn11384.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (2-methylacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) reaction introducing a C2-C3 double bond into 2-methylbutyryl-CoA (from isoleucine catabolism), transferring two hydrogens to FAD to form FADH2. Physiologically it proceeds in the oxidation (forward) direction.

rxn07358.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction (CrtF) in carotenoid biosynthesis of purple bacteria. Rhodopin (1-OH carotenoid) is methylated at its hydroxyl group to form the methoxy carotenoid 3,4-dihydroanhydrorhodovibrin. SAM donates the methyl group, becoming S-adenosyl-homocysteine, with release of a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: transfer of a CH3 group from SAM to the carotenoid hydroxyl, generating SAH and H+. The enzyme name mentions demethylspheroidene, but the listed substrate is rhodopin; both are analogous hydroxyl-bearing carotenoid intermediates for this O-methyltransferase, so the chemistry is consistent.

rxn08125.other_comments: This is an L,D-carboxypeptidase reaction cleaving the terminal D-alanine from the tetrapeptide stem of an anhydro-N-acetylmuramyl (1,6-anhydroMurNAc) peptidoglycan fragment, yielding the tripeptide plus free D-Ala. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water is consumed to hydrolyze the peptide bond, producing one D-Ala and the tripeptide. Such anhydro-muropeptide processing occurs during peptidoglycan recycling. Hydrolytic peptidase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (hydrolysis) direction.

rxn10625.other_comments: This reaction describes a hydroxymethylpyrimidine kinase using CTP as the phosphate donor. Toxopyrimidine (4-amino-5-hydroxymethyl-2-methylpyrimidine, HMP) is phosphorylated to 4-amino-5-phosphomethyl-2-methylpyrimidine (HMP-P), with CTP converted to CDP and a proton released. Atoms and charges balance: one phosphoryl group is transferred from CTP to the hydroxymethyl group, producing CDP and H+. This is part of the thiamine biosynthesis pathway. Kinase reactions of this type (NTP-driven phosphorylation) are essentially irreversible in vivo, favoring the forward direction.

errors: Volemulose (sedoheptulose) is a 7-carbon ketose sugar; phosphorylation by ATP at the C7 position yields sedoheptulose 7-phosphate. The stoichiometry (ATP + sedoheptulose -> ADP + H+ + sedoheptulose 7-phosphate) is balanced for atoms and charge, so no major stoichiometric error is present. The only concern is nomenclature: 'Volemulose' is an uncommon synonym for sedoheptulose.
rxn01344.other_comments: This is a sedoheptulokinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.14), transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to sedoheptulose to form sedoheptulose 7-phosphate, releasing ADP and a proton. Kinase reactions driven by ATP hydrolysis are strongly exergonic and proceed in the forward (phosphorylation) direction in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric inconsistency: the substrate is named '2-Octaprenyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinol' (octaprenyl = 8 isoprenoid units) but is annotated as having '5 repeating units', which is contradictory; the prenyl chain length descriptor and the explicit unit count should match for both substrate and product
rxn09572.other_comments: This is an S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM)-dependent C-methyltransferase step in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis, transferring a methyl group from SAM to the benzoquinol ring carbon, producing S-adenosyl-homocysteine (SAH) and a proton. The reaction corresponds to the COQ5 (or E. coli UbiE) methylation step. Atom balance for the methyl transfer (CH3 from SAM, leaving SAH + H+) is consistent. The main issue is the ambiguous/contradictory prenyl chain length notation.

rxn06181.other_comments: This is a protein tyrosine kinase reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to a tyrosine residue on a protein substrate, yielding ADP, a phosphorylated tyrosine residue, and a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ATP donates a phosphoryl group to the tyrosine hydroxyl, with release of H+. In vivo, protein kinase reactions are strongly favored thermodynamically due to ATP hydrolysis-driven phosphoryl transfer and proceed in the phosphorylation direction; dephosphorylation is carried out by separate phosphatases.

errors: Mass and atom balance is incorrect. The reaction as written cannot balance. 2,4,5-Trichlorophenoxyacetic acid (C8H5Cl3O3) cleaves at the ether bond to yield 2,4,5-trichlorophenol (C6H3Cl3O) plus glyoxylate (C2H2O3). With one O2 (2 oxygen atoms) and 2 substrate molecules, oxygen and hydrogen do not balance.

Stoichiometry: balanced cleavage of one 2,4,5-T to one trichlorophenol + one glyoxylate requires only 0.5 O2 per substrate molecule (i.e. 1 O2 per 2 substrates), but atom-level checking still fails because cleaving the ether bond and oxidizing the glycolyl side chain to glyoxylate requires additional reducing equivalents/water not shown.
Product name 'Glyoxalate' is a misspelling of 'Glyoxylate'.
Likely intermediate is glyoxylate only after further oxidation; the immediate cleavage product of the side chain is glyoxylate, but cofactors (NADH/FADH2, H2O) are missing.
rxn03718.other_comments: This represents the oxygenase-catalyzed cleavage of the herbicide 2,4,5-trichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4,5-T) to 2,4,5-trichlorophenol plus a two-carbon fragment (glyoxylate), an O2-dependent dioxygenase/monooxygenase step in microbial degradation. Such oxygenase reactions are physiologically essentially irreversible (forward).

errors: The reaction is not balanced for hydrogen. 5-Chloro-1,2,4-trihydroxybenzene (C6H5ClO3) yields Hydroxybenzoquinone (2-hydroxy-1,4-benzoquinone, C6H4O3) plus Cl- plus 2 H+. Reactant H count = 5, product H count = 4 (quinone) + 2 (H+) = 6, so there is a 1 H imbalance.
Charge appears unbalanced: left side neutral (0), right side = 2(+1) + 1(-1) = +1, so a net +1 charge mismatch.
Reductive dehalogenation/dehydrogenation typically requires a redox cofactor or electron acceptor to convert the trihydroxybenzene to the quinone; no oxidant/electron acceptor is shown.
rxn06908.other_comments: This represents the chlorohydroxyquinol dehalogenation step in chlorophenol degradation, where 5-chloro-1,2,4-trihydroxybenzene loses chloride to form hydroxybenzoquinone (2-hydroxy-1,4-benzoquinone). The conversion involves loss of HCl and oxidation of the aromatic ring to a quinone, so atom/charge balance as written is off and the loss of the aromatic OH/quinone formation needs proper accounting.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the conversion of the 13(1)-oxo (keto) group to the divinyl protochlorophyllide isocyclic ring closure does not consume 2 H+ as written; with NADPH + O2 the proton balance is off (typically NADPH + O2 + H+ -> NADP+ + H2O + product for a monooxygenase reaction)

The substrate name in the reaction title (magnesium-protoporphyrin-IX 13-monomethyl ester) does not match the actual listed substrate (13(1)-Oxo-Mg-protoporphyrin IX 13-monomethyl ester); the EC class name appears to describe the prior cyclase step
rxn04154.other_comments: This represents a step in the aerobic Mg-protoporphyrin IX monomethyl ester oxidative cyclase pathway (BchE/AcsF-type chemistry), forming the isocyclic E ring to yield divinyl protochlorophyllide. The oxygen-dependent reaction consumes NADPH and O2. As written it shows oxidation of the 13(1)-oxo intermediate with NADPH and O2 producing water and divinyl protochlorophyllide.

rxn00756.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of choline sulfate by choline sulfatase (choline-sulfatase, EC 3.1.6.6), an arylsulfatase-type reaction. Choline sulfate + H2O yields choline + sulfate. The reaction as written is mass- and charge-balanced: choline-O-SO3- (neutral zwitterion overall as choline is +1 and sulfate ester -1) plus water gives choline+ (cation) and sulfate (SO4 2-) plus H+, balancing charge. As a hydrolysis of a sulfate ester, it is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, typically functioning to liberate sulfate or choline for use as a nutrient source.

rxn11712.other_comments: This is a thioester hydrolysis reaction: linoleoyl-CoA is hydrolyzed by water to yield free linoleate (linoleic acid) plus coenzyme A. The reaction is stoichiometrically and charge-balanced: the thioester bond cleavage releases CoA (with its free thiol) and the carboxylate of linoleate, with a proton released to balance charge. Acyl-CoA thioester hydrolases (acyl-CoA hydrolases/thioesterases) catalyze this essentially irreversible hydrolysis driven by the favorable free energy of thioester bond cleavage.

rxn01132.other_comments: This is maltose phosphorylase (EC 2.4.1.8), which catalyzes the phosphorolysis of maltose. Maltose (Glc-alpha-1,4-Glc) reacts with inorganic phosphate to yield D-glucose and beta-D-glucose 1-phosphate (note the inversion of configuration at the anomeric carbon, which is characteristic of this inverting glycosyltransferase). The stoichiometry is balanced: maltose (C12H22O11) + phosphate (HPO4 / Pi) yields glucose (C6H12O6) + glucose 1-phosphate (C6H13O9P). Mass and charge balance hold when protonation states are properly accounted for.

rxn06509.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 2,2-dialkylglycine decarboxylase (pyruvate-dependent transaminase, EC 4.1.1.64). It performs decarboxylation of 2,2-dialkylglycine yielding a dialkyl ketone and CO2, while transferring the amino group to pyruvate to form L-alanine. The atoms balance: 2,2-dialkylglycine (R2C(NH2)COOH) loses CO2 and the amino group transfers to pyruvate. The proton consumed accounts for the decarboxylation/protonation. This is a coupled decarboxylation-transamination and is physiologically essentially irreversible due to CO2 release.

rxn04737.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction: 2-naphthaldehyde is oxidized to 2-naphthoic acid with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (C11H8O) plus water plus NAD+ yields the carboxylic acid (C11H8O2), NADH, and 2 H+. Atom and charge balance check out (NAD+ accepts a hydride, releasing NADH and the protons accompany the oxidation). Aldehyde dehydrogenases are typically physiologically irreversible, strongly favoring acid formation.

rxn07230.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the 4-phosphate from PtdIns(3,4)P2 to yield PtdIns(3)P plus inorganic phosphate, catalyzed by an inositol polyphosphate 4-phosphatase. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O cleaves the 4-position phosphate ester, releasing one Pi. Mass and charge balance hold (one phosphomonoester removed as Pi). [directionality_note] Phosphatase-catalyzed hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the standard oxidoreductase half-reaction should be written as Dihydrophloroglucinol + NADP+ <=> Phloroglucinol + NADPH + H+; the H+ is missing

Reaction direction as written corresponds to dehydrogenation (oxidation of dihydrophloroglucinol), whereas the physiological enzyme (phloroglucinol reductase) typically catalyzes reduction of phloroglucinol to dihydrophloroglucinol using NADPH
rxn03619.other_comments: This represents the phloroglucinol/dihydrophloroglucinol redox couple linked to NADP+/NADPH. As written it oxidizes dihydrophloroglucinol to phloroglucinol. In vivo, the well-characterized enzyme (e.g., in anaerobic phloroglucinol fermentation by Eubacterium oxidoreducens) runs in the reductive direction: phloroglucinol + NADPH + H+ -> dihydrophloroglucinol + NADP+. A proton should be included to balance the redox reaction.

rxn00563.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of N-amidino-L-aspartate (also known as N-guanidino-L-aspartate or arguably the carbamoyl/amidino derivative) by an amidinohydrolase (arginase-family enzyme), cleaving the amidino group to release urea and yield L-aspartate. Atom and charge balance: substrate carbons (5) + water gives L-aspartate (4 C) + urea (1 C); nitrogens (3 from amidino-aspartate) split as 1 N in aspartate amino group and 2 N in urea; balanced. Hydrolytic amidinohydrolase reactions are strongly exergonic and physiologically essentially irreversible in the hydrolysis direction.

rxn02829.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction transferring an amino group between 2-oxoglutarate/L-glutamate and the substrate pair. The aminotransferase converts 6-Acetamido-3-aminohexanoate (amino donor) to 6-Acetamido-3-oxohexanoate while 2-oxoglutarate is converted to L-glutamate. Stoichiometry is balanced: one amino group transferred, atoms conserved (C, N, O match on both sides). Note: the enzyme name references the 2-oxohexanoate at position 6, but the listed substrate has the keto/amino group at position 3, a minor naming inconsistency. Aminotransferases are generally reversible due to near-equilibrium thermodynamics.

rxn05389.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid (here, branched-chain methyl-branched) biosynthesis. NADPH reduces the 3-oxo (beta-keto) group of 7-methyl-3-oxo-octanoyl-ACP to the 3-hydroxy product, yielding NADP+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (the 2 H from NADPH + H+ are accounted for by the C=O to C-OH reduction). In vivo this fatty acid synthesis reduction proceeds toward the hydroxy-acyl product.

rxn02366.other_comments: This is the homoprotocatechuate 2,3-dioxygenase (3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate 2,3-dioxygenase) reaction, EC 1.13.11.15. It incorporates molecular oxygen into the aromatic ring of homoprotocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate), cleaving it extradiol to form 5-carboxymethyl-2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde. The atom balance is consistent: O2 adds two oxygen atoms during ring cleavage, and one proton is released. Stoichiometry appears correct.

N-Hydroxyarylamine (e.g., phenylhydroxylamine, C6H7NO) and o-aminophenol (2-aminophenol, C6H7NO) are indeed isomers with the same molecular formula, so atom/charge balance is technically satisfied. However, the enzyme name 'hydroxyaminobenzene hydroxymutase' (HAB mutase) specifically catalyzes the rearrangement of hydroxylaminobenzene (phenylhydroxylamine) to 2-aminophenol, so the substrate/product order should be N-hydroxyarylamine (hydroxylaminobenzene) as substrate and o-aminophenol as product.
rxn03684.other_comments: This is an intramolecular rearrangement (mutase reaction) converting phenylhydroxylamine (hydroxylaminobenzene) to 2-aminophenol, a key step in nitrobenzene/aniline degradation pathways in bacteria. Both species share formula C6H7NO, so the reaction is mass-balanced. The physiological direction is from N-hydroxyarylamine to o-aminophenol; as written, the substrate and product are reversed relative to the conventional direction.

rxn03765.other_comments: This is the clavaminate synthase (CAS) reaction, a 2-oxoglutarate/Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenase step in clavulanic acid biosynthesis. Proclavaminate is oxidatively cyclized to dihydroclavaminate (clavaminate), with 2-oxoglutarate decarboxylated to succinate plus CO2 and O2 reduced to water. Atom balance checks: C5H8N2O3 (proclavaminate) + C5H4O5 (2-OG) + O2 yields C5H6N2O3 (dihydroclavaminate) + C4H4O4 (succinate) + CO2 + H2O. Carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and nitrogen all balance.

errors: Carbon imbalance: reactants contain Acetyl-CoA (2 C in acyl portion) + 3 Malonyl-CoA (3 C each in acyl/malonyl portion). Octanoyl-CoA has an 8-carbon acyl chain. Counting acyl carbons: acetyl (2) + 3x(malonyl contributes 2 C after decarboxylation) = 2 + 6 = 8 C, which matches octanoyl. CO2 release of 3 accounts for the 3 lost carbons. Carbon balance is actually correct.
H balance should be verified but appears consistent with 9 H+ and 6 NADPH consumed producing 3 H2O and 6 NADP.
rxn09421.other_comments: This is a lumped fatty acid synthase reaction producing octanoyl-CoA (C8:0) from acetyl-CoA primer plus 3 malonyl-CoA extender units, with 6 NADPH for reduction and release of 3 CO2 and 3 CoA. Stoichiometry (carbon, CoA, redox) is internally consistent. FAS reactions are strongly thermodynamically driven forward in vivo by NADPH consumption and decarboxylation of malonyl-CoA.

rxn03493.other_comments: This reaction represents the ring-cleavage of 6-chlorohydroxyquinol (6-chlorobenzene-1,2,4-triol, a chlorinated dihydroxy/triol aromatic) by a ring-cleaving dioxygenase (hydroxyquinol 1,2-dioxygenase type), incorporating molecular O2 to open the aromatic ring and yield 2-chloromaleylacetate. The atoms appear to balance: incorporation of two oxygen atoms from O2 cleaves the ring, and the two released protons reflect the carboxylate/keto products. Such intradiol/ortho-cleavage dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, driven by O2 consumption and ring cleavage.

errors: Atom/mass imbalance: a methylation by SAM transfers a CH2 (or CH3) group, but here the carbon chain grows from C56 to C57 with addition of a methyl-derived carbon; however the inclusion of H2O as a substrate is inconsistent with a simple SAM-dependent methyltransferase reaction and is not balanced

Stoichiometry cannot be verified: ACP-bound meromycolic acid intermediates (cis-19-cis-39-C56oyl-ACP and cis-39-C57oyl-ACP) are given as generic placeholders without explicit formulas, so elemental balance of C, H, O, N, S cannot be confirmed
H2O role unclear: SAM-dependent methyl/methylene transfer reactions (e.g., cyclopropane synthase / mycolic acid methyltransferases) typically do not consume water
rxn13481.other_comments: This appears to be a SAM-dependent methyltransferase reaction in mycolic acid (meromycolate) biosynthesis, converting a C56 ACP-bound intermediate to a C57 (additional carbon from SAM methyl group), releasing S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. Such methyltransferase steps are physiologically essentially irreversible in the forward direction due to SAH release.

rxn01186.other_comments: This reaction describes the transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl-phosphate to the N6-amino group (epsilon-amino) of L-lysine, producing N6-acetyl-L-lysine and releasing phosphate plus a proton. Mass and charge are balanced: acetyl-phosphate carries the acetyl group and a high-energy phosphoanhydride bond; cleavage releases inorganic phosphate and transfers acetyl to lysine's side-chain amine, releasing a proton. Atoms balance (C, H, N, O, P) and the net charge is conserved. This is an acetyltransferase using acetyl-phosphate as the acetyl donor, analogous to acetyl-phosphate dependent protein/amino acid acetylation. While written as reversible, the energetically favorable hydrolysis of the acetyl-phosphate anhydride bond tends to drive the acetylation forward in vivo.

rxn09123.other_comments: This represents phospholipase A1 hydrolysis of phosphatidic acid (1,2-didodecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) at the sn-1 position, releasing the sn-1 fatty acid (dodecanoate/ddca, C12:0) and producing the 2-acyl lysophosphatidate (2-dodecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate). The stoichiometry is balanced: water is consumed to cleave the ester bond, yielding a free carboxylate (ddca, as the anion) plus a proton, accounting for charge/mass balance. Phospholipase A1 reactions are hydrolytic and thermodynamically favorable in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn09027.other_comments: This is a galactofuranosyltransferase reaction in LPS O16 antigen biosynthesis (E. coli). UDP-galactofuranose (the galactofuranose donor, written here as UDP-D-galacto-1,4-furanose, i.e. UDP-Galf) transfers a galactofuranosyl unit onto the growing undecaprenyl-PP-linked oligosaccharide acceptor (glucosyl-O-acetyl-rhamnosyl-GlcNAc-undecaprenyl diphosphate), releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one sugar unit transferred from nucleotide-sugar to acceptor with release of UDP. The transferred galactose is retained in the furanose form. Glycosyltransferase reactions of this type are essentially irreversible due to the energy of the UDP-sugar bond.

rxn10966.other_comments: This represents a thioredoxin-dependent nitrate reductase reaction, reducing nitrate to nitrite using reduced thioredoxin (trdrd) as electron donor, oxidizing it to trdox. Stoichiometry is balanced: nitrate (NO3-) plus 2 H+ and 2 electrons from trdrd yields nitrite (NO2-) plus H2O. Charge and mass balance check out (N:1, O:3 left vs O:1+2=3 right; H:2 left, 2 in H2O right). Nitrate assimilation/reduction is strongly favored thermodynamically in the reductive direction.

rxn13795.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing 3-aminopropanaldehyde (3-aminopropionaldehyde) to beta-alanine. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (C3H7NO) plus H2O plus NAD+ yields the carboxylic acid beta-alanine (C3H7NO2) plus NADH plus H+. Mass and charge balance check out (oxygen from water added, two electrons and one proton transferred to NAD+, one H+ released). NAD+-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenases are essentially irreversible in vivo, strongly favoring oxidation of the aldehyde to the carboxylate.

errors: Stoichiometric inconsistency: the reaction as written shows transfer of lysine to phosphatidylglycerol but loses one acyl (isoheptadecanoyl) group from the diacyl substrate (Diisoheptadecanoylphosphatidylglycerol -> Isoheptadecanoyllysylphosphatidylglycerol), which is not accounted for; a free fatty acid or acyl-bearing product is missing

Mass/atom imbalance: lysine addition via aminoacyl-tRNA-independent or tRNA-dependent mechanism is not consistent with direct ATP -> AMP + PPi activation as written without a tRNA or carrier; the lysylation of phosphatidylglycerol normally uses Lys-tRNA(Lys), not free lysine plus ATP directly
Product name spelling: 'Isoheptadecanoyllysylphophatidylglycerol' is misspelled (phophatidyl)
rxn10328.other_comments: This represents synthesis of lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (Lys-PG), a membrane lipid modification. The biological aminoacylation of PG is typically catalyzed by MprF using Lys-tRNA(Lys), not free lysine + ATP directly. As written the carbon/acyl balance does not close because the di-acyl PG appears to become a mono-acyl lysyl-PG without releasing the second acyl chain.

rxn08128.other_comments: This is an amylomaltase (4-alpha-glucanotransferase) reaction. Maltose (Glc2) plus maltopentaose (Glc5) yields D-glucose (Glc1) plus maltohexaose (Glc6). The transferase moves a glucosyl unit from the donor to the acceptor: maltose donates a glucose to maltopentaose, extending it to maltohexaose and releasing free glucose. Carbon balance checks out (2+5 = 7 = 1+6 glucose units), and glycosidic bonds are conserved. Such glucanotransferase reactions are freely reversible.

rxn11079.other_comments: This is the cystathionine beta-lyase (cystathionine gamma-lyase reverse / cystathionine beta-lyase) type reaction. Cystathionine is hydrolyzed with water to yield cysteine, 2-oxobutyrate (alpha-ketobutyrate), and ammonia. The reaction is balanced: cystathionine (C7H14N2O4S) + H2O yields cysteine (C3H7NO2S) + 2-oxobutyrate (C4H5O3-, or C4H6O3) + NH3 + H+. Atoms and charges balance with the H+ released. This is the L-cystathionine gamma-lyase (CGL/CSE) cleavage producing cysteine, alpha-ketobutyrate, and ammonia.

errors: Atomic imbalance: HCN (CHN) + Thioglycol/2-mercaptoethanol (C2H6OS) gives C3H7NOS on the left; products H+ + Ethanol (C2H6O) + Thiocyanate (SCN-, CNS) give C3H7NOS with charge -1 on right vs neutral left, so charge is unbalanced by the explicit H+. Counting: left has 7 H (1 from HCN + 6 from thioglycol), right has H+ (1) + ethanol (6 H) = 7 H, balanced for H; carbons: 1+2=3 left, 2+1=3 right OK; N 1=1 OK; O 1=1 OK; S 1=1 OK. Charge: left 0, right = +1 (H+) plus -1 (thiocyanate) = 0, balanced. Reaction is actually balanced.
rxn03524.other_comments: This is a sulfurtransferase (rhodanese-type) reaction transferring sulfur from 2-mercaptoethanol (thioglycol) to cyanide, producing thiocyanate and ethanol. Mass and charge balance check out when thiocyanate is treated as the anion balancing the H+. The cyanide-to-thiocyanate detoxification reaction is thermodynamically favorable and typically proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn05188.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction for ferrichrome (a siderophore). It is written as a transport reaction where ferrichrome appears on both sides, representing the same metabolite in different compartments (e.g., extracellular/periplasm to cytoplasm). The energy is provided by ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Phosphate + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP hydrolysis with water yields ADP, inorganic phosphate, and a proton, and ferrichrome is conserved across compartments. The reaction as displayed lacks explicit compartment annotations, but the intent is clear.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides without compartment designations, making it appear as a null reaction; a proper proton symport transport reaction must specify two compartments, e.g., H+[e] + 3-Hydroxyisobutyrate[e] <=> H+[c] + 3-Hydroxyisobutyrate[c]
rxn12561.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction for 3-hydroxyisobutyrate (3-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoate). The metabolite mass and charge balance are trivially satisfied since the same species appear on both sides, but the lack of compartment labels means no actual transport is represented. Transport via proton symport is typically reversible thermodynamically but driven by the proton motive force in vivo.

rxn13489.other_comments: This is the 2-methylcitrate synthase reaction (PrpC), the first step of the methylcitrate cycle for propionate catabolism. Propionyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate, and water hydrolyzes the resulting thioester intermediate to release CoA and form 2-methylcitrate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: left side has Propionyl-CoA (carrying the propionyl group) plus oxaloacetate (4C) yielding the 7-carbon 2-methylcitrate, with CoA and H+ released. Analogous to citrate synthase, the highly exergonic thioester hydrolysis drives the reaction essentially irreversibly in the synthesis direction in vivo.

rxn02820.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of a galactose moiety from UDP-galactose to a galactosylceramide (cerebroside, a monogalactosylceramide), producing UDP and digalactosylceramide (galabiosylceramide). This is catalyzed by a galactosyltransferase. The stoichiometry is balanced: UDP-galactose donates one galactose unit, leaving UDP, while the acceptor cerebroside gains one galactose to become digalactosylceramide. Glycosyltransferase reactions using sugar nucleotide donors are thermodynamically favorable due to the energy released upon cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The product should be D-ribose-5-phosphate only if the transferred two-carbon unit comes off correctly; sedoheptulose-7-phosphate (7C) minus a glycolaldehyde unit (2C) yields a 5-carbon aldose, which is correct as ribose-5-phosphate, so carbon balance holds (7 = 5 + 2)
Stoichiometrically the reaction is balanced for the transketolase half-reaction (TPP carbanion accepts the glycolaldehyde unit forming 2-(1,2-dihydroxyethyl)-TPP)
rxn04678.other_comments: This is the first half-reaction of transketolase (EC 2.2.1.1). Sedoheptulose-7-phosphate donates a 2-carbon (glycolaldehyde) unit to TPP, forming the 2-(1,2-dihydroxyethyl)-TPP intermediate and releasing ribose-5-phosphate. Carbon count balances (7C = 5C + 2C). Transketolase reactions are freely reversible in vivo as part of the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway.

rxn01423.other_comments: This is the aminotransferase (transaminase) reaction transferring an amino group between L-2-aminoadipate and 2-oxoglutarate to yield 2-oxoadipate and L-glutamate. The reaction is balanced: both sides have matching carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. Aminotransferases use pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP) as cofactor; PLP is typically omitted as it is tightly bound and regenerated. The enzyme (e.g., AADAT/2-aminoadipate aminotransferase) operates in lysine degradation, converting 2-aminoadipate to 2-oxoadipate. Like most transaminases, it is freely reversible, though physiologically it often runs toward 2-oxoadipate formation in lysine catabolism.

rxn01074.other_comments: This is the UDP-xylose pyrophosphorylase (UTP:alpha-D-xylose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase, EC 2.7.7.11) reaction. UTP reacts with alpha-D-xylose 1-phosphate to form UDP-xylose plus pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: a uridylyl group (UMP) is transferred to the xylose-1-phosphate, releasing pyrophosphate. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn01972.other_comments: This is the N-acetyl-LL-2,6-diaminopimelate deacetylase reaction (EC 3.5.1.47) in the acetylase pathway of lysine/DAP biosynthesis. Hydrolysis of the N-acetyl group yields acetate and LL-2,6-diaminopimelate. The atoms balance: the acetyl-amide is cleaved by water into a free amine plus acetate. As a hydrolytic amidohydrolase reaction, it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (hydrolysis) direction in vivo.

rxn01733.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA ligase reaction forming itaconyl-CoA from itaconate and CoA, using ITP (the inosine analog of ATP) which is hydrolyzed to IDP and orthophosphate. The atoms balance: itaconate carboxyl is activated, CoA thiol forms the thioester, and the ITP gamma-phosphate is released as inorganic phosphate while IDP is produced. Stoichiometry of phosphate, CoA, and the thioester product is consistent. Note that NTP:NDP + Pi cleavage of this type is typical of CoA ligases of the ADP-forming class (here using IDP instead of ADP).

errors: The transported Ca2+ should appear on both sides with a compartment distinction (e.g., Ca2+[cytosol] -> Ca2+[extracellular]); as written, Ca2+ appears identically on both sides and cancels out, making the transport meaningless without compartment labels
Charge and mass balance cannot be fully verified without compartment annotation, but the ATP hydrolysis component (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) is balanced
rxn10447.other_comments: This is an ABC-type primary active transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis to Ca2+ translocation across a membrane. The chemistry of ATP hydrolysis is correct, but the reaction as written lacks compartment identifiers for Ca2+, so the actual vectorial transport is not represented. ATP-driven transporters are effectively irreversible in vivo, driving Ca2+ movement against its gradient.

errors: Electron/charge imbalance: the standard fatty acyl-CoA desaturase reaction requires 2 electrons from NAD(P)H plus 2 H+ to reduce O2 to 2 H2O. With NADPH providing a hydride (effectively 2 electrons and 1 H+) the proton stoichiometry should be NADPH + O2 + H+ -> NADP+ + 2 H2O (the substrate provides the other 2 H). As written with 2 H+, the equation is not charge-balanced: left side net charge differs from right side by +1.
rxn09460.other_comments: This is a stearoyl-CoA desaturase-type reaction introducing a cis double bond into myristoyl-CoA (C14:0) to give tetradecenoyl-CoA (C14:1), consuming O2 and NADPH. Atom balance for C/N/P is fine; the issue is the H+/charge balance. Desaturation is essentially irreversible in vivo (O2-dependent oxidation), so it proceeds in the forward direction.

rxn03655.other_comments: This is the cis-dihydrodiol dehydrogenase step in styrene/aromatic degradation pathways. Styrene cis-glycol (cis-1,2-dihydroxy-3-vinylcyclohexa-3,5-diene) is oxidized/rearomatized by NAD-dependent dehydrogenase to yield 3-vinylcatechol, NADH, and H+. The reaction is balanced: the cis-diol loses 2 hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+ giving NADH, one as a proton) upon dehydrogenation/aromatization. Atom and charge balance are consistent. In vivo this catabolic dehydrogenation proceeds essentially irreversibly toward catechol formation, driven by aromatization.

rxn02039.other_comments: This reaction represents the delta4-3-ketosteroid reductase (5beta-reductase) reaction in the cortisol catabolism direction, written in reverse. Cortisol contains a delta4 double bond (4-pregnene-11beta,17alpha,21-triol-3,20-dione), and 5beta-Pregnane-11beta,17alpha,21-triol-3,20-dione (5beta-dihydrocortisol) is the saturated 5beta-reduced product. The forward written direction reduces NADP-dependent oxidation of the saturated steroid to cortisol, but in vivo the 5beta-reductase (AKR1D1) catalyzes the irreversible reduction of the delta4 double bond using NADPH, i.e., Cortisol + NADPH + H+ -> 5beta-dihydrocortisol + NADP. Thus the physiological direction is the reverse of how this equation is written. Stoichiometry is balanced (2 H added across the double bond accounted for by NADPH + H+).

errors: Hydrogen atoms are unbalanced: the oxidation of a secondary alcohol (4-hydroxy-L-proline) to a ketone (4-oxoproline) releases only 1 H+ along with NADH, not 2 H+. The reaction as written shows 2.0 H+ on the product side, which violates proton/charge balance.
Charge balance is incorrect as a consequence of the extra proton.
rxn04944.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent oxidation of the 4-hydroxyl group of 4-hydroxy-L-proline to a 4-oxo (keto) group, producing NADH. The correct balanced form should be: NAD+ + 4-hydroxy-L-proline -> NADH + H+ + 4-oxoproline. In vivo, NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase reactions of this type typically proceed in the oxidative (forward) direction driven by NADH consumption downstream.

errors: Charge and hydrogen imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance protons. For a monooxygenase reaction, the correct form is Estradiol + NAD(P)H + H+ + O2 -> 2-OH-Estradiol + NAD(P)+ + H2O; the cofactor here is typically NADPH rather than NADH for cytochrome P450 estrogen 2-hydroxylase (CYP1A1/CYP1B1)
Cofactor likely incorrect: estradiol 2-hydroxylation in vivo uses NADPH (via P450 reductase), not NADH
rxn02214.other_comments: This is an aromatic hydroxylation (monooxygenase) reaction converting estradiol to 2-hydroxyestradiol (2-OH-estradiol). One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate as a hydroxyl group and the other is reduced to water, consuming reducing equivalents. Such P450-catalyzed oxygenations are physiologically irreversible.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (H+ + L-Lactate) on both sides with no compartment annotation, making it appear as a null reaction. For a proper transport reaction, the metabolites should be assigned to distinct compartments, e.g., H+[c] + L-Lactate[c] <=> H+[e] + L-Lactate[e].

The reaction name indicates a 'proton antiport' but the stoichiometry written shows symport-like behavior (both H+ and L-Lactate would move in the same direction). A true antiport would have H+ and L-Lactate moving in opposite directions.
rxn10818.other_comments: This is intended to be a transmembrane transport reaction moving L-lactate out of the cell coupled with proton movement. The chemical formula is balanced trivially (same species both sides), but without compartment tags the reaction is meaningless as written. The name says antiport but lactate-proton transporters (e.g., monocarboxylate transporters) are typically symporters; the mechanism described should be clarified.

errors: Charge and mass imbalance: two molecules of glucose-1-phosphate (each C6H11O9P, with phosphate) contain 2 phosphate groups, but the products D-glucose (C6H12O6, no phosphate) plus glucose-1,6-bisphosphate (2 phosphates) account for the phosphates; however the carbon count is unbalanced - reactants have 12 carbons (2 x C6) while products have 12 carbons (6 + 6), so carbon balances, but hydrogen/charge with 2 H+ is questionable
The 2.0 H+ on the reactant side appears unnecessary/unbalanced for this phosphotransfer reaction

The enzyme name indicates a phosphotransferase transferring a phosphate from one glucose-1-phosphate to another, which would yield glucose-1,6-bisphosphate + free glucose (after dephosphorylation); but a direct phosphotransfer should give glucose-1,6-bisphosphate + glucose, not requiring added protons
rxn00705.other_comments: This reaction represents a phosphotransferase where one glucose-1-phosphate donates its phosphate to the 6-position of another glucose-1-phosphate, producing alpha-D-glucose-1,6-bisphosphate and releasing D-glucose. The phosphotransfer logic is sound, but the inclusion of 2 H+ on the substrate side is not properly balanced for this group-transfer reaction.

rxn02778.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction where T3 (3,5,3'-triiodothyronine) transfers its amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and the keto-acid analog 3,5,3'-triiodothyropyruvate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the amino group from T3 is transferred to 2-oxoglutarate forming glutamate, while T3's alpha-carbon becomes a keto group. Atom and charge balance are maintained in this classic aminotransferase mechanism. Thyroid hormone aminotransferases catalyze this as part of thyronine catabolism.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass/atom balanced. 4-Hydroxybutyryl-CoA (C4 acyl portion C4H7O2-CoA) dehydration should yield crotonyl-CoA (trans-2-butenoyl-CoA) or vinylacetyl-CoA (3-butenoyl-CoA) plus water. The enzyme 4-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydratase actually produces crotonyl-CoA (2-butenoyl-CoA) via a radical mechanism, with vinylacetyl-CoA (3-butenoyl-CoA) as an intermediate; '3-Butenoyl-CoA' is a synonym for vinylacetyl-CoA so the product naming may be acceptable, but the canonical net product is crotonyl-CoA.
rxn03642.other_comments: This represents 4-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydratase, which removes water from 4-hydroxybutyryl-CoA. The atoms do balance for a simple dehydration (loss of H2O), so stoichiometry is essentially correct; my main concern is the product identity. The enzyme is bifunctional (dehydratase/vinylacetyl-CoA delta-isomerase), interconverting vinylacetyl-CoA (3-butenoyl-CoA) and crotonyl-CoA.

rxn01181.other_comments: This is the cinnamoyl-CoA reductase (CCR) reaction. 4-Coumaroyl-CoA is reduced by NADPH to p-coumaraldehyde (4-hydroxycinnamaldehyde), releasing free CoA and NADP+. The reaction is balanced: charges, carbon, and the thioester-to-aldehyde conversion with hydride transfer from NADPH are consistent. Stoichiometry is correct. [directionality_note] In vivo this reductive direction (producing p-coumaraldehyde) is favored as part of the monolignol biosynthesis pathway

rxn02323.other_comments: This represents an intradiol/ring-cleavage dioxygenase reaction where molecular oxygen cleaves the aromatic ring of pyrogallol (1,2,3-trihydroxybenzene), incorporating both oxygen atoms. Dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to O2 consumption and ring cleavage.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: conversion of 2-hydroxy-vitamin K (the 2-hydroxy-2,3-dihydronaphthoquinone hydrate intermediate) to vitamin K1 2,3-epoxide (vitamin K1 oxide) involves loss/rearrangement of water, but the reaction as written pairs it with reduction of oxidized DTT to DTT (which requires adding 2 H), making redox and atom balance inconsistent

rxn04063.other_comments: This appears to be a step in the vitamin K cycle, where a 2-hydroxy-2,3-dihydronaphthoquinone (vitamin K hydrate intermediate) is dehydrated to vitamin K 2,3-epoxide (vitamin K oxide). DTT/oxidized DTT are commonly used as artificial thiol redox partners in VKOR assays. I understand the reaction couples a thiol oxidation/reduction to a vitamin K oxide interconversion.

rxn03975.other_comments: This is an FMNH2:NADP+ oxidoreductase reaction (EC 1.5.1.-). FMNH2 (reduced flavin mononucleotide) transfers a hydride to NADP+ to form NADPH and FMN (oxidized flavin mononucleotide). The stoichiometry is balanced: NADP+ + FMNH2 yields NADPH + FMN + H+. Both atoms and charge balance, since FMNH2 carries 2 H more than FMN, with one H going to NADPH (as hydride) and one released as H+. NADP is interpreted as NADP+. This flavin reductase activity is physiologically reversible depending on the NADPH/NADP+ ratio, though in many systems it operates to reduce flavin (i.e., reverse as written, consuming NADPH).
