This is a retro-aldol/aldolase-type reaction analogous to enzymes in aromatic compound degradation (e.g., HpaI/HpcH family). Such aldolases are typically reversible, though physiologically they often operate in the cleavage (degradative) direction.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is incorrect; the cyclization of 5-formiminotetrahydrofolate to 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate with release of ammonia does not consume 2 protons. The balanced reaction is 5-formiminotetrahydrofolate + H+ <=> 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate + NH3 (releasing NH4+ if a proton is consumed, or NH3 with no net proton change). Including 2.0 H+ on the substrate side leaves the equation unbalanced in charge and hydrogen.
rxn01654.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by formimidoyltetrahydrofolate cyclodeaminase (EC 4.3.1.4), which converts 5-formiminotetrahydrofolate to 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate, releasing ammonia. In vivo it proceeds in the deaminating/cyclizing direction as part of histidine degradation. The proton balance as written is incorrect (should involve one proton, not two).

rxn10276.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to a monoglucosyl-diacylglycerol (with isotetradecanoyl/iso-C14 acyl chains), producing diglucosyl-diacylglycerol and UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose, releasing UDP, and adding one glucose to the monoglucosyl substrate to form the diglucosyl product.

rxn04073.other_comments: This is the glycine N-acyltransferase (GLYAT) reaction where phenylacetyl-CoA transfers its phenylacetyl group to the amino group of glycine, producing phenylacetylglycine and releasing free CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: the thioester bond cleavage releases CoA, and a proton is released upon amide bond formation with the glycine amino group. This is a Phase II conjugation/detoxification reaction; in vivo it proceeds in the direction of phenylacetylglycine formation (excretion product), driven by the favorable hydrolysis of the high-energy thioester bond.

rxn03129.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA oxidase / dehydrogenase step in peroxisomal bile acid synthesis (DHCA pathway). The trihydroxycholestanoyl-CoA oxidase (ACOX2) introduces a double bond at the 24,25 position of 3alpha,7alpha-dihydroxy-5beta-cholestanoyl-CoA, reducing FAD to FADH2. Stoichiometry is balanced: one dehydrogenation removes two hydrogens (one H from C24 and C25), captured by FAD to form FADH2 and the cholest-24-enoyl-CoA. Note the product double bond is more correctly the 24,25-unsaturated species (delta-24); the naming 'cholest-24-enoyl' is consistent. In vivo this flavoprotein oxidase reaction proceeds in the forward direction toward the unsaturated product.

rxn04844.other_comments: This represents the 12-lipoxygenase reaction, where arachidonate (C20H31O2-, arachidonic acid carboxylate) is oxygenated by molecular O2 to form 12(R)-HPETE (12(R)-hydroperoxy-eicosatetraenoate). Stoichiometry is balanced: arachidonate (C20H31O2) plus O2 yields the hydroperoxide product (C20H31O4) - both carbon (20) and the added two oxygen atoms are accounted for, and hydrogen/charge are conserved as a peroxidation/dioxygenation. Lipoxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to incorporation of O2 and the thermodynamically favorable oxygenation. Note: most mammalian 12-lipoxygenases produce 12(S)-HPETE; the 12(R) stereochemistry is characteristic of specific isoforms (e.g., epidermal 12R-LOX).

rxn00554.other_comments: This reaction is a CTP-dependent phosphorylation of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, analogous to phosphofructokinase but using CTP instead of ATP as the phosphate donor. The stoichiometry is balanced: CTP donates a phosphate group, producing CDP and the bisphosphate, with release of one H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly. The phosphoryl transfer to fructose-6-phosphate is highly exergonic and physiologically committed, so in vivo it runs essentially irreversibly in the forward direction.

errors: Incorrect cofactor/mechanism: biotin synthase does not use NAD/NADH; it is a radical SAM enzyme that uses S-adenosylmethionine (SAM/AdoMet) and a [2Fe-2S] cluster as the sulfur source.
Incorrect sulfur donor: free H2S is not the physiological sulfur source; the sulfur is derived from an iron-sulfur cluster of the enzyme.
Incorrect substrates/products: the true reaction consumes 2 SAM and produces 2 methionine and 2 5'-deoxyadenosine, not ATP/AMP/PPi/NAD.
Stoichiometric imbalance: as written the redox and atom balance does not reflect the actual chemistry (e.g., NAD/NADH inclusion and ATP hydrolysis to AMP + PPi are not part of biotin synthesis).
rxn12868.other_comments: The input is labeled as biotin synthase converting dethiobiotin to biotin (BIOT). While biotin synthase indeed catalyzes the insertion of sulfur into dethiobiotin to form biotin, the cofactors shown (ATP, NAD, H2S) are incorrect. The accepted reaction is: dethiobiotin + 2 SAM + sulfur(from [2Fe-2S]) -> biotin + 2 methionine + 2 5'-deoxyadenosine. The conversion direction (dethiobiotin to biotin) is biologically correct and essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: This reaction as written is not stoichiometrically balanced or mechanistically complete. The conversion of 2,3-oxidosqualene to euphol is a cyclization that does not change molecular formula (both are C30H50O), so atomically it can balance, but euphol is the protostane/euphane-type tetracyclic triterpene product of oxidosqualene cyclase and the KEGG R08376 product should be checked - the canonical cyclization typically yields multiple possible products
No cofactors are consumed in this cyclization, which is correct (oxidosqualene cyclases require no cofactor), so no missing-cofactor error applies
rxn11887.other_comments: This represents an oxidosqualene cyclase-type reaction converting (S)-2,3-oxidosqualene (squalene 2,3-oxide) into the tetracyclic triterpenoid euphol. Both substrate and product share formula C30H50O, so the cyclization is isomerization-like and conserves atoms. In vivo, oxidosqualene cyclase reactions are essentially irreversible due to the large free energy release from polyene cyclization.

errors: Charge and electron imbalance: reducing 2 cob(I)alamin (Cbl) to 2 cob(II)alamin (B12r) is an oxidation requiring loss of 2 electrons, but the reaction as written shows NAD+ being reduced to NADH (which consumes electrons), so electrons do not balance

Direction of redox is reversed: cob(I)alamin -> cob(II)alamin is oxidation, which should be coupled to NAD+ reduction giving NADH, but then no H+ should be consumed on the left; instead the proton stoichiometry and electron count are inconsistent (2 e- released vs 2 e- needed for NAD+ + H+ -> NADH)
Proton/hydride balance issue: a 1-electron oxidation of 2 cobalamins yields 2 electrons but NAD+ + H+ + 2e- -> NADH; the H+ placement appears inconsistent with a balanced half-reaction
rxn00074.other_comments: This is the cob(I)alamin:NAD+ oxidoreductase reaction interconverting cob(I)alamin (Cbl) and cob(II)alamin (Vitamin B12r) with the NAD+/NADH couple. As written, 2 cob(I)alamin are oxidized (each losing 1 electron) to 2 cob(II)alamin, providing 2 electrons to reduce NAD+ to NADH along with one proton. The stoichiometry of cobalamin (2:2) and NAD couple (1:1) is plausible, but care must be taken that the redox direction and proton/electron accounting are internally consistent.

rxn05050.other_comments: This is a generic 5'-ribonucleotide phosphohydrolase (5'-nucleotidase) reaction: a 5'-ribonucleotide (e.g., AMP, GMP) is hydrolyzed by water to release inorganic phosphate and the corresponding ribonucleoside. The stoichiometry is balanced as written for a generic monophosphate substrate (one phosphoester bond cleaved by one water yielding one phosphate and one nucleoside). Because it is a hydrolysis of a phosphomonoester, it is thermodynamically favorable and operates essentially irreversibly in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

errors: The product should be D-sorbitol 6-phosphate (D-glucitol 6-phosphate), but there is a positional inconsistency: L-sorbose 1-phosphate reduction would yield a hexitol phosphate with the phosphate at a position derived from C1 of sorbose. The standard reaction R03234 is NADPH + H+ + L-sorbose 1-phosphate <=> NADP+ + D-glucitol 6-phosphate, so the carbon numbering reversal (C1 of sorbose becomes C6 of glucitol) is actually correct upon reorientation. No true stoichiometric imbalance is evident.
Charge/notation: NADP should be written as NADP+ for clarity, but this is a minor notation issue.
rxn02313.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by sorbitol-6-phosphate 2-dehydrogenase (glucitol-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.140), part of L-sorbose utilization. L-sorbose 1-phosphate is reduced by NADPH to D-glucitol (sorbitol) 6-phosphate; carbon numbering inverts because the molecule is read from the opposite end. Atoms appear balanced.

rxn10450.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter reaction for Cob(I)alamin-HBI (a corrinoid/cobalamin precursor). The reaction couples ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to substrate translocation. Mass and charge are balanced because the transported substrate (Cob(I)alamin-HBI) appears on both sides, representing movement across a membrane between two compartments; the ATP hydrolysis terms are stoichiometrically correct and balanced. ABC import/export driven by ATP hydrolysis is effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Carbon imbalance: hexadecenoyl-CoA (16 carbons in the acyl chain) plus the CoA priming cannot yield 8 acetyl-CoA (16 acetyl carbons) AND consume 7 additional CoA correctly; the acetyl-CoA count and CoA stoichiometry are internally inconsistent for proper beta-oxidation.

Redox/cofactor mismatch: peroxisomal beta-oxidation uses O2 with the acyl-CoA oxidase producing H2O2, but the same reaction should not also generate NADH from the same dehydrogenation step. Mixing 7 O2/H2O2 with 7 NAD/NADH in one lumped reaction double-counts the dehydrogenation steps.

For a monounsaturated substrate (hexadecenoyl-CoA, one double bond), one acyl-CoA oxidase (O2-dependent) step is bypassed/altered by enoyl-CoA isomerase; thus 6 O2 plus 7 NAD does not correctly represent 7 dehydrogenation cycles for a 16-carbon unsaturated chain.
Hydrogen/oxygen and charge balance cannot be verified as consistent given the cofactor double-counting; the 8 H+ produced does not balance against the lumped half-reactions.

Complete oxidation of 16-carbon chain requires 7 cycles producing 8 acetyl-CoA, but each cycle consumes only 1 CoA, so 7 CoA consumed is consistent with 8 acetyl-CoA only if substrate already bears 1 CoA - acceptable - but the oxidase O2 count (should be 7 for fully saturated, fewer for unsaturated) and NAD count are not reconciled.
rxn09469.other_comments: This is a lumped fatty acid beta-oxidation reaction degrading a 16-carbon monounsaturated acyl-CoA (hexadecenoyl-CoA) to 8 acetyl-CoA over 7 cycles. It appears to be a peroxisomal-style formulation (O2 + H2O2 from acyl-CoA oxidase) but inconsistently also includes NAD/NADH. The CoA-in (1 thioester + 7 free) to acetyl-CoA-out (8) bookkeeping is plausible, but the simultaneous use of O2/H2O2 and NAD/NADH double-counts the dehydrogenation steps, and the unsaturation should reduce the O2-dependent oxidation steps by one.

rxn01580.other_comments: This is L-pipecolate oxidase (EC 1.5.3.7), which oxidizes L-pipecolate using molecular oxygen to produce delta1-piperideine-6-carboxylate (also called 2,3,4,5-tetrahydropyridine-2-carboxylate) plus hydrogen peroxide. The reaction oxidizes the C-N bond, releasing 2 electrons/2 protons that reduce O2 to H2O2. Stoichiometry is balanced: L-pipecolate (C6H11NO2) loses 2 H (one from N, one from C6) to form the imine; these reduce O2 to H2O2. Mass and charge balance: left side has O2 + pipecolate anion (-1 charge); right side H2O2 + H+ + piperideine-6-carboxylate (-1 charge), so net charge -1 on both sides.

rxn11838.other_comments: This reaction describes the NAD+-dependent oxidation of 4-hydroxy-5-phenyltetrahydro-1,3-oxazin-2-one to 5-phenyl-1,3-oxazinane-2,4-dione, converting a hemiaminal/alcohol carbon (C4-OH) to a ketone/carbonyl. The oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone with concomitant reduction of NAD+ to NADH plus a proton is stoichiometrically balanced: one hydride and one proton are removed from the substrate. Carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen atoms balance, and charge balances (NAD+ to NADH plus H+).

rxn08409.other_comments: This reaction represents ECA (enterobacterial common antigen) polymerization in the periplasm. The polymerase transfers an ECA trisaccharide repeat unit (GlcNAc-ManNAcA-Fuc4NAc) from the lipid-linked donor (undecaprenyl-diphospho trisaccharide) onto a growing ECA chain carrying x2 repeat units, extending it to x3 repeat units and releasing undecaprenyl/bactoprenyl diphosphate. Stoichiometry of lipid carriers and chain length is consistent: one repeat donor consumed, chain grows by one unit, one undecaprenyl-PP released.

rxn03008.other_comments: This reaction represents 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase / 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type activity. Androstan-3alpha,17beta-diol (5alpha-androstane-3alpha,17beta-diol) is oxidized at the 3alpha position to yield androstanolone (dihydrotestosterone, DHT), which has a 3-keto group and a 17beta-hydroxyl. NAD+ is reduced to NADH + H+. The atom and charge balance is consistent: removal of two hydrogens (oxidation of secondary alcohol to ketone) is accounted for by NADH + H+. Stoichiometry is correct as written.

rxn01092.other_comments: This is the ethanolaminephosphotransferase reaction (EC 2.7.8.1/related), transferring the phosphoethanolamine moiety from CDP-ethanolamine to ceramide to form ceramide phosphoethanolamine (sphingosylphosphoethanolamine-type product) plus CMP. The atom balance works: ceramide-OH + CDP-ethanolamine yields ceramide-O-P-ethanolamine + CMP, releasing a proton. Stoichiometry and charge balance are consistent. CDP-alcohol phosphotransferases are driven forward in vivo by the high-energy CDP linkage and subsequent metabolism.

errors: Stoichiometric/mass imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced. Tyrosine (C9H11NO3) plus O2 converting to dopaquinone (C9H9NO3) plus water (H2O) does not balance for hydrogen and oxygen. Tyrosinase actually catalyzes two distinct steps: (1) monooxygenase hydroxylation of tyrosine to L-DOPA (Tyrosine + O2 + reductant -> L-DOPA + H2O), and (2) oxidation of L-DOPA to dopaquinone (L-DOPA + 1/2 O2 -> dopaquinone + H2O). Combining them, the correct overall reaction is: L-Tyrosine + 3/2 O2 -> Dopaquinone + 2 H2O (or with whole numbers: 2 L-Tyrosine + 3 O2 -> 2 Dopaquinone + 4 H2O). As written with only 1 O2 and 1 H2O it is unbalanced.
rxn01497.other_comments: This represents tyrosinase (monophenol monooxygenase/polyphenol oxidase) activity converting L-tyrosine through L-DOPA to dopaquinone, a key step in melanin biosynthesis. The reaction is physiologically irreversible (oxidation driven by O2 consumption).

errors: The product 'acyl phosphatidylglycerol hexadecanoyl' implies addition of one acyl group to phosphatidylglycerol, but phosphatidylglycerol dihexadecanoyl is already fully acylated (diacyl); the acceptor for the transferred acyl group should be a monoacyl (lyso) phosphatidylglycerol, not the diacyl form, otherwise the acyl balance is inconsistent

Carbon/acyl mass balance appears unbalanced: the single acyl group removed from the 2-acyl-GPE should be transferred to a lyso-PG to form a diacyl-PG, but here the starting PG is already diacyl and the product gains an additional acyl chain (would yield a triacyl species), which is chemically incorrect for a glycerophospholipid
rxn08827.other_comments: This represents a lysophospholipase L2 / acyltransferase reaction where an acyl group is transferred from a 2-acyl-glycerophosphoethanolamine (palmitoyl) onto a phosphatidylglycerol acceptor, releasing glycerophosphoethanolamine (the deacylated GPE). The transacylation logic is understood, but the acyl balance on the PG acceptor/product seems off as written.

rxn07775.other_comments: This reaction describes the NAD-dependent oxidoreductase interconverting 2-formylglutarate (an aldehyde) and (S)-2-(hydroxymethyl)glutarate (a primary alcohol). As written, NADH + H+ reduce the aldehyde to the alcohol, regenerating NAD+. The atoms balance: reduction of the formyl (CHO) group to hydroxymethyl (CH2OH) consumes 2 H (one hydride from NADH plus one proton). This enzyme (EC 1.1.1.291) is part of the nicotinate degradation pathway in Eubacterium barkeri.

rxn09923.other_comments: This represents an L-amino acid ligase (Lal/RizA-type) reaction forming the dipeptide Ala-Trp from L-alanine and L-tryptophan, driven by ATP hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (charge -4) + Ala (neutral) + Trp (neutral) = ADP (-3) + Pi (-2) + H+ (+1) + Ala-Trp dipeptide (neutral); both sides sum to -4. Atom balance for the peptide bond formation (loss of water captured by Pi formation) is consistent. The ATP-to-ADP+Pi cleavage indicates an ADP-forming ligase mechanism.

errors: The substrate and product are named '2-Octaprenyl' but specified as having 5 repeating units, which is internally inconsistent; octaprenyl implies 8 isoprenoid units, not 5. The naming should match the actual chain length (e.g., pentaprenyl for 5 units).
rxn09568.other_comments: This represents a monooxygenase/hydroxylase step in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis, where 2-octaprenylphenol is hydroxylated to 2-octaprenyl-6-hydroxyphenol. The use of 0.5 O2 reflects incorporation of one oxygen atom from molecular oxygen into the hydroxyl group. Stoichiometrically, the hydroxylation adds one oxygen atom (consistent with 0.5 O2). However, typical monooxygenase reactions also require a reductant (e.g., NADH/NADPH) and produce water; this reaction as written omits the reducing cofactor and any water product, making the mass/redox balance incomplete.

errors: The product name in the reaction string (Neoabietadiene) does not match the enzyme annotation, which specifies ent-abieta-8(14),12-diene as the product
Substrate specificity mismatch: enzyme is annotated for ent-Copalyl-diphosphate but the reaction lists generic Copalyl diphosphate (stereochemistry not specified)
Charge/mass balance cannot be fully verified due to ambiguous product identity, but a simple intramolecular cyclization releasing PPi should be balanced if the correct diterpene is used
rxn04177.other_comments: This is a class II/I diterpene synthase-type reaction where copalyl diphosphate undergoes ionization and cyclization with loss of diphosphate to form a tetracyclic/tricyclic diterpene. The released diphosphate makes this effectively irreversible in vivo. The main concern is the inconsistency between the named product (Neoabietadiene) and the enzyme's stated product (ent-abieta-8(14),12-diene).

rxn01951.other_comments: This is the ManNAc kinase reaction (part of NagK/sialic acid metabolism). ATP phosphorylates N-acetyl-D-mannosamine at the 6-position, producing N-acetylmannosamine 6-phosphate, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge: ATP + ManNAc yields ADP + H+ + ManNAc-6-P. Kinase reactions of this type, with ATP-driven phosphoryl transfer, are strongly exergonic and proceed in the phosphorylation (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02726.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP4F)-catalyzed omega-hydroxylation of leukotriene B4 (LTB4) at C20, producing 20-hydroxy-LTB4. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + LTB4 -> H2O + NADP+ + 20-OH-LTB4. One atom of molecular oxygen is incorporated into the substrate as the hydroxyl group, the other is reduced to water using reducing equivalents from NADPH. This is a monooxygenase reaction.

rxn12170.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of (+)-bornyl diphosphate by a phosphohydrolase, yielding pyrophosphate (PPi), a proton, and (+)-borneol (d-borneol). The stoichiometry is balanced: water cleaves the diphosphate ester bond, releasing PPi and the free monoterpene alcohol. Mass and charge balance check out, with the proton accounting for charge balance. Hydrolytic cleavage of a high-energy phosphoanhydride/phosphoester is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn02429.other_comments: This is the 2-dehydro-3-deoxygalactonokinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.58), part of the De Ley-Doudoroff pathway for D-galactonate catabolism. ATP phosphorylates 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-galactonate at the C6 position to form 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-galactonate 6-phosphate, producing ADP and a proton. The reaction is balanced: the phosphate transfer from ATP accounts for the new phosphate group on the product, and the proton release is consistent with kinase chemistry. Atoms and charges balance.

rxn01743.other_comments: This is the hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA:shikimate hydroxycinnamoyltransferase (HCT) reaction in the phenylpropanoid/lignin biosynthesis pathway. 4-Coumaroyl-CoA transfers its coumaroyl group to the hydroxyl of shikimate, releasing free CoA and forming 4-coumaroylshikimate (p-coumaroylshikimate). The reaction is balanced: the coumaroyl moiety is transferred intact from the CoA thioester to the shikimate, with one CoA released. Atom and charge balance hold. In vivo the reaction proceeds toward coumaroylshikimate formation as part of lignin/chlorogenic acid biosynthesis, though HCT can act reversibly in vitro.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the reaction shows production of 2.0 H+, but the amide bond formation between sphinganine and hexacosanoyl-CoA (ceramide synthase reaction) releases only CoA and 1 H+, not 2 H+

Misannotation: this is a ceramide synthase (N-acyltransferase) reaction, not a ceramidase reaction; an alkaline ceramidase would hydrolyze ceramide to sphingoid base and free fatty acid, not condense them with acyl-CoA
rxn09606.other_comments: The reaction depicts N-acylation of sphinganine with hexacosanoyl-CoA (C26:0) to form a dihydroceramide (Ceramide-1), releasing CoA. This is mechanistically a ceramide synthase reaction. In vivo it proceeds strongly toward ceramide synthesis (forward) driven by thioester hydrolysis.

rxn04078.other_comments: This reaction (R05846) is part of monoterpenoid indole alkaloid biosynthesis. 4,21-Dehydrogeissoschizine cyclizes to form cathenamine (an iminium intermediate), releasing a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: the substrate loses a proton during the intramolecular cyclization, so H+ appears as a product. Cathenamine has one fewer net positive (or is the neutral form relative to the protonated substrate). The atoms balance with H+ accounting for the difference.

rxn02943.other_comments: This is the CMP-N-glycoloylneuraminate (CMP-NeuNGc) synthase reaction, analogous to CMP-sialic acid synthase. CTP reacts with N-glycoloylneuraminate (NeuNGc) to form CMP-NeuNGc plus pyrophosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the cytidylyl group (CMP) is transferred from CTP to the anomeric carboxyl/hydroxyl region of the sialic acid, releasing PPi and a proton. Charge and atoms balance correctly. Although the chemical reaction is reversible, subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase drives it strongly toward CMP-NeuNGc formation in vivo, hence forward directionality.

errors: Carbon imbalance: Octadecynoyl-CoA (C18 acyl chain) plus 8 acetyl-CoA-generating cycles would yield 9 acetyl-CoA only if fully oxidized, but octadecynoyl is C18 = 9 acetyl-CoA, which is consistent; however the O2/H2O2 stoichiometry is inconsistent with standard beta-oxidation chemistry

Beta-oxidation uses FAD (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase), not O2 directly; production of 6 H2O2 is mechanistically wrong for mitochondrial beta-oxidation (peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase produces H2O2 but the stoichiometry here is unbalanced)
Redox/electron balance inconsistent: for 8 oxidation cycles you need 8 dehydrogenation steps (FAD or O2) plus 8 NAD+ reduction steps; mixing 8 NAD and 6 O2 does not balance the electrons removed
Oxygen atom balance does not close: 8 H2O + 6 O2 (=8+12=20 O on left from these) versus 6 H2O2 (=12 O) on right leaves oxygen unaccounted
Hydrogen/charge balance appears off given the H+ count
rxn09464.other_comments: This represents complete beta-oxidation of an 18-carbon acetylenic fatty acyl-CoA (octadecynoyl-CoA, C18 with a triple bond) into 9 acetyl-CoA. The intent is 8 rounds of beta-oxidation, but the use of O2 to produce H2O2 (peroxisomal-style) combined with NAD/NADH and the given coefficients does not yield a balanced equation in mass, oxygen, or electrons.

rxn10271.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction where UDP-glucose serves as the glucosyl donor, transferring a glucose moiety to monoglucosyl-diacylglycerol (specifically dipalmitoyl) to form the diglucosyl-diacylglycerol product, releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose (leaving UDP) to the monoglucosyl acceptor, yielding the diglucosyl product. UDP-glucose to UDP plus glycoside transfer is correctly balanced for the sugar moiety. In vivo, glycosyltransferases using UDP-sugar donors are strongly driven forward due to the favorable hydrolysis/cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond.

rxn06725.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphorylation of HMG-CoA reductase (NADPH) enzyme by an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), transferring a phosphate group from ATP to a serine residue on the enzyme, producing ADP, H+, and the phosphorylated (inactivated) form of HMG-CoA reductase. This is a regulatory protein phosphorylation event. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP donates a phosphate to the protein substrate, yielding ADP, a proton, and the phosphoprotein. In vivo, protein kinase reactions are essentially irreversible (forward), as the reverse reaction is catalyzed by separate phosphatases via hydrolysis rather than ATP synthesis.

rxn14327.other_comments: This is the CYP7B1-catalyzed 7alpha-hydroxylation of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA/DHA, 3beta-hydroxyandrost-5-en-17-one) to 7alpha-hydroxy-DHEA. The monooxygenase reaction incorporates one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate and reduces the other to water, consuming NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + DHA -> H2O + NADP+ + 7alpha-OH-DHEA. As a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase, this reaction is physiologically irreversible in the forward direction.

errors: Charge and proton imbalance: with NADPH carrying negative charges and CoA/methylmalonyl-CoA also charged, the proton count (3 H+ on left) does not balance correctly for a typical fatty acid synthase elongation step

Methylmalonyl-CoA stereochemistry concern: the (2S)-methylmalonyl-CoA (often the S form) is the substrate used by methylmalonyl-CoA-dependent polyketide/mycocerosate synthases; D-(R)-methylmalonyl-CoA may be incorrect for this elongation

Product naming inconsistency: substrate 'dimethyl lignoceric acid' (C24 dimethyl) extended by a methylmalonyl unit should give a C26+ with three methyl branches; verify the carbon count of 'tri-methyl hexacosanoate' (C26) is consistent with dimethyl-C24 + C2 backbone from methylmalonyl-CoA
rxn10715.other_comments: This represents a mycocerosic-acid-synthase-type elongation: a methyl-branched fatty acid (dimethyl lignoceric acid) is extended by a methylmalonyl-CoA-derived unit using 2 NADPH to reduce the beta-keto intermediate, releasing CO2, CoA, and water, yielding a tri-methyl-branched C26 product. The condensation/decarboxylation and NADPH-driven reduction make this effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Missing proton (H+) on the product side. The glycosyltransferase reaction transfers glucose from UDP-glucose to the diacylglycerol hydroxyl, releasing UDP. A proton should be balanced: UDP-glucose + diacylglycerol -> monoglucosyldiacylglycerol + UDP + H+
rxn10282.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase forming monoglucosyldiacylglycerol (here with two stearoyl/distearoyl C18:0 chains). UDP-glucose donates glucose to the sn-3 hydroxyl of 1,2-diacylglycerol, releasing UDP. The core mass balance (glucose transfer, UDP release) is consistent aside from the proton.

rxn03862.other_comments: This is a sialyltransferase reaction (ST6Gal, EC 2.4.99.1) transferring N-acetylneuraminate from CMP-Neu5Ac donor to the 6-position of the terminal galactose of an N-acetyllactosamine unit on a glycoprotein, releasing CMP and a proton. Stoichiometry and charge balance are correct: the sialyl group is transferred and CMP plus H+ are released. Glycosyltransferase reactions using CMP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Charge imbalance: the left side has 2 H+ giving net charge that does not match the right side; the reaction as written is not properly balanced for H and charge

rxn00037.other_comments: The reaction shown is the hydroxylation/decarboxylation of 6-hydroxynicotinate to 2,5-dihydroxypyridine, a monooxygenase step in nicotinate catabolism (typically using NAD(P)H + O2). The associated name (FAD7 omega-3 fatty acid desaturase) is completely unrelated to this chemistry, indicating a mislabeling. The proper monooxygenase reaction normally consumes O2 plus a reductant (NADH/NADPH) and releases CO2 and H2O; the version given omits the reductant cofactor and water.

rxn03389.other_comments: This is the SAM-dependent O-methylation step in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis, catalyzed by 2-polyprenyl-6-hydroxyphenol methylase (UbiG/Coq3). SAM donates a methyl group to the hydroxyl, producing the methoxy product, SAH, and a proton. The atom and charge balance is correct: the methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to the phenolic hydroxyl yields the methyl ether plus S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a released proton.

rxn06947.other_comments: This reaction represents peptide deformylase (PDF) activity, hydrolyzing the N-terminal formyl group from formyl-methionyl peptides to yield formate and the free methionyl peptide. The stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the formamide bond, releasing formate (HCOO-/HCOOH) and exposing the methionine amino group. In vivo this is an essential, effectively irreversible deformylation step in N-terminal protein maturation in bacteria, mitochondria, and chloroplasts.

rxn01815.other_comments: This is the cinnamaldehyde dehydrogenase (CoA-acylating) reaction, EC 1.2.1.44. The aldehyde (cinnamaldehyde) is oxidized to the CoA thioester (cinnamoyl-CoA) with concomitant reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The atoms balance: cinnamaldehyde (C9H8O) + CoA + NADP+ -> cinnamoyl-CoA (C9H7O-S-CoA) + NADPH + H+. The acyl-CoA forming aldehyde dehydrogenases incorporate CoA and release NADPH and a proton, which is consistent here. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn10435.other_comments: This reaction is part of the AksA/homocitrate synthase-type pathway involved in lysine/coenzyme B biosynthesis (the alpha-aminoadipate or methanogen AAA pathway). 2-oxoheptanedioic acid (2-oxopimelate/alpha-ketopimelate) condenses with acetyl-CoA and water to form (R)-(homo)3citrate (trihomocitrate), releasing CoA and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: acetyl-CoA contributes a 2-carbon acetyl group, water hydrolyzes the thioester, and CoA plus H+ are released. This is a Claisen-type condensation catalyzed by a homocitrate synthase homolog. Note the enzyme name given ('CoA ligase') is misleading since this is a synthase/condensation, not an ATP-dependent ligation.

rxn13865.other_comments: This is a transport reaction (proton symport) for 2-oxohexanedioic acid (2-oxoadipate). The reactants and products are identical because compartment labels are not shown, but the reaction represents co-transport of H+ and the substrate across a membrane (e.g., extracellular to cytosol). Stoichiometry is balanced (1 H+ : 1 substrate). Such transport reactions are typically modeled as reversible unless driven by an electrochemical gradient.

rxn10602.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of (R)-sulfolactate (L-sulfolactate / (2R)-3-sulfolactate) to 3-sulfopyruvate, coupled with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The enzyme is (R)-sulfolactate dehydrogenase / sulfolactate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.272 / ComC). The stoichiometry is balanced: removal of two H from the secondary alcohol/CH yields the keto acid 3-sulfopyruvate, with one hydride transferred to NADP+ (forming NADPH) and one proton released. Carbon (C3), sulfur, and charge balance correctly.

rxn10774.other_comments: This is the MurE reaction (UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide synthetase) variant using N-glycolylmuramoyl substrate (as found in Mycobacteria). It adds meso-DAP to the UDP-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-Glu dipeptide, forming the tripeptide via an ATP-dependent amide ligation. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + amino acid + carboxylate donor yields ADP + Pi + H+ + new amide bond product. Charge and atoms balance with one H+ released, consistent with ADP/Pi formation.

rxn02057.other_comments: This reaction is hexokinase-type phosphotransfer where ATP phosphorylates sorbitol (D-glucitol) at the 6-position to yield D-glucitol 6-phosphate (sorbitol 6-phosphate), ADP, and a proton. Note that 'Sorbitol' and 'D-glucitol' are synonyms, so the substrate is the sugar alcohol and the product is its 6-phosphate ester. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: ATP transfers a gamma-phosphate to the C6 hydroxyl, releasing ADP and H+. Kinase reactions coupled to ATP hydrolysis are strongly exergonic and proceed in the phosphorylation direction in vivo.

errors: The chlorine count appears unbalanced: the substrate is named '2,5-Dichloro' (2 Cl) but the carbon skeleton and product naming are inconsistent; the substrate 'carboxymethylenebut-2-en-4-olide' has 6 carbons while the product 'hex-2-enedioate' also has 6 carbons, which is consistent, but proper atom-by-atom balancing of Cl, C, H, and O cannot be confirmed from the names without explicit formulas

Charge balance: the product is written as a dianion (dioate) releasing only one H+, while ring opening of a lactone by water typically yields a hydroxyl/carboxyl; the single H+ release suggests a charge/proton imbalance that should be verified
rxn04650.other_comments: This is a lactonohydrolase (EC 3.1.1.x) reaction analogous to dienelactone hydrolase, where water hydrolyzes (opens) the lactone ring of a chlorinated muconolactone-type compound to give the corresponding open-chain oxo-dicarboxylate. Hydrolytic ring opening of lactones is strongly favored thermodynamically and physiologically driven forward.

errors: Electron/charge imbalance: oxidized minus reduced ferredoxin accounts for only 1 electron, but reduction of O2 to H2O with hydroxylation requires 2 electrons; two reduced ferredoxin (one-electron carriers) should be consumed, producing two oxidized ferredoxin
As written, the H+ stoichiometry (2 H+) does not balance with a single one-electron transfer; with 2 reduced ferredoxin and 2 H+ the proton and electron balance is consistent
rxn11982.other_comments: This is the steroid 11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) reaction converting 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone to 21-deoxycortisol using O2 and electrons from adrenodoxin (ferredoxin). The chemistry (monooxygenase hydroxylation) is correct, but ferredoxin is a one-electron carrier, so 2 reduced ferredoxin are needed per O2 to balance electrons. Mitochondrial P450 hydroxylations are physiologically irreversible.

rxn03340.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing 3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde (homovanillin) to homovanillate, using NAD+ as the electron acceptor with water as the source of the added oxygen. The reaction is balanced: an aldehyde (RCHO) plus H2O plus NAD+ yields a carboxylate (RCOO-) plus NADH plus 2 H+. Mass and charge balance check out (the carboxylate carries a negative charge, accounting for the second proton).

errors: Charge imbalance: the H+ on the left side is incorrect; UDP-glucosyltransferase reactions do not consume a proton. The standard reaction is UDP-glucose + flavonol 3-O-glucoside <=> UDP + flavonol 3-O-sophoroside, with no free H+ required
rxn04619.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.x) transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the 2''-position of the existing glucose on kaempferol 3-O-glucoside, forming sophoraflavonoloside (kaempferol 3-O-sophoroside). Aside from the spurious H+, the glucose/UDP stoichiometry is balanced.

rxn01711.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by beta-pyrazolylalanine synthase (a serine hydro-lyase, EC 4.2.1.50). L-serine condenses with pyrazole, eliminating water, to form beta-(pyrazol-1-yl)-L-alanine, a non-protein amino acid found in cucumber and watermelon seedlings. The atom balance checks out: L-serine (C3H7NO3) + pyrazole (C3H4N2) yields beta-pyrazol-1-ylalanine (C6H9N3O2) + H2O. Carbon: 3+3=6; nitrogen: 1+2=3; matches the product plus water. The reaction is biosynthetic and proceeds in the direction of beta-pyrazol-1-ylalanine formation in vivo (water elimination/condensation is thermodynamically favored as the product accumulates).

rxn12708.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 4-oxalmesaconate hydratase (EC 4.2.1.83), part of the protocatechuate 4,5-cleavage pathway for aromatic compound degradation. The substrate 4-carboxy-2-hydroxyhexa-2,4-dienedioate (4-oxalmesaconate, the enol/hydrated tautomer) undergoes hydration of the double bond by water to yield 4-oxalcitramalate (4-carboxy-4-hydroxy-2-oxohexanedioate / 4-oxalcitromalate). Both substrate and product are C7 dicarboxylic acid intermediates; addition of one H2O accounts for the mass and stoichiometry, which balances correctly.

rxn01408.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of L-carnitinamide (the amide of carnitine) by an amidohydrolase, yielding carnitine and ammonia with consumption of water. The atoms balance: L-carnitinamide (C7H16N2O2) + H2O -> carnitine (C7H15NO3) + NH3. Charges and elements are consistent. As an amide hydrolysis, the reaction is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

errors: The substrate '100-2' is not a properly identified chemical compound; it appears to be a placeholder or incomplete identifier, making full stoichiometric verification impossible.
Without explicit molecular formulas for the aglycone acceptor (100-2) and Urdamycin G, atom and charge balance cannot be definitively confirmed.
rxn04502.other_comments: This represents a glycosyltransferase reaction in which an L-rhodinose moiety is transferred from the activated sugar donor dTDP-beta-L-rhodinose to an aglycone/glycoside acceptor (denoted 100-2), releasing dTDP and producing the angucycline antibiotic Urdamycin G. This is consistent with the urdamycin biosynthetic pathway (e.g., UrdGT enzymes in Streptomyces fradiae).

rxn00429.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD-dependent oxidation of formaldehyde to formate. Mass and charge balance check: Left side - H2O (H2O), NAD+ (charge +1), formaldehyde (CH2O); Right side - NADH (charge 0 in this notation), formate (CHO2-, charge -1), 2 H+. Carbon: 1 on each side (formaldehyde to formate). Oxygen: 1 (H2O) + 1 (formaldehyde) = 2 on left; 2 (formate) on right - balanced. Hydrogen: 2 (H2O) + 2 (formaldehyde) = 4 on left; 1 (NADH transfers H) + 1 (formate) + 2 (H+) = 4 on right - balanced. Charge: left +1 (NAD+); right -1 (formate) + 2 (H+) = +1 - balanced. The reaction is well-balanced.

rxn01999.other_comments: This is a transaminase (aminotransferase) reaction interconverting dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-glucose (dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose) and its 4-amino derivative, dTDP-4-amino-4,6-dideoxy-D-glucose, using the glutamate/2-oxoglutarate amino donor/acceptor pair. The reaction is stoichiometrically and atom-balanced (amino group transferred between the sugar and the C5 dicarboxylate). In the biosynthesis of deoxyamino sugars (e.g., dTDP-D-fucosamine, dTDP-L-vancosamine pathways), the physiological direction is the amination of the 4-keto sugar: L-glutamate + dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose -> 2-oxoglutarate + dTDP-4-amino-4,6-dideoxy-D-glucose. As written, this is the reverse direction.

rxn03228.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction (norcoclaurine 6-O-methyltransferase, 6OMT). It transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to the 6-hydroxyl of the substrate, producing the 6-O-methylated product and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine plus a proton. Norlaudanosoline (tetrahydroxy substrate) is an accepted alternative substrate in addition to norcoclaurine. Stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl transferred, SAM to SAH, with release of H+. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are essentially irreversible in vivo, favoring methyl transfer.

rxn08764.other_comments: This is the ketol-acid reductoisomerase (KARI, IlvC) reaction in the isoleucine biosynthesis pathway. The substrate (S)-2-aceto-2-hydroxybutanoate is reduced and isomerized to (R)-2,3-dihydroxy-3-methylvalerate (2,3-dihydroxy-3-methylpentanoate), consuming NADPH and producing NADP+. Atom and charge balance check out: NADPH provides the hydride and H+ is consumed, yielding NADP+ and the reduced/rearranged product. In vivo this proceeds in the biosynthetic direction toward the product.

rxn04611.other_comments: This is a malonyltransferase reaction transferring the malonyl group from malonyl-CoA to the 6''-OH of the glucose moiety of biochanin A-7-O-glucoside, releasing CoA and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: malonyl group (C3H2O3 portion) is transferred, the thioester bond to CoA is replaced by an ester bond to the glucoside, releasing free CoA and H+. Acyl-CoA-dependent acyltransferases are thermodynamically driven by thioester hydrolysis and operate in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The product cardiolipin should retain all four acyl chains from two phosphatidylglycerol molecules. Two PG molecules each containing C16:0 and C19:0(methylstearoyl) chains would yield a cardiolipin with two C16:0 and two C19:0 chains; the naming 'dihexadecanoyl, dimethylstearoyl' is consistent with this, so acyl-chain balance is acceptable. However, the byproduct should be glycerol (released from one PG headgroup), which is correctly shown. The main concern is whether mass/atom balance fully holds: 2 PG -> CL + glycerol is the canonical bacterial reaction and is balanced.
rxn10678.other_comments: This represents bacterial-type cardiolipin synthase (CLS) from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, condensing two phosphatidylglycerol molecules into cardiolipin with release of one free glycerol. The stoichiometry 2 PG -> CL + glycerol is correct for the prokaryotic PG-dependent CLS mechanism (a phospholipase D-type enzyme).

errors: Atom and charge imbalance: the formation of 1,3-dihydroxy-N-methylacridone from N-methylanthraniloyl-CoA plus 3 malonyl-CoA releases 4 CoA, 3 CO2, but the H/O balance and H+ stoichiometry as written do not balance correctly. The correct ACS (acridone synthase) reaction produces 1,3,5-trihydroxy-N-methylacridone, not the dihydroxy product; the standard reaction is 3 malonyl-CoA + N-methylanthraniloyl-CoA -> 4 CoA + 3 CO2 + 1,3,5-trihydroxy-N-methylacridone. The product name/formula here appears inconsistent with the standard PKS condensation.
rxn05016.other_comments: This is an acridone synthase (type III PKS) reaction: a starter N-methylanthraniloyl-CoA is extended by three malonyl-CoA units with decarboxylation, then cyclized to form the acridone. The decarboxylative Claisen condensations make this essentially irreversible in vivo, hence forward.

errors: The product 'Phthalate' is incorrect for amide hydrolysis; hydrolysis of one amide bond of phthalylamide (phthalamide/phthalimide-type) would yield a phthalic acid monoamide (phthalamic acid) plus the amine, or full hydrolysis would require two water molecules to yield phthalate plus ammonia/amine. As written with a single H2O, the stoichiometry and product identity are inconsistent.

Mass balance cannot be confirmed because 'Substituted amine' and 'Phthalylamide' are generic placeholders without defined R groups, but the loss of only one water while cleaving to a fully free dicarboxylate (phthalate) implies an unaccounted second hydrolysis step.
rxn03503.other_comments: This represents an amidohydrolase cleaving an amide bond of a phthalyl-amide to release phthalate (or phthalamic acid) and the corresponding amine. Amide hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, hence forward direction.

rxn01715.other_comments: This is the amine oxidase (flavin-containing) reaction acting on tyramine. Oxidative deamination: tyramine + O2 + H2O yields 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde + NH3 + H2O2. The stoichiometry is balanced (C8H11NO + O2 + H2O -> C8H8O2 + NH3 + H2O2), with C8, H13, N1, O4 on each side. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven forward by oxidation.

rxn00133.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of P1,P4-bis(5'-adenosyl)-tetraphosphate (Ap4A) by an asymmetrically-cleaving Ap4A hydrolase (e.g., EC 3.6.1.17), yielding ATP and AMP. Stoichiometry is balanced: Ap4A contains two adenosines and four phosphates; cleavage of a phosphoanhydride bond with water gives ATP (one adenosine, three phosphates) plus AMP (one adenosine, one phosphate), with release of a proton. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: Reaction is unbalanced: allantoate carries a net negative charge, so the equation should produce both NH3 (or NH4+) and a proton, or be written with charge balance. As written, hydrolysis of allantoin (C4H6N4O3) with H2O yields allantoate (C4H7N4O4, as the anion C4H6N4O4-) but the nitrogen/atom and charge balance is not satisfied by simply adding one H+.
rxn01748.other_comments: This is allantoinase (allantoin amidohydrolase, EC 3.5.2.5), which hydrolyzes the ureido ring of allantoin to give allantoate. Allantoin C4H6N4O3 + H2O -> allantoate C4H8N4O4 (or its anion + H+). The ring-opening hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively unidirectional in vivo as part of purine catabolism.

rxn04965.other_comments: This is a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase reaction (GA 20-oxidase) converting gibberellin GA44 to GA19. The reaction couples oxidation of the substrate with decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate to succinate and CO2, consuming O2. Atoms balance: 2-oxoglutarate (C5) yields succinate (C4) plus CO2 (C1), with one oxygen atom incorporated and the other forming the hydroxylated/oxidized product or water. The H+ accounts for charge balance. GA20-oxidases catalyze successive oxidations and this step (GA44 to GA19) is one such step.

rxn03920.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic cleavage reaction catalyzed by 2'-hydroxybenzalpyruvate hydratase-aldolase (or trans-o-hydroxybenzylidenepyruvate hydratase-aldolase, EC 4.1.2.45) in the naphthalene degradation pathway. The substrate cis-4-(1'-hydroxynaphth-2'-yl)-2-oxobut-3-enoate undergoes aldol cleavage with water to yield pyruvate and 1-hydroxy-2-naphthaldehyde. Atom and charge balance: the C-C bond cleavage with water addition produces a 3-carbon pyruvate plus the aromatic aldehyde, which accounts for all atoms. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. [directionality_note] In vivo this aldolase operates in the catabolic (degradative) direction toward pyruvate and the naphthaldehyde during naphthalene/PAH degradation.

rxn01548.other_comments: This is the purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) reaction acting on guanosine. Phosphate + guanosine yields guanine + alpha-D-ribose 1-phosphate. The reaction is correctly balanced: guanosine (C10H13N5O5) plus phosphate breaks the N-glycosidic bond to give guanine (C5H5N5) and ribose 1-phosphate (C5H11O8P). Atoms and charges balance.

rxn01386.other_comments: This is an aldose-ketose isomerization between D-lyxose (an aldose) and D-lyxulose (a ketose), both C5 sugars (C5H10O5). The reaction is mass-balanced and stoichiometrically correct (1:1, same molecular formula). Aldose-ketose isomerases (e.g., L-arabinose/D-lyxose isomerase family) catalyze freely reversible reactions near equilibrium; the in vivo direction depends on substrate availability. The reaction as written shows D-Lyxulose to D-Lyxose, but isomerases typically act on the aldose substrate; regardless, it is reversible.

rxn09886.other_comments: This is the cysteine synthase (O-acetylserine sulfhydrylase) reaction using selenide instead of sulfide as the nucleophile, producing L-selenocysteine. O-Acetyl-L-serine + selenide yields acetate + L-selenocysteine, with a proton released. Atoms balance: O-acetylserine (C5H9NO4) plus HSe(-) gives selenocysteine (C3H7NO2Se) plus acetate (C2H3O2-) plus H+. C: 5 = 3+2; N: 1=1; Se: 1=1; charge and O balance check out. The beta-replacement reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven forward by release of the good acetate leaving group.

rxn04849.other_comments: This reaction (R07043) represents the conversion of 15(S)-HPETE (15(S)-hydroperoxy-eicosatetraenoic acid) to 11H-14,15-EETA (an epoxyalcohol, specifically a hepoxilin-type/epoxyhydroxy eicosatetraenoic acid). This is an intramolecular rearrangement catalyzed by hepoxilin synthase / lipoxygenase activity, converting the hydroperoxide into an epoxyalcohol. The reaction is balanced (isomerization with no net atom change, both being C20H32O4). Mechanistically the hydroperoxide is the high-energy substrate that is converted to the more stable epoxyalcohol, so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn12088.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of N-demethylnarwedine to norgalanthamine, a step in Amaryllidaceae alkaloid (galanthamine) biosynthesis. The carbonyl group of the narwedine-type ketone is reduced to a hydroxyl group. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ provides the hydride and proton for reduction of the ketone to the secondary alcohol, yielding NADP+. In vivo, this reductase step proceeds toward the alcohol product (norgalanthamine/galanthamine pathway).

rxn11998.other_comments: This is the GGGP synthase (geranylgeranylglyceryl phosphate synthase, EC 2.5.1.41) reaction, the first committed step in archaeal ether lipid biosynthesis. It transfers a geranylgeranyl group from GGPP to the sn-3 hydroxyl of glycerol-1-phosphate (note: archaea use sn-glycerol-1-phosphate, not the glycerol-3-phosphate stereoisomer used in bacteria/eukaryotes; the input lists Glycerol-3-phosphate, which may be a stereochemical naming issue). The atoms balance: GGPP (C20 diphosphate) + G1P -> ether-linked product + PPi + H+, which is correct. The release of pyrophosphate makes the reaction thermodynamically favorable in the forward (biosynthetic) direction.

errors: The product N2-Acetyl-L-lysine is incorrect; the transamination of N2-Acetyl-L-aminoadipate semialdehyde produces N2-Acetyl-L-aminoadipate (the alpha-aminoadipate derivative), not N2-Acetyl-L-lysine. The carbon/nitrogen balance does not support formation of lysine, which has a different carbon skeleton end-group.
rxn04659.other_comments: This is intended as a glutamate-dependent transamination (aminotransferase) reaction interconverting an aldehyde/keto-acid pair with the L-glutamate/2-oxoglutarate couple. Aminotransferase reactions are generally reversible. However, the listed product appears mismatched: amination of the semialdehyde would yield N2-acetyl-LL-2-aminoadipate, while N2-acetyl-L-lysine would derive from a different (saccharopine/diaminopimelate-type) pathway. As written, the transformation is not a simple, mass-balanced transamination.

rxn07978.other_comments: This is a beta-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase (FabA/FabZ-type) reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis. The (R)-3-hydroxy-cis-9-palmitoleoyl-ACP (C16:1) is dehydrated to form the trans-2,cis-9 enoyl-ACP (here written as trans-3,cis-9, likely a nomenclature/numbering artifact) plus water. The stoichiometry is balanced: removal of one water yields the unsaturated acyl-ACP. In vivo, this dehydration/isomerization step (especially the FabA-mediated branch generating cis double bonds for unsaturated fatty acid synthesis) proceeds in the dehydration direction toward elongation.

rxn06484.other_comments: This represents the PCIF1/CAPAM methyltransferase reaction that converts the 2'-O-methyladenosine cap (Am) at the first transcribed nucleotide into N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am), using SAM as the methyl donor and producing SAH. The cap is correctly written as m7G(5')pppAm becoming m7G(5')pppm6Am. Stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group transferred from SAM, yielding SAH and a proton, consistent with SAM-dependent N6-adenosine methyltransferase reactions.

errors: Electron/stoichiometry balance issue: flavodoxin carries one electron per molecule in its semiquinone form, but NADPH delivers two electrons (a hydride). A balanced reaction typically requires 2 oxidized flavodoxin to accept the 2 electrons from one NADPH: NADPH + 2 flavodoxin(ox) -> NADP+ + H+ + 2 flavodoxin(sq), or 1 flavodoxin if going between oxidized quinone and hydroquinone forms. As written with 1:1 ratio and an H+ on the left, charge/proton balance is questionable.
rxn08519.other_comments: This represents flavodoxin/ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase (Fpr) type chemistry, where NADPH reduces flavodoxin. The enzyme is generally reversible in vitro, but in vivo it predominantly runs in the direction of reducing flavodoxin using NADPH. The main concern is the redox stoichiometry between the 2-electron NADPH donor and the 1-electron-capable flavodoxin redox states.

errors: Stoichiometric inconsistency: forming tetrahydropteroyltri-L-glutamate (3 glutamate residues) from tetrahydrofolate (1 glutamate residue) requires the addition of 2 glutamate residues, which is correct (2.0 L-Glutamate). However, each glutamate addition consumes 1 ATP and produces 1 ADP + 1 Pi, so 2 ATP/2 ADP/2 Pi is balanced. The water needed for hydrolysis is not shown; technically the reaction should include water as a reactant or be balanced with the gamma-glutamyl bond formation. The H+ stoichiometry should be checked: 2 H+ produced is approximately consistent with the ligase mechanism.

Mass/charge balance: as written, water is missing as a reactant; ATP-dependent ligation releasing ADP + Pi typically does not require water explicitly but the amide bond formation releases the equivalent; the overall atom balance for adding 2 glutamate residues with loss of 2 water (condensation) should be verified. The reaction omits the 2 water molecules released during peptide bond formation.
rxn12216.other_comments: This represents folylpolyglutamate synthase adding two L-glutamate residues to tetrahydrofolate (1 glu) to yield the triglutamate form, consuming 2 ATP. The carbon backbone count for added glutamates is correct (1 -> 3 glutamates needs +2). The main concern is the missing water molecules in the condensation/balance. [directionality_note] Folylpolyglutamate synthase reactions are ATP-driven and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo, adding glutamate residues.

rxn02548.other_comments: This reaction describes an O-methyltransferase using S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) as the methyl donor to methylate the 4'-hydroxyl group of apigenin (5,7,4'-trihydroxyflavone), producing acacetin (4'-methoxy derivative) and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). Apigenin (C15H10O5) gains a methyl group to become acacetin (C16H12O5); SAM loses a methyl to become SAH. Mass and charge balance are consistent with the released H+. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of methyl transfer.

rxn07586.other_comments: This reaction represents the cobalt-precorrin-5A acetaldehyde-lyase (hydrolase) step in anaerobic cobalamin (vitamin B12) biosynthesis, catalyzed by CbiG. Cobalt-precorrin-5A is hydrolyzed with water to yield cobalt-precorrin-5B plus the release of acetaldehyde (and the deacylation/ring contraction associated with extrusion of the C-20 fragment as acetic acid in some annotations). The mass balance is approximately consistent: the loss of a two-carbon acetaldehyde unit accompanied by addition of water. In vivo this deacylating/ring-contraction step is part of a committed biosynthetic pathway and proceeds in the forward direction.

rxn11931.other_comments: This reaction represents the PQQ-dependent oxidation of betaine aldehyde to betaine (glycine betaine, BET) by a quinoprotein dehydrogenase. The reaction is balanced: betaine aldehyde (C5H11NO) + H2O is oxidized while PQQ accepts a hydride/two electrons and two protons to form PQQH2 (reduced PQQ), with betaine and a proton released. Atoms balance: C, H, N, O are conserved when accounting for PQQ (C14H6N2O8) becoming PQQH2 (C14H8N2O8), and charge is balanced. Note the enzyme name 'Choline oxidoreductase' typically refers to the choline-to-betaine pathway; betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase activity is the second oxidation step.

rxn00581.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of a galactosyl group from UDP-galactose to sucrose, forming planteose (a trisaccharide: galactose-fructose-glucose) and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one galactose unit is transferred from UDP-galactose to the fructose moiety of sucrose. The reaction is mass-balanced (UDP-galactose + sucrose yields UDP + planteose). Glycosyltransferase reactions using sugar nucleotides as donors are strongly exergonic due to hydrolysis of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, so they proceed in the biosynthetic direction in vivo.

rxn10865.other_comments: This represents the PEP:carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS) for lactose uptake. Extracellular lactose is transported and phosphorylated to lactose-6-phosphate using phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) as the phosphoryl donor, which is converted to pyruvate. Stoichiometry is balanced (one phosphate transferred from PEP to lactose). Although group translocation involves a phosphorelay (EI, HPr, EIIA, EIICB), the net reaction shown is correct. In vivo, the large drop in free energy from PEP hydrolysis coupled to sugar import makes this essentially irreversible in the import/phosphorylation direction.
