However, the water is placed on the wrong side: a C-C bond-forming condensation usually releases water as a product, so the stoichiometry seems inverted.

rxn02608.other_comments: This is a dehydratase (hydro-lyase) reaction. D-Fuconate (a 6-carbon sugar acid, C6H12O6) loses a water molecule to form 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-fuconate (C6H10O5). Mass balance: C6H12O6 = H2O (H2O) + C6H10O5, which checks out for both carbon (6=6), hydrogen (12=2+10), and oxygen (6=1+5). Stoichiometry is correct. This is part of the L-fucose/D-fuconate degradation pathway, where the dehydration step is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward the deoxy-keto acid.

rxn03741.other_comments: This is a flavin-dependent monooxygenase (aromatic ring hydroxylation) reaction. 4-chlorophenol is hydroxylated to 4-chlorocatechol, incorporating one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate while the other oxygen is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: O2 provides two oxygens (one to the ring, one to water), NADPH+H+ provides the reducing equivalents, yielding NADP+ and H2O. Atoms and charges balance.

rxn01249.other_comments: This reaction represents pyridoxine 4-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.65), oxidizing pyridoxine (pyridoxol) at the 4-position to pyridoxal, with NADP+ as the electron acceptor producing NADPH. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: NADP+ + pyridoxine yields NADPH + H+ + pyridoxal. Atoms and charges balance, as the alcohol (CH2OH) is oxidized to an aldehyde (CHO), removing two H (one as hydride to NADP+, one as H+).

errors: Stereochemistry mismatch: substrate is the D-glucose (gluco) configuration at C4 while the product is named as D-galactose (galacto) configuration; an N-acetyltransferase does not epimerize C4, so the product should be dTDP-4-acetamido-4,6-dideoxy-D-glucose unless a coupled epimerase activity is intended
rxn09289.other_comments: This is an N-acetyltransferase transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the C4 amino group of dTDP-4-amino-4,6-dideoxy-D-glucose, forming the acetamido sugar plus CoA and releasing a proton. Carbon, nitrogen, and CoA balance are otherwise consistent. Such acetyl-CoA-dependent acyl transfers are strongly exergonic and physiologically essentially irreversible toward the acetamido product.

rxn13223.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADPH-dependent reduction of 2-methylbutanal to 2-methyl-1-butanol, despite the enzyme name suggesting aldehyde dehydrogenase activity. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (C5H10O) is reduced by NADPH + H+ to the primary alcohol (C5H12O), with NADP+ released. Carbon (5), hydrogen, and oxygen balance, and the redox electron transfer (2 electrons from NADPH) is accounted for. Note that this is functionally an alcohol dehydrogenase/aldehyde reductase reaction. Such NAD(P)-dependent oxidoreductases are generally reversible, though the high cytosolic NADPH/NADP+ ratio typically favors the reductive (alcohol-forming) direction in vivo.

rxn00893.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD+-dependent oxidation of N-Acetyl-D-glucosamine (an aldose) to N-Acetyl-D-glucosaminate (the corresponding aldonic acid). The aldehyde group at C1 is oxidized to a carboxylate, consuming one water and reducing NAD+ to NADH with release of 2 protons. The atoms balance: oxidation of the hemiacetal/aldehyde to carboxylic acid adds one oxygen (from water) and removes two hydrogens (one to NADH, two H+ released net accounting for the dehydrogenation and the dissociation of the carboxylic acid). Charge and mass appear balanced.

rxn00266.other_comments: This is the keto-enol tautomerization of oxaloacetate, interconverting the keto form (2-oxosuccinate) and the enol form (2-hydroxybut-2-enedioate). Both species share the same molecular formula (C4H4O5 in their respective protonation states), so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a 1:1 isomerization. Tautomerizations are inherently reversible, though the keto form is thermodynamically favored at equilibrium; oxaloacetate keto-enol isomerase (EC 5.3.2.2) accelerates this interconversion.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction includes an extra H+ on the product side that is not justified. SAM (net +1) reacting with glutamine (neutral) yields SAH (net -1 or neutral depending on protonation state) plus methylated glutamine. A standard SAM-dependent methyltransfer is: SAM + acceptor -> SAH + methyl-acceptor + H+, so the H+ may actually be balanced; however the listed N5-methyl product implies methylation of the amide nitrogen, which is chemically unusual
rxn12661.other_comments: This represents a SAM-dependent methyltransferase transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to the N5 (amide) nitrogen of L-glutamine, producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine and N5-methyl-L-glutamine. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are generally treated as effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo due to the favorable thermodynamics and removal of SAH.

errors: Atom/charge balance fails as written. Isovaleryl-CoA (C5 acyl) plus 3 malonyl-CoA condensations with decarboxylation builds a polyketide, but the phloroglucinol-type product 3-Methyl-1-(2,4,6-trihydroxyphenyl)butan-1-one requires aldol/Claisen cyclization and loss of water, which is not represented; no H2O appears on the product side.
Proton stoichiometry is inconsistent: type III PKS reactions typically release CoA and CO2 but the 3 H+ on the substrate side do not balance the charge change of releasing 4 CoA thiolate and 3 CO2.

Carbon count should be checked: isovaleryl (C5 acyl, C6 with carbonyl) + 3 x malonyl (each contributes C2 after decarboxylation) = C5+6 = ~C11 product backbone; the named C11 product (C11H14O4) is plausible in carbon count, but the equation lacks the water released during ring formation.
rxn03637.other_comments: This represents a type III polyketide synthase (PKS) reaction: a phloroglucinol synthase using isovaleryl-CoA as starter and 3 malonyl-CoA extenders, with sequential decarboxylative condensation and cyclization to form a phloroglucinol (e.g., a precursor in bitter acid/humulone-type or related biosynthesis). The committed, decarboxylation-driven biosynthetic direction is forward.

errors: Charge and proton balance not explicitly accounted for; at physiological pH the adenylyltransferase reaction typically requires a H+ on the appropriate side to balance, though the core mass balance of nucleotidyl transfer (ATP + sugar-1-P -> ADP-sugar + PPi) is correct
rxn03916.other_comments: This is a nucleotidyltransferase (adenylyltransferase) reaction in which the AMP/adenylyl moiety of ATP is transferred to D-glycero-beta-D-manno-heptose 1-phosphate, producing ADP-heptose and releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). Note the product should be the ADP-D-glycero-beta-D-manno-heptose to match the substrate stereochemistry. In vivo the reaction is driven forward by hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by pyrophosphatase, part of the ADP-L-glycero-beta-D-manno-heptose biosynthesis pathway for LPS inner core.

rxn03035.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of D-myo-inositol-3,4-bisphosphate at the 4-position, removing the 4-phosphate to yield inositol 3-phosphate and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water hydrolyzes one phosphoester bond, releasing one phosphate and leaving the monophosphate product. This is a phosphatase reaction.

rxn04968.other_comments: This is a 2-oxoglutarate/Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenase reaction (IDS3 enzyme in graminaceous plants) that hydroxylates 2'-deoxymugineic acid to form 3-epihydroxy-2'-deoxymugineic acid, part of the mugineic acid phytosiderophore biosynthesis pathway. The stoichiometry is balanced: O2 provides one oxygen for hydroxylation of the substrate and one for the conversion of 2-oxoglutarate to succinate + CO2. Atom and charge balance check: carbons (5 from 2OG + substrate C = product succinate C4 + CO2 + hydroxylated substrate) account correctly, and the H+ release is consistent. Such dioxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible.

rxn04124.other_comments: This represents the condensation of tryptamine with protoemetine to form deoxytubulosine, releasing water. The reaction is a Pictet-Spengler type condensation: the primary amine of tryptamine reacts with the aldehyde group of protoemetine to form an iminium intermediate, followed by cyclization onto the indole ring to yield the tetrahydro-beta-carboline-type alkaloid deoxytubulosine. The stoichiometry is balanced (loss of one water during imine/amine bond formation). This is a biosynthetic step in the formation of ipecac alkaloids and proceeds in the direction of deoxytubulosine synthesis in vivo.

rxn11510.other_comments: This is the fructoselysine kinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.- , encoded by frlD in E. coli and related organisms). ATP phosphorylates fructoselysine on the C6 position of the glucose moiety to yield fructoselysine 6-phosphate, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (one phosphate transferred) yields ADP plus the phosphorylated substrate plus H+. As a kinase reaction coupling ATP hydrolysis, it is essentially irreversible in vivo and proceeds in the phosphorylation (forward) direction.

errors: No net transformation: identical species (H+ and Cysteamine) appear on both sides with the same stoichiometry, so the reaction is empty/null

A proton antiport reaction should show the transported species and protons moving in opposite directions across compartments (e.g., Cysteamine[c] + H+[e] <=> Cysteamine[e] + H+[c]); compartment labels are missing
As written, the antiport mechanism (opposite directionality of H+ and substrate) is not represented
rxn12622.other_comments: The reaction is intended to be a proton antiport transport of cysteamine, but as written both sides are identical with no compartment distinction, making it a null reaction. Transport reactions require compartment annotations (e.g., cytosol vs extracellular) and, for antiport, protons and the substrate should cross in opposite directions.

errors: Oxygen atom imbalance: the conversion of zeaxanthin to antheraxanthin adds one epoxide oxygen, but only one H2O is produced from O2 (which has two oxygen atoms). With NADH + O2 + H+ -> NAD+ + H2O, one oxygen atom must be incorporated into the substrate (antheraxanthin = zeaxanthin + O). The balance requires zeaxanthin + O2 + NADH + H+ -> antheraxanthin + H2O + NAD+, which is consistent only if antheraxanthin carries the extra oxygen. As written the oxygen balance is correct (2 O from O2 = 1 in H2O + 1 in epoxide), so this is acceptable.
Cofactor note: zeaxanthin epoxidase physiologically uses NADPH/ferredoxin rather than NADH, so the use of NADH may be biologically inaccurate.
rxn04755.other_comments: This is the zeaxanthin epoxidase reaction of the xanthophyll cycle, converting zeaxanthin to antheraxanthin by introducing one epoxide group. It is a monooxygenase-type reaction consuming O2 and a reductant. Atom balance is essentially correct (one O incorporated into the carotenoid, one O released as water). In vivo it proceeds toward antheraxanthin (and onward to violaxanthin) under low light, while the reverse de-epoxidation is catalyzed by a separate enzyme.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the reaction transfers one acyl group from phosphatidylglycerol (dioctadecanoyl) to the lyso-PE acceptor, but the products shown indicate a net deacylation of the lyso-PE (producing glycerophosphoethanolamine, which has no acyl chains) while only adding one acyl to phosphatidylglycerol. The acyl group counts do not balance: starting acyl groups = 1 (lyso-PE) + 2 (PG) = 3; product acyl groups = 0 (GPE) + 3 (acyl-PG, i.e. tri-acyl) = 3 only if the PG product carries three acyls, which is structurally unusual and the naming 'acyl phosphatidylglycerol octadecanoyl' is ambiguous

The acyltransferase mechanism (Lysophospholipase L2 / PldB) typically transfers the acyl group from a lyso-phospholipid (2-acyl-GPE) onto another lyso-acceptor or PG to form a diacyl product; here PG is already diacyl, so adding a third acyl is chemically inconsistent with standard PG structure
rxn08829.other_comments: This represents an acyltransferase (lysophospholipase L2, PldB-type) reaction: the C18:0 acyl group of 2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine is transferred to phosphatidylglycerol, yielding free glycerophosphoethanolamine and an acylated phosphatidylglycerol. The overall logic (deacylation of lyso-PE coupled to transacylation onto PG) is plausible, but the product naming for acyl-PG is ambiguous and the acyl-group bookkeeping should be verified.

errors: The hydrogen (H+) stoichiometry is incorrect; chalcone synthase-type reactions with 3 malonyl-CoA release 3 CO2 and consume CoA but do not typically require 3 H+ as written. The proton balance should be re-derived from the molecular formulas.

Eriodictyol chalcone formation from caffeoyl-CoA requires the correct hydroxylation pattern; the canonical chalcone synthase product from p-coumaroyl-CoA is naringenin chalcone, while caffeoyl-CoA would yield the corresponding trihydroxy/dihydroxy chalcone (eriodictyol chalcone), so the product identity is plausible but the overall mass/charge balance should be verified.
rxn07778.other_comments: This is a chalcone synthase (CHS) type polyketide condensation: one starter caffeoyl-CoA condenses with 3 malonyl-CoA units, releasing 3 CO2 and 4 CoA total (3 from malonyl-CoA plus 1 from the starter), followed by cyclization to form a chalcone. The product from caffeoyl-CoA is eriodictyol chalcone. The reaction is strongly favored forward in vivo due to decarboxylation.

rxn02194.other_comments: This reaction is the conjugation of glutathione (GSH) to leukotriene A4 (LTA4), the epoxide-containing precursor, to form leukotriene C4 (LTC4), catalyzed by LTC4 synthase (a glutathione S-transferase). The epoxide ring of LTA4 (5,6-epoxyeicosatetraenoate) is opened by nucleophilic attack of the glutathione thiol, with the proton balancing the stoichiometry. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written.

errors: Charge imbalance: NAD+ should be written as NAD+ with +1 charge; product side has NADH plus 2 H+ which does not balance charge correctly. Standard oxidation produces NADH + 1 H+, not 2 H+

Atom/redox accounting: oxidation of phosphonate (P-H bond, +3 oxidation state) to phosphate (+5) involves a 2-electron transfer, but the proton/hydrogen balance with one water and two H+ needs verification - the equation as written appears to have an extra proton
rxn04004.other_comments: This represents an NAD-dependent oxidation of phosphonate (HPO3 2-, with a P-H bond) to phosphate, analogous to phosphite dehydrogenase chemistry. The reaction consumes water and NAD+, producing phosphate, NADH and protons. Such NAD+-coupled oxidations are strongly favored thermodynamically in the oxidative (forward) direction in vivo, regenerating reducing equivalents.

rxn03382.other_comments: This reaction is analogous to cystathionine gamma-synthase (O-acetylhomoserine + cysteine -> acetate + cystathionine), but with selenocysteine substituting for cysteine, yielding selenocystathionine. The thiol/selenol group of selenocysteine displaces the acetate from O-acetylhomoserine via a gamma-replacement reaction. Atoms balance: O-acetylhomoserine contributes the acetyl group released as acetate, and the homoserine moiety is joined to selenocysteine through the selenium atom. Stoichiometry is 1:1:1:1 and appears balanced.

errors: Hydrogen/charge imbalance: reducing one aromatic nitro group (-NO2) to an amino group (-NH2) requires 3 NADH + 3 H+ but releases 2 H2O; however the proton balance is off. The reduction of one nitro group to amine consumes 6 electrons (3 NADH provide 6 electrons) and 6 H+, producing 2 H2O. The written 3 H+ undercounts protons. Balanced form should be: 4-Amino-2,6-dinitrotoluene + 3 NADH + 7 H+ -> 2,4-Diamino-6-nitrotoluene + 3 NAD+ + 2 H2O.
Charge imbalance as written: left side net charge from 3 NADH (3-) + 3 H+ (3+) = 0 plus neutral substrate = 0; right side 3 NAD+ (3+) = +3 with neutral products, so charges do not balance.
rxn07836.other_comments: This is the nitroreductase-type reduction of one of the two nitro groups of 4-amino-2,6-dinitrotoluene (a TNT degradation intermediate) to yield 2,4-diamino-6-nitrotoluene. NADH serves as the electron donor. The overall transformation (nitro to amine) is correct in concept, but the stoichiometry of protons/charge is not properly balanced as written.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction for the named enzyme; a hydrolase cleaves the substrate by adding water, so 2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde + H2O should yield formate + 2-oxopent-4-enoate, not the reverse
Proton (H+) balance is questionable; the hydrolytic cleavage of 2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde produces formate and 2-oxopent-4-enoate without requiring an explicit H+ on the formate side as written
rxn01896.other_comments: This is 2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde hydrolase (EC 3.7.1.9) from the meta-cleavage pathway of catechol/aromatic degradation. The hydrolytic C-C bond cleavage of 2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde releases formate and 2-oxopent-4-enoate (oxopent-4-enoate). As written here, the substrates and products are reversed: the in vivo direction is hydrolysis of 2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde + H2O -> formate + oxopent-4-enoate. Stoichiometry of carbon (C7 = C1 + C6) is consistent, but the listed direction is backwards.

rxn05547.other_comments: This is an ABC-type oligopeptide importer reaction. ATP is hydrolyzed (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to power the transport of the dipeptide Gly-Gln across the membrane. The dipeptide appears on both sides because it represents the substrate being translocated (external to internal compartment); in a properly annotated transport reaction the two Gly-Gln species would carry compartment labels (e.g., Gly-Gln[out] -> Gly-Gln[in]). Stoichiometry of the ATP hydrolysis is balanced. The lack of explicit compartment tags is the only ambiguity, but the mass/charge balance is consistent.

rxn12629.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for (S)-2-aminobutanoate (L-2-aminobutyrate). As written, the same species (H+ and the amino acid) appear on both sides, indicating a transport process across a membrane. Typically these would be annotated with compartment labels (e.g., H+[e] + substrate[e] <=> H+[c] + substrate[c]) to show movement from extracellular to cytoplasmic compartments. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (identical species on both sides). Proton symport transporters are generally reversible thermodynamically, but the physiological direction (uptake) is driven by the proton motive force into the cell.

rxn01753.other_comments: This is the xylonate dehydratase reaction (EC 4.2.1.82), part of the oxidative non-phosphorylative D-xylose catabolic pathway (Dahms/Weimberg-type). D-Xylonate is dehydrated to 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-pentonate (2-keto-3-deoxy-xylonate) with release of water. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: D-xylonate (C5H9O6-/C5H10O6) loses one H2O to form the 2-keto-3-deoxy product (C5H8O5/C5H7O5-). Mass and charge balance accordingly.

rxn09082.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of a phosphoethanolamine group from phosphatidylethanolamine (with C16:1 diacyl chains) onto Kdo2-lipid A, producing phosphoethanolamine-modified Kdo2-lipid A and a 1,2-diacylglycerol (DAG, also C16:1). This is the EptA/PmrC-type enzyme reaction in Gram-negative bacteria that decorates the lipid A phosphates with pEtN, contributing to polymyxin/cationic antimicrobial peptide resistance. The phosphoethanolamine donor is the polar headgroup of phosphatidylethanolamine, and the lipid backbone is released as diacylglycerol, so the atoms balance conceptually (pEtN transferred, DAG released). Stoichiometry of one PE consumed yielding one DAG and one pEtN-modified product is consistent.

errors: Stoichiometrically inconsistent: thioester hydrolysis of acyl-CoA yields the free fatty acid plus CoA, but the proton balance shown is incorrect. Hydrolysis of an acyl-CoA thioester (R-CO-S-CoA + H2O -> R-COOH + CoA-SH) does not release an extra H+; the displayed H+ on the product side is spurious because both the carboxylic acid (deprotonated state) and CoA thiol balance without an additional free proton in the neutral formulation.
rxn11721.other_comments: This is a thioester hydrolysis (acyl-CoA hydrolase / thioesterase) acting on icosenoyl-CoA (a C20:1 monounsaturated acyl-CoA) to give icosenoic acid (gondoic/eicosenoic acid) and free CoA. Hydrolysis of a high-energy thioester bond is strongly exergonic and physiologically essentially irreversible in vivo, hence forward.

errors: The reaction is incorrectly written. Methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (EC 1.2.1.27) is a CoA-dependent enzyme that catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation: methylmalonate semialdehyde + NAD+ + CoA -> propionyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH. It does NOT produce methylmalonate.

The substrate '3-Oxo-2-methylpropanoate' is not methylmalonate semialdehyde; methylmalonate semialdehyde is 2-methyl-3-oxopropanoate (2-methyl-3-oxopropanoic acid), not 3-oxo-2-methylpropanoate as a free 'oxo' carbonyl naming is ambiguous/incorrect.

If interpreted as a simple aldehyde-to-acid oxidation (semialdehyde -> methylmalonate), then the proton balance is wrong: oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid with NAD+ and H2O yields NADH + 1 H+ (RCHO + H2O + NAD+ -> RCOOH + NADH + H+), not 2 H+.
Charge/mass balance is inconsistent as written.
rxn02729.other_comments: The input describes (S)-methylmalonate semialdehyde:NAD+ oxidoreductase, which I interpret as oxidation of methylmalonate semialdehyde. The written products (methylmalonate + NADH + 2 H+) suggest a simple aldehyde-to-carboxylate oxidation, but the proton stoichiometry is off and the physiological enzyme is typically the CoA-dependent oxidative decarboxylation to propionyl-CoA.

rxn13216.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of an ester (isobutyl acetate) by an esterase, yielding acetate, a proton, and isobutyl alcohol (isobutanol). The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: isobutyl acetate (C6H12O2) + H2O yields acetate (C2H3O2-) + H+ + isobutanol (C4H10O). Carbons: 6 = 2 + 4; oxygens: 2 + 1 = 2 + 1; hydrogens: 12 + 2 = 3 + 1 + 10; charge: 0 = -1 + 1 + 0. All balanced. Hydrolytic esterase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn02226.other_comments: This is the oxidation of L-2-aminoadipate-6-semialdehyde (allysine) to L-2-aminoadipate, catalyzed by aminoadipate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (NAD+-dependent, part of the lysine degradation/saccharopine pathway). The aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylic acid using water, reducing NAD+ to NADH and releasing 2 H+. Atom and charge balance check out: aldehyde (CHO) + H2O -> COOH + 2H+ + 2e- (carried to NADH). In vivo this oxidation reaction proceeds forward toward 2-aminoadipate in lysine catabolism.

errors: Reaction is not mass/charge balanced as written. Adding a single malonyl-CoA unit to palmitate (C16:0) to form stearate (C18:0, ocdca) requires 2 NADPH and 2 H+ (net), releasing CO2, CoA, and H2O. Carbon balance: palmitate C16 + malonyl-CoA C3 = C19; products stearate C18 + CO2 C1 = C19, which balances. However proton balance is off: with 2 NADPH the correct stoichiometry uses 2 H+ on the substrate side (one for each reduction), not 3 H+. Need to verify charge balance: 2 NADPH(2-) + 3 H+ + malonyl-CoA + palmitate(-1) vs 2 NADP(-1) + CoA + CO2 + H2O + stearate(-1).
rxn09429.other_comments: This represents the fatty acid synthase elongation step converting palmitate (C16:0) to stearate (C18:0, octadecanoate/ocdca) using malonyl-CoA as the two-carbon donor with decarboxylation and NADPH-dependent reductions. Biosynthetic elongation is strongly forward in vivo due to malonyl-CoA decarboxylation driving the reaction.

rxn14031.other_comments: This is the chlorophyll(ide) b synthase / chlorophyllide a oxygenase pathway-related reaction. 7-hydroxychlorophyllide a is oxidized at the C7 hydroxymethyl group to the C7 formyl group, yielding chlorophyllide b, with NAD+ serving as the electron acceptor and producing NADH + H+. The atoms balance: oxidation of -CH(OH)- to -C(=O)- removes two hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one as H+), so the equation is stoichiometrically consistent. As written with NAD as the abbreviation for NAD+, the reaction is balanced.

rxn02931.other_comments: This is the oxidative deamination of D-threo-2,4-diaminopentanoate at the C4 amino position, producing 2-amino-4-oxopentanoate, ammonia, and NADPH. It is part of the ornithine/lysine fermentation pathway (2,4-diaminopentanoate dehydrogenase). The stoichiometry is balanced: the substrate amino group is replaced by a keto group with release of NH3, water provides the oxygen, and NADP+ is reduced to NADPH + H+. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn02115.other_comments: This reaction represents acetoin racemase activity, interconverting the (R)- and (S)-stereoisomers of acetoin (3-hydroxy-2-butanone). The substrate ACTN is interpreted as (R)-acetoin based on the enzyme name. Racemases/epimerases interconvert stereoisomers with no change in atomic composition, so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (both species are C4H8O2). As an isomerization between enantiomers with no thermodynamic driving force, the reaction is freely reversible in vivo.

rxn10547.other_comments: This appears to be an ATP-dependent kinase/phosphotransferase step in tetrahydromethanopterin (H4MPT) biosynthesis, where a ribofuranosyl 5'-monophosphate intermediate is phosphorylated to the corresponding 5'-diphosphate, with ATP converted to ADP. The phosphate transfer is balanced (ATP + monophosphate -> ADP + diphosphate), so stoichiometry is consistent. The substrate/product naming refers to the dihydropterin-aminophenyl-ribitol-ribofuranosyl phosphate intermediates characteristic of the methanopterin pathway.

rxn03748.other_comments: This is a monooxygenase/hydroxylase-type reaction (R05448) where 2,6-dichlorophenol is hydroxylated to 2,6-dichlorohydroquinone using O2, with NADH serving as electron donor (oxidized to NAD+). Stoichiometric check: Left side has NADH + O2 + 2 H+ + dichlorophenol; right side has H2O + NAD+ + dichlorohydroquinone. The phenol (C6H4Cl2O) is converted to hydroquinone (C6H4Cl2O2), gaining one O atom. O2 provides two O atoms: one inserted into substrate, one reduced to H2O. Charge and atom balance are consistent with NADH + 2H+ providing reducing equivalents. The reaction is balanced for C, Cl, O, and H/charge.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides (L-Methionine + H+ <=> L-Methionine + H+) with no compartment annotation, making it appear to have zero net change. A proton antiport transport reaction must specify distinct compartments for the metabolites, e.g. L-Methionine[c] + H+[e] <=> L-Methionine[e] + H+[c], to represent the actual translocation.
rxn05615.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction (L-methionine export via proton antiport). The name indicates methionine moves out while a proton moves in (or vice versa). As written, however, the metabolites lack compartment labels, so the equation is formally a null/empty reaction. Stoichiometry is balanced trivially but biologically meaningless without compartmentalization. Directionality cannot be properly assessed without knowing the driving proton gradient and compartment assignments.

errors: The reaction has identical substrate and product (Acetylated Alginate <=> Acetylated Alginate), which is stoichiometrically trivial and represents no chemical transformation

No spatial/compartmental distinction is shown; if this is a transport reaction (export through outer membrane porin), the substrate and product should be annotated with different compartments, e.g., Acetylated Alginate [periplasm] <=> Acetylated Alginate [extracellular]
rxn13920.other_comments: This appears to represent the transport/secretion of acetylated alginate through an outer membrane protein (likely AlgE/AlgK-type porin in Pseudomonas aeruginosa alginate biosynthesis). As written it is a null reaction because both sides are identical. For a transport reaction, export to the extracellular space is the biologically relevant direction.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass/charge balanced; the stated reactants and products cannot be reconciled stoichiometrically. The named substrate '6-(2-Amino-2-carboxyethyl)-7,8-dioxo-7,8-dihydroquinoline-2,4-dicarboxylate' contains an extra amino-carboxyethyl side chain plus extra carboxylates that are not accounted for in the products (PQQ formation requires ring cyclization and loss of carbons/nitrogen).

Atom balance fails: counting C, N, O between substrate plus 3 O2 versus PQQ plus 2 H2O plus 2 H2O2 plus H+ does not balance. PQQ biosynthesis is a complex multistep oxidative process not captured by this single equation.
rxn05086.other_comments: This represents a late step in pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) biosynthesis, an oxidative ring cyclization/oxidation converting a quinoline precursor into PQQ with O2 consumption. The oxidative, O2-driven nature makes it physiologically essentially irreversible (forward), but the equation as presented appears to be an oversimplified/unbalanced lumped reaction.

rxn06143.other_comments: This reaction describes a 5'-phosphopolynucleotide 5'-phosphohydrolase (a 5'-polynucleotidase / 5'-nucleotidase-type activity) hydrolyzing the terminal 5'-phosphate of a polynucleotide. rxn02431.other_comments: This is the formylmethanofuran:tetrahydromethanopterin formyltransferase (Ftr) reaction in methanogenesis/methanotrophy. rxn06565.other_comments: This represents the UDP-glucose:poly(glycerol-phosphate) alpha-D-glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.52), which transfers a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the polyglycerophosphate backbone of teichoic acid, releasing UDP. Glycosyltransferases using sugar-nucleotide donors are strongly exergonic due to cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, driving the reaction toward glucosyl transfer in vivo.

rxn03704.other_comments: This is the extradiol (meta) ring cleavage of 3-vinylcatechol (3-vinylbenzene-1,2-diol) by a catechol 2,3-dioxygenase type enzyme, incorporating molecular O2 to open the aromatic ring and yield the semialdehyde/oxo ring-fission product 2-hydroxy-6-oxoocta-2,4,7-trienoate. rxn06984.other_comments: This is a phenanthrene dioxygenase (aromatic ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase) reaction. NADH + O2 + H+ + phenanthrene yields NAD+ + (+)-cis-3,4-dihydrophenanthrene-3,4-diol. rxn01714.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of sinapine (sinapoylcholine), an ester between sinapic acid and choline, by sinapine esterase (sinapoylcholine sinapohydrolase, EC 3.1.1.49). rxn13422.other_comments: This is the 3-hydroxyisobutyrate dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.31), part of the valine catabolism pathway. rxn04106.other_comments: This is the vinorine synthase reaction (EC 2.3.1.160), which catalyzes the acetyl-CoA dependent acetylation and cyclization of 16-epivellosimine to form vinorine in the ajmaline biosynthetic pathway. rxn04042.other_comments: This is an ADP-dependent glucokinase (ADP:D-glucose 6-phosphotransferase, EC 2.7.1.147), found in some archaea and protists, which uses ADP rather than ATP as the phosphoryl donor, producing AMP. rxn00728.other_comments: This reaction is kynureninase (EC 3.7.1.3), which hydrolyzes L-kynurenine into anthranilate and L-alanine. rxn01482.other_comments: This is the (R)-3-amino-2-methylpropanoate:pyruvate aminotransferase reaction (EC 2.6.1.40). rxn02613.other_comments: This represents the conversion of ergosterol to vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol). rxn03709.other_comments: This is a catechol 1,2-dioxygenase (intradiol ring cleavage) type reaction acting on 3,6-dichlorocatechol (a chlorocatechol). rxn02492.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3, galabiosylglucosylceramide / digalactosylglucosylceramide) by alpha-galactosidase A, removing the terminal galactose to yield lactosylceramide (LacCer) plus free galactose. rxn02950.other_comments: This is the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH, E1 component) reaction acting on 3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (3MOP, the keto acid derived from isoleucine). rxn10548.other_comments: This reaction is part of tetrahydromethanopterin (H4MPT) biosynthesis in methanogens/archaea. rxn07904.other_comments: This is a muconate cycloisomerase-type reaction involving the cyclization/decyclization of a fluorinated muconate. 3-Fluoro-cis,cis-muconate (a dicarboxylic acid with formula C6H2F O4 in anionic form, plus a proton) undergoes intramolecular lactonization to form 4-fluoromuconolactone. rxn02592.other_comments: This reaction represents the indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase-type cleavage of melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) by molecular oxygen to yield N1-acetyl-N2-formyl-5-methoxykynuramine (AFMK), with the indole ring decyclized. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the feruloyl moiety is transferred from glucose to betanin, releasing glucose. Atoms and the feruloyl group are conserved on both sides.

rxn02094.other_comments: This is a kinase reaction (ATP-dependent phosphorylation of D-tagatose at the 6-position, analogous to tagatose kinase / ketohexokinase activity). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP + tagatose yields ADP + H+ + tagatose 6-phosphate. The released proton correctly balances the charge from phosphate transfer. ATP-dependent sugar kinase reactions are strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the phosphorylation (forward) direction.

rxn12544.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport secondary active transport reaction for the dipeptide methionyl-alanine (met-L-ala-L) coupled to proton movement. rxn06209.other_comments: This is the first committed step of GPI anchor biosynthesis catalyzed by the GPI-GlcNAc transferase (PIG-A complex), transferring N-acetylglucosamine from UDP-GlcNAc to phosphatidylinositol to form GlcNAc-PI and releasing UDP. rxn01341.other_comments: This is the 17,20-lyase reaction cleaving the C17-C20 bond of 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone (C21 steroid) to yield androstenedione (C19 steroid) plus a two-carbon fragment. Note this enzyme requires O2 and NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase, which are not shown in the equation.

rxn12584.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction for 4-aminobenzenesulfonate (sulfanilic acid) coupled to proton symport. The substrates and products are the same species without compartment labels, making it stoichiometrically meaningless as currently written. rxn09961.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing pentadecanal (C15 aldehyde) to pentadecanoate (C15 fatty acid), with NAD+ reduced to NADH. The reaction is balanced: the aldehyde RCHO + H2O is oxidized to carboxylate RCOO- plus 2 H+ (one from the water-derived proton and one freed as the carboxylate is deprotonated at physiological pH), and the hydride goes to NAD+ forming NADH. Mass and charge balance check out.

rxn05463.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI/FabK type) step in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing trans-2-octadecenoyl-ACP (C18 enoyl-ACP) to octadecanoyl-ACP (stearoyl-ACP) using NADPH. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: NADPH + H+ provides the hydride and proton needed to reduce the C2-C3 double bond, yielding NADP+ and the saturated acyl-ACP. In vivo this reductive step is essentially irreversible and drives fatty acid elongation forward.

rxn01617.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADP+-dependent oxidation of 1,2-propanediol to L-lactaldehyde (or the reverse reduction). Stoichiometry is balanced: the diol loses 2 hydrogens (one as hydride to form NADPH, one as proton H+) to yield the aldehyde. Atoms and charge balance correctly. While the enzyme name implies oxidation, aldehyde reductases/oxidoreductases of this type typically operate in vivo in the reductive direction (lactaldehyde to propanediol) under fermentative conditions, but the reaction is thermodynamically reversible and direction depends on cofactor ratios.

rxn01696.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-catalyzed (CYP3A4/CYP1A2) 16alpha-hydroxylation of estrone. The reaction is a monooxygenase reaction where one atom of O2 is incorporated into estrone to form 16alpha-hydroxyestrone, and the other oxygen atom is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + Estrone -> H2O + NADP+ + 16alpha-Hydroxyestrone. Charge and atom balance are consistent for a typical monooxygenase reaction. In vivo, this hydroxylation proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction.

rxn02262.other_comments: This is a fuculokinase/fucokinase-type reaction where ATP phosphorylates L-fucose (6-deoxy-L-galactose) at the 1-position to form L-fucose 1-phosphate, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is balanced: ATP + L-fucose yields ADP + H+ + L-fucose 1-phosphate. Atoms and charges balance (the phosphate transfer releases one proton).

rxn07140.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in nogalamycin biosynthesis. SAM donates a methyl group to nogalonic acid (carboxyl group), producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine and the methylated product. The stoichiometry appears balanced (1 SAM + 1 substrate -> 1 SAH + 1 methylated product), but the product name is missing. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are generally thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in the forward direction.

rxn13799.other_comments: This is a transport reaction for 5-methylthioadenosine (MTA) between two compartments, likely extracellular import or export. Both sides show the same metabolite (5-Methylthioadenosine), which is correct for a transport reaction where the species is identical but located in different compartments. Stoichiometry is balanced (1:1). The reaction is annotated as irreversible, indicating unidirectional transport. Note: the compartment labels are not explicitly shown in the formula, but a proper transport reaction should distinguish them (e.g., MTA[e] <=> MTA[c]).

rxn03983.other_comments: This describes adenylyl-sulfate reductase (glutathione) (EC 1.8.4.9), which physiologically catalyzes the reductive direction: APS + 2 GSH -> AMP + sulfite + GSSG + H+ (assimilatory sulfate reduction). The reaction as written (AMP + sulfite + GSSG -> 2 GSH + H+ + APS) is the oxidative reverse direction. Charge and atom balance are consistent: oxidation of 2 GSH to GSSG releases 2 electrons used to reduce sulfite to the sulfonyl group of APS, with the H+ accounting for proton balance. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn00627.other_comments: This is the fructokinase (1-phosphotransferase, ketohexokinase-type) reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the C1 hydroxyl of D-fructose, yielding fructose 1-phosphate, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (-4) + fructose (0) -> ADP (-3) + H+ (+1) + fructose-1-phosphate (-2), giving -4 on each side. Atoms also balance with the released proton accounting for the ionization upon phosphorylation. As an ATP-driven kinase step, it is essentially irreversible in vivo and proceeds in the direction of phosphorylation.

rxn02655.other_comments: This reaction represents strictosidine synthase (EC 4.3.3.2) running in reverse. The physiological reaction is the condensation of tryptamine and secologanin to form strictosidine with release of water (a Pictet-Spengler condensation). The reaction as written (hydrolytic cleavage of strictosidine into tryptamine and secologanin) is the lyase reverse direction. Stoichiometry is balanced: strictosidine (C27H34N2O9) + H2O yields tryptamine (C10H12N2) + secologanin (C17H24O10). In vivo, the synthase direction (tryptamine + secologanin -> strictosidine + H2O) is strongly favored as the committed step of monoterpene indole alkaloid biosynthesis.

Ambiguous/nonstandard product: 'Caffeoquinone' is not a standard metabolite name; the expected product of 4-coumarate 3-hydroxylation is caffeate (3,4-dihydroxycinnamate).
rxn11971.other_comments: This appears intended to represent the oxygenase-catalyzed hydroxylation of 4-coumarate (para-coumarate) at the meta position to yield caffeate, consistent with the enzyme name '4-coumarate:oxygen oxidoreductase'. Such O2-dependent hydroxylations are essentially irreversible in vivo and proceed in the forward direction. However, the equation as written is not balanced and the product name is nonstandard.

rxn13834.other_comments: This is glucose 1-dehydrogenase (NADP+), oxidizing D-glucose to D-glucono-1,5-lactone with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH and release of a proton. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: glucose (C6H12O6) loses two hydrogens (as hydride to NADP+ giving NADPH, plus H+) to form gluconolactone (C6H10O6). Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn14173.other_comments: This is the nitrite oxidoreductase (NXR) reaction, oxidizing nitrite to nitrate using water as the oxygen source and reducing cytochrome c (electron acceptor). Mass balance: left has N, 3 O (1 from H2O, 2 from nitrite), 2 H (from H2O); right has N, 3 O (nitrate), 3 H. Charge: left = nitrite(-1) + 2*Fe3+(+6) = +5; right = 3 H+(+3) + 2*Fe2+(+4) + nitrate(-1) = +6. There is a charge imbalance of 1 (left +5, right +6), suggesting the proton stoichiometry should be 2 H+ rather than 3, or an electron accounting issue.

rxn12058.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of geranyl diphosphate (GPP) by a phosphohydrolase, releasing geraniol and inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: GPP (C10H20O7P2) + H2O yields geraniol (C10H18O), PPi (HP2O7^3-), and a proton. Charges and atoms balance correctly. Hydrolysis of the phosphoanhydride/phosphoester bond is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the direction of geraniol formation in vivo.

rxn00263.other_comments: This is D-aspartate oxidase (EC 1.4.3.1). It oxidatively deaminates D-aspartate using molecular oxygen, producing the imino acid which hydrolyzes (consuming H2O) to oxaloacetate plus ammonia, with O2 reduced to H2O2. The balance is correct: D-aspartate (C4H7NO4) + O2 + H2O yields oxaloacetate (C4H4O5) + NH3 + H2O2. Atoms balance (C4, N1, and H/O check out). In vivo this oxidase reaction is essentially irreversible in the forward direction because O2 consumption and H2O2 release drive it forward.

rxn10421.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction moving 4-aminobenzoate (ABEE) together with a proton across the mitochondrial membrane. rxn04324.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (PikC) catalyzed hydroxylation of YC-17 (10-deoxymethynolide glycoside) to form methymycin. rxn03547.other_comments: This is the p-cumic alcohol dehydrogenase reaction (CymB) from the cumene/p-cymene degradation pathway. p-Cumic alcohol (4-isopropylbenzyl alcohol) is oxidized to cuminaldehyde (4-isopropylbenzaldehyde) with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. rxn08085.other_comments: This is the second acyltransferase step in phosphatidic acid biosynthesis, transferring a tetradecenoyl (C14:1) group from acyl-ACP to the sn-2 position of 1-acyl-glycerol-3-phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) to form phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-glycerol-3-phosphate). Mass and charge balance correctly when standard ionization states are considered. The hydrolysis of a thioester bond is highly exergonic (releasing roughly -7 to -8 kcal/mol), so it is essentially irreversible in vivo and proceeds in the direction of hydrolysis.

rxn02591.other_comments: This reaction represents linoleate isomerase activity, converting linoleic acid (9Z,12Z-octadecadienoic acid) to rumenic acid / conjugated linoleic acid (9Z,11E-octadecadienoic acid). rxn14218.other_comments: This represents a deoxyribonucleoside kinase reaction (ATP-dependent 5'-phosphorylation of a deoxynucleoside, EC 2.7.1.145-type). rxn01345.other_comments: This is the sedoheptulose-1,7-bisphosphatase (SBPase) reaction from the Calvin-Benson cycle. It hydrolyzes sedoheptulose 1,7-bisphosphate at the 1-position, releasing inorganic phosphate and yielding sedoheptulose 7-phosphate. rxn01113.other_comments: This is the D-ribitol-5-phosphate:NADP+ 2-oxidoreductase reaction, where ribitol 5-phosphate (a polyol/sugar alcohol phosphate) is oxidized at C2 to the ketose D-ribulose 5-phosphate, with NADP+ reduced to NADPH plus a proton. rxn08220.other_comments: This represents a phospholipase D-type (cardiolipin hydrolase, e.g. ClsC or a cardiolipin-specific phospholipase) cleavage of cardiolipin (tetratetradecanoyl, i.e. four C14:0 acyl chains) into phosphatidic acid (1,2-ditetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) and phosphatidylglycerol (ditetradecanoyl). The reaction is a hydrolysis, thermodynamically favorable in the forward direction.

rxn04246.other_comments: This reaction (KEGG R06380, EC 5.1.99.5) is a racemase/epimerase interconverting two diastereomers of dihydrocarvone: (1R,4R)-dihydrocarvone and (1S,4R)-iso-dihydrocarvone. rxn05645.other_comments: This is intended to be a riboflavin uptake via proton symport, where one proton and one riboflavin are co-transported from the extracellular to the cytoplasmic compartment. With proper compartmentalization, the 1:1 H+:riboflavin stoichiometry is reasonable. In vivo, driven by the proton motive force, the reaction proceeds in the import direction (extracellular to cytoplasm).

rxn05237.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter reaction coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the import of a polar amino acid (L-Cysteine). The ATP hydrolysis part is correctly balanced in mass and charge. The L-Cysteine is meant to be translocated across a membrane, but the compartment labels are missing, making the transport step appear as a null reaction.

rxn05429.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthase elongation (condensation) step (KAS-type, beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase). Malonyl-ACP condenses with a 12-methyl-tridecanoyl-ACP primer, releasing CO2 and free ACP, and producing the 3-oxo (beta-keto) elongated product. Adding the 2-carbon unit (minus CO2) to the C14 branched acyl chain yields a 16-carbon branched 3-oxo-acyl-ACP (14-methyl-3-oxo-pentadecanoyl-ACP). Atom and carbon balance is consistent, and the loss of CO2 makes the condensation effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn07662.other_comments: This reaction involves the conversion of 12-oxo-9(Z)-dodecenoic acid to traumatin (12-oxo-10-trans-dodecenoic acid). Both are C12 oxo-fatty acids with a single double bond, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a simple isomerization (cis-9 to trans-10 double bond shift). Traumatin is a wound hormone in plants derived from this pathway. The conversion typically proceeds toward traumatin formation in vivo.

errors: The product 'Adenosylcobalamin-HBI' is unusual nomenclature; the standard product is adenosylcobalamin 5'-phosphate (also called adenosyl-5-hydroxybenzimidazolylcobamide 5'-phosphate). The reaction with 5-hydroxybenzimidazole as base produces a cobamide analog rather than true adenosylcobalamin, but the name appears stoichiometrically consistent if HBI denotes the hydroxybenzimidazolyl base.
rxn10429.other_comments: This is the cobalamin synthase step (CobS/CobV-type), where adenosylcobinamide-GDP reacts with an alpha-ribazole base (here the 5-hydroxybenzimidazole ribotide variant) to form the cobamide nucleotide loop, releasing GMP and a proton. Stoichiometry of phosphate transfer (loss of GMP from the GDP moiety) is balanced.

rxn04437.other_comments: This is a CoA ligase (acyl-activating enzyme) reaction in which 5-hydroxyferulate is activated to its CoA thioester. ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi (AMP-forming), consistent with the EC 6.2.1.12 class (4-coumarate:CoA ligase). The atom and charge balance is correct: the carboxylic acid combines with CoA to form a thioester, releasing AMP, PPi, and a proton. Although written as reversible, in vivo the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase, favoring CoA-thioester formation in phenylpropanoid metabolism.

rxn06109.other_comments: This is the succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) reaction. Succinate is oxidized to fumarate, transferring two electrons and two protons to ubiquinone (Q) to form ubiquinol (QH2). The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: succinate (C4H4O4^2-) + Q + 2H -> fumarate (C4H2O4^2-) + QH2, with the 2H/2e- accounted for by the Q/QH2 couple. As written (Succinate + Q <=> Fumarate + QH2), it is stoichiometrically correct.

errors: Oxygen/mass imbalance: removal of the 7-alpha hydroxyl group from chenodeoxycholate (chenodiol) to give lithocholate eliminates an oxygen atom, but the only oxygen-containing product shown is one H2O while FADH2 -> FAD does not account for the removed oxygen and hydrogens correctly. The dehydroxylation (C-OH to C-H) is a reductive process consuming reducing equivalents, so FADH2 -> FAD (an oxidation) is the wrong direction for the cofactor; reduction of the substrate should consume reducing power.

Redox inconsistency: 7-dehydroxylation is a multi-step pathway (oxidation, dehydration, then reduction) and cannot be represented as a single FAD/FADH2 oxidoreductase step; the net transformation removes an O and replaces it with H, which requires net input of reducing equivalents, not their generation.
rxn02797.other_comments: The reaction represents bacterial 7-alpha-dehydroxylation converting chenodeoxycholic acid (chenodiol) to lithocholic acid (lithocholate). This is a well-known gut-microbial conversion that proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo, but the cofactor stoichiometry as written (FADH2 oxidized to FAD producing water) is chemically backwards for a reductive deoxygenation and the reaction is not balanced.

rxn03837.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of paraoxon (an organophosphate) by paraoxonase/phosphotriesterase. Water cleaves the P-O-aryl bond, releasing p-nitrophenol (PNP) and diethyl phosphoric acid (diethyl phosphate). The H+ accounts for the proton balance from the released phosphate/phenol. The atom balance is consistent: paraoxon (C10H14NO6P) + H2O yields PNP (C6H5NO3) + diethyl phosphate (C4H11O4P) + H+; checking: C 10=6+4, N 1=1, P 1=1, and H/O balance with the released proton. Hydrolytic ester cleavage is strongly thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn03944.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in puromycin biosynthesis. SAM donates a methyl group to N-Acetyl-N6,O-didemethylpuromycin-5'-phosphate, producing the O-methylated product (N-Acetyl-O-demethylpuromycin-5'-phosphate, which now bears an O-methyl group), plus SAH and a proton. The atoms balance: transfer of one CH3 group from SAM converts it to SAH, and the methyl acceptor gains the methyl group; the H+ released is consistent with methyl transfer chemistry.

rxn00373.other_comments: This is the oxalate decarboxylase (carboxy-lyase) reaction, EC 4.1.1.2. Oxalate (C2O4, charge -2) plus a proton yields CO2 plus formate (CHO2, charge -1). Mass balance: left side C2H1O4 (charge -1), right side CO2 + CHO2 = C2H1O4 (charge -1). The reaction is balanced for both atoms and charge. Note: oxalate decarboxylase typically uses O2 as a cofactor and produces CO2 + formate; the catalytic decarboxylation as written is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn13823.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 2-amino-2-deoxyisochorismate (ADIC) lyase (PhzD), part of phenazine biosynthesis. ADIC is hydrolyzed with addition of water and elimination of pyruvate to form trans-2,3-dihydro-3-hydroxyanthranilate (DHHA). Atom balance checks out: ADIC (C10H11NO5) + H2O (H2O) yields pyruvate (C3H4O3) + DHHA (C7H9NO3). Carbon: 10 = 3+7; nitrogen 1 = 1; this balances. The reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly toward DHHA due to release of pyruvate and the favorable hydrolytic step.

rxn11289.other_comments: This is an aldose 1-epimerase (mutarotase) reaction interconverting the anomeric forms of L-arabinose. The substrate 'L-Arabinose' here represents the alpha-anomer (or open-chain) form, and the product is beta-L-arabinose; the enzyme catalyzes anomeric interconversion at the C1 (anomeric) carbon. Stoichiometry is balanced as this is an isomerization (1:1, same molecular formula C5H10O5). Mutarotase reactions are freely reversible and driven toward equilibrium between anomers.

errors: Reaction is not stoichiometrically balanced. Ergothioneine (C9H15N3O2S) cannot decompose simply into trimethylamine ((CH3)3N, C3H9N) plus thiourocanic acid. The atom counts do not balance: ergothioneine has 9 carbons, while the products would need to account for all C, H, N, O, S atoms. Thiourocanic acid (the thiol analog of urocanic acid) would derive from the imidazole/histidine portion, but the loss of trimethylamine plus formation of thiourocanic acid leaves carbon, oxygen, and the carboxylate/amino group unaccounted for.

Charge balance is also not addressed; trimethylamine is shown as free amine while ergothioneine contains a betaine-like trimethylammonium group.
rxn03331.other_comments: I understand this to be a proposed degradation of ergothioneine (a betaine derivative of 2-mercaptohistidine) into trimethylamine and a thiourocanic acid (the thiol/2-thio analog of urocanate). Conceptually this resembles an elimination/deamination type cleavage, but the equation as written does not balance.

rxn00123.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) by a phosphatase (e.g., pyridoxal phosphatase, PDXP), producing pyridoxal and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: H2O + PLP yields pyridoxal + Pi. Phosphomonoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible.

rxn11806.other_comments: This reaction represents the tautomeric interconversion between 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide (a cyclic hemiaminal/carbinolamine form) and aldophosphamide (the open-chain aldehyde form). These are the two key activated metabolites of the prodrug cyclophosphamide, formed after hepatic CYP-mediated 4-hydroxylation. The ring-opening to the aldehyde is a spontaneous, non-enzymatic equilibrium, so the stoichiometry is balanced (isomerization) and the process is genuinely reversible. Aldophosphamide subsequently fragments to phosphoramide mustard (the cytotoxic species) and acrolein, but that is a separate downstream step.

rxn02028.other_comments: This reaction represents betaine-homocysteine S-methyltransferase (BHMT, EC 2.1.1.5). Betaine (BET, trimethylglycine) donates a methyl group to homocysteine, producing L-methionine and dimethylglycine (DMG). The stoichiometry is balanced 1:1:1:1 with one methyl transfer. Note the substrate is L-homocysteine (typo 'homosysteine' in enzyme name). In vivo this reaction strongly favors methionine formation, contributing to the regeneration of methionine and serving as an alternative to folate-dependent remethylation.

errors: Mass/atom balance is questionable; the conversion of 2,3-diketo-5-methylthio-1-phosphopentane to 4-methylthio-2-oxobutyrate plus formate plus phosphate does not appear to balance with the indicated water, NAD/NADH, and proton stoichiometry. The carbon balance (5C substrate -> 4C product + 1C formate = OK on carbon) but the redox/oxygen accounting with 2 NAD and 3 H2O is inconsistent.
Charge/proton balance likely incorrect with the stated 4 H+ given the phosphate release.
rxn08349.other_comments: This represents a step in the methionine salvage (5-methylthioadenosine) pathway, where the 1-phosphate intermediate is metabolized toward 4-methylthio-2-oxobutyrate (the alpha-keto acid precursor of methionine via transamination). The depicted oxidative/hydrolytic cleavage releasing formate and phosphate is plausible in concept but the NAD-dependent oxidation steps and water/proton stoichiometry as written do not cleanly balance.

errors: The glucose product should be beta-D-glucose, not D-glucose, since the sinapoyl group is transferred from 1-O-sinapoyl-beta-D-glucose, releasing the intact glucose moiety as beta-D-glucose (which may then mutarotate). The stoichiometry of atoms is otherwise balanced: the sinapoyl group is transferred from glucose to malate.
rxn02382.other_comments: This is the sinapoylglucose:malate sinapoyltransferase (SMT) reaction (EC 2.3.1.92) common in Brassicaceae. 1-O-sinapoyl-beta-D-glucose acts as an activated acyl donor, transferring the sinapoyl moiety to (S)-malate (L-malate) to form sinapoylmalate, releasing free glucose. [directionality_note] In vivo this reaction proceeds toward sinapoylmalate synthesis (transfer of sinapoyl from the glucose ester acyl donor to malate), driven by the energy-rich acyl-glucose bond.

rxn01967.other_comments: This is the beta-phosphoglucomutase (EC 5.4.2.6) reaction, an intramolecular phosphotransfer interconverting beta-D-glucose 1-phosphate and beta-D-glucose 6-phosphate. It is a mutase/isomerase reaction with 1:1 stoichiometry that is balanced for atoms and charge. Note: catalysis typically requires a phosphorylated enzyme intermediate and a beta-glucose 1,6-bisphosphate intermediate, but these are not net reactants/products. The reaction is thermodynamically reversible, though it tends to favor the 6-phosphate (more stable) under physiological conditions.

rxn01515.other_comments: This reaction represents a phosphotransferase (kinase) activity where dTTP (TTP) donates a phosphate group to cytidine, producing CMP and dTDP, with release of a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: the gamma-phosphate transfer from dTTP yields dTDP, and phosphorylation of cytidine yields CMP. The H+ accounts for the proton released during phosphoryl transfer. In vivo, kinase-mediated phosphoryl transfer from a nucleoside triphosphate to a nucleoside is thermodynamically favorable and typically proceeds in the direction of nucleoside monophosphate formation.

errors: The direction is mislabeled relative to the enzyme name. The named oxidoreductase (flavan-4-ol:NADP+ 4-oxidoreductase) catalyzes oxidation of the flavan-4-ol using NADP+, producing the 4-oxo (flavanone) product plus NADPH. However, the biosynthetic/physiological role of this enzyme class (dihydroflavonol/flavanone 4-reductase type) is reduction. As written, Luteoforol (a flavan-4-ol, reduced form) plus NADP+ giving Eriodictyol (the flavanone, oxidized form) plus NADPH is chemically consistent with the oxidation direction, so stoichiometry is balanced.
Atom/charge balance check: flavan-4-ol oxidation to the corresponding ketone (flavanone) loses 2 H (2 e- + 2 H+), which matches NADP+ -> NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry appears balanced.
rxn03352.other_comments: The reaction couples interconversion of Luteoforol (a (2S)-flavan-4-ol) and Eriodictyol (a flavanone) via NADP/NADPH. In vivo these reductases typically run in the reductive direction (flavanone + NADPH -> flavan-4-ol), i.e., the reverse of how written here.

errors: L-Arabitol (L-Lyxitol) is oxidized at C2/C4 position not C1 in this enzyme system; the product L-Arabinose is incorrect. L-Arabitol:NAD+ 1-oxidoreductase (EC 1.1.1.12) oxidizes L-arabitol to L-xylulose, not L-arabinose. The correct product should be L-Xylulose.
L-Lyxitol is a synonym for L-arabitol, so the substrate naming is acceptable, but the product mismatch breaks the reaction logic.
rxn01290.other_comments: The reaction is a NAD+-dependent oxidation of the pentitol L-arabitol (L-lyxitol). The stoichiometry of the redox couple (NAD+/NADH + H+) is balanced, but the carbon product is wrong: oxidation of L-arabitol yields a ketose (L-xylulose), not the aldose L-arabinose. Polyol dehydrogenases of this type are generally reversible in vitro, though physiological flux often favors oxidation (sugar reduction in reverse depending on cofactor balance).

As written, the reaction oxidizes methionine using oxidized thioredoxin, which is thermodynamically and mechanistically incorrect.
Proton (H+) balance is questionable; the standard MsrA reaction does not typically require a free H+ as written here.
rxn06595.other_comments: The reaction describes the thioredoxin-dependent methionine sulfoxide reductase (MsrA) system. The physiological reaction is the reduction of peptide methionine-(S)-S-oxide back to methionine, consuming reduced thioredoxin and producing oxidized thioredoxin plus water. The substrate and reductant pairings are inverted relative to the in vivo direction.

rxn01927.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 3-hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-dioxygenase (EC 1.13.11.6), part of the kynurenine pathway of tryptophan degradation. It incorporates molecular oxygen (O2) into 3-hydroxyanthranilate, cleaving the aromatic ring to form 2-amino-3-carboxymuconate-6-semialdehyde (ACMS). The stoichiometry is balanced: 3-hydroxyanthranilate (C7H7NO3) plus O2 yields the ring-opened dioxygenation product (C7H7NO5). As a dioxygenase reaction, both oxygen atoms are incorporated into the substrate, making it essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: The reaction name '2-dehydro-L-idonate:NADP+ 5-oxidoreductase' does not match the listed substrate/product (2-Dehydro-L-gulonate). The standard 2,5-diketo-D-gluconate reductase reaction produces 2-keto-L-gulonate (2-dehydro-L-gulonate), so the product is consistent, but the enzyme name referring to 2-dehydro-L-idonate appears inconsistent.
rxn08345.other_comments: This is a 2,5-diketo-D-gluconate reductase reaction. NADPH reduces one of the keto groups of 2,5-diketo-D-gluconate (2,5-DKG) to yield 2-keto-L-gulonate (2-dehydro-L-gulonate), an important intermediate in vitamin C biosynthesis. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: NADPH + H+ + 2,5-DKG -> NADP+ + 2-keto-L-gulonate; the H atoms and charges balance. Biologically it runs in the reductive (forward) direction toward 2-keto-L-gulonate.

rxn03313.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent oxidoreductase (dehydrogenase) reaction. The substrate 3alpha,20alpha,21-Trihydroxy-5beta-pregnane-11-one has a secondary alcohol at C20 that is oxidized to a ketone, yielding 5beta-Pregnane-3alpha,21-diol-11,20-dione. NAD+ is reduced to NADH + H+. The reaction is balanced: one hydroxyl converted to a carbonyl, removing 2 H (one as hydride to NADH, one as proton). Atoms and charges balance with the standard H+ release.

errors: The reaction is not balanced. Conversion of 7,8-dihydroneopterin 3'-triphosphate to 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin involves loss of triphosphate but also requires net redox/atom changes that are not captured. The correct GTP cyclohydrolase/PTPS-type chemistry differs from this single-step lyase representation.

Atom imbalance: the trihydroxypropyl side chain (C3) becoming a pyruvoyl group (C3 with two carbonyls) implies a net loss of hydrogen/water that is not accounted for; carbon, hydrogen and oxygen counts do not balance after removal of only triphosphate and a proton.

The named enzyme (triphosphate lyase releasing the triphosphate) does not produce 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin in one step; that product is generated by 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase (PTPS), which involves an internal redox isomerization.
rxn02986.other_comments: This reaction purports to convert 7,8-dihydroneopterin 3'-triphosphate into 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin with release of triphosphate and a proton, resembling the PTPS step of tetrahydrobiopterin biosynthesis. However, the stoichiometry as written does not balance and conflates triphosphate elimination with the internal redox/isomerization chemistry of PTPS.

rxn02347.other_comments: This is an alcohol dehydrogenase-type oxidation: the secondary hydroxyl of 2-hydroxycyclohexan-1-one is oxidized to a ketone, yielding cyclohexane-1,2-dione. NAD+ is reduced to NADH + H+. The reaction is balanced for carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge (the alcohol loses 2 H, NAD+ gains H- as hydride and one H+ is released). NAD(H)-dependent dehydrogenases are typically reversible, with direction set by cellular NAD+/NADH ratio and substrate concentrations.

rxn03623.other_comments: This is the dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.3.1.-) converting the 5,6-dihydroxy-3-methyl-2-oxo-1,2,5,6-tetrahydroquinoline (a cis-dihydrodiol) to the aromatic 5,6-dihydroxy-3-methyl-2-oxo-1,2-dihydroquinoline catechol, using NAD+ as electron acceptor. This is part of the quinaldine/methylquinoline degradation pathway. Atoms balance: oxidation removes 2 H (2H+ + 2e-) from the substrate, transferred to NAD+ giving NADH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced in both mass and charge.

rxn03462.other_comments: This is a glycosphingolipid galactohydrolase (beta-galactosidase) reaction. GA1 (asialo-GM1, Gal-beta1->3GalNAc-beta1->4Gal-beta1->4Glc-beta1->1'Cer) is hydrolyzed by addition of water to remove the terminal beta1->3 galactose, yielding free galactose and GA2 (asialo-GM2, GalNAc-beta1->4Gal-beta1->4Glc-beta1->1'Cer). The stoichiometry is balanced: one water cleaves one glycosidic bond releasing one galactose monosaccharide. Hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds by glycosidases is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in vivo.

rxn04167.other_comments: This is part of the ent-kaurene oxidase (KO, CYP701A) pathway, a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that performs sequential oxidations of ent-kaurene to ent-kaurenoic acid via the alcohol and aldehyde. The step shown (kaurenal/aldehyde -> kaurenoic acid) is the final oxidation. As an irreversible P450 oxygenation consuming NADPH and O2, it proceeds in the forward (oxidation) direction in vivo.

rxn12893.other_comments: This represents D-lactate dehydrogenase (cytochrome), EC 1.1.2.4, which oxidizes D-lactate to pyruvate while transferring two electrons to two molecules of ferricytochrome c (Fe3+), reducing them to ferrocytochrome c (Fe2+). The stoichiometry is balanced: 2 electrons are donated by lactate during its 2-electron oxidation to pyruvate, reducing 2 cytochrome c3+ to 2 cytochrome c2+, with release of 2 H+. Charge and atom balance are consistent.

rxn13182.other_comments: This is the kynureninase reaction acting on 3-hydroxy-L-kynurenine. Hydrolytic cleavage of the C-C bond yields 3-hydroxyanthranilate and L-alanine. Stoichiometry is balanced: 3-hydroxykynurenine (C10H12N2O4) + H2O gives L-alanine (C3H7NO2) + 3-hydroxyanthranilate (C7H7NO3) + H+. Atoms balance (C10, H14, N2, O5 on each side accounting for proton/charge). This step is part of the tryptophan degradation / kynurenine pathway leading to NAD biosynthesis and is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn05423.other_comments: This is a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase reaction in the fatty acid synthesis (FAS) elongation cycle, applied to a branched-chain (10-methyl) substrate. The hydro-lyase removes water from the 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP to form the trans-2-enoyl-ACP. Stoichiometry is balanced: a 3-hydroxy group plus an alpha hydrogen are eliminated as H2O, producing the trans-2-enoyl double bond. Carbon count (C12 backbone with branch) and ACP carrier are conserved on both sides.

rxn03100.other_comments: This is the beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase reaction (B4GALT family). UDP-galactose donates galactose to the C4 position of a terminal N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl residue on a glycopeptide, forming a beta-1,4 glycosidic bond and releasing UDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one galactosyl unit transferred from UDP-galactose to the GlcNAc acceptor, yielding the galactosylated product and free UDP. Glycosyltransferase reactions using sugar-nucleotide donors are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic (forward) direction due to the energy released upon cleaving the UDP-sugar bond.

rxn11985.other_comments: This describes p-cresol 2-hydroxylase, a flavin-dependent aromatic monooxygenase that uses NADPH and O2 to hydroxylate p-cresol (4-cresol) at the 2-position, yielding 4-methylcatechol and water. The stoichiometry is balanced: one atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (forming the hydroxyl group) and the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Charge and atoms balance correctly (NADPH + H+ provides the reducing equivalents, NADP+ released). In vivo, monooxygenase reactions consuming O2 and NADPH are essentially irreversible and proceed in the hydroxylation (forward) direction.

rxn01010.other_comments: This is the UDP-glucuronate 5-epimerase reaction (EC 5.1.3.12), interconverting UDP-D-glucuronate and UDP-L-iduronate by epimerization at C5 of the uronic acid. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a simple epimerization (same molecular formula on both sides, no cofactors consumed). As an epimerase reaction it is freely reversible in principle; in vivo the C5 epimerization of glucuronate to iduronate residues occurs predominantly at the polymer level during glycosaminoglycan (dermatan/heparan sulfate) biosynthesis, but the free UDP-sugar epimerization is reversible.

rxn04628.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.-) transferring a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the acceptor flavonol glycoside (QUOSP = quercetin 3-sophoroside or related glucoside), producing UDP and quercetin 3-sophorotriroside (a triglucoside). The stoichiometry balances: one glucosyl unit is transferred, UDP-glucose becomes UDP, and the acceptor gains one glucose. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugars are strongly exergonic (cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond) and operate in the biosynthetic forward direction in vivo.

rxn11661.other_comments: This represents a step in sterol C4-demethylation, where the 4alpha-methyl group (already oxidized to an aldehyde) is further oxidized to a carboxylic acid by a monooxygenase using O2 and reducing equivalents. The oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylate consuming O2 and NAD(P)H is essentially irreversible in vivo and proceeds in the forward direction toward the carboxylate.

A monooxygenase incorporates one atom of O2 into the substrate while reducing the other to water, requiring a reduced cofactor (e.g., NAD(P)H or FADH2) and producing water. Missing reducing cofactor (NAD(P)H + H+) typically required for monooxygenase activity.
Missing water (H2O) as a product if one oxygen atom is reduced.
Hydrogen and oxygen atom balance cannot be verified/closed as written.
rxn07345.other_comments: This reaction is part of nicotine degradation, where 6-hydroxypseudooxynicotine is hydroxylated to 2,6-dihydroxypseudooxynicotine. Monooxygenase-catalyzed hydroxylations using O2 and a reductant are strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, hence forward direction.

rxn11391.other_comments: This reaction is the hydration of methylacrylyl-CoA (2-methylprop-2-enoyl-CoA / methacrylyl-CoA), an intermediate in valine catabolism, to 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA. Water adds across the double bond. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: methacrylyl-CoA (C4 acyl portion, one C=C) plus H2O yields the 3-hydroxy product with the same atoms. In valine degradation, the pathway proceeds toward 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA (which is subsequently hydrolyzed), so the physiological direction is forward as written, though enoyl-CoA hydratase reactions are inherently reversible.

rxn04019.other_comments: This is the beta-pinene synthase reaction, where geranyl diphosphate (GPP) undergoes ionization, cyclization, and deprotonation to form the bicyclic monoterpene beta-pinene, releasing diphosphate (PPi). Stoichiometry balances: GPP (C10H20O7P2) yields beta-pinene (C10H16), diphosphate (HP2O7^3-), and a proton. Charge and atoms balance. Terpene synthase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to loss of the diphosphate leaving group and formation of a stable cyclic product.

rxn07909.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolytic dehalogenation/lactone ring opening of 4-fluoromuconolactone (a fluorinated cycloisomerization intermediate in chloro/fluoroaromatic degradation pathways). Charge balance: left side is neutral (H2O + neutral lactone, assuming the carboxylate is protonated); right side has 2 H+ (+2), F- (-1), and maleylacetate carrying -1 net charge for balance, giving net 0. Mass balance for C, H, O, and F appears consistent with loss of HF equivalent and addition of water. This type of reaction is essentially irreversible because spontaneous halide elimination and ring opening are thermodynamically favorable.

rxn01593.other_comments: This is the streptomycin 6-phosphotransferase reaction (an aminoglycoside-modifying kinase, e.g., StrA/AphE), transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the 6-hydroxyl of streptomycin. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP + streptomycin yields ADP + H+ + streptomycin 6-phosphate. The proton released accounts for the charge balance of the phosphoryl transfer.

rxn06499.other_comments: This is the mRNA capping guanylyltransferase reaction (EC 2.7.7.50). GTP reacts with the 5'-diphosphate end of nascent mRNA (ppPur-mRNA) to form the GpppN cap structure with release of pyrophosphate. The atom and charge balance is consistent: the alpha phosphate of GTP is transferred to the diphosphate RNA end, releasing PPi (the beta and gamma phosphates of GTP). A proton is released, consistent with the formation of the new phosphoanhydride bond. In vivo this reaction is driven forward as part of co-transcriptional cap formation, with the PPi typically hydrolyzed to drive the overall capping process.

rxn01135.other_comments: This is an oxalate:CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction where oxalate is activated by ATP to form oxalyl-CoA, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the AMP moiety to form the acyl-CoA thioester, releasing PPi. The proton (H+) balance is correct as one H+ is released. Mass and charge are balanced. In vivo, this type of acyl-CoA synthetase reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible toward oxalyl-CoA formation.
