rxn03219.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in the benzophenanthridine alkaloid pathway. SAM donates a methyl group to the 12-hydroxyl, producing SAH, a proton, and the O-methylated product (dihydromacarpine). The cofactor stoichiometry (SAM -> SAH + H+) is balanced and standard.

rxn04442.other_comments: This reaction represents an aldose-ketose isomerization between kanosamine 6-phosphate (3-amino-3-deoxy-D-glucose 6-phosphate) and aminofructose 6-phosphate (3-amino-3-deoxy-D-fructose 6-phosphate). Both species are C6 sugar phosphates with one amino group; the isomerization interconverts an aldose and a ketose, conserving all atoms (C6H14NO8P for both). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. Sugar phosphate isomerases generally catalyze near-equilibrium, freely reversible reactions, so directionality depends on metabolic context.

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: free fatty acids cannot be directly esterified to trehalose-2-sulfate with only release of water; in vivo the acyl groups are donated as acyl-CoA or via polyketide synthase (Pks2)/acyltransferase (PapA) mechanisms, not as free acids plus H+. As written, esterification of 4 acyl chains onto trehalose-2-sulfate would release 4 H2O, but free carboxylic acids do not provide the activation energy, so the stoichiometry implies a thermodynamically unfavorable direct condensation.

Proton balance is questionable: esterification of 4 hydroxyls with 4 free acids would consume the acid OH groups and trehalose OH groups producing 4 H2O, but the 4.0 H+ on the substrate side is not clearly balanced by charge changes (sulfate group remains anionic on both sides).
The product 'sulfonated tetra-acyl trehalose' should be 'sulfated' (O-sulfate, sulfolipid SL-1) rather than 'sulfonated' (C-S bond); terminology error if SL-1 is intended.
rxn10742.other_comments: This represents biosynthesis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis sulfolipid-1 (SL-1), a tetra-acylated trehalose-2-sulfate. The intended reaction is acylation of trehalose-2-sulfate with one palmitate and three methyl-branched (phthioceranic/hydroxyphthioceranic) acyl chains. The biological direction is toward SL-1 synthesis (forward). However, in vivo acyl transfer uses activated acyl-CoA or PKS-bound acyl donors, so writing free fatty acids + H+ -> ester + H2O misrepresents the true stoichiometry and energetics.

rxn06910.other_comments: This is the muconate cycloisomerase-type reaction (chloromuconate cycloisomerase, part of the modified ortho-cleavage / chloroaromatic degradation pathway). 3-Chloro-cis,cis-muconate undergoes cycloisomerization and dehalogenation, releasing chloride and forming the dienelactone (4-carboxymethylenebut-2-en-4-olide, also called cis-dienelactone). The reaction is balanced: 3-chloro-cis,cis-muconate (C6H4ClO4, as anion) loses Cl- to form the lactone C6H4O4. Carbon (6), hydrogen, and oxygen are conserved, and one chlorine leaves as chloride. Charge is balanced.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: capecitabine has the formula C15H22FN3O6. The carbamate group (N-CO-O-pentyl) hydrolyzes to release a carbamic acid which decomposes to CO2 and the free amine; the products listed (CO2 + 5'-deoxy-5-fluorocytidine + 1-pentanol = C2O2 + C9H12FN3O4 + C5H12O) sum to C16H24FN3O7, while reactant + water (C15H22FN3O6 + H2O = C15H24FN3O7) gives C15. There is a one-carbon discrepancy: the products contain one extra carbon (C16 vs C15), so the reaction as written is mass-unbalanced.
Carbon imbalance specifically: reactant side has 15 C, product side has 16 C (2 from CO2 + 9 from deoxyfluorocytidine + 5 from pentanol).
rxn12023.other_comments: This represents the carboxylesterase/carbamate hydrolysis step in capecitabine activation, cleaving the pentyl carbamate to yield 5'-deoxy-5-fluorocytidine (with subsequent loss of CO2 from the carbamic acid intermediate) plus 1-pentanol. The decarboxylation makes it physiologically irreversible (forward). However, the stoichiometry does not balance as written.

rxn02350.other_comments: This reaction is the oxidation of 4-trimethylammoniobutanal (4-trimethylaminobutyraldehyde) to gamma-butyrobetaine (4-trimethylaminobutyrate), catalyzed by trimethylaminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase (TMABA-DH, EC 1.2.1.47), an NAD+-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase in the carnitine biosynthesis pathway. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylate with incorporation of water, transfer of a hydride to NAD+ (forming NADH), and release of 2 protons. Mass and charge balance check out (aldehyde + H2O - 2[H] -> carboxylic acid; NAD+ + H- -> NADH; net 2 H+ released).

rxn00163.other_comments: This is the acetylenedicarboxylate decarboxylase (acetylenedicarboxylate carboxy-lyase, EC 4.1.1.78) reaction. Acetylenedicarboxylate (2-butynedioic acid, HOOC-C#C-COOH, C4H2O4) undergoes hydration and decarboxylation to yield pyruvate and CO2. Mass balance: left = C4H2O4 + H2O + H+ = C4H5O5; right = CO2 (CO2) + pyruvate (C3H3O3, the anion). Sum right = C4H3O5. The charge/H balance suggests pyruvate should be C3H4O3 (neutral pyruvic acid) or the H+ should be reconsidered, but with anionic forms (acetylenedicarboxylate 2- + H+ + H2O -> pyruvate anion + CO2) the atoms balance reasonably depending on protonation states.

errors: Atom/charge imbalance: the conversion of (S)-canadine (tetrahydroberberine) to berberine is a 4-electron oxidation (removal of 4 H, i.e. two H2). With 2 O2 producing 2 H2O2 this accounts for 4 H atoms transferred, but the proton (H+) on the substrate side is unbalanced - berberine is a quaternary cation (+1), so charge does not balance as written; an extra H+ should appear on the product side rather than the substrate side
rxn02067.other_comments: This is the (S)-tetrahydroberberine oxidase (STOX) reaction, oxidizing (S)-canadine to the fully aromatic protoberberine alkaloid berberine, with molecular oxygen as electron acceptor producing hydrogen peroxide. The two-step oxidation removes two pairs of hydrogens. Biologically this is a committed oxidative aromatization step in berberine biosynthesis.

rxn08891.other_comments: This is a D,D-carboxypeptidase reaction acting on murein (peptidoglycan). It hydrolytically removes the terminal D-alanine from a pentapeptide side chain, converting it to a tetrapeptide. The substrate is a three-disaccharide murein unit containing a pentapeptide-crosslinked-tetrapeptide and a tetrapeptide-crosslinked-tetrapeptide; the product converts the pentapeptide to a tetrapeptide, releasing one D-alanine. Stoichiometry is balanced: one water consumed, one D-Ala released, single peptide bond hydrolyzed. Carboxypeptidase hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically unidirectional.

errors: Charge imbalance: the equation as written does not balance charge correctly. Nitrite reduction to ammonia: NO2- + 6 Fd(red) + 8 H+ -> NH3 + 2 H2O + 6 Fd(ox). In the reverse (oxidation) direction shown, balancing gives NH3 + 2 H2O + 6 Fd(ox) -> NO2- + 6 Fd(red) + 8 H+, but the reaction lists only 7 H+, indicating a proton/charge imbalance depending on ferredoxin charge convention
Proton count inconsistency: with NO2- bearing a -1 charge and 6 ferredoxin one-electron transfers, the H+ stoichiometry should be 8 (for the standard ferredoxin-nitrite reductase reaction), not 7
rxn05893.other_comments: This is the ferredoxin-nitrite reductase reaction. Physiologically it operates in the assimilatory reductive direction (nitrite + reduced ferredoxin -> ammonia), i.e., the reverse of the way it is written here. The written direction (ammonia oxidation to nitrite) is thermodynamically unfavorable with ferredoxin as acceptor in vivo.

rxn05000.other_comments: This reaction represents the aureusidin synthase (a polyphenol oxidase) reaction, converting the chalcone isosalipurpol (2',4,4',6'-tetrahydroxychalcone, also known as naringenin chalcone) to the aurone aureusidin, with O2 as the oxidant and water as a product. The stoichiometry (one O2 reduced to one H2O coupled with oxidative cyclization/hydroxylation) is consistent with the oxidoreductase mechanism. As an O2-dependent oxidative biosynthetic step, it proceeds in the forward (oxidative) direction in vivo.

rxn05376.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase step in branched-chain (iso/anteiso) fatty acid biosynthesis. NADPH reduces the 3-oxo (beta-keto) group of the 12-methyl-3-oxo-tetradecanoyl-ACP to the corresponding 3-hydroxy product, regenerating NADP+. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: NADPH + H+ provides the hydride and proton to convert C=O to CHOH, and ACP is conserved on both sides.

rxn01373.other_comments: This is guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT, EC 2.1.1.2). SAM donates a methyl group to glycocyamine (guanidinoacetate) producing creatine and S-adenosyl-homocysteine. The atom and charge balance is correct: the methyl transfer releases a proton, and the stoichiometry is consistent. In vivo this is the final step of creatine biosynthesis and proceeds strongly in the methylation direction.

rxn01123.other_comments: This is the 2-keto-3-deoxygluconate (KDG) kinase reaction (kdgK, EC 2.7.1.45), part of the modified Entner-Doudoroff and hexuronate degradation pathways. ATP phosphorylates 2-keto-3-deoxygluconate at the 6-position to form 2-keto-3-deoxy-6-phosphogluconate (KDPG), producing ADP and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced in terms of atoms and charge: ATP transfers a phosphoryl group to the substrate's C6 hydroxyl, releasing ADP and H+.

errors: Thermodynamically infeasible cofactor: succinate oxidation to fumarate uses FAD (as in succinate dehydrogenase), not NAD+. The redox potential of the fumarate/succinate couple (~+30 mV) is incompatible with NAD+/NADH (~-320 mV), making this reaction with NAD as electron acceptor highly unfavorable.
rxn00284.other_comments: The reaction depicts oxidation of succinate to fumarate with reduction of NAD+ to NADH and release of a proton. Atoms balance (succinate C4H6O4 -> fumarate C4H4O4 + 2[H], i.e. 2e- + 2H+, captured as NADH + H+). Stoichiometry and charge are balanced, but the physiological electron acceptor for succinate dehydrogenase is FAD/ubiquinone, not NAD+.

rxn03148.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA oxidase (or oxidase-type dehydrogenation) step in peroxisomal bile acid synthesis (side-chain shortening of cholestanoyl-CoA). THCA-CoA is oxidized to the 24-ene-CoA (24,25-dehydro) intermediate. The reaction abstracts two hydrogens from C24-C25, transferring them to FAD to form FADH2. Stoichiometry is balanced: one double bond introduced into the substrate matches FAD -> FADH2 (2H). In vivo this is catalyzed by branched-chain acyl-CoA oxidase, where FADH2 is reoxidized by molecular oxygen producing H2O2, driving the reaction strongly forward.

rxn02108.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of aspirin (acetylsalicylate) by aspirin esterase/acetylsalicylate O-acetylhydrolase. Water cleaves the acetyl ester bond, yielding acetate and salicylate (SALC), with release of a proton. Aspirin C9H7O4(-) + H2O -> salicylate C7H5O3(-) + acetate C2H3O2(-) + H+. Atom and charge balance check: C9H8O4 (neutral form) splits into C7H6O3 (salicylic acid) + C2H4O2 (acetic acid); the deprotonated/ionic representation given (water + aspirate -> acetate + H+ + salicylate) is balanced for C, H, O, and charge.

rxn01842.other_comments: This is the phenylacetate-CoA ligase (PaaK) reaction, which activates phenylacetate (PACT) using ATP and CoA to form phenylacetyl-CoA, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the AMP moiety and releases PPi, CoA's thiol displaces to form the thioester, and 2 protons are released (consistent with the ionization states of the carboxylate substrate and thioester product). In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making the acyl-CoA synthetase reaction effectively irreversible toward phenylacetyl-CoA formation.

errors: The reaction is not balanced. The conversion of (S)-1-phenylethanol (C8H10O) to acetophenone (C8H8O) is a 2-electron oxidation removing 2 H (2H+ + 2e-). With O2 as electron acceptor along with NADH, the oxygen and hydrogen atoms do not balance. For a monooxygenase using O2 + NADH, only one O atom would be incorporated and one water produced, but here no oxygen is incorporated into the product (alcohol to ketone needs no extra O). The correct alcohol-to-ketone oxidation is simply: (S)-1-phenylethanol + NAD+ <=> acetophenone + NADH + H+. The presence of O2 and 2 H2O is inconsistent.

Oxygen balance error: 2 O atoms enter via O2 plus 1 O in substrate = 3 O on left; right side has 2 H2O + 1 O in acetophenone = 3 O. Oxygen actually balances, but hydrogen/electron accounting is inconsistent with the redox cofactor usage shown (NADH appears as a reactant being oxidized while also driving reduction of O2, which conflicts with the dehydrogenation direction).
Direction of NADH/NAD+ is inconsistent: oxidizing an alcohol to a ketone should produce NADH from NAD+, not consume NADH.
rxn11657.other_comments: The reaction depicts oxidation of (S)-1-phenylethanol to acetophenone. As written it pairs NADH consumption with O2 reduction to water, which resembles an oxidase/oxygenase formulation, but the cofactor redox direction conflicts with the alcohol-to-ketone dehydrogenation. A standard alcohol dehydrogenase reaction would be (S)-1-phenylethanol + NAD+ <=> acetophenone + NADH + H+.

rxn01151.other_comments: This is the aldol cleavage of 3-deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate (KDO, an 8-carbon sugar acid, C8H14O8) into pyruvate (C3H4O3) and D-arabinose (C5H10O5). Carbon balance: 3+5=8, correct. Atom balance checks: C8H14O8 vs C3H4O3 + C5H10O5 = C8H14O8, fully balanced. The enzyme is KDO aldolase (a lyase forming pyruvate); aldolases are generally reversible, though metabolic context (KDO degradation vs synthesis) determines net flux. In vivo this catabolic aldolase typically favors cleavage but the equilibrium permits both directions.

rxn07949.other_comments: This reaction represents acyl-CoA-independent (or rather direct ATP-dependent) acylation of a lyso-phosphatidylethanolamine. Mechanistically, palmitate is activated by ATP (forming an acyl-adenylate, releasing PPi), and the palmitoyl group is then transferred to the sn-2-acyl-glycerophosphoethanolamine (a lysophospholipid) to form the diacyl phosphatidylethanolamine (dihexadecanoyl/dipalmitoyl PE), releasing AMP. The atoms balance: ATP provides AMP + PPi, the carboxylate of palmitate forms an ester bond with the free hydroxyl of the lyso-PE, and one H+ is released. Stoichiometry is consistent.

errors: Oxygen atom imbalance: monooxygenase reactions incorporating one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate (forming a hydroxyl) release the other oxygen as water, but here the standard stoichiometry requires accounting; with NADH + O2 -> NAD + H2O the balance of H and O needs the product hydroxylation. As written: left has O2 (2 O) + NADH; right has H2O (1 O) + hydroxylated product (1 O from OH). Carbon side: PACT (phenylacetate) -> 2-hydroxyphenylacetate adds one O. This appears atom-balanced overall, but charge/proton balance should include H+ (NADH + H+ + O2 -> NAD+ + H2O + product).
Likely missing a proton (H+) on the substrate side for proper charge balance, since NAD+ is positively charged.
rxn03783.other_comments: This is a NADH-dependent monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction converting phenylacetate (PACT) to 2-hydroxyphenylacetate using O2 and NADH, releasing water and NAD+. Such oxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydroxylation (forward) direction.

errors: The reaction is not charge-balanced as written: the substrate 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-(2-hydroxyphenyl)-hexa-2,4-dienoate carries a -1 charge, and hydrolysis should yield 2-oxopent-4-enoate (-1) plus salicylate (-1) plus an H+ (+1); the net product charge (-1) does not match unless the H+ is accounted for properly. As written with H+ explicitly on the product side, charges balance (-1 = -1 -1 +1), so the main concern is verifying atom balance.

Mass/atom balance should be checked: the C-C hydrolytic cleavage adds H2O and splits the C12 substrate into a C5 (2-oxopent-4-enoate) and a C7 (salicylate) fragment; carbon count 12 = 5 + 7 is consistent.
rxn03661.other_comments: This is the meta-cleavage pathway hydrolase reaction (analogous to dihydroxybiphenyl/HOPDA hydrolase). The substrate 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-(2-hydroxyphenyl)-hexa-2,4-dienoate is hydrolytically cleaved with water to yield 2-oxopent-4-enoate (2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate tautomer) and salicylate (SALC = 2-hydroxybenzoate / salicylaldehyde-related; here likely salicylate). The C-C bond hydrolysis is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn02317.other_comments: This reaction is an ITP-dependent phosphorylation of D-tagatose 6-phosphate at the C1 position, yielding D-tagatose 1,6-bisphosphate, IDP, and a proton. The reaction is analogous to the 1-phosphofructokinase (tagatose-6-phosphate kinase) reaction, but uses ITP instead of ATP as the phosphoryl donor. Stoichiometrically the reaction is balanced: a phosphoryl group is transferred from ITP (yielding IDP) to the sugar phosphate (yielding the bisphosphate), with release of a proton, consistent with kinase chemistry. Phosphotransfer from a nucleoside triphosphate to a sugar phosphate is highly exergonic and physiologically essentially irreversible, hence the forward direction.

errors: Charge and proton imbalance: CoA (typically -4 at physiological pH) hydrolyzes to 3',5'-ADP (-2) plus phosphopantetheine (-2 with terminal thiol); the 2.0 H+ on the product side does not balance unless protonation states are reconsidered. The reaction as written likely has a proton imbalance.

The enzyme name 'acyl carrier protein synthase' (holo-ACP synthase, AASD-HPP) actually transfers the 4'-phosphopantetheine moiety from CoA to apo-ACP, releasing 3',5'-ADP; the reaction shown is the simple hydrolysis of CoA to free phosphopantetheine, which represents a pantetheine-phosphate adenylyltransferase / nudix hydrolase type activity, not the ACP synthase transfer reaction. The apo-ACP substrate and holo-ACP product are missing.
rxn09532.other_comments: The reaction depicts hydrolytic cleavage of coenzyme A into 3',5'-ADP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate) and 4'-phosphopantetheine, consuming water. Atom-wise the C/N/P backbone splits correctly at the pyrophosphate bond, but the true holo-ACP synthase reaction should transfer phosphopantetheine onto a serine of apo-ACP rather than releasing it as a free product. CoA hydrolysis to ADP-3',5'-P plus phosphopantetheine is strongly favored thermodynamically and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric/mass imbalance as written: polymerization of two O16-antigen-undecaprenyl-diphosphate units should release one undecaprenyl phosphate (or the lipid carrier) rather than bactoprenyl (undecaprenyl) diphosphate; the released carrier from the donor is typically undecaprenyl phosphate, not the diphosphate form, so the phosphate balance is questionable

rxn09022.other_comments: This is the Wzy-type O-antigen polymerase reaction in the periplasm: it transfers the growing O16-antigen chain from one undecaprenyl-PP carrier onto another, elongating the chain by one repeat unit and releasing a lipid carrier. The block-transfer mechanism makes it effectively irreversible (committed polymerization) in vivo.

The two C9 fragments together total C18, but oxygen accounting from the hydroperoxide (O-O cleavage) must be verified.
rxn07658.other_comments: This is a hydroperoxide lyase (HPL) reaction in the oxylipin/lipoxygenase pathway. 9(S)-HPOT (9(S)-hydroperoxy-(10E,12Z,15Z)-octadecatrienoic acid) is cleaved at the C9-C10 bond, producing 9-oxononanoic acid and a C9 unsaturated aldehyde (3,6-nonadienal). HPL-catalyzed cleavage of fatty acid hydroperoxides is essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Stereochemistry mismatch: substrate is specified as generic Glucose-1-phosphate but the enzyme name indicates alpha-D-glucose 1-phosphate; the product is beta-D-glucose 6-phosphate, whereas phosphoglucomutase normally yields alpha-D-glucose 6-phosphate
The reaction as written lacks the catalytic intermediate/cofactor (glucose 1,6-bisphosphate) typically associated with phosphomutase mechanism, though this is often implicit
rxn12204.other_comments: This is a phosphoglucomutase-type reaction interconverting glucose 1-phosphate and glucose 6-phosphate by transferring the phosphate group between the C1 and C6 positions. Atom and charge balance for the phosphate transfer itself is fine (intramolecular isomerization), but the anomeric designations are inconsistent between substrate, product, and enzyme name.

rxn10545.other_comments: This is a hydrolysis (dephosphorylation) step in the tetrahydromethanopterin (H4MPT) biosynthesis pathway in methanogenic archaea. Water hydrolyzes the 5'-phosphate ester of the dihydropterin-aminophenyl-ribitol phosphate intermediate, releasing inorganic phosphate and yielding the dephosphorylated ribitol product. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: a phosphomonoester bond is cleaved by water, transferring the phosphate group to water (yielding Pi) and leaving a free hydroxyl on the ribitol. Stoichiometry is correct (one H2O consumed, one Pi released).

rxn00435.other_comments: This is a Cannizzaro-type dismutation of formaldehyde: two molecules of formaldehyde (CH2O) react with water, with one being oxidized to formate (HCOO-) and the other reduced to methanol (CH3OH). Atom and charge balance check: left side C2H6O3 (2 CH2O + H2O), right side formate CHO2- + H+ + methanol CH4O = C2H6O3 with net charge 0. The reaction is stoichiometrically and charge balanced.

errors: The reaction as written is unbalanced/mislabeled relative to its name: the name 'alcophosphamide:NAD+ oxidoreductase' implies oxidation of alcophosphamide (alcohol) to aldophosphamide (aldehyde) with reduction of NAD+ to NADH, but the equation written shows the opposite (NADH-driven reduction of aldophosphamide to alcophosphamide).
NAD should be written as NAD+ for charge/electron balance consistency with NADH + H+.
rxn11809.other_comments: This is an aldo-keto reductase / alcohol dehydrogenase type reaction interconverting aldophosphamide (an aldehyde intermediate of cyclophosphamide metabolism) and alcophosphamide (the corresponding alcohol). As written, NADH + H+ reduces the aldehyde (aldophosphamide) to the alcohol (alcophosphamide), regenerating NAD+. This is a standard redox couple and is thermodynamically reversible; in vivo aldo-keto reductases typically favor reduction (forward as written) given high NADPH/NADH and substrate context.

errors: Reaction is written in the reverse direction relative to the enzyme's physiological function; berbamunine synthase (CYP80A1) consumes the two N-methylcoclaurine monomers, O2, and NADPH to produce berbamunine, water, and NADP+
As written, it implies water and NADP+ regenerate the substrates plus O2 and NADPH, which is thermodynamically unfavorable for a P450 monooxygenase phenol-coupling reaction
rxn03210.other_comments: This is berbamunine synthase, a cytochrome P450 (CYP80A1) catalyzing oxidative C-O phenol coupling of (S)- and (R)-N-methylcoclaurine to form the bisbenzylisoquinoline alkaloid berbamunine. The atom balance is consistent (2 H2O, NADP+, berbamunine on one side; NADPH, O2, H+, and the two monomers on the other), so stoichiometry appears balanced. However, the biological direction is monomers + O2 + NADPH -> berbamunine + 2 H2O + NADP+, i.e., the reverse of how it is written here.

rxn04620.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.x) that transfers a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the flavonol glycoside Sophoraflavonoloside (kaempferol 3-sophoroside), extending the sugar chain to form kaempferol 3-sophorotrioside, releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucosyl unit is transferred from UDP-glucose (yielding UDP) to the acceptor, increasing its glucose count by one. Glycosyltransferase reactions of this type are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic (glucosylation) direction in vivo due to the high-energy UDP-sugar donor.

rxn02537.other_comments: This is the cytochrome P450 (CYP72A1, secologanin synthase pathway; specifically 7-deoxyloganin 7-hydroxylase) catalyzed monooxygenation of 7-deoxyloganin (deoxyloganin) to loganin. A monooxygenase reaction incorporates one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate (the 7-hydroxyl) while the other oxygen is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. The stoichiometry NADPH + O2 + H+ + substrate -> H2O + NADP+ + hydroxylated product is balanced and standard for P450 hydroxylation. As an oxygen- and NADPH-dependent oxygenation, this is physiologically irreversible, proceeding in the forward (hydroxylating) direction.

rxn00164.other_comments: This is the oxaloacetate decarboxylase/carboxylase type reaction. As written, pyruvate plus CO2 forms enol-oxaloacetate and a proton. The atoms balance: pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + CO2 (CO2) gives oxaloacetate (C4H3O5-) which is consistent with the enol form, plus H+. Charge balances (pyruvate -1 + CO2 0 = enol-oxaloacetate -2 + H+ +1 = -1). The name in the input ('2-Hydroxyethylenedicarboxylate carboxy-lyase, pyruvate-forming') refers to enol-oxaloacetate as the 2-hydroxyethylenedicarboxylate, with decarboxylation yielding pyruvate.

rxn09442.other_comments: This is a mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) elongation cycle reaction extending octanoyl-ACP (C10:0... wait, C8:0) to decanoyl-ACP (C10:0). The reaction combines condensation (Octanoyl-ACP + Malonyl-ACP yields beta-ketoacyl-ACP + CO2 + ACP), then reduction, dehydration, and a second reduction. Carbon balance: 8 (octanoyl) + 3 (malonyl) = 11, minus 1 CO2 = 10 carbons (decanoyl), correct. Two NADPH are consumed for the two reduction steps, one H2O released in dehydration. ACP released from the malonyl donor. Stoichiometry and redox balance are consistent.

errors: Substrate mismatch: CDP-diacylglycerol synthetase uses phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate), not glycerol 3-phosphate (sn-glycerol 3-phosphate). The listed substrate lacks the two acyl chains required to form CDP-diacylglycerol.
Atomic/mass imbalance: the two acyl groups (C16:0 and C19:0) appear in the product but are not accounted for in the substrates, so the reaction as written is not mass-balanced.
Charge/proton balance should be re-checked once the correct phosphatidic acid substrate is used; the reaction CTP + phosphatidate -> CDP-DAG + PPi is typically written without a free H+ release.
rxn10679.other_comments: This is intended to be the CDP-diacylglycerol synthase (CDS) reaction, where CTP reacts with phosphatidic acid to form CDP-diacylglycerol plus pyrophosphate. The input incorrectly lists sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (lacking acyl chains) instead of the diacyl phosphatidic acid bearing the C16:0/C19:0 chains. In vivo the reaction is driven forward by subsequent pyrophosphate hydrolysis.

errors: Reaction is unbalanced: a typical cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (C6-oxidase) reaction requires O2 plus NADPH and H+ as reducing equivalents, producing the oxidized product, water, and NADP+. As written, only one oxygen atom from O2 is accounted for (one goes into substrate, one into H2O), but the second oxygen of O2 requires two electrons and two protons that must come from a cofactor (NADPH); these are missing.

Mass/atom balance is incomplete because the conversion of 3-Dehydro-6-deoxoteasterone (lacking C6 oxo) to 3-Dehydroteasterone (bearing C6 ketone) adds an oxygen but the hydrogen/electron bookkeeping does not close without NADPH/NADP+.
If only the carbonyl oxygen is introduced, water release as the sole co-product implies a 2-electron oxidation requiring an electron donor that is not shown.
rxn07289.other_comments: This represents the brassinosteroid biosynthetic step where a 6-deoxo (C6-deoxygenated) intermediate is oxidized at C6 to introduce the 6-oxo group, catalyzed by a P450 brassinosteroid C6-oxidase (e.g., CYP85). Such monooxygenase reactions proceed essentially irreversibly toward oxidation in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: oxygen atoms do not balance. The azoxy product contains an N-O bond, but the overall O balance is off. Left side: O2 (2 O) plus 4 hydroxylamino groups (each contributing OH, ~4 O from NHOH) = ~6 O from those groups plus 2 = consider carefully; Right side: 4 H2O (4 O) + 2 azoxy (2 O in azoxy linkages) = 6 O. Hydrogen balance also questionable: each 4-hydroxylamino-2,6-dinitrotoluene NHOH contributes 2 H (N-H and O-H); 4 molecules give 8 H, right side 4 H2O gives 8 H, so H may balance. The main concern is the nitrogen and carbon coupling: 2 hydroxylamino monomers condense to form 1 azoxy dimer, so 4 monomers give 2 dimers, which is consistent.
Charge/atom verification recommended: while C, H, N may balance, the role of O2 as oxidant and the precise O count should be double-checked
rxn11690.other_comments: This represents the oxidative dimerization (condensation) of two 4-hydroxylamino-2,6-dinitrotoluene molecules to form an azoxy compound (2,2',6,6'-tetranitro-4,4'-azoxytoluene), a known abiotic/biotic transformation in TNT degradation pathways. Two hydroxylamino monomers combine into one azoxy dimer, hence the 4:2 ratio. O2 serves as oxidant and water is released.

rxn10251.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction where UDP-glucose donates a glucose moiety to diglucosyldiacylglycerol (with anteiso-pentadecanoyl acyl chains) to form the triglucosyl product, releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose, converting it to UDP, while the acceptor lipid gains one glucose (di to tri glucosyl). Such glycosyltransferase reactions using activated sugar-nucleotide donors are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species and stoichiometry on both sides (H+ + Citrate-Mg <=> H+ + Citrate-Mg), making it a null/empty reaction with no net transformation
Compartment designations are missing; a transport reaction must distinguish extracellular and cytoplasmic (intracellular) species, e.g. H+[e] + Citrate-Mg[e] <=> H+[c] + Citrate-Mg[c]
Without compartment tags the proton symport cannot be represented
rxn10855.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport (proton symport) importing the magnesium-citrate complex along with a proton, driven by the proton motive force. As written it lacks compartment labels, so it appears as a trivial identity reaction. Properly written it should be: H+[e] + Citrate-Mg[e] -> H+[c] + Citrate-Mg[c]. Mass and charge balance only if the same species move between compartments. Symport import driven by the proton gradient is typically modeled as effectively irreversible (forward, into the cell) in vivo.

rxn04660.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of N2-acetyl-L-lysine (acetylation on the alpha-amino group) by an acylase/deacetylase, yielding acetate and L-lysine. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: substrate C8H16N2O3 plus H2O yields acetate C2H3O2(-)/C2H4O2 plus L-lysine. Hydrolytic deacylation reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the deacetylation direction in vivo.

errors: Charge imbalance: left side has 2 H+ plus quinol (neutral) plus MnO2 (neutral) giving net +2; right side has Mn2+ (+2) plus water and quinone (neutral) giving net +2, so charge actually balances, but the proton/electron accounting needs care. MnO2 + 2 H+ + 2 e- -> Mn2+ + H2O requires only 1 H2O, not 2 (Mn has only 2 oxygens shared)
Oxygen imbalance: MnO2 supplies 2 O atoms but product side shows 2 H2O (2 O) which is consistent, however the standard reaction MnO2 + 4 H+ + 2 e- -> Mn2+ + 2 H2O requires 4 H+, not 2 H+
Hydrogen imbalance: with 2 H2O on the right (4 H) plus the 2 H released from quinol oxidation, the left needs 4 H+ to balance, but only 2 H+ are provided
Likely misspelling: 'methymenaquinol 7' should be 'methylmenaquinol 7'
rxn13724.other_comments: This represents a manganese oxide reductase coupling oxidation of methylmenaquinol-7 to methylmenaquinone-7 with reduction of Mn(IV) oxide to Mn(II). The redox couple direction (quinol oxidation driving Mn(IV)->Mn(II) reduction) is biologically favorable, but the equation is not properly balanced.

rxn04012.other_comments: This is the jasmonate carboxyl methyltransferase (JMT) reaction, EC 2.1.1.141. SAM donates a methyl group to the carboxyl group of jasmonate, producing methyl jasmonate and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. The stoichiometry is balanced 1:1:1:1 and mass/charge conserved. Physiologically this proceeds in the methyl-ester-forming direction.

rxn04749.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of N-cyclohexylformamide (an amide bond) into formate and cyclohexanamine (cyclohexylamine). The reaction is balanced: N-cyclohexylformamide (C7H13NO) + H2O (H2O) -> formate (CHO2-) + cyclohexanamine (C6H14N+, as protonated amine). Mass and charge balance hold when accounting for protonation states. This corresponds to a formamidase/amidohydrolase-type activity. Amide hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Mass and atom imbalance: the reaction as written shows 2 hydroxylated substrates yielding 2 dehydroxylated products plus O2, but oxygen balance is incorrect. A hydroxylation reaction should consume O2 and reducing equivalents, not produce O2. As written, removing OH groups from 2 substrates would release 2 O atoms (as water with reductant), not molecular O2 with no other reactant
Missing cofactors/reductants (e.g., NAD(P)H, H+) typically required for the monooxygenase hydroxylation step
The direction implies generation of free O2 from phenolic hydroxyls, which is biochemically implausible
rxn05768.other_comments: This appears to be a step in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis involving 2-polyprenylphenol and its 6-hydroxy derivative. The biologically relevant reaction is the hydroxylation of 2-polyprenylphenol to form 6-hydroxy-2-polyprenylphenol (here named 5-hydroxy-2-polyprenylphenol), which consumes O2 and reductant. The reaction as written runs backward (producing O2) and is stoichiometrically unbalanced.

errors: Mass imbalance: ACP and AMP are present on both sides in a way that does not balance the acyl-carrier transfer; the alpha-meroacyl group is transferred from ACP to AMP, but the AMP appearing as a free reactant plus the AMP-bound product implies AMP is both consumed and produced, which is contradictory
Charge/proton imbalance: 2.0 H+ on the substrate side has no clear counterpart, indicating the equation is not balanced for hydrogen/charge

rxn13464.other_comments: This appears to be a fatty-acid AMP ligase reaction involved in mycolic acid biosynthesis, transferring an alpha-meroacyl chain between ACP and AMP carriers (the cyclopropane rings indicate a mycobacterial meromycolate). However, the metabolites are poorly defined/generic and the equation does not balance as written.

rxn01623.other_comments: This reaction represents prostaglandin D synthase (PGDS), which catalyzes the isomerization of prostaglandin H2 (PGH2, the endoperoxide intermediate (5Z,13E)-(15S)-9alpha,11alpha-epidioxy-15-hydroxyprosta-5,13-dienoate) to prostaglandin D2 (PGD2). This is an intramolecular isomerization/rearrangement of the endoperoxide bridge, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced 1:1 with no additional substrates or products required (though some isoforms use glutathione as a cofactor, it is not consumed net). Biologically, this proceeds in the forward direction toward PGD2 formation.

rxn03021.other_comments: This is the nitrilase/nitrile hydratase-amidase type hydrolysis of bromoxynil (3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxybenzonitrile). The nitrile group (C-N) is hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid with release of ammonia. The reaction R-CN + 2 H2O -> R-COOH + NH3 is balanced: the nitrile carbon plus two waters yields the carboxylate (as 3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxybenzoate) and ammonia. Mass and charge balance check out (carboxylate deprotonated and NH3 protonation considerations aside, the atom balance is consistent). Hydrolytic nitrilase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn00606.other_comments: This is trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase (TPS2/OtsB, EC 3.1.3.12). The reaction hydrolyzes trehalose 6-phosphate, cleaving the phosphate-ester bond to yield free trehalose. However, as written, the products are D-glucose + D-glucose-6-phosphate, which would correspond to hydrolysis of the glycosidic bond rather than the phosphoester bond. The correct product of EC 3.1.3.12 is trehalose + phosphate (H2O + trehalose-6-phosphate -> trehalose + Pi). The atoms are balanced for the written reaction (C12H23O14P + H2O = C6H12O6 + C6H13O9P), so it is stoichiometrically balanced, but it does not match the named enzyme activity (phosphoglucohydrolase/phosphatase). The named reaction should produce trehalose + inorganic phosphate.

rxn02711.other_comments: This is the 4'-O-methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.116) in benzylisoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis. SAM donates a methyl group to 3'-hydroxy-N-methyl-(S)-coclaurine, producing (S)-reticuline (the product should properly be (S)-reticuline; the listing as (+)-Reticuline may be a stereochemical naming concern, but (+)-reticuline corresponds to the (R) form, so this could be flagged) and SAH plus a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced for the methyl transfer with one H+ released.

rxn00531.other_comments: This reaction describes the conversion of L-tyrosine (an alpha-amino acid) to beta-tyrosine (3-amino-3-(4-hydroxyphenyl)propanoic acid) catalyzed by tyrosine 2,3-aminomutase (TAM). The enzyme migrates the amino group from the alpha (C2) to the beta (C3) carbon. The reaction is balanced (it is an intramolecular isomerization, so no atoms are gained or lost). In vivo, this is a biosynthetic step (e.g., in production of secondary metabolites) and proceeds predominantly toward beta-tyrosine.

rxn00487.other_comments: This is the L-phenylalanine dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.4.1.20). L-phenylalanine undergoes oxidative deamination using water and NAD+ to yield phenylpyruvate, ammonia, NADH, and a proton. The reaction is balanced for atoms (C9 in both phenylalanine and phenylpyruvate) and charge. While catalogued as reversible, in vivo it typically favors reductive amination (phenylpyruvate to phenylalanine) for amino acid synthesis, though deamination occurs under appropriate conditions.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: NADPH oxidation by a Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase should consume a proton (NADPH + H+ + O2 ...), the H+ is missing on the substrate side

Incorrect product identity: 4-hydroxyacetophenone monooxygenase produces an ester (4-hydroxyphenyl acetate, i.e. 4-acetoxyphenol / the acetate ester of hydroquinone), NOT 4-hydroxyphenylacetate (a carboxylic acid). These are different molecules with different formulas
Oxygen balance is incorrect as written because the wrong product is used; a Baeyer-Villiger reaction inserts one oxygen atom into the substrate and reduces the other oxygen to water
rxn04701.other_comments: This is intended to be the EC 1.14.13.84 Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase reaction, oxidizing 4'-hydroxyacetophenone to its acetate ester (4-hydroxyphenyl acetate) with insertion of oxygen between the carbonyl and the methyl group. The enzyme name (ester-forming) confirms an ester product, but the listed product '4-Hydroxyphenylacetate' is an arylacetic acid, not the ester, indicating a product identity error.

rxn12610.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for glycerol 2-phosphate. The metabolites (H+ and glycerol 2-phosphate) on both sides represent extracellular and intracellular compartments, with both species cotransported in the same direction. Mass and charge are balanced. Transport reactions are typically written as reversible unless the proton motive force or concentration gradients dictate a specific direction; in vivo, proton symport usually drives uptake (extracellular to cytoplasmic) using the proton gradient.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides (H+ + D-Fructose on both reactant and product sides), so there is no net chemical transformation. For a proton symport transport reaction, the metabolites should be distinguished by compartment, e.g., H+[extracellular] + D-Fructose[extracellular] <=> H+[cytosol] + D-Fructose[cytosol]. Without compartment annotations the reaction is not meaningful as a transport step.
rxn09681.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction moving D-fructose into the cell coupled to a proton symport. Stoichiometry (1 H+ : 1 fructose) is balanced and reasonable for a symporter, but the equation lacks compartment designations, making it appear as a null reaction.

rxn04548.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction (MtmGIV in the mithramycin biosynthetic pathway) transferring D-olivose from the activated sugar donor dTDP-beta-D-olivose onto the aglycone acceptor premithramycinone, forming premithramycin A1 and releasing dTDP. The atom balance is consistent: the olivosyl moiety is transferred from the nucleotide sugar to the polyketide acceptor, and the dTDP leaving group accounts for the donor's remaining portion. Glycosyltransferases using NDP-sugar donors strongly favor the glycosyl transfer direction in vivo due to release of NDP and the thermodynamics of the glycosidic bond formation.

rxn02182.other_comments: This is the beta-alanyl-CoA ammonia-lyase reaction (EC 4.3.1.6). Beta-alanyl-CoA is deaminated to yield acryloyl-CoA (acrylyl-CoA) and ammonia. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: beta-alanyl-CoA (C3 amino-acyl moiety) loses NH3 to form the alpha,beta-unsaturated acryloyl-CoA. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1). This enzyme operates in propionate/3-hydroxypropionate and beta-alanine metabolism, and in organisms such as Clostridium propionicum it functions physiologically in the aminating (reverse) direction to fix ammonia onto acryloyl-CoA, but it is enzymatically reversible.

rxn02300.other_comments: This is a PAPS-dependent sulfotransferase reaction (EC 2.8.2.-) that catalyzes the final step of glucosinolate biosynthesis, transferring a sulfate group from 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) to a desulfoglucosinolate (desulfoglucotropeolin) to form the glucosinolate (glucotropeolin/benzylglucosinolate) plus adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate (PAP) and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: one sulfate group is transferred, and the release of H+ accounts for charge balance. Sulfotransferase reactions using PAPS are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the sulfation direction in vivo.

rxn11616.other_comments: This is an aromatase (CYP19) catalyzed step. The reaction oxidizes the 19-hydroxyl group of 19-hydroxyandrostenedione to the 19-oxo (aldehyde) form, consuming NADPH, O2, and a proton, producing NADP+ and 2 water. Atom and charge balance check: C19H26O3 (19-OH-androstenedione) + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> C19H24O3 (19-oxo-androstenedione) + NADP+ + 2 H2O. Carbon (19=19), the substrate loses 2 H (26->24) which together with NADPH's hydrogens and O2/H+ accounts for the 2 H2O produced. Stoichiometry is balanced.

rxn12028.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of irinotecan (CPT-11) by carboxylesterase, cleaving the carbamate ester to yield the active metabolite SN-38 and the leaving group 4-piperidinopiperidine carbamic acid, which is represented here as 1,4'-bipiperidine-1'-carboxylic acid. The atoms balance: water adds across the carbamate bond, releasing SN-38 (the phenolic active form) plus the dipiperidinyl carbamic acid and a proton. Carboxylesterase-catalyzed hydrolysis is physiologically essentially irreversible (forward) in vivo. Note that the dipiperidinyl carbamic acid is unstable and spontaneously decarboxylates to 1,4'-bipiperidine plus CO2, but as written the carbamic acid form keeps the equation balanced.

rxn03414.other_comments: This is a flavanone 3-hydroxylase (F3H) type reaction, a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase. It hydroxylates the flavanone dihydrotricetin (5,7,3',4',5'-pentahydroxyflavanone) at the C-3 position to yield the dihydroflavonol ampelopsin (dihydromyricetin). The cosubstrate 2-oxoglutarate is oxidatively decarboxylated to succinate plus CO2, with one O2 consumed. The stoichiometry is balanced: O2 provides one O atom to the substrate hydroxyl and one to CO2/succinate.

rxn02924.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of (S)-3-(imidazol-5-yl)lactate to imidazole pyruvate (imidazol-5-yl-pyruvate) coupled to reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the lactate has a secondary alcohol oxidized to a ketone, releasing 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH, one as H+). Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and charge balance check out.

rxn14104.other_comments: This is sucrose synthase (ADP-glucose:D-fructose 2-alpha-D-glucosyltransferase, EC 2.4.1.13 with ADP). The reaction as written (ADP + Sucrose -> D-Fructose + ADPglucose) is the sucrose-cleavage direction producing ADP-glucose. Stoichiometry is balanced: glucose and fructose moieties of sucrose are conserved, and ADP is converted to ADP-glucose. In vivo, sucrose synthase predominantly catalyzes sucrose breakdown to produce nucleotide-sugar (here ADP-glucose) plus fructose, so the dominant physiological direction is the forward-written cleavage of sucrose. Note that the EC name lists the synthesis direction (ADP-glucose:fructose transferase), which is opposite to the written equation; the enzyme is generally considered reversible but favors sucrose cleavage in many tissues.

rxn05173.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction for L-arabinose. The substrate L-Arabinose appears on both sides because it represents transport across the membrane (extracellular to intracellular); compartment labels are implied but not shown explicitly in this notation. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) drives the import. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced.

rxn05473.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for 2-phosphoglycolate. The same species (H+ and 2-phosphoglycolate) appear on both sides, representing movement across a membrane (e.g., extracellular to cytoplasm). Although compartment labels are not shown explicitly here, the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (1 H+ and 1 2-phosphoglycolate on each side). Proton symport transport reactions are typically reversible thermodynamically, though the net direction in vivo depends on the proton motive force and substrate concentration gradients.

rxn00226.other_comments: This is the first step of the acetyl-CoA synthetase (AMP-forming) mechanism, where ATP reacts with acetate to form acetyl-AMP (acetyl adenylate) and release pyrophosphate (PPi). The reaction is balanced: ATP provides AMP to acetate forming acetyl-adenylate, and the beta-gamma phosphates leave as PPi. Atoms and charges balance. In vivo, the enzyme-bound acetyl-adenylate intermediate normally proceeds forward because PPi is subsequently hydrolyzed by inorganic pyrophosphatase, pulling the overall reaction toward acetyl-CoA formation; however, the isolated adenylylation step itself is chemically reversible.

rxn09065.other_comments: This is phosphatidate phosphatase (PAP) hydrolyzing phosphatidic acid (1,2-dihexadecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) to diacylglycerol (1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol dihexadecanoyl) and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the phosphomonoester bond, releasing Pi and H+. Atom and charge balance are consistent. Phosphoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible, proceeding in the dephosphorylation direction.

errors: Proton imbalance: hydrolysis of GDP (a phosphoanhydride bond) to GMP and phosphate releases 1 H+ at physiological pH, not 2 H+. The charge/proton stoichiometry as written is incorrect.
rxn00236.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of GDP to GMP and inorganic phosphate (a nucleoside diphosphatase / GDP phosphohydrolase reaction). Water cleaves the terminal phosphoanhydride bond. Such hydrolytic reactions are strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction. The main issue is the proton balance: cleavage of one phosphoanhydride bond typically liberates a single proton.

errors: No spatial compartment annotation distinguishes substrates from products; as written both sides are identical (H+ + cGMP = H+ + cGMP), making the reaction a null/zero-net transformation unless compartments are specified
A proton symport transport reaction should show the same species in two compartments, e.g. H+[e] + cGMP[e] <=> H+[c] + cGMP[c]; the stoichiometry is balanced only because it is trivially identical
rxn05720.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction importing cyclic GMP (cGMP) coupled to proton symport, using the inwardly directed proton motive force. The mass and charge balance trivially, but the lack of compartment labels means the reaction is degenerate as written. With proper compartmentalization (extracellular -> cytoplasm), it represents 1:1 H+/cGMP symport driven into the cell.

rxn01880.other_comments: This is the 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (NAD+) reaction (EC 1.1.1.141). Dinoprostone is PGE2, which has a 15-hydroxyl group. NAD+ oxidizes the 15-OH to a 15-keto group, producing 15-keto-PGE2 (11alpha-hydroxy-9,15-dioxoprost-13-enoate), NADH, and H+. The reaction is balanced: one hydroxyl is oxidized to ketone, with hydride transfer to NAD+ and release of a proton. Atoms and charges balance.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced for hydrogen and charge. A monooxygenase reaction inserting one oxygen atom as a hydroxyl typically requires an additional proton, e.g. NADPH + H+ + O2 + L-Tyrosine -> H2O + NADP+ + N-Hydroxy-L-tyrosine
rxn00523.other_comments: This is an N-hydroxylating flavin/NADPH-dependent monooxygenase reaction (e.g. early step of glucosinolate/cyanogenic glycoside biosynthesis via CYP79 enzymes) that incorporates one atom of O2 into the substrate as an N-hydroxyl group, with the other oxygen reduced to water. The carbon skeleton (tyrosine -> N-hydroxytyrosine) is consistent.

errors: The reaction as written appears unbalanced. Pelargonidin 3-O-(6-caffeoyl-beta-D-glucoside) plus a glucosyl unit from UDP-glucose should yield a diglucoside product, but Bisdemalonylsalvianin is a more complex anthocyanin (pelargonidin 3-O-(6-O-caffeoyl-glucoside)-5-O-glucoside). The product matches a 5-O-glucosylation, so the glucose count is consistent (UDP-glucose donates one glucose), but atom balance should be verified for H and charge.
rxn07665.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose-dependent glucosyltransferase reaction (5-O-glucosyltransferase) transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the anthocyanin acceptor, releasing UDP. Glucosyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favored toward glycosylation in vivo due to the high-energy UDP-sugar donor.

errors: Charge imbalance: hydrolysis of one phosphodiester bond by water yields one H+ (a 5'-phosphate and a free hydroxyl), not 2.0 H+
Stoichiometric ambiguity: 'Dinucleotide' and 'Mononucleotide' are generic placeholders without defined formulas, so mass/charge balance cannot be rigorously verified
If 2.0 Mononucleotide each bear a terminal phosphate, the proton count and water count may be inconsistent depending on the exact bond cleaved
rxn05763.other_comments: This represents hydrolysis of a dinucleotide into two mononucleotides by a nucleotidohydrolase (phosphodiesterase-type) reaction, consuming water and breaking the phosphodiester linkage. Hydrolytic phosphodiester cleavage is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn10440.other_comments: This is an archaeal phosphatidylserine decarboxylase analog. The substrate archaetidylserine (2,3-O-phytanyl-sn-glycero-1-phosphoserine) is decarboxylated to archaetidylethanolamine, consuming one proton and releasing CO2. The reaction is balanced: serine head group (C3) loses CO2 to become ethanolamine (C2), with the proton consumed for the decarboxylation. Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and charge all balance.

rxn01046.other_comments: This is the decarboxylation of L-valine to form isobutylamine (2-methylpropanamine) and CO2. The reaction consumes one proton along with L-valine to produce CO2 and isobutylamine. The stoichiometry is balanced: L-valine (C5H11NO2) plus H+ yields CO2 (CO2) plus isobutylamine (C4H11N). Carbon: 5 = 1 + 4; Nitrogen: 1 = 1; Oxygen: 2 = 2; Hydrogen: 11+1 = 0+12. The reaction is balanced for mass and charge. Amino acid decarboxylations are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the release of CO2.

rxn00829.other_comments: This is diphosphomevalonate decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.33), which catalyzes the ATP-dependent decarboxylation of (R)-5-diphosphomevalonate to isopentenyl diphosphate in the mevalonate pathway. The reaction is balanced: ATP + 5-diphosphomevalonate yields ADP + Pi + CO2 + IPP. Mass and charge balance hold, with the ATP phosphorylating the 3-hydroxyl, followed by decarboxylation and loss of the phosphate as Pi. In vivo this is a committed, essentially irreversible step driven by ATP hydrolysis and CO2 release.

errors: The product should be Morphine-6-glucuronide or, more commonly for the 3-position, Morphine-3-glucuronide; the conjugation occurs at a phenolic/hydroxyl group, so this is acceptable. The main stoichiometric concern is the UDP product: glucuronidation by UGT enzymes releases UDP, which is correct here. No atom-balance error is evident if the glucuronyl moiety is transferred correctly.
rxn11790.other_comments: This represents a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) reaction, specifically UGT2B7-mediated glucuronidation of morphine. UDP-glucuronate (UDP-glucuronic acid) donates a glucuronyl group to the 3-hydroxyl (phenolic) position of morphine, forming morphine-3-glucuronide and releasing UDP. This is a phase II conjugation/detoxification reaction.

errors: The substrate is named 'S-thiohydroximoyl-L-cysteine' in the enzyme name but written as 'S-Alkyl-thiohydroximate' in the reaction equation - these appear inconsistent

The reaction as written is not mass/atom balanced; cleaving a cysteine conjugate (S-alkyl-thiohydroximate where the alkyl moiety is derived from cysteine) should release the thiohydroximate plus a C3 fragment - the products NH3 + pyruvate account for the cysteine-derived portion, but the carbon/sulfur balance depends on the exact alkyl group definition which is ambiguous
rxn13991.other_comments: This represents a C-S lyase (cysteine conjugate beta-lyase type) reaction in the glucosinolate biosynthesis pathway, where an S-alkyl-thiohydroximate (a cysteine conjugate) is hydrolytically/eliminatively cleaved to yield the thiohydroximate, pyruvate, and ammonia via a beta-elimination on the cysteine moiety. The 'deaminating; pyruvate-forming' designation indicates conversion of the cysteine side chain to pyruvate + NH3.

rxn04560.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of methylecgonine (ecgonine methyl ester) to ecgonine and methanol, releasing a proton. The reaction is balanced: methylecgonine (C10H17NO3) + H2O yields ecgonine (C9H15NO3) + methanol (CH4O) + H+. Carbon: 10 = 9+1; the mass and charge balance correctly. This is an esterase-catalyzed hydrolysis step in cocaine degradation.

errors: The product should be 5-deoxy-alpha-D-ribose-1-phosphate (2-deoxyribose is incorrect; doxifluridine is a 5-deoxyribose derivative, not 2-deoxyribose). The name '5-Deoxyribose-1-phosphate' is acceptable but should specify the alpha-D-ribose configuration and the 5-deoxy modification.
Stoichiometry is otherwise balanced: phosphate cleaves the N-glycosidic bond releasing 5-fluorouracil and 5-deoxyribose-1-phosphate.
rxn11750.other_comments: This is a phosphorolysis reaction catalyzed by thymidine/pyrimidine phosphorylase. Doxifluridine (5'-deoxy-5-fluorouridine) is phosphorolyzed to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) plus 5-deoxy-alpha-D-ribose-1-phosphate. This is the basis for prodrug activation of doxifluridine to the active cytotoxic agent 5-FU. Note the sugar is 5-deoxyribose (not 2-deoxyribose), so the product name as written ('5-Deoxyribose-1-phosphate') is appropriate but should be alpha-configured.

rxn01722.other_comments: This reaction represents the interconversion between bilirubin and biliverdin coupled to NAD+/NADH. The atoms balance: biliverdin (C33H34N4O6) plus 2H (as NADH + H+) yields bilirubin (C33H36N4O6), and the redox cofactors are balanced. The named enzyme (Bilirubin:NAD+ oxidoreductase) is biliverdin reductase, which physiologically reduces biliverdin to bilirubin using NADPH (or NADH for some isoforms). As written (oxidizing bilirubin to biliverdin), the in vivo flux runs predominantly in the reverse direction, i.e., biliverdin + NADH + H+ -> bilirubin + NAD+.

rxn07525.other_comments: This reaction represents a NADPH-dependent flavonoid hydroxylase (cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase) that hydroxylates liquiritigenin at the 6 position to form 6,7,4'-trihydroxyflavanone. Liquiritigenin is 7,4'-dihydroxyflavanone, so addition of one hydroxyl group is consistent with a monooxygenase reaction. Stoichiometry is balanced: one oxygen atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (hydroxylation) and the other is reduced to water using two electrons and protons supplied by NADPH. The mass and charge balance check out with NADPH + O2 + H+ consumed and H2O + NADP+ produced.

rxn02470.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 3,9-dihydroxypterocarpan 6a-monooxygenase (EC 1.14.13.28), which converts (6aR,11aR)-3,9-dihydroxypterocarpan to (-)-glycinol (the 6a-hydroxylated product) in the glyceollin biosynthetic pathway. The stoichiometry is balanced: a typical NADPH-dependent monooxygenase incorporates one oxygen atom into the substrate as a hydroxyl group and reduces the other to water, consuming NADPH + H+ and O2, producing NADP+ and H2O. Charge balance is consistent with NADP+ written as NADP. As a P450/NADPH-dependent monooxygenase, this hydroxylation is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction toward glycinol.

rxn09521.other_comments: This is a gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) reaction where the gamma-glutamyl group of glutathione (GSH, gamma-L-Glu-L-Cys-Gly) is transferred to an acceptor amino acid (L-alanine), yielding 5-L-glutamyl-L-alanine (gamma-glutamyl-alanine) and the dipeptide Cys-Gly. The atoms balance: GSH donates its gamma-glutamyl moiety to alanine, releasing cysteinylglycine. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1:1). Physiologically, GGT initiates extracellular glutathione catabolism and the transpeptidation reaction proceeds in the direction of gamma-glutamyl transfer to the amino acid acceptor.

rxn06555.other_comments: This is a gamma-glutamyltransferase-type reaction where the gamma-glutamyl group of D-glutamine is transferred to a D-glutamyl-peptide acceptor, releasing ammonia. The reaction is mass-balanced: D-glutamine (C5H10N2O3) plus the glutamyl-peptide donates a glutamyl moiety; the amide nitrogen is released as NH3, and a proton is liberated. Atom and charge balance appear consistent as written.

rxn00868.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of butyryl-CoA to crotonyl-CoA (trans-2-enoyl-CoA), the first step of fatty acid beta-oxidation, coupled to reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Stoichiometry is balanced: butyryl-CoA (C4 acyl-CoA) loses 2 H (one as H+ and a hydride to NAD+) to form crotonyl-CoA. In vivo, the physiological enzyme acyl-CoA dehydrogenase uses FAD rather than NAD+; the NAD+-dependent direction as written is thermodynamically unfavorable. The reverse direction (crotonyl-CoA reduction to butyryl-CoA via crotonyl-CoA reductase, e.g., in butyrate fermentation) is the biologically favored direction with this cofactor pair.

rxn04741.other_comments: This represents a ring-cleavage (extradiol dioxygenase) type reaction on a dihydroxynaphthalene, incorporating molecular O2 to open the aromatic ring and form a 2-hydroxychromene-2-carboxylate, analogous to naphthalene degradation pathways (e.g., 1,2-dihydroxynaphthalene dioxygenase). Such oxygenase-catalyzed ring cleavages are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn06696.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by H2-forming methylenetetrahydromethanopterin dehydrogenase (Hmd), found in methanogenic archaea. It reduces 5,10-methenyl-H4MPT (a cation, carrying a positive charge) using H2 to form 5,10-methylene-H4MPT, releasing a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the methenyl cation plus H2 yields the neutral methylene compound plus H+ (mass and charge balanced, since the methenyl form carries a +1 charge that is neutralized upon reduction). In vivo this enzyme operates near equilibrium during methanogenesis and can run in either direction depending on the H2 partial pressure and metabolic demand (CO2 reduction pathway).

rxn07746.other_comments: This represents the N-demethylation of caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) to theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine), catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (e.g., CYP1A2). The demethylation removes the N1-methyl group, releasing it as formaldehyde. The reaction consumes NADPH and O2, with one oxygen atom incorporated into water (consistent with monooxygenase chemistry). Stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl carbon lost from caffeine is recovered as formaldehyde, and N/O/H atoms balance correctly. Such oxidative demethylations are physiologically irreversible.

rxn00572.other_comments: This reaction represents nitrate reductase (NADPH) written in the oxidative direction: nitrite + NADP+ + H2O <=> nitrate + NADPH + 2 H+. The atoms balance: left has N, 2 O (nitrite) + 1 O (water) = 3 O matching nitrate; H balance is 2 H (water) on left and 2 H+ on right (plus NADP+/NADPH H accounting). The charges and elements balance correctly. In vivo, assimilatory/dissimilatory nitrate reductase strongly favors the reductive direction (nitrate -> nitrite, consuming NADPH), so the spontaneous physiological flux is the reverse of how this is written.

rxn02140.other_comments: This is a CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction activating 2-furoate to 2-furoyl-CoA. ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi, with the carboxylate of 2-furoate forming a thioester bond with CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + 2-furoate yields AMP + PPi + H+ + 2-furoyl-CoA. Charge and atoms balance with the H+ released. While written as reversible, AMP-forming ligases are driven forward in vivo by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making the activation effectively irreversible.

rxn02265.other_comments: This reaction represents the non-enzymatic cyclization of hydroxymethylbilane (preuroporphyrinogen, a linear tetrapyrrole) to form uroporphyrinogen I with release of water. However, in the absence of this enzyme, hydroxymethylbilane spontaneously cyclizes to the non-physiological uroporphyrinogen I isomer. The stoichiometry (1 hydroxymethylbilane -> 1 H2O + 1 uroporphyrinogen I) is balanced and correct. This spontaneous cyclization proceeds in the forward (cyclization) direction and is effectively irreversible.

rxn04153.other_comments: This is the second oxidation step of the Mg-protoporphyrin IX monomethyl ester oxidative cyclase (encoded by AcsF/BchE-type enzymes, EC 1.14.13.81) in chlorophyll/bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis. rxn04956.other_comments: This is the (R)-6-hydroxynicotine oxidase (flavoprotein) reaction from nicotine degradation in Arthrobacter/Paenarthrobacter. rxn07605.other_comments: This is a PAPS-dependent sulfotransferase reaction (EC 2.8.2.-) transferring a sulfate group from 3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) to the hydroxyl group of 5beta-scymnol, producing 5beta-scymnol sulfate and adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate (PAP). Sulfotransferase reactions are strongly favored in the forward (sulfo-transfer) direction in vivo due to the high energy of the phosphosulfate bond in PAPS.

rxn07623.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction where the CoA moiety is transferred from acetyl-CoA to 3-hydroxy-5-oxohexanoate, producing acetate and 3-hydroxy-5-oxohexanoyl-CoA. The CoA group is conserved on one side (one thioester reactant, one thioester product), and the carbon skeletons balance: acetyl-CoA donates CoA to the carboxylate of the hexanoate substrate. Atom and charge balance are maintained. CoA-transferases typically operate near equilibrium and are reversible in vivo, with direction governed by relative concentrations of the acyl-CoA/free acid pairs.

rxn07355.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in the spirilloxanthin biosynthesis pathway of purple bacteria. SAM donates a methyl group to the hydroxyl of hydroxyspirilloxanthin, producing methoxylated spirilloxanthin plus S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl transfer from SAM to the substrate hydroxyl forms a methyl ether, releasing SAH and H+. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are strongly forward-driven in vivo due to the high transfer potential of SAM and favorable thermodynamics.

rxn11719.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of behenoyl-CoA (docosanoyl-CoA, C22:0 acyl-CoA) by a thioesterase. rxn06296.other_comments: This reaction describes an acetyltransferase transferring the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to a monoterpenol (a generic monoterpene alcohol), producing CoA and the corresponding monoterpenol acetate ester. rxn14025.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase (PAPS-dependent) reaction transferring a sulfate group from 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) to desulfo-p-hydroxybenzylglucosinolate, producing the glucosinolate sinalbin (p-hydroxybenzylglucosinolate) and PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate). rxn02478.other_comments: This is the biphenyl-2,3-diol 1,2-dioxygenase reaction (BphC, EC 1.13.11.39) in the biphenyl/PCB degradation pathway. rxn04787.other_comments: This is the L-2,4-diaminobutyrate acetyltransferase (EctA) reaction in ectoine biosynthesis. rxn11758.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by thymidine phosphorylase (pyrimidine-nucleoside phosphorylase), acting on the fluorinated analog. 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) plus 2-deoxy-alpha-D-ribose-1-phosphate yields floxuridine (5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine, FdUrd) plus inorganic phosphate. Checking H balance: glycine (C2H5NO2) + THF provides the methylene carbon; release of NH3 and CO2 plus NADH typically requires an additional H+ on the product side to balance protons (NAD+ + Glycine + THF <=> NADH + H+ + CO2 + NH3 + 5,10-CH2-THF).

Like most P450 oxygenations, this is physiologically irreversible in the hydroxylation direction.

rxn00718.other_comments: This reaction represents dihydrouracil dehydrogenase (oxidase) activity, oxidizing 5,6-dihydrouracil to uracil using molecular oxygen, producing hydrogen peroxide. In vivo this oxidase reaction proceeds in the oxidative direction toward uracil with O2 as electron acceptor.

rxn14245.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolytic deamination of 2-aminoacrylate (dehydroalanine, the enamine/imine tautomer 2-iminopropanoate), yielding ammonia and pyruvate. The reaction is balanced: dehydroalanine (C3H5NO2) plus water (H2O) gives pyruvate (C3H4O3) plus ammonia (NH3). Atoms balance: C3, N1, O3, and H7 on each side. This is the spontaneous/enzyme-assisted (RidA/2-iminobutanoate deaminase) hydrolysis of a reactive enamine intermediate to a stable keto acid, which is strongly favored thermodynamically in vivo.

rxn08711.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by ADP-heptose:LPS heptosyltransferase II (WaaF/RfaF, EC 2.4.99.-). It transfers the second L-glycero-D-manno-heptose residue from ADP-L-glycero-beta-D-manno-heptose onto the heptosyl-Kdo2-lipid A acceptor (forming heptosyl-heptosyl-Kdo2-lipid A), releasing ADP. Stoichiometry is balanced: a single heptose moiety is transferred from the ADP-heptose donor to the LPS inner core acceptor, yielding ADP and the di-heptose product. As a glycosyltransferase reaction utilizing a high-energy ADP-sugar donor, it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass/charge balanced. Oxidation of the 5'-CH2OH to a carboxylic acid (uronic acid) is a 4-electron oxidation and cannot be accomplished by a single O2 producing only one H2O. A typical alcohol-to-aldehyde oxidation by an oxidase consumes O2 and produces H2O2 (R-CH2OH + O2 -> R-CHO + H2O2); a further aldehyde-to-acid step requires additional oxidant/water. As written with only one O2 -> one H2O + H+, oxygen and hydrogen atoms do not balance for full conversion of a primary alcohol (CH2OH) to carboxylate (COOH/COO-).
rxn04054.other_comments: The reaction proposes oxidation of inosine at the 5' position, converting the ribose 5'-hydroxymethyl group to a carboxyl group, yielding 9-riburonosylhypoxanthine (the glucuronic-acid-like uronate analog). O2-dependent oxidations of alcohols to acids are thermodynamically strongly favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn04360.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction transferring an L-oleandrose sugar from dTDP-L-oleandrose to the avermectin A1b monosaccharide aglycone-derived acceptor, producing the disaccharide-bearing Avermectin A1b and releasing dTDP. The atom balance is consistent: the sugar moiety is transferred while dTDP departs, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. Glycosyltransferases using NDP-sugar donors strongly favor the transfer direction in vivo because dTDP-sugar bond hydrolysis/transfer is thermodynamically favorable and the released dTDP is rapidly recycled.

ABC import is energetically driven by ATP hydrolysis and is effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo.

rxn03596.other_comments: This is the haloalkane dehalogenase (DhlA) reaction. 'Dutch liquid' is a synonym for 1,2-dichloroethane (ClCH2-CH2Cl). Hydrolytic dehalogenation replaces one chlorine with a hydroxyl: H2O + 1,2-dichloroethane -> 2-chloroethanol (ClCH2-CH2OH) + Cl- + H+. The stoichiometry balances for C (2=2), H (water 2 + DCE 4 = 6; products: H+ 1 + 2-chloroethanol 5 = 6), O (1=1), and Cl (2 = 1 + 1), with charge balanced (0 = +1 -1 + 0).

rxn07498.other_comments: This represents a dioxygenase-catalyzed extradiol (meta) ring cleavage of a dihydroxynaphthalene sulfonate. Such dioxygenase reactions consume molecular O2 and are physiologically irreversible (committed catabolic step), proceeding in the direction of ring opening.

rxn03290.other_comments: This is a hydro-lyase (dehydratase/hydratase) reaction in bile acid biosynthesis. The reaction as written shows dehydration of the 24-hydroxyl group to form the 24-enoyl-CoA, releasing water. The atoms balance: removal of H2O from the tetrahydroxy substrate yields the trihydroxy-cholest-24-enoyl-CoA. However, in vivo (peroxisomal bile acid synthesis), the enzyme (D-bifunctional protein / 2-enoyl-CoA hydratase 2) catalyzes the hydration direction, adding water across the 24,25 double bond of 3alpha,7alpha,12alpha-trihydroxy-5beta-cholest-24-enoyl-CoA to form the 24-hydroxy intermediate. Thus the physiological flux is from right to left as written (hydration), i.e., reverse of the written dehydration.

rxn07445.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of malonurate (3-oxo-3-ureidopropanoate, i.e. N-carbamoyl malonate) by malonurate hydrolase. Malonuric acid (C4H5N2O4-) + H2O yields urea (CH4N2O) + malonate (C3H2O4 2-) + H+. Checking atoms: malonuric acid HOOC-CH2-CO-NH-CO-NH2 (C4H6N2O4 neutral) plus H2O gives malonate (C3H4O4 neutral) + urea (CH4N2O); C:4=3+1, N:2=0+2, O:4+1=4+1, H:6+2=4+4. Mass balanced. The released H+ accounts for deprotonation states. This is part of pyrimidine (uracil) degradation via the reductive pathway, where amidohydrolases catalyze essentially irreversible hydrolytic cleavages.

rxn06620.other_comments: This represents the oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) reaction in N-linked glycosylation. The dolichyl-diphosphooligosaccharide (Glc3Man9GlcNAc2-PP-Dol) donor transfers the oligosaccharide en bloc to the asparagine residue (in the Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequon) of a nascent polypeptide, releasing dolichyl diphosphate. The reaction is written generically (Protein asparagine, Oligosaccharide-PP-Dol) so explicit atomic balance cannot be verified, but stoichiometrically it is balanced as written: the oligosaccharide moiety is transferred from the dolichol carrier to the protein, with dolichyl diphosphate released.

rxn03714.other_comments: This is the carbazole 1,9a-dioxygenase reaction (CarAa) that initiates carbazole degradation. It is a dioxygenase that incorporates both oxygen atoms, hydroxylating carbazole at the angular position (1,9a positions), leading to ring cleavage and formation of 2'-aminobiphenyl-2,3-diol. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + O2 + H+ + carbazole (C12H9N) yields NAD+ + 2'-aminobiphenyl-2,3-diol (C12H11NO2). Carbon (12), nitrogen (1), and the addition of two oxygen atoms and a net of two H from NADH/H+ all balance. Note the systematic name says (2,3-hydroxylating) but the actual product reflects angular dioxygenation; the product formula is consistent with addition of O2 and reduction.

rxn13126.other_comments: This is annotated as a transport reaction (extracellular import of fucose), apparently a proton-coupled symport. Functionally, proton symporters are typically driven by the proton motive force toward import, but they can be reversible thermodynamically; with no compartment-specific driving forces shown I default to reversible.

rxn02972.other_comments: This represents the conversion of 7alpha-hydroxycholesterol to 7alpha-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one, a key step in the classic (neutral) bile acid biosynthesis pathway, catalyzed by 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD3B7). The enzyme oxidizes the 3beta-hydroxyl and isomerizes the delta5 double bond to delta4. In vivo it proceeds toward bile acid synthesis (forward), driven by downstream metabolism.

rxn02623.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydration of mesaconate (2-methylfumarate / methylfumarate) to form L-threo-3-methylmalate (beta-methylmalate), catalyzed by mesaconate hydratase (EC 4.2.1.34). The stoichiometry is balanced: mesaconate (C5H4O4 as dianion) plus H2O yields 3-methylmalate (C5H6O5). One water adds across the C=C double bond. As a hydratase/lyase reaction, it is thermodynamically reversible, though physiological flux often favors hydration (forward) in pathways such as L-leucine/methylaspartate metabolism.

rxn12087.other_comments: This is the final step of galantamine biosynthesis where norgalanthamine is N-methylated to form galantamine. SAM serves as the methyl donor, producing SAH and a proton. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are typically thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in the forward direction.

rxn01407.other_comments: This describes carnitine 3-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.108), which oxidizes carnitine to 3-dehydrocarnitine using NAD+ as the electron acceptor. rxn00901.other_comments: This is the valine dehydrogenase (NADP+) reaction (EC 1.4.1.8). rxn05135.other_comments: This reaction represents glucosylation of DIBOA (2,4-dihydroxy-1,4-benzoxazin-3-one) by UDP-glucose, catalyzed by a UDP-glucose:DIBOA glucosyltransferase, producing UDP and DIBOA-glucoside (DIBOA-Glc). This is part of benzoxazinoid biosynthesis in grasses (e.g., maize, BX8/BX9 enzymes). Glucosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn00986.other_comments: This reaction represents the adenylylation of propionate (propanoate) by ATP to form propionyl-AMP (propionyladenylate) with release of pyrophosphate (PPi). It is the first step of propionyl-CoA synthetase-type activation. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + propionate yields propionyl-adenylate + PPi, with the AMP moiety transferred to the carboxylate and the beta-gamma phosphates leaving as PPi. Charges and atoms balance. The acyl-adenylate intermediate is high-energy; although the chemical step is reversible, the overall process is typically driven forward in vivo by subsequent PPi hydrolysis and CoA transfer.

rxn07719.other_comments: This reaction represents the acylation of mirtillin (delphinidin 3-O-glucoside) with a p-coumaroyl group transferred from 4-coumaroyl-CoA, producing delphinidin 3-(6-p-coumaroyl)glucoside and releasing free CoA. The reaction is catalyzed by an anthocyanin acyltransferase (BAHD family). Stoichiometry is balanced: the coumaroyl moiety is transferred from CoA to the 6-position of the glucose unit. Acyl-CoA-dependent acyltransferases are thermodynamically driven by thioester bond cleavage, favoring the acylation (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn04823.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase reaction converting naphthalene 1,2-dihydrodiol to the 1,2-dihydroxy-3,4-epoxide (a bay-region diol epoxide intermediate). Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ provide reducing equivalents and one oxygen atom is incorporated into the epoxide while the other is reduced to water, regenerating NADP+. Atom and charge balance are consistent with a typical monooxygenase mechanism.

rxn00795.other_comments: This reaction represents biotinidase (EC 3.5.1.12), which hydrolyzes biocytin (N6-D-biotinyl-L-lysine) into free biotin (BIOT) and L-lysine using water. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water molecule cleaves the amide bond, releasing one L-lysine and one biotin. As a hydrolase, the reaction strongly favors the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo, recycling biotin from biocytin during protein turnover.

rxn02787.other_comments: This is a BAHD-type acyltransferase reaction transferring the sinapoyl group from sinapoyl-CoA to the hydroxyl group of tartronic acid (2-hydroxymalonate), releasing free CoA and forming sinapoyltartronate ester. Atoms balance: sinapoyl-CoA donates the acyl group via thioester cleavage, esterifying the hydroxyl of tartronate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (one acyl-CoA + one acceptor yields one ester + one CoA). Acyl-CoA transferase reactions are thermodynamically driven by thioester hydrolysis and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn05412.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase reaction in fatty acid biosynthesis (branched-chain). NADPH and H+ reduce the trans-2 double bond of 4-methyl-trans-pent-2-enoyl-ACP to yield the saturated 4-methyl-pentanoyl-ACP plus NADP+. Stoichiometry and atom/charge balance are consistent: the C=C double bond is reduced by addition of two H (one as hydride from NADPH, one as proton). In vivo, enoyl reductase steps in FAS strongly favor the reductive (forward) direction.

rxn06906.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by trans-3-chloroacrylic acid dehalogenase (CaaD, EC 3.8.1.6). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: left side has C3H3ClO2 + H2O; right side has C3H4O3 + H+ + Cl-. Carbon (3=3), hydrogen (3+2=4+1), oxygen (2+1=3), and chlorine (1=1) all balance, and charge balances (acid neutral form gives -1 on right from Cl- offset by H+, consistent). The enzyme operates in the catabolism of 1,3-dichloropropene, committing the substrate toward central metabolism.
