rxn10215.other_comments: This is intended to be a phosphatidic acid biosynthesis step: a 1-acyl-glycerol-3-phosphate (LPA) is acylated at the sn-2 position by an acyl-CoA (LPAAT/AGPAT reaction) to form phosphatidic acid (diacyl-glycerol-3-phosphate), releasing CoA. rxn09949.other_comments: This reaction describes spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferase (SSAT, SAT1) acting on spermine. The atom and charge balance is correct: each acetyl transfer releases CoA and a proton, so 2 acetyl-CoA yields 2 CoA, 2 H+, and the diacetylated polyamine. In vivo, SSAT-catalyzed acetylation is the committed, essentially irreversible step in polyamine catabolism, driving the reaction in the forward (acetylation) direction.

The reaction is intrinsically reversible, but its biological flux usually favors NADH consumption.

rxn13438.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylinositol synthase (CDP-diacylglycerol-inositol 3-phosphatidyltransferase) reaction. It transfers the phosphatidyl group from CDP-diacylglycerol (here the dipalmitoyl, C16:0 species) onto myo-inositol, releasing CMP and a proton, and forming phosphatidylinositol with the corresponding C16:0 acyl chains. The stoichiometry is balanced: the phosphatidyl moiety is transferred from CDP-DAG to inositol, with CMP and H+ released. The substrate should properly be myo-inositol rather than 'L-Inositol', but the intended substrate is clear.

rxn03612.other_comments: This reaction describes the interconversion of 4-methylmuconolactone (a cyclic lactone) and 3-methyl-cis,cis-muconate (an open-chain dicarboxylic acid) with release/uptake of a proton. In the protocatechuate/beta-ketoadipate pathway of methylaromatic degradation, muconolactone-type cycloisomerases catalyze lactonization of muconates; however, for the methyl-substituted branch the equilibrium and physiological flux favor formation of the lactone (cyclization). rxn04094.other_comments: This is an amine oxidase (sarcosine oxidase-like) reaction acting on N-ethylglycine. rxn14090.other_comments: This is a prenyltransferase reaction transferring a dimethylallyl group from DMAPP to leachianone G, producing sophoraflavanone G with release of diphosphate (PPi). rxn03699.other_comments: This reaction couples NADH oxidation to the reduction of hydroxybenzoquinone (2-hydroxy-1,4-benzoquinone) to hydroxyquinol (1,2,4-trihydroxybenzene). Although named as an oxidoreductase acting on the trihydroxybenzene, in vivo such NAD(P)H-dependent quinone reductases strongly favor reduction of the quinone, so the forward direction as written (consuming NADH) is the physiological direction. The redox chemistry and carbon balance are otherwise consistent.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the hydration of methyl-cis-aconitate to methylisocitrate adds the elements of water (H2O) across the double bond, so atoms should balance one-to-one; if the formulas as written do not account for all H and O atoms, the equation is unbalanced
Possible naming/charge inconsistency: 2-methylaconitate/methylisocitrate are typically carboxylate anions at physiological pH, and charge balance should be verified
rxn13424.other_comments: This is the 2-methylcitrate cycle reaction catalyzed by aconitase (or 2-methylcitrate dehydratase/2-methylaconitate hydratase, AcnD/PrpD-type), interconverting 2-methyl-cis-aconitate and water with 2-methylisocitrate. Aconitase-type hydratase reactions are reversible in vivo.

errors: The reaction is not mass-balanced as written; the molecular formula of the 'Blue pigment' product is undefined/ambiguous, making it impossible to verify stoichiometric balance of C, H, N, and O atoms. In the known reaction (R07948), 2 molecules of 2,3,6-trihydroxypyridine combine oxidatively to form the blue pigment (a dimeric quinone-imine type compound), and the atom balance depends on the exact structure of the pigment.
rxn12015.other_comments: This corresponds to KEGG R07948, part of nicotinate degradation. 2,3,6-trihydroxypyridine is oxidized by O2 (autoxidation/oxidative coupling) to form a blue pigment with release of hydrogen peroxide. The dimerization to a colored quinonoid product driven by O2 consumption is effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: This reaction is mislabeled as '3-keto-steroid reductase' but the conversion to zymosterol does not involve reduction of a 3-keto group; the naming/EC association appears inconsistent with the actual chemistry
The metabolite name 'zymosterol intermediate 2' is ambiguous and undefined, making stoichiometric verification difficult

If a 3-keto group is being reduced to a 3-hydroxyl, the stoichiometry of NADPH + H+ -> NADP+ is consistent for a single reduction step, but the substrate identity must be a 3-ketosteroid for this to balance
rxn09623.other_comments: This represents an NADPH-dependent reductase step in post-squalene sterol biosynthesis leading to zymosterol. The reaction reduces a substrate using NADPH as cofactor, oxidizing it to NADP+. In vivo, NADPH-dependent sterol biosynthetic reductions are essentially irreversible toward product (zymosterol) formation. Note that 'NADP' should be written as 'NADP+' to reflect proper charge balance.

errors: Reaction is not balanced. The standard reaction interconverting hydantoin-propionate (4-imidazolone-5-propanoate is actually the same family) involves hydrolysis, not O2 release. As written, mass and oxygen/hydrogen atoms do not balance: production of O2 from two substrates without an oxygen source/sink is chemically incorrect.
Atom balance fails: the difference between hydantoin-propionate and 4-imidazolone-5-propanoate corresponds to a hydrolysis (addition/removal of H2O), not release of molecular O2.
Charge/proton balance not accounted for.
rxn00050.other_comments: The reaction relates hydantoin-propionate and 4-imidazolone-5-propanoate, intermediates in histidine degradation. The physiological reaction (imidazolonepropionase, EC 3.5.2.7) is a hydrolytic ring-opening using H2O, converting 4-imidazolone-5-propanoate to N-formimino-L-glutamate, or interconverts urocanate hydratase products. Generating O2 here is not biochemically valid and indicates a malformed/auto-generated equation.

rxn01339.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity (here NADP-dependent), interconverting dehydroepiandrosterone (DHA/DHEA, a 3beta-hydroxy-delta5 steroid) and androstenedione. Stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of the 3-hydroxyl group to a ketone transfers a hydride to NADP+ giving NADPH + H+. As written (DHA -> androstenedione), this is the oxidation direction. In vivo, 3beta-HSD physiologically converts DHEA to androstenedione (with concomitant delta5->delta4 isomerization), so the favored direction is toward androstenedione formation.

errors: Mass imbalance: the conversion of juvenile hormone III acid (which contains an epoxide) to its diol by hydrolysis adds H2O across the epoxide ring. The product written as a 'diol' is consistent with epoxide hydrolase activity, so atom balance may be correct if the substrate epoxide opens to a vicinal diol. However, the reaction name/identifier (R08152) corresponds to epoxide hydrolase acting on juvenile hormone, and stereochemistry/atom counts should be verified.
rxn11538.other_comments: This represents an epoxide hydrolase (juvenile hormone epoxide hydrolase, EC 3.3.2.x) reaction in which water hydrolyzes the 10,11-epoxide of juvenile hormone III acid to yield the corresponding vicinal diol. Epoxide hydrolysis is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of diol formation (a degradative/inactivation step in JH metabolism).

rxn09245.other_comments: This is an aminoacyl-adenylate formation reaction (serine activation), where ATP reacts with L-serine to form L-seryl-AMP (seryl-adenylate) plus pyrophosphate. Atoms balance: ATP provides AMP moiety, the carboxyl of serine is adenylated, releasing PPi. The H+ accounts for charge balance. In vivo this is driven forward by subsequent PPi hydrolysis by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making the aminoacylation effectively irreversible toward the aminoacyl-adenylate.

rxn06588.other_comments: This is the 4-chlorobenzoyl-CoA dehalogenase reaction (EC 3.8.1.6), a hydrolytic dehalogenation. Water attacks the aromatic ring (via a Meisenheimer-like intermediate with an active-site aspartate), replacing the chlorine at the para position to give 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA, releasing chloride and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: substrate side has the C-Cl bond and incoming H2O; product side has the C-OH plus released Cl- and H+. This is part of the bacterial degradation pathway of 4-chlorobenzoate.

rxn04868.other_comments: This is an intramolecular oxygen transfer (hydroperoxide isomerase/hydroxymutase) reaction. 8(R)-HPODE (8R-hydroperoxyoctadeca-9,12-dienoate) is converted to (7S,8S)-DiHODE (7,8-dihydroxyoctadeca-9,12-dienoate). The hydroperoxide is rearranged: one oxygen remains at C8 as a hydroxyl and the other oxygen is transferred to C7 as a hydroxyl, forming a vicinal diol. Both substrate and product contain the same C18 backbone with two C=C double bonds (9Z,12Z) and a carboxylate. Atoms are balanced - the two oxygens of the peroxide become two hydroxyls, no net atom change, so the equation is stoichiometrically correct as an isomerization.

rxn00010.other_comments: This is the glyoxylate carboligase reaction (EC 4.1.1.47). Two glyoxylate molecules condense, releasing CO2 and forming tartronate semialdehyde, consuming a proton. Atoms balance: 2 glyoxylate (C2H1O3 each, as anions) = C4H2O6; products CO2 (CO2) + tartronate semialdehyde (C3H3O4) = C4H3O6, with the H+ on the left balancing. Charge: 2(-1) + 1(+1) = -1 on left; CO2 (0) + tartronate semialdehyde (-1) = -1 on right. Balanced. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo due to CO2 release in glyoxylate utilization pathways.

errors: No compartment information is provided; a transport reaction requires distinct compartments (e.g., periplasm/extracellular vs cytoplasm) for both H+ and butanesulfonate. As written, both sides are identical and the net reaction is null (no actual transport or chemical change).
rxn12559.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transporter for butanesulfonate, where H+ and butanesulfonate are co-transported across a membrane. The stoichiometry (1 H+ : 1 substrate) is plausible, but the reaction string lacks compartment tags, so it reduces to an identity with no net transformation. To be correct it should read something like: H+[e] + butanesulfonate[e] <=> H+[c] + butanesulfonate[c]. Symport direction in vivo is typically driven by the proton motive force (inward), but transporters can be modeled as reversible.

rxn00084.other_comments: This reaction represents NADPH-dependent reduction of hydrogen peroxide to water (glutathione/thioredoxin peroxidase-type or NADPH peroxidase activity). Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH (C21H29N7O17P3) + H2O2 + H+ yields 2 H2O + NADP+ (C21H27N7O17P3). Atoms balance (the 2 H from NADPH and 1 H from H+ plus the 2 O and 2 H of H2O2 account for the 2 water molecules), and charge is balanced. Physiologically this proceeds in the direction of detoxifying H2O2.

errors: The product 'Cortell' is not a recognized chemical entity; the correct product of cortisol O-acetylation should be cortisol 21-acetate (acetyl-cortisol)
Reaction as written is unbalanced because the product is undefined/misnamed
rxn02036.other_comments: This represents an acetyl-CoA-dependent O-acetyltransferase transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the 21-hydroxyl of cortisol, releasing CoA and producing cortisol 21-acetate. The mechanism and overall transfer logic are correct, but the product name 'Cortell' appears to be a truncated or corrupted name for cortisol acetate. CoA-dependent acetyl transfers are thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy thioester bond, hence forward directionality.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the conversion of an aldoxime (C8H9NO2) to a hydroxynitrile/cyanohydrin (C8H7NO2) requires loss of two hydrogen atoms and water elimination; with NADPH + O2 + H+ as substrates and 2 H2O + NADP+ as products, the hydrogen and oxygen balance does not close properly. Left side O: NADPH O-content + 2 (O2) + oxime (2 O); right side: 2 H2O (2 O) + NADP + product (2 O). The single oxime-to-nitrile oxidation typically consumes one O2 and one NADPH yielding only one H2O for a monooxygenase dehydration, not two.
rxn03993.other_comments: This represents a cytochrome P450 (CYP79/CYP71-type) reaction in cyanogenic glucoside/dhurrin biosynthesis, converting 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldoxime to the cyanohydrin (S)-4-hydroxymandelonitrile via a dehydration and C-hydroxylation. Such P450-catalyzed oxidations are physiologically irreversible (forward). The overall transformation is a two-step process (dehydration to nitrile then hydroxylation), so the lumped stoichiometry should be checked carefully.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (NH3 + K+) on both sides with no compartment annotation, making it stoichiometrically meaningless as a chemical transformation. For a transport reaction, the substrates and products must be distinguished by compartment (e.g., NH3[external] + K+[internal] <=> NH3[internal] + K+[external]). As written, there is no net change.

An NH3/K+ antiport mechanism is unusual; ammonium transport is typically described with NH4+ (the charged species) rather than neutral NH3, and antiport coupling to K+ for a neutral molecule would not be charge-balanced or biologically sensible.
If this is intended as an antiport, the two species should move in opposite directions across the membrane, which requires explicit compartment labels that are missing.
rxn10868.other_comments: This is annotated as an ammonium transport reaction coupled to K+ antiport. As written, both sides are identical (NH3 + K+ <=> NH3 + K+) with no compartment specification, so no actual transport or transformation is represented. Proper transport reactions require compartment tags to indicate the direction of solute movement.

rxn02890.other_comments: This reaction represents 3-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity acting on lithocholate (3alpha-hydroxy-5beta-cholanate). The 3-alpha-hydroxyl group is oxidized to a 3-oxo group, with NAD+ being reduced to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance correctly (the oxidation releases one hydride to NAD+ and one proton). 3alpha-HSD enzymes are typically reversible NAD(P)-dependent oxidoreductases, with directionality depending on the NAD+/NADH ratio and substrate concentrations.

rxn04949.other_comments: This is an L-2-hydroxy acid oxidase (likely 2-hydroxyacid oxidase / L-alpha-hydroxyacid oxidase family) reaction oxidizing the alpha-hydroxyl group of L-2-hydroxyphytanate to a 2-oxo (keto) group, with molecular oxygen as the electron acceptor producing hydrogen peroxide. The stoichiometry is balanced: O2 + R-CH(OH)-COO- -> H2O2 + R-C(=O)-COO-, with two H transferred from substrate to oxygen. This step is part of the phytanic acid alpha-oxidation pathway in peroxisomes.

rxn02420.other_comments: This is the rosmarinic acid synthase (hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA:hydroxyphenyllactate transferase) reaction. Caffeoyl-CoA transfers its caffeoyl group to the hydroxyl of 3-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)lactate, forming an ester bond to yield rosmarinic acid (rosmarinate) and releasing free CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: one acyl group is transferred from CoA to the lactate acceptor, and free CoA is released. In vivo this proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward rosmarinate due to the favorable thermodynamics of thioester cleavage.

rxn09940.other_comments: This reaction represents methionine sulfoxide reductase B (MsrB), which reduces the R-stereoisomer of L-methionine sulfoxide back to L-methionine using reduced thioredoxin (trdrd) as the electron donor, producing oxidized thioredoxin (trdox) and water. Stoichiometry is balanced: the proton plus the oxygen from the sulfoxide combine with the thiol-derived electrons to release water, and the disulfide forms in oxidized thioredoxin. In vivo this reaction proceeds toward methionine and oxidized thioredoxin, driven by NADPH/thioredoxin reductase regeneration of reduced thioredoxin.

rxn01282.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of 2-phospho-D-glycerate (2PG) to glycerate and inorganic phosphate, consuming one water molecule. The stoichiometry is balanced: 2PG (C3H4O7P with appropriate protonation) + H2O yields D-glycerate (C3H5O4) + phosphate (HPO4/H2PO4). As a phosphohydrolase (phosphatase) reaction, hydrolysis of a phosphate monoester is highly exergonic and proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

errors: Oxygen balance issue: NADH + O2 + 1-methylxanthine should yield H2O plus the demethylated/hydroxylated product; only one H2O is produced but the reaction as written does not fully balance hydrogen and oxygen. A demethylase (N-demethylation) typically converts N-CH3 to N-H plus formaldehyde, consuming O2 and NAD(P)H and producing two H2O (one from O2 reduction). As written, only one H2O appears, leaving oxygen/hydrogen unbalanced.
Charge/proton balance not explicitly shown (NADH/NAD+ couple usually involves an H+ that is unaccounted for).
rxn07759.other_comments: This represents an oxidative N-demethylation of 1-methylxanthine to xanthine (XAN), releasing formaldehyde from the N-methyl group, with NADH and O2 as cosubstrates (cytochrome P450 / monooxygenase-type chemistry). The general transformation is biologically sensible.

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: the reaction transfers one acyl chain from the 2-acyl-glycerophosphoethanolamine to phosphatidylglycerol, but the products are written as fully deacylated glycerophosphoethanolamine (loss of one acyl) and an acyl-phosphatidylglycerol that has gained only one acyl, while the substrate PG already has two acyl chains; the carbon/acyl bookkeeping does not balance as written

Product naming is ambiguous: 'acyl phosphatidylglycerol hexadec-9-enoyl' should specify a triacyl (acyl-PG) species if one acyl is transferred from the lyso-PE, but the donor here is a 2-acyl-GPE (monoacyl) whose acyl moves, leaving glycerophosphoethanolamine - the receiving PG would become a tri-acyl-PG; the stoichiometry of acyl groups (in 16:1 + 32:1 = 48:1 carbons total) must be conserved on the product side
rxn08828.other_comments: This represents a lysophospholipase L2 transacylase activity: an acyl group from 2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (a lyso-PE, monoacyl, palmitoleoyl 16:1) is transferred to phosphatidylglycerol (dipalmitoleoyl, di-16:1), yielding deacylated glycerophosphoethanolamine and an acyl-(tri-acyl-)PG. The transacylation/hydrolysis tends to run toward acyl removal from the lyso-lipid in vivo.

rxn05428.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase reaction in branched-chain fatty acid (iso-fatty acid) biosynthesis. NADPH reduces the trans-2 double bond of the 12-methyl-tridec-2-enoyl-ACP to give the saturated 12-methyl-tridecanoyl-ACP, consuming NADPH + H+ and producing NADP+. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the two-electron reduction of the C2=C3 double bond is accounted for by NADPH + H+ -> NADP+ plus addition of 2 H to the substrate. In vivo, enoyl-ACP reductase strongly drives fatty acid elongation in the reductive direction.

rxn02878.other_comments: This reaction represents the ring-cleavage of 1,2-dihydroxynaphthalene (naphthalene-1,2-diol) catalyzed by 1,2-dihydroxynaphthalene dioxygenase (EC 1.13.11.56), a key step in the bacterial naphthalene degradation pathway. The dioxygenase incorporates both atoms of O2, cleaving the diol ring to yield 2-hydroxy-2H-chromene-2-carboxylate (also written as 2-hydroxychromene-2-carboxylate). The atom balance is consistent: O2 provides the two oxygens incorporated into the carboxylate/hydroxyl, and the loss of one proton (H+) reflects the overall mass/charge balance for the product written in its ionized form.

rxn06356.other_comments: This represents the dephosphorylation of phosphorylated Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) by a protein phosphatase. Water hydrolyzes the phosphoester bond on the phospho-ACC, releasing inorganic phosphate and yielding the dephosphorylated (active) enzyme. Stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphate group is transferred from the enzyme to water, yielding free Pi. Phosphoprotein phosphatase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo (the reverse would require a kinase and ATP).

rxn09903.other_comments: This represents an ATP-dependent dipeptide ligase forming the Ala-Leu dipeptide bond. The reaction couples ATP hydrolysis to ADP + inorganic phosphate, releasing a proton consistent with amide bond formation and net charge balance. Mass and charge appear balanced: ATP + Ala + Leu yields ADP + Pi + H+ + dipeptide. The H+ released is consistent with deprotonation during peptide bond synthesis. Such L-amino acid ligases (e.g., RimK-type/Lal enzymes) catalyze ATP-grasp dependent ligation. Although written as reversible, the strong thermodynamic drive from ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi makes the reaction effectively unidirectional toward dipeptide formation in vivo.

rxn00682.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by (3S)-malyl-CoA/beta-methylmalyl-CoA lyase (also known as L-malyl-CoA/beta-methylmalyl-CoA lyase). It performs an aldol condensation between glyoxylate and propionyl-CoA to form L-erythro-3-methylmalyl-CoA (also called (2R,3S)-beta-methylmalyl-CoA). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: glyoxylate (C2H1O3) plus propionyl-CoA condense via aldol addition to give the C4 dicarboxylic acid-CoA thioester, with no atoms gained or lost. This is a key step in the 3-hydroxypropionate cycle and the ethylmalonyl-CoA pathway. As an aldol/retro-aldol lyase, the reaction is thermodynamically reversible.

rxn05673.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for D-galacturonate. The same species (H+ and D-Galacturonate) appear on both sides because the equation does not distinguish compartments (e.g., extracellular vs cytoplasmic). Stoichiometrically it is balanced (1 H+ and 1 D-galacturonate on each side). For a proper transport reaction representation, the metabolites should be annotated with their respective compartments, such as H+[e] + D-Galacturonate[e] <=> H+[c] + D-Galacturonate[c], to make the proton symport directionality meaningful.

rxn06740.other_comments: This is a sialyltransferase (ST3Gal family) reaction transferring N-acetylneuraminate (sialic acid) from CMP-N-acetylneuraminate to the 3-position of the terminal beta-D-galactose of a glycan acceptor, producing the sialylated product plus CMP and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the CMP-Neu5Ac donates Neu5Ac, leaving CMP, and a proton is released. The acceptor (Gal-beta-1,3-GalNAc-R, a T-antigen-like core) gains the alpha-2,3-linked sialic acid.

errors: The reaction is not charge balanced as written. 3-Chloro-cis,cis-muconate is a dicarboxylate dianion (charge -2) at physiological pH. Products are CO2 (neutral), Cl- (charge -1), and Protoanemonin (neutral). With one H+ on the left (charge +1), left side total = -2 + 1 = -1, right side total = -1. Actually charge balances to -1 on each side.

Mass/atom balance check: 3-Chloro-cis,cis-muconate (C6H2ClO4 as dianion, or C6H4ClO4 protonated form) should yield Protoanemonin (C5H4O2) + CO2 (CO2) + Cl-. Carbon: 6 = 5 + 1, OK. The reaction corresponds to chloromuconate cycloisomerase / dienelactone forming pathway leading to protoanemonin via decarboxylation and dehalogenation - this is a recognized transformation.
rxn03691.other_comments: This represents the conversion of 3-chloro-cis,cis-muconate to protoanemonin with release of CO2 and chloride, part of the modified ortho-cleavage (chlorocatechol degradation) pathway. The dechlorination/decarboxylation step is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo due to loss of CO2 and Cl-.

errors: Charge imbalance: the left side includes an extra H+ that is not balanced; phenylacetonitrile + 2 H2O -> phenylacetate (PACT) + NH3 (or NH4+) does not require an additional proton if products are neutral. If NH4+ and phenylacetate (anion) are intended, the H+ should be reconsidered. As written with neutral NH3 and protonated acid (phenylacetic acid), the H+ on the left is unbalanced.
Atom balance check: phenylacetonitrile (C8H7N) + 2 H2O = C8H11NO2; products NH3 (NH3) + phenylacetic acid (C8H8O2) = C8H11NO2 - this balances only if no extra H+ is added
rxn07645.other_comments: This is a nitrilase-type reaction converting phenylacetonitrile (benzyl cyanide) to phenylacetate (PACT) plus ammonia, consuming 2 water molecules. Nitrilases hydrolyze nitriles directly to carboxylic acids and ammonia without forming a free amide intermediate. In vivo this proceeds essentially irreversibly toward hydrolysis.

rxn02918.other_comments: This represents the protein glucosylation reaction catalyzed by UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucose-1-phosphotransferase (Glc-1-P transferase, EC 2.7.8.19). The enzyme transfers a glucose-1-phosphate moiety from UDP-glucose to a mannose residue on a glycoprotein, forming a phosphodiester linkage (6-(D-glucose-1-phospho)-D-mannose) and releasing UMP plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: UDP-glucose donates Glc-1-P, leaving UMP, and the glucose-1-phospho group is appended to the glycoprotein mannose. Charge and atoms balance with H+ release.

errors: The substrate/product naming is inconsistent with the enzyme annotation; the enzyme (precorrin-6Y C5,15-methyltransferase) acts on precorrin-6Y to form precorrin-7, not precorrin-6B to precorrin-8. The correct EC 2.1.1.132 reaction is: 2 SAM + precorrin-6Y -> 2 SAH + precorrin-7 + CO2
Precorrin-8 (precorrin-8X/8W) is the product of a separate mutase/methyltransferase step, not of this reaction
rxn03491.other_comments: This represents the cobalamin (vitamin B12) biosynthesis double methylation/decarboxylation step using two SAM molecules and releasing two SAH, one CO2, and a proton. The double methyltransferase/decarboxylase reactions in this pathway are physiologically irreversible (forward) due to CO2 release and SAM consumption.

rxn06701.other_comments: This reaction represents alpha-galactosidase hydrolysis of digalactosyldiacylglycerol (DGDG) to release one galactose and yield monogalactosyldiacylglycerol (MGDG). The stoichiometry is balanced: DGDG (two galactose units on a diacylglycerol) plus water yields free galactose plus MGDG (one galactose unit). Hydrolytic glycosidase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo, though many databases annotate them as reversible. The bond cleaved is the alpha-galactosidic linkage between the two galactose residues.

rxn05037.other_comments: This is the nicotianamine aminotransferase (NAAT) reaction, key in the biosynthesis of mugineic acid family phytosiderophores in graminaceous plants. Nicotianamine donates an amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and the 3''-keto (oxo) intermediate. The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: nicotianamine loses an amine (converted to a ketone) while 2-oxoglutarate gains it to form glutamate. The H+ accounts for charge balance of the transamination. In vivo, NAAT drives the committed step toward deoxymugineic acid synthesis, so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction as written.

errors: The reaction name states 'unlinked' but the substrate and product are both 'linked', creating an inconsistency between the reaction description and the metabolites

Mass/charge balance is questionable: D-alanylation of lipoteichoic acid via D-alanine carrier protein (DltA/DltC) typically proceeds through D-alanyl-AMP intermediate releasing PPi, but the direct condensation onto LTA usually releases AMP only without additional PPi in the final esterification step; the combined stoichiometry of producing both 24 PPi and 24 AMP per D-Ala may double-count or omit intermediate carrier steps
The 48 H+ should be checked against the actual protonation states; each D-Ala ester bond formation with release of AMP+PPi from ATP would not straightforwardly yield exactly 2 H+ per reaction
rxn10324.other_comments: This represents D-alanylation of lipoteichoic acid (LTA), a Gram-positive cell envelope modification carried out by the Dlt pathway (DltABCD). D-alanine is activated by ATP (DltA) to D-alanyl-AMP, transferred to DltC carrier protein, then esterified to LTA glycerophosphate backbone. Here n=24 indicates 24 substitutable positions, hence the 24x multipliers. ATP activation releases PPi and AMP.

rxn11530.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) by farnesyl diphosphate diphosphatase (EC 3.1.7.6), cleaving the diphosphate group to yield farnesol and inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: FPP (C15H28O7P2 with appropriate protonation) + H2O yields farnesol (C15H26O) + PPi + H+. Mass and charge balance check out. As a hydrolase reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable in the hydrolytic direction.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the acyl group transferred is 14-methyl-hexadecanoyl (C17 branched-chain), but the product 'fa12coa' typically denotes a C12 (dodecanoyl/lauroyl)-CoA, so the carbon counts do not match between substrate acyl-ACP and product acyl-CoA
Charge/proton imbalance: a simple thioester transacylation from ACP to CoA does not consume 2 H+; the inclusion of 2.0 H+ on the substrate side is incorrect for this exchange reaction
Product CoA-ester identity mismatch: the acyl moiety on the product CoA should be 14-methyl-hexadecanoyl, not a generic C12 fatty acyl-CoA
rxn05452.other_comments: This is an acyl group transfer (transacylation) reaction moving a branched-chain fatty acyl group from acyl-carrier protein (ACP) to coenzyme A, yielding an acyl-CoA and free ACP. Such thioester exchanges are generally near-equilibrium and reversible. The main concern is the mismatch between the named substrate (14-methyl-hexadecanoyl, C17) and the product label 'fa12coa' (a C12 acyl-CoA), plus the spurious 2 H+.

errors: The reaction as written has identical species (H+ and ACTN) on both sides without compartment distinction; for a transport reaction, substrates and products must be in different compartments (e.g., H+[e] + ACTN[e] <=> H+[c] + ACTN[c]). As shown, it is a null/empty reaction with no net change.
rxn10426.other_comments: This represents (R)-acetoin uptake via proton symport, where acetoin is co-transported with a proton across the membrane. The intended reaction is H+[extracellular] + ACTN[extracellular] <=> H+[cytoplasm] + ACTN[cytoplasm]. Proton symport transport reactions are typically modeled as reversible, though physiologically uptake (import) is driven by the proton motive force.

rxn01607.other_comments: This is mevalonate kinase (EC 2.7.1.36), which phosphorylates (R)-mevalonate at the 5-hydroxyl using ATP to yield 5-phosphomevalonate (mevalonate 5-phosphate) and ADP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP + mevalonate -> ADP + 5-phosphomevalonate + H+. The released proton correctly balances charge since the transferred phosphoryl group adds two negative charges relative to ATP-to-ADP conversion accounting. In vivo this kinase reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward isoprenoid synthesis.

errors: PPi appears on both sides of the reaction as an unchanged spectator and should be removed
Charge and mass balance only works after removing PPi; the net reaction is ATP hydrolysis: ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+
rxn05635.other_comments: This appears to be an ATP hydrolysis reaction (likely coupled to a transport process, given the TRANS-RXN identifier). PPi is listed identically on both sides and contributes nothing to the net transformation. The core reaction ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+ is correctly balanced and strongly exergonic, hence essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Charge imbalance: nitrite reduction to ammonia is a 6-electron reduction requiring 8 protons; the balanced equation should be 8 H+ + NO2- + 3 Menaquinol-8 -> 2 H2O + NH4+ + 3 Menaquinone-8 (each menaquinol provides 2 electrons and releases 2 H+ upon oxidation). The stoichiometry is balanced: xanthine (C5H4N4O2) + H2O + O2 yields urate (C5H4N4O3 / C5H3N4O3-) + H2O2 + H+. Atoms and charge balance correctly. This reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding strongly in the forward direction toward urate formation.

errors: SALC is not a standard metabolite abbreviation; in KEGG R06603 the product is salicylate (2-hydroxybenzoate), so SALC likely denotes salicylate

The reaction as written is unbalanced: conversion of chorismate (C10H8O6, after deprotonation states) to pyruvate (C3H3O3) plus salicylate (C7H5O3) requires an additional water loss/elimination; salicylate synthase (isochorismate-derived) typically proceeds via isochorismate, not directly from chorismate in a single balanced step as shown
rxn04455.other_comments: This appears to represent salicylate (SALC) formation with pyruvate release from chorismate, a reaction catalyzed by salicylate synthase (e.g., MbtI/Irp9). Physiologically this is essentially irreversible due to the energetically favorable aromatic product and pyruvate elimination, driving it strongly toward salicylate and pyruvate.

rxn09478.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA oxidase reaction (first step of peroxisomal beta-oxidation). Lauroyl-CoA (C12 saturated acyl-CoA) is oxidized to (2E)-dodecenoyl-CoA (trans-2-enoyl-CoA), with O2 reduced to H2O2 via the FAD cofactor. Atom and charge balance is correct: a C-H bond pair is removed from the substrate and transferred (via FADH2) to O2 forming H2O2. In vivo this reaction is essentially irreversible in the oxidative direction because H2O2 is rapidly degraded by catalase.

rxn04066.other_comments: This reaction represents secologanin synthase (SLS)-type chemistry acting on loganate (the carboxylic acid form), a cytochrome P450 (CYP72A1) monooxygenase that oxidatively cleaves the cyclopentane ring of loganate to yield secologanate. The stoichiometry is consistent with a P450 monooxygenase: one O2 is consumed, one oxygen atom is incorporated/used and the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH, producing 2 H2O, NADP+, and the ring-cleaved product. Atoms and charges balance (NADPH + H+ provides reducing equivalents; the second oxygen of O2 plus 2H+ from NADPH/H+ gives water). The native CoA/acid substrate for this enzyme is typically loganin, but loganate is an accepted variant.

errors: The reaction shows the same metabolite (D-Glucosamine phosphate) on both sides without any compartment distinction in the written equation; a transport reaction must specify distinct compartments, e.g., D-Glucosamine phosphate[e] <=> D-Glucosamine phosphate[c]

No coupling ion or energy source (e.g., ATP, H+, PEP via PTS) is shown, which is typically required for phosphorylated sugar transport since charged phosphosugars do not freely diffuse across membranes
rxn05568.other_comments: This is annotated as a transport reaction for D-glucosamine 6-phosphate between the extracellular space and cytoplasm. As written, both sides are identical because compartment tags are missing, making it impossible to verify the transport direction. Phosphorylated sugars are generally imported via group translocation (PTS system) producing the phosphorylated form intracellularly from the free sugar, so a simple symmetric exchange of the phospho-form is biochemically unusual.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: combining 2 (R)-3-hydroxybutanoyl-CoA with a polymer of (n-2) units should yield a polymer of n units, but the product is written generically as Poly-beta-hydroxybutyrate without explicit chain-length bookkeeping (n) on the product side

CoA release count should match the number of monomers added; if 2 monomeric CoA esters are incorporated, 2 CoA are released, which is consistent, but the polymer notation (n-2) vs product n is inconsistent/ambiguous
Mass balance cannot be verified because the polymer terms lack defined chain-length variables that reconcile reactant (n-2) and product (n)
rxn11920.other_comments: This represents PHB (polyhydroxybutyrate) synthase (PhaC) elongation, where (R)-3-hydroxybutanoyl-CoA monomers are polymerized onto a growing chain with release of free CoA. In vivo this is a biosynthetic (polymerizing) reaction driven forward. The chain-length notation is the main issue: a polymer of (n-2) plus 2 monomers should give a polymer of n, so the product should be denoted as the (n)-length polymer.

rxn03116.other_comments: This reaction represents the dehydrochlorination (dehydrohalogenation) of DDT (1,1,1-trichloro-2,2-bis(4-chlorophenyl)ethane) to DDE (1,1-dichloro-2,2-bis(4-chlorophenyl)ethylene), catalyzed by DDT-dehydrochlorinase. The reaction eliminates HCl, producing H+ and Cl- as shown. Stoichiometry is balanced: DDT (C14H9Cl5) loses one HCl to form DDE (C14H8Cl4), releasing one H+ and one Cl-. This is an essentially irreversible elimination reaction (a known detoxification/metabolic pathway in insects), proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn04636.other_comments: This is a malonyl-CoA dependent acyltransferase reaction. Cosmetin (apigenin 7-O-beta-D-glucoside, also known as apigetrin) serves as the acceptor, and the malonyl group is transferred from malonyl-CoA to the 6'' position of the glucose moiety, yielding apigenin 7-(6''-malonylglucoside) and free CoA. The reaction is atom-balanced: one malonyl group is transferred, releasing CoASH. Acyltransferase reactions of this type are strongly favored in the biosynthetic (forward) direction due to the high-energy thioester bond of malonyl-CoA driving acyl transfer.

rxn04865.other_comments: This reaction (R07059) represents the epimerization of GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy sugars. GDP-4-dehydro-D-rhamnose (also known as GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose) is converted to GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-L-galactose (GDP-4-keto-6-L-deoxygalactose). This is part of the GDP-L-fucose biosynthesis pathway, catalyzed by GDP-L-fucose synthase (FX protein / GFUS, EC 1.1.1.271), which performs both 3,5-epimerization and 4-reduction. The epimerization step shown here is an intramolecular rearrangement (same molecular formula on both sides), so it is stoichiometrically balanced. As an epimerase/isomerase-type interconversion, it is reversible, though metabolic flux in vivo typically proceeds toward L-fucose synthesis.

rxn03391.other_comments: This is the ubiquinone biosynthesis C-methyltransferase reaction (COQ5 / UbiE), where S-adenosyl-L-methionine donates a methyl group to 2-hexaprenyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinone to form the 3-methyl product, generating S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The atom balance is consistent: the methyl group transferred adds CH2 to the acceptor (one C and two H net, with the third methyl H accounted for by the released H+), matching the SAM to SAH conversion. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are thermodynamically driven strongly toward methyl transfer in vivo.

rxn04356.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction (avermectin biosynthesis) where dTDP-L-oleandrose serves as the sugar donor, transferring the L-oleandrose moiety onto the Avermectin A2b monosaccharide acceptor to yield the disaccharide product (Avermectin A2b) and releasing dTDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced with one sugar nucleotide donor producing one dTDP and one glycosylated product. Glycosyltransferase reactions using nucleotide-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo due to the energy released upon cleavage of the high-energy sugar-nucleotide bond.

rxn00404.other_comments: This is the glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT/GATM) reaction, EC 2.1.4.1, the first committed step of creatine biosynthesis. It transfers the amidino group from L-arginine to glycine, producing L-ornithine and guanidinoacetate (glycocyamine/guanidinoacetic acid). The stoichiometry is balanced (1:1:1:1). In vivo it proceeds toward guanidinoacetate formation, driven by downstream methylation to creatine.

rxn04021.other_comments: This is the mannosylglycerate biosynthesis reaction catalyzed by MPG synthase (GDP-mannose:3-phosphoglycerate 3-alpha-D-mannosyltransferase, EC 2.4.1.217). GDP-mannose donates a mannosyl group to 3-phosphoglycerate, producing mannosyl-3-phosphoglycerate (the phosphorylated intermediate) and GDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the mannosyl unit (C6H10O5) transfers from GDP-mannose to 3-phosphoglycerate, leaving GDP. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: The reaction as written has identical reactants and products on both sides (H+ + Salicin <=> H+ + Salicin), representing no net chemical change; it fails to distinguish intracellular from extracellular compartments. A proper proton symport transport reaction should show the species in different compartments, e.g., H+[extracellular] + Salicin[extracellular] <=> H+[cytoplasm] + Salicin[cytoplasm].
rxn12540.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction moving salicin into the cell coupled with proton symport. As written without compartment annotations, both sides are identical and the reaction is meaningless. With proper compartmentalization, salicin uptake via proton symport is typically driven by the proton motive force in the import direction.

rxn05101.other_comments: This is a flavin-containing monooxygenase (FMO) / cytochrome P450-type N-oxygenation reaction converting the pyrrolizidine alkaloid senecionine to its N-oxide. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH provides reducing equivalents, one atom of O2 is incorporated into the N-oxide while the other is reduced to water, and NADP+ is released. Atom and charge balance hold (NADPH + H+ + O2 + amine -> NADP+ + H2O + N-oxide). Such monooxygenase reactions consuming NADPH and O2 are physiologically irreversible in vivo.

rxn04413.other_comments: This is the adenosylcobinamide kinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.156, CobU bifunctional enzyme). GTP transfers its gamma-phosphate to the hydroxyl group of adenosylcobinamide, producing adenosylcobinamide-phosphate and GDP, with release of a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphate group is transferred from GTP to the cobinamide, GTP becomes GDP, and the proton is released from the phosphorylated hydroxyl. This is part of the cobalamin (vitamin B12) biosynthesis pathway. As a kinase using GTP as phosphoryl donor in a committed biosynthetic step, it proceeds in the forward (phosphorylation) direction in vivo.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction for the standard beta-oxidation/peroxisomal hydratase reaction; the hydratase (enoyl-CoA hydratase) normally adds water across the double bond, so the physiological convention is trans-2-Enoyl-OPC4-CoA + H2O -> 3-Hydroxy-OPC4-CoA. As written, it represents the dehydration direction.
Stoichiometry is otherwise balanced: dehydration of a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA yields a trans-2-enoyl-CoA plus one water.
rxn07687.other_comments: This is the enoyl-CoA hydratase (crotonase-type) step in the jasmonic acid biosynthesis beta-oxidation pathway, acting on the OPC4-CoA intermediate. The conversion between 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA and trans-2-enoyl-CoA plus water is enzymatically reversible, though in the JA biosynthetic flux the hydration direction (toward 3-hydroxy-OPC4-CoA) predominates as part of chain shortening.

rxn01006.other_comments: This is the formation of UDP-glucuronate from UTP and alpha-D-glucuronate 1-phosphate, releasing pyrophosphate (analogous to UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase chemistry). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: UTP (C9H11N2O15P3 with charges) + glucuronate-1-phosphate yields UDP-glucuronate + PPi + H+. Mass and charge balance correctly with one H+ released. Although the enzymatic reaction is intrinsically reversible, in vivo the rapid hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase drives the reaction toward UDP-glucuronate synthesis.

rxn03929.other_comments: This is the epoxide hydrolase reaction (EC 3.3.2.x) in which water hydrolytically opens the arene oxide (phenanthrene-9,10-oxide) to yield the trans-9,10-dihydrodiol of phenanthrene. The stoichiometry is balanced: addition of H2O across the epoxide gives the trans-dihydrodiol with no atoms unaccounted for. As an enzymatic hydration of an epoxide, the reaction is thermodynamically strongly favorable and proceeds in the forward (hydrolysis) direction in vivo.

rxn07495.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of L-galactono-1,4-lactone (a lactone) to L-galactonate. The atoms balance: H2O + C6H10O6 (lactone) yields C6H11O7 (galactonate, dissociated form) + H+. Mass and charge are balanced when the carboxylate is written as the anion with the released proton. Lactone hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and generally proceeds in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02077.other_comments: This is the phloretin hydrolase reaction (EC 3.7.1.4), which hydrolyzes the C-C bond in phloretin (a dihydrochalcone) to yield phloretate (3-(4-hydroxyphenyl)propionate / phloretic acid) and phloroglucinol (1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene). The reaction consumes one water and produces one proton, which is consistent and balanced. As a hydrolytic C-C bond cleavage, this proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn01467.other_comments: This is the (-)-endo-fenchol synthase reaction (EC 4.2.3.10), a monoterpene cyclase that converts geranyl diphosphate (GPP, C10) into the bicyclic monoterpene alcohol (-)-endo-fenchol with consumption of water and release of diphosphate (PPi) and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: GPP (C10H17O7P2, charge -3) + H2O yields fenchol (C10H18O) + PPi (HP2O7, charge -3) + H+. Carbon (10=10), oxygen (7+1=7+1), phosphorus (2=2), and charge (-3 = -3 + 0 + 1... ) balance appropriately. The PPi-releasing cyclization is strongly exergonic and physiologically irreversible.

rxn02564.other_comments: This reaction represents flavone synthase I (FNS I, EC 1.14.20.5), a 2-oxoglutarate/Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenase that converts the flavanone eriodictyol to the flavone luteolin by introducing a C2-C3 double bond. The reaction couples decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate to succinate and CO2 with consumption of O2. The desaturation removes two hydrogen atoms (as the new double bond forms), which combine with one oxygen atom of O2 to form H2O; the other O atom is incorporated into the carboxylation/decarboxylation chemistry of 2-oxoglutarate. Stoichiometry is mass and charge balanced. The H+ produced balances the loss of two H from the substrate combined with water formation.

errors: Reaction is missing a proton (H+) on the substrate side; the balanced reaction should be: Acetoacetyl-ACP + NADPH + H+ <=> (R)-3-Hydroxybutyryl-ACP + NADP+
Product name is generic '(R)-3-Hydroxyacyl-[acyl-carrier protein]' but should specifically be (R)-3-Hydroxybutyryl-ACP (n-C4:0) to match the acetoacetyl-ACP (C4) substrate
rxn07994.other_comments: This is the FabG-catalyzed step of fatty acid synthesis, reducing the 3-oxo group of acetoacetyl-ACP (a C4 beta-ketoacyl-ACP) to the (R)-3-hydroxy form using NADPH. In vivo this proceeds in the reductive (forward) direction as part of the FAS elongation cycle.

rxn01938.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of tryptophol (indole-3-ethanol) to indole-3-acetaldehyde, coupled with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: the primary alcohol (tryptophol) loses two hydrogens (effectively a hydride to NAD+ giving NADH, plus a proton H+) to form the aldehyde. Atoms and charges balance correctly. Alcohol dehydrogenase-type NAD-dependent oxidoreductases are generally reversible enzymes; the physiological direction depends on cellular NAD+/NADH ratio and substrate concentrations. In the context of indole-3-acetic acid (auxin) biosynthesis, the aldehyde-to-alcohol (reductive) direction is also relevant, supporting overall reversibility.

errors: This reaction as written is not balanced. Combining CoA + mesaconate to form mesaconyl-CoA releases water, but this thioester-forming dehydration condensation is not how mesaconyl-CoA is biologically made and the H+ stoichiometry/balance is inconsistent. The direct ligation of a free acid with CoA to release only water is thermodynamically unfavorable and does not occur without ATP or a CoA-transfer mechanism.
Mesaconyl-CoA is physiologically generated via CoA transfer (e.g., from succinyl-CoA) or other activated intermediates, not by direct dehydrative condensation of mesaconate with free CoA.
rxn02624.other_comments: The input is the activation/CoA-thioester formation of mesaconate (a methyl-substituted fumarate, 2-methylfumarate) to mesaconyl-CoA. While atom counts (C, the methylbutenedioate plus CoA losing water) can superficially appear to balance for a generic acid+CoA->acyl-CoA+H2O thioesterification, such direct condensation is not energetically realistic in vivo.

rxn14112.other_comments: This is an epimerization reaction interconverting dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose (dTDP-4-keto-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose) and the corresponding L-mannose epimer via a 3,5-epimerase (analogous to RmlC/RfbC type enzymes). The substrate and product are isomers with identical molecular formulas, so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (1:1 stoichiometry, no cofactors required). Epimerases of this type are mechanistically reversible, though in deoxysugar biosynthetic pathways flux typically proceeds toward the L-configured product as the subsequent reactions pull the equilibrium forward.

errors: The reaction as written is missing a required reductant cofactor and electron donor; cytochrome P450-type hydroxylations/oxidations typically require NADPH and produce NADP+ along with water (e.g., O2 + RH + NADPH + H+ -> ROH + H2O + NADP+). As written, only O2 is consumed with one water produced, leaving oxygen and hydrogen atoms unbalanced.
Atom balance cannot be satisfied with a single O2 and one H2O between Abomacetin and Erythromycin E unless an additional reductant supplies two electrons and protons.
rxn03808.other_comments: This corresponds to a P450 (EryK-type) oxidation/hydroxylation step in erythromycin biosynthesis, converting an erythromycin intermediate (Abomacetin = 3-O-alpha-mycarosylerythronolide-related precursor / EryF context) toward a hydroxylated product. Such monooxygenase reactions consume molecular oxygen and a reduced cofactor; biologically they proceed essentially irreversibly in the oxidative (forward) direction.

errors: Atom imbalance: hydrolysis of a phosphate monoester releases inorganic phosphate but the substrate carries a 5-phosphoribosyl group whose phosphate is at the 5' position; removing only phosphate to give a ribosyl group is consistent, but the standard reaction is a phosphatase removing Pi from the ribose-5-phosphate moiety. Charge/H balance should be checked: H2O + R-O-PO3 -> R-OH + Pi (HPO4), which is balanced only if protonation states are accounted for.
rxn03090.other_comments: This is the dephosphorylation step in histidine degradation (imidazolepropionate/imidazoleacetate pathway). A phosphatase hydrolyzes the 5'-phosphate of 1-(5-phosphoribosyl)imidazole-4-acetate to yield 1-ribosylimidazole-4-acetate plus inorganic phosphate. The overall atom mapping (one phosphate transferred to water as Pi) is reasonable.

rxn05387.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2 double bond of 5-methyl-trans-hex-2-enoyl-ACP to give the saturated 5-methylhexanoyl-ACP. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ provides the hydride and proton needed to reduce the C2=C3 double bond, yielding NADP+ and the saturated acyl-ACP. In vivo, enoyl-ACP reductases (FabI/InhA-type, NADPH-dependent) drive the reaction strongly toward the reduced product, consistent with the biosynthetic elongation cycle.

errors: Stoichiometry is unbalanced. Elongation of myristic acid (C14:0) by malonyl-CoA adds 2 carbons to give a C16 chain; combined with one desaturation (O2-dependent) this could yield C16:1 (hexadecenoate), but the H/charge and oxygen balance are off.

Carbon balance: myristate (C14) + malonyl-CoA (3 carbons in malonyl moiety, one lost as CO2 = net +2 C) yields C16, consistent with hexadecenoate, but the overall mass balance with NADPH/O2/H2O should be checked. As written, NADPH count appears inconsistent: elongation condensation/reduction normally consumes 2 NADPH, and desaturation consumes 1 NADPH (or NADH) + O2, totaling ~3 NADPH which is plausible, but H+ and H2O balance need verification.
Proton (H+) balance is questionable: with 3 NADPH oxidized to 3 NADP+ plus O2 reduction, the consumed 4 H+ and produced 3 H2O do not clearly balance hydrogen and charge.

This conflates two distinct enzymatic activities (fatty acid elongation and acyl desaturation) into a single fatty acid synthase reaction, which is biochemically inaccurate; desaturation is typically performed by a separate desaturase.
rxn10665.other_comments: The reaction represents elongation of myristic acid (C14:0) by malonyl-CoA combined with an oxygen-dependent desaturation to give hexadecenoate (C16:1), releasing CoA and CO2. Biosynthetically this proceeds in the forward (synthesis) direction, driven by NADPH and decarboxylation of malonyl-CoA.

rxn03050.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 4-carboxy-4-hydroxy-2-oxoadipate aldolase / dehydratase region of the protocatechuate degradation pathway. The reaction as written shows dehydration of 4-carboxy-4-hydroxy-2-oxoadipate to form 4-carboxy-2-hydroxy-cis,cis-muconate plus water. In the protocatechuate 4,5- or 3,4-cleavage degradation pathway, the in vivo flux runs in the catabolic direction toward the oxoadipate (i.e., hydration of the muconate), so physiologically the reverse direction (consuming water, forming the hydroxy-oxoadipate) predominates. Stoichiometry is balanced: loss of one water molecule converts the hydroxy compound to the unsaturated muconate.

rxn06381.other_comments: This is the dinitrogen reductase activating glycohydrolase (DraG) reaction. It hydrolyzes the ADP-ribose moiety from an arginine residue of dinitrogen reductase (Fe protein of nitrogenase), reactivating the enzyme. Water is consumed, releasing free ADP-D-ribose and the unmodified protein. Stoichiometry is balanced as a hydrolysis reaction.

errors: This reaction as written is not balanced for hydrogen/electrons in a consistent way for a typical dehydrogenase. An aldehyde-to-acid oxidation (sinapaldehyde -> sinapate) consumes H2O and produces NADPH + 2 H+, which is consistent with an aldehyde dehydrogenase mechanism, so atom balance is approximately correct. However, the enzyme name 'sinapoyl aldehyde:NADP oxidoreductase' implies oxidation of the aldehyde, which matches the written direction.
rxn05143.other_comments: The reaction oxidizes sinapaldehyde to sinapate using NADP+ as electron acceptor, consuming water and releasing NADPH plus two protons. This is a sinapaldehyde dehydrogenase-type reaction. The mass and electron balance appears correct (one O incorporated from water, two H removed: one as H+ and one transferred to NADP+ as hydride, yielding NADPH + 2 H+). [directionality_note] Aldehyde dehydrogenase reactions oxidizing an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid with NADP+ are strongly favored in the forward (oxidative) direction in vivo and are essentially irreversible.

rxn07538.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction. Daidzein (7,4'-dihydroxyisoflavone) is methylated at the 7-OH position to give isoformononetin (7-methoxy-4'-hydroxyisoflavone), with SAM converted to S-adenosyl-homocysteine. The atom balance is consistent: a methyl group is transferred from SAM to daidzein. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the thermodynamically favorable transfer of the methyl group and the typically rapid removal/hydrolysis of SAH.

rxn06196.other_comments: This is the methylesterase reaction (CheB in chemotaxis) that hydrolyzes a protein-L-glutamate-O4-methyl-ester (methylated glutamate residue) using water to yield methanol and a free protein glutamate carboxylate, releasing a proton. Mass and charge balance hold: the methyl ester (neutral) plus water gives methanol plus carboxylate (-1) plus H+ (+1), net neutral on both sides. The reaction is a hydrolysis and is thermodynamically favorable in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn07894.other_comments: This is the NAD-dependent dehydrogenation (aromatization) of cis,cis-4-fluorocyclohexadiene-1,2-diol to 4-fluorocatechol, catalyzed by a cis-dihydrodiol dehydrogenase as part of fluorobenzene/halogenated aromatic degradation. The dihydrodiol (a cis-diol with two double bonds) is oxidized, removing 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+ yielding NADH, one as H+) to form the aromatic catechol. Stoichiometry is balanced: C, H, F, O and the redox couple (NAD+/NADH + H+) are consistent. The strongly favorable aromatization makes this essentially irreversible in the forward (catabolic) direction in vivo.

rxn05388.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthesis (FAS) condensation step (3-ketoacyl-ACP synthase / KAS type reaction). A 5-methyl-hexanoyl primer (C7 branched acyl-ACP) condenses with malonyl-ACP, releasing CO2 and free ACP, yielding 7-methyl-3-oxo-octanoyl-ACP (a C9 branched 3-ketoacyl-ACP). Carbon balance checks: C7 acyl + C3 malonyl (minus 1 C as CO2) = C9 product, consistent. The decarboxylative Claisen condensation is essentially irreversible in vivo due to CO2 release, driving chain elongation forward.

rxn03337.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of 5,6-dihydroxyindole (DHI) by molecular oxygen, catalyzed by enzymes such as tyrosinase or laccase, producing indole-5,6-quinone (an intermediate in melanin biosynthesis). Stoichiometry is balanced: O2 + 2 DHI yields 2 H2O + 2 quinone. Each DHI loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) to form the quinone; 2 DHI provide 4 electrons and 4 protons, and O2 (4 electrons) is reduced to 2 H2O. Mass and charge balance check out.

errors: Water stoichiometry is incorrect: each elongation cycle (condensation + reduction + dehydration + reduction) releases one H2O from the dehydration step. For 6 cycles, 6 H2O is produced, which matches; however the overall carbon balance must be checked carefully.
Carbon balance check: starting C5-ACP + 6 malonyl-ACP each adding 2 carbons gives C5 + 12 = C17, which is correct for heptadecanoyl-ACP.

Reducing equivalent count is too low: each elongation cycle requires 2 NADPH (one for the ketoreductase and one for the enoyl reductase). For 6 cycles that is 12 NADPH, which matches the stated 12 NADPH, so this is acceptable.

The label 'b-ketoacyl synthetase' describes only the condensation step, but the reaction as written lumps together condensation, two reductions, and dehydration (full fatty acid synthase cycles); the enzyme name is therefore misleading/incorrect for the overall reaction.
rxn13673.other_comments: This is a lumped fatty acid elongation reaction extending a C5-ACP primer to C17-ACP via 6 rounds of malonyl-ACP condensation. Atom balance: carbon (5 + 6x3 = 23 on left vs 17 + 6 CO2 = 23 on right) balances, 6 CO2 released from decarboxylative condensation, 6 ACP released, 6 H2O from dehydrations, and 12 NADPH/12 H+ -> 12 NADP for the 12 reduction steps. Stoichiometry appears mass- and redox-balanced; main issue is the enzyme naming which only covers condensation.

rxn02543.other_comments: This is the esterification reaction forming littorine (Daturine, also known as hyoscyamine/littorine precursor). Tropine (3-tropanol) is esterified with tropate (phenyllactate) to yield the ester littorine plus water, consuming a proton. The reaction is a condensation/dehydration: Tropine + Tropate + H+ -> Littorine + H2O. Stoichiometry and mass/charge balance are reasonable as written (the carboxylic acid form of tropate would be protonated and lose water upon esterification). In vivo this ester-forming reaction is biosynthetically driven toward product (littorine) in the tropane alkaloid pathway.

rxn07278.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (DWF4/CYP90B1) monooxygenase reaction in the brassinosteroid biosynthesis pathway, hydroxylating campesterol at the C22 alpha position. The stoichiometry is balanced: one atom of O2 is incorporated into the hydroxyl group of the product, the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Mass and charge balance: NADPH + O2 + H+ + campesterol yields H2O + NADP+ + 22alpha-hydroxy-campesterol, which is correct for a typical P450 monooxygenase. P450 oxidations are physiologically irreversible.

rxn04736.other_comments: This is an alcohol dehydrogenase-type reaction oxidizing (2-naphthyl)methanol (a primary alcohol) to 2-naphthaldehyde, with NAD+ reduced to NADH. Stoichiometry is balanced: the alcohol loses two hydrogens (as a hydride to NAD+ giving NADH, plus a proton H+), correctly yielding the aldehyde. Atoms and charges balance. Alcohol dehydrogenases are thermodynamically reversible enzymes; direction in vivo depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio and substrate concentrations.

rxn01404.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis (amidase) reaction of glutathionylspermidine, where the amide bond linking the glycine carboxyl of glutathione (GSH) to spermidine is cleaved by water, yielding GSH and spermidine. The bifunctional glutathionylspermidine synthetase/amidase (GspSA) catalyzes both the ATP-dependent synthesis and the hydrolysis. As written (hydrolysis direction), the equation is stoichiometrically balanced: H2O hydrolyzes the amide bond to release free GSH (with its glycine carboxyl restored) and free spermidine (with its amine restored). The reaction is reversible in the sense that the enzyme has both synthetase and amidase activities, but the synthetic direction physiologically requires ATP, which is not shown here. The amidase reaction itself favors hydrolysis.

rxn02527.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADH-dependent reduction of butanal (butyraldehyde) to n-butanol, catalyzed by an alcohol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.1). The stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + H+ + butanal (C4H8O) yields NAD+ + n-butanol (C4H10O), with two electrons and a proton transferred to the aldehyde. While alcohol dehydrogenases are intrinsically reversible enzymes, in vivo the high NADH/NAD+ ratio and aldehyde toxicity typically drive the reaction toward alcohol formation (the reductive, forward direction as written), as seen in solventogenic fermentation pathways (e.g., Clostridium ABE fermentation).

rxn04778.other_comments: This is the ammeline aminohydrolase (deaminase) reaction in the cyanuric acid/melamine degradation pathway. rxn07579.other_comments: This is the enoyl-ACP reductase step of fatty acid biosynthesis (FabI-type, NADH-dependent), reducing trans-2-octadecenoyl-ACP to stearoyl-ACP. rxn11407.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for L-threonine phosphate. rxn03481.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 6-phospho-beta-glucosidase (arbutin 6-phosphate glucohydrolase, often encoded by ascB/bglA-type genes). As a hydrolysis reaction it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn05746.other_comments: This reaction represents maltodextrin glucosidase (MalZ) hydrolyzing maltotriose (amylotriose, a trisaccharide of three glucose units linked by alpha-1,4 bonds). rxn00564.other_comments: This reaction represents urea hydro-lyase (EC 4.2.1.69), which interconverts urea with cyanamide plus water. In vivo, the enzyme (cyanamide hydratase) physiologically catalyzes the hydration of cyanamide to urea, so the biologically favored direction as written (Urea -> H2O + Cyanamide) is the reverse direction. The hydration of cyanamide to urea is thermodynamically favorable, making urea formation the dominant in vivo direction.

rxn04380.other_comments: This is an SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction. Homoprotocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate) is methylated on one hydroxyl group by S-adenosyl-L-methionine, producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) and the O-methylated product 3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenylacetate (homovanillate). The stoichiometry is balanced: methyl transfer from SAM yields SAH, and a proton is released from the phenolic oxygen upon methylation. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn07435.other_comments: This is the second step of branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex (E1/E2 type chemistry) acting on 2-methylbutanoyl (derived from isoleucine catabolism, the 2-keto-3-methylvalerate decarboxylation product). The hydroxyalkyl-TPP intermediate transfers the acyl group to lipoamide, generating the S-acyl-dihydrolipoamide and regenerating TPP. In vivo this oxidative acyl transfer proceeds in the catabolic forward direction.

rxn01738.other_comments: This is the galactinol-sucrose galactosyltransferase (raffinose synthase) reaction. rxn00394.other_comments: This is the arginase reaction (EC 3.5.3.1), which hydrolyzes L-arginine into L-ornithine and urea using one water molecule. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: L-arginine (C6H14N4O2) + H2O yields L-ornithine (C5H12N2O2) + urea (CH4N2O). Atoms balance for C (6=5+1), N (4=2+2), and O (2+1=2+1). Charges are also consistent at physiological pH. As a hydrolysis reaction in the urea cycle, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction toward ornithine and urea.

rxn02960.other_comments: This represents the interconversion between 2-aminoethylphosphonate (ciliatine) and 2-amino-3-phosphonopropanoate (phosphonoalanine), conceptually a carboxylation/decarboxylation step. rxn05919.other_comments: This is the glycerone-phosphate (dihydroxyacetone phosphate, DHAP) acyltransferase reaction (DHAPAT, EC 2.3.1.42), the first committed step in ether lipid (plasmalogen) biosynthesis occurring in peroxisomes. rxn07769.other_comments: This represents an oxidase reaction where 7-methylxanthine is oxidized at C8 to 7-methyluric acid, consuming O2 and water and producing hydrogen peroxide and a proton. rxn14052.other_comments: This is the CYP8B1 (sterol 12-alpha-hydroxylase) reaction in bile acid biosynthesis. It converts 7alpha-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one to 7alpha,12alpha-dihydroxycholest-4-en-3-one (4-cholesten-7alpha,12alpha-diol-3-one). As a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase, it incorporates one atom of O2 into the substrate as a hydroxyl group and reduces the other to water, consuming NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: one O from O2 goes into the product hydroxyl, the other forms water; NADPH/H+ provide reducing equivalents yielding NADP+.

rxn04599.other_comments: This is the dihydrodiol dehydrogenase reaction in the phenylpropanoid/biphenyl degradation pathway (HcaB-like). The cis-dihydrodiol of 3-phenylpropanoate is oxidized (rearomatized) to 2,3-dihydroxyphenylpropanoate (DHPP), with NAD+ reduced to NADH + H+. The reaction is balanced in C, H, O, N and charge: the substrate diol loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+, one as proton) to form the catechol product. In vivo this dehydrogenase step strongly favors aromatization toward the diol/catechol product.

rxn11621.other_comments: This represents a cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase (epoxidation) reaction where 5-cholestene (cholest-5-ene) is converted to 5,6alpha-epoxy-5alpha-cholestane. One atom of molecular O2 is incorporated into the epoxide product, the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + substrate yields H2O + NADP+ + epoxide. This monooxygenase-driven epoxidation is effectively irreversible in vivo, consuming O2 and NADPH.

rxn02738.other_comments: This is an oxidoreductase reaction (EC 1.3.1.-) where 1,2-dihydrosantonin is oxidized to alpha-santonin, reducing NAD+ to NADH. rxn06476.other_comments: This is the arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT, EC 2.3.1.87) reaction. Acetyl-CoA transfers its acetyl group to the primary amine of a 2-arylethylamine, producing N-acetyl-2-arylethylamine and CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred to the amine nitrogen, releasing the thiol of CoA and one proton. The released H+ comes from the amine NH2 becoming an amide NH. rxn00421.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of a phosphate group from diphosphate (pyrophosphate, PPi) to L-serine, producing O-phospho-L-serine (phosphoserine), phosphate (Pi), and a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: PPi (P2O7H) contributes one phosphate to serine forming phosphoserine and releasing inorganic phosphate plus a proton. Mass and charge balance: PPi (HP2O7^3-) + serine -> Pi (HPO4^2-) + H+ + phosphoserine. Atom and charge balance appear consistent. While diphosphate hydrolysis-coupled reactions are typically thermodynamically driven forward in vivo (PPi hydrolysis favors product formation), the reaction is formally written as reversible and the EC class (a phosphotransferase) can operate in both directions depending on conditions.

rxn02678.other_comments: This reaction is the oxidation/reduction couple between octanoyl-CoA and trans-2-octenoyl-CoA (2E-octenoyl-CoA). As written, NADP+ + octanoyl-CoA -> NADPH + H+ + trans-2-octenoyl-CoA represents oxidation (introduction of a C2-C3 double bond) with reduction of NADP+. The enzyme name 'trans-Oct-2-enoyl-CoA reductase' (enoyl-CoA reductase / trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase, e.g. fatty acid synthesis or mitochondrial FAS) physiologically catalyzes the reverse direction: reduction of trans-2-octenoyl-CoA to octanoyl-CoA using NADPH. Thus in vivo the favored direction is reverse relative to how it is written.

rxn12560.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-symport transport reaction moving hypotaurine across a membrane coupled with a proton. rxn13794.other_comments: This represents an ABC-type transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the import of 4-aminobutyrate (GABA). rxn14235.other_comments: This reaction describes the ring-cleaving oxygenase (extradiol/seco-type dioxygenase) acting on L-Dopa (3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine). Stoichiometry is balanced: both oxygen atoms of O2 are incorporated into the ring-cleaved product, consistent with a dioxygenase mechanism.

rxn03230.other_comments: This is a CoA-independent transacylase reaction transferring an arachidonoyl group from the sn-2 position of an alkyl-phosphocholine donor to a lyso-phosphoethanolamine acceptor, producing the lyso-phosphocholine and the arachidonoyl-phosphoethanolamine. rxn09156.other_comments: This is phospholipase A2 acting on phosphatidylethanolamine (di-C18:0 / distearoyl), hydrolyzing the sn-2 ester bond to yield free stearate (octadecanoate, ocdca) and 1-acyl-lyso-phosphatidylethanolamine. rxn04266.other_comments: This represents a Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase oxidation of a hydroxy-oxo limonene derivative using NADPH and molecular oxygen, incorporating one oxygen atom and releasing the other as water. rxn01730.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA synthetase (ADP-forming) reaction: ATP + CoA + glutarate yields ADP + phosphate + glutaryl-CoA. The reaction is mass and charge balanced as written. ATP provides energy via hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi), which couples to thioester (glutaryl-CoA) formation. ADP-forming ligases of this type (analogous to ADP-forming acetyl-CoA synthetase / succinyl-CoA synthetase) are typically reversible in vivo, in contrast to AMP+PPi-forming ligases which are driven forward. Direction depends on cellular concentrations and metabolic context.

errors: Mass and electron imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced. 6-Pyruvoyltetrahydropterin is more oxidized than tetrahydrobiopterin, so oxidation would consume NADP+ (reducing it to NADPH), but the stoichiometry of 2 NADP/2 NADPH is incorrect for this two-step conversion

rxn11742.other_comments: The reaction relates tetrahydrobiopterin and 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin via NADP/NADPH. In de novo biopterin biosynthesis, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin is reduced by sepiapterin reductase using NADPH to form tetrahydrobiopterin. rxn07809.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of 4-hydroxylamino-2,6-dinitrotoluene to 4-amino-2,6-dinitrotoluene, releasing water. The conversion of a hydroxylamino group (R-NHOH) to an amino group (R-NH2) requires removal of one oxygen (as water) and addition of 2 H, supplied by NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry balances: NADPH (provides hydride) plus H+ reduces the substrate, oxidizing NADPH to NADP+ and releasing H2O. This is part of the bacterial nitrotoluene/TNT degradation pathway. Such nitroreductase/hydroxylaminoreductase reactions strongly favor the reductive direction in vivo.

rxn08167.other_comments: This is the L-aspartate oxidase (NadB) reaction, the first committed step in de novo NAD biosynthesis. L-Aspartate is oxidized to iminoaspartate (alpha-iminosuccinate) with two electrons and two protons transferred to the quinone acceptor (menaquinone-8 reduced to menaquinol-8). The reaction is balanced for carbon, nitrogen, and redox: aspartate loses 2H (2e- + 2H+) which reduces menaquinone to menaquinol. Under anaerobic conditions NadB uses quinones (fumarate/menaquinone) rather than O2 as the electron acceptor. Stoichiometry is correct as written.

rxn03643.other_comments: This is the 3-hexulose-6-phosphate synthase (HPS) reaction (EC 4.1.2.43), an aldol condensation between formaldehyde and D-ribulose-5-phosphate yielding D-arabino-3-hexulose-6-phosphate (D-arabino-6-phospho-hex-3-ulose). The stoichiometry is balanced (CH2O + C5H11O8P = C6H13O9P) and atomically correct. As a lyase it is intrinsically reversible, but in formaldehyde-assimilating organisms (RuMP pathway) it operates physiologically in the condensation/forward direction toward the hexulose-phosphate, driven by formaldehyde detoxification and assimilation.

rxn09454.other_comments: This is a fatty-acyl-ACP thioesterase (hydrolase) reaction. Water hydrolyzes the thioester bond between the octadecynoyl group (an 18-carbon acyl chain bearing a triple bond) and acyl carrier protein (ACP), releasing free octadecynoate (the fatty acid) and holo-ACP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one water and one acyl-ACP yield one free ACP (with its regenerated thiol) and one carboxylate. Thioester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and these reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn00690.other_comments: This is the formate-tetrahydrofolate ligase (formyltetrahydrofolate synthetase, EC 6.3.4.3) reaction. ATP + formate + tetrahydrofolate yields ADP + Pi + 10-formyltetrahydrofolate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written: ATP provides the energy to condense formate onto THF. The enzyme is well known to operate reversibly in vivo, particularly important in anaerobes and one-carbon metabolism (e.g., acetogens, where it can run toward formate fixation, or in folate-mediated one-carbon catabolism running the other direction).

rxn00977.other_comments: Epimelibiose (galactosyl-mannose, specifically alpha-D-galactopyranosyl-(1->6)-D-mannose) is hydrolyzed by an alpha-galactosidase-type activity. The water cleaves the glycosidic bond yielding free D-galactose and D-mannose. Stoichiometry is balanced: the disaccharide plus water gives two monosaccharides. Hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, so this proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction.

rxn08438.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of octanoyl-ACP (the acyl carrier protein thioester of octanoate) by a thioesterase, releasing free octanoate, ACP, and a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: water cleaves the thioester bond, the carboxylic acid is formed, and a proton is released consistent with mass and charge balance at physiological pH. Acyl-ACP thioesterases catalyze chain termination in fatty acid biosynthesis.

rxn01173.other_comments: This is the malonate semialdehyde (3-oxopropanoate) dehydrogenase reaction. The reaction as written oxidizes 3-oxopropanoate (malonate semialdehyde) to malonate, consuming H2O and NADP+ and producing NADPH and 2 H+. Mass balance: left side C3H3O3 (3-oxopropanoate) + H2O = C3H5O4; right side malonate C3H3O4 (2-) + 2 H+ accounts for H balance. Carbon (3=3), oxygen (3+1=4=4), and charge balance check out, so stoichiometry is correct. Physiologically, the aldehyde dehydrogenase-type oxidation of malonate semialdehyde to malonate proceeds in the direction of NADPH formation (i.e., toward malonate as written here).

rxn05182.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis to the import of tungstate/tungsten. rxn10696.other_comments: This represents a mannosyltransferase reaction in Mycobacterium tuberculosis phosphatidylinositol mannoside (PIM) / lipomannan biosynthesis. Polyprenyl phosphate mannose (decaprenyl/polyprenol monophosphomannose, PPM) serves as the mannosyl donor, transferring one mannose residue to the acyl-PIM3 acceptor to form acyl-PIM4, releasing decaprenyl phosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: one mannose group is transferred from the donor to the acceptor, accounting for the loss of phosphate-mannose from the lipid donor.

rxn00243.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of GDP-glucose (GDP-alpha-D-glucose) by GDP-glucose glucohydrolase (EC 3.2.2.x). As a hydrolysis reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn04979.other_comments: This represents the zeaxanthin epoxidase (ZEP) reaction in the xanthophyll cycle, specifically the second epoxidation step converting antheraxanthin (mono-epoxide) to violaxanthin (di-epoxide). In vivo this monooxygenase reaction strongly favors the forward (epoxidation) direction; de-epoxidation back to antheraxanthin/zeaxanthin is catalyzed by a separate enzyme (violaxanthin de-epoxidase, using ascorbate), not by reversal of this reaction.

rxn14275.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADPH-dependent reduction of dTDP-3,4-dioxo-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose at the C3 position, yielding dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose and NADP+. rxn04301.other_comments: This reaction describes a dimethyltransferase (EC 2.1.1.-) that uses two molecules of SAM to transfer two methyl groups onto the 3-amino group of dTDP-3-amino-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose, producing dTDP-D-mycaminose (which bears a 3-dimethylamino group). rxn06771.other_comments: This is a protein arginine N-methyltransferase (PRMT) reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to an arginine residue on myelin basic protein, producing S-adenosyl-homocysteine (SAH) and methylated arginine. The methyl transfer to nitrogen releases a proton, so the H+ on the product side is balanced. Stoichiometry is correct: the methyl group (CH3) lost by SAM (becoming SAH) is transferred to the omega nitrogen of arginine, and the released proton balances charge/mass.

rxn02418.other_comments: This reaction describes a phytase (myo-inositol-hexakisphosphate phosphohydrolase) hydrolyzing phytate (myo-inositol hexakisphosphate, InsP6) at the 4-position, releasing inorganic phosphate and yielding myo-inositol 1,2,3,5,6-pentakisphosphate (Ins(1,2,3,5,6)P5).
