rxn00978.other_comments: This reaction describes the phosphorylation of D-mannose to D-mannose 6-phosphate using dATP as the phosphoryl donor, producing dADP and a proton. The reaction is analogous to hexokinase activity but using dATP instead of ATP. The atoms balance: the gamma-phosphate is transferred from dATP to the C6 hydroxyl of mannose, releasing H+. Phosphate, charge, and mass are conserved.

rxn03685.other_comments: This reaction represents the reductive dechlorination/dehydrochlorination of DDD (1,1-dichloro-2,2-bis(4-chlorophenyl)ethane, also called TDE) to DDMU (1-chloro-2,2-bis(4-chlorophenyl)ethylene). The reaction eliminates HCl, releasing H+ and Cl-, which is consistent with a chloride-lyase (dehydrohalogenation) mechanism. Atom and charge balance appear consistent: DDD loses HCl to form the unsaturated DDMU.

rxn01180.other_comments: This is the stilbene synthase (resveratrol synthase) reaction. It condenses one 4-coumaroyl-CoA with three malonyl-CoA units, releasing 4 CoA and 4 CO2 (3 from decarboxylation of malonyl-CoA extender units, 1 from the final aldol-type cyclization/decarboxylation) to form resveratrol. Carbon: resveratrol is C14H12O3. The H+ stoichiometry of 3 balances the protons consumed; mass and charge balance is consistent. Reaction is essentially irreversible due to multiple decarboxylations.

rxn02324.other_comments: This is the gallate decarboxylase (carboxy-lyase) reaction. Gallate (3,4,5-trihydroxybenzoate) is decarboxylated to pyrogallol (1,2,3-trihydroxybenzene, benzene-1,2,3-triol) with release of CO2. rxn11213.other_comments: This is the third step of the shikimate pathway, catalyzed by 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase (DHQ dehydratase). rxn07608.other_comments: This is an extradiol ring-cleavage dioxygenase reaction (BphC-type). rxn11876.other_comments: This represents an aldehyde oxidase (or molecular oxygen-dependent oxidase) reaction oxidizing citalopram aldehyde to citalopram propionic acid (the carboxylic acid metabolite). Atom and charge balance check out, since the aldehyde gains one O (from water) and loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons), with O2 reduced to H2O2. Aldehyde oxidase reactions are physiologically irreversible in the oxidative direction.

rxn09516.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of dGTP (deoxyguanosine triphosphate) to dGDP, releasing inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O attacks the terminal phosphoanhydride bond, yielding dGDP + Pi + H+. Mass and charge balance: dGTP (charge -4) + H2O -> dGDP (charge -3) + Pi (charge -2) + H+ (charge +1), which balances to -4 on both sides. Atoms also balance. The hydrolysis of a phosphoanhydride bond is highly exergonic, strongly favoring the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn02833.other_comments: This is phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT, EC 2.1.1.28), which transfers a methyl group from SAM to the amino group of phenylethanolamine (or noradrenaline in vivo), producing S-adenosyl-homocysteine and the N-methylated amine. errors: The substrate 'Laminariaceae' is incorrect; Laminariaceae is a family of brown algae, not a chemical compound. rxn00699.other_comments: This is a disaccharide phosphorylase reaction (laminaribiose phosphorylase, EC 2.4.1.31). Phosphorylase reactions of this type are generally reversible in vivo, with direction depending on phosphate and sugar-1-phosphate concentrations.

rxn01456.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of D-galacturonate to D-mucic acid (galactaric/meso-tartaric... actually galactaric acid) by an NAD+-dependent uronate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.203). The aldehyde group at C1 of D-galacturonate is oxidized to a carboxylate, yielding the dicarboxylic acid (D-glucaric/galactaric type, mucic acid). The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + NAD+ + galacturonate -> NADH + 2 H+ + mucic acid. Carbon (C6 each side), redox, and charge balance are consistent (the aldehyde + H2O is oxidized losing 2 electrons/2 H to NAD+, with one proton released plus the proton from carboxylic acid ionization accounted for).

rxn01776.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by D-mannonate oxidoreductase (related to fructuronate reductase, EC 1.1.1.57). The reaction oxidizes the C6 (or relevant carbon) of D-mannonate using NAD+ as the electron acceptor, producing D-mannuronate, NADH, and a proton. The atoms balance: oxidation of an alcohol to an aldehyde/acid moiety transfers a hydride to NAD+ and releases a proton, so the stoichiometry (NAD+ + mannonate <=> NADH + H+ + mannuronate) is correct. NAD-dependent dehydrogenases are generally reversible, though physiological flux often favors the reductive direction (mannuronate/fructuronate reduction to mannonate) using NADH.

errors: The H+ on the substrate side is questionable. In a sulfotransferase reaction (PAPS + acceptor-OH -> PAP + acceptor-OSO3-), a proton is typically released when the hydroxyl oxygen is sulfated, so an H+ would appear on the product side, not the substrate side. The reaction as written may have a charge/proton balance error.
rxn01907.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase (SULT) reaction transferring a sulfo group from PAPS (3'-phosphoadenylylsulfate) to the 3'-OH of quercetin 3-sulfate, producing quercetin 3,3'-bissulfate and PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate). Sulfotransferase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the sulfo-transfer direction.

rxn06304.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by NocL (nocardicin biosynthesis), an SAM-dependent 3-amino-3-carboxypropyltransferase. SAM donates its 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl (homoserine) moiety to the phenol oxygen of nocardicin E, producing isonocardicin A and 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA). The stoichiometry is balanced: SAM transfers the ACP group, leaving MTA, with release of a proton. Unlike typical SAM methyltransferases (which yield S-adenosylhomocysteine), this transfers the aminocarboxypropyl group, correctly yielding MTA. The reaction is biologically driven toward the transferase product.

rxn05570.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction for gamma-butyrobetaine. The gamma-butyrobetaine on the left represents the extracellular/periplasmic substrate and on the right the cytoplasmic product (transported in). ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) is stoichiometrically balanced and energetically drives the import. The metabolite is conserved across the membrane. ABC import is effectively irreversible in vivo due to ATP hydrolysis.

errors: Charge imbalance: the right side has an extra positive charge from H+ that is not balanced. Mass appears balanced (C3H7NO3 + NAD+H2O vs C3H4O4 + NH3 + NADH + H+), but the redox/oxidation logic is internally inconsistent.

A true 'deaminating' oxidoreductase (like serine dehydratase/deaminase analogs) yields a 2-oxo acid plus NH3, which from serine would give hydroxypyruvate, but this requires both oxidation AND deamination consuming/producing water in a way that does not match a single NAD+ reduction cleanly.
rxn00419.other_comments: The reaction proposes oxidative deamination of L-serine using NAD+ and water to yield hydroxypyruvate, NH3, and NADH. I understand it as combining oxidation (NAD+ to NADH) with deamination releasing ammonia. While atom counts roughly balance, the combined oxidation-plus-deamination on serine to give 3-hydroxypyruvate is mechanistically unusual; serine is typically converted to hydroxypyruvate via transamination (with 2-oxoglutarate) or its deamination yields pyruvate (serine dehydratase). An NAD+-dependent route to hydroxypyruvate is atypical.

rxn04937.other_comments: This describes the NADP+-dependent oxidation of lactaldehyde (CH3-CHOH-CHO) to methylglyoxal/2-oxopropanal (CH3-CO-CHO). rxn08380.other_comments: This reaction represents the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of 1-deoxy-D-xylulose to 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate, catalyzed by a D-xylulokinase-type/1-deoxy-D-xylulose kinase activity (EC 2.7.1.-). Kinase reactions involving ATP-to-ADP phosphoryl transfer are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (phosphorylation) direction.

rxn09912.other_comments: This reaction represents an L-amino acid ligase (LAL, RimK-type) catalyzing the ATP-dependent condensation of two L-methionine molecules to form the dipeptide Met-Met. rxn00026.other_comments: This represents an oxidase reaction in which molecular oxygen oxidizes thiamine to thiamine aldehyde with production of hydrogen peroxide. O2-dependent oxidations producing H2O2 are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the reaction forward.

rxn00092.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of ADP to AMP and inorganic phosphate, catalyzed by an ADP phosphohydrolase (apyrase-type activity). rxn00458.other_comments: This is the decarboxylation of L-methionine to form 3-methylthiopropylamine (3-methylthiopropanamine) and CO2. rxn10706.other_comments: This is a fatty acid-CoA ligase (acyl-CoA synthetase) reaction activating arachidic acid (C20:0) to arachidyl-CoA. ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi, with CoA thioester formation. rxn10332.other_comments: This represents synthesis of lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (Lys-PG), a membrane lipid modification that increases bacterial resistance to cationic antimicrobial peptides. Physiologically, Lys-PG synthesis (MprF/multiple peptide resistance factor) uses lysyl-tRNA(Lys) as the amino acid donor rather than ATP + free lysine. The reaction as written uses ATP activation of free lysine analogous to aminoacyl-adenylate chemistry.

rxn01532.other_comments: This reaction represents the isomerization of all-trans-retinal to 11-cis-retinal, catalyzed by retinal isomerase. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as it is a simple isomerization (C20H28O on both sides, same molecular formula, just a configurational change at the 11-12 double bond). In the visual cycle, the thermodynamically favored direction is generally toward all-trans-retinal (the trans isomer is more stable), and biological conversion to 11-cis typically requires energy input, often via the retinoid isomerase RPE65 acting on retinyl esters rather than free retinal directly. As written between free aldehydes, the simple isomerization can be considered reversible, though in vivo the energetically uphill 11-cis formation usually relies on coupled processes.

rxn10275.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction that transfers a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to monoglucosyl-diacylglycerol (with anteisoheptadecanoyl chains), forming the diglucosyl-diacylglycerol and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose is transferred, UDP-glucose becomes UDP, and the monoglucosyl acceptor gains one glucose to become diglucosyl. Glycosyltransferases using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically driven toward glycoside formation due to the energy released from cleaving the UDP-sugar bond, so the reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02516.other_comments: This is beta-cyanoalanine synthase (EC 4.4.1.9), which condenses L-cysteine with hydrogen cyanide (HCN) to form 3-cyano-L-alanine and release hydrogen sulfide (H2S). The reaction is mass and charge balanced: L-cysteine (C3H7NO2S) + HCN (CHN) yields H2S (H2S) + L-3-cyanoalanine (C4H6N2O2). Atoms balance (C4H8N2O2S on each side). In vivo this enzyme functions in cyanide detoxification, strongly favoring beta-cyanoalanine formation.

rxn10494.other_comments: This reaction represents an NADH-dependent reduction of 4,5-diketo-6-deoxyfructose 1-phosphate to 6-deoxy-5-ketofructose 1-phosphate, part of the F420 coenzyme biosynthesis pathway. The keto group at C4 is reduced to a hydroxyl. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + H+ provides two electrons and one proton to reduce a single ketone to an alcohol, consistent with a 2-electron reduction. Carbon, phosphate, and redox balances are consistent. In vivo, the strong negative free energy of NADH-coupled ketone reduction and the metabolic role in biosynthesis drives the reaction toward the alcohol product.

errors: The reaction name (Hexadecanoyl-[acyl-carrier protein]:malonyl-CoA C-acyltransferase) does not match the written reaction, which is an oxidation/desaturation, not an acyltransfer involving malonyl-CoA

rxn07223.other_comments: This is GnT-I (MGAT1), EC 2.4.1.101, which transfers GlcNAc from UDP-GlcNAc to the alpha-1,3 mannose of the trimannosyl core in N-glycan biosynthesis. The reaction is written with the generic acceptor 'R' representing the glycoprotein. Mass balance holds: UDP-GlcNAc donates a GlcNAc residue to the beta-D-mannosyl acceptor, releasing UDP and forming the GlcNAc-beta-1,4-Man linkage. Glycosyltransferase reactions using nucleotide-sugar donors are strongly exergonic (cleavage of the high-energy sugar-nucleotide bond) and proceed in the biosynthetic forward direction in vivo.

rxn07481.other_comments: This is the oxidation of 3-hydroxybenzaldehyde to 3-hydroxybenzoate, catalyzed by an aldehyde dehydrogenase (NADP+ dependent). The aldehyde group (CHO) is oxidized to a carboxylic acid (COOH), consuming water and NADP+, producing NADPH and 3-hydroxybenzoate plus 2 protons. The reaction is balanced for atoms (the added oxygen and hydrogens come from H2O) and charge: left side NADP+ (-1) + neutral substrates = -1; right side NADPH (-2) + 2 H+ (+2) + 3-hydroxybenzoate (-1) = -1. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn04074.other_comments: This is the epoxide hydrolase reaction where ethylene oxide (oxirane) is hydrolyzed by water to form ethylene glycol (1,2-ethanediol). Stoichiometry is balanced: ethylene oxide (C2H4O) + water (H2O) yields 1,2-ethanediol (C2H6O2). Carbon (2=2), hydrogen (4+2=6), and oxygen (1+1=2) all balance. Epoxide hydrolysis is highly thermodynamically favorable due to relief of ring strain in the epoxide, so the reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn07674.other_comments: This reaction represents a malonyltransferase (acyltransferase) reaction transferring a malonyl group from malonyl-CoA to the 3'' position of the glucose moiety of pelargonidin 3-O-(6-O-malonyl-beta-D-glucoside), yielding the 3'',6''-dimalonyl diester and free CoA. Atom and charge balance is consistent: one malonyl group is transferred from CoA to the glucoside, releasing free CoA. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1:1). Biologically, BAHD-type malonyltransferases drive acyl transfer in the synthetic direction.

errors: Proton stoichiometry appears unbalanced: left side has 2.0 H+ plus formate (HCOO-), right side has 1 H+; for the reaction Formate -> CO2 + H+ (2 electrons) coupled to methylmenaquinone + 2 H+ + 2 e- -> methylmenaquinol, the proton balance should be checked - net the equation as written does not clearly balance charge/protons
Typographical error: 'methymenaquinol 7' should be 'methylmenaquinol 7'

rxn13700.other_comments: This is a formate dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing formate to CO2 with two electrons transferred to methylmenaquinone-7, reducing it to methylmenaquinol-7. In vivo this typically proceeds in the direction of formate oxidation (forward). Standard balanced form: Formate + methylmenaquinone-7 -> CO2 + methylmenaquinol-7 (with appropriate proton handling depending on membrane sidedness).

rxn12182.other_comments: This is the beta-caryophyllene synthase reaction. (2E,6E)-Farnesyl diphosphate (FPP, C15H25O7P2 with appropriate charge) undergoes cyclization with loss of diphosphate to form the bicyclic sesquiterpene beta-caryophyllene (C15H24). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: FPP releases PPi (diphosphate) and the cyclization/deprotonation accounts for the H+. Terpene cyclase reactions are essentially irreversible due to release of the high-energy diphosphate leaving group, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (caryophyllene-forming) direction in vivo.

rxn03573.other_comments: This is a biphenyl 2,3-dioxygenase reaction acting on 4-chlorobiphenyl. The enzyme incorporates both atoms of O2 into the substrate to form the cis-dihydrodiol, using NADH + H+ as the electron donor which is oxidized to NAD+. Atom balance: substrate gains 2 O (from O2) and 2 H (net), consistent with NADH + H+ providing reducing equivalents and O2 being fully consumed. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced and, as an oxygenase-catalyzed step driven by O2 consumption and NADH oxidation, is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn02843.other_comments: This reaction is an N-malonyltransferase transferring the malonyl group from malonyl-CoA to the aromatic amine 3,4-dichloroaniline, releasing free CoA and forming N-(3,4-dichlorophenyl)malonamate. The atom balance is consistent: the malonyl moiety (C3H2O3-derived) is transferred to the aniline nitrogen with loss of the thioester linkage to CoA. This is a xenobiotic detoxification/conjugation reaction (notably in plants). Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and sulfur balance check out across the thioester-to-amide exchange.

rxn10457.other_comments: This is a CDP-alcohol phosphatidyltransferase-type reaction where CTP activates a glycerol-derived hydroxyl group to form a CDP-linked intermediate, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: the cytidylyl (CMP) group is transferred from CTP to the free hydroxyl of the diether glycerol substrate, with the beta and gamma phosphates leaving as PPi. This appears to be part of an archaeal-type ether lipid biosynthesis pathway. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charges as written.

errors: Acetyl-ACP (acetyl-acyl carrier protein) is not the correct acetyl donor for alginate O-acetylation; the physiological donor is acetyl-CoA (via the AlgI/AlgJ/AlgF/AlgX machinery in Pseudomonas, or analogous systems). ACP carries fatty acyl groups for fatty acid synthesis, not short acetyl groups for polysaccharide acetylation.

Stoichiometry is ambiguous: 'Epimerized Alginate Dimer' as a substrate and 'Acetylated Alginate' as a product are not mass-balanced because the product is described as a generic polymer rather than the specific acetylated dimer; the acetyl group transfer should be tracked explicitly (one acetyl per modified residue).

Alginate acetylation typically occurs before epimerization in vivo; acetylated residues are generally protected from epimerization by AlgG, so an 'epimerized' substrate being acetylated may be biologically inconsistent.
rxn13806.other_comments: This represents an alginate O-acetyltransferase reaction transferring an acetyl group from an acyl carrier to an alginate polymer, releasing the deacylated carrier. Acetyltransferase reactions of this type are strongly thermodynamically favored toward acetyl transfer and are effectively irreversible in vivo. However, the acetyl donor is biochemically questionable (should be acetyl-CoA, not acetyl-ACP).

rxn07781.other_comments: This reaction represents the chalcone isomerase (CHI) catalyzed intramolecular cyclization of eriodictyol chalcone (a 2',3,4,4',6'-pentahydroxychalcone) to the flavanone eriodictyol. It is an isomerization, so atom counts are conserved (both are C15H12O6) and the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced with a 1:1 ratio. Although CHI accelerates the reaction, ring closure to the flavanone is thermodynamically favorable and the reaction can also proceed spontaneously; in vivo it strongly favors flavanone formation.

errors: This reaction as written conflates two distinct biochemical conversions. The actual conversion of pregnenolone to progesterone is catalyzed by 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase (3-beta-HSD), which uses NAD+ (not NADP+) as cofactor and involves both an oxidation of the 3-beta-hydroxyl group AND an isomerization of the double bond from delta-5 to delta-4. The simple NADP-dependent oxidoreductase shown here does not account for the delta-5 to delta-4 isomerization step.
Cofactor specificity issue: the physiological enzyme (3-beta-HSD) predominantly uses NAD+/NADH rather than NADP+/NADPH.
rxn01587.other_comments: The reaction depicts oxidation of pregnenolone (a 3-beta-hydroxy delta-5 steroid) to progesterone (a 3-keto delta-4 steroid) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometrically the atoms and redox balance (one 2-electron oxidation, one hydride transfer plus a proton) are consistent. In vivo the 3-beta-HSD reaction strongly favors product formation (progesterone), so the forward direction dominates.

errors: The product name 'dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-L-glucose' is chemically problematic. A 5-epimerase acting on dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose epimerizes the C5 stereocenter, converting a D-sugar to an L-sugar configuration. The actual product of such 3,5-epimerases/5-epimerases in dTDP-sugar pathways is typically dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-L-mannose or similar; calling it 'L-glucose' by simple C5 inversion may not match standard nomenclature, but a single C5 inversion would change the sugar identity (e.g., to an L-allo/L-galacto configuration), not merely add an L prefix to glucose.
rxn03816.other_comments: This is an epimerization reaction at C5 of a dTDP-4-keto-2,6-dideoxyhexose. Stoichiometry is balanced (a single intramolecular epimerization, no atoms gained or lost). Epimerases are generally reversible enzymes operating near equilibrium, with directionality driven by downstream consumption.

rxn14043.other_comments: This is an N-acetyltransferase reaction transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the amino group of demethylphosphinothricin, producing N-acetyl-demethylphosphinothricin (N-Adpt), CoA, and a proton. The reaction is part of the phosphinothricin tripeptide (bialaphos) biosynthesis pathway in Streptomyces. Stoichiometry is balanced: the acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred from acetyl-CoA to the amine, releasing CoA-SH and H+. The released proton accounts for the deprotonation balance of the thiol/amide formation.

rxn05397.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase step in branched-chain (iso) fatty acid biosynthesis. The 3-oxo (beta-keto) group of 11-methyl-3-oxo-dodecanoyl-ACP is reduced by NADPH to the 3-hydroxy (R-3-hydroxyacyl) product, consuming NADPH + H+ and yielding NADP+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (one NADPH/H+ provides the hydride and proton; carbon, oxygen, and ACP carrier are conserved). In vivo this proceeds in the reductive direction of fatty acid synthesis.

errors: The product 'Galactose' is ambiguous; aldose-1-epimerase interconverts the anomers, so the product should specifically be alpha-D-galactose, not generic 'Galactose'
As written with an unspecified anomer, atom/anomeric specificity is incomplete though the overall stoichiometry (1:1 isomerization) is balanced
rxn08582.other_comments: This represents aldose-1-epimerase (mutarotase), which catalyzes the interconversion of the alpha and beta anomers of D-galactose. The reaction is a 1:1 anomeric isomerization and is freely reversible, approaching the equilibrium anomeric ratio. The substrate is beta-D-galactose and the proper product should be alpha-D-galactose.

rxn04644.other_comments: This is a rhamnosyltransferase reaction transferring an L-rhamnosyl group from UDP-L-rhamnose to the 2'' position of the glucose moiety of luteolin 7-O-glucoside, producing scolymoside (luteolin 7-O-rutinoside) and UDP. The atoms balance: UDP-rhamnose donates the rhamnosyl group via glycosidic bond formation, releasing UDP and a proton. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn05012.other_comments: This is the acetylornithine transcarbamylase reaction (AOTCase, EC 2.1.3.9), found in arginine biosynthesis of certain organisms (e.g., Xanthomonas, Bacteroides). It transfers a carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to N-acetylornithine, producing N-acetylcitrulline and releasing phosphate plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the carbamoyl group (NH2-CO-) is transferred to the delta-amino group of acetylornithine, with phosphate and a proton released. Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and charge balance check out.

rxn11202.other_comments: This is a branched-chain/aromatic aminotransferase reaction. L-Tryptophan donates its amino group to 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (4MOP, the keto acid of leucine), producing L-Leucine and indolepyruvate (the keto acid of tryptophan). The reaction is balanced: each side has one amino acid and one 2-oxo acid, and atoms are conserved (transfer of NH2 from one carbon skeleton to another). PLP-dependent aminotransferase reactions of this type are freely reversible in vivo, with net direction determined by relative substrate/product concentrations.

errors: The product '1-Radyl-2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine' uses 'Radyl' as a generic term encompassing both alkyl and acyl substituents at sn-1; given the substrate is specifically 1-alkyl, the product should be named '1-alkyl-2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine' for stoichiometric/nomenclature precision
rxn06379.other_comments: This is the acyltransferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.63) transferring an acyl group from acyl-CoA to the sn-2 position of 1-alkyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (lyso-PAF), producing 1-alkyl-2-acyl-GPC and free CoA. Atom balance is otherwise consistent: an acyl group is transferred and CoA-SH is released.

rxn03307.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of tetrahydrocorticosterone (3alpha,11beta,21-trihydroxy-5beta-pregnan-20-one) at the 3-hydroxyl group to form a 3-oxo group, yielding 5beta-pregnane-11beta,21-diol-3,20-dione, coupled to reduction of NAD+ to NADH + H+. This is consistent with a 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (B-specific, transferring hydride to the B-face of the nicotinamide ring). Stoichiometry is balanced: a secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, removing 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+, one as H+).

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction is not mass-balanced. Anabasine (C10H14N2) cannot be split into Niacin (nicotinic acid, C6H5NO2) plus Piperideine (C5H9N) with only CO2 and H+ on the other side; atoms (C, H, N, O) do not balance.

rxn03477.other_comments: This reaction describes the interconversion of anabasine with niacin (nicotinic acid) and a piperideine (delta-1-piperideine / dihydropyridine) unit. Biologically, anabasine is synthesized by condensation of nicotinic acid (niacin) with a piperideine derived from lysine/cadaverine, so the biosynthetic flux goes toward anabasine formation, i.e. the reverse of the written direction. As written, the equation is also not atom-balanced.

rxn10456.other_comments: This is a CDP-archaeol synthase-type reaction in archaeal ether lipid biosynthesis. CTP reacts with 2,3-bis-O-(geranylgeranyl)-sn-glycerol 1-phosphate (DGGGP) to form CDP-2,3-bis-O-(geranylgeranyl)-sn-glycerol with release of pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: a CMP group is transferred to the phosphate of the substrate and PPi is released, conserving phosphate and the nucleotide moiety. The reaction proceeds in the forward direction in vivo, driven by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by inorganic pyrophosphatase.

errors: Oxygen atom imbalance: TNT (C7H5N3O6) reduction to 4-hydroxylamino-2,6-dinitrotoluene (C7H6N3O5) removes one oxygen as water, but the equation as written does not balance H/O properly. Reduction of a nitro group (-NO2) to a hydroxylamino group (-NHOH) requires 2 NAD(P)H and consumes the equivalent removal of one oxygen as water; check that H+ and H2O counts close the balance.

Hydrogen/charge balance should be verified: nitro-to-hydroxylamine reduction is a 4-electron, 2 NADPH process producing 1 H2O, which appears consistent, but the listed H+ stoichiometry (2 H+) and product H count must be reconciled with the actual molecular formulas.
rxn07804.other_comments: This is the reduction of one nitro group of 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT) to a hydroxylamino group, yielding 4-hydroxylamino-2,6-dinitrotoluene, catalyzed by nitroreductases/oxygen-insensitive nitroreductases. The overall reduction (nitro to hydroxylamine) is a 4-electron reduction consuming 2 NADPH and producing 1 H2O, which is broadly consistent. Such nitroreductase reactions are strongly thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn07789.other_comments: This reaction (leucoanthocyanidin/flavanonol interconversion) describes dihydroflavonol 4-reductase (DFR) activity. Fisetinidin-3,4-diol (5-deoxyleucocyanidin, a leucoanthocyanidin/flavan-3,4-diol) is the reduced product, while Fustin (a dihydroflavonol, specifically dihydrofisetin) is the more oxidized substrate. As written, the equation shows oxidation of the flavan-3,4-diol to the dihydroflavonol with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry (atoms and charge) balances: the diol loses two H (one as electrons/hydride to NADP+, one as H+) to become the ketone (dihydroflavonol). However, DFR physiologically operates in the reductive direction (dihydroflavonol + NADPH -> leucoanthocyanidin + NADP+), so the biologically favored direction is the reverse of what is written.

rxn02940.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of an oxalyl group from oxalyl-CoA to the N3 (beta-amino) position of L-2,3-diaminopropionate, producing CoA and N3-oxalyl-L-2,3-diaminopropanoate (beta-ODAP/BOAA), the neurotoxin found in Lathyrus sativus (grass pea). The atoms balance: oxalyl-CoA (C2O3 acyl-CoA) transfers the oxalyl moiety to the amine, releasing free CoA and forming an amide bond. The H+ accounts for the proton released/consumed during amide bond formation, and the overall mass and charge are balanced. Acyl-CoA transferase reactions of this type are thermodynamically favorable due to cleavage of the high-energy thioester bond.

rxn02258.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction transferring the CoA moiety from succinyl-CoA to citramalate, producing succinate and citramalyl-CoA. The atom balance is consistent: the CoA group is transferred between the two acyl carriers, and succinyl loses CoA while citramalate gains it. CoA-transferases of this type catalyze reactions with relatively small free energy changes and are generally reversible in vivo.

rxn13709.other_comments: This is glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase coupling oxidation of glycerol-3-phosphate (sn-glycerol-3-phosphate) to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerone phosphate) with reduction of methylmenaquinone-7 to methylmenaquinol-7. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (2 electrons and 2 protons transferred from G3P to the quinone). In vivo, this is a catabolic respiratory step driving glycerol-3-phosphate oxidation coupled to the quinone pool, so it proceeds in the forward (oxidative) direction.

rxn09423.other_comments: This represents one cycle of fatty acid elongation: a C24 (tetracosanoate) fatty acid is extended by two carbons using malonyl-CoA and 2 NADPH to give a C26 (hexacosanoate) fatty acid, releasing CO2, CoA, and H2O. rxn04584.other_comments: This represents a biosynthetic step in coumermycin assembly involving two glycosyltransfer reactions (using dTDP-activated deoxysugar donors) and two SAM-dependent methylations on the coumermic acid (pyrrole dicarboxylic acid) scaffold to form Coumermycin D. Such glycosylation/methylation steps are biosynthetic and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn00228.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by phosphonoacetate hydrolase (EC 3.11.1.2), which cleaves the C-P bond of phosphonoacetate (Fosfonet). Hydrolysis of phosphonoacetate yields acetate and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: phosphonoacetate (C2H2O5P, charge -2) plus H2O yields acetate (C2H3O2, charge -1) plus phosphate (HPO4, charge -2) plus H+. Carbon: 2=2, phosphorus: 1=1. As a C-P bond hydrolysis, this proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (hydrolytic) direction.

errors: Oxygen mass imbalance: O2 provides 2 oxygen atoms, but the product 2,2',3-trihydroxydiphenyl ether requires incorporation of 2 hydroxyl oxygens while the dibenzo-p-dioxin ring contains 2 ether oxygens; ring-opening dioxygenase chemistry should yield 3 hydroxyl/phenolic oxygens from the substrate plus O2, so the oxygen balance needs verification

This appears to be an angular dioxygenase reaction (dibenzo-p-dioxin dioxygenase), which usually incorporates both atoms of O2 and requires NAD(P)H plus formation of a cis-dihydrodiol or hydroxylated/ring-cleaved product; the stoichiometry as written likely omits H2O
rxn03739.other_comments: This is the initial oxygenation/angular dioxygenation of dibenzo-p-dioxin to a trihydroxydiphenyl ether, a key step in dibenzo-p-dioxin degradation. Such NAD(P)H-dependent oxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, driven forward by O2 consumption and NADH oxidation.

rxn07847.other_comments: This reaction represents the condensation of formaldehyde with tetrahydromethanopterin (H4MPT) to form 5,10-methylenetetrahydromethanopterin and water. This is a spontaneous/enzyme-independent or formaldehyde-activating enzyme (Fae) catalyzed reaction in methylotrophic and methanogenic archaea/bacteria. The stoichiometry is balanced: formaldehyde (CH2O) provides the methylene carbon that bridges N5 and N10 of H4MPT, releasing one water molecule. Atom and charge balance are consistent. The reaction is generally considered reversible, though under physiological conditions in methylotrophs it often proceeds in the direction of formaldehyde detoxification/oxidation, while in methanogens reduction direction is favored depending on context.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the inclusion of 3.0 H+ on the left side is not balanced. For a monooxygenase reaction (UbiH/UbiF type) using NADPH + O2 to hydroxylate the substrate, only 1 H+ is consumed: NADPH + O2 + H+ + substrate -> H2O + NADP+ + hydroxylated-substrate. Three protons overcharges the left side.
Oxygen atom balance: one atom of O2 is incorporated into the product hydroxyl group and the other is reduced to H2O; this part is correct, but verify with corrected proton count.
rxn04139.other_comments: This is a flavin-dependent aromatic ring hydroxylase step in ubiquinone biosynthesis (analogous to UbiH/UbiF), adding a hydroxyl group to the benzoquinone ring using NADPH as electron donor and molecular oxygen as the oxygen source. Such monooxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (forward).

rxn01254.other_comments: This is a pyridoxamine-oxaloacetate transaminase (half-reaction type) where pyridoxamine (PM) donates its amino group to oxaloacetate, forming L-aspartate and pyridoxal (PL). Stoichiometry is balanced: oxaloacetate (C4H4O5) provides the keto acceptor, pyridoxamine carries the amino group; products are L-aspartate (C4H7NO4) and pyridoxal. The carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen atoms balance. Such pyridoxal/pyridoxamine transamination reactions are freely reversible.

rxn09358.other_comments: This is the Mpl reaction (murein peptide ligase / EC 6.3.2.45), which recycles the tripeptide L-Ala-gamma-D-Glu-meso-DAP by ligating it onto UDP-MurNAc in a single ATP-dependent step. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + UDP-MurNAc + tripeptide yields ADP + Pi + H+ + UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide. As an ATP-dependent amide ligase, this proceeds in the biosynthetic/forward direction in vivo.

rxn05098.other_comments: This appears to be a cytochrome P450-type (or flavonoid hydroxylase) monooxygenase reaction adding a hydroxyl group at the 5' position of 3'-hydroxyflavanone to yield 3',5'-dihydroxyflavanone. The reaction consumes NADPH, O2, and H+, incorporating one oxygen atom into the substrate and releasing the other as water, with NADP+ produced. The stoichiometry is balanced: a monooxygenase incorporates one O atom into substrate and reduces the other to water using NADPH (one electron pair) plus a proton.

rxn05299.other_comments: This is a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN) representing the movement of L-Histidine across a membrane, likely coupled with a proton (H+ symport/antiport). The reactants and products are identical (H+ + L-Histidine on both sides), which is typical notation for a transport process where the same species appear in different cellular compartments. Stoichiometrically the reaction is balanced (1 H+ and 1 L-Histidine on each side). The directionality depends on the proton-motive force and substrate concentration gradients; as written it is reversible.

rxn09462.other_comments: This represents peroxisomal beta-oxidation of octanoyl-CoA (C8) to 4 acetyl-CoA via 3 cycles. Peroxisomal beta-ox uses acyl-CoA oxidase (O2 -> H2O2) for step 1 and NAD-linked 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase for step 3 of each cycle, then thiolytic cleavage adds CoA. The lumped equation captures 3 cycles producing 3 NADH, 3 H2O2, 4 acetyl-CoA. The reaction is physiologically irreversible (driven by O2 consumption and H2O2 release).

errors: This reaction as written is not balanced. A decarboxylation (loss of CO2) would require removing a carboxyl group, but the substrate is named '2-Decarboxy' (already lacking the carboxyl), so converting it to Tetrangomycin (which has a carboxyl/CO2-related group) by RELEASING CO2 is contradictory. rxn04484.other_comments: The reaction depicts an apparent decarboxylation interconverting 2-decarboxytetrangomycin and tetrangomycin with CO2 and H+, part of angucycline antibiotic biosynthesis. Without exact molecular formulae I cannot fully verify atom balance, and the naming (decarboxy substrate giving CO2) is internally inconsistent, suggesting a direction/labeling error.

rxn02164.other_comments: This is an alcohol dehydrogenase-type oxidation of the 2-hydroxyl group of (S)-2-hydroxystearate (a C18 fatty acid) to the corresponding 2-oxo (keto) group, with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is balanced: a secondary alcohol (CHOH) is oxidized to a ketone (C=O), releasing 2 [H] which are carried as NADH + H+. Atoms and charges balance. NAD/NADH dehydrogenase reactions of this type are typically reversible thermodynamically, though physiological direction may favor oxidation depending on NAD+/NADH ratio.

rxn01822.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 4-hydroxyphenylacetate 3-monooxygenase (a flavin-dependent monooxygenase, EC 1.14.13.3). It hydroxylates 4-hydroxyphenylacetate at the 3-position to yield homogentisate (2,5-dihydroxyphenylacetate), incorporating one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate and reducing the other to water using NADPH. rxn02219.other_comments: This is the nitrilase reaction converting 3-indoleacetonitrile to indole-3-acetate (IAA) plus ammonia. rxn00552.other_comments: This is the glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminase (NagB, EC 3.5.99.6) reaction. D-Glucosamine 6-phosphate + H2O is converted to D-fructose 6-phosphate + ammonia (NH3). In vivo it typically runs in the deaminative direction to feed amino sugar catabolism into glycolysis, but it is biochemically reversible (and the reverse aminating direction is favored at high ammonia under anabolic conditions).

rxn07331.other_comments: This is the homogentisate phytyltransferase (HPT/VTE2) reaction in tocopherol biosynthesis. rxn01857.other_comments: This is the altronate oxidoreductase reaction (EC 1.1.1.58), part of the hexuronate/galacturonate catabolism pathway. Stoichiometry is balanced: the substrate loses two hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+, one as proton). In vivo this enzyme typically operates in the catabolic direction reducing tagaturonate to altronate (i.e., reverse as written) during fructuronate/galacturonate degradation, but it is thermodynamically reversible.

rxn05409.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthesis condensation (Claisen) reaction catalyzed by a beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (KAS III type). rxn07157.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent methyltransferase reaction transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to a beta-keto-L-tyrosyl carrier protein (pcp) substrate, forming the 3-methyl product, S-adenosyl-homocysteine, and a proton. rxn02290.other_comments: This is the oxidosqualene cyclase (lanosterol synthase, EC 5.4.99.7) reaction, which converts (S)-2,3-epoxysqualene (squalene 2,3-oxide) into lanosterol via a polycyclization cascade. rxn11901.other_comments: This reaction represents the epoxidation of all-trans-retinoic acid (Tretin M = retinoic acid) to all-trans-5,6-epoxyretinoic acid, catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. rxn05363.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthesis condensation step (KAS/beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase type). Atoms and charges balance: malonyl (C3) + acyl chain - CO2 = chain + 2 carbons, consistent with Claisen condensation chemistry.

rxn00617.other_comments: This reaction describes a phosphotransfer from sn-glycerol-3-phosphate to D-glucose, producing D-glucose-6-phosphate and glycerol. This corresponds to EC 2.7.1.142 (glycerol-3-phosphate-glucose phosphotransferase). In vivo, the high-energy phosphate transfer and metabolic context favor the forward direction (glucose phosphorylation), though such transfer reactions can be near-equilibrium.

rxn09436.other_comments: This represents one round of mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) elongation: Dodecanoyl-ACP (C12) is condensed with malonyl-ACP, with loss of CO2, then reduced (2 NADPH) and dehydrated (H2O released) to yield Myristoyl-ACP (C14) plus free ACP. rxn00547.other_comments: This is ketohexokinase/fructokinase-type phosphorylation: ATP transfers a phosphate to D-fructose, producing ADP, a proton, and D-fructose-6-phosphate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (ATP4- + fructose -> ADP3- + H+ + F6P2-). Note: the enzyme name 'ATP:D-fructose 6-phosphotransferase' is technically incorrect terminology since classical fructokinase yields fructose-1-phosphate, but the written stoichiometry forming F6P is self-consistent and balanced.

rxn03954.other_comments: This is the IdnD/IdnO-type reaction (L-idonate 5-dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.264) in which the C5 hydroxyl of L-idonate is oxidized to a ketone, yielding 5-dehydro-D-gluconate (5-ketogluconate). Note that the physiological E. coli enzymes IdnD/IdnO are often NAD-linked; if the actual cofactor specificity is NAD rather than NADP, that would be an error.

rxn03000.other_comments: This reaction represents a 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase acting on etiocholan-3alpha-ol-17-one (3alpha-hydroxy-5beta-androstan-17-one), oxidizing the 3alpha-hydroxyl group to a ketone to form 5beta-androstane-3,17-dione, with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. rxn10475.other_comments: This reaction describes the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of 7-mercaptoheptanoylthreonine to form HTP (7-mercaptoheptanoylthreonine phosphate, also known as coenzyme M-7-mercaptoheptanoylthreonine phosphate / CoB), catalyzed by 2-phospho-L-lactate transferase or specifically the kinase in coenzyme B biosynthesis in methanogenic archaea. rxn12948.other_comments: This is 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (EC 2.4.1.34), which transfers a glucose residue from UDP-glucose to the non-reducing end of a growing 1,3-beta-D-glucan chain. The reaction is balanced: a phosphoryl group is transferred from the protein N-phosphohistidine to the C6 hydroxyl of glucose. Stoichiometry is correct (one phosphate transferred, atoms balanced). Note the nomenclature: N-pros (tau, N3) vs N-pai (pi, N1) refers to the histidine ring nitrogen position; the reaction name references N(pai) while the substrate is written as N-pros, which is a minor inconsistency in labeling but does not affect mass balance.

rxn00803.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by maleate cis-trans isomerase (EC 5.2.1.1), which converts maleate (cis-butenedioate) to fumarate (trans-butenedioate). It is a geometric isomerization with identical molecular formula (C4H4O4) on both sides, so it is stoichiometrically balanced. In vivo, the reaction proceeds toward fumarate because fumarate is the thermodynamically more stable trans isomer and is readily consumed by downstream metabolism (e.g., the TCA cycle), making the conversion effectively irreversible in the forward direction.

rxn08647.other_comments: This reaction is glycerate kinase (ATP:(R)-glycerate 2-phosphotransferase, EC 2.7.1.165) producing 2-phospho-D-glycerate. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP donates a phosphate to D-glycerate yielding 2-phospho-D-glycerate, ADP, and a proton. Mass and charge are balanced. As an ATP-dependent kinase reaction, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the phosphorylation (forward) direction.

rxn02760.other_comments: This is sucrose-6-phosphate hydrolase (sucrose-6-phosphate fructohydrolase). It hydrolyzes sucrose-6-phosphate (6-phosphosucrose) with water to yield D-glucose-6-phosphate and D-fructose. The stoichiometry is balanced: the glucose moiety retains the 6-phosphate while the fructose is released free. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn11513.other_comments: This reaction represents a beta-glucuronidase-type hydrolysis where water cleaves a beta-D-glucuronosyl linkage from luteolin triglucuronide. The substrate Luteolin 7-O-[beta-D-glucuronosyl-(1->2)-beta-D-glucuronide]-4'-O-beta-D-glucuronide carries three glucuronic acid moieties; hydrolysis removes the terminal 4'-O glucuronide releasing one free glucuronate and yielding Luteolin 7-O-beta-D-diglucuronide. Stoichiometry appears balanced (one water consumed, one glucuronate released). Hydrolases acting on glycosidic bonds are essentially irreversible in vivo because hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable.

rxn02602.other_comments: This is a flavanone 3-hydroxylase (F3H, a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase) reaction. Eriodictyol (a flavanone) is hydroxylated at C3 to form taxifolin (dihydroquercetin, a dihydroflavonol). The reaction couples substrate hydroxylation with decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate to succinate and CO2, consuming one O2. The stoichiometry is balanced: one O atom goes into the substrate hydroxyl and the other into the succinate/CO2 (one O from O2 ends in CO2, one in the product hydroxyl). Atoms balance correctly.

errors: Reaction is not stoichiometrically balanced. Pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + Glyceraldehyde3-phosphate (C3H5O6P2-) gives 6 carbons on the left, but products CO2 (1 C) + 1-Deoxy-D-xylulose (C5H10O4, 5 C) = 6 C, so carbon balances. rxn13147.other_comments: This appears to be a corrupted version of the 1-deoxy-D-xylulose-5-phosphate synthase (DXS) reaction, which condenses pyruvate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate with loss of CO2 to form DXP. The given reaction incorrectly produces dephosphorylated 1-deoxy-D-xylulose plus free phosphate and adds spurious H2O/H+.

rxn12039.other_comments: This represents oxidative deamination of demethylcitalopram (the desmethyl metabolite of citalopram) by a flavin-containing amine oxidase (MAO-type chemistry). The reaction consumes O2 and H2O, releasing H2O2, the amine (methanamine/methylamine), and an aldehyde product (citalopram aldehyde / propionaldehyde derivative). Demethylcitalopram has a secondary amine (N-methyl); oxidative deamination cleaves the C-N bond yielding an aldehyde plus methylamine. Stoichiometry of atoms balances for the generic amine oxidase mechanism (R-CH2-NHCH3 + O2 + H2O -> R-CHO + CH3NH2 + H2O2).

rxn12179.other_comments: This is an O-methyltransferase reaction (xanthotoxol/bergaptol-type methyltransferase in furanocoumarin biosynthesis). SAM donates a methyl group to the 5-hydroxyl of 5-hydroxyxanthotoxin, producing isopimpinellin (5,8-dimethoxypsoralen) and S-adenosyl-homocysteine. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one methyl group transferred, SAM converted to SAH. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are strongly favored in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn04330.other_comments: This reaction represents the cyclization of 2,3-oxidosqualene (squalene 2,3-epoxide) to beta-amyrin, catalyzed by beta-amyrin synthase (a member of the oxidosqualene cyclase family, EC 5.4.99.39). The substrate and product are isomers with the same molecular formula (C30H50O), so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a single intramolecular cyclization/rearrangement. In vivo this is an essentially irreversible, thermodynamically driven cyclization (the energy from the epoxide opening drives the polycyclization), so it proceeds in the forward direction.

errors: Stoichiometric/mass imbalance: lytic transglycosylases are intramolecular reactions that do not consume or release water; rather they cleave the glycosidic bond and form a 1,6-anhydro ring with no net addition of H2O. H2O should not appear as a product (it should be on the substrate side if hydrolysis, but transglycosylase forms anhydroMurNAc, releasing no water).
Water is shown on the product side, which is chemically incorrect for an anhydro-product-forming transglycosylase; the formation of the 1,6-anhydro bond is intramolecular and net water-neutral.

Likely atom imbalance: one disaccharide-tripeptide dimer should yield two anhydro-MurNAc tripeptide products only if the bond cleavage and ring closure balance; the explicit free H2O term suggests an unbalanced equation.
rxn08939.other_comments: This represents a murein (peptidoglycan) lytic transglycosylase acting on uncrosslinked, mid-chain disaccharide-tripeptide units to produce 1,6-anhydro-N-acetylmuramyl (GlcNAc-anhMurNAc) tripeptide fragments. In vivo these enzymes cleave the beta-1,4 glycosidic bond between MurNAc and GlcNAc and form an intramolecular 1,6-anhydro bond, acting degradatively in the forward direction. The named species and process are recognizable.

rxn00466.other_comments: This is the N5-(L-1-carboxyethyl)-L-ornithine synthase reaction (EC 1.5.1.24). The reaction as written is the oxidative (hydrolytic deamination/cleavage) direction: N5-(L-1-carboxyethyl)-L-ornithine + NADP+ + H2O -> ornithine + pyruvate + NADPH + H+. Atoms and charges balance: the reductive amination joining ornithine and pyruvate consumes NADPH and forms the secondary amine linkage with loss of water. In vivo this enzyme functions biosynthetically in the reductive (condensation) direction, forming N5-(L-1-carboxyethyl)-L-ornithine from ornithine and pyruvate using NADPH; thus relative to the way the reaction is written here (cleavage), the physiological flux is in the reverse direction.

No definitive atom-balance error detected given the formyl-to-carboxyl conversion
rxn03366.other_comments: This represents an NADP-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase oxidizing the formyl (aldehyde) group of 5-(2'-formylethyl)-4,6-dihydroxypicolinate to the corresponding carboxylic acid (5-(2'-carboxyethyl)-4,6-dihydroxypicolinate), with water providing the oxygen and NADP being reduced to NADPH plus release of 2 protons. This is a classic aldehyde dehydrogenase step in nicotinate/pyridine degradation pathways.

rxn14034.other_comments: This is the dinitrogen reductase activating glycohydrolase (DraG) reaction, which removes the ADP-ribose moiety from an arginine residue of dinitrogen reductase (NifH/Fe protein), reactivating nitrogenase. Hydrolysis of the ADP-ribosyl-protein bond using water yields free ADP-ribose and the unmodified reductase. Stoichiometry is balanced as written (the ADP-ribosyl group plus water gives ADP-ribose plus the deribosylated protein).

rxn02421.other_comments: This is a cytidylyltransferase reaction (EC 2.7.7.-) analogous to ethanolamine-phosphate cytidylyltransferase. CTP reacts with N-methylethanolamine phosphate to form CDP-N-methylethanolamine plus pyrophosphate (PPi). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the cytidylyl group (CMP) is transferred to the phosphate of N-methylethanolamine phosphate, releasing PPi. In vivo, the subsequent hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase drives the reaction toward CDP-aminoalcohol formation.

errors: This is a null/identity reaction: L-Sorbose appears identically on both sides with no transformation, no transport compartment distinction shown, and no change in chemical species
No net chemical change occurs, making the reaction biochemically meaningless as written

The reaction ID suggests this may be intended as a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN), where the same metabolite moves between compartments (e.g., periplasm to cytoplasm), but no compartment annotations are provided in the equation itself. rxn00804.other_comments: This is leucine dehydrogenase (EC 1.4.1.9), catalyzing the oxidative deamination of L-leucine to 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (4MOP, also known as ketoleucine/alpha-ketoisocaproate) with reduction of NAD+ to NADH and release of ammonia. The reaction is balanced: atoms and charges are conserved. L-Leucine (C6H13NO2) + H2O + NAD+ yields 4MOP (C6H10O3, the 2-oxo acid anion) + NADH + NH3 + H+. The enzyme is physiologically reversible and can run in the reductive amination direction (forming leucine) depending on substrate concentrations.

rxn01053.other_comments: This is the aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.2.1.22, lactaldehyde dehydrogenase) oxidizing L-lactaldehyde to L-lactate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylic acid using water, with NAD+ reduced to NADH and 2 protons released. Atoms (C, H, O, N) and charge balance correctly. In vivo, NAD+-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenases are essentially irreversible in the oxidative direction.

rxn00075.other_comments: This is the NAD nucleosidase (NAD glycohydrolase, EC 3.2.2.5) reaction, which hydrolyzes the N-glycosidic bond of NAD+ to yield nicotinamide and ADP-ribose. The stoichiometry is balanced: NAD+ + H2O yields nicotinamide + ADP-ribose + H+ (the H+ accounts for charge/proton balance). As a hydrolysis reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in the forward direction.

rxn00967.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the hydroxyl group of 4-hydroxybenzoate, forming 4-(beta-D-glucosyloxy)benzoate and releasing UDP. The reaction is balanced: UDP-glucose (C15H24N2O17P2) provides glucose to the phenolic acceptor; carbon, oxygen, and the glycosidic bond formation are consistent. A proton balance check: UDP-glucose + acceptor-OH -> glucoside + UDP, with glucose transferred from the diphosphate linkage to the oxygen, which is stoichiometrically consistent.

rxn01792.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of pantothenate (PAN) by pantothenase (pantothenate amidohydrolase, EC 3.5.1.22). Pantothenate consists of pantoate joined to beta-alanine via an amide bond. Hydrolysis with water cleaves this amide bond to yield pantoate and beta-alanine. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (note: at physiological pH the carboxylates would be ionized, but the atom balance holds).

rxn02340.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.91) transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the 3-O position of a flavonol, producing flavonol 3-O-D-glucoside and UDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (one glucosyl unit transferred, UDP released). Glycosyltransferase reactions of this type are thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy UDP-sugar bond and proceed essentially in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn08607.other_comments: This reaction transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the 6-position hydroxyl of D-glucose, producing CoA and 6-acetyl-D-glucose (6-O-acetyl-D-glucose). The atoms balance: acetyl-CoA (C23H38N7O17P3S) + glucose (C6H12O6) yields CoA (C21H36N7O16P3S) + 6-acetyl-glucose (C8H14O7). Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur are conserved. Acetyltransferase reactions using acetyl-CoA as the acyl donor are strongly exergonic due to the high-energy thioester bond, driving the reaction toward acetylation.

rxn03490.other_comments: This is a terephthalate 1,2-dioxygenase (TPDO) reaction, an aromatic ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase. Terephthalate (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylate) is converted to the cis-1,2-dihydrodiol (1,2-dihydroxy-3,5-cyclohexadiene-1,4-dicarboxylate, often abbreviated as DCD or 1,2-dihydroxyterephthalate dihydrodiol), incorporating both atoms of molecular oxygen. NADH provides the two reducing equivalents. The reaction is atom-balanced: NADH + O2 + H+ + terephthalate yields NAD+ + the cis-dihydrodiol. Charge and atom balance are consistent assuming NAD is written as NAD+.

rxn02461.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate (Ins(1,3,4,5)P4) by a 3-phosphatase, removing the phosphate at the 3-position to yield inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (Ins(1,4,5)P3) and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphate group is removed via hydrolysis, consuming one water and releasing one phosphate. Phosphomonoester hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of hydrolysis.

rxn03957.other_comments: This reaction describes the interconversion of dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-glucose (dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose) and dTDP-D-fucose. As written, NADP+ oxidizes dTDP-D-fucose to the 4-keto sugar. Stoichiometry is balanced: the reductase reaction couples reduction of the 4-keto group with oxidation of NADPH, so charges and atoms balance (NADP+ + reduced sugar = NADPH + H+ + keto sugar). The enzyme name 'dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxyglucose reductase' indicates the physiological direction is reduction of the 4-keto sugar to dTDP-D-fucose, which consumes NADPH. Thus the biologically favored direction is opposite to how the reaction is written (i.e., the reverse: NADPH + H+ + dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose -> NADP+ + dTDP-D-fucose).

rxn11040.other_comments: This is the oxidative decarboxylation of 6-phospho-D-gluconate to ribulose-5-phosphate in the pentose phosphate pathway, catalyzed by 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.44 with NADP+; EC 1.1.1.343 is the NAD+-dependent variant). Carbon balance (6 C -> 5 C + 1 CO2) is correct; the decarboxylation drives the reaction strongly forward in vivo.

rxn02163.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of (R)-2-hydroxystearate (a C18 2-hydroxy fatty acid) to 2-oxostearate (2-oxooctadecanoate), coupled to the reduction of NAD+ to NADH + H+. The reaction is stoichiometrically and redox balanced: the secondary alcohol at C2 is oxidized to a ketone, releasing two electrons and a proton to NAD+, with the second proton released into solution. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and charge are conserved. This is a 2-hydroxyacid dehydrogenase type reaction. Such NAD-dependent alcohol/hydroxyacid dehydrogenases are typically reversible in vitro, though physiological direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio and downstream consumption of products.

rxn04891.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-catalyzed monooxygenation of 1,1-dichloroethylene (vinylidene chloride). One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate (here forming the epoxide which rearranges to 2,2-dichloroacetaldehyde / chloroacetyl chloride pathway), while the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Stoichiometry balances: C2H2Cl2 + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> C2H2Cl2O + H2O + NADP+. Atoms balance (C2, H, Cl2, O, plus NADPH/NADP+ and water). P450 oxidations are physiologically irreversible.

rxn07776.other_comments: This is the 2-methyleneglutarate hydratase (2-hydroxymethylglutarate dehydratase) reaction, EC 4.2.1.85, involved in nicotinate fermentation in anaerobic bacteria such as Clostridium barkeri. It interconverts (S)-2-(hydroxymethyl)glutarate and 2-methyleneglutarate plus water. The stoichiometry is balanced: removal/addition of one water molecule across the substrate. As a hydro-lyase, it is reversible in vivo, though in the nicotinate degradation pathway it operates in the dehydration direction (toward 2-methyleneglutarate).

errors: The substrate name '2,4,5-Trichloro-2,5-cyclohexadiene-1-ol' is chemically inconsistent: a 2,5-cyclohexadiene-1-ol with substituents at 2,4,5 implies a carbon (C4) bearing both a ring double bond participant and a chloro substituent, but the actual KEGG R05370 substrate is 2,4,5-trichloro-2,5-cyclohexadien-1-ol (a chlorinated dienol intermediate in lindane/gamma-HCH degradation). Naming aside, stoichiometry should be checked: replacing one Cl by OH via hydrolytic dehalogenation releases HCl (H+ + Cl-) and consumes H2O, which balances mass and charge.
Carbon count: substrate C6Cl3O (one OH), product C6Cl2O2 (two OH). One Cl is replaced by OH. Balanced as written: H2O in, H+ + Cl- out, net one Cl-to-OH swap. Atom balance appears correct.
rxn03671.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic dehalogenation step catalyzed by LinB (haloalkane/halidohydrolase) in the gamma-hexachlorocyclohexane (lindane) degradation pathway, converting a trichlorocyclohexadienol to a dichlorocyclohexadienediol with release of chloride. Such dehalogenations are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn05124.other_comments: This is the gamma-glutamylputrescine oxidase reaction (PuuB/YgjG, EC 1.4.3.-) in the putrescine utilization (Puu) pathway. It oxidizes the primary amine of gamma-L-glutamylputrescine to an aldehyde, releasing ammonia and producing hydrogen peroxide via O2 and water. The reaction is balanced: gamma-L-glutamylputrescine (C9H19N3O3) + H2O + O2 yields gamma-glutamyl-gamma-aminobutyraldehyde (C9H16N2O3) + NH3 + H2O2, with C, H, N, O all balanced. As an FAD-dependent amine oxidase coupled to O2 reduction to H2O2, it is physiologically irreversible in the oxidative (forward) direction.

errors: Mass imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced. Ureidoglycine (C3H7N3O3) + H2O (H2O) yields C3H9N3O4, but NH3 (NH3) + Ureidoglycolate (C3H5N2O4 as deprotonated, or C3H6N2O4 neutral) accounts for only C3H9N3O4 if ureidoglycolate is C3H6N2O4; check protonation states

rxn03842.other_comments: This is the ureidoglycine aminohydrolase (UGlyAH) reaction in the purine degradation pathway, where (S)-ureidoglycine is hydrolytically deaminated to (S)-ureidoglycolate, releasing ammonia. With correct neutral formulas (ureidoglycine C3H7N3O3 + H2O = ureidoglycolate C3H6N2O4 + NH3) the reaction is actually atom-balanced.

rxn08025.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 6-phospho-beta-glucosidase (arbutin-6-phosphate glucohydrolase, EC 3.2.1.86). It hydrolyzes the glycosidic bond of arbutin-6-phosphate, releasing glucose-6-phosphate and the aglycone hydroquinone (quinol). As a hydrolase acting on a phosphorylated substrate during sugar catabolism (PTS uptake), it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo. Note: 'quinol' is a synonym for hydroquinone, so the naming is acceptable.

rxn12748.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by N-formylmaleamate deformylase (NicD) in the aerobic nicotinate degradation pathway. N-formylmaleamic acid is hydrolyzed to release formate and produce maleamate. The reaction is balanced: N-formylmaleamate (C5H5NO4) + H2O yields formate (CHO2-) + H+ + maleamate (C4H4NO3-). Carbon (5=1+4), nitrogen (1=1), and charge balance correctly. The hydrolytic deformylation is essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the pathway forward.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction as written is not charge-balanced. GSH (neutral thiol) reacting with an acyl chloride should release HCl (H+ + Cl-), but only Cl- is shown as a product. A proton (H+) is missing from the product side to balance charge and mass.

rxn07181.other_comments: This is a thioester-forming reaction in which glutathione's thiol attacks the acyl chloride carbon, displacing chloride and forming 2-(S-glutathionyl)acetyl glutathione (a bis-glutathione thioester adduct). Acyl chlorides are highly reactive electrophiles and this nucleophilic acyl substitution is essentially irreversible under physiological conditions, strongly favoring the forward direction. Note that acyl chlorides are not typical biological metabolites, which raises questions about the in vivo relevance of this reaction.

errors: Carbon balance is incorrect. Each malonyl-ACP elongation cycle adds 2 carbons to the acyl chain (net, after CO2 release). 8 cycles add 16 carbons to a C22 (docosanoyl) substrate, giving C38, which matches. However, the elongation of an acyl-ACP by malonyl-ACP releases the holo-ACP from malonyl-ACP and consumes one malonyl-ACP per cycle, so 8 ACP released is consistent; this part balances.

Reducing equivalent count is wrong. A standard fatty acid elongation cycle (condensation, ketoreduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction) requires 2 reducing equivalents (NAD(P)H) per 2-carbon unit added, i.e., 2 per cycle. For 8 cycles that is 16 NAD(P)H total. The reaction provides 8 NADH + 8 NADPH = 16 reducing equivalents, which is consistent in total, but mixing 8 NADH AND 8 NADPH oxidized to BOTH 8 NAD AND 8 NADP per cycle implies 2 reductions per cycle - acceptable, though specific cofactor usage (NADPH for both reductions in FAS-II type systems) may be inaccurate.

Oxygen/hydrogen balance: dehydration step yields H2O. 8 cycles should yield 8 H2O, which matches. Proton (H+) balance should be checked; 16 H+ consumed corresponds to 16 NAD(P)H oxidations, consistent.

Product name 'cis-C38oyl-ACP' with a single cis double bond from a 'cis-19-docosanoyl-ACP' (C22:1) elongated by saturated 2C units is reasonable, but the double bond position relabeling is not explicit.
rxn13454.other_comments: This is a fatty-acid elongation (meromycolate/methoxy-meroacid synthesis, mycobacterial-type) reaction extending a C22:1 (cis-19-docosanoyl) acyl-ACP by 8 two-carbon malonyl units to form a C38:1 acyl-ACP, releasing 8 CO2 and 8 holo-ACP, consuming 16 reducing equivalents. The overall carbon stoichiometry (22 + 8x2 = 38) is consistent, and reducing equivalents (16) match 2 per cycle. The use of malonyl-ACP and decarboxylative condensation makes this strongly forward (biosynthetic) in vivo.

rxn01448.other_comments: This is the indolepyruvate C-methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.106) involved in indolmycin biosynthesis. SAM donates a methyl group to indolepyruvate, producing S-adenosyl-homocysteine and (S)-beta-methylindolepyruvate, with release of a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl group transferred from SAM accounts for the additional CH2 (CH3 added minus the H lost as proton) in the methylated product. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are typically thermodynamically favorable and physiologically driven in the methyl-transfer (forward) direction.

rxn10348.other_comments: This represents alpha-amylase (EC 3.2.1.1) catalyzing the endohydrolysis of internal alpha-1,4-glucosidic bonds in amylose. As a hydrolytic reaction in vivo, it proceeds in the direction of polymer breakdown to shorter oligosaccharides.

rxn06981.other_comments: This is the ferredoxin-dependent bilin reductase (PcyA-type/related) reaction reducing biliverdin IXalpha across the 15,16 double bond to form 15,16-dihydrobiliverdin. The reaction is a 2-electron reduction, so it requires 2 ferredoxin (reduced) and yields 2 ferredoxin (oxidized); the stated 1:1 ferredoxin stoichiometry is unbalanced.

rxn14075.other_comments: This is the betanidin 5-O-glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.174). UDP-glucose donates a glucose moiety to the 5-hydroxyl of betanidin, producing betanin (betanidin 5-O-beta-D-glucoside) and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose to betanidin, with UDP and the glucosylated product formed. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward betanin formation in betalain pigment biosynthesis.

rxn02428.other_comments: This is the MHPCO reaction (EC 1.14.13.-/oxygenase) where 3-hydroxy-2-methylpyridine-5-carboxylate is oxidatively cleaved (ring opening) using NADPH and O2 to form 2-(acetamidomethylene)succinate. As an oxygenase-catalyzed ring-cleavage step in vitamin B6 degradation, it is physiologically essentially irreversible in the forward direction.

Charge/proton balance appears incorrect as written (2.0 H+ overstated for a simple thioester hydrolysis)
rxn04927.other_comments: This represents hydrolysis of a thioester bond in 2-(S-glutathionyl)acetyl glutathione, releasing free GSH and forming the carboxylate (2-S-glutathionyl acetate) as part of glyoxalase/glutathione-dependent detoxification pathways. Thioester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable, so it proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn00661.other_comments: This reaction represents an amide bond ligase forming beta-alanyl-L-arginine from beta-alanine and L-arginine, using ATP hydrolyzed to AMP + PPi. Mass and charge balance check out: ATP (charge -4) + NH3 (0) + substrate (-1) on left = -5; products PPi (-3) + AMP (-2) + 2 H+ (+2) + amide product (-1) = -4 + 2 = ... let me note charge balances as -5 = -4, so charge is consistent if 2 H+ are released. Atoms (C, N, O, P) balance with water-free AMP-forming ligase convention. The subsequent pyrophosphate release makes this reaction thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn10283.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction transferring glucose from UDP-glucose to a diacylglycerol (1,2-diisoheptadecanoyl-sn-glycerol), forming a monoglucosyldiacylglycerol and releasing UDP. Glycosyltransferases using UDP-sugar donors are strongly thermodynamically driven toward glycoside formation due to the high group-transfer potential of the UDP-sugar bond.

rxn10008.other_comments: This is a lumped/aggregate reaction intended to represent pimelate (a C7 dicarboxylic acid, precursor of biotin) synthesis from pyruvate and oxaloacetate. rxn10434.other_comments: This is the homocitrate synthase reaction (EC 2.3.3.14) in the lysine biosynthesis (AAA) pathway. The product listed here, trans-homoaconitate (also called cis-homoaconitate depending on convention), is actually the product of the subsequent homoaconitase dehydration step, not the direct condensation product. The reaction as written appears to combine condensation with dehydration; if it represents that net conversion, water should be released. As written, the atoms do not balance: acetyl-CoA (C23H38N7O17P3S) + 2-oxoglutarate (C5H6O5) yields CoA (C21H36N7O16P3S) + H+ + homocitrate (C7H10O7), not homoaconitate. Producing homoaconitate (C7H8O7) would require loss of H2O, which is missing on the product side.

rxn12171.other_comments: This is an acetyl-CoA-dependent O-acetyltransferase (BAHD-type) reaction transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the hydroxyl of (L-)menthol, producing menthyl acetate and free CoA. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the acetyl moiety is transferred from CoA to menthol, so atoms and the thioester-to-ester linkage are conserved. In vivo, acetyltransferase reactions using acetyl-CoA as the acyl donor are thermodynamically driven by the high-energy thioester bond and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward the acetylated ester.

rxn00034.other_comments: This is the oxidative cleavage of the alpha-beta carbon-carbon double bond of a dehydrodivanillin-type stilbene-like compound (1,2-bis(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)ethylene) by O2, yielding two molecules of vanillin (4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde). The stoichiometry is balanced: cleaving the central C=C double bond with insertion of two oxygen atoms (one per carbon) converts each half to an aldehyde, consistent with a dioxygenase-type cleavage producing 2 vanillin from 1 substrate plus 1 O2.

rxn03846.other_comments: This is the AtzC reaction in the atrazine degradation pathway. N-isopropylammelide (a hydroxylated triazine) is hydrolyzed by the metal-dependent amidohydrolase to yield cyanuric acid and isopropylamine (2-propanamine, 2-aminopropane). Mass and atom balance: N-isopropylammelide (C6H10N4O2) + H2O + H+ -> cyanuric acid (C3H3N3O3) + isopropylamine (C3H9N, which becomes C3H10N+ when protonated). Checking atoms: C6 -> C3+C3 ok; the deamination replaces the isopropylamino group with a hydroxyl/keto oxygen. The reaction is balanced if isopropylamine is protonated to consume the H+. Direction is physiologically committed forward toward cyanuric acid (a hydrolytic, essentially irreversible amidohydrolase step).

rxn10649.other_comments: This appears to be part of methoxy mycolic acid biosynthesis in Mycobacterium, where SAM-dependent methyltransferases (e.g., MmaA family) modify the meromycolate chain. SAM is the methyl donor producing SAH and H+. The reaction as written introduces both a methyl and a hydroxyl group, which is mechanistically inconsistent with a single methyltransferase step.

rxn06527.other_comments: This reaction represents glutathione:protein-disulfide oxidoreductase (thiol-disulfide exchange). Oxidized glutathione (GSSG) oxidizes a protein dithiol to a protein disulfide, releasing 2 reduced glutathione (GSH). The stoichiometry is balanced: one disulfide bond is broken in GSSG and one is formed in the protein, with the two thiol equivalents conserved (2 GSH produced from GSSG, and protein dithiol oxidized to disulfide). Mass and redox balance are correct.

The explicit H+ on the product side creates a hydrogen imbalance (left 15 H vs right 16 H) and a charge imbalance unless glucosaminate is written as the deprotonated carboxylate anion. If glucosaminate carries a -1 charge, then H+ balances charge, but the H count must be reconciled accordingly.
rxn01440.other_comments: This is an oxidase reaction (D-glucosamine oxidase) oxidizing the C1 of D-glucosamine to D-glucosaminic acid using molecular O2 and producing H2O2. The stoichiometry is approximately correct if glucosaminate is the carboxylate anion balancing the released H+, but the H/charge accounting as written should be verified.

rxn06106.other_comments: This is Complex III (cytochrome bc1 / ubiquinol:cytochrome c oxidoreductase). Note that this simplified equation omits the additional protons translocated across the membrane via the Q-cycle (vectorial transport), but the chemical balance shown is correct.

rxn03986.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 3-hydroxy-2-methyl-4(1H)-quinolone 2,4-dioxygenase (a cofactor-independent dioxygenase, EC 1.13.11.47). rxn09964.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing octadecanal (a C18 fatty aldehyde) to octadecanoate (ocdca, stearate) using NAD+ as the electron acceptor. rxn04651.other_comments: This reaction describes an ATP-dependent phosphotransferase converting ribose-1,5-bisphosphate to PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate). rxn07688.other_comments: This is a beta-oxidation step in the jasmonic acid biosynthesis pathway (OPC-8:0 to jasmonate conversion). rxn11608.other_comments: This represents a lignin peroxidase (or related peroxidase) catalyzed oxidative cleavage of a beta-O-4 or beta-1 type lignin model compound. rxn14375.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADPH-dependent reduction of the 3-keto group of allopregnan-20alpha-ol-3-one (5alpha-pregnan-20alpha-ol-3-one) to yield 5alpha-pregnane-3alpha,20alpha-diol (allopregnanediol). The A-specific designation refers to pro-R hydride transfer from the nicotinamide ring.

rxn01814.other_comments: This represents pinosylvin (stilbene) synthase, a type III polyketide synthase that condenses cinnamoyl-CoA with three malonyl-CoA units, followed by cyclization to form the stilbene pinosylvin. rxn01508.other_comments: This is a deoxyadenosine kinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.76). ATP phosphorylates deoxyadenosine at the 5' position, producing dAMP and ADP, with release of a proton. rxn03502.other_comments: This is the lacto-N-biosidase reaction (EC 3.2.1.140). rxn07970.other_comments: This is the L-idonate 5-dehydrogenase (NADP+) reaction (EC 1.1.1.264 / idonate:NADP+ 2-oxidoreductase). It interconverts L-idonate and 5-keto-D-gluconate / 2-dehydro-L-gulonate using NADPH/NADP+. The stoichiometry is balanced: reduction of the keto group to a hydroxyl consumes NADPH + H+ and releases NADP+, with mass and charge conserved. Note: the enzyme name says NADP+ but standard naming for this activity is L-idonate 5-dehydrogenase; the substrate '2-dehydro-L-gulonate' is the oxidized form corresponding to L-idonate.

rxn08926.other_comments: This is intended to be a murein (peptidoglycan) L,D-carboxypeptidase acting in the periplasm, converting a crosslinked tetrapeptide stem to a tripeptide by removing the terminal D-alanine, consuming water. The reaction is written on a dimeric (two disaccharide-linked) murein unit.

rxn01996.other_comments: This is the methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase (racemase) reaction interconverting the (S)-/(R)- (L-/D-) stereoisomers of methylmalonyl-CoA. Both species have identical molecular formulas (C25H40N7O19P3S), so the reaction is inherently mass- and charge-balanced. As an epimerase catalyzing a stereochemical inversion, the reaction is thermodynamically near-equilibrium and freely reversible. In the propionate/odd-chain fatty acid catabolism pathway, net flux proceeds from (S)-methylmalonyl-CoA (formed by propionyl-CoA carboxylase) to (R)-methylmalonyl-CoA (substrate for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase). Note: nomenclature conventions for L/D vs R/S can vary across databases, so verify the stereochemical labels match the intended substrate/product.

rxn03583.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of 4-sulfobenzyl alcohol (4-(hydroxymethyl)benzenesulfonate) to 4-sulfobenzaldehyde, with NAD+ acting as the electron acceptor and being reduced to NADH. Carbon, oxygen, sulfur, and the sulfonate group are conserved on both sides; hydrogen and charge balance with the H+ released. This is part of toluenesulfonate/p-toluenesulfonate degradation pathways in bacteria such as Comamonas testosteroni.

rxn09992.other_comments: This is the 6-phospho-beta-glucosidase reaction (EC 3.2.1.86). Salicin-6-phosphate is hydrolyzed by water to yield D-glucose-6-phosphate and saligenin (2-hydroxybenzyl alcohol, the aglycone).
