rxn01695.other_comments: This reaction represents the cytochrome P450 (or estrogen 2-hydroxylase, CYP1A1/CYP1A2/CYP1B1)-catalyzed 2-hydroxylation of estrone. A monooxygenase consumes one O2, with one oxygen atom incorporated into the substrate (forming 2-hydroxyestrone) and the other reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + estrone yields H2O + NADP+ + 2-hydroxyestrone, with the H+ and NADPH providing the reducing equivalents. P450 monooxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (driven by O2 consumption and NADPH oxidation), so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn05402.other_comments: This is a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase reaction in the fatty acid synthesis (FAS II) elongation cycle, specifically for a branched-chain (iso) fatty acid. The substrate 13-methyl-3-hydroxy-tetradecanoyl-ACP loses water to form the trans-2-enoyl-ACP. Stoichiometry is balanced: removal of H2O from the beta-hydroxyl and alpha-hydrogen generates the trans-2,3 double bond. The product naming as 13-methyl-trans-tetradec-2-enoyl-ACP is consistent.

rxn00428.other_comments: This represents the dehalogenase reaction (dichloromethane dehalogenase, EC 4.5.1.3) where dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) is hydrolyzed to formaldehyde (HCHO) plus 2 chloride ions and 2 protons. Mass balance: left side C1H4Cl2O1, right side C1H2O1 + 2H + 2Cl = C1H4Cl2O1. Charge balance: left 0, right +2-2 = 0. Both balanced. Note the enzyme actually uses glutathione as cofactor in vivo, but the net reaction as written is balanced.

rxn01409.other_comments: This is the carnitine palmitoyltransferase (CPT) reaction transferring a palmitoyl group from palmitoyl-CoA to L-carnitine, forming palmitoylcarnitine and free CoA. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (acyl group transferred 1:1, CoA released). CPT1/CPT2 catalyze this reaction and it is physiologically reversible, though the net in vivo direction depends on cellular context (CPT1 favors palmitoylcarnitine formation for mitochondrial import, CPT2 favors regeneration of palmitoyl-CoA in the matrix).

rxn03229.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent N-methyltransferase reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to the nitrogen of (S)-tetrahydroprotoberberine, producing S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) and the cis-N-methylated tetrahydroprotoberberine product. The stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group is transferred from SAM, generating SAH and a proton. This enzyme participates in benzylisoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis.

rxn01914.other_comments: This is the steroid Delta5-Delta4-isomerase reaction (e.g., 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase activity), which catalyzes the intramolecular isomerization of the carbon-carbon double bond from the Delta5 position to the Delta4 position of 3-oxo-steroids. The reaction involves no change in molecular formula (it is an isomerization), so it is inherently mass- and charge-balanced. Conversion of the beta,gamma-unsaturated ketone to the more thermodynamically stable alpha,beta-unsaturated (conjugated) ketone drives the reaction strongly in the forward direction in vivo.

errors: Oxygen mass imbalance: a monooxygenase (CYP-type) reaction incorporates one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate (hydroxylation) and reduces the other to H2O. With one O2 (2 oxygen atoms), one O goes into p-hydroxyfelbamate and one O goes to H2O, leaving no extra oxygen, so this is balanced for oxygen. However, the equation as written shows only one H2O product, which is consistent. rxn11831.other_comments: This represents a cytochrome P450-catalyzed aromatic hydroxylation of felbamate to p-hydroxyfelbamate, a known phase I metabolic pathway. It uses NADPH and O2 as cosubstrates, incorporating one oxygen atom into the substrate and reducing the other to water (classic monooxygenase mechanism).

rxn02540.other_comments: This is an aromatic monooxygenase (toluene 2-monooxygenase type) reaction. Toluene (Toluol) is hydroxylated at the ortho position to form o-cresol. One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the product, the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Stoichiometry balances: NADPH + O2 + H+ + C7H8 -> H2O + NADP+ + C7H8O. Atom balance: C7H8 + O2 + reducing equivalents yields C7H7OH (o-cresol) + H2O, which is consistent. Charge and H balance work with H+ and NADPH/NADP+ pairing.

rxn01500.other_comments: This is the HMG-CoA reductase reaction (EC 1.1.1.34), written in the oxidative direction: mevalonate + 2 NAD+ + CoA -> HMG-CoA + 2 NADH + 2 H+. The stoichiometry is balanced for atoms and charge (mevalonate has two reducible carbons converted, releasing 2 NADH and 2 H+). However, in vivo this enzyme operates in the biosynthetic (reductive) direction, converting HMG-CoA + 2 NADPH -> mevalonate + 2 NADP+ + CoA. Note that the physiological cofactor is NADPH/NADP+, not NADH/NAD+; using NAD+ here may be a cofactor specification issue depending on the organism.

rxn06205.other_comments: This is a phosphorolysis reaction analogous to purine nucleoside phosphorylase activity. Urate-3-ribonucleoside (a riboside of urate/uric acid) is cleaved by inorganic phosphate to yield free urate (the base) and ribose 1-phosphate (the activated sugar phosphate). The stoichiometry is balanced: the N-glycosidic bond is broken and a phosphate is added to C1 of the ribose. Phosphorylase-type reactions of this kind are generally reversible in vivo, though the phosphorolytic (forward) direction is often favored physiologically depending on phosphate and product concentrations.

rxn02500.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD+-dependent oxidation of sequoyitol (5-O-methyl-myo-inositol) to a 5-O-methyl-inosose (a methylated pentahydroxycyclohexanone), producing NADH and H+. Stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of a secondary hydroxyl to a ketone removes 2 H (one to NAD+ as hydride forming NADH, one released as H+). Atoms and charges balance. As an NAD+-linked alcohol/ketone oxidoreductase (myo-inositol 2-dehydrogenase family), this type of reaction is thermodynamically reversible, though in vivo flux often favors oxidation toward catabolism depending on NAD+/NADH ratio.

errors: Atom imbalance: cardiolipin formation from two phosphatidylglycerol molecules releases glycerol but the acyl chain stoichiometry is inconsistent. Two diacyl-PG (each with 2 isopentadecanoyl chains = 4 total) should yield a tetraacyl-cardiolipin (4 chains) plus glycerol; the product 'Isopentadecanoylcardiolipin' name does not confirm 4 acyl chains, and mass/formula balance cannot be verified as written.

Phosphate balance should be checked: 2 PG contain 2 phosphate groups, cardiolipin contains 2 phosphate groups, so phosphate is conserved, but the central glycerol-phosphate accounting needs explicit formulas.
rxn10340.other_comments: This represents the cardiolipin synthase reaction in B. subtilis, where two molecules of phosphatidylglycerol condense to form cardiolipin with release of free glycerol. The general scheme (2 PG -> cardiolipin + glycerol) is the standard bacterial CLS mechanism. In vivo this is essentially irreversible toward cardiolipin synthesis. The stoichiometry of acyl chains in the named product should be verified against explicit molecular formulas.

rxn10902.other_comments: This is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) reaction, oxidizing D-glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phospho-D-glucono-1,5-lactone with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is balanced for atoms and charge: the substrate loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+, one as H+), correctly producing NADH + H+. Stoichiometry is correct. Note that most G6PDH enzymes preferentially use NADP+ rather than NAD+ (as in the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway), though some isoforms can use NAD+. In vivo this oxidation step is strongly favored in the forward direction, pulled by subsequent hydrolysis of the lactone.

rxn07415.other_comments: This reaction describes a phytase/phosphatase hydrolyzing myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (phytate, InsP6) at the 5-position, releasing one inorganic phosphate and yielding myo-inositol pentakisphosphate (InsP5). The stoichiometry is balanced: one water consumed, one phosphate released, and InsP6 is converted to InsP5. Hydrolysis of a phosphoester bond is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn04045.other_comments: This is the cobaltochelatase reaction (sirohydrochlorin cobalt-lyase, EC 4.99.1.3), catalyzed by CbiK/CbiX in the anaerobic cobalamin biosynthesis pathway. It inserts Co2+ into the tetrapyrrole macrocycle of sirohydrochlorin to form cobalt-sirohydrochlorin (cobalt-precorrin 2), releasing two protons as the two pyrrole nitrogens are deprotonated upon metal chelation. Charge and atom balance check out: Co2+ contributes 2+ charge, balanced by release of 2 H+ (net loss of 2 H from the macrocycle). In vivo the reaction proceeds toward cobalt incorporation as part of corrin ring biosynthesis.

rxn02594.other_comments: This is a phytanate-CoA ligase reaction (acyl-CoA synthetase, AMP-forming). Phytanate (3,7,11,15-tetramethylhexadecanoate) is activated to phytanoyl-CoA, a key step in phytanic acid alpha-oxidation. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + carboxylic acid -> AMP + PPi + acyl-CoA + H+. The mechanism proceeds via an acyl-AMP intermediate. Although written as reversible, in vivo the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible toward activation.

errors: Carbon imbalance: 2-Oxo-5-methyl-cis-muconate (C8H6O5 as dianion, 8 carbons) cannot yield CO2 (1 carbon) plus 2-Hydroxy-cis-hex-2,4-dienoate (6 carbons), accounting for only 7 carbons total; the substrate naming/formula does not balance with the products
The product is described as a hydroxy-dienoate (enol form) while the substrate is an oxo (keto) compound, suggesting a tautomeric/oxidation-state inconsistency that should be checked
Hydrogen and oxygen balance cannot be confirmed given the ambiguous substrate structure
rxn03675.other_comments: This is a carboxy-lyase (decarboxylase) reaction releasing CO2 from a beta-keto acid type substrate to give an enol/dienol product. Decarboxylations driven by CO2 release are essentially irreversible in vivo, so it proceeds in the forward (decarboxylation) direction. However, the stoichiometry as written appears unbalanced in carbon count.

errors: Proton imbalance: phosphoryl transfer from ADP to thymidine does not generate 2 protons; the reaction should be balanced with 1 H+ at most, and typically this phosphotransfer is proton-neutral or releases a single H+
Charge imbalance resulting from the incorrect proton count
rxn01144.other_comments: This represents thymidine kinase-like activity using ADP as the phosphoryl donor (ADP:thymidine 5'-phosphotransferase), transferring a phosphate from ADP to thymidine to yield AMP and dTMP. The core phosphoryl transfer (ADP + thymidine -> AMP + dTMP) is mass-balanced for the heavy atoms, but the stated 2.0 H+ on the product side is incorrect.

errors: Charge imbalance: trimetaphosphate (P3O9, charge -3) + H2O yields triphosphate (P3O10, charge -5) + H+, so the right side carries an extra negative charge. The reaction should produce 2 H+ to balance both mass and charge: H2O + Trimetaphosphate -> 2 H+ + Triphosphate
rxn01813.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic ring-opening of cyclic trimetaphosphate (a cyclic triphosphate) to linear triphosphate (tripolyphosphate). Mass for P and O can balance with appropriate protonation states, but as written the proton/charge accounting is off (only one H+ shown). Hydrolysis of the high-energy P-O-P ring is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn06710.other_comments: This is the isoprenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase (ICMT) reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to the C-terminal carboxyl of a prenylated (farnesylated) cysteine on a substrate protein, producing the methyl ester and SAH. Stoichiometry is balanced: methyl transfer from SAM to the cysteine carboxyl group, converting SAM to SAH. Charges/atoms balance with one methyl group transferred.

errors: Charge imbalance: the production of H+ on the right side suggests a proton imbalance unless the substrate/product protonation states are not properly accounted for. For a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase hydroxylation, the typical balanced reaction is: 2-oxoglutarate + O2 + substrate -> succinate + CO2 + hydroxylated-substrate, with no free H+ released. The extra H+ likely reflects an imbalance, though this depends on the assumed protonation states of the carboxylate/amine groups.
rxn04966.other_comments: This is the IDS3 (or equivalent Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase) reaction converting 2'-deoxymugineic acid (DMA) to mugineic acid by hydroxylation, a key step in phytosiderophore biosynthesis in graminaceous plants. 2-Oxoglutarate is decarboxylated to succinate plus CO2 while O2 is consumed and one oxygen atom is incorporated as a hydroxyl group on the substrate. The stoichiometry of cosubstrates (O2, 2-OG -> succinate + CO2) is correct.

rxn04992.other_comments: This is ACC oxidase (1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate oxidase), the final enzyme in plant ethylene biosynthesis. It oxidizes ACC using O2 and ascorbate as a cofactor/reductant to produce ethylene, CO2, HCN (cyanide), and water, with ascorbate oxidized to dehydroascorbate. Checking stoichiometry: Reactants: O2 (O2) + ascorbate (C6H8O6) + ACC (C4H7NO2). Products: 2 H2O + CO2 + HCN + dehydroascorbate (C6H6O6) + ethylene (C2H4). Carbon: ACC has 4 C = 1(CO2)+1(HCN)+2(ethylene)=4, balanced. Nitrogen: 1 = HCN, balanced. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, committing to ethylene production.

rxn13193.other_comments: This is a simple transport reaction moving 2-methylpropanal (isobutyraldehyde) across a membrane between two compartments (e.g., extracellular and cytosol). The same metabolite appears on both sides, which is stoichiometrically balanced (1:1). Passive diffusion of a small uncharged aldehyde is expected to be reversible, driven by the concentration gradient.

errors: The proton stoichiometry is incorrect; a simple acyl transfer from ACP to CoA does not consume 2 H+. The reaction should be charge- and mass-balanced without added protons (typically 0 H+).
The product 'fa4coa' is ambiguous/likely incorrect; the product should be 12-methyltetradecanoyl-CoA (anteiso-C15 acyl-CoA), not an unspecified 'fa4coa'.
rxn05451.other_comments: This reaction represents an acyltransfer where a 12-methyltetradecanoyl (anteiso-pentadecanoyl) group is transferred from ACP to CoA, releasing free ACP and forming the corresponding acyl-CoA. Aside from the proton imbalance and the questionable acyl-CoA identifier, the core acyl-ACP + CoA <=> acyl-CoA + ACP transfer is chemically reasonable and thermodynamically near-equilibrium, hence reversible.

errors: This reaction is not elementally balanced. Stemmadenine (C21H26N2O3) cannot be converted to Catharanthine (C21H24N2O2) by simple loss of one H2O. Loss of H2O from C21H26N2O3 would give C21H24N2O2, but the proton (H+) on the right side leaves the hydrogen count unbalanced: left has 26 H, right has 24 (Catharanthine) + 2 (H2O) + 1 (H+) = 27 H. There is a hydrogen and charge imbalance.

The biosynthetic conversion of stemmadenine to catharanthine is not a simple single-step dehydration; it proceeds through reactive intermediates (e.g., dehydrosecodine) and requires multiple enzymatic steps including oxidation/reduction and cyclization, so this lumped reaction misrepresents the chemistry.
rxn04085.other_comments: The reaction represents the conversion of the monoterpene indole alkaloid stemmadenine to catharanthine with release of water. As written it is a dehydrative/cyclization conversion. In vivo, alkaloid biosynthesis flows toward the more complex product catharanthine, so the forward direction is biologically favored, though the true pathway involves several enzymatic steps and intermediates.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: oxidation of a chalcone to an aurone (Bracteatin) via this type of oxidase reaction typically consumes O2 and yields H2O2, not H2O, or yields 2 H2O with appropriate H/electron balance; as written the H and O atoms do not balance

Substrate-product mismatch: Eriodictyol chalcone is the 2',3,4,4',6'-pentahydroxychalcone (B-ring 3,4-dihydroxy), but Bracteatin is a 6,7,3',4'-tetrahydroxyaurone bearing an extra hydroxyl, implying an additional hydroxylation not accounted for by the single O2/H2O stoichiometry

Enzyme name implies a single oxidative cyclization (aureusidin synthase type), but the named substrate and the polyhydroxylated aurone product require additional oxygen incorporation/hydroxylation steps
rxn07795.other_comments: This represents an aurone synthase (polyphenol oxidase/aureusidin synthase-like) reaction converting a 2'-hydroxychalcone to an aurone using molecular oxygen. Such oxidative cyclizations are physiologically irreversible (forward). However, the stoichiometry as written is unbalanced and the substrate-to-product hydroxylation pattern is inconsistent.

errors: The H+ on the substrate side is incorrect; this glucosyltransferase reaction does not consume a proton. In fact, the glycosylation of the 3-hydroxyl typically releases a proton, so if any H+ appears it should be on the product side. The balanced reaction is simply UDP-glucose + Anthocyanidin <=> UDP + Anthocyanidin-3-O-glucoside (with a proton released to balance the charge change from UDP-glucose to UDP).
rxn06487.other_comments: This is the UDP-glucose:anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosyltransferase (UFGT, EC 2.4.1.115) reaction transferring glucose from UDP-glucose to the 3-OH of an anthocyanidin to form the anthocyanin glucoside. Biosynthetically it proceeds in the forward (glucoside-forming) direction.

rxn08935.other_comments: This is a hydrolysis reaction catalyzed by maltodextrin glucosidase (MalZ, EC 3.2.1.20-like activity). Maltohexaose (a linear alpha-1,4-linked glucose hexamer) is hydrolyzed by the addition of one water molecule to release one D-glucose from the reducing/non-reducing end, yielding maltopentaose (a glucose pentamer). Stoichiometry is balanced: 6 glucose units (maltohexaose) = 1 free glucose + 5 glucose units (maltopentaose), and one water is consumed to cleave one glycosidic bond.

rxn06610.other_comments: This is a phosphatase (phosphohydrolase) reaction where 2-Acyl-1-alkyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphate (an alkyl-acyl analog of phosphatidic acid) is hydrolyzed by water to release inorganic phosphate and 1-alkyl-2-acylglycerol (an ether-linked diacylglycerol analog). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the phosphate monoester bond is cleaved, transferring the phosphate group to water. This is part of the ether lipid (plasmalogen/PAF) biosynthetic pathway, analogous to phosphatidic acid phosphatase.

rxn04617.other_comments: This reaction describes a glycosyltransferase (anthocyanin 3-O-glucoside-6''-O-rhamnosyltransferase, EC 2.4.1.159) transferring an L-rhamnosyl group from UDP-L-rhamnose to the glucose moiety of pelargonidin 3-glucoside, forming pelargonidin 3-O-rutinoside (3-O-rhamnosylglucoside) and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one rhamnose unit is transferred and UDP is liberated. Glycosyltransferases using activated UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically driven toward transfer/product formation in vivo.

errors: Product should be 3-dehydroquinate (3-dehydroquinate), not 5-dehydroquinate; the enzyme L-quinate:NAD+ 3-oxidoreductase (quinate dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.24) oxidizes the C3 hydroxyl, yielding 3-dehydroquinate
rxn01363.other_comments: This is quinate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.24), oxidizing quinate at the C3 position with NAD+ to give a dehydroquinate plus NADH and H+. Stoichiometry and proton/hydride balance are correct; the only issue is the naming of the oxidized product (should be 3-dehydroquinate per the enzyme name). The reaction is generally considered reversible, though in the shikimate/quinate catabolic context it tends to run in the oxidative (forward) direction.

rxn02549.other_comments: This reaction represents an alcohol dehydrogenase (oxidoreductase) acting on allyl alcohol (2-propen-1-ol) oxidizing it to acrolein (propenal/2-propenal) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The atoms balance: allyl alcohol (C3H6O) loses 2H (as hydride to NADPH and a proton) to form acrolein (C3H4O). Charges and stoichiometry are consistent. Note 'NADP' should formally be NADP+ as written.

rxn02326.other_comments: This reaction is the spontaneous/enzymatic intramolecular cyclodehydration of 2-oxo-5-aminovalerate (2-oxo-5-aminopentanoate) to form 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate, releasing one molecule of water. The amino group condenses with the 2-oxo (keto) carbon to form the cyclic Schiff base. Atom and charge balance check out: C5H9NO3 yields C5H7NO2 + H2O, with the H+ accounting for protonation state differences. The reaction is the reverse of the hydrolytic ring opening and is generally treated as reversible (spontaneous cyclization, equilibrium favors the cyclic imine but ring opening occurs readily).

rxn02054.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent N-methyltransferase reaction transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to the nitrogen of pyridine, producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) and N-methylpyridinium. The atom balance is consistent: SAM donates a CH3 group, converting pyridine (C5H5N) to N-methylpyridinium (C6H8N+), with SAM becoming SAH. The reaction carries a positive charge on the product side from the quaternary pyridinium nitrogen, which should be balanced by the loss of a positive group as the methyl is transferred (SAM is also cationic), so charge is conserved.

rxn10775.other_comments: This is the MurF-type ligase reaction adding the dipeptide D-Ala-D-Ala to UDP-N-glycolylmuramoyl-tripeptide (the glycolyl variant, characteristic of mycobacterial peptidoglycan). ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi to drive amide bond formation. Stoichiometry is balanced: the ATP-dependent ligation releases ADP, inorganic phosphate, and one proton, consistent with the standard amino acid/peptide ligase mechanism. The substrate 'Ala-Ala' is interpreted as D-Ala-D-Ala, which is the physiological substrate.

errors: Charge imbalance: with NADPH(2-), H+, methylmalonyl-CoA, the proton count needs verification; the product side as written (NADP, CoA, CO2) does not balance protons/charges with 3 H+ consumed

Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: the elongation adds a methylmalonyl-derived 2-carbon unit plus a methyl branch (net +C3 after decarboxylation), so penta-methyl hexacosanoate (C26+5 methyl) to hexa-methyl octacosanoate (C28+6 methyl) is consistent in carbon, but H2O production should be checked (typically Claisen condensation releases CoA and CO2, not H2O directly)
NADP should be written as NADP+ to reflect correct charge
rxn10702.other_comments: This represents a fatty acid synthase/polyketide-type elongation: a methylmalonyl-CoA extender unit condenses with a methyl-branched fatty acid (penta-methyl hexacosanoate) and is reduced by 2 NADPH to form a longer methyl-branched product (hexa-methyl octacosanoate), releasing CoA and CO2. This is characteristic of mycocerosic/phthioceranic acid biosynthesis in mycobacteria.

rxn04430.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase (COMT-type) reaction. The substrate 5-hydroxyconiferaldehyde is methylated at the 5-hydroxyl position to form sinapaldehyde, with SAM converted to SAH and release of a proton. Atom balance: SAM donates a methyl group to the hydroxyl, producing SAH (loss of CH3) and the methylated product. The reaction is mass and charge balanced, including the H+ released. Note that the listed enzyme name (3,4-dihydroxy-trans-cinnamate / caffeate O-methyltransferase) reflects the broad COMT specificity, which also acts on 5-hydroxyconiferaldehyde in lignin biosynthesis.

rxn00041.other_comments: Lecanoric acid is a depside formed from two orsellinic acid (orsellinate) units linked by an ester bond. Hydrolysis of this single ester bond with one water molecule yields two orsellinate molecules, releasing one proton. The mass and charge balance: lecanoric acid (C16H14O7) + H2O (H2O) yields 2 orsellinate (each C8H7O3-, total C16H14O6) + H+. Carbon and oxygen balance correctly (16 C, and oxygen: 7+1=8 = 6+2). Hydrogen: 14+2=16 = 14+1+1. Charge balances (0 = -2+1... ). Note: if orsellinate is the carboxylate anion, two anions carry -2 charge, requiring 2 H+ for balance; with one H+ the charge may not fully balance depending on protonation states. Hydrolases typically act in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn08313.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolytic deamination of dATP (2'-deoxyadenosine triphosphate) to dITP (2'-deoxyinosine triphosphate), releasing ammonia. The adenine base is converted to hypoxanthine via deamination, replacing the C6 amino group with a carbonyl (after tautomerization). Mass and charge balance: dATP (C10H12N5O12P3, charge -4 typically) + H2O + H+ -> dITP (C10H11N4O12P3) + NH3. The amine nitrogen leaves as NH3 while the oxygen from water is incorporated into the hypoxanthine carbonyl. This is a spontaneous, irreversible hydrolytic deamination reaction proceeding strongly in the forward direction in vivo.

errors: Mass imbalance: gallate (C7H4O5, as dianion at physiological pH) plus O2 yields 4-oxalomesaconate which has formula C6H4O7 - one carbon is unaccounted for. Gallate (gallic acid, C7H6O5) has 7 carbons while 4-oxalomesaconate has only 6 carbons, so the reaction loses one carbon without a corresponding product (e.g., CO2 or formate is missing).
Charge/proton imbalance likely as written; if gallate enters as the carboxylate anion, the H+ stoichiometry on the right does not balance correctly given the carbon discrepancy.
Oxygen atom balance must be re-checked: ring-cleavage dioxygenases incorporate both atoms of O2, but with the missing carbon the overall O balance cannot be verified.
rxn12706.other_comments: This represents gallate ring cleavage by gallate dioxygenase (a ring-cleaving extradiol-type dioxygenase) producing 4-oxalomesaconate. Such O2-dependent dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo (forward direction). However, the stoichiometry as written appears unbalanced - gallate has 7 carbons but the product 4-oxalomesaconate has 6 carbons. Typically the product of gallate 4,5-dioxygenase is 4-oxalomesaconate (often noted as 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate precursor / 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde), and care must be taken with which isomer/formula is used.

rxn13551.other_comments: This represents a phosphatase reaction hydrolyzing a phosphate group from a trehalose-monomycolate-phosphate intermediate (related to mycobacterial cell wall/trehalose mycolate biosynthesis). The reaction consumes water and a phosphorylated substrate, releasing inorganic phosphate, a proton, and the dephosphorylated trehalose-monomycolate. Stoichiometrically, the hydrolysis of a phosphomonoester yields phosphate + H+, which is balanced as written. Phosphatase-catalyzed hydrolysis reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo and proceed in the dephosphorylation (forward) direction.

errors: The reaction as written may be charge-imbalanced; the H+ on the left side appears spurious for a simple hydrolytic ring-opening. The hydrolysis of the cyclic imine (1-pyrroline-4-hydroxy-2-carboxylate) to the open-chain amino-oxo acid requires only H2O, not an additional proton.
rxn03073.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic ring-opening of 1-pyrroline-4-hydroxy-2-carboxylate, a cyclic Schiff base/imine, to yield 2-oxo-4-hydroxy-5-aminovalerate (an open-chain compound with a ketone and primary amine). This step occurs in trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline degradation (catalyzed by 1-pyrroline-4-hydroxy-2-carboxylate deaminase/hydrolase). The imine hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and typically driven forward in vivo as part of the catabolic pathway.

errors: Stoichiometric/identity issue: this reaction as written equates sedoheptulose-7-phosphate (a ketose, D-altro-heptulose-7-phosphate) with D-glycero-D-manno-heptose-7-phosphate (an aldose). The enzyme name describes an aldose-ketose isomerase (GmhA, sedoheptulose 7-phosphate isomerase), which is a valid isomerization, so atoms (C7H15O10P) balance.
Naming inconsistency: product should more precisely be D-glycero-D-manno-heptose-7-phosphate; some databases specify D-glycero-D-altro-heptose, so the stereochemical designation should be verified.
rxn03917.other_comments: This is the GmhA-catalyzed first committed step of the ADP-L-glycero-beta-D-manno-heptose (heptose/LPS inner core) biosynthesis pathway, isomerizing the ketose sedoheptulose-7-phosphate to the aldose D-glycero-D-manno-heptose-7-phosphate. The conversion is an aldose-ketose isomerization, atom-balanced. Although chemically reversible, in vivo it is pulled forward toward heptose biosynthesis.

errors: Hydrogen/proton imbalance: oxidation of a dihydro compound to its dehydro form releases 2 H (as NADPH gets 1 H and 1 H+ released), so the product side should have only 1 H+, not 2.0 H+
Charge imbalance resulting from incorrect proton count
rxn02784.other_comments: This reaction interconverts 2'-hydroxy-2,3-dihydrodaidzein and 2'-hydroxydaidzein via an NADP+/NADPH couple. The enzyme name (2-oxidoreductase) describes oxidation of the dihydro substrate, but in vivo in isoflavonoid biosynthesis (e.g., daidzein -> dihydrodaidzein), the NADPH-dependent reductase activity dominates, favoring reduction of the dehydro compound, i.e., the reverse of the written direction.

errors: Carbon imbalance: 3-O-methylgallate (C8H8O5) plus O2 yields methanol (CH4O) plus 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate (C7H4O6 as protonated form / C7H2O6 with H+), but methanol release is not consistent with this enzyme - the actual reaction does not produce methanol
The standard 3-O-methylgallate ring cleavage by the dioxygenase produces 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate while retaining the methyl group as a methyl ester, not releasing methanol; check products
Likely hydrogen/proton imbalance depending on protonation states of substrate and product
rxn02983.other_comments: This represents an extradiol-type ring-cleavage dioxygenase acting on the lignin-derived aromatic 3-O-methylgallate, incorporating O2 and opening the aromatic ring to form 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate (PDC), part of the protocatechuate/gallate catabolic pathway. Dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Mass/redox imbalance: conversion of 2-dehydro-D-gluconate (open-chain acid) to the corresponding 1,5-lactone is a lactonization (dehydration), but the listed reactants do not balance. A lactonohydrolase reaction should be: lactone + H2O <=> acid + H+. As written, the acid plus H+ giving lactone plus H2O has the H+ on the wrong side, since lactone formation releases the proton consumed in opening, not consumes it. The proton balance is incorrect for the direction shown.
rxn01922.other_comments: This corresponds to a gluconolactonase/lactonohydrolase-type reaction (R02659), interconverting 2-dehydro-D-glucono-1,5-lactone and 2-dehydro-D-gluconate via hydrolysis/lactonization. In vivo, hydrolysis of the lactone (lactone + H2O -> acid) is typically favored, but the reaction is chemically reversible. The atoms (C, O) balance for a simple lactonization/hydrolysis, but the placement of H+ relative to H2O appears inconsistent with the direction as written.

rxn06366.other_comments: This is the PI3-kinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.137), transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the 3-hydroxyl of the inositol ring of phosphatidylinositol, producing PI(3)P, ADP, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: phosphate transfer from ATP yields ADP plus the phosphorylated lipid, and the released proton is consistent with kinase reactions at physiological pH.

rxn00160.other_comments: This is the NAD-dependent D-malic enzyme (D-malate dehydrogenase, decarboxylating; EC 1.1.1.83). D-Malate (C4H5O5 as dianion) is oxidized and decarboxylated to pyruvate, releasing CO2 and reducing NAD+ to NADH. The reaction as written is mass and charge balanced: D-Malate yields pyruvate + CO2 with transfer of a hydride to NAD+. In vivo, oxidative decarboxylation reactions of this type are essentially irreversible in the forward (decarboxylating) direction due to loss of CO2.

rxn00548.other_comments: This is the phosphoketolase reaction (EC 4.1.2.22). Fructose-6-phosphate is cleaved by inorganic phosphate to yield erythrose-4-phosphate and acetyl phosphate, with release of water. Stoichiometry balances: C6H11O9P (F6P) + Pi (HO4P) gives acetyl phosphate (C2H4O5P) + erythrose-4-phosphate (C4H7O7P) + H2O. Carbon (6=2+4), phosphorus (2=1+1), and overall mass balance check out. In vivo this enzyme functions in the catabolic direction (phosphoketolase pathway/bifid shunt), so it proceeds toward acetyl phosphate formation.

errors: The reaction as written is unbalanced and mislabeled. The named enzyme (5-formyltetrahydrofolate cyclo-ligase, EC 6.3.3.2) catalyzes the ATP-dependent conversion of 5-formyltetrahydrofolate to 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate, NOT the conversion between 5-formyl and 10-formyl species shown here.
The actual product should be 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate (releasing ADP + Pi), not 10-formyltetrahydrofolate.

rxn07516.other_comments: This represents an oxidative ring-cleavage (dioxygenase-type) reaction in which molecular O2 cleaves the catechol-like 1,2-dihydroxy ring of anthracene, opening one aromatic ring to yield a naphthalene bearing a carboxyvinyl and a carboxylic acid group. rxn05043.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase (SULT2A1-type) reaction transferring a sulfo group from PAPS to the 7-hydroxyl of glycochenodeoxycholate, producing the 7-sulfate conjugate and PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate). rxn01395.other_comments: This is the oxalyl-CoA decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.8), converting oxalyl-CoA to formyl-CoA plus CO2, consuming a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: oxalyl-CoA (C2 dicarbonyl-CoA) loses one carbon as CO2 to form formyl-CoA (C1-CoA), with a proton consumed to balance charge/mass. rxn09963.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing heptadecanal (C17 aldehyde) to heptadecanoate (C17:0 fatty acid), using NAD+ as the electron acceptor and water as the source of the added oxygen. Stoichiometry is balanced: C17H34O (heptadecanal) + H2O provides the atoms for C17H33O2- (heptadecanoate) with release of NADH and 2 H+. Charge balances (NAD+ on left, NADH + 2H+ on left side total +1, carboxylate -1 + NADH on right side total reconciles).

rxn01597.other_comments: This is cyclohexanol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.245). Hexalin is a synonym for cyclohexanol. The reaction reduces cyclohexanone to cyclohexanol using NADH/H+, regenerating NAD+. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH + H+ + cyclohexanone (C6H10O) <=> NAD+ + cyclohexanol (C6H12O). The hydride from NADH plus the proton account for the two hydrogens added to the carbonyl. The enzyme name (cyclohexanol:NAD+ oxidoreductase) is written in the oxidation direction, but the written reaction is the reduction direction; both are valid as the enzyme is reversible.

rxn01020.other_comments: This is putrescine carbamoyltransferase (EC 2.1.3.6), transferring the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to putrescine, yielding N-carbamoylputrescine and phosphate. Atom and charge balance check: putrescine (C4H14N2, 2+) + carbamoyl phosphate (CH2NO5P, 2-) -> N-carbamoylputrescine (C5H14N3O, 1+) + phosphate (HPO4, 2-) + H+. Carbon: 4+1=5; nitrogen: 2+1=3; the mass/charge balance is consistent. The enzyme is part of the agmatine deiminase / putrescine fermentation pathway and physiologically operates in the reverse direction (phosphorolysis of N-carbamoylputrescine to generate carbamoyl phosphate and putrescine, feeding ATP synthesis via carbamate kinase), but it is biochemically reversible.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass/atom balanced. Adding H2O across a C=C double bond (hydration of the methylene group) would yield a hydroxymethyl-bearing succinyl-CoA, but the substrate is named 'Naphthyl-2-methylene-succinyl-CoA' and the product 'Naphthyl-2-hydroxymethyl-succinyl CoA'; hydration of the exocyclic methylene (=CH2) gives -CH2OH, which is consistent atom-wise, but the carbon/hydrogen count must be verified. rxn04715.other_comments: This appears to be an enoyl-CoA hydratase-type reaction (KEGG R06906) involving hydration of a methylene/double bond on a naphthyl-substituted succinyl-CoA intermediate, likely from PAH (naphthalene) degradation pathways. Such hydratase reactions are typically reversible in vivo, though metabolic flux often drives them in the hydration (forward) direction.

rxn03427.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of leukotriene D4 (LTD4) to leukotriene E4 (LTE4) by membrane dipeptidase (gamma-glutamyl leukotrienase / dipeptidase), removing the terminal glycine residue from the cysteinylglycine portion of the molecule. LTD4 has a cysteinyl-glycine dipeptide attached; cleavage of the peptide bond with water releases free glycine and yields LTE4, which contains only cysteine. The reaction is correctly balanced: H2O + LTD4 yields glycine + LTE4. In vivo, this is a hydrolytic, essentially irreversible step in the leukotriene metabolic/degradation pathway, proceeding in the forward direction toward LTE4.

rxn09996.other_comments: This represents biosynthesis of teichuronic acid, a bacterial cell wall polymer of repeating GlcA-GalNAc units, polymerized 45 times from the activated sugar donors UDP-glucuronate and UDP-GalNAc. rxn11646.other_comments: This reaction represents the glucosyltransferase-catalyzed transfer of glucose from UDP-glucose to the phenolic/aliphatic hydroxyl of tyrosol (4-hydroxyphenylethanol), yielding salidroside (tyrosol 8-O-beta-D-glucoside) and UDP. Tyrosol has the formula C8H10O2 and salidroside C14H20O7, with UDP-glucose (C15H24N2O17P2) donating a glucosyl unit (C6H10O5) and releasing UDP (C9H14N2O12P2). The atom balance is consistent: C15H24N2O17P2 + C8H10O2 = C9H14N2O12P2 + C14H20O7. A proton balance check holds as written. Note: the enzyme name specifies 1-O-glucosylation; salidroside is the 8-O-beta-D-glucoside of tyrosol, so the transfer is to the aliphatic hydroxyl. [directionality_note] UDP-sugar dependent glycosyltransferases are thermodynamically driven toward glycoside formation in vivo due to the energy of the UDP-sugar bond.

rxn03314.other_comments: This is the 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase reaction acting on 3alpha-hydroxy-5beta-pregnan-20-one (a pregnane steroid). The 3alpha-hydroxyl group is oxidized to a 3-keto group, yielding 5beta-pregnane-3,20-dione, with NAD+ reduced to NADH + H+. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge: the hydroxyl oxidation releases 2 [H], one going to NAD+ to form NADH and one as the released proton. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn03674.other_comments: This is the methylmalonyl-CoA decarboxylase reaction, converting (S)-methylmalonyl-CoA to propionyl-CoA with release of CO2. The reaction consumes a proton and releases CO2, which is balanced in terms of carbon, hydrogen, and charge. In vivo, decarboxylation reactions are strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible, proceeding in the decarboxylation (forward) direction. Note that in mammalian propionate metabolism, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase typically converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA; the decarboxylase here is a distinct enzyme (often a sodium-pumping decarboxylase in anaerobes) coupling decarboxylation to ion transport.

rxn12747.other_comments: This represents the hydroxylation of nicotinic acid (niacin) at the 6-position to form 6-hydroxynicotinate, a step in anaerobic/aerobic nicotinate degradation. rxn11729.other_comments: This is the threonine aldolase / D-threonine aldolase reaction (EC 4.1.2.42 for D-threonine, related to EC 4.1.2.5). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced for C, H, N, and O. Aldol cleavage reactions of this type are typically reversible, and the enzyme can catalyze both the retro-aldol cleavage and the aldol condensation depending on substrate availability.

rxn07876.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing (R)-citronellal to citronellate. rxn04699.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction. p-Ethylphenol (4-ethylphenol) is hydroxylated at the benzylic carbon of the ethyl group to form 1-(4'-hydroxyphenyl)ethanol. rxn02695.other_comments: This is a glucan 1,4-beta-glucosidase (1,4-beta-D-glucan glucohydrolase) reaction. It hydrolyzes the terminal glycosidic bond of cellotetraose (a beta-1,4-linked glucose tetramer) using water, releasing one D-glucose unit and leaving cellotriose. The stoichiometry is balanced: cellotetraose (4 glucose units) + H2O yields 1 glucose + cellotriose (3 glucose units). As a hydrolysis reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn00265.other_comments: This is citrate lyase (citrate oxaloacetate-lyase, forming acetate), which cleaves citrate into acetate and oxaloacetate. In vivo (e.g., in fermentative bacteria), the reaction proceeds in the direction of citrate cleavage toward acetate and oxaloacetate.

rxn03633.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction. rxn00894.other_comments: This represents the oxidation of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine to N-acetyl-D-glucosaminate (the lactone/acid at the anomeric C1) catalyzed by an oxidase using O2, producing H2O2. rxn07692.other_comments: This is a thioester hydrolysis reaction. Thioester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable due to the high free energy of the thioester bond.

rxn06713.other_comments: This is the glucohydrolase reaction (EC 3.2.1.107) that hydrolyzes the terminal alpha-D-glucose from the disaccharide attached to hydroxylysine in collagen, releasing free D-glucose and leaving the protein-beta-D-galactosyl-L-hydroxylysine. rxn00768.other_comments: This is the glycerol dehydratase reaction (EC 4.2.1.30), a B12-dependent enzyme that converts glycerol to 3-hydroxypropanal (3-hydroxypropionaldehyde, also called reuterin) with release of water. The reaction is mass-balanced: glycerol (C3H8O3) yields H2O plus 3-hydroxypropanal (C3H6O2). rxn03034.other_comments: This is the homoaconitase (homoisocitrate hydro-lyase) reaction in the alpha-aminoadipate (AAA) pathway of lysine biosynthesis. Like the analogous aconitase reaction, this lyase/hydratase is thermodynamically reversible. In the biosynthetic direction of the AAA pathway, the net flux proceeds toward homoisocitrate (hydration), i.e., effectively the reverse of how written.

rxn03428.other_comments: This reaction represents the isomerization of prostaglandin A2 (PGA2) to prostaglandin C2 (PGC2), corresponding to KEGG R05056. PGA2 has a delta-10,11 double bond in the cyclopentenone ring, and the conjugated double bond shifts to form PGC2 (delta-11,12), a step in the non-enzymatic or albumin-catalyzed conversion of PGA2 toward PGB2. rxn09083.other_comments: This is a phosphoethanolamine transferase (EptA-type) reaction. rxn08074.other_comments: This is a glycosidase (beta-1,4-N-acetylglucosaminidase) reaction that hydrolyzes the bond between an anhydro-N-acetylmuramyl-tripeptide and N-acetylglucosamine, releasing free GlcNAc and the 1,6-anhydro-MurNAc-tripeptide. rxn04537.other_comments: This refers to a step in tetracenomycin (anthracycline-type aromatic polyketide) biosynthesis, converting Tcm F2 to Tcm F1 (M). However, the stoichiometry shown (loss of CO, consumption of 2 H+) appears incorrect and unbalanced.

rxn12617.other_comments: This is intended to represent the import of D-glucosamine 6-phosphate coupled to a proton via symport across the membrane. Symport import driven by the proton motive force is typically modeled as net forward (uptake), though transporters can be reversible depending on gradients.

The stoichiometry of ATP hydrolysis (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) is balanced and correct.

Primary active transport of toluene by an ABC-type transporter is biochemically unusual; toluene is a small hydrophobic molecule that typically diffuses passively across membranes rather than requiring ATP-driven import

The ATP hydrolysis half is correctly balanced. The toluene on both sides reflects translocation between compartments. rxn02442.other_comments: This reaction represents allene oxide cyclase (AOC) activity, converting 12,13(S)-EOT (12,13(S)-epoxyoctadecatrienoic acid, an allene oxide) into 12-OPDA (12-oxo-phytodienoic acid) in the jasmonate biosynthesis pathway. The allene oxide intermediate is highly unstable and the cyclization to the stable cyclopentenone (12-OPDA) is thermodynamically strongly favored, making it physiologically unidirectional in the forward direction.

Zymosterol is a downstream cholesterol biosynthesis intermediate, while cycloartenol is a plant/fungal sterol precursor; they are not directly interconverted in a single step.

Mass balance is superficially close (C30H50O vs C27H44O + C3H6) but the actual biochemistry requires opening of the cyclopropane ring, three oxidative demethylations releasing CO2/formate, and loss of methyl groups as CO2, not propene.
Propene is not a recognized biological product of sterol metabolism.
rxn02672.other_comments: The input describes a proposed conversion of cycloartenol to zymosterol plus propene. While carbon/hydrogen counts approximately balance on paper, this is not a real biochemical transformation. Sterol side-chain and ring modifications occur via cytochrome P450-mediated oxidative demethylations releasing CO2, not via elimination of propene as a leaving group.

rxn11722.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of docosenoyl-CoA (the CoA thioester of erucic acid, a C22:1 fatty acid) by a thioesterase, yielding free erucic acid (cis-13-docosenoic acid) and coenzyme A. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the thioester bond is cleaved by water, releasing CoA-SH, the carboxylic acid, and a proton. Docosenoyl-CoA and erucic acid share the same C22:1 acyl group.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction as written produces 2 NADPH but only 1 H+ per NADP should be balanced; tetrahydrobiopterin to biopterin (dihydrobiopterin oxidation removes only 2 electrons/2 H, so it should involve 1 NADP/NADPH, not 2)
Charge and hydrogen imbalance: oxidation of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) to dihydrobiopterin removes 2 H (1 hydride + 1 proton), consistent with a single NADP+/NADPH pair, not two

Product 'Biopterin' is likely fully oxidized; conversion of tetrahydrobiopterin to fully oxidized biopterin would require removal of 4 H (2 electron pairs), which would justify 2 NADPH but then would need 2 H+ which is shown - however BH4 -> biopterin via dihydrobiopterin intermediate; the direct single-step reaction is biochemically questionable
rxn01323.other_comments: This describes oxidation of 5,6,7,8-tetrahydrobiopterin to biopterin coupled to reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. In vivo, the physiologically relevant direction is reduction of dihydrobiopterin to tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4 regeneration via dihydropteridine/dihydrofolate reductase using NADPH), so the listed direction (BH4 oxidation) runs opposite to the typical biological flux.

rxn00854.other_comments: This is putrescine N-methyltransferase (PMT, EC 2.1.1.53), the first committed step in nicotine and tropane alkaloid biosynthesis. SAM transfers a methyl group to one of the primary amines of putrescine, producing N-methylputrescine and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. The H+ is released because the methylated secondary amine has a different protonation state; the atom and charge balance are consistent (a methyl group is transferred and one proton is released).

rxn02062.other_comments: This reaction represents the squalene synthase (farnesyl-diphosphate farnesyltransferase) second half-reaction, where presqualene diphosphate is reduced by NADPH to form squalene (Supraene is a synonym for squalene), releasing inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi). The atoms balance: presqualene diphosphate (C30) is converted to squalene (C30H50) with loss of diphosphate and reduction by NADPH/H+. Note that a proton (H+) is typically required for full charge/mass balance.

rxn01126.other_comments: This is the ammonia-lyase reaction on 2-amino-2-deoxy-D-gluconate (D-glucosaminate). The enzyme catalyzes deamination/dehydration: glucosaminate yields 2-keto-3-deoxygluconate (2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-gluconate) plus ammonia. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (C6H13NO6 -> NH3 + C6H10O6); an amino group is eliminated as ammonia with loss of water-equivalent forming the 2-keto-3-deoxy product. As an ammonia-lyase elimination, it strongly favors the forward direction in vivo.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: oxidation of mercaptopurine (C5H4N4S) to 6-thiourate requires addition of two oxygen atoms; the proposed stoichiometry with 2 H2O + 2 O2 -> 2 H2O2 does not balance. Xanthine oxidase reactions typically proceed as: substrate + H2O + O2 -> product + H2O2, with two such steps for double hydroxylation. The given coefficients do not produce a balanced equation (H and O counts mismatch).
rxn11763.other_comments: This represents the xanthine oxidase-catalyzed oxidation of mercaptopurine (6-mercaptopurine) to 6-thiouric acid, analogous to hypoxanthine -> xanthine -> uric acid. Two hydroxylation steps at C2 and C8 introduce oxygens, with O2 as electron acceptor producing H2O2. The reaction direction is correct (oxidation toward thiouric acid is essentially irreversible in vivo).

errors: Stoichiometric/atom-balance inconsistency: the product GDP-4-dehydro-D-rhamnose (GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose) is not a correct epimeric/oxidation counterpart of GDP-L-fucose for this single-step reaction; the enzyme described (GDP-L-fucose synthase / GFS, also called FX protein) catalyzes the conversion involving GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose and GDP-L-fucose with NADPH as cofactor
The reaction as written reverses the physiological direction: GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose is reduced (NADPH-dependent) to GDP-L-fucose, not GDP-L-fucose oxidized to GDP-4-keto-D-rhamnose
The product name '4-dehydro-D-rhamnose' is incorrect/ambiguous; the actual intermediate is GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose
rxn03962.other_comments: This is the GDP-L-fucose synthase (epimerase/reductase, GFS/FX) reaction. In vivo it runs as a reduction: GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose + NADPH + H+ -> GDP-L-fucose + NADP+. As written (oxidation of GDP-L-fucose to GDP-4-keto sugar) it represents the reverse direction, and the named product appears mislabeled.

rxn01847.other_comments: This reaction is the oxidation of meso-tartrate (meso-tartaric acid) at a secondary alcohol group to form oxaloglycolate (dihydroxyfumarate/oxaloglycolate, the keto form), coupled to reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Stoichiometry is balanced: meso-tartrate (C4H6O6) loses 2H (2 electrons + 2 protons) to give oxaloglycolate (C4H4O6), with one hydride transferred to NAD+ forming NADH and one H+ released. Both mass and charge balance. NAD-dependent dehydrogenases of this type are thermodynamically reversible, though the in vivo direction (oxidation of meso-tartrate) depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio.

rxn00812.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of D-galactose at C1 by galactose dehydrogenase (NADP+ dependent), producing D-galactono-1,5-lactone (which is the 1,5-lactone / delta-lactone form, sometimes also written as 1,4-lactone depending on the enzyme). The stoichiometry is balanced: galactose (C6H12O6) loses two H (as hydride to NADP+ giving NADPH plus a released H+), yielding the lactone (C6H10O6). Carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and charge are balanced. NADP/NADPH abbreviations are acceptable shorthand for NADP+/NADPH. In vivo this oxidation typically proceeds toward lactone formation as part of galactose/oxidative metabolism, though some dehydrogenases can operate reversibly.

errors: Atom/mass imbalance: each fatty acid elongation cycle (Claisen condensation + 2 reductions + dehydration) consumes 2 NADPH and releases 1 CO2 and 1 H2O per malonyl-ACP added. For 3 cycles (C7 to C13, adding 3 x C2 units), the correct stoichiometry should be 6 NADPH, 6 H+, 3 malonyl-ACP, 1 Iso-C7:0-ACP yielding 3 H2O, 6 NADP+, 3 CO2, 3 ACP, and 1 Iso-C13:0-ACP. This actually appears balanced in carbon/cofactor accounting.
Charge/proton balance should be checked: NADP should be written as NADP+; H+ count (6) is consistent with 6 NADPH oxidations.
rxn13666.other_comments: This represents three rounds of bacterial type II fatty acid elongation (FabB/FabG/FabA/FabI-type chemistry) extending an iso-C7:0-ACP to iso-C13:0-ACP by adding three malonyl-ACP-derived C2 units. The cofactor and CO2/H2O/ACP stoichiometry (6 NADPH, 3 malonyl-ACP -> 3 CO2, 3 ACP, 3 H2O, iso-C13:0-ACP) is internally consistent for 3 elongation cycles. Fatty acid biosynthesis is essentially irreversible in vivo due to decarboxylation of malonyl groups driving the condensation.

rxn08228.other_comments: This is a bacterial cardiolipin synthase reaction (phospholipase D-type, e.g., ClsA) where two molecules of phosphatidylglycerol (each with two tetradec-7-enoyl/C14:1 acyl chains) are combined. One PG donates its phosphatidyl group to the headgroup glycerol of the second PG, forming cardiolipin (with four C14:1 acyl chains, hence tetratetradec-7-enoyl) and releasing free glycerol. The stoichiometry is balanced: 2 PG (each C2 glycerophosphate backbone + 2 acyl chains) yields cardiolipin (3 glycerols linked via 2 phosphates, 4 acyl chains) plus one free glycerol. The atom and acyl-chain bookkeeping is consistent.

rxn06652.other_comments: This is the final step of the de novo (remodeling-independent) pathway for platelet-activating factor (PAF) synthesis. CDP-choline donates a phosphocholine group to 1-alkyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycerol, producing CMP and 1-alkyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (PAF). The atoms balance: the phosphocholine moiety is transferred from CDP-choline to the diradylglycerol hydroxyl, releasing CMP and a proton. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn01337.other_comments: This reaction represents 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/delta5-delta4-isomerase (3beta-HSD) acting on dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA, here written as DHA). The enzyme oxidizes the 3-hydroxyl group using NAD+ to NADH and isomerizes the delta5 double bond to delta4, yielding androstenedione (androst-4-ene-3,17-dione). Stoichiometry is balanced: one hydride and one proton are transferred to NAD+, giving NADH + H+, while the substrate is oxidized and isomerized. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn01025.other_comments: This is the deamination of 5-methylcytosine to thymine (cytosine deaminase-type reaction on the methylated base). H2O attacks, releasing ammonia and converting the amino group to a keto group, yielding thymine (5-methyluracil). Stoichiometry is balanced: 5-methylcytosine (C5H7N3O) + H2O + H+ gives thymine (C5H6N2O2) + NH3 (as NH4+). The H+ accounts for charge balance when ammonia is protonated to ammonium under physiological conditions. Hydrolytic deaminations are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward thymine formation.

errors: Product mismatch: galactosylation of luteolin would yield a luteolin galactoside, not trifolin (which is kaempferol 3-O-beta-D-galactoside)
Substrate inconsistency: the enzyme name specifies kaempferol as the acceptor, but the reaction lists luteolin
To produce trifolin, the aglycone substrate should be kaempferol, not luteolin
rxn04623.other_comments: This is a UDP-galactose dependent galactosyltransferase. The named product trifolin is kaempferol 3-O-beta-D-galactoside, which requires kaempferol as the acceptor substrate. The listed acceptor luteolin is a different flavone and would give a luteolin galactoside instead. The cofactor/byproduct stoichiometry (UDP-galactose -> UDP + H+) is correct, but the aglycone substrate does not match the product. Glycosyltransferases of this type proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn00408.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of CTP to CDP and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O (H2O) + CTP yields CDP + Phosphate (HPO4) + H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly (CTP4- + H2O -> CDP3- + HPO4^2- + H+). Thermodynamically, phosphoanhydride bond hydrolysis is highly exergonic and proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written involves [enzyme]-lysine on the substrate side but [eIF5A-precursor]-deoxyhypusine on the product side, creating an inconsistency in the enzyme/protein carrier. The deoxyhypusine synthase mechanism transfers the 4-aminobutyl moiety to the eIF5A lysine; the imine intermediate N-(4-aminobutylidene) should be on the eIF5A-precursor lysine, not a generic [enzyme]-lysine.
NAD should be written as NAD+ to balance charge with the consumed NADH + H+.
rxn07309.other_comments: This represents the final reductive step of deoxyhypusine synthase, in which the enzyme-bound imine intermediate (N-(4-aminobutylidene)-lysine on the eIF5A precursor) is reduced by NADH to form deoxyhypusine. In vivo, deoxyhypusine biosynthesis proceeds toward the formation of deoxyhypusine residue, so the reaction runs in the forward direction as written.

rxn08918.other_comments: This reaction represents methionine sulfoxide reductase (Msr) activity, reducing L-methionine sulfoxide (S-oxide) back to L-methionine using reduced thioredoxin (trdrd) as the electron donor, which becomes oxidized thioredoxin (trdox). The stoichiometry is balanced: the sulfoxide oxygen is released as water, with H+ and 2 electrons (from thioredoxin's dithiol-to-disulfide conversion) consumed. In vivo this is part of the oxidative damage repair system and proceeds in the reduction direction (sulfoxide to methionine).

rxn01247.other_comments: This is the oxidation of hexadecanal (palmitaldehyde) to palmitate by a fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase, using NAD+ and water. The reaction is balanced: the aldehyde (C16H32O) plus water minus 2H (as NADH + H+) yields the carboxylate (palmitate, C16H31O2-). Charge and mass balance check out, with NAD+ + aldehyde + H2O producing NADH + palmitate + 2 H+.

rxn00729.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of N-formylanthranilate (also known as N-formylanthranilic acid) to formate and anthranilate, catalyzed by formylanthranilate amidohydrolase (kynurenine formamidase-related activity is similar but acts on N-formylkynurenine; here the substrate is N-formylanthranilate). The reaction is a hydrolytic amide bond cleavage: H2O is consumed, formate, anthranilate, and a proton are produced. The stoichiometry balances in terms of atoms and charge (the amide C-N bond is hydrolyzed, releasing formate as the carbon-containing leaving group and anthranilate). Hydrolysis of an amide bond is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: hydrolysis of a phosphoanhydride bond (TPP to TMP + Pi) releases only 1 H+ at physiological pH, not 2 H+, depending on protonation states; the stoichiometry of 2 H+ is likely incorrect for a simple anhydride hydrolysis
rxn00436.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of thiamine diphosphate (TPP/ThDP) to thiamine monophosphate (TMP) plus inorganic phosphate, cleaving the terminal phosphoanhydride bond. Mass balance for the heavy atoms (P, the thiamine moiety) is consistent: TPP + H2O yields TMP + Pi. Phosphoanhydride hydrolysis is thermodynamically highly favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Nitrobenzene (Nitrobenzol) reduction to nitrosobenzene removes one oxygen atom; the reaction as written is missing one water on the product side. Balanced form: Nitrobenzene + NADPH + H+ -> Nitrosobenzene + NADP+ + H2O accounts for only one O removal, but nitro group (NO2) to nitroso (NO) loses one O which forms one H2O - this requires 2 H and produces 1 H2O, so the single NADPH/H+ provides the needed 2 electrons and 2 protons. Oxygen balance: left O = 2 (nitro), right O = 1 (nitroso) + 1 (H2O) = 2, OK. Hydrogen: left = NADPH(H) + H+ = 2 H from cofactor; right = H2O = 2 H, OK. The equation is actually balanced as written.
No actual stoichiometric error detected upon balancing.
rxn03701.other_comments: This represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of nitrobenzene to nitrosobenzene, an early step in nitroaromatic metabolism/xenobiotic reduction. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (C6H5NO2 + NADPH + H+ -> C6H5NO + NADP+ + H2O). In vivo, nitroreductases drive this reductively toward nitrosobenzene.

errors: Stoichiometry is not mass-balanced: (E)-cinnamate (C9H7O2-) plus water (H2O) gives C9H9O3-, but tropate is C9H9O3- only if oxygen is added; cinnamate has no hydroxyl groups while tropate (3-hydroxy-2-phenylpropanoate) has a hydroxyl, requiring net addition of one oxygen which water alone cannot provide without an additional acceptor/redox partner

Atom balance fails: cinnamate (C9H8O2) + H2O (H2O) = C9H10O3 expected, but tropate is C9H10O3 - this appears balanced by formula but the chemical transformation (reduction of a C=C double bond plus hydroxylation) is not achievable by simple hydration
The transformation from cinnamate to tropate involves both saturation of the double bond and introduction of a hydroxyl, which is not a single hydration reaction
rxn04575.other_comments: The reaction proposes converting (E)-cinnamate to tropate (3-hydroxy-2-phenylpropanoate / tropic acid) with water. Cinnamate is an alpha,beta-unsaturated aromatic acid; tropate is a saturated beta-hydroxy acid. Converting one to the other is more complex than a hydration and likely requires additional cofactors or multiple steps. As written it does not represent a clean, balanced biochemical hydratase reaction.

rxn02221.other_comments: This is an ATP-dependent amide bond formation between the carboxyl group of indole-3-acetate (IAA) and the epsilon-amino (N6) group of L-lysine, producing IAA-lysine conjugate. The reaction is an ADP-forming ligase (acid-amino acid ligase). Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides energy via hydrolysis to ADP + phosphate + H+, and the amide bond formation releases the products. Charge and mass appear balanced.

rxn01946.other_comments: This is an AMP-forming CoA ligase (acyl-CoA synthetase) reaction. 4-Hydroxyphenylacetate is activated by ATP, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate (PPi), and the carboxyl group is coupled to CoA to form 4-hydroxyphenylacetyl-CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + carboxylic acid yields AMP + PPi + H+ + acyl-CoA, consistent with the EC 6.2.1.x family. Mass and charge are balanced as written.

rxn03213.other_comments: This reaction represents salutaridine reductase (EC 1.1.1.248), part of the morphine biosynthesis pathway in opium poppy. The reaction as written shows oxidation of salutaridinol to salutaridine with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: the C7 hydroxyl (salutaridinol) is oxidized to a ketone (salutaridine), releasing 2 electrons and a proton, consistent with NADP+ + H- transfer. In vivo, the enzyme operates in the reductive direction (salutaridine + NADPH -> salutaridinol), which is the morphine biosynthetic direction. As written here, the favored physiological direction is the reverse.

errors: The substrate and product are identical (Thyminose appears on both sides), which is incorrect for a transport reaction representation; a proper ABC transporter reaction should distinguish the substrate by compartment, e.g. Thyminose[external] => Thyminose[cytoplasm]
As written, the sugar substrate cancels out, leaving only ATP hydrolysis, making the net reaction stoichiometrically meaningless as a transporter
rxn05549.other_comments: This is intended to be a monosaccharide-transporting ATPase (ABC transporter) coupling ATP hydrolysis to import of Thyminose (2-deoxyribose). Thyminose is the trivial name for 2-deoxy-D-ribose. The ATP hydrolysis half (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) is balanced and correct. The reaction should show the sugar moving between compartments rather than being identical on both sides.

rxn00534.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction (EC 2.8.3.-) transferring the CoA moiety from acetyl-CoA to malonate, yielding acetate and malonyl-CoA. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and the CoA group are conserved on both sides. CoA-transferases generally operate near equilibrium and are reversible, with direction depending on relative substrate/product concentrations. Note that malonyl-CoA is also produced by acetyl-CoA carboxylase using ATP/bicarbonate; this transferase route is an alternative, ATP-independent path.

errors: Mass imbalance: NADH + O2 + H+ + ethylbenzene should yield NAD+ + cis-dihydrodiol (cis-2,3-dihydro-2,3-dihydroxyethylbenzene), not a catechol; the proper product of a Rieske dioxygenase is the cis-dihydrodiol, which retains both oxygen atoms from O2 and consumes NADH. The named product 'cis-1,2-dihydro-3-ethylcatechol' appears to be a misnomer

Cofactor balance: the standard naphthalene/ethylbenzene dioxygenase uses NADH + H+ + O2 to give the cis-dihydrodiol + NAD+; if the product is truly a catechol (aromatic with two OH), then one oxygen atom is unaccounted for and atoms do not balance
Charge/notation: NAD should be written as NAD+ for proper charge balance
rxn03740.other_comments: This represents an aromatic-ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase reaction on ethylbenzene, consuming NADH and molecular O2. Both atoms of O2 are incorporated into the cis-dihydrodiol product in canonical Rieske dioxygenase chemistry. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo due to O2 consumption and NADH oxidation.

rxn04017.other_comments: This is the trans-aconitate 3-methyltransferase (Tmt1) reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to trans-aconitate, producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine and the methyl ester (E)-2-(methoxycarbonylmethyl)butenedioate, i.e. trans-aconitate 3-methyl ester. The atoms balance: SAM transfers a CH3 to one carboxylate of trans-aconitate forming the methyl ester, with SAM converted to SAH. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1:1).

rxn05378.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase step in branched-chain fatty acid biosynthesis (FabI/FabL-type). NADPH and a proton reduce the trans-2 double bond of the 12-methyl-tetradec-2-enoyl-ACP substrate to give the saturated 12-methyl-tetradecanoyl-ACP (anteiso-C15 acyl-ACP) and NADP+. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: NADPH provides the hydride and the H+ balances the saturation of the C2=C3 double bond. In vivo, enoyl-ACP reductase strongly favors the reductive direction during fatty acid elongation.

rxn01848.other_comments: This reaction represents the epimerization of (R,R)-tartrate to meso-tartrate, catalyzed by tartrate epimerase (EC 5.1.2.5). The reaction interconverts stereoisomers of tartrate by inverting the configuration at one stereocenter. As an epimerization/isomerization, there is no net change in molecular formula or atom count, so stoichiometry is balanced (1:1). Epimerase-catalyzed reactions are typically freely reversible since they have a small standard free energy change between stereoisomers.

rxn02866.other_comments: This is the isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase (IVD) reaction in leucine catabolism. Isovaleryl-CoA (3-methylbutanoyl-CoA) is oxidized to 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA (dimethylacryloyl-CoA / beta-methylcrotonyl-CoA) with reduction of FAD to FADH2. The stoichiometry is balanced: a C-C single bond is dehydrogenated to a double bond, transferring two hydrogens (2H) to FAD. In vivo the electrons from FADH2 are passed to electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF), so the physiological acceptor is ETF rather than free FAD; the written form using FAD/FADH2 is an acceptable abstraction. The reaction proceeds in the catabolic (oxidative) direction physiologically.

errors: Reaction is not mass-balanced as written: alpha-terpineol (C10H18O) and 1,8-cineole (C10H18O) have the same molecular formula, so cyclization (ether formation) involves loss and re-addition of water; if shown as direct isomerization without H2O the atom balance is fine, but the mechanism is an intramolecular dehydration/cyclization that should be checked for explicit cofactors/water in the source database
rxn04284.other_comments: This represents conversion of alpha-terpineol to 1,8-cineole (eucalyptol) via intramolecular cyclization (ether bridge formation between the C1 hydroxyl/cation and the C8 isopropyl group). Both are C10H18O monoterpenoids, so they are formal isomers. In vivo, cineole synthases convert the terpinyl cation/alpha-terpineol intermediate to 1,8-cineole, making this strongly directional toward cineole.

errors: Atom imbalance: caffeine (C8H10N4O2) demethylation to theobromine (C7H8N4O2) removes a CH2 group, but the products list formaldehyde (CH2O) plus H2O which introduces an extra oxygen. Checking O: reactants O2 (2 O); products H2O (1 O) + formaldehyde (1 O) = 2 O, oxygens balance. Checking C: caffeine 8 C; theobromine 7 C + formaldehyde 1 C = 8 C, balanced. Checking N: 4 = 4, balanced. Checking H: reactants NADH(H not counted separately, use net) - net hydrogen balance is consistent. Reaction appears balanced for a typical N-demethylase oxidation; however the canonical caffeine N-demethylase products are 7-methylxanthine/theobromine/paraxanthine plus formaldehyde, and the cofactor should be NADPH rather than NADH for the CYP-type enzyme in many organisms.
rxn07745.other_comments: This represents an oxidative N-demethylation of caffeine to theobromine, releasing formaldehyde, consuming O2 and a reduced nicotinamide cofactor. The reaction as written is essentially atom-balanced (C8, N4, O2 conserved). Such monooxygenase/demethylase reactions are physiologically unidirectional toward demethylation. [directionality_note] irreversible oxidative N-demethylation

rxn01320.other_comments: This is the sialate O-acetyltransferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.45), transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the 9-O position of N-acetylneuraminate (Neu5Ac), producing N-acetyl-9-O-acetylneuraminate (Neu5,9Ac2) and CoA. The reaction is balanced: one acetyl group is transferred from CoA to the hydroxyl, conserving carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and the thiol/ester groups. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1:1).

rxn02228.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 3-mercaptopyruvate reductase / 3-mercaptolactate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.-). 3-Mercaptolactate is oxidized to 3-mercaptopyruvate with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is balanced: the secondary alcohol (CHOH) of mercaptolactate is oxidized to the ketone (C=O) of mercaptopyruvate, releasing 2 electrons and 1 H+ as written (one H+ on the product side accounts for the proton, with the hydride transferred to NAD+). Mass and charge are consistent. NAD-dependent dehydrogenases of this type are generally reversible in vivo depending on the NAD+/NADH ratio.

rxn00304.other_comments: This reaction represents the GTP-dependent phosphorylation of pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), analogous to PEP synthase/pyruvate-phosphate dikinase chemistry but using GTP. Atom and charge balance check: Pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + GTP (C10H12N5O14P3 4-) gives GDP (C10H12N5O11P2 3-) + PEP (C3H2O6P 3-) + H+ (1+). Carbon: 3+10=13 = 3+10. Phosphorus: 3 = 2+1. Charge: (-1)+(-4) = -5 on left; (-3)+(-3)+(+1) = -5 on right. The reaction is balanced as written. Thermodynamically, phosphoryl transfer to form the high-energy PEP enol phosphate is generally unfavorable, so in vivo the reverse (PEP -> pyruvate, GDP -> GTP) direction is typically favored; however it is formally listed as reversible.

rxn02599.other_comments: This reaction describes a flavonoid 8-hydroxylase activity acting on taxifolin (dihydroquercetin). The product 2,3-dihydrogossypetin is the 8-hydroxylated taxifolin. The stoichiometry is consistent with a NADH-dependent monooxygenase (likely a flavonoid 8-hydroxylase / cytochrome P450 or flavin monooxygenase type mechanism): one oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate as the hydroxyl group, and the other is reduced to water using two electrons from NADH and protons. Atom and charge balance: NADH + O2 + H+ + taxifolin yields H2O + NAD+ + hydroxylated product, which is balanced for a typical monooxygenase reaction.

errors: Charge imbalance: left side has net charge 0, right side has net charge +3 (from H+) -1 (Cl-) -2 (2-chloromaleylacetate carboxylates) = 0, but stoichiometry needs careful check; the standard reaction R05408 is catalyzed by 2,6-dichlorohydroquinone 1,2-dioxygenase and typically balanced as: 2,6-dichlorohydroquinone + O2 -> 2-chloromaleylacetate + H+ + Cl-, so the inclusion of H2O and the coefficient of 3 H+ likely produces mass/charge imbalance
Possible oxygen/mass imbalance: ring cleavage dioxygenases incorporate both atoms of O2 without requiring additional H2O
rxn03708.other_comments: This is a ring-cleavage dioxygenase reaction (2,6-dichlorohydroquinone 1,2-dioxygenase) in chlorophenol degradation pathways. O2 cleaves the aromatic ring of 2,6-dichlorohydroquinone, releasing a chloride and forming 2-chloromaleylacetate. Oxygenase reactions consuming O2 are essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Atomic/charge balance issue: the reaction as written does not balance. Combining (Z)-phenylacetaldehyde oxime (C8H9NO) with L-cysteine (C3H7NO2S) to form S-(phenylacetothiohydroximoyl)-L-cysteine should be a formal dehydration/condensation introducing a thiohydroximate. Two H2O are released, requiring two oxygen atoms from substrates, but NADPH + O2 provides extra reducing equivalents and oxygen that must be carefully accounted; the H and O counts do not reconcile with only 2 H2O produced.
Charge balance: NADPH (-4) + 2 H+ + cysteine (zwitterion ~0) vs NADP (-3) and the product (anionic) needs verification; net charge appears unbalanced.
rxn14259.other_comments: This is a CYP79/CYP83-type step in glucosinolate biosynthesis: the aldoxime is oxidized and conjugated with cysteine to give an S-alkyl-thiohydroximate (here S-(phenylacetothiohydroximoyl)-L-cysteine). The reaction is a cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenation, which in vivo proceeds toward thiohydroximate formation and is effectively irreversible.

errors: The reaction shows identical substrates and products (H+ + 5-Aminolevulinate on both sides), representing no net chemical transformation. For a proton-coupled permease/symport reaction, the metabolite and proton should be transported across a membrane, which is typically represented with compartment labels (e.g., 5-Aminolevulinate[e] + H+[e] <=> 5-Aminolevulinate[c] + H+[c]). Without compartmentalization, this reaction is meaningless.

The reaction is labeled as a GABA-specific permease but the substrate is 5-Aminolevulinate, not GABA (4-aminobutyrate). This is a mismatch between the annotated enzyme/transporter specificity and the actual metabolite, though 5-ALA is a structural analog of GABA and may be a genuine substrate of this permease.
rxn09702.other_comments: This appears to be a proton-coupled transport (symport) reaction for 5-aminolevulinate via a GABA permease. As written, it lacks compartment annotations, so substrates and products are identical, making it a null reaction. Transport reactions are generally reversible thermodynamically but driven directionally in vivo by the proton motive force and substrate gradients.

errors: Stoichiometry appears balanced for a typical cytochrome P450 monooxygenase hydroxylation: NADPH + O2 + H+ + substrate -> H2O + NADP+ + hydroxylated product. However, the substrate/product identities should be verified - the reaction name refers to sophoraflavanone-B as substrate and a 2'-hydroxylation, while the listed substrate is Flavaprenin and product is Leachianone G, which creates a naming inconsistency.
Verify that Flavaprenin and Leachianone G differ by exactly one hydroxyl group (one oxygen atom incorporation) consistent with a monooxygenase reaction.
rxn14186.other_comments: This is described as a NADPH/O2-dependent oxygenase (hydroxylating) reaction, characteristic of a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. The overall atom balance follows the standard monooxygenase pattern (one O incorporated into product, one O reduced to water). Such NADPH/O2-consuming hydroxylations are essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Oxygen atom imbalance: O2 provides 2 oxygen atoms; products account for one in H2O and one in the N-oxide, which is consistent, but the typical CYP-mediated N-hydroxylation/N-oxidation requires correct accounting. As written, mass/charge balance appears plausible if IAOx N-oxide is the N-oxide of indole-3-acetaldoxime. Charge balance: NADPH (-4) + H+ + O2 = NADP (-3) + H2O + N-oxide; charges balance if N-oxide is neutral.
rxn14107.other_comments: This describes a cytochrome P450 (CYP)-type monooxygenase reaction converting indole-3-acetaldoxime (3-indoleacetaldoxime) to its N-oxide, consuming NADPH and O2 and releasing NADP+ and water. Such oxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (forward), driven by O2 consumption and NADPH oxidation. This is relevant to glucosinolate/camalexin biosynthesis in plants.

errors: Substrate mismatch: 'Phycite' is a synonym for erythritol (meso-erythritol), the C4 sugar alcohol. The product D-Erythritol 4-phosphate is consistent with phosphorylation of erythritol, so the substrate naming is acceptable if Phycite = erythritol. No stoichiometric imbalance detected (ATP phosphate transferred to erythritol, yielding ADP + H+ + erythritol 4-phosphate). Mass and charge appear balanced.
rxn01754.other_comments: This is an ATP-dependent kinase reaction phosphorylating erythritol (Phycite) at the 4-position to give D-erythritol 4-phosphate, consuming ATP and releasing ADP plus a proton. Phycite is an older common name for erythritol.

rxn08328.other_comments: This is a hydrolysis reaction where 2,3-dihydroxybenzoylserine (an ester/amide linkage between 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate and L-serine) is cleaved by water into L-serine and 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate (2,3-DHB). This is part of enterobactin/siderophore degradation and iron-recycling pathways. The stoichiometry is balanced: the amide/ester bond is broken with addition of water, yielding the free amino acid and the carboxylic acid. Hydrolases acting on such bonds are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo (forward direction toward hydrolysis).

rxn09066.other_comments: This is a phosphatidate phosphatase reaction hydrolyzing 1,2-dihexadec-9-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a phosphatidic acid with two C16:1 acyl chains) to the corresponding diacylglycerol, releasing inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: PA + H2O -> DAG + Pi. The H+ accounts for charge/protonation balance upon phosphate release. Hydrolysis of a phosphomonoester is thermodynamically favorable and strongly drives the reaction toward DAG formation in vivo.

errors: Maltose appears on both sides of the reaction as substrate and product, which is stoichiometrically inconsistent for a chemical transformation; this represents a transport reaction where the compartment labels were lost in the parsing, making it appear that maltose is unchanged.
Without compartment designations, the net reaction shows ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+ with maltose unchanged, which has no net biological meaning as written.
