rxn01934.other_comments: This represents (S)-4-hydroxymandelate oxidase / mandelate oxidation, an oxidative decarboxylation using O2 to produce p-hydroxybenzaldehyde, CO2, and H2O2. Such flavin-dependent oxidase reactions consuming O2 and releasing CO2 are physiologically irreversible (forward direction).

rxn08604.other_comments: This is the gamma-glutamylputrescine synthetase (PuuA) reaction, the first step of the putrescine degradation pathway in E. coli. ATP-dependent ligation of glutamate and putrescine forms gamma-glutamyl-putrescine, releasing ADP, inorganic phosphate, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written.

rxn01600.other_comments: This is cyclohexylamine oxidase (EC 1.4.3.12), an amine oxidase that oxidatively deaminates cyclohexylamine. The reaction uses O2 and H2O to convert the primary amine to the ketone (cyclohexanone), releasing ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. Atoms balance: C6H13N (cyclohexanamine) + H2O + O2 -> C6H10O (cyclohexanone) + NH3 + H2O2. Carbon: 6=6; Nitrogen: 1=1; checking H: 13+2 = 15 on left, cyclohexanone 10 + NH3 3 + H2O2 2 = 15; O: 1+2 = 3 on left, 1 (ketone) + 0 + 2 (H2O2) = 3. Balanced.

rxn04988.other_comments: This represents the cytochrome P450 (CYP7B1)-catalyzed 7alpha-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxycholesterol. A monooxygenase reaction: one oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate (forming the 7alpha-hydroxyl) and the other is reduced to water, using NADPH as the electron donor. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + 25-hydroxycholesterol -> H2O + NADP+ + 7alpha,25-dihydroxycholesterol. Atoms and charges balance correctly (one O incorporated, one O to water).

rxn07860.other_comments: This is a phosphatase/nucleotidase reaction (5'-nucleotidase type activity) hydrolyzing dihydrozeatin riboside monophosphate to dihydrozeatin riboside plus inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the phosphomonoester bond, releasing one phosphate and the dephosphorylated nucleoside. Hydrolysis reactions of this type are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the direction of phosphate release in vivo, representing a step in cytokinin metabolism/activation.

rxn10250.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose-dependent glucosyltransferase reaction that transfers a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to a diglucosyldiacylglycerol acceptor (with isopentadecanoyl acyl chains), forming a triglucosyldiacylglycerol product and releasing UDP. Atom/charge balance is consistent: one glucosyl unit is transferred, UDP-glucose becomes UDP, and the acceptor gains one glucose. Such glycolipid biosynthesis reactions proceed in the synthetic (forward) direction in vivo, driven by cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond.

rxn02582.other_comments: This is the galactosylceramidase (GALC) reaction, EC 3.2.1.46, which hydrolyzes galactocerebroside (D-galactosyl-N-acylsphingosine) into ceramide and free beta-D-galactose. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water hydrolyzes the glycosidic bond, releasing one galactose and one ceramide. As a hydrolase, it proceeds strongly in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02571.other_comments: This reaction represents O-acetyl-L-serine sulfhydrylase (cysteine synthase) acting on selenide instead of sulfide, producing selenocysteine and acetate. O-acetyl-L-serine (C5H9NO4) + selenide (HSe-/Se2-) yields acetate (C2H3O2-) + H+ + selenocysteine (C3H7NO2Se). The atoms balance: acetyl group is released as acetate while the selenol replaces the acetoxy group via beta-replacement. Note that selenide protonation state affects the H+ balance; if written as HSe-, the H+ on the product side balances correctly with acetate as the anion.

rxn03107.other_comments: This is the bile acid CoA ligase reaction (THCA-CoA synthetase) activating 3alpha,7alpha-dihydroxy-5beta-cholestanate (DHCA) to its CoA thioester. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + carboxylic acid -> AMP + PPi + H+ + acyl-CoA. The H+ accounts for charge/proton balance. AMP-forming ligase reactions are thermodynamically driven forward in vivo by subsequent PPi hydrolysis, favoring activation of the bile acid intermediate for peroxisomal beta-oxidation.

errors: Charge imbalance: left side has 3 H+ plus 2 NADPH (each -2 net relative to NADP) and the malonyl-CoA/octanoate/CoA charges; the proton count does not balance a standard fatty acid elongation cycle. A single elongation cycle (C8 -> C10) consumes 2 NADPH + 2 H+, not 3 H+, when written with CO2 and H2O released.

The reaction shows free octanoate and free decanoate (acids) rather than ACP- or CoA-bound acyl thioesters; fatty acid synthase normally operates on acyl-ACP/acyl-CoA intermediates, so using free acids is mechanistically inaccurate, though it can be acceptable as a lumped reaction.
H balance check: counting H from 2 NADPH, 3 H+, malonyl-CoA, octanoate vs products (H2O, 2 NADP, CoA, CO2, decanoate) appears off by one proton given the 3 H+ stoichiometry.
rxn09443.other_comments: This represents one round of fatty acid elongation converting octanoate (C10:0 product, decanoate) using malonyl-CoA as the two-carbon donor, releasing CO2, CoA, and H2O, with 2 NADPH used for the reduction steps. Net carbon balance (C8 + C3 malonyl - CO2 = C10) is correct. The main concern is proton/charge balance and the use of free acids instead of thioester-bound intermediates.

rxn01608.other_comments: This reaction describes mevalonate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.-), oxidizing (R)-mevalonate to mevaldate (the semialdehyde) using NAD+ as electron acceptor, producing NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced: mevalonate (C6H11O4-) loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one as the released H+) to form mevaldate (the aldehyde). Atoms and charges balance. In vivo, the thermodynamically favored direction is reduction (mevaldate + NADH -> mevalonate), so as written (oxidation) the favored direction is the reverse. Note that the standard mevalonate pathway uses NADPH-dependent HMG-CoA reductase, not this NAD-linked enzyme.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the listed substrates and products do not balance. Azoxytoluene dimers are formed by condensation of two hydroxylamino-dinitrotoluene molecules each, so producing 2 azoxy dimers requires 4 hydroxylamino monomers total (matching the 2 + 2 given), but the oxygen and water stoichiometry is inconsistent for a simple condensation; an azoxy bond formation from two hydroxylamines typically releases one H2O per dimer, not requiring molecular O2 as written

Stoichiometric inconsistency: 2 azoxy products from mixed monomers (4-hydroxylamino and 2-hydroxylamino) cannot both yield the single named product 2,4',6,6'-tetranitro-2',4-azoxytoluene without producing additional cross- and homo-coupled isomers
rxn11691.other_comments: This represents the abiotic/enzyme-assisted condensation of hydroxylamino-dinitrotoluene intermediates (from TNT reduction) into an azoxy-coupled dimer. The intent is coupling of two arylhydroxylamines to form an azoxy compound with loss of water; the inclusion of O2 and the exact water count appear unbalanced.

rxn02148.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 / Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase-type reaction. 6-Oxocineole is oxidized using NADPH and molecular O2, incorporating one oxygen atom into the substrate (forming the lactone 1,6,6-Trimethyl-2,7-dioxabicyclo[3.2.2]nonan-3-one) and reducing the other to water. Stoichiometry balances: one O from O2 goes into the product, the other becomes H2O, NADPH and H+ are consumed yielding NADP+. Atoms and charges balance with the typical monooxygenase scheme.

rxn10978.other_comments: The reaction as written (rxn10978/OROATP) shows H+ and Orotate on both sides with no change. The identifier 'OROATP' and the proton presence suggest this is intended to be an orotate antiporter/transport reaction (likely orotate-proton symport or exchange across a membrane), but the compartment designations (e.g., cytosol vs extracellular) are missing, so it appears as a meaningless identity reaction. Without compartment tags, no net reaction is represented.

errors: Charge imbalance: hydrolysis of a mixed acyl-phosphate anhydride (5'-butyrylphosphoinosine) with water yields IMP, butyrate, and one proton, not two protons. The 2.0 H+ stoichiometry does not balance charge correctly for this hydrolysis.
rxn01238.other_comments: This describes hydrolysis of the mixed anhydride bond between butyrate and the 5'-phosphate of inosine monophosphate (IMP), releasing free butyrate and IMP. Hydrolysis of an energy-rich acyl-phosphate anhydride is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, favoring the forward (hydrolysis) direction.

rxn01506.other_comments: This is an epimerization reaction interconverting N-Acetyl-D-glucosamine 6-phosphate and N-Acetyl-D-mannosamine 6-phosphate at the C2 position. Both substrate and product are C8H16NO9P with identical molecular formulas, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (1:1). Epimerases are typically reversible enzymes; in the sialic acid catabolic pathway the flux is generally toward GlcNAc-6-P, but the enzyme itself catalyzes a near-equilibrium reversible interconversion.

rxn02554.other_comments: This is a ferulate 5-hydroxylase (F5H/CYP84A1) reaction, a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that hydroxylates ferulate at the 5-position to form 5-hydroxyferulate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate (hydroxylation) and the other is reduced to water, consuming NADPH + H+ as the electron donor. As a P450 monooxygenase reaction, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydroxylation direction.

errors: The proton (H+) stoichiometry is incorrect; this acyl transfer from ACP to CoA does not consume or produce 2 protons. The reaction should be charge- and mass-balanced without the addition of 2 H+.
The product 'fa1coa' is an ambiguous/generic identifier; the product should specifically be 12-methyl-tridecanoyl-CoA (iso-myristoyl-CoA) to match the named substrate.
rxn05455.other_comments: This is an acyl-ACP:CoA transacylase reaction transferring the 12-methyl-tridecanoyl (iso-C14) group from ACP to CoA, releasing free ACP and forming the branched-chain acyl-CoA. The core transfer (acyl-ACP + CoA <=> acyl-CoA + ACP) is correct in concept, but the 2 H+ are spurious and the product ID is generic.

rxn02816.other_comments: This is a beta-glucosidase hydrolysis reaction. Water hydrolyzes the glucosidic bond of p-coumaryl alcohol 4-O-glucoside, releasing D-glucose and p-coumaryl alcohol (the aglycone). The stoichiometry is balanced: the glucoside (aglycone + glucosyl) plus water yields the free aglycone plus free glucose. Hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02074.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.185) transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to the 7-O position of naringenin (a flavanone), producing prunin (naringenin 7-O-glucoside) and UDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the glucosyl group is transferred from UDP-glucose to the hydroxyl of naringenin, releasing UDP. Glycosyltransferase reactions of this type are strongly thermodynamically favorable due to the high energy of the UDP-sugar bond, driving them in the glucosylation direction in vivo.

rxn01233.other_comments: This is the taurine--2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase (taurine:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase, EC 2.6.1.55) reaction. It transfers the amino group from taurine to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and sulfoacetaldehyde (2-sulfoacetaldehyde). The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: taurine (C2H7NO3S) plus 2-oxoglutarate (C5H6O5 / C5H4O5 as dianion) give L-glutamate (C5H9NO4) plus sulfoacetaldehyde (C2H4O4S). Carbon (7=7), nitrogen (1=1), and sulfur (1=1) are conserved. As an aminotransferase reaction, it is mechanistically reversible.

rxn00156.other_comments: This is pyruvate oxidase (CoA-acetylating), which uses molecular oxygen to oxidatively decarboxylate pyruvate, producing acetyl-CoA, CO2, and hydrogen peroxide. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: left side has C24 (CoA ~C21 plus pyruvate C3) and right side acetyl-CoA (C23) plus CO2 (C1), oxygens and hydrogens balance with the H+ and H2O2. The use of O2 with reduction to H2O2 strongly favors the forward (oxidative) direction in vivo.

rxn02102.other_comments: This is the (S)-ureidoglycolate dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.154), oxidizing the secondary alcohol of ureidoglycolate to a carbonyl to form oxalurate (oxaluric acid), with concomitant reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Stoichiometry is balanced: ureidoglycolate (C3H6N2O4) loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+, one as H+), giving oxalurate (C3H4N2O4). Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen, and charge all balance. NAD+/NADH dehydrogenases of this type are generally reversible, though physiological flux is often in the oxidative direction in purine degradation pathways.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance as written: NADP should be NADP+ (carries a positive charge); the equation as literally written with neutral 'NADP' would be unbalanced in charge. With proper NADP+, the reaction balances: L-menthol + NADP+ -> menthone + NADPH + H+
rxn01566.other_comments: This is a menthol dehydrogenase (secondary alcohol oxidoreductase) reaction oxidizing (-)-menthol to (-)-menthone with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry of atoms is correct (menthol C10H20O -> menthone C10H18O, losing 2 H, i.e. 2H+ + 2e- transferred as hydride + proton). NADP-dependent alcohol/ketone oxidoreductases are typically reversible in vivo; in biosynthesis of menthol from menthone the reverse (reductive) direction operates.

errors: Likely water stoichiometry mismatch: cleavage of a single L,D crosslink (A2pm-A2pm bond) is a single hydrolysis event requiring 1.0 H2O, not 2.0 H2O. Unless two crosslinks are being hydrolyzed, the coefficient of 2.0 H2O is inconsistent with breaking one peptide bond.
rxn08932.other_comments: This is a murein L,D-endopeptidase reaction that hydrolyzes the cross-link between two diaminopimelate (A2pm) residues connecting adjacent peptidoglycan strands, converting a crosslinked pentapeptide-tripeptide structure into uncrosslinked separate strands. Hydrolytic peptide-bond cleavage of this type is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: L-Mimosine (C8H10N2O4) hydrolysis should yield 3-hydroxy-4-pyridone (3,4-dihydroxypyridine) plus a 3-carbon amino acid. The reaction as written produces L-Serine (C3H7NO3), but balancing requires the product to be a non-hydroxylated 3-carbon amino acid. L-Mimosine is beta-(3-hydroxy-4-pyridone-1-yl)-alanine; cleavage of the N-C bond yields 3-hydroxy-4-pyridone plus pyruvate/alanine-type backbone (typically 3-hydroxy-4-pyridone + pyruvate + NH3, or alanine), not serine

Atom balance check: Left side C8H12N2O5 (mimosine + water); Right side L-Serine C3H7NO3 + 3-hydroxy-4-pyridone C5H5NO2 = C8H12N2O5. The formulas actually balance, but biochemically the alanine-derived moiety of mimosine would yield pyruvate + ammonia (after deamination) or alanine, not serine
rxn03022.other_comments: This is a hydrolytic cleavage of L-mimosine (a non-protein amino acid) into the heterocyclic moiety 3-hydroxy-4-pyridone and an amino acid fragment. The given products are atom-balanced (C8H12N2O5 on both sides), so stoichiometry is technically correct, but the identity of the amino acid product is biochemically questionable; mimosine degradation typically yields 3-hydroxy-4-pyridone (3,4-DHP) plus pyruvate and ammonia rather than serine. Hydrolytic amidohydrolase reactions are essentially irreversible under physiological conditions.

rxn03063.other_comments: This is the sterol C-24 methyltransferase reaction (ERG6 in yeast). SAM donates a methyl group to zymosterol at C-24, producing fecosterol, S-adenosyl-homocysteine, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl group transferred from SAM accounts for the carbon difference between zymosterol (C27) and fecosterol (C28), and a proton is released. In vivo this SAM-dependent methylation is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the methyl-transfer (forward) direction as part of ergosterol biosynthesis.

rxn05035.other_comments: This reaction represents O-phosphoserine sulfhydrylase (also known as O-phospho-L-serine:hydrogen-sulfide 2-amino-2-carboxyethyltransferase, EC 2.5.1.65), which converts O-phospho-L-serine and hydrogen sulfide into L-cysteine and phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2S provides the sulfur and hydrogens, the phosphate group is released as inorganic phosphate, and the amino-carboxyethyl moiety is transferred to sulfide forming cysteine. This pathway is the dominant route for cysteine biosynthesis in some archaea (e.g., Aeropyrum pernix, Mycobacterium tuberculosis).

errors: The reaction shows identical species on both sides (H+ + D-Cysteine on each side), so no net chemical transformation or transport is represented. A proper transport reaction must distinguish compartments, e.g., H+[e] + D-Cysteine[e] <=> H+[c] + D-Cysteine[c]. As written, the reaction is a null/empty reaction with zero net flux.
rxn12613.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-symport transport reaction for D-cysteine (importing D-cysteine coupled to proton movement across the membrane). However, the equation lacks compartment annotations, so substrates and products are identical and the reaction is trivially balanced but biologically meaningless as written.

rxn07713.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction. UDP-glucose serves as the sugar donor, transferring a glucosyl moiety to the acceptor (Delphinidin 3-glucoside 5-caffoyl-glucoside) at the 3'-O position of the B-ring, producing Albireodelphin and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: the glucose from UDP-glucose is added to the acceptor, leaving UDP as the byproduct. UDP-glucosyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable in the glucosylation direction due to the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, so the reaction proceeds physiologically toward the glucosylated product.

rxn11711.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of oleoyl-CoA (a thioester) by oleoyl-CoA hydrolase (a long-chain acyl-CoA thioesterase, EC 3.1.2.2). Water cleaves the thioester bond, releasing free CoA and oleate. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + oleoyl-CoA yields CoA + oleate + H+ (the proton is released from the carboxylic acid of oleate). Mass and charge are balanced.

rxn02740.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction where the CoA group is transferred from acetyl-CoA to glutaconate, producing acetate and glutaconyl-CoA. Stoichiometry is balanced: both sides carry one CoA, and the carbon/charge balance is maintained as the thioester bond energy is conserved during transfer. (E)-Glutaconate CoA-transferase (EC 2.8.3.12) catalyzes this reversible CoA transfer. In Acidaminococcus fermentans glutamate fermentation, the physiological direction favors activation of glutaconate to glutaconyl-CoA using acetyl-CoA, but CoA-transferases are mechanistically reversible.

rxn02394.other_comments: This reaction is the NADP-dependent oxidation of 4-hydroxyphenyllactate (HPL) to p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate), with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: the secondary alcohol/hydroxyl group on the lactate carbon is oxidized to a ketone, releasing 2 electrons and a proton; NADP+ accepts a hydride to form NADPH, and a free H+ is released. Atoms and charges balance. As an NAD(P)-dependent oxidoreductase acting on a hydroxy acid/keto acid pair, the reaction is thermodynamically reversible and direction depends on the NADPH/NADP+ ratio and substrate concentrations in vivo.

errors: The product L-Galactono-1,4-lactone is a lactone (cyclic ester), but oxidation of the aldehyde group of L-galactose at C1 would yield L-galactonic acid (open-chain), which then cyclizes; the direct enzymatic product is typically written as L-galactono-1,4-lactone, so this is acceptable. However, oxidation of an aldose to its lactone is a 2-electron oxidation requiring loss of 2 H, consistent with NAD+ to NADH + H+, so atoms balance.
Strictly, the reaction as written is stoichiometrically balanced if L-galactono-1,4-lactone is the cyclized aldonolactone form.
rxn07490.other_comments: This is the NAD-dependent oxidation of L-galactose (aldehyde at C1) to L-galactono-1,4-lactone, a key step in the plant (Smirnoff-Wheeler) ascorbate biosynthesis pathway. The reaction is generally driven forward toward lactone formation in vivo, feeding ascorbate synthesis.

errors: The reaction name specifies '3-oxopropanoate' as the amino acceptor, but the listed substrate is '3-Oxo-2-methylpropanoate' (2-methyl-3-oxopropanoate / methylmalonate semialdehyde). These are different compounds; the enzyme name and substrate are inconsistent.

If the substrate is indeed 3-Oxo-2-methylpropanoate, the product should be L-3-Amino-isobutyrate (beta-aminoisobutyrate), which is consistent; but then the reaction name should read 'L-Alanine:3-oxo-2-methylpropanoate aminotransferase'.
rxn02925.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction transferring an amino group from L-alanine to 3-oxo-2-methylpropanoate (methylmalonate semialdehyde), yielding pyruvate and L-3-aminoisobutyrate. Atom and charge balance appear correct for the listed substrate/product pair. Transaminations are generally reversible, though physiologically this often operates in the direction of beta-aminoisobutyrate formation/degradation depending on context (valine/thymine catabolism). The main issue is the naming mismatch with '3-oxopropanoate'.

rxn02748.other_comments: This reaction is the decarboxylation of (3S)-3-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (3MOP, the 2-oxo acid derived from isoleucine) to 2-methylbutanal, catalyzed by a 2-oxo acid (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid) decarboxylase, releasing CO2. Stoichiometry is balanced: 3MOP (C6H9O3-) + H+ yields CO2 (CO2) + 2-methylbutanal (C5H10O). Carbon: 6 = 1 + 5; oxygen: 3 = 2 + 1; hydrogen: 9 + 1 = 10; charge: -1 + 1 = 0. Balanced. Decarboxylation reactions releasing CO2 are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the reaction forward (e.g., in Ehrlich pathway fusel alcohol/aldehyde production).

rxn00204.other_comments: This is the oxalate oxidase reaction (EC 1.2.3.4), oxidizing oxalate using molecular oxygen to produce two CO2 and hydrogen peroxide. Mass balance: left side C2H2O6 (oxalate C2O4H2- with 2 H+ gives C2H4O4 plus O2 = C2H4O6); right side 2 CO2 (C2O4) + H2O2 (H2O2) = C2H2O6. Wait, checking: oxalate as C2O4(2-) plus 2 H+ = C2H2O4, plus O2 = C2H2O6. Right side 2 CO2 = C2O4, H2O2 = H2O2, total C2H2O6. Atoms balance C2 H2 O6 on both sides. Charge balances (neutral both sides if oxalate written as dianion plus 2 H+).

errors: Stoichiometric/entity inconsistency: the substrate is written as free 'Dihydrolipoamide' but the product is the enzyme-bound 'S-(3-Methylbutanoyl)-dihydrolipoamide-E' (an E2-lysine-bound lipoyl group); the substrate should correspondingly be the enzyme-bound dihydrolipoyllysine residue (Dihydrolipoamide-E) for mass/charge balance
An H+ is generated as product but no proton donor is balanced on the substrate side; the thiol transacylation does not net release a free proton in this representation, so the H+ is questionable
rxn06586.other_comments: This is the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex E2 (dihydrolipoyllysine-residue acyltransferase) reaction, transferring the isovaleryl (3-methylbutanoyl) group from isovaleryl-CoA onto the dihydrolipoyl moiety, releasing free CoA. Acyl transfer between CoA thioesters and dihydrolipoamide thiols is energetically near-equilibrium and can run reversibly, though in vivo within BCKDH it proceeds in the catabolic (forward) direction.

rxn01725.other_comments: This is the carnitine 3-dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.108), oxidizing the hydroxyl group of carnitine to a keto group, yielding 3-dehydrocarnitine. The reaction is balanced: carnitine (C7H15NO3) loses 2 H (as hydride to NAD+ giving NADH plus a free H+) to form 3-dehydrocarnitine (C7H13NO3). Atoms and charge balance correctly. NAD+/NADH-dependent alcohol-to-ketone oxidations are typically reversible thermodynamically, though physiological flux often favors carnitine oxidation under conditions of carnitine catabolism.

errors: Product identity/inconsistency: the substrate is specified as trans-3-cis-7-tetradecadienoyl (a diene, trans-3-cis-7), but the product 'Tetradecenoyl-ACP' is a monoene (C14:1); reduction of one double bond by enoyl-ACP reductase should yield a cis-7-tetradecenoyl-ACP, so the product should be explicitly cis-7-tetradecenoyl-ACP
Naming ambiguity: 'Tetradecenoyl-ACP' lacks position/geometry specification (should be cis-7-tetradecenoyl-[acyl-carrier protein])
rxn08391.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase (NADPH-dependent) step in fatty acid elongation/biosynthesis. It reduces the trans-3 (2,3 in enoyl numbering) double bond using NADPH, consuming NADPH + H+ and producing NADP+. Stoichiometry of cofactors and protons is balanced (one double bond reduced per NADPH). The cis-7 double bond is retained, giving the monounsaturated C14:1 product. In vivo, FabI-type enoyl-ACP reductase reactions are essentially irreversible toward the reduced (saturated/elongated) product.

errors: The substrate is written generically as 'Cyanohydrin' and the product as 'Cyanoglycoside', but the enzyme name specifies (S)-4-hydroxymandelonitrile as the acceptor and the product should be the dhurrin (the beta-D-glucoside of (S)-4-hydroxymandelonitrile). Generic naming makes the reaction non-specific.

A proton (H+) is typically released when UDP-glucose transfers the glucosyl moiety; however, glucosylation of a hydroxyl group generally does not net-release a free proton because the acceptor -OH oxygen forms the glycosidic bond. Charge balance should be checked, but the main atom balance via 'glucose moiety transfer' is consistent.
rxn06822.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose-dependent glucosyltransferase (UGT) that transfers a beta-D-glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the hydroxyl of a cyanohydrin (here (S)-4-hydroxymandelonitrile), forming a cyanogenic glucoside (dhurrin) and releasing UDP. The generic placeholders 'Cyanohydrin' and 'Cyanoglycoside' are stoichiometrically consistent as a glucosyl transfer (one glucose moiety moved from UDP-glucose to the acceptor).

rxn03203.other_comments: This reaction (R04686) represents the intramolecular cyclization/lactonization of beta-D-glucosyl-2-coumarate (the glucoside of the open-chain o-coumaric acid, i.e. trans-2-hydroxycinnamate glucoside) to beta-D-glucosyl-2-coumarinate, which leads toward coumarin biosynthesis. Both substrate and product carry the same beta-D-glucosyl moiety and the same C/H/O atoms, so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (an isomerization/configurational change at the double bond, trans to cis, enabling later lactone formation). Stoichiometry appears correct with a 1:1 conversion.

rxn04633.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by anthocyanin 3-O-glucoside 6''-O-rhamnosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.159). UDP-L-rhamnose donates a rhamnosyl group to the glucose moiety of cyanidin 3-O-glucoside, forming the rutinoside (rhamnosyl-(1->6)-glucoside) and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: rhamnose is transferred from UDP-rhamnose to the acceptor sugar.

errors: Charge and hydrogen imbalance: 12.0 H+ on the product side is incorrect for this condensation

Incorrect substrate: enterobactin biosynthesis uses L-serine (not L-seryl-AMP) which is adenylated and condensed; the correct activated serine intermediate in the EntF mechanism is serine loaded onto the carrier protein, and water/AMP balance is not properly represented
Stoichiometric water release not accounted for: trilactone (triester) ring formation and amide bond formation release water molecules
Carrier protein/PPi and ATP usage not represented, making the overall adenylate-based stoichiometry unbalanced
rxn08420.other_comments: This represents enterobactin biosynthesis from 3 molecules of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoyl-adenylate (DHB-AMP) and 3 molecules of an activated serine, forming the cyclic trilactone siderophore enterobactin with release of AMP. The overall direction toward enterobactin is correct in vivo, but the proton count (12 H+) and the use of L-seryl-AMP as written likely do not balance mass/charge correctly.

rxn01795.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) reaction transferring the glucuronosyl moiety from UDP-glucuronate to androsterone, producing androsterone glucuronide and UDP. The atoms balance: UDP-glucuronate donates glucuronate to the acceptor hydroxyl, releasing UDP. The reaction is correctly written as UDPglucuronate + Androsterone -> UDP + Androsterone glucuronide. In vivo, glucuronidation is a phase II conjugation reaction that proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (conjugating) direction.

errors: Substrate and product names are inconsistent: the substrate is a glyceroserine ether lipid lacking a phosphate, while the product is a glycero-l-phosphoserine (phospho) compound - the phosphate group is unbalanced

Stoichiometry is not balanced: reducing two C20 geranylgeranyl-type chains to fully saturated phytanyl chains requires reduction of multiple double bonds; the geranyl/3-hydroxygeranyl groups (C10 units) shown do not match the C20 phytanyl products in the product name
Phosphate (Pi or equivalent) is missing from the substrate side to account for the phosphoserine product
NADP should be written as NADP+ to balance charge
rxn10556.other_comments: This is intended to be a saturation (hydrogenation) reaction reducing unsaturated isoprenoid ether chains (geranyl-type) to saturated phytanyl chains using NADPH, a step in archaeal ether lipid biosynthesis. However, the substrate and product names are mismatched (geranyl vs phytanyl chain lengths, and absence vs presence of a phosphate group), making the reaction as written stoichiometrically unbalanced.

errors: Charge imbalance: UDP (-3) + H2O (0) on left should equal UMP (-2) + Phosphate (-2) + 2 H+ (+2) on right. Left side charge = -3; right side charge = -2. The reaction as written produces 2 H+ but hydrolysis of a phosphoanhydride bond releases only 1 H+ at physiological pH. Correct form should generate 1 H+: H2O + UDP -> UMP + Phosphate + H+, which balances charge (-3 = -2 + -2 + 1 = -3).
rxn00116.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of UDP to UMP and inorganic phosphate by a UDP phosphohydrolase (nucleoside diphosphatase). Mass appears balanced for P (one anhydride cleaved), but proton/charge stoichiometry is off as written; should release 1 H+ rather than 2. Hydrolysis of the phosphoanhydride bond is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Charge imbalance: phospholipase A2 hydrolysis of one ester bond produces one fatty acid (ddca, dodecanoate) and one lysophospholipid plus one proton, but this reaction shows 2.0 H+ being released for cleavage of a single ester bond
Proton stoichiometry incorrect: cleavage of one acyl ester yielding a carboxylic acid should release at most 1 H+ at physiological pH, not 2
rxn09144.other_comments: This is a phospholipase A2 reaction hydrolyzing the sn-2 ester bond of 1,2-didodecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a phosphatidic acid with two C12:0 chains), releasing dodecanoate (ddca, lauric acid) and producing 1-dodecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a lysophosphatidic acid). Hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn04395.other_comments: This is the anthocyanidin synthase / leucoanthocyanidin dioxygenase (ANS/LDOX) type reaction, a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase. It uses O2 and 2-oxoglutarate, producing CO2 and succinate as expected for this enzyme class. cis-3,4-leucopelargonidin (leucopelargonidin, a flavan-3,4-diol) is oxidized; aromadendrin (dihydrokaempferol) is the dihydroflavonol product. Mass and atom balance is consistent: 2-oxoglutarate (C5H6O5) + O2 yields succinate (C4H6O4) + CO2, accounting for the oxidative decarboxylation, and the substrate loses water to become the more oxidized product, balancing the extra H2O on the product side.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance for oxygen and hydrogen. Reactant side has 2 H2O2 (4 O, 4 H) + 1 H+ + palmitate (C16H31O2-). Product side has 3 H2O + CO2 + pentadecanal (C15H30O). Carbon balances (16 = 15 + 1), but oxygen: left 4(from H2O2)+2(palmitate) = 6 O; right 3(H2O)+2(CO2)+1(aldehyde) = 6 O - oxygen balances. Hydrogen: left 4(H2O2)+1(H+)+31(palmitate) = 36 H; right 6(H2O)+30(aldehyde) = 36 H - hydrogen balances. Charge: left -1(palmitate)+1(H+) = 0; right 0 - charge balances. The reaction is actually balanced.
Re-examination shows no clear imbalance; original concern unfounded.
rxn01246.other_comments: The reaction represents a peroxide-driven oxidative decarboxylation of palmitate (C16) to pentadecanal (C15) plus CO2, consuming 2 H2O2 and releasing 3 H2O. Upon checking, atoms and charge balance: C 16=16, O 6=6, H 36=36, charge 0=0. [directionality_note] This is an alpha-oxidation / oxidative decarboxylation type reaction (a fatty acid peroxygenase producing a one-carbon-shorter aldehyde), which proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction given consumption of H2O2.

rxn04780.other_comments: This is a hydrolytic deamination reaction where N-cyclopropylammeline is converted to N-cyclopropylammelide, replacing an amino group with a hydroxyl/keto group and releasing ammonia. The reaction consumes water and a proton, releasing NH3 (or NH4+). The atom balance is consistent: an amino group (-NH2) is replaced by an oxygen from water, with the nitrogen leaving as ammonia. Such amidohydrolase/deaminase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction toward ammonia release.

rxn01527.other_comments: This is the zeatin O-glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.203). UDP-glucose serves as the glycosyl donor, transferring a glucose moiety to the hydroxyl group of the zeatin side chain to form O-beta-D-glucosylzeatin, releasing UDP. The reaction is balanced: UDP-glucose (C15H24N2O17P2) + zeatin (C10H13N5O) yields UDP (C9H14N2O12P2) + O-glucosylzeatin (C16H23N5O6). Glucosyltransferases using UDP-sugar donors are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the direction of glycoside formation due to the high-energy UDP-glucose bond.

rxn08943.other_comments: This is the maltodextrin phosphorylase reaction (MalP, EC 2.4.1.1), which catalyzes the phosphorolytic cleavage of an alpha-1,4-glucosidic bond at the non-reducing end of maltoheptaose, releasing glucose-1-phosphate and shortening the chain to maltohexaose. The stoichiometry is balanced: maltoheptaose (G7) plus inorganic phosphate yields G1P plus maltohexaose (G6). The reaction is freely reversible in vitro; in vivo direction depends on the ratio of phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate, but it generally proceeds in the degradative (phosphorolytic) direction during maltodextrin catabolism.

rxn00151.other_comments: This is pyruvate, orthophosphate dikinase (PPDK, EC 2.7.9.1). The reaction ATP + Pi + pyruvate -> AMP + PPi + PEP is mass and charge balanced: ATP (C10H12N5O13P3, charge -4) + Pi (HPO4, -2) + pyruvate (C3H3O3, -1) gives PEP (C3H4O6P, -3) + AMP (-2) + PPi (-3) + 2 H+. Charge: left -7, right -8+2 = -6; note that net proton count balances charge. Atoms balance overall. In C4/CAM plants and many bacteria this enzyme operates in the gluconeogenic direction (pyruvate to PEP) physiologically, though it is biochemically reversible.

rxn07315.other_comments: This reaction (KEGG R07484) is part of the ergosterol/phytosterol biosynthesis pathway. It represents a delta(8) to delta(7) sterol isomerase step (or related rearrangement) converting 4alpha-methylfecosterol to 24-methylenelophenol. Both substrates are C29 sterol intermediates with the same molecular formula (C29H48O), so the reaction is an isomerization and is mass/stoichiometrically balanced as a 1:1 conversion. In vivo this proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward the sterol end product.

rxn01024.other_comments: The reaction is the condensation of acetaldehyde, ammonia, and hydrogen cyanide (a Strecker-type synthesis) to form alpha-aminopropionitrile (2-aminopropanenitrile) with release of water. Mass balance: reactants C2H4O (acetaldehyde) + NH3 + HCN = C3H8N2O; products H2O + H+ + alpha-aminopropiononitrile (C3H6N2). C: 2+1=3 vs 3 OK. N: 1+1=2 vs 2 OK. O: 1 vs 1 OK. H: acetaldehyde 4 + NH3 3 + HCN 1 = 8; products H2O 2 + H+ 1 + nitrile 6 = 9. There is a hydrogen imbalance of 1 (charge also unbalanced by the extra H+ on product side). The reaction appears to be charge/H imbalanced as written.

rxn11346.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction between L-methionine and 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (4MOP, the keto acid of leucine). The amino group is transferred from L-methionine to 4MOP, yielding L-leucine and 4-methylthio-2-oxobutyrate (the keto acid of methionine, also known as KMB). The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: each side has one amino acid and one 2-oxo acid, and the carbon/nitrogen/sulfur atoms balance. Aminotransferase (transaminase) reactions are near-equilibrium and freely reversible in vivo, with direction governed by relative substrate/product concentrations.

rxn02536.other_comments: This is the secologanin synthase (CYP72A1) reaction, a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that oxidatively cleaves the cyclopentane ring of loganin to form secologanin. The stoichiometry is balanced: loganin (C17H26O10) + O2 + NADPH + H+ yields secologanin (C17H24O10) + NADP+ + 2 H2O. This is consistent with a typical P450 reaction where one oxygen atom is incorporated/released and two waters are produced (one from the cleaved O2 oxygen and one from the consumed reducing equivalents).

rxn07684.other_comments: This is a NAD+-dependent oxidation of a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA to a 3-oxoacyl-CoA, part of the jasmonic acid biosynthesis beta-oxidation pathway. OPC6-CoA refers to 3-oxo-2-(2-pentenyl)cyclopentane-1-hexanoyl-CoA derivatives. The reaction is catalyzed by 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase. Stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of a secondary alcohol (3-hydroxy) to a ketone (3-oxo) removes 2 hydrogens, transferred as a hydride to NAD+ (forming NADH) plus a released proton (H+).

errors: Hydrogen (H+) is not balanced: left side has 3 H+ plus 2 NADPH contributing hydride; the product side accounts for H2O and 2 NADP but the proton/charge balance is inconsistent. A typical fatty acid synthase elongation cycle (one methylmalonyl-CoA elongation) consumes 2 NADPH + 2 H+ (not 3 H+) per round, releasing CO2, CoA, and H2O.
Oxygen balance should be rechecked: methylmalonyl-CoA elongation produces one H2O, but the proton stoichiometry suggests an off-by-one error in H+.

Use of D-methylmalonyl-CoA: typically the (S)/(2S) or specifically the methylmalonyl-CoA stereoisomer used by fatty acid synthase-type elongation should be verified; methylmalonyl-CoA-based chain extension adds a C2 unit plus a methyl branch (a propionate-derived C3 increment), so the carbon increment from C22 (behenic, tri-methyl) to C24 (lignoceric, tetra-methyl) plus an extra methyl should be checked against +3 carbons.
rxn13473.other_comments: This represents a fatty acid synthase-type chain elongation using methylmalonyl-CoA as the extender unit, adding a methyl-branched two-carbon unit to tri-methyl behenic acid (C22) to yield a tetra-methyl lignoceric acid (C24)-type product, with release of CO2, CoA, and H2O and consumption of NADPH for the reductive steps. The biosynthetic reductive elongation is essentially irreversible in vivo (driven by decarboxylation of the malonyl/methylmalonyl unit), hence forward.

rxn04152.other_comments: This is the first step of the aerobic Mg-protoporphyrin IX monomethyl ester oxidative cyclase reaction (EC 1.14.13.81), catalyzed by AcsF/BchE-type enzymes in bacteriochlorophyll/chlorophyll biosynthesis. The aerobic cyclase hydroxylates the 13(1) position using O2 and NADPH as reductant. Stoichiometry balances: one O atom from O2 is incorporated as the hydroxyl, the other is reduced to water; NADPH provides reducing equivalents to NADP+. Atoms and charges balance with NADPH + O2 + H+ -> H2O + NADP+ + hydroxylated product.

errors: Reaction is unbalanced. The oxidation of bis(glutathionyl)spermine (dithiol) to bis(glutathionyl)spermine disulfide releases 2 H and 2 electrons. As written, NADP+ + H+ on the left and NADPH on the right does not balance H atoms or charge. The correct form should be: Bis(glutathionyl)spermine disulfide + NADPH + H+ <=> 2 Bis(glutathionyl)spermine + NADP+ (reduction direction), or with proper coupling. The stated reductant/oxidant pairing is reversed relative to thiol/disulfide chemistry.

Hydrogen/proton balance incorrect: reduction of a disulfide consumes NADPH + H+, while as written NADPH appears on the product (oxidized) side alongside the disulfide, which is chemically inconsistent.
rxn12046.other_comments: This describes a glutathionylspermine reductase-type reaction (analogous to glutathione/trypanothione reductase). Physiologically these enzymes use NADPH to reduce the disulfide form back to the dithiol; thus in vivo the favored direction is disulfide + NADPH + H+ -> 2 thiol-conjugate + NADP+, i.e. the reverse of how it is written here.

errors: Unbalanced as written: GSH + trichloroethene (C2HCl3) -> S-(1,2-dichlorovinyl)glutathione (DCVG) + Cl- + H+. The reaction releases one chloride and a proton; the displayed equation omits the H+ and the mass/charge balance should be verified. Net: GSH + TCE -> DCVG + Cl- + H+.
rxn04903.other_comments: This is a glutathione S-transferase (GST)-catalyzed conjugation of reduced glutathione (GSH) to trichloroethylene (TCE), producing the conjugate S-(1,2-dichlorovinyl)glutathione (DCVG) with displacement of a chloride ion. Conjugation reactions of this type are strongly thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Atom imbalance: 4-Hydroxyphenylacetate (C8H8O3) + H2O (H2O) gives C8H10O4, but products Acetate (C2H3O2-) + Quinol/hydroquinone (C6H6O2) sum to C8H9O4, which does not balance in carbon distribution or hydrogen/charge
Mechanistically implausible: hydrolysis of 4-hydroxyphenylacetate at the ester/amide bond would not cleave the carbon-carbon bond required to release acetate and hydroquinone
4-Hydroxyphenylacetate is a carboxylic acid (phenylacetate derivative), not an aryl ester, so it is not a valid substrate for an aryl-ester hydrolase
rxn04702.other_comments: The reaction proposes hydrolysis of 4-hydroxyphenylacetate into acetate and quinol (hydroquinone). This requires breaking a C-C bond between the aromatic ring and the acetate side chain, which a simple hydrolase cannot do. An aryl-ester hydrolase cleaves ester bonds (O-acyl linkages), not the C-C bond present here. The stoichiometry also does not properly balance.

errors: Atom imbalance: 3-oxoadipate (C6H8O5, as dianion C6H6O5) loses only 2 H to form maleylacetate; the reaction as written with NAD+/NADH is not balanced. 3-oxoadipate is a saturated dicarboxylate while maleylacetate contains a C=C double bond, so the conversion is a dehydrogenation, but the proper redox partner and H balance must be verified.

Maleylacetate is normally produced by oxidative reactions involving O2 (e.g., from chlorocatechols via ring cleavage), not by simple NAD+ dehydrogenation of 3-oxoadipate; this NAD-coupled interconversion is biochemically questionable.
rxn02141.other_comments: The reaction proposes oxidation of 3-oxoadipate by NAD+ to give maleylacetate (introducing a C=C double bond) plus NADH and H+. While the redox bookkeeping of a dehydrogenation (removing 2 H as NADH + H+) could in principle balance, the assignment of 3-oxoadipate as the direct NAD-dependent precursor of maleylacetate is biologically dubious; maleylacetate is typically formed in chlorocatechol/aromatic degradation pathways and reduced (by maleylacetate reductase) to 3-oxoadipate using NADH, i.e., the physiological flow is the reverse.

rxn05072.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by myo-inositol-1-phosphate synthase (MIPS, also called 1L-myo-inositol-1-phosphate synthase / inositol-3-phosphate synthase). It converts D-glucose-6-phosphate to 1L-myo-inositol-1-phosphate (equivalently 1D-myo-inositol-3-phosphate). The reaction requires NAD+ as a tightly bound cofactor (intramolecular oxidation-reduction, aldol cyclization), but NAD+ is regenerated so it is not consumed net. Stoichiometry of the C6 phosphorylated sugar to inositol phosphate is balanced 1:1, so the equation is atom-balanced as written. In vivo this is the committed, essentially irreversible step in de novo inositol biosynthesis, proceeding in the direction glucose-6-phosphate to inositol-3-phosphate.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the formation of a phosphoanhydride-to-aminoacyl-adenylate linkage releasing PPi typically does not generate 2 H+; the proton stoichiometry appears incorrect. Standard aminoacyl-adenylate formation (ATP + amino acid -> aminoacyl-AMP + PPi) is essentially charge-balanced with at most a single proton change depending on protonation states.
rxn00486.other_comments: This represents the activation of L-phenylalanine via adenylylation, forming phenylalanyl-adenylate (Phe-AMP) and releasing pyrophosphate, analogous to the first half-reaction of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (or NRPS adenylation domains). In vivo this step is reversible at the adenylate level but is typically pulled forward by subsequent PPi hydrolysis and transfer of the aminoacyl group.

rxn02665.other_comments: This is the 7beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.201), oxidizing the 7beta-hydroxyl group of a steroid to a 7-oxo (keto) group, with NADP+ reduced to NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADP+ + 7beta-hydroxysteroid <=> NADPH + H+ + 7-oxosteroid. The hydride and proton accounting (one H to NADPH, one H+ released) is correct. The enzyme catalyzes a reversible oxidoreduction; physiological direction depends on the NADPH/NADP+ ratio and substrate availability.

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: cobalt-precorrin-5B to cobalt-precorrin-6A conversion is a methylation at C1 that releases an acetyl group (as acetaldehyde), so simple methyl transfer plus 2 H+ does not balance; the C and H atoms do not reconcile
Proton stoichiometry of 2.0 H+ appears incorrect for a methyltransferase reaction; typically SAM-dependent methylation releases SAH and H+ in a 1:1 manner at most
Product should be cobalt-precorrin-6A (the immediate product of CbiF), not generically 'cobalt-precorrin 6'
rxn07587.other_comments: This is the CbiF reaction in the anaerobic (cobalt-early) cobalamin/B12 biosynthesis pathway, a SAM-dependent C1 methyltransferase converting cobalt-precorrin-5B to cobalt-precorrin-6A. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are strongly forward-driven in vivo. The stoichiometry as written (especially the H+ count and atom balance) should be verified against the actual chemical formulas of the precorrin intermediates.

rxn12294.other_comments: This represents L-lactate oxidation by a quinone-dependent lactate dehydrogenase (e.g., LldD/respiratory L-lactate dehydrogenase). L-Lactate is oxidized to pyruvate, transferring 2 electrons and 2 protons to ubiquinone (Q), reducing it to ubiquinol (QH2). The reaction is balanced: lactate (C3H5O3-) loses 2H to become pyruvate (C3H3O3-), and Q + 2H -> QH2. Stoichiometry and electron balance are correct. In vivo, the strong driving force from quinone reduction and downstream respiratory electron flow makes this effectively irreversible in the oxidative direction.

errors: Substrate/product stoichiometry and identity mismatch: enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI) reduces a 2,3-trans-enoyl-ACP double bond using NADH, but the substrate is listed as 'trans-3-cis-11' (a 3-position and 11-position double bond), which is inconsistent with the standard enoyl-ACP reductase substrate (trans-2-enoyl-ACP)

The substrate has two double bonds (trans-3 and cis-11) while the product (octadecenoyl-ACP, n-C18:1) has only one, implying only one double bond is reduced; this is not the typical FabI reaction which fully saturates the 2,3 position to acyl-ACP without leaving residual unsaturation unless this is the special cis-vaccenate (anaerobic) pathway
Product name 'Octadecenoyl-ACP' is ambiguous regarding double-bond position/geometry; for cis-vaccenoyl-ACP it should specify cis-11-octadecenoyl-ACP
rxn08398.other_comments: This represents an enoyl-ACP reductase (NADH-dependent, FabI-type) step in fatty acid elongation producing an unsaturated C18:1 acyl-ACP (vaccenoyl-ACP). The NADH-driven reduction of an enoyl group is strongly exergonic and physiologically proceeds toward the reduced acyl-ACP product, retaining the cis-11 double bond from the anaerobic unsaturated fatty acid pathway.

errors: The reaction is missing water (H2O) as a substrate; the decyclization (ring-opening hydrolysis) of 2-hydroxy-2-hydropyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate to 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde requires the addition of one water molecule to balance both mass and atoms
rxn03097.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate lactonase (PDC hydrolase) in the protocatechuate 4,5-cleavage pathway. The enzyme hydrolyzes the lactone ring of 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate to yield 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde (in its enol/hydrated form). The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward the open-chain product as part of aromatic compound degradation.

rxn11718.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of arachidonoyl-CoA (a long-chain acyl-CoA) to free arachidonate and CoA, catalyzed by a thioesterase (acyl-CoA hydrolase, EC 3.1.2.2). The thioester bond hydrolysis: H2O + arachidonoyl-CoA -> arachidonate + CoA + H+. Mass and charge appear balanced (the thioester C-S bond is cleaved, water adds, releasing the carboxylate, a proton, and free CoA-SH). In vivo, thioester hydrolysis is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn02274.other_comments: This is a decarboxylation of 2-oxo-5-guanidinopentanoate (the alpha-keto acid derived from arginine) yielding 4-guanidinobutanal and CO2. Stoichiometry balances: substrate C6H11N3O3 plus H+ gives CO2 (CO2) plus 4-guanidinobutanal (C5H11N3O). Carbon: 6 = 1 + 5; nitrogen 3 = 3; oxygen 3 = 2 + 1; hydrogen 11 + 1 = 12 = 11 + 1 (CO2 has no H, aldehyde has 11). Balanced. Alpha-keto acid decarboxylations releasing CO2 are essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written using FAD/FADH2 as the free cofactor pair is questionable; the enzyme name specifies '(acceptor)', indicating a generic electron acceptor rather than free FAD/FADH2. Gluconate 2-dehydrogenase is typically a flavoprotein with covalently/tightly bound FAD that transfers electrons to an external acceptor (e.g., cytochrome, ubiquinone, or PMS/DCIP in vitro), so free FAD should not appear as a soluble substrate.
Charge/protonation conventions: GLCN (gluconate) is the anion while '2-Keto-D-gluconic acid' is written as the protonated acid; nomenclature should be consistent (2-dehydro-D-gluconate).
rxn14117.other_comments: This represents gluconate 2-dehydrogenase, oxidizing D-gluconate at C2 to 2-keto(2-dehydro)-D-gluconate with concomitant reduction of a flavin/acceptor. Atom balance for the C6 backbone is fine (oxidation of a CHOH to C=O), and FAD + 2H = FADH2 balances the two electrons/hydrogens. In vivo this oxidation runs in the forward direction (gluconate -> 2-ketogluconate).

rxn06012.other_comments: This reaction represents ceramide synthase (acyl-CoA:sphingosine N-acyltransferase), where an acyl group from acyl-CoA is transferred to the amino group of a sphingoid base (sphingosine/sphinganine) to form ceramide, releasing CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: the amide bond formation releases CoA and a proton (H+). In vivo, this biosynthetic acylation is thermodynamically driven by the high-energy thioester bond of acyl-CoA and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction toward ceramide synthesis.

rxn00862.other_comments: This is histidine aminotransferase (histidine:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase), transferring the amino group from L-histidine to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and imidazol-5-yl-pyruvate (imidazole pyruvate). The reaction is balanced: both sides carry the amino group transfer, with C, N, and charge conserved. Like most aminotransferase (transaminase) reactions, the near-equilibrium thermodynamics make it physiologically reversible, though it commonly proceeds toward histidine degradation (forming imidazole pyruvate and glutamate).

rxn03978.other_comments: This is the hydroxylamine/ammonia oxidation to nitrite reaction catalyzed by enzymes like hydroxylamine oxidoreductase / ammonia-related oxidoreductases (EC 1.7.2.6 type, ammonia:ferricytochrome-c oxidoreductase). Checking mass balance: NH3 has N, 3H; 2 H2O adds 2O, 4H. Total left (excluding cytochrome): N, 7H, 2O. Right: nitrite NO2- has N, 2O; plus 7 H+. So N:1=1, O:2=2, H:7=7. Charge: left has 6x(3+)=+18 from cytochrome, others neutral, total +18. Right: 7 H+ (+7) + nitrite (-1) + 6x(2+)=+12, total +18. Mass and charge balanced.

rxn11984.other_comments: This is a histone acetyltransferase (HAT) reaction transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the epsilon-amino group of a lysine residue in histone, producing CoA, a proton, and acetylated histone. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred from CoA to the lysine, and the released proton accounts for the loss of a positive charge on the lysine amino group upon acetylation. In vivo, acetyl-CoA is the acetyl donor and the reaction proceeds toward histone acetylation; deacetylation is carried out by a separate enzyme class (HDACs), so this acetyltransferase reaction is effectively unidirectional.

rxn00529.other_comments: This is the tyrosine decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.25), a PLP-dependent enzyme that decarboxylates L-tyrosine to form tyramine and CO2. The stoichiometry is balanced: L-tyrosine (C9H11NO3) plus a proton yields tyramine (C8H12NO, as the protonated amine cation) plus CO2. Mass and charge balance correctly with the proton consumed to balance the loss of the carboxylate.

errors: This is a transport reaction representing the same metabolite (D-Ribose) and a proton (H+) on both sides; as written with identical compartments it is a null reaction (no net change). For a proper transport reaction, the species should be annotated with different compartments, e.g., H+[out] + D-Ribose[out] <=> H+[in] + D-Ribose[in].
rxn09663.other_comments: The reaction appears to be a proton-coupled D-ribose transport (symport) across a membrane. As written, both sides are identical (no compartment distinction), making it stoichiometrically null. Atomically/charge balanced trivially. If compartments are added it represents H+/ribose symport.

rxn06468.other_comments: This reaction represents protoaphin-aglucone hydro-lyase (cyclizing), EC 4.2.1.104, which converts protoaphin aglucone to xanthoaphin via dehydration and cyclization. The reaction as written shows H+ + protoaphin aglucone yielding H2O + xanthoaphin, consistent with a hydro-lyase removing water. Stoichiometry is balanced for the lyase-type elimination of water with cyclization. This is part of the aphin pigment biosynthesis pathway in aphids, proceeding protoaphin to xanthoaphin to chrysoaphin to erythroaphin.

rxn01877.other_comments: This is the guanidinoacetate kinase reaction (analogous to creatine kinase). ATP phosphorylates glycocyamine (guanidoacetate) to form phosphoguanidinoacetate (N-phospho-guanidinoacetate) and ADP, releasing a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (-4) + guanidoacetate (0 net at relevant pH, zwitterionic carboxylate plus guanidinium) yields ADP (-3) + phosphoguanidinoacetate (-2 with phosphoryl group) + H+, consistent with the typical phosphagen kinase formulation.

rxn01130.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADP-dependent secondary alcohol dehydrogenase (Propan-2-ol:NADP+ oxidoreductase). It interconverts acetone and 2-propanol (isopropanol). The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ + acetone (C3H6O) yields NADP+ + 2-propanol (C3H8O). Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance correctly. The named direction (alcohol oxidase by EC convention, 2-propanol -> acetone) is written here in the reduction direction (acetone -> 2-propanol). Alcohol dehydrogenases of this type are typically reversible, with actual in vivo direction depending on cofactor and substrate ratios.

rxn04299.other_comments: This reaction represents the epimerization of dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-glucose to dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-allose, an interconversion at the C-3 position catalyzed by a 3-epimerase (EC 5.1.3.-, e.g. dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxyglucose 3-epimerase). Both substrate and product are isomers with identical molecular formulas (C16H24N2O15P2), so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced. As an epimerase/isomerase reaction, it is thermodynamically near-equilibrium and freely reversible, though in vivo flux is typically pulled toward the allose derivative for downstream deoxysugar biosynthesis.

rxn01762.other_comments: This reaction represents the interconversion (mutarotation/ring isomerization) between the open-chain or pyranose form of L-rhamnose and its furanose ring form (L-rhamnofuranose). Both are isomers of the same sugar (C6H12O5), so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced with a 1:1 ratio and conserves all atoms. Such ring tautomerization is spontaneous in solution and freely reversible.

rxn11710.other_comments: This is the thioester hydrolysis of icosanoyl-CoA (arachidoyl-CoA, C20:0 acyl-CoA) catalyzed by an acyl-CoA thioesterase. Stoichiometry is balanced: water cleaves the thioester bond releasing free CoA (with thiol) and arachidic acid (icosanoic acid, C20:0). The H+ accounts for proton balance from the carboxylic acid/CoA thiol. Mass and charge balance correctly.

rxn00909.other_comments: This is methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), which catalyzes the reduction of 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate to 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the methylene group is reduced to a methyl group using two reducing equivalents from FADH2, which is oxidized to FAD. In vivo, this reaction is physiologically irreversible in the forward direction (toward 5-methyl-THF), committing one-carbon units to methionine synthesis. Note that the physiological electron donor is NAD(P)H, with FAD serving as the bound prosthetic group; this representation uses FADH2/FAD as the redox couple.

rxn10699.other_comments: This represents a thioesterase/hydrolase reaction in which water hydrolyzes the thioester bond linking the phthiocerol precursor to the acyl carrier protein (ACP), releasing the free phthiocerol precursor and regenerating holo-ACP. The mass balance appears reasonable as written, assuming the bound and free precursor masses differ only by the ACP thioester linkage and the added water. Thioester hydrolysis is strongly exergonic and thermodynamically favored in the direction of hydrolysis, so it proceeds essentially irreversibly in vivo toward product release.

rxn08948.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of D-mannose-6-phosphate by a phosphatase, yielding D-mannose and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: H2O + mannose-6-phosphate (C6H13O9P) gives D-mannose (C6H12O6) + phosphate (HPO4/Pi). Atoms balance with water adding across the phosphoester bond. Phosphatase-catalyzed hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

errors: Mass imbalance: the meta-cleavage of a catechol-type diol (2'-aminobiphenyl-2,3-diol) by an extradiol dioxygenase incorporates both atoms of O2 to open the aromatic ring; the product 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-(2'-aminophenyl)-hexa-2,4-dienoate should not also release an H+ unless protons are explicitly balanced. As written, oxygen and hydrogen balance should be verified - ring fission products of this type are typically charge/proton balanced without a free H+, suggesting the H+ may be erroneous or the substrate protonation state inconsistent.
rxn03715.other_comments: This is an extradiol (meta) ring-cleavage dioxygenase reaction (analogous to the carbazole degradation pathway, e.g. CarBaBb), where 2'-aminobiphenyl-2,3-diol undergoes O2-dependent meta-cleavage to form a 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-hexadienoate (HOPDA-type) product. Such dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to O2 incorporation and ring opening.

errors: Stoichiometric/chemical inconsistency: gamma-carotene (an acyclic/monocyclic carotene, C40H56) cannot be directly converted to alpha-carotene (a bicyclic carotene with one beta-ring and one epsilon-ring) in a single step; these differ in cyclization and the reaction as written omits required intermediates
Molecular formulas are not balanced as a simple isomerization without specifying the ring-forming/cyclase activities and any required cofactors
rxn04774.other_comments: The input is a carotenoid biosynthesis interconversion between gamma-carotene (monocyclic, beta-ring) and alpha-carotene (bicyclic, beta- plus epsilon-ring). In typical biosynthetic pathways gamma-carotene is cyclized further toward beta- or alpha-carotene; lycopene cyclases catalyze ring formation, which is biosynthetically forward (toward the cyclized product). However, the direct gamma-to-alpha step is mechanistically questionable since alpha-carotene formation usually proceeds via delta-carotene or through separate epsilon/beta cyclase actions.

rxn00561.other_comments: This reaction describes guanidinoacetate (glycocyamine) amidinohydrolase / amidohydrolase activity. Glycocyamine is guanidinoacetate (H2N-C(=NH)-NH-CH2-COOH). Hydrolysis cleaves the guanidino group. The mass balance checks out: glycocyamine (C3H7N3O2) + H2O (H2O) yields glycine (C2H5NO2) + urea (CH4N2O). Carbon: 3 = 2+1; Nitrogen: 3 = 1+2; the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. Note that this is more precisely an amidinohydrolase, transferring the amidino group; the products as written (glycine + urea) require an amidinohydrolase yielding urea, which is consistent with hydrolytic cleavage of the C-N bond.

errors: Water stoichiometry imbalance: each round of fatty acid elongation (condensation, ketoreduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction) releases one H2O, so 5 cycles produce 5 H2O, but the dehydration step plus other balances need verification; the elongation from C7 to C17 adds 10 carbons (5 malonyl units), consistent with 5 cycles
NADPH/NADP balance: 2 NADPH per cycle x 5 cycles = 10 NADPH, consistent

Proton (H+) balance appears off: condensation/reduction net proton accounting should be checked; 10 H+ consumed with 10 NADPH is plausible but CO2 release and ACP regeneration may require rebalancing of H+ and H2O
Carbon balance: Iso-C7 (7C) + 5 malonyl (5x3=15C, but 5 CO2 lost = 5C) yields net 7+10 = 17C, consistent with Iso-C17:0
rxn13672.other_comments: This represents iterative fatty acid elongation by beta-ketoacyl synthase + associated FAS reductase/dehydratase activities, extending Iso-C7:0-ACP to Iso-C17:0-ACP via 5 malonyl-ACP additions. Carbon, NADPH, and CO2 stoichiometry are internally consistent (5 cycles), but the H2O and H+ balance should be carefully verified.

rxn07852.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of trans-zeatin riboside triphosphate to the diphosphate plus inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: H2O hydrolyzes a terminal phosphoanhydride bond, releasing phosphate and a proton. Phosphoanhydride hydrolysis is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction written (triphosphate to diphosphate).

rxn04941.other_comments: This reaction represents D-arabinitol:NADP+ oxidoreductase (EC 1.1.1.11). D-Lyxitol is a synonym for D-arabinitol, and D-Lyxulose corresponds to the oxidized ketose product (D-xylulose region). The reaction oxidizes the polyol to the ketose, transferring a hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced: one secondary alcohol oxidized to ketone, with NADP+ reduced to NADPH and release of one proton. Charge and mass appear balanced.

rxn14246.other_comments: This is a homocysteine desulfhydrase / gamma-lyase type reaction (L-homocysteine hydrogen-sulfide-lyase). L-homocysteine (C4H9NO2S) is cleaved to release H2S and form 2-aminobut-2-enoate (dehydrobutyrate / 2-aminocrotonate, the enamine tautomer that hydrolyzes to 2-oxobutanoate + NH3). Stoichiometry balances: C4H9NO2S yields H+ + H2S (H2S) + C4H6NO2- (2-aminobut-2-enoate). C: 4=4, N: 1=1, O: 2=2, S: 1=1, H: 9 = 1+2+6, charge: 0 = +1 + 0 + (-1). The reaction is mass and charge balanced.

errors: NAD/NADH should not be involved in this reaction; the enzyme is a prenyltransferase, not an oxidoreductase
The reaction couples a decarboxylation and prenylation; the redox cofactors (NAD/NADH) are spurious and unbalanced
Atom balance is incorrect: with NAD->NADH added, hydrogen and electron counts do not balance with the prenylation/decarboxylation chemistry

Prenyl donor should be all-trans-octaprenyl diphosphate (C40) for octaprenyltransferase, not heptaprenyl diphosphate (C35); product 2dmmq7 (demethylmenaquinone-7) would correspond to a heptaprenyl chain, creating an inconsistency with the enzyme name 'octaprenyltransferase'
rxn05267.other_comments: This is the MenA-type reaction converting 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoate (DHNA) to demethylmenaquinone via prenylation and concomitant decarboxylation, releasing CO2 and PPi. The correct reaction is: DHNA + polyprenyl-PP -> demethylmenaquinol (DMK) + CO2 + PPi. No NAD/NADH should participate. Also the prenyl chain length notation is inconsistent (heptaprenyl vs product 2dmmq7 vs the enzyme name octaprenyltransferase).

rxn07573.other_comments: This is the second step of the fatty acid elongation cycle (a beta-ketoacyl-CoA reductase / 3-oxoacyl-CoA reductase reaction). NADPH + H+ reduces the 3-oxo group of 3-oxostearoyl-CoA (C18 3-ketoacyl-CoA) to the 3-hydroxyl, producing (R)-3-hydroxystearoyl-CoA and NADP+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: NADPH(2H from NADPH + proton) reduces the ketone to alcohol. In vivo this NADPH-dependent reduction within the elongation cycle proceeds in the reduction direction (toward 3-hydroxystearoyl-CoA).

rxn04863.other_comments: This reaction represents the action of a 9-lipoxygenase (linoleate 9S-lipoxygenase), which catalyzes the dioxygenation of linoleate (linoleic acid) using molecular O2 to form 9(S)-HPOD (9(S)-hydroperoxy-10,12-octadecadienoic acid). The stoichiometry is balanced: linoleate (C18H31O2-) plus O2 incorporates both oxygen atoms as a hydroperoxide group, yielding 9(S)-HPOD (C18H31O4-). Both oxygen atoms from O2 are retained in the product. The reaction is physiologically driven in the forward direction because the dioxygenation is highly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn07751.other_comments: This reaction represents an N-demethylation of theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine) to form 7-methylxanthine, catalyzed by an N-demethylase (monooxygenase). The methyl group removed appears as formaldehyde. NADH and O2 serve as cosubstrates, with O2 split between H2O and the oxidized methyl carbon. Atom balance checks out: theobromine (C7H8N4O2) loses a CH2 (released as formaldehyde, CH2O) to give 7-methylxanthine (C6H6N4O2). NADH + H+ + O2 -> NAD+ + H2O accounts for the redox/oxygen chemistry. C, H, N, O all balance. Monooxygenase reactions consuming O2 and NADH are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the demethylation direction.

errors: The reaction shows H+ + D-Gulitol on both sides with no compartment distinction; as written it is a null reaction (identical reactants and products). A proper symport transport reaction should specify compartments, e.g. H+[e] + D-Gulitol[e] <=> H+[c] + D-Gulitol[c]. Note also that D-Gulitol (D-glucitol/sorbitol) is the same molecule named differently; the description references 'glucitol' while the metabolite is named 'D-Gulitol'.
rxn13127.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport (transport) of the sugar alcohol D-glucitol/sorbitol from the extracellular to the cytoplasmic compartment. As written, however, the compartments are not indicated, making it a trivial identity reaction. Biologically, proton-coupled sugar uptake is typically directional into the cell.

rxn14156.other_comments: This is an isomerase (hydroxymutase/isomerase) reaction in the methionine chain-elongation pathway for glucosinolate biosynthesis, analogous to the isopropylmalate isomerase (LeuCD) reaction in leucine biosynthesis. It converts 2-(7'-methylthio)heptylmalate to 3-(7'-methylthio)heptylmalate via a dehydration/rehydration mechanism. The reaction is balanced (intramolecular rearrangement, same molecular formula on both sides). Note: the enzyme name says (3'-methylthio) but the substrates say (7'-methylthio); this naming inconsistency may reflect different elongation cycle numbering but is not a stoichiometric error.

rxn04822.other_comments: This is the oxidation of cis-1,2-dihydronaphthalene-1,2-diol to 1,2-naphthalenediol (naphthalene-1,2-diol), part of the naphthalene degradation pathway (EC 1.3.1.29, cis-1,2-dihydro-1,2-dihydroxynaphthalene dehydrogenase). The reaction is properly balanced: removal of two hydrogens (2H = 2e- + 2H+, with one H+ released and a hydride transferred to NADP+ forming NADPH) aromatizes the ring. Atoms and charges balance correctly. Note that the physiological enzyme typically uses NAD+ rather than NADP+, but the NADP-dependent stoichiometry as written is internally consistent.

errors: Reaction is not balanced as written; beta-carotene (C40H56) and lycopene (C40H56) are isomers with identical formulas, but the conversion involves cyclization requiring no net atom change in formula yet the enzymatic reaction actually proceeds in the opposite biosynthetic direction
Missing cofactors/electron carriers are not strictly required since this is an isomerization-cyclization, but the directionality is misrepresented
rxn11573.other_comments: Both beta-carotene and lycopene share the molecular formula C40H56, so the reaction is formula-balanced (isomerization via cyclization at both ends). However, in vivo the biosynthetic pathway proceeds from lycopene to beta-carotene, catalyzed by lycopene beta-cyclase, which cyclizes both ends of the linear lycopene to form the two beta-ionone rings of beta-carotene. The reaction as written (beta-carotene -> lycopene) is therefore the reverse of the natural direction.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the conversion of arachidonate (C20H32O2 / C20H31O2-) to prostaglandin G2 (PGG2, C20H32O6 / C20H31O6-) requires only 2 O2 to add four oxygen atoms (one hydroperoxy group and the endoperoxide bridge). However, PGG2 formation also requires abstraction of two hydrogen atoms; the net mass balance for cyclooxygenase reaction is arachidonate + 2 O2 -> PGG2, which IS balanced if PGG2 is the hydroperoxide form. No additional reductant is consumed at the cyclooxygenase step, so the atoms balance as written.
Note: the second (peroxidase) step converting PGG2 to PGH2 is not included here, which is fine since this reaction only describes the cyclooxygenase activity.
rxn01163.other_comments: This is the cyclooxygenase (PGHS/COX) reaction: arachidonate plus two molecules of dioxygen yields prostaglandin G2 (PGG2). The reaction adds an endoperoxide bridge and a 15-hydroperoxy group. It is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding strongly in the direction of PGG2 formation.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-L-mannose (the 4-keto sugar) reduced at C4 yields a 2,6-dideoxyhexose; the product naming requires careful checking. The substrate name 'dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-L-mannose' has a 6-deoxy plus a keto at C4, and reduction of the 4-oxo to 4-hydroxyl gives a fully balanced product. However dTDP-L-olivose is a 2,6-dideoxy sugar (deoxy at C2), whereas the listed substrate is 2,6-dideoxy as well, so atom balance between substrate and dTDP-L-olivose is consistent. The main concern is correct identity matching of the 4-keto reductase substrate.
rxn04296.other_comments: This is a NADPH-dependent 4-ketoreductase reaction converting a dTDP-4-keto-2,6-dideoxyhexose into dTDP-L-olivose, part of deoxysugar biosynthesis. The reduction of the C4 keto group consumes NADPH + H+ to give NADP+ and the 4-hydroxy product.

rxn00522.other_comments: This is an L-amino acid oxidase reaction (deaminating oxidative deamination) acting on L-tyrosine. The substrate amino group is oxidized to an imino intermediate, which is hydrolyzed to the 2-oxo acid (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate) with release of ammonia, while O2 is reduced to H2O2. Atom balance checks out: L-tyrosine (C9H11NO3) + H2O + O2 yields p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (C9H8O4) + NH3 + H2O2. C: 9=9, N: 1=1; H: 11+2 = 13 on left vs 8+3+2 = 13 on right; O: 3+1+2 = 6 on left vs 4+2 = 6 on right. Mass and charge balanced.

rxn02706.other_comments: This reaction represents the second amide bond formation catalyzed by glutathionylspermidine synthetase (GspS), or the activity of trypanothione synthetase. ATP-dependent ligation of a second glutathione (GSH) molecule to glutathionylspermidine (Gsp) yields trypanothione (TSH, also known as N1,N8-bis(glutathionyl)spermidine), with release of ADP and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the ATP gamma-phosphate is hydrolyzed to drive amide bond formation, releasing ADP, Pi, and H+. In vivo, ATP-dependent ligase reactions of this type are strongly driven forward.

errors: The reaction is identical on both sides; substrates and products are the same, so no net transport or transformation is represented
If this is meant to be a transport reaction, the two sides should be distinguished by compartment labels (e.g., extracellular vs cytoplasmic), which are missing

Proton symport stoichiometry: typically the transported solute moves with protons in the same direction across the membrane; here protons are unchanged on both sides indicating no symport gradient is captured
rxn12519.other_comments: This is annotated as carbamoyl phosphate transport via proton symport, but as written it shows 2 H+ and carbamoylphosphate on both sides with no compartmental distinction, making it a null (no-net-change) reaction. A valid representation would be: 2 H+[extracellular] + Carbamoylphosphate[extracellular] <=> 2 H+[cytoplasm] + Carbamoylphosphate[cytoplasm].

errors: Atom imbalance: 1,2-dihydroxyfluorene (C13H10O2) plus O2 gives C13H10O4, but the product 2-hydroxy-4-(2-oxo-1,3-dihydro-2H-inden-1-ylidene)but-2-enoic acid (C13H10O4) plus H+ implies an extra proton and charge imbalance; the product should be the carboxylate anion to balance, or H+ should not be a separate product without indicating a deprotonated species
Charge imbalance: left side neutral, right side has a free H+ producing net +1 unless the acid is written as the anion
rxn03712.other_comments: This is an extradiol-type ring-cleavage dioxygenase reaction: 1,2-dihydroxyfluorene is cleaved by molecular O2 to form a ring-opened meta-cleavage product. Both oxygen atoms of O2 are incorporated, consistent with a dioxygenase mechanism. Such oxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn07352.other_comments: This is the SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in spheroidene/carotenoid biosynthesis (CrtF). SAM donates a methyl group to the hydroxylated carotenoid (3,4-dehydrorhodopin), producing the methoxy carotenoid anhydrorhodovibrin and S-adenosyl-homocysteine plus a proton. Atom and charge balance are consistent: the methyl from SAM converts a hydroxyl to a methoxy group, releasing SAH and H+. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the methyl-transfer (forward) direction.

errors: Reaction is not balanced as written; the conversion of UDP-glucose plus sulfite to UDP-sulfoquinovose requires removal of a hydroxyl/oxygen and addition of sulfonate, but no oxidant or proper redox/leaving group accounting is shown
Oxygen and hydrogen atoms do not balance: UDP-glucose (C6 sugar with OH at C6) plus sulfite cannot form a C-S sulfonate bond and only release H2O without an additional oxidized/reduced partner
