errors: Substrate mismatch: the reaction name refers to 4-Hydroxyphenyllactate:NAD+ oxidoreductase, but the listed substrate is 3-(3,4-Dihydroxyphenyl)lactate (a dihydroxy/catechol compound), not the monohydroxy 4-hydroxyphenyllactate
rxn02419.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent oxidation of a 2-hydroxy acid (lactate derivative) to the corresponding 2-oxo acid (pyruvate derivative). Atoms and charges balance: the secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, transferring 2 electrons and a hydride to NAD+ giving NADH + H+. The stoichiometry is correct for the molecules as written; the issue is the inconsistency between the enzyme name (4-hydroxyphenyl) and the actual substrate (3,4-dihydroxyphenyl).

rxn02126.other_comments: This reaction is the oxidation of tartronic acid (hydroxymalonate, 2-hydroxymalonic acid) at its hydroxyl group to form oxomalonate (2-oxomalonate / mesoxalic acid), coupled to reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Tartronate (HOOC-CHOH-COOH) loses two hydrogens (one from the C-OH, one as the hydride to NAD+) to yield mesoxalate (HOOC-CO-COOH). The atom and charge balance is correct: the substrate carbon goes from a secondary alcohol to a ketone, electrons transferred to NAD+ giving NADH + H+. NAD+ NADH oxidoreductases of this type are typically reversible, though in vivo direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance. Theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine, C7H8N4O2) + H2O + O2 should yield 3,7-dimethyluric acid (C7H8N4O3) + H2O2. Checking: left = C7H8N4O2 + H2O + O2 = C7 H10 N4 O5; right = C7H8N4O3 + H2O2 = C7 H10 N4 O5. Atoms actually balance.

Charge imbalance: an extra H+ appears on the left side that is not balanced on the right; removing the H+ gives a balanced neutral equation. As written with the additional H+, the equation has a net +1 charge excess on the left.
rxn07768.other_comments: This is an oxidase reaction in which theobromine is hydroxylated at C8 to form 3,7-dimethyluric acid, consuming molecular oxygen and water and producing hydrogen peroxide. Oxidase reactions producing H2O2 from O2 are strongly exergonic and physiologically irreversible, proceeding in the direction of urate formation.

rxn06720.other_comments: This reaction represents the dephosphorylation of HMG-CoA reductase (NADPH-dependent) by a protein phosphatase. Water hydrolyzes the phosphoester bond on the phosphorylated enzyme, releasing inorganic phosphate and yielding the dephosphorylated (active) form of HMG-CoA reductase. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + protein-phosphate yields phosphate + dephosphorylated protein. Phosphoprotein phosphatase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the dephosphorylation direction.

rxn07849.other_comments: This reaction hydrolyzes formylmethanofuran (N-formyl group attached to the amino terminus of methanofuran) into formate and free methanofuran, consuming one water molecule. The atoms and charges balance: the formyl group (CHO) plus water (H2O) yields formate (HCOOH/HCOO-) while regenerating the free amine of methanofuran. Stoichiometry is correct. In the context of methanogenesis/CO2 reduction, formylmethanofuran is normally formed from CO2 and methanofuran by formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase; this hydrolytic reaction is thermodynamically reversible but its physiological flux direction depends on the organism and pathway context.

rxn00845.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of the methyl ester at the 4-position of oxaloacetate, yielding oxaloacetate, a proton, and methanol. The stoichiometry is balanced: the ester (C5H5O5-) plus H2O gives oxaloacetate (C4H2O5 2-), H+, and methanol (CH4O). Mass and charge are conserved. Ester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the forward (hydrolytic) direction is appropriate.

errors: The substrate is written as 'Diphthamide' but the product refers to 'EF-2 N-(ADP-D-ribosyl)diphthamide'; the substrate should consistently be the diphthamide residue on EF-2 (i.e., 'peptide-diphthamide' or 'EF-2 diphthamide') for proper mass and atom balance
rxn06577.other_comments: This is the ADP-ribosylation of the diphthamide residue of elongation factor 2 (EF-2), the reaction catalyzed by diphtheria toxin and exotoxin A. NAD+ donates the ADP-ribose group to diphthamide, releasing nicotinamide and a proton. Stoichiometry is otherwise balanced if the substrate is taken to be the EF-2 diphthamide residue. The reaction is effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo, releasing nicotinamide.

errors: Carbon and hydrogen atoms do not balance between substrates and product. trans-2-Methyl-5-isopropylhexa-2,5-dienoyl-CoA (C10 acyl portion) plus H2O should give a hydroxy acyl-CoA with the same carbon count, but the named product 3-Hydroxy-2,6-dimethyl-5-methylene-heptanoyl-CoA implies a C10 acyl chain whose formula appears inconsistent with simple hydration of the named substrate; the naming/structure correspondence should be verified for atom balance.
rxn04275.other_comments: This is described as a hydro-lyase (enoyl-CoA hydratase-type) reaction: water adds across a C=C double bond of an unsaturated acyl-CoA to give a 3-hydroxy acyl-CoA. Such hydratase reactions are generally reversible. The main concern is whether the substrate and product names correspond to the same carbon skeleton and balance atomically.

rxn07609.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic cleavage step in phenanthrene/biphenyl-type degradation pathways, catalyzed by a meta-cleavage product hydrolase (e.g., PhdJ/related). Water attacks the C-C bond of the 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-(2-carboxyphenyl)-hexa-2,4-dienoate (a meta-cleavage product / HOPDA analog), yielding 2-oxopent-4-enoate (2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate tautomer) and phthalate, plus a proton. Carbon balance: substrate has 15 C; phthalate (8 C) + 2-oxopent-4-enoate (5 C) = 13 C. There is a discrepancy of 2 carbons, suggesting the products should sum to 15 C (the ring product is typically 2-carboxybenzaldehyde or the dienoate fragment should be 6-7 C). Please verify the carbon balance of the listed products.

errors: Carbon mass imbalance: desmosterol (C27) plus two methyl groups from SAM would yield a C29 sterol, but stigmasterol is C29 with a 22,23-double bond. The conversion of desmosterol to stigmasterol is not a simple double methylation. Desmosterol has a 24,25-double bond; stigmasterol has a 24-ethyl group plus a 22-double bond. The transformation requires C24 methylation (twice) plus desaturation and reduction steps, not captured here.

Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: bis-methylation of the 24 position consumes 2 SAM and produces 2 SAH plus 2 H+, but the resulting sterol would be a 24-ethyl sterol; producing the 22-double bond of stigmasterol requires an additional desaturation (loss of 2 H), which is not accounted for. Hydrogen balance is therefore incorrect.
Reaction appears to conflate multiple enzymatic steps (sterol C-24 methyltransferase reactions plus C-22 desaturase) into one, which is biologically inaccurate as written.
rxn02644.other_comments: The reaction depicts conversion of desmosterol to stigmasterol using 2 SAM as methyl donors, generating 2 SAH and 2 H+. This is meant to represent the phytosterol C-24 ethylation pathway, but it omits the required desaturation/reduction chemistry and is not properly balanced. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn08209.other_comments: This is cyclopropane fatty acid synthase acting on phosphatidylglycerol with two C18:1 (cis-vacenic/oleic type, dioctadec-11-enoyl) acyl chains. Each unsaturated double bond receives a methylene group from SAM to form a cyclopropane ring. With two unsaturated acyl chains, 2 SAM are consumed yielding 2 SAH and 2 H+, and both double bonds are converted to cyclopropane rings (dioctadec-11,12-cyclo). The stoichiometry of SAM:SAH:H+ (2:2:2) is balanced and consistent with two methylation/cyclopropanation events.

rxn09139.other_comments: This is a phospholipase A1 reaction hydrolyzing the sn-1 ester bond of phosphatidylglycerol (with two tetradec-7-enoyl/C14:1 chains). Water cleaves the sn-1 acyl group, releasing one free tetradecenoate fatty acid and yielding 2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol (a lysophospholipid retaining the sn-2 acyl chain). The H+ accounts for protonation balance from the carboxylate release. Mass and charge appear balanced: one acyl group is removed and one fatty acid plus the lyso-product are produced.

rxn02422.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphorylation of 5-hydroxy-L-lysine (5-hydroxylysine) at its hydroxyl group, transferring the gamma-phosphate from GTP to form 5-phosphonooxy-L-lysine and GDP. This is catalyzed by hydroxylysine kinase (FLJ36724/AGPHD1, EC 2.7.1.81), part of the hydroxylysine degradation pathway. The stoichiometry is balanced: a phosphate group is transferred from GTP to the hydroxyl of hydroxylysine, yielding GDP and the phosphorylated product. Charges and atoms balance.

errors: Oxygen/hydrogen mass imbalance: with NADH + O2 + 2 H+ + phenazine-1-carboxylic acid on the left and H2O + NAD+ + CO2 + 1-hydroxyphenazine on the right, the equation does not balance. PCA (C13H8N2O2) to 1-hydroxyphenazine (C12H8N2O) loses one carbon (as CO2) and the hydroxyl is added. Balancing C: 13 = 12 + 1 (OK). Balancing O: left = 2 (O2) + 2 (PCA carboxyl) = 4; right = 1 (H2O) + 2 (CO2) + 1 (1-OH-phenazine) = 4 (OK). Balancing H: left = 1 (NADH) + 2 (H+) + 8 (PCA) = 11; right = 2 (H2O) + 8 (1-OH-phenazine) = 10, plus NAD+ carries the H normally counted -> charge/H accounting must be checked carefully, and as written there is a 1 H discrepancy unless NAD vs NADH protons are reconciled. Charge: left has +2 (from 2 H+) plus NADH(-1) = +1 net; right NAD+ is +1, H2O and others neutral = +1 (charge balances).
rxn13787.other_comments: This represents an oxidative decarboxylation/hydroxylation of phenazine-1-carboxylic acid (PCA) to 1-hydroxyphenazine, a monooxygenase-type reaction consuming NADH and O2. The carbon balance and oxygen balance work; the main concern is exact hydrogen/proton bookkeeping between NADH and NAD+. Such oxygenase reactions are physiologically essentially irreversible in the forward direction.

rxn07466.other_comments: This reaction represents D-Ala-D-Ala dipeptidase activity, hydrolyzing the D-alanyl-D-alanine dipeptide into two D-alanine molecules using one water molecule. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O cleaves the peptide bond, yielding 2 D-Alanine. Note the substrate label 'Ala-Ala' is generic; for this specific enzyme it should be D-Ala-D-Ala. Hydrolysis of a peptide bond is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the forward direction dominates.

errors: The product of the inositol moiety should be myo-inositol, not L-inositol. Galactinol is 1-alpha-D-galactosyl-myo-inositol, so upon transfer of the galactosyl group, free myo-inositol is released.
rxn02451.other_comments: This is the galactinol-dependent stachyose synthase reaction. Galactinol (galactosyl-myo-inositol) donates a galactose unit to raffinose (melitose = raffinose, a trisaccharide of Gal-Glc-Fru), producing stachyose (a tetrasaccharide) and releasing free myo-inositol. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as 1:1:1:1, but the inositol product should be myo-inositol rather than L-inositol. In vivo this galactinol-dependent transfer proceeds toward stachyose biosynthesis.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the phenol-coupling oxidation produces only one H2O per electron pair, not two; for forming one C-C bond between two molecules with loss of 2 H and 2 electrons, the balanced reaction should yield 2 H2O when consuming O2 and NADPH, but the H balance must be checked - actual berbamunine synthase reaction is 2 (R)-N-methylcoclaurine + NADPH + H+ + O2 -> dimer + NADP+ + 2 H2O which is balanced
Substrate name mismatch: enzyme is named for (S)-N-methylcoclaurine but reaction uses (R)-N-methylcoclaurine
rxn03530.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP80) phenol-coupling oxidative dimerization forming a bisbenzylisoquinoline alkaloid (guattegaumerine) from two N-methylcoclaurine units, consuming NADPH and O2. P450-mediated oxidative couplings are physiologically irreversible.

rxn10054.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolytic deamination of CMP (cytidine monophosphate) to UMP (uridine monophosphate), releasing ammonia. The reaction as written is mass- and charge-balanced: H2O + CMP (C9H13N3O8P, charge -1 typically as CMP2- but here shown protonated) + H+ yields NH3 + UMP. Cytosine (with an amino group) is converted to uracil (with a carbonyl), with the amino nitrogen leaving as ammonia. Note: the enzyme name says 'dCMP deaminase' but the substrate is CMP/UMP (ribonucleotides), so there may be an annotation mismatch. Deamination reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is incorrect; an NAD-dependent dehydrogenase oxidizing a secondary alcohol to a ketone releases only 1 H+, not 2. Balanced reaction: NAD+ + 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutyryl-CoA <=> NADH + H+ + 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA
rxn13419.other_comments: This is the 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase step in isoleucine degradation, oxidizing the 3-hydroxyl group to a ketone (2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA) with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Carbon, CoA, and redox balance are otherwise consistent.

rxn06680.other_comments: This represents the phosphorylation of isocitrate dehydrogenase (NADP+) by the bifunctional enzyme AceK (isocitrate dehydrogenase kinase/phosphatase). ATP transfers a phosphate to a serine residue on IDH, producing ADP, a proton, and the phosphorylated (inactive) form of the enzyme. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: ATP donates the gamma-phosphate to the protein, yielding ADP, H+, and the phosphoprotein. Note this is a protein post-translational modification reaction, where IDH and IDH-phosphate are macromolecular substrate/product. In vivo, the kinase activity drives phosphorylation (inactivation) to redirect flux through the glyoxylate shunt; the reverse dephosphorylation is catalyzed by the phosphatase activity hydrolytically, not by reversing this ATP-dependent reaction. Thus the kinase reaction proceeds essentially in the forward (phosphorylating) direction.

errors: The H+ on the left side is not balanced; the methyl transfer from O6-methylguanine to cysteine does not produce or consume a free proton. The reaction as written has an unbalanced charge/hydrogen due to the extraneous H+.
rxn06647.other_comments: This describes the O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT/ada) reaction, where a methyl group is transferred from O6-methylguanine in DNA to a cysteine residue in the protein, repairing the DNA to guanine and forming S-methylcysteine. The methyl transfer itself is stoichiometrically correct except for the spurious H+. MGMT is a suicide enzyme that is irreversibly alkylated, so the reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction.

errors: Proton (H+) imbalance: deamination of the adenine amino group consumes water and releases ammonium (NH4+), the net charge/proton balance is incorrect as written; a typical balanced form is H2O + ADP -> NH3 + IDP, or with NH4+: H2O + ADP -> IDP + NH4+ (no extra H+ consumed). Including H+ on the substrate side does not balance hydrogen/charge.
rxn00093.other_comments: This is an adenosine/AMP-type deaminase activity acting on ADP, converting adenine to hypoxanthine, thus producing IDP (inosine diphosphate) and ammonia from ADP plus water. Hydrolytic deaminations are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the deamination (forward) direction.

rxn00387.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase (SULT) reaction transferring the sulfo group from PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate) to the 3-hydroxyl (phenolic) position of 2-methoxyestradiol, producing PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate) and the 3-sulfate ester plus a proton. The atoms balance: the sulfate group and its charge transfer to the steroid, and a proton is released from the phenolic hydroxyl. Stoichiometry and charge appear balanced.

rxn00618.other_comments: This reaction is a galactosyltransferase transferring a galactosyl group from UDP-galactose to glycerol-3-phosphate, producing UDP and 2-(alpha-D-galactosyl)-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate. The atoms balance: the galactosyl moiety is transferred and UDP is released, with no net loss of atoms. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable in the synthetic (forward) direction due to cleavage of the high-energy glycosidic phosphate bond.

errors: This is an exchange reaction with identical species (Acrylamide) on both sides; it represents transport/exchange across the system boundary rather than a chemical transformation
No actual stoichiometric conversion occurs; both sides are the same metabolite
rxn10941.other_comments: This is labeled as an exchange reaction (EX_C01659_e), which in metabolic models represents the uptake or secretion of a metabolite (acrylamide, C01659) across the model boundary. Such reactions conventionally show the same metabolite on both sides and are formally balanced. They are typically written as reversible to allow both import and export, with the actual direction constrained by flux bounds in the model.

rxn02216.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP1A1/CYP1A2/CYP1B1) catalyzed aromatic hydroxylation of estradiol at the 2-position, producing 2-hydroxyestradiol (a catechol estrogen). The monooxygenase reaction incorporates one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate and reduces the other to water, consuming NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: one O atom goes into 2-OH-estradiol and the other O combines with 2H (from NADPH/H+) to form water. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: Mass imbalance: the reaction transfers a single lysine residue onto phosphatidylglycerol, but the substrate is named 'Diisohexadecanoyl' (two acyl chains) while the product is named 'Isohexadecanoyl' (single acyl chain), implying loss of one fatty acyl group that is not accounted for among the products
If both substrate and product carry two isohexadecanoyl chains, the product name is simply abbreviated and there is no acyl imbalance; the naming inconsistency must be resolved

Lysyl-PG synthases (MprF-type) typically use lysyl-tRNA(Lys) as the lysine donor, not free L-lysine plus ATP directly; however, aminoacyl-PG synthesis via an aminoacyl-tRNA route is the documented in vivo mechanism. The ATP + free lysine -> AMP + PPi formulation represents the activation step (aminoacyl-adenylate formation) lumped with transfer
rxn10333.other_comments: This represents synthesis of lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (Lys-PG), an aminoacylation of the membrane lipid PG head group. The ATP -> AMP + PPi (with H+) stoichiometry indicates amino acid activation via an adenylate intermediate, which is energetically favorable and drives the reaction toward Lys-PG formation in vivo.

errors: The substrate name '(Hydroxymethylphenyl)succinyl-CoA' is inconsistent with the product 'Benzoylsuccinyl-CoA'; oxidation of a (3S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA to a 3-oxoacyl-CoA would require a hydroxyl on the acyl chain carbon being converted to a keto group, not a hydroxymethyl/benzoyl conversion as written. If the intended substrate is (1-hydroxy...)succinyl-CoA the naming is ambiguous and likely incorrect.

The transformation as named would need to remove 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+, one as proton), which is consistent for an alcohol-to-ketone oxidation, but the atom balance cannot be confirmed because the substrate/product structures implied by the names do not match (hydroxymethylphenyl vs benzoyl implies loss of additional atoms).
rxn03860.other_comments: This appears to be a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase-type reaction (NAD+-dependent oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone), likely part of an aromatic compound beta-oxidation pathway. Such dehydrogenases are typically reversible, with direction depending on NAD+/NADH ratio. The main concern is naming consistency between substrate and product.

rxn03291.other_comments: This reaction represents the 3-oxo-delta4-steroid 5beta-reductase (AKR1D1) step in bile acid biosynthesis. The enzyme catalyzes the reduction of 7alpha-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one (delta4 double bond) using NADPH to form 7alpha-hydroxy-5beta-cholestan-3-one. As written, the forward direction (oxidation of the 5beta-cholestanone to the delta4-en-3-one with NADP+ reduction) is thermodynamically unfavorable. The stoichiometry is balanced: addition of hydride and proton (2H) reduces the C4-C5 double bond. In vivo this proceeds in the reverse direction (right to left), i.e., NADPH-dependent reduction.

rxn12709.other_comments: This is the 4-oxalomesaconate tautomerase/isomerase reaction (EC 5.3.2.8) in the protocatechuate 4,5-cleavage (meta) pathway. It interconverts the keto form of 4-oxalomesaconate (4-oxalmesaconate) and its enol form, 4-carboxy-2-hydroxyhexa-2,4-dienedioate (also called 2-hydroxy-4-carboxymuconate / the enol tautomer). Both species share the formula C7H4O7 (as dianions/depending on protonation state), so the keto-enol isomerization is mass- and charge-balanced. As a tautomerization, it is thermodynamically reversible, though metabolic flux in the meta-cleavage pathway proceeds toward the downstream hydratase reaction.

rxn09604.other_comments: This represents a fatty acid 2-hydroxylase (FA2H-type) reaction acting on a ceramide containing an N-linked C26:0 acyl chain (sphinganine backbone). The enzyme uses molecular oxygen and NADPH to introduce a 2-hydroxyl group onto the amide-linked fatty acid, producing the 2'-hydroxy ceramide, water, and NADP+. The stoichiometry (NADPH + O2 + H+ + substrate -> H2O + NADP+ + 2-OH product) is consistent with a typical monooxygenase/hydroxylase reaction: one oxygen atom is incorporated into the product hydroxyl and the other is reduced to water.

rxn05092.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by acireductone dioxygenase (ARD/MtnD) in the methionine salvage pathway. The Ni-dependent enzyme catalyzes an off-pathway reaction converting 1,2-dihydroxy-3-keto-5-methylthiopentene (acireductone) plus O2 into formate, 2-oxo-4-methylthiobutyrate (the alpha-keto acid precursor of methionine), and carbon monoxide. Note: the stoichiometry as written appears to be missing CO as a product. Charge and atom balance: acireductone (C6H10O3S) + O2 = formate (CHO2-) + 2 H+ + 2-oxo-4-methylthiobutyrate (C5H7O3S-) requires accounting for carbon; the difference of one carbon and one oxygen indicates CO should also be a product.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: SAM carries a net positive charge (sulfonium), and the methyl transfer to a neutral phenol oxygen yielding neutral anisole and neutral SAH should not release an H+. The phenol oxygen is methylated, not deprotonated, so the free H+ on the product side creates a charge imbalance.
rxn00922.other_comments: This is an O-methyltransferase reaction transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to the hydroxyl oxygen of phenol, producing anisole (methoxybenzene) and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). The carbon skeleton (one methyl transferred) balances correctly; the main concern is the extra H+.

rxn01389.other_comments: This is a kinase reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to L-xylulose (note: the enzyme name uses 'L-xylulose' as substrate; 'L-Lyxulose' is a synonym for L-xylulose, so the substrate naming is consistent). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP + L-xylulose -> ADP + L-xylulose 5-phosphate + H+. ATP-dependent phosphorylation reactions are thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in the direction of phosphate transfer.

rxn03932.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphorylation of 5-dehydro-2-deoxy-D-gluconate (DKH) by ATP to form 5-dehydro-2-deoxy-D-gluconate 6-phosphate (DKHP), ADP, and a proton. This is catalyzed by 2-dehydro-3-deoxygluconokinase-type enzymes (EC 2.7.1.92, 5-dehydro-2-deoxygluconokinase). The stoichiometry is balanced: a phosphate group is transferred from ATP to the sugar acid, with release of ADP and H+. The reaction is part of inositol/myo-inositol degradation pathways in some organisms.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: 2 NADPH + 2 H+ provides reducing equivalents, but the stoichiometry of H+ and water needs verification; the net redox balance for an N-hydroxylating decarboxylating oxidation should be checked
NADP should be written as NADP+ to reflect correct charge
rxn14161.other_comments: This is a CYP79-type cytochrome P450 reaction converting a chain-elongated methionine derivative (hexahomomethionine) into the corresponding aldoxime (9-methylthiononanaldoxime), a step in glucosinolate biosynthesis. The reaction involves two successive N-hydroxylations followed by decarboxylation and dehydration, consuming 2 NADPH and 2 O2, releasing CO2 and water.

rxn02311.other_comments: This is the final step of vindoline biosynthesis in Catharanthus roseus, catalyzed by deacetylvindoline 4-O-acetyltransferase (DAT). Acetyl-CoA transfers an acetyl group to deacetylvindoline (17-O-deacetylvindoline) to yield vindoline and CoA. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA is added to the hydroxyl of deacetylvindoline. In vivo, acetyltransferase reactions using acetyl-CoA are strongly driven toward acetylation due to the high group-transfer potential of the thioester bond.

errors: Carbon balance incorrect: Nonane-4,6-dione (C9) hydrolyzed should yield C4 (butyrate) + C5 fragment, but 2-pentanone is C5H10O while the C5 portion of the diketone with a ketone group should retain proper atoms. Checking: Nonane-4,6-dione C9H16O2 + H2O (H2O) -> butyrate C4H7O2(-) + H+ + product. Butyrate accounts for C4H8O2 (as acid). Remaining C5H10O = 2-pentanone. Carbon: 4+5=9 OK. Hydrogen: C9H16O2 + H2O = H18; products butyrate(C4H7O2-) H7 + H+ + 2-pentanone C5H10O H10 = H18 OK. Oxygen: 2+1=3; butyrate 2 + pentanone 1 = 3 OK. Reaction is actually balanced.
rxn02683.other_comments: This is a hydrolytic cleavage of a 1,3-diketone (beta-diketone) into butyrate and 2-pentanone. Hydrolases acting on C-C bonds of beta-diketones cleave irreversibly. After re-checking, the atom balance (C9, H18, O3 on each side) is correct.

rxn11965.other_comments: This reaction (R02780) represents a PTS (phosphoenolpyruvate-dependent phosphotransferase system) trehalose transport/phosphorylation step. TRHL (trehalose) accepts a phosphate from a phospho-histidine carrier protein (likely PtsH/HPr or enzyme II), yielding trehalose 6-phosphate and the dephosphorylated protein histidine. The phosphoryl transfer from N-pros (N1/tele-pi)-phosphohistidine to the sugar hydroxyl is stoichiometrically balanced: one phosphate moves from the protein histidine to trehalose, giving trehalose 6-phosphate plus protein histidine.

rxn04032.other_comments: This reaction represents cyclic-imide amidohydrolase (imidase, EC 3.5.2.16) hydrolyzing maleimide (a cyclic imide) by ring-opening to form maleamate. The reaction adds H2O across one of the imide C-N bonds, opening the five-membered ring to yield the linear monoamide-monoacid (maleamate). Stoichiometry balances: maleimide (C4H3NO2) + H2O (H2O) yields maleamate (C4H4NO3, the carboxylate anion) + H+. Atom and charge balance check out, with the product carboxylate deprotonated and a free proton released. This hydrolytic ring-opening is thermodynamically favorable and biologically essentially irreversible in the direction of hydrolysis.

errors: Atom/charge imbalance in cofactors: the reaction lists NADH + NADPH on the left and NAD + NADP on the right, but the proper oxidized forms are NAD+ and NADP+; only one of the two pyridine nucleotides is typically used per fatty acid elongation/synthesis cycle (one NADPH for the ketoreduction and one NADPH for the enoyl reduction), not one NADH plus one NADPH.

Proton/hydrogen balance is incorrect as written; with 2 H+ consumed and water and CO2 released, the H balance does not close given a 2-carbon (C20 -> C22) elongation typically requires 2 reducing equivalents (2 NADPH) and releases 1 CO2 and 1 H2O.
Standard fatty acid elongation uses 2 NADPH (not 1 NADH + 1 NADPH); using NADH here is biochemically atypical/likely wrong.
Stoichiometry of water: a full elongation cycle (condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction) releases 1 H2O and 1 CO2, but the redox cofactor count must match the two reduction steps (2 NADPH).
rxn13451.other_comments: This represents a fatty acid elongation step adding a 2-carbon unit from malonyl-ACP to a C20 (eicosanoyl) chain to yield C22 (docosanoyl)-ACP, releasing CO2 and ACP. The overall condensation/reduction is thermodynamically driven forward by malonyl-ACP decarboxylation, so in vivo it proceeds in the synthesis (forward) direction. The cofactor usage as written (NADH + NADPH) is questionable; canonical FAS/elongase chemistry uses 2 NADPH.

errors: Product name is inconsistent with substrate: the substrate '3,5,7,9,11,13,15,17,19-Nonaoxo' lists nine oxo groups, while the product '9-Hydroxy-3,5,7,11,13,15,17,19-nonaoxo' lists only eight oxo positions plus one hydroxyl, but still calls it 'nonaoxo' (literal naming error)

Atom/oxygen balance is internally consistent for a ketoreduction (one C=O reduced to C-OH at position 9 using NADH + H+), but the product name retains 'nonaoxo' prefix which contradicts the loss of one oxo group
Charge/proton balance: NADH + H+ -> NAD typically written as NAD+; reduction of ketone to alcohol consumes NADH + H+ correctly
rxn07138.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP reductase type reaction reducing a keto group at position 9 of a polyketo fatty acyl-ACP chain to a hydroxyl, using NADH as the reductant. Such NAD(P)H-dependent ketoreductions in fatty acid/polyketide biosynthesis proceed in the reductive (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Charge imbalance: left side has net charge 0 (H2O neutral, bromochloromethane neutral), but right side has net charge of +2 (2 H+) -1 (Cl-) = +1, plus HBr written as neutral; the reaction as written is not charge-balanced. If Br is released as Br- (bromide), then product side has 2 H+ + Cl- + Br- = net 0, but HBr is written instead of H+ + Br-, creating inconsistency.
rxn02515.other_comments: This is a halidohydrolase (dehalogenase) reaction. Bromochloromethane (CH2BrCl) is hydrolyzed by water, releasing both halides. Atom balance: C: 1=1, H: 2(H2O)+2(CH2BrCl)=4 vs 2(formaldehyde)+2(H+)+1(HBr)=5 H, so hydrogen count is off by one as written. Mass-balanced version would be H2O + CH2BrCl -> HCHO + 2 H+ + Cl- + Br-, giving H: 4 = 2+2, balanced, and net charge 0=0. The product should be Br- not HBr to balance properly.

errors: Substrate Gly-Tyr appears unchanged on both sides of the reaction; for a transport reaction the dipeptide should be distinguished by compartment (e.g., Gly-Tyr[extracellular] -> Gly-Tyr[cytoplasm]). As written, the transported metabolite has no compartment annotation, making the equation appear to consume and produce the same species.
Reaction name says 'Gly-Try' (tryptophan) but the substrate is Gly-Tyr (tyrosine); inconsistent naming.
rxn12851.other_comments: This is an ABC-type peptide importer coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to translocation of the dipeptide Gly-Tyr. The ATP hydrolysis portion is stoichiometrically balanced. ABC import driven by ATP hydrolysis is effectively irreversible in vivo (forward toward import).

rxn03166.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction transferring an N-acetylglucosamine residue from UDP-GlcNAc to a mannotetraose acceptor, releasing UDP. The product gains a GlcNAc moiety and UDP loses the GlcNAc. Stoichiometry is balanced: the GlcNAc transferred from the UDP-sugar donor appears on the oligosaccharide acceptor. Glycosyltransferases using nucleotide-sugar donors are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the high energy of the sugar-nucleotide bond, driving the reaction forward.

errors: Proton imbalance: 2 H+ appear on both sides and cancel out, leaving the net reaction as H2 + Menaquinone6 -> Menaquinol6; the explicit H+ terms are redundant/incorrect as written

Charge and hydrogen accounting: menaquinone reduction to menaquinol requires 2 H (2 H+ + 2 e-); if H2 provides both electrons and protons, no additional free H+ should be consumed, so the canceling H+ pairs indicate a stoichiometric error
rxn10968.other_comments: This represents a hydrogenase-coupled reduction of menaquinone-6 by molecular hydrogen, forming menaquinol-6. The core chemistry (H2 + MK -> MKH2) is sound, but the symmetric 2 H+ on both sides is redundant and should be removed for proper balancing.

errors: Stoichiometric and elemental imbalance: L-cysteine (C3H7NO2S) + sulfite (SO3 2-) cannot yield L-cysteate (C3H7NO5S) + H2S while balancing oxygen, hydrogen, charge and sulfur. L-cysteate has three oxygens on its sulfonate group, but the substrates provide insufficient oxygen and the reaction as written does not balance.

The named enzyme reaction (cysteine + sulfite -> H2S + cysteate) implies replacement of the cysteine thiol sulfur with a sulfonate derived from sulfite, but this requires oxidation/redox partners not shown; no cofactors (e.g., O2, NAD) are present to account for the oxidation state change.
rxn00651.other_comments: The reaction is presented as a cysteine hydrogen-sulfide lyase adding sulfite to form L-cysteate plus H2S. I understand it as a thiol-for-sulfonate exchange, but as written the equation is not mass/charge balanced and lacks needed redox cofactors.

rxn01197.other_comments: This is the 4-sulfobenzoate 3,4-dioxygenase reaction (EC 1.14.12.8), a two-component flavin-dependent monooxygenase/dioxygenase that converts 4-sulfobenzoate to protocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxybenzoate). NADH provides reducing equivalents, O2 is incorporated, and sulfite is released. The mass and charge balance: 4-sulfobenzoate (C7H4O5S, charge -2 with carboxylate and sulfonate) + O2 + NADH + H+ yields protocatechuate (C7H5O4, -1), sulfite (SO3, -2), and NAD+. Atoms balance for C, S; the dioxygenase incorporates one O into the ring hydroxyl and the other contributes to release as part of the desulfonation, with NADH reducing the second oxygen to water-equivalent. Stoichiometry is consistent with the established enzymatic reaction.

rxn02232.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in the aflatoxin/sterigmatocystin biosynthesis pathway (catalyzed by OmtB/AflO type enzymes in Aspergillus). It transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to the 6-hydroxyl of 6-demethylsterigmatocystin, producing sterigmatocystin and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. Stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl transfer converts an O-H to an O-CH3, and the released proton accounts for charge/mass balance.

errors: Allysine is not the product of L-Lysine transamination at the epsilon-amino group via standard nomenclature here; the reaction as written transaminates the epsilon-amino group of lysine to yield 2-aminoadipate-6-semialdehyde (allysine), which is correct, but the molecular charges/formulas should be balanced. As written the atom and charge balance is essentially correct: Pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + L-Lysine (C6H14N2O2) -> L-Alanine (C3H6NO2-) + Allysine (C6H11NO3). Carbon balances (9=9), but nitrogen does not appear balanced if allysine retains only one N - check: lysine has 2 N, alanine gains 1 N, allysine retains 1 N, so N balances (2=1+1). Oxygen: pyruvate 3 + lysine 2 = 5; alanine 2 + allysine 3 = 5, balances. Hydrogen approximately balances. The reaction is stoichiometrically acceptable.
rxn00315.other_comments: This is a transamination (aminotransferase) reaction transferring the epsilon-amino group of L-lysine to pyruvate, producing L-alanine and allysine (2-aminoadipate-6-semialdehyde). Aminotransferase reactions are generally reversible due to small free energy change.

rxn10485.other_comments: This is the second prenyltransfer step in archaeal ether lipid biosynthesis (digeranylgeranylglyceryl phosphate synthase, DGGGP synthase). It transfers a geranylgeranyl group from geranylgeranyl diphosphate to the sn-2 hydroxyl of (S)-3-O-geranylgeranylglyceryl phosphate (GGGP), releasing diphosphate (PPi) and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the GGPP donates its geranylgeranyl moiety forming the new ether bond, with PPi and H+ released. In vivo it proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction, driven thermodynamically by PPi hydrolysis.

rxn05112.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of glutaryl-7-aminocephalosporanic acid (GL-7-ACA) by glutaryl-7-ACA acylase, cleaving the amide bond between the glutaryl side chain and 7-aminocephalosporanic acid (7-ACA). One water hydrolyzes the amide, releasing glutarate and 7-ACA. Atoms balance: the amide C-N bond is split, with OH added to the carbonyl carbon (forming glutarate carboxylate) and H added to the nitrogen (forming the free amino group of 7-ACA). Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: Stoichiometry is incorrect: nucleoside triphosphatase typically hydrolyzes only the terminal (gamma) phosphate, releasing 1 phosphate and 1 H+ to yield dGDP, not deoxyguanosine. Complete hydrolysis of dGTP to deoxyguanosine plus 3 phosphates would require 3 H2O but is not the standard reaction of EC 3.6.1.15.

The hydrogen ion balance for full hydrolysis to nucleoside plus 3 inorganic phosphates does not correctly reflect the actual proton release at physiological pH for sequential phosphoanhydride and phosphoester cleavage.
rxn13140.other_comments: The reaction depicts complete hydrolysis of dGTP to deoxyguanosine releasing three inorganic phosphates with three water molecules. Nucleoside triphosphatase normally removes only the terminal phosphate to form dGDP. Phosphoanhydride bond hydrolysis is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Proton balance is incorrect: the reaction as written with 2 H+ on the left does not balance charge/mass. For the standard 4-hydroxybenzoate 3-monooxygenase (decarboxylating) reaction, the correct stoichiometry is NADPH + O2 + H+ + 4-hydroxybenzoate -> NADP+ + H2O + CO2 + hydroquinol, requiring only 1 H+
rxn00963.other_comments: This is the 4-hydroxybenzoate 1-hydroxylase (decarboxylating) reaction (EC 1.14.13.64), a flavin-dependent monooxygenase that converts 4-hydroxybenzoate to hydroquinone (quinol) with decarboxylation, consuming NADPH and O2. The hydroxylation occurs at C1 with displacement of the carboxyl as CO2.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: a standard SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction transfers a methyl group to a hydroxyl/carboxyl acceptor and typically does not release a free H+ as written; if the acceptor is an oxygen nucleophile, the proton balance should be checked, but methyl transfer (CH3, neutral) from SAM+ to an O-acceptor yields SAH (neutral) and would release one H+, so the H+ may actually be correct depending on protonation states

Carbon mass balance must be verified: cis-39-C57oyl to cis-39-C58oyl indicates net addition of one carbon (a methyl), consistent with methylation from SAM; this is acceptable if the acceptor gains a CH3 group
rxn13493.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent methyltransferase (methoxylation/O-methylation) reaction acting on a mycolic-acid/meromycolate intermediate carried on ACP. SAM is the methyl donor, producing S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) and an acceptor extended by one carbon (C57 -> C58). The carbon increment is consistent with methyl transfer. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are strongly favored in the methylation direction in vivo due to the high group-transfer potential of SAM and rapid removal of SAH.

errors: This is a transport reaction representing the movement of xylitol coupled with a proton across a membrane; however, as written, both sides are identical (H+ + Xylitol on both sides), so there is no net chemical transformation indicated. The compartmental designations (e.g., H+[in]/H+[out] and Xylitol[in]/Xylitol[out]) are missing, which makes the reaction appear as a null/identity reaction.
rxn12532.other_comments: The reaction appears to be a proton-coupled symport/transport of xylitol across a membrane (TRANS-RXN prefix indicates a transport reaction). The stoichiometry is balanced for H+ and xylitol, but without compartment annotations the two sides are literally identical and the reaction conveys no net change. Proton-coupled sugar/polyol transporters can operate reversibly depending on electrochemical gradients.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction as written does not conserve carbon, hydrogen, or CoA moieties. A thiolase reaction (3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase) cleaves a 3-ketoacyl-CoA into acetyl-CoA (or propionyl-CoA) and a shorter acyl-CoA; here the substrate/product carbon counts do not match. Chenodeoxyglycocholoyl-CoA contains a glycine conjugate, which is inconsistent with a CoA thioester thiolytic reaction.
The substrate 'Chenodeoxyglycocholoyl-CoA' (a glyco-conjugated bile acid) cannot simultaneously be a glycine conjugate and a CoA thioester; this appears to be a mis-annotated metabolite.

In the physiological bile acid side-chain shortening (peroxisomal) pathway, the thiolase cleaves the C27 3-keto bile acid-CoA (e.g., 24-oxo-trihydroxycholestanoyl-CoA) to yield propionyl-CoA plus the C24 bile acyl-CoA (cholyl-CoA/chenodeoxycholoyl-CoA). The direction shown (consuming propionyl-CoA to build a longer chain) is opposite to the in vivo thiolytic direction.
rxn03288.other_comments: This is intended to represent the final thiolytic step of peroxisomal bile acid side-chain shortening, where a 3-keto-C27 bile acyl-CoA is cleaved into propionyl-CoA and a C24 bile acyl-CoA. In vivo the thiolase runs in the cleavage (thiolytic) direction, i.e., the reverse of how written. The named substrate is also chemically inconsistent (glyco-conjugate vs CoA thioester).

rxn04884.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP1A1)-mediated monooxygenase reaction that epoxidizes benzo[a]pyrene to benzo[a]pyrene-4,5-oxide. The stoichiometry is balanced: one atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (forming the epoxide), the other is reduced to water using two electrons from NADPH plus one proton. Mass and charge balance: NADPH (charge -4) + O2 + H+ + benzpyrene yields H2O + NADP (charge -3) + epoxide. The hydrogen and oxygen atoms balance correctly for a monooxygenase reaction.

errors: Charge and electron imbalance: ferredoxin-dependent sulfite reductase reduces sulfite (SO3^2-) to sulfide (H2S) requiring 6 electrons, so 6 reduced ferredoxin should be consumed, not 3. As written with 3 ferredoxin only 3 electrons are transferred, which is insufficient.
Proton/charge balance is inconsistent with the 6-electron transfer; the H+ stoichiometry does not balance with the correct electron count.
rxn05902.other_comments: This represents assimilatory/dissimilatory sulfite reductase using ferredoxin as the electron donor. As written the reaction shows sulfide oxidation to sulfite (left to right), but in vivo the physiological direction is sulfite reduction to sulfide, consuming reduced ferredoxin. The proper balanced reaction is: Sulfite + 6 Reduced ferredoxin + ~7-8 H+ -> H2S + 3 H2O + 6 Oxidized ferredoxin.

rxn14002.other_comments: This reaction represents the conversion of L-tryptophan to indole-3-acetaldoxime catalyzed by cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP79B2/CYP79B3 in plants). It involves two sequential N-hydroxylations followed by decarboxylation and dehydration. Checking mass balance: Left side C11H12N2O2 (Trp) + 2 NADPH + 2 O2 + 2 H+. Right side: indole-3-acetaldoxime (C10H10N2O) + CO2 + 3 H2O + 2 NADP+. Carbon: 11 (Trp) = 10 (oxime) + 1 (CO2), balanced. The NADPH/NADP+ couple and oxygen consumption are consistent with two monooxygenase cycles. The reaction is balanced for C, N, and redox.

rxn02874.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the hydroxyl group of a hydroxyanthraquinone, producing a glucosyloxyanthraquinone (O-glucoside) and releasing UDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written: the glucose moiety is transferred and UDP is the leaving group. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugars are highly exergonic due to cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, and they proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass-balanced. Cardiolipin synthase in Bacillus subtilis (and most bacteria) condenses two phosphatidylglycerol molecules to form one cardiolipin plus one glycerol, but the products do not balance with the given dihexadecanoyl (dipalmitoyl) substrate stoichiometry. Two dipalmitoyl-PG (each carrying 2 palmitoyl chains, total 4 chains) should yield a cardiolipin bearing 4 acyl chains, which is consistent, but the product 'Palmitoylcardiolipin' must explicitly carry all four palmitoyl chains for the atoms to balance.
No charge/proton balance is shown; cardiolipin carries additional phosphate groups whose protonation states should be specified.
rxn10334.other_comments: This represents bacterial cardiolipin synthase (Cls), which catalyzes the transesterification of two phosphatidylglycerol molecules to produce one cardiolipin and release one glycerol. The substrate is specified as the dipalmitoyl (dihexadecanoyl) species, giving tetrapalmitoyl-cardiolipin. In B. subtilis this reaction proceeds toward cardiolipin synthesis, especially under stationary phase and sporulation conditions.

rxn01910.other_comments: This is the UDP-galacturonate decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.67), which converts UDP-D-galacturonate to UDP-L-arabinose. The reaction is a decarboxylation: the C6 carboxyl group of the galacturonate is removed as CO2, yielding the pentose sugar arabinose attached to UDP. Stoichiometry balances: UDP-galacturonate (a UDP-hexuronic acid) loses CO2, and a proton is consumed to balance charge/mass for the decarboxylation, giving UDP-arabinose. Decarboxylations releasing CO2 are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn00659.other_comments: This reaction represents the ATP-dependent ligation of L-lysine and beta-alanine to form the dipeptide beta-alanyl-L-lysine, with release of AMP and pyrophosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides AMP + PPi, the peptide bond formation between the carboxyl of beta-alanine and the epsilon-amino (or alpha-amino) group of lysine releases water-equivalent protons. The charge and atom balance with 2 H+ released is consistent with AMP-forming ligase chemistry. This enzyme produces the dipeptide found in carnosine-related/homocarnosine metabolism. ATP-dependent ligase reactions (AMP-forming) are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic direction due to subsequent PPi hydrolysis, so they proceed forward in vivo.

errors: Substrate stereochemistry mismatch: the enzyme name specifies (S)-Reticuline as the substrate, but the reaction lists (+)-Reticuline. (S)-Reticuline corresponds to the (-) form; the (+) form is (R)-Reticuline, which is not the substrate of berberine bridge enzyme.

Charge/proton balance: berberine bridge enzyme (EC 1.21.3.3) reaction is typically written as (S)-reticuline + O2 -> (S)-scoulerine + H2O2; the additional H+ on the product side creates a charge imbalance unless reticuline is written in its protonated cationic form.
rxn02710.other_comments: This is the berberine bridge enzyme (EC 1.21.3.3) reaction, which forms the methylenedioxy/berberine bridge converting (S)-reticuline to (S)-scoulerine, consuming O2 and producing H2O2. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo (forward direction toward scoulerine).

errors: The reaction shows the same compound (Epsilcapramine) and proton (H+) on both sides without any compartment designation, making it stoichiometrically trivial/null as written. A proton symport transport reaction must indicate distinct compartments, e.g., H+[e] + Epsilcapramine[e] <=> H+[c] + Epsilcapramine[c].

The metabolite name 'Epsilcapramine' (epsilon-aminocaproate / 6-aminohexanoate) does not match the reaction title's substrate '6-Aminohexanoate' consistently; epsilon-aminocaproic acid is 6-aminohexanoate, but the naming should be standardized.
No compartmental transfer is represented, so this is not actually a transport reaction as labeled.
rxn12573.other_comments: The reaction is intended to be a proton symport import of 6-aminohexanoate (epsilon-aminocaproate). As written, both sides are identical with no extracellular/cytosolic compartment tags, so it represents no net transformation. A proton symporter would typically be driven by the inward proton gradient (extracellular to cytosol), favoring import in vivo, but with proper compartments it could be modeled as reversible.

rxn02318.other_comments: This reaction represents galactose-6-phosphate isomerase (EC 5.3.1.26), which interconverts D-galactose 6-phosphate (an aldose) and D-tagatose 6-phosphate (a ketose). This is an aldose-ketose isomerization. Both substrate and product are single phosphorylated hexose molecules (C6H13O9P), so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced 1:1. As an isomerase reaction, it is freely reversible, though in vivo it typically proceeds toward tagatose 6-phosphate as part of the tagatose 6-phosphate pathway for galactose catabolism.

rxn04276.other_comments: This is a NAD+-dependent oxidation of a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA to a 3-oxoacyl-CoA (a beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase-type reaction). The hydroxyl group at C3 is oxidized to a ketone, with reduction of NAD+ to NADH and release of one proton. Mass and charge balance: the substrate loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one released as H+), consistent with the products. Stoichiometry appears correct and balanced.

errors: Charge/naming inconsistency: NADP should be written as NADP+ to balance charge with NADPH + H+
rxn14321.other_comments: This represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of clavulanate-9-aldehyde to clavulanate (clavulanic acid), catalyzed by clavaldehyde dehydrogenase (CAD) in the clavulanic acid biosynthesis pathway of Streptomyces clavuligerus. The reaction reduces the aldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol. Stoichiometry is otherwise balanced with one hydride from NADPH plus one proton reducing the aldehyde.

rxn02765.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to the 6-hydroxyl of 6-hydroxymellein, producing 6-methoxymellein and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). This is part of the dihydroisocoumarin/6-methoxymellein biosynthesis pathway in carrot. The stoichiometry is balanced: methyl transfer converts the OH to OCH3, with H+ released. SAM-dependent methylations are thermodynamically favorable and generally considered essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the methylation (forward) direction.

rxn09967.other_comments: This is the oxidation of propanal (propionaldehyde) to propionate, catalyzed by an aldehyde dehydrogenase using NAD+ as the electron acceptor. Stoichiometry is balanced: propanal (C3H6O) + H2O + NAD+ yields propionate (C3H5O2-) + NADH + 2 H+. Carbon (3=3), oxygen (1+1=2), and charge balance check out (NAD+ at 0 here, products: NADH neutral, propionate -1, 2 H+ = +2, net +1; reactants net 0 if NAD written as neutral). Note charge balance depends on the protonation/charge convention used for the cofactors, but with standard NAD+/NADH (+1/0) and propionate (-1) it balances.

rxn00031.other_comments: This is the galactinol-independent raffinose-to-stachyose-type reaction catalyzed by raffinose:raffinose galactosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.166). Melitose is a synonym for raffinose. Two raffinose molecules react: one acts as galactosyl donor, transferring an alpha-D-galactosyl unit to the other raffinose (the acceptor), yielding sucrose (the leftover from the donor) and stachyose, which is named here as 1F-alpha-D-galactosylraffinose. Stoichiometry balances: each raffinose is Gal-Glc-Fru (C18H32O16); 2 raffinose = C36H64O32; products sucrose (C12H22O11) + stachyose (C24H42O21) = C36H64O32. Mass balanced.

rxn01664.other_comments: This reaction describes the spontaneous, reversible interconversion between allysine ((S)-2-amino-6-oxohexanoate, an open-chain amino aldehyde) and delta1-piperideine-6-L-carboxylate (P6C, a cyclic Schiff base / dehydropiperidine carboxylate). Allysine undergoes intramolecular cyclization where the alpha-amino group condenses with the C6 aldehyde, releasing water to form the cyclic imine P6C. As written, the forward direction is the hydration/ring-opening of P6C to allysine, consuming H2O and H+. Stoichiometry is balanced: P6C (C6H9NO2) + H2O + H+ = allysine (C6H12NO3+); atoms and charge balance. Physiologically, the cyclic P6C form is favored at neutral pH, so the spontaneous equilibrium tends toward cyclization (the reverse of the written direction, i.e., allysine to P6C).

rxn04425.other_comments: This is a cinnamyl-alcohol dehydrogenase (CAD, EC 1.1.1.195) type reaction reducing caffeyl aldehyde (3,4-dihydroxycinnamaldehyde) to caffeyl alcohol using NADPH. The reaction is balanced: NADPH + H+ donates a hydride and proton to reduce the aldehyde group (CHO) to a primary alcohol (CH2OH), regenerating NADP+. Atoms and charges balance correctly. CAD enzymes are formally reversible, though in vivo during lignin/monolignol biosynthesis the reduction direction (aldehyde to alcohol) is favored.

rxn06199.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent histidine N-methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.85). SAM donates a methyl group to a protein histidine residue, producing S-adenosyl-homocysteine and the methylated histidine. Note: the enzyme name specifies N-tele (N-pros, the tau/N1 position is sometimes ambiguous in nomenclature), while the product is written as Ntau-methyl-L-histidine; the tele/tau designation appears slightly inconsistent but refers to ring nitrogen methylation. Stoichiometry is balanced with one methyl transferred and one H+ released.

rxn00964.other_comments: This is a CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction activating 4-hydroxybenzoate to 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA. ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi, consistent with the AMP-forming mechanism. Mass and charge balance check: left side ATP(-4) + CoA(-4) + 4-hydroxybenzoate(-1) = -9; right side PPi(-3) + AMP(-2) + H+(+1) + 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA(-4) = -8. There is a charge imbalance of 1, suggesting the H+ should be on the left side or the proton stoichiometry needs adjustment depending on protonation states used.

rxn04846.other_comments: This reaction represents the intramolecular rearrangement of 12(S)-HPETE (12(S)-hydroperoxyeicosatetraenoic acid) to Hepoxilin B3, catalyzed by hepoxilin synthase activity (12-HPETE hydroxymutase). Both molecules share the same molecular formula (C20H32O4), so this is an isomerization/intramolecular rearrangement that conserves all atoms, making it stoichiometrically balanced. The hydroperoxide group is converted into an epoxide and a hydroxyl group.

rxn04684.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of phosphocholine by a phosphatase (e.g., phosphocholine phosphatase, EC 3.1.3.75). The reaction is balanced: phosphocholine + water yields choline + inorganic phosphate. Mass and charge balance are maintained when accounting for protonation states. Hydrolysis of a phosphomonoester is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction toward choline and phosphate.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides (H+ + Glucosaminate <=> H+ + Glucosaminate), so no net transformation is represented. For a proton symport transport reaction, the compartments must be distinguished, e.g., H+[e] + Glucosaminate[e] <=> H+[c] + Glucosaminate[c]. Without compartment annotations the reaction is stoichiometrically trivial/null.
rxn05696.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction importing D-glucosaminic acid (glucosaminate) coupled to proton symport. As written it lacks compartment labels, making both sides identical. Biologically, proton symport import is driven by the proton motive force (inward H+ gradient), so the net direction is uptake (extracellular to cytoplasm).

rxn12777.other_comments: This is the oxidative decarboxylation of 2-oxobutyrate (2-oxobutanoate) by the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex (or similar 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase). The reaction is balanced: 2-oxobutyrate (C4H5O3-) + NAD+ + CoA-SH yields propionyl-CoA (C3H5O-S-CoA), CO2, and NADH. Carbon balance: 4 carbons in 2-oxobutyrate = 3 (propionyl) + 1 (CO2). This irreversible oxidative decarboxylation strongly favors the forward direction in vivo.

rxn02557.other_comments: This is the oxidation of geraniol (a primary allylic alcohol) to geranial (the corresponding aldehyde) using NADP+ as the electron acceptor. The reaction NADP+ + Geraniol <=> NADPH + H+ + Geranial is stoichiometrically and redox-balanced: the alcohol loses two hydrogens (2e- + 2H+), with NADP+ accepting a hydride (becoming NADPH) and one proton released. Although written as alcohol oxidation, NADP-dependent alcohol/aldehyde oxidoreductases (e.g., geraniol dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.183) are typically catalytically reversible; in vivo the favored direction depends on the NADPH/NADP+ ratio, often favoring aldehyde reduction (reverse).

rxn00254.other_comments: This is the omega-amidase (or related amidohydrolase) reaction acting on 2-oxosuccinamate (oxaloacetate monoamide), hydrolyzing the amide to release ammonia and yield oxaloacetate. Atom balance checks: 2-oxosuccinamate (C4H5NO4) + H2O (H2O) = oxaloacetate (C4H4O5) + NH3 (NH3). Left: C4 H7 N1 O5; Right: C4 H7 N1 O5. Mass and charge balanced. Hydrolysis of an amide to a carboxylic acid plus ammonia is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, so it proceeds in the forward direction.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: malonyl-ACP elongation should release CO2 and produce a C18 chain, but the redox/oxygen bookkeeping is inconsistent for the stated product.
Product naming inconsistency: reaction title indicates n-C18:2-ACP (linoleoyl, two double bonds) but the product listed is Octadecynoyl-ACP (an alkynyl/triple-bond C18 species), which do not match.

Carbon balance issue: elongation of palmitoyl-ACP (C16) by one malonyl unit yields a C18 product, releasing 1 CO2, but the desaturation/oxygenation steps to introduce unsaturation with O2 are not properly accounted for in a single combined step.
Cofactor balance for combined elongation plus aerobic desaturation is ambiguous; NADPH and O2 stoichiometry cannot be cleanly reconciled with a single net product.
rxn09425.other_comments: This is presented as a combined fatty-acyl-ACP synthase step elongating palmitoyl-ACP (C16) with malonyl-ACP to a C18 unsaturated acyl-ACP, with concomitant O2-dependent desaturation. The condensation/elongation releases CO2 and NADPH reduces the beta-keto intermediate; O2 and NADPH drive aerobic desaturation. rxn14262.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADPH/NADH-dependent reduction of CDP-4-keto-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose (CDP-4-dehydro-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose) to CDP-ascarylose, catalyzed by an oxidoreductase (Asc enzyme, e.g. AscD/AscE type). Atom and charge balance check out (NADH + H+ + O2 reduce one O to water, insert one OH). As an NAD(P)H-dependent monooxygenase coupling oxygen activation to NADH oxidation, this is physiologically irreversible.

Carbon counts for the organic substrate/product (pinobanksin C15H12O5 to galangin C15H10O5) and the 2-oxoglutarate (C5) to succinate (C4) + CO2 (C1) appear consistent.

rxn10601.other_comments: This represents the oxidation of L-sulfolactate to 3-sulfopyruvate coupled to reduction of NAD+ to NADH, catalyzed by L-sulfolactate dehydrogenase (ComC, EC 1.1.1.272). The stoichiometry is balanced: the secondary alcohol of sulfolactate is oxidized to a ketone, releasing 2 electrons and 1 H+ to NAD+ (net 1 H carried as NADH plus 1 H+ released). Atoms and charges balance. This enzyme functions in coenzyme M biosynthesis. As a typical NAD-dependent dehydrogenase the reaction is thermodynamically reversible, though physiological direction depends on NAD+/NADH ratio.

rxn01366.other_comments: This is uridine phosphorylase (EC 2.4.2.3), catalyzing the phosphorolysis of uridine to uracil and alpha-D-ribose 1-phosphate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: uridine (C9H12N2O6) plus phosphate yields uracil (C4H4N2O2) plus ribose 1-phosphate (C5H9O8P, as ribose-1-P carries the phosphate group). Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn07332.other_comments: This is the MPBQ/MSBQ methyltransferase (VTE3) reaction in tocopherol/plastoquinone biosynthesis. SAM donates a methyl group to 2-methyl-6-phytylquinol (MPBQ), producing 2,3-dimethyl-5-phytylquinol (DMPBQ) plus S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group transferred from SAM to the quinol substrate, with H+ released. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are generally thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the methylation direction in vivo.

rxn03260.other_comments: This is the catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT, EC 2.1.1.6) reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to the 2-hydroxyl of 2-hydroxyestradiol (2-OH-estradiol), producing 2-methoxyestradiol and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). Stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl transfer to the catechol hydroxyl releases one proton, and atoms balance correctly (SAM -> SAH loses a CH3, which is added to the substrate -OH to form -OCH3, with H+ release). Biologically this methylation proceeds in the forward (catabolic) direction.

rxn02992.other_comments: This reaction represents the interconversion of pyrogallol (1,2,3-trihydroxybenzene) and phloroglucinol (1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene), catalyzed by a hydroxyl transferase (pyrogallol-phloroglucinol transhydroxylase, EC 1.97.1.4). Both are C6H6O3 isomers, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced with respect to atoms. In the actual enzymatic mechanism (e.g., in Pelobacter acidigallici), a cosubstrate such as 1,2,3,5-tetrahydroxybenzene serves as the hydroxyl donor/acceptor, which the reaction name implies but does not show explicitly. As written with only the two isomers, the net mass balance holds. The transhydroxylase reaction is physiologically reversible but operates in the pyrogallol-to-phloroglucinol direction during anaerobic gallate degradation.

rxn12742.other_comments: This represents the hydrolytic ring-opening/oxidation of 1-piperideine (a cyclic imine, the dehydrated/cyclized form related to lysine catabolism) to 5-aminopentanoate (5-aminovalerate), coupled to reduction of NAD+ to NADH. This is consistent with the lysine degradation pathway producing 5-aminovalerate via an aminopentanal dehydrogenase / piperideine intermediate. In vivo this oxidative, NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase step proceeds toward 5-aminopentanoate formation.

rxn13196.other_comments: This represents a transport reaction for 2-phenylethanol, where the same metabolite appears on both sides of the equation, indicating movement across a membrane (e.g., extracellular to cytosol). The stoichiometry is balanced (1:1) since transport reactions move a molecule without chemical modification. 2-phenylethanol is a small, uncharged, lipophilic aromatic alcohol that can diffuse passively across membranes, consistent with reversible transport. Note: compartment annotations are not shown in this input string, but are implied by the transport designation.

rxn09456.other_comments: This is the thioesterase reaction (acyl-ACP thioesterase, e.g. EC 3.1.2.14) hydrolyzing octadecanoyl-ACP (stearoyl-ACP) into free stearate (ocdca, octadecanoic acid) and ACP. Stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the thioester bond, releasing the fatty acid and holo-ACP. Mass and charge balance hold (one C18 acyl group transferred to a hydroxyl from water, releasing free ACP with its thiol).

rxn04475.other_comments: This is a transaminase (aminotransferase) reaction transferring an amino group from L-tyrosine to 4-hydroxybenzoylformate (4-hydroxyphenylglyoxylate). L-tyrosine is converted to its 2-oxo acid (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate), while the keto acid 4-hydroxybenzoylformate is aminated to L-4-hydroxyphenylglycine. This corresponds to 4-hydroxyphenylglycine aminotransferase (EC 2.6.1.72). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (atoms and charges conserved between substrate/product amino-acid and 2-oxo-acid pairs).

ATP hydrolysis makes this strongly thermodynamically driven and effectively irreversible in vivo (forward direction).

rxn12177.other_comments: This reaction represents a sorbitol/polyol dehydrogenase-type oxidation. D-Gulitol (also called L-glucitol or L-gulitol, a hexitol) is oxidized at C2 by NAD+ to yield L-fructose (a ketose), with production of NADH and H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: the hydride and proton removed from the alcohol (CHOH -> C=O) are accounted for by NADH + H+. Mass and charge balance hold. Polyol dehydrogenases are typically reversible enzymes; physiological direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio and substrate concentrations, so reversible is the most appropriate assignment in vivo, though oxidation (forward) is often favored under cytosolic NAD+-rich conditions.

rxn03170.other_comments: This is a sialyltransferase reaction (ST6GalNAc family, EC 2.4.99.7) transferring N-acetylneuraminate from CMP-Neu5Ac to the GalNAc residue via an alpha-2,6 linkage on a sialylated O-glycan acceptor. The acceptor substrate already bears an alpha-2,3-linked sialic acid on galactose, and the enzyme adds a second sialic acid in alpha-2,6 to GalNAc.

rxn01060.other_comments: This reaction represents the epoxidation of cholesterol to cholesterol-5beta,6beta-epoxide, consuming NADPH, O2, and H+, producing water and NADP+. Stoichiometry is balanced: oxygen, hydrogen, and the redox carriers are accounted for. Mechanistically, NADPH-dependent oxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo and proceed in the direction of substrate oxidation.

rxn01993.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (EC 1.2.1.85) in the meta-cleavage pathway of catechol/aromatic compound degradation. rxn00312.other_comments: This is lysine 2-monooxygenase (EC 1.13.12.2), which catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of L-lysine to 5-aminopentanamide (delta-aminovaleramide). Stoichiometry is balanced: one UDP-GlcNAc donates one GlcNAc and releases UDP, with the acceptor gaining one GlcNAc residue.

The reaction is stoichiometrically and elementally balanced: C5H14N2 + O2 + H2O -> C5H11NO + NH3 + H2O2. In vivo this oxidase reaction is essentially irreversible, proceeding in the forward (oxidative) direction.

rxn06197.other_comments: This is a histidine kinase autophosphorylation/phosphotransfer reaction where ATP donates a phosphoryl group to a histidine residue on a protein, forming phosphohistidine (N-pros/N-tau form) and ADP plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the gamma-phosphate to the histidine, releasing ADP and H+. Histidine kinase reactions are generally reversible since phosphohistidine is a high-energy phosphoramidate bond, and these enzymes (two-component signaling) can catalyze both forward phosphorylation and reverse phosphotransfer/dephosphorylation depending on cellular conditions. Note the name says N(pi) (N-tele) while the product is named N-pros-phosphohistidine; this is a minor naming inconsistency regarding which nitrogen is phosphorylated.

rxn01890.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by N-acylneuraminate-9-phosphate phosphatase (EC 3.1.3.29), hydrolyzing the 9-phosphate group of N-acylneuraminate 9-phosphate to yield N-acylneuraminate (sialic acid) and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water hydrolyzes one phosphate ester bond, releasing one phosphate and the dephosphorylated product. As a phosphatase hydrolysis reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo, committing the final step of sialic acid biosynthesis.

rxn02118.other_comments: This is the phenylacrylic acid decarboxylase (PAD)/ferulic acid decarboxylase type reaction. 4-Coumarate (4-hydroxycinnamate, C9H8O3) undergoes non-oxidative decarboxylation to give 4-vinylphenol (4-hydroxystyrene, C8H8O). Hydrogen: 8 (substrate) + 1 (H+) = 9 on the left; right side CO2 (0 H) + 4-vinylphenol (8 H) = 8. There is a one-hydrogen discrepancy; if the anionic form of 4-coumarate is used, the H+ correctly protonates/neutralizes, but as written with neutral acid the H balance is slightly off. Decarboxylations are essentially irreversible in vivo due to release of CO2.

The NAD-dependent (cytosolic/fumarate-independent class 1A) enzymes such as those in some bacteria can operate reversibly; however, in many organisms the physiological dihydroorotate dehydrogenase uses ubiquinone rather than NAD+. As written with NAD+/NADH, the reaction is generally treated as reversible in flux models.
