rxn10310.other_comments: This reaction represents glycosylation (GlcNAc substitution) of the glycerophosphate backbone of lipoteichoic acid with 24 repeating units. UDP-GlcNAc serves as the sugar donor, transferring GlcNAc to the unsubstituted LTA and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry appears balanced (24 UDP-GlcNAc in, 24 UDP out, 24 GlcNAc added). Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible.

rxn02291.other_comments: This is the cycloartenol synthase reaction (EC 5.4.99.8), which cyclizes (S)-2,3-oxidosqualene (squalene 2,3-oxide) into the tetracyclic triterpene cycloartenol. It is an intramolecular isomerase/cyclase reaction; both substrate and product are C30H50O, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced 1:1. In vivo this cyclization is thermodynamically highly favorable and essentially irreversible, committing the substrate to phytosterol biosynthesis in plants and algae.

errors: The substrate (R)-N-Methylcoclaurine appears incorrect; the enzyme (berbamunine synthase, CYP80A1) couples (R)-N-methylcoclaurine with (S)-N-methylcoclaurine (not (S)-coclaurine) to form berbamunine, or two molecules of (R)-N-methylcoclaurine. The named product 2'-norberbamunine arises specifically from (R)-N-methylcoclaurine + (S)-coclaurine, so the listed (S)-Coclaurine is consistent for that product but the reaction name and product should be checked for consistency.

Charge/proton balance should be verified: the phenol oxidative coupling consumes O2 and NADPH to form a C-O bond, producing 2 H2O; the H+ stoichiometry as written (NADPH + H+ -> NADP + 2 H2O) is consistent with a P450 monooxygenase-type reaction.
rxn03525.other_comments: This is the berbamunine synthase (CYP80A1)-type cytochrome P450 reaction performing oxidative phenol coupling of two benzylisoquinoline alkaloid monomers to form a bisbenzylisoquinoline (here 2'-norberbamunine), consuming NADPH and O2. As an oxygen- and NADPH-dependent P450 oxidation, it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the synthetic (forward) direction.

errors: This reaction is not balanced as written; the conversion of an aldehyde-amide (3-carbamoyl-2-phenylpropionaldehyde, C10H11NO2) to the cyclic carbamate/oxazinone (4-hydroxy-5-phenyltetrahydro-1,3-oxazin-2-one, C10H11NO3) implies addition of an oxygen atom, so an oxidant/water and possibly other species are missing
Atom balance discrepancy: product contains one more oxygen than the substrate
rxn11837.other_comments: The input is a single-substrate, single-product transformation in which a carbamoyl-aldehyde cyclizes to a tetrahydro-1,3-oxazin-2-one. Mechanistically this represents intramolecular cyclization of the amide nitrogen/oxygen onto the aldehyde carbon to form a hemiaminal-type ring (4-hydroxy oxazinone). The reaction as drawn appears unbalanced in oxygen.

rxn01369.other_comments: This is an alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase reaction. The enzyme hydroxylates 2-deoxyuridine at the 2' position, converting it to uridine, while 2-oxoglutarate is oxidatively decarboxylated to succinate and CO2, consuming one molecule of O2. Atom and charge balance check: deoxyuridine (C9H12N2O5) + O2 + 2-oxoglutarate (C5H6O5/C5H4O5) yields uridine (C9H12N2O6) + succinate (C4H6O4/C4H4O4) + CO2. The added oxygen atom on uridine and the CO2 carbon are accounted for. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced.

errors: The Na+ ions are listed on both sides with the same stoichiometry (1.7) and same compartment notation, which cancels out and renders them meaningless as written; the sodium translocation should reflect movement across a membrane (e.g., Na+[in] on one side, Na+[out] on the other) to represent the ion-pumping function of this enzyme
rxn10576.other_comments: This is the N5-methyltetrahydrosarcinapterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase (Mtr) reaction, a key step in methanogenesis from the Methanosarcina pathway. The methyl group is transferred from N5-methyl-H4SPT to CoM (coenzyme M), producing methyl-CoM (CH3-S-CoM) and regenerating tetrahydrosarcinapterin. This exergonic methyl transfer is coupled to the translocation of sodium ions across the membrane, generating a sodium-motive force. The carbon/methyl balance is correct (one methyl transferred, free thiol of CoM methylated).

rxn01143.other_comments: This is thymidine kinase (EC 2.7.1.21), which phosphorylates thymidine using ATP to form dTMP, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is balanced: ATP (C10H12N5O13P3 charge -4) + thymidine (C10H14N2O5) yields ADP (C10H12N5O10P2 charge -3) + dTMP (C10H13N2O8P charge -2) + H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: Charge imbalance: formate (HCOO-) oxidation to CO2 releases 2 electrons and the products show only 1 H+; the reaction as written is not balanced. Formate -> CO2 + H+ + 2e-, so two electrons must be transferred to ferredoxin. Ferredoxin should typically be balanced as a 2-electron carrier here (or written with 2 single-electron ferredoxins). As written, electron/charge balance is inconsistent.
rxn13775.other_comments: This represents formate dehydrogenase activity coupling formate oxidation to CO2 with reduction of ferredoxin. Ferredoxin-dependent formate dehydrogenases are typically reversible and can also run in the CO2-reduction direction in many anaerobes.

errors: This is a transport reaction; without compartment labels (e.g., [e] extracellular vs [c] cytoplasmic) the reaction appears as identical species on both sides, making it a null/empty reaction as written

Proton symport stoichiometry not represented: a symport of triphosphate with H+ should show H+ and triphosphate being co-transported in the same direction (both consumed on one side and produced on the other), not balanced as written
rxn05717.other_comments: The reaction is intended to represent tripolyphosphate (triphosphate, P3O10) uptake driven by proton symport. As written it lists H+ + Triphosphate on both sides without compartmental distinction, so it is trivially balanced but conveys no net transport. Proper form: H+[e] + Triphosphate[e] <=> H+[c] + Triphosphate[c].

rxn01856.other_comments: This is a Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase reaction (cyclopentanone monooxygenase, EC 1.14.13.16). It oxygenates cyclopentanone using NADPH and O2 to form the lactone (5-valerolactone, also called delta-valerolactone or tetrahydro-2H-pyran-2-one). Stoichiometry is balanced: one O2 atom is incorporated into the lactone (ring expansion inserting an oxygen) and the other is reduced to water. NADPH and a proton are oxidized to NADP+. Atom and charge balance check out.

rxn03635.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucosyl group from ADP-glucose to sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, forming 2-(beta-D-glucosyl)-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate and releasing ADP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: glycerol-3-phosphate (C3H7O6P, with charges aside) plus ADP-glucose donates a glucose moiety, yielding the glucosylated glycerophosphate and ADP. Atoms and charges balance when accounting for the glucosyl transfer. Such NDP-sugar glycosyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo due to the high group-transfer potential of the ADP-glucose glycosidic bond.

rxn04653.other_comments: This is the dienelactone hydrolase reaction (EC 3.1.1.45). It hydrolyzes the lactone ring of trans-4-carboxymethylenebut-2-en-4-olide (dienelactone) to yield maleylacetate, part of the chlorocatechol/protocatechuate degradation pathway. The reaction adds one water across the lactone, opening the ring. Stoichiometry is balanced: dienelactone (C6H4O4) + H2O gives maleylacetate (C6H5O5 as anion) + H+, with carbons (6=6), and mass conserved. As a hydrolase acting on a lactone, it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the catabolic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the methyl transfer from SAM to precorrin-3B releases one H+ (from the methylated carbon), not 2 H+; the stoichiometry of 2.0 H+ is incorrect for a single C-methylation step

Precorrin-4 is the product of C11 methylation (precorrin-3B to precorrin-4), but the enzyme is named C17-methyltransferase, which corresponds to precorrin-6A formation in some pathways; the substrate/product/enzyme naming should be checked for consistency
rxn03513.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent C-methyltransferase reaction (CobL/CobM-type) in the cobalamin/siroheme biosynthesis pathway, converting precorrin-3B to precorrin-4 with transfer of a methyl group from SAM to produce SAH. The reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic forward direction in vivo.

rxn06716.other_comments: This reaction represents the PTEN-catalyzed hydrolysis of the 3-phosphate from PIP3 (phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate) yielding PIP2 (phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate) and inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water hydrolyzes one phosphoester bond, releasing one phosphate and converting the trisphosphate to the bisphosphate. As a phosphohydrolase, the reaction is thermodynamically driven toward hydrolysis and proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn00610.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of sn-glycerol-3-phosphate by glycerol-3-phosphatase (glycerophosphatase, EC 3.1.3.21). The reaction is balanced: H2O + glycerol-3-phosphate (C3H7O6P, with appropriate protonation) yields glycerol (C3H8O3) + inorganic phosphate. Mass and charge balance correctly when standard protonation states are accounted for.

rxn09487.other_comments: This is the P5C dehydrogenase (ALDH4A1) reaction, oxidizing L-glutamate 5-semialdehyde to L-glutamate using NADP+ (it can also use NAD+). The aldehyde + H2O is oxidized to the carboxylate, releasing 2 H+ and reducing the cofactor to NADPH. Mass and charge balance are correct: the aldehyde-to-acid oxidation removes 2 H (as 2 e- + 2 H+ to NADP+ giving NADPH + H+, plus the extra H+ from the carboxyl), and water provides the added oxygen. In vivo this irreversible oxidation proceeds in the direction of glutamate formation (part of proline/arginine catabolism).

rxn01647.other_comments: This is the purine-nucleoside phosphorylase-type reaction acting on nicotinate ribonucleoside (EC 2.4.2.1 family). Phosphate attacks the N-glycosidic bond, releasing nicotinate (niacin) and ribose 1-phosphate. The atoms balance: nicotinate ribonucleoside (C11H13NO6) + phosphate (HPO4^2-) yields nicotinate (C6H4NO2^- / niacin) + ribose 1-phosphate (C5H11O8P) + H+. Charge and mass are consistent. Phosphorolysis reactions of this type are generally reversible in vivo, though they often favor nucleoside cleavage depending on phosphate and ribose-1-phosphate concentrations.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance. The substrate (6-(2-Amino-2-carboxyethyl)-7,8-dioxo-1,2,3,4,7,8-hexahydroquinoline-2,4-dicarboxylate, the PQQ precursor often called AHQQ) being oxidized to PQQ loses the side-chain amino acid moiety, but no amino acid leaving group (e.g., release of carbon/nitrogen as a separate product) is shown, so C and N atoms are not conserved
Charge imbalance: substrate and PQQ are polyanions; only a single H+ is shown on the product side, which is insufficient to balance protons released during the oxidative cyclization
Stoichiometry of O2 vs H2O/H2O2 likely inconsistent with the actual oxidation chemistry without proper accounting of the cleaved fragment
rxn11680.other_comments: This represents the final oxidative step(s) of pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) biosynthesis, converting the cyclized precursor (AHQQ) to PQQ using molecular oxygen, releasing H2O and H2O2. PqqB/PqqC-type chemistry. The oxidative cyclization/aromatization is essentially irreversible in vivo, so forward is correct, but the equation as written is not properly balanced.

errors: Atomic/mass imbalance: arachidic acid (C20) plus methylmalonyl-CoA (3-carbon extender contributing C2 backbone + methyl branch = C3 added) should yield a C23 methyl-branched product, not C22 (behenic = C22). The product 'methyl behenic acid' nomenclature is ambiguous and the carbon count does not balance cleanly.

Hydrogen/charge imbalance: with 2 NADPH + 3 H+ consumed and only 2 NADP released, the proton and overall charge balance is not satisfied; one elongation cycle uses 2 NADPH but typically with a different proton stoichiometry.

CO2 and CoA release is consistent with methylmalonyl-CoA condensation (releases CO2 and CoA), but the water count and reductive steps need rechecking - a single elongation/full reduction normally produces 1 H2O, which is present, but redox balance still does not close.
rxn10705.other_comments: This represents a fatty acid synthase-type elongation using methylmalonyl-CoA as the extender unit to add a methyl-branched two-carbon equivalent to arachidic acid (C20), with full reduction (2 NADPH) yielding a saturated methyl-branched fatty acid plus CO2, CoA, water, and NADP. Biosynthetic elongation/reduction is essentially irreversible in vivo (driven by CoA-thioester cleavage and decarboxylation), so it proceeds forward.

rxn06567.other_comments: This is a hydrolase reaction (acetylhydrolase) cleaving the acetyl ester bond at the sn-2 position of 1-alkyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycerol, releasing acetate and producing 1-alkyl-sn-glycerol. The stoichiometry is balanced: water adds across the ester bond, yielding the free alcohol and acetate plus a proton (acetic acid pKa ~4.76, so it is ionized at physiological pH, hence acetate + H+). Mass and charge are balanced.

rxn02150.other_comments: This is a transferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.103, chlorogenate:D-glucarate 2-O-caffeoyltransferase) that transfers the caffeoyl group from chlorogenate (5-O-caffeoylquinate) to D-glucarate. Products are quinate (the deacylated acceptor portion of chlorogenate) and 2-O-caffeoylglucarate. The reaction is balanced: the caffeoyl moiety is simply transferred from quinate to glucarate, conserving atoms. Acyltransferase reactions of this type are generally reversible in vitro/in vivo since they involve transesterification with comparable bond energies.

rxn00899.other_comments: This is the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase reaction acting on 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate (the deaminated product of valine). It performs oxidative decarboxylation: 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate + NAD+ + CoA -> isobutyryl-CoA (2-methylpropanoyl-CoA) + CO2 + NADH. Carbon balance: substrate C5 -> isobutyryl-CoA acyl group C4 + CO2 C1, correct. Redox and CoA stoichiometry are balanced. The reaction also typically releases H+ which is not shown but commonly omitted.

errors: Reaction lacks compartment annotation; substrates and products are identical (Mn2+ + H+ on both sides), so as written there is no net chemical transformation. A proper transport reaction should specify compartments, e.g., Mn2+[e] + H+[e] <=> Mn2+[c] + H+[c]
rxn05618.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction where Mn2+ is imported across a membrane coupled to proton symport (H+ moving down its electrochemical gradient drives Mn2+ uptake). Without compartment labels the equation appears as a null reaction. With proper extracellular/cytoplasmic annotation, the stoichiometry (1 Mn2+ : 1 H+) is balanced for mass and charge.

rxn01487.other_comments: This is the geranylgeranyl reductase reaction, which reduces geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP) to phytyl diphosphate by sequential reduction of three of its four double bonds. GGPP (C20H36O7P2) has four double bonds; reducing three with 3 NADPH yields phytyl-PP, which retains one double bond. Stoichiometry is balanced: 3 NADPH + 3 H+ provide 6 H equivalents (3 H2 added across 3 double bonds), and 3 NADP+ are released. In vivo this reaction is essentially irreversible in the forward (reductive) direction, consuming NADPH for chlorophyll and tocopherol biosynthesis.

rxn08023.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction (Fuc4NAc transferase, WecF/WzxE pathway) involved in enterobacterial common antigen (ECA) biosynthesis. dTDP-4-acetamido-4,6-dideoxy-D-galactose (dTDP-Fuc4NAc) donates its Fuc4NAc sugar to the lipid-linked acceptor Undecaprenyl-diphospho-GlcNAc-ManNAcA (Lipid II precursor), producing the trisaccharide-lipid and releasing dTDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the sugar transferred from the nucleotide donor appears on the product lipid carrier, and dTDP is released.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: hydrolysis of the pyrophosphate (PPi) group from PRPP should yield PPi (diphosphate) and ribose-5-phosphate, or alternatively a single phosphate plus ribose product, but the products as written do not balance. PRPP (ribose with 1-pyrophosphate at C1 and 5-phosphate) has 3 phosphorus atoms total. Products list only 1 Phosphate + Ribose 1,5-bisphosphate (2 P) = 3 P, which balances P, but the bisphosphate naming is inconsistent with simple pyrophosphatase action.
Charge/proton balance questionable: release of 2 H+ from simple hydrolysis of a phosphoanhydride bond typically yields 1 H+; the stated 2 H+ should be checked against the protonation states used.

Reaction logic error: a 'pyrophosphatase' cleaving PRPP would normally produce inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi) and ribose-5-phosphate, not a single Phosphate plus Ribose 1,5-bisphosphate. The product identity appears incorrect for the named enzyme.
rxn10591.other_comments: The input is a hydrolytic cleavage of PRPP using water. Hydrolysis reactions of phosphoanhydride bonds are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so written direction (forward) is reasonable. However, the product set is chemically inconsistent with the enzyme name; a true PRPP pyrophosphatase should give ribose-5-phosphate + PPi.

errors: Atom and CoA balance issue: with two CoA on the left (free CoA + Naphthyl-2-oxomethyl-succinyl-CoA) and two CoA-thioesters on the right (Succinyl-CoA + 2-Naphthoyl-CoA), the free CoA on the substrate side is consumed but no free product CoA is released, which is consistent with a thiolytic cleavage; however the carbon balance should be checked: the naphthyl-2-oxomethyl-succinyl moiety cleaved into 2-naphthoyl and succinyl appears to account for atoms, so the main concern is verifying that the keto/methylene carbon is properly partitioned
rxn04717.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-CoA thiolytic cleavage (thiolase-type reaction, R06908) involved in naphthalene/PAH degradation. The 2-(2-naphthoyl)methyl-succinyl-CoA type intermediate is cleaved by free CoA into 2-naphthoyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA. Such thiolase reactions are formally reversible but strongly favor cleavage in the catabolic direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written shows no net transformation or transport; both substrates and products are identical (H+ + L-Xylose on both sides). For a proton symport transport reaction, the metabolites should be distinguished by compartment, e.g., H+[e] + L-Xylose[e] <=> H+[c] + L-Xylose[c]. Without compartment annotations, this is a null reaction.
rxn12620.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transporter moving L-xylose across a membrane coupled to proton movement (typically down the proton gradient). As written, no compartmental distinction is given, so it appears as an identity (no-op) reaction. Stoichiometrically the atoms balance trivially, but biologically the transport is meaningless without separate compartments.

rxn00891.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine by an amidohydrolase, cleaving the acetamido group to yield acetate and glucosamine (GLUM). The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (C8H15NO6) gives acetate (C2H3O2-/C2H4O2) plus glucosamine (C6H13NO5). The amide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically proceeds in the deacetylation direction.

errors: Charge imbalance: the product side includes H+ but trans-L-3-hydroxyproline (zwitterion, net 0) gives 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (net -1) plus H2O; the products carry an extra positive charge unless the H+ accompanies a -1 product, in which case net charge balance requires careful accounting. As written, left side net charge ~0, right side net charge ~0 only if 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate is treated as anion (-1) plus H+ (+1); this is balanceable but ambiguous as written.

Mass/atom check: trans-L-3-hydroxyproline (C5H9NO3) -> 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (C5H7NO2 as acid / C5H6NO2- as anion) + H2O. Removing H2O from C5H9NO3 yields C5H7NO2, consistent, but the extra H+ on the product side is not balanced by atoms unless the carboxylate deprotonation is invoked.
rxn03037.other_comments: This is a dehydration (hydro-lyase) reaction: trans-L-3-hydroxyproline loses water to form the cyclic imine 1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (a delta-1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate). Atom-wise the dehydration is correct (loss of one H2O). The H+ is included presumably for charge balance with the anionic carboxylate form. Hydro-lyase reactions are often reversible thermodynamically but typically proceed in the dehydration direction in vivo as part of hydroxyproline catabolism.

rxn02469.other_comments: This is the trimethyllysine dioxygenase (TMLHE/TMLD) reaction, the first step of carnitine biosynthesis. It is an Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase that hydroxylates N6,N6,N6-trimethyl-L-lysine at the C3 position to form 3-hydroxy-N6,N6,N6-trimethyl-L-lysine. Stoichiometry is balanced: O2 splits with one oxygen incorporated into the hydroxylated product and one into succinate (via oxidative decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate, releasing CO2). Atoms and charges balance.

rxn01719.other_comments: This is the arylamine N-acetyltransferase (NAT) reaction, transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the amine nitrogen of an arylamine. Using aniline as the arylamine substrate, the product N-acetylarylamine (acetanilide) is formed along with free CoA. The reaction is balanced: acetyl-CoA + aniline -> CoA + acetanilide, with the acetyl group (C2H3O) transferred from CoA to the aniline amino group. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn14137.other_comments: This represents an isomerase/mutase reaction interconverting 2-alkylmalate and 3-alkylmalate, analogous to the aconitase-type interconversion of citrate and isocitrate via a hydroxyl/carboxyl group shift. The reaction is an intramolecular rearrangement (hydroxymutase), so it is mass- and charge-balanced as written (same molecular formula on both sides, isomers). Such isomerization reactions are typically near-equilibrium and reversible in vivo, with direction determined by downstream metabolite consumption. Note that 'alkyl' is a generic placeholder, so exact atom counts depend on the R group, but as an isomerization the balance holds regardless.

errors: Reaction appears unbalanced as written; an intramolecular rearrangement of 2,4-dihydroxylamino-6-nitrotoluene to 4-amino-6-hydroxylamino-3-methyl-2-nitrophenol would require redox/hydroxyl transfer that is not mass-balanced without additional atoms (e.g., loss/gain of O or H equivalents). No cofactors or water shown.

The product introduces a phenolic hydroxyl group while one hydroxylamino group is converted to an amino group, implying an intramolecular Bamberger-type rearrangement that changes atom positions but the overall formula change should be checked; as written no balancing species are provided.
rxn07838.other_comments: This is the Bamberger-type rearrangement step in the bacterial degradation of 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT). A dihydroxylamino-nitrotoluene undergoes an intramolecular rearrangement where one hydroxylamino group is converted to an amino group and a ring hydroxyl (phenol) is introduced, yielding an aminohydroxylaminonitrophenol. The reaction (R08048) is part of TNT catabolism and proceeds in the degradative direction in vivo.

errors: Atom imbalance: D-serine (C3H7NO3) oxidation to 2-aminomalonate semialdehyde (2-amino-3-oxopropanoate, C3H5NO3) requires removal of 2 H atoms (i.e. loss of H2); the reaction as written balances H only if water is not involved, but the oxidation of a hydroxyl (CH2OH) to an aldehyde (CHO) removes 2 hydrogens. Products show NADPH + H+ which accounts for 2 H, so the reaction appears H-balanced; however charge/oxygen accounting should be verified - oxidation of CH2OH to CHO removes 2 H and yields NADPH+H+, which is consistent, so the main concern is whether the named product structure (2-aminomalonate semialdehyde) is correct for serine oxidation
rxn08371.other_comments: This represents an NADP-dependent dehydrogenase oxidizing the hydroxymethyl group of D-serine to an aldehyde, forming 2-amino-3-oxopropanoate (aminomalonate semialdehyde) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry of hydrogen transfer (2 H removed = NADPH + H+) is internally consistent.

rxn04757.other_comments: This reaction represents the conversion of violaxanthin to neoxanthin, a step in the carotenoid/xanthophyll and abscisic acid biosynthetic pathway. Both violaxanthin (C40H56O4) and neoxanthin (C40H56O4) are isomeric C40 xanthophylls with the same molecular formula, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. The conversion involves opening of one of the 5,6-epoxide groups of violaxanthin to form an allenic neoxanthin, catalyzed by neoxanthin synthase. In vivo this proceeds toward neoxanthin as part of biosynthesis.

rxn01088.other_comments: This is the UDP-glucose ceramide glucosyltransferase (UGCG) reaction, transferring glucose from UDP-glucose to ceramide (N-acylsphingosine) to form glucosylceramide (glucocerebroside) plus UDP. The reaction is balanced as written, with one glucose moiety transferred. In vivo, this glycosyltransfer reaction is essentially irreversible in the forward direction (synthesis of glucosylceramide) due to release of UDP and the thermodynamics of glycosidic bond formation; degradation occurs hydrolytically via glucocerebrosidase rather than reversal.

rxn02196.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the acetyl ester group of Cephalosporin C by cephalosporin-C acetylhydrolase (deacetylase, EC 3.1.1.41). Water hydrolyzes the acetate ester, releasing acetate, a proton, and deacetylcephalosporin C. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acetyl ester (O-CO-CH3) is cleaved, water adds an OH to the deacetyl product and the acetyl is released as acetate plus a proton. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides (H+ + Ethylamine on each side), which makes it a null/empty reaction with no net transformation. For a proper transport reaction, the compartments must be specified, e.g., H+[extracellular] + Ethylamine[extracellular] <=> H+[cytosol] + Ethylamine[cytosol]. Without compartment annotations, the reaction is stoichiometrically meaningless (everything cancels).
rxn05710.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction moving ethylamine into the cell coupled with a proton, driven by the proton motive force. As written it lacks compartment designations, so no net change occurs. In vivo, uptake via proton symport is typically directional (import).

rxn02117.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the 4-hydroxyl group of 4-coumarate (trans-4-hydroxycinnamate), producing 4-O-beta-D-glucosyl-4-hydroxycinnamate and releasing UDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: glucose is transferred and UDP is released. The product is a 4-O-beta-D-glucoside ester/ether of the phenolic hydroxyl. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugars are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic (glucosylation) direction due to the high group-transfer potential of the UDP-glucose bond.

errors: This reaction appears to involve an oxidative decarboxylation, but the stoichiometry is unbalanced. Converting a 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (with a 2-oxo carboxylic acid side chain, -CO-COOH) to a mandelic acid (with a -CHOH-COOH side chain) while releasing CO2 requires loss of one carbon. The pyruvate side chain (CH2-CO-COOH) becoming a mandelate side chain (CH(OH)-COOH) plus CO2 removal is not mass-balanced as written; hydrogen and oxygen atoms do not balance.

Only one O2 is shown but the transformation (decarboxylation plus hydroxylation) would alter the oxygen/hydrogen count inconsistently; water (H2O) is likely missing as a product or reactant to balance H and O.
rxn04579.other_comments: This is intended as an O2-dependent oxidative decarboxylation analogous to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase-type chemistry, converting a prenylated (dimethylallyl) hydroxyphenylpyruvate to the corresponding mandelate with release of CO2. Oxygenase reactions consuming O2 and releasing CO2 are essentially irreversible in vivo, hence forward direction.

rxn03380.other_comments: This reaction represents cystathionine beta-synthase-type activity using selenohomocysteine instead of homocysteine. L-Serine condenses with selenohomocysteine, releasing water and forming Se-cystathionine (selenocystathionine). The stoichiometry is balanced: serine (C3H7NO3) + selenohomocysteine (C4H9NO2Se) yields water (H2O) + selenocystathionine (C7H14N2O4Se). Atom balance: C 3+4=7, N 1+1=2, O 3+2=5 (4 in product + 1 in water), Se 1=1, H 7+9=16 (14 in product + 2 in water). The reaction is balanced. The beta-replacement/condensation reaction is thermodynamically driven forward by the elimination of water and is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn05504.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction for arsenobetaine, coupling ATP hydrolysis to substrate import. The arsenobetaine appears on both sides representing the extracellular (substrate) and intracellular (product) compartments, which is the standard convention for transport reactions even when compartment tags are not shown. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + ATP yields ADP + phosphate (Pi) + H+, which is the canonical ATP hydrolysis stoichiometry. ATP-driven transport is thermodynamically forced in the import direction in vivo.

rxn14189.other_comments: This is a kinase reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the 6-position hydroxyl of 1D-1-guanidino-3-amino-1,3-dideoxy-scyllo-inositol, yielding N1-amidinostreptamine 6-phosphate and ADP. This is part of streptomycin biosynthesis. The reaction is balanced: ATP + acceptor -> ADP + phosphorylated acceptor. The substrate is also known as N1-amidino-scyllo-inosamine, and the product is N1-amidinostreptamine 6-phosphate (the phosphorylated form). Kinase reactions of this type are essentially irreversible in vivo due to ATP hydrolysis thermodynamics.

rxn07454.other_comments: This is the dehydration of (Z)-phenylacetaldoxime to phenylacetonitrile (benzyl cyanide), catalyzed by an aldoxime dehydratase (OxdA-type, EC 4.99.1.7). The reaction is balanced: the oxime C8H9NO loses H2O to yield benzyl cyanide C8H7N plus water. Atoms balance (C8, H9, N1, O1 on both sides). In vivo this dehydration proceeds essentially irreversibly toward nitrile formation.

rxn12038.other_comments: This represents oxidative deamination of citalopram by a flavin-containing amine oxidase, cleaving the tertiary dimethylaminopropyl side chain to yield an aldehyde, dimethylamine, and hydrogen peroxide. Citalopram is actually metabolized in vivo mainly to demethylcitalopram (CYP-mediated N-demethylation) and to citalopram propionic acid / propionaldehyde via MAO-catalyzed deamination. [directionality_note] Oxidative deamination reactions consuming O2 and producing H2O2 are essentially irreversible under physiological conditions.

rxn01751.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of D-xylono-1,4-lactone (D-xylonolactone) to D-xylonate, catalyzed by a lactonohydrolase (lactonase). The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O attacks the lactone, opening the ring to yield the open-chain D-xylonate carboxylate plus a proton (released because the carboxylic acid is deprotonated near physiological pH). Atoms and charge balance: lactone is neutral, water is neutral, products are D-xylonate (-1) plus H+ (+1), so net charge is conserved.

rxn06282.other_comments: This is the C-S lyase (cysteine desulfhydrase-type) reaction acting on S-alkyl-L-cysteine. The enzyme is a PLP-dependent lyase that performs an alpha,beta-elimination releasing the alkyl thiol, plus deamination yielding ammonia and pyruvate. Mass and charge balance: S-alkyl-L-cysteine (C3H6NO2-S-R) + H2O yields pyruvate (C3H3O3-), NH3/NH4+, and R-SH. Atoms balance with one water consumed. Note that the actual mechanism does not strictly require water as a co-substrate in the classical PLP elimination (the alpha-aminoacrylate intermediate hydrolyzes to pyruvate and ammonia, which does incorporate water), so the inclusion of H2O is consistent with net hydrolytic release of pyruvate.

rxn12897.other_comments: Urea carboxylase (EC 6.3.4.6) catalyzes the ATP-dependent carboxylation of urea to form allophanate (urea-1-carboxylate). The reaction consumes ATP, CO2 (or bicarbonate), urea, and water, producing ADP, inorganic phosphate, and allophanate. Stoichiometry of mass and charge balances: substrates carry net charge (ATP -4) and products (ADP -3, Pi -2, plus 2 H+) balance correctly when CO2 is the carbon source. Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and phosphorus atoms balance. As an ATP-driven ligase reaction, it is biologically essentially irreversible in the forward (biosynthetic/carboxylation) direction.

rxn00723.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction: anthranilate is activated by ATP, releasing PPi and AMP, with formation of a thioester bond to CoA to yield anthranilyl-CoA. The reaction is balanced for mass and charge: ATP provides AMP + PPi, the carboxylate of anthranilate is esterified to CoA, and one H+ is released. Atom counts and charges (ATP -4, CoA -4, anthranilate -1 on left; PPi -3, AMP -2, H+ +1, anthranilyl-CoA -4 on right) balance correctly.

rxn04818.other_comments: This reaction represents the non-enzymatic (or epoxide hydrolase-independent) isomerization/rearrangement of naphthalene 1,2-oxide (1,2-epoxy-1,2-dihydronaphthalene) to 2-naphthol via the NIH shift. Both species are C10H8O, so the conversion is balanced as a simple intramolecular rearrangement with no other atoms required. In vivo, the unstable arene oxide spontaneously rearranges to the aromatic phenol, making this strongly favored in the forward direction.

rxn02091.other_comments: This is the D-amino acid oxidase reaction acting on D-arginine. The substrate D-arginine is oxidatively deaminated, consuming O2 and H2O, producing the corresponding 2-oxo acid (2-oxo-5-guanidinopentanoate, also known as 5-guanidino-2-oxopentanoate), ammonia (NH3), and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Mass and charge balance: D-Arginine (C6H14N4O2) + H2O + O2 -> 2-oxo-5-guanidinopentanoate (C6H11N3O3) + NH3 + H2O2 (C6H14N4O2 + H2O + O2 = C6H16N4O5; products C6H11N3O3 + NH3 + H2O2 = C6H16N4O5). The reaction is balanced.

rxn00374.other_comments: This is formamidase (EC 3.5.1.49), catalyzing the hydrolysis of formamide. The reaction H2O + Formamide -> NH3 + Formate is balanced: formamide (CH3NO) plus water (H2O) yields ammonia (NH3) and formate (CHO2-/HCOOH). Atoms and charge balance correctly. As a hydrolase, it proceeds in the hydrolytic direction in vivo.

rxn00817.other_comments: This is the alpha-galactosidase reaction (melibiose galactohydrolase, EC 3.2.1.22). Melibiose is a disaccharide (galactose alpha-1,6-glucose), and hydrolysis with water cleaves it into D-glucose and D-galactose. The reaction is balanced: melibiose (C12H22O11) + H2O (H2O) yields glucose (C6H12O6) + galactose (C6H12O6). As a hydrolysis reaction, it proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo and is thermodynamically favorable.

rxn00669.other_comments: This is propionate:CoA ligase (ADP-forming), analogous to acetate:CoA ligase (ADP-forming). ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi (rather than AMP + PPi) to drive thioester bond formation between propionate and CoA, yielding propionyl-CoA. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: ATP + CoA + propionate yields ADP + phosphate + propionyl-CoA. ADP-forming acyl-CoA synthetases are typically found in archaea and some anaerobes and can operate reversibly depending on cellular energetics, though physiologically they often favor acyl-CoA formation.

rxn07122.other_comments: This represents glucose dehydrogenase (membrane-bound, quinone-dependent), oxidizing D-glucose to D-glucono-1,5-lactone (gluconolactone) with reduction of ubiquinone (Q) to ubiquinol (QH2). The reaction is balanced: glucose (C6H12O6) loses 2 H (2H+ + 2e-) to become gluconolactone (C6H10O6), and Q gains 2 H to become QH2. In vivo, periplasmic/membrane quinoprotein glucose dehydrogenases drive this oxidation toward gluconolactone formation, feeding electrons into the respiratory chain.

rxn06037.other_comments: This is the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.35) from the beta-oxidation pathway. It oxidizes (S)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA to 3-oxoacyl-CoA using NAD+ as electron acceptor, producing NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced for mass, charge, redox, and CoA/hydrogen atoms. In the context of beta-oxidation it proceeds in the oxidative direction, but the enzyme is intrinsically reversible and the reverse direction operates in fatty acid synthesis-related contexts; net direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio.

rxn00181.other_comments: This is glutamate 5-kinase (EC 2.7.2.11), the first committed step of proline biosynthesis. ATP phosphorylates the gamma-carboxyl group of L-glutamate to form L-glutamyl 5-phosphate (gamma-glutamyl phosphate). Note: the product is conventionally named L-glutamate 5-phosphate (gamma) rather than 1-phosphate (alpha), so the substrate naming here may reflect a naming/positional convention difference, but the atoms balance. The reaction is mass and charge balanced as written.

rxn02460.other_comments: This is the inositol-trisphosphate 3-kinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.127), phosphorylating Ins(1,4,5)P3 at the 3-position to form Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 using ATP. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP donates a phosphate to IP3 yielding IP4, ADP, and a proton. Mass and charge balance check out as written.

rxn13218.other_comments: This is the trans-aconitate 3-methyltransferase (Tam, EC 2.1.1.144) reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to trans-aconitate to form a methyl ester product (trans-aconitate methyl ester) and SAH. The stoichiometry is balanced: SAM transfers one methyl group to a carboxylate of trans-aconitate, producing the monomethyl ester and SAH. The product named 'E-3-carboxyl-2-pentenedioate 5-methyl ester' is consistent with methylation of trans-aconitate. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the thermodynamic favorability of SAM methyl transfer.

rxn03856.other_comments: This is the galactitol-1-phosphate 5-dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.251), part of the galactitol degradation pathway in E. coli (gatD gene). Galactitol 1-phosphate is oxidized by NAD+ to D-tagatose 6-phosphate, producing NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced in atoms (oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes 2 H, captured as NADH + H+) and charge.

rxn02659.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of (+)-cis-sabinol (a secondary allylic alcohol) to (+)-sabinone (a ketone) by an NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase/oxidoreductase. The stoichiometry is balanced: the alcohol loses two hydrogens (one as a hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one as a proton H+), converting the C-OH to C=O. Atoms and charges balance. Although dehydrogenases of this type are intrinsically reversible, in vivo the oxidation direction (toward the ketone) is often favored in monoterpene biosynthetic contexts, but the thermodynamics are close to equilibrium so reversible is the safest assignment.

rxn01793.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD+-dependent oxidation of androsterone (a 3-hydroxy steroid) to androstanedione (5alpha-androstane-3,17-dione), catalyzed by a 3-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase. The reaction is balanced in mass and charge: oxidation of an alcohol to a ketone removes two hydrogens (one as hydride to NAD+, one as H+), consistent with the products shown.

rxn01026.other_comments: This is the thymine 7-hydroxylase (EC 1.14.11.6) reaction, an alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase. It oxidizes thymine (5-methyluracil) at the methyl group to give 5-hydroxymethyluracil, with concomitant oxidative decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate to succinate + CO2, consuming one O2. Atom balance: thymine C5H6N2O2 + 2OG C5H6O5 + O2 yields 5-hydroxymethyluracil C5H6N2O3 + succinate C4H6O4 + CO2. C: 5+5=10 vs 5+4+1=10; N: 2 vs 2; H: 6+6=12 vs 6+6=12; O: 2+5+2=9 vs 3+4+2=9. Balanced.

rxn04379.other_comments: This is the vetispiradiene synthase reaction, a sesquiterpene cyclase that converts trans,trans-farnesyl diphosphate (C15) into the bicyclic sesquiterpene vetispiradiene with release of diphosphate (PPi) and a proton. Mass and charge balance: FPP (C15H25O7P2, charge -3) ionizes/cyclizes to vetispiradiene (C15H24, neutral) plus PPi (HP2O7, charge -3) plus H+ (charge +1). Carbon (15=15), and overall atom/charge balance checks out.

rxn07554.other_comments: This reaction describes a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to (-)-medicarpin, producing (-)-medicocarpin (the 3-O-glucoside of medicarpin) and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: the glucose is transferred from UDP-glucose to the acceptor, with UDP as byproduct. Glycosyltransferase reactions of this type are highly exergonic due to cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, so they proceed essentially in the forward (glucosylation) direction in vivo.

rxn01043.other_comments: This reaction represents xylitol:NADP+ oxidoreductase (xylose reductase running in reverse, or NADP-dependent xylitol dehydrogenase). Xylitol is oxidized to xylose (D-xylose) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: xylitol (C5H12O5) loses 2 H (as hydride to NADP+ giving NADPH and a free H+) to form xylose (C5H10O5). Atoms and charges balance correctly. In vivo, NADPH-dependent xylose reductase strongly favors xylose reduction to xylitol (reverse of written direction); however, the enzyme catalyzes a reversible redox interconversion thermodynamically, so directionality depends on cofactor ratios. Many curated databases treat this as reversible.

rxn04338.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction. Avermectin B1a aglycone has a 5-hydroxyl group that is methylated to give the 5-methoxy derivative (Avermectin A1a aglycone), with SAM converted to S-adenosyl-homocysteine and release of a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl group transferred from SAM accounts for the conversion of the OH to OCH3, and the proton released balances the charge/mass. The reaction is catalyzed by AveD (avermectin B O-methyltransferase) in Streptomyces avermitilis.

rxn02440.other_comments: This reaction describes GDP-D-rhamnose being oxidized at the 4-position to form GDP-4-dehydro-D-rhamnose (also called GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose), with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The enzyme name (GDP-6-deoxy-D-mannose:NADP+ 4-oxidoreductase) corresponds to the EC 1.1.1.281 type activity. Stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of an alcohol to a ketone releases 2H, transferring a hydride to NADP+ (giving NADPH) and a proton. In vivo, the biosynthetic flux runs in the reverse direction as written here, i.e., the reductase converts GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-mannose to GDP-D-rhamnose using NADPH, which is the physiologically favored direction.

rxn03747.other_comments: This represents an oxidative dehalogenation of 2,4,5-trichlorophenol to 2,5-dichlorohydroquinone, catalyzed by a flavin/NADH-dependent monooxygenase (e.g., chlorophenol 4-monooxygenase). One chlorine is replaced by a hydroxyl group, releasing Cl-, with O2 and NADH consumed.

rxn13967.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to curcumin, producing curcumin monoglucoside and releasing UDP. The reaction is balanced: a glucose unit (C6H10O5) is transferred from UDP-glucose to curcumin, accounting for the gain of glucose on the product and the loss of glucose from UDP-glucose to yield UDP. Stoichiometry and mass balance are correct.

rxn00502.other_comments: This is the malonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (acylating/decarboxylating) reaction, oxidatively decarboxylating 3-oxopropanoate (malonate semialdehyde) using CoA and NADP+ to form acetyl-CoA, CO2, and NADPH. It is part of beta-alanine/propanoate metabolism. The strongly exergonic decarboxylation drives it toward acetyl-CoA formation in vivo.

rxn06820.other_comments: This reaction describes the formation of Se-cystathionine (selenocystathionine) from O-phosphohomoserine and selenocysteine, with release of phosphate and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the homoserine carbon skeleton transfers to the selenol of selenocysteine, the phosphate group leaves as inorganic phosphate, and a proton balances charge. This gamma-replacement reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo due to release of inorganic phosphate.

rxn00222.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of cellobiose (CELB), a beta-1,4-linked glucose disaccharide, into two molecules of D-glucose with the consumption of one water molecule. The stoichiometry is balanced: cellobiose (C12H22O11) + H2O (H2O) yields 2 glucose (2x C6H12O6 = C12H24O12), which checks out for both carbon (12=12) and hydrogen/oxygen. Glycoside hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable due to the energy released from breaking the glycosidic bond, so this proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn10592.other_comments: This is the ComB reaction (2-phosphosulfolactate phosphatase, EC 3.1.3.71) in coenzyme M biosynthesis. It hydrolyzes (2R)-O-phospho-3-sulfolactate (L-sulfolactyl phosphate) to give (2R)-3-sulfolactate and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: water cleaves the phosphate ester bond, yielding phosphate plus the free hydroxyl-bearing sulfolactate. Mass and charge are conserved. As a phosphatase (hydrolysis), it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn07307.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by (2R)-O-phospho-3-sulfolactate sulfo-lyase (ComC, EC 4.4.1.19), part of coenzyme M biosynthesis. It eliminates sulfite from (2R)-phospho-3-sulfolactate to yield phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) and sulfite. Stoichiometry is balanced: the sulfolactate phosphate (C3 backbone with phosphate and sulfonate) loses sulfite to form PEP. Atoms and charges balance. The reaction is a beta-elimination and proceeds in the direction of sulfite release in vivo.

rxn02611.other_comments: This reaction represents the decarboxylation/tautomerization of L-dopachrome to 5,6-dihydroxyindole (DHI), part of the melanin biosynthesis pathway. The conversion of dopachrome to DHI involves loss of CO2 (decarboxylative tautomerization), which can occur spontaneously or via dopachrome tautomerase (though that enzyme typically favors DHICA formation, retaining the carboxyl). The non-enzymatic/spontaneous route yields DHI with decarboxylation. Atoms balance: L-dopachrome (C9H5NO3, as the deprotonated/charged form) plus H+ yields CO2 (C1O2) + DHI (C8H7NO2). The decarboxylation releasing CO2 makes this strongly favored in the forward direction.

rxn04892.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase reaction epoxidizing 1,1-dichloroethylene (vinylidene chloride) to 2,2-dichlorooxirane. rxn14074.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose-dependent S-glucosyltransferase (S-GT, e.g. UGT74B1) in glucosinolate biosynthesis. rxn00621.other_comments: This is CTP:glycerol-3-phosphate cytidylyltransferase (TagD/GlpD-type, EC 2.7.7.39). It transfers a cytidylyl group from CTP to sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, producing CDP-glycerol and releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). The reaction is balanced: CTP (one cytidine + 3 phosphates) reacts with glycerol-3-phosphate; CMP moiety attaches to glycerol-3-phosphate forming CDP-glycerol (CMP-glycerol-3-phosphate, i.e., cytidine + 2 phosphates linked to glycerol-3-phosphate), and the beta-gamma phosphates leave as PPi. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn05123.other_comments: This is the glutamate-putrescine ligase reaction (PuuA, EC 6.3.1.11), the first step in the putrescine degradation pathway. It conjugates the gamma-carboxyl of L-glutamate to putrescine, forming gamma-L-glutamylputrescine, driven by ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi. The stoichiometry is balanced for mass and charge: the amide bond formation releases one H+, and ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi accounts for the energetics. ATP-dependent ligase reactions of this type are strongly exergonic and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02652.other_comments: This is a homocitrate-synthase-type (re-citrate synthase / 2-methylcitrate synthase family) condensation/cleavage reaction analog. The substrate (2S,3S)-2-hydroxytridecane-1,2,3-tricarboxylate is the aldol condensation product of oxaloacetate and lauroyl-CoA (C12 acyl-CoA). The lyase reaction cleaves it into oxaloacetate and lauroyl-CoA while consuming CoA and releasing H2O, regenerating the thioester. Stoichiometry balances: in the synthesis direction, lauroyl-CoA (C12 acyl) + oxaloacetate (C4) + H2O condense to give the C16 hydroxy-tricarboxylate plus CoA and H+. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn01067.other_comments: This is the CYP7A1-catalyzed reaction (cholesterol 7alpha-monooxygenase, EC 1.14.14.23), the rate-limiting step in the classic bile acid synthesis pathway. A monooxygenase incorporates one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate (forming the 7alpha-hydroxyl group) and reduces the other to water, using NADPH as electron donor. Stoichiometry balances: NADPH + O2 + H+ + cholesterol yields H2O + NADP+ + 7alpha-hydroxycholesterol. Charges and atoms are consistent. As a P450 monooxygenase reaction, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

For 2 ethylbenzene only 2 O atoms (1 O2) are consumed, which balances oxygen, but hydrogen is unbalanced. Ethylbenzene C8H10 + [O] -> C8H10O; 2 C8H10 + O2 -> 2 C8H10O is actually atom-balanced (C16H20O2 on both sides). rxn06913.other_comments: Reaction depicts oxygen-dependent benzylic hydroxylation of ethylbenzene to (S)-1-phenylethanol (ethylbenzene dehydrogenase or monooxygenase chemistry). The written 2:1:2 stoichiometry (2 ethylbenzene + O2 -> 2 (S)-1-phenylethanol) is atom-balanced for C, H, and O.

rxn04333.other_comments: This is an NADPH-dependent ketoreductase reaction. The 5-oxo (5-keto) group of 5-oxoavermectin '2a' aglycone is reduced to a hydroxyl group, yielding avermectin B2a aglycone. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ reduce the ketone to a secondary alcohol, regenerating NADP+. In vivo, NADPH-dependent reductions of this kind typically proceed in the reductive direction (ketone to alcohol), consistent with avermectin biosynthesis.

rxn01441.other_comments: This is the sulfamidase (N-sulfoglucosamine sulfohydrolase, SGSH) reaction involved in heparan sulfate degradation. It hydrolytically cleaves the N-sulfate group from N-sulfo-D-glucosamine, yielding free glucosamine (GLUM) and sulfate. The stoichiometry is balanced: water provides the OH and H needed, the N-S bond is cleaved releasing sulfate and protonating the amino group. This hydrolysis is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the catabolic (forward) direction.

Hydrogen/charge balance not verified; the 3 H+ on the left appear inconsistent with proper mass and charge balance
rxn04370.other_comments: This represents a type III PKS (chalcone synthase-like) condensation of three malonyl-CoA units with a caffeoyl-CoA starter, releasing 3 CO2 and 4 CoA. The biosynthetic decarboxylative condensation is strongly favored in the forward (biosynthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn01336.other_comments: This is the 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.51 family), oxidizing the 17-hydroxyl of testosterone to the 17-keto group of androstenedione (androst-4-ene-3,17-dione), with NAD+ serving as the hydride acceptor producing NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced in atoms (testosterone C19H28O2 - 2H gives androstenedione C19H26O2) and in charge/redox (one hydride to NAD+ plus one released proton). Enzymes of this class are intrinsically reversible; the in vivo net direction depends on the specific isozyme, cofactor (NAD vs NADP), and tissue NAD+/NADH ratio.

Inclusion of H+ as a product is questionable; condensation of an allylic diphosphate with IPP releases one diphosphate (PPi) but typically does not net release a proton in standard balanced formulations.
rxn05287.other_comments: This is a prenyltransferase (transtransferase) reaction adding a C5 isopentenyl unit to the C20 geranylgeranyl diphosphate to elongate the prenyl chain (to C25), releasing inorganic pyrophosphate. Such chain-elongation condensations are thermodynamically driven by PPi release and are physiologically essentially irreversible (forward).

rxn00818.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of raffinose (melitose, a trisaccharide of galactose-glucose-fructose) by alpha-galactosidase (raffinose galactohydrolase, EC 3.2.1.22). Water cleaves the alpha-1,6 glycosidic bond between galactose and glucose, releasing free galactose and sucrose (glucose-fructose). The stoichiometry is balanced: one water hydrolyzes the trisaccharide into galactose plus sucrose. As a hydrolase reaction, it proceeds in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn12543.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction moving sebacate (the dianion of sebacic acid, a C10 dicarboxylate) across a membrane coupled with the symport of 2 protons. rxn02693.other_comments: This is the aspulvinone E dimethylallyltransferase reaction (EC 2.5.1.35), which transfers two dimethylallyl groups from DMAPP onto aspulvinone E to form the diprenylated aspulvinone H, releasing two molecules of diphosphate (PPi). The stoichiometry is balanced: each prenyl transfer adds a C5H8 unit and releases one PPi and one H+, and with two transfers this gives 2 DMAPP consumed, 2 PPi and 2 H+ released. Prenyltransferase reactions are essentially irreversible due to release of diphosphate (and its subsequent hydrolysis), driving the reaction forward.

rxn00540.other_comments: This is the 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase reaction (EC 4.1.3.39), an aldol condensation between pyruvate and acetaldehyde forming 4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate (4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate). The reaction is mass and charge balanced as written (C3 pyruvate + C2 acetaldehyde = C5 product). It is part of the meta-cleavage pathway for aromatic compound degradation; physiologically it operates in the cleavage (aldolase) direction, i.e. reverse as written here, but the enzyme is freely reversible.

rxn03467.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the ganglioside GT1b by a sialidase (neuraminidase), removing one terminal N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) residue and producing GD1b plus free Neu5Ac. rxn03985.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 3-hydroxy-2-methylquinolin-4-one 2,4-dioxygenase-type enzymes (here acting on 3-hydroxy-4(1H)-quinolinone). rxn01694.other_comments: This is an aromatic hydroxylation of estrone at the 2-position to form 2-hydroxyestrone, catalyzed by a monooxygenase (e.g., CYP1A1/CYP1A2/CYP3A4 in estrogen 2-hydroxylation). The stoichiometry is balanced as a monooxygenase reaction: one oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate (hydroxyl group) and the other is reduced to water, with NADH/NAD+ providing reducing equivalents. Note that P450 estrogen 2-hydroxylation physiologically uses NADPH rather than NADH.

rxn01615.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD+-dependent oxidation of 1,2-propanediol (propylene glycol) to L-lactaldehyde, catalyzed by propanediol oxidoreductase (EC 1.1.1.77). The stoichiometry is balanced: 1,2-propanediol (C3H8O2) loses two hydrogens (one H- to NAD+ forming NADH, plus one H+ released) to form L-lactaldehyde (C3H6O2). Mass and charge balance correctly. rxn01712.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction (caffeic acid O-methyltransferase, COMT-type activity). 5-Hydroxyferulate is methylated to sinapate, with SAM converted to SAH and release of a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically correct.

rxn04044.other_comments: This is a deoxynucleoside kinase reaction (ATP:deoxynucleoside 5'-phosphotransferase, EC 2.7.1.145). ATP donates a phosphate group to the 5' hydroxyl of a generic deoxynucleoside, producing the deoxynucleoside 5'-monophosphate, ADP, and a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: a phosphoryl group is transferred from ATP to the deoxynucleoside, and the released proton accounts for charge balance. Kinase reactions coupled to ATP hydrolysis of the gamma-phosphate are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the phosphorylation (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn14376.other_comments: This represents an N-hydroxylating, oxidative decarboxylation of L-leucine to form 3-methylbutyraldehyde oxime (isovaleraldoxime), a flavin-dependent monooxygenase reaction (e.g., CYP79-type) producing an aldoxime from an amino acid. rxn09463.other_comments: This represents three rounds of peroxisomal beta-oxidation converting lignoceroyl-CoA (C24:0-CoA) to stearoyl-CoA (C18:0-CoA, 'strcoa') with release of 3 acetyl-CoA. Peroxisomal beta-oxidation uses an O2-dependent acyl-CoA oxidase generating H2O2, which is physiologically essentially irreversible in the catabolic (forward) direction.

rxn07414.other_comments: This reaction describes a phytase/phosphohydrolase removing the 5-phosphate group from myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (phytate, InsP6). The stoichiometry is balanced: phytate (C6H18O24P6) plus H2O gives free phosphate plus the pentakisphosphate (C6H17O21P5). Hydrolysis reactions of this type are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the direction of dephosphorylation in vivo.

rxn05493.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport of 2-oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate) across a membrane (extracellular to cytoplasm). Symport with one H+ suggests electrogenic transport driven by the proton motive force; such transporters are typically reversible depending on substrate and proton gradients.

rxn00918.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of P1,P4-bis(5'-guanosyl)-tetraphosphate (Gp4G, GppppG) by a guanylylhydrolase (asymmetric Ap4A/Gp4G hydrolase type activity). Water cleaves the molecule to yield GTP and GMP, with release of a proton. Atom and charge balance: Gp4G (C20H25N10O21P4 at relevant protonation) + H2O yields GTP + GMP + H+. The stoichiometry of one water consumed producing GTP, GMP, and one proton is consistent with phosphoanhydride hydrolysis.

rxn02501.other_comments: This is D-pinitol:NADP+ oxidoreductase (EC 1.1.1.-). D-Pinitol is 3-O-methyl-D-chiro-inositol (a methylated cyclitol). The reaction oxidizes a secondary hydroxyl group of pinitol to a ketone (a methyl-pentahydroxycyclohexanone), transferring a hydride to NADP+ to give NADPH plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one hydroxyl-to-ketone oxidation releases 2H (2e- + 2H+), of which one hydride goes to NADP+ (forming NADPH) and one proton is released, consistent with the written H+ on the product side. Atoms (C, H, O) and charges balance for an inositol-dehydrogenase-type reaction.

rxn03541.other_comments: This describes adenosylcobinamide amidohydrolase (CbiZ), which cleaves the amide-linked aminopropanol from adenosylcobinamide, yielding adenosylcobyric acid and 1-aminopropan-2-ol, consuming water. The reaction as listed has water and the substrates/products positioned as if running biosynthetically; the true hydrolytic direction is adenosylcobinamide + H2O -> adenosylcobyric acid + 1-aminopropan-2-ol.

rxn14253.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction transferring a D-olivose sugar moiety from the activated nucleotide-sugar donor dTDP-D-olivose to the acceptor aglycone/glycoside Urdamycin G, producing Urdamycin A and releasing dTDP. Urdamycin G is a precursor in the urdamycin biosynthetic pathway (angucycline antibiotics from Streptomyces fradiae), and the addition of the D-olivose unit yields Urdamycin A. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the glycosyl group (C minus dTMP portion) transferred from dTDP-sugar equals the difference between the two urdamycin species, with dTDP released as the leaving group.

errors: Reaction is not mass/redox balanced as written. The conversion of vitamin K1 (phylloquinone) to vitamin K1 2,3-epoxide (vitamin K1 oxide) is an oxidation requiring an oxygen atom incorporation, while oxidized dithiothreitol being reduced to dithiothreitol is also a reduction. Both vitamin K1 and DTT are being oxidized/reduced in a way that does not balance electrons/atoms properly.
