Oxygen and hydrogen balance: epoxide formation/removal involves an oxygen atom; H2O placement on the substrate side with oxidized DTT and vitamin K1 does not yield a balanced equation.
rxn02509.other_comments: The reaction describes vitamin K oxidation to its 2,3-epoxide coupled to dithiothreitol redox chemistry, resembling vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR). Vitamin K1 = phylloquinone, vitamin K1 oxide = phylloquinone 2,3-epoxide; DTT serves as the dithiol/disulfide redox couple.

rxn10247.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to a diglucosyldiacylglycerol (with two isoheptadecanoyl/C17 branched acyl chains) to form the triglucosyl product, releasing UDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one glucose unit is transferred, UDP-glucose donates glucose and becomes UDP, while the acceptor gains one glucose (di- to tri-glucosyl). Atoms and charges balance accordingly.

rxn05544.other_comments: This represents an ABC-type oligopeptide import system coupled to ATP hydrolysis. The dipeptide Ala-Leu appears on both sides because the transport reaction typically denotes the substrate moving across the membrane (e.g., periplasmic/extracellular to cytoplasmic), but as written without compartment annotation the peptide appears unchanged. The ATP hydrolysis portion (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) is stoichiometrically balanced. In vivo, ATP-driven importers run in the direction of substrate uptake powered by ATP hydrolysis, so the reaction proceeds forward.

errors: Casbene is a diterpene (C20H32) formed by cyclization of geranylgeranyl diphosphate (C20H36O7P2) with loss of diphosphate. The balanced reaction is: GGPP -> casbene + PPi. Checking H balance: GGPP (C20H36O7P2) -> PPi (HP2O7, i.e. H1P2O7 as anion or H4P2O7) + casbene (C20H32). The inclusion of a separate H+ depends on the protonation states assumed. With diphosphate written as PPi (HP2O7^3-) and casbene C20H32, the proton balance is correct only if H+ is included; mass/charge should be verified against the chosen protonation states.
Possible charge/proton imbalance depending on the ionic forms used for diphosphate.
rxn01488.other_comments: This is the casbene synthase reaction, a class II/I terpene cyclase converting geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP) to the macrocyclic diterpene casbene with release of diphosphate. The overall carbon skeleton is conserved (C20 to C20) and PPi is released. Such terpene synthase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to loss of the diphosphate leaving group and energetically favorable cyclization.

errors: Reaction is unbalanced: an oxygen atom is missing on the product side. Adding H2O (one O) to 15-hydroperoxy-11,12-EET (epoxyeicosatrienoic acid) followed by epoxide hydrolysis should yield a trihydroxy product; the listed substrate 15H-11,12-EETA likely refers to 15-hydroperoxy-11,12-epoxyeicosatrienoic acid, and the product 11,12,15-THETA (trihydroxyeicosatrienoic acid) does not balance simply by addition of one H2O without accounting for the hydroperoxide-derived oxygen and reduction
rxn04850.other_comments: This appears to be an epoxide hydrolase type reaction where water opens the 11,12-epoxide of a hydroperoxy/hydroxy eicosatrienoate to form a vicinal diol, generating a trihydroxy fatty acid (THETA). Epoxide hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, so it proceeds in the forward direction. However, the atom balance as written needs verification because the abbreviations for the hydroxy/hydroperoxy substituents are ambiguous.

rxn01437.other_comments: This is the kynurenine formamidase (arylformamidase, EC 3.5.1.9) reaction in the tryptophan degradation pathway. It hydrolyzes N-formyl-L-kynurenine to formate and L-kynurenine. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + N-formylkynurenine yields formate + H+ + L-kynurenine. Mass and charge balance check out (the formyl carbon leaves as formate, releasing a proton).

errors: Acyl chain inconsistency: the substrate acyl-ACP is named 'Hexadecenoyl-ACP' (double bond position unspecified) while the product is '1,2-dihexadec-9-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate', implying both acyl chains are C16:1 delta-9; the reaction name references C16:1 (n-C16:1) but the acceptor lipid is '1-hexadec-9-enoyl' so the transferred group should be hexadec-9-enoyl to yield a homogeneous 1,2-dihexadec-9-enoyl product

Reaction name mismatch: the name specifies '1-hexadec-7-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate' as substrate, but the actual substrate listed is '1-hexadec-9-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate' (delta-7 vs delta-9 discrepancy)
rxn08087.other_comments: This is an acylglycerophosphate acyltransferase (LPAAT/PlsC-type) reaction transferring a hexadecenoyl group from acyl-ACP onto the sn-2 position of lyso-phosphatidic acid (1-acyl-G3P) to form phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-G3P), releasing ACP and a proton. Atom/charge balance is reasonable if the acyl groups are matched. Acyltransferase reactions of this type are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward PA synthesis.

rxn03625.other_comments: This is the toluate/o-toluate degradation pathway reaction catalyzed by 1,2-dihydroxy-6-methylcyclohexa-3,5-dienecarboxylate dehydrogenase (toluene/xylene pathway, e.g. XylL). The cis-dihydrodiol carboxylate is oxidized by NAD+ to NADH, with concomitant rearomatization, decarboxylation (release of CO2), yielding 3-methylcatechol. Stoichiometry balances: substrate (C8H10O4-) + NAD+ -> 3-methylcatechol (C7H8O2) + CO2 + NADH, with charge and H/C/O/N accounting consistent.

rxn04912.other_comments: This reaction represents soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH/EPHX2) acting on 11,12-epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (11,12-EET). The epoxide ring is opened by addition of water (H2O) across the epoxide, yielding the vicinal diol 11,12-dihydroxyeicosatrienoic acid (11,12-DHET). Stoichiometry is balanced: the C20 EET plus one water gives the C20 diol, with all atoms accounted for (the epoxide oxygen plus the two atoms of water become two hydroxyl groups). In vivo this hydrolysis is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the direction of DHET formation, which inactivates the bioactive EET signaling lipid.

rxn06325.other_comments: This is the myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) reaction, transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to a serine/threonine residue on myosin light chain, producing phosphorylated myosin light chain, ADP, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced as written, assuming the generic metabolite names represent properly charged species (the released H+ accounts for the proton liberated upon phosphoester formation). Kinase reactions of this type are strongly exergonic due to ATP hydrolysis coupling and proceed in the phosphorylation direction in vivo; dephosphorylation is carried out by a separate phosphatase rather than reversal of this enzyme.

rxn04995.other_comments: This is a fatty acyl-CoA desaturase reaction introducing a cis double bond at position 11 of myristoyl-CoA (14:0-CoA), producing (11Z)-tetradecenoyl-CoA (14:1). Desaturases use molecular O2 and electrons from NAD(P)H; both atoms of O2 are reduced to two water molecules. Stoichiometry is balanced: the two electrons removed from the substrate plus two electrons from NADPH reduce O2 to 2 H2O. Charge/proton balance is consistent with H+ and NADPH consumption.

errors: This reaction as written is not stoichiometrically or biochemically correct. Glycosylation reactions in vivo do not use free D-glucose as the glycosyl donor; they use an activated sugar nucleotide, typically UDP-glucose. The correct reaction is: UDP-glucose + tyrosol <=> UDP + salidroside.

If free glucose were the donor, the products would be salidroside + H2O, which is formally a condensation, but this is thermodynamically and enzymatically not how glycosides are synthesized biologically.
rxn03444.other_comments: Salidroside is the 8-O-beta-D-glucoside of tyrosol (2-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethanol). The reaction depicts glucosylation of tyrosol with release of water. While formally balanced (glucose + tyrosol joined via glycosidic bond, releasing one water), the use of free glucose as donor is biologically incorrect; UDP-glucose-dependent glucosyltransferases (e.g., UGT73B6) catalyze salidroside biosynthesis in vivo. If interpreted as written, it would proceed toward salidroside synthesis.

rxn01115.other_comments: This is the 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (decarboxylating) reaction, the third step of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway. 6-phospho-D-gluconate is oxidatively decarboxylated to D-ribulose 5-phosphate, releasing CO2 and reducing NADP+ to NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: substrate carbons (6) split into ribulose-5-phosphate (5C) plus CO2 (1C); a hydride is transferred to NADP+. The H+ is sometimes shown explicitly but the net balance holds.

rxn03460.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of a galactose residue from UDP-galactose to the ganglioside GD2, producing UDP and the ganglioside GD1b. This is catalyzed by beta-1,3-galactosyltransferase (B3GALT4, GD1b/GM1/GA1 synthase). The stoichiometry is balanced: one UDP-galactose donates a galactosyl group to GD2, releasing UDP and forming GD1b. The galactosyl unit is added in a beta-1,3 linkage. In vivo, glycosyltransferase reactions using activated sugar nucleotides are essentially irreversible due to the favorable hydrolysis of the high-energy sugar-nucleotide bond, so this proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn01435.other_comments: This is kynurenine aminotransferase (KAT, EC 2.6.1.7). It transfers the amino group from L-kynurenine to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and the corresponding 2-oxo acid. The product 4-(2-aminophenyl)-2,4-dioxobutanoate is the deaminated keto acid of kynurenine, which spontaneously cyclizes to kynurenic acid. The reaction is balanced in carbon, nitrogen, and charge for an aminotransferase, with one amino group exchanged between the two substrate/product pairs.

rxn14335.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase reaction where a feruloyl group from 1-O-feruloyl-beta-D-glucose is transferred to amaranthin (a betacyanin glucoside), producing celosianin II (the feruloylated betacyanin) and releasing free D-glucose. The mass balance is consistent: the feruloyl moiety is transferred and the glucose donor becomes free glucose. Stoichiometry appears balanced (1:1:1:1). Such 1-O-acyl-glucose-dependent acyltransferases (serine carboxypeptidase-like, SCPL enzymes) typically operate in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo, driven toward acylation of the secondary metabolite.

errors: Charge imbalance: NADPH + 2 H+ + Quinidinone (carbonyl) reducing to Quinidine (alcohol) requires only 1 H+ for a typical ketone reduction; the standard form is NADPH + H+ + ketone <=> NADP+ + alcohol. Using 2 H+ creates a +1 charge imbalance unless NADP is written without its proper charge.
NADP should carry its correct protonation/charge state (NADP+) to balance the redox couple; written as 'NADP' it is ambiguous.
rxn14213.other_comments: This is a carbonyl reductase / ketoreductase reaction reducing quinidinone (a ketone) to quinidine (a secondary alcohol) using NADPH as the electron donor. The reverse direction (alcohol -> ketone) would require NADP+ as oxidant. For the equation as written to balance, the correct stoichiometry is NADPH + H+ + Quinidinone <=> NADP+ + Quinidine.

rxn09977.other_comments: This is the oxidation of nonanal (a 9-carbon aldehyde) to nonanoate by an NAD-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase. The reaction RCHO + NAD+ + H2O -> RCOO- + NADH + 2 H+ is correctly balanced for atoms and charge: water provides the oxygen, NAD+ is reduced to NADH, and two protons are released. Aldehyde dehydrogenases catalyze essentially irreversible oxidation in vivo, strongly favoring the forward (acid-forming) direction.

rxn10427.other_comments: This is the deoxyribose form of adenylate kinase: dATP + dAMP <=> 2 dADP. The reaction is mass-balanced for adenine, ribose, and phosphate. The H+ inclusion is a minor protonation-state detail; the core transfer of a phosphate group between dATP and dAMP to form two dADP is correct. Adenylate kinase reactions equilibrate near unity and are physiologically reversible, with direction depending on cellular nucleotide ratios.

rxn08491.other_comments: This reaction describes the reduction of two ferric ions (Fe3+) to two ferrous ions (Fe2+) coupled to the oxidation of FADH2 to FAD. The stoichiometry is balanced: FADH2 provides 2 electrons and 2 protons. On the left, FADH2 contributes 2 H atoms which are released as 2 H+ on the right while the 2 electrons reduce 2 Fe3+ to 2 Fe2+. Mass balance (FAD core, H, Fe) and charge balance are correct: left side charge = 2(+3) = +6; right side = 0 (FAD) + 2(+1) + 2(+2) = +6. The reaction is written in the thermodynamically favorable direction (FADH2 oxidation driving Fe3+ reduction).

rxn02860.other_comments: This is the cis-toluene dihydrodiol dehydrogenase (TodD) reaction, the second step of toluene degradation. The substrate cis-1,2-dihydroxy-3-methylcyclohexa-3,5-diene (toluene-cis-1,2-dihydrodiol) is oxidized by NAD+ to yield 3-methylcatechol, NADH, and H+. The reaction is balanced: the diol substrate (C7H10O2) loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) to form the aromatic catechol (C7H8O2), with one H pair captured as NADH + H+. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: Reaction is not mass-balanced as written; the conversion of stemmadenine (C21H26N2O2) to tabersonine (C21H24N2O2) plus water (H2O) does not balance because removing H2O from stemmadenine would give C21H24N2O, not tabersonine; additionally this transformation in reality involves multiple enzymatic steps (oxidation, deglycosylation, cyclization) and intermediates such as dehydrosecodine, precondylocarpine acetate, and others, not a simple dehydration
rxn04084.other_comments: This represents the late stages of monoterpene indole alkaloid biosynthesis where stemmadenine is converted toward tabersonine. The reaction as written is a gross oversimplification; the actual pathway requires several oxidoreductases and reductases (e.g., precondylocarpine acetate synthase, dihydroprecondylocarpine acetate synthase) and is not a single dehydration step. Stoichiometrically a simple loss of water cannot directly yield tabersonine.

rxn09938.other_comments: This reaction represents an ATP-dependent L-amino acid ligase (RimK-type / YwfE-like) forming a dipeptide bond between glycine and L-cysteine, yielding the dipeptide Gly-Cys (glycyl-L-cysteine). The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + inorganic phosphate, consistent with peptide bond formation where the carboxyl group is first activated as an acyl-phosphate intermediate releasing ADP, then attacked by the amine to form the peptide and release Pi. Mass and charge are conserved (one water-equivalent is consumed during the condensation reaction releasing the amide bond, accounted for by the ADP+Pi split of ATP). The reaction is consistent with biological dipeptide biosynthesis.

rxn00040.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of digallate (a depside/ester linkage between two gallate units) by tannase (digallate acylhydrolase, EC 3.1.1.20). Water cleaves the ester bond yielding two molecules of gallate plus a proton. Mass and charge balance: digallate (C14H9O9, -1) + H2O = 2 gallate (C7H5O5, -1 each) + H+; carbons (14=14), and atoms/charge balance correctly. As a hydrolase reaction, it proceeds in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02755.other_comments: This reaction represents glycyrrhizin (glycyrrhizinate) being hydrolyzed by glycyrrhizinate glucuronosylhydrolase (glycyrrhizinic acid hydrolase, EC 3.2.1.169). Glycyrrhizin consists of the aglycone enoxolone (glycyrrhetinic acid, 18-beta-glycyrrhetinic acid) attached to a disaccharide of two glucuronic acid units. Hydrolysis with one water molecule cleaves the glycosidic bond, releasing enoxolone and the 1,2-beta-D-glucuronosyl-D-glucuronate disaccharide. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water adds across the cleaved glycosidic bond yielding the aglycone plus the intact diglucuronide.

errors: This is a transport reaction but both H+ and L-Homoserine appear identical on both sides with no compartment designation, making the reaction a null/identity reaction as written
No compartment annotations (e.g., [c]/[e]) are present to indicate the direction of transport across the membrane
As written, the reaction has zero net transformation: substrates equal products
rxn05684.other_comments: The reaction ID (TRANS-RXN) and name suggest a proton-coupled L-homoserine transport across a membrane (likely a symport). For it to be meaningful, the species must be split between two compartments, e.g., H+[e] + L-Homoserine[e] <=> H+[c] + L-Homoserine[c]. As written without compartment tags, it is a trivial identity reaction.

rxn04431.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction (caffeic acid O-methyltransferase, COMT-type). It methylates the 5-hydroxyl of 5-hydroxyconiferyl alcohol to produce sinapyl alcohol, a monolignol precursor in lignin biosynthesis. The methyl group transfers from SAM to the substrate, yielding SAH and a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group is transferred, carbon/hydrogen/charge balance with the released H+. Note the enzyme name references the cinnamate substrate but the reaction shown uses the alcohol form; both are accepted COMT substrates.

rxn09068.other_comments: This is a phosphatidate phosphatase (lipin/PAP) reaction hydrolyzing phosphatidic acid (1,2-dioctadec-11-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate, i.e., di-C18:1 PA) to diacylglycerol (di-C18:1 DAG) plus inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: a phosphate monoester is cleaved by water, releasing Pi and producing the free hydroxyl-bearing DAG. Atoms and charge balance correctly with the proton released. The hydrolysis of a phosphate monoester is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so it proceeds in the forward (dephosphorylation) direction.

errors: Stoichiometric inconsistency: esterification of trehalose with four acyl groups should release water per ester bond formed, but with free fatty acids as substrates the products should include the acyl-CoA or direct ester linkage; if free acids condense with hydroxyls, 4 H2O are produced (consistent), however the H+ should be consumed/balanced differently - 4 H+ on the substrate side with 4 H2O on product side is not properly charge/mass balanced for an esterification

Mass balance cannot be verified: 'tetra-acyl trehalose' is a generic lumped metabolite without defined formula, so atom balance for the four distinct acyl chains (palmitate + hepta-methyl C30 + 2x octa-methyl C34) cannot be confirmed
Naming inconsistency: 'octa-methyl tetracontatricosanoic acid (C34:0...)' is contradictory - tetraconta = 40, tricosa = 23, neither matches a C34 backbone

Direction of proton usage is questionable: condensation (ester formation) typically does not consume protons; 4 H+ as a reactant alongside 4 H2O as product suggests the equation is reversed or mis-specified
rxn10674.other_comments: This appears to represent the biosynthesis of a tetra-acylated trehalose (a polyacyltrehalose-type cell-wall lipid of Mycobacterium), formed by esterifying trehalose (TRHL) with palmitate and three long methyl-branched (mycolipenic/mycosanoic-type) fatty acids, releasing water. The reaction is biosynthetic and would proceed in the forward direction toward the acylated trehalose product in vivo.

rxn03876.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydration of cyclohexa-1,5-diene-1-carbonyl-CoA (also known as cyclohexa-1,5-dienecarbonyl-CoA or dienoyl-CoA) to 6-hydroxycyclohex-1-ene-1-carbonyl-CoA, catalyzed by dienoyl-CoA hydratase (EC 4.2.1.100), a key step in anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation. The stoichiometry is balanced: addition of one water molecule across the C5-C6 double bond yields the hydroxylated product, conserving atoms and charge. In vivo, as part of the benzoyl-CoA catabolic pathway, this hydration step proceeds in the forward direction toward ring cleavage.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass/atom balanced. CDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-D-glucose has a 3-OH group while CDP-4-dehydro-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose lacks the 3-position oxygen. Converting the dideoxy (3-deoxy) substrate to the 6-deoxy (3-hydroxy) product requires net addition of an oxygen/hydroxyl, but oxidation of a C-H to C-OH coupled to NAD+ reduction is chemically inconsistent. A typical NAD+-dependent oxidoreduction does not hydroxylate a carbon; the redox bookkeeping (water consumed + NAD+ reduced to NADH) does not balance for a simple dehydrogenase reaction.
rxn02432.other_comments: The reaction is named as an oxidoreductase acting on CDP-4-dehydro-3,6-dideoxy-D-glucose with NAD+, producing NADH and CDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-D-glucose. The substrate and product differ at the 3-position (deoxy vs hydroxy), so this implies a hydroxylation/dehydration-type interconversion rather than a clean dehydrogenase reaction; the stoichiometry and cofactor usage appear inconsistent.

rxn01128.other_comments: This is a phosphotransferase (kinase) reaction where dATP donates a phosphate to cytidine, producing CMP and dADP plus a proton. Atoms balance: dATP (C10H16N5O12P3) + cytidine (C9H13N3O5) yields CMP (C9H14N3O8P) + dADP (C10H14N5O9P2) + H+. Phosphate transfer and charge are balanced. Cytidine kinase reactions are strongly favored in the forward (phosphorylation) direction in vivo due to the high phosphoryl transfer potential of the deoxynucleoside triphosphate, though such enzymes typically use ATP rather than dATP as the canonical donor.

rxn01396.other_comments: This is pyridoxal kinase activity (EC 2.7.1.35) acting on pyridoxine (pyridoxol). ATP phosphorylates the 5'-hydroxyl group of pyridoxine to form pyridoxine 5'-phosphate (pyridoxine phosphate), producing ADP and a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ATP + pyridoxine -> ADP + pyridoxine-5'-P + H+. Kinase reactions of this type are strongly favored in the forward (phosphorylation) direction in vivo.

rxn06031.other_comments: This is the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase (E1 component) reaction acting on 4-methyl-2-oxopentanoate (4MOP, the keto acid derived from leucine). The decarboxylation of the 2-oxo acid yields CO2 and transfers the resulting acyl group (3-methylbutanoyl/isovaleryl) onto the dihydrolipoamide moiety of the E2 lipoyl-lysine. The carbon balance works: 4MOP (C6) loses one CO2 to give a 3-methylbutanoyl (C5) acyl group attached to the lipoamide. Note the enzyme name references 2-methylpropanoyl (from valine pathway), but the substrate 4MOP corresponds to the leucine pathway yielding a 3-methylbutanoyl group, which is consistent with the products shown.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (Formate + H+) on both sides with no compartment distinction, making it a null/identity reaction. To represent a transport reaction, the metabolites must be assigned to different compartments, e.g., Formate[c] + H+[c] <=> Formate[e] + H+[e].

The name states 'proton antiport' but the stoichiometry shows formate and proton moving in the same direction (symport), which is contradictory. A true antiport would have the proton moving in the opposite direction to formate.
rxn10860.other_comments: This is intended to be a formate transport reaction (efflux of formate). However, as written there is no compartmentalization, so it reduces to a trivial identity equation. Additionally, the stated mechanism (proton antiport) is inconsistent with the implied symport stoichiometry. Formate transport across the membrane is often near-equilibrium and can be reversible, though physiological efflux of formate (e.g., via FocA) typically occurs outward.

rxn10600.other_comments: This is the cobaltochelatase (CbiK/CbiX) reaction inserting Co2+ into precorrin-2 to form cobalt-precorrin-2, part of the anaerobic cobalamin biosynthesis pathway. Mass and charge balance check: Co2+ (+2) + precorrin-2; products are cobalt-precorrin-2 plus 2 H+ released upon chelation (insertion of a divalent metal displaces 2 pyrrole protons). The reaction as written shows 4 H+, which appears stoichiometrically incorrect; metal chelation into a tetrapyrrole-derived macrocycle typically releases 2 H+, giving charge balance (left +2, right would need +2 from 2 H+ if cobalt-precorrin-2 retains the same net charge as precorrin-2). The value 4.0 H+ likely reflects a protonation-state convention difference, but as written it does not balance.

rxn04483.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction between pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate (PMP) and 3,5-dihydroxyphenylglyoxylate, producing pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) and 3,5-dihydroxyphenylglycine. This is the half-reaction of an aminotransferase where the amino group is transferred from PMP to the 2-oxo acid (glyoxylate derivative), regenerating PLP and forming the amino acid. Atoms balance: the amine on PMP is transferred to the keto group, converting it to an amine (glycine derivative) while PMP is oxidized to the aldehyde PLP. This is part of vancomycin/balhimycin biosynthesis (DpgC/HpgT pathway). Transaminase reactions are inherently reversible.

errors: The reaction as written has identical reactants and products (PPi + 2.0 H+ on both sides), so there is no net chemical transformation. For a transport reaction, the compartments must be distinguished, e.g., PPi[e] + 2 H+[e] <=> PPi[c] + 2 H+[c]. As written, no compartment labels are present, making it a null reaction.
rxn11395.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport (proton symport) moving pyrophosphate (PPi) across a membrane coupled to the movement of 2 protons down their electrochemical gradient. The stoichiometry of substrates is balanced, but without compartment annotations the reaction is trivially identical on both sides and represents no real process. Proton symport transporters are typically driven by the proton motive force, so directionality (import vs export) depends on the gradient and compartment definitions, which are missing here.

rxn01707.other_comments: This reaction represents ecdysone oxidase (EC 1.1.3.16) activity, oxidizing the 3-hydroxyl group of ecdysone to a 3-keto group (3-dehydroecdysone), using molecular oxygen as the electron acceptor and producing hydrogen peroxide. The stoichiometry is balanced: ecdysone (C27H44O7) + O2 -> 3-dehydroecdysone (C27H42O7) + H2O2. The H and O atoms balance correctly.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: 6 NADPH (6-) + 6 H+ + 3 Malonyl-ACP (each ~2-) + Acetyl-ACP does not balance against products with 6 NADP (6-) plus anionic ACP species; explicit H+ accounting appears off by the protons consumed in the 4 elongation cycles

Hydrogen atom balance should be rechecked given the lumped condensation/reduction/dehydration/reduction cycles; water count of 3 may be inconsistent with 3 dehydration steps that should accompany 4 condensation rounds (acetyl + 3 malonyl gives C8, which is consistent), so verify each dehydration releases exactly the stated water
rxn09422.other_comments: This is a lumped fatty acid synthase elongation: acetyl-ACP (C2) primed with 3 malonyl-ACP units, each adding 2 carbons (with loss of CO2) to yield octanoyl-ACP (C8). Three condensation steps with 3 malonyl-ACP correctly give C8 (2 + 3*2 = 8). Each cycle uses 2 NADPH, so 3 cycles = 6 NADPH, consistent. 3 CO2 and 3 regenerated ACP from the malonyl units are correct. The reaction is biosynthetic and effectively irreversible in vivo due to NADPH consumption and CO2 release.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: oxygen is unbalanced. The reaction 4-CPA (4-chlorophenoxyacetate) + O2 -> glyoxylate + p-chlorophenol requires proper accounting. 4-CPA (C8H6ClO3) + 1/2 O2 + H2O could give glyoxylate (C2H1O3) + 4-chlorophenol (C6H5ClO), but as written with stoichiometry 1 O2 : 2 4-CPA : 2 glyoxylate : 2 chlorophenol, hydrogen and oxygen do not balance without added water
Likely missing H2O as a substrate and possible H+ balancing
Glyoxalate is a misspelling of glyoxylate
rxn03786.other_comments: This represents the etherase/oxygenase-type cleavage of 4-chlorophenoxyacetate (4-CPA) into glyoxylate and p-chlorophenol (KEGG R05493). The C-O ether bond cleavage is an oxygenase reaction that proceeds in the catabolic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02855.other_comments: This is the imidazole acetate phosphoribosyltransferase/ligase reaction. Imidazole-4-acetate is conjugated with PRPP to form 1-(5-phosphoribosyl)imidazole-4-acetate, driven by ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi, releasing PPi. Checking atom/charge balance: ATP hydrolysis provides energy, the carboxylate of imidazoleacetate is activated and attached to the ribose phosphate. Mass balance: H2O + ATP + PRPP + imidazoleacetate yields ADP + Pi + PPi + product. The 2 H+ and water account for proton/charge balance of the coupled hydrolysis and condensation. The reaction appears balanced.

rxn01921.other_comments: This is a kinase reaction (2-dehydro-D-gluconate kinase / 2-ketogluconate kinase) transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the 6-position of 2-dehydro-D-gluconate (2-ketogluconate), yielding 6-phospho-2-dehydro-D-gluconate, ADP, and a proton. Atoms and charges balance: ATP provides the phosphate to the C6 hydroxyl, and the H+ released accounts for the proton liberated upon phosphorylation. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn00121.other_comments: This reaction is FAD nucleotidohydrolase (also known as FAD pyrophosphatase, EC 3.6.1.18), which hydrolyzes FAD into FMN and AMP. The balance: FAD has the structure FMN linked to AMP via a pyrophosphate bond. Hydrolysis of this phosphoanhydride bond by water yields FMN + AMP. The mass balance is correct (FAD + H2O -> AMP + FMN), and charge balance accounts for the 2 H+ released, consistent with the deprotonation of the newly formed phosphate groups at physiological pH. As a hydrolysis of a high-energy pyrophosphate bond, this reaction is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn01594.other_comments: This is the streptomycin 3''-adenylyltransferase (aminoglycoside adenylyltransferase) reaction, an antibiotic resistance enzyme. ATP donates an AMP moiety to the 3'' hydroxyl of streptomycin, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). The mass and charge balance is correct: ATP (transfers AMP) + Streptomycin -> 3''-Adenylylstreptomycin + PPi. The proton (H+) accounts for charge balance from the released hydroxyl proton and phosphate group transfer. In vivo this proceeds in the adenylylation direction (drug inactivation), and PPi hydrolysis drives it forward.

rxn10707.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction in LPS O16 antigen biosynthesis. dTDP-rhamnose serves as the rhamnose donor, transferring a rhamnosyl group to the GlcNAc-PP-undecaprenyl acceptor (the lipid carrier intermediate), releasing dTDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: one rhamnose unit is transferred and dTDP is released. Glycosyltransferase reactions using activated nucleotide-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn01296.other_comments: This is the hydroxynitrile lyase (mandelonitrile lyase, EC 4.1.2.10) reaction. Mandelonitrile (the cyanohydrin of benzaldehyde) dissociates into hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and benzaldehyde. Stoichiometry and atom balance are correct: mandelonitrile (C8H7NO) = HCN (CHN) + benzaldehyde (C7H6O), with C, H, N, and O all balanced. Although classified as a lyase favoring cleavage, the reaction is intrinsically reversible and these enzymes are widely exploited synthetically in the reverse (cyanohydrin-forming) direction.

rxn06367.other_comments: This reaction represents the dephosphorylation of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) at the D3 position of the inositol ring, catalyzed by a 3-phosphatase (e.g., myotubularin family enzymes). Water hydrolyzes the 3-phosphate group, yielding inorganic phosphate and phosphatidylinositol (PI). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one water plus the substrate monophosphate yields free phosphate plus the dephosphorylated lipid.

rxn02794.other_comments: This is a bile acid-CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction. Chenodiol (chenodeoxycholate/chenodeoxycholic acid) is activated to its CoA thioester at the expense of ATP, yielding AMP and PPi. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides AMP + PPi, CoA is attached to the carboxyl group of chenodeoxycholate forming the thioester, and an H+ is released. Mass and charge balance are consistent. In vivo, AMP-forming ligase reactions are driven forward thermodynamically by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by pyrophosphatase.

rxn02208.other_comments: This is a nucleotidyltransferase reaction (EC 2.7.7.-) where UTP reacts with L-arabinose 1-phosphate to form UDP-L-arabinose and release pyrophosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the uridylyl (UMP) group is transferred to the sugar phosphate, releasing PPi. Charges and atoms balance correctly. Although the reaction is written as reversible and such transferases are intrinsically reversible, in vivo the rapid hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase typically drives the reaction toward UDP-sugar synthesis.

errors: Mass imbalance: AMP appears on the reactant side and an acyl-AMP product is formed, but AMP cannot simultaneously be a substrate and be incorporated into the product; the reaction as written is contradictory
Charge/proton imbalance: addition of 2 H+ is not justified by the transacylation from ACP to AMP
An ACP-to-AMP acyl transfer is mechanistically unusual; typically ATP activates the fatty acid to acyl-AMP releasing PPi, then the acyl group is transferred to ACP, not the reverse
rxn10661.other_comments: This reaction depicts a fatty-acyl-AMP ligase (FAAL) type step on a cyclopropanated methoxy-meroacid (mycolic acid biosynthesis intermediate), transferring the acyl group between ACP and AMP. As written, AMP appearing as a free substrate while also being part of the acyl-AMP product is inconsistent, suggesting the intended reaction should involve ATP -> acyl-AMP + PPi, not AMP as a free reactant.

rxn05411.other_comments: This is a dehydratase (hydro-lyase) reaction in fatty acid/branched-chain acyl-ACP biosynthesis. A 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP loses water to form a trans-2-enoyl-ACP. The atoms balance: removal of H2O from the beta-hydroxy substrate yields the alpha,beta-unsaturated (trans-2-enoyl) product. Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn02012.other_comments: This reaction represents the 7-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (7alpha-HSDH) activity oxidizing the 7-hydroxyl group of cholate (3alpha,7alpha,12alpha-trihydroxy-5beta-cholanate) to a 7-oxo group, producing 3alpha,12alpha-dihydroxy-7-oxo-5beta-cholanate, with NAD+ reduced to NADH + H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes 2 H (one to NAD+, one released as H+), and atom/charge balance is consistent. NAD-dependent HSDHs are characteristically reversible enzymes; the in vivo direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio and substrate concentrations, though the oxidative direction is often favored under typical cellular conditions.

rxn03315.other_comments: This reaction represents a 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (AKR family) oxidizing the 3alpha-hydroxyl group of 3alpha-hydroxy-5beta-pregnane-20-one to a ketone, yielding 5beta-pregnane-3,20-dione, with NADP+ reduced to NADPH + H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH, one as H+). Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance are consistent.

rxn02384.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 20-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.149). The substrate 17alpha,20alpha-dihydroxypregn-4-en-3-one is oxidized at the C20 hydroxyl to a ketone, yielding 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone, while NADP+ is reduced to NADPH + H+. The atom and charge balance is consistent: oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes 2H (one as hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH, one as a proton). Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn07653.other_comments: This is the allene oxide synthase (AOS, CYP74A) reaction in the plant oxylipin/jasmonate pathway. 13(S)-HPOT (13S-hydroperoxy-9Z,11E,15Z-octadecatrienoate) is dehydrated to form the allene oxide 12,13(S)-EOT (12,13S-epoxy-9Z,11E,15Z-octadecatrienoate), releasing water. The atoms balance: removal of H2O from the hydroperoxide forms the epoxide. Note: the product retains the 11E double bond (the lyase naming 9Z,15Z omits the conjugated 11-double bond present in the allene oxide), but the chemistry is the standard AOS reaction.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: this reaction combines two unrelated oxidations. NAD-dependent oxidation of L-glutamine to 2-oxoglutaramate releases ammonia (omitted), and the conversion of L-inositol (myo-inositol) to scyllo-inosamine requires an amino group and does not balance with the glutamine oxidation as written.
Nitrogen imbalance: scyllo-inosamine contains an amino group not accounted for by simple oxidation of inositol; the released NH3 from glutamine deamidation is not shown.
Likely two distinct reactions improperly merged into one.
rxn03802.other_comments: The reaction as written couples NAD-dependent oxidation of L-glutamine to 2-oxoglutaramate with conversion of inositol to an amino-inositol (scyllo-inosamine). These do not constitute a single balanced redox/transfer step; an ammonia molecule and proper redox bookkeeping appear missing.

rxn04953.other_comments: This is aspartate dehydrogenase (EC 1.4.1.21), catalyzing the oxidative deamination of L-aspartate to oxaloacetate with NADP+ as cofactor. Stoichiometry is balanced: atoms (C4H7NO4 aspartate + H2O - 2H to NADPH gives C4H4O5 oxaloacetate + NH3) and charges balance. In vivo this enzyme functions predominantly in the reductive direction, catalyzing aspartate biosynthesis from oxaloacetate and ammonia (the reverse of the written reaction) as part of NAD biosynthesis.

rxn01082.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of D-glucurono-6,2-lactone (D-glucurono-gamma-lactone) by glucuronolactonase (EC 3.1.1.19), opening the lactone ring to yield D-glucuronate. Atom and charge balance check: D-glucurono-6,2-lactone (C6H8O6) + H2O (H2O) = C6H10O7, which equals glucuronate (C6H9O7-) + H+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced. As a hydrolase reaction in vivo, it strongly favors the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn02868.other_comments: This is an NADP+-dependent oxidoreductase reaction (EC 1.1.1.-) oxidizing the 3alpha-hydroxyl group of glycyrrhetinate to a 3-oxo (ketone) group, transferring a hydride to NADP+ to form NADPH plus a released proton. The reaction is balanced: the 3-OH loses two hydrogens (one as H- to NADP forming NADPH, one as H+), correctly accounting for the conversion of hydroxyl to oxo. Stoichiometry of cofactors (NADP/NADPH/H+) is standard and correct.

rxn00047.other_comments: This is the oligogalacturonide lyase / unsaturated digalacturonate reaction. The unsaturated disaccharide 4-(4-deoxy-beta-D-gluc-4-enuronosyl)-D-galacturonate is converted into 2 molecules of 5-dehydro-4-deoxy-D-glucuronate (the saturated galacturonate residue tautomerizes/rearranges and the unsaturated residue hydrates to give the same product). Mass and atom balance work out: the disaccharide (C12H16O12) plus water yields 2 C6H8O6, so technically a water molecule is consumed; if water is omitted the reaction as written is slightly unbalanced by one H2O.

rxn03519.other_comments: This is the inositol-pentakisphosphate 2-kinase (IPK1) reaction. The enzyme name indicates ATP + Ins(1,3,4,5,6)P5 -> ADP + phytate (InsP6). The reaction as written is in the reverse direction (showing phytate -> InsP5). Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP transfers a phosphate to the 2-position of InsP5 to form InsP6 (phytate), releasing ADP and H+. The biosynthetic direction in vivo is phosphorylation (InsP5 -> InsP6), so relative to how it is written (ADP + H+ + Phytate <=> ATP + InsP5), the physiological flux runs in reverse.

errors: Substrate-enzyme mismatch: alpha-methyl-D-glucoside is an alpha-glycoside, but beta-glucosidase acts on beta-glycosidic bonds. Hydrolysis of methyl-alpha-D-glucoside would require an alpha-glucosidase, not a beta-glucosidase.
rxn09978.other_comments: The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: H2O + methyl-alpha-D-glucoside yields D-glucose + methanol (C7H14O6 + H2O = C6H12O6 + CH4O). Hydrolysis of the glycosidic bond is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, so the forward direction is correct. The main issue is the enzyme annotation, since the anomeric configuration (alpha) does not match a beta-glucosidase.

rxn08040.other_comments: This is the MraY-type / WecA reaction (UDP-GlcNAc:undecaprenyl-phosphate GlcNAc-1-phosphate transferase). Undecaprenyl-phosphate attacks UDP-GlcNAc, transferring GlcNAc-1-phosphate to the lipid carrier and releasing UMP, yielding undecaprenyl-PP-GlcNAc (lipid I/II precursor in enterobacterial common antigen and O-antigen synthesis). The reaction is balanced: the phosphate from UDP-GlcNAc is transferred to undecaprenyl-phosphate forming the diphosphate linkage, with UMP released. Atoms and charges balance.

errors: Product should be ent-kaur-16-en-19-ol (ent-kaurenol), not generic 'Kaurenol'; stereochemistry/nomenclature inconsistent with substrate ent-kaurene
Charge/proton balance is acceptable as written (NADPH + H+ -> NADP+ + H2O with monooxygenase using O2)
rxn04165.other_comments: This represents the first hydroxylation step of ent-kaurene oxidase (CYP701A, KO), a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. It converts ent-kaurene to ent-kaurenol using NADPH and O2, with one oxygen atom incorporated into the product and the other reduced to water. P450 monooxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible, so the forward direction is correct.

rxn05044.other_comments: This is the formyl-CoA transferase (Frc) reaction (EC 2.8.3.16), a CoA-transferase that moves the CoA moiety from formyl-CoA to oxalate, producing oxalyl-CoA and formate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written: each side has the oxalate/oxalyl-CoA carbon skeleton and a formate/formyl-CoA unit, with CoA transferred between them. In vivo it is part of the oxalate degradation pathway in organisms like Oxalobacter formigenes, working together with oxalyl-CoA decarboxylase; it is mechanistically reversible.

rxn12025.other_comments: This is a kinase reaction transferring a phosphate from ATP to 6-thioinosine 5'-monophosphate (a thiopurine drug metabolite, also called thioIMP) to form 6-thioinosine 5'-diphosphate (thioIDP), with ADP as the byproduct. The H+ on the substrate side balances the proton released during phosphoryl transfer. Atoms balance: phosphate transferred from ATP to the monophosphate. As a typical NMP/NDP kinase-type phosphorylation, this proceeds in the direction of ADP and the diphosphate product under physiological conditions, though such kinase reactions can be reversible in principle.

errors: The reaction name (N-Acetyl-D-Galactosamine transport) does not match the metabolite in the reaction (beta-Methylglucoside)
No compartment distinction is shown; a transport reaction must indicate substrates in different compartments (e.g., extracellular vs cytoplasmic) for both H+ and the sugar
As written, both sides are identical (H+ + beta-Methylglucoside on each side), so the reaction represents no net chemical change and is meaningless without compartment labels
rxn11397.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction importing a sugar across the membrane. However, as written it lacks compartment annotations, so the substrates and products are identical. Additionally, the reaction name references N-Acetyl-D-Galactosamine while the actual metabolite is beta-Methylglucoside, indicating an inconsistency. Proton symport transporters driven by the proton motive force typically operate in the import (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written is not balanced if 'Alkenate' refers to the free aldehyde/fatty species released; for a 1-(1-alkenyl) vinyl ether linkage, hydrolysis of the alkenyl ether typically yields a long-chain aldehyde plus glycerophosphocholine, not a free 'alkenate' carboxylate, so the product identity and charge balance are questionable
Proton (H+) generation is inconsistent with vinyl-ether hydrolysis, which does not release a carboxylic acid; an H+ would be expected only if a carboxylate is formed
rxn03102.other_comments: This is a lysophospholipase-type / alkenyl hydrolase reaction acting on 1-alkenyl-glycerophosphocholine (a lyso-plasmalogen derivative). Water hydrolyzes the sn-1 alkenyl (vinyl ether) linkage to give glycerophosphocholine and the released alkenyl moiety. Hydrolysis reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (hydrolytic) direction.

rxn00393.other_comments: This reaction represents a phosphotransfer from glucose-1-phosphate to riboflavin, producing free D-glucose and FMN (riboflavin 5'-phosphate). Stoichiometry is balanced: glucose-1-phosphate (C6H11O9P) + riboflavin (C17H20N4O6) yields D-glucose (C6H12O6) + FMN (C17H21N4O9P), with both atoms and charges conserved. The transfer of the phosphate group is thermodynamically favorable since glucose-1-phosphate is a high-energy phosphate donor and the released glucose is stabilized, driving the reaction toward FMN formation in vivo.

errors: The product of L-idonate oxidation at C5 is 5-keto-D-gluconate, not L-sorbosonate. L-idonate 5-dehydrogenase (IdnD) oxidizes L-idonate to 5-keto-D-gluconate using NAD(P)+.
The conventional name for this enzyme corresponds to oxidation at C5; the product name 'L-sorbosonate' appears incorrect for this substrate-cofactor pairing.
rxn14148.other_comments: This is intended to be the L-idonate dehydrogenase reaction (part of the L-idonate degradation pathway in E. coli, idnD). The reaction oxidizes a secondary hydroxyl of L-idonate to a ketone with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometrically the redox couple and proton balance (NADP+ + R-CHOH-R' <=> NADPH + H+ + R-CO-R') are correct, but the named oxidized product is questionable.

rxn01554.other_comments: This is histamine N-methyltransferase (HNMT, EC 2.1.1.8). SAM donates a methyl group to histamine to form N-tele-methylhistamine (3-methylhistamine, methylated on the tele/N-tau ring nitrogen) and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. The mass balance is correct: the methyl group transfer plus release of a proton accounts for atoms and charge correctly. In vivo this is the primary histamine inactivation pathway in the CNS and other tissues and proceeds in the methylation (forward) direction.

rxn02061.other_comments: This is spermine synthase (EC 2.5.1.22), transferring an aminopropyl group from decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (S-adenosylmethioninamine) to spermidine, producing spermine and 5-methylthioadenosine plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aminopropyl moiety is added to spermidine to form spermine, leaving MTA. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward spermine production.

errors: Carbon/mass imbalance: lanosterol (C30) is converted to 4,4-dimethylcholesta-8,14,24-trienol (C29) with loss of one carbon, but the byproduct should be formic acid (HCOOH) released as the demethylation product, not 'Formate' alone without proper charge/proton balancing; the equation produces formate (CHO2-) but the proton/charge balance is inconsistent

Proton/charge imbalance: with 2 H+ consumed and formate (anion) produced, net charge does not balance (3 NADP+ on product side vs 3 NADPH on reactant side already accounts for charge, but formate adds an extra negative charge)
Hydrogen balance should be rechecked: the standard lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase reaction yields formate plus the demethylated sterol with water; verify H atoms across all species
rxn09617.other_comments: This represents the CYP51 (lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase) reaction, a three-step oxidative demethylation removing the 14-alpha-methyl group of lanosterol using 3 NADPH and 3 O2 per turnover, releasing the carbon as formate and forming a 14,15-double bond to give 4,4-dimethylcholesta-8,14,24-trienol (FF-MAS). The reaction is physiologically essentially irreversible in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn07343.other_comments: This reaction describes the isomerization of 7,9,7',9'-tetra-cis-lycopene (prolycopene) to all-trans-lycopene, catalyzed by carotenoid isomerase (CRTISO) in plants or by light/photoisomerization in some systems. Stoichiometrically it is a simple 1:1 isomerization where the molecular formula (C40H56) is conserved on both sides, so it is balanced. In vivo, the conversion proceeds toward all-trans-lycopene because the all-trans isomer is the biologically required substrate for downstream cyclization into carotenoids, making the forward direction strongly favored.

errors: Charge imbalance: left side (NADP+ has charge, H+ is +1, Hg is 0) does not balance with right side (NADPH plus Hg2+ which is +2); the reduction of Hg2+ to Hg0 is a 2-electron transfer but NADPH provides only a hydride (2 electrons plus a proton), so electron count must be checked carefully
The reaction as written is reversed relative to the actual mercuric reductase mechanism: NADPH reduces Hg2+ to Hg0, so the physiological direction is NADPH + Hg2+ -> NADP+ + H+ + Hg0
Notation issue: NADP should be written as NADP+ to reflect its oxidized charged form
rxn02021.other_comments: This represents the mercuric reductase (MerA) reaction, an FAD-containing enzyme that uses NADPH to reduce ionic mercury Hg2+ to elemental mercury Hg0. As written, the equation shows oxidation of Hg0 coupled to NADP+ reduction, which is the non-physiological direction. The two-electron transfer (Hg2+ + 2e- -> Hg0) is consistent with NADPH oxidation.

errors: Stachydrine (proline betaine) appears identically on both the substrate and product sides without a compartment distinction; for a transport reaction these should be labeled with different compartments (e.g., Stachydrine[periplasm/extracellular] -> Stachydrine[cytoplasm]). As written, the substrate is consumed and reproduced with no net transport indicated.
rxn10073.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transporter for proline betaine (stachydrine) coupled to ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+). ATP hydrolysis stoichiometry is balanced. The transport itself should show stachydrine moving from outside (periplasm/extracellular) into the cytoplasm; the lack of compartment tags is the main issue. ABC importers driven by ATP hydrolysis are physiologically unidirectional (uptake).

rxn02069.other_comments: This reaction describes the interconversion between 4,5alpha-dihydrocortisone and cortisone, catalyzed by a delta4-3-ketosteroid 5alpha-reductase type enzyme using the NADP+/NADPH redox pair. The named enzyme '4,5alpha-dihydrocortisone:NADP+ delta4-oxidoreductase' is the oxidoreductase reading. As written, the dihydro substrate is oxidized to introduce the delta4 double bond (cortisone), reducing NADP+ to NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced: removal of two hydrogens from the saturated steroid yields the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone, with electrons transferred to NADP+. In vivo, 5alpha-reductases are essentially physiologically irreversible and run in the reductive direction (cortisone + NADPH -> dihydrocortisone). Therefore the biologically favored direction is the reverse of how this reaction is written.

errors: The product side should include carbon dioxide (CO2). The conversion of the 2-succinyl-... (SSA-TPP) addition to isochorismate followed by elimination of pyruvate also releases CO2 in the menaquinone biosynthesis pathway. Mass/charge balance is not satisfied as written.
SHCHC formation here is typically coupled to release of pyruvate AND CO2; verify whether a water molecule is consumed/produced.
rxn03398.other_comments: This is the MenD/MenH-type step in menaquinone (vitamin K2) biosynthesis. SHCHC = (1R,6R)-6-hydroxy-2-succinyl-cyclohexa-2,4-diene-1-carboxylate (or 2-succinyl-6-hydroxy-2,4-cyclohexadiene-1-carboxylate). The succinic semialdehyde-thiamine diphosphate anion is the activated succinyl-semialdehyde TPP intermediate (from MenD) that condenses with isochorismate, regenerating TPP and eliminating pyruvate. The reaction is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, driven toward menaquinone synthesis.

errors: Product identity questionable: 'Bisdemalonylsalvianin' is not a standard product name for caffeoylation of pelargonin; the naming convention is inconsistent. Salvianin derivatives typically involve malonylated pelargonidin glycosides, and the relationship between substrate and product (added caffeoyl group) versus the 'bisdemalonyl' prefix needs verification.
rxn07666.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase reaction (hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA dependent) transferring a caffeoyl group from caffeoyl-CoA onto an anthocyanin (pelargonin, a pelargonidin diglucoside) to form an acylated anthocyanin, releasing free CoA. Stoichiometry of CoA and acyl transfer (1:1) is balanced in principle. Such CoA-dependent acyltransfer reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo due to the high-energy thioester bond cleavage.

errors: Mass and charge imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced. Geranyl diphosphate (C10H20O7P2, often written with appropriate protonation) converts to PPi (diphosphate) plus the cyclized hydrocarbon product, but the proton/charge accounting requires care. Geranyl diphosphate is C10H17(OPP); cyclization to a monoterpene (C10H16) releases diphosphate. The product 'Car-3-ene' (3-carene, C10H16) is correct in carbon count, but the listed extra H+ leads to a hydrogen imbalance unless ionic forms are specified consistently.
rxn12057.other_comments: This represents a monoterpene cyclase (carene synthase / 3-carene synthase) reaction in which geranyl diphosphate (GPP, C10H20O7P2) is converted via ionization and cyclization into the bicyclic monoterpene 3-carene (car-3-ene, C10H16) with release of pyrophosphate (PPi). The carbon skeleton (C10) is conserved. Such terpene synthase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to loss of the diphosphate leaving group.

errors: The product decaprenylphosphoryl-beta-D-5-phosphoribofuranose/arabinofuranose contains a furanose form, but the substrate is named '5-phosphoarabinose pyrophosphate' without specifying furanose; the donor in this pathway is properly 5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose-1-diphosphate (PRPP) used in DPA biosynthesis, so substrate naming is inconsistent

Charge/proton balance: transfer of a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP releasing PPi typically does not release an additional H+; the H+ balance should be checked - the product retains a phosphate group and the reaction as written may not be proton-balanced

Stoichiometry concern: decaprenyl phosphate has 10 isoprene units but the lipid carrier in Mycobacterium DPA synthesis is decaprenyl phosphate (C50); the stereochemistry descriptor lists only 9 configurations (E,E,E,E,E,E,E,Z,Z) for what should be a decaprenyl (10-unit) chain
rxn10740.other_comments: This appears to be the DPA (decaprenylphosphoryl-D-arabinose) biosynthesis step in mycobacteria, where a phosphoribosyl/phosphoarabinosyl group is transferred from a PRPP-like donor to decaprenyl phosphate, releasing pyrophosphate. The release of PPi (which is hydrolyzed in vivo) drives this reaction forward.

rxn07200.other_comments: This is the hydrogenase reaction (NADP+ oxidoreductase) where molecular hydrogen reduces NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2 (2 H) provides 1 hydride (H-) to NADP+ forming NADPH plus 1 H+. Atoms and charge balance (left: NADP+ charge balanced by H2 neutral; right: NADPH plus H+). The enzyme (e.g., NAD(P)H-dependent hydrogenase) catalyzes this reversibly, though physiological direction depends on H2 partial pressure and redox state of the cell.

rxn14380.other_comments: This represents N-glycosylation, transfer of a GlcNAc moiety from UDP-GlcNAc onto a protein asparagine residue, releasing UDP. The product is N-(N-acetyl-D-glucosaminyl)-L-asparagine residue (linkage to the asparagine amide nitrogen). Stoichiometry is balanced: the GlcNAc group transferred from UDP-GlcNAc plus the asparagine acceptor yields UDP plus the glycosylated protein. The enzyme name describes a beta-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase. Glycosyltransferase reactions using sugar nucleotide donors are thermodynamically favorable and operate in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Substrate mismatch: the enzyme name 'ATP:pyridoxal 5'-phosphotransferase' (pyridoxal kinase, EC 2.7.1.35) refers to phosphorylation of pyridoxal, but the reaction shows PM (pyridoxamine) being converted to pyridoxamine phosphate

Stoichiometric inconsistency relative to enzyme name: pyridoxal kinase produces pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, not pyridoxamine phosphate; if the reaction intends pyridoxamine kinase activity, the product is correct but the name is wrong
rxn01807.other_comments: This represents an ATP-dependent kinase reaction phosphorylating pyridoxamine (PM) to pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate, producing ADP and H+. The atom/charge balance of the written reaction (ATP + PM -> ADP + H+ + PMP) is correct for a kinase. The issue is the enzyme name references pyridoxal, not pyridoxamine.

rxn06874.other_comments: This is the nitrogenase reaction reducing dinitrogen (N2) to ammonia (NH3) with obligate hydrogen evolution. Stoichiometry is balanced: N2 + 8 e- (from 8 reduced ferredoxin) + 8 H+ + 16 ATP -> 2 NH3 + H2 + 16 ADP + 16 Pi. Atom balance: N (2=2), H balance accounts for 16 H2O providing protons and the 6 H+ released plus H2; charge and electron balance are consistent with 8 electrons transferred. ATP hydrolysis makes this strongly exergonic and physiologically irreversible.

errors: Charge and proton imbalance: with 5 H+ on the left and 4 H+ on the right, the net proton transfer is only 1, but NADH oxidation transfers 2 electrons (2 H equivalents) to the quinone. For a redox-balanced reaction, NADH + H+ + MMK-7 -> NAD+ + MMK-7-H2 (quinol) should consume 1 H+ for the chemical reduction, plus any translocated protons should appear symmetrically (e.g., n H+[in] -> n H+[out]). The given 5 vs 4 split does not represent a balanced chemical + translocation scheme.
Mass balance issue: the quinol product 'methymenaquinol 7' has a misspelling and the H balance does not close correctly given the 5/4 proton split.
NAD should be written as NAD+ to reflect correct charge.
rxn13729.other_comments: This represents respiratory Complex I-type NADH:quinone oxidoreductase using methylmenaquinone-7 as the electron acceptor, reducing it to methylmenaquinol-7 while NADH is oxidized to NAD+. Proton translocation across the membrane is implied by the asymmetric H+ counts.

rxn01475.other_comments: This is the 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (non-decarboxylating) reaction, EC 1.1.1.343, oxidizing the C2 hydroxyl of 6-phospho-D-gluconate to a ketone (6-phospho-2-dehydro-D-gluconate) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Note this is distinct from the classic oxidative pentose phosphate pathway enzyme (EC 1.1.1.44) which is decarboxylating and yields ribulose-5-phosphate plus CO2. The stoichiometry shown is balanced in atoms and charge: a 2-electron oxidation transfers a hydride to NADP+ and releases one proton.

errors: Stoichiometric/elemental imbalance: Glycerol (C3H8O3) does not balance against H2O + Lactaldehyde. Lactaldehyde is C3H6O2 and water is H2O, giving C3H8O3 on the right, so carbon and oxygen actually balance, but the typical product of glycerol dehydration by glycerol dehydratase is 3-hydroxypropionaldehyde (3-HPA), not lactaldehyde
Mislabeled product: glycerol dehydratase (EC 4.2.1.30) converts glycerol to 3-hydroxypropionaldehyde + H2O, not to lactaldehyde
rxn00769.other_comments: This represents glycerol dehydratase activity (hydro-lyase removing water from glycerol). The elemental formulas of glycerol (C3H8O3) and H2O + lactaldehyde (H2O = H2O; lactaldehyde = C3H6O2) do sum correctly (C3H8O3), so it is formally balanced. However, the biologically correct product of glycerol dehydration is 3-hydroxypropionaldehyde, not lactaldehyde; both are C3H6O2 isomers. The dehydration is strongly favored in the forward direction in vivo (coenzyme B12-dependent, essentially irreversible).

rxn07240.other_comments: This is a heparan/heparin biosynthesis glucuronyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.225). UDP-glucuronate donates a glucuronosyl residue to the non-reducing end N-acetyl-alpha-D-glucosaminyl terminus of the growing glycosaminoglycan chain, forming a beta-1,4 linkage and releasing UDP. The reaction is balanced: one glucuronosyl group is transferred from UDP-glucuronate (yielding UDP) to the acceptor proteoglycan, elongating it by one GlcA unit.

rxn00129.other_comments: This reaction describes the conversion of S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) into 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA) and 2-aminobutan-4-olide (homoserine lactone), catalyzed by an enzyme of the type that cleaves SAM intramolecularly. The atoms balance: SAM (C15H22N6O5S) splits into MTA (C11H15N5O3S) plus the aminobutyrolactone moiety (C4H7NO2), which accounts for the homoserine lactone portion derived from the methionine carbon skeleton. Stoichiometry and elemental balance appear correct.

errors: The reaction as written is not mass/charge balanced. A direct ATP-dependent phosphotransfer (ATP + cellobiose -> ADP + cellobiose 6-phosphate + H+) is atomically balanced, but cellobiose phosphorylation in vivo is typically performed by the PTS (phosphoenolpyruvate-dependent phosphotransferase system) using PEP rather than ATP, so the enzyme/substrate context may be incorrect.

rxn01049.other_comments: The reaction depicts phosphorylation of cellobiose to cellobiose 6-phosphate using ATP, releasing ADP and a proton. rxn00282.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction catalyzed by aminotransferase (EC 2.6.1.12, alanine-oxaloacetate transaminase). The amino group from L-alanine is transferred to oxaloacetate, yielding pyruvate and L-aspartate. The reaction is balanced: both sides have matching atoms and charges. Carbon balance: oxaloacetate (C4) + alanine (C3) = pyruvate (C3) + aspartate (C4). Nitrogen and other atoms balance as well. Like most aminotransferase reactions, the equilibrium constant is near unity, making it freely reversible in vivo with direction determined by relative substrate/product concentrations.

rxn03354.other_comments: This is the aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction converting 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde to 5-hydroxyindoleacetate (5-HIAA), part of serotonin degradation. Stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde + H2O + NAD+ yields the carboxylate + NADH + 2 H+. Mass and charge balance are correct (aldehyde RCHO + H2O - 2H -> RCOOH releasing 2 electrons and 2 protons; one proton/hydride to NAD+, net 2 H+ on product side). In vivo, aldehyde dehydrogenase reactions are essentially irreversible and proceed in the oxidative (forward) direction.

rxn08255.other_comments: This reaction represents the ATP-dependent activation of carnitine to carnitinyl-CoA (an acyl-adenylate forming/thioester forming ligase). The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + carnitine yields ADP + inorganic phosphate + carnitinyl-CoA, releasing the carboxyl group of carnitine to form a thioester bond with CoA. This is consistent with a ligase mechanism that hydrolyzes ATP to ADP + Pi. In vivo, ATP-driven CoA-ligase/synthetase reactions are typically pushed in the synthesis (activation) direction, favoring carnitinyl-CoA formation.

rxn01840.other_comments: This is phenylacetaldehyde dehydrogenase. Alpha-tolualdehyde is a synonym for phenylacetaldehyde, and PACT denotes phenylacetate (the product acid). The reaction oxidizes phenylacetaldehyde with NAD+ and water to phenylacetate, producing NADH and H+. The atoms and charges balance: aldehyde (RCHO) + H2O + NAD+ -> RCOOH (as carboxylate) + NADH + H+. In vivo, aldehyde dehydrogenases are essentially irreversible in the oxidative (forward) direction.

errors: Carbon and hydrogen are not balanced: a complete iso-C16:1 fatty acid (16 carbons, 1 double bond) synthesis from isobutyryl-CoA (4 C) plus 6 malonyl-CoA (each contributing 2 C after decarboxylation = 12 C) gives 16 C, which is correct, but the NADPH count is inconsistent. rxn10034.other_comments: This represents iterative fatty acid (type I/II) biosynthesis: a primer (isobutyryl-CoA) extended by 6 malonyl-CoA units to yield a branched iso-C16:1 fatty acid, releasing 6 CO2 and 7 CoA. Such biosynthetic chain-elongation reactions are physiologically irreversible (forward), driven by malonyl-CoA decarboxylation and NADPH consumption.

rxn04706.other_comments: This is the HpcH/HpaI-type hydratase reaction in the homoprotocatechuate (4-hydroxyphenylacetate) degradation pathway. The hydro-lyase (water addition across the 4,5 double bond) converts 2-hydroxyhepta-2,4-dienedioate (2-oxo form / enol of 2-oxohept-3-enedioate) plus water into 2,4-dihydroxyhept-2-enedioate. The reaction is balanced: addition of one H2O across a C=C bond yields one hydroxyl. In vivo, within the catabolic pathway, the hydration runs in the direction of substrate breakdown (toward the dihydroxy product, which is subsequently cleaved to pyruvate and succinic semialdehyde).

rxn01125.other_comments: This is the oxidation of 2-keto-3-deoxy-D-gluconate (2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-gluconate) at the C6 position by NADP+, producing NADPH, H+, and the 6-aldehyde/6-oxo product (4,5-dihydroxy-2,6-dioxohexanoate). The substrate has a free primary alcohol at C6 that is oxidized to an aldehyde, consistent with a 6-oxoreductase (EC 1.1.1.127-type). Stoichiometry balances: one hydride and one proton are removed from the alcohol, transferred to NADP+ giving NADPH + H+. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance. As a typical NAD(P)-dependent alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenase, the reaction is thermodynamically reversible, though the in vivo direction depends on cofactor ratios and pathway context.

errors: Mass/charge imbalance: hydrolysis of ADP-ribose by H2O yields AMP + D-ribose 5-phosphate, not ribose 1-phosphate; the products as written do not balance phosphate placement and the H+ stoichiometry is incorrect. Correct reaction (R01885, EC 3.6.1.13): H2O + ADP-ribose -> AMP + D-ribose 5-phosphate + 2 H+
rxn01375.other_comments: This is ADP-ribose diphosphatase (Nudix hydrolase) cleaving the diphosphate bond of ADP-ribose. The hydrolysis is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward AMP and ribose 5-phosphate. The given product 'Ribose 1-phosphate' appears to be a misannotation; it should be ribose 5-phosphate.

errors: This reaction as written (dehydration forming the beta-lactam ring from the penicilloic acid) is not stoichiometrically or chemically correct for penicillinase/beta-lactamase chemistry; the physiological reaction is the hydrolytic ring-opening of Penicillin G to benzylpenicilloic acid, which consumes water rather than releasing it

The proton (H+) balance is questionable: hydrolysis of the beta-lactam generates a carboxylate, so a proton may be released, but the direction shown (ring closure releasing H2O) does not properly account for the carboxyl group of penicilloic acid
rxn11599.other_comments: This corresponds to the beta-lactamase (penicillinase) reaction. Penicillin G (benzylpenicillin) is hydrolyzed by water to give benzylpenicilloic acid via opening of the beta-lactam ring. As written (Benzylpenicilloic acid -> Penicillin G + H2O) it depicts ring closure, which is thermodynamically unfavorable and not the in vivo direction. In vivo the reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly toward hydrolysis (ring opening), i.e., the reverse of the written direction.

rxn08913.other_comments: This reaction represents the spontaneous oxidation of L-methionine by hydrogen peroxide to form methionine sulfoxide (specifically the R-diastereomer) plus water. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O2 provides one oxygen atom to the sulfur of methionine, releasing H2O. Atoms balance (H2O2 + Met -> H2O + Met-sulfoxide; the extra O is incorporated into the thioether sulfur). As a spontaneous oxidation by a strong oxidant (H2O2), this proceeds essentially irreversibly in vivo; reduction back to methionine requires enzymatic action by methionine sulfoxide reductases (MsrB for the R-form), not simple reversal.

errors: Atom/hydrogen imbalance: phytoene (C40H64) cannot be converted to zeta-carotene (C40H56) by releasing 2 H2; the desaturation introduces two double bonds, removing 4 H atoms (2 H2), but in vivo this is a dehydrogenation requiring an electron/hydrogen acceptor (e.g., quinone/FAD), not free H2
Free molecular H2 is not a physiological product of carotenoid desaturation; the reaction as written misrepresents the redox cofactor chemistry
rxn07341.other_comments: This represents the phytoene desaturase (PDS/CRTI-type) step converting 15-cis-phytoene to 9,9'-di-cis-zeta-carotene via two desaturation (dehydrogenation) events. Carbon stoichiometry is consistent (both C40), and removal of two pairs of hydrogens (2 H2 equivalent) matches the introduction of two new double bonds, but the hydrogens are transferred to an acceptor rather than released as H2.

errors: Product name misspelled: 'methymenaquinol 7' should be 'methylmenaquinol 7'
Iminoaspartate is typically written as iminosuccinate (2-iminosuccinate) in the L-aspartate oxidase reaction, though iminoaspartate is an accepted synonym
rxn13761.other_comments: This is the L-aspartate oxidase (NadB) reaction, the first step in de novo NAD biosynthesis. L-aspartate is oxidized to iminoaspartate (2-iminosuccinate) with the reduction of a quinone electron acceptor. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: aspartate loses 2 H (2e- and 2H+) which are transferred to the quinone forming the quinol. Under anaerobic conditions the enzyme uses menaquinone derivatives (here methylmenaquinone-7) rather than O2 as the electron acceptor. In vivo this proceeds in the oxidative direction toward iminoaspartate for NAD synthesis.

errors: The reaction as written is unbalanced because water is missing; oxidation of spermidine by NAD+ to form a dehydro (imine) product typically does not consume water, but if the product is the aminoaldehyde, water must be included as a reactant

Charge/mass balance cannot be fully verified without explicit formulas for spermidine and dehydrospermidine, but the proton balance (NAD+ + RH2 -> NADH + H+ + R) is consistent for a simple dehydrogenation
rxn07308.other_comments: This represents an NAD+-dependent oxidation of spermidine to a dehydrogenated (imine) product, generating NADH and a proton. The core hydride-transfer stoichiometry (NAD+ + substrate-H2 -> NADH + H+ + dehydro-substrate) is internally consistent. NAD+/NADH oxidoreductase reactions are generally written as reversible, though in vivo the direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio.

errors: Hydrogen and charge imbalance: the reaction consumes 14 H+ but produces NADP (written without charge); using 10 NADPH + 14 H+ -> 10 NADP+ leaves a proton imbalance that does not close cleanly

rxn10708.other_comments: This represents a polyketide synthase (PKS)-type iterative elongation producing a phenolic phthiocerol precursor on ACP, using malonyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA as extender units with NADPH-driven reductions, starting from phenol palmitic acid ACP. The chemistry is biosynthetic and committed (driven by decarboxylation and NADPH consumption), so it runs in the forward (anabolic) direction in vivo.

rxn05370.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase reaction (FabI-type) in fatty acid biosynthesis, reducing the trans-2 double bond of 8-methyl-trans-dec-2-enoyl-ACP to the saturated 8-methyl-decanoyl-ACP using NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ provides the two electrons and proton needed to reduce the C=C double bond, regenerating NADP+. This is a branched-chain fatty acid elongation cycle step. The enoyl reductase step is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the reductive (biosynthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn01153.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of D-glutamine to D-glutamate, releasing ammonia. Stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + D-glutamine (C5H10N2O3) yields NH3 + D-glutamate (C5H9NO4). Atoms balance (C5, H12, N2, O4 on each side when accounting for the ammonia and water). Amidohydrolase reactions of glutamine to glutamate are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn07865.other_comments: This is the zeatin O-glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.203), transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to the hydroxyl group of dihydrozeatin to form dihydrozeatin-O-glucoside, releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: glucose is transferred from UDP-glucose to the acceptor, leaving UDP. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the direction of glycoside formation in vivo.

Substrate naming inconsistency: the reaction name references leucocyanidin but the substrate listed is leucodelphinidin
Charge/proton balance cannot be fully verified due to the unidentified product 'Ephdine'

rxn03412.other_comments: This appears to be a leucoanthocyanidin dioxygenase (LDOX/ANS) type 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase reaction. Such reactions consume O2 and 2-oxoglutarate, releasing CO2 and succinate, and oxidize the leucoanthocyanidin substrate. The standard product is an anthocyanidin (e.g., delphinidin from leucodelphinidin) plus water, not 'Ephdine', which seems to be a corrupted or erroneous compound name.

The balanced form should be: Fluorene + NADH + H+ + O2 -> cis-dihydrodiol + NAD+. The product name is truncated, making full balance verification impossible.

Charge/proton balance cannot be fully verified due to truncated product name; written reaction lacks explicit water if any monooxygenase mechanism were involved, but for dioxygenase both O atoms go into product so no water is expected.
rxn11655.other_comments: This represents an aromatic-ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase acting on fluorene to form a cis-3,4-dihydrodiol, consuming NADH, O2, and a proton. This is the initial step in bacterial fluorene degradation and is essentially irreversible in vivo due to O2 consumption and the energetic favorability of dioxygenation.

rxn00437.other_comments: This reaction represents the phosphorylation of thiamine diphosphate (TPP/ThDP) to thiamine triphosphate (ThTP) using ATP as the phosphate donor, catalyzed by thiamine-diphosphate kinase (EC 2.7.4.15). Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + TPP -> ADP + thiamine triphosphate, with one phosphate transferred from ATP to TPP. In vivo, the reaction proceeds in the direction of ThTP synthesis, though ThTP levels are typically low and tightly regulated, with hydrolysis occurring via separate phosphatases.

As written, the products/substrates use 'Aminofructose 6-phosphate' and 'Iminoerythrose 4-phosphate', which are non-standard/incorrect amino-sugar derivatives not consistent with transketolase chemistry.

The presence of nitrogen (amino/imino groups) in both an oxygenated substrate and product is inconsistent with the named glycolaldehyde transfer; nitrogen balance and identity of these species are dubious.
rxn04443.other_comments: This is annotated as a transketolase-type reaction (sedoheptulose-7-phosphate:glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate glycolaldehydetransferase). The enzyme name implies a standard non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway reaction, but the listed metabolites (aminofructose-6-phosphate and iminoerythrose-4-phosphate) do not match the canonical substrates/products, suggesting the substituted name fields are inconsistent or the reaction definition is corrupted.

rxn01708.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase reaction transferring a palmitoyl group from palmitoyl-CoA to the steroid hormone ecdysone, forming ecdysone palmitate (a fatty acyl ester) and releasing free CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: the palmitoyl group (C16 acyl) transfers from the thioester of CoA to a hydroxyl group on ecdysone, with CoA-SH released. This is the storage/conjugation pathway for ecdysteroids and is thermodynamically favorable in the acylation direction due to cleavage of the high-energy thioester bond.

rxn04622.other_comments: This is intended to be an S-adenosyl-L-methionine-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction (SAM -> SAH plus methylation of a flavonoid). The catabolic transfer of a methyl group from SAM is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward (methylation) direction in vivo. However, the substrate (luteolin) and product (kaempferide) are inconsistent with each other and with the enzyme name (kaempferol). The correct substrate should be kaempferol to yield kaempferide.

rxn01800.other_comments: This is the deoxycytidine deaminase reaction (EC 3.5.4.14), hydrolytic deamination of deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine plus ammonia. The stoichiometry is balanced: deoxycytidine (C9H13N3O4) + H2O + H+ yields deoxyuridine (C9H12N2O5) + NH4+ (written here as NH3 plus the consumed H+). Mass and charge balance appropriately when ammonia is treated as NH4+. As a hydrolytic deamination, the reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo and proceeds in the forward (deamination) direction.

rxn03663.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic cleavage of 2-hydroxy-6-oxoocta-2,4,7-trienoate (a meta-cleavage product in styrene/aromatic degradation pathways) by a C-C hydrolase (formylhydrolase/MhpC-type). Water attacks the dienol/keto system, cleaving the C-C bond to yield 2-oxopent-4-enoate (2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate / oxopent-4-enoate) plus acrylate (2-propenoate). The atom and charge balance check out: substrate C8H7O4(-) plus H2O gives oxopentenoate C5H5O3(-) plus acrylate C3H3O2(-) plus H+. Carbon (8 = 5+3), and overall mass/charge are balanced.

rxn02675.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of L-rhamno-1,4-lactone to L-rhamnonate by a lactonohydrolase. The lactone ring is opened by adding water, producing the open-chain rhamnonate (a sugar acid). Stoichiometry is balanced: the lactone (C6H10O5) plus H2O (H2O) yields rhamnonate (C6H11O6 as the acid, or C6H10O6 minus H+ as the anion). Releasing H+ along with the carboxylate anion is consistent with formation of the deprotonated acid at physiological pH. Mass and charge balance check out: left side neutral, right side H+ (+1) plus rhamnonate (-1) = 0.

rxn06490.other_comments: This is the mRNA cap guanine-N7 methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.56). SAM transfers a methyl group to the N7 position of the 5'-terminal guanosine of the GpppN-capped RNA, producing m7G-capped RNA and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. The atoms balance: a single methyl group is transferred from SAM to the guanine N7, converting SAM to SAH and G-cap to m7G-cap. Stoichiometry is correct (1:1:1:1).
