The oxidation of mevalonate to mevaldate (as written, forward) is thermodynamically unfavorable; in vivo the physiologically relevant direction is reduction of mevaldate to mevalonate (i.e., the reverse of the written direction).

rxn07710.other_comments: This is the caffeine synthase reaction, methylation of theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine) at the N1 position to form caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine), using SAM as methyl donor and producing SAH. Atom and charge balance are correct: methyl transfer from SAM to theobromine yields caffeine plus SAH plus a proton. SAM methyltransferase reactions are strongly favored in the forward direction in vivo due to the favorable thermodynamics of SAM-to-SAH conversion.

rxn01461.other_comments: This is the arginine:4-aminobutanoate amidinotransferase reaction (EC 2.1.4.-). It transfers the amidino (guanidino) group from L-arginine to the amino group of 4-aminobutanoate (GABA), producing L-ornithine and 4-guanidinobutanoate (guanidinobutyrate). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: arginine donates its amidino group, becoming ornithine, while GABA accepts it to become 4-guanidinobutyrate. Atoms and charges balance on both sides. This reaction is part of the arginine/guanidinobutyrate catabolic pathway in certain bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas).

errors: The reaction is identical on both sides (H+ + Arsenate <=> H+ + Arsenate), making it a null/trivial reaction with no net chemical change
No compartment annotation is provided; a transport reaction must specify distinct compartments (e.g., periplasm vs cytoplasm) for the substrate to indicate translocation
The reaction is named 'Arsenite transport' but the metabolite listed is Arsenate, not arsenite - this is a naming/metabolite inconsistency
rxn13759.other_comments: This appears to be intended as a transmembrane transport reaction for an arsenic oxyanion. As written, identical species and identical (or absent) compartments on both sides mean it transports nothing. For a valid transporter, the substrate and accompanying ion should appear in different compartments, e.g., Arsenite[c] + H+[c] <=> Arsenite[p] + H+[p]. Also the metabolite (arsenate) does not match the reaction name (arsenite).

rxn03528.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.128, related to benzylisoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis). SAM donates a methyl group to (S)-6-O-methylnorlaudanosoline, producing the further methylated product and S-adenosyl-homocysteine plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group is transferred from SAM to the acceptor hydroxyl, releasing SAH and H+. The biosynthetic flow in vivo proceeds toward alkaloid formation.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the standard fatty acid elongation cycle (condensation + reduction + dehydration + reduction) consumes 2 NADPH, not 1, to fully reduce the beta-keto group to a methylene/saturated carbon.

The product is described as containing a cis double bond (cis-21-tetracosanoyl-ACP), which is inconsistent with a fully reduced elongation product; if a cis-unsaturated bond is introduced, the second reduction step is skipped, but then only 1 NADPH is used and the dehydration product retains a double bond - the labeling and intermediate handling are inconsistent.

Carbon balance: docosanoyl (C22) + malonyl (adds C2 with loss of CO2) yields a C24 chain (tetracosanoyl), which is correct, but the degree of saturation/H accounting must match the NADPH count; as written H/electron balance is questionable.

ACP/holo-ACP bookkeeping: malonyl-ACP and docosanoyl-ACP are consumed, one free ACP released - net acyl-carrier balance appears off (two ACP-bound substrates in, one ACP-bound product + one free ACP out, which is balanced; but verify the CoA/ACP forms).
rxn13432.other_comments: This is intended to be a fatty acid elongation step (FAS-type) extending docosanoyl-ACP (C22) by a malonyl-ACP-derived C2 unit, releasing CO2 and forming a C24 (tetracosanoyl) product, here drawn as a cis-unsaturated species. Biosynthetic elongation/condensation steps are effectively irreversible in vivo due to decarboxylation, so it runs forward.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: chlorophyllase hydrolysis of an ester bond releases the phytol alcohol and the free carboxylic acid (chlorophyllide), which deprotonates to release at most 1 H+, not 2.0 H+
Mass/charge balance should be verified; ester hydrolysis adds H2O across the bond yielding one -OH (phytol) and one -COOH (chlorophyllide)
rxn03895.other_comments: This is the chlorophyllase reaction (EC 3.1.1.14), hydrolyzing the phytyl ester bond of chlorophyll a to yield phytol and chlorophyllide a. As a hydrolase acting on a water-rich environment, the reaction proceeds in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo. The main issue is the 2.0 H+ stoichiometry, which appears incorrect for a single ester hydrolysis.

rxn08460.other_comments: This is the glutathione-dependent formaldehyde dehydrogenase (ADH5/class III ADH) reaction. The substrate hydroxymethylglutathione (S-hydroxymethylglutathione, the spontaneous adduct of formaldehyde and glutathione) is oxidized by NAD+ to S-formylglutathione, with production of NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced: the C-H of the hydroxymethyl group is removed as a hydride to NAD+ along with a proton, converting the hemithioacetal alcohol to a thioester. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn02569.other_comments: This is the selenophosphate synthetase (SelD) reaction. ATP reacts with selenide and water to produce selenophosphate, AMP, and orthophosphate. Mass and charge balance check: left side ATP(4-) + selenide(HSe-, charge -1) + H2O gives products AMP(2-) + phosphate(HPO4 2-) + selenophosphate(SePO3 2-) + 3 H+. Atom and charge balance are consistent as written. In vivo the reaction is driven forward to generate selenophosphate, the active selenium donor for selenocysteine and selenouridine biosynthesis.

errors: The transported substrate (gly-asp-L) appears on both sides of the reaction with identical compartment designation; a proper transport reaction must distinguish the substrate by compartment (e.g., gly-asp-L[external] <=> gly-asp-L[cytosol]). As written, the peptide cancels out and the net reaction is simply ATP hydrolysis, which does not represent transport.
rxn05537.other_comments: This is intended to be an ABC-type oligopeptide importer that couples ATP hydrolysis (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the translocation of the dipeptide glycyl-aspartate. The ATP hydrolysis stoichiometry is balanced and correct, but the transport aspect is not properly represented because the substrate is not assigned to different compartments.

errors: Stoichiometric/redox inconsistency: the conversion shown corresponds to a reduction (loss of a double bond, addition of 2 H to give 4,5beta-dihydrocortisone), which should consume NADH + H+ and produce NAD+. As written, NAD+ is consumed and NADH produced (an oxidation), which contradicts the direction of substrate transformation.

Substrate naming inconsistency: 'Urocortisone' is an unusual/non-standard name; the reaction appears to interconvert cortisone and 4,5beta-dihydrocortisone via the C4-C5 double bond reduction, so the oxidized substrate should be the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone (cortisone) rather than the dihydro form being the product of an NAD+-dependent oxidation.
rxn03299.other_comments: This appears to be a 5-beta-reductase (steroid 5beta-reductase, AKR1D1-type) type transformation reducing the C4=C5 double bond of a 3-oxo-delta4 steroid. Such reactions use NADPH/NADH as the electron donor. The cofactor usage as written (NAD+ -> NADH while reducing the steroid) is internally inconsistent; the reducing reaction should run with NAD(P)H as reductant, i.e., effectively the reverse of the written direction.

errors: The reaction as written shows free palmitate (hexadecanoate) condensing with the lipid A acceptor and releasing water, but in vivo acyltransferases use an activated acyl donor (typically acyl-ACP or a phospholipid such as a palmitoyl-phosphatidylethanolamine/PagP-type donor), not free fatty acid; free palmitate plus a proton cannot directly acylate to release only water under physiological conditions

The likely physiological PagP reaction transfers a palmitate from a glycerophospholipid (e.g., phosphatidylethanolamine) to lipid A, producing the deacylated lysophospholipid as a coproduct; that coproduct is missing

Mass/charge balance is questionable: a simple H+ + carboxylate + acceptor -> H2O condensation does not balance the carbon/atom budget of attaching a C16 acyl group unless the donor's leaving group is accounted for
rxn08789.other_comments: This represents palmitoyltransferase (PagP-like) acylation of core oligosaccharide-lipid A to form the hepta-acylated species. Acyl transfer to lipid A is essentially irreversible and physiologically proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction, even though stated as reversible.

rxn03155.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of 5-(L-alanin-3-yl)-2-hydroxy-cis,cis-muconate 6-semialdehyde to stizolobinate, coupled with reduction of NAD to NADH and release of a proton. The semialdehyde group is oxidized to a carboxylate/cyclized to form stizolobinate. The named enzyme 'DOPA:oxygen 2,3-oxidoreductase (recyclizing)' is actually the ring-cleaving dioxygenase that produces the semialdehyde substrate; the dehydrogenase step shown here (stizolobinate synthase pathway) converts that semialdehyde to stizolobinate. Stoichiometry is balanced: aldehyde oxidation transfers a hydride to NAD with release of H+. This is consistent with NAD-dependent semialdehyde dehydrogenase chemistry, which strongly favors the oxidative (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn08199.other_comments: This is a CDP-diacylglycerol pyrophosphatase (phosphatase) reaction with C12:0 (dodecanoyl/lauroyl) acyl chains. Hydrolysis of CDP-diacylglycerol cleaves the pyrophosphate bond, yielding CMP and phosphatidic acid (1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate). Atom and charge balance: CDP-DAG carries CMP-PP linked to DAG; water adds across the diphosphate to release CMP and leave a single phosphate on the glycerol (phosphatidate), with one H+ released. Stoichiometry and charge are balanced.

rxn01565.other_comments: This is an amine N-methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.49 family) where SAM donates a methyl group to the primary amine of tryptamine, producing N-methyltryptamine and S-adenosyl-homocysteine. The methyl transfer to the amine nitrogen releases a proton, so the H+ on the product side is correct. Atom and charge balance: SAM (C15H22N6O5S, +1) + tryptamine (C10H12N2) gives SAH (C14H20N6O5S) + N-methyltryptamine (C11H14N2) + H+. Carbon: 25 = 25; the methyl group (CH3) transfers correctly, and the released H+ balances charge.

rxn02741.other_comments: This is a nucleoside hydrolase reaction where 1-methyladenosine is hydrolyzed at the N-glycosidic bond, yielding the free base 1-methyladenine and D-ribose. The reaction is balanced: 1-methyladenosine (C11H15N5O4) plus water (H2O) gives 1-methyladenine (C6H7N5) plus D-ribose (C5H10O5). Atom balance: C11/C11, H17/H17, N5/N5, O5/O5. Hydrolytic cleavage of glycosidic bonds is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: This reaction describes an intradiol (1,2) cleavage as indicated by the enzyme name '1,2-oxidoreductase (decyclizing)', but the product '3-Chloro-2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde' is the product of extradiol (2,3) meta-cleavage, not intradiol (ortho) cleavage. Intradiol cleavage of 3-chlorocatechol yields 2-chloromuconate (a dicarboxylic acid), whereas the muconic semialdehyde product corresponds to a catechol 2,3-dioxygenase reaction.

Charge/proton imbalance: intradiol catechol dioxygenase reactions consume the catechol and O2 to give the muconate without releasing a free H+ in the manner shown; the H+ stoichiometry depends on the actual product and protonation states.
Mismatch between the named product and the named mechanism means the stoichiometry cannot be both correct and consistent with the EC name.
rxn07618.other_comments: The reaction is a ring-cleaving dioxygenase acting on 3-chlorocatechol with molecular oxygen. The enzyme name specifies intradiol (1,2, ortho) cleavage producing a chloromuconate, but the listed product (3-chloro-2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde) is the extradiol (2,3, meta) cleavage product. Dioxygenase reactions incorporating O2 with ring opening are physiologically essentially irreversible (forward).

rxn07337.other_comments: This is an oxidoreductase reaction (KEGG R07506) involving the C-22 desaturation in the ergosterol biosynthesis pathway. The reaction as written shows NADP being reduced to NADPH while a saturated sterol (5,7,24(28)-ergostatrienol) is oxidized to introduce a 22,23 double bond (5,7,22,24(28)-ergostatetraenol). Stoichiometrically the reaction is balanced: introducing a double bond removes 2 H (one to NADP forming NADPH, one as H+). In vivo, the C-22(23) desaturase (Erg5/CYP61) drives this conversion toward formation of the additional double bond, so the biologically favored direction is the reverse of how it is written (i.e., from the trienol to the tetraenol with consumption of reducing equivalents conceptually, though desaturation typically uses O2/cytochrome systems). Given the written orientation, the in vivo flux proceeds from left-side substrate toward the tetraenol product but with NADPH on the substrate side, hence the net direction favors the reverse as written.

errors: Stoichiometric oxygen imbalance: oxidation of a methylene (CH2) to a ketone (C=O) requires introduction of an oxygen atom; this reaction as written removes 2 H (as NADH + H+) but adds an oxygen with no source, so atoms are not balanced. A keto group formation by NAD+-dependent dehydrogenation typically requires an adjacent hydroxyl (oxidation of an alcohol to a ketone), not a bare CH2.
rxn13486.other_comments: This appears to be a custom/synthetic biosynthetic step (mycolic-acid-like very-long-chain ACP intermediate, C59) introducing a keto group at position 19 using NAD+ as the oxidant. If the substrate already bears a 19-hydroxyl, then oxidation of the secondary alcohol to a ketone with NAD+ -> NADH + H+ would be balanced; as written with a generic 'C59oyl' precursor the oxygen balance cannot be verified.

rxn07991.other_comments: This is the 3-oxoacyl-ACP reductase (FabG) step of fatty acid biosynthesis (type II FAS). It reduces the 3-oxo (beta-keto) group of the cis-palmitoleoyl (C16:1, delta-9) ACP intermediate using NADPH to yield the (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-ACP plus NADP+. The reaction is balanced: the carbonyl is reduced to a hydroxyl, consuming NADPH + H+ and producing NADP+. Stoichiometry of hydride and proton transfer is correct. Note: bacterial FabG typically produces the (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-ACP stereochemistry, consistent with the product shown.

rxn02825.other_comments: This is the arylamine N-hydroxylamine O-acetyltransferase (NAT, O-acetyltransferase activity) reaction (EC 2.3.1.118). Acetyl-CoA transfers its acetyl group to the oxygen of an N-hydroxyarylamine, producing an N-acetoxyarylamine (an unstable reactive ester) and free CoA. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written: one acetyl group is transferred from Acetyl-CoA to the hydroxyl oxygen, releasing CoA. In vivo this is a metabolic activation/bioactivation step (relevant to carcinogen activation) that proceeds in the acetyl-transfer (forward) direction.

errors: Atom and charge balance issue: H2O + phosphonate (HPO3^2-, i.e. one H on P) does not balance against phosphate (PO4^3-) + H+ + H2. Left side has H: 2 (water) + 1 (phosphonate H-P) = 3 H plus 1 O from water = 4 O total on left (3 from phosphonate + 1 water); right side phosphate has 4 O, but H count is 1 (H+) + 2 (H2) = 3 H. Charge: left -2 (phosphonate), right -3 (phosphate) +1 (H+) = -2, charge balances but the redox accounting is questionable.

Phosphonate to phosphate conversion is an oxidation of the C-P/H-P bond; producing molecular H2 as the reductant byproduct from a simple hydrolysis is biochemically implausible. Real phosphonate degradation uses C-P lyase or oxidative pathways, not H2 release.
rxn09184.other_comments: The reaction depicts conversion of phosphonate plus water to phosphate, proton, and molecular hydrogen. While the heavy-atom (P, O) balance can be made to work, the generation of free H2 as a product of a hydrogenase-type cleavage is unusual and the H balance is borderline; such a reaction is not a standard well-characterized in vivo process.

rxn02912.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction (kynurenine aminotransferase, KAT) acting on 3-hydroxy-L-kynurenine. The amino group of 3-hydroxy-L-kynurenine is transferred to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and the corresponding 2-oxo (alpha-keto) acid, 4-(2-amino-3-hydroxyphenyl)-2,4-dioxobutanoate, which is the deaminated keto product of 3-hydroxykynurenine. The keto product can cyclize spontaneously to form xanthurenic acid. Stoichiometry is balanced: one amino donor (3-hydroxy-L-kynurenine) and one amino acceptor (2-oxoglutarate) give one new amino acid (glutamate) and one new keto acid. Like most PLP-dependent aminotransferases, this reaction is freely reversible, though in vivo it tends to proceed toward keto product/xanthurenate formation.

errors: The reaction as written is mass-unbalanced in formula representation only if products/substrates differ; however maltooligosyltrehalose synthase (MTSase, EC 5.4.99.15) is an intramolecular transglycosylase that converts the terminal alpha-1,4 glycosidic bond at the reducing end into an alpha,alpha-1,1 bond, so maltoheptaose and its product are isomers with identical molecular formula (C42H72O36) - thus the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced

The product name is imprecise: the maltooligosyltrehalose formed from maltoheptaose would specifically be 'maltopentaosyltrehalose' (a 7-glucose-unit oligosaccharide bearing a terminal trehalose moiety)
rxn10815.other_comments: This is the MTSase (EC 5.4.99.15) reaction, an intramolecular transglucosylation/isomerization. It transglycosylates the reducing-end alpha-1,4 linkage of a linear malto-oligosaccharide (here maltoheptaose, 7 glucose units) into an alpha,alpha-1,1 (trehalose-type) linkage, yielding a maltooligosyltrehalose of the same chain length. Because it is an isomerase (mutase), substrate and product have the same molecular formula and the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced 1:1.

errors: This reaction as written is incomplete/unbalanced; the tautomerization/ring-opening of 4-hydroxyifosfamide to aldoifosfamide does not require additional substrates, but mass balance should be explicitly checked - the two species are constitutional isomers (ring-closed carbinolamine vs open-chain aldehyde), so atoms should balance, however no water or other species are shown which is consistent with an intramolecular isomerization
rxn11816.other_comments: This represents the interconversion of 4-hydroxyifosfamide (a cyclic carbinolamine/hemiaminal hydroxylation product of ifosfamide) and its open-chain tautomer aldoifosfamide. These are tautomers in equilibrium; aldoifosfamide subsequently fragments to the active isophosphoramide mustard plus acrolein. The ring-open/ring-closed equilibrium is a spontaneous chemical tautomerization, hence reversible.

rxn01426.other_comments: This is caffeoyl-CoA O-methyltransferase (CCoAOMT), EC 2.1.1.104. SAM donates a methyl group to the 3-hydroxyl of caffeoyl-CoA, producing feruloyl-CoA and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine, with release of a proton. The atoms balance: SAM transfers CH3 to the substrate hydroxyl, converting caffeoyl (3,4-dihydroxycinnamoyl) to feruloyl (3-methoxy-4-hydroxycinnamoyl). The H+ released balances the loss of the phenolic proton upon methylation. Stoichiometry and charge balance are correct.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: octadecenoyl-CoA (C18:1, an 18-carbon monounsaturated acyl-CoA) yields 9 acetyl-CoA, requiring 8 rounds of beta-oxidation, but the cofactor stoichiometry is inconsistent. Standard beta-oxidation of an 18-carbon acyl-CoA uses 8 FAD and 8 NAD+, not O2/H2O2, and produces 8 FADH2 + 8 NADH.

Incorrect electron acceptor: mitochondrial beta-oxidation uses FAD (via acyl-CoA dehydrogenase), not O2, and does not produce H2O2. Peroxisomal beta-oxidation uses O2 and produces H2O2 via acyl-CoA oxidase, but then O2/H2O2 stoichiometry should equal the number of dehydrogenation (acyl-CoA oxidase) steps, here 8, not 7.

Stoichiometric inconsistency: O2 (7) and H2O2 (7) do not match the 8 oxidation cycles needed; 8 acetyl-CoA cleavages from C18 require 8 thiolytic cuts producing 9 acetyl-CoA, with 8 FAD-type oxidations and 8 NAD-dependent oxidations.
Charge/proton imbalance likely given the mismatched cofactor counts.
rxn09467.other_comments: The reaction represents beta-oxidation of an 18-carbon monounsaturated acyl-CoA (octadecenoyl-CoA, e.g., oleoyl-CoA) into 9 acetyl-CoA. The framing with O2/H2O2 suggests a peroxisomal-style oxidation, but the cofactor and O2/H2O2 counts (7 vs expected 8) are inconsistent with the 8 cycles required, and a double bond in the substrate would further alter the dehydrogenation step count.

rxn06314.other_comments: This is the cholinephosphotransferase reaction (EC 2.7.8.2-related) transferring the phosphocholine group from CDP-choline onto a 1-alkenyl-2-acylglycerol (a plasmalogen-type diradylglycerol) to form plasmenylcholine (choline plasmalogen), releasing CMP and a proton. The mass and charge balance are correct: the phosphocholine moiety is transferred and CMP plus H+ are released. The reaction is part of the CDP-choline (Kennedy) pathway for plasmalogen biosynthesis.

errors: Stoichiometry appears balanced in count (NADH + H+ reducing one double bond), but the product identity is ambiguous: reducing the trans-3 enoyl double bond of trans-3-cis-7-myristoleoyl-ACP should yield cis-7-tetradecenoyl-ACP (still containing the cis-7 double bond), so the product 'Tetradecenoyl-ACP' is acceptable only if it specifically denotes the cis-7-tetradecenoyl species
Product naming is underspecified (position/geometry of remaining double bond not stated)
rxn08390.other_comments: This is the FabI/enoyl-ACP reductase step of fatty acid elongation (unsaturated, n-C14:1 branch). NADH reduces the trans-2 (here labeled trans-3) enoyl double bond to give the saturated bond while retaining the cis-7 double bond, producing a monounsaturated tetradecenoyl-ACP. In vivo this reductive step is essentially irreversible toward fatty acid synthesis.

rxn01079.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of L-gulonate to D-glucuronate with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH, catalyzed by glucuronate reductase (EC 1.1.1.19). The stoichiometry is balanced: NADP+ + L-gulonate <=> NADPH + H+ + D-glucuronate. Both carbon substrates are C6 sugar acids and the redox cofactor pair balances (one hydride to NADPH plus one proton released). The enzyme physiologically operates in the glucuronate-to-gulonate direction (reduction) as part of the glucuronate/uronic acid pathway, but the enzyme is reversible and direction depends on NADPH/NADP+ ratio.

errors: Oxaloglycolate is not a standard recognized metabolite name; the enzyme D-glycerate:NADP+ oxidoreductase (carboxylating) corresponds to hydroxypyruvate reductase / tartronate semialdehyde reductase related chemistry, but the product of carboxylating oxidation of glycerate would be 2-hydroxy-3-oxopropanoate (tartronate semialdehyde) or a beta-keto acid, not 'Oxaloglycolate'

Charge/proton balance appears inconsistent: a carboxylating oxidoreductase producing NADPH should yield an oxidized carboxylated product; the listed product 'Oxaloglycolate' is ambiguous and its formula cannot be verified to balance carbon and oxygen with Glycerate + CO2
Atom balance cannot be confirmed because the product identity is undefined
rxn01284.other_comments: The reaction is described as a carboxylating NADP-dependent oxidoreductase acting on D-glycerate, oxidizing glycerate while incorporating CO2 to form a more oxidized carboxylated product, with NADP+ reduced to NADPH and release of protons. The main issue is the non-standard product 'Oxaloglycolate', preventing verification of mass and charge balance.

rxn02749.other_comments: This reaction describes the dehydration of (R)-2-methylmalate (D-citramalate) to form citraconate (2-methylfumarate / methylmaleate) plus water, catalyzed by a hydro-lyase. The stoichiometry is balanced: citramalate (C5H8O5) yields water (H2O) plus citraconate (C5H6O4). Hydro-lyases (dehydratases) of this type, such as the citramalate/2-methylmalate dehydratase family, catalyze reversible dehydration reactions in vivo, with the direction depending on metabolic context.

errors: DMAPP (dimethylallyl diphosphate) is not the correct mannose acceptor; the substrate should be a polyprenol phosphate (e.g. dolichyl phosphate or undecaprenyl phosphate), not DMAPP
Mass/atom imbalance: DMAPP is a 5-carbon prenyl diphosphate and cannot directly yield a polyprenyl-mannose product; the carbon count does not balance

Phosphate balance is inconsistent: if a polyprenol monophosphate were the acceptor, the products should be GDP + polyprenyl-phosphate-mannose, but using DMAPP (a diphosphate) the phosphate accounting is incorrect
rxn13530.other_comments: This is intended to be a polyprenol-monophosphomannose synthase (dolichyl-phosphate mannosyltransferase) reaction, transferring mannose from GDP-mannose to a polyprenol phosphate to form polyprenyl(dolichyl)-phosphate-mannose plus GDP. The acceptor listed (DMAPP) is wrong; it should be a polyprenol/dolichol monophosphate. These mannosyltransferase reactions proceed essentially irreversibly in the forward (biosynthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn06160.other_comments: This is acyl-CoA:retinol O-acyltransferase (ARAT), which transfers an acyl group from acyl-CoA to retinol to form a retinyl ester plus free CoA. The reaction is mass and charge balanced as written (the acyl group is transferred from CoA to the retinol hydroxyl, releasing CoASH). In vivo, this reaction proceeds in the direction of retinyl ester synthesis for vitamin A storage, making it effectively forward (biosynthetic/storage direction).

rxn03204.other_comments: This is the 2,5-diaminohexanoate dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.4.1.10), part of the lysine fermentation pathway in Clostridium. It oxidatively deaminates the 5-amino group of 2,5-diaminohexanoate using NAD+ as cofactor, producing 2-amino-5-oxohexanoate, NADH, and ammonia. Atoms balance: substrate C6H14N2O2 + H2O loses NH3 and 2H (to NADH+H+) to give C6H11NO3 (2-amino-5-oxohexanoate). Charges and mass are consistent. The deaminating oxidation strongly favors the forward direction in vivo.

errors: Mass and charge imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance. Transfer of an acyl group from ACP to AMP to form an acyl-AMP (acyl-adenylate) typically releases ACP and consumes the acyl-ACP, but the 2.0 H+ and the lack of any other co-substrate/product (e.g. pyrophosphate, ATP, or water) make this unbalanced.

Stoichiometric inconsistency: forming acyl-AMP from AMP + acyl-ACP is energetically unfavorable without ATP/pyrophosphate involvement; an acyl-adenylate is normally generated from a free fatty acid + ATP (releasing PPi), not from AMP + acyl-ACP.
rxn13470.other_comments: The reaction appears to represent transfer of a keto-meroacid acyl chain from ACP to AMP to form an acyl-adenylate (keto-meroacid-2-AMP), with release of holo-ACP. This is plausibly part of mycolic acid biosynthesis (FadD32-type activation), but the depicted use of free AMP as the acceptor with 2 H+ and no pyrophosphate/ATP is chemically problematic.

rxn10243.other_comments: This is a phosphatidic acid phosphatase (lipin-type) reaction where a diacylglycerol 3-phosphate (phosphatidic acid with two isohexadecanoyl/branched C16 chains) is hydrolyzed by water to yield diacylglycerol and inorganic phosphate. Stoichiometry and charge balance are correct: H2O + PA -> DAG + Pi + H+. The released phosphate accounts for the proton balance.

rxn02521.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of 2',3'-cyclic AMP to 3'-AMP by 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide 3'-phosphodiesterase (EC 3.1.4.16). The phosphodiester bond is opened by water addition, releasing a proton. Stoichiometry balances: the cyclic phosphate plus H2O yields the linear 3'-monophosphate, with the consumed hydroxyl/proton bookkeeping accounting for the H+ released. Hydrolysis of the strained cyclic phosphodiester is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn04908.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADH-dependent reduction of chloral hydrate (2,2,2-trichloro-1,1-ethanediol) to trichloroethanol, catalyzed by alcohol dehydrogenase (or aldehyde reductase). Chloral hydrate is the hydrated form of trichloroacetaldehyde; the carbonyl carbon is reduced to an alcohol, releasing water. Atoms balance: NADH + H+ + C2HCl3O2 -> H2O + NAD+ + C2H3Cl3O. The named enzyme (trichloroethanol:NAD+ oxidoreductase) formally describes the oxidation direction, but in vivo the reaction proceeds toward trichloroethanol formation (detoxification/metabolism of chloral hydrate in mammals).

errors: The acyl chain descriptor is inconsistent between substrate and product: the substrate is labeled 'dituberculostearoyl' while the product is labeled 'dimethylstearoyl'. Tuberculostearic acid is 10-methylstearic acid (10-methyloctadecanoic acid), so both should carry the same acyl groups; the naming should be consistent. Aside from this labeling discrepancy, the mass/charge balance is consistent with a phosphomonoester hydrolysis.
rxn10714.other_comments: This is a phosphatidylglycerophosphate phosphatase (PgpA/PgpB-type) reaction that hydrolyzes the terminal phosphate of phosphatidylglycerophosphate to yield phosphatidylglycerol plus inorganic phosphate. The acyl chains are tuberculostearic (10-methyl-C18) fatty acids. Hydrolysis releasing Pi and H+ is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn03114.other_comments: This is the second prenyltransferase step in archaeal ether lipid biosynthesis, catalyzed by geranylgeranylglyceryl phosphate synthase / digeranylgeranylglyceryl phosphate synthase (DGGGP synthase). Geranylgeranyl diphosphate transfers its geranylgeranyl group to the sn-2 hydroxyl of 3-O-geranylgeranyl-sn-glycerol-1-phosphate, forming 2,3-bis-O-(geranylgeranyl)-sn-glycerol-1-phosphate, releasing PPi and H+. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (carbon from C20 prenyl transfer accounted for, diphosphate released as PPi, and the proton balances the new ether linkage/condensation).

rxn04064.other_comments: This is the xylitol:NAD oxidoreductase reaction (EC 1.1.1.10, L-xylulose reductase, or related polyol dehydrogenase). Xylitol is oxidized at a secondary hydroxyl group to a ketose (L-xylulose) with NAD+ as the electron acceptor, generating NADH and a proton. The reaction shown produces L-Lyxulose; note that the canonical product of xylitol oxidation by L-xylulose reductase (EC 1.1.1.10) is L-xylulose, while D-xylulose is produced by sorbitol/xylitol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.9). L-Lyxulose (L-threo-2-pentulose) is a recognized product for certain polyol dehydrogenases acting on xylitol. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: oxidation of a CHOH to C=O removes 2 H, accounted for by NADH + H+. Carbon (C5 to C5), hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance.

rxn07493.other_comments: This is the GDP-L-galactose phosphorylase reaction (VTC2/VTC5) in the Smirnoff-Wheeler ascorbate biosynthesis pathway in plants. Stoichiometry is balanced: phosphate attacks the glycosidic bond of GDP-L-galactose, releasing GDP and forming L-galactose 1-phosphate. Atoms and charges balance. In vivo this committed step proceeds in the forward direction toward ascorbate (vitamin C) synthesis.

rxn05382.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid elongation, reducing the trans-2 double bond of 14-methyl-hexadec-2-enoyl-ACP to the saturated 14-methyl-hexadecanoyl-ACP using NADPH. The reaction is balanced: NADPH+H+ provides two electrons and a proton, NADP+ is released, and the C=C is reduced to C-C. Atoms and charges balance correctly. In vivo, enoyl reductases strongly favor the reductive (forward) direction as part of biosynthesis.

rxn07239.other_comments: This is the heparan/heparosan chain elongation reaction (EC 2.4.1.224, alpha-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase, EXTL/EXT family). UDP-GlcNAc transfers a GlcNAc residue in alpha-1,4 linkage onto the non-reducing terminal GlcUA of the growing proteoglycan chain, releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: the GlcNAc moiety is transferred from UDP-GlcNAc to the acceptor, with UDP as the leaving group.

rxn04634.other_comments: This is a Leloir-type glycosyltransferase reaction. UDP-glucose donates a glucosyl moiety to the 5-O position of cyanidin 3-O-rutinoside, producing cyanidin 3-O-rutinoside 5-O-beta-D-glucoside and releasing UDP. The reaction is balanced: the glucose transferred from UDP-glucose is accounted for by the new 5-O-glucoside, and UDP is the byproduct. Atoms and charges balance.

errors: Atom imbalance: the product side does not balance with the substrate plus O2. The dihydroxy aromatic ring opening to a muconate-type semialdehyde/oxo-acid typically requires incorporation of both oxygen atoms from O2, but the chlorine count and carbon/hydrogen accounting between the given substrate and product are inconsistent as written.
Charge/proton balance appears off: a single H+ on the product side is insufficient to balance the conversion of a catecholic substrate to a ring-cleaved carboxylate product.
rxn03569.other_comments: This represents a dioxygenase-type extradiol (or related) ring-cleavage reaction of a chlorinated catechol derivative (a DDE/DDT metabolite) using molecular O2 to open the aromatic ring and form an oxo-hydroxy-trienoate (muconate semialdehyde-like) product. Such oxygenase ring cleavages are physiologically irreversible.

rxn00406.other_comments: This is an amino acid racemase reaction interconverting L-arginine and D-arginine. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (same molecular formula and charge on both sides, as it is a simple stereochemical inversion at the alpha-carbon). Racemase/epimerase reactions are inherently reversible and are typically driven toward racemic equilibrium, so directionality is reversible. Arginine racemase (EC 5.1.1.9) is a PLP-dependent enzyme found mainly in bacteria.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance atoms and charge. The condensation of 2-oxoglutarate and glyoxylate yields 2-hydroxy-3-oxoadipate, but the decarboxylation (release of CO2) means the carbon counts do not match. 2-Oxoglutarate (C5) + glyoxylate (C2) = C7, while 2-hydroxy-3-oxoadipate is C6, so one carbon (CO2) must be lost on the synthesis side, not added. The reaction direction/placement of CO2 is inconsistent with a balanced equation.
rxn00332.other_comments: This is the 2-hydroxy-3-oxoadipate synthase / oxoglutarate:glyoxylate carboligase reaction (EC 2.2.1.5). Physiologically, 2-oxoglutarate is decarboxylated and condensed with glyoxylate to form 2-hydroxy-3-oxoadipate (or its precursor), releasing CO2. As written, the equation appears to run in the direction of consuming CO2 and 2-hydroxy-3-oxoadipate to form 2-oxoglutarate + glyoxylate, which is the reverse of the biologically favored decarboxylating direction. The balance issue must be confirmed: a proper equation is 2-oxoglutarate + glyoxylate -> 2-hydroxy-3-oxoadipate + CO2.

rxn07685.other_comments: This is the 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (beta-ketothiolase) step in the peroxisomal beta-oxidation spiral of jasmonic acid biosynthesis (OPC metabolism). OPC4-CoA (8-[(1R,2R)-3-oxo-2-(pent-2-enyl)cyclopentyl]octanoyl-CoA with shortened side chain) condenses with acetyl-CoA. As written, the thiolytic cleavage direction is reverse (3-oxo-acyl-CoA + CoA -> acyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA), so the forward arrow here represents the Claisen condensation. Stoichiometry is balanced: a two-carbon unit from acetyl-CoA is added and CoA is released, converting the C6 side chain (3-Oxo-OPC6-CoA) to OPC4-CoA upon the subsequent thiolytic shortening. The carbon and CoA balance is consistent.

rxn04674.other_comments: This reaction is the final step of phylloquinone (vitamin K1) biosynthesis, catalyzed by demethylphylloquinone methyltransferase (MenG/UbiE-type, EC 2.1.1.329). SAM donates a methyl group to demethylphylloquinone (2-phytyl-1,4-naphthoquinone) to form vitamin K1 (phylloquinone), producing S-adenosyl-homocysteine. Stoichiometry is balanced: a methyl group transferred from SAM yields SAH plus a proton, with the methyl added to the naphthoquinone ring. SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving forward.

rxn11399.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for L-gulonolactone. The same species (H+ and L-Gulonolactone) appear on both sides, which is the standard notation for transport reactions where compartments are not shown explicitly in the string. Stoichiometry is balanced (1 H+ and 1 L-gulonolactone cotransported). In a proper metabolic model, the two sides would be in different compartments (e.g., extracellular vs cytosol). Transport via proton symport is typically driven by the proton motive force and is often modeled as reversible, though net flux is usually inward (uptake).

rxn01004.other_comments: This is a keto-enol tautomerization of phenylpyruvate. The reaction interconverts the keto form (phenylpyruvate) and the enol form (enol-phenylpyruvate). Both species have identical molecular formula (C9H8O3), so the reaction is mass-balanced. Keto-enol tautomerizations are inherently reversible, though the keto form is typically thermodynamically favored.

rxn02566.other_comments: This reaction represents morphine 6-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.218), which oxidizes the C6 hydroxyl of morphine to a ketone, producing morphinone, with NADP+ as the electron acceptor. Stoichiometry is balanced: morphine (C17H19NO3) loses 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+ giving NADPH, one as a proton), yielding morphinone (C17H17NO3). Charge and atoms balance. Note that the enzyme name indicates dual NAD(P)+ specificity, though the written reaction uses NADP+ specifically.

rxn02075.other_comments: This is the chalcone isomerase (CHI) reaction, an intramolecular cyclization/ring-opening interconverting a chalcone (2'-hydroxychalcone) and the corresponding flavanone via Michael-type addition. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as a simple isomerization (no atoms added or lost). In vivo, CHI strongly favors flavanone formation (cyclization direction, i.e., chalcone -> flavanone), though the spontaneous (non-enzymatic) reaction is also possible and the enzyme accelerates an inherently reversible equilibrium. The enzyme name 'flavanone lyase (decyclizing)' describes the ring-opening direction.

rxn04900.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of 2-(S-glutathionyl)acetyl chloride, an acyl chloride, to yield 2-S-glutathionyl acetate, releasing chloride and protons. Stoichiometry balances: the acyl chloride (R-CO-Cl) plus H2O gives the carboxylate (R-COO-) plus Cl- plus 2 H+ (one from water becoming the carboxylate OH-derived proton, with the carboxylic acid then deprotonated). Charge and atom balance are consistent. Acyl chloride hydrolysis is highly thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in aqueous conditions.

rxn05107.other_comments: This reaction corresponds to the methionine salvage pathway enzyme acireductone synthase / DK-MTP-1-P enolase-phosphatase (MtnC, EC 3.1.3.77). It hydrolyzes 2,3-diketo-5-methylthiopentyl-1-phosphate (DK-MTP-1-P) with water, releasing inorganic phosphate and yielding the enol product 1,2-dihydroxy-3-keto-5-methylthiopent-1-ene (acireductone). The reaction couples enolization and dephosphorylation. Stoichiometry balances: the phosphate group is removed as Pi and water is consumed. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven by phosphate hydrolysis, proceeding toward acireductone formation.

errors: Stoichiometric inconsistency: this reaction combines fatty acid elongation (Palmitate C16 + Malonyl-CoA -> C18) with a desaturation step (introduction of the double bond requiring O2). These are separate enzymatic processes (elongase vs desaturase) and should not be lumped as a single fatty acid synthase reaction.

Carbon balance check: Palmitate (C16) + Malonyl-CoA (C3 in the malonyl moiety) = C19; releasing CO2 (C1) yields C18 octadecenoate, which is consistent for carbon. However the simultaneous use of O2 and 3 NADPH mixes elongation (2 NADPH per cycle) and desaturation (1 NADPH/NADH + O2), making the combined stoichiometry biochemically misleading.
Cofactor/charge balance should be verified: H+ count of 4 and the NADPH/NADP balance require careful checking given the mixed reduction/oxidation steps.
rxn10667.other_comments: The reaction depicts conversion of palmitate to an octadecenoate (C18:1, e.g. oleate) by adding a 2-carbon unit from malonyl-CoA (elongation), with loss of CO2 and CoA, plus an oxygen-dependent desaturation. It is a lumped reaction combining elongation and desaturation. In vivo, fatty acid elongation and biosynthesis are strongly forward-driven (committed, ATP/NADPH-consuming) processes.

rxn01622.other_comments: This reaction represents the isomerization of Prostaglandin H2 (PGH2, the 9,11-endoperoxide intermediate) to Dinoprostone (Prostaglandin E2, PGE2), catalyzed by prostaglandin E synthase. The endoperoxide bridge of PGH2 is rearranged to yield the 9-keto, 11-hydroxy configuration characteristic of PGE2. This is an intramolecular isomerization with no net change in atoms, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (C20H32O5 on both sides).

rxn01552.other_comments: This is gamma-glutaminylhistamine synthetase, which catalyzes the ATP-dependent ligation of L-glutamate to histamine forming gamma-glutamylhistamine, with hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: ATP + glutamate + histamine yields ADP + Pi + H+ + the gamma-glutamyl-histamine conjugate. The amide bond formation consumes ATP (cleaved to ADP + Pi), releasing one proton. Atom and charge balance are consistent with a glutamine-synthetase-type ligase mechanism.

rxn00150.other_comments: This reaction is the oxidation of methylglyoxal (2-oxopropanal) to pyruvate with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The aldehyde carbon is oxidized to a carboxylic acid, consuming water and releasing 2 protons (one from NADP+ reduction balance and one from the carboxylic acid). Atoms balance: methylglyoxal C3H4O2 + H2O = pyruvate C3H4O3 with 2 H+ and 2 electrons transferred to NADP+. Charge and mass appear balanced. Aldehyde dehydrogenase-type oxidations are strongly favored thermodynamically toward the carboxylic acid product.

errors: The product '4-Carboxy-2-oxo-4-pentanoate' appears to be a mislabeled species. The actual product of 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (decarboxylating) pathway / or the hydratase-aldolase steps differ. For the enzyme EC 4.1.1.68 (5-carboxymethyl-2-hydroxymuconate isomerase) or the LigK/related reactions, no water is consumed and no formate is released. The release of formate from a semialdehyde via hydrolysis is not the documented chemistry for this intermediate.

Carbon/atom balance is questionable: cleaving a single carbon as formate from 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde would require oxidative or hydrolytic C-C cleavage chemistry not consistent with simple addition of one H2O. The carbon counts of the named substrate and product plus formate do not clearly balance.
rxn03096.other_comments: The reaction is presented as a water-dependent conversion of 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde to a pentanoate-type keto acid with release of formate and a proton. In the canonical meta-cleavage / protocatechuate 4,5-cleavage pathway, 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde is oxidized (NADP-dependent) to 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate, not hydrolyzed to release formate. The stated products and the use of only water do not match well-characterized enzymology, and the product nomenclature is ambiguous, so I cannot confirm mass balance.

rxn02482.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 1-hydroxy-2-naphthoate dioxygenase (EC 1.13.11.38), a ring-cleavage dioxygenase in the bacterial naphthalene/phenanthrene degradation pathway. It incorporates both atoms of molecular oxygen, cleaving the aromatic ring of 1-hydroxy-2-naphthoate to yield trans-2'-carboxybenzalpyruvate (2-(2-carboxyphenyl)-4-oxo-2-butenoate). The atom balance is consistent: the substrate (C11H8O3, as the acid) plus O2 yields the product (C11H8O5) plus the released proton when accounting for the anionic forms. As a dioxygenase consuming O2 in an irreversible ring-cleavage step, this reaction proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn10244.other_comments: This reaction describes a glucosyltransferase transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to the diglucosyl diacylglycerol acceptor, producing triglucosyl diacylglycerol and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose (forming UDP) to the diglucosyl acceptor, extending it to triglucosyl. Glycosyltransferases using UDP-sugars are thermodynamically driven toward glycoside formation due to the high-energy nucleotide-sugar bond, so the reaction proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the product 'Polyprenyl-mannose' shares no obvious moiety with any substrate (no mannose or polyprenyl group on the substrate side), making the carbon/sugar balance impossible to reconcile

The mycolate-carrier substrate 'trans-cyclopropane-methoxy-meroacid-1-mycolate-ppm' (PPM = polyprenyl-phosphomannose carrier) should yield a polyprenyl-phosphate or polyprenyl-phosphomannose product after mycolate transfer, not free 'Polyprenyl-mannose'; the phosphate accounting is inconsistent

Phosphate balance questionable: Trehalose 6-phosphate contributes one phosphate; the product 'trans-methoxy-1-trehalose-monomyclolate-phosphate' retains a phosphate, yet a phosphorylated carrier/mannose product is also implied, suggesting an extra or unbalanced phosphate

Likely the trehalose substrate for mycolate transfer should be free trehalose (or trehalose-6-P with explicit handling), and the mycolate donor is typically trehalose monomycolate (TMM) in vivo via Antigen 85 complex, not the PPM intermediate shown
rxn13556.other_comments: This is intended to represent a step in mycobacterial trehalose monomycolate (TMM) biosynthesis, transferring a meromycolate/mycolate chain onto a trehalose moiety. The biosynthetic mycolyltransfer step is effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo. However, the written stoichiometry does not balance: the carrier byproduct should be a polyprenyl-phosphate/phosphomannose species derived from the donor, and the phosphate/sugar atoms do not map cleanly between substrates and products.

errors: Cofactor mismatch: the enzyme name specifies NAD+/NADH (Propane-1,2-diol:NAD+ 1-oxidoreductase, EC 1.1.1.77), but the reaction uses NADP/NADPH

Product specificity issue: oxidation of 1,2-propanediol at C1 yields (S)- or (R)-lactaldehyde, which should be specified; the generic lactaldehyde is acceptable but the carbon being oxidized should be the primary alcohol (C1)
rxn01879.other_comments: This is the oxidoreductase interconverting 1,2-propanediol and lactaldehyde with a nicotinamide cofactor. The atom balance for the redox half is correct (one alcohol oxidized to aldehyde, releasing 2[H] captured as NADH/NADPH + H+). The main problem is the cofactor identity does not match the named enzyme (NAD-dependent). EC 1.1.1.77 (lactaldehyde reductase) physiologically runs in the reductive direction (lactaldehyde -> propanediol) during anaerobic fucose/rhamnose fermentation, but the enzyme is reversible in vitro.

errors: Stereochemistry inconsistency: the substrate is named as a 5beta-epoxide (5,6beta-epoxy-5beta-cholestane) while the product is a 5alpha,6beta-diol; epoxide hydrolysis of a 5,6beta-epoxide should yield the trans-diol with consistent stereochemistry, suggesting a naming/stereo mismatch
Atom balance: hydrolytic opening of an epoxide by H2O is otherwise stoichiometrically balanced (epoxide + H2O -> vicinal diol), so the mass balance itself is fine if stereochemistry is ignored
rxn11622.other_comments: This is an epoxide hydrolase type reaction in which water opens the steroid 5,6-epoxide ring to form a vicinal diol (cholestane-5,6-diol). Such hydrolytic ring-opening reactions are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of diol formation.

rxn06805.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent methyltransferase reaction transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to a protein lysine residue (cytochrome c lysine), converting N6,N6-dimethyl-L-lysine to N6,N6,N6-trimethyl-L-lysine, producing S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The atom and charge balance are consistent: one methyl is transferred, SAM becomes SAH, and a proton is released. Methyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable in the direction of methylation due to the high group-transfer potential of SAM and are physiologically essentially irreversible.

rxn01837.other_comments: This reaction represents phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to norepinephrine (Arterenol/noradrenaline), producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH), a proton, and epinephrine (L-Adrenaline). The stoichiometry is balanced: SAM donates a methyl group, converting the secondary amine of norepinephrine to the N-methylated tertiary amine (epinephrine), with release of one proton. Mass and charge are conserved.

errors: Reaction is not charge-balanced; NADP should be written as NADP+ and the product NADPH carries a different net charge. As written (NADP <=> NADPH) a proton (H+) is missing on the product side, so the reaction is not H/charge balanced.

Mass/atom balance is questionable: acetoacetate (C4H7O3-) decarboxylation yields CO2 plus a 3-carbon acetone-derived moiety; coupling to CoM to form 2-oxopropyl-CoM is plausible for carbon, but the formula consistency and proton accounting must be verified.
rxn03979.other_comments: The reaction is a proposed NADP-dependent reductive carboxylation/decarboxylation linking acetoacetate, CoM (coenzyme M, 2-mercaptoethanesulfonate), and 2-oxopropyl-CoM. The named enzyme is an oxidoreductase (decarboxylating). The chief issue is missing H+ for the NADP+/NADPH couple; if H+ is included the redox half is balanced. Reductive carboxylation of 2-oxopropyl-CoM to acetoacetate (epoxyalkane/propylene metabolism in bacteria such as Xanthobacter) is part of the propylene degradation pathway and the physiologically favored direction is often the carboxylation (reductive) direction, i.e., reverse as written, but the enzyme can operate reversibly.

rxn01876.other_comments: This is the DMSP lyase (DddL/DddD-type) reaction, EC 4.4.1.3, cleaving dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) into dimethyl sulfide (DMS, 'methyl sulfide' here likely refers to dimethyl sulfide) and acrylate, releasing a proton. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: DMSP is a zwitterion/cation (net +1 charge as the sulfonium), products are acrylate (-1), DMS (neutral), and H+ (+1), giving net +1 on both sides. As a lyase eliminating a stable volatile product (DMS), it proceeds in the cleavage direction in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric/redox imbalance: reduction of disulfide consumes NADPH and 2 H+ (one captured per thiol), not just one H+; the reaction as written treats NADP+ reduction direction incorrectly

Naming/direction inconsistency: 'Homotrypanothione' (dithiol, reduced) being converted to 'Homotrypanothione disulfide' (oxidized) is an oxidation, which should consume NADP+ and produce NADPH plus H+, but the proton bookkeeping should be balanced (typically: 2 reduced thiol substrate + NADP+ <=> disulfide + NADPH + H+)

Proton count likely wrong: oxidation of a dithiol to disulfide releases 2 e- and 2 H+; coupled to NADP+ -> NADPH consumes one H+, net +1 H+ on product side, so H+ should appear with NADPH not with NADP+
rxn12047.other_comments: This is the homotrypanothione reductase reaction (an NADPH-dependent flavoenzyme of the glutathione/trypanothione reductase family). Physiologically these enzymes run in the direction of reducing the disulfide using NADPH (i.e., disulfide + NADPH + H+ -> dithiol + NADP+). As written the left-to-right direction shows oxidation of the dithiol coupled to NADP+ reduction, which is the non-physiological direction; in vivo the reductive (reverse of written) direction dominates.

rxn01305.other_comments: This is the oxidation of ethylene glycol (1,2-ethanediol) to glycolaldehyde, catalyzed by an alcohol dehydrogenase using NAD+ as the electron acceptor. Stoichiometry is balanced: ethylene glycol (C2H6O2) loses two H (one as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, one released as H+) to form glycolaldehyde (C2H4O2). Mass and charge are balanced. Although written as reversible (alcohol dehydrogenases are intrinsically reversible), in vivo the direction depends on the NAD+/NADH ratio and substrate availability; the oxidation direction (forward as written) is typically favored under aerobic conditions, but this can proceed in reverse for reductive metabolism.

rxn04184.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 10-deacetylbaccatin III 10-O-acetyltransferase (DBAT), a key enzyme in the Taxol (paclitaxel) biosynthetic pathway. Acetyl-CoA donates an acetyl group to the 10-beta-hydroxyl of 10-deacetylbaccatin III, producing baccatin III and CoA. The atoms balance: the acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred from CoA to the substrate hydroxyl, and the reaction is stoichiometrically correct (1:1:1:1). Acetyl-CoA thioester transfer reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn03971.other_comments: This is the coniferyl aldehyde dehydrogenase (REF/CALDH) reaction oxidizing ferulaldehyde (coniferyl aldehyde) to ferulate (ferulic acid). The aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylic acid using NADP+ as the electron acceptor, with incorporation of one oxygen from water. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (RCHO) plus H2O loses 2 H and 2 e- to form the carboxylate (RCOO-) plus H+; NADP+ gains the hydride to form NADPH, with a net release of 2 H+ accounting for charge and mass balance. In vivo this aldehyde-to-acid oxidation is strongly thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible.

errors: Water stoichiometry is incorrect: fatty acid elongation by 5 cycles releases 5 H2O from the dehydration step, but the reduction of the keto group consumes water balance differently; net atom balance should be checked. For 5 elongation cycles, the reaction produces 5 H2O (one per dehydration), consistent here.
Carbon balance check: Iso-C6:0 (6 C) + 5 malonyl groups (each adds 2 C after decarboxylation) = 6 + 10 = 16 C, matching Iso-C16:0. This is correct.
Charge/proton balance should be verified: 10 NADPH + 10 H+ -> 10 NADP+; typical FAS uses 2 NADPH per cycle (one for ketoreduction, one for enoyl reduction) = 10 NADPH for 5 cycles, correct.
rxn13671.other_comments: This is a lumped fatty acid synthesis reaction representing 5 rounds of elongation (KS, KR, DH, ER) converting Iso-C6:0 ACP to Iso-C16:0 ACP. Each cycle adds a malonyl-ACP, releasing CO2 and consuming 2 NADPH. The overall stoichiometry (10 NADPH, 5 malonyl-ACP, 5 CO2, 5 H2O, 5 ACP regenerated) is consistent with 5 elongation cycles and is essentially correct. The reaction name mentions only the ketoacyl synthase step but the full stoichiometry covers all four enzymatic steps.

errors: Atomic balance issue: trihomomethionine (the chain-elongated amino acid with three additional methylene groups, C8H17NO2S) converting to 6-methylthiohexanaldoxime requires loss of the carboxyl group as CO2 and conversion of the amino group to an aldoxime; the listed products should be checked - the reaction loses one C (as CO2) and the N is retained in the oxime, which is consistent, but the H balance should be verified
Charge/proton balance should be re-checked: NADPH is typically written with its appropriate charge; the 2 H+ consumed plus 2 NADPH may not perfectly balance the 2 NADP+ and water production
rxn14285.other_comments: This represents a CYP79 family cytochrome P450 reaction in glucosinolate biosynthesis, converting a chain-elongated methionine derivative (trihomomethionine) to the corresponding aldoxime (6-methylthiohexanaldoxime). The enzyme N-hydroxylates the amino acid twice, then performs oxidative decarboxylation to yield the aldoxime, consuming 2 NADPH and 2 O2. This is physiologically a committed, essentially irreversible oxidative step.

rxn04777.other_comments: This is the melamine deaminase reaction (TrzA/AtzA-type hydrolytic deamination). Melamine (C3H6N6) is hydrolyzed: one amino group is replaced by a hydroxyl/oxo group, releasing ammonia and yielding ammeline (C3H5N5O). The atoms balance: melamine + H2O + H+ -> ammeline + NH3 (as NH4+/NH3). The hydrolytic deamination is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of ammonia release as part of the s-triazine degradation pathway.

rxn09153.other_comments: This is a phospholipase A2 reaction that hydrolyzes the sn-2 ester bond of a diacyl phosphatidylethanolamine (with two tetradec-7-enoyl chains, C14:1). Water cleaves one acyl chain, releasing a free tetradecenoate fatty acid and yielding the 1-acyl lysophospholipid (1-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine). Mass and charge balance: H2O + diacyl-PE -> H+ + tetradecenoate (carboxylate anion) + lyso-PE; the released proton balances the deprotonated carboxylate, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced.

rxn06388.other_comments: This is a sialyltransferase reaction transferring N-acetylneuraminate from CMP-N-acetylneuraminate (the activated sugar nucleotide donor) to the galactose moiety of monogalactosyldiacylglycerol (MGDG), producing CMP, a proton, and the sialylated galactolipid. The stoichiometry is balanced: the sialyl group (minus CMP) is transferred to the acceptor, releasing CMP and H+. Sialyltransferase reactions using CMP-sialic acid donors are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: this reaction conflates two distinct steps (condensation by KAS/3-ketoacyl-ACP synthase and reduction by 3-ketoacyl-ACP reductase). A single condensation+reduction cannot be written this way without the ketoacyl intermediate.

Atom balance issue: the condensation of palmitoyl-ACP (C16) with malonyl-ACP releases CO2 and forms 3-oxo-stearoyl-ACP (C18 beta-ketoacyl-ACP); subsequent NADPH reduction yields R-3-hydroxyoctadecanoyl-ACP. Combining both into one reaction gives one extra ACP on the product side that does not balance with reactant ACPs (two ACP-bound substrates in, three ACP species out).
rxn10994.other_comments: This represents fatty acid elongation: condensation of palmitoyl-ACP (C16) with malonyl-ACP, loss of CO2, then NADPH-dependent reduction to the 3-hydroxy-C18 acyl-ACP. In vivo fatty acid synthesis proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction. The reaction as written merges two enzymatic steps (KAS condensation + ketoreductase) and is not properly balanced as a single equation.

rxn07756.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidative N-demethylation of 7-methylxanthine to xanthine (XAN), catalyzed by a cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase. The methyl group is released as formaldehyde. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + 7-methylxanthine yields H2O + NADP+ + formaldehyde + xanthine. This is a typical monooxygenase mechanism where one oxygen atom is incorporated into water and one into the substrate (forming an unstable carbinolamine that decomposes to formaldehyde and the demethylated product). Such P450/monooxygenase demethylations are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the consumption of O2 and NADPH.

errors: Atom/mass balance cannot be fully verified without explicit formulas for the ACP-bound substrate and product, but the proton stoichiometry appears inconsistent: cyclopropanation via SAM-dependent methyltransferase typically releases 1 H+ per methyl transfer/ring formation, so 2 cyclopropane rings would balance with 2 H+ which is shown; however the carbon addition (2 CH2 groups added from 2 SAM) should increase the acyl chain by 2 carbons, which is not reflected in the named product unless the C52 backbone is modified accordingly
rxn13441.other_comments: This represents cyclopropane ring formation on a mycobacterial meromycolate (alpha-meroacyl-ACP) precursor. Two SAM molecules donate two methylene-derived cyclopropane rings to the two cis double bonds (cis-21 and cis-37) of the C52 acyl-ACP, producing SAH plus the dicyclopropanated product. This is a SAM-dependent cyclopropane synthase (e.g., cmaA/pcaA-type) reaction.

rxn01626.other_comments: This is the dihydropyrimidinase (5,6-dihydrouracil amidohydrolase) reaction, the second step of reductive pyrimidine degradation. It hydrolytically opens the ring of 5,6-dihydrouracil (hydrouracil) to form N-carbamoyl-beta-alanine (3-ureidopropanoate). The reaction is balanced: dihydrouracil (C4H6N2O2) + H2O (H2O) yields 3-ureidopropanoate (C4H7N2O3-) + H+, so atoms and charge are conserved. Although the enzyme can catalyze ring closure in vitro, in the catabolic (degradative) pathway the flux proceeds in the ring-opening (forward) direction.

errors: The reaction shows dATP being converted to dATP with no net change; substrate and product are identical, making this a null/identity reaction with no chemical transformation
No transport compartments are specified, so this does not represent a valid transport reaction either
rxn12647.other_comments: The reaction lists dATP (deoxyadenosine triphosphate) on both sides of the equation. If this were intended as a transport reaction (suggested by the TRANS-RXN identifier), it would require distinct compartment annotations (e.g., dATP[cytosol] <=> dATP[extracellular]) to be meaningful. As written, it is stoichiometrically trivial and biologically uninformative.

rxn00495.other_comments: This is the phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) reaction, EC 4.3.1.24/4.3.1.5. L-Phenylalanine is deaminated to form trans-cinnamate (E-cinnamate) and ammonia. The reaction is stoichiometrically and atomically balanced: C9H11NO2 yields NH3 (NH3) plus C9H7O2 (trans-cinnamate, as the anion). In vivo it proceeds in the forward direction as the committed step of the phenylpropanoid pathway in plants and some microbes.

rxn03924.other_comments: This is the taurine:pyruvate aminotransferase (taurine-pyruvate aminotransferase, EC 2.6.1.77) reaction. Taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonate) transfers its amino group to pyruvate, yielding L-alanine and sulfoacetaldehyde (2-oxoethanesulfonate). The reaction is balanced: each side has the equivalent carbons, nitrogen, and sulfur. Taurine (C2H7NO3S) + pyruvate (C3H4O3) gives L-alanine (C3H7NO2) + sulfoacetaldehyde (C2H4O4S), which balances atoms and charge. In vivo, this reaction proceeds in the direction of taurine degradation (catabolism), so it operates primarily forward toward sulfoacetaldehyde production, although aminotransferases are mechanistically reversible.

rxn01239.other_comments: This reaction represents L-sorbose:NADP+ 5-oxidoreductase (EC 1.1.1.123), which interconverts L-sorbose and 5-dehydro-D-fructose using the NADP+/NADPH cofactor pair. The oxidation of L-sorbose at C5 yields 5-dehydro-D-fructose with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH plus a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: carbon (C6 sugar on both sides), redox equivalents, and the proton are accounted for.

rxn04195.other_comments: This is a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase (gibberellin oxidase) reaction. GA12 is oxidized to GA15 (open lactone form) with consumption of O2 and 2-oxoglutarate, producing succinate and CO2. The stoichiometry is balanced: one O2 incorporates one oxygen into the substrate and decarboxylates 2-oxoglutarate to succinate + CO2. These Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate dioxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (forward direction) due to the decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate.

rxn05025.other_comments: This is a phosphorylase-type reaction (kojibiose phosphorylase, EC 2.4.1.230). Kojibiose (2-alpha-D-glucosyl-D-glucose) is cleaved with inorganic phosphate to yield D-glucose and beta-D-glucose 1-phosphate. The stoichiometry balances: a disaccharide plus phosphate gives one free glucose monomer and one glucose-1-phosphate, conserving carbon, oxygen, and phosphate atoms. The anomeric configuration (alpha to beta inversion) is consistent with an inverting glycoside phosphorylase mechanism.

errors: The molecular formulas are not balanced; producing catechol (C6H6O2) plus HF and H+ from 1-fluoro-cyclohexa-3,5-diene-1,2-diol (C6H7FO2) requires loss of water to aromatize, but no H2O is shown. The reaction as written loses only HF (as H+ + F-), which would not yield aromatic catechol. Carbon and oxygen balance (C6, O2) but hydrogen and the aromatization chemistry are inconsistent without elimination of water.

Charge/atom balance check: left side has 7 H, right side has H+ (1) + catechol (6 H) = 7 H, so H balances, but the conversion of a non-aromatic diol-diene to aromatic catechol with only HF elimination is chemically implausible (a dehydrofluorination yielding an aromatic ring would need formal loss of HF only if the substrate were a dihydrodiol, which it appears to be; reconsider substrate degree of unsaturation).
rxn07895.other_comments: This represents a dehydrofluorination/aromatization step converting a fluorinated cis-dihydrodiol intermediate (from microbial fluorobenzene degradation) into catechol, releasing fluoride and a proton. Such spontaneous/enzymatic rearomatization with halide elimination is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn04026.other_comments: This is the sulfopyruvate decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.79), which converts 3-sulfopyruvate into sulfoacetaldehyde and CO2, consuming a proton. The reaction is balanced: 3-sulfopyruvate (C3H3O6S-) plus H+ yields CO2 plus sulfoacetaldehyde (C2H3O4S-). Atoms (C3, H4, O6, S1) and charge balance. This enzyme is part of coenzyme M biosynthesis in methanogens.

rxn10597.other_comments: This is a phosphatase reaction analogous to alpha-ribazole 5-phosphate phosphatase (CobC), hydrolyzing the 5-phosphate group from N1-(5-phospho-alpha-D-ribosyl)-5-hydroxybenzimidazole to yield the dephosphorylated alpha-ribosyl compound plus inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: water and a phosphate ester yield free phosphate and the dephosphorylated product. Phosphate ester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and typically irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of dephosphorylation.

rxn05924.other_comments: This is the 2-halobenzoate 1,2-dioxygenase reaction (EC 1.14.12.13). 2-Chlorobenzoate is oxidized using O2 and NADH to yield catechol, with release of CO2 and chloride. Checking the atom and charge balance: Left side carbons = 1 (NADH) ... actually let me verify net mass: 2-chlorobenzoate (C7H4ClO2-) + O2 + NADH + H+ -> catechol (C6H6O2) + CO2 + Cl- + NAD+. Carbons: 7 on left (substrate) = 6 (catechol) + 1 (CO2) = 7, balanced. Chlorine: 1 = 1, balanced. The transformation is a dioxygenation/dehalogenation/decarboxylation consistent with the named enzyme. Stoichiometry appears reasonable and balanced.

rxn02137.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of dTDP-D-glucose to dTDP-D-glucuronate, a four-electron oxidation of the primary alcohol (C6) to a carboxylic acid. This requires 2 NADP+ and produces 2 NADPH, consuming 1 H2O. Mass and charge balance: left side has dTDP-glucose plus H2O plus 2 NADP+; right side has dTDP-glucuronate plus 2 NADPH plus 3 H+. The 4 electrons removed are carried by 2 NADPH, and the proton count (3 H+) balances the charge and hydrogen, making this stoichiometrically correct. Such UDP/dTDP-sugar dehydrogenases are typically physiologically driven in the oxidative (forward) direction.

rxn14314.other_comments: This is an epimerase reaction converting dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose to its 5-epimer dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-L-glucose. The epimerization at C5 changes the D/L configuration. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a simple intramolecular isomerization with identical molecular formulas on both sides. Epimerases typically catalyze reversible reactions, and the direction in vivo depends on the downstream consumption of products in deoxysugar biosynthesis pathways.

rxn01162.other_comments: This reaction represents methylguanidine amidinohydrolase (EC 3.5.3.16), which hydrolyzes methylguanidine. The atoms balance: methylguanidine (CH3-NH-C(=NH)-NH2, C2H7N3) plus H2O (H2O) yields urea (CH4N2O) plus methylamine (CH5N). Counting C: 2 = 1+1; N: 3 = 2+1; O: 1 = 1; H: 7+2=9 = 4+5=9. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced. As a hydrolase cleaving an amidine bond, the reaction is essentially irreversible under physiological conditions, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn04297.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent C-methyltransferase reaction. SAM donates a methyl group to the C-3 position of the dTDP-4-oxo-2,6-dideoxy-L-mannose (sugar nucleotide), producing SAH and the 3-C-methylated product plus a proton. The atom and charge balance is consistent: one methyl group is transferred from SAM to the sugar, SAM becomes SAH, and the H+ released accounts for the deprotonation at the methylated carbon. The naming change from mannose to glucose configuration reflects the stereochemical descriptor at the new methylated/branched center. This type of reaction is involved in deoxysugar biosynthesis (e.g., mycarose/noviose-type branched-chain sugars in antibiotic glycosylation).

rxn03926.other_comments: This represents a monooxygenase (flavoprotein/cytochrome P450-type) reaction where one atom of molecular oxygen is incorporated into phenanthrene to form the 1,2-epoxide (arene oxide), the other oxygen atom is reduced to water using two electrons from NADH. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH (H+ source) provides 2 electrons and 2H+ overall (NADH + H+), O2 splits into the epoxide oxygen and water. Mass and charge balance: NADH + O2 + H+ + C14H10 -> H2O + NAD+ + C14H10O. This checks out atomically.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction as written produces 2 H+ but only one aminopropyl transfer occurs, which should release a single H+. The decarboxylated SAM (S-adenosylmethioninamine) transfers one aminopropyl group to the primary amine of 1,3-diaminopropane, releasing 5-methylthioadenosine and a net of 1 H+, not 2.
rxn02343.other_comments: This is the spermidine synthase-type reaction (aminopropyltransferase). Decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (S-adenosylmethioninamine) donates an aminopropyl group to 1,3-diaminopropane (propane-1,3-diamine), producing bis(3-aminopropyl)amine (norspermidine) and 5-methylthioadenosine (MTA). The atom balance for the core transfer is correct; the issue is the proton count.

rxn03056.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 5-carboxymethyl-2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (EC 1.2.1.60), part of the meta-cleavage pathway of aromatic compound degradation (e.g., 4-hydroxyphenylacetate catabolism). The aldehyde group of 5-carboxymethyl-2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde is oxidized to a carboxylate, consuming H2O and reducing NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid (CHO + H2O -> COOH + 2H+ + 2e-), with the two electrons and one proton going to form NADPH, releasing 2 H+ overall. Atoms and charges balance.

rxn13201.other_comments: This represents a transport reaction for 3-methylbutanal (isovaleraldehyde) moving between compartments (extracellular and cytosol). The metabolite is identical on both sides, which is expected for a simple transport/diffusion reaction where the only difference is the cellular compartment. Stoichiometry is balanced (1:1). As a small, lipophilic aldehyde, 3-methylbutanal likely crosses membranes by passive diffusion, consistent with reversible directionality.

rxn02863.other_comments: This reaction represents the FAD-dependent desaturation/oxidation converting 3-dehydrosphinganine (3-ketodihydrosphingosine) to 3-ketosphingosine (3-ketosphingenine), introducing a trans double bond (delta-4) into the sphingoid backbone. FAD is reduced to FADH2 as the electron acceptor. The reaction as written is balanced in terms of the hydrogen transfer (two H removed from substrate to form the C=C double bond, accepted by FAD to form FADH2). In vivo this dihydroceramide/sphingolipid desaturase-type oxidation is driven in the forward (oxidative) direction.

rxn13717.other_comments: This represents D-lactate dehydrogenase (respiratory, membrane-bound, FAD-dependent quinone oxidoreductase, e.g. EC 1.1.5.12). It oxidizes D-lactate to pyruvate while reducing menaquinone-7 (MK-7) to menaquinol-7 (mql7). The reaction is balanced: D-lactate (C3H5O3-) plus the oxidized quinone yields pyruvate (C3H3O3-) plus the reduced quinol (a 2H transfer, H- plus H+). Stoichiometry of carbon, oxygen, and the redox-coupled hydrogen transfer is consistent. In vivo this respiratory dehydrogenase operates in the direction of D-lactate oxidation, feeding electrons into the quinone pool, so it is physiologically essentially unidirectional toward pyruvate and menaquinol.

errors: The H+ on the product side is likely incorrect; SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reactions transfer a methyl group to a hydroxyl oxygen, and the typical balanced reaction is SAM + acceptor-OH -> SAH + acceptor-O-CH3 without net release of a proton. The methyl transfer to an oxygen nucleophile does not generate a free H+ in the standard formulation.
rxn07366.other_comments: This is the O-methyltransferase step in spheroidene biosynthesis (carotenoid pathway, e.g., CrtF in purple bacteria), where demethylspheroidene is O-methylated using SAM to produce spheroidene, releasing S-adenosyl-homocysteine. [directionality_note] SAM-dependent methyltransferases are strongly biased toward methyl transfer in vivo due to the high group-transfer potential of SAM and the much weaker methyl donor capacity of SAH.

errors: This reaction is not stoichiometrically balanced. Dimethylallyltryptophan (C16H20N2O2) cannot be converted to Elymoclavine (C16H18N2O) by simply removing water and adding a proton.

The conversion from dimethylallyl-L-tryptophan to elymoclavine requires multiple enzymatic steps (decarboxylation, oxidation, cyclization) and additional cofactors/substrates (e.g., loss of CO2, NAD(P)H, O2), not a single dehydration.
Mass balance fails: the carboxyl group of tryptophan must be lost as CO2 during ergot alkaloid biosynthesis, which is not accounted for here.
Charge and atom balance are not satisfied as written.
rxn03448.other_comments: The reaction describes a step in ergot alkaloid biosynthesis, where 4-dimethylallyl-L-tryptophan (the product of DMATS/FgaPT2) is eventually converted to elymoclavine. However, this is a multi-step pathway, not a single dehydration reaction. The proposed transformation with only H+, H2O, and the two metabolites is chemically and stoichiometrically incorrect.

errors: Stoichiometry is unbalanced. The correct urate oxidase (uricase) pathway converts urate + O2 + H2O to 5-hydroxyisourate + H2O2, but the overall conversion of urate to allantoin requires additional steps. For the lumped overall reaction (urate + O2 + 2 H2O -> allantoin + CO2 + H2O2), check balance: Urate C5H4N4O3, plus 2 H2O (H4O2), plus O2; products allantoin C4H6N4O3, CO2, H2O2 (H2O2). Carbon: left 5, right 4+1=5 OK. Nitrogen: left 4, right 4 OK. Oxygen: left 3+2+2=7, right 3+2+2=7 OK. Hydrogen: left 4+4=8 (plus extra H+ makes 9), right 6+0+2=8. The extra H+ on the left makes hydrogen unbalanced (9 vs 8).
Charge imbalance: the H+ on the left side is unbalanced relative to neutral products.
rxn09370.other_comments: This represents the overall (lumped) conversion of urate to allantoin via the uricase pathway, releasing CO2 and producing H2O2. Apart from the spurious extra H+, the atoms balance. In vivo this oxidative degradation is essentially irreversible and proceeds toward allantoin.

errors: Succinate appears on both sides of the equation without distinguishing intracellular and extracellular compartments; a proper transport reaction should show Succinate[external] being moved to Succinate[internal] (or vice versa). As written, succinate cancels out, leaving only ATP hydrolysis with no net transport.
Charge/proton balance is questionable: the H+ on the product side is not balanced by the reactant side, and without compartment annotation the proton release cannot be properly assigned.
rxn10138.other_comments: This is intended to be an ABC-type transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the import/export of succinate across a membrane. The core ATPase chemistry is correct, but the substrate (succinate) is not differentiated by compartment, so no net translocation is represented. ABC transporters are typically modeled as irreversible (forward, driven by ATP hydrolysis).

rxn02248.other_comments: This reaction represents a beta-substitution reaction catalyzed by a cysteine synthase-like (O-acetylserine sulfhydrylase) enzyme, where pyrazole acts as a nucleophile replacing the acetyl group of O-acetyl-L-serine. The products are beta-(pyrazol-1-yl)-L-alanine (a known non-protein amino acid found in cucumber/watermelon seeds), acetate, and a proton. The atoms balance: O-acetyl-L-serine (C5H9NO4) + pyrazole (C3H4N2) yields beta-pyrazol-1-ylalanine (C6H9N3O2) + acetate (C2H3O2-) + H+. Charge and mass are balanced.

errors: Charge and atom balance issue: the conversion of UTP to dUTP removes one oxygen atom (2'-OH to 2'-H), which is released as water, but this requires two electrons and two protons. The flavodoxin (reduced)/flavodoxin (oxidized) couple typically transfers electrons, and the proton balance (H+) is missing on the substrate side. As written, the equation is unbalanced for hydrogen.

Proton (H+) balance: reduction of the ribose 2'-OH to 2'-deoxy releases the oxygen as water but the two protons needed are not accounted for; typically 2 H+ should appear with the reduced electron donor.
