It hydrolytically deaminates D-galactosamine 6-phosphate to D-tagatose 6-phosphate plus ammonia, with water as a reactant. The atom and charge balance is correct: galactosamine 6-phosphate (C6H14NO8P) + H2O yields tagatose 6-phosphate (C6H13O9P) + NH3, balancing C, H, N, O, and P. In vivo this deaminase reaction proceeds toward sugar phosphate plus ammonia release as part of amino sugar catabolism.

rxn01187.other_comments: This is the phosphoketolase reaction (EC 4.1.2.9), where xylulose-5-phosphate is cleaved using inorganic phosphate to yield acetyl phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, releasing water. Atom balance checks: D-Xylulose-5-phosphate (C5H11O8P) + Phosphate (HPO4 or H2PO4 depending on protonation) gives Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (C3H7O6P) + Acetyl phosphate (C2H5O5P) + H2O. Carbon (5=3+2), phosphorus (2=1+1), and oxygen/hydrogen balance appropriately when proper protonation states are considered.

rxn01104.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by bisphosphoglycerate phosphatase (often a function of bisphosphoglycerate mutase, BPGM). It hydrolyzes 2,3-bisphospho-D-glycerate (DPG/2,3-BPG) to 3-phosphoglycerate and inorganic phosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: 2,3-BPG (C3H8O10P2) + H2O yields 3-phosphoglycerate (C3H7O7P) + phosphate (HPO4/H3PO4). Mass and charge balance correctly. Physiologically this hydrolysis is essentially irreversible in the forward (hydrolytic) direction.

rxn02218.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidative decarboxylation of indole-3-acetate (indoleacetate) by indoleacetate monooxygenase or a related oxidase. One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated and CO2 is released, with formation of 3-methyleneoxindole or 3-methyldioxyindole-type product. Checking stoichiometry: indoleacetate (C10H9NO2) + O2 + H+ -> CO2 + product. The product 3-methyldioxyindole would be approximately C9H9NO2 (indole ring with methyl and dioxy groups). Carbon balance: 10 C in indoleacetate = 1 (CO2) + 9 (product), consistent. Oxygen balance is approximately satisfied with O2 incorporation plus the carboxylate oxygens; some ambiguity exists around the exact protonation/water involvement, but the overall scheme is broadly consistent. Oxygenase-driven decarboxylations are essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Electron balance is incorrect: reduced ferredoxin (typically a one-electron carrier, [2Fe-2S]) provides only 1 electron, but the monooxygenase reaction requires 2 electrons. The stoichiometry should use 2 reduced ferredoxin and produce 2 oxidized ferredoxin.
Charge/proton balance is inconsistent with the 1:1 ferredoxin stoichiometry as written; with 2 electrons needed, 2 H+ are consumed correctly but must be paired with 2 ferredoxin.
rxn06262.other_comments: This is the steroid 11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) type monooxygenase reaction converting 11-deoxycortisol (Cortodoxone/cortexolone) to cortisol, using O2 and reducing equivalents from ferredoxin (adrenodoxin), releasing water. The hydroxylation chemistry and substrate/product identities are correct.

errors: Stoichiometry is incorrect: CMP (cytidine monophosphate) consists of cytosine + ribose-5-phosphate connected by an N-glycosidic bond. Hydrolysis of this bond yields cytosine + ribose-5-phosphate, but the masses do not balance as written. CMP is C9H14N3O8P; cytosine is C4H5N3O; ribose-5-phosphate is C5H11O8P. Sum of products (C9H16N3O9P) versus reactant CMP + H2O (C9H16N3O9P) - this actually balances correctly.
rxn00362.other_comments: This is a nucleotide N-glycosidic bond hydrolysis: CMP is cleaved by water into cytosine (the free base) and ribose-5-phosphate. Upon recomputation the atoms balance (CMP C9H14N3O8P + H2O = C9H16N3O9P; cytosine C4H5N3O + ribose-5-phosphate C5H11O8P = C9H16N3O9P), so the reaction is stoichiometrically correct.

rxn09124.other_comments: This is a phospholipase A1 reaction hydrolyzing the sn-1 ester bond of 1,2-ditetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (dimyristoyl phosphatidic acid). Water cleaves the sn-1 myristoyl ester, releasing myristic acid (C14:0) and yielding 2-tetradecanoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a 2-acyl lysophosphatidic acid) plus a proton. Mass and charge balance: both sides carry the two C14 acyl groups distributed correctly, and the proton accounts for the carboxylic acid release. Stoichiometry is balanced.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (H+ + ala-L-glu-L) on both sides without any compartment designations, making it a null/empty reaction. For a proton symport transport reaction, the metabolites must have distinct compartment labels, e.g. H+[e] + ala-L-glu-L[e] <=> H+[c] + ala-L-glu-L[c]. As written, no net transport or transformation occurs.
rxn12523.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction where the dipeptide L-alanyl-L-glutamate is imported across a membrane coupled to proton symport (using the proton motive force). The stoichiometry of 1 H+ to 1 dipeptide is plausible, but the reaction string lacks compartment annotations, so it appears as a non-transformation. Proton symport import is typically driven forward (extracellular to cytoplasm) by the proton gradient.

rxn03609.other_comments: This reaction (R05297) is the hydration of 2-oxohex-trans-4-enoate (2-oxo-5-hexenoate type unsaturated keto acid) by addition of water across the C4-C5 double bond to give 4-hydroxy-2-oxohexanoate. It is catalyzed by 2-keto-4-pentenoate hydratase family enzymes (e.g., OphA/related hydratases) in aromatic/meta-cleavage degradation pathways. Stoichiometry is balanced: water (H2O) adds across the double bond, one substrate gives one product, atoms and charges are conserved.

errors: Product mismatch: the enzyme name specifies (E)-alpha-bisabolene as the product, but the reaction lists Levomenol (alpha-bisabolol) as the product. These are different compounds.

Levomenol (alpha-bisabolol) is a hydroxylated sesquiterpene alcohol, consistent with water addition; alpha-bisabolene is a hydrocarbon and would NOT consume H2O. The stoichiometry (H2O consumed) matches Levomenol but contradicts the bisabolene-forming enzyme annotation.
If the intended product is (E)-alpha-bisabolene, then H2O should not appear as a reactant and the products should be PPi + H+ + bisabolene only.
rxn14233.other_comments: This is a terpene synthase reaction converting farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) to a sesquiterpene with release of diphosphate (PPi). The cyclization/hydrolysis of the allylic diphosphate is essentially irreversible due to PPi release. The core issue is the inconsistency between the enzyme name (alpha-bisabolene-forming) and the listed product (Levomenol = alpha-bisabolol), which require different reactant sets (alcohol formation needs H2O, hydrocarbon does not).

rxn08018.other_comments: This is the acyl-ACP synthetase reaction activating oleate (C18:1, octadecenoate) to oleoyl-ACP. The mechanism proceeds via an acyl-AMP intermediate, consuming ATP and releasing PPi and AMP. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + ACP + fatty acid yields PPi + AMP + acyl-ACP. The H+ balance is consistent (the carboxylate forms a thioester, and proton release accompanies the reaction). In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate, making it effectively irreversible toward acyl-ACP formation.

rxn06677.other_comments: This is a PTS (phosphoenolpyruvate-dependent phosphotransferase system) reaction transferring a phosphoryl group from a phosphohistidine residue on a protein (such as the lactose-specific EIIA/EIIB components) to lactose, producing lactose-6-phosphate as the sugar is transported into the cell. LACT is lactose. The stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphoryl group is transferred from the phospho-histidine protein to lactose, yielding lactose-6-phosphate and the dephosphorylated protein histidine. Note a minor nomenclature inconsistency: the enzyme name specifies N(pai) (N-pi/tele, the N3/tau nitrogen) phosphohistidine while the substrate text reads 'N-pros' (N-pros = pros/N1/pi tautomer); these should be consistent, but this is a naming detail rather than a stoichiometric error.

errors: The reaction as written is not balanced in terms of compartments; substrates and products are identical, indicating missing compartment designations (e.g., periplasm vs cytoplasm)
Without distinct compartment labels, this represents a null/identity reaction with no net transport
rxn12562.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction moving itaconate together with 2 protons across a membrane. The molecular stoichiometry (1 itaconate : 2 H+) is internally consistent, but the reaction string lacks compartment annotations, so both sides appear identical. Properly written it should be: 2.0 H+[e] + Itaconate[e] <=> 2.0 H+[c] + Itaconate[c]. Symport driven by the proton motive force typically favors import into the cytoplasm, but transporters can be reversible depending on gradients.

rxn05189.other_comments: This represents an ABC-type transporter for Fe(III)dicitrate, coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to substrate translocation across a membrane. The Fe(III)dicitrate appears on both sides because it represents the same metabolite in different cellular compartments (e.g., extracellular/periplasmic to cytoplasmic), which is standard notation for transport reactions. The ATP hydrolysis component is stoichiometrically balanced, and the transported species is conserved. The reaction is correctly formulated as a transport process.

rxn09150.other_comments: This is a phospholipase A2 reaction hydrolyzing the sn-2 ester bond of a phosphatidic acid (1,2-dioctadec-11-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate, dioleoyl-PA). Water cleaves the acyl ester releasing one octadecenoate (oleate, C18:1) fatty acid and generating the lyso-phosphatidic acid (1-octadec-11-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate) plus a proton. The mass and atom balance is consistent: C39H73O8P + H2O -> C18H33O2 (oleate, deprotonated) + C21H40O7P (lyso-PA, deprotonated) + H+. The charges balance with the released proton.

rxn04874.other_comments: This is the epoxide hydrolase reaction (EC 3.3.2.x) where bromobenzene-3,4-oxide (an arene oxide) is hydrolyzed by addition of water to form the trans-3,4-dihydrodiol. Stoichiometry is balanced: the arene oxide (C6H5BrO) plus H2O yields the dihydrodiol (C6H7BrO2). Epoxide hydrolases catalyze hydrolytic ring opening of epoxides/arene oxides, a thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible detoxification reaction in vivo.

rxn01732.other_comments: This is an itaconate:CoA ligase reaction forming itaconyl-CoA from itaconate and CoA, coupled to GTP hydrolysis to GDP and phosphate. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: GTP (C10H12N5O14P3) is converted to GDP (C10H12N5O11P2) plus inorganic phosphate, and the CoA thiol (C21H32N7O16P3S) is joined to itaconate (C5H4O4) forming itaconyl-CoA (C26H35N7O19P3S) with loss of nothing extra. The standard mechanism for nucleotide-dependent CoA ligases (acyl-CoA synthetase, GDP-forming type, EC 6.2.1.5-like) proceeds via an acyl-phosphate intermediate. Note: many physiological CoA ligases produce AMP+PPi (ATP-forming type), but GDP-forming succinyl-CoA-type ligases (EC 6.2.1.4/6.2.1.5) are well established and reversible in vivo.

rxn09040.other_comments: This reaction represents the UbiF (or UbiH/UbiI family) hydroxylase step in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis. It adds a hydroxyl group at the 5-position of the benzoquinol ring using molecular oxygen as the oxygen donor. The stoichiometry is balanced: one oxygen atom from 0.5 O2 is incorporated into the product as the new hydroxyl group (a monooxygenase-type insertion). In many flavin-dependent monooxygenase formulations, NAD(P)H and H2O would also be involved, but as written with 0.5 O2 the oxygen atom balance for the net hydroxylation is consistent.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the disproportionation of two monodehydroascorbate (ascorbate) radicals into ascorbate plus dehydroascorbate does not require 4 H+. The balanced reaction is 2 Ascorbate radical (monodehydroascorbate) + H+ <=> Ascorbate + Dehydroascorbate, or written neutrally 2 MDHA -> Ascorbate + DHA. The stoichiometry of 4 H+ is incorrect.
Mass imbalance results from the incorrect proton count given the redox/protonation states of the species involved.
rxn02280.other_comments: This represents the non-enzymatic (or enzyme-catalyzed) disproportionation of the ascorbate free radical (monodehydroascorbate/ascorbyl radical) into ascorbate and dehydroascorbate. Two radicals undergo a one-electron transfer to yield one fully reduced and one fully oxidized molecule. In vivo this disproportionation proceeds spontaneously in the forward direction.

rxn05709.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction moving D-Lysine across a membrane (typically extracellular to cytoplasm) coupled to proton movement down its electrochemical gradient. As written, both sides are identical because compartment tags are missing; the proton motive force normally drives such symport inward. With proper compartmentalization the stoichiometry (1 H+ : 1 D-Lysine) is plausible for a symporter.

rxn01671.other_comments: This is the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK/Nrk) reaction (EC 2.7.1.22). ATP phosphorylates the 5'-hydroxyl of N-ribosylnicotinamide (nicotinamide riboside) to yield NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide) plus ADP and a proton. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge (transfer of a phosphate group with release of H+), and is stoichiometrically correct. As a kinase reaction coupled to ATP hydrolysis, it proceeds essentially in the forward (phosphorylation) direction in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric/structural error: the product 'ADPribose' (ADP-ribose) is a glycosidic compound where AMP is linked to ribose, but the substrate provided is ADP (which has a beta-phosphate). An adenylyltransferase transfers an adenylyl (AMP) group, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi), not inorganic phosphate. The reaction as written (ADP + ribose-5-P -> Pi + ADP-ribose) does not balance phosphate atoms correctly: ADP has 2 phosphates, ribose-5-P has 1 phosphate (total 3 P on left); ADP-ribose has 2 phosphates and Pi has 1 (total 3 P on right) - so phosphorus count balances, but the chemistry is implausible.

Mechanistic inconsistency: forming ADP-ribose from ADP + ribose-5-phosphate with release of inorganic phosphate is not a standard biochemical reaction; ADP-ribose is normally generated from NAD+ hydrolysis or via ADP-ribosyl transfer, not by this condensation.
rxn00773.other_comments: The reaction proposes that ADP and ribose-5-phosphate combine to form ADP-ribose plus inorganic phosphate, named as an adenylyltransferase. While the phosphorus atom count appears balanced, the proposed mechanism is biochemically questionable, since an adenylyltransferase typically transfers AMP and releases pyrophosphate, and ADP-ribose is not normally synthesized this way.

rxn02171.other_comments: This is the vinylacetyl-CoA delta3-delta2-isomerase reaction (EC 5.3.3.3), which catalyzes the isomerization of vinylacetyl-CoA (3-butenoyl-CoA, with a beta-gamma double bond) to crotonyl-CoA (2-butenoyl-CoA, with an alpha-beta double bond). Both species share the molecular formula C25H40N7O17P3S and the same number of atoms, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as an intramolecular double-bond migration. The conjugated alpha-beta unsaturated crotonyl-CoA is thermodynamically more stable, but as an isomerase the reaction is generally treated as reversible, with the in vivo direction (e.g., in lysine/gamma-aminobutyrate fermentation pathways) typically favoring crotonyl-CoA formation.

rxn02413.other_comments: This is the ring-cleavage dioxygenation of caffeate (3,4-dihydroxy-trans-cinnamate). A protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase-type intradiol cleavage incorporates O2 across the catechol ring, opening it to yield the muconate derivative 3-(2-carboxyethenyl)-cis,cis-muconate. The atom and charge balance is consistent: O2 provides 2 oxygens incorporated into the two new carboxyl groups, and 2 H+ are released from the two phenolic/carboxyl protons. Stoichiometry appears balanced.

rxn03641.other_comments: This is a CoA transferase reaction (EC 2.8.3.-) transferring the CoA moiety from acetyl-CoA to 4-hydroxybutanoate, yielding acetate and 4-hydroxybutyryl-CoA. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the CoA group is simply transferred between two carboxylate acceptors, conserving all atoms. This step is part of the 4-aminobutyrate/succinate fermentation pathway in anaerobes such as Clostridium kluyveri. CoA transferases are typically reversible and the in vivo direction depends on the relative concentrations of acetyl-CoA/acetate and 4-hydroxybutyryl-CoA/4-hydroxybutanoate. In the catabolic/fermentative context the forward direction (activating 4-hydroxybutanoate) is favored, but the enzyme itself catalyzes a near-equilibrium thioester exchange.

errors: The H+ on the substrate side is not balanced; the phosphoryl transfer from ATP to 5-phosphomevalonate does not consume a proton. The reaction is more correctly written as ATP + 5-phosphomevalonate <=> ADP + 5-diphosphomevalonate (the small charge/proton balance depends on protonation states, but a free H+ as reactant is not standard for this kinase reaction)
rxn02322.other_comments: This is phosphomevalonate kinase (EC 2.7.4.2), which transfers the gamma-phosphate of ATP to (R)-5-phosphomevalonate to yield 5-diphosphomevalonate (mevalonate 5-diphosphate) and ADP, a step in the mevalonate pathway for isoprenoid biosynthesis. The ATP/ADP and phosphomevalonate/diphosphomevalonate pairs are otherwise correctly matched.

rxn02844.other_comments: This is the transamination reaction catalyzed by 2-aminoethylphosphonate-pyruvate transaminase (or phosphonoalanine biosynthesis). L-Glutamate donates an amino group to 3-phosphonopyruvate, forming 2-oxoglutarate and phosphonoalanine (2-amino-3-phosphonopropionate). The reaction is atom- and charge-balanced: the amino group transfer between glutamate/2-oxoglutarate and phosphonopyruvate/phosphonoalanine is stoichiometrically correct. As a PLP-dependent aminotransferase, this reaction is thermodynamically near-equilibrium and freely reversible in vivo, though the physiological direction in phosphonate biosynthesis often favors formation of the phosphonoamino acid.

rxn12302.other_comments: This is the tricarballylate dehydrogenase (TcuA) reaction, which oxidizes tricarballylate to cis-aconitate using a quinone (Q) electron acceptor, producing the reduced quinol (QH2). The reaction is balanced: tricarballylate (C6H8O6 as trianion) is dehydrogenated by removal of two hydrogens (2H), introducing a double bond to form cis-aconitate, with Q accepting 2[H] to become QH2. Carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen atoms balance with the 2-electron/2-proton transfer to the quinone. This is a key step in citrate fermentation/tricarballylate degradation in organisms like Salmonella.

rxn01630.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of 5-aminopentanamide (an amide) to 5-aminopentanoate (5-aminovalerate) plus ammonia, consuming one water. The reaction is balanced: C5H12N2O + H2O = NH3 + C5H11NO2. Amidohydrolase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo in the hydrolytic direction.

rxn00599.other_comments: This is the ALA synthase (5-aminolevulinate synthase) reaction, the first committed step of heme/tetrapyrrole biosynthesis in the C4 (Shemin) pathway. Glycine condenses with succinyl-CoA, releasing CoA and CO2 to form 5-aminolevulinate. The atom and charge balance check out: glycine (C2H5NO2) + succinyl-CoA + H+ yields CoA + CO2 + 5-aminolevulinate (C5H9NO3). Carbons: 2 (glycine) + 4 (succinyl portion) = 6 = 1 (CO2) + 5 (ALA). The reaction is strongly exergonic due to thioester hydrolysis and decarboxylation, driving it essentially irreversibly toward ALA in vivo.

errors: The reaction appears unbalanced as written. R03298 is the conversion of 2,3-bisphospho-D-glycerate (DPG) to 2,3-cyclic-bisphospho-D-glycerate (cDPG) coupled to ATP hydrolysis. The proper balanced form is ATP + 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate <=> ADP + phosphate + 2,3-cyclic-bisphosphoglycerate. The inclusion of an explicit H+ on the substrate side is questionable for proton/charge balance and may make the reaction unbalanced.
rxn02362.other_comments: This is the 2,3-cyclic-bisphosphoglycerate synthetase (cyclic 2,3-diphosphoglycerate synthetase) reaction found in methanogenic archaea. It uses ATP to form an intramolecular phosphoanhydride (cyclic) bond in DPG, releasing ADP and inorganic phosphate. The ATP-driven phosphate elimination makes it strongly favorable in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward cDPG.

rxn01786.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (limonene 6-monohydroxylase, e.g. EC 1.14.14.x) reaction. (-)-Limonene is hydroxylated at the C6 position to yield (-)-trans-carveol. The monooxygenase incorporates one atom of O2 into the substrate (forming the hydroxyl group) while the other oxygen atom is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Stoichiometry balances: NADPH + O2 + H+ + Limonene (C10H16) -> H2O + NADP+ + carveol (C10H16O). Atoms and charges are balanced.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the product side shows only one isotetradecanoyl group transferred to lysylphosphatidylglycerol, but the substrate is named 'Diisotetradecanoylphosphatidylglycerol' (two acyl chains). The lysyl-PG product should retain both acyl chains of the phosphatidylglycerol backbone plus the added lysine; the naming inconsistency (Di- in substrate vs single 'Isotetradecanoyl' prefix in product) suggests a mass/atom imbalance.

Mechanistic concern: aminoacyl-PG synthases (MprF/LysX-type) use aminoacyl-tRNA(Lys) as the lysine donor, not free L-Lysine + ATP directly. If this reaction represents the lysyl-tRNA synthetase-like activation, the lysine should be charged onto tRNA, and a separate transfer step esterifies it to PG. The combined reaction as written omits tRNA.
Charge/proton balance should be verified: aminoacylation releasing AMP + PPi typically does not also release a free H+ unless explicitly balanced against protonation states.
rxn10330.other_comments: This is intended to be the biosynthesis of lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (a membrane lipid modification conferring resistance to cationic antimicrobials) using isotetradecanoyl (anteiso/iso C14) acyl chains. The general scheme is ATP-dependent attachment of L-lysine to the phosphatidylglycerol head group, releasing AMP and PPi. [directionality_note] ATP hydrolysis to AMP + PPi (subsequently hydrolyzed by pyrophosphatase) makes this reaction strongly favored in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn14319.other_comments: This is the 3beta-hydroxy-Delta5-C27-steroid oxidoreductase (HSD3B7) type reaction acting on a bile acid biosynthesis intermediate. The substrate (24S)-cholest-5-ene-3beta,7alpha,24-triol is oxidized at the 3-OH to a 3-oxo group with concomitant isomerization of the Delta5 double bond to Delta4, yielding 7alpha,24-dihydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one. NAD+ is reduced to NADH. Atoms balance: oxidation of the 3beta-OH removes 2 H (one to NAD+ as hydride, one released as H+), and the double bond shifts from 5,6 to 4,5 position, which is consistent. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: The reaction is not stoichiometrically balanced. The coupling of two iodinated tyrosine residues (3,5-diiodo-L-tyrosine + 3-iodo-L-tyrosine) to form T3 (3,5,3'-triiodothyronine) plus dehydroalanine requires careful accounting of atoms. T3 (C15H12I3NO4) contains a diphenyl ether linkage. The atoms from DIT and MIT do not balance against T3 + dehydroalanine + 2 H2O; specifically the iodine count (DIT has 2 I, MIT has 1 I = 3 I total = matches T3's 3 I), but the oxygen, hydrogen, and carbon balance with dehydroalanine and water need verification and the redox role of H2O2 is not properly represented as an oxidant (water as the only reduced product is insufficient).

Thyroid hormone synthesis (thyroperoxidase-catalyzed coupling) occurs on thyroglobulin-bound tyrosyl residues, not on free amino acids; representing free DIT and MIT coupling is biochemically imprecise.
rxn02779.other_comments: This represents the oxidative coupling step of thyroid hormone biosynthesis, where a diiodotyrosine and a monoiodotyrosine residue are coupled by thyroid peroxidase using H2O2 to form triiodothyronine (T3), leaving a dehydroalanine residue on the donor. The reaction is physiologically driven forward by peroxide-dependent oxidation.

rxn07763.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 / NADH-dependent monooxygenase (N-demethylase) reaction. Theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) is N-demethylated to 3-methylxanthine, with the removed methyl group released as formaldehyde. The reaction consumes O2 and NADH (with H+) and produces H2O, NAD+, formaldehyde, and the demethylated xanthine. Atom balance checks out: theophylline (C7H8N4O2) loses a CH2 (carried by formaldehyde, CH2O) using one O from O2 and the other O incorporated into water; NADH+H+ provides the reducing equivalents to form NAD+ and H2O. Monooxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (driven by O2 consumption and oxidative demethylation).

rxn05180.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction for carnitine. The substrate carnitine appears on both sides because the reaction represents translocation across the membrane (carnitine[external] transported to carnitine[internal]), with ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) providing the energy. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced if the two carnitine entries are in different compartments. ABC importers are driven by ATP hydrolysis and are physiologically unidirectional (uptake), so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn03602.other_comments: This is the toluate 1,2-dioxygenase reaction (toluate cis-dihydrodiol formation). Toluate (4-methylbenzoate / o-toluate) is dioxygenated using O2, with NADH + H+ providing reducing equivalents, yielding the cis-dihydrodiol and NAD+. The stoichiometry is balanced: both oxygen atoms from O2 are incorporated (one as the carboxyl-bearing carbon hydroxyl, one as the adjacent hydroxyl), and NADH provides 2 electrons + H+. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance. The product name suggests a methylcyclohexadiene cis-diol carboxylic acid consistent with toluate dioxygenation. In vivo this dioxygenase reaction is essentially irreversible (driven by O2 incorporation), proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn06773.other_comments: This is a transacetylase reaction (CoA-independent transacetylase, EC 2.3.1.147) that transfers the acetyl group from the sn-2 position of platelet-activating factor (PAF, 2-acetyl-1-alkyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine) to a lysophospholipid acceptor (1-radyl-2-lyso-sn-glycero-3-phospholipid). The product names appear inconsistent: the acceptor is described as '1-Radyl-2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phospholipid' rather than the 2-lyso (acceptor) form, but the product '1-Radyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycero-3-phospholipid' correctly shows the acetylated acceptor, and the PAF is correctly converted to its 2-lyso form (1-alkyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine). The acetyl group is conserved across both sides, so stoichiometry/mass balance for the acetyl transfer holds.

rxn09399.other_comments: This represents the 1,4-alpha-glucan branching enzyme (EC 2.4.1.18) reaction, which introduces alpha-1,6 glycosidic branch points into a linear alpha-1,4-glucan (amylose-like) to form a branched glucan (glycogen-like). The branching reaction is effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward branch formation. As written, the polymeric substrates lack defined stoichiometry and the equation is overly simplified.

errors: Unbalanced as written: cyclopropanation of a cis double bond by SAM produces S-adenosyl-homocysteine plus a proton, but the carbon count must increase by one (CH2 transfer from the methyl group of SAM). rxn06306.other_comments: This is a nucleotidyltransferase (uridylyltransferase) reaction. rxn01450.other_comments: This is indolepyruvate decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.74), which catalyzes the decarboxylation of 3-(indol-3-yl)pyruvate to 2-(indol-3-yl)acetaldehyde plus CO2. rxn02519.other_comments: This represents the oxidation of 2-hydroxyglutarate to 2-oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate), catalyzed by 2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase (an FAD-dependent enzyme, e.g., L2HGDH or D2HGDH-type activity). Note that physiologically the actual electron acceptor is often a flavoprotein/quinone (the '(acceptor)' in the name), with FAD as the bound prosthetic group rather than a free cosubstrate.

rxn01905.other_comments: This is an oxidative deamination of 3-sulfinoalanine (cysteine sulfinate) to 3-sulfinopyruvate, catalyzed by a glutamate dehydrogenase-like or amino acid dehydrogenase activity. rxn10295.other_comments: This reaction represents the polymerization step of lipoteichoic acid (LTA) synthesis, where 24 CDP-glycerol units are transferred sequentially onto the diglucosyldiacylglycerol (Glc2-DAG) membrane anchor to build the poly(glycerophosphate) backbone. Glycosyltransferase/polymerase reactions of this type using activated CDP-sugar/CDP-glycerol donors are strongly thermodynamically favorable and physiologically committed in the forward (biosynthetic) direction.

rxn07463.other_comments: This is a sesquiterpene synthase reaction converting farnesyl diphosphate (FPP, C15) into the cyclic sesquiterpene (-)-Germacrene D, releasing pyrophosphate (PPi). DTT/oxidized-DTT is an artificial redox couple commonly used in vitro, so 'in vivo' directionality is somewhat artificial; thermodynamically these dehydratase/epoxidase-type steps can be written reversibly in databases.

rxn10273.other_comments: This reaction describes a glycosyltransferase that transfers a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to monoglucosyl-1,2-distearoylglycerol, producing diglucosyl-1,2-distearoylglycerol and UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucosyl unit is transferred from the nucleotide sugar donor to the glycolipid acceptor, releasing UDP. This represents the biosynthesis of diglucosyldiacylglycerol (a membrane glycolipid common in bacteria). Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are strongly exergonic due to cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

However, the product of adenine deamination is hypoxanthine (loss of NH3 from C6 amino group), so the proton (H+) on the reactant side is not balanced - deamination of an amino group (NH2) by hydrolysis yields NH3 and replaces NH2 with =O, consuming H2O but not requiring an additional H+; the H+ should not be on the substrate side
Charge/proton balance is questionable: hydrolytic deamination is H2O + R-NH2 -> R=O + NH3, no extra free H+ is needed
rxn00142.other_comments: This represents a hydrolytic deamination of S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine, converting the adenine moiety to a hypoxanthine moiety (inosyl), releasing ammonia. Such adenine/adenosine-type deaminations are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (deamination) direction.

Charge/redox cofactor missing: aromatic ring dioxygenases incorporate both atoms of O2 and consume NAD(P)H; the reaction as written lacks the reducing equivalents and the cis-dihydrodiol intermediate

rxn03830.other_comments: This represents the dioxygenase-catalyzed oxidation of fluorene incorporating molecular oxygen to form a dihydroxylated fluorene, an early step in microbial PAH degradation. As written it is unbalanced because it omits the required reducing cofactor (NAD(P)H + H+) and oversimplifies the cis-dihydrodiol intermediate.

rxn14273.other_comments: This is the CYP83 (e.g., CYP83A1/B1) reaction in glucosinolate biosynthesis, converting an aldoxime to an aci-nitro/S-alkyl-thiohydroximate intermediate via cysteine conjugation. It is a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase using NADPH and O2, which is physiologically irreversible (forward) in vivo.

rxn07464.other_comments: This is the germacrene A synthase reaction (EC 4.2.3.23), a terpene cyclase that converts (2E,6E)-farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) into (+)-germacrene A, releasing diphosphate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: FPP (C15H25O7P2, charge -3) yields germacrene A (C15H24), PPi (HP2O7, charge -3), and H+. Carbon, oxygen, phosphorus, and charge all balance.

rxn00652.other_comments: This is a racemase reaction interconverting L-Cysteine and D-Cysteine. The two are stereoisomers (enantiomers) with identical molecular formula C3H7NO2S, so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced. Racemases catalyze epimerization at the alpha-carbon and are inherently reversible, with the equilibrium favoring no particular direction thermodynamically (ratio driven toward racemic mixture). Note: '2-Amino-3-mercaptopropionic acid' is indeed the systematic name for cysteine.

rxn03330.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADH-dependent reduction of imidazole pyruvate (3-(imidazol-4-yl)pyruvate, a keto acid) to imidazole lactate (3-(imidazol-4-yl)lactate, the corresponding hydroxy acid), with concomitant oxidation of NADH to NAD+. The stoichiometry is balanced: the keto group (C=O) is reduced to a hydroxyl (CH-OH) using the hydride from NADH plus a proton, consuming one H+. This is a typical NAD(H)-linked dehydrogenase/reductase reaction (analogous to lactate dehydrogenase chemistry). Such reactions are generally reversible thermodynamically, though physiological direction depends on the NADH/NAD+ ratio and substrate concentrations.

rxn01945.other_comments: This is 4-hydroxyphenylacetate 3-monooxygenase (EC 1.14.14.9/1.14.13.3), a flavin-dependent two-component monooxygenase. It hydroxylates 4-hydroxyphenylacetate at the 3-position to form homoprotocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate). One atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate and the other is reduced to water, with NADH (via FADH2) providing reducing equivalents. The equation is balanced: NADH + O2 + H+ + substrate -> H2O + NAD+ + hydroxylated product. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: The reaction name refers to caffeate (3,4-dihydroxy-trans-cinnamate) as the substrate, but the actual substrates listed are caffeyl alcohol and its product coniferol (coniferyl alcohol); name/substrate mismatch

rxn04429.other_comments: This is a caffeoyl-CoA / caffeic acid O-methyltransferase (COMT)-type reaction. As written it methylates caffeyl alcohol at the 3-hydroxyl to form coniferyl alcohol (coniferol), with SAM converted to SAH. The atom mapping for the methyl transfer (C of methyl, plus loss of one OH proton) is otherwise consistent.

rxn01530.other_comments: This is retinol dehydrogenase activity: retinol is oxidized to retinal (retinaldehyde) using NAD+ as the electron acceptor, producing NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: retinol (C20H30O) loses two H (as hydride to NAD+ and a proton), yielding retinal (C20H28O). NAD+ + retinol -> NADH + H+ + retinal is stoichiometrically correct.

rxn03881.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydration of 6-hydroxycyclohex-1-ene-1-carbonyl-CoA across the C1-C2 double bond, adding water to yield 2,6-dihydroxycyclohexane-1-carbonyl-CoA. This is part of the anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: water provides the OH and H needed to saturate the enoyl-CoA double bond. Enoyl-CoA hydratase-type reactions of this kind are typically reversible, though in the degradative pathway flux proceeds in the hydration direction.

errors: Substrate name mismatch: the reaction name refers to 3-Oxopropanoate (malonate semialdehyde) but the equation lists 3-Oxo-2-methylpropanoate (methylmalonate semialdehyde / 2-methyl-3-oxopropanoate).

Product identity error: oxidative decarboxylation (CoA-acetylating) of methylmalonate semialdehyde yields propionyl-CoA + CO2, not (L)-methylmalonyl-CoA. The decarboxylating mechanism requires loss of CO2.
Missing CO2 product: a 'decarboxylating' reaction must release CO2, which is absent from the equation.
Carbon imbalance: methylmalonate semialdehyde (C4) + CoA should give propionyl-CoA (C3) + CO2; the written product methylmalonyl-CoA (C4-CoA) does not balance with loss of decarboxylation.
If propionyl-CoA were the product, atoms do not balance as written either since no CO2 is shown.
rxn02424.other_comments: This is intended to be methylmalonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (acylating), EC 1.2.1.27, which oxidatively decarboxylates 2-methyl-3-oxopropanoate to propionyl-CoA + CO2 using NAD+ and CoA. The correct equation is: 2-methyl-3-oxopropanoate + CoA + NAD+ -> propionyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH + H+. As written, the product (methylmalonyl-CoA) and the omission of CO2 are incorrect, and the enzyme name references the wrong (unmethylated) substrate.

rxn01230.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of hypotaurine to taurine, catalyzed by hypotaurine dehydrogenase (EC 1.8.1.3), coupling the oxidation to reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Atom balance: hypotaurine (C2H7NO2S) + H2O provides the additional oxygen, NAD+ is reduced to NADH with release of one H+. Taurine is C2H7NO3S. The mass and charge balance is correct: O and H account for the water incorporation and the proton released. In vivo, hypotaurine is converted to taurine, so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction as written.

rxn01499.other_comments: This is the aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (DOPA decarboxylase) reaction converting L-Dopa to dopamine. The reaction is balanced: L-Dopa (C9H11NO4) plus H+ yields CO2 (CO2) plus dopamine (C8H12NO2+, the protonated amine form). Carbon balance: 9 = 1 + 8. The H+ consumption accounts for the charge/proton balance with the protonated amine product. Decarboxylations are essentially irreversible due to release of CO2.

With NADH + 2 H+ + O2 yielding NAD+ + H2O + hydroxylated product, the H balance is correct (NADH provides 1 H, plus 2 H+, total 3 H on reactant H side; products H2O has 2 H plus 1 H added as OH = 3 H). No clear stoichiometric error detected.
Minor: NAD should be written as NAD+ to reflect correct charge state.
rxn03532.other_comments: This is the precorrin-3A C20-monooxygenase (CobG) reaction in aerobic cobalamin (vitamin B12) biosynthesis. It is an oxygen-dependent hydroxylation/monooxygenase step converting precorrin-3A to precorrin-3B using NADH and molecular oxygen. As an O2-consuming monooxygenase reaction, it is physiologically irreversible (forward).

errors: Apiin is flavone-7-O-apiosylglucoside, not a simple flavone-7-O-beta-D-glucoside; the substrate name in the enzyme designation does not strictly match apiin, though the malonylation chemistry of the glucosyl moiety is plausible
The reaction as written produces H+, but malonyl transfer (esterification of a hydroxyl with the malonyl group) does not typically release a free proton; the proton balance should be verified
rxn03165.other_comments: This is a malonyl-CoA-dependent acyltransferase reaction transferring a malonyl group to a sugar hydroxyl (6''-O position) of the glycosylated flavone, releasing CoA. Acyl-CoA transferases are thermodynamically driven forward by the energy-rich thioester bond.

rxn03122.other_comments: This is the aminotransferase (transaminase) reaction catalyzed by enzymes such as WecE/PglE/QdtB (EC 2.6.1.-). It transfers an amino group between UDP-2-acetamido-4-amino-2,4,6-trideoxyglucose (UDP-4-amino sugar) and 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and the corresponding UDP-4-keto sugar (UDP-2-acetamido-4-dehydro-2,6-dideoxyglucose). Atom and charge balance hold: the amino-for-oxo exchange is stoichiometrically consistent. As written, the reaction runs left-to-right toward forming the keto sugar plus glutamate; however, the biosynthetic direction in vivo is typically the reverse (amination of the 4-keto sugar using glutamate as amino donor). PLP is the cofactor but is regenerated and not shown.

rxn04037.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of 2-(alpha-D-mannosyl)-3-phosphoglycerate (MPG) by the phosphatase MpgP (EC 3.1.3.70), yielding alpha-mannosylglycerate (the compatible solute) and inorganic phosphate. Water is consumed. The stoichiometry is balanced (the phosphate group plus the H from water are released as Pi, with mannosylglycerate retaining the hydroxyl). As a phosphohydrolase reaction, it is strongly exergonic and proceeds essentially irreversibly in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

The balanced reaction should be: 13(1)-Hydroxy-Mg-protoporphyrin IX 13-monomethyl ester + NAD+ <=> 13(1)-Oxo-Mg-protoporphyrin IX 13-monomethyl ester + NADH + H+
rxn11941.other_comments: This represents a step in chlorophyll biosynthesis, the oxidation of the C13(1) hydroxyl group of Mg-protoporphyrin IX monomethyl ester to a keto group, part of the formation of the isocyclic E-ring (catalyzed by Mg-protoporphyrin IX monomethyl ester cyclase pathway). The redox direction (hydroxyl -> ketone with NAD+ -> NADH) is correct in vivo, but the H+ count is wrong (should be 1 H+, not 3).

rxn09071.other_comments: This represents the oxidation of pyridoxine 5'-phosphate (PNP) to pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP). The conversion of the hydroxymethyl group at C4 to an aldehyde is a 2-electron oxidation, releasing 2 H (as a hydride to NAD+ giving NADH, plus one H+). The stoichiometry NAD + PNP -> NADH + PLP + H+ is balanced for both atoms and charge. Typically this reaction is catalyzed by an FMN-dependent oxidase (PdxH) using O2 as the electron acceptor; here it is framed as an anaerobic NAD-linked variant.

rxn05061.other_comments: This is the 4-hydroxyphenylacetate decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.83), a glycyl radical enzyme. It converts 4-hydroxyphenylacetate to p-cresol (4-methylphenol) with release of CO2, consuming a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: 4-hydroxyphenylacetate (C8H7O3-) plus H+ yields p-cresol (C7H8O) plus CO2. This decarboxylation is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward p-cresol formation, which is a characteristic anaerobic gut bacterial reaction.

rxn07793.other_comments: This is a prenyltransferase reaction (chalcone prenyltransferase) where dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) transfers a prenyl group to isosalipurpol (naringenin chalcone), producing desmethylxanthohumol with release of pyrophosphate (PPi) and a proton. Mass and charge balance check: DMAPP (C5H11O7P2, charge -3 typically) plus the chalcone, yielding the prenylated chalcone plus PPi (charge -3) and H+. The prenyl group (C5H8) is transferred, and PPi plus H+ accounts for the diphosphate leaving group. The stoichiometry of carbon, hydrogen, and phosphate appears consistent with a standard prenyltransferase mechanism. Prenyltransferase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the loss of pyrophosphate and its subsequent hydrolysis, driving the reaction strongly forward.

rxn01410.other_comments: This is the carnitine dehydratase (carnitine hydro-lyase) reaction (EC 4.2.1.89). L-carnitine (4-hydroxy-trimethylammonio-butanoate) loses water to form crotonobetaine (4-(trimethylammonio)but-2-enoate). Stoichiometry is balanced: carnitine (C7H15NO3) = water (H2O) + crotonobetaine (C7H13NO2). The reaction is part of carnitine metabolism in bacteria such as E. coli.

rxn00320.other_comments: This is a racemase reaction interconverting the L and D stereoisomers of lysine. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced (both sides are C6H14N2O2, same net charge), so it is stoichiometrically correct. Racemases catalyze stereochemical inversion at the alpha carbon and are thermodynamically reversible, driven toward the racemic equilibrium based on substrate/product concentrations.

rxn14164.other_comments: This is the CYP7B1-catalyzed 7alpha-hydroxylation of pregnenolone, a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase reaction. One atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate as the 7alpha-hydroxyl group, while the other oxygen atom is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + pregnenolone yields H2O + NADP+ + 7alpha-hydroxypregnenolone, conserving atoms and charge. P450 monooxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible, proceeding in the hydroxylation direction.

rxn08113.other_comments: This is an aldose-ketose isomerization between D-allose 6-phosphate (an aldose sugar phosphate) and allulose 6-phosphate (also known as D-psicose 6-phosphate, a ketose). Both species share the molecular formula C6H13O9P and the reaction is balanced 1:1, so it is stoichiometrically correct. Aldose-ketose isomerases (e.g., AlsE-type enzymes in the allose utilization pathway) catalyze a near-equilibrium reaction, hence freely reversible in vivo with the net direction determined by substrate/product concentrations.

rxn01055.other_comments: This is a sulfatase reaction hydrolyzing the sulfate ester bond of 2-O-sulfolactate to release free lactate and inorganic sulfate. The reaction is balanced (C3H5O6S- + H2O -> C3H5O3- + SO4^2- + H+). Sulfatase hydrolysis of sulfate esters is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

Oxygen: O2 provides 2 O, both incorporated as the two hydroxyls - balanced. The equation as written is essentially balanced for a dioxygenase reaction.
rxn03574.other_comments: This is a biphenyl 2,3-dioxygenase type reaction (Rieske non-heme iron dioxygenase) converting 4-chlorobiphenyl to the cis-dihydrodiol, incorporating both atoms of molecular O2 and consuming NADPH. Such dioxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (forward only).

rxn05214.other_comments: This is intended to represent a citrate-Mg2+:H+ symporter (CitMHS family), which co-transports a magnesium-citrate complex together with a proton across the membrane. The stoichiometry of one H+, one citrate, and one Mg2+ is plausible for such a symporter. Transport is driven by the proton motive force; as written without compartments it is a trivial identity, but the underlying transport process is generally reversible and direction depends on the electrochemical gradients.

rxn05474.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction moving 2-phospho-D-glycerate together with a proton across a membrane. rxn01356.other_comments: This represents 4-aminobenzoate carboxy-lyase (decarboxylase), converting 4-aminobenzoate to aniline plus CO2 with consumption of a proton. Decarboxylation releasing CO2 is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn02467.other_comments: This reaction represents the cyclization/dehydration of 4-(2-aminophenyl)-2,4-dioxobutanoate (the tautomer/open-chain form derived from kynurenine pathway intermediates) to form kynurenate with release of water. The intramolecular condensation between the aromatic amino group and a keto carbonyl forms the quinoline ring of kynurenate. Stoichiometry is balanced: the substrate loses one H2O to cyclize into kynurenate. This is a non-enzymatic or spontaneous cyclization step in tryptophan catabolism that strongly favors the cyclic product.

rxn03305.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD+-dependent oxidation of a 3-alpha-hydroxyl group to a 3-oxo (keto) group on a pregnane steroid derivative bearing an 18-aldehyde. The substrate 3alpha,11beta,21-trihydroxy-20-oxo-5beta-pregnan-18-al is oxidized at the C3 position, producing the 3,20-dioxo product, with NAD+ reduced to NADH + H+. Atoms balance: the 3-OH loses two hydrogens (one to NAD+ as hydride, one released as H+), consistent with a B-specific hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase reaction. Stoichiometry is correct and charge/mass are balanced.

rxn04643.other_comments: This reaction describes the transfer of a glucuronosyl group from UDP-glucuronate to luteolin 7-O-beta-D-diglucuronide, forming luteolin triglucuronide (with the new glucuronide at the 4' position) and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucuronate moiety is transferred from UDP-glucuronate to the acceptor, yielding UDP. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are strongly exergonic due to cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, so they proceed essentially irreversibly in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

Atom imbalance: as written, the carbon/oxygen skeleton of Luteolin does not match that of Kaempferol, so the reaction is not balanced.
rxn04463.other_comments: This is a flavonol 3-O-glucosyltransferase reaction transferring glucose from UDP-glucose to the 3-OH of a flavonol, releasing UDP and a proton. The correct sugar acceptor for kaempferol 3-O-glucoside is Kaempferol, not Luteolin.

rxn00457.other_comments: This represents a racemase reaction interconverting L-methionine and D-methionine. The stoichiometry is balanced (1:1), as racemization simply inverts the stereochemistry at the alpha carbon without changing molecular formula. Racemases/epimerases are inherently reversible reactions that approach an equilibrium near a 1:1 ratio of the two enantiomers. Note that methionine racemase activity is rare and not well characterized in most organisms.

rxn14363.other_comments: This reaction describes the NAD+-dependent oxidation of menth-8-ene-1,2-diol (a vicinal diol) to a hydroxy-ketone (1-hydroxymenth-8-en-2-one). One of the secondary hydroxyl groups is oxidized to a ketone. The stoichiometry is balanced: NAD+ + diol yields NADH + H+ + ketone, which is correct for a two-electron, two-proton (one H- transferred to NAD+, one H+ released) alcohol-to-ketone oxidation. NAD is written as NAD which I interpret as NAD+.

rxn07960.other_comments: This reaction represents the acylation of a 2-acyl-glycerophosphoglycerol (1-position) using dodecanoate (lauric acid, ddca = C12:0) to form a diacyl phosphatidylglycerol (didodecanoyl-PG). The mechanism is an ATP-dependent fatty acid activation/transfer, consistent with acyl-AMP intermediate formation: ATP + fatty acid -> acyl-AMP + PPi, then acyl transfer to the lysophospholipid releasing AMP. Stoichiometry of ATP -> AMP + PPi (two-bond cleavage) plus release of one proton is consistent. Carbon balance: a C12 acyl group is added to a monoacyl-PG bearing one C12 chain to give a diacyl-PG with two C12 chains, which is correct.

The balanced reaction is Undecaprenyl-phosphate + UDP-Fuc2NAc -> Fuc2NAc-PP-undecaprenyl + UMP, which as written is actually balanced. No stoichiometric error if the diphosphate bridge is accounted for.
rxn13833.other_comments: This is a phospho-sugar transferase (e.g., WecA/WbpL-type) reaction transferring FucNAc-1-phosphate from UDP-Fuc2NAc onto undecaprenyl phosphate to form the lipid-linked diphosphate intermediate, releasing UMP. The reaction is essentially balanced as written (one P from the UDP-sugar ends up in the PP bridge, the rest leaves as UMP). It is strongly driven forward in vivo toward lipid-linked saccharide synthesis.

rxn07225.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction catalyzed by diamine:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase (omega-amino acid--pyruvate or similar aminotransferase family). An alpha,omega-diamine donates an amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and the corresponding omega-aminoaldehyde. The stoichiometry is balanced (1:1:1:1) since the amino group transferred from the diamine converts 2-oxoglutarate to L-glutamate while the diamine loses one amine to become an aminoaldehyde. Aminotransferase reactions are generally freely reversible.

rxn10763.other_comments: This represents an acyltransferase reaction in Mycobacterium tuberculosis phosphatidylinositol mannoside (PIM) biosynthesis. The reaction transfers a palmitoyl group from palmitoyl-CoA to a mono-acylated dimannosyl-PIM (Ac1PIM2), producing the di-acylated form (Ac2PIM2) and releasing free CoA. This is catalyzed by acyltransferases such as PatA/Rv2611c. Stoichiometry is balanced at the level of acyl group transfer: one acyl group moves from CoA to the PIM acceptor, with CoA released. Note that exact atom balance cannot be fully verified without explicit molecular formulas, but the acyl-transfer logic is consistent. Acyltransferase reactions consuming acyl-CoA thioesters are strongly exergonic due to thioester bond hydrolysis and are physiologically unidirectional toward the acylated product.

rxn13706.other_comments: This is the fumarate reductase direction of the succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase enzyme. Fumarate is reduced to succinate using reduced menaquinol-7 (mql7) as the electron donor, regenerating oxidized menaquinone-7. The reaction is balanced: fumarate (C4H2O4) + menaquinol (reduced, +2H) yields succinate (C4H4O4) + menaquinone (oxidized). Note the enzyme name mentions a proton, which is consistent with the redox chemistry of the menaquinone/menaquinol couple. In organisms using fumarate as a terminal electron acceptor (anaerobic respiration), the reaction proceeds in the written direction (fumarate reduction). The same enzyme complex can run in reverse (succinate oxidation) under aerobic/quinone-pool conditions, making it physiologically reversible depending on the redox poise.

errors: Oxygen atom balance issue: a monooxygenase incorporates one atom of O2 into the substrate (forming the hydroxyl of hydroquinone) and reduces the other to water. For 2,3,5,6-tetrachlorophenol -> tetrachlorohydroquinone, one ring H is replaced by OH. Balance check: C6HCl4OH (phenol C6H2Cl4O) + O -> tetrachlorohydroquinone C6H2Cl4O2. The substrate already has the proper H count; adding one OH and removing one ring H gives correct product. Reaction as written is essentially balanced for a hydroxylase using NADPH and O2.
rxn04972.other_comments: This is a flavin/NADPH-dependent monooxygenase (hydroxylase) converting tetrachlorophenol to tetrachlorohydroquinone, consuming NADPH and O2. Such oxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (driven forward by O2 consumption and NADPH oxidation).

rxn00551.other_comments: This is pyrophosphate-dependent phosphofructokinase (PFP, EC 2.7.1.90), which catalyzes the reversible transfer of a phosphate from PPi to fructose-6-phosphate, forming fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and inorganic phosphate plus a proton. The reaction is balanced for mass and charge: PPi provides the phosphoryl group, and the products account for Pi, H+, and FBP. Unlike ATP-dependent PFK (EC 2.7.1.11), this enzyme is freely reversible because the PPi/Pi couple has a small free energy change, allowing it to function in both glycolytic and gluconeogenic directions depending on metabolic conditions.

errors: Reaction as written is incomplete/unbalanced; the conversion of strictosidine aglucone to the dialdehyde (or related rearranged intermediate) requires explicit accounting of atoms, but only generic compound names ('Strictosidine aglycone' and 'Dialdehyde') are given with no molecular formulas, making stoichiometric verification impossible
The term 'Dialdehyde' is ambiguous and does not specify a defined chemical structure
rxn04076.other_comments: This reaction refers to a step in monoterpenoid indole alkaloid biosynthesis where strictosidine aglucone (formed after deglucosylation of strictosidine) spontaneously rearranges into a reactive dialdehyde intermediate, which feeds into downstream alkaloid pathways (e.g., cathenamine, ajmalicine, vindoline). The transformation is largely a non-enzymatic tautomerization/rearrangement of the unstable aglucone. Without explicit molecular formulas, stoichiometric balance cannot be confirmed.

rxn02083.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent N-methyltransferase reaction transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to the primary amine of serotonin, producing N-methylserotonin and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). The stoichiometry is balanced: SAM donates a methyl (CH3) to serotonin's amine; the proton released balances charge/mass. Methyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable in the methyl-transfer direction due to SAM's high group-transfer potential, so the reaction proceeds toward N-methylserotonin in vivo.

rxn02002.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADP+-dependent oxidation of dTDP-6-deoxy-L-talose at the C4 position, yielding dTDP-4-oxo-L-rhamnose (also known as dTDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-L-mannose) plus NADPH and H+. The atoms balance: removal of two hydrogens (a hydride to NADPH plus a proton) converts the C4 hydroxyl to a keto group. dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-L-mannose and dTDP-4-oxo-L-rhamnose refer to the same compound since rhamnose is 6-deoxy-L-mannose. This is the EC 1.1.1.- type oxidoreductase reaction (dTDP-6-deoxy-L-talose 4-dehydrogenase), which physiologically often runs in the reductive direction (forming the deoxy sugar) but is enzymatically reversible.

errors: Stoichiometry is not mass-balanced as written; the reaction lacks defined coefficients and the atoms of substrates and products do not balance.

Dextrin 6-alpha-D-glucanohydrolase (pullulanase/limit dextrinase, EC 3.2.1.142 / debranching enzymes) hydrolyzes alpha-1,6 glucosidic linkages, not a generic conversion of starch to free D-glucose plus amylose.
D-Glucose as a free product is not the typical product of a debranching endohydrolase acting on alpha-1,6 bonds; it cleaves branch points to release linear chains.
Starch and Amylose are generic polymer entities without specified degree of polymerization, making the equation impossible to balance properly.
rxn06094.other_comments: The reaction is annotated as a 6-alpha-D-glucanohydrolase, implying hydrolysis of alpha-1,6 branch linkages in starch/glycogen/dextrins. As a hydrolase, it operates essentially irreversibly in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo. However, the substrate/product set shown (water + starch giving free glucose + amylose) is chemically inconsistent with the named activity and is not balanced.

rxn06649.other_comments: This is an N-terminal acetyltransferase (RimI-type) reaction transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the alpha-amino group of the N-terminal alanine of a ribosomal protein. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: acetyl-CoA donates the acetyl group, producing CoA, an H+ (released from the amino group upon acetylation), and the N-acetylated protein. In vivo, protein N-terminal acetylation is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the forward direction due to the thioester bond energy of acetyl-CoA.

errors: Charge and proton balance appears incorrect: reduction of sulfite (SO3^2-) to H2S (sulfide) is a 6-electron reduction, but 3 menaquinol provide only 6 electrons via 3 quinol oxidations which is consistent for electrons; however the proton balance is not shown - the reaction as written does not balance H/charge. Sulfite + 6 H+ + 6 e- -> H2S + 3 H2O, so additional protons are required on the substrate side that are not accounted for.
Inconsistent spelling: 'methymenaquinol 7' should be 'methylmenaquinol 7'.

Quinol/quinone hydrogen accounting: each methylmenaquinol carries 2 H, so 3 quinol -> 3 quinone releases 6 H, but explicit proton balance is still not shown and oxygen/water balance should be rechecked.
rxn13746.other_comments: This is a sulfite reductase reaction using methylmenaquinol as the electron donor to reduce sulfite to hydrogen sulfide, producing water and oxidized methylmenaquinone. The 6-electron reduction of sulfite to sulfide is consistent with oxidation of 3 quinol molecules. In vivo this dissimilatory/assimilatory-type sulfite reduction proceeds in the reductive (forward) direction.

rxn01417.other_comments: This reaction describes the NAD-dependent interconversion of 2-oxoadipate (2-oxoadipate) and 2-hydroxyadipate. The reaction as written shows reduction: NADH + H+ + 2-oxoadipate -> NAD+ + 2-hydroxyadipate. The enzyme name (2-hydroxyadipate:NAD+ 2-oxidoreductase) formally defines the oxidation direction (2-hydroxyadipate + NAD+ -> 2-oxoadipate + NADH). Stoichiometry is balanced: the carbonyl is reduced to a hydroxyl group with transfer of a hydride from NADH plus a proton. Atoms and charges balance. NAD is written without explicit charge but represents NAD+.

rxn13368.other_comments: This is the alcohol acetyltransferase reaction (e.g., yeast ATF1/ATF2) transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to isoamyl alcohol (3-methyl-1-butanol) to produce isoamyl acetate and free CoA. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: acetyl-CoA (C-O-S thioester) transfers the C2 acetyl moiety to the alcohol hydroxyl, releasing CoA-SH. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn04683.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of phosphoethanolamine (O-phosphoethanolamine) by a phosphohydrolase (e.g., phosphoethanolamine/phosphocholine phosphatase, PHOSPHO1). Water cleaves the phosphate ester bond yielding inorganic phosphate and ethanolamine (aminoethanol). The stoichiometry is balanced: phosphoethanolamine (C2H8NO4P) + H2O yields ethanolamine (C2H7NO) + phosphate (H3PO4/HPO4). Phosphohydrolase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and physiologically run in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn04602.other_comments: This is a flavin-dependent monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction. 3-Coumaric acid (m-coumarate, (2E)-3-(3-hydroxyphenyl)prop-2-enoate) is hydroxylated at the 2-position to yield 2,3-dihydroxycinnamic acid. One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the product, the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADH. The reaction is balanced: NADH + O2 + H+ provide reducing equivalents and oxygen; products are H2O, NAD+, and the dihydroxylated aromatic acid. Atom and charge balance are consistent (NADH + H+ -> NAD+ + 2[H]; O2 + substrate-H + 2[H] -> product-OH + H2O).

errors: Carbon/atom balance cannot be verified because 'phthiocerol precursor bound ACP' is an undefined generic product, making rigorous mass balance impossible

rxn10723.other_comments: This represents an iterative/modular polyketide synthase (PKS) elongation starting from eicosanoyl-ACP (C20) extended by 2 malonyl-CoA and 2 methylmalonyl-CoA units, with NADPH-dependent reductions, releasing CoA and CO2 to build a phthiocerol precursor (relevant to mycobacterial PDIM/phthiocerol biosynthesis). Each chain extension via Claisen condensation should release one CO2 per extender unit (expected 4 CO2 for 4 extensions), so the listed 2 CO2 looks stoichiometrically inconsistent.

rxn00355.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by UTP:galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (UDP-galactose pyrophosphorylase, EC 2.7.7.10). UTP reacts with alpha-D-galactose 1-phosphate to form UDP-galactose and inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi). The reaction is balanced: UTP (uridine triphosphate) transfers a UMP moiety to galactose-1-phosphate, releasing PPi. Atoms and charges balance correctly. Like most nucleotidyltransferase reactions, it is thermodynamically reversible, though in vivo the hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase typically drives it toward UDP-galactose synthesis.

rxn04873.other_comments: This represents glutathione S-transferase-mediated conjugation of bromobenzene-2,3-oxide (a reactive epoxide metabolite of bromobenzene) with glutathione, opening the epoxide to give a 2-S-glutathionyl-3-hydroxy dihydro adduct. The reaction name labels it as an epoxide-forming lyase, but the forward biological direction is conjugation (epoxide consumption), a detoxification step that is effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written does not match the enzyme name; the name describes a full fatty acid synthase elongation cycle (condensation with malonyl-CoA, decarboxylation, reduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction), but the written reaction is only an enoyl-ACP reductase reverse step (oxidation of dodecanoyl-ACP to 2-trans-dodecenoyl-ACP)
Charge/proton imbalance: oxidation of a saturated acyl-ACP to a 2-enoyl-ACP removes 2 [H], which should be NADP+ + dodecanoyl-ACP <=> NADPH + H+ + (2E)-dodecenoyl-ACP, not 2 H+
Missing all substrates/products implied by the enzyme name (malonyl-CoA, CoA, CO2, H2O)
rxn05355.other_comments: The written reaction is the enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI) reaction running in the oxidative (reverse) direction: dodecanoyl-ACP being dehydrogenated to trans-2-dodecenoyl-ACP using NADP+. In vivo, fatty acid synthesis runs in the opposite direction (enoyl-ACP + NADPH -> acyl-ACP). The enzyme name supplied corresponds to a multi-step FAS elongation, which is inconsistent with the simple single-step reaction written.

rxn03868.other_comments: This is a CoA-transferase reaction (succinyl-CoA:(R)-benzylsuccinate CoA-transferase, EC 2.8.3.15) involved in anaerobic toluene degradation. CoA is transferred from succinyl-CoA to benzylsuccinate (the product of toluene addition to fumarate), yielding succinate and benzylsuccinyl-CoA. The atoms balance: a single CoA moiety is exchanged between the two acid groups, so C, H, N, O, P, S are all conserved. In vivo, this reaction proceeds in the direction of benzylsuccinyl-CoA formation as part of the catabolic toluene/benzylsuccinate degradation pathway, regenerating succinate for the TCA cycle.

rxn03286.other_comments: This is a hydro-lyase (hydratase) reaction in bile acid synthesis. Water is added across the C24-C25 double bond of 3alpha,7alpha-dihydroxy-5beta-cholest-24-enoyl-CoA to form the 24-hydroxy product. The reaction as written shows hydration (H2O + enoyl-CoA <=> hydroxy-CoA), which is the reverse of the named hydro-lyase direction (which would form the enoyl-CoA). Atoms balance: addition of one water accounts for the gain of two H and one O converting the C24 double bond to a C24-hydroxyl. This step is catalyzed by D-bifunctional protein (HSD17B4) hydratase domain. Such enoyl-CoA hydratase reactions are generally reversible in vitro, though metabolic flux in bile acid beta-oxidation favors hydration toward the 24-hydroxy intermediate.

errors: Stereochemistry mismatch: the enzyme name specifies ent-copalyl diphosphate as substrate and ent-sandaracopimara-8(14),15-diene as product, but the reaction lists generic 'Copalyl diphosphate' and '(+)-Sandaracopimaradiene', which is the opposite enantiomer convention; substrate and product stereochemistry should be consistent (ent-CPP -> ent-product)
rxn04174.other_comments: This is a class I diterpene synthase reaction: a copalyl diphosphate undergoes ionization-dependent cyclization with loss of diphosphate to form a tetracyclic/tricyclic diterpene (sandaracopimaradiene). Stoichiometry is balanced (one substrate yields one diphosphate, one proton, and the cyclized hydrocarbon). The H+ accounts for the deprotonation terminating the carbocation. Diphosphate-lyase cyclizations are essentially irreversible in vivo due to loss of PPi.

rxn02900.other_comments: This is the (2-aminoethyl)phosphonate:pyruvate aminotransferase reaction (EC 2.6.1.37). Ciliatine is 2-aminoethylphosphonate (AEP). The transamination transfers the amino group from AEP to pyruvate, yielding L-alanine and phosphonoacetaldehyde. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charges (one amino group transferred, one keto/oxo group exchanged). As a PLP-dependent aminotransferase, it is reversible; however, in vivo it typically operates in the direction of phosphonoacetaldehyde formation to feed into the phosphonatase degradation pathway, where the irreversible downstream phosphonatase step pulls flux forward.

errors: The reaction as written is unbalanced in terms of oxygen and hydrogen if interpreted as a simple oxidoreduction; the azoxy product (4-(dimethylamino)phenylazoxybenzene) contains an additional oxygen relative to the azo substrate (Methyl yellow, an azobenzene derivative), so the conversion of azo to azoxy requires incorporation of an oxygen atom. The written direction (NADP + H2O consumed to make NADPH) represents an oxidation of the azo compound but the cofactor stoichiometry is inverted - NADPH-dependent enzymes typically oxidize substrate using NADPH as reductant, here NADPH is shown as a product.
rxn02995.other_comments: The reaction describes interconversion between Methyl yellow (4-(dimethylamino)azobenzene, an azo compound) and its azoxy derivative. The enzyme name 'NADPH:...oxidoreductase' indicates NADPH is the electron donor, so the physiological direction should consume NADPH (NADPH + H+ + azoxy compound -> NADP + H2O + azo compound), i.e., the reductive cleavage/reduction of the azoxy group. As written (left-to-right) it shows the reverse (oxidation) direction.

rxn00455.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of N-formyl-L-methionine by N-formylmethionine deformylase/amidohydrolase, cleaving the formyl group to yield formate and L-methionine. The stoichiometry is balanced: N-Formyl-L-methionine (C6H11NO3S) + H2O (H2O) yields Formate (CH2O2, i.e., HCOO- + H) + L-Methionine (C5H11NO2S). Atoms balance for C, H, N, O, and S. As a hydrolysis of an amide/formamide bond, the reaction is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the deformylation direction in vivo.

rxn00513.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of ITP (inosine triphosphate) to IDP (inosine diphosphate) plus inorganic phosphate, catalyzed by an ITP phosphohydrolase (e.g., ITPA/NTP pyrophosphatase-type activity, though true ITPA typically yields IMP + PPi). The reaction as written is mass and charge balanced: H2O + ITP yields Pi + H+ + IDP. ITP (charge -4) + H2O gives IDP (-3) + phosphate (HPO4 2-) + H+, which balances atoms and charge.

errors: Incorrect product: fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (EC 3.1.3.11) hydrolyzes the 1-phosphate to yield D-fructose-6-phosphate, not D-fructose-1-phosphate. The phosphate at position 1 is removed, leaving the 6-phosphate.

The product as written (D-fructose-1-phosphate) implies removal of the 6-phosphate, which is not the reaction catalyzed by this enzyme name (D-fructose 1,6-bisphosphate phosphohydrolase typically cleaves the C1 phosphate).
rxn01491.other_comments: This is intended to be the fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase reaction (FBPase), a key gluconeogenic enzyme. The correct reaction is: H2O + D-fructose-1,6-bisphosphate -> phosphate + D-fructose-6-phosphate. As written the product is wrong; it should be fructose-6-phosphate. The hydrolysis is essentially irreversible (highly exergonic) and proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn02841.other_comments: This reaction represents pyranose oxidase (EC 1.1.3.10) acting on 2-dehydro-D-glucose. Wait, more precisely: pyranose oxidase oxidizes D-glucose at C2 to form 2-dehydro-D-glucose (glucosone). The reaction as written shows O2 + 2-dehydro-D-glucose forming H2O2 + 2-dehydro-D-glucono-1,5-lactone, which corresponds to oxidation at C1 of the 2-keto sugar. The substrate-product pairs (O2/H2O2 and aldose/lactone) are balanced for atoms: each side has consistent C, H, and O counts since the oxidation removes 2 H from the sugar (forming a lactone) and reduces O2 to H2O2. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced.

rxn00216.other_comments: This is the hexokinase/glucokinase reaction (EC 2.7.1.1/2.7.1.2). ATP phosphorylates D-glucose at the 6-position, producing D-glucose-6-phosphate and ADP, releasing a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (C10H12N5O13P3, charge -4) + glucose (C6H12O6, neutral) -> ADP (charge -3) + G6P (C6H11O9P, charge -2) + H+. Atoms balance and charges balance (-4 = -3 + -2 + 1 = -4). [directionality_note] Although written as reversible, in vivo the large negative free energy of ATP-dependent phosphorylation drives this strongly in the forward direction (glucose -> G6P).

rxn03471.other_comments: This is R05122, a step in the biosynthesis of a modified pterin (related to the methanopterin/H4MPT biosynthetic pathway). Two SAM molecules act as methyl donors, producing two SAH and two H+, with release of water during cyclization to form the 7-methyl-7,8-dihydrobiopterin-type product. SAM-dependent methylations are strongly forward in vivo.

errors: The product 'Serine phosphoethanolamine' is not a standard recognized metabolite for this reaction; the enzyme transfers a phosphoethanolamine group, but the canonical acceptor is typically a lipid (diacylglycerol) yielding phosphatidylethanolamine, not free L-serine

rxn01865.other_comments: The reaction depicts a phosphotransferase transferring a phosphoethanolamine moiety from CDP-ethanolamine to the hydroxyl of L-serine, releasing CMP and a proton. Atom balance (C, N, O, P) appears consistent if 'Serine phosphoethanolamine' = O-phosphoethanolamine-serine. CDP-dependent transfer reactions are strongly exergonic due to CMP release and are essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Reaction is unbalanced as written; zymosterol has one more double bond than zymostenol, so reduction would consume NADPH and produce NADP, not the reverse

Zymosterol has a delta-24 double bond while zymostenol (5-alpha-cholest-8-en-3-beta-ol) is the saturated counterpart. In vivo, the relevant sterol reductase (e.g., DHCR24/sterol delta-24 reductase) reduces the double bond using NADPH, converting zymosterol to zymostenol. Thus the physiological direction with NADPH consumption is zymosterol -> zymostenol, opposite to how this equation is written.

rxn07806.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADPH-dependent reduction of a hydroxylamino group to an amino group in the degradation pathway of 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT). 2,4-Dihydroxylamino-6-nitrotoluene is reduced, with one hydroxylamino group converted to an amino group, producing 4-Amino-2-hydroxylamino-6-nitrotoluene. The stoichiometry balances: the reduction of -NHOH to -NH2 consumes NADPH + H+ and releases water, which is consistent. Atom and charge balance are consistent with a 2-electron reduction.

errors: The reaction as written appears unbalanced without explicit molecular formulas; 2-inosose (2,4,6/3,5-pentahydroxycyclohexanone, C6H10O6) losing one H2O would yield a product of formula C6H8O5, which should be verified against DKDI

rxn02007.other_comments: This is a hydro-lyase (dehydratase) reaction in the myo-inositol catabolic pathway. 2-Inosose (scyllo-inosose / 2-keto-myo-inositol) undergoes dehydration catalyzed by inosose dehydratase to remove water and form a downstream intermediate (commonly 2-deoxy-5-keto-D-gluconic acid via ring opening, sometimes abbreviated in models). Hydro-lyases typically catalyze elimination of water in the forward (dehydration) direction in vivo.

rxn07482.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing 3-hydroxybenzaldehyde to 3-hydroxybenzoate, coupled to reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (CHO) is oxidized to a carboxylate (COOH) using water as the oxygen source, releasing 2 electrons and 2 protons; one H- (as hydride) goes to NAD+ forming NADH, and 2 H+ are released. Mass and charge balance check out (aldehyde + H2O -> acid releases 2 [H], giving NADH + H+ net, with the extra H+ from the carboxylic acid/water).

rxn05395.other_comments: This is an enoyl-ACP reductase step in fatty acid biosynthesis (branched-chain, iso/anteiso type). NADPH reduces the trans-2 double bond of the 9-methyl-dec-2-enoyl-ACP to yield the saturated 9-methyl-decanoyl-ACP. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + H+ donate a hydride and proton to reduce the C2-C3 double bond, regenerating NADP+. The reaction is correctly written.

rxn11961.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of glycerol 1,2-cyclic phosphate by addition of water, opening the cyclic phosphate ring to yield a glycerophosphate (sn-glycerol 1-phosphate / DL-glyceryl 1-phosphate) and releasing a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the cyclic phosphate has one phosphate, and water addition opens the ring. Charge balance is consistent with release of H+ as the phosphate group is protonated/ionized. This is a phosphodiesterase/cyclic phosphate hydrolase type reaction.

rxn09522.other_comments: This is the second half-reaction of succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II), where the FADH2 generated from succinate oxidation transfers electrons to ubiquinone-6, regenerating FAD and producing ubiquinol-6. The reaction is balanced: FADH2 (carries 2H, 2e-) reduces ubiquinone to ubiquinol while FADH2 is oxidized back to FAD. Hydrogen/electron balance is consistent. In vivo this proceeds in the forward direction (FADH2 oxidation coupled to quinone reduction), as part of the electron transport chain and TCA cycle flux.

rxn06728.other_comments: This is a sialyltransferase reaction (ST8Sia family, EC 2.4.99.8) transferring N-acetylneuraminate from the CMP-sialic acid donor onto the terminal sialic acid of an alpha-2,3-sialylated galactoside acceptor, forming an alpha-2,8 linkage and producing CMP and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the sialyl group transferred from CMP-Neu5Ac to the acceptor accounts for the mass and the released CMP plus H+.

rxn01319.other_comments: This is the O-acetyltransferase reaction transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the 7-O position of N-acetylneuraminate (Neu5Ac), producing CoA and N-acetyl-7-O-acetylneuraminate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: acetyl-CoA donates an acetyl group, leaving free CoA, while Neu5Ac gains an acetyl group. Atom and charge balance are consistent. Acetyl-CoA-dependent acetyltransferases are thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy thioester bond, driving the reaction in the acetylation (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn14324.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction transferring an L-mycarose sugar from the activated donor dTDP-beta-L-mycarose onto the 4'-OH of demethyllactenocin (the acceptor), producing demethylmacrocin and releasing dTDP. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: the mycarosyl group is transferred from dTDP to the acceptor hydroxyl. Glycosyltransferases using NDP-sugar donors are strongly thermodynamically driven toward glycoside formation in vivo due to the favorable hydrolysis of the sugar-nucleotide bond.

rxn12739.other_comments: This is the dimethylglycine dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.5.8.4 / 1.5.99.2), which oxidatively demethylates N,N-dimethylglycine to sarcosine. The stoichiometry is balanced: dimethylglycine (C4H9NO2) + H2O + FAD yields formaldehyde (CH2O) + sarcosine (C3H7NO2) + FADH2. Note that in vivo the electron acceptor for this flavoenzyme is typically the electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF) rather than free FAD/FADH2 (the FAD is enzyme-bound covalently), and tetrahydrofolate often captures the C1 unit instead of releasing free formaldehyde. The reaction proceeds in the catabolic (demethylation) direction physiologically.

rxn02310.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in the vindoline/terpenoid indole alkaloid biosynthetic pathway. SAM donates a methyl group to the 11-hydroxyl of 11-O-demethyl-17-O-deacetylvindoline, producing deacetylvindoline (the 11-O-methylated product) plus S-adenosyl-homocysteine and a proton. The atom balance is consistent: one methyl group transferred from SAM to the substrate, generating SAH, and the released proton balances charge.
