rxn04501.other_comments: This appears to be a glycosyltransferase reaction in which a rhodinose sugar is transferred from the dTDP-activated donor (dTDP-beta-L-rhodinose) onto the aglycone acceptor (aquayamycin), releasing dTDP. This is part of angucycline/aquayamycin-type antibiotic biosynthesis. Such NDP-sugar glycosyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward the glycosylated product plus dTDP. The acceptor 'aquayamycin' and product '100-2' suggest formation of a rhodinosylated aquayamycin derivative.

rxn02463.other_comments: This reaction describes the NADH- and O2-dependent dihydroxylation of kynurenate to 7,8-dihydro-7,8-dihydroxykynurenate, consistent with a kynurenate 7,8-dioxygenase/dihydrodiol-forming dioxygenase reaction (as in bacterial kynurenate degradation). Stoichiometry is balanced: one NADH provides reducing equivalents, O2 supplies both hydroxyl oxygens, and NAD+ is released. Atom and charge balance check out (NADH + O2 + H+ + kynurenate yields NAD+ + the cis-dihydrodiol).

errors: Pyridoxine (pyridoxol) to pyridoxal is an oxidation of a primary alcohol (4-hydroxymethyl group) to an aldehyde, not a deamination; the enzyme name 'deaminating' is incorrect for this substrate

The reaction as written is missing the proper H accounting (pyridoxol C8H11NO3 + O2 -> pyridoxal C8H9NO3 + H2O2 actually balances for C/N/O but should be checked: left H = 11, right H = 9 + 2 = 11, so H balances)
On recheck the atom balance (C8H11NO3 + O2 = C8H9NO3 + H2O2) is balanced; the main error is the misleading enzyme name (deaminating)
rxn01252.other_comments: This represents an oxidase reaction converting pyridoxine (pyridoxol) to pyridoxal using molecular oxygen and producing hydrogen peroxide. The atoms actually balance (C8H11NO3 + O2 -> C8H9NO3 + H2O2). The reaction is essentially the alcohol-to-aldehyde oxidation catalyzed by pyridoxine 4-oxidase; the substrate has no amine to deaminate, so the EC name 'deaminating' is a misnomer.

rxn06531.other_comments: This is the cap 1 methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.57), transferring a methyl group from SAM to the 2'-O position of the first transcribed nucleotide (a purine) of the m7G-capped mRNA, producing SAH and a 2'-O-methylated cap. The stoichiometry is balanced: one methyl group transferred from SAM yields SAH, a proton, and the methylated RNA product. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are thermodynamically driven and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn10605.other_comments: This represents the diffusion/transport of elemental sulfur (S) across a boundary, with identical species on both sides. Such transport reactions are stoichiometrically balanced by definition (S = S) and are typically modeled as reversible since diffusion can occur in either direction depending on concentration gradients. If intended to represent compartmental transport, the two S species would normally carry different compartment labels (e.g., S[e] <=> S[c]); as written without compartment distinction, the reaction is trivial.

errors: The product name 'Desmethyldescarbamoylnovobiocin' is not the correct product; transfer of the noviosyl sugar moiety to novobiocic acid yields descarbamoyl-demethyl-novobiocin (the glycosylated product). The naming here is somewhat nonstandard but refers to the glycoside.
Stoichiometry of dTDP-sugar to dTDP is balanced for a glycosyltransfer (sugar moiety transferred, dTDP released), so this aspect is correct.
rxn04586.other_comments: This is the NovM-catalyzed glycosyltransferase reaction in novobiocin biosynthesis, transferring the L-noviose-derived sugar (dTDP-5-dimethyl-L-lyxose, i.e., dTDP-noviose) onto novobiocic acid to form the noviosylated aglycone, releasing dTDP. The transfer of the sugar from the dTDP-activated donor to the aglycone acceptor proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn00170.other_comments: This is the acetyl-CoA hydrolase reaction (EC 3.1.2.1), hydrolyzing the thioester bond of acetyl-CoA to yield CoA and acetate. The reaction is stoichiometrically and charge-balanced: H2O + Acetyl-CoA gives CoA + Acetate + H+ (the proton balances the charge from cleavage of the thioester releasing the carboxylate). Thioester hydrolysis is highly exergonic (large negative delta G, ~-31 kJ/mol), so it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn07880.other_comments: This is a thiolase (C-acyltransferase) reaction in the beta-oxidation direction. The 3-oxoacyl-CoA (7-methyl-3-oxo-6-octenoyl-CoA, a C9 beta-ketoacyl-CoA) is cleaved by CoA to release acetyl-CoA and a shortened acyl-CoA (5-methylhex-4-enoyl-CoA, C7). Carbon balance: the C9 oxo-acyl chain (9C) minus acetyl (2C) gives the 7C product, consistent. CoA is added and one acetyl-CoA is released, stoichiometry is correct. Thiolytic cleavage of beta-ketoacyl-CoA is strongly favored thermodynamically in the cleavage (forward, as written) direction during beta-oxidation.

rxn07173.other_comments: This reaction represents glycerol-3-phosphate 2-O-acyltransferase activity, transferring an acyl group from acyl-CoA to the sn-2 position of glycerol-3-phosphate, yielding 2-acyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate and free CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced (one acyl group transferred, one CoA released). Note that the more common physiological reaction is acylation at the sn-1 position (GPAT, EC 2.3.1.15); 2-acylation is less typical but enzymatically valid. Acyltransferases of this type are thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic direction due to the high-energy thioester bond of acyl-CoA.

errors: N-Acetyl-D-chondrosamine is a synonym for N-acetyl-D-galactosamine; the product should be named consistently as N-acetyl-D-galactosamine (the dephosphorylated sugar), though this is a naming/synonym issue rather than a true stoichiometric error
Charge/mass balance should be verified: phosphate ester hydrolysis yields inorganic phosphate and the free sugar; protonation states (HPO4^2- vs H2PO4^-) should be specified for proper balancing
rxn08035.other_comments: This is a phosphatase reaction hydrolyzing the phosphate ester bond of N-acetyl-D-galactosamine 1-phosphate to release inorganic phosphate and free N-acetyl-D-galactosamine (chondrosamine is an old synonym for galactosamine). Phosphate ester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn02459.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent oxidation of 3-(3,5-diiodo-4-hydroxyphenyl)lactate (a 2-hydroxy acid) to the corresponding 2-oxo acid (3,5-diiodo-4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate). The conversion of the secondary alcohol/hydroxy group to a keto group is a 2-electron oxidation, consistent with reduction of one NAD+ to NADH plus one H+. Atoms and charges balance: the substrate loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+, one as H+). This is a typical 2-hydroxyacid dehydrogenase / aromatic lactate dehydrogenase type reaction. Such NAD-dependent dehydrogenases are generally reversible, with directionality dependent on the NADH/NAD+ ratio and substrate concentrations.

rxn04726.other_comments: This is an alcohol dehydrogenase-type oxidation: 1-naphthalenemethanol (a primary alcohol) is oxidized to 1-naphthaldehyde, with NAD+ reduced to NADH. The reaction is balanced: the alcohol (CH2OH) loses two hydrogens (as one hydride to NAD+ and one proton) to form the aldehyde (CHO). Atom and charge balance are correct. NAD-dependent alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenases are generally reversible thermodynamically, though in vivo the direction depends on NAD+/NADH ratio and downstream metabolism.

rxn00550.other_comments: This is the fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase reaction (the FBPase-2 activity of the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme). It hydrolyzes the 2-phosphate group of fructose 2,6-bisphosphate using water, yielding fructose 6-phosphate and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: H2O + C6H11O12P2 (Fru-2,6-P2) -> Pi (HPO4) + C6H11O9P (Fru-6-P). Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn03345.other_comments: This is the amine oxidase (copper-containing) reaction acting on L-normetanephrine. The deamination consumes one water and one O2, releasing ammonia, hydrogen peroxide, and the corresponding aldehyde (3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenylglycolaldehyde). Atom and charge balance: substrate amine carbon becomes aldehyde, the amino group leaves as NH3, and O2 is reduced to H2O2 using water/the amine hydrogen. The stoichiometry is balanced.

rxn07841.other_comments: This is the adenylate isopentenyltransferase (IPT) reaction in cytokinin biosynthesis, transferring the dimethylallyl (prenyl) group from DMAPP (dimethylallyl diphosphate) to the N6 position of the adenine moiety of ATP, producing N6-(dimethylallyl)-ATP (isopentenyl-ATP) and releasing pyrophosphate. The stoichiometry is mass and charge balanced: ATP + DMAPP yields the prenylated ATP plus PPi and a proton. Despite the EC name referencing 2-isopentenyl-diphosphate, the actual donor in this enzyme is DMAPP. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven forward by PPi release/hydrolysis, and is the committed/rate-limiting step of cytokinin biosynthesis.

rxn03127.other_comments: This is the methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR) reaction, the terminal step of methanogenesis. Methyl-CoM (2-(methylthio)ethanesulfonate) reacts with coenzyme B (HTP, N-7-mercaptoheptanoylthreonine phosphate, here described as the thiol form) to yield methane and the heterodisulfide CoM-S-S-CoB. The stoichiometry is balanced (the methyl group becomes methane, and the two thiols of CoM and CoB form the mixed disulfide). In vivo this reaction strongly favors methane formation under methanogenic conditions.

rxn06400.other_comments: This is a fucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.152, related to alpha-1,3-fucosyltransferase activity) transferring an L-fucose residue from the donor GDP-L-fucose to the N-acetylglucosamine moiety of the acceptor glycan (type 2 LacNAc, Gal-beta-1,4-GlcNAc-R), forming the Lewis x (Le-x) type structure with an alpha-1,3 fucosyl linkage and releasing GDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: a single fucosyl group is transferred and GDP is released. Glycosyltransferase reactions using activated nucleotide-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn01859.other_comments: This is the purine nucleoside phosphorylase (deoxyadenosine phosphorylase) reaction: deoxyadenosine + phosphate <=> adenine + 2-deoxy-D-ribose-1-phosphate. The reaction is correctly balanced in atoms (C10H13N5O3 deoxyadenosine + HPO4 phosphate yields C5H5N5 adenine + C5H11O7P deoxyribose-1-phosphate) and charges. Although the equilibrium favors nucleoside synthesis (reverse direction), in vivo the reaction is generally considered reversible, with the physiological direction depending on substrate concentrations and downstream salvage/degradation pathways.

rxn00194.other_comments: This is glutamate decarboxylase (GAD, EC 4.1.1.15), which decarboxylates L-glutamate to form GABA (4-aminobutanoate) and CO2. The reaction consumes a proton along with glutamate to produce GABA plus CO2. Stoichiometry is balanced: glutamate (C5H8NO4-) + H+ yields GABA (C4H9NO2) + CO2. Charge and atoms balance correctly. As a decarboxylation releasing CO2, this reaction is essentially irreversible in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn05055.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of N-benzylformamide (an amide bond) by water, yielding formate and benzylamine. Mass and charge balance check: N-benzylformamide (C8H9NO) + H2O (H2O) -> formate (CHO2-, i.e., formate anion) + benzylamine (C7H9N, which at physiological pH would be protonated benzylammonium, C7H10N+). Atom balance: C8H9NO + H2O = C8H11NO2 on left; right = CHO2 + C7H9N = C8H9NO2, plus the proton/protonation states account for the remaining 2 H. So with formate as the anion and benzylamine protonated, the reaction is balanced. Amidohydrolases catalyzing amide hydrolysis are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo due to the energy released in amide bond cleavage.

rxn03265.other_comments: This reaction represents methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to the selenium atom of selenomethionine, producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) and Se-methylselenomethionine. The stoichiometry is balanced: SAM donates a methyl group to selenomethionine, becoming SAH, while selenomethionine gains the methyl group to form Se-methylselenomethionine. This is analogous to the methionine S-methyltransferase reaction (EC 2.1.1.12) which normally methylates methionine to form S-methylmethionine; here selenomethionine is the selenium analog substrate. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

rxn10887.other_comments: This is annotated as the TagO/TarO reaction initiating wall teichoic acid synthesis. The true reaction is UDP-GlcNAc + undecaprenyl-phosphate -> undecaprenyl-PP-GlcNAc + UMP, a transferase reaction. The equation provided instead depicts hydrolysis releasing free GlcNAc and phosphate, which is not the actual biochemistry and is unbalanced.

The product of an ATP-dependent amide bond formation between a carboxylic acid and an amine is usually accompanied by AMP and diphosphate, releasing one water as well.

If the reaction is taken as written (ATP -> ADP + Pi), the proton balance and the mass balance for amide bond formation (which releases water) are questionable; a water molecule should appear on the product side.
rxn01097.other_comments: The reaction describes amide bond formation between the carboxyl group of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate and the amino group of L-serine to yield 2,3-dihydroxy-N-benzoyl-L-serine, an intermediate in enterobactin/siderophore biosynthesis. ATP hydrolysis drives the condensation. In vivo this biosynthetic ligation proceeds essentially in the forward (synthesis) direction.

Without explicit compartment labels, the reaction conveys no net transformation.

rxn00177.other_comments: This is the citramalyl-CoA lyase reaction (EC 4.1.3.25), part of the citramalate/(S)-citramalyl-CoA pathway and the ethylmalonyl-CoA pathway. (3S)-citramalyl-CoA is cleaved to pyruvate and acetyl-CoA. The reaction is stoichiometrically and atom-balanced: citramalyl-CoA (a C5 dicarboxylic acid thioester linked to CoA) splits into pyruvate (C3) and acetyl-CoA (C2 + CoA). Carbon, charge, and CoA moiety balance. As an aldol-type lyase reaction, it is reversible, though in pathways like the methylaspartate/citramalate cycle it typically runs in the cleavage (forward) direction.

rxn07889.other_comments: This is a benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase type reaction acting on 2-fluorobenzoate. The dihydrodiol dioxygenase incorporates both oxygen atoms from O2 (one into the ring as hydroxyl, the other reduced to the second hydroxyl via NADH), producing the cis-dihydrodiol carboxylate. Stoichiometry balances: NADH provides the reducing equivalents and H+, O2 supplies both oxygen atoms incorporated into the diol product, and NAD+ is released. Atom and charge balance are consistent. Such NAD(P)H/O2-dependent dioxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (forward) due to O2 consumption and the thermodynamics of NADH oxidation.

rxn00380.other_comments: This reaction is ADP sulfurylase (ADP:sulfate adenylyltransferase, EC 2.7.7.5), interconverting ADP + sulfate with phosphate + adenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (APS). The reaction is mass-balanced: ADP provides the AMP moiety that combines with sulfate to form APS, releasing the beta-phosphate as inorganic phosphate. Atom and charge balance are consistent. In vivo, the physiological direction favors APS hydrolysis/phosphorolysis (APS + phosphate -> ADP + sulfate), i.e. the reverse of the written direction, releasing free sulfate. The enzyme is generally considered to operate toward sulfate liberation.

rxn11775.other_comments: This represents D-ribose pyranase (RbsD), which catalyzes the interconversion between the pyranose and furanose forms of D-ribose. The substrate 'Ribose' here refers to beta-D-ribopyranose, and the product is beta-D-ribofuranose. This is an isomerization (ring-form interconversion), so it is mass- and atom-balanced (both are C5H10O5). Such anomerase/mutarotase-type reactions are inherently reversible, though physiologically the enzyme converts pyranose to furanose to feed ribose into ribokinase-mediated phosphorylation. The substrate name 'Ribose' is ambiguous and ideally should be specified as beta-D-ribopyranose.

errors: Reaction is not mass-balanced as written. 4-Coumaroyl-CoA (p-coumaroyl-CoA) is the CoA thioester of 4-hydroxycinnamic acid (C9 acid). Cleavage of the side chain typically yields 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde (C7) plus acetyl-CoA (C2), but this requires both a hydratase and a retro-aldol/lyase step, and the atom balance does not close with a single water. A proper hydratase/aldolase (HCHL-type) mechanism gives 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde + acetyl-CoA, but accounting requires careful tracking: p-coumaroyl-CoA (C18 including CoA portion conceptually) + H2O -> 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde (C7H6O2) + acetyl-CoA. Carbon: coumaroyl moiety C9 = C7 (benzaldehyde) + C2 (acetyl) checks; however hydrogen/oxygen balance should be verified - the published HCHL reaction is 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde + acetyl-CoA with one water consumed, so this is essentially balanced.
rxn12676.other_comments: This is the p-hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA hydratase/lyase (HCHL) reaction. The enzyme first hydrates the enoyl-CoA double bond then performs a retro-aldol (lyase) cleavage to release 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde and acetyl-CoA. Carbon skeleton balances (C9 coumaroyl = C7 aldehyde + C2 acetyl). In vivo it proceeds toward aldehyde formation (degradation/biosynthesis of phenolic aldehydes like vanillin precursors).

rxn04235.other_comments: This is an ADP-forming CoA ligase reaction: perillic acid is activated to perillyl-CoA at the expense of ATP, which is hydrolyzed to ADP + inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + perillic acid yields ADP + Pi + perillyl-CoA (the thioester bond is formed via cleavage of ATP into ADP and Pi). Charge and atom balance are consistent assuming standard protonation states. ADP-forming acyl-CoA ligases (as opposed to AMP-forming ones) typically drive CoA-thioester formation in the forward (activation) direction in vivo.

As written here, the equation is in the reverse orientation. Glycosyltransferase reactions using sugar nucleotides are essentially irreversible in vivo, driven forward toward the glycosylated product.

rxn06576.other_comments: This is an aspartate beta-hydroxylase (EC 1.14.11.16) reaction, a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase. O2 is split: one oxygen atom hydroxylates the peptidyl L-aspartate at C3, and the other is incorporated into the decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate yielding succinate and CO2. Stoichiometry is balanced (O2 + 2OG + Asp-peptide -> CO2 + succinate + 3-hydroxy-Asp-peptide), with both atoms of molecular oxygen accounted for and carbon/charge conserved.

As a hydration/dehydration, it is in principle reversible, but the in vivo direction depends on the metabolic context (carotenoid biosynthesis typically drives toward the hydroxylated product).

rxn02127.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction transferring an amino group between aminomalonate and pyruvate. Aminomalonate (2-aminomalonate, HOOC-CH(NH2)-COOH) donates its amino group, becoming oxomalonate (2-oxomalonate/ketomalonate, HOOC-CO-COOH), while pyruvate (CH3-CO-COOH) accepts it to become L-alanine (CH3-CH(NH2)-COOH). Atom balance: C: 3 (pyruvate) + 3 (aminomalonate) = 3 (alanine) + 3 (oxomalonate), balanced. N: 1 = 1, balanced. The reaction is stoichiometrically correct.

rxn01037.other_comments: This is the hippuricase (aminoacylase/benzoylglycine amidohydrolase, EC 3.5.1.32) reaction. Hippurate (N-benzoylglycine) is hydrolyzed by water to yield glycine and benzoate. The reaction is balanced: hippurate (C9H9NO3) + H2O (H2O) = glycine (C2H5NO2) + benzoate (C7H6O2 / C7H5O2- depending on protonation). Atoms and charges balance correctly. As a hydrolysis reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn07568.other_comments: This is a malonyltransferase reaction transferring a malonyl group from malonyl-CoA to the 6''-hydroxyl of the glucose moiety of trifolirhizin (a pterocarpan glucoside, the glucoside of maackiain). Products are CoA and the 6''-O-malonate derivative. Stoichiometry is balanced: the malonyl group transfers from CoA to the sugar hydroxyl. Acyltransferase reactions using acyl-CoA donors are strongly driven forward by the thioester bond energy.

rxn06721.other_comments: This is the PI3K (phosphoinositide 3-kinase) reaction, transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the 3-position of PI(4,5)P2 to form PI(3,4,5)P3. Stoichiometry is balanced: ATP donates a phosphate, yielding ADP, H+, and the trisphosphate product. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced.

The reaction transfers a methyl group from SAM to a hydroxyl of myo-inositol. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are generally physiologically forward (highly exergonic) due to the high methyl-transfer potential of SAM.

rxn01496.other_comments: This is a transamination reaction transferring an amino group from L-Dopa (3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine) to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding L-glutamate and 3-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)pyruvate (the keto acid corresponding to L-Dopa). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: carbons, nitrogens, and the amino/keto group exchange are all consistent. Aminotransferase (transaminase) reactions are typically reversible in vivo due to small free energy changes.

rxn02947.other_comments: This is the glycosyltransferase step in streptomycin biosynthesis. dTDP-L-dihydrostreptose transfers the dihydrostreptose moiety onto streptidine 6-phosphate, producing O-1,4-alpha-L-dihydrostreptosyl-streptidine 6-phosphate and releasing dTDP. The reaction is balanced: the dihydrostreptosyl group is transferred from the nucleotide-sugar donor to the acceptor, with dTDP as leaving group. Glycosyltransferase reactions using NDP-sugars are strongly exergonic and physiologically drive biosynthesis in the forward direction.

rxn12174.other_comments: This reaction represents UDP-glucose:sinapate glucosyltransferase activity, transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the carboxyl group of sinapate, forming sinapoyl glucose (1-O-sinapoyl-beta-D-glucose / 4-O-beta-D-glucosyl-sinapate) and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose moiety transferred, UDP-glucose -> UDP. Glycosyltransferase reactions using activated UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable and typically proceed in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo. Note: the enzyme name suggests O-glucosylation; sinapoyl glucose is the typical product serving as an activated acyl donor in downstream reactions.

rxn01584.other_comments: This is the 20-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (AKR1C family) reaction. Progesterone (4-pregnene-3,20-dione) is reduced at the C20 ketone to 20alpha-hydroxyprogesterone (20alpha-hydroxy-4-pregnen-3-one), with NADPH+H+ serving as the electron donor and being oxidized to NADP+. The stoichiometry is balanced: a 2-electron reduction of one carbonyl consumes one NADPH and one proton. The enzyme name correctly describes the oxidoreductase acting on the C20 position. Although named as the oxidoreductase, in vivo AKR1C enzymes preferentially catalyze NADPH-dependent ketosteroid reduction, so the forward (reductive) direction predominates physiologically, but the reaction is thermodynamically reversible.

rxn02643.other_comments: This is the fucosterol-epoxide lyase reaction (EC 4.1.2.33), a key step in phytosterol-to-cholesterol conversion in insects. The enzyme cleaves the C24-C28 bond of fucosterol epoxide, releasing acetaldehyde and producing desmosterol. The C/H/O atoms balance: fucosterol epoxide (C29H48O2) yields desmosterol (C27H44O) plus acetaldehyde (C2H4O), which is stoichiometrically consistent. Physiologically this is a lyase committed step driving sterol dealkylation toward cholesterol synthesis.

rxn01703.other_comments: This represents the isomerization of all-trans-retinol to 11-cis-retinol, a key step in the visual cycle catalyzed by RPE65 (the retinoid isomerase) in the retinal pigment epithelium. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as both species are isomers (C20H30O). In vivo, the reaction proceeds in the direction of 11-cis-retinol formation; thermodynamically the trans isomer is more stable, but RPE65 couples ester hydrolysis (all-trans-retinyl ester) to drive isomerization toward the 11-cis product. As written from free retinol, the reaction is endergonic and physiologically driven forward by the coupled system.

rxn05160.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction (monosaccharide-transporting ATPase) coupling ATP hydrolysis to the import of D-Ribose. The D-Ribose appears on both sides because, in a properly annotated transport reaction, the substrate is shown in different cellular compartments (e.g., extracellular/periplasmic on the left, cytoplasmic on the right). The chemical stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + H2O yields ADP + Phosphate + H+, with the sugar translocated rather than chemically modified. In vivo, ATP-driven import is essentially irreversible (forward), driven by ATP hydrolysis.

rxn00039.other_comments: This is the beta-glucogallin O-galloyltransferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.90), where two molecules of beta-glucogallin (1-O-galloyl-beta-D-glucose) react: one serves as galloyl donor and the other as acceptor, producing 1,6-digalloyl-beta-D-glucose and releasing free D-glucose. The stoichiometry is balanced: 2 galloyl-glucose units yield one diglucose-galloyl ester (carrying 2 galloyl groups on one glucose) plus one free glucose. This is a key step in gallotannin biosynthesis and proceeds toward digalloylglucose formation in vivo.

rxn02199.other_comments: This is the chloramphenicol acetyltransferase (CAT) reaction, which transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the 3-hydroxyl of chloramphenicol, producing CoA and chloramphenicol 3-acetate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred from acetyl-CoA to chloramphenicol, conserving atoms and charge. In vivo, this reaction proceeds strongly in the forward (acetylation) direction as a detoxification mechanism conferring antibiotic resistance.

rxn10288.other_comments: This reaction describes a glucosyltransferase transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to 1,2-diacylglycerol (with isohexadecanoyl/branched C16 acyl chains), forming monoglucosyldiacylglycerol and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: UDP-glucose donates glucose to the diacylglycerol hydroxyl, yielding UDP and the monoglucosyl-DAG product. The glycosyl transfer from a UDP-sugar is thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy nucleotide-sugar bond, driving the reaction toward synthesis of the glucolipid in vivo.

rxn11880.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the N9 position of an N6-alkylaminopurine, producing the 9-beta-D-glucoside and releasing UDP. rxn01212.other_comments: This is the dimethylallyltryptophan synthase (DMATS) reaction, the first committed step in ergot alkaloid biosynthesis. L-tryptophan is prenylated at C4 of the indole ring using dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP), releasing pyrophosphate and a proton. The product is 4-dimethylallyl-L-tryptophan (4-DMA-Trp). Atoms balance: the prenyl group (C5H8) transfers from DMAPP to tryptophan, with the diphosphate leaving as PPi and a proton released. Carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and charge are balanced.

rxn05024.other_comments: This is the DHNA-CoA synthase (MenB) reaction in menaquinone biosynthesis. rxn00844.other_comments: This is the soluble/particulate methane monooxygenase (MMO) reaction catalyzing the first step of methane oxidation in methanotrophs. Carbon (1 each side), oxygen (3 on left: 2 from O2 + included in NADPH balance; 1 methanol O + 1 water O on right derived from O2), hydrogen, and charge all balance. rxn03224.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction in ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) biosynthesis, corresponding to UbiG/Coq3 activity. rxn10468.other_comments: This is the hydration of cis-homoaconitate (with two homo extensions, i.e. (homo)2aconitate) to form (-)-threo-iso(homo)2citrate, analogous to the aconitase/homoaconitase reactions in the alpha-aminoadipate/extended carbon-chain pathways. Aconitase-family enzymes catalyze reversible dehydration/hydration, so the reaction is thermodynamically reversible in vivo.

rxn12947.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of PtdIns(3,5)P2 to PtdIns(3)P by removal of the 5-phosphate, catalyzed by a polyphosphoinositide 5-phosphatase (e.g., Sac-domain or related phosphatases such as Fig4/Sac3). rxn02725.other_comments: This reaction represents the NADP+-dependent oxidation of leukotriene B4 (LTB4) at the 12-hydroxyl group to form 12-keto-LTB4 (12-oxo-LTB4), catalyzed by 12-hydroxydehydrogenase/15-oxo-prostaglandin 13-reductase (or a related dehydrogenase). rxn09605.other_comments: This represents fatty acid 2-hydroxylase (FA2H) type chemistry, where a ceramide-bound N-linked C24:0 fatty acyl chain is hydroxylated at the alpha (2') position to form a 2-hydroxy ceramide. The substrate is a C24:0 ceramide and the product is the 2-hydroxylated (2'-OH) C24:0 ceramide.

rxn02604.other_comments: This reaction describes the glucosyltransferase/glycosyltransferase-type condensation of mandelonitrile with the disaccharide vicianose (6-O-alpha-L-arabinopyranosyl-D-glucose) to form the cyanogenic glycoside (R)-vicianin, releasing water. The written stoichiometry is balanced as a formal condensation (loss of one water upon glycosidic bond formation). However, in vivo glycoside biosynthesis is driven by activated sugar donors (e.g., UDP-glucose), not by direct dehydrative condensation with free sugar plus water release; thermodynamically the hydrolytic (reverse, glycoside breakdown) direction is favored in aqueous cellular conditions. As written here with free vicianose and water as a product, the favorable in vivo direction is the reverse (hydrolysis of vicianin).

rxn14130.other_comments: This is the C-S lyase (SUR1/CYP-independent step) in glucosinolate biosynthesis. It cleaves S-(hydroxyphenylacetothiohydroximoyl)-L-cysteine using water to release the thiohydroximate, pyruvate, and ammonia. Mass and charge appear balanced: the cysteine conjugate provides the cysteine moiety that is converted to pyruvate + NH3, releasing the thiohydroximic acid product. The reaction is driven essentially irreversibly in the biosynthetic direction.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the conversion of terephthalate-1,2-cis-dihydrodiol to protocatechuate involves dehydrogenation (aromatization) with loss of a carboxyl group, but the reaction as written does not balance carbon, hydrogen, or charge. The dehydrogenase reaction (rxn01194) named is the NAD+ oxidoreductase converting the cis-dihydrodiol to a dihydroxy aromatic intermediate plus NADH and H+, not directly to protocatechuate with CO2 release.
Missing H+ on the NADH product side (oxidation by NAD+ typically yields NADH + H+).

CO2 release (decarboxylation) is not catalyzed by an NAD+ oxidoreductase as named; the proper product of the dehydrogenase is 1,2-dihydroxy-3,5-cyclohexadiene-1,4-dicarboxylate or the aromatized 2-hydroxy intermediate, with decarboxylation occurring in a separate step.
rxn01194.other_comments: This appears to be from the terephthalate degradation pathway, where terephthalate cis-dihydrodiol is oxidized by an NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase. The enzyme name refers to the (3S,4R)-3,4-dihydroxycyclohexa-1,5-diene-1,4-dicarboxylate:NAD+ oxidoreductase. The written reaction combines dehydrogenation and decarboxylation into one step and is not properly balanced.

rxn10280.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction transferring glucose from UDP-glucose to a diacylglycerol (dipalmitoylglycerol) to form a monoglucosyldiacylglycerol plus UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucosyl unit is transferred, UDP-glucose donates glucose and becomes UDP, and the glucose is added to the diacylglycerol hydroxyl. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are highly exergonic due to cleavage of the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, so the reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn11007.other_comments: This is the FAD-dependent thymidylate synthase (ThyX/TMDS) reaction. Unlike classical thymidylate synthase (ThyA), ThyX uses reduced flavin (FADH2 or FMNH2 here) as a hydride source, so 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate is regenerated to tetrahydrofolate (the methylene carbon is reduced to methyl by the flavin rather than by the folate itself). The reaction methylates dUMP to dTMP. Stoichiometry is balanced: the methylene group is transferred to dUMP and reduced to a methyl, FMNH2 is oxidized to FMN providing the hydride, and tetrahydrofolate is released. Reaction is biologically driven in the dTMP-forming direction.

rxn00314.other_comments: This is the oxidative deamination (hydrolytic) reaction of lysopine (N2-(D-1-carboxyethyl)-L-lysine) by opine dehydrogenase. The reaction as written shows the breakdown of lysopine into pyruvate and L-lysine using NADP+ and water, producing NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: lysopine (C9H18N2O4) + H2O + NADP+ yields pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + L-lysine (C6H14N2O2) + NADPH + H+. Charge and atom balance check out. Opine dehydrogenases physiologically favor the reductive condensation (synthesis) direction, forming lysopine from pyruvate and lysine with NADPH consumption; thus the written direction (lysopine breakdown) is the reverse of the typical in vivo flow.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species (H+ and Phenethylamine) on both sides without any compartment designation, making it a null reaction. A proton antiport transport reaction should show species in different compartments, e.g., H+[extracellular] + Phenethylamine[cytoplasm] <=> H+[cytoplasm] + Phenethylamine[extracellular]. As written, there is no net chemical or spatial change.
True antiport implies the proton and substrate move in opposite directions across the membrane; the written reaction does not reflect opposing transmembrane movement.
rxn12533.other_comments: This is annotated as a phenethylamine:H+ antiport transport reaction. Transport reactions are mass-balanced but should encode compartment changes to be meaningful. As written, both sides are identical with no compartment labels, so it represents no net transformation. Antiporters are typically driven by the proton motive force and can operate reversibly depending on gradients.

errors: Carbon balance is incorrect: starting C22 acyl-ACP (cis-19-docosanoyl) with 9 rounds of 2-carbon elongation from malonyl-ACP should yield a C40 product, but each malonyl condensation adds only 2 carbons to the chain (C22 + 9*2 = C40), which is consistent; however the CO2 release count is correct at 9, so chain carbon is balanced

Redox/cofactor stoichiometry is unbalanced for a standard fatty acid elongation: each elongation cycle (ketoacyl synthesis, ketoreduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction) typically consumes 2 reducing equivalents (commonly 2 NADPH), so 9 cycles would require ~18 NAD(P)H, but only 9 NADH + 9 NADPH (18 total) are provided, while the product here is a keto-meroacid (cis-19-C40oyl) implying only the keto group remains, not a fully reduced chain
Mixing of NADH and NADPH as cofactors is biochemically unusual; fatty acid/polyketide elongation typically uses NADPH exclusively for both reduction steps
Water balance: dehydration steps release water, and the consumption of 9 H2O on the product side rather than production is inconsistent with elongation chemistry (dehydration produces water)

If the product is a keto intermediate (named 'keto-meroacid'), then ketoreduction/dehydration/enoyl reduction were NOT all performed, so consuming 18 reducing equivalents is inconsistent with retaining a keto/unsaturated functionality
rxn13452.other_comments: This represents a mycobacterial mycolic acid meromycolate elongation step (FAS-II type), extending a C22 acyl-ACP by 9 two-carbon units via malonyl-ACP to a C40 keto-meroacid. The reaction is written as a lumped 9-cycle elongation. The major concern is internal consistency of the redox cofactor and water stoichiometry relative to the stated 'keto' product: water appears on the wrong side (should be produced by dehydration, not consumed), and the count of reducing equivalents does not match retention of a keto group.

errors: Oxygen atom balance is incorrect: O2 provides two oxygen atoms, but the products account for only one new oxygen in the hydroxymethyl group plus one in water. Actually for a methyl-to-hydroxymethyl hydroxylation, one O atom is incorporated into the substrate (as -OH) and one O is reduced to water, which balances O2 correctly
Stoichiometry as written appears balanced for a monooxygenase reaction; no major imbalance detected
rxn04001.other_comments: This is the first hydroxylation step in the C4-demethylation of sterols, catalyzed by a methylsterol monooxygenase (CYP51-related/SMO, e.g. ERG25/SC4MOL). A 4,4-dimethyl sterol has one of its 4-methyl groups (the 4alpha or 4beta methyl) oxidized to a hydroxymethyl group using NADPH and molecular O2, with formation of water. This is a cytochrome P450/monooxygenase-type reaction that is physiologically irreversible and proceeds in the direction of hydroxylation.

rxn02191.other_comments: This is the AAC(2') aminoglycoside N-acetyltransferase reaction, transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the 2'-amino position of gentamicin C1a, yielding CoA, a proton, and N2'-acetylgentamicin C1a. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acetyl group (C2H3O) and a proton are transferred from acetyl-CoA to the substrate amine, releasing free CoA. Acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase reactions are thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy thioester bond and are physiologically driven toward acetylation (antibiotic inactivation).

rxn06686.other_comments: This reaction represents the acylation of 1-alkenylglycerophosphoethanolamine (lyso-plasmenylethanolamine, a vinyl-ether lysophospholipid) at the sn-2 position using acyl-CoA, producing CoA and plasmenylethanolamine (the diacyl/alkenyl-acyl ethanolamine plasmalogen). The stoichiometry is balanced 1:1:1:1 in terms of the major substrates/products: one acyl group is transferred from CoA to the free hydroxyl, releasing free CoA. This is a remodeling step (Lands cycle analog for plasmalogens) and biologically proceeds in the direction of plasmalogen synthesis.

rxn12744.other_comments: This is a pyridoxal-5'-phosphate dependent aminotransferase reaction. The amino group from D-Lysine is transferred to Pyruvate, producing D-Alanine and the corresponding 2-oxo acid of lysine (2-Oxo-6-aminocaproate, also known as 2-keto-6-aminocaproate or allysine amine form). Stoichiometry is balanced: Pyruvate (C3H4O3) + D-Lysine (C6H14N2O2) -> D-Alanine (C3H7NO2) + 2-Oxo-6-aminocaproate (C6H11NO3). Atom count: C9, and balanced for H, N, O. Aminotransferase reactions are typically freely reversible due to similar energetics of the transamination.

errors: The dipeptide substrate gly-pro-L appears identical on both sides of the reaction; for a proper transport reaction, the substrate should be distinguished by compartment (e.g., gly-pro-L[e] on the reactant side and gly-pro-L[c] on the product side). Without compartment labels the reaction shows no net transport and appears to cancel out the substrate.
rxn05538.other_comments: This is an ABC-type dipeptide (glycyl-proline) transport reaction coupled to ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+). The ATP hydrolysis portion is stoichiometrically and charge balanced. ABC importers driven by ATP hydrolysis are physiologically unidirectional (import into the cytoplasm), so the reaction proceeds forward in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written is not balanced for protons/hydrogens. Oxidation of 1-acyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a secondary alcohol at C2) to acylglycerone phosphate (a ketone) removes 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+ and one as H+). The correct stoichiometry should produce NADPH + 1 H+, not 2 H+.
rxn06233.other_comments: This is the acylglycerone-phosphate reductase reaction (EC 1.1.1.101), interconverting 1-acyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (alcohol) and acylglycerone phosphate (acyl-DHAP, a ketone) using the NADP+/NADPH couple. The redox logic is correct (alcohol/ketone oxidation-reduction coupled to NADPH), but the H+ stoichiometry is wrong. In vivo this enzyme typically operates in the reductive direction (ketone to alcohol, consuming NADPH) in ether lipid biosynthesis, though it is biochemically reversible.

rxn09132.other_comments: Phospholipase A1 hydrolyzes the sn-1 ester bond of phosphatidylethanolamine. The substrate has two tetradec-7-enoyl chains; cleavage of the sn-1 acyl chain releases one tetradecenoate (free fatty acid) and yields the 2-acyl-lysophospholipid (2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine) bearing the remaining tetradec-7-enoyl at sn-2. Stoichiometry balances: water hydrolyzes the ester, producing one free fatty acid plus a proton and the lyso-PE.

errors: Stoichiometry is incorrect: the canonical Na+/K+-ATPase transports 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP hydrolyzed, but the reaction shows only 1 Na+ and 1 K+ with no compartment distinction
Na+ and K+ appear on both sides without indicating transport across a membrane (no in/out or cytosol/extracellular compartments specified), making the transport function uninterpretable
Without compartmentalization, the ions cancel out and the reaction reduces to simple ATP hydrolysis, which does not represent the actual pump activity
rxn10578.other_comments: This is intended to represent the Na+/K+-exchanging ATPase, which couples ATP hydrolysis to the export of 3 Na+ and import of 2 K+. As written, the ions are not separated into compartments and the stoichiometry (1 Na+, 1 K+) does not match the well-established 3:2 ratio. ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi + H+ is correct and drives the reaction strongly forward in vivo.

rxn00585.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of trans-1,2-dihydrobenzene-1,2-diol (trans-1,2-dihydroxy-1,2-dihydrobenzene) to catechol, with concomitant reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The reaction is catalyzed by trans-1,2-dihydrobenzene-1,2-diol dehydrogenase (EC 1.3.1.20). Stoichiometry is balanced: the dihydrodiol loses two hydrogen atoms (two electrons plus the protons) to aromatize, transferring a hydride to NADP+ and releasing one proton. Atom and charge balance are consistent (substrate C6H8O2 to catechol C6H6O2, NADP+ to NADPH + H+).

errors: Stoichiometric/elemental imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance. A C-acyltransferase (thiolase-type) condensation of propionyl-CoA with an acyl-CoA forms a new C-C bond releasing CoA, but the carbon count does not match - chenodeoxycholoyl-CoA (C24 bile acid acyl-CoA) condensed with propionyl-CoA (C3) would give a C27 product, whereas 3alpha,7alpha-dihydroxy-5beta-24-oxocholestanoyl-CoA is a C27 (cholestanoyl) species formed from a 3-oxo condensation. The correct beta-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase reaction requires a 2-carbon (acetyl-CoA) not 3-carbon donor for many steps, and a CO2 or proton balance/oxo group needs to be accounted for
Mislabeled enzyme name vs substrates: the listed enzyme 'Propanoyl-CoA:acetyl-CoA C-acyltransferase' references acetyl-CoA as a substrate, but acetyl-CoA does not appear in the reaction
rxn14138.other_comments: This appears to be a peroxisomal bile-acid side-chain synthesis step where a propionyl/acetyl-CoA condensation extends or modifies the cholestanoyl-CoA skeleton, producing a 24-oxo intermediate and releasing free CoA. Thiolase-type Claisen condensations are typically driven in the condensation (forward) direction in vivo as written, but the equation as given is not properly balanced and the named substrate (acetyl-CoA) is inconsistent with the listed reactants.

rxn07453.other_comments: This is the aldoxime dehydratase (Oxd) reaction, where an aliphatic aldoxime (R-CH=N-OH) is converted to the corresponding aliphatic nitrile (R-C#N) with release of water. The atom balance is correct: the aldoxime loses H2O to form the nitrile. The reaction is generic (R group unspecified) but stoichiometrically consistent for any aliphatic substituent. In vivo, aldoxime dehydratases catalyze the irreversible dehydration of aldoximes to nitriles as part of the aldoxime-nitrile pathway, so the physiological direction strongly favors nitrile formation.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction includes 2.0 H+ on the product side, but sulfotransferase reactions transferring a sulfo group from PAPS to a hydroxyl group typically release only 1 H+ (from the hydroxyl group being sulfated). The transfer of the SO3 group from PAPS to the acceptor hydroxyl generates PAP plus one proton, so the stoichiometry of 2 H+ appears incorrect and creates a charge imbalance.
rxn02354.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase (EC 2.8.2.-) reaction in which a sulfo group is transferred from PAPS (3'-phosphoadenylylsulfate) to the 7-hydroxyl of quercetin 3,3'-bissulfate, producing quercetin 3,3',7-trissulfate and PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate). PAPS-dependent sulfotransfer reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, driven toward sulfation of the acceptor.

rxn01911.other_comments: This represents the oxidation of 3-dehydro-L-gulonate to 2,3-dioxo-L-gulonate, with NAD+ serving as the electron acceptor (reduced to NADH). The reaction is catalyzed by 3-dehydro-L-gulonate 2-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.130). Atoms and charges balance: oxidation of a hydroxyl group to a keto group transfers a hydride to NAD+ and releases a proton.

rxn01943.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde to 4-hydroxyphenylacetate using NAD+ as electron acceptor. Mass and charge are balanced: aldehyde (C8H8O2) + H2O + NAD+ yields carboxylate (C8H7O3, -1 charge) + NADH + 2 H+. The carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge all balance correctly. Aldehyde dehydrogenases are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the favorable thermodynamics of aldehyde oxidation to carboxylic acid.

rxn01665.other_comments: This is an epimerase reaction interconverting two diastereomers of isocitrate (D-threo and D-erythro forms), differing in configuration at one stereocenter. The substrate name '(1R,2S)-1-Hydroxypropane-1,2,3-tricarboxylate 1-epimerase' describes an isocitrate epimerase. Stoichiometry is balanced as an isomerization (one molecule to one molecule, same molecular formula C6H8O7). Epimerases catalyze reversible interconversion of stereoisomers, driven by relative concentrations.

rxn02932.other_comments: This is a hydrolase reaction (EC 3.1.1.60, bis(2-ethylhexyl)phthalate acylhydrolase) cleaving one of the two ester bonds of di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP, dioctyl phthalate). Hydrolysis of one ester linkage releases 2-ethyl-1-hexanol and the monoester mono(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (here written as 2-ethylhexyl phthalate). Stoichiometry balances: H2O is consumed and an H+, the alcohol, and the monoester are produced, consistent with ester hydrolysis. The formula and charge balance is plausible for this hydrolytic cleavage.

rxn02766.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of the dipeptide beta-alanyl-L-arginine into its constituent amino acids beta-alanine and L-arginine. The reaction is balanced: H2O cleaves the peptide bond, yielding one molecule each of L-arginine and beta-alanine. Atoms and charges balance. Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: The reaction as written has identical species on both sides (H+ and L-Fucose appear on both the substrate and product side with the same stoichiometry), so no net chemical change is represented. To properly represent a proton symport transport reaction, the compounds must be distinguished by compartment, e.g., H+[extracellular] + L-Fucose[extracellular] <=> H+[cytosol] + L-Fucose[cytosol]. Without compartment annotations the reaction is a null/identity reaction.
rxn05691.other_comments: This is intended to be a secondary active transport reaction (L-fucose:H+ symport), coupling proton movement down its electrochemical gradient to fucose uptake. As written without compartmental designations it is a trivial identity equation. Biologically, fucose import is driven by the inward proton-motive force, so it is typically directed inward (forward = uptake into the cell), though transporters can in principle run reversibly depending on gradients.

errors: Charge imbalance: hexadecenoyl-CoA hydrolysis should release only 1 H+ (the carboxylic acid proton), not 2. The reaction as written generates excess positive charge. Balanced form: H2O + Hexadecenoyl-CoA -> CoA + H+ + hexadecenoate
rxn08443.other_comments: This is a thioesterase reaction hydrolyzing the thioester bond of hexadecenoyl-CoA to yield free CoA and hexadecenoate (a C16:1 fatty acid). Thioester hydrolysis is highly exergonic and physiologically irreversible, proceeding in the direction of hydrolysis.

rxn02399.other_comments: This represents the demethylation of N,N-dimethylaniline N-oxide, yielding formaldehyde and N-methylaniline. Atom balance: substrate C8H11NO breaks into formaldehyde (CH2O) plus N-methylaniline (C7H9N), giving C8H11NO on the product side, so the reaction is mass-balanced. This type of N-oxide rearrangement/dealkylation (Meisenheimer-type or via cytochrome P450/FMO-mediated N-demethylation) is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the demethylation direction in vivo.

rxn07709.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent N3-methyltransferase reaction in caffeine biosynthesis. 7-Methylxanthine is methylated at N3 to form theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine), with SAM converted to S-adenosyl-homocysteine. The atom balance is correct: methyl transfer from SAM to the substrate, releasing SAH and a proton. Stoichiometry and charge balance are consistent.

rxn03545.other_comments: This reaction represents the carbamoylation of deacetylcephalosporin C (DAC) by carbamoyl phosphate, catalyzed by carbamoyltransferase (CmcH/EC 2.1.3.7), transferring the carbamoyl group to the 3-hydroxymethyl group to form O-carbamoyl-DAC, releasing inorganic phosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: the carbamoyl group (NH2-CO-) is transferred from the phosphate to the hydroxyl, and phosphate is released. This is a step in cephamycin C biosynthesis.

rxn03855.other_comments: This is a hydrolytic deamination reaction. Deisopropyldeethylatrazine (2-chloro-4,6-diamino-1,3,5-triazine, also called desethyldesisopropylatrazine/DEDIA) is hydrolyzed, replacing one amino group with a hydroxyl group, releasing ammonia and forming 2-chloro-4-hydroxy-6-amino-1,3,5-triazine. Atoms balance: substrate C3H4ClN5 + H2O + H+ yields product C3H3ClN4O + NH3 (as NH4+ with the H+). The reaction is mass-balanced (counting the H+ for the protonation of ammonia), and hydrolytic deaminations releasing ammonia are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the reaction in the forward direction. This is part of the atrazine degradation pathway in bacteria.

rxn05081.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.x) transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to a flavonol triglucoside precursor, extending the sugar chain. The mass and charge balance: UDP-glucose donates a glucose to the acceptor, producing UDP and the elongated triglucoside. One glucose unit is transferred, and stoichiometry of 1:1 substrates to 1:1 products is correct. A proton may technically be released but is often omitted in these representations.

rxn00255.other_comments: This is the aldolase reaction (4-carboxy-4-hydroxy-2-oxoadipate aldolase, EC 4.1.3.17), part of the protocatechuate/gallate degradation pathway. The substrate 4-carboxy-4-hydroxy-2-oxoadipate (2-hydroxy-4-oxo-1,2,4-butanetricarboxylate) is cleaved into pyruvate and oxaloacetate. Stoichiometry is balanced: the C7 substrate (C7H8O8) splits into pyruvate (C3H4O3) and oxaloacetate (C4H4O5), conserving atoms and charge.

rxn14263.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by futalosine hydrolase (MqnB) in the menaquinone (vitamin K2) biosynthesis pathway via futalosine. Futalosine is hydrolyzed at the N-glycosidic bond, releasing hypoxanthine (HYXN) and producing dehypoxanthinyl futalosine (DHFL). The stoichiometry is balanced: water is consumed and the bond cleavage yields the two products. Hydrolytic reactions of this type are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the pathway forward.

rxn06198.other_comments: This is a histidine kinase autophosphorylation-type reaction (EC 2.7.13.3 family). ATP transfers its gamma-phosphate to the tele (N-tau/N-tele) nitrogen of a protein histidine residue, producing ADP, a proton, and the phosphohistidine. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + His-protein yields ADP + H+ + phosphohistidine-protein. Phosphate, adenine, and charge balance are correct, with the released proton accounting for the phosphoryl transfer.

rxn00965.other_comments: This is the thioester hydrolysis of 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA by 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA thioesterase (EC 3.1.2.23). The reaction: H2O + 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA -> CoA + H+ + 4-hydroxybenzoate. Stoichiometry is balanced: the thioester bond is hydrolyzed, releasing free CoA (with its thiol) and the carboxylic acid (4-hydroxybenzoate), with a proton released consistent with mass and charge balance. Thioester hydrolysis is highly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of CoA release. This step is part of the bacterial 4-chlorobenzoate degradation pathway.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: ornithine has two amino groups (alpha and delta), and L-ornithuric acid (N2,N5-dibenzoylornithine) is the di-benzoylated product, so 2 Benzoyl-CoA yielding 2 CoA is correct for the acyl transfer; however the proton balance is incorrect - benzoylation of two amine groups releases 2 H+ as written, which is consistent, but charge/atom balance should be verified
Substrate should be specified as L-Ornithine to match the L-Ornithuric acid product (the reactant is listed only as 'Ornithine')
rxn00464.other_comments: This is a benzoyltransferase reaction transferring two benzoyl groups from 2 Benzoyl-CoA to the two amino groups of L-ornithine, producing L-ornithuric acid (dibenzoylornithine) plus 2 CoA and 2 H+. The 1:2 stoichiometry for ornithine:benzoyl-CoA is appropriate for double acylation. CoA thioester hydrolysis/acyl transfer makes this thermodynamically favorable in the synthetic (forward) direction.

errors: Carbon balance is incorrect: the substrate (3S,4S)-3-Hydroxytetradecane-1,3,4-tricarboxylate has 17 carbons, while products 2-oxoglutarate (5 C) plus lauroyl-CoA acyl portion (12 C) total 17 C, so carbon balances on the substrate side; however the reaction as written includes a spurious H2O on the product side. A retro-aldol/lyase cleavage releasing CoA-acylated product should consume rather than produce water, suggesting a water/H+ balance error.
Hydrogen and oxygen balance should be rechecked: the H+ on the substrate side and H2O on the product side appear inconsistent with a CoA-acylating cleavage mechanism.
rxn02721.other_comments: This reaction is an aldol-type carbon-carbon lyase (analogous to homocitrate/citrate synthase-type chemistry in reverse). It cleaves a hydroxy-tricarboxylate into 2-oxoglutarate and a long-chain (lauroyl, C12) acyl-CoA, with CoA as a substrate. Such aldol cleavage/condensation reactions are typically thermodynamically reversible, though physiological direction depends on metabolite concentrations.

errors: The reaction as written shows no mass balance issue per se, but it is incomplete/abstract: it does not specify the transfer of an alpha-1,4-linked glucan segment to an alpha-1,6 branch point. No explicit atoms or groups are shown being transferred, so stoichiometric correctness cannot be verified.
Glycogen and 'branching glycogen' are not defined chemical entities with explicit formulas, making elemental balance impossible to confirm.
rxn08605.other_comments: This represents the 1,4-alpha-glucan branching enzyme (EC 2.4.1.18), which cleaves an alpha-1,4 glucan chain and reattaches it via an alpha-1,6 glycosidic bond to create branch points in glycogen. In vivo this is part of glycogen synthesis and proceeds in the direction of branch formation (glycogen -> branched glycogen).

errors: Substrate mismatch: the donor is UDP-galactose and the acceptor should be procollagen-bound 5-hydroxy-L-lysine residue, not free 5-hydroxylysine. The product name (Procollagen 5-(D-galactosyl)-L-lysine) implies a protein-bound substrate, so the free amino acid 5-hydroxylysine on the left is inconsistent with the product on the right.

Charge/proton balance: glycosyltransferase reactions transferring from UDP-sugar typically should be checked, though as written galactosyl transfer with UDP release is mass-balanced if acceptor is correctly specified.
rxn02423.other_comments: This is procollagen galactosyltransferase (galactosylhydroxylysyl glucosyltransferase pathway precursor; EC 2.4.1.50), which transfers galactose from UDP-galactose to hydroxylysine residues in collagen. The main issue is that the acceptor should be the procollagen 5-hydroxy-L-lysyl residue, not the free amino acid, to be consistent with the product. Glycosyltransfer from a UDP-sugar is strongly thermodynamically favorable and physiologically unidirectional.

errors: This is a transport reaction representing movement across a membrane (extracellular to cytoplasmic compartment), but the compartment annotations are missing. As written without compartment labels, both sides are identical (L-Leucine + Na+ = L-Leucine + Na+), making it a null/trivial reaction with no net chemical change.
Proper representation should be: L-Leucine[e] + Na+[e] <=> L-Leucine[c] + Na+[c]
rxn05240.other_comments: This is a sodium-coupled symport reaction for L-leucine uptake. The intended biology is co-transport of one L-leucine with one Na+ ion across the membrane, driven by the sodium electrochemical gradient. The 1:1 leucine:Na+ stoichiometry is plausible for such symporters. As written the equation is degenerate because compartment tags are omitted.

rxn02391.other_comments: This reaction represents an intramolecular acyl migration (transacylation) in lysophosphatidylcholine, where the single acyl chain migrates between the sn-2 and sn-3 (commonly designated sn-1) hydroxyl positions of the glycerophosphocholine backbone. 3-Lysolecithin (acyl at sn-3/sn-1) interconverts with 2-Lysolecithin (acyl at sn-2). Stoichiometrically this is a 1:1 isomerization with no net atoms gained or lost, so it is balanced. Acyl migration in lysophospholipids is a well-known spontaneous, reversible chemical process that does not strictly require enzyme catalysis; thermodynamically it tends to favor the more stable sn-1 (primary hydroxyl) acyl ester, but both forms coexist and interconvert readily.

rxn04845.other_comments: This reaction represents the conversion of 12(S)-HPETE (12(S)-hydroperoxy-eicosatetraenoic acid) to Hepoxilin A3, catalyzed by hepoxilin synthase (also known as 12-HPETE hydroxymutase, an activity of 12-lipoxygenase). It is an intramolecular rearrangement of the hydroperoxide into an epoxy-alcohol, so it is mass-balanced and atom-balanced (isomerization, no net atoms gained or lost). In vivo this proceeds in the direction of hepoxilin formation.

rxn06207.other_comments: This represents the oxidation of N-acyl-D-mannosamine at the C1 position to form N-acyl-D-mannosaminolactone (a 1,5-lactone), with NAD+ accepting the hydride to form NADH plus a proton. This corresponds to EC 1.1.1.233 (N-acylmannosamine 1-dehydrogenase). The reaction is balanced in mass and charge: one hydride and one proton are released from the substrate, accounting for the NADH and H+ products. While written as reversible (typical for NAD-dependent dehydrogenases), in vivo the oxidation direction (forward as written) is often favored for catabolic flux, though the lactone can be reduced or hydrolyzed depending on conditions.

rxn14077.other_comments: This is the putrescine:pyruvate aminotransferase (also known as PatA/SpuC) reaction. Carbon (7=7), nitrogen (2=2), and oxygen (3=3) balance, and hydrogen balances (16=16). This enzyme is part of the putrescine degradation pathway, with the aldehyde subsequently oxidized toward GABA.

rxn09924.other_comments: This represents an L-amino acid ligase (Lal/RizA-type) reaction forming the dipeptide Ser-Trp. The H+ release is consistent with the proton stoichiometry of ATP-grasp ligation.

rxn01406.other_comments: This is the spermidine synthase reaction (EC 2.5.1.16). rxn08103.other_comments: This is the first half-reaction of the ping-pong mechanism of alanine transaminase (ALT/GPT). rxn09622.other_comments: This represents the ERG25-type C-4 sterol methyl oxidase step in sterol biosynthesis, oxidizing a 4-methyl group through hydroxymethyl, formyl, to carboxyl using O2 and NADPH. rxn01919.other_comments: This is the gentisate 1,2-dioxygenase reaction (EC 1.13.11.4), which incorporates molecular O2 into gentisate (2,5-dihydroxybenzoate) and cleaves the aromatic ring to form maleylpyruvate. Carbon (7=7) and oxygen (4+2=6) balance, and hydrogen balances when the released H+ is accounted for. As a dioxygenase ring-cleavage reaction, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn01446.other_comments: This is the purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) reaction acting on deoxyguanosine. Atoms and charges balance with appropriate protonation states. The enzyme catalyzes a phosphorolysis and is thermodynamically near-equilibrium, hence freely reversible in vitro, though in vivo flux is typically directed toward base salvage/degradation (phosphorolysis direction).

rxn01350.other_comments: This represents methanethiol oxidase activity (methanethiol:oxygen oxidoreductase, EC 1.8.3.4), oxidizing methanethiol (CH3SH) to formaldehyde, hydrogen sulfide, and hydrogen peroxide using molecular oxygen.
