As written (NADP+ + CoA + GSH -> NADPH + CoA-glutathione), the electron bookkeeping is backwards: forming a disulfide is an oxidation that should not produce NADPH from NADP+. A proton is also missing.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: this reaction combines two distinct steps (condensation and reduction) but lacks proper atom/charge balance.

The condensation step (KAS, beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase) produces a 3-oxoacyl-ACP (3-oxopalmitoyl-ACP), not directly a 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP. A separate ketoreductase step with NADPH is required to form the 3-hydroxy product.
Only one NADPH is shown, but if the product is the 3-hydroxy form, the NADPH consumption matches the reduction step; however the combined reaction should not occur as a single reaction.

ACP balance issue: condensation of myristoyl-ACP (C14) with malonyl-ACP should release one ACP and CO2, yielding a 3-oxopalmitoyl-ACP (C16); the equation only releases one ACP which is correct for the condensation but the hydrogen/charge balance with NADPH/NADP+ needs verification.
rxn10937.other_comments: This is presented as a beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (KAS) reaction extending myristoyl-ACP (C14) by two carbons using malonyl-ACP to give a C16 product, with concomitant NADPH-dependent reduction. In reality, fatty acid elongation in FAS proceeds via discrete steps: condensation (KAS) to 3-oxoacyl-ACP, then ketoreduction (FabG/KAR) to 3-hydroxyacyl-ACP. The decarboxylative condensation makes the overall direction essentially irreversible toward elongation.

rxn07413.other_comments: This is a phosphomonoesterase (phosphohydrolase) reaction hydrolyzing the 9-phosphate group of (9S,10S)-10-hydroxy-9-(phosphonooxy)octadecanoate to yield (9S,10S)-9,10-dihydroxyoctadecanoate and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is balanced: one water and one phosphomonoester bond are cleaved, releasing one phosphate and converting the phosphooxy group to a hydroxyl. Atoms and charges balance with phosphate carrying the released group. Phosphatase reactions involving hydrolysis of a phosphomonoester are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn01959.other_comments: This is a lactonohydrolase reaction where D-arabinono-1,4-lactone is hydrolyzed by water to yield D-arabinonate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the lactone (C5H8O5) plus H2O (H2O) gives the open-chain acid anion D-arabinonate (C5H9O6-) plus a proton (H+). Carbon (5=5), oxygen (5+1=6) and charge (0 = -1+1) all balance. Hydrolysis of the lactone ring is thermodynamically favorable due to relief of ring strain and the irreversibility typical of lactone hydrolysis in vivo, so the reaction proceeds in the forward direction physiologically, though hydrolases are often written as reversible.

errors: This reaction as written is incomplete/imbalanced. The C-3 sterol dehydrogenase (decarboxylase) step in sterol biosynthesis (ERG26/NSDHL) is a 3-keto reduction associated with decarboxylation of the 4-carboxyl group. The substrate that is decarboxylated is the 4alpha-carboxy intermediate, and the product is the 3-keto sterol. A proton (H+) is typically required to balance the equation: NAD+ + 4alpha-carboxysterol -> NADH + CO2 + 3-keto sterol + H+ is not balanced unless the named metabolites carry the correct formulas. As written with generic 'intermediate-methylzymosterol-I/II' names, charge and H balance cannot be verified.
Missing H+ on the product side for proper charge/mass balance of the NAD+/NADH oxidative decarboxylation.
rxn09626.other_comments: This represents the C3 sterol dehydrogenase/C4 decarboxylase reaction in ergosterol/cholesterol biosynthesis, in which a 4-carboxy sterol intermediate is oxidatively decarboxylated using NAD+ to give a 3-keto sterol, NADH and CO2. The release of CO2 makes this reaction essentially irreversible in vivo, driving it in the forward direction.

errors: This reaction is mislabeled - the name describes an aminotransferase (transamination) but the equation combines two distinct chemical events: deacetylation and transamination, with incorrect stoichiometry/products.

The product dTDP-4-oxo-6-deoxy-D-glucose (a keto sugar) cannot be directly formed from dTDP-4-acetamido-4,6-dideoxy-D-glucose by simple transamination plus deacetylation; the correct aminotransferase product would be dTDP-4-amino-4,6-dideoxy-D-glucose forming from the keto sugar, i.e. the reaction is conceptually reversed.

The acetamido-to-keto conversion requires removal of an acetamido group, which involves both deacetylation (releasing acetate, not generating acetyl-CoA from CoA) and transamination/oxidation; coupling CoA + acetamido sugar to give acetyl-CoA is chemically implausible as written.
Atom/charge balance is questionable: a true aminotransferase should be 2-oxoglutarate + amino-sugar <=> L-glutamate + keto-sugar (1:1 amine transfer) without CoA or acetyl-CoA involvement.
rxn01998.other_comments: The named enzyme is a dTDP-4-amino-sugar:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase. The canonical reaction transfers an amino group between an amino sugar and 2-oxoglutarate/glutamate. The equation as given improperly mixes a CoA/acetyl-CoA acetyl transfer with the transamination and uses the acetamido sugar with a keto sugar product, which is inconsistent both stoichiometrically and mechanistically.

errors: The H+ on the substrate side is stoichiometrically incorrect; glucosyltransferase reactions of this type typically release a proton rather than consume one, so H+ should appear on the product side: UDP-glucose + Biochanin A <=> UDP + Biochanin A-glucoside + H+
rxn04610.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent O-glucosyltransferase transferring a glucosyl moiety to the 7-OH position of the isoflavone Biochanin A, yielding the 7-O-beta-D-glucoside (sissotrin) and releasing UDP. The glycosyl transfer from the high-energy UDP-sugar donor strongly favors the forward (biosynthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn01068.other_comments: This is the L-threonine dehydrogenase (TDH, EC 1.1.1.103) reaction. L-threonine is oxidized at its beta-hydroxyl group, with NAD+ as the electron acceptor, producing L-2-amino-3-oxobutanoate (L-2-amino-acetoacetate), NADH, and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically and redox balanced: the secondary alcohol of threonine is oxidized to a ketone, transferring a hydride to NAD+ and releasing one H+. In vivo this is the first step of the threonine degradation pathway, with the unstable 2-amino-3-oxobutanoate subsequently consumed by 2-amino-3-ketobutyrate CoA ligase, pulling the reaction forward.

errors: Reaction is trivial/identity: identical species and stoichiometry on both sides (H+ + SALC = H+ + SALC), so no net chemical or transport change is represented
Compartment annotations are missing; a proton symport transport reaction should distinguish extracellular vs cytoplasmic species (e.g., H+[e] + SALC[e] <=> H+[c] + SALC[c])
rxn12589.other_comments: This is intended to be a salicylate proton-symport transport reaction, where salicylate is co-transported with a proton across the membrane. As written, both sides are identical because compartment tags are absent, making it a null reaction. With proper compartments it would represent import driven by the proton motive force.

rxn02546.other_comments: This is the decarboxylation of 6-methylsalicylate (6-methyl-2-hydroxybenzoate) catalyzed by 6-methylsalicylate decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.52). The reaction removes the carboxyl group, yielding m-cresol (3-methylphenol) and CO2. Atom and charge balance: 6-methylsalicylate (C8H7O3-, as carboxylate) plus H+ gives C8H8O3, which fragments to CO2 (CO2) and m-cresol (C7H8O). C: 8 = 1+7, H: 8 = 0+8, O: 3 = 2+1. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced.

rxn01549.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of guanosine 3'-monophosphate (Gp, 3'-GMP) by a phosphohydrolase, cleaving the phosphoester bond to yield free phosphate and guanosine. The stoichiometry is balanced: H2O + guanosine 3'-phosphate yields inorganic phosphate + guanosine. Phosphomonoester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

rxn14176.other_comments: This is the reduction of the 3-oxo group of allopregnane-21-ol-3,20-dione (5alpha-dihydrodeoxycorticosterone) by NADPH to yield 5-alpha-THDOC (3alpha,21-dihydroxy-5alpha-pregnan-20-one, tetrahydrodeoxycorticosterone), catalyzed by a 3alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (AKR family). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: NADPH + H+ reduces the ketone to a hydroxyl, consuming the proton and converting NADPH to NADP+. As an aldo-keto reductase reaction it is thermodynamically reversible in vitro, though in vivo it favors the reductive (NADPH-dependent) direction toward 5-alpha-THDOC formation.

rxn04898.other_comments: This is the hydration of dichloroacetaldehyde (CHCl2-CHO) by water to form the geminal diol dichloroacetaldehyde hydrate (CHCl2-CH(OH)2). The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: H2O (H2O) plus C2H2Cl2O equals C2H4Cl2O2. Aldehyde hydration to a gem-diol is a spontaneous, near-equilibrium chemical process, and for electron-poor aldehydes like dichloroacetaldehyde the hydrate (diol) form is strongly favored in aqueous solution.

rxn02059.other_comments: This is a hexose 6-phosphotransferase (hexokinase-like) reaction using ITP instead of ATP as the phosphate donor. Sorbitol and D-glucitol are synonyms for the same molecule (D-sorbitol = D-glucitol), so the substrate is phosphorylated at the 6-position to yield D-glucitol 6-phosphate (sorbitol 6-phosphate). Stoichiometry is balanced: ITP donates a phosphate to sorbitol, producing IDP, the phosphorylated sugar alcohol, and a proton. Mass and charge are conserved.

errors: The hydrogen ion stoichiometry appears incorrect; a typical NADPH-dependent reduction of an iminium/enamine in cathenamine consumes one proton (NADPH + H+), not 2 H+. Balanced form: NADPH + H+ + Cathenamine -> NADP+ + Tetrahydroalstonine
Charge/notation: NADP should be written as NADP+ to maintain charge balance
rxn04080.other_comments: This is the reduction of cathenamine by NADPH (cathenamine reductase, EC 1.3.1.x) yielding tetrahydroalstonine, a step in monoterpenoid indole alkaloid biosynthesis (e.g., in Catharanthus roseus). The reductive direction toward the tetrahydro product is strongly favored in vivo.

errors: Unbalanced reaction as written: methylation of cobalt-precorrin 3 to cobalt-precorrin 4 (catalyzed by CbiH) also incorporates a lactone/ring contraction step involving water and loss of a proton; the simple SAM/SAH transfer shown does not balance C, H, O atoms between cobalt-precorrin 3 and cobalt-precorrin 4
rxn04047.other_comments: This is the CbiH-catalyzed C-17 methylation step in the anaerobic (cobalt-early) cobalamin/vitamin B12 biosynthesis pathway, transferring a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to cobalt-precorrin 3, yielding cobalt-precorrin 4 and S-adenosyl-homocysteine.

errors: The reaction lacks an enzyme/cofactor context, but stoichiometrically it represents an isomerization (PGA1 to PGC1) where the molecular formula is conserved (C20H32O4 = C20H32O4), so it is balanced as written.
rxn03138.other_comments: This reaction represents the isomerization of prostaglandin A1 (PGA1) to prostaglandin C1 (PGC1). Both are cyclopentenone-type prostaglandins differing in the position of the double bond in the cyclopentane ring. This conversion is a double-bond migration (delta-isomerization), commonly catalyzed by PGA isomerase. It is an intramolecular rearrangement that conserves atomic composition.

rxn02506.other_comments: This reaction is part of the bile acid biosynthesis pathway, oxidizing the C26 hydroxyl group of 5beta-cholestane-3alpha,7alpha,12alpha,26-tetrol to the corresponding aldehyde (3alpha,7alpha,12alpha-trihydroxy-5beta-cholestan-26-al) using NAD+ as the electron acceptor, producing NADH and H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: the alcohol is oxidized to an aldehyde with removal of two hydrogen atoms (transferred as hydride to NAD+ forming NADH plus a released proton). This is catalyzed by an alcohol dehydrogenase activity (EC 1.1.1.-). In vivo, the strongly committed flux toward bile acid synthesis and the favorable consumption of the aldehyde by downstream steps drive this in the forward (oxidative) direction, though the alcohol dehydrogenase reaction is thermodynamically reversible in isolation.

errors: Carbon imbalance: Acetylacetone (C5H8O2) has 5 carbons, but products Acetate (C2H3O2) + 2-Oxopropanal/methylglyoxal (C3H4O2) sum to 5 carbons, so carbon is balanced. However, the equation is not mass/charge balanced as written: reactant side O2 + C5H8O2 = C5H8O4; product side C2H3O2(-) + H+ + C3H4O2 = C5H8O4. Atoms actually balance (C5 H8 O4 each side, charge 0 each side).
On careful inspection the reaction is balanced; no stoichiometric error.
rxn04964.other_comments: This is acetylacetone-cleaving dioxygenase (Dke1-type), which uses O2 to cleave the 1,3-diketone acetylacetone into acetate and methylglyoxal (2-oxopropanal). Both O atoms of O2 are incorporated. The dioxygenase reaction is essentially irreversible in the forward (oxygenation) direction.

rxn09638.other_comments: This is the alpha-aminoadipate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (AASS / LYS2-type) reaction, which activates L-2-aminoadipate via adenylation (ATP -> AMP + PPi) and then reduces the activated carboxyl group using NADPH to yield L-2-aminoadipate 6-semialdehyde (allysine), NADP+, AMP, and PPi. Mass and charge balance: ATP donates the adenylyl group giving AMP + PPi, NADPH reduces the carboxyl to an aldehyde giving NADP+. The atoms balance (the carboxylic acid OH is lost as part of the reduction, with the corresponding oxygen going to AMP during the adenylation/displacement). Note water is sometimes shown explicitly depending on how the adenylated intermediate is treated, but the overall stoichiometry is standard. In vivo this reductive step is essentially irreversible, driven by ATP hydrolysis (PPi release), so it proceeds in the forward direction.

rxn03504.other_comments: This is the deacetylation (amidohydrolase/deacetylase) reaction of N-acetyl-D-galactosamine 6-phosphate, hydrolyzing the acetamido group to yield D-galactosamine 6-phosphate and acetate. The stoichiometry is balanced: water cleaves the amide bond, releasing acetate. This corresponds to AgaA/NagA-type deacetylase activity in galactosamine catabolism. The hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the catabolic (forward) direction.

rxn02158.other_comments: This is a gibberellin 3-beta-hydroxylase (GA3ox) reaction, a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase. It hydroxylates GA20 to GA1 at the 3-beta position, consuming O2 and 2-oxoglutarate, producing succinate and CO2. The stoichiometry is balanced: one O2 atom is incorporated into the hydroxyl group of the product, the other oxidatively decarboxylates 2-oxoglutarate to succinate and CO2. Such 2OG-dependent dioxygenases are effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn01693.other_comments: This reaction represents 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.62), oxidizing estradiol-17beta at the 17-OH position to the 17-keto group of estrone, with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: estradiol (C18H24O2) loses 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH, one as H+) yielding estrone (C18H22O2). The enzyme is bidirectional in vivo, with directionality depending on the isozyme and cellular redox/cofactor ratios; some isoforms favor reduction (estrone to estradiol) while others favor oxidation.

rxn01028.other_comments: This is dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (NADP+) (EC 1.3.1.2), interconverting thymine and 5,6-dihydrothymine. The reaction as written shows oxidation of dihydrothymine to thymine, generating NADPH. Stoichiometrically it is balanced (atoms and charge: NADP+ + dihydrothymine -> NADPH + H+ + thymine, with two H transferred). However, in vivo the physiologically relevant direction is the reductive one: thymine + NADPH + H+ -> dihydrothymine + NADP+, as the first step of pyrimidine degradation. Thus relative to how it is written (oxidation), the favored physiological flux is the reverse.

rxn09455.other_comments: This is a fatty-acyl-ACP thioesterase (hydrolase) reaction. Water hydrolyzes the thioester bond between octadecenoyl (oleoyl, C18:1) and acyl carrier protein (ACP), releasing free octadecenoate (oleate) and holo-ACP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one water consumed, one thioester cleaved, yielding free fatty acid and free ACP. Thioester hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible, proceeding in the direction of free fatty acid release.

errors: Substrate specificity mismatch: the reaction name specifies alpha-D-aldose-1-phosphate but the equation uses beta-L-Aldose 1-phosphate (stereochemistry/configuration inconsistency)

Mechanistic/stoichiometric error: a nucleotidyltransferase (adenylyltransferase) transferring an adenylyl (AMP) group from ATP to a sugar-1-phosphate should release pyrophosphate (PPi), not free phosphate; if ADP is the nucleotide donor, the leaving group would be phosphate but the product naming as ADP-aldose (which contains a diphosphate bridge) is inconsistent with releasing only one phosphate
rxn06322.other_comments: This is intended to be an adenylyltransferase reaction forming a nucleotide-sugar (ADP-aldose) from a nucleotide donor and an aldose-1-phosphate. As written it uses ADP + aldose-1-phosphate to give Pi + ADP-aldose, which is atom-imbalanced relative to standard nucleotidyltransferase chemistry and has a sugar stereochemistry mismatch between the enzyme name and the substrate.

errors: Atom and charge imbalance: the reaction as written is not mass balanced. Oxidation of vanillin (an aldehyde) to vanillate (a carboxylic acid) adds one oxygen atom; balancing requires NAD+ as a substrate (not product) since the aldehyde dehydrogenase oxidizes the substrate while reducing NAD+ to NADH. The given direction has NADH as substrate and NAD as product, which is backward for an oxidation.

The enzyme name '4-Hydroxy-3-methoxybenzoate:oxygen oxidoreductase' (vanillate monooxygenase / vanillate degradation) does not match the written substrates/products; that name implies a monooxygenase acting on vanillate, not on vanillin.
rxn03585.other_comments: The reaction depicts oxidation of vanillin (4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde) to vanillate (4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzoate). This is an aldehyde-to-carboxylic-acid conversion. As written, the redox cofactor usage is inverted (NADH consumed, NAD produced) which contradicts an oxidation; a correct NAD-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase would consume NAD+ and produce NADH (NAD+ + Vanillin + H2O -> NADH + Vanillate + H+), and O2 would not be required.

rxn09579.other_comments: This reaction represents the dephosphorylation of phytosphingosine 1-phosphate by sphingosine-1-phosphate phosphatase (SGPP1/SGPP2), releasing inorganic phosphate and phytosphingosine. The reaction is balanced: water hydrolyzes the phosphate monoester bond, yielding free phosphate, a proton, and the free sphingoid base. Phytosphingosine 1-phosphate is a known substrate of these phosphatases. Mass and charge are balanced (the proton released accounts for the charge from the liberated phosphate group).

rxn13191.other_comments: This is a transport reaction moving 2-methyl-1-butanol across a membrane (extracellular to intracellular or vice versa). The same metabolite appears on both sides, representing the same compound in different compartments. Stoichiometry is balanced (1:1). As a small uncharged alcohol, 2-methyl-1-butanol can diffuse passively across membranes, so the reaction is appropriately modeled as reversible.

rxn06616.other_comments: This is the alpha-tubulin acetyltransferase (ATAT1) reaction transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the epsilon-amino group of a lysine residue (K40) on alpha-tubulin, producing acetyl-lysine, CoA, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred from CoA to the lysine, the released proton accounts for the loss of one H from the lysine amine upon acetylation, and atoms/charges balance.

rxn04990.other_comments: This is the tyrosine hydroxylase reaction (EC 1.14.16.2). L-Tyrosine is hydroxylated to L-DOPA using molecular oxygen and the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin, which is oxidized to 4a-hydroxytetrahydrobiopterin (carbinolamine). One oxygen atom is incorporated into the aromatic ring (3-hydroxylating) and the other into the pterin cofactor. Atoms balance: O2 provides both oxygens. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the catabolic/biosynthetic forward direction toward catecholamine synthesis.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction for the named enzyme reaction; the oxidoreductase reduces protochlorophyllide to chlorophyllide, consuming NADPH, not producing it

Substrate/product naming inconsistency: the enzyme reduces the D-ring 17,18 (7,8) double bond, converting divinyl protochlorophyllide to divinyl chlorophyllide; as written it shows oxidation of chlorophyllide back to protochlorophyllide
rxn04162.other_comments: This corresponds to the light-dependent (or dark-operative) protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase (POR) step in chlorophyll biosynthesis. Physiologically the reaction proceeds as divinyl protochlorophyllide + NADPH + H+ -> divinyl chlorophyllide a + NADP+. As written (left to right) it is the unfavorable reverse oxidation and would consume chlorophyllide while producing NADPH.

rxn00268.other_comments: This reaction is the oxidative deamination of glycine to glyoxylate, coupling NAD+ reduction to NADH and releasing ammonia. Mass and charge balance check: left side has Glycine (C2H5NO2) + H2O + NAD+; right side has Glyoxylate (C2HO3-) + NH3 + NADH + H+. Carbon (2=2), nitrogen (1=1), and oxygen balance, and charge is conserved when accounting for the H+ released. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as written.

rxn02238.other_comments: This reaction describes leucopelargonidin (a leucoanthocyanidin/flavan-3,4-diol) and aromadendrin (dihydrokaempferol, a dihydroflavonol). The conversion of dihydrokaempferol to leucopelargonidin is the well-known dihydroflavonol 4-reductase (DFR) step, which consumes NADPH and reduces the 4-keto group to a 4-hydroxyl. As written (NADP+ + leucopelargonidin -> NADPH + H+ + aromadendrin), this is the oxidation direction. In vivo the physiological flux is the reduction direction (aromadendrin + NADPH -> leucopelargonidin + NADP+), so relative to the written equation the favored direction is reverse. Stoichiometry and redox balance are correct.

rxn02596.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of stachyose by alpha-galactosidase. Stachyose (a tetrasaccharide: Gal-Gal-Glc-Fru) is hydrolyzed by adding water across the terminal alpha-1,6 galactosidic bond, releasing one galactose and yielding raffinose (Melitose/Melibiose+sucrose; raffinose = Gal-Glc-Fru). The stoichiometry balances: stachyose (C24H42O21) + H2O (H2O) gives galactose (C6H12O6) + raffinose (C18H32O16). Note that 'Melitose' is a synonym for raffinose, the expected product. Hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the forward (hydrolytic) direction in vivo.

rxn00742.other_comments: This reaction represents cystathionine gamma-lyase (cystathionase, EC 4.4.1.1) acting on L-cystathionine. The enzyme cleaves cystathionine with water to yield L-cysteine, 2-oxobutyrate (2-ketobutyrate), and ammonia. The stoichiometry is balanced: cystathionine (C7H14N2O4S) + H2O yields L-cysteine (C3H7NO2S) + 2-oxobutyrate (C4H5O3-) + NH3 + H+. Atoms balance (C7, N2, S1, O5 on each side) and charge balances. This is the transsulfuration pathway step. In vivo it proceeds in the degradative direction.

errors: The reaction name describes a delta5-delta4 isomerase, but the written reaction is a redox reaction involving NADPH/NADP+, which is inconsistent with an isomerization
An isomerase reaction (delta5 to delta4 double bond shift) does not require NADPH or produce NADP+; the cofactor stoichiometry is incorrect for the named enzyme

Cortodoxone (11-deoxycortisol) is the delta4-3-keto form, while 17alpha,21-dihydroxypregnenolone is the delta5-3beta-hydroxy form; their interconversion involves both a 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase oxidation AND a delta5-delta4 isomerization, not a simple NADPH-dependent step
rxn03319.other_comments: The substrates 17alpha,21-dihydroxypregnenolone (delta5-3beta-OH steroid) and 11-deoxycortisol/cortodoxone (delta4-3-keto steroid) are interconverted by the 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/delta5-delta4-isomerase (3beta-HSD) complex. The physiological conversion uses NAD+ (oxidation) plus isomerization, producing NADH, and proceeds in the direction toward 11-deoxycortisol. The reaction as written incorrectly couples it to NADPH and runs in the reverse (reductive) direction, which is not how 3beta-HSD operates in vivo.

rxn04658.other_comments: This reaction represents the reduction of N2-acetyl-L-aminoadipyl-delta-phosphate (an acyl phosphate) to N2-acetyl-L-aminoadipate semialdehyde, with release of phosphate, using NADPH as the reductant. This is a step in the alpha-aminoadipate (AAA) pathway of lysine biosynthesis (in fungi, this corresponds to the acetylated variant via N-acetyl intermediates). The stoichiometry is balanced: the acyl phosphate is reduced to an aldehyde, releasing inorganic phosphate and oxidizing NADPH to NADP+. This is analogous to the aspartate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase and glutamate-5-semialdehyde reactions, which physiologically proceed in the reductive (biosynthetic) direction consuming NADPH.

errors: Proton stoichiometry is questionable; an acyltransferase reaction transferring an acyl group from ACP to a hydroxyl/amino acceptor typically does not release 3 H+. At most one proton may be involved, and many such transferase reactions are balanced with no net proton change.
rxn08417.other_comments: This is a Kdo2-lipid IVA acyltransferase reaction (analogous to LpxL/LpxM, here using palmitoleoyl/hexadecenoyl-ACP instead of the usual lauroyl/myristoyl donor). It transfers the hexadecenoyl (palmitoleoyl) chain from acyl-ACP onto Kdo2-lipid IVA, releasing free ACP, as part of lipid A (endotoxin) biosynthesis. Acyl-ACP-dependent acyltransfer is thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn13842.other_comments: This is the gastric H+/K+-ATPase (P-type ATPase). It hydrolyzes ATP (H2O + ATP -> ADP + Pi) to drive electroneutral exchange of cytoplasmic H+ for extracytoplasmic K+. The equation shows ATP hydrolysis coupled to ion transport: one K+ is imported and one H+ is exported (net one extra H+ appears on the product side reflecting the transported proton). The stoichiometry shown (K+ consumed and K+ produced on both sides representing import, and the additional H+ on the product side representing the exported proton) is mass and charge balanced. ATP-driven pumps operate in the hydrolysis (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: 2-hydroxypropylphosphonate (C3H7O4P, 3 carbons) cannot be converted to phosphonoacetaldehyde (C2H3O4P, 2 carbons) without accounting for the missing carbon; the lost methyl group does not balance with the conversion of aquacobalamin to methylcobalamin in a charge/atom-consistent manner as written

Charge imbalance: aquacobalamin (cob(III)alamin, water coordinated) to methylcobalamin involves a redox/methyl transfer that is not stoichiometrically balanced with a single H+ and H2O on the product side

The conversion of aquacobalamin (Co(III)) to methylcobalamin (Co(III)-methyl) requires a methyl donor; here the substrate provides a methyl via C-C bond cleavage, but the redox electrons are unaccounted for
rxn11649.other_comments: This appears to be the HppE/PhpA-type radical SAM or cobalamin-dependent step in fosfomycin or 2-aminoethylphosphonate-related biosynthesis. The intent is a methyl/electron transfer where 2-hydroxypropylphosphonate is converted to phosphonoacetaldehyde with the methyl group going to the cobalamin cofactor. As written the carbon and charge balance do not cleanly close.

rxn02249.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase (PAPS-dependent) reaction transferring a sulfo group from 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) to Renilla luciferin, producing luciferyl sulfate and adenosine-3',5'-bisphosphate (PAP) plus a proton. The atom balance is consistent: the sulfate group transfers from PAPS to the luciferin hydroxyl, leaving PAP, and a proton is released. Sulfotransferases using PAPS are generally strongly exergonic and operate in the forward (sulfation) direction in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the reaction consumes 1 O2 (2 oxygen atoms) but only incorporates 1 oxygen atom into the product (hydroxyl group) and 1 into water, which actually balances oxygen; however the hydrogen/charge balance should be checked. With NADPH + H+ providing reducing equivalents, one O atom goes to the 20-OH and the other to H2O, so atoms balance. Main concern is the enzyme name 'side-chain-cleaving' does not match the reaction, which is a simple hydroxylation, not a C-C bond cleavage.
rxn01061.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (likely CYP11A1/scc) monooxygenase-type hydroxylation of cholesterol at C20 to form 20alpha-hydroxycholesterol, using NADPH and molecular O2. The true side-chain cleavage (scc) involves sequential 20- and 22-hydroxylations followed by C20-C22 bond cleavage to yield pregnenolone; this reaction only represents the first hydroxylation step, so the 'side-chain-cleaving' label is misleading for this specific equation.

rxn02790.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of a phosphate group from 3-(ADP)-2-phosphoglycerate, yielding inorganic phosphate and 3-(ADP)-glycerate. The substrate has both a 2-phosphate (being hydrolyzed) and an ADP moiety linked at position 3. Removal of the 2-phosphate as inorganic phosphate via water-mediated hydrolysis is stoichiometrically balanced (water added, phosphate released, one phosphoester bond cleaved). As a phosphohydrolase reaction, it is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo.

rxn10319.other_comments: This represents D-alanylation of lipoteichoic acid (LTA), where D-alanine is activated by ATP (forming D-alanyl-AMP + PPi) and transferred onto the polyglycerophosphate backbone of LTA. The n=24 indicates 24 glycerophosphate repeat units, each receiving one D-alanine, hence the 24x stoichiometry. The ATP -> AMP + PPi cleavage (releasing 2 H+ per reaction) drives the reaction forward.

rxn02019.other_comments: This reaction represents the dehydration of Prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) to form Prostaglandin J2 (PGJ2). PGD2 (C20H32O5) loses a water molecule to form PGJ2 (C20H30O4), which involves dehydration of the hydroxyl group at the cyclopentane ring to create the cyclopentenone (alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone) characteristic of the J-series prostaglandins. The atoms balance: C20H32O5 = H2O (H2O) + C20H30O4. This dehydration occurs non-enzymatically (spontaneously) in vivo and is essentially irreversible under physiological conditions because formation of the conjugated enone is thermodynamically favorable and water loss is not readily reversed.

rxn04006.other_comments: This is a Pictet-Spengler type condensation between secologanin (a secoiridoid glucoside with an aldehyde) and dopamine (a beta-arylethylamine), forming the tetrahydroisoquinoline alkaloid deacetylipecoside with release of water. The reaction is mass-balanced: the C-N bond formation and ring closure between the aldehyde of secologanin and the amine of dopamine releases one water molecule. Stoichiometry appears correct. This condensation step in ipecac (Cephaelis) alkaloid biosynthesis proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward alkaloid formation.

rxn04432.other_comments: This is a caffeoyl-CoA O-methyltransferase (CCoAOMT)-type reaction where SAM donates a methyl group to the 5-hydroxyl of 5-hydroxyferuloyl-CoA, producing sinapoyl-CoA and S-adenosyl-homocysteine. The stoichiometry is balanced: a methyl group is transferred from SAM to the substrate hydroxyl, converting 5-hydroxyferuloyl-CoA (one free OH) to sinapoyl-CoA (now methylated). The released proton accounts for the deprotonation accompanying methylation. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn03915.other_comments: This reaction is the NAD+-dependent oxidation of 2-formylbenzoate (o-formylbenzoic acid) to phthalate (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylate). The aldehyde group is oxidized to a carboxylate, consuming H2O and NAD+, producing NADH, phthalate, and 2 H+. Atom and charge balance: aldehyde (CHO) + H2O -> COOH releases 2 electrons and 2 H+; NAD+ + 2e- + H+ -> NADH; net produces NADH + 2 H+ alongside the carboxylate. This is stoichiometrically and charge balanced. Aldehyde dehydrogenase-type reactions are strongly favored thermodynamically in the oxidative direction in vivo, typically part of aromatic compound degradation pathways.

errors: The reaction as written is not stoichiometrically balanced for a simple hydration. The conversion of 16-Methoxytabersonine to 16-Methoxy-2,3-dihydro-3-hydroxytabersonine involves addition of a hydroxyl group at C3 and a hydrogen at C2 (saturation of the 2,3-double bond). This is actually a monooxygenase/hydroxylase reaction requiring O2 and NADPH, not a hydratase reaction with water alone.

If treated strictly as hydration (H2O addition across the C2-C3 double bond), the atoms could balance, but the actual enzymatic step (T16H2/3-hydroxylase in vindoline biosynthesis) consumes O2 and NADPH and produces NADP+ and H2O, which are missing.
rxn04087.other_comments: This corresponds to a step in the vindoline/vindorosine biosynthetic pathway in Catharanthus roseus, converting 16-methoxytabersonine to its 3-hydroxy-2,3-dihydro derivative. In vivo this is catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 (a hydroxylase), so the biological direction is toward the hydroxylated product.

rxn01990.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 5-dehydro-4-deoxy-D-glucarate dehydratase/aldolase (EC 4.1.2.20), part of the D-glucarate/galactarate degradation pathway. 5-Dehydro-4-deoxy-D-glucarate (a 6-carbon dicarboxylic acid sugar, C6H8O7) is cleaved into pyruvate (C3H4O3) and tartronate semialdehyde (C3H4O4). Carbon count: 6 = 3 + 3, balanced. The C, H, and O atoms balance correctly. This is a lyase (aldol cleavage) reaction; physiologically it operates in the degradative (forward) direction to channel carbon into central metabolism.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: with 2 NADPH and 3 H+ consumed producing 2 NADP+, the proton balance is off. The standard fatty acid elongation step (condensation + reduction + dehydration + reduction) consumes 2 NADPH + 2 H+ and releases 2 NADP+, H2O, CO2, and CoA. The 3.0 H+ should be 2.0 H+.
The product NADP should be written as NADP+ (oxidized form) to be explicit; as written 'NADP' is ambiguous but presumably NADP+.
rxn10733.other_comments: This represents a methylmalonyl-CoA-dependent chain elongation (mycocerosic-type/PKS-like or methyl-branched FAS) step: a penta-methyl C28 substrate is extended by a methylmalonyl-CoA unit (Claisen condensation releasing CO2, then ketoreduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction using 2 NADPH) to give the hexa-methyl C30 product. Carbon balance (C28 acid + 3-carbon contribution from methylmalonyl-CoA minus decarboxylation -> C30 plus extra methyl branch) is consistent. The main issue is proton stoichiometry.

For 2-hydroxycyclohexan-1-one (C6H10O2) + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> product + H2O + NADP+, the product should be C6H10O3 (a 7-membered lactone bearing the hydroxyl). The named product '1-Oxa-2-oxo-3-hydroxycycloheptane' (a 7-membered ring lactone with a hydroxyl) corresponds to C6H10O3, which balances C, H, and O correctly.
Charge/proton accounting: as written with NADP (not NADP+) and H+ on the left, the net charge balance is consistent if NADP is interpreted as NADP+.
rxn04472.other_comments: This is a Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase (BVMO) type reaction: a flavin/NADPH-dependent monooxygenase oxidizes the cyclic alpha-hydroxy ketone (2-hydroxycyclohexanone) by oxygen insertion to form a 7-membered ring lactone (the named 1-oxa-2-oxo-3-hydroxycycloheptane = 6-membered-to-7-membered ring expansion lactone). The reaction consumes NADPH, O2, and H+ and releases NADP+ and water.

The reaction as written does not balance, since cleavage of the carbamate ester bond should release the bipiperidine moiety along with CO2 or as a carbamic acid intermediate.
Mass/atom balance cannot be satisfied with the stated products.
rxn12030.other_comments: This represents the carboxylesterase-catalyzed hydrolysis of irinotecan (NPC/CPT-11) to its active metabolite SN-38. Such ester/carbamate hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, hence forward direction. However, the leaving-group product is misidentified.

rxn07521.other_comments: This reaction represents the non-enzymatic (or epoxide hydrolase-independent) isomerization/rearrangement of phenanthrene-9,10-oxide (an arene oxide) to 9-phenanthrol (9-hydroxyphenanthrene) via the NIH shift mechanism. Both species are C14H10O, so the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced as a simple intramolecular rearrangement. The aromatization to the phenol is strongly thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn03351.other_comments: This reaction describes a flavonol glycosyltransferase (UDP-rhamnose:flavonol-3-O-glucoside rhamnosyltransferase, e.g. EC 2.4.1.159). It transfers an L-rhamnosyl group from UDP-L-rhamnose to the 3-O-glucoside of a flavonol. Isotrifoliin (quercetin 3-O-glucoside, isoquercitrin) is rhamnosylated to form rutin (quercetin 3-O-rutinoside), releasing UDP. Note: isotrifoliin is sometimes used to denote kaempferol 7-O-glucoside, but in this rutin-producing context it refers to quercetin 3-O-glucoside (isoquercitrin). The stoichiometry is balanced: a rhamnose unit is transferred and UDP plus H+ are released. The H+ on the substrate side is conventional for charge balance.

rxn06108.other_comments: This represents the reaction between NAD+/NADH and ubiquinone (Q)/ubiquinol (QH2). As written (NAD+ + QH2 -> NADH + H+ + Q), it depicts ubiquinol reducing NAD+, which is the reverse of the physiological Complex I direction. The atoms and charges balance: QH2 + NAD+ yields Q + NADH + H+ (2 electrons and 2 protons transferred, one proton released as H+, one retained on NADH). In vivo, Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) operates in the direction NADH + H+ + Q -> NAD+ + QH2, coupled to proton pumping. Note: the equation as written omits the proton translocation across the membrane, which is the energetically relevant coupling.

rxn03171.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction (UDP-GlcNAc:O-glycosyl-glycoprotein beta-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase) transferring GlcNAc from UDP-GlcNAc to the beta-D-galactosyl residue of a core 2 O-glycan acceptor, producing UDP and the elongated glycoprotein. Mass balance is consistent: one GlcNAc moiety is transferred from UDP-GlcNAc to the galactose via a new beta-1,3 linkage, releasing UDP.

rxn00541.other_comments: This is the threonine aldolase reaction (EC 4.1.2.5). L-Threonine is cleaved into glycine and acetaldehyde via a PLP-dependent aldol cleavage. Stoichiometry is balanced: L-threonine (C4H9NO3) yields glycine (C2H5NO2) plus acetaldehyde (C2H4O), with C, H, N, and O atoms conserved. The enzyme is a retro-aldol reaction and is inherently reversible, though physiological direction depends on substrate availability; aldol condensation (reverse) is often exploited synthetically.

errors: The substrate and product roles appear inverted relative to the reaction name. rxn05084.other_comments: This represents an oxidoreductase acting on the cyclic ether of usnic acid, where NAD(H) couples to formation/cleavage of an ether bond. (S)-usnate is the closed dibenzofuran-type ring, and the named product is the ring-opened biphenyl/bis-phenol acetyl compound. The biological direction depends on whether the enzyme forms the ether (oxidative, NAD+ direction) or cleaves it (reductive, NADH direction); the name says ether-bond-forming but the written equation shows reductive cleavage.

rxn02245.other_comments: This reaction describes the synthesis of willardiine (a non-protein amino acid, 3-(1-uracil)-L-alanine) from uracil and O-acetyl-L-serine, catalyzed by a beta-substituted alanine synthase (cysteine synthase-like enzyme). The transferase transfers the 1-(2-amino-2-carboxyethyl) group from O-acetyl-L-serine to the N1 of uracil, releasing acetate and a proton. The reaction is balanced: O-acetyl-L-serine (C5H9NO4) provides the alanyl moiety, uracil (C4H4N2O2) is the acceptor, yielding willardiine (C7H9N3O4) plus acetate (C2H3O2-) and H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn01393.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 3-dehydro-L-gulonate decarboxylase (also called keto-gulonate decarboxylase, EC 4.1.1.85), part of the L-ascorbate utilization pathway in bacteria such as E. coli (UlaD). 3-Dehydro-L-gulonate (a 6-carbon keto-acid) is decarboxylated to produce L-xylulose (often written as L-lyxulose interchangeably in databases) plus CO2. The proton consumed balances the carboxylate group. Atom and charge balance: 3-dehydro-L-gulonate (C6H9O7-) + H+ yields CO2 (CO2) + L-xylulose (C5H10O5), which balances C6, H10, O7 on both sides. Stoichiometry is correct. [directionality_note] Decarboxylations releasing CO2 are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the decarboxylation direction.

rxn09152.other_comments: This is a phospholipase A2 reaction hydrolyzing the sn-2 ester bond of phosphatidylethanolamine (ditetradecanoyl, i.e., dimyristoyl PE). Water cleaves the sn-2 fatty acyl group, releasing myristic acid (C14:0) and yielding the 1-acyl lysophospholipid (1-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine). The mass and charge balance: one acyl group plus a proton are released along with the free fatty acid. Stoichiometry is balanced.

errors: Naming inconsistency: the reaction is labeled '2-octaprenyl-6-methoxyphenol hydroxylase' implying an 8-prenyl (octaprenyl) substrate, but the metabolites are annotated with '5 repeating units', which corresponds to a pentaprenyl side chain; the prenyl chain length should be consistent.

Atom/mass balance issue as written: addition of a single oxygen atom (0.5 O2) to a phenol to form a benzoquinol (hydroquinone, a dihydroxylated species) requires that the new hydroxyl oxygen and the corresponding hydrogens balance; with a monooxygenase, reducing equivalents (e.g., NAD(P)H + H+) and a second water product are typically required and are missing here.
rxn09570.other_comments: This represents a monooxygenase (hydroxylase) step in ubiquinone biosynthesis, converting 2-octaprenyl-6-methoxyphenol to 2-octaprenyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinol by inserting a hydroxyl group at the para position. Such O2-dependent hydroxylations are essentially irreversible in vivo and proceed in the forward direction.

rxn06592.other_comments: This is a PTS (phosphoenolpyruvate-dependent phosphotransferase system) reaction transferring a phosphoryl group from a phosphohistidine residue on the EIIA/HPr protein component to maltose, producing maltose-6-phosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphoryl group is transferred, maltose becomes maltose-6-phosphate, and protein N-phospho-histidine becomes protein histidine. The reaction couples sugar uptake with phosphorylation. In vivo, PTS-mediated sugar import/phosphorylation is effectively unidirectional toward the phosphorylated sugar.

rxn11601.other_comments: This is the methanol:corrinoid methyltransferase (MtaB-type) reaction, where the methyl group of methanol is transferred to the cobalt of 5-hydroxybenzimidazolylcob(I)amide, generating methyl-cobamide and water. This is the first step of methanol-dependent methanogenesis. In vivo it proceeds toward methylation of the corrinoid (methanol consumption).

rxn01924.other_comments: This is the isobutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction in valine catabolism. It oxidizes isobutyryl-CoA to methacrylyl-CoA (2-methylacrylyl-CoA), transferring two electrons and reducing FAD to FADH2. The stoichiometry is balanced (one FAD reduced per substrate dehydrogenated). In vivo, like other acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, the reaction proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction, with electrons typically passed to ETF rather than free FADH2; representing the cofactor as FADH2 is a simplification but the atom/charge balance holds.

rxn02981.other_comments: This reaction represents 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate lactonase pathway intermediate oxidation. The substrate 2-hydroxy-2-hydropyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate (the hydrated/gem-diol form) is oxidized by NAD+ to 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate (PDC), producing NADH and H+. This is part of the protocatechuate 4,5-cleavage pathway in bacteria (e.g., LigC, 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylic acid dehydrogenase). The atom and charge balance is consistent: oxidation removes 2H (as hydride to NAD+ and a proton), converting the hydrated species to the lactone form. Stoichiometry appears balanced.

For a typical monooxygenase: substrate + O2 + NADH + H+ -> hydroxylated product + H2O + NAD+. Here one oxygen atom goes into product and one into water, but the carbon skeleton change from BPA (gem-dimethyl) to a propanol (hydroxymethyl) means a methyl group was hydroxylated, which is consistent with monooxygenation. Hydrogen balance should be rechecked: NADH(H) + H+ + BPA(16H) + O2 vs H2O(2H) + NAD + product(16H). Left non-cofactor H = 16+1 = 17 (plus NADH transfers H); right = 2 + 16 = 18. Appears off by ~1 H depending on cofactor accounting.
rxn04693.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 / monooxygenase-type reaction converting Bisphenol A into a hydroxymethyl derivative (2,2-bis(4-hydroxyphenyl)-1-propanol), consuming O2 and NADH. The substrate is the well-known endocrine disruptor BPA, and this represents an oxidative biotransformation/detoxification step.

rxn01142.other_comments: This is the creatinase (creatine amidinohydrolase, EC 3.5.3.3) reaction. Creatine is hydrolyzed with water to yield urea and sarcosine (N-methylglycine). The reaction is balanced: creatine (C4H9N3O2) + H2O (H2O) yields urea (CH4N2O) + sarcosine (C3H7NO2). Atom counts balance (C4, H11, N3, O3 on each side). As a hydrolytic amidinohydrolase reaction, it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn11640.other_comments: This reaction (R04978) represents the interconversion between (3Z)-phycoerythrobilin and (3Z)-phycocyanobilin, catalyzed by 15,16-dihydrobiliverdin:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PebB) or related ferredoxin-dependent bilin reductases (FDBRs). As written, both species are isomeric C33H38N4O6 tetrapyrroles, so the reaction is mass/atom balanced. However, the actual enzymatic conversion involves a 2-electron reduction step using reduced ferredoxin and is not a simple isomerization; the standard KEGG R04978 includes reduced/oxidized ferredoxin as cofactors, which are missing here. The biologically relevant direction is the reductive formation of phycoerythrobilin from a precursor, so as written (phycocyanobilin to phycoerythrobilin) it would proceed in the reverse direction.

errors: The reaction shows identical metabolites on both sides without compartment specification; a transport reaction must indicate distinct compartments (e.g., extracellular vs cytoplasm) for both H+ and ala-L-asp-L, otherwise it represents no net change.
rxn12628.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction for the dipeptide L-alanyl-L-aspartate coupled to H+ co-transport. As written, both substrates and products are identical (no compartment tags), making it a null reaction. Atomically the two sides balance trivially, but biologically it is meaningless without compartment annotation like [e] and [c].

rxn00629.other_comments: This reaction represents mannitol 2-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.67), oxidizing D-mannitol to D-fructose with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The stoichiometry is balanced: D-mannitol (C6H14O6) is oxidized to D-fructose (C6H12O6), releasing 2 H (one as H+ and one transferred to NADH as hydride). Atoms and charges balance correctly. Although thermodynamically reversible, in vivo direction depends on organism and metabolic context; many bacteria use it in the reductive direction (fructose to mannitol) for storage, while oxidative direction occurs during mannitol catabolism.

errors: Stoichiometric/mass imbalance: the abbreviation 'DMAP' is ambiguous; if it denotes dimethylallyl phosphate (C5H11O4P), then DMAP -> phosphate (HPO4/H2PO4) + isoprene (C5H8) is unbalanced unless water and protons are accounted for. The correct substrate for isoprene synthase is dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP), which yields isoprene + diphosphate (pyrophosphate, PPi), not a single phosphate.
If the intended substrate is DMAPP, the product should be diphosphate (PPi), not phosphate (Pi).
Charge balance not explicitly shown; phosphate/diphosphate species carry charges at physiological pH.
rxn13774.other_comments: This represents isoprene synthase, which physiologically catalyzes the conversion of dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) to isoprene plus diphosphate. The reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo because volatile isoprene escapes and the elimination is thermodynamically favorable. As written, 'DMAP' likely should be DMAPP and the leaving group should be diphosphate rather than a single phosphate.

rxn07870.other_comments: This is the flavone synthase I (FNS I) reaction, a 2-oxoglutarate/Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenase that converts the flavanone pinocembrin into the flavone chrysin by introducing a C2-C3 double bond. The reaction couples decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate to succinate and CO2 with O2 consumption. Stoichiometry is balanced: pinocembrin (C15H12O4) loses 2 H (one as H2O incorporating an O, the other as H+) to form chrysin (C15H10O4). Atoms and charge balance: O2 (2 O) provides one O to H2O and one to the C2-C3 desaturation/CO2 pathway; carbons balance (5+15 = 1+4+15), oxygens balance (2+5+4 = 1+2+4+4), and hydrogens/charge balance with the released H+.

rxn06854.other_comments: This is a PAPS-dependent sulfotransferase reaction transferring a sulfate group from 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) to digalactosylceramide, producing the sulfated glycolipid and PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate) plus a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: the sulfate moiety is transferred from PAPS to the lipid, with PAP and H+ released. Sulfotransferase reactions using PAPS are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the sulfate-donor direction in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: a single myristoyl transfer reaction should release only 1 H+, not 2.0 H+, unless two acyl transfers occur. The reaction transfers one myristoyl group from Myristoyl-ACP, which should yield 1 ACP and 1 H+ (myristoyl ester formation releases one proton).

Atom balance cannot be fully verified because the substrate/product structures (KDO2-lipid IVA with palmitoleoyl vs cold-adapted KDO2-lipid A) are not given as explicit formulas; the difference should correspond to addition of one myristoyl chain (C14 acyl), loss of one H.
rxn08418.other_comments: This represents LpxM/MsbB-type myristoyl transferase (acyltransferase) action in lipid A biosynthesis, transferring a myristoyl (C14) group from myristoyl-ACP onto KDO2-lipid IVA bearing a palmitoleoyl group (cold-adapted modification, as in LpxP-modified lipid A), producing acylated KDO2-lipid A and releasing holo-ACP. Acyl-ACP-dependent acyltransferases are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving acylation forward.
