The main concern is consistency of carbon/oxygen counts between Pregnanediol (C21H36O2) and 3alpha-Hydroxy-5beta-pregnane-20-one (C21H34O2), which is consistent with a 2-H oxidation. No clear stoichiometric error if formulas match.
rxn03316.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent oxidoreductase (dehydrogenase) reaction interconverting the 20-hydroxyl of pregnanediol with the 20-ketone, producing 3alpha-hydroxy-5beta-pregnan-20-one (pregnanolone/allopregnanolone-type steroid). Such hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase reactions are generally reversible, though the in vivo direction depends on NAD+/NADH ratio and tissue context.

errors: Atom/electron imbalance: standard fatty acid elongation by two carbons (malonyl-ACP condensation) consumes 2 NADPH and yields a saturated acyl-ACP; producing an unsaturated product (Hexadecenoyl-ACP, C16:1) plus consuming 3 NADPH and O2 is inconsistent. A typical elongation cycle to make C16:0 from C14:0 (myristoyl) gives palmitoyl-ACP, not hexadecenoyl-ACP.

Redox/oxygen imbalance: combining a reductive elongation (NADPH-driven) with an O2-dependent desaturation in a single lumped reaction misrepresents the stoichiometry; mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) uses NADPH-dependent reduction but does not typically include an O2-dependent desaturase step in the same condensing reaction.
Charge/proton balance likely incorrect given the mixed reductive and oxidative half-reactions.
rxn09430.other_comments: This is presented as a mitochondrial fatty-acyl-ACP synthase elongation step converting myristoyl-ACP (C14) plus malonyl-ACP into a C16 product with release of CO2, ACP, water and NADP+. The intended chemistry is a 2-carbon elongation cycle (condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction). Biosynthetic elongation runs in the forward (anabolic) direction in vivo.

errors: The substrate should be L-glutamyl 5-phosphate (gamma-glutamyl phosphate), not 'alpha-D-Glutamyl phosphate'. Glutamate is an L-amino acid (chiral center is L, not D), and the phosphate is on the gamma-carboxyl (5-position), not the alpha position. The naming is incorrect.
rxn13072.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by gamma-glutamyl phosphate reductase (glutamate-5-semialdehyde dehydrogenase, ProA), part of proline/ornithine biosynthesis. It reduces L-glutamyl 5-phosphate to L-glutamate 5-semialdehyde, releasing inorganic phosphate. The atom balance is essentially correct: NADPH provides the hydride, the acyl phosphate is reduced to an aldehyde with loss of Pi. As written (from NADPH + glutamyl phosphate to NADP + Pi + semialdehyde), the equation describes the physiological biosynthetic direction. In vivo the flux runs toward glutamate-5-semialdehyde (the direction written here), so 'forward' as written = reductive/biosynthetic direction.

errors: Proton imbalance: the reaction shows 2.0 H+ on the product side, but hydrolysis of 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA to 3-hydroxyisobutyrate and CoA should release only 1 H+ (the carboxylic acid proton balances with the thioester cleavage).
rxn11392.other_comments: This is the 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase reaction (EC 3.1.2.4), part of valine catabolism. The thioester bond is hydrolyzed by water to yield free CoA and 3-hydroxyisobutyrate. Thioester hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolysis direction.

rxn02542.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of atropine (an ester of tropine and tropic acid) by atropine acylhydrolase (atropinesterase, EC 3.1.1.10). Water cleaves the ester bond, yielding tropine and tropate (tropic acid). The reaction is balanced: atropine (C17H23NO3) + H2O yields tropine (C8H15NO) + tropate (C9H9O3-) + H+. Mass and charge balance check out, with the carboxylate of tropate accounting for the released proton.

rxn14177.other_comments: This is a 20-oxidoreductase (aldo-keto reductase type) reaction. The substrate 5alpha-pregnan-20alpha-ol-3-one (allopregnan-20alpha-ol-3-one) has its 20-hydroxyl group oxidized to a ketone, yielding 5alpha-pregnane-3,20-dione (dihydroprogesterone). NADP+ is reduced to NADPH + H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone removes 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH, one as proton). Carbon, hydrogen, and redox balance are correct.

errors: The reaction as written is not charge or proton balanced correctly. The transfer of a phosphate from ATP to adenosine yields ADP + AMP, but this reaction does not release a proton. ATP + Adenosine <=> ADP + AMP is the correct balanced form; the extra H+ on the product side creates a charge imbalance.
rxn00134.other_comments: This is adenosine kinase (ATP:adenosine 5'-phosphotransferase, EC 2.7.1.20), which phosphorylates adenosine to AMP using ATP, producing ADP. Atomically the phosphoryl transfer is balanced (ATP donates a gamma-phosphate to adenosine's 5'-OH), but the inclusion of an extra H+ on the product side introduces a charge imbalance unless the protonation states are specified. Physiologically the reaction strongly favors AMP formation (adenosine salvage).

rxn06453.other_comments: This is the glycogenin autoglucosylation initiation reaction (EC 2.4.1.186). Glycogenin transfers a glucose residue from UDP-glucose to a tyrosine hydroxyl on itself, producing the first glucose unit of the glycogen primer and releasing UDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (one glucosyl transferred, UDP released). In vivo it proceeds toward glucosylation, driven by the energetically favorable cleavage of the UDP-glucose glycosidic bond and continued chain elongation.

rxn03036.other_comments: This is the second step in the uncovering of the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker on lysosomal enzymes. The enzyme N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphodiester alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase (EC 3.1.4.45, the 'uncovering enzyme') hydrolyzes the GlcNAc-phosphodiester bond, releasing N-acetyl-D-glucosamine and exposing the phospho-D-mannose (mannose-6-phosphate) residue on the glycoprotein. The reaction is a hydrolysis: water cleaves the phosphodiester linkage, releasing free GlcNAc, a proton, and leaving the phosphomonoester on mannose. Stoichiometry is balanced: the GlcNAc moiety and its glycosidic phosphate linkage are properly accounted for, with water consumed and H+ produced.

errors: Electron and charge balance issue: the reductive carboxylation of succinyl-CoA to 2-oxoglutarate requires 2 electrons. Reduced ferredoxin typically carries 1 electron, so the balanced reaction should use 2 reduced ferredoxin and produce 2 oxidized ferredoxin. As written with single ferredoxin species, the electrons are not balanced.
Proton balance should be rechecked depending on ferredoxin convention (often 2 H+ consumed for the 2-electron reduction).
rxn05939.other_comments: This is 2-oxoglutarate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (OGOR/KGOR), shown in the reductive (carboxylating) direction forming 2-oxoglutarate from succinyl-CoA and CO2. It is a key enzyme of the reductive TCA cycle. The named direction ('rev') represents reductive carboxylation; physiologically the enzyme is reversible and the direction depends on ferredoxin redox state.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: tetrahymanol (C30H52O) requires only one water addition to squalene (C30H50); H2O + C30H50 = C30H52O, so the atom balance is actually correct for a single cyclization-hydration
rxn02064.other_comments: Supraene is a synonym for squalene (C30H50). Tetrahymanol is a pentacyclic triterpenoid (gammacerane-type) alcohol, C30H52O. The enzyme tetrahymanol synthase (squalene-tetrahymanol cyclase) catalyzes the cyclization of squalene with addition of one water molecule to form tetrahymanol. The reaction H2O + C30H50 -> C30H52O is mass-balanced. In vivo this is a highly exergonic cyclization driving the reaction toward tetrahymanol formation.

errors: Stoichiometric/mass imbalance: a single methyl transfer from S-adenosyl-L-methionine adds one CH2 group (forming a mono-methyl, i.e. 5-C-methyl or 5-methyl derivative), not two methyl groups. The product named 'dTDP-5-dimethyl-L-lyxose' implies addition of two methyl groups, which would require two equivalents of SAM and produce two SAH. As written with 1 SAM -> 1 SAH, the carbon balance does not match a 'dimethyl' product.

Product naming/structure inconsistency: conversion of dTDP-rhamnose (a 6-deoxyhexose) to a 'lyxose' (a pentose) skeleton is chemically inconsistent with a simple methyltransferase reaction; the sugar backbone identity appears altered beyond methylation.
rxn04577.other_comments: This is intended to be a SAM-dependent C-methyltransferase acting on a dTDP-activated deoxysugar, producing SAH, a proton, and a methylated dTDP-sugar. The general format (methyl donor -> methylated acceptor + SAH + H+) is recognizable, but the specific stoichiometry of methyl groups and the sugar identity in the product name are problematic. [directionality_note] SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to release of SAH and the favorable thermodynamics of methyl transfer; written direction (SAM consumed) is correct.

rxn01559.other_comments: This is the flavonol synthase (FLS) reaction, a 2-oxoglutarate/Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenase. It converts the dihydroflavonol taxifolin (dihydroquercetin) to the flavonol quercetin by introducing a C2-C3 double bond. The reaction couples to oxidative decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate, yielding succinate and CO2, with one O2 atom incorporated into succinate/water. Stoichiometry is balanced: substrate loses 2H (desaturation), 2-oxoglutarate is decarboxylated to succinate + CO2, O2 consumed, H2O produced. This dioxygenase reaction is physiologically irreversible (forward).

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: oxidation of pyridoxal (an aldehyde) to a carboxylic acid (4-pyridoxic acid) by NAD+ requires incorporation of water and produces 2 H+, not formation of a lactone. The product 4-pyridoxolactone is formed from 4-pyridoxic acid by a separate lactonase, or pyridoxal is oxidized directly to the lactone by an O2-dependent oxidase (pyridoxal 4-dehydrogenase/oxidase), not NAD+
If the intended product is 4-pyridoxic acid: NAD+ + pyridoxal + H2O <=> NADH + 2 H+ + 4-pyridoxic acid (water missing, H+ count wrong)
If the intended product is 4-pyridoxolactone via the FAD/O2 enzyme (EC 1.1.3.12), NAD+ is the wrong cofactor (O2 should be the acceptor, producing H2O2)
rxn01248.other_comments: This represents NAD-dependent oxidation of pyridoxal in the degradative pyridoxal catabolism pathway. As written it directly yields 4-pyridoxolactone with NADH, but the aldehyde-to-lactone conversion is not balanced (oxygen/hydrogen accounting is incorrect, and water is omitted). The physiological direction is oxidation (forward) under catabolic conditions.

rxn00267.other_comments: This is the glycine dehydrogenase (cytochrome) reaction (EC 1.4.2.1), oxidatively deaminating glycine to glyoxylate with reduction of two cytochrome c. Mass balance: left side has C2H5NO2 (glycine) + H2O contributing C2, N1, O3, H7; right side NH3 + glyoxylate (C2H2O3, as the anion CHOCOO-) + 2 H+. Carbon (2=2), nitrogen (1=1), and oxygen (2+1=3 = 3) balance. Hydrogen: glycine 5 + water 2 = 7 on left; NH3 3 + glyoxylate (CHO-COO- = 2 H) + 2 H+ = 7 on right. Charge balances if cytochrome reduction accounts for the 2 electrons. The reaction is well balanced. ('Glyoxalate' is a spelling variant of glyoxylate.)

rxn04531.other_comments: This reaction (R06699) represents the conversion of Tetracenomycin F2 to Tetracenomycin F1 with release of water, catalyzed by Tetracenomycin F2 cyclase (TcmI, EC 4.2.1.154). It is an intramolecular aldol condensation/cyclization step in the biosynthesis of tetracenomycin C in Streptomyces. The stoichiometry is balanced as the loss of water accompanies the dehydration/cyclization. As a biosynthetic dehydration/cyclization step, it proceeds in the forward direction in vivo.

rxn00309.other_comments: This reaction represents lysine 6-dehydrogenase (EC 1.4.1.18), which oxidatively deaminates the epsilon-amino group of L-lysine. The product is 2-aminoadipate 6-semialdehyde (allysine, the semialdehyde). The reaction first yields an imine intermediate which spontaneously hydrolyzes; the net equation L-lysine + NAD+ + H2O -> allysine + NH3 + NADH + H+ is stoichiometrically balanced for atoms and charge. Although written as oxidative deamination, the enzyme is generally classed as reversible in vitro; in vivo it typically operates in the oxidative (forward) direction.

rxn02802.other_comments: This is the trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase reaction. As written, it shows the oxidative direction: Myristoyl-CoA (tetradecanoyl-CoA, saturated C14) + NADP -> (2E)-tetradecenoyl-CoA (trans-Dec-2-enoyl-CoA, C14) + NADPH + H+. The stoichiometry is balanced (atoms and charge: NADP+ accepts a hydride and a proton is released, consistent with the redox couple). However, in vivo this enzyme operates in the reductive direction (enoyl-CoA reduction during fatty acid elongation/synthesis), reducing the trans-2-enoyl-CoA to the saturated acyl-CoA using NADPH. Therefore relative to how it is written, the biologically favored direction is the reverse.

rxn11768.other_comments: This represents IMP dehydrogenase acting on a thio-substituted substrate analog (6-thioinosine 5'-monophosphate, the active metabolite of azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine). The reaction oxidizes the C2 position, adding an oxygen from water and removing two hydrogens (transferred as hydride to NAD+ plus a proton), converting the inosine analog to a xanthine analog. Atom balance: substrate gains O (from H2O) and loses 2 H overall (one as NADH hydride, one as released H+), consistent with the IMPDH-type dehydrogenation. Stoichiometry is balanced for C, H, O, N, S, P, and charge.

rxn00892.other_comments: This is the GlcNAc kinase (NagK, EC 2.7.1.59) reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the 6-hydroxyl of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, yielding N-acetyl-D-glucosamine 6-phosphate and ADP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: a phosphate group is transferred from ATP to the sugar, releasing ADP and a proton. In vivo, ATP-dependent sugar kinase reactions are essentially irreversible and proceed in the phosphorylation direction.

rxn01321.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of an O-acetyl ester on N-acetyl-O-acetylneuraminate (an O-acetylated sialic acid), catalyzed by sialate O-acetylesterase (EC 3.1.1.53). Water hydrolyzes the acetyl ester bond, releasing acetate (and a proton) and yielding N-acetylneuraminate (Neu5Ac). The stoichiometry is balanced: the O-acetyl group is transferred from the substrate to water, producing free acetate plus the deacetylated sialic acid.

rxn04578.other_comments: This is a prenyltransferase reaction transferring a dimethylallyl group from DMAPP (dimethylallyl diphosphate) onto 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, producing 3-dimethylallyl-4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate and releasing pyrophosphate (PPi) plus a proton. This corresponds to KEGG R06757, an early step in some prenylated phenolic/menaquinone-related or natural product biosynthesis pathways. The stoichiometry is balanced: the prenyl group (C5H9 from DMAPP) is transferred to the aromatic ring with loss of the diphosphate as PPi and release of H+ from the aromatic substitution. Aromatic prenylation via release of inorganic pyrophosphate is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (biosynthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn12193.other_comments: This reaction represents the isomerization step catalyzed by 3-isopropylmalate dehydratase (isopropylmalate isomerase, LeuCD) in the leucine biosynthesis pathway. It converts 2-isopropylmalate to 3-isopropylmalate via the intermediate 2-isopropylmaleate (dehydration followed by rehydration). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written since it is an isomerization (both isomers share formula C7H12O5). In the biosynthetic direction (toward leucine), flux proceeds from 2-isopropylmalate to 3-isopropylmalate, but the enzyme catalyzes a near-equilibrium reversible isomerization.

rxn04819.other_comments: This reaction represents the non-enzymatic (or spontaneous) rearrangement of naphthalene 1,2-oxide (1,2-epoxide) to 2-naphthol via the NIH shift. Both species are single molecules with molecular formula C10H8O, so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as a simple intramolecular isomerization. The epoxide opens and aromatizes to the stable phenol.

rxn06658.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolytic deamidation of a peptidyl-L-glutamine residue to peptidyl-L-glutamate, releasing ammonia (protein-glutamine glutaminase / peptidyl-glutaminase, EC 3.5.1.43/3.5.1.44). The atoms balance: glutamine side chain amide (C(=O)NH2) plus water yields carboxylate (C(=O)OH) plus NH3. Mass and charge are conserved when NH3 is the product (note that at physiological pH the free species is NH4+ and the glutamate carboxylate would be deprotonated, which can introduce a proton/charge imbalance depending on protonation conventions).

errors: Mass imbalance: Heme C is formed by covalent attachment of heme to two cysteine residues of apocytochrome c via thioether bonds; the substrate is the apocytochrome c protein (its Cys residues), not free L-cysteine
Atom/charge imbalance: heme b (Heme, with two vinyl groups) plus protein thiols yields heme c plus released protons; the equation as written does not balance vinyl groups against cysteine thiols
The product should be protein-bound heme c (holocytochrome c), not a free 'Heme C' species
Protons should be products (released upon thioether bond formation), not reactants on the left side
rxn10001.other_comments: This represents cytochrome c heme lyase / heme C synthase activity, which covalently links heme b to the CXXCH motif of apocytochrome c via two thioether bonds with the cysteine thiols. As written it uses free L-cysteine and an undefined 'Heme C', which is not chemically/biologically accurate; the proton stoichiometry and direction are also off.

rxn02096.other_comments: This is the L-glutamate:ethylamine ligase (gamma-glutamylethylamide synthetase) reaction forming L-theanine. ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + phosphate as glutamate and ethylamine are condensed via an amide bond at the gamma-carboxyl. Atom and charge balance check out: ATP + Glu + ethylamine yields ADP + Pi + H+ + theanine. This ligase reaction is driven forward by ATP hydrolysis in vivo for theanine biosynthesis.

rxn03960.other_comments: This is the 2-(S)-hydroxypropyl-CoM dehydrogenase reaction from the bacterial epoxide/propylene metabolism pathway (e.g., Xanthobacter autotrophicus Py2). It oxidizes the secondary alcohol of 2-(S)-hydroxypropyl-CoM to the ketone 2-oxopropyl-CoM using NAD+ as electron acceptor. The reaction is balanced: atoms and charges balance with NAD+ + alcohol giving NADH + H+ + ketone (a 2-electron, 2-proton oxidation releasing one H+ as is standard for NAD-dependent dehydrogenases).

rxn00720.other_comments: This is dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (NADP+), catalyzing the interconversion of uracil and 5,6-dihydrouracil. As written, dihydrouracil is oxidized to uracil with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The reaction is balanced in atoms (uracil C4H4N2O2 + 2[H] = dihydrouracil C4H6N2O2) and charge with the H+ included. In vivo, this enzyme (EC 1.3.1.2, the first step of pyrimidine catabolism) strongly favors the reductive direction, converting uracil to dihydrouracil using NADPH. Thus, relative to the way the reaction is written, the biological direction is the reverse.

errors: Mass imbalance: the substrate 'two linked disaccharide tetrapeptide murein units' represents a glycan chain segment that upon lytic transglycosylase action yields anhydro-MurNAc-containing products plus the remaining chain; producing exactly 2 anhydro-GlcNAc-MurNAc-tetrapeptide monomers from a single linked dimer is not stoichiometrically balanced because each lytic transglycosylase cleavage generates only one new 1,6-anhydro bond per cut, not one per monosaccharide unit

Lytic transglycosylases cleave the beta-1,4 glycosidic bond between MurNAc and GlcNAc with intramolecular formation of a 1,6-anhydro-MurNAc, so the product designation 'N-Acetyl-D-glucosamine(anhydrous)' appears mislabeled; the anhydro ring forms on the muramic acid (MurNAc), not on GlcNAc
rxn08937.other_comments: This represents a murein (peptidoglycan) lytic transglycosylase reaction that cleaves uncrosslinked glycan strands to release 1,6-anhydro-MurNAc disaccharide-tetrapeptide products in the periplasm. Lytic transglycosylases are non-hydrolytic glycosidases that catalyze cleavage with concomitant intramolecular anhydro-ring formation. In vivo this degradative/remodeling step proceeds in the direction of bond cleavage (forward).

rxn02227.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of allysine (L-2-aminoadipate-6-semialdehyde) to L-2-aminoadipate, using NADP+ as the electron acceptor and water as the oxygen source for the carboxylate. This is catalyzed by aminoadipate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (e.g., LYS9/AASS-type activity in the lysine degradation pathway). The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde plus water is oxidized to a carboxylic acid, releasing 2 H+ and 2 electrons captured as NADPH. Atom and charge balance check out (aldehyde CHO + H2O -> COOH + 2H+ + 2e-).

errors: Carbon balance error: 10-methyl-dodecanoyl (C13 acyl) + malonyl (C3 acyl) should give a 3-oxo product with 16 carbons (3-oxo-hexadecanoyl backbone), but the product is named as 12-methyl-3-oxo-tetradecanoyl, which corresponds to a C15 chain (C14 tetradecanoyl + 1 methyl). The product should be 12-methyl-3-oxo-tetradecanoyl only if the substrate were 10-methyl-dodecanoyl (C13: 12 + methyl = 13 C); condensation with malonyl adds 2 C and loses CO2, giving a 15-C acyl. The 'tetradecanoyl' (C14) + methyl = C15 product is consistent. Net atoms appear balanced; methyl branch position shifts from C10 to C12 due to chain extension at carboxyl end, which is correct.
On closer accounting the reaction is actually balanced and consistent; the apparent naming discrepancy resolves correctly.
rxn05375.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (condensing enzyme) step in fatty acid elongation. Malonyl-ACP condenses with the acyl-ACP, releasing CO2 and free ACP, extending the chain by two carbons and adding a 3-oxo group. The branched-methyl numbering shifts from position 10 to 12 because two carbons are added at the carboxyl (thioester) end. The reaction is biologically driven forward by decarboxylation.

rxn00430.other_comments: This is the NAD-dependent oxidation of methanol to formaldehyde (methanol dehydrogenase / alcohol dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.244). The reaction is balanced for atoms and charge: methanol (CH3OH) + NAD+ yields formaldehyde (CH2O) + NADH + H+. Two electrons and two protons are removed from methanol; one proton ends up on NADH (hydride) and one is released. Although written reversibly, in vivo the thermodynamically and physiologically favored direction is methanol oxidation to formaldehyde.

errors: Incorrect product: sarcosine oxidase produces glycine, not glyoxylate
Incorrect amine product: the demethylation yields formaldehyde, not methanamine (methylamine)
Mass/atom imbalance resulting from the wrong products
rxn04093.other_comments: This is sarcosine oxidase (EC 1.5.3.1). The correct reaction is sarcosine + H2O + O2 -> glycine + formaldehyde + H2O2. Sarcosine is N-methylglycine; oxidative demethylation cleaves the N-methyl group to formaldehyde and leaves glycine, with O2 reduced to H2O2. The listed products glyoxylate and methanamine are incorrect.

errors: Stoichiometric/product error: sphingomyelinase (EC 3.1.4.12) hydrolyzes sphingomyelin to ceramide + phosphocholine, not choline + ceramide phosphate. The products listed are inconsistent with the enzyme name and with mass/group balance.

If the intended enzyme is the listed 'ceramide-phosphohydrolase', then phosphocholine should be released (not free choline), and the remaining product should be ceramide. As written, splitting off choline would leave ceramide phosphate, but free choline plus ceramide phosphate does not balance with a single water hydrolysis of the phosphodiester (this would require breaking the other phosphoester bond and would not yield ceramide phosphate plus free choline from one hydrolysis step).
rxn01845.other_comments: This is meant to be sphingomyelin hydrolysis by sphingomyelinase. The correct reaction is: H2O + sphingomyelin -> H+ + phosphocholine + ceramide. The given products (choline + ceramide phosphate) are mislabeled; correct products are phosphocholine + ceramide. Hydrolysis reactions of this type are effectively irreversible (forward) in vivo.

rxn00859.other_comments: This is histidinol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.23), the final step of histidine biosynthesis, catalyzing a four-electron oxidation of L-histidinol to L-histidine via the aldehyde intermediate. It uses 2 NAD+ and 1 H2O. Mass and charge balance check: C atoms (histidinol C6H11N3O = 6, histidine C6H9N3O2 = 6), the reaction consumes 2 NAD+ and water and produces 2 NADH plus 3 H+, which balances hydrogen and charge correctly. The reaction is stoichiometrically correct.

rxn11720.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of lignoceroyl-CoA (a C24:0 fatty acyl-CoA, tetracosanoyl-CoA) by a thioesterase, yielding free CoA and tetracosanoate (lignocerate, the C24:0 carboxylate). The stoichiometry is balanced: water hydrolyzes the thioester bond, producing the free fatty acid and CoA-SH, with release of a proton consistent with the carboxylate being deprotonated at physiological pH. Lignocerate and tetracosanoate are synonyms for the same C24 saturated fatty acid.

rxn03707.other_comments: This is the ring-cleavage reaction catalyzed by chlorocatechol 1,2-dioxygenase (intradiol dioxygenase, EC 1.13.11.x) in the modified ortho-cleavage pathway for degradation of chloroaromatics. O2 incorporates both oxygen atoms into the substrate, cleaving the catechol ring between the two hydroxyl-bearing carbons to yield the cis,cis-muconate derivative. Stoichiometry balances: 3,5-dichlorocatechol (C6H4Cl2O2) plus O2 gives 2,4-dichloro-cis,cis-muconate (C6H2Cl2O4 as the dianion) plus 2 H+. Atoms and charge balance correctly (the two carboxylate protons released account for the 2 H+).

errors: Oxygen mass imbalance: left side has O2 (2 O atoms) plus the phenol's hydroxyl O, right side has H2O (1 O) plus the hydroquinone's two hydroxyl O atoms; the dechlorination/hydroxylation with O2 reduction needs careful balancing. 2,4,6-trichlorophenol (C6H3Cl3O) being converted to 2,6-dichlorohydroquinone (C6H4Cl2O2) requires replacement of one Cl by OH; one O from O2 is incorporated, the other reduced to water. With 2 NADH consumed only 1 O2 should yield H2O plus incorporated O, which balances; check H: left NADH(2H from 2 NADH as hydride+) + 2 H+ ... overall H appears slightly off but within typical formulation.
Charge balance should be verified: NAD shown without charge (should be NAD+); product Cl- is anionic so a proton balance is needed.
rxn03749.other_comments: This is a flavin/monooxygenase-type reductive dehalogenation of 2,4,6-trichlorophenol (TCP) to 2,6-dichlorohydroquinone (chlorophenol 4-monooxygenase, TcpA-type), using O2 and NADH, releasing chloride. The general chemistry (oxidative para-dechlorination/hydroxylation) is correct in concept.

rxn03215.other_comments: This is the protopine synthase (CYP82N2v2 / P450-type monooxygenase) reaction converting (S)-cis-N-methylstylopine to protopine. It is a cytochrome P450-catalyzed oxidative reaction (14-hydroxylation/ring rearrangement) consuming NADPH and O2, producing protopine, NADP+, and H2O. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 provide the reducing equivalents and oxygen for the monooxygenation, with one oxygen atom going to water and the substrate being oxidized. As a P450 monooxygenase reaction, it is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn11761.other_comments: This is a kinase (phosphotransferase) reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to floxuridine (5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine), producing FdUMP (5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate), ADP, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP donates a phosphate to the 5'-hydroxyl of floxuridine, and the released H+ accounts for the proton balance from the phosphoester bond formation. This is the activation step relevant to 5-FU/floxuridine antimetabolite metabolism, where FdUMP inhibits thymidylate synthase. Kinase reactions of this type are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the phosphorylation direction in vivo.

rxn07580.other_comments: This is the octanoyltransferase (LipB) reaction transferring an octanoyl group from octanoyl-ACP to a specific lysine residue of the lipoyl-domain apoprotein, releasing holo-ACP and a proton. The substrate Apoprotein has its lysine epsilon-amino group acylated to form Protein N6-(octanoyl)lysine; the freed sulfhydryl of ACP and the released proton balance reasonably given the thioester-to-amide conversion. Stoichiometry is plausible if Apoprotein and Protein are treated as the same polypeptide differing only by the octanoyl-lysine modification.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: oxidation of isethionate (HOCH2-CH2-SO3-) to sulfoacetaldehyde (OHC-CH2-SO3-) removes 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons), but the reaction as written must also balance oxygen and hydrogen. Isethionate C2H5O4S yields sulfoacetaldehyde C2H3O4S, a difference of 2 H, which matches the 2 H+ and 2 electrons accepted by 2 cytochrome c. Atom balance is actually correct.
Charge balance check: 2 Cyt c3+ (+6) + isethionate (-1) = +5 on left; 2 H+ (+2) + 2 Cyt c2+ (+4) + sulfoacetaldehyde (-1) = +5 on right. Charge is balanced. No errors found.
rxn04790.other_comments: This represents isethionate dehydrogenase (IslA/IseJ type) coupling oxidation of isethionate to sulfoacetaldehyde with reduction of cytochrome c. The reaction is correctly balanced for both mass and charge. Physiologically it proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction during isethionate catabolism.

rxn02157.other_comments: This is a gibberellin 2-beta-hydroxylase (GA 2-oxidase) type reaction, a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase. It consumes O2 and 2-oxoglutarate, producing CO2 and succinate while hydroxylating the gibberellin substrate (GA1 to GA8). The stoichiometry is balanced: one O2 atom is incorporated into the hydroxyl group of the product, the other into CO2 from decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate. 2-Oxoglutarate (C5H6O5) + O2 yields succinate (C4H6O4) + CO2, accounting for the consumed oxygen and carbon. These dioxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible due to the decarboxylation step.

errors: Charge imbalance: left side has NADH (2-) x2, H+, Cl- absent on left; right side has NAD (-1) x2 and Cl-. Net charge does not balance.

Hydrogen/atom balance issue: the conversion of 2,5-dichlorohydroquinone (C6H4Cl2O2) to 5-chloro-1,2,4-trihydroxybenzene (C6H5ClO3) replaces one Cl with OH (hydroxylation/dehalogenation), but the H and O accounting with O2, H2O and 2 NADH needs verification - as written it does not cleanly balance.
Stoichiometry of reducing equivalents: a monooxygenase hydroxylative dehalogenation typically uses 1 NAD(P)H + O2, not 2 NADH; using 2.0 NADH likely overcounts reducing power.
rxn03746.other_comments: This is a hydroxylative/oxygenolytic dehalogenation: 2,5-dichlorohydroquinone is converted to 5-chloro-1,2,4-trihydroxybenzene (chlorohydroxyquinol), releasing chloride, consuming O2 and NADH. The overall transformation (oxygenase replacing Cl with OH) is essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn07346.other_comments: This is the hydrolytic cleavage step in nicotine degradation (e.g., Arthrobacter nicotinovorans pathway). 2,6-Dihydroxypseudooxynicotine is hydrolyzed by 2,6-dihydroxypseudooxynicotine hydrolase to yield 2,6-dihydroxypyridine and 4-methylaminobutyrate (also called gamma-N-methylaminobutyrate). The reaction consumes water and cleaves a C-C bond beta to the carbonyl. Atom balance: substrate (C12H18N2O3) + H2O yields 2,6-dihydroxypyridine (C5H5NO2) + 4-methylaminobutyrate (C5H11NO2, as the anion C5H10NO2-) + H+. The charge and mass balance with the released proton is consistent. Hydrolases of this type are effectively irreversible in vivo.

errors: Atom/mass imbalance: nine rounds of fatty acid elongation by malonyl-ACP add 9 x C2 = 18 carbons, so a C38 acyl-ACP should yield a C56 acyl-ACP, not C58. The product designation (C58) is inconsistent with 9 malonyl-ACP additions from a C38 substrate.

Redox stoichiometry imbalance: each elongation cycle (condensation, ketoreduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction) consumes 2 reducing equivalents per cycle, i.e. 9 cycles require 18 NAD(P)H total. Here only 9 NADH + 9 NADPH = 18 are provided, which is the correct count, but the H+ balance (18 H+ consumed vs none released) needs checking against the standard FAS reaction; typically 18 H+ are consumed, so this part may be acceptable.
Charge/proton balance should be re-verified given the carbon discrepancy.
rxn13461.other_comments: This represents a multi-step type-I/mycobacterial FAS or PKS-like meromycolate elongation, condensing 9 malonyl-ACP units onto a cis-19,cis-37-C38 acyl-ACP with concomitant CO2 release and NAD(P)H-dependent reduction, producing a longer-chain acyl-ACP and free ACP. Such biosynthetic elongations are physiologically irreversible (driven by decarboxylation and reduction).

rxn13960.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.188) transferring a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the 6-O position of betanidin, producing gomphrenin I and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: the glucose moiety is transferred from UDP-glucose to betanidin, conserving atoms. A proton (H+) may technically be released but is often omitted. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugars are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic (glucosylation) direction due to cleavage of the high-energy UDP-glucose bond.

rxn04625.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the 7-O position of quercetin, forming quercimeritrin (quercetin 7-O-glucoside), UDP, and a proton. Stoichiometry is balanced: UDP-glucose provides the glucose moiety, the glycosidic bond formation releases UDP and a proton. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugars are thermodynamically favorable in the direction of glycoside formation due to the high-energy nucleotide-sugar bond, so in vivo it proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn02593.other_comments: This is the phthalate 4,5-dioxygenase reaction. It is a Rieske-type aromatic ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase that incorporates both atoms of O2 into the substrate, forming the cis-dihydrodiol (phthalate 4,5-cis-dihydrodiol) while oxidizing NADH to NAD+. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADH provides the 2 electrons and protons needed for reductive activation of O2, and both oxygen atoms end up in the cis-diol product. Such dioxygenase reactions are physiologically irreversible (forward) due to the irreversible reductive activation of molecular oxygen.

rxn01551.other_comments: This is the histamine N-acetyltransferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.5), transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the primary amine of histamine, producing N-acetylhistamine (4-(beta-acetylaminoethyl)imidazole) plus CoA and a proton. The atoms balance: acetyl-CoA donates the acetyl group to histamine's amine, releasing free CoA and H+. Acetyltransferase reactions of this type are thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy thioester bond and are physiologically essentially irreversible in the acetylation direction.

rxn01027.other_comments: This is dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (NAD+) acting on dihydrothymine. The reaction as written shows oxidation of dihydrothymine to thymine with reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Stoichiometry is balanced: dihydrothymine (C5H8N2O2) + NAD+ -> thymine (C5H6N2O2) + NADH + H+. In vivo, the physiological direction of pyrimidine catabolism is the reduction of thymine to dihydrothymine (using NADPH typically by DPD), so the catabolic flux runs opposite to the way written here, favoring dihydrothymine formation.

errors: Incorrect water stoichiometry: full fatty acid elongation cycles should release 5 H2O for the dehydration steps but the overall mass/oxygen balance must be checked - actually 5 dehydration steps yield 5 H2O which is consistent

The reaction lumps 5 cycles of fatty acid elongation but a beta-ketoacyl synthase only catalyzes the condensation (Claisen) step, not the full reductive cycle; the name is inconsistent with the multi-step chemistry shown (condensation + ketoreduction + dehydration + enoyl reduction)
NADPH stoichiometry: 5 elongation cycles require 2 NADPH each = 10 NADPH, which is consistent
CO2 stoichiometry: 5 malonyl-ACP condensations release 5 CO2, consistent; ACP released = 5, consistent
rxn13669.other_comments: This represents the net elongation of C5:0-ACP to C15:0-ACP via 5 rounds of fatty acid synthesis (each adding a C2 unit from malonyl-ACP). Atom balance: carbon: 5(C5 ACP) start + 5 malonyl(3C each in the acyl portion) = adds 5x2C = 10C net (after 5 CO2 loss), giving C15, consistent. The main issue is that the enzyme label (beta-ketoacyl synthase) only catalyzes condensation, while the written reaction is the full FAS reductive cycle lumped together.

rxn04858.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (epoxygenase, e.g. CYP2C/CYP2J) catalyzed monooxygenation of arachidonate. Arachidonate (C20H32O2) is epoxidized at the 5,6 double bond to form 5,6-EET (5,6-epoxyeicosatrienoic acid, C20H32O3). One atom of O2 is incorporated into the product as the epoxide oxygen, and the other oxygen atom is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Mass and charge balance: NADPH + O2 + H+ + C20H32O2 -> H2O + NADP+ + C20H32O3. Carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and charge all balance correctly.

rxn00130.other_comments: This is the AMP deaminase (AMP aminohydrolase, EC 3.5.4.6) reaction, hydrolytically deaminating AMP to IMP. The reaction is correctly balanced: H2O + AMP (C10H12N5O7P) + H+ yields NH3 (as NH4+) + IMP (C10H11N4O8P). Mass and charge balance hold when accounting for the proton consumed and ammonium produced. In vivo this hydrolytic deamination is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the forward direction.

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: nebularine (purine riboside, 9-beta-D-ribofuranosylpurine) reacting with PPi should yield a ribonucleotide 5'-monophosphate plus orthophosphate (Pi), but the masses do not balance as written. PPi (P2O7) minus one phosphate group transferred to the nucleoside leaves Pi, which is consistent, but the product 'Purine mononucleotide' is ambiguous and the proton balance is questionable.
Ambiguous product: 'Purine mononucleotide' is not a defined species; it should be specified as the 5'-monophosphate of nebularine (purine ribonucleoside 5'-phosphate).
rxn06458.other_comments: This represents a diphosphate:purine nucleoside phosphotransferase reaction, where pyrophosphate acts as a phosphoryl donor to phosphorylate the nucleoside nebularine (a purine riboside lacking the typical 6-amino/oxo substituent), producing the corresponding nucleoside monophosphate and releasing orthophosphate. The transfer of a phosphoryl from PPi to the 5'-OH of the ribose is the intended chemistry.

rxn10501.other_comments: This reaction represents an oxidative deamination of 3,7-dideoxy-D-threo-hepto-2-amino-6-ulosonate, converting the C2 amino group to a keto group (forming the 2,6-diulosonate). It is part of the methanogenesis/coenzyme biosynthesis pathway (related to methanofuran biosynthesis). The stoichiometry is balanced: NAD+ accepts a hydride (forming NADH + H+), water provides oxygen, and ammonia is released from the amine. Atoms (C, H, N, O) and charges balance correctly for a transamination/deamination coupled to NAD reduction.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: the reverse of an aminotransferase reaction should be an oxidative deamination-type conversion. LL-2,6-diaminopimelate to tetrahydrodipicolinate requires loss of an amino group and cyclization, which is a transamination producing a 2-amino-6-oxopimelate intermediate, not directly tetrahydrodipicolinate. The shown reaction conflates transamination with the subsequent dehydratase/cyclization step.

Atom balance issue: tetrahydrodipicolinate (C7H7NO4 as 2,3,4,5-tetrahydrodipicolinate) plus glutamate plus water does not balance with 2-oxoglutarate plus LL-DAP. The single transamination should yield L-2-amino-6-oxoheptanedioate (a linear oxo acid), with cyclization/dehydration releasing water separately.
Water appears on the product side but a simple transamination does not release water.
rxn07441.other_comments: This corresponds to the DapL/LL-DAP aminotransferase pathway in reverse. The enzyme normally transfers an amino group from glutamate to a tetrahydrodipicolinate-derived oxo acid to form LL-DAP during lysine biosynthesis. As written (LL-DAP -> tetrahydrodipicolinate), it represents the catabolic/reverse direction; in vivo the biosynthetic direction (forming LL-DAP) is favored.

rxn07905.other_comments: This is a CoA ligase (acyl-CoA synthetase) reaction activating 4-fluorobenzoate to 4-fluorobenzoyl-CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + carboxylic acid yields acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi + H+. This is the standard adenylate-forming mechanism (releasing AMP and PPi rather than ADP and Pi). Mass and charge balance check out, with the H+ released accounting for the deprotonation upon thioester formation. In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible toward acyl-CoA synthesis.

rxn04744.other_comments: This reaction represents the NAD-dependent oxidation of an aldehyde (4-hydroxymethylsalicylaldehyde) to its corresponding carboxylic acid (4-hydroxymethylsalicylate), catalyzed by an aldehyde dehydrogenase. The stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde group (-CHO) plus water is oxidized to a carboxylate (-COO-), with NAD reduced to NADH and release of 2 H+. Atom and charge balance are consistent (one hydride transferred to NAD, one proton released from water addition, and accounting for the carboxylate anion). Aldehyde dehydrogenase reactions are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the oxidative direction.

errors: Charge imbalance: the left side has a net +1 charge from the explicit H+, while the products (H2O2 and Rifamycin O) are neutral; the proton should not appear as a free reactant in this oxidase reaction

Hydrogen/atom balance issue: oxidation of Rifamycin B to Rifamycin O removes 2 H (from the hydroquinone/glycolic moiety); the balanced reaction is Rifamycin B + O2 -> Rifamycin O + H2O2, with no separate free H+ needed
rxn02653.other_comments: This is the rifamycin-B oxidase reaction, which oxidizes Rifamycin B to Rifamycin O using molecular oxygen and producing hydrogen peroxide. As an O2-dependent oxidase reaction, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (oxidation) direction.

rxn08919.other_comments: This is the MsrB (methionine sulfoxide reductase B) reaction, which reduces L-methionine-R-sulfoxide back to L-methionine using reduced thioredoxin (trdrd) as the electron donor. The products are water, L-methionine, and oxidized thioredoxin (trdox). The stoichiometry is balanced: the proton and reduced thioredoxin provide the reducing equivalents to remove the oxide oxygen as water. In vivo this proceeds in the reductive (forward) direction as written, repairing oxidized methionine residues.

rxn02185.other_comments: This reaction represents the reversal of the acetolactate synthase (ALS) decarboxylation/condensation step. Written left-to-right, TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) plus 2-acetolactate (ALCTT) yields pyruvate plus 2-hydroxyethyl-ThPP (the resonance-stabilized enamine/carbanion intermediate, often written as alpha-lactyl-ThPP or hydroxyethyl-ThPP). Stoichiometry is balanced as a lyase reaction where ALCTT is cleaved to release one pyruvate, leaving the two-carbon acetaldehyde-derived unit on TPP. Note: the enzyme name says 'carboxylating' but the lyase mechanism is non-carboxylating (C-C bond cleavage), so the annotation is slightly misleading. In vivo, acetolactate synthase strongly favors acetolactate formation (the reverse of this written direction) because the physiological flux is condensation of two pyruvate molecules.

rxn02612.other_comments: This is a dehydration (hydro-lyase) reaction in the ergosterol biosynthesis pathway. The C-5 hydroxyl group of 5alpha-Ergosta-7,22-diene-3beta,5-diol is eliminated along with a hydrogen from C-6 to form a 5,6-double bond, yielding ergosterol and releasing water. Both sides have one steroid molecule, and removal of one OH plus one H accounts for the loss of one H2O, so the reaction is mass-balanced. EC 4.2.1.- type C5 sterol desaturase/dehydratase step (ERG3-related chemistry). Dehydration leading to conjugated diene formation drives the reaction in the direction of ergosterol production.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the reduction of a ketone to an alcohol by NADPH consumes one H+, not two. The balanced form should be NADPH + H+ + Cinchoninone <=> NADP+ + Cinchonine.
rxn14101.other_comments: This is a ketoreductase reaction: Cinchoninone (a ketone) is reduced by NADPH to Cinchonine (a secondary alcohol), with NADPH oxidized to NADP+. Cinchonine and cinchonidine are diastereomeric reduction products of cinchoninone in Cinchona alkaloid biosynthesis. Thermodynamically, NADPH-dependent carbonyl reductions strongly favor the reduction (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn00819.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of galactosylglycerol (a galactoside) by galactosylglycerol galactohydrolase (EC 3.2.1.22, alpha-galactosidase activity), cleaving the glycosidic bond with water to yield free glycerol and galactose. The stoichiometry is balanced: galactosylglycerol (C9H18O8) + H2O (H2O) yields galactose (C6H12O6) + glycerol (C3H8O3). Hydrolysis reactions of glycosides are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the hydrolytic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: The reaction shows identical species (H+ and gly-asn-L) on both sides without compartment designations; a proton symport transport reaction must specify distinct compartments (e.g., extracellular vs cytosol) for both the proton and the dipeptide. As written, it is a null reaction with no net change and no transport occurring.
rxn12542.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction for the glycyl-L-asparagine dipeptide coupled to proton symport across a membrane. The chemistry is balanced trivially (same on both sides), but the lack of compartment labels (such as gly-asn-L[e] + H+[e] <=> gly-asn-L[c] + H+[c]) makes it meaningless as a transport process. With proper compartments, proton symport peptide uptake is typically driven inward (extracellular to cytosol) by the proton motive force.

errors: The reaction name refers to 'coenzyme F430 precursor synthase' but the substrate is named 'coenzyme F390 precursor 1', which is inconsistent (F390 vs F430). This likely indicates a naming/identifier error in either the substrate or the enzyme name.

Charge and mass balance cannot be confirmed without explicit molecular formulas for the precursor metabolites; the proton stoichiometry (2 H+) should be verified against the actual redox half-reaction (a typical NADH-dependent two-electron reduction consumes NADH + 1 H+, releasing NAD+).
rxn10509.other_comments: This is presented as an NADH-dependent reductive step in the biosynthesis of coenzyme F430 (the nickel-containing cofactor of methyl-coenzyme M reductase). NADH is oxidized to NAD+ while a precursor is reduced. Such NAD(P)H-driven reductions in cofactor biosynthesis are typically physiologically irreversible in the reductive (forward) direction.

errors: Acyl-CoA carboxylase reactions require ATP and bicarbonate (HCO3-), not free CO2; the correct mechanism is ATP + HCO3- + acyl-CoA -> ADP + Pi + carboxy-acyl-CoA
Missing ATP substrate
Missing ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) products
Free CO2 should be HCO3- (bicarbonate) as the carboxyl donor
Charge and atom balance cannot be satisfied as written; the spurious H+ on the product side does not balance the missing ATP hydrolysis components
rxn13423.other_comments: This represents a biotin-dependent carboxylation of a very-long-chain acyl-CoA (hexacosanoyl-CoA, C26) to form a malonyl-CoA-like 2-carboxy derivative. As written it is unbalanced because carboxylases use ATP-driven carboxylation from bicarbonate rather than direct addition of CO2. In vivo such ATP-coupled carboxylations proceed in the carboxylation (forward) direction.

errors: Atom imbalance: 13(S)-HPOT (13(S)-hydroperoxy-9(Z),11(E),15(Z)-octadecatrienoic acid, C18H30O4) cleaves into cis-3-hexenal (C6H10O) and 12-oxo-9(Z)-dodecenoic acid (C12H20O3); summing products gives C18H30O4, which actually balances. However the listed product '3-Hexenal' should specify the (Z)/cis-3-hexenal isomer for biological accuracy
rxn07660.other_comments: This is the hydroperoxide lyase (HPL) reaction acting on 13(S)-hydroperoxylinolenic acid (13-HPOT), cleaving the carbon-carbon bond to yield (Z)-3-hexenal and 12-oxo-(Z)-9-dodecenoic acid. The reaction is a lyase cleavage that is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding strongly in the forward (cleavage) direction in the green leaf volatile / oxylipin pathway.

rxn13251.other_comments: This represents the fumarate-dependent dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (class 1B DHODH) reaction, where dihydroorotate is oxidized to orotate while fumarate serves as the terminal electron acceptor, being reduced to succinate. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: dihydroorotate (C5H6N2O4) loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) to become orotate (C5H4N2O4), and fumarate (C4H4O4) gains 2 H to become succinate (C4H6O4). Atoms and charges balance. In vivo, this is part of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis and proceeds in the direction of orotate formation.

rxn05725.other_comments: This is a transport reaction (proton symport) for 2-aminoethylphosphonic acid (ciliatine). The notation shows H+ and Ciliatine on both sides, representing the same species moving across a membrane (extracellular to intracellular compartments). Stoichiometrically it is balanced (1:1 symport of H+ with ciliatine). Although written as reversible, proton symport import is typically driven forward (into the cell) by the proton motive force in vivo; however, without compartment labels the directionality defaults to reversible as written.

errors: The reaction has identical substrates and products (D-Alanine + Na+ on both sides), so there is no net chemical transformation; this is not a valid metabolic reaction as written
rxn13660.other_comments: This appears to be intended as a sodium-coupled symport transport reaction for D-Alanine across a membrane. However, as written, both sides of the equation are identical (D-Alanine + Na+), so it lacks compartment annotations (e.g., extracellular vs cytosolic) that are required to represent transport. A proper symport would be: D-Alanine[out] + Na+[out] <=> D-Alanine[in] + Na+[in].

errors: Stoichiometric/atom imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance. Nicotinamide riboside kinase phosphorylates nicotinamide riboside (NR) to give nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), not free nicotinamide + D-Ribose. The correct reaction is ATP + nicotinamide riboside -> ADP + nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN). The listed substrates (D-Ribose + Nicotinamide) are not joined and no glycosidic bond formation is catalyzed by a kinase.
Spurious H2O product: a kinase phosphotransfer reaction does not release water; phosphate is transferred from ATP to the hydroxyl acceptor.
Wrong substrate: should be nicotinamide riboside (a single molecule), not separate nicotinamide and ribose.
rxn11355.other_comments: The reaction is labeled nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK/NMRK, EC 2.7.1.22/2.7.1.173), which transfers a phosphate from ATP to the 5' hydroxyl of nicotinamide riboside to form NMN + ADP. As written here the substrates are incorrect (free nicotinamide + ribose instead of nicotinamide riboside) and an erroneous H2O is produced.

rxn02694.other_comments: This is the blasticidin-S deaminase (aminohydrolase) reaction, which hydrolytically deaminates blasticidin S to deaminohydroxyblasticidin S, releasing ammonia. The reaction consumes water and converts the amino/amidine group to a hydroxyl group (deamination), producing ammonia. Stoichiometrically, one water is consumed and one ammonia released, which balances the conversion of an amino group to a hydroxyl. The H+ accounting is approximately reasonable for an aqueous deamination. As a detoxification/hydrolytic deamination, this reaction proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward (deaminating) direction in vivo.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: the reaction as written likely does not balance protons correctly. The N5-CAIR forming reaction (PurK, the ATPase subunit) typically is written as AIR + ATP + HCO3- -> N5-CAIR + ADP + Pi with 1 H+ released, not 3 H+. Using CO2 instead of HCO3- changes the proton/water balance.
rxn12362.other_comments: This is the PurK reaction (N5-carboxyaminoimidazole ribonucleotide synthetase, the ATP-dependent subunit of the bacterial AIR carboxylase system). It converts AIR plus bicarbonate/CO2 to N5-CAIR (5-phosphoribosyl-5-carboxyaminoimidazole) using ATP. The substrate is normally bicarbonate (HCO3-) rather than CO2.

rxn09931.other_comments: This is an ATP-dependent L-amino acid ligase (Lal/RizA-type) forming the dipeptide L-alanyl-L-histidine (Ala-His) from L-alanine and L-histidine. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi (with release of H+) coupling peptide bond formation. Mass and charge balance hold (one peptide bond forms releasing water equivalent captured in the ADP+Pi+H+ products). ATP-dependent ligation drives the reaction toward dipeptide synthesis in vivo.

rxn00186.other_comments: This is the 5-oxoprolinase reaction (EC 3.5.2.9), where 5-oxo-L-proline (pyroglutamate) is hydrolytically opened to L-glutamate, driven by ATP hydrolysis to ADP + phosphate. The stoichiometry balances: 5-oxoproline (C5H6NO3-) + 2 H2O + ATP yields L-glutamate (C5H8NO4-) + ADP + Pi + H+. Atoms (C, N, P) and charge balance. The ATP-driven hydrolysis makes this effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding toward glutamate formation.

rxn02638.other_comments: This reaction represents bile acid conjugation catalyzed by bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase (BAAT). Glycine attacks the thioester bond of choloyl-CoA, releasing CoA and forming the amide-linked conjugate glycocholate, with release of a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: glycine (C2H5NO2) + choloyl-CoA yields CoA-SH + glycocholate (C26H42NO6-, the amide product) + H+. Mass and charge balance are consistent. In vivo, this thioester-to-amide conjugation is thermodynamically favorable and physiologically drives bile acid conjugation in the forward direction.

rxn00007.other_comments: This is trehalase (alpha,alpha-trehalose glucohydrolase, EC 3.2.1.28), which hydrolyzes the non-reducing disaccharide trehalose (TRHL, alpha,alpha-trehalose, C12H22O11) using one water molecule to yield two molecules of D-glucose. The stoichiometry is balanced: trehalose (C12H22O11) + H2O (H2O) gives 2 glucose (2 x C6H12O6 = C12H24O12), with C12H22O11 + H2O = C12H24O12 confirming mass and atom balance.

errors: D-Gulitol (D-glucitol/D-sorbitol) is not the correct substrate to produce L-sorbose; L-sorbose is formed by oxidation of D-sorbitol (D-glucitol) at C5, but the proper substrate-product relationship and naming is inconsistent. The enzyme name 'L-sorbitol dehydrogenase' is a misnomer since sorbitol exists as D-glucitol; however, the C5 oxidation of D-sorbitol does yield L-sorbose, so the substrate-product pairing is actually chemically valid.
rxn09395.other_comments: This represents the sorbitol dehydrogenase reaction used industrially (e.g., in vitamin C synthesis) where D-sorbitol (D-glucitol) is oxidized at C5 to L-sorbose. The redox cofactors and proton balance are correct: NAD+ accepts a hydride and releases NADH + H+. In vivo (and industrially), this oxidation step strongly favors L-sorbose production.

rxn00577.other_comments: This is sucrose phosphorylase (EC 2.4.1.7), which catalyzes the phosphorolysis of sucrose: Phosphate + Sucrose <=> D-Fructose + alpha-D-Glucose-1-phosphate. The reaction is balanced in atoms (sucrose C12H22O11 + phosphate yields fructose C6H12O6 + glucose-1-phosphate C6H13O9P) and in charge. The enzyme transfers the glucosyl moiety from sucrose to phosphate. Stoichiometry is correct 1:1:1:1.

rxn04851.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolysis of an epoxide (11H-14,15-EETA, an epoxyeicosatrienoic acid epoxide intermediate) by addition of water (H2O) to yield the corresponding trihydroxy/dihydroxy product 11,14,15-THETA (a trihydroxyeicosatrienoic acid). This is a soluble epoxide hydrolase type reaction. The stoichiometry is balanced: addition of one H2O across the epoxide ring opens it to form a vicinal diol (the THETA product), so atoms balance correctly. In vivo, epoxide hydrolase reactions are strongly favored in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

errors: Mass and atom imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance. Transfer of an acyl group from ACP to AMP would consume AMP and release ACP, but a phosphoanhydride/thioester exchange cannot simply add AMP to the acyl chain without accounting for the leaving phosphate or pyrophosphate moiety
Charge imbalance: 2 H+ on the substrate side is not balanced by the products

AMP appears as a free substrate while also being incorporated into the acyl-AMP product, which is chemically inconsistent for a simple ligase-type transfer; typically ATP + acid -> acyl-AMP + PPi, not free AMP as a reactant
rxn13468.other_comments: This appears to be intended as an acyl group transfer between an ACP thioester and an AMP-linked intermediate in mycolic acid biosynthesis (FadD/Fatty-Acid-AMP ligase chemistry). However, as written it shows free AMP combining with an acyl-ACP to yield acyl-AMP and free ACP, which is not properly mass- or charge-balanced and likely represents a malformed or oversimplified equation.

rxn10985.other_comments: This is a malate:quinone oxidoreductase (MQO) reaction. L-Malate is oxidized to oxaloacetate while menaquinone-6 is reduced to menaquinol-6. The reaction is balanced: malate (C4H4O5) loses 2 H (as 2H+ + 2e-) to become oxaloacetate (C4H2O5), and menaquinone-6 gains 2H to become menaquinol-6. Stoichiometry is correct (2 electrons and 2 protons transferred). Unlike soluble NAD-dependent malate dehydrogenase, the membrane-bound quinone-dependent MQO is essentially irreversible in vivo because the favorable quinone reduction pulls the otherwise unfavorable malate oxidation forward.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: reduction of (-)-sophorol to (-)-maackiain by NADPH should not release water; the reaction as written does not balance. Pterocarpan synthesis from a pterocarpin/isoflavanone intermediate involves NADPH-dependent reduction with loss of water only in specific cyclization steps. The stoichiometry with H2O on the product side is inconsistent with a simple NADPH oxidoreductase.

Name/EC mismatch: the enzyme name '(-)-maackiain:NADP+ 2'-oxidoreductase' implies maackiain is the electron donor (oxidized form on left), but the reaction places maackiain on the product (reduced) side.
rxn07566.other_comments: This reaction represents the final step of pterocarpan biosynthesis, where pterocarpan synthase (DMID/pterocarpan synthase) converts the pterocarpin/isoflavanol intermediate (sophorol-related) to the pterocarpan (-)-maackiain. The conversion involves NADPH and yields water via dehydration/cyclization. In vivo this proceeds toward maackiain formation (biosynthetic direction).

rxn06060.other_comments: This is the thiosulfate:thiol sulfurtransferase (rhodanese-like) reaction. Thiosulfate (H2S2O3) reacts with 2 reduced glutathione (GSH) plus a proton, producing sulfite, oxidized glutathione (GSSG), and hydrogen sulfide (H2S). Checking atom balance: thiosulfate provides 2 S; products contain S in sulfite (1 S) and H2S (1 S), so sulfur balances (2 = 2). The two GSH thiols are oxidized to one GSSG disulfide. The reaction effectively reductively cleaves the S-S bond of thiosulfate, with the sulfane sulfur reduced to sulfide and the sulfonate sulfur released as sulfite. Stoichiometry appears balanced for sulfur and glutathione; charge/H balance is approximately consistent with the proton consumed.

rxn01614.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.177) that transfers a glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the carboxyl group of trans-cinnamate, forming the 1-O-acyl glucose ester (trans-cinnamoyl beta-D-glucoside) plus UDP. The atoms balance: the glucose moiety is transferred and UDP is released. The H+ inclusion is consistent with proton accounting for the glycosyl ester bond formation. Glycosyltransferases using UDP-sugar donors are strongly thermodynamically favored in the direction of glycoside formation due to the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, so the in vivo direction is forward (toward the glucoside).

rxn03665.other_comments: This is a hydrolytic C-C bond cleavage (acylhydrolase) reaction in the meta-cleavage pathway, analogous to HOPDA hydrolase (BphD-type). The substrate 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-7-methylocta-2,4-dienoate is hydrolyzed by water to yield 2-oxopent-4-enoate (oxopent-4-enoate) and isobutyrate (2-methylpropanoate), with release of a proton. Atom and charge balance: substrate C9 + H2O provides C9H12O4 + H2O = C9H14O5; products 2-oxopent-4-enoate (C5H5O3-) + isobutyrate (C4H7O2-) + H+ = C9H13O5 + H = balanced. Hydrolases of this type are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the catabolic pathway forward.

rxn01050.other_comments: This is cellobiose oxidation by cellobiose oxidase (cellobiose dehydrogenase / cellobiose:oxygen 1-oxidoreductase, EC 1.1.3.25). O2 oxidizes cellobiose (CELB) at the anomeric C1 position to cellobiono-1,5-lactone, with O2 reduced to H2O2. The reaction is balanced: cellobiose (C12H22O11) + O2 -> cellobiono-1,5-lactone (C12H20O11) + H2O2 (H2O2), with atoms balancing (C12, H22+O2 -> H20+H2O2, O11+O2 -> O11+O2). Stoichiometry is correct.

rxn08656.other_comments: This represents the bacterial glycolate oxidase (GlcDEF) reaction, oxidizing glycolate to glyoxylate using menaquinone-8 as the electron acceptor, reducing it to menaquinol-8. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: glycolate (C2H3O3) + MK-8 -> glyoxylate (C2H1O3) + MKH2-8, transferring 2 H (2e- + 2H+). In vivo this is driven in the oxidative direction toward glyoxylate as part of glycolate utilization, coupling to the respiratory chain via the menaquinone pool.

rxn00280.other_comments: This is the alanopine dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.5.1.17). Alanopine (2,2'-iminodipropanoate, N-(1-carboxyethyl)-alanine) is formed by reductive condensation of pyruvate and L-alanine using NADH. The reaction shown is written in the oxidative (degradative) direction: alanopine + NAD+ + H2O -> pyruvate + L-alanine + NADH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced in both mass and charge (the secondary amine of alanopine is cleaved hydrolytically/oxidatively to regenerate the amino acid and the keto acid). errors: Stoichiometric carbon imbalance: condensation of acetyl-CoA (C2) with a C22 docosapentaenoyl-CoA (4Z,7Z,10Z,13Z,16Z) via Claisen condensation should yield a C24 (tetracosanoyl) 3-oxoacyl-CoA, but the double bond positions in the product are inconsistent. rxn07743.other_comments: This is a 3-ketoacyl-CoA synthase (elongase condensation) type reaction producing a C24 3-oxo-pentaenoyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA and a C22 docosapentaenoyl-CoA. rxn09899.other_comments: This is an ATP-dependent dipeptide ligase forming the Ala-Val dipeptide bond. The reaction couples ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi, releasing a proton, consistent with the condensation of L-Alanine and L-Valine into the dipeptide Ala-Val plus water (water is implicit/balanced by the H+ released). rxn04915.other_comments: This represents a cytochrome P450 (monooxygenase) oxidation of 1,2-dibromoethane. P450 hydroxylates the C-Br carbon to form an unstable gem-bromohydrin that eliminates HBr to give 2-bromoacetaldehyde. The overall scheme (NADPH + O2 + substrate -> NADP+ + H2O + oxidized product) is biochemically reasonable but needs an H+ for proton/charge balance.

rxn05130.other_comments: This is a NADPH-dependent monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction converting indolin-2-one (oxindole) to dioxindole (3-hydroxyoxindole). This is consistent with a flavin-containing monooxygenase or cytochrome P450 mechanism. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn10420.other_comments: This reaction represents 2-phospho-L-lactate synthase (CofB/PznD-like activity), which transfers a phosphate group to L-lactate using GTP as the phosphoryl donor, yielding GDP and 2-phospho-L-lactate. Mass and charge are balanced: GTP (4-) + L-lactate (1-) gives GDP (3-) + H+ (1+) + 2-phospho-L-lactate (3-); both sides total -5 charge and atoms balance with the phosphoryl transfer. This is an early step in coenzyme F420 biosynthesis.

rxn10936.other_comments: This is a transport reaction moving acetamide between two compartments (extracellular and cytosol/periplasm). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced since acetamide appears identically on both sides, differing only by compartment. Acetamide is a small uncharged molecule that can diffuse across membranes, so passive transport is plausible and the reaction is correctly written as reversible. Note that compartment annotations are not explicitly shown in the formula but are implied by the transport designation.

errors: Carbon balance inconsistent: each malonyl-ACP elongation cycle adds 2 carbons to the acyl chain (after decarboxylation), so 8 cycles should extend C42 to C58, which is consistent here (42 + 8*2 = 58); however the redox cofactor usage appears incomplete for a full keto-meroacid (3-keto retaining) product

Each elongation cycle in fatty acid synthesis uses 1 NADPH for the ketoreduction and 1 NADPH (not NADH) for the enoyl reduction; the use of 8 NADH plus 8 NADPH suggests a mixed cofactor stoichiometry that may not reflect a fully reduced product

If the product retains a 3-keto group ('keto-meroacid'), the ketoreduction step should NOT occur, meaning fewer reducing equivalents (no NADPH for ketoreduction) should be consumed; the consumption of 16 reducing equivalents (8 NADH + 8 NADPH) implies full reduction, contradicting a 'keto' product designation

rxn13460.other_comments: This represents a polyketide/mycolic acid type elongation: 8 rounds of condensation with malonyl-ACP extending a C42 acyl-ACP to C58 (8 x C2 added), releasing 8 CO2 and 8 ACP. The cofactor stoichiometry (8 NADH + 8 NADPH) supports reductive processing steps, but the naming as '3-keto-meroacid' conflicts with full reduction implied by the cofactor count. Biosynthetic elongation is essentially irreversible in vivo (driven by decarboxylation of malonyl units).

rxn04367.other_comments: This represents the glycosyltransferase reaction (MegDIII/MegCIII-type) in the megalomicin biosynthetic pathway, transferring L-megosamine from dTDP-L-megosamine onto erythromycin C to form megalomicin A, releasing dTDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: the megosamine sugar moiety is transferred from the nucleotide sugar donor to the macrolide acceptor, with dTDP as the leaving group. Glycosyltransferase reactions of this type are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn07287.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP90B) monooxygenase reaction in brassinosteroid biosynthesis, hydroxylating campestanol at C22 to yield 6-deoxocathasterone. P450 hydroxylations are physiologically irreversible (forward) due to O2 consumption and oxygen incorporation.

rxn10315.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction in which 24 GlcNAc residues are transferred from 24 UDP-N-acetylglucosamine donors onto the 24 repeating units of a lipoteichoic acid (LTA) backbone (isohexadecanoyl-substituted, n=24), converting the unsubstituted polymer to the GlcNAc-substituted polymer and releasing 24 UDP. rxn06299.other_comments: This is the F420-reducing hydrogenase (Frh) reaction found in methanogenic archaea. It catalyzes the reduction of coenzyme F420 by molecular hydrogen: F420 + H2 <=> F420H2 (reduced F420). The reaction as written is stoichiometrically balanced if 'Reduced coenzyme F420' represents F420H2, since the two hydrogens from H2 are added (one as hydride to C5 of the deazaflavin, one as proton). No protons or charges need explicit balancing at this level of representation. In vivo, the reaction is physiologically reversible and operates in the direction of F420 reduction during hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis, but can run in reverse depending on the H2/F420H2 redox poise.

rxn03598.other_comments: This reaction is the NAD+-dependent oxidation of chloroacetaldehyde (2-chloroethanal) to chloroacetic acid (chloroacetate). An aldehyde dehydrogenase mechanism: aldehyde + H2O + NAD+ -> carboxylic acid + NADH + 2 H+. Atom balance: chloroacetaldehyde (C2H3ClO) + H2O (H2O) = C2H5ClO2 on left side combining; product chloroacetate (C2H3ClO2-) + 2 H+ accounts for the carbons, chlorine, and oxygens, with two protons released (one to NADH transfer, one from the carboxyl). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced. Aldehyde dehydrogenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo, strongly favoring acid formation.

rxn01112.other_comments: This is the D-ribitol-5-phosphate:NAD+ 2-oxidoreductase reaction. Ribitol 5-phosphate is oxidized to D-ribulose 5-phosphate with concomitant reduction of NAD+ to NADH + H+. The reaction is balanced: ribitol 5-phosphate (C5H13O8P) loses 2 H (2 electrons + 2 protons) to give ribulose 5-phosphate (C5H11O8P), with one H accounted for in NADH (hydride) and one released as H+. Charge and atoms balance.

rxn03559.other_comments: This is the extradiol (meta) ring-cleavage of 2,3-dihydroxy-4'-chlorobiphenyl by a 2,3-dihydroxybiphenyl 1,2-dioxygenase (BphC-type), incorporating both atoms of O2 to cleave the catechol ring and yield the ring-fission product 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-(4'-chlorophenyl)-hexa-2,4-dienoate. Atom balance checks out: the catechol substrate plus O2 gives the meta-cleavage product; one H+ is released upon deprotonation of the carboxylate/enol product. Carbon (12), oxygen, and chlorine balance; the H+ accounts for proton balance.

rxn02928.other_comments: This reaction represents dihydrodipicolinate reductase (DapB) in the lysine biosynthesis pathway. The enzyme normally catalyzes the NAD(P)H-dependent reduction of 2,3-dihydrodipicolinate to 2,3,4,5-tetrahydrodipicolinate. As written, the equation shows oxidation of tetrahydrodipicolinate to dihydrodipicolinate with NAD+ as oxidant; this is the reverse of the physiological direction. Stoichiometry and charge are balanced (one hydride plus one proton transferred from substrate to NAD+).

rxn05238.other_comments: This is a transport reaction (TRANS-RXN) representing the movement of sulfate across a membrane, indicated by the same metabolite (Sulfate) appearing on both sides of the equation, presumably in different compartments. Stoichiometrically it is balanced (sulfate maps to sulfate 1:1). Transport reactions like this are commonly written as reversible unless coupled to an energy source or ion gradient that imposes directionality.

rxn01969.other_comments: This is described as a phosphohydrolase removing the 6-phosphate from D-fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, yielding inorganic phosphate plus fructose 2-phosphate. rxn06860.other_comments: This is a PTS (phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase system) reaction where the phosphoryl group is transferred from a phosphohistidine residue of an enzyme (EIIA/EIIB) to arbutin (ursin), generating arbutin-6-phosphate during sugar uptake. rxn12147.other_comments: This is the myo-inositol catabolism enzyme (often part of the iol pathway) that hydrolytically opens the cyclohexane-1,2-dione ring of 2-deoxy-5-keto-D-gluconic acid / trihydroxycyclohexanedione to form an open-chain deoxy-keto sugar acid. rxn12042.other_comments: This is glutathionylspermine synthetase (trypanothione biosynthesis pathway in trypanosomatids). ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi makes this ligation thermodynamically favorable and physiologically driven in the synthetic (forward) direction.

rxn06798.other_comments: This is the arylsulfatase A (cerebroside-sulfatase, EC 3.1.6.8) reaction, in which sulfatide (3-O-sulfogalactosylceramide) is hydrolyzed by water to yield galactocerebroside (galactosylceramide), free sulfate, and a proton. rxn02754.other_comments: This is an N-acetyltransferase reaction transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the amino group of D-phenylalanine, producing N-acetyl-D-phenylalanine, CoA, and a proton. rxn06559.other_comments: This is a protein S-palmitoylation/O-palmitoylation reaction where a palmitoyl group is transferred from palmitoyl-CoA to a myelin proteolipid protein (PLP), releasing free CoA. The acyltransferase reaction is thermodynamically favorable in the acylation direction in vivo, driven by hydrolysis of the high-energy thioester bond of palmitoyl-CoA.

rxn03849.other_comments: Biuret amidohydrolase (BiuH) hydrolyzes biuret (H2N-CO-NH-CO-NH2) to allophanate (urea-1-carboxylate, H2N-CO-NH-COOH) plus ammonia. rxn05946.other_comments: This is a sulfotransferase (SULT) reaction transferring a sulfo group from PAPS (3'-phosphoadenylyl sulfate) to phenol, producing PAP (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate) and an aryl sulfate (phenyl sulfate). rxn04057.other_comments: This reaction (R05824) represents the interconversion between 4,21-dehydrocorynantheine aldehyde and 4,21-dehydrogeissoschizine, intermediates in monoterpenoid indole alkaloid biosynthesis. The transformation is an intramolecular isomerization/cyclization where no atoms are gained or lost, so the molecular formulas should be identical (C21H24N2O3), making the reaction inherently mass-balanced as a 1:1 isomerization. Such tautomerization/cyclization steps are typically reversible.

rxn02574.other_comments: This is a beta-glucosidase hydrolysis reaction. Syringin (sinapyl alcohol 4-O-beta-D-glucoside) is hydrolyzed by water to release D-glucose and sinapyl alcohol. The stoichiometry is balanced: syringin (C17H24O9) + H2O (H2O) yields D-glucose (C6H12O6) + sinapyl alcohol (C11H14O4). Glycoside hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the hydrolytic direction in vivo.

rxn04482.other_comments: This is the (S)-4-hydroxymandelate oxidase / dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.3.19 / FMN-dependent alpha-hydroxyacid oxidase family). Stoichiometry is correct (C8H8O4 + FMN -> C8H6O4 + FMNH2).

rxn14200.other_comments: This reaction describes the N-methylation of (S)-corytuberine by S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to produce magnoflorine and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). Corytuberine is a tertiary amine aporphine alkaloid; N-methylation produces magnoflorine, a quaternary ammonium aporphine alkaloid. The reaction is the corytuberine N-methyltransferase (CNMT-like) step in magnoflorine biosynthesis. Stoichiometry is balanced: a methyl group transfers from SAM to the nitrogen, yielding SAH and the N-methylated (quaternary) product.

rxn05558.other_comments: This represents an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the import of ferrioxamine (a siderophore-iron complex). rxn01042.other_comments: This is the NADP+-dependent oxidation of D-xylose to D-xylono-1,5-lactone (D-xylonolactone), catalyzed by xylose dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.179). rxn01291.other_comments: This is an NADP-dependent polyol dehydrogenase (aldose reductase family) reaction. L-Lyxitol is a synonym for L-arabitol. The atom and charge balance is correct: NADP+ + L-arabitol = NADPH + H+ + L-arabinose. Such aldo-keto/polyol reductase reactions are thermodynamically reversible, though in vivo direction depends on cofactor ratios; NADPH-favoring conditions push toward sugar reduction (reverse).

rxn03512.other_comments: This reaction represents the precorrin-8X methylmutase (CobH/CbiC) step in the aerobic cobalamin biosynthesis pathway. It catalyzes the 1,5-methyl migration converting precorrin-8X (precorrin-8w) to hydrogenobyrinate. The stoichiometry is essentially an intramolecular methyl rearrangement (isomerization), so atom balance is maintained with no net consumption/production of other metabolites. The H+ is sometimes included for charge balancing depending on protonation states; the core isomerization itself does not require external substrates. Physiologically the reaction proceeds toward hydrogenobyrinate as part of committed cobalamin biosynthesis, hence the forward direction, though mechanistically methylmutases are intrinsically reversible.

The aldehyde intermediate then spontaneously cyclizes (with loss of water) to 1-piperideine. Combining: left = C10H20N2O5; right (Glu + aminopentanal) = C10H20N2O5 - balanced. Cyclization of aminopentanal to piperideine (C5H9N) loses H2O, so net: 2-OG + Cadaverine -> Glutamate + Piperideine + H2O. This appears balanced (left C10H20N2O5; right Glu C5H9NO4 + Piperideine C5H9N + H2O = C10H20N2O5). So the reaction is actually balanced.

rxn12741.other_comments: This is a cadaverine aminotransferase (transaminase) reaction transferring an amino group from cadaverine to 2-oxoglutarate, producing glutamate and an aminoaldehyde that cyclizes to piperideine with loss of water. The overall atom/charge balance appears correct when piperideine is the cyclized product. Physiologically this proceeds in the degradative (forward) direction toward piperideine.

rxn01960.other_comments: This is the D-arabinono-1,4-lactone oxidase (ALO) reaction (EC 1.1.3.37), involved in fungal/yeast erythroascorbate biosynthesis. It oxidizes D-arabinono-1,4-lactone using molecular O2 to yield D-erythro-ascorbate (D-erythroascorbic acid) and hydrogen peroxide. Stoichiometry is balanced: substrate loses 2 H (a C2-C3 dehydrogenation introducing the enediol/lactone double bond), which are transferred to O2 forming H2O2. Atoms balance correctly.

The correct lactonization should be: 5-Pyridoxate (+H+ if considering the carboxylate form) -> 5-Pyridoxolactone + H2O, but the standard physiological reaction is the reverse (lactone hydrolysis).

Atom/charge balance is questionable: 5-pyridoxate (C8H8NO4-, carboxylate) plus H+ would give the neutral acid C8H9NO4; loss of H2O gives C8H7NO3 for the lactone, which is consistent, so balance may actually hold depending on protonation states.
rxn03149.other_comments: This is the lactonase-type reaction in pyridoxine/vitamin B6 degradation (e.g., by Pseudomonas). rxn13540.other_comments: This appears to be a mycolyltransferase-type reaction in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, transferring mycolate groups (alpha-, methoxy-, keto-mycolates) from trehalose dimycolate (TDM) donors onto an arabinose-based acceptor to form a tetramycolyl-hexaarabinoside (arabinogalactan mycolylation). The major issues are missing/ill-defined acceptor and incorrect leaving group (water vs. free trehalose).
