The product should likely be a cyclic imine intermediate or the reaction requires release of H2O which is not shown

Biologically, 5-aminopentanoate (5-aminovalerate) is a linear amino acid; its oxidative cyclization to proline (a 5-membered ring) is not a recognized physiological reaction - the carbon skeleton/ring size relationship is questionable

Forming a ring from the linear amine would require loss of water plus an oxidation, so the atom balance as written is incomplete.

rxn11964.other_comments: This is an aldehyde oxidase reaction (indole-3-acetaldehyde oxidase, EC 1.2.3.7) converting indole-3-acetaldehyde to indole-3-acetate (IAA, auxin). The stoichiometry is balanced: aldehyde + H2O + O2 yields carboxylic acid + H2O2. Carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and charge balance correctly (left: indoleacetaldehyde neutral + H2O + O2; right: indoleacetate(-1) + H2O2 + H+). Oxidase reactions using molecular O2 are physiologically irreversible.

rxn02852.other_comments: This is the hydroxyquinol 1,2-dioxygenase reaction (EC 1.13.11.37). It catalyzes ortho ring cleavage of benzene-1,2,4-triol (hydroxyquinol) using molecular O2 to yield 3-hydroxy-cis,cis-muconate (maleylacetate precursor). The stoichiometry balances: hydroxyquinol (C6H6O3) + O2 yields 3-hydroxy-cis,cis-muconate (C6H4O5 as the dianion) + 2 H+, with both C, O, and H/charge balanced when the product is considered as the deprotonated dicarboxylate. [directionality_note] Dioxygenase reactions incorporating O2 with ring cleavage are essentially irreversible in vivo.

rxn01683.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of nebularine (9-beta-D-ribofuranosylpurine, the purine riboside) by N-D-ribosylpurine ribohydrolase. Water cleaves the N-glycosidic bond, yielding D-ribose and the free base purine. The reaction is balanced: nebularine (C10H12N4O4) + H2O (H2O) gives D-ribose (C5H10O5) + purine (C5H4N4). Carbon (10=5+5), nitrogen (4=4), and oxygen (4+1=5) balance, and hydrogen (12+2=14 vs 10+4=14) balances.

rxn02385.other_comments: This reaction represents 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase activity converting 17alpha-hydroxypregnenolone to 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone. The enzyme oxidizes the 3-beta-hydroxyl group using NAD+ as cofactor, producing NADH and H+. Note that the full physiological conversion also involves a delta-5 to delta-4 isomerization (3beta-HSD is a bifunctional enzyme), but the stoichiometry shown for the oxidoreductase step is balanced in terms of atoms and charge. The substrate (delta-5, 3-OH) is oxidized to the 3-keto product. Carbon counts (C21 steroids) match, and the redox couple is balanced.

rxn02235.other_comments: This is the oxidation of 1,3-propanediol to 3-hydroxypropanal (3-hydroxypropionaldehyde) using NAD+ as electron acceptor. The reaction is balanced: 1,3-propanediol (C3H8O2) loses 2 H (one as H+ and two electrons going to NAD+ to form NADH) to give 3-hydroxypropanal (C3H6O2). Mass and charge balance check out. This is catalyzed by 1,3-propanediol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.202). Although written as oxidation, in vivo (e.g., glycerol fermentation pathways in Klebsiella, Clostridium) the physiological direction is typically the reverse, reducing 3-hydroxypropanal to 1,3-propanediol to regenerate NAD+. The enzyme reaction itself is thermodynamically reversible.

rxn00632.other_comments: This reaction describes a phosphatase hydrolyzing the phosphate ester bond of beta-D-fructose 2-phosphate, producing D-fructose and inorganic phosphate. Note that fructose 2-phosphate is an unusual metabolite; the more common biologically relevant species is fructose-2,6-bisphosphate or fructose-6-phosphate.

rxn09979.other_comments: This is a hydrolysis reaction catalyzed by beta-glucosidase, cleaving the glycosidic bond of beta-methylglucoside (methyl beta-D-glucoside) using water to yield D-glucose and methanol. rxn02434.other_comments: This is the inositol polyphosphate 1-phosphatase reaction (EC 3.1.3.57). rxn02977.other_comments: This is alpha-L-fucosidase (EC 3.2.1.63) acting on 2-alpha-L-fucopyranosyl-beta-D-galactoside. rxn03622.other_comments: This reaction is an acyl-CoA dehydrogenase/oxidoreductase step that oxidizes pimeloyl-CoA to 6-carboxyhex-2-enoyl-CoA (introducing a 2,3-double bond), reducing NAD+ to NADH. rxn04952.other_comments: This is L-aspartate oxidase (or aspartate dehydrogenase, EC 1.4.1.21) catalyzing the oxidative deamination of L-aspartate to oxaloacetate, using NAD+ as electron acceptor and releasing ammonia. rxn11938.other_comments: This represents the formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase reaction, which interconverts CO2 + methanofuran (+ reduced carrier) and formylmethanofuran (+ oxidized carrier + H2O). rxn13371.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to 2-phenylethanol (2-phenylethyl alcohol), producing phenethyl acetate (2-phenylethyl acetate) and free CoA. Alcohol acetyltransferases (e.g., yeast ATF1/ATF2) catalyze ester formation, which is thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy thioester bond of acetyl-CoA, driving the reaction toward ester synthesis in vivo.

rxn00945.other_comments: This reaction represents the reduction of (2E)-hexadecenoyl-CoA (trans-2-hexadecenoyl-CoA) to palmitoyl-CoA using NADPH, equivalent to the enoyl-CoA reductase step in fatty acid elongation. rxn10252.other_comments: This reaction describes a glucosyltransferase transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose to a diglucosyl-diacylglycerol acceptor, forming a triglucosyl-diacylglycerol and releasing UDP. rxn03369.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of the 2-aminoethylphosphonate (ciliatine) moiety from CMP-ciliatine (CMP-2-aminoethylphosphonate) onto a ceramide hydroxyl, producing ceramide aminoethylphosphonate (ceramide ciliatine) and releasing CMP. rxn06704.other_comments: This is the galactolipid:galactolipid galactosyltransferase/acyltransferase-type reaction (processive galactolipid metabolism). rxn02337.other_comments: This is an alcohol dehydrogenase-type oxidation: farnesol (primary alcohol) is oxidized to farnesal (aldehyde) with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. rxn04018.other_comments: This is the pinene synthase reaction, where geranyl diphosphate (GPP, C10H20O7P2 with charge -2 at physiological pH) is cyclized to (-)-alpha-pinene (C10H16) with release of diphosphate (PPi). rxn03101.other_comments: This is the beta-glucogallin-dependent galloyltransferase that builds pentagalloylglucose from 1,2,3,6-tetragalloylglucose, transferring a galloyl group from beta-glucogallin (the activated acyl donor) and releasing free D-glucose. The core stoichiometry (donor + acceptor -> glucose + pentagalloylglucose) is correct and atom-balanced; the extra H+ appears spurious. In vivo this proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward gallotannin synthesis, driven by the consumption of beta-glucogallin.

rxn09148.other_comments: This is a Phospholipase A2 reaction: water hydrolyzes the sn-2 ester bond of 1,2-dihexadec-9-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (phosphatidic acid with two C16:1 acyl chains), releasing one hexadecenoate (C16:1 fatty acid) and a proton, yielding 1-hexadec-9-enoyl-sn-glycerol 3-phosphate (a lysophosphatidic acid). The stoichiometry is mass and charge balanced: one acyl chain is removed and the carbon/hydrogen/oxygen/phosphate accounting is consistent.

rxn02020.other_comments: This represents a generic Ap4A (diadenosine tetraphosphate) hydrolase-type reaction using placeholder 'X' for the nucleoside moiety. The asymmetric hydrolase cleaves the P1,P4-bis(5'-nucleosyl)-tetraphosphate (XppppX) into a nucleoside monophosphate (XMP) and a nucleoside triphosphate (XTP). Stoichiometry balances: the tetraphosphate bridge (4 phosphates) is split as 1 + 3, water adds across the cleaved anhydride bond, and one proton is released. Mass and charge are conserved.

rxn01474.other_comments: This reaction represents 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (2-oxidizing), oxidizing 6-phospho-D-gluconate at C2 to 6-phospho-2-dehydro-D-gluconate (2-keto-6-phosphogluconate), reducing NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is balanced: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphate, and charge are conserved (NAD+ + 6-phosphogluconate yields NADH + H+ + the 2-keto product). Note this is distinct from the more common 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (decarboxylating) in the pentose phosphate pathway, which produces ribulose-5-phosphate and CO2.

rxn00203.other_comments: This is a decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate, C5H4O5 as the dianion) yielding CO2 and 4-oxobutanoate (succinic semialdehyde, C4H5O3 as the anion). Atom/charge balance checks out: left side C5H5O5 (1- net, after adding H+ to the 2- dianion), right side CO2 (C1O2) + C4H5O3 (1-) = C5H5O5 with 1- charge. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced. Decarboxylations releasing CO2 are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the favorable loss of gaseous/dissolved CO2 and the thermodynamics of C-C bond cleavage.

errors: Reaction is written in the wrong direction for a phosphohydrolase; hydrolysis should consume H2O and release phosphate, not the reverse
As written, this is a phosphorylation/condensation (PM + Phosphate -> Pyridoxamine phosphate + H2O), which is the opposite of what the enzyme name describes
rxn01808.other_comments: The reaction involves pyridoxamine (PM) and pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate (PMP). A phosphohydrolase cleaves the phosphate from PMP using water: Pyridoxamine phosphate + H2O -> PM + Phosphate. The given equation lists the substrates and products reversed relative to the stated hydrolase activity. Atom balance is consistent for a phosphoester hydrolysis (water in, phosphate and free pyridoxamine out).

errors: No net transformation: substrates and products are identical (H+ + Taurine on both sides), so no compartmental information is conveyed in this representation
rxn12554.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-symport transport reaction for taurine, where a proton and taurine are co-transported across a membrane (e.g., extracellular to cytoplasm). As written, both sides are identical with no compartment annotations, making it a null reaction with no net change. To be meaningful, it should specify compartments, e.g., H+[e] + Taurine[e] -> H+[c] + Taurine[c]. Stoichiometry of 1 H+ to 1 taurine is plausible for a symporter.

errors: This reaction is incorrectly written as an NAD-dependent oxidoreductase. Melilotate (3-(2-hydroxyphenyl)propanoate) is converted to 2-coumarate (trans-2-hydroxycinnamate / 2-coumarate) by introduction of a double bond, but the actual enzyme melilotate dehydrogenase / 2-coumarate reductase uses NADH to reduce 2-coumarate to melilotate, and physiologically the reaction is a flavin-dependent reductase rather than a direct NAD+ oxidoreductase. The atom/H balance for an oxidative desaturation requires loss of 2 H (as in dehydrogenation), which is consistent with NAD+ -> NADH + H+, so stoichiometry of redox equivalents balances.

The systematic name implies oxidation of melilotate to 2-coumarate, but the biological enzyme (EC 1.3.1.11) operates as a reductase in the reductive direction (2-coumarate + NADH -> melilotate + NAD+).
rxn14383.other_comments: The reaction interconverts melilotate (3-(2-hydroxyphenyl)propanoate, saturated) and 2-coumarate (2-hydroxycinnamate, an alpha,beta-unsaturated acid) coupled to NAD/NADH. The redox stoichiometry (loss/gain of 2H) balances. Biologically (EC 1.3.1.11, 2-coumarate reductase) the favored direction is reduction of 2-coumarate to melilotate, i.e., the reverse of how it is written here.

rxn11696.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis (dephosphorylation) of trans-zeatin riboside 5'-monophosphate to trans-zeatin riboside plus inorganic phosphate, catalyzed by a phosphatase/nucleotidase activity. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: a phosphomonoester bond is cleaved by water, releasing one phosphate group. This is part of cytokinin metabolism. Phosphatase-catalyzed hydrolysis reactions are thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction of dephosphorylation.

errors: The reaction is not mass-balanced as written. The condensation of two phosphatidylglycerol molecules to form cardiolipin releases glycerol but the atom balance is not correct without accounting for water/phosphate; in the bacterial cardiolipin synthase reaction (cardiolipin synthase, EC 2.7.8.-/2.7.8.41), 2 phosphatidylglycerol yield cardiolipin plus 1 glycerol, which is balanced only if the headgroup glycerol is the leaving group. As written with generic 'Glycerol' the formula balance depends on R-group definitions, but the transesterification stoichiometry (2 PG -> CL + glycerol) is the accepted form.
rxn07267.other_comments: This represents the cardiolipin synthase reaction in which two phosphatidylglycerol molecules condense to form cardiolipin (diphosphatidylglycerol) with release of one free glycerol. The phosphate-bearing glycerol headgroup of one PG is transferred to the other PG's phosphate, releasing glycerol.

errors: The dipeptide Gly-Leu appears on both the substrate and product sides without any change, which makes the transport step ambiguous in a single-compartment representation. A proper ABC transport reaction should distinguish compartments, e.g. Gly-Leu[external] -> Gly-Leu[cytoplasm]. As written, the dipeptide is not actually transformed or moved, so the reaction is not balanced in a biological sense (no net transport indicated).
rxn12849.other_comments: This represents an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter for the dipeptide Gly-Leu. The chemistry of ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) is mass- and charge-balanced. The intent is import of the dipeptide coupled to ATP hydrolysis, which is energetically driven and effectively irreversible in vivo. The reaction would be improved by adding compartment tags to the Gly-Leu species to show the transport.

rxn07241.other_comments: This is a glucuronosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.226-type) in glycosaminoglycan/chondroitin sulfate biosynthesis. UDP-glucuronate donates a glucuronosyl residue via beta-1,3 linkage to the terminal N-acetyl-beta-D-galactosaminyl residue of the growing proteoglycan chain, releasing UDP. The atom balance is consistent: a glucuronosyl unit is transferred from UDP-glucuronate to the acceptor, and UDP is released. The stoichiometry (1 UDP-glucuronate + 1 acceptor -> 1 UDP + 1 extended acceptor) is correct.

rxn06465.other_comments: This is the 24-sterol C-methyltransferase reaction (sterol 24-C-methyltransferase, EC 2.1.1.41), found in plants and fungi. SAM donates a methyl group to the C24 position of desmosterol, producing 24-methylenecholesterol (the methylene group arises from methyl transfer followed by loss of a proton from the methyl carbon, giving an exocyclic =CH2). Products are S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine, a proton, and 24-methylenecholesterol. The stoichiometry is balanced: SAM contributes a CH3 (net CH2 added after H+ release) to desmosterol's C24=C25 double bond. SAM-dependent methyltransferases are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the reaction forward.

errors: The reaction is unbalanced for hydrogen and oxygen. The sterol 14-demethylase (CYP51) reaction removes the 14-methyl group as formate via three sequential monooxygenation steps. Balanced form: Obtusifoliol + 3 O2 + 3 NADPH + 3 H+ -> 4,4-dimethyl-5alpha-cholesta-8,14,24-trien-3beta-ol (delta8,14-sterol) + formate + 3 NADP+ + 4 H2O. The given equation omits one H+ on the substrate side (3 H+ needed, only 2 given), making protons/charge unbalanced.
NADP should be written as NADP+ for correct charge accounting.
rxn03996.other_comments: This represents sterol 14alpha-demethylase (CYP51), a cytochrome P450 that performs three successive monooxygenations to remove the 14-methyl group from obtusifoliol, releasing it as formate and introducing a delta8,14 double bond. Each oxidation step consumes one O2 and one NADPH. The reaction is physiologically irreversible (P450 monooxygenase, formate-releasing).

rxn07667.other_comments: This reaction represents the glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.-) where UDP-glucose donates a glucose moiety to pelargonidin 3-glucoside, forming pelargonidin 3-O-sophoroside (a diglucoside with a 1->2 glucosidic linkage) and releasing UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose to the acceptor, with UDP released. This corresponds to anthocyanin 3-O-glucoside 2'''-O-glucosyltransferase activity.

errors: L-Isoleucine appears on both sides without compartment designation; for a transport reaction the substrate should be shown in distinct compartments (e.g., L-Isoleucine[external] -> L-Isoleucine[cytosol]). As written, the transported solute cancels out, making the reaction stoichiometrically meaningless beyond ATP hydrolysis.
rxn05179.other_comments: This represents an ABC-type ATPase coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the import of the nonpolar amino acid L-isoleucine. The ATP hydrolysis portion is balanced, but the transport is not represented because the same metabolite appears on both sides without compartment tags.

rxn00477.other_comments: This is an L-amino acid oxidase reaction (EC 1.4.3.2) acting on L-tryptophan. The enzyme oxidatively deaminates the amino acid: L-tryptophan + O2 + H2O yields the corresponding 2-oxo acid (indole-3-pyruvate), ammonia, and hydrogen peroxide. Atom and charge balance: substrates contribute C11H12N2O2 (Trp) + O2 + H2O = C11H14N2O5; products give NH3 + H2O2 + indolepyruvate (C11H9NO3) = C11H14N2O5. Mass balanced.

rxn03187.other_comments: This is the GnT-V (MGAT5) reaction, transferring a GlcNAc from UDP-GlcNAc to the alpha-1,6-linked mannose arm of an N-glycan acceptor. The substrate already bears a beta-1,2-GlcNAc on the alpha-1,6-mannose, and the enzyme adds a beta-1,6-GlcNAc to form the 2,6-branched product. Stoichiometry is balanced: UDP-GlcNAc donates a GlcNAc residue to the acceptor, releasing UDP. The mass balance holds with the GlcNAc moiety transferred to R-bearing glycoprotein acceptor.

rxn09694.other_comments: This is the ATP hydrolysis reaction (H+-exporting ATPase), where ATP + H2O yields ADP + inorganic phosphate + H+. The mass and charge balance: ATP (charge -4) + H2O yields ADP (-3) + Pi (-2) + H+ (+1), giving -4 on both sides. Atom balance is correct. Note that for a proton-pumping ATPase, the full physiological reaction also includes vectorial transport of H+ across a membrane (e.g. nH+[in] -> nH+[out]); this representation omits the transported protons but the chemical ATP hydrolysis portion is balanced. In vivo, ATP-driven proton pumps run in the hydrolysis (forward) direction to translocate protons against their gradient.

rxn01372.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of phosphocreatine (creatine phosphate) to creatine and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is correctly balanced: phosphocreatine (C4H8N3O5P, with charge considerations) plus water yields creatine (C4H9N3O2) and phosphate. The hydrolysis of the high-energy N-P phosphoramidate bond is strongly exergonic (large negative delta-G), so it proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction as written. Note that in vivo, the physiologically relevant enzyme is creatine kinase, which transfers the phosphate to ADP to form ATP rather than performing simple hydrolysis; direct hydrolysis to inorganic phosphate is thermodynamically favorable but wastes the high-energy bond.

rxn02372.other_comments: This reaction represents the conversion of provitamin D3 (7-dehydrocholesterol) to vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol). The process involves two steps: a photochemical reaction where UVB light opens the B-ring of 7-dehydrocholesterol to form previtamin D3, followed by a thermal isomerization to vitamin D3. As written, the reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (an isomerization, same molecular formula C27H44O for both species). In vivo, this proceeds essentially irreversibly toward vitamin D3 because the photochemical ring-opening step is driven by UV photon absorption and the subsequent thermal isomerization is spontaneous; vitamin D3 is then removed from the equilibrium by binding proteins. Note that the input combines the photochemical and thermal steps into a single net transformation.

rxn13394.other_comments: This represents the acetoin-forming reaction catalyzed by pyruvate decarboxylase (or acetolactate synthase-like activity). Pyruvate is decarboxylated to a hydroxyethyl-TPP intermediate, which condenses with acetaldehyde to form acetoin (ACTN) and release CO2. Stoichiometry balances: pyruvate (C3H3O3-) + H+ + acetaldehyde (C2H4O) yields CO2 + acetoin (C4H8O2). Carbon: 3+2 = 1+4 = 5. The release of CO2 makes this thermodynamically favorable and essentially irreversible in the forward direction.

rxn03415.other_comments: This is a step in the visual phototransduction cascade. After 11-cis-retinal in rhodopsin absorbs a photon and isomerizes to all-trans-retinal, a series of thermally-driven conformational intermediates proceed spontaneously: photorhodopsin -> bathorhodopsin -> lumirhodopsin -> metarhodopsin I -> metarhodopsin II. The bathorhodopsin to lumirhodopsin transition is a unimolecular thermal relaxation that proceeds essentially irreversibly in the forward direction in vivo, releasing stored strain energy. Stoichiometry is balanced as it is a simple conformational/isomeric interconversion (1:1).

rxn08393.other_comments: This reaction represents the enoyl-ACP reductase step of fatty acid biosynthesis (FAS), reducing the trans-2 double bond of (2E)-hexadecenoyl-[acp] to yield palmitoyl-ACP using NADPH as the electron donor (B-specific hydride transfer). Atoms balance: NADPH + H+ provides two electrons and protons to saturate the C2-C3 double bond, producing NADP+ and the saturated acyl-ACP. Stoichiometry is correct.

errors: Nomenclature inconsistency: the enzyme precorrin-6Y:NADP+ oxidoreductase corresponds to precorrin-6X reductase (EC 1.3.1.54), which reduces precorrin-6X (precorrin-6A) to precorrin-6Y (precorrin-6B); the substrate/product naming appears reversed relative to the reductive physiological direction

Charge/atom balance: as written NADPH + H+ on the product side implies oxidation of precorrin-6B, but reduction of NADP+ to NADPH requires consumption of 2 electrons and a proton from the substrate, so the redox direction is inconsistent with the named oxidoreductase reaction
rxn03492.other_comments: This is the cobalamin (vitamin B12) biosynthesis step catalyzed by precorrin-6X reductase (CobK/CbiJ), EC 1.3.1.54. The physiological reaction is reductive: precorrin-6A (precorrin-6X) + NADPH + H+ -> precorrin-6B (precorrin-6Y) + NADP+. As written here it is presented in the oxidative direction (NADP+ + precorrin-6B -> NADPH + H+ + precorrin-6A), which is the reverse of the biological direction.

rxn03660.other_comments: This is the meta-cleavage hydrolase step in the degradation of chlorinated biphenyls (BphD-type reaction). The substrate 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-(4'-chlorophenyl)-hexa-2,4-dienoate (a 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-6-aryl-hexa-2,4-dienoate, HOPDA analog) is hydrolyzed by water to yield 2-oxopent-4-enoate (2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate tautomer) plus 4-chlorobenzoate, with release of a proton. The C-C bond cleavage and atom balance are consistent: C12H8ClO4 (substrate) + H2O yields C5H6O3 (oxopentenoate) + C7H5ClO2 (4-chlorobenzoate) + H+. Mass and charge balance check out.

rxn11656.other_comments: This reaction describes a monooxygenase-type hydroxylation of ethylbenzene to (S)-1-phenylethanol, using molecular oxygen and NADH as the reductant. The stoichiometry is balanced: one atom of O2 is incorporated into the product (as the hydroxyl), the other oxygen is reduced to water using two electrons from NADH plus protons. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge balance are consistent. In vivo, monooxygenase reactions consuming O2 and NAD(P)H are essentially irreversible and proceed in the hydroxylation direction.

errors: The reaction as written is unbalanced. Standard stoichiometry for 2-aminophenol oxidation to 2-aminophenoxazin-3-one (isophenoxazine type) is 3 O2 + 2 o-aminophenol -> 2-amino-3H-phenoxazin-3-one + 4 H2O. As written (3 O2 + 4 aminophenol -> 6 H2O + 2 isophenoxazine), oxygen and hydrogen atoms do not balance correctly.

Atom balance check: 4 o-aminophenol (C6H7NO each = C24H28N4O4) + 3 O2 (O6) gives C24H28N4O10 on left; right side 6 H2O (H12O6) + 2 isophenoxazine. Each phenoxazinone product (C12H8N2O2) x2 = C24H16N4O4, plus H12O6 = C24H28N4O10. Carbon/nitrogen balance but the proposed product formula and H2O count need precise definition of 'isophenoxazine' to confirm.
rxn00054.other_comments: This describes the oxidative dimerization of 2-aminophenol by molecular oxygen to form a phenoxazinone (isophenoxazine) chromophore, with water as byproduct. The reaction is strongly exergonic (O2-driven oxidation) and physiologically irreversible in the oxidative direction.

rxn07720.other_comments: This is an acyltransferase reaction transferring a caffeoyl group from caffeoyl-CoA to the 6'''-OH of the 5-O-glucose of pelargonin (pelargonidin 3,5-diglucoside), yielding the 5-caffeoylglucoside product and free CoA. The acyl group balance (caffeoyl in donor matches caffeoyl in product) and CoA release are consistent. Thioester-driven acyltransfer reactions are thermodynamically favorable and proceed in the acylation direction in vivo.

rxn02534.other_comments: This is a methyltransferase-type reaction where methanol acts as methyl donor to gallate, producing water and 3-O-methylgallate. The atoms balance: gallate (C7H6O5) + methanol (CH4O) = 3-O-methylgallate (C8H8O5) + H2O. Stoichiometry is correct. However, in vivo this reaction typically proceeds in the demethylation direction (3-O-methylgallate -> gallate + methanol), catalyzed by demethylases in anaerobic methanol-forming bacteria such as Acetobacterium dehalogenans, where the methyl group is transferred to a cobalt corrinoid cofactor and methanol is the actual product. Thus relative to how it is written, the dominant in vivo direction is reverse.

rxn01801.other_comments: This is an alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase reaction (thymine/uracil oxygenase family-like). Deoxyuridine is hydroxylated at the 1'-position using O2 and 2-oxoglutarate, which is decarboxylated to succinate and CO2. The unstable 1'-hydroxy intermediate collapses, releasing the uracil base and yielding 2-deoxyribonolactone. Atoms balance: C9H12N2O5 (deoxyuridine) + C5H4O5 (2-OG) + O2 -> CO2 + C4H6O4 (succinate) + C4H4N2O2 (uracil) + C5H8O4 (deoxyribonolactone). C: 9+5=14 vs 1+4+4+5=14; N: 2 vs 2; balances.

errors: Oxidation of D-arabinose at C1 to a lactone (D-arabinono-1,4-lactone) is a 2-electron oxidation that produces NADPH + H+, but this requires removal of two hydrogens (effectively oxidizing the aldehyde/hemiacetal to a lactone). The atom/electron balance is consistent for a dehydrogenase-type oxidation, so stoichiometry is correct as written.
Reaction name says 'D-Arabinose:NADP+ 1-oxidoreductase' implying oxidation at C1, consistent with lactone formation.
rxn01150.other_comments: This is an aldose dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing the C1 of D-arabinose to form D-arabinono-1,4-lactone, transferring electrons to NADP+ to form NADPH. The stoichiometry (NADP+ + sugar -> NADPH + H+ + lactone) is balanced and biochemically sound. Many such NADP-dependent sugar/aldose dehydrogenases can operate reversibly in vitro, though in vivo direction is often driven toward lactone formation (oxidation) depending on cofactor ratios.

rxn04097.other_comments: This reaction represents the epoxidation of tabersonine to lochnericine, catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (tabersonine 6,7-epoxidase). The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ provide reducing equivalents and one oxygen atom is incorporated into the substrate (forming the 6,7-epoxide of lochnericine), while the other oxygen atom is reduced to water. NADP+ is the oxidized cofactor product. This is consistent with a typical P450 monooxygenase reaction.

errors: The proton balance appears inconsistent: 5 H+ on the left and 4 H+ on the right yields a net consumption of 1 H+, but the redox reaction NADH + menaquinone + H+ -> NAD+ + menaquinol consumes 1 scalar proton chemically (2 e- + 2 H+ transferred, with 1 H from NADH). The stoichiometry should distinguish chemical protons from translocated protons; as written without compartment labels the proton accounting is ambiguous.
Charge/atom balance cannot be fully verified without compartment (cytoplasmic vs periplasmic) annotation for the translocated protons.
rxn13727.other_comments: This is a respiratory NADH:menaquinone oxidoreductase reaction where NADH reduces menaquinone-7 (MK-7) to menaquinol-7 (mql7), with associated proton movement. The redox chemistry (NADH + MK + 2H -> NAD+ + menaquinol) is correct in principle; the asymmetric H+ likely represents proton translocation across the membrane.

rxn14308.other_comments: This is the homocitrate-synthase-like condensation reaction in the methionine chain-elongation pathway (relevant to glucosinolate biosynthesis). Acetyl-CoA condenses with the 2-oxo acid 2-oxo-6-methylthiohexanoate, with hydrolysis of the thioester to release CoA, forming 2-(4'-methylthio)butylmalate. Stoichiometry balances: the acetyl group (C2H3O) plus water adds to the oxo acid carbonyl, the CoA thioester is cleaved giving free CoA and a new C-C bond plus carboxymethyl group. Atom and charge balance are consistent (H2O + acetyl-CoA + substrate -> CoA + H+ + product). Such isopropylmalate/methylthioalkylmalate synthase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to thioester hydrolysis driving the reaction forward.

errors: The product is named 5-Dehydroquinate but the enzyme (quinate:NADP+ 3-oxidoreductase, EC 1.1.1.24) oxidizes the C3 hydroxyl, yielding 3-dehydroquinate (also commonly written as 5-dehydroquinate depending on numbering convention; 3-dehydroquinate is the standard name). The product should be 3-dehydroquinate.
rxn04661.other_comments: This is quinate dehydrogenase (NADP+), EC 1.1.1.24, oxidizing quinate to dehydroquinate with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written (NADP+ + quinate <=> NADPH + H+ + dehydroquinate). The enzyme is generally reversible, though in vivo direction depends on the metabolic context (quinate catabolism favors oxidation/forward).

rxn07288.other_comments: This reaction represents a cytochrome P450 (BR6ox) catalyzed C6-oxidation step in brassinosteroid biosynthesis, converting 6-deoxoteasterone to teasterone. The conversion of a C6-deoxy (CH2/CH) intermediate to the corresponding C6-oxo (ketone) compound is an oxidation. However, the stoichiometry as written is incomplete/unbalanced: a monooxygenase or oxidase reaction of this type requires additional reducing equivalents (typically NADPH + H+ yielding NADP+) and the O2 consumption with only one H2O product does not balance the oxygen and hydrogen atoms. A balanced form would be approximately: 6-deoxoteasterone + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> teasterone + 2 H2O + NADP+. The reaction as shown omits the NADPH/NADP+ cofactor pair.

errors: Cofactor mismatch: reaction name specifies NAD but the equation uses NADP/NADPH
Proton stoichiometry appears unbalanced: a two-electron oxidation of a hydroquinone to a quinone (NADP+ + QH2 -> NADPH + H+ + Q) should release only 1 H+, not 2 H+
rxn10850.other_comments: This is a quinone oxidoreductase reaction where reduced phthiocol (phthiocol hydroquinone) is oxidized to oxidized phthiocol (quinone) with concomitant reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. Such NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductases are typically reversible in vitro, though in vivo they usually operate to reduce quinones using NAD(P)H.

errors: Nomenclature inconsistency between substrate and product: substrate is written as 'diacylchitobiosyl' while product is written as 'diacetylchitobiosyl'; these should be the same moiety (N,N'-diacetylchitobiose). This is likely a typographical error rather than a stoichiometric one.
A proton (H+) is typically released in glycosyltransferase reactions but charge/mass balance depends on the protonation states used; minor balance concern.
rxn09506.other_comments: This is an alpha-1,3 (or alpha-1,6) mannosyltransferase step in N-glycan biosynthesis (dolichol-linked oligosaccharide assembly). GDP-mannose donates a mannosyl residue to the lipid-linked Man-Man-GlcNAc2-PP-Dol acceptor, producing Man2-Man-GlcNAc2-PP-Dol and GDP. The mannosyl group is transferred 1:1, and the overall stoichiometry is balanced aside from the naming inconsistency.

errors: Stoichiometry is incorrect: the reaction as written shows 2 molecules of 2-oxoglutarate, 2 succinate, 2 CO2, and 2 O2, but this enzyme (deacetoxycephalosporin C synthase / DAOCS, EC 1.14.20.1) couples a single ring-expansion to one round of 2-oxoglutarate decarboxylation, giving 1 O2, 1 2-oxoglutarate, 1 succinate, and 1 CO2

Product mismatch: ring expansion of penicillin N yields deacetoxycephalosporin C (DAOC), not deacetylcephalosporin C; deacetylcephalosporin C is produced by a subsequent hydroxylation step (DACS, EC 1.14.11.26)
Direction as written is reversed: the physiological substrates are penicillin N + 2-oxoglutarate + O2, and the products are the cephalosporin + succinate + CO2
rxn06888.other_comments: This is intended to represent the 2-oxoglutarate/O2-dependent ring-expansion of penicillin N to a cephalosporin by an Fe(II)/2OG oxygenase. As written, the equation runs in the wrong direction (penicillin N should be a substrate), has doubled stoichiometry, and lists deacetylcephalosporin C instead of deacetoxycephalosporin C as the product.

rxn00794.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of biotin amide (biotinamide) to release ammonia and free biotin (BIOT). The reaction is balanced: water adds across the amide bond, converting the carboxamide (-CONH2) to a carboxylic acid (-COOH) with release of NH3. Stoichiometry of H/N/O atoms is consistent. Amidohydrolases catalyze essentially irreversible hydrolytic cleavage under physiological conditions, so the reaction proceeds in the hydrolysis (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02100.other_comments: This reaction is the hydrolysis of L-gulono-1,4-lactone to L-gulonate, catalyzed by a lactonohydrolase. The lactone ring is opened by water, producing the free carboxylic acid (gulonate) and releasing a proton. Stoichiometry and mass/charge balance are correct: H2O + neutral lactone yields a carboxylate anion (gulonate) plus H+. Lactone hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the hydrolytic (forward) direction.

errors: Reaction is not mass-balanced; reduction of a vinyl group to ethyl requires addition of 2 H (one H2 equivalent), and the proper redox cofactor (e.g., NADPH) is missing

rxn05038.other_comments: This reaction represents a kinase (ATP:1D-myo-inositol 3-phosphotransferase) transferring a phosphate from ATP to myo-inositol to form inositol 3-phosphate (1D-myo-inositol 3-phosphate), producing ADP and a proton. The naming 'L-Inositol' is somewhat nonstandard; the substrate should be myo-inositol. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP (phosphate donor) + inositol -> ADP + H+ + inositol-monophosphate, which conserves atoms and charge (the transferred phosphoryl group plus the released proton account for charge balance).

errors: Reaction as written is not mass/atom balanced; TCE (trichloroethylene) epoxide has formula C2HCl3O while dichloroacetyl chloride is C2HCl3O - need to verify atom balance. Both share formula C2HCl3O, so the rearrangement is balanced for atoms but no chlorine migration details are shown.
No cofactors or catalytic species indicated; this is an intramolecular rearrangement (chlorine 1,2-shift / NIH shift type) and may proceed non-enzymatically.
rxn04905.other_comments: This represents the spontaneous intramolecular rearrangement of trichloroethylene oxide (TCE epoxide), a reactive intermediate formed during CYP-mediated TCE metabolism, into dichloroacetyl chloride via a chlorine migration. Both species are isomers (C2HCl3O), so the transformation is atom-balanced as an isomerization. [directionality_note] The epoxide is a high-energy, unstable intermediate that rearranges essentially irreversibly to the more stable acyl chloride.

rxn09908.other_comments: This is the L-amino acid ligase (Lal) reaction forming the dipeptide L-alanylglycine from L-alanine and glycine, coupled to ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: ATP (C10H12N5O13P3, charge -4) + Glycine (neutral, C2H5NO2) + L-Alanine (zwitterion neutral, C3H7NO2) yields ADP (-3) + Phosphate (HPO4 2-) + H+ + L-alanylglycine (neutral dipeptide, C5H10N2O3) plus the water released in peptide bond formation is accounted for by the ATP hydrolysis. Atoms and charges balance.

rxn04700.other_comments: This is an NAD+-dependent oxidation of a secondary alcohol (1-(4'-hydroxyphenyl)ethanol) to the corresponding ketone (4'-hydroxyacetophenone). Stoichiometry is balanced: the secondary alcohol loses two hydrogens (a hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, and a proton released to solution), yielding the ketone. Both atoms and charge balance correctly.

rxn14332.other_comments: This is the acetyl-CoA:tropine O-acetyltransferase reaction, transferring an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the hydroxyl of tropine, yielding acetyltropine (O-acetyltropine) and free CoA. The atom balance is correct: the acetyl group (C2H3O) is transferred to tropine, with CoA-SH released. In vivo, acetyltransferase reactions using the thioester of acetyl-CoA are thermodynamically favorable due to the high-energy thioester bond, driving the reaction toward acetylation.

rxn10743.other_comments: This represents a glycosyltransferase reaction (PimB/related mannosyltransferase) transferring a mannose residue from GDP-mannose donor to a phosphatidylinositol mannoside (PIM) acceptor, producing GDP and the di-mannosylated PIM. This is part of the PIM/LAM biosynthesis pathway in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The stoichiometry is balanced conceptually (one mannose added, GDP-mannose converted to GDP). Note that the substrate/product names are generic descriptions of PIM species; without explicit chemical formulas a precise atom balance cannot be verified, but the transfer logic is sound.

errors: Biotin (BIOT) appears unchanged on both sides of the reaction; for a transport reaction the substrate should be distinguished by compartment, e.g. BIOT[external] -> BIOT[cytoplasm]. As written, biotin is not actually transported and the compartmental designation is missing.
rxn05223.other_comments: This is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter for biotin uptake. The reaction couples ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) to the import of biotin across the membrane. ATP hydrolysis portion is stoichiometrically balanced, but the biotin should be shown moving between two compartments rather than appearing identically on both sides.

errors: Reaction is incomplete/unbalanced: squalene cyclization to a hopanoid (diploptene) requires water as a reactant. Squalene (C30H50) cyclizes; diploptene (hop-22(29)-ene) is C30H50, so by formula they are isomers and the atoms balance, but the named enzyme is misleading.
The enzyme name 'squalene mutase (cyclizing)' is nonstandard; the correct enzyme is squalene-hopene cyclase (EC 4.2.1.129), which catalyzes a cyclization/isomerization, not a true mutase reaction.
rxn05070.other_comments: Supraene is a synonym for squalene (C30H50). Diploptene (hop-22(29)-ene) is a pentacyclic triterpene (hopanoid), also C30H50, so this is an intramolecular cyclization/isomerization with the same molecular formula. Atom balance holds (C30H50 = C30H50). The reaction is catalyzed by squalene-hopene cyclase. [directionality_note] Cyclization of squalene to diploptene is thermodynamically highly favorable and essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Charge imbalance: the product contains H+ plus the carboxylic acid form; if the substrate diol is neutral and O2 is neutral, generating a free H+ alongside a neutral acid leaves a net charge imbalance unless the acid is written as the carboxylate anion

Atom balance should be verified: ring-cleavage dioxygenase reactions incorporate both oxygen atoms of O2 into the product, which appears consistent here, but the explicit formulas should be checked for C, H, O counts
rxn03710.other_comments: This represents an extradiol (or meta) ring-cleavage dioxygenase acting on a dihydroxylated aromatic substrate (3,4-dihydroxyfluorene), incorporating molecular O2 to cleave the catechol ring and yield a 2-hydroxy-muconate-type semialdehyde/keto-acid product. Such dioxygenase reactions are essentially irreversible in vivo due to O2 incorporation.

rxn00488.other_comments: This is an L-amino acid oxidase reaction (oxidative deamination of L-phenylalanine). It uses O2 and water to convert L-phenylalanine to phenylpyruvate (the 2-oxo acid), releasing ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. Atom balance: L-Phe (C9H11NO2) + H2O + O2 -> phenylpyruvate (C9H8O3) + NH3 + H2O2. Carbon: 9=9; Nitrogen: 1=1; checking H: left 11+2+0=13, right 8+3+2=13; O: 2+1+2=5, right 3+0+2=5. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced.

rxn05033.other_comments: This is a prenyltransferase reaction transferring a dimethylallyl group from dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) to the pterocarpan (-)-glycinol (3,6a,9-trihydroxypterocarpan), producing 4-dimethylallylglycinol plus pyrophosphate (PPi). Stoichiometry is balanced: the prenyl moiety is transferred to the aromatic ring and the diphosphate leaving group plus the displaced proton account for the products. This is involved in glyceollin (phytoalexin) biosynthesis in soybean.

rxn02742.other_comments: This is an alcohol dehydrogenase-type oxidation of the terminal hydroxyl group of 10-hydroxydecanoate to the corresponding aldehyde (10-oxodecanoate), using NAD+ as the electron acceptor. The reaction is balanced: the primary alcohol (C-OH) loses two hydrogens (a hydride to NAD+ forming NADH, and a proton H+) to become an aldehyde (C=O). Atoms and charges balance. NAD-dependent alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenases are generally reversible, though in vivo the direction depends on the NADH/NAD+ ratio and substrate concentrations.

rxn08000.other_comments: This is a beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (KAS) reaction in fatty acid elongation. Malonyl-ACP condenses with the C14:1 acyl-ACP (tetradecenoyl-ACP) to form a C16:1 3-oxoacyl-ACP (3-oxo-cis-palmitoleoyl-ACP), releasing CO2 and free ACP. Atom and charge balance hold: the malonyl two-carbon unit is added to the growing chain (C14 to C16) with decarboxylation, and one ACP is released. The decarboxylative Claisen condensation is essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the reaction in the elongation (forward) direction.

rxn02499.other_comments: This reaction represents the hydrolytic dephosphorylation of N-amidino-scyllo-inosamine 4-phosphate (1-guanidino-1-deoxy-scyllo-inositol-4-phosphate) by a phosphohydrolase (phosphatase). Note that N-amidino-scyllo-inosamine and 1-guanidino-1-deoxy-scyllo-inositol are synonyms, so the substrate is the 4-phosphate form and the product is the dephosphorylated form. This step occurs in the biosynthesis of streptomycin. Stoichiometry is balanced: one water consumed, one inorganic phosphate released, one phosphoester bond cleaved.

rxn01887.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of coniferyl alcohol (coniferol) to coniferaldehyde (ferulaldehyde) using NADP+ as the electron acceptor, producing NADPH and H+. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: coniferyl alcohol (C10H12O3) loses 2 H (2e- + 2H+) to form coniferaldehyde (C10H10O3), with NADP+ accepting a hydride and one proton released. This is catalyzed by cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase (CAD) family enzymes. In vivo, during lignin/monolignol biosynthesis, the dominant physiological direction is the reduction of coniferaldehyde to coniferyl alcohol (i.e., the reverse of how this reaction is written), using NADPH. Thus as written (alcohol oxidation), the in vivo flux favors the reverse direction.

rxn11717.other_comments: This is a thioesterase (acyl-CoA hydrolase) reaction. Water hydrolyzes the thioester bond of dihomo-gamma-linolenoyl-CoA (8,11,14-icosatrienoyl-CoA, 20:3) to release free CoA and the free fatty acid (8,11,14-icosatrienoate, dihomo-gamma-linolenate), plus a proton. The atom and charge balance are consistent: the thioester C-S bond is cleaved with addition of H2O, yielding the carboxylate, free CoA thiol, and one H+. Hydrolysis of a thioester is strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction written (CoA release).

rxn03020.other_comments: This is the methyl-transfer reaction catalyzed by N5-methyltetrahydromethanopterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase (Mtr) in methanogenic archaea. It transfers the methyl group from 5-methyl-H4MPT to coenzyme M (CoM, 2-mercaptoethanesulfonate), producing methyl-CoM and free H4MPT. The reaction is correctly balanced (one methyl group transferred). In vivo, during methanogenesis it proceeds in the methyl-CoM-forming direction and is coupled to sodium ion translocation, making it strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible toward methyl-CoM formation.

rxn13533.other_comments: This reaction represents the synthesis of trehalose dimycolate (TDM, cord factor) from two trehalose monomycolate (TMM) molecules. In mycobacteria, antigen 85 complex (Ag85) mycolyltransferases catalyze transfer of a mycolyl group from one TMM to another, generating TDM and releasing free trehalose (TRHL). Here one alpha-mycolate-bearing TMM and one methoxy-mycolate-bearing TMM combine to form a TDM containing both an alpha-mycolate and a methoxymycolate, plus free trehalose. Stoichiometry is balanced in principle: two TMM (each = trehalose + one mycolate) yield one TDM (trehalose + two mycolates) + one free trehalose. Note minor spelling inconsistency in the input ('monomyclolate' vs monomycolate), but the intended species are clear.

rxn06392.other_comments: This is the de-N-acetylation step in GPI anchor biosynthesis (catalyzed by PIG-L). N-acetyl-D-glucosaminyl-PI is hydrolyzed with water to release acetate, yielding glucosaminyl-PI. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: an amide/acetamido C-N bond is cleaved, transferring the acetyl group to water to form acetate while the amine remains on the sugar. Stoichiometry is correct (1 H2O consumed, 1 acetate produced).

rxn01761.other_comments: This reaction represents the aldose-ketose isomerization catalyzed by L-rhamnose isomerase (RhaA, EC 5.3.1.14), converting the aldose L-rhamnose into the ketose L-rhamnulose. Both are C6 deoxyhexoses (C6H12O5) and the reaction is balanced 1:1 with no additional substrates or cofactors required. As an isomerase reaction it is freely reversible; in vivo it operates in the rhamnose catabolic direction (toward L-rhamnulose), which is then pulled forward by phosphorylation via rhamnulokinase (RhaB).

rxn06313.other_comments: This reaction represents the acylation at the sn-2 position of 1-alkenyl(plasmalogen)-glycerophosphocholine (lyso-plasmenylcholine) using an acyl-CoA donor, producing plasmenylcholine (a choline plasmalogen) and free CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: one acyl group is transferred from acyl-CoA to the free hydroxyl of the lysophospholipid, releasing CoA. This is the Lands cycle remodeling/reacylation step. In vivo, acyltransferases driven by acyl-CoA hydrolysis (thioester cleavage) proceed strongly in the biosynthetic (forward) direction toward the intact plasmalogen.

errors: The enzyme name '(E)-Glutaconate CoA-transferase' (EC 2.8.3.12) catalyzes CoA transfer involving glutaconate, not 2-hydroxyglutarate; the substrate listed appears mismatched with the named enzyme.

The physiological CoA donor for this CoA-transferase system is typically acetyl-CoA or glutaconyl-CoA paired with the corresponding acid; the specific named reaction usually involves (E)-glutaconyl-CoA / glutaconate or 2-hydroxyglutarate / 2-hydroxyglutaryl-CoA interconversion - check substrate-product pairing.
rxn02810.other_comments: This represents a CoA-transferase reaction transferring the CoA moiety from acetyl-CoA to 2-hydroxyglutarate, yielding acetate and 2-hydroxyglutaryl-CoA. Stoichiometrically the atoms balance (CoA and acetyl/2-hydroxyglutaryl groups are conserved). CoA-transferases are generally reversible enzymes operating near equilibrium, with direction governed by relative substrate concentrations. In the glutaconate fermentation pathway (e.g., Acidaminococcus fermentans), CoA transfer onto 2-hydroxyglutarate is an early activation step.

rxn07728.other_comments: This is a malonyltransferase reaction (EC 2.3.1.171-type) transferring a malonyl group from malonyl-CoA to the 6'' position of the glucose moiety of mirtillin (delphinidin 3-O-beta-D-glucoside). Products are CoA and delphinidin 3-O-(6-O-malonyl-beta-D-glucoside). Stoichiometry is balanced: the malonyl group is transferred and CoA is released. Acyltransferases using acyl-CoA donors strongly favor acyl transfer in vivo due to the high-energy thioester bond.

errors: Cofactor mismatch: the enzyme name specifies NADPH/NADP+ (N,N,N-trimethylamine,NADPH:oxygen oxidoreductase), but the reaction is written with NADH/NAD+
Charge/proton imbalance: the reaction as written is not balanced for protons/charge. A proper balancing requires an H+ on the substrate side, e.g. NADPH + H+ + O2 + (CH3)3N -> H2O + NADP+ + (CH3)3NO
rxn03899.other_comments: This represents trimethylamine monooxygenase (flavin-containing monooxygenase) activity, oxidizing trimethylamine (TMA) to trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), consuming O2 and NAD(P)H. The reduced cofactor should be NADPH per the enzyme name, not NADH as written. As an oxygenase reaction coupled to O2 consumption, it is physiologically irreversible in the direction of N-oxide formation.

rxn04631.other_comments: This reaction describes an O-methyltransferase using S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) as methyl donor to methylate laricitrin, producing syringetin (the 3',5'-dimethylated flavonol) and S-adenosyl-homocysteine (SAH). Laricitrin is the 3'-O-methyl derivative of myricetin; methylation at the 5'-OH yields syringetin. Stoichiometry is balanced: SAM transfers a methyl group (CH3) to the substrate, and a proton (H+) is released, consistent with standard SAM-dependent methyltransferase reactions. Although the enzyme is named for myricetin, the listed substrate laricitrin is a plausible physiological substrate for the second methylation step.

errors: Stereochemistry mismatch: substrate listed as 'Copalyl diphosphate' but the enzyme name specifies 'ent-Copalyl-diphosphate'; the correct substrate for ent-kaurene synthesis is ent-copalyl diphosphate

Charge/proton balance issue: cyclization of copalyl diphosphate to ent-kaurene releases diphosphate (PPi) but does not net produce a free H+; the reaction is typically written as ent-CPP -> ent-kaurene + PPi without an extra proton
rxn03452.other_comments: This is the ent-kaurene synthase (KS) step in gibberellin/diterpene biosynthesis, converting ent-copalyl diphosphate to the tetracyclic diterpene ent-kaurene with release of diphosphate. Loss of the stable diphosphate leaving group makes the cyclization essentially irreversible in vivo.

errors: Atoms are not balanced. 2 3-hydroxyanthranilate (C7H5NO3 each, total C14H10N2O6) plus 3 O2 (O6) gives C14H10N2O12. Products: 3 H2O2 (H6O6) plus cinnavalininate. This requires cinnavalininate to be C14H4N2O6, which does not match its known formula. The reaction as written does not balance.
The enzyme name 'Hydrogen-peroxide:hydrogen-peroxide oxidoreductase' does not correspond to the substrates/products shown (3-hydroxyanthranilate oxidation), so the annotation is inconsistent.

Oxygen/hydrogen balance is questionable; producing 3 H2O2 from 3 O2 would require 6 H atoms abstracted, and the carbon condensation to a single cinnavalininate from two anthranilate units is not properly accounted.
rxn01932.other_comments: This appears to describe the oxidative dimerization/condensation of two molecules of 3-hydroxyanthranilate (a tryptophan catabolite) with molecular oxygen to form cinnavalininate (a quinoline-type pigment) and hydrogen peroxide. The chemistry (O2-dependent oxidation forming H2O2) is biologically plausible and would proceed essentially irreversibly in the forward direction, but the stoichiometry given does not mass-balance.

rxn02783.other_comments: This is an oxidative deamination of L-beta-leucine (3-amino-4-methylpentanoate) by NAD+, producing beta-ketoisocaproate (4-methyl-3-oxopentanoate), NADH, NH3, and H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: the amino group is removed as ammonia and the resulting amine carbon is oxidized to a ketone, with H2O providing the oxygen and NAD+ accepting the hydride. Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen, and charge all balance. Note: the enzyme name specifies the (3R)-beta-leucine configuration while the substrate is written as L-beta-leucine; this stereochemical naming should be verified for consistency. Amino acid dehydrogenases of this type are typically reversible in vivo, often functioning in the reductive amination direction (ammonia assimilation), but can operate either way depending on redox and ammonia levels.

If 'Cysteine' refers to D-cysteine or unspecified cysteine, this would be a racemization/isomerization, but as written it appears to convert generic Cysteine to L-Cysteine, which is redundant or ill-defined.
The H+ on both sides is superfluous and provides no net transformation.
No cofactor or enzyme requirement indicated for what would be an isomerization (racemase) reaction.

This is either a trivial identity (if Cysteine already means L-Cysteine) or an implied racemization/isomerization (e.g., D- to L-cysteine), which would require a racemase enzyme.
