Atoms balance (C15H22N5O18P3 on each side) and charge balances (-4 = -3 -2 +1 = -4). ATP-dependent sugar phosphorylation is strongly exergonic and physiologically essentially irreversible, proceeding in the forward direction as written.

rxn11766.other_comments: This reaction describes a phosphoribosyltransferase activity where 6-methylmercaptopurine (6-methylthiopurine) reacts with PRPP to form 6-methylthioinosine-5'-monophosphate (6-MeTIMP) plus PPi and H+. This is analogous to the HGPRT/APRT salvage reaction mechanism, where the purine N9 nitrogen attacks the C1 of the ribose phosphate, displacing pyrophosphate. The proton is released from the purine base nitrogen. Atom and charge balance is consistent: PRPP (5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate) donates the ribose-5-phosphate moiety, releasing PPi. 6-Methylmercaptopurine is a drug metabolite of thiopurine therapy (e.g., 6-mercaptopurine methylation), and its conversion to 6-MeTIMP is well documented. PRPP-dependent transferase reactions are strongly thermodynamically driven forward by PPi release and subsequent hydrolysis by pyrophosphatase in vivo.

rxn12749.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by 2,5-dihydroxypyridine 5,6-dioxygenase (EC 1.13.11.9), a key enzyme in nicotinate degradation. It incorporates molecular O2 into 2,5-dihydroxypyridine, cleaving the pyridine ring to yield N-formylmaleamic acid (N-formylmaleamate). The atom balance checks out: 2,5-dihydroxypyridine (C5H5NO2) plus O2 gives N-formylmaleamate (C5H5NO4) plus H+ accounting requires balancing. Counting atoms: substrate C5H5NO2 + O2 = C5H5NO4; product N-formylmaleamic acid is C5H5NO4. Carbon (5=5), nitrogen (1=1), oxygen (2+2=4=4), hydrogen (5=5 on product, but H+ released would give 6). The proton is likely from acid dissociation of the carboxyl/amide product.

rxn04793.other_comments: This is an enoyl-CoA reductase reaction reducing the C2-C3 double bond of trans-2-hexenoyl-CoA to form hexanoyl-CoA, using NADPH as the electron donor. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: NADPH + H+ + enoyl-CoA -> NADP+ + acyl-CoA. The trans-2,3 double bond is reduced and two reducing equivalents (hydride from NADPH plus proton) are consumed. This is the reductive step of fatty acid biosynthesis/elongation (enoyl reductase, e.g. trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase, TER/FabI-type chemistry).

rxn06206.other_comments: This is the ManNAc kinase reaction (NanK, EC 2.7.1.60), transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the 6-hydroxyl of N-acyl-D-mannosamine. The reaction is balanced for mass and charge: ATP + ManNAc -> ADP + H+ + ManNAc-6-phosphate. The proton release is consistent with phosphoryl transfer chemistry.

rxn04890.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450 (CYP)-catalyzed monooxygenase reaction. One atom of O2 is incorporated into the substrate (epoxidation at the 4,5 position of 9-hydroxybenzo[a]pyrene) and the other is reduced to water, with NADPH serving as the electron donor. The stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ provides the two electrons and protons needed, yielding H2O, NADP+, and the epoxide product. Mass and charge balance are consistent (NADPH carries the H, and the H+ balances charge with NADP+).

rxn07900.other_comments: This reaction represents a dihydrodiol dehydrogenase (decarboxylating) acting on a fluorinated cyclohexadiene cis-diol carboxylate, analogous to the benzoate/dihydroxycyclohexadiene carboxylate dehydrogenase step in aromatic degradation pathways. The substrate (5-fluoro-1,2-dihydroxycyclohexa-3,5-diene-1-carboxylate) is oxidized and decarboxylated to yield 4-fluorocatechol, with concomitant reduction of NAD+ to NADH and release of CO2. Stoichiometry is balanced: the diol-carboxylate loses CO2 and 2H (as NADH + H+, though the proton is often omitted in such databases) to aromatize into the catechol. Atom and charge balance are consistent aside from the commonly omitted H+. Decarboxylating dehydrogenases of this type are essentially irreversible in vivo due to CO2 release and NADH formation, driving the reaction forward toward catechol formation.

rxn06695.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of the acetyl-form of citrate (pro-3S)-lyase to regenerate the thiol-form, releasing acetate. The acetyl group is attached via a thioester bond to the prosthetic group (2-(5-triphosphoribosyl)-3-dephospho-CoA), and water hydrolyzes it to acetate and the free thiol form, plus a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: water provides OH to acetate and H to the proton/thiol. This is part of the deactivation/regeneration cycle of citrate lyase. Hydrolysis of a thioester is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward direction.

rxn14076.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction. UDP-glucose serves as the glucosyl donor, transferring a glucose moiety to the 3-O position of sarsasapogenin (a steroidal sapogenin, (25S)-5beta-spirostan-3beta-ol) to form the 3-O-beta-glucoside (asparagoside A) and releasing UDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose, yielding UDP and the monoglucosylated product. Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are typically thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn10442.other_comments: This is a geranylgeranyl reductase-type reaction saturating the isoprenoid chains of an archaeal phospholipid precursor (archaetidylinositol biosynthesis). NADPH-dependent reductions of double bonds are strongly favored in the reductive direction in vivo.

rxn04817.other_comments: This reaction represents the non-enzymatic (or epoxide hydrolase-independent) rearrangement of naphthalene 1,2-oxide (1,2-epoxy-1,2-dihydronaphthalene) to 1-naphthol via the NIH shift. The atoms balance: naphthalene 1,2-oxide (C10H8O) isomerizes to 1-naphthol (C10H8O), so the reaction is an intramolecular rearrangement with identical molecular formula on both sides. This is a downstream step in naphthalene metabolism/detoxification.

rxn00959.other_comments: This is an aromatic monooxygenase (hydroxylase) reaction. Benzoate is hydroxylated at the 4-position to form 4-hydroxybenzoate. One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate, the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Mass and charge balance: left side has Benzoate (C7H5O2-) + NADPH + O2 + H+; right side has 4-Hydroxybenzoate (C7H5O3-) + NADP+ + H2O. Carbon: 7=7. The extra O in product plus the O in water account for the two atoms of O2. H: NADPH provides H, H+ added, balanced with H2O and product hydroxyl. The reaction is stoichiometrically consistent with a typical NADPH-dependent monooxygenase.

rxn03705.other_comments: This is an aminophenol 2-aminophenol 1,6-dioxygenase reaction (EC 1.13.11.74) cleaving the aromatic ring of 2-aminophenol using molecular O2 to form 2-aminomuconate-6-semialdehyde. Both oxygen atoms of O2 are incorporated. Upon re-checking atoms, the equation is balanced.

errors: The enzyme name '3-sn-phosphatidate phosphohydrolase' does not match the substrate; phosphatidate phosphohydrolase (EC 3.1.3.4) acts on phosphatidate, not sphinganine 1-phosphate. The reaction shown is hydrolysis of sphinganine 1-phosphate, which is catalyzed by a sphingosine-1-phosphate phosphatase (EC 3.1.3.-).
The substrates are otherwise stoichiometrically balanced: sphinganine 1-phosphate + H2O yields sphinganine + inorganic phosphate.
rxn04376.other_comments: The reaction is the hydrolytic dephosphorylation of sphinganine 1-phosphate to sphinganine plus inorganic phosphate. rxn04208.other_comments: This is a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase reaction (gibberellin 13-oxidase / GA 20-oxidase family activity) where O2 and 2-oxoglutarate drive the oxidation of GA24 to GA36, producing CO2 and succinate. The carbon and oxygen counts are consistent with a typical Fe(II)/2OG oxygenase mechanism. These enzymes are essentially irreversible in vivo due to the decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate.

rxn05125.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction activating N-methylanthranilate. ATP is cleaved to AMP and PPi, with the carboxylate of N-methylanthranilate being thioesterified to CoA. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP + CoA + carboxylic acid yields AMP + PPi + thioester + H+. The released proton accounts for the charge balance of forming the thioester from the carboxylate. Such adenylate-forming ligase reactions are typically driven forward in vivo by subsequent pyrophosphate hydrolysis, though the enzyme itself is often reversible. This activation step in alkaloid (e.g., acridone/quinoline alkaloid) biosynthesis proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction.

rxn01447.other_comments: This reaction describes the oxidation of indolelactate (indole-3-lactate) to indolepyruvate (indole-3-pyruvate) coupled with the reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reaction is a 2-electron, 2-hydrogen transfer: the secondary alcohol/CHOH of the lactate is oxidized to a ketone. Stoichiometry is balanced: indolelactate (C11H11NO3) loses 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+, one as H+) to form indolepyruvate (C11H9NO3). NAD+ + 2[H] -> NADH + H+. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

rxn14183.other_comments: This is the methylthioalkylmalate synthase (MAM)-type reaction analogous to 2-isopropylmalate synthase, involved in chain-elongation of methionine-derived amino acids in glucosinolate biosynthesis. Acetyl-CoA condenses with the 2-oxo acid (2-oxo-5-methylthiopentanoate) via an aldol-type addition followed by thioester hydrolysis, yielding the substituted malate (2-(3'-methylthio)propylmalate), CoA, and H+. Atom and charge balance: C2H3O-CoA + C6H10O3S + H2O -> CoASH + H+ + C9H15O5S(-)... the carbon (2+6=8 vs product 9? recheck). Acetyl contributes 2 C, oxo acid 6 C = 8 C total in product malate, consistent with 2-(methylthio)propylmalate core; balance appears correct.

rxn08231.other_comments: This represents bacterial cardiolipin synthase (Cls), which condenses two phosphatidylglycerol molecules to form one cardiolipin plus free glycerol. With dioctadecanoyl (di-C18:0) phosphatidylglycerol as substrate, two PG (each contributing two C18:0 acyl chains) yield tetraoctadecanoyl cardiolipin (four C18:0 chains) and glycerol. The mass balance is consistent: the head-group glycerol of one PG is released while its phosphatidyl moiety is transferred to the other PG. In bacteria the reaction is driven forward physiologically (transphosphatidylation), though the prokaryotic Cls reaction is thermodynamically near-equilibrium and can be reversible in vitro; in vivo it proceeds toward cardiolipin synthesis.

rxn11725.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of (11Z,14Z)-icosadienoyl-CoA (a C20:2 acyl-CoA thioester) to free icosadienoic acid and CoA, catalyzed by an acyl-CoA thioesterase/hydrolase. Stoichiometry is balanced: the thioester bond is cleaved by water, releasing the fatty acid, CoA-SH, and a proton. Mass and charge balance check out (H2O + acyl-CoA -> CoA + H+ + fatty acid).

rxn00662.other_comments: This is the guanidinobutyrase/amidinotransferase-type hydrolysis of 3-guanidinopropanoate (guanidinopropionate). Water hydrolyzes the guanidino group, releasing urea and yielding beta-alanine. Atom balance checks out: 3-guanidinopropanoate (C4H9N3O2) + H2O (H2O) gives urea (CH4N2O) + beta-alanine (C3H7NO2). C: 4=1+3; N: 3=2+1; O: 2+1=1+2; H: 9+2=4+7. Balanced. As a hydrolytic reaction it is thermodynamically favorable and proceeds in the forward (hydrolysis) direction in vivo.

rxn03333.other_comments: This reaction describes the NAD+-dependent oxidation of 3,4-dihydroxyphenylethyleneglycol (a vicinal diol, DOPEG) to 3,4-dihydroxymandelaldehyde. SAM-dependent methylations are essentially irreversible in vivo, driving the reaction forward toward methylation.

errors: Electron/charge imbalance: reduced ferredoxin carries reducing equivalents that must be represented stoichiometrically. The reaction as written transfers 2 electrons (NADP+ + H+ + 2e- -> NADPH), so 2 reduced ferredoxin (each 1e-) are required: NADP+ + H+ + 2 Reducedferredoxin -> NADPH + 2 Oxidizedferredoxin. The 1:1 ferredoxin stoichiometry shown is unbalanced in electrons and charge.
NADP should be written as NADP+ to reflect correct protonation/charge state
rxn05937.other_comments: This is the ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase (FNR) reaction, transferring electrons between reduced ferredoxin and NADP+ to form NADPH. In photosynthetic organisms it typically operates forward (toward NADPH) but the enzyme is catalytically reversible and direction depends on the redox poise of the cell.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: the cardiolipin product should contain four acyl chains derived from two phosphatidylglycerol molecules, but 'Anteisopentadecanoylcardiolipin' as named/implied appears to carry only the acyl content consistent with a tetra-acyl species; check that the product formula accounts for all 8 anteisopentadecanoyl chains from 2 substrate PG molecules (each diacyl PG = 2 chains x 2 = 4 chains, so a tetra-acyl cardiolipin is correct only if the name denotes four chains).
Leaving group should be glycerol (free glycerol head group released), which is shown; however, charge/proton balance is not explicitly verifiable from the names provided.
rxn10341.other_comments: This is the bacterial cardiolipin synthase reaction in which two phosphatidylglycerol molecules condense, releasing one free glycerol and forming one cardiolipin. The 2:1:1 stoichiometry (2 PG -> 1 cardiolipin + 1 glycerol) is the standard mechanism. In B. subtilis (PG/PLD-type Cls), the reaction is essentially driven forward toward cardiolipin synthesis in vivo.

errors: The substrate should be 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate (DXP) and 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine, but the cofactor is incorrect: PNP synthase (PdxJ) does not use NAD/NADH. The actual PdxJ reaction is: 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate + 3-amino-2-oxopropyl phosphate (1-amino-propan-2-one 3-phosphate) -> pyridoxine 5'-phosphate + phosphate + 2 H2O. The reaction as written conflates multiple steps of the deoxyxylulose-5-phosphate-dependent (DXP) pathway

Nitrogen is not balanced: pyridoxine phosphate contains a ring nitrogen, but no nitrogen-containing substrate provides it in a balanced way unless 4-phosphohydroxy-threonine is the N donor; however the released atoms do not account for loss of the amino group correctly
Mass/atom balance cannot be verified as written - if NAD/NADH are removed and the proper PdxJ substrates used, the equation differs substantially
CO2 release and NADH production correspond to the PdxA/PdxB oxidative decarboxylation steps, not to PNP synthase (PdxJ)
rxn09072.other_comments: This is labeled as Pyridoxine 5'-phosphate synthase (PdxJ), which condenses 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate with 1-amino-acetone 3-phosphate (3-amino-1-hydroxyacetone phosphate) to form pyridoxine 5'-phosphate plus phosphate and water. The written reaction appears to merge the PdxA-catalyzed oxidative decarboxylation of 4-phosphohydroxy-threonine (which uses NAD and releases CO2/NADH) with the PdxJ condensation, producing an incorrect lumped equation.

rxn11896.other_comments: This is an aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizing 9-cis-retinal to 9-cis-retinoic acid using NAD+ as electron acceptor, with water added as the oxygen source. Stoichiometry is balanced: the aldehyde (CHO) is oxidized to a carboxylic acid (COOH), consuming H2O and NAD+, producing NADH and 2 H+. Atom and charge balance check out (one H+ from the carboxylic acid proton, one from the hydride transfer that becomes NADH releasing a proton). Such retinal-to-retinoic-acid oxidations are essentially irreversible in vivo, driven physiologically in the forward direction toward retinoic acid synthesis.

errors: The reaction shows identical species (H+ and Gp) on both sides without compartment designations; a transport reaction must distinguish the two compartments (e.g., H+[e] + Gp[e] <=> H+[c] + Gp[c]) to be meaningful
As written, both sides are identical, making this a null/trivial reaction with no net transformation or transport
rxn05478.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton symport transport reaction for guanosine 3'-phosphate (Gp), moving Gp together with a proton across a membrane. The 1:1 H+:Gp stoichiometry is plausible for symport, but compartment labels are missing, so the reaction is formally balanced but biologically uninformative as written. Transport reactions are commonly treated as reversible thermodynamically, though net direction depends on the proton motive force and substrate gradients.

rxn06711.other_comments: This reaction represents the dehydrochlorination of 2-chloro-5-oxo-2,5-dihydrofuran-2-acetate (also known as 2-chloro-4-carboxymethylenebut-2-en-4-olide or chloromaleylacetate-derived lactone) to form 4-carboxymethylenebut-2-en-4-olide (cis-dienelactone), releasing HCl (as H+ and Cl-). This is part of the modified ortho-cleavage (chlorocatechol) degradation pathway, catalyzed by chloromuconolactone dehalogenase (EC 5.5.1.11 / related). The atoms balance: removal of HCl from the chlorolactone yields the unsaturated dienelactone plus H+ and Cl-.

rxn08894.other_comments: This is a murein (peptidoglycan) D,D-carboxypeptidase reaction. It hydrolyzes the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala bond of a pentapeptide stem, removing the terminal D-alanine to yield a tetrapeptide stem. The substrate is a linked disaccharide unit bearing one pentapeptide and one tripeptide; the product has the pentapeptide converted to a tetrapeptide plus free D-alanine. Stoichiometry is balanced: one water consumed, one D-Ala released, and one peptide bond cleaved.

rxn05003.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction (COQ3/Coq3 in ubiquinone biosynthesis). S-adenosyl-L-methionine donates a methyl group to the hydroxyl of 3-demethylubiquinone-9 (2-nonaprenyl-3-methyl-5-hydroxy-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinone), producing ubiquinone-9 and S-adenosyl-homocysteine. The stoichiometry is balanced 1:1:1:1, with the methyl group transferred from SAM converting the hydroxyl to a methoxy group.

rxn02595.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction (DmpM in puromycin biosynthesis) that transfers a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to O-demethylpuromycin, yielding S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine and puromycin. The stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl group transferred to the hydroxyl/oxygen acceptor accounts for the conversion of SAM to SAH, and the released proton (H+) is consistent with O-methylation chemistry. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced.

rxn08458.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of reducing equivalents from NADH to FAD, producing NAD+ and FADH2. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADH (carries 2 electrons, 1 hydride) + FAD + H+ yields NAD+ + FADH2. Atoms and charges balance (NADH + H+ provides 2 H and 2 electrons to FAD). The name 'FADH2:NAD+ oxidoreductase' is written in the direction of the reverse reaction (FADH2 oxidation), but biologically NADH typically reduces FAD in flavoenzymes. Note: 'NAD' should formally be 'NAD+'.

errors: Puromycin appears on both the substrate and product sides with no change, indicating it is a transported substrate; in a proper transport reaction the species should be distinguished by compartment (e.g., Puromycin[c] vs Puromycin[e]). As written without compartment labels, the metabolite cancels out and the reaction is stoichiometrically uninformative/incorrect.
rxn05641.other_comments: This is an ABC-type xenobiotic-transporting ATPase coupling ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi + H+) to the export of puromycin across a membrane. The ATP hydrolysis portion is balanced. The reaction needs compartment annotations on puromycin (in vs out) to be meaningful; ATP-driven efflux pumps operate essentially irreversibly in the export direction.

rxn10437.other_comments: This is a decarboxylation reaction. 2-oxooctanedioic acid (also called alpha-ketosuberate, an 8-carbon dicarboxylic acid with a 2-oxo group) loses CO2 to form 7-oxoheptanoic acid (a 7-carbon compound with an aldehyde/oxo group). Carbon balance: 8 carbons = 1 (CO2) + 7 carbons. The alpha-keto acid loses its carboxyl group adjacent to the keto group, yielding an aldehyde. The reaction is mass and charge balanced with consumption of a proton. This type of alpha-keto acid decarboxylation (e.g., in biotin/coenzyme biosynthesis pathways) is essentially irreversible.

rxn02439.other_comments: This reaction describes GDP-6-deoxy-D-talose:NADP+ 4-oxidoreductase. As written, the substrate GDP-6-deoxy-D-talose (4-hydroxyl, with C6 deoxygenated) is oxidized at C4 to form the 4-keto sugar GDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-D-mannose (also called GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-D-mannose; the name GDP-4-dehydro-D-rhamnose is consistent). Stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone releases 2 H (as NADPH + H+). The atom and charge balance are correct. Biologically, this enzyme functions in the reductive direction, using NADPH to reduce the 4-keto intermediate to the deoxy sugar; thus in vivo the favored direction is the reverse of the way it is written here (i.e., reduction of GDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-mannose to GDP-6-deoxy-talose).

rxn02862.other_comments: This is a beta-substitution reaction in which O-acetyl-L-serine reacts with 3,4-dihydroxypyridine (acting as a nitrogen nucleophile via its ring N) to form the non-protein amino acid mimosine-like product 3-(3,4-dihydroxypyridin-1-yl)-L-alanine, releasing acetate and a proton. This is the classic mimosine biosynthesis-type step catalyzed by an O-acetylserine (thiol) lyase / cysteine synthase-like enzyme. Atom balance: O-acetyl-L-serine (C5H9NO4) + 3,4-dihydroxypyridine (C5H5NO2) gives acetate (C2H3O2-) + H+ + product (C8H10N2O4); C, H, N, O, and charge balance.

errors: The reaction is written identically on both sides (H+ + Tyramine on both substrate and product sides) with no compartment distinction shown, making it appear as a null/identity reaction. For a proton symport transport reaction, the metabolites should be labeled with distinct compartments, e.g., H+[e] + Tyramine[e] <=> H+[c] + Tyramine[c].
rxn05686.other_comments: This is intended to be a transport reaction moving tyramine into the cell coupled to proton symport (driven by the proton motive force). As written, it is mass- and charge-balanced trivially since both sides are identical, but it lacks the compartmental annotation needed to represent actual transport. Proton symport uptake is typically directional (uptake into the cytoplasm) due to the inward proton gradient.

rxn10425.other_comments: This reaction represents the ATP-dependent ligation of 7-mercaptoheptanoic acid (the precursor of coenzyme B / N-(7-mercaptoheptanoyl)threonine phosphate pathway) with L-threonine to form 7-mercaptoheptanoylthreonine, catalyzed by 7-mercaptoheptanoylthreonine ligase. ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP + phosphate, releasing a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: the carboxylic acid of 7-mercaptoheptanoic acid condenses with the amino group of threonine forming an amide bond with loss of water, energetically driven by ATP cleavage to ADP + Pi. Charge and atom balance are consistent with the H+ release.

rxn02352.other_comments: This is the anserine synthase reaction (carnosine N-methyltransferase pathway variant), where beta-alanine is ligated to N(pi)-methyl-L-histidine (1-methylhistidine) using ATP, forming anserine (beta-alanyl-N(pi)-methyl-L-histidine), with release of AMP and PPi. The reaction is an ATP-dependent amide bond ligase (AMP-forming). Stoichiometry: ATP provides AMP + PPi; the condensation forms a peptide bond releasing water, and the proton balance of 2 H+ is consistent with deprotonation states at physiological pH. Mass and charge appear balanced.

errors: Charge/proton imbalance: NADPH is typically written as NADPH and consumes an additional H+ in the reaction; the equation as written (NADPH + O2 + MPTP -> H2O + NADP + N-oxide) is missing an H+ on the substrate side. A balanced flavin/P450 monooxygenase N-oxidation would be: MPTP + NADPH + H+ + O2 -> MPTP N-oxide + NADP+ + H2O. Without the explicit H+, the equation is unbalanced in hydrogen and charge.
rxn06719.other_comments: This is a flavin-containing monooxygenase (FMO)-type N-oxidation of MPTP (1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine) to its N-oxide, using NADPH and molecular oxygen, producing water and NADP+. One oxygen atom is incorporated into the product (N-oxide) and the other reduced to water, consistent with monooxygenase chemistry.

rxn00911.other_comments: This reaction represents the transfer of a hydroxymethyl group from 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate to D-alanine, producing 2-methylserine (2-methyl-DL-serine) and tetrahydrofolate, with consumption of water. Checking atoms: D-alanine (C3H7NO2) + 5,10-methylene-THF (C20H21N7O6, which carries a CH2 bridge) + H2O. The methylene group is transferred and hydrated to form a CH2OH, yielding 2-methylserine (C4H9NO3) and THF (C19H21N7O6). The carbon and hydrogen balance is consistent: the CH2 from methylene-THF plus an O and H from water are added to alanine. This is the serine hydroxymethyltransferase-type chemistry (EC 2.1.2.7 for the D-form). Stoichiometry appears balanced.

rxn08410.other_comments: This represents the ECA polymerase (WzyE) reaction that elongates the enterobacterial common antigen chain by transferring an ECA trisaccharide repeat unit. A lipid-linked ECA polymer carrying 3 repeat units accepts an additional repeat unit from the undecaprenyl-diphospho-linked trisaccharide (GlcNAc-ManNAcA-Fuc4NAc), yielding the 4-repeat polymer and releasing undecaprenyl (bactoprenyl) diphosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: one repeat unit is added and one bactoprenyl-PP is released, consistent with the polymerization mechanism.

rxn04086.other_comments: This is the tabersonine 16-hydroxylase (T16H, CYP71D12/CYP71D351) cytochrome P450 monooxygenase reaction in the vindoline biosynthesis pathway. A P450 monooxygenase incorporates one atom of molecular O2 into the substrate (hydroxylation at position 16) and reduces the other O atom to water using NADPH/H+ as electron donor. Stoichiometry is balanced: one O atom goes into the hydroxyl group of 16-hydroxytabersonine, the other O is reduced to H2O; NADPH supplies the two electrons and is oxidized to NADP+. Atom and charge balance are consistent.

errors: Atom imbalance: lathosterol (C27H46O) loses two hydrogens to form 7-dehydrocholesterol/provitamin D3 (C27H44O), introducing a double bond. This is a desaturation, not a hydroxylation. The product side has 2 H2O plus NADP+, but the stoichiometry as written does not balance hydrogen/oxygen correctly. For a desaturase using O2 and NADPH: Lathosterol + NADPH + H+ + O2 -> 7-dehydrocholesterol + NADP+ + 2 H2O is actually correctly balanced (O2 accepts 4 H: 2 from substrate, 2 from NADPH+H+, forming 2 H2O).

On recheck the mass balance: C27H46O + O2 + NADPH + H+ -> C27H44O + 2H2O + NADP+. Carbon: 27=27 OK. The reaction is essentially balanced; the main concern is naming (Provitamin D3 = 7-dehydrocholesterol).
rxn04993.other_comments: This represents lathosterol oxidase (SC5DL / sterol-C5-desaturase), introducing a C5-6 double bond into lathosterol to yield 7-dehydrocholesterol (provitamin D3) in cholesterol biosynthesis. It is an O2- and NADPH-dependent desaturation. In vivo this biosynthetic step proceeds in the forward direction.

errors: The product alpha,beta-didehydrotryptophan is not the correct product of this oxidoreductase reaction. The L-amino acid oxidase / dehydrogenase reaction with O2 typically yields the 2-imino acid (then hydrolyzed to the 2-oxo acid, indolepyruvate, plus ammonia) rather than an alpha,beta-didehydro (dehydro) amino acid. Oxidation of the Calpha-Camino bond gives an imine at the alpha carbon, not a Calpha-Cbeta double bond.

If interpreted as written, the reaction is mass-balanced (C11H12N2O2 + O2 -> C11H10N2O2 + H2O2), but the chemistry of forming an alpha,beta double bond by O2 with H2O2 release is not the standard amino acid oxidase mechanism.
rxn03627.other_comments: This is described as an L-tryptophan:oxygen oxidoreductase, i.e., an amino acid oxidase using molecular O2 and producing H2O2. Such flavin-dependent oxidase reactions are strongly exergonic and physiologically irreversible in the oxidative (forward) direction, but the listed dehydro product appears chemically incorrect.

errors: Reaction is not balanced as written: NADP should be NADP+ to balance charge; the oxidation of 3-nitropropanoate to 3-nitroacrylate removes 2 hydrogen atoms (2 H and 2 electrons), which is consistent with NADP+ -> NADPH + H+, so atom balance is acceptable if charges are correct
rxn02753.other_comments: This describes a dehydrogenation (oxidoreductase) interconverting 3-nitropropanoate and 3-nitroacrylate coupled to NADP+/NADPH. The transformation introduces a C=C double bond (CH2-CH2 to CH=CH), releasing 2 reducing equivalents captured by NADP+. The half-reaction stoichiometry (one NADP+ to NADPH + H+) matches a 2-electron oxidation.

rxn11894.other_comments: This is a retinol dehydrogenase reaction interconverting 9-cis-retinol and 9-cis-retinal using the NADP+/NADPH cofactor pair. The oxidation of the primary alcohol (retinol) to the aldehyde (retinal) removes two hydrogens, transferring a hydride to NADP+ to form NADPH and releasing one proton. The stoichiometry (NADP+ + retinol <=> NADPH + H+ + retinal) is balanced for both atoms and charge. While written with NADP, many retinol dehydrogenases are NAD-dependent; either cofactor is biochemically plausible. These dehydrogenase reactions are generally reversible, though the physiological direction often favors retinal formation when coupled to downstream retinoic acid synthesis.

rxn03511.other_comments: This is the HldD (formerly GmhD/RfaD) ADP-L-glycero-D-manno-heptose-6-epimerase reaction in the LPS inner core heptose biosynthesis pathway. It converts ADP-D-glycero-D-manno-heptose to ADP-L-glycero-D-manno-heptose by epimerization at C6. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced (substrate and product are isomers with identical molecular formulas). Although epimerases are mechanistically reversible, in vivo this step is committed toward the L-glycero product, which is the activated sugar donor used by heptosyltransferases for LPS assembly.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: aristolochene (C15H24) is formed from one molecule of FPP, but the reaction as written shows only one farnesyl diphosphate yielding one PPi plus aristolochene, which is mass-balanced only if cyclization with loss of diphosphate occurs - however aristolochene synthase uses FPP (C15H28O7P2) to give aristolochene (C15H24) + PPi; charge/proton balance: FPP3- -> PPi3- (or HPPi) requires careful proton accounting
The released diphosphate is typically PPi (charge state dependent); the H+ stoichiometry needs verification against protonation states

Reaction name says 'farnesyltransferase (bicyclizing)' but the product aristolochene is an eremophilane bicyclic sesquiterpene formed by aristolochene synthase, a terpene cyclase, not a farnesyltransferase - naming/EC mismatch
rxn01658.other_comments: This represents aristolochene synthase (a sesquiterpene cyclase, EC 4.2.3.9) converting farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) into the bicyclic sesquiterpene aristolochene with release of inorganic pyrophosphate. The ionization-cyclization mechanism makes this strongly favored in vivo.

rxn11802.other_comments: This is a cytochrome P450-catalyzed monooxygenase (hydroxylation) reaction converting N-desmethyltamoxifen to alpha-hydroxy-N-desmethyltamoxifen. One oxygen atom from O2 is incorporated into the substrate (hydroxylation), while the other is reduced to water using electrons from NADPH. Stoichiometry is balanced: one O2 provides one O for the hydroxyl group and one O for water; NADPH plus H+ supplies the reducing equivalents, yielding NADP+. This is a standard CYP-mediated phase I metabolism step in tamoxifen biotransformation.

rxn09351.other_comments: This is UDP-glucuronate decarboxylase (UDP-glucuronic acid decarboxylase / UDP-apiose synthase-like; EC 4.1.1.35 type, UDP-xylose synthase family). The enzyme uses tightly-bound NAD+ as a cofactor, oxidizing the C4 hydroxyl, decarboxylating C6, and the NAD+ is regenerated. The product 'UDP-4-keto-pyranose' represents the UDP-4-keto-pentose intermediate (UDP-4-keto-arabinose/xylose). Stoichiometry balances: UDP-glucuronate (C15H22N2O18P2) loses CO2 and 2H (to NADH/H+) yielding the UDP-4-keto-pentose. Note the catalytic NAD+ is recycled in the full physiological reaction, so net NAD/NADH may not change, but as written the redox couple balances the oxidation/decarboxylation.

rxn13832.other_comments: This is an ABC-type transport reaction for N-formyl-L-methionine. The substrate appears on both sides because transport reactions typically represent the same metabolite in different compartments (e.g., extracellular/periplasmic to cytoplasmic). ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Phosphate + H+) drives the import. The stoichiometry is balanced and consistent with ABC transporter energetics. ABC transporters using ATP hydrolysis are effectively irreversible in vivo, hence forward directionality.

rxn01343.other_comments: This reaction describes the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of sedoheptulose 7-phosphate at the C1 position to form sedoheptulose 1,7-bisphosphate, producing ADP and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the phosphate group, transferring it to the sugar, with ADP and H+ released. This is a kinase reaction (sedoheptulose-7-phosphate kinase / phosphofructokinase-like activity), and ATP-driven phosphorylations are thermodynamically favorable and typically irreversible in vivo, driving the reaction in the forward direction.

rxn05646.other_comments: This is a proton symport transport reaction for L-rhamnose. The notation shows H+ and L-Rhamnose on both sides, representing movement across a membrane (extracellular to cytoplasmic compartments). Although compartment labels are not explicitly shown in the input, the reaction is mass and charge balanced since the same species appear on both sides. As a secondary active transporter coupling proton movement to rhamnose uptake, it is typically modeled as reversible, with the in vivo direction driven by the proton motive force favoring rhamnose import.

errors: The reaction as written shows identical species on both sides (H+ + Lactate <=> H+ + Lactate), so it appears mass-balanced but is biologically meaningless unless compartment annotations are included to indicate transport across a membrane.
Missing compartment labels: a proton-coupled lactate transporter should be written as H+[side1] + Lactate[side1] <=> H+[side2] + Lactate[side2].
rxn11116.other_comments: This represents a proton-coupled monocarboxylate (lactate) transporter (MCT-like, symport of H+ and lactate). As written it is a symport antiport-style transport reaction; chemically the two sides are identical so it is trivially balanced but lacks the compartment distinction needed to represent actual transport. Such transporters typically operate reversibly depending on the proton and lactate concentration gradients.

errors: Hydrogen and charge are unbalanced. The reaction as written produces 3 H+ on the left and only releases CO2, CoA, H2O on the right. Balancing the fatty acid elongation cycle (Lauroyl-CoA C12 to Myristoyl-CoA C14): Malonyl-CoA (C24H33N7O19P3S, accounting charge) + Lauroyl-CoA + 2 NADPH + 2 H+ should yield Myristoyl-CoA + CoA + CO2 + 2 NADP+ + H2O. The proton count of 3 H+ appears incorrect; for the canonical fatty acid synthase elongation, 2 H+ are consumed along with 2 NADPH.
rxn09435.other_comments: This represents a single round of fatty acid chain elongation (condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction) converting a C12 acyl-CoA (lauroyl) to a C14 acyl-CoA (myristoyl) using malonyl-CoA as the two-carbon donor and 2 NADPH as reductant, releasing CO2 and CoA. Biosynthetic elongation is essentially irreversible in vivo, driven by decarboxylation of malonyl-CoA.

errors: Charge imbalance: the reaction as written produces an extra H+ on the product side without a corresponding source. The standard SAM-dependent methyltransferase reaction (SAM + acceptor -> SAH + methylated acceptor) is typically balanced without releasing a free H+; the methyl group is transferred intact. Including H+ on the product side creates a proton imbalance unless explicitly accounted for in protonation states.
rxn05004.other_comments: This is gamma-tocopherol methyltransferase (VTE4), which methylates gamma-tocopherol at the 5-position to form alpha-tocopherol (the most biologically active form of Vitamin E), using S-adenosyl-L-methionine as the methyl donor and producing S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine. The carbon/methyl transfer stoichiometry is correct; the main issue is the explicit H+ which may cause an imbalance depending on protonation conventions.

errors: Stoichiometry is not balanced; addition of a palmitate (C16:0) acyl chain to KDO2-lipid A proceeds via an ester/amide bond formation releasing water, but the 3.0 H+ on the substrate side is incorrect and unbalanced
Mass and charge balance cannot be verified because formulae of the lipid species are not provided, but the free 3 H+ are spurious

Acyltransferases typically use an acyl carrier (acyl-ACP or acyl-CoA) rather than free palmitate as the acyl donor; using free palmitate plus water release is thermodynamically/mechanistically questionable
rxn08790.other_comments: This represents the transfer of a hexadecanoate (palmitate, C16:0) group onto KDO2-lipid A to form a hepta-acylated KDO2-lipid A, an outer membrane LPS biosynthesis step. Acylation reactions of lipid A are biosynthetically committed and run in the direction of the more acylated product in vivo.

rxn01923.other_comments: This is the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase / oxidase reaction converting isobutyryl-CoA (2-methylpropanoyl-CoA) to methacrylyl-CoA, part of valine catabolism. The stoichiometry is balanced: O2 + 2 isobutyryl-CoA -> 2 H2O + 2 methacrylyl-CoA, where O2 accepts 4 electrons (2 H2 equivalents) to form 2 H2O while introducing a double bond in each substrate. This represents an oxidase formulation (FAD reoxidized directly by O2). In mitochondrial dehydrogenases electrons go to ETF rather than O2, but as written this is an acyl-CoA oxidase-type reaction.

rxn02982.other_comments: This reaction corresponds to 4-carboxy-2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde dehydrogenase activity (EC 1.1.1.312 / related), part of the protocatechuate meta-cleavage / 4,5-cleavage pathway. The hemiacetal form (2-hydroxy-2-hydropyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate, i.e. the cyclic hemiacetal of CHMS) is oxidized by NADP+ to 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate (PDC), generating NADPH + H+. Stoichiometry is balanced: oxidation of a hemiacetal (C-OH) to a lactone removes 2 H (one as hydride to NADPH, one as proton), which is consistent. Atom and charge balance appear correct.

rxn01394.other_comments: This is an aldose-ketose isomerization between L-lyxose (an aldose) and L-lyxulose (the corresponding ketose, also called L-xylulose isomer). Both are C5 sugars (C5H10O5), so the reaction is mass- and charge-balanced 1:1. Aldose-ketose isomerases (like the related L-arabinose/L-fucose isomerase family) catalyze freely reversible reactions whose direction in vivo depends on substrate/product concentrations.

rxn03968.other_comments: This is mannitol oxidase (EC 1.1.3.40), which oxidizes D-mannitol using molecular oxygen to produce D-mannose and hydrogen peroxide. The reaction is mass-balanced: O2 + C6H14O6 -> H2O2 + C6H12O6, with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen all conserved (12 H and 8 O on each side). The 'cyclizing' descriptor reflects that the acyclic mannose product cyclizes. As an O2-dependent oxidase, this reaction is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward (oxidation) direction.

rxn03517.other_comments: This represents the quinoprotein alcohol dehydrogenase reaction where ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde, transferring two electrons (and protons) to the PQQ cofactor, reducing it to PQQH2 (reduced pyrroloquinoline quinone). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as a 2-electron, 2-proton transfer: PQQ + ethanol -> acetaldehyde + PQQH2. Note that the enzyme name (ethanol:cytochrome c oxidoreductase) implies cytochrome c is the ultimate electron acceptor, but the written reaction uses PQQ directly, which is the bound cofactor.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: NH3 (NH3) + Hydroxylamine (NH2OH) gives N2H5O on the left, while H2O + Hydrazine (N2H4) gives N2H6O on the right; hydrogen and electron balance are incorrect
Charge/redox imbalance: the reaction as written does not balance electrons or protons; hydrazine synthase requires reducing equivalents (e.g., ferredoxin) that are not shown
rxn04959.other_comments: This appears to be the hydrazine synthase (HZS) reaction from anammox metabolism, condensing ammonia and hydroxylamine (or NO) to form hydrazine and water. The reaction strongly favors hydrazine formation in vivo as part of the anammox pathway, but as written it is not balanced and omits the required electron donors/protons.

rxn11728.other_comments: This is an NADP-dependent oxidoreductase reaction. 1,5-anhydro-D-mannitol is oxidized at C2 to 1,5-anhydro-D-fructose, with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH + H+. The stoichiometry is balanced: the secondary alcohol (CHOH) is converted to a ketone (C=O), releasing 2 H (one as hydride to NADP+ forming NADPH, one as H+). Carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen counts balance. Reaction written with NADP (=NADP+) and product NADPH + H+.

rxn01294.other_comments: This is the benzoylformate decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.7), a thiamine diphosphate-dependent enzyme. Benzoylformate (phenylglyoxylate, C6H5-CO-COO-) is decarboxylated to benzaldehyde (C6H5-CHO) plus CO2, consuming one proton. Atom balance: benzoylformate (C8H5O3-) + H+ = C8H6O3; products CO2 (CO2) + benzaldehyde (C7H6O) = C8H6O3. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and charge all balance.

errors: The reaction combines two distinct catalytic steps into one. As written, the acyl group attached to CoA or ACP is not used; instead free dodecanoate (ddca) is shown being directly transferred. A proper acyltransferase uses an activated acyl donor (acyl-CoA or acyl-ACP), not free fatty acid plus ATP in a single step.

Atom/charge balance is questionable: activating ddca with ATP yields dodecanoyl-AMP + PPi, releasing AMP only upon subsequent transfer. Combining activation and transfer can be written, but the H+ balance and the omission of any CoA/ACP carrier should be verified. A single H+ is unlikely to balance protons across the activation and acyl-transfer steps.
rxn07946.other_comments: This is intended as a 2-acyl-glycerophosphoethanolamine acyltransferase (lysophospholipid reacylation) for the n-C12:0 (lauroyl/dodecanoyl) species, producing didodecanoyl-phosphatidylethanolamine. The hydrolysis of ATP to AMP + PPi (with subsequent PPi hydrolysis in vivo) makes the reaction thermodynamically driven forward.

rxn01596.other_comments: This reaction describes the hydrolysis of streptomycin 6-phosphate by streptomycin-6-phosphate phosphohydrolase (StrK / EC 3.1.3.39), removing the phosphate group from the 6-position to yield free streptomycin plus inorganic phosphate. The stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphomonoester bond is cleaved by water, releasing one phosphate and the dephosphorylated streptomycin. This is the final activation step in streptomycin biosynthesis in Streptomyces griseus.

rxn02718.other_comments: This reaction represents 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11beta-HSD) activity. Corticosterone is oxidized to 11-dehydrocorticosterone with reduction of NADP+ to NADPH. The stoichiometry is balanced: the 11-hydroxyl group loses two hydrogens (one as H+, one as hydride to NADPH), so the mass and charge balance correctly. In vivo, the NADP-dependent isoform (11beta-HSD type 1) predominantly operates as a reductase (favoring corticosterone formation), so the physiological direction is often the reverse of as written, but the enzyme is intrinsically reversible and direction depends on cofactor availability and isoform.

rxn06365.other_comments: This is the phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase (PI4K) reaction (EC 2.7.1.67), transferring the gamma-phosphate of ATP to the 4-position of the inositol ring of phosphatidylinositol, yielding PI4P, ADP, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: one phosphate is transferred from ATP to PI, generating ADP and releasing one H+. In vivo, kinase reactions consuming ATP are essentially irreversible and proceed in the direction of phosphorylation.

rxn02024.other_comments: This reaction represents pterin deaminase activity (EC 3.5.4.11), in which pterin (2-amino-4-hydroxypteridine) undergoes hydrolytic deamination. Water attacks the C2 amino group, releasing ammonia and producing lumazine (2,4-dihydroxypteridine / 2,4(1H,3H)-pteridinedione). Stoichiometry is balanced: pterin (C6H5N5O) + H2O yields lumazine (C6H4N4O2) + NH3. Hydrolytic deaminations are essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the direction written.

rxn05042.other_comments: This is a PAPS-dependent sulfotransferase (SULT) reaction transferring a sulfo group from 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) to the 3-hydroxyl of glycolithocholate, yielding adenosine-3',5'-bisphosphate (PAP), a proton, and sulfoglycolithocholate. The stoichiometry is balanced: the sulfonate group is transferred from PAPS to the bile acid hydroxyl, releasing PAP and H+. Sulfotransferase reactions are thermodynamically driven toward sulfoconjugation in vivo due to the high group-transfer potential of PAPS.

errors: Charge and proton balance not explicitly shown; glycosyltransferase reactions typically release H+ but none is indicated
Product name 'phosphatidylinositol mannoside (tuberculosis)' is ambiguous and does not specify the exact mannoside species (e.g., PIM1 vs PIM2)
Acyl chain specification (C16:0, C19:0) appears only on the substrate, not carried through to the named product, creating ambiguity
rxn10734.other_comments: This reaction represents an alpha-mannosyltransferase transferring a mannose residue from GDP-mannose to phosphatidylinositol, forming a phosphatidylinositol mannoside (PIM, relevant to Mycobacterium tuberculosis cell wall biosynthesis) with release of GDP. Mannosyl group balance: one mannose moves from GDP-mannose to PI, which is consistent.

rxn07655.other_comments: This is the allene oxide synthase (AOS) reaction in the oxylipin/jasmonate pathway. 9(S)-HPOT (9(S)-hydroperoxy-10,12,15-octadecatrienoic acid) is converted to an unstable allene oxide, 9,10-EOT (9,10-epoxy-octadecatrienoic acid / 12,13(S)-epoxylinolenic acid analog), with release of water. The stoichiometry is balanced: the hydroperoxide (-OOH) is dehydrated to form the epoxide plus H2O. Atomically, removal of H2O from the hydroperoxide group yields the allene oxide epoxide, so C, H, and O atoms balance. In vivo, AOS catalyzes this as an essentially irreversible dehydration; the allene oxide product is highly unstable and is rapidly cyclized or hydrolyzed, driving the reaction strongly forward.

rxn07588.other_comments: This is the cobalt-precorrin-6B (C5)-methyltransferase reaction (CbiE, EC 2.1.1.289) in the anaerobic cobalamin biosynthesis pathway. SAM acts as the methyl donor, transferring a methyl group to cobalt-precorrin-6B to yield cobalt-precorrin-7, with SAH and a proton released. The stoichiometry is balanced: a single methyl group is transferred, generating one SAH and one H+. The reaction is driven forward in vivo by the energetically favorable SAM-dependent methylation in the committed biosynthetic pathway.

rxn09937.other_comments: This reaction represents an ATP-dependent L-amino acid ligase forming a dipeptide bond between two L-serine molecules, producing Ser-Ser (a dipeptide), ADP, inorganic phosphate, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP provides the energy via hydrolysis to ADP + Pi, and the condensation of two serines releases one water that is consumed in ATP hydrolysis, with a net release of H+. Mass and charge balance check out: two serines (each C3H7NO3) condense to a dipeptide losing one H2O, while ATP -> ADP + Pi releases energy. The H+ accounts for the charge balance from peptide bond formation and phosphate release.

rxn07749.other_comments: This is a paraxanthine N-demethylase reaction (cytochrome P450 / oxidative N-demethylation, e.g. CYP1A2). Paraxanthine (1,7-dimethylxanthine) undergoes N7-demethylation to form 1-methylxanthine, releasing formaldehyde. The monooxygenase mechanism consumes O2 and NADH (or NADPH) with one oxygen atom incorporated into the leaving methyl group (released as formaldehyde) and the other reduced to water. Stoichiometry balances: C8H10N4O2 + O2 + NADH + 2H+ yields C7H8N4O2 + HCHO + H2O + NAD+. Atoms and charges balance correctly.

errors: The reaction as written is mass/charge unbalanced and mechanistically inconsistent. The conversion of 17alpha,21-Dihydroxypregnenolone (a delta5-3-hydroxysteroid) to Cortodoxone (11-deoxycortisol, a delta4-3-ketosteroid) is catalyzed by 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/delta5-delta4-isomerase, which oxidizes the 3-hydroxyl to a 3-keto group AND isomerizes the double bond. This requires NAD+ as oxidant being reduced to NADH, not the reverse as written.
If interpreted as the named isomerase function (delta5 to delta4 isomerization only), no NAD(H) should be involved at all; the isomerization step is redox-neutral.
The cofactor usage is backwards: the oxidation of the hydroxyl to ketone should produce NADH from NAD+, but here NADH is consumed to produce NAD+.
rxn03317.other_comments: This represents the 3beta-HSD/isomerase combined activity converting 17alpha,21-dihydroxypregnenolone to 11-deoxycortisol (cortodoxone). The physiological direction is steroidogenic, going from the pregnenolone derivative to 11-deoxycortisol, producing NADH. As written (NADH consumed, going toward the pregnenolone derivative), the cofactors are reversed relative to the in vivo direction.

errors: This reaction as written is not balanced. Epsilon-caprolactam-related transamination should produce an aminotransferase product; the standard KEGG R05507 is: 2-Oxoglutarate + 6-Aminohexanoate <=> L-Glutamate + 6-Oxohexanoate. 'Epsilcapramine' is not the correct substrate; the amino donor should be 6-aminohexanoate (6-aminohexanoic acid). As written with 'Epsilcapramine', the atoms do not balance with the products L-Glutamate + 6-Oxohexanoate.
rxn03797.other_comments: This is an aminotransferase (transaminase) reaction transferring an amino group from a 6-amino fatty acid to 2-oxoglutarate, producing L-glutamate and the corresponding oxo-acid (6-oxohexanoate). The correct amino donor for KEGG R05507 is 6-aminohexanoate, not the listed 'Epsilcapramine'. Transaminations are generally reversible.

rxn01080.other_comments: This is the aldose-ketose isomerase reaction (UxaC, EC 5.3.1.12) interconverting D-glucuronate (an aldose) and D-fructuronate (a ketose) in the hexuronate catabolic pathway. The reaction is balanced 1:1 with both substrate and product being C6H10O7 isomers; no cofactors or additional metabolites are required. As an isomerase, it is intrinsically reversible, though in vivo the flux is typically toward fructuronate as part of glucuronate degradation feeding into the Entner-Doudoroff-related route.

rxn00168.other_comments: This is the pyruvate decarboxylase reaction (EC 4.1.1.1), which converts pyruvate to acetaldehyde and CO2. The reaction is mass and charge balanced: Pyruvate (C3H3O3, charge -1) + H+ yields CO2 (CO2, neutral) + Acetaldehyde (C2H4O, neutral). Carbons (3 = 1+2), hydrogens (3+1=4), oxygens (3=2+1), and charge (-1+1=0) all balance. The enzyme requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) and Mg2+ as cofactors, though these are catalytic and not consumed.

errors: This reaction as written conflates two distinct enzymatic activities. The conversion of 17alpha-Hydroxypregnenolone to 17alpha-Hydroxyprogesterone is NOT a simple NADP-dependent 3-oxidoreductase reaction; it is catalyzed by 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase (3-beta-HSD), which uses NAD+ (not NADP+) as the cofactor and involves both an oxidation of the 3-beta-hydroxyl group and an isomerization of the delta-5 double bond to delta-4.
Cofactor error: physiological 3-beta-HSD uses NAD+/NADH, not NADP+/NADPH.
The name '3-oxidoreductase' does not capture the obligatory delta-5 to delta-4 isomerization step required to form the delta-4 product (17alpha-Hydroxyprogesterone).
rxn02386.other_comments: The substrates and products are isomeric C21 steroids: 17alpha-Hydroxypregnenolone (a delta-5, 3-beta-ol) is oxidized/isomerized to 17alpha-Hydroxyprogesterone (a delta-4, 3-keto steroid). The atom balance for a simple 3-hydroxyl oxidation (loss of 2H captured as NAD(P)H + H+) is internally consistent, though the reaction also requires isomerization. In vivo, 3-beta-HSD strongly favors the forward (oxidation/isomerization) direction toward the 3-keto-delta-4 product.

rxn02063.other_comments: This is squalene monooxygenase (squalene epoxidase, EC 1.14.14.17). Supraene is a synonym for squalene. The reaction converts squalene to (S)-2,3-epoxysqualene (squalene 2,3-oxide) using molecular oxygen and NADPH as reductant, incorporating one oxygen atom into the substrate and reducing the other to water. Stoichiometry is balanced: NADPH + O2 + H+ + squalene -> H2O + NADP+ + squalene-2,3-epoxide.

errors: DOC (11-deoxycorticosterone) is a 3-keto, 4-ene steroid with 21-hydroxyl, but 21-hydroxypregnenolone is a 3-hydroxy, 5-ene steroid; conversion requires both a 3-oxidoreduction and a delta5-delta4 isomerization (i.e., 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase activity), so the stated single oxidoreductase step is incomplete/mislabeled

Atom/charge balance issue: the simple oxidation of the 3-OH to 3-keto is consistent (loss of 2H), but the accompanying double-bond migration (5,6 to 4,5) is not accounted for as a separate isomerization; written as a pure NADP-dependent dehydrogenation it does not fully balance with the product DOC
rxn02906.other_comments: This represents the 3beta-HSD/isomerase-type conversion of 21-hydroxypregnenolone to 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC). The enzyme uses NAD(P)+ to oxidize the 3beta-hydroxyl and isomerizes the delta5 double bond to delta4, producing the 3-keto-4-ene steroid. In vivo this proceeds in the oxidative (forward) direction toward DOC.

rxn01014.other_comments: This is a decarboxylation reaction where hydroxypyruvate (3-carbon: HOCH2-CO-COOH) loses CO2 to form glycolaldehyde (2-carbon: HOCH2-CHO). Carbon balance: 3 = 1 (CO2) + 2 (glycolaldehyde), correct. Atom and charge balance check: hydroxypyruvate anion (C3H3O4-, charge -1) plus H+ gives C3H4O4; products CO2 (CH0O2... CO2) plus glycolaldehyde (C2H4O2) = C3H4O4. Mass and charge balance correctly. Decarboxylation reactions releasing CO2 are essentially irreversible in vivo due to loss of gaseous/stable CO2, so the reaction strongly favors the forward direction.

errors: The reaction as written shows H+ and 4-Hydroxyphenylacetate on both sides without compartment labels, making it appear as a null reaction. For a proton symporter transport reaction, the species should be in different compartments (e.g., H+[e] + 4-Hydroxyphenylacetate[e] <=> H+[c] + 4-Hydroxyphenylacetate[c]). Without compartmental annotation, the reaction is stoichiometrically trivial/empty and biologically meaningless.
rxn10559.other_comments: This is intended to be a proton-coupled symport reaction importing 4-hydroxyphenylacetate from the extracellular space into the cytoplasm, driven by the proton motive force. The 1:1 H+ to substrate stoichiometry is plausible for a symporter, but the lack of compartment designations renders the written reaction equivalent on both sides.

errors: Hydrogen and charge imbalance: oxidation of trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline (C5H9NO3) by NAD+ to the cyclic imine 3-hydroxy-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (C5H7NO3) releases 2 H (one as hydride to NAD+, one as proton), so the balanced form should produce NADH + 1 H+, not 2 H+. As written there is an extra H+ on the product side.
rxn02356.other_comments: This is hydroxyproline 2-epimerase/dehydrogenase-type oxidation: NAD+-dependent dehydrogenation of trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline at C5 (the alpha-amino carbon) to give the cyclic Schiff base 1-pyrroline derivative (3-hydroxy-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate) plus NADH. The chemistry is correct but the proton count appears off.

errors: Atomically unbalanced: naringenin (C15H12O5) cannot be converted to daidzein (C15H10O4) by simply releasing H2O and H+; the mass/charge does not balance.
Loss of H2O plus H+ from C15H12O5 would yield C15H9O4 (charge -1), not neutral daidzein C15H10O4.

Biochemically these are distinct flavonoid skeletons: naringenin is a flavanone (2-phenylchromanone) while daidzein is an isoflavone (3-phenylchromone); their interconversion requires aryl migration and oxidation, not a simple dehydration.
rxn04407.other_comments: The reaction proposes converting naringenin to daidzein with release of water and a proton. Naringenin and daidzein are different flavonoid classes (flavanone vs isoflavone) and the transformation cannot be a single dehydration; the equation is not balanced.

rxn06038.other_comments: This is the NADP-dependent oxidation of (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA to 3-oxoacyl-CoA. The reaction is balanced: NADP+ oxidizes the secondary hydroxyl group to a ketone, releasing NADPH and a proton. Atoms and charges balance (2 H removed from substrate, transferred as hydride to NADP+ plus released H+). Note the stereochemistry: this enzyme acts on the (R)-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA, distinct from the (S)-specific enzymes of canonical beta-oxidation.

errors: Stoichiometric imbalance: ATP provides a pyrophosphate group, so the product should be AMP plus ppGpp (guanosine 3',5'-bis(diphosphate)). The phosphate balance requires checking: ATP (3 phosphates) + GDP (2 phosphates) = 5 P; AMP (1 phosphate) + ppGpp (4 phosphates) = 5 P, so phosphorus balances. However the H+ stoichiometry of 2.0 H+ is questionable; transfer of a pyrophosphoryl group typically releases 0 or 1 H+ depending on protonation states, not 2.
rxn08598.other_comments: This is the GDP pyrophosphokinase (RelA/SpoT) reaction synthesizing ppGpp by transferring a pyrophosphate group from ATP to the 3'-OH of GDP, yielding AMP and guanosine 3',5'-bis(diphosphate). The carbon/phosphorus skeleton appears balanced; the main concern is the proton count.

rxn01556.other_comments: This is a SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase reaction. Quercetin (3,5,7,3',4'-pentahydroxyflavone) is methylated at the 3-O position to yield 3-O-methylquercetin, with S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) serving as the methyl donor and being converted to S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH). The stoichiometry is balanced: the methyl group transferred from SAM to a hydroxyl of quercetin releases a proton, consistent with the H+ on the product side. Methyltransferase reactions are generally driven forward in vivo because SAM is a high-energy methyl donor and SAH is removed/hydrolyzed, making them effectively irreversible.

rxn03143.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase reaction. Nuatigenin is the aglycone (20S,22S,25S)-22,25-epoxyfurost-5-ene-3beta,26-diol, which is glucosylated at the 3-O position to yield the 3-O-beta-D-glucoside, releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: the glucosyl group is transferred from UDP-glucose to the acceptor hydroxyl, converting UDP-glucose to UDP and adding glucose to the aglycone. Glycosyltransferases of this type are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the synthetic (forward) direction due to the high-energy UDP-sugar linkage.

rxn01473.other_comments: This is the limonene synthase reaction (EC 4.2.3.20), where geranyl diphosphate (GPP, C10H17O7P2 with appropriate charge) undergoes ionization, cyclization, and deprotonation to form (4S)-limonene. The products are diphosphate (PPi), a proton (H+), and limonene. Atom and charge balance: GPP (formal charge -3) yields limonene (neutral C10H16) + PPi (charge -3 at physiological pH, releasing the diphosphate) + H+. The C, H, O, P balance is consistent. The reaction is effectively irreversible in vivo because it proceeds through a highly favorable ionization of the allylic diphosphate and loss of PPi, which is subsequently hydrolyzed, driving the reaction forward.

errors: Stoichiometry appears unbalanced: UDP-L-rhamnose donates a rhamnosyl group, but the product Tulipanin (delphinidin 3-rutinoside) versus substrate Mirtillin (delphinidin 3-galactoside or 3-glucoside) implies the acceptor must contain a glucoside moiety to receive rhamnose, forming the rutinoside (rhamnosyl-(1->6)-glucoside); check that the acceptor is delphinidin 3-glucoside rather than 3-galactoside
rxn07693.other_comments: This represents a rhamnosyltransferase reaction: UDP-rhamnose transfers a rhamnosyl group onto an anthocyanin glucoside (Mirtillin/delphinidin glucoside) to yield UDP and the rutinoside (Tulipanin, delphinidin 3-rutinoside). Glycosyltransferases using activated UDP-sugar donors are strongly thermodynamically favorable in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

The naming hexa-methyl octacosanoate (C28) to hepta-methyl triacontanoic acid (C30) implies addition of only 2 backbone carbons plus 1 methyl = consistent with C28->C30 backbone + extra methyl, but verify carbon count: octacosanoate=C28, triacontanoate=C30, difference is 2 carbons in backbone; methylmalonyl contributes 2 backbone C + 1 methyl C = 3 C total, so 1 carbon must leave as CO2 - this is accounted for. Carbon balance appears approximately correct.
Charge/proton balance should be checked: typical FAS-type elongation uses 2 NADPH + 2 H+ per cycle, not 3 H+. The extra H+ may be incorrect.
H2O production: standard fatty acid elongation via Claisen condensation, ketoreduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction releases 1 H2O - this is consistent.
rxn10746.other_comments: This is a polyketide/methyl-branched fatty acid elongation cycle using D-methylmalonyl-CoA as the extender unit, adding a methyl-branched two-carbon unit to a C28 hexa-methyl substrate to yield a C30 hepta-methyl product, releasing CoA and CO2. The reductive elongation (condensation, ketoreduction, dehydration, enoyl reduction) consumes 2 NADPH and is biosynthetically driven forward.

rxn00478.other_comments: This is the reaction catalyzed by tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO, EC 1.13.11.11) or indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO, EC 1.13.11.52), the first and rate-limiting step of the kynurenine pathway. It incorporates both atoms of molecular oxygen (a dioxygenase) into L-tryptophan, cleaving the indole ring to form N-formyl-L-kynurenine. The stoichiometry is balanced: L-tryptophan (C11H12N2O2) + O2 yields N-formylkynurenine (C11H12N2O3)... note the oxygen count - one oxygen atom appears unaccounted, but in fact N-formylkynurenine has formula C11H12N2O3, so both O atoms are incorporated only if formula is checked carefully; actual product formula accounts for the added oxygens via ring cleavage.

rxn10200.other_comments: This is a biomass-type lumped reaction that pools many lipoteichoic acid (LTA) species, differing by their acyl chain (palmitoyl, myristoyl, stearoyl, iso/anteiso branched chains) and by their headgroup substitutions (unsubstituted, glucose, GlcNAc, D-alanine), into a single generic 'Lipoteichoic acid content' pseudo-metabolite. The fractional stoichiometric coefficients represent relative molar contributions of each species, consistent with a biomass composition equation rather than a true enzymatic transformation. As such, mass/charge balance in the conventional sense does not apply since the product is a defined-pool placeholder. Although written as reversible, biomass aggregation reactions proceed in the synthetic/forward direction toward the pooled component.

rxn01805.other_comments: This is a hydro-lyase (dehydratase) reaction: (3S)-citramalyl-CoA (L-citramalyl-CoA) loses water to form itaconyl-CoA. The reaction is balanced - C16H26N7O20P3S (citramalyl-CoA) yields itaconyl-CoA (C26H38N7O18P3S after losing H2O). Atoms balance: removing H2O from the citramalyl-CoA gives the unsaturated itaconyl-CoA. This enzyme (EC 4.2.1.56, citramalyl-CoA lyase/dehydratase context, often associated with itaconate degradation via Ict/CitE pathways) catalyzes a freely reversible dehydration/hydration. In itaconate catabolism it runs toward citramalyl-CoA (hydration), while in itaconyl-CoA formation it runs as written.

rxn00127.other_comments: This is adenosylmethionine decarboxylase (AdoMetDC, EC 4.1.1.50). S-adenosyl-L-methionine is decarboxylated, consuming a proton and releasing CO2 to form S-adenosylmethioninamine (decarboxylated SAM), which serves as the aminopropyl donor in polyamine biosynthesis. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written. As a decarboxylation releasing CO2, it is essentially irreversible in vivo, proceeding in the forward direction.

rxn04015.other_comments: This reaction represents the lyase 2-(S)-hydroxypropyl-CoM:2-mercaptoethanesulfonate lyase (epoxyalkane-ring-forming), which is part of the bacterial epoxide/alkene metabolism pathway (e.g., propylene metabolism in Xanthobacter and Rhodococcus). The enzyme EpoxyalkaneCoM transferase normally operates in the direction of opening the epoxide ring by adding CoM, converting (S)-1,2-epoxypropane + CoM into 2-(S)-hydroxypropyl-CoM during propylene degradation. Stoichiometry is balanced: the C3H6O hydroxypropyl group is split off from CoM, and reforming the epoxide releases free CoM (2-mercaptoethanesulfonate). As written (hydroxypropyl-CoM to CoM + epoxypropane), this is the epoxide-forming direction, which is the reverse of the physiologically favored catabolic direction.

rxn02023.other_comments: This is a hydro-lyase (hydratase) reaction. (R)-10-Hydroxystearate is dehydrated to form oleate (cis-9-octadecenoate) plus water. The reverse reaction is the hydration of the oleate double bond to yield the 10-hydroxy fatty acid. Stoichiometry is balanced: C18H36O3 (hydroxystearate) <=> H2O + C18H34O2 (oleate). Fatty acid hydratases (e.g., oleate hydratase, EC 4.2.1.53) typically catalyze the hydration direction in vivo, but the enzyme is generally considered reversible. The named enzyme (10-hydro-lyase) emphasizes the dehydration direction.

rxn00445.other_comments: This is L-galactono-1,4-lactone dehydrogenase/oxidase type reaction, the final step of ascorbate biosynthesis. The reaction shows oxidation of L-galactono-1,4-lactone to L-ascorbate. Note: in plants, the physiological enzyme (L-galactono-1,4-lactone dehydrogenase, EC 1.3.2.3) uses cytochrome c rather than O2 as electron acceptor. However, as written with O2 -> H2O2 (an oxidase, EC 1.3.3.12), the stoichiometry is balanced: L-galactono-1,4-lactone (C6H10O6) loses 2 H to form L-ascorbate (C6H8O6), and O2 + 2H gives H2O2. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen all balance.

rxn10634.other_comments: This represents a fatty-acid-AMP ligase / acyltransfer step in mycolic acid biosynthesis, transferring a cyclopropanated meromycolate chain from ACP to an AMP carrier. The intent is acyl-ACP + AMP -> acyl-AMP + ACP, but the stoichiometry as written (free AMP consumed AND AMP-acyl produced, plus 2 H+) appears unbalanced. rxn07668.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction (EC 2.4.1.x) where UDP-glucose donates a glucose moiety to cyanidin 3-O-glucoside, forming cyanidin 3-O-sophoroside (a 1->2 linked diglucoside) and releasing UDP. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: one glucose unit is transferred from UDP-glucose to the acceptor, with UDP released. Atom and charge balance are conserved.

For palmitoleate (C16:1) synthesis from 1 acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA with 13 NADPH, the standard balance requires consuming ~14 H+ on the reactant side, not 19; the proton count is inconsistent with charge balance.

NADPH stoichiometry: full saturated palmitate (C16:0) synthesis uses 14 NADPH; for the monounsaturated hexadecenoate (C16:1) with one fewer reduction, 13 NADPH is reasonable, but this must be paired with corrected H+ and the appropriate degree of unsaturation, which is internally inconsistent here.
rxn10036.other_comments: This represents de novo fatty acid synthesis producing hexadecenoate (palmitoleate, C16:1) from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA, consuming NADPH and releasing CO2, CoA, and water.
