Without the actual substrate identity and likely cofactors (e.g., NADPH, O2, or SAM depending on the step), no reliable assessment is possible.

rxn03134.other_comments: This reaction corresponds to prostaglandin 13,14-reductase (EC 1.3.1.48), interconverting the 13,14-dihydro (saturated C13-C14) and the delta13 (unsaturated) prostanoate forms. The right side bears the delta13 double bond (13E) while the left side is the saturated 13,14-dihydro compound. NADP+/NADPH and H+ balance the redox: saturation of the C13=C14 double bond consumes NADPH+H+. The substituents (11alpha-hydroxy, 9,15-dioxo, 5Z) are conserved on both sides, so the reaction is stoichiometrically and elementally balanced (atoms and charge balance with one H+). [directionality_note] As written (NADP+ on left, NADPH on right), the equation describes oxidation/double-bond introduction, but in vivo prostaglandin reductase enzymes catalyze reduction (saturation) of the enone double bond using NADPH. Thus the biologically favored direction is right-to-left (reverse) relative to how it is written.

rxn11293.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of xylobiose (a disaccharide of two xylose units linked by a beta-1,4 glycosidic bond) by beta-1,4-xylosidase (beta-xylosidase, EC 3.2.1.37). One water molecule hydrolyzes the single glycosidic bond, yielding two molecules of xylose. The stoichiometry is balanced: xylobiose (C10H18O9) + H2O (H2O) gives 2 xylose (2x C5H10O5 = C10H20O10). As a hydrolase reaction under physiological conditions, it strongly favors hydrolysis (forward direction).

rxn04352.other_comments: This reaction represents a glycosyltransferase step in avermectin biosynthesis, where a second sugar (oleandrose) is transferred from dTDP-L-oleandrose onto the avermectin A1a monosaccharide to form the disaccharide-containing avermectin A1a, releasing dTDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: the glycosyl moiety is transferred from the activated nucleotide sugar to the acceptor, and dTDP is the leaving group. Catalyzed by an avermectin glycosyltransferase (e.g., AveBI). In vivo, glycosyltransferases using NDP-sugars strongly favor the glycosyl transfer (forward) direction due to the thermodynamically favorable cleavage of the sugar-nucleotide bond.

errors: Mass/atom imbalance: combining glutamate-1-semialdehyde with phosphate and oxidizing with NADP+ does not yield glutamyl-1-phosphate plus NADPH; the oxidation of an aldehyde to an acyl-phosphate requires loss of water/proper accounting, and the atoms do not balance as written

The enzyme name '(S)-4-Amino-5-oxopentanoate:NADP+ 5-oxidoreductase' describes oxidoreductase activity on glutamate-1-semialdehyde, but the actual substrate of glutamyl-phosphate formation should be glutamate-5-semialdehyde / glutamate-5-phosphate (this corresponds to glutamate-5-semialdehyde dehydrogenase / GSA reductase chemistry), so the metabolite naming is inconsistent
rxn02990.other_comments: This appears intended to represent the reductive acylation step in proline/arginine biosynthesis (glutamate-5-semialdehyde + NADP+ + Pi <=> glutamyl-5-phosphate + NADPH + H+), catalyzed by glutamate-5-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (ProA). The reaction as written mislabels the semialdehyde position (1- vs 5-) and pairs it with an oxidoreductase name for 4-amino-5-oxopentanoate (glutamate-1-semialdehyde), which is normally the substrate of glutamate-1-semialdehyde aminomutase, not a phosphorylating dehydrogenase.

rxn10760.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction transferring a rhamnose moiety from dTDP-rhamnose (the activated sugar donor) to the mono-rhamnosylated phenolphthiocerol dimycocerosate acceptor, producing the di-rhamnosylated product plus dTDP. This is part of the biosynthesis of phenolic glycolipids in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Stoichiometry is balanced: the rhamnosyl group plus dTDP accounts for the dTDP-rhamnose donor. Glycosyltransferases using NDP-sugar donors are strongly favored in the biosynthetic (forward) direction due to release of the nucleotide diphosphate.

rxn10701.other_comments: This represents a glycosyltransferase reaction adding a mannose residue from GDP-mannose to phosphatidylinositol dimannoside (PIM2) to form the trimannoside (PIM3), releasing GDP. This is part of the PIM/LM/LAM biosynthetic pathway in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Stoichiometry is balanced: one mannosyl unit is transferred, and the GDP-mannose to GDP conversion accounts for the donor sugar. Glycosyltransferases using activated nucleotide-sugar donors are strongly exergonic due to cleavage of the high-energy GDP-sugar bond, so this proceeds in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn08232.other_comments: This represents bacterial cardiolipin synthase (cls), which condenses two molecules of phosphatidylglycerol (each with two C18:1 oleoyl/cis-vaccenoyl chains) to form one molecule of cardiolipin (with four C18:1 chains) plus one free glycerol. Stoichiometry is balanced: 2 PG (each contributing one glycerol headgroup and one diacylglycerophosphate moiety) yields cardiolipin (two phosphatidyl units bridged by one glycerol) plus released glycerol. The four acyl chains in cardiolipin equal the four chains from the two PG substrates.

rxn09902.other_comments: This represents an ATP-dependent dipeptide ligase forming the dipeptide Ser-Leu from L-serine and L-leucine, with hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP + Ser + Leu yields ADP + Pi + H+ + dipeptide (releasing one water equivalent of bond formation while consuming ATP). The atoms balance, since peptide bond formation releases water that combines with the gamma-phosphate cleavage. The single H+ accounts for charge balance. L-amino acid ligases (RimK/YwfE-type) typically drive synthesis toward dipeptide formation coupled to ATP hydrolysis.

rxn13978.other_comments: This is a UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.114) that transfers a beta-D-glucosyl group from UDP-glucose to the carboxyl/hydroxyl group of trans-2-hydroxycinnamate (2-coumarate), producing UDP and beta-D-glucosyl-2-coumarate. The reaction is balanced: one glucose unit is transferred, UDP-glucose becomes UDP, and the acceptor gains a glucosyl moiety. Note that the proton balance may need explicit accounting depending on the protonation states of the carboxylate groups, but the core glucosyl transfer is correctly represented.

rxn10274.other_comments: This is a glucosyltransferase reaction transferring a glucose moiety from UDP-glucose (the activated sugar donor) to monoglucosyldiacylglycerol (diisoheptadecanoyl variant), forming diglucosyldiacylglycerol and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: one glucose unit is transferred, UDP-glucose becomes UDP, and the acceptor gains one glucose. Glycosyltransferases using UDP-sugars are thermodynamically driven toward glycosyl transfer due to the high-energy UDP-sugar bond, so the reaction proceeds in the forward (biosynthetic) direction in vivo.

rxn02018.other_comments: This reaction is catalyzed by 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (NADP+), oxidizing the 15-hydroxyl group of Prostaglandin D2 to a 15-keto group, producing the 11,15-dioxo product. NADP+ is reduced to NADPH with release of H+. The atoms and charges balance: removal of two hydrogens (as hydride to NADP+ giving NADPH plus a proton) from the C15 hydroxyl yields the ketone. Stoichiometry is correct. Although 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenases typically favor oxidation (forward) in vivo due to NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios and rapid product turnover, the enzyme reaction is formally reversible.

rxn04662.other_comments: This is the shikimate dehydrogenase reaction (EC 1.1.1.25), oxidizing shikimate to 3-dehydroshikimate using NAD+ as electron acceptor, producing NADH and H+. The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: shikimate loses two hydrogens (an oxidation of the 3-hydroxyl to a ketone), accounting for NADH + H+. In the biosynthetic shikimate pathway, the enzyme typically operates in the reverse direction (NADPH-dependent reduction of 3-dehydroshikimate to shikimate), though the NAD-linked isoform shown here is generally catabolic and thermodynamically reversible.

rxn11760.other_comments: This is a kinase reaction transferring the gamma-phosphate from ATP to the 5'-hydroxyl of 5-fluorouridine, producing 5-fluorouridine monophosphate (5-FUMP), ADP, and a proton. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: ATP provides the phosphoryl group, and one H+ is released upon phosphoester bond formation. This represents the activation step of the antimetabolite 5-fluorouridine, likely catalyzed by uridine-cytidine kinase (a non-specific reaction on the fluorinated analog).

rxn01935.other_comments: This reaction describes the cleavage of (S)-4-hydroxymandelonitrile (a hydroxynitrile/cyanohydrin) into hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde (p-hydroxybenzaldehyde), catalyzed by a hydroxynitrile lyase (mandelonitrile lyase, EC 4.1.2.11 family). The stoichiometry is balanced: the cyanohydrin C(OH)(CN) group dissociates into the aldehyde C=O plus HCN. Hydroxynitrile lyases catalyze a reversible reaction; the synthetic (condensation) direction is industrially exploited for chiral cyanohydrin production, while in planta the degradative (release of HCN, cyanogenesis) direction is favored upon tissue damage.

rxn06383.other_comments: This is the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase reaction, which phosphorylates and inactivates the E1 component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. ATP donates a phosphate to a serine residue on PDH, producing the phosphorylated enzyme, ADP, and a proton. The stoichiometry is balanced: ATP transfers one phosphoryl group, yielding ADP, H+, and the phosphoprotein. In vivo, kinase phosphorylation reactions driven by ATP hydrolysis are strongly favored in the forward direction; the reverse is catalyzed separately by a phosphatase, not by simple reversal.

errors: The fatty acid substrate is labeled generically as 'fa1' rather than specifying the iso-C14:0 fatty acid (12-methyltridecanoic acid) that corresponds to the product; substrate and product acyl chains should match
rxn10404.other_comments: This is a fatty acid-CoA ligase (acyl-CoA synthetase) reaction activating an iso-branched C14:0 fatty acid. The mechanism proceeds via an acyl-AMP intermediate, releasing PPi and then AMP, forming the acyl-CoA thioester. Stoichiometry is balanced (ATP + CoA + fatty acid -> AMP + PPi + acyl-CoA), assuming fa1 is the iso-C14:0 acid. In vivo, subsequent pyrophosphate hydrolysis drives the reaction toward acyl-CoA formation.

rxn04346.other_comments: This is a glycosyltransferase reaction (KEGG R06485) where dTDP-L-oleandrose donates an oleandrose sugar to Avermectin B2a monosaccharide, producing the disaccharide Avermectin B2a and releasing dTDP. The stoichiometry is balanced: the sugar moiety is transferred from the nucleotide-diphospho-sugar donor to the acceptor, releasing dTDP. This is the second glycosylation step in avermectin biosynthesis.

rxn00619.other_comments: This reaction describes a galactosyltransferase transferring galactose from UDP-galactose to sn-glycerol-3-phosphate, forming galactosylglycerol-3-phosphate and releasing UDP. The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced as written: UDP-galactose donates the galactosyl moiety, leaving UDP, and the galactose is attached to glycerol-3-phosphate. Atoms balance because the glycosidic bond formation releases no additional water (the acceptor hydroxyl and the sugar anomeric carbon combine directly). [directionality_note] Glycosyltransferase reactions using activated nucleotide-sugar donors (UDP-sugars) are strongly exergonic due to the high group-transfer potential of the UDP-glycosidic bond, driving the reaction essentially irreversibly in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

errors: Stoichiometric ambiguity: the reaction combines two distinct trehalose dimycolate (TDM) species (tdm1 and tdm4) plus TRHL (trehalose) but the atom balance cannot be verified without explicit molecular formulas; the production of only 2 H2O from condensation of multiple large mycolyl-containing substrates is unlikely to mass-balance the carbon/oxygen of the mycolate transfers

Mechanistic concern: mycolyl transfer reactions (catalyzed by Antigen 85 / mycolyltransferases) typically transfer mycolate groups onto arabinogalactan or trehalose using TMM/TDM as donors, releasing free trehalose rather than consuming free trehalose; the role of free TRHL as a substrate here is questionable
The product naming (tetramycolyl-hexaarabinoside) implies an arabinan acceptor, but no arabinose/arabinan acceptor appears explicitly on the substrate side
rxn13539.other_comments: I understand this is intended to represent mycobacterial cell-wall biosynthesis: assembly of a tetra-mycolylated hexaarabinoside (arabinan terminal motif) by transfer of mycolate groups from trehalose dimycolate (TDM) donors bearing alpha- and methoxy-mycolates, with release of water. The reaction is written as a condensation/transesterification toward the mycolylated arabinan product.

rxn08014.other_comments: This is an acyl-ACP synthetase (ligase) reaction activating myristic acid (C14 fatty acid) onto acyl carrier protein. The mechanism proceeds via a myristoyl-AMP intermediate, releasing PPi, then transferring the acyl group to the ACP thiol to form myristoyl-ACP plus AMP. The stoichiometry is balanced: one ATP is cleaved to AMP + PPi (one H+ released), and the carboxylate of myristate is condensed with the ACP phosphopantetheine thiol. Atom and charge balance are consistent. In vivo, the reaction is driven forward by subsequent hydrolysis of PPi to 2 Pi by inorganic pyrophosphatase, making it effectively irreversible.

rxn10301.other_comments: This reaction represents glucosylation of a lipoteichoic acid backbone bearing 24 glycerophosphate repeat units. Each of the 24 repeats is substituted with a glucose moiety donated from UDP-glucose, yielding 24 UDP. The stoichiometry is balanced (24 glucose transferred, 24 UDP released). Glycosyltransferase reactions using UDP-sugar donors are thermodynamically favorable due to hydrolysis of the high-energy glycosidic bond of the nucleotide sugar, so the reaction proceeds in the synthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn14294.other_comments: This represents alpha-farnesene synthase activity, where (2E,6E)-farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) undergoes ionization and deprotonation to form (3E,6E)-alpha-farnesene plus diphosphate (PPi). The reaction is mass- and charge-balanced: FPP (C15H25O7P2, charge -3) yields alpha-farnesene (C15H24), PPi (HP2O7, charge -3), and a proton (H+). Carbon (15=15), phosphorus (2=2), oxygen (7=7), and hydrogen (25 = 24+1) all balance, as does charge (-3 = -3+0+1+0... note the H+ provides +1, so left -3, right -3+1=-2). Recheck: PPi at this protonation state carries -3 and adding H+ gives net -2 on the right while left is -3, indicating a possible charge imbalance depending on protonation states assumed.

errors: Charge imbalance: with 3 H+ on left and the stated species, charge does not balance. NADPH (-4) + 3 H+ (+3) + Malonyl-CoA (-5) + Decanoate (-1) = -7 on left; H2O (0) + 2 NADP (-2 each = -4) + CoA (-4) + CO2 (0) + ddca/dodecanoate (-1) = -9 on right. A charge imbalance of 2 exists, suggesting 2 H+ rather than 3 H+ would balance.
Hydrogen mass balance should be rechecked given the H+ stoichiometry issue.
rxn09440.other_comments: This represents one elongation cycle of fatty acid synthesis, extending decanoate (C10) to dodecanoate/laurate (ddca, C12:0) by addition of a malonyl-CoA-derived two-carbon unit. Carbon balance is correct (C10 + C3 acyl from malonyl - CO2 = C12), and 2 NADPH are consumed for the reductive steps (ketoreduction and enoyl reduction). The reaction is written and operates in the biosynthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02035.other_comments: This reaction represents the oxidation of cortisol to cortisone, catalyzed by 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11-beta-HSD). The 11-beta-hydroxyl group of cortisol is oxidized to a ketone, with NADP+ accepting the hydride to form NADPH and a proton. The reaction is stoichiometrically balanced: carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, and redox equivalents are conserved (cortisol C21H30O5 loses 2 H to become cortisone C21H28O5, balanced by NADP+ to NADPH + H+). Note that 11-beta-HSD type 1 (which uses NADP/NADPH) predominantly catalyzes the reverse reaction (reduction of cortisone to cortisol) in vivo due to high local NADPH availability, while 11-beta-HSD type 2 uses NAD+ and favors oxidation. The enzyme is bidirectional in principle.

rxn05128.other_comments: This is the hydrolysis of gamma-glutamyl-GABA (4-(glutamylamino)butanoate) by an amidohydrolase (PuuD/related enzyme in the putrescine utilization pathway). Water cleaves the amide bond linking the gamma-carboxyl of glutamate to the amino group of GABA, yielding L-glutamate and GABA (4-aminobutanoate). The reaction is balanced in atoms and charge: the amide plus water gives a free carboxylate (glutamate) and a free amine (GABA). Hydrolytic amidohydrolase reactions are thermodynamically favorable and run in the direction of hydrolysis in vivo.

rxn10677.other_comments: This is a mannosyltransferase reaction in Mycobacterium tuberculosis where a mannose residue is transferred from polyprenyl-phosphate-mannose (decaprenyl/polyprenyl phosphomannose, the activated sugar donor) to an acyl phosphatidylinositol dimannoside (Ac-PIM2), producing the trimannoside (Ac-PIM3) and releasing decaprenyl phosphate. Stoichiometry is balanced: one mannose unit is transferred from the lipid-linked donor to the acceptor, with corresponding conversion of the mannosyl-phosphate donor to free phosphate-lipid. Glycosyltransferase reactions using lipid-phospho-sugar donors are essentially irreversible in vivo (driven toward product, biosynthetic direction toward PIM/LM/LAM synthesis).

rxn05421.other_comments: This is a fatty acid synthase elongation (condensation) step, a beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (KAS) reaction. A C10 branched acyl-ACP (8-methyl-nonanoyl-ACP) condenses with malonyl-ACP, releasing CO2 and free ACP, to form the elongated beta-ketoacyl product (10-methyl-3-oxo-undecanoyl-ACP, a C12 branched chain). The stoichiometry balances: the acyl primer (C10) plus the acetyl unit derived from malonate (C2 after decarboxylation) yields a C12 3-oxo product, with loss of one CO2 from malonate and release of the carrier ACP that delivered the malonyl group. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen balance.

rxn14131.other_comments: This is arylamine N-acetyltransferase (NAT, EC 2.3.1.5), which transfers the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to the aromatic amine of aniline, producing acetanilide and free CoA. The reaction is balanced: acetyl-CoA (C23H38N7O17P3S) + aniline (C6H7N) yields acetanilide (C8H9NO) + CoA (C21H36N7O16P3S). Atoms balance correctly with the acetyl group transferred to the nitrogen.

rxn03751.other_comments: This is an acyl-CoA ligase (AMP-forming) reaction: 2,4-dichlorobenzoate is activated by ATP to form an acyl-adenylate intermediate, then thioesterified with CoA, releasing AMP and PPi. The H+ accounts for proton balance. Atoms and charges balance: ATP + CoA-SH + RCOOH -> RCO-SCoA + AMP + PPi + H+.

rxn10020.other_comments: This is a fatty acid-CoA ligase (acyl-CoA synthetase) reaction activating anteiso-C17:1 fatty acid. The mechanism: ATP + fatty acid + CoA yields acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi (+ H+). Stoichiometry is balanced for atoms and charge: ATP provides AMP plus PPi, and the carboxylate is esterified to CoA releasing a proton. The reaction is correctly written with one H+ produced.

rxn16614.other_comments: This is the HldE/GmhB-associated nucleotidyltransferase reaction (EC 2.7.7.105) where GTP and D-glycero-alpha-D-manno-heptose 1-phosphate combine to form GDP-D-glycero-alpha-D-manno-heptose plus pyrophosphate, a step in ADP/GDP-heptose biosynthesis for LPS inner core. The reaction is balanced: GTP contributes the GMP moiety to the sugar phosphate, releasing PPi. In vivo, subsequent rapid hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase drives the reaction forward.

errors: The product name 'di-mannose' implies addition of two mannose residues, but only one GDP-mannose is consumed, which would add only a single mannose. Stoichiometry of mannose transferred (1) does not match a 'di-mannose' product unless the substrate already contained one mannose and the name refers to the total count after addition.
Missing H+ may be needed for charge/proton balance depending on the protonation states used, though glycosyltransfer reactions of this type are typically balanced as written.
rxn10757.other_comments: This is a GDP-mannose-dependent alpha-mannosyltransferase reaction relevant to Mycobacterium tuberculosis phosphatidylinositol mannoside (PIM) biosynthesis, transferring a single mannosyl residue from GDP-mannose to an acylated PIM acceptor and releasing GDP. Biosynthetic glycosyltransfer using activated sugar nucleotide donors is essentially irreversible and proceeds in the synthetic (forward) direction in vivo.

rxn02530.other_comments: This reaction describes UDP-glucose:methylazoxymethanol beta-D-glucosyltransferase (EC 2.4.1.171). It transfers a glucosyl moiety from UDP-glucose to the hydroxyl group of methylazoxymethanol (CH3-N(O)=N-CH2OH), producing cycasin (the beta-D-glucoside) and releasing UDP. Stoichiometry is balanced: the glucose is transferred to the acceptor, with UDP as the leaving group. A proton (H+) is typically also released but is often omitted in such notation.

errors: No chemical transformation occurs; substrate and product are identical (phenolic phthiocerol dimycocerosate on both sides)
Transport reactions should indicate a change in compartment (e.g., cytoplasm to periplasm/extracellular), but no compartments are specified
Missing energy/coupling component if this is an ABC-type translocase (e.g., ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi)
rxn10825.other_comments: This is annotated as a translocase (ppdima translocase) moving phenolic glycolipid/PDIM-related lipid (phenolphthiocerol dimycocerosate, a Mycobacterium tuberculosis cell-envelope lipid). As written, the reaction is degenerate because identical species appear on both sides with no compartment labels, so it conveys no net change. Transport reactions of cell-envelope lipids like PDIM/PGL are typically directional (export to the cell envelope/outer membrane), often coupled to ATP hydrolysis (e.g., MmpL/DrrABC systems).

errors: The reaction is not elementally balanced as written. The product 'tetramycolyl-hexaarabinoside' implies a hexaarabinose (six arabinose) scaffold acceptor, but no arabinose-containing acceptor (e.g., arabinogalactan or hexaarabinofuranosyl unit) appears on the substrate side; only TRHL (trehalose) and two trehalose dimycolate (TDM) species are listed.

Mycolyl transfer reactions (catalyzed by antigen 85 / mycolyltransferases) transfer a mycolate from a donor (e.g., trehalose monomycolate/dimycolate) to an acceptor, releasing the deacylated trehalose sugar; they do not produce water as a byproduct. Mycolyl ester transfer is a transesterification, not a condensation releasing 2 H2O.

Stoichiometry of mycolate groups is inconsistent: combining one alpha,keto-TDM and one alpha,methoxy-TDM (four total mycolates) plus trehalose to yield a single tetramycolyl-hexaarabinoside does not account for the trehalose moieties or the carbon/mycolate balance.
The molecular formulae of these complex lipid species are not specified, so a precise mass balance cannot be verified, but the qualitative group accounting is inconsistent.
rxn13542.other_comments: This appears to be a Mycobacterium tuberculosis cell-envelope reaction proposing assembly of a tetramycolylated hexaarabinoside from trehalose (TRHL) and two trehalose dimycolate species bearing alpha/keto and alpha/methoxy mycolates. The intended chemistry is mycolic acid transfer onto an arabinan acceptor, but as written the acceptor and byproducts are biochemically inconsistent.

rxn10721.other_comments: This is a rhamnosyltransferase reaction transferring rhamnose from dTDP-rhamnose (the activated sugar donor) to the phenolic glycolipid phenol phthiocerol dimycocerosate (the aglycone acceptor), producing the rhamnosylated phenolic glycolipid and releasing dTDP. This corresponds to a step in phenolic glycolipid (PGL) biosynthesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, catalyzed by a glycosyltransferase such as Rv2962c. The stoichiometry is balanced: one rhamnosyl unit is transferred, the nucleotide diphosphate leaving group accounts for the rest of the donor. Glycosyltransferase reactions using sugar nucleotide donors are thermodynamically favorable and physiologically irreversible in the synthetic direction.

rxn10756.other_comments: This reaction represents the final esterification step in PDIM A (phthiocerol dimycocerosate) biosynthesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phthiocerol A has two free hydroxyl groups that are each esterified with a mycocerosic acid (tetra-methyl octacosanoate / mycocerosate), catalyzed by the polyketide-associated protein PapA5. Each esterification releases one water molecule, so two esterifications produce 2 H2O, consistent with 2 acyl donors. The proton balance (2 H+ on left) accounts for the deprotonated/protonated states of the carboxylic acids in the esterification. Stoichiometry of carbons and the 2:1:2 ratio of substrates appears balanced for forming a diester from a diol and two fatty acids.
